lymph node metastasis and microscopic extrathyroidal extension. 
The age criterion for defining high-risk disease has been raised 
from 45 years to 55 years. This change increases the proportion 
of relatively young patients whose mortality risk can be defined 
solely on the basis of the absence or presence of distant metastases 
(stages I and II, respectively). As for microscopic extension of the 
tumor to the perithyroidal soft tissues, this finding is no longer 
considered an absolute indication for assigning the tumor to the 
T3 category. The ability to recognize this minimal extrathyroidal 
invasion can vary widely, even between skilled pathologists. The 
T3 category now includes tumors whose largest diameter exceeds 
4 cm and those that invade the perithyroidal muscles (sternohy­
oid, sternothyroid, thyroidhyoid, omohyoid). Upper mediastinal 
lymph node metastases (level VII) are now considered features of 
N1a disease, which was formerly used solely in the presence of 
central neck node lesions. The expanded definition reflects the 
well-known difficulties in distinguishing level VI and VII nodes 
from an anatomic point of view. Stage I thyroid cancer now refers 
exclusively to T1 or T2 tumors with no lymph node metastases, 
whereas stage II includes T3, N0, M0 tumors and any T1 to T3 
tumor with metastatic lymph node disease (either N1a or N1b).
To date, prognostic differences and, especially, the differing risk 
of cause-specific mortality between central lymph node metastases 
(N1a) and other regional metastases (N1b) have yet to be widely 
validated. Indeed, the risk of persistent/recurrent disease appears 
to be more closely related to the number and size of involved 
lymph nodes and the number of lymph nodes with extracapsu­
lar extension. These characteristics, however, are not taken into 
account in the TNM AJCC staging system.216,217 Stages III and 
IVa include T4a and T4b tumors, respectively, regardless of their 
lymph node status. Stage IVb includes any tumor with distant 
metastases, and stage IVc has been eliminated entirely in the new 
eighth edition system. 
Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma
PTC is considered a type of well-differentiated thyroid cancer and 
is defined as “a malignant epithelial tumor showing evidence of 
follicular cell differentiation and a set of distinctive nuclear fea­
ture. Papillae, invasion or cytologic features of papillary thyroid 
carcinoma are required.”183,218 As the most common thyroid 
malignancy, PTC constitutes 50% to 90% of DTCs world­
wide.97,219 The 2022 WHO classification recognizes many PTC 
subtypes, including classic, infiltrative follicular, tall cell, colum­
nar cell, hobnail, solid, diffuse sclerosing, warthin-like, oncocytic, 
and solid/trabecular.210 Less common subtypes include clear cell, 
spindle cell, and PTC with fibromatosis/fasciitis-like/desmoid-
type stroma.
Classic PTCs appear as firm, unencapsulated or partially encap­
sulated tumors. PTCs may be partly necrotic, and some are cystic. 
The presence of necrosis and a high mitotic rate are associated with 
aggressive behavior similar to that of poorly differentiated thyroid 
cancer (PDTC).47,220 Typically, PTC shows a predominance of 
papillary structures, consisting of a fibrovascular core lined by a 
single layer of epithelial cells, but the papillae are usually admixed 
with neoplastic follicles having characteristic nuclear features. The 
nuclei of PTC cells have a distinctive appearance, which has a 
diagnostic significance comparable to that of the papillae. Indeed, 
the preoperative diagnosis of PTC can often be made on the basis 
of the characteristic nuclear changes seen in FNA material: nuclei 
are larger than in normal follicular cells and overlap, they may be 
fissured like coffee beans, chromatin is hypodense (ground-glass 
nuclei), limits are irregular, and they frequently contain an inclu­
sion corresponding to a cytoplasmic invagination. Psammoma 
bodies are often present in the core of papillae or in the tumor 
stroma; they are microscopic structures of calcified layers.
The diffuse sclerosing variant of PTC is characterized by diffuse 
involvement of one or both thyroid lobes, widespread lymphatic 
permeation, prominent fibrosis, and lymphoid infiltration. The 
tall cell variant of PTC is characterized by well-formed papillae 
that are covered by cells that are twice to three times tall as they 
are wide. Other subtypes of PTC include the columnar cell variant, 
which differs from other forms of PTC because of the presence 
of prominent nuclear stratification of elongated cells. Tall cell, 
columnar cell, and hobnail subtypes are typically more aggressive 
than classic PTC.210
In children, PTC represents the large majority of newly diag­
nosed thyroid cancer cases, and histologic subtypes include the 
classic PTC, the presence of the solid/trabecular variant features (of 
unknown prognostic significance), the follicular variant (now con­
sidered separately from PTC), and the diffuse sclerosing variant. 
Tumor extension can be substantial at diagnosis: tumors can be

Presenting Features of Papillary Thyroid 
Carcinoma
PTC is frequently multifocal when it occurs in a single lobe and 
is bilateral in 20% to 80% of cases, depending on whether the 
thyroid is meticulously examined. Extrathyroidal invasion of 
adjacent soft tissues is present in about 15% (range 5%–34%) 
at the time of primary diagnosis.219,223 About 35% to 50% of 
excised neck lymph nodes have histologic evidence of involvement 
(microscopic foci of metastases in most of the cases), although in 
patients 17 years of age or younger, nodal involvement may be 
present in up to 90%.215,221,222,224 Only 1% to 7% of patients 
with PTC have distant metastases at diagnosis.219 Spread to supe­
rior mediastinal nodes is usually associated with extensive neck 
nodal involvement. 
Prediction of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma 
Recurrence
For most patients with PTC, survival is near 100% (https://seer.
cancer.gov/) (Figs. 12.10 and 12.11).225 However, there is a small 
subset of patients with a higher risk of death from thyroid can­
cer. Illustrative of the excellent survival of the majority of patients 
with PTC, using the eighth edition of AJCC staging, at presen­
tation, most PTCs are classified as TNM stage I or II tumors, 
with fewer than 10% of all PTCs classified as stage III or IV (Fig. 
12.12).226,227 The current staging system dichotomizes age, with 
patients ages 55 and older considered at greater risk for death and 
therefore staged higher.228 Although age is categorized for staging, 
prior work has found that patient age is associated with death in a 
linear fashion.225,229
Despite the high survival, approximately 10% to 30% of 
patients will have recurrences.230–236 Thyroid cancer recurrence can 
be classified as biochemical or structural recurrence. Biochemical 
recurrence is based on serum markers, specifically an elevated thy­
roglobulin. Thyroglobulin is only made by normal thyroid tissue 
or well-differentiated thyroid cancer; therefore, it is a useful tumor 
marker after the entire thyroid is removed (i.e., after total thyroid­
ectomy). Structural recurrence can be detected with imaging, but 
the gold standard is pathology confirmation, either with biopsy or 
surgical resection. Many patients with structural recurrence first 
present with biochemical recurrence. Prior studies suggest that of 
all recurrences, 75% or more occur in the first 5 years and almost 
all in the first 10 years after initial treatment.230,231,237–239
In 2015 the ATA proposed a stratification system predicting 
the risk of recurrence after initial treatment.1 The stratification 
is based on individual factors from various studies and reports a 
continuous increasing risk of recurrence according to each factor 
(Fig. 12.13). No multivariate analysis is thus far available. Of 
note, the age of the patient at the time of initial treatment is not

taken into account for the risk of recurrence, but many other 
prognostic factors for thyroid cancer death are also prognostic 
for the risk of recurrence, such as some histologic characteris­
tics, the size of the thyroid tumor, the extension of the tumor 
beyond the thyroid capsule, the presence of lymph node metas­
tases, and the presence of residual disease as a result of either 
incomplete surgical resection or presence of distant metastases. 
Aggressive histologic subtypes, the presence of necrosis, a high 
mitotic count, and vascular invasion are associated with higher 
recurrence risk. Indeed, the risk of recurrence is minimal (<2%) 
for unifocal micropapillary carcinoma but higher for multifocal 
micropapillary carcinoma (∼4%), and it increases with the size 
of the thyroid tumor but is still low (∼5%) in patients with an 
intrathyroid tumor of 3 to 4 cm without extension beyond the 
thyroid capsule.240
The prognostic impact of extension beyond the thyroid cap­
sule is low in micropapillary carcinomas that are classified as 
N0. This risk increases with the size of the thyroid tumor and 
with the extent of the extension.241–243 Minimal lymph node 
involvement (i.e., less than three lymph node metastases, each 
<2 mm) is associated with a low risk of recurrence. This risk 
again increases with the number of lymph node metastases, with 
the size of the lymph node metastases, and with the presence of 
extranodal extension.216,217,244 Therefore, minimal lymph node 
involvement that is usually found at prophylactic lymph node 
dissection may have a minimal prognostic impact and may not 
change the indication for postoperative treatment with radio­
iodine. However, large lymph node metastases that are usually 
palpable and easily visualized on neck ultrasonography and are 
frequently multiple and associated with extracapsular nodal 
extension have a major prognostic impact on recurrence that 
may occur in up to 40% of patients.
A limitation of the existing ATA risk stratification system is that 
most of the existing studies on recurrence focus on patients treated 
with total thyroidectomy and RAI. In recent years there has been 
a paradigm shift, with more treatment with total thyroidectomy 
without RAI or with lobectomy alone.245–247 In the setting of less 
intensive initial management, there is a need to assess recurrence 
risk and refine the existing risk stratification system.
The risk of PTC recurrence is also associated with the molec­
ular profile and with the presence of a BRAF V600E mutation, 
which is associated with a higher risk of recurrence for most 
tumor stages.143,248,249 This risk is even higher when both BRAF 
and telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) mutations are pres­
ent in the tumor.143,250 Each of these characteristics is associated 
with a risk of tumor recurrence that may range from less than 
2% up to more than 40%. However, despite correlating with 
a greater risk for mortality, thus far, studies have not found a

In 2022 the WHO determined that FVPTC should be sep­
arated from the other subtypes of PTC because it has RAS-like 
mutations as opposed to BRAF-like mutations.210 The two dis­
tinct variants of FVPTC are infiltrative and encapsulated forms 
with invasion of blood vessels or of the tumor capsule. Infiltrative 
FVPTC has features of classic PTC except no papillae. The encap­
sulated subtype of FVPTC resembles follicular thyroid cancer 
(FTC). The distinction between the FTC and the encapsulated 
subtype of FVPTC is based on nuclear morphology: FTC lacks 
nuclear features of PTC.210 
Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma
The WHO defines FTC as a malignant epithelial tumor charac­
terized by follicular cell differentiation and absence of the nuclear 
features typical of PTC.188 This definition excludes the follicu­
lar variant of PTC, and it is also customary to exclude both the 
poorly differentiated carcinoma252 and the rare mixed medullary 
and follicular carcinoma.253
Thus, FTC is a relatively rare neoplasm whose identification 
requires invasion of the capsule, blood vessel, or adjacent thyroid. 
In initial epidemiologic surveys, FTC constituted 5% to 50% 
of DTCs and tended to be more common in areas with iodine 
deficiency.254 Changing diagnostic criteria and increases in the 
incidence of PTC associated with dietary iodine supplementa­
tion have reduced the frequency of FTC diagnoses. Data from 
the SEER program from 1980 to 2009 show incidence rates for 
FTCs (1.19 per 100,000 woman-years, 0.55 per 100,000 man-
years) that are markedly lower than those for PTCs (9.21 per 
100,000 woman-years, 3.10 per 100,000 man-years).255
The microscopic appearance of FTC varies from well-formed 
follicles to a predominantly solid growth pattern.183 Poorly 
formed follicles and atypical patterns (e.g., cribriform) may occur, 
and multiple architectural types may coexist. FTC is best divided 
into three categories on the basis of degree of invasiveness: (1) 
minimally invasive or encapsulated, (2) encapsulated angioin­
vasive, and (3) widely invasive. Minimally invasive FTC is an 
encapsulated tumor whose growth pattern resembles that of a 
trabecular or solid microfollicular or atypical adenoma. The diag­
nosis of malignancy depends on the demonstration of capsular 
invasion. The criteria for invasion must therefore be strict.183,188 
Interruption of the capsule must involve the full thickness to 
qualify as capsular invasion. Penetration of only the inner half 
or the presence of tumor cells embedded in the capsule does not 
qualify for the diagnosis of FTC. Foci of capsular invasion must 
be distinguished from the capsular rupture that can result from 
FNA. Extensive histologic sampling may be required to distin­
guish minimally invasive FTCs from follicular adenomas, and the 
ability to discriminate between the two varies substantially from 
one pathologist to another.256
In contrast, the rare, widely invasive form of FTC can be dis­
tinguished easily from benign lesions. Although the tumor may 
be partially encapsulated, the margins are infiltrative even on 
gross examination, and vascular invasion is often extensive. The 
structural features are variable, but a follicular element is always 
present. When follicular differentiation is poor or absent, or 
in the presence of trabecular, insular, or solid components, the 
tumor may be classified as a poorly differentiated carcinoma (see 
later).183,252 Focal or extensive clear cell changes can also be seen 
on histologic analysis. 
Presenting Features of Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma
FTC tends to occur in slightly older individuals as compared to 
PTC.254 As in most thyroid malignancies, women outnumber men 
(>2:1). Most patients with FTC present with a painless thyroid 
nodule, with or without background thyroid nodularity, and they 
rarely (2%–8%) have clinically evident lymphadenopathy at presen­
tation.254 Lymph node metastases to the neck in FTC are so excep­
tional that “wherever they are observed, the alternative possibilities 
of follicular variant papillary carcinoma, oncocytic carcinoma, and 
poorly differentiated carcinoma should be considered.”183
In most series in which tumor sizes were reported, the average 
tumor in FTC was larger than those seen with PTC.257 Direct 
extrathyroidal extension, by definition, does not occur with mini­
mally invasive FTC but is common in the rare patients with widely 
invasive FTC. Between 15% and 27% of patients may have dis­
tant metastases at presentation, although other series suggest lower 
percentages.254 The most common sites for distant metastases in 
FTC are the lung and bone.254 The bones most often involved 
are long bones (e.g., femur), flat bones (particularly the pelvis, 
sternum, and skull), and vertebrae. When a distant metastasis is 
the first manifestation of the disease, definitive proof of its thy­
roid origin should be obtained, usually by biopsy of a metastasis, 
before performing any thyroid surgery. It is unusual but possible 
for patients with FTC to have thyrotoxicosis caused by a massive 
tumor burden producing thyroid hormone.258 
Risk of Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma Recurrence 
and Mortality
Recurrence rates reported in patients with FTCs vary widely, from 
3% to 43.5%, and recurrence is most frequent in widely invasive 
FTC. Over half of all FTC recurrences are detected within the 3 
years after diagnosis, and 80% are found within the first 6 years. 
The vast majority of recurrences (up to 85%) occur at distant sites, 
but lesions can also be found in the thyroid bed and regional lymph 
nodes. Nodal metastases are rare in typical FTC, and the nodal 
recurrence rate at 20 postoperative years is the lowest among dif­
ferentiated thyroid carcinoma, being around 2%.259
The mortality rate from FTC exceeds that of PTC (Fig. 12.14). 
Carcinoma-specific mortalities vary with the presenting TNM stage 
in both FTC and Hürthle cell carcinoma (HCC) (Fig. 12.15). The 
death rates tend to parallel the curves for the development of distant 
metastases (Fig. 12.16).
The risk factors that predict outcome in FTC are similar to those 
recognized in PTC260–263 and include distant metastases at presen­
tation, advanced age at diagnosis (>45 years for most studies), large 
primary tumors (>4 cm), the presence and extent of local (extra­
thyroidal) invasion, and the completeness of excision. To a lesser 
degree, increased mortality risk is associated with male sex. The 
number of vessels involved (<4 or ≥4) also has prognostic value for 
both cancer-specific survival and disease-free survival.254,262 Incon­
sistencies between the results of different studies in predicting the 
outcome of patients with FTC may reflect the use of different clas­
sification systems over long follow-up periods, the quality of the 
pathologic reviews, and/or the small sample sizes. 
Molecular Pathogenesis of Follicular Cell–
Derived Neoplasms
Nearly all PTCs arise as the result of alterations in genes encoding 
components of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) 
453
CHAPTER 12  Nontoxic Diffuse Goiter, Nodular Thyroid Disorders, and Thyroid Malignancies
and PI3K/PTEN/AKT/mTOR signaling pathways. The gene 
most frequently mutated in PTCs is the protooncogene BRAF, 
which encodes a serine-threonine protein kinase that plays a cen­
tral role in regulating signaling through the MAPK pathway. In 
most cases, BRAF is activated as a result of a point mutation 
that causes a glutamate-for-valine substitution at residue 600 
(p.V600E). This alteration is found in up to 40% to 60% of 
all PTCs,148,264,265 primarily the classic and tall cell subtypes.148 
The BRAF V600E mutation occurs early in tumorigenesis,266 
inducing loss of differentiation267 and promoting tumor inva­
sion and progression.268
The second most prevalent mutations found in PTCs involve 
the RAS family of genes, which encode proteins that act as sig­
nal transduction switches to regulate diverse cytoplasmic signal­
ing pathways.269 Although RAS is a classic activator of both the 
MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways, the RAS mutations associated 
with thyroid tumorigenesis seem to preferentially activate the 
PI3K-AKT pathway. Missense mutations at codons 12, 13, and 
61 result in constitutive RAS signaling, and they are found in 10% 
to 30% of PTCs148,270 (FVPTCs and NIFTPs in particular).132,271
Of all PTCs, 5% to 10% are characterized by genetic 
recombination of the RET protooncogene, which encodes a 
transmembrane receptor with a tyrosine kinase domain.148,272 
These alterations are characteristic of PTCs linked to radiation 
exposure (environmental or therapeutic).272 There are >25 differ­
ent types of RET/PTC, all resulting from the fusion of the tyrosine 
kinase domain of RET to the 5′ portion of different genes.273 RET/
PTC1 (now referred to as CCDC6/RET) and RET/PTC3 (now 
referred to as NCOA4/RET) are the most common types, followed 
by RET/PTC2 (now referred to as PRKAR1A/RET). CCDC6/
RET is formed by an intrachromosomal rearrangement fusing the 
RET tyrosine kinase domain to a gene designated H4 (CCDC6). 
PRKAR1A/RET is formed by an interchromosomal rearrangement 
fusing the RET tyrosine kinase domain to a gene located on chro­
mosome 17 encoding the RIα regulatory subunit of protein kinase 
A. NCOA4/RET is formed by an intrachromosomal rearrange­
ment fusing the RET tyrosine kinase domain to a gene designated 
RFG (NCOA4). NCOA4/RET was more frequently found in 
aggressive tumors that occurred early after the Chernobyl disaster,

and CCDC6/RET was found in classic variant tumors that are less 
aggressive and occurred later.
In addition to RET/PTC rearrangements, PTCs have been 
found to harbor fusion genes involving NRTK1,274 NTRK3,275 
BRAF,276 ALK,277 FGFR2, THADA, MET, LTK,148 and ROS1.278 
PTCs with oncogenic gene fusions are closely associated with 
radiation exposure, and these tumors usually have distinctive 
clinicopathologic features.275 Fusions (especially those involv­
ing NRTK1/3) are particularly common in PTCs that develop 
in pediatric patients, where they are associated with more aggres­
sive disease.279,280 On the whole, adult PTCs with gene fusions 
are usually associated with an intermediate risk of recurrence.1 
Fusions involving the PAX8 and PPARG genes, which are fre­
quently found in FTCs, have also been reported in a small subset 
of PTCs, particularly FVPTCs.148,281
TERT-promoter mutations are identified in 8% to 27% of 
PTCs, particularly those that also harbor mutations affecting 
the MAPK pathways (e.g., BRAF V600E, activating RAS muta­
tions).282–285 They upregulate the expression of TERT, thereby 
reactivating telomerase to promote cellular immortality. The 
C228T substitution is the most common (7%), and the C228A 
and C250T substitutions are less common (0.3% and 2.1%, 
respectively).148 TERT mutations are associated with aggressive 
clinicopathologic features and a high risk of recurrence, particu­
larly when coexisting with BRAF, suggesting a synergistic interac­
tion between BRAF and TERT.286
Mutations in the DNA repair genes CHEK2 and PPMID have 
also been found in PTCs, each affecting approximately 1% of all 
tumors. These mutations occurred concomitantly with MAPK-
pathway driver mutations, suggesting that they are late genetic 
events in PTC tumorigenesis and that the development of particu­
larly aggressive phenotypes may be triggered by an acquired defect 
in DNA repair.148
There is still no accepted paradigm for the pathogenesis of 
FTC. A multistep adenoma-to-carcinoma pathogenesis, simi­
lar to that for colon cancer and other adenocarcinomas, is not 
universally accepted because pathologists do not recognize fol­
licular carcinoma in situ, and documentation of the evolution of 
adenoma to carcinoma is rare. Nevertheless, several facts about 
the pathogenesis of FTC are firmly established.143,187,287,288 First, 
most follicular adenomas and all FTCs are probably of mono­
clonal origin. Second, oncogene activation, particularly by point 
mutation of the RAS oncogene, is common both in follicular 
adenomas (∼20%) and in FTCs (∼40%), supporting a role for 
these mutations in early tumorigenesis.288,289 This commonality 
suggests that follicular thyroid adenoma (FTA) and FTC are etio­
logically related or, more specifically, that FTAs are premalignant 
neoplasms that can (at least in some cases, but likely not all) prog­
ress to become FTC.288 Moreover, the fact that RAS mutations 
are common in FTA, FTC, and FVPTC implies that all these 
follicular-patterned neoplasms share a common pathogenesis.290 
The RET and BRAF oncogenes do not appear to be involved in 
follicular tumors.143,187,291 Third, cytogenetic abnormalities and 
evidence of genetic loss are more common in FTC than in PTC 
and also occur in follicular adenomas.287,291
Genes encoding components of the PI3K/PTEN/AKT sig­
naling pathway are also likely to be genetically altered or epige­
netically silenced in FTCs.292 Somatic mutations involving the 
tumor suppressor gene PTEN are found in up to 1 of 10 sporadic 
FTCs,293 and germline PTEN mutations are associated with the 
Cowden syndrome (CS). Up to 10% of all FTCs also harbor acti­
vating PIK3CA mutations.294 
Hürthle Cell Carcinoma/Oncocytic Carcinoma of 
the Thyroid
Until recently, HCCs were considered a subtype of FTCs. How­
ever, two recent landmark studies have now provided definitive 
evidence that HCCs result from unique molecular alterations 
distinct from other thyroid neoplasias.295,296 The characteristic 
accumulation of mitochondria seen in HCC histology led to 
parallel analyses of somatic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and 
nuclear DNA, yielding several findings. First, recurrent mtDNA 
mutations coding for subunits of the electron transport chain 
complex I within the mitochondrial structure were found. As 
yet, the functional consequences of these mtDNA alterations and 
their relationship to oncogenesis have not been elucidated. In the 
genomic DNA studied, recurrent mutations in tumor suppressor 
genes were found in DAXX, TP53, CDK1A, and ARHGAP35. 
Mutations in genes converging upon the RAS/RAF/MAPK and 
mTOR/PI3K/AKT pathways were also identified, in addition 
to TERT-promoter mutations. Additional mutations involving 
transcription and translation, such as EIF1AX and ATRX, were 
found in a subset of cases. Mutations involving DNA repair and 
the DNA damage response were also found in some cases. Impor­
tantly, unique to HCCs among thyroid cancer histologies, DNA 
copy number analysis revealed that widespread chromosomal loss 
was common in HCCs, resulting in near-haploid chromosomal 
content, which may facilitate the oncogenic consequences of sin­
gle tumor suppressor gene hits and result in complete tumor sup­
pressor inactivation. 
Presenting Features of Oncocytic Carcinoma of 
the Thyroid
Oncocytic carcinoma of the thyroid (OCA) has replaced the 
term Hürthle cell carcinoma because Hürthle cell carcinoma was 
considered a misnomer.297 OCA is a rare subtype of follicu­
lar-derived thyroid carcinoma, distinguished from other his­
tologies by a marked accumulation of mitochondria, creating 
an abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. By definition, 
OCAs are composed of at least 75% oncocytic cells with abun­
dant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm that also lack the typical 
nuclear features of PTC. Because of differences in outcomes, 
OCAs are histologically subclassified into minimally invasive 
cancers with capsular invasion only, encapsulated angioinva­
sive cancers, and widely invasive cancers with gross invasion 
through the gland.
On US, there are no specific abnormalities characteristic of 
OCA; the spectrum of suspicious findings is similar to that seen 
in other DTCs. By cytology alone, it is usually impossible to dis­
tinguish between a benign oncocytic process and OCA. Thus, 
histologic evaluation of a surgical specimen is generally neces­
sary to make the diagnosis. Compared to other DTCs, OCAs are 
diagnosed in older patients, with a median age of approximately 
55 to 60 years, and although they are more frequently diagnosed 
in women than men, the female-to-male ratio is lower than that 
seen in other thyroid cancers. Most patients present with resect­
able, widely invasive cancers, with a median primary tumor size 
of approximately 3.5 cm. Lymph node metastasis is found in a 
minority of patients, and up to 10% of patients will have distant 
metastasis at presentation, the risk of which is almost entirely con­
centrated in patients with widely invasive OCA. The most com­
mon sites of distant metastasis include the lungs, followed by the 
bones and the mediastinum.298–303

Risk of Recurrence and Mortality
Although some studies have shown that patients with OCA have 
a worse prognosis than that of patients with FTC, not all have 
found this to be the case.304–306 A recent SEER database analysis 
of 2279 OCA cases demonstrates cancer-specific survival rates at 
5, 10, and 15 years of 96.9%, 93.2%, and 90.3%, respectively.303 
Among patients with OCA, independent risk factors for recur­
rence and/or death include widely invasive histology, male sex, 
and TNM stage III to IV.298 Although ablative or treatment doses 
of 131I have historically been administered postoperatively to a 
majority of patients with OCA, the benefits of 131I in OCA are 
debated.298–299 In a National Cancer Data Base (NCDB) analy­
sis of 1909 OCA cases, 60.6% of patients received 131I. Patients 
with stage I disease were more likely to receive 131I, but otherwise, 
131I treatment did not vary based on pathologic features. Treated 
patients were also younger, more often had private medical insur­
ance, and were more likely to receive treatment at an academic 
center. Of note, 131I administration was associated with a statisti­
cally significant 30% reduction in mortality (HR = 0.703, p = 
0.001). Further data on the responsiveness of OCA to 131I may 
be gleaned from evidence of 131I uptake in treated patients with 
distant metastatic disease. In a series including 22 patients with 
metastatic OCA treated with 131I, 131I avidity was present in only 
13.6% of cases, a rate that was lower compared to all other DTC 
histology studies.307 Moreover, despite 131I avidity in some cases, 
95.5% of patients with OCA experienced progressive disease, with 
a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 9 months. 
Poorly Differentiated Thyroid Carcinoma
Following publication of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) analy­
sis detailing the molecular landscape of PTCs, the need for similar 
analyses in more aggressive follicular-derived thyroid cancers was 
clear.308 Next generation sequencing (NGS) by a 341-gene assay 
was performed in 84 PDTCs and 33 ATCs.309 Findings support 
the hypothesis of PDTCs and ATCs arising from more well-differ­
entiated DTCs, particularly as shown in the increasing frequency 
and clonality of TERT-promoter mutation from PTC to PDTC to 
ATC. TERT-promoter mutations in PDTC and ATC were found 
to coexist with BRAF and RAS mutations, suggesting an interplay 
between MAPK-pathway activation and transcription factor regu­
lation. TP53 was far more common in ATC than PDTC, whereas 
mutations in other tumor suppressor genes or genes related to 
DNA damage response and repair, including ATM, RB1, NF2, 
and MEN1, were seen uncommonly in both. Mutations in PI3K/
AKT/mTORpathway genes were seen more frequently in ATCs 
than PDTCs, as were mutations in genes encoding components 
of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex. Mutations 
involving the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) pathway, includ­
ing MSH2, MSH6, and MLH1, were found occasionally in ATCs 
and less commonly in PDTCs. These tumors were more likely to 
harbor a high tumor mutational burden. Of note, gene rearrange­
ments involving the targetable oncogenic kinases RET and ALK 
were found in several PDTC cases. 
Presenting Features of PDTC
A consensus meeting of international pathologists was held in 
Turin, Italy, in 2007 to establish the diagnostic criteria for PDTCs 
that carry an intermediate prognosis between the favorable out­
comes of DTC and the very poor prognosis of ATC.310 Following 
this, the WHO recently recognized two groups of high-grade non­
anaplastic follicular-derived carcinomas: PDTC and differentiated 
high-grade thyroid carcinoma (DHGTC).297 Both subtypes tend 
to exhibit aggressive pathologic features, such as widely invasive 
behavior, hemorrhagic foci, vascular invasion, and tumor necrosis, 
but can be distinguished by histologic features. Hallmark charac­
teristics of PDTCs are their solid, trabecular, and insular growth 
patterns (or combination of these features), whereas DHGTCs 
retain the well-differentiated histologic appearance of DTCs, such 
as nuclear features of PTCs or the follicular growth pattern of 
FTCs.297,311
PDTC and DHGTC are rare, accounting for up to 6.7% of 
all thyroid carcinomas. The median age at diagnosis of PDTC 
is approximately 60 years, and as seen in OCA, the female-to-
male ratio is lower than that which occurs in other thyroid can­
cers. Locally invasive extrathyroidal disease is frequently found 
at presentation, and lymph node metastasis is common in both. 
Approximately 25% to 45% of patients will have distant metas­
tasis at diagnosis, with sites including lung, bone, and brain. Of 
note, distant metastatic PDTC can concentrate 131I at fairly high 
rates, although information on structural response to 131I treat­
ment is lacking.311–314 
Risk of Recurrence and Mortality
Disease-specific survival rates for PDTC and DHGTC are similar, 
with a 5-year disease-specific survival rate of 66% to 76% and 10- 
and 20-year disease-specific survival rates of approximately 60% 
and 35%, respectively.311,312,315 Risk factors for poor outcomes 
include older age, advanced T stage, extensive necrosis, high 
mitotic count, lack of encapsulation, high ATA risk stratification, 
and the presence of distant metastasis.311,312,314,315 Molecular risk 
factors that in turn predict poor outcomes include TERT pro­
moter, TP53, and a high-molecular-risk gene signature on Thyro­
Seq analysis.309–311,314 
Anaplastic Carcinoma
NGS studies defining the molecular landscape of ATCs have now 
been conducted. Overall and not unexpectedly, ATCs harbor a 
higher tumor mutational burden than more well-differentiated 
thyroid carcinomas, with a median of six alterations per tumor. 
This likely results, at least in part, from a higher rate of DNA 
mismatch repair and APOBEC mutation signatures seen in some 
ATCs. The two most commonly mutated genes in ATC are TP53, 
seen in approximately 65% of cases versus rarely in other thy­
roid cancers, and the TERT promoter, also seen in approximately 
65%; 41% of ATCs harbor BRAF gene alterations, whereas 27% 
harbor RAS mutations. EIF1AX mutations are less common than 
and mutually exclusive with TERT-promoter mutations. They 
tend to co-occur with RAS mutations. ATCs are also enriched for 
mutations in other tumor suppressor genes (e.g., NF2, NF1, and 
RB1) and are more likely to harbor mutations in genes involved 
in the PI3K/AKT pathway. Alterations in genes involved in his­
tone modification and the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling 
complex, as well as alterations in cell cycle genes (e.g., CDKN2A, 
CDKN2B, and CCNE1) are also more common in ATCs com­
pared to DTCs.309
Interestingly, hierarchical clustering revealed four main groups 
of ATCs. TP53 mutations were seen across all four clusters. One 
cluster featured tumors with BRAF V600E mutations, often with 
co-mutations in PIK3CA, AKT1, or ARID2. These ATCs are 
SECTION III    Thyroid
456
thought to have devolved from more well-differentiated PTCs. A 
second cluster was characterized by NRAS mutations, frequently 
with CCNE1 copy number alterations, and likely represent­
ing tumors that have devolved from FTCs. Another cluster was 
found to harbor PTEN mutations, frequently with NF1 and RB1 
co-mutations. ATCs in this cluster also often had KIT/KDR/
PDGFR amplifications and DNA MMR mutations. This cluster 
tended to have a higher tumor mutational burden than ATCs in 
the other clusters and was thought to most likely have arisen out 
of preexisting OCAs or FTCs. Finally, a group of mixed ATCs 
clustered together, harboring alterations involving CDKN2A and/
or CDKNB, co-occurring with mutually exclusive BRAF, NRAS, 
or PTEN/NF1/RB1 mutations, thus not seeming to arise from one 
common, more well-differentiated precursor.316
With an emerging role for immunotherapy as a treatment 
modality in ATC, increasing attention is being paid to the tumor 
microenvironment of ATC. Early reports described rich infiltra­
tion of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), particularly with 
an M2 cancer-promoting immunosuppressive phenotype.317,318 
Now, a deeper understanding of the adaptive tumor microen­
vironment that allows ATCs to escape immune surveillance is 
unfolding.319 Infiltration of both cytotoxic and regulatory T cells 
is significantly greater in ATCs compared to DTCs. The tumor 
microenvironment of DTCs is rarely positive for PD-L1, whereas 
most ATCs are PD-L1–positive, and a generous subset of ATCs 
exhibit high PD-L1 expression.320 
Presenting Features of ATC
ATC typically presents in patients in the sixth or seventh decade 
of life as a rapidly enlarging neck mass that may be associ­
ated with hoarseness, dyspnea, dysphagia, and pain.321 Most 
patients have large primary tumors at diagnosis, with frequent 
regional nodal involvement. Approximately 40% will have dis­
tant metastasis. Given the frequency of distant metastasis in 
ATC, PET/CT imaging is considered essential in the staging 
workup.322 The diagnosis is slightly more common in women 
than men. Because of the aggressive nature of the disease, all 
ATCs are stage IV by the AJCC 8th edition criteria. Stage IVA 
disease is confined within the capsule of the thyroid, with no 
nodal or distant metastasis. Stage IVB disease exhibits extension 
beyond the capsule and/or lymph nodes are involved. Stage IVC 
patients present with distant metastasis.
Approximately two-thirds of patients with ATC will have 
potentially resectable disease at diagnosis. The resectability of ATC 
should be carefully assessed upon presentation, given the frequency 
with which ATC invades locoregional structures, including the 
internal jugular vein, carotid artery, recurrent laryngeal and other 
nerves, esophagus, trachea, and larynx. Although metastasis to the 
lungs, mediastinum, bones, and liver are the most common, ATC 
can metastasize anywhere, including the brain.
Histologically, about 60% of ATCs arise in patients with an ear­
lier history of a more well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma, or the 
ATC is found coexisting with a more well-differentiated thyroid 
carcinoma. Although ATCs exhibit a wide range of histologic fea­
tures, including pleomorphic, spindle cell, epithelioid, squamous 
cell carcinoma, rhabdoid, osteoclast giant cell-rich, and tumor 
giant cells, other features, such as invasiveness, extensive necro­
sis, marked nuclear pleomorphism, and high mitotic activity, are 
common to most ATCs.297,323 Some of these ATC cytomorpho­
logic features can be shared in common with other thyroid cancer 
histologies, and thus FNA sampling alone may prove insufficient 
in confirming a diagnosis of ATC, although clinical suspicion of 
aggressive disease is often apparent at time of presentation, allow­
ing surgical planning to nonetheless occur.324,325 FNA often pro­
vides high suspicion of aggressive disease, although core-needle 
biopsy can also be considered because this also may improve the 
yield for biomarker testing. 
Risk of Recurrence and Mortality
Despite the rarity of ATC, accounting for less than 2% of all 
thyroid tumors, ATC is responsible for up to 40% of all thyroid 
cancer deaths.326,327 The 5-year disease-specific survival of ATC 
is <15%, and the median OS is 3 to 9 months.323,328 The most 
powerful predictor of survival in ATC is resectability. A number 
of studies have shown that survival is possible only when patients 
have undergone an R0 or R1 surgery with complete resection 
with negative microscopic margins, or all gross tumor is resected, 
but margins are microscopically positive, respectively. For those 
patients presenting with unresectable disease or who undergo an 
R2 resection with gross disease left behind, the chance of long-
term survival is poor.323,329 Additional prognostic factors in ATC 
include age, performance status, socioeconomic status, respira­
tory compromise by the tumor, the presence of distant metastasis, 
receipt of chemotherapy or multimodal therapy, and the presence 
of a TERT-promoter co-mutation in BRAF- and RAS-mutated dis­
ease.322,323,328,330,331 Although survival rates have not improved in 
the past several decades, there is hope that new precision targeted 
therapy approaches will improve outcomes, at least for a subset of 
patients with ATC with targetable molecular alterations.328,332,333 
Lymphoma and Rare Malignancies of Other Cell 
Types
Rarely, other malignant processes not derived from follicular or C 
cells can arise in the thyroid. Large case series suggest such find­
ings represent <3% of all thyroid cancers, and the most common 
of these rare malignancies is thyroid lymphoma.334 Primary thy­
roid lymphomas account for less than 2% of all extranodal lym­
phomas. The peak incidence is during the seventh decade of life, 
and the male-to-female ratio is 1:2 to 8.335
Primary thyroid lymphoma almost always has a B-cell lin­
eage.335 The majority of thyroid malignant lymphomas are 
mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphomas that usu­
ally arise in a background of Hashimoto thyroiditis. These small 
cell lymphomas are characterized by a low grade of malignancy, a 
slow growth rate, and a tendency for recurrence at other MALT 
sites, such as the gastrointestinal or respiratory tract, the thymus, 
or the salivary glands. At diagnosis, diffuse large cell lymphomas 
account for about 70% to 80% of tumors, and a substantial pro­
portion of clinical cases arise from the transformation of low-
grade MALT lymphoma to high-grade B-cell lymphoma. Other 
histologic findings are rare.
Clinical thyroid lymphomas almost invariably present as a rap­
idly enlarging, painless neck mass. One-third of the patients have 
compressive symptoms. The mass is often fixed to surrounding 
tissues, and half of the patients have unilateral or bilateral cervi­
cal lymph node enlargement. Clinically evident distant disease is 
uncommon. About 20% of patients already have a long-standing 
goiter, and hypothyroidism is reported in up to 40% of cases. The 
palpated mass is solid and hypoechoic on ultrasonography, which 
often depicts a characteristic asymmetric pseudocystic pattern. 
Most patients have serum antiperoxidase and anti-Tg antibodies. 
457
CHAPTER 12  Nontoxic Diffuse Goiter, Nodular Thyroid Disorders, and Thyroid Malignancies
US typically demonstrates a hypoechoic enlarged thyroid, often 
with associated abnormal lymphadenopathy.
The diagnosis of lymphoma can often be established by FNA 
cytologic and flow cytometric tests, particularly in diffuse large 
B-cell type. The need for core-needle or surgical biopsies has 
decreased, but they can still be helpful for distinguishing thyroid­
itis from low-grade MALT lymphoma and for reliably excluding 
aggressive histologies because histology, immunostaining, and 
testing for gene rearrangements may be needed.
Accurate staging is critical for treatment planning. Staging 
includes a physical examination; complete blood count; serum 
lactate dehydrogenase; liver function tests; bone marrow biopsy; 
CT scan or MRI of the neck; CT scan of the thorax, abdomen, 
and pelvis; and appropriate biopsies at other sites where tumor is 
suspected. [18F]FDG-PET scanning may be useful for the initial 
diagnosis and for monitoring responses to treatment. Involvement 
of the Waldeyer ring and the gastrointestinal tract has been associ­
ated with thyroid lymphomas, and therefore upper gastrointesti­
nal tract radiographs or endoscopy should be performed.
Treatment is guided by the histologic subtype, the extent of the 
disease, and (in the case of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) the age-
adjusted international prognostic index.336,337 Surgical debulk­
ing of thyroid lymphomas is neither feasible nor necessary. Small 
tumors are often treated initially as primary thyroid carcinomas 
with surgery, and additional radiotherapy may be necessary in case 
of indolent lymphoma.
For high-grade B-cell lymphoma, chemotherapy combined 
with rituximab (chimeric human-mouse anti-CD20 monoclonal 
antibody) has become the standard treatment.338 The chemo­
therapy prescribed should be an anthracycline-based regimen. It 
usually consists of four to six cycles of the CHOP regimen (cyclo­
phosphamide 750 mg/m2 on day 1, doxorubicin 50 mg/m2 on 
day 1, vincristine 1.4 mg/m2 on day 1, and prednisone 40 mg/m2 
per day on days 1–5) every 3 weeks. For localized aggressive lym­
phoma, the combination of chemotherapy and radiotherapy used 
before the era of rituximab reduced distant recurrence compared 
with radiotherapy alone, which should be used only for elderly 
patients who cannot receive medical treatment because a recur­
rence at distant sites will occur in one-third of the patients and 
generally within the first year of treatment.
For MALT lymphomas, if disease is localized after accurate 
staging, total thyroidectomy (predicted OS rate and disease-free 
survival, 100% at 5 years) or involved field radiation therapy 
alone, 2 Gy per fraction for 5 days per week up to a total dose 
of 30 to 40 Gy (5-year OS rate, 90%) may be adequate.339 For 
disseminated MALT lymphoma, chemotherapy alone with a sin­
gle agent such as chlorambucil or combined with local radiation 
therapy can be proposed.
When other nonlymphomatous solid tumors have metasta­
sized to the thyroid, advanced and other distant disease should be 
expected. Specific therapy for such metastatic disease (e.g., breast 
cancer, renal cell carcinoma, esophageal carcinoma) must be driven 
by data specific to each malignancy and often benefits from molecu­
lar analysis and specific targeted tyrosine kinase therapy if available. 
Immediate resection, as would be considered for a primary follicular 
cell–derived thyroid malignancy, is often not favored unless immi­
nent compression or invasion of neck structures occurs. 
Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma
MTC is rare, accounting for less than 4% of all thyroid cancers. 
Yet MTC has a more aggressive natural history than that of DTC, 
therefore accounting for approximately 10% of thyroid cancer 
deaths.340 Remarkable progress has been made over the last several 
decades in understanding molecular underpinnings of MTC and 
optimizing treatment approaches.
Molecular Pathogenesis
MTC arises from parafollicular C cells embedded in the thyroid 
gland.341,342 Because C cells are of neural crest origin, MTC is 
considered a neuroendocrine tumor. The majority of MTCs are 
sporadic, whereas 25% arise in the setting of the hereditary MEN 
syndromes MEN2A and MEN2B (also referred to as MEN3). 
Germline mutations in the rearranged in transfection (RET) pro­
tooncogene are causative in essentially all hereditary MTCs. RET 
encodes a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase that, when acti­
vated by ligand binding to its coreceptor, homodimerizes, leading 
to phosphorylation and activation of the kinase domain. In turn, 
activated RET promotes signaling via several cellular pathways 
regulating cell growth, differentiation, and metastasis, includ­
ing the phospholipase Cγ/protein kinase C (PLCγ/PKC), c-Jun 
N-terminal kinases (c-Jun/JNK), phosphatidyl-inositol-3-kinase 
(PI3K-AKT), and MAPK pathways.343 More than 100 mutations, 
duplications, insertions, or deletions have been identified across 
seven RET exons. In MEN2A, the most common germline muta­
tion occurs at RET codon C634 in the extracellular cysteine-rich 
domain. MEN2B, most often caused by a germline RET M918T 
mutation in the kinase domain, is far less common than MEN2A, 
likely because of the aggressive nature of the MTC associated 
with this mutation, arising very early in life, even in infancy.342 
Consequently, many MEN2B cases result from de novo rather 
than inherited germline RET M918T mutations.344 First-degree 
relatives of patients harboring any germline RET mutation should 
be encouraged to receive genetic counseling and testing. Newly 
identified carriers should then enter further screening evaluations, 
and treatment should be based on the specific RET alteration and 
screening findings.342
A distinct genotype-phenotype correlation across the various 
germline RET mutations has been described.344,345 For example, 
patients with MEN2A RET C634 mutations are at high risk for 
early-onset MTC that may arise before 5 years of age, leading 
to the recommendation that carriers begin screening by US and 
serum calcitonin by 3 years of age to determine when prophylac­
tic thyroidectomy is needed.342,346 These patients are also at high 
risk for pheochromocytoma and parathyroid adenoma. On the 
other hand, germline RET V804 mutations are considered mod­
erate risk, with a more variable onset of MTC that may even be 
diagnosed in later adulthood, suggesting that screening alone may 
be appropriate for some carriers; not all may require prophylac­
tic thyroidectomy. Patients with RET V804 mutations are also at 
risk for pheochromocytoma and parathyroid adenoma, although 
the risk is lower than that seen with RET C634 mutations. The 
phenotype of patients with MEN2B includes the very high risk 
of early-onset MTC, in addition to a distinct marfanoid habitus, 
mucosal neuromas, medullated corneal fibers, and intestinal auto­
nomic ganglion dysfunction leading to diverticulae and megaco­
lon. Because MTC may arise even in the first months of life in 
germline RET M918T carriers, genetic testing should be done 
soon after birth in at-risk infants, and prophylactic thyroidectomy 
should be performed within the first year of life.
Of the 75% of MTC cases that are sporadic, approximately 
60% harbor somatic RET mutations.347 RET M918T is the 
most common sporadic mutation, followed by RET codon C634 
SECTION III    Thyroid
458
and other mutations. In RET wild-type sporadic MTC, H- and 
N-RAS are the most common driver molecular alterations found. 
Of note, germline RET mutations have been identified in up to 
6% of apparently sporadic MTCs, highlighting the need for deter­
mination of germline RET status in every patient diagnosed with 
MTC.344 
Presenting Features of MTC
The age range at diagnosis is wide for MTCs, but most patients are 
in the fourth and fifth decades of life when diagnosed. The gender 
distribution is roughly equivalent. Sporadic MTC most frequently 
presents with a neck mass and less commonly with paraneoplastic 
diarrhea and/or flushing secondary to elevated calcitonin secreted 
by the tumor. Rarely, MTCs produce ectopic adrenocorticotropic 
hormone (ACTH), leading to paraneoplastic Cushing syndrome. 
A majority of familial MTC cases are diagnosed by familial screen­
ing after identification of an index case.
Thyroid US and FNA of a suspicious lesion are the most 
common initial diagnostic tests, although cytologic identifica­
tion of MTC can be challenging.348 The diagnostic accuracy can 
be improved by measuring serum calcitonin when MTC is sus­
pected, and now molecular diagnostics that can be incorporated 
into FNA analysis are highly sensitive and specific for MTC.349,350 
When MTC is identified preoperatively, screening for pheochro­
mocytoma is critical to allow for careful perioperative pheochro­
mocytoma management.
Preoperative serum calcitonin levels predict extent of disease. 
Serum calcitonin of less than 20 to 50 pg/mL indicates a low like­
lihood of occult nodal metastases, whereas calcitonin greater than 
500 pg/mL predicts a high likelihood of nodal metastasis, which 
can involve the bilateral central and lateral neck compartments 
and mediastinum.351–353 When serum calcitonin is >1000 pg/mL, 
the possibility of distant metastatic disease is high, and the staging 
workup should include comprehensive structural imaging. When 
preoperative calcitonin levels are high, in addition to thyroid US, 
CT imaging of the neck and chest may be helpful in identify­
ing nodal disease not evaluable by US, such as retropharyngeal 
and/or substernal, mediastinal, and hilar adenopathy.342 When 
preoperative calcitonin exceeds 200 pg/mL, some advocate for 
contralateral neck dissection in addition to total thyroidectomy 
and ipsilateral neck dissection, although this is controversial. The 
most common sites of distant metastases are the liver (most com­
mon), lung, bone, and brain. Metastatic deposits to the liver and 
bone can be very small and challenging to detect on routine CT. 
Thus, liver-directed imaging by MRI or CT and PET/CT imaging 
with [18F]FDOPA or 68Ga-DOTA-peptides may be indicated.354 
Because brain metastasis is rare at initial presentation, brain MRI 
to rule out brain metastasis is typically reserved for patients with 
more advanced disease. 
Risk of MTC Recurrence and Mortality
The natural history of MTC is quite variable, whether diagnosed 
when the disease is limited to the locoregional area or when dis­
tant metastasis is already present. MTC is staged according to the 
AJCC TNM staging system.355 For MTC, T1 N0 M0 carcinoma 
is stage I, but T2 to T3 N0 M0 is stage II, and a T1 to T3 N1a 
M0 tumor is stage III, underlying the prognostic impact of lymph 
node involvement. There is no age distinction for MTC, although 
age is a significant independent prognostic indicator in most mul­
tivariate analyses.356,357 Approximately 70% of MTC cases are 
confined to the thyroid, with or without regional nodal metastasis, 
at the time of diagnosis.358
Standard pathologic findings, including the TNM stage, extra­
thyroidal extension, margin status, nodal involvement, and extra­
nodal extension, are important prognostic factors.359,360 A new 
International MTC Grading System (IMTCGS) evaluating Ki-67 
proliferative index, mitotic count, and the presence of necrosis 
has been proposed to provide more accurate prognostic informa­
tion on disease relapse and OS by stratifying MTCs into low- and 
high-grade tumors.361 
Outcome Prediction for MTC
Approximately 70% of patients with MTC will have locoregion­
ally confined stage I to III disease at presentation. Of these patients 
who undergo complete resection, very few will experience struc­
tural locoregional recurrence or distant metastatic disease over 
time.362 On the other hand, the prognosis for the approximately 
10% to 30% of patients who present with distant metastasis is 
poor, with a 5-year OS rate of approximately 15%. Tumor grade 
is also predictive of outcomes. In IMTCGS high-grade MTC, 
the 10-year OS was 47%, versus 91% in patients with low-grade 
MTC.361
Serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels 
have utility beyond predicting the preoperative extent of disease. 
Postoperatively, calcitonin and CEA are followed as biochemical 
markers of residual disease. Following complete resection, if a bio­
chemical complete response is achieved (i.e., serum calcitonin and 
CEA levels normalize), the long-term likelihood of biochemical 
recurrence is less than 5%, and the risk of structural recurrence 
is even lower.358 In patients who experience a postoperative bio­
chemical incomplete response, the risk of structural disease recur­
rence is approximately 10% to 15%. Calcitonin and CEA DT 
calculated by serial measurement are also helpful in risk-stratifying 
patient outcomes in long-term follow-up, with shorter DTs pre­
dicting worse outcomes. A meta-analysis of six studies found that 
a DT cutoff of 1 year provided the most accurate prognostic infor­
mation.363 The 10-year survival for patients with a calcitonin DT 
of ≤1 year was 18%, whereas 10-year survival for patients with 
calcitonin DT >1 year was 95%. When the CEA DT was ≤1 year, 
the 10-year survival was 21%, compared to 100% when CEA 
DT was >1 year. Even when patients have structurally metastatic 
MTC, the natural history of the disease varies. Tumor volume DT 
is predictive in this group, with all patients surviving in long-term 
follow-up when tumor volume DT was >3 years, whereas those 
with tumor volume DT ≤1 year experienced a median OS of 11 
years, and those with intermediate tumor volume DTs experi­
enced a median OS of 17 years.364 Lastly, tumor mutational status 
correlates with outcomes. In sporadic MTC, patients with tumors 
harboring a RET mutation, particularly RET M918T, have worse 
clinical outcomes, whereas those with RAS mutations experience 
better outcomes.340,365 
Initial Treatment of Thyroid Malignancy
Active Surveillance of Thyroid Malignancy
Given the indolent nature of many (especially small, <1 cm) 
PTCs, active surveillance, which involves close monitoring with 
intervention only if there is disease progression, has been proposed 
as a viable management option for low-risk PTC. This manage­
ment option avoids surgical morbidity and overtreatment. A 
459
CHAPTER 12  Nontoxic Diffuse Goiter, Nodular Thyroid Disorders, and Thyroid Malignancies
recent systematic review of seven studies and two cross-sectional 
studies of active surveillance versus immediate surgery and seven 
uncontrolled treatment series of active surveillance found that 
for small, low-risk PTCs, active surveillance and immediate sur­
gery may be associated with similar mortality, risk of recurrence, 
and other outcomes, but that methodology limitations prevent 
strong conclusions.366 Most of the studies to date have focused on 
cancers <1 cm, a tumor size where FNA is not routinely recom­
mended. More studies are needed to assess the safety and utility of 
active surveillance in larger tumors (>1 cm). 
Surgical Therapy: Selecting Total or Lobectomy 
for Differentiated Thyroid Cancer
Before deciding on extent of surgery for well-differentiated thy­
roid cancer, appropriate imaging to assess size of tumor, evidence 
of local invasion, and metastases should be performed.367 In addi­
tion, a history of compressive symptoms, hoarseness, hypothyroid­
ism, radiation exposure, prior head and neck surgery, and family 
history of thyroid cancer or syndromes should be ascertained. 
Finally, a laryngoscopy should be performed preoperatively, if 
warranted, and a TSH level measured. Evidence of multinodular 
disease, local invasion, metastatic disease, history of head and neck 
irradiation, current hypothyroidism, strong family history of thy­
roid cancer, or tumor >4 cm generally warrants a total thyroidec­
tomy (Table 12.5).367 The extent of lymph node dissection should 
be guided by US imaging and FNA biopsy results of lateral neck 
nodes in levels II to VI. If positive, a unilateral or bilateral modi­
fied radical neck dissection should be performed. For a tumor >1 
cm and <4 cm without any of the associated features or history, 
thyroid lobectomy alone should suffice.
Before surgery, the inherent potential risks should be 
thoroughly reviewed by the surgeon with the patient. These 
include the following: (1) for thyroidectomy—bleeding, infec­
tion, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, superior laryngeal nerve 
injury, voice changes, hypoparathyroidism, need for thyroid 
hormone replacement, need for more surgery; (2) for central 
neck dissection (CND)—recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, hypo­
parathyroidism, need for parathyroid gland removal and auto­
transplantation; (3) for a lateral neck dissection (LND)—ear or 
shoulder numbness, marginal mandibular nerve injury and facial 
droop, spinal accessory nerve injury and inability to shrug the 
shoulder, Horner syndrome, vagus nerve and recurrent laryngeal 
nerve injury, thoracic duct injury, tumor recurrence, and need 
for additional surgery. 
Determining the Extent of Initial Cervical Lymph 
Node Dissection in Differentiated Thyroid Cancer
Most often, the surgeon can determine the likelihood of the need 
for CND based on the size of the tumor and any evidence of local 
invasion. However, occasionally one can identify a positive central 
lymph node during surgery, proven by frozen section. In these 
cases, either a unilateral or bilateral CND should be performed 
concomitantly with total thyroidectomy.367 Almost always, a 
CND should also be considered when an LND is indicated 
because “skip metastases” are extremely rare. 
Surgical Approach to Medullary Thyroid Cancer
Patients who present with MTC should be biochemically screened 
for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism.342 Patients 
should also have baseline calcitonin levels measured. All patients 
with MTC should also be screened for the presence of a MEN2 
syndrome and RET protooncogene mutations. Any pheochro­
mocytoma should be surgically removed before thyroidectomy.

Surgical Approach to Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer
ATC is a disease with a very high mortality, and patients with 
this diagnosis require immediate multidisciplinary care (Fig. 
12.17).368 The diagnosis is often suspected on FNA biopsy, as well 
as the initial clinical context. Core biopsy may provide further 
diagnostic information in certain circumstances and can facilitate 
molecular testing, which is indicated for adequate management. 
CT scans of the neck and chest are paramount for making opera­
tive plans. Should the tumor be completely resectable (only R0 
or R1) without compromising vital structures such as the carotid 
artery, trachea, or esophagus, then one should proceed immedi­
ately to surgery. Adjunctive radiation and/or targeted molecular 
therapy is next often considered (see later section on advanced 
therapeutics). New forms of systemic therapies have substantially 
improved the outcomes in a subset of patients with ATC. 
Postoperative Management of Thyroid 
Malignancy
In view of disease-specific uncertainties and the unique needs of 
individual patients, the postoperative treatment of thyroid carci­
noma does not follow a rigid algorithm.1 Clinicians must consider 
the extent of disease at surgery, the histopathology and differentia­
tion of the tumor, the age of the patient and his or her risk group 
category for tumor-related death and recurrence, and the results 
of postoperative serum Tg determination with neck ultrasonog­
raphy. Furthermore, any relevant patient comorbidities (e.g., 
Sjögren syndrome) that may affect the choice of RAI therapy or 
preparation for the procedure, in addition to individual patient 
preferences about treatment, need to be considered.
131I and the Role of RAI Administration
131I is an effective agent for delivering high radiation doses tar­
geted to the thyroid tissue with relatively low radiation exposure 
to other organs. The radiation dose to the thyroid tissue is related 
to the tissue concentration (the ratio between the total tissue 
uptake and the volume of functional tissue) and the effective half-
life of 131I in the tissue.124,369 Concentration of iodine in thyroid 
tissue is significantly augmented by TSH stimulation, but even 
after optimal TSH stimulation, iodine uptake in neoplastic tis­
sue remains lower than in normal thyroid tissue and may not be 
detectable in about one-third of cases.124

CHAPTER 12  Nontoxic Diffuse Goiter, Nodular Thyroid Disorders, and Thyroid Malignancies
131I therapy may be administered postoperatively for one of 
three reasons, depending on the postoperative risk stratification.1 
Remnant ablation, or the destruction of any residual thyroid tis­
sue, was traditionally performed to facilitate detection of recurrent 
disease and/or initial staging by thyroglobulin measurement or 
whole-body RAI scan. This is no longer routinely recommended 
because disease surveillance may be satisfactorily accomplished 
without RAI ablation using neck US and high-sensitivity Tg 
(with Tg antibody) measurements while the patient is on thyroid 
hormone therapy. Adjuvant therapy, involving the destruction of 
suspected but unproven residual disease, is performed in patients 
at increased risk of disease recurrence to improve the duration of 
disease-free survival. RAI therapy involves the treatment of known 
persistent disease in high-risk patients with the intent to improve 
disease-specific and disease-free survival. Importantly, the post­
therapy WBS also provides an opportunity to accurately stage the 
extent of RAI-avid disease and, in combination with SPECT/CT, 
document the presence (or absence) of RAI uptake at any sites of 
structural disease. 
Preparation for RAI Therapy
Several measures are utilized to optimize RAI uptake at sites of 
disease. A low-iodine diet is recommended for 1 to 2 weeks to 
augment RAI uptake, acknowledging there is conflicting evi­
dence on its impact on successful thyroid remnant ablation.370 
TSH stimulation is traditionally performed after thyroid hor­
mone withdrawal for a period of 3 to 4 weeks, and the TSH level 
should be >30 mIU/L before RAI administration.1,371,372 rhTSH 
preparation is an alternative to thyroid hormone withdrawal for 
remnant ablation of patients with ATA low- or intermediate-risk 
disease372–377 or for patients with comorbidities that preclude thy­
roid hormone withdrawal.378 Intramuscular injections of rhTSH 
(0.9 mg for 2 consecutive days, with 131I administered 1 day after 
the second injection) given while on levothyroxine treatment may 
achieve an equally effective stimulation of RAI uptake by normal 
thyroid remnant, with ablation rates similar to those obtained 
with withdrawal using either a high (100 mCi) or a low (30 
mCi) activity.374,376,377 The use of rhTSH prevents hypothyroid­
ism (because the patient remains on levothyroxine) and induces 
lower radiation exposure to the body, permitting an earlier dis­
charge from the hospital.374,376,377,379–381 However, it is important 
to note that remnant ablation (or destruction of normal thyroid 
remnant tissue) is not a meaningful oncologic outcome, and both 
the intrinsic iodine avidity and response to TSH stimulation of 
thyroid cancer cells differs from that of normal thyroid tissue. In 
patients with ATA high-risk disease, thyroid hormone withdrawal 
remains the preferred preparation for RAI therapy in most major 
thyroid cancer guidelines.1,382–384 
Postoperative Disease Status and RAI Decision 
Making
In addition to clinicopathologic risk stratification (see Fig. 12.13), 
the postoperative serum Tg measured at 6 to 12 weeks can be 
used to guide RAI therapy decision making. Although there is a 
lack of consensus regarding actionable Tg levels, if RAI is being 
considered, an unstimulated Tg of <1 ng/mL in the absence of 
detectable anti-Tg antibodies confers a highly favorable prognosis 
without RAI ablation,385 whereas RAI is typically recommended 
if unstimulated Tg is >5 to 10 ng/mL.386–389 Pretreatment RAI 
scanning (see “Structural and Functional Imaging of the Thyroid”) 
can also be considered if it will influence clinical management. 
The role of molecular marker status in postoperative RAI decision 
making continues to evolve, with some guidelines incorporating 
BRAF V600E and TERT mutations into the risk stratification of 
PTC.382 
ATA Recurrence Risk Stratification to Guide 
Postoperative RAI Decision Making
The updated 2015 ATA DTC guidelines provide a practical 
approach to disease recurrence risk stratification, which is a useful 
framework to guide RAI decision making (Box 12.4).1 RAI rem­
nant ablation is not recommended for patients with ATA low-risk 
disease because of the long-term favorable prognosis after surgery 
alone.1,42,390–393 Patients with intermediate-risk disease may be 
treated with administered activities of 30 to 150 mCi (or 1.1–5.5 
GBq) 131I.394–397 An activity of 30 mCi (1.1 GBq) is typically 
used in patients with intermediate-risk disease with lower-risk fea­
tures, whereas higher activities are used for patients where adju­
vant therapy is intended.398
Patients with ATA high-risk or known metastatic disease should 
be treated with higher administered activities of 100 to 200 mCi 
(or 3.7–7.4 GBq).1 RAI therapy is strongly recommended for 
treatment of RAI-avid pulmonary metastases, typically involv­
ing repeated doses at 6- to 12-month intervals for 1 to 2 years, 
provided there is satisfactory iodine uptake, there is evidence of 
continued clinical benefit (e.g., improved symptoms, reduced size 
of pulmonary nodules and declining Tg), and the side effects are 
tolerable.399–402 Dosimetric approaches to therapy with a limit of 
80-mCi whole-body retention at 48 hours and 2 Gy to the bone 
marrow should be considered in patients with diffuse RAI-avid 
pulmonary uptake to minimize the risk of pulmonary pneumo­
nitis and fibrosis,403 but it is only available at high-volume spe­
cialist centers. Whole-body and blood clearance dosimetry can 
also be used to determine a maximum tolerable activity higher 
than 200 mCi (7.4 GBq) and to safely treat patients with renal 
impairment395 or those over 70 years of age,404 for whom empiri­
cally administered RAI above 150 mCi (5.5 GBq) may exceed the 
maximum tolerable dose and should be avoided. RAI therapy at 
similar doses is recommended for RAI-avid bone metastases.1
Empiric therapy with activities ranging between 100 and 200 
mCi (or 3.7–7.4 GBq 131I) may be considered for patients with 
significantly elevated Tg levels (Tg > 10 ng/mL with thyroxine 
withdrawal or Tg > 5 ng/mL with rhTSH stimulation, particu­
larly if progressively rising) but no imaging evidence of structural 
disease (including on RAI diagnostic scans).1,405 It should be 
noted that some guidelines do not support this approach in the 
absence of identifiable structural disease.406 If there is no identifi­
able RAI-avid disease on the posttreatment scan, [18F]FDG-PET/
CT is recommended to identify sites of RAI-refractory disease.
131I ablation therapy has no role in the management of patients 
with ATC, MTC, or thyroid lymphoma. 
External Radiotherapy
External radiotherapy to the neck and mediastinum is indicated 
only for older patients (>55 years) with extensive and aggressive 
pathology subtypes in whom complete surgical excision is impos­
sible, invasion of critical neck structures is likely, and tumor tis­
sue does not take up 131I. Retrospective studies have shown that 
in these selected patients, external radiotherapy decreases the risk 
of neck recurrence.407,408 The target volume encompasses the 
SECTION III    Thyroid
462
thyroid bed, bilateral neck lymph node areas, and the upper part 
of the mediastinum. Typically, 50 Gy (5000 rad) is delivered in 
25 fractions over 5 weeks, with a boost of 5 to 10 Gy on any 
residual macroscopic focus. The current approach with intensity-
modulated radiation therapy permits the delivery of 63 to 66 Gy 
to gross disease and high-risk areas and 54 to 56 Gy in 30 to 33 
fractions to cervical and mediastinal nodal regions. This approach 
may decrease late morbidity.
In patients with ATC, when the extent of disease is limited and 
surgery is feasible, accelerated external radiotherapy in combina­
tion with chemotherapy permits local control of the disease in two-
thirds of the patients and long-term survival in about 20%.409–411 
TSH-Suppressive Therapy
The growth of thyroid tumor cells is controlled by TSH, and inhi­
bition of TSH secretion with levothyroxine is thought to improve 
the recurrence and survival rates.42,174,390 Therefore, levothy­
roxine should be given to all patients with FCTC, whatever the 
extent of thyroid surgery and other treatment. The initial effec­
tive dose is about 1.6 to 2 μg/kg body weight in adults, although 
children require a higher dose and elderly patients a lower dose. 
The adequacy of therapy is monitored by measuring serum TSH 
approximately 3 months after initiation. The initial goal is a serum 
TSH concentration that is below about 0.1 mU/L for patients 
with high-risk thyroid cancer or 0.1 to 0.5 mU/L for patients with 
intermediate risk, and the TSH may be maintained at the lower 
end of the reference range (0.5–2 mU/L) for low-risk patients. 
All TSH targets must also weigh the individual risks associated 
with TSH-suppressive therapy. The dose of levothyroxine is then 
modified (and often deescalated) according to the ATA initial 
response to therapy.412 In patients with no evidence of disease, 
the dose of levothyroxine is decreased to maintain the serum TSH 
level within the reference range. Thus, the dosing of levothyroxine 
(and target TSH concentration) must be continually reevaluated 
based on disease risk and potential side effects of long-term TSH 
suppression.413,414
In patients with MTC or thyroid lymphoma, a replacement 
dose of levothyroxine is given with the aim of obtaining a serum 
TSH level in the normal range. 
Long-Term Follow-Up of Patients With 
Thyroid Cancer After Initial Therapy
Determining Response to Therapy
Although initial thyroid cancer treatment is individualized to the 
best extent possible through use of staging data obtained at the 
time of diagnosis and surgery, it has long been noted that two or 
more patients with similar disease may nonetheless demonstrate 
different outcomes over time. Broadly, this led to the understand­
ing that a patient’s response to initial therapy may provide equally 
prognostic data as that obtained at the time of initial diagnosis. 
Although originally conceived to be used as a restaging system to 
be utilized after 2 years of follow-up, the dynamic risk assessment 
approach has evolved such that the response to therapy defini­
tions can be used at any point during follow-up to describe the 
clinical status of a patient (Fig. 12.18).415–417 Thus, it is appropri­
ate even within the first year of follow-up to describe the clinical 
status of a patient using the response to therapy nomenclature 
(excellent response, biochemical incomplete response, structural 
incomplete response, indeterminate) (Box 12.5). Even at these early 
time points, the response to therapy can be used to alter the ini­
tial management plans. This is most apparent in patients who 
have ATA intermediate-risk disease who manifest an excellent 
response within the first year of initial therapy and can therefore 
have their management intensity decreased. Or alternatively, ATA 
low-risk or intermediate-risk patients demonstrating a biochemi­
cal or structural incomplete response may require more aggres­
sive follow-up, disease detection studies, or therapy. Importantly, 
a patient’s response to therapy is also not predicted by the tumor’s 
genomic or mutational status,418 although certain oncogenic pat­
terns are associated with a worsened prognosis.419
In oncologic terms, excellent response can be thought of as 
“remission” because it describes patients who have no biochemi­
cal, clinical, or structural evidence of disease (see Box 12.5). 
Patients with abnormal thyroglobulin values or rising antithy­
roglobulin antibodies in the absence of localizable disease are

described as having a biochemical incomplete response. Struc­
tural incomplete response is used to describe patients who have 
persistent or recurrent imaging evidence of disease. The inde­
terminate response category describes patients who have non­
specific either low-level thyroglobulin values (or thyroglobulin 
antibodies) or nonspecific findings on imaging that cannot be 
confidently classified as either benign or malignant. Over time, 
most patients can be moved out of the indeterminate response 
category as follow-up studies help to define whether the nonspe­
cific findings are benign or malignant.
The precise definitions for each of the response to therapy 
categories and the management implications are given in Table 
12.6.1 An excellent response to therapy should lead to an early 
decrease in the intensity and frequency of follow-up and the 
degree of TSH suppression because these patients do exception­
ally well, with essentially no mortality and very low recurrence 
rates. Interestingly, at least 30% of the patients with a biochemi­
cal incomplete response will eventually evolve to having no evi­
dence of disease with observation alone. Unfortunately, patients 
with a structural incomplete response usually maintain persistent 
disease (either biochemical or structural incomplete response) 
despite additional therapies. Fortunately, the majority of patients 
classified as having an indeterminate response remain disease-
free, with only 15% to 20% of these patients eventually being 
classified as having either biochemical or structural incomplete 
response. Factors such as patient age or the presence of micro­
scopic extrathyroidal extension can influence the likelihood of 
achieving an excellent response to therapy,420,421 although obesity 
does not.422
In the past, stimulated thyroglobulin values were a key compo­
nent of follow-up testing. However, with the development of new 
ultrasensitive assays, the definition of excellent response to therapy 
can be established with the suppressed thyroglobulin value of less 
than 0.2 ng/mL.1 For most patients, stimulated thyroglobulin 
values provide no additional prognostic information.423 Because 
the response to therapy definitions rely heavily on serum thyro­
globulin measurements, patients with antithyroglobulin antibod­
ies present a challenge. In these cases, the serum thyroglobulin 
measurement may or may not be reliable and therefore cannot 
be trusted. Antithyroglobulin antibodies that decline by at least 
50% over the first 6 months usually indicate the absence of persis­
tent disease.424 Conversely, rising thyroglobulin values over time 
are often an early indicator of subsequent structural incomplete 
response and would lead to additional structural or functional 
imaging.425
Additionally, the response to therapy definitions were origi­
nally developed for patients who had a total thyroidectomy 
and RAI ablation. These definitions have also been modi­
fied slightly to accommodate patients who were treated with 
lobectomy alone or total thyroidectomy without RAI.426,427 In 
patients who underwent total thyroidectomy without RAI, an 
excellent response to therapy requires a unstimulated thyro­
globulin of less than 0.2 ng/mL, an indeterminate response is 
defined as a serum thyroglobulin of 0.2 to 5 ng/mL, and a bio­
chemical incomplete response requires a serum thyroglobulin 
of greater than 5 ng/mL. In patients treated only with lobec­
tomy, absolute thyroglobulin values have proven insensitive to 
determine response to therapy. However, a negative US in such 
patients, combined with a downward trend in thyroglobulin or 
thyroglobulin antibodies, signals an excellent response428,429; 
conversely, a persistently rising thyroglobulin or thyroglobu­
lin antibody may signal a biochemical incomplete response to 
therapy.
ATA low-risk and intermediate-risk patients who demonstrate 
an excellent response to therapy can transition to low-intensity 
follow-up. In the long term, patients with an excellent response 
to therapy are followed primarily with serum thyroglobulin, 
thyroglobulin antibody, and physical examination every 1 to 2 
years. Routine use of neck ultrasonography in the follow-up of 
these patients with excellent response to therapy is likely to yield 
more false-positive findings than true structural disease and there­
fore is not routinely recommended.430,431 Although an excellent
