response to therapy almost always leads to less intense follow-up, 
it is important to note that ATA high-risk patients can still have 
a risk of recurrence in the range of 5% to 10%, despite having 
been classified as an excellent response to therapy, because they 
often manifest distant sites of disease that are not apparent on 
early imaging or they are poor thyroglobulin producers, leading 
to them being inappropriately classified as having an excellent 
response to therapy.415,416 Consequently, it is not unreasonable to 
consider cross-sectional imaging in ATA high-risk patients every 3 
to 5 years, depending on the specifics of individual cases.
The evaluation of the patient with biochemical incomplete 
response begins first with an assessment of whether appropriate 
imaging studies have been done. The level of serum thyroglobulin 
roughly correlates with the location of disease, with unstimulated 
Tg values of less than 10 ng/mL usually identifying persistent/
recurrent disease in the neck, values in the range of 10 to 100 sug­
gesting pulmonary metastasis, and values in the thousands suggest­
ing bone metastases.432 In addition to meticulous cross-sectional 
imaging, functional imaging with RAI or [18F]FDG-PET may 
identify the source of the abnormal thyroglobulin. Once appro­
priate imaging has been done to definitively rule out structurally 
identifiable disease, then the follow-up of patients with biochemi­
cal incomplete response depends on the trend over time in their 
thyroglobulin and thyroglobulin antibodies. Patients with stable 
or declining thyroglobulin and thyroglobulin antibodies are usu­
ally followed with observation. Patients with rising thyroglobulin 
or thyroglobulin antibodies are followed with additional cross-sec­
tional imaging, with the type, intensity, and frequency of testing 
dependent on the rate of rise of the biochemical markers. Studies 
have now verified a correlation between thyroglobulin DT and 
clinical outcomes.433
Patients with a structural incomplete response are particu­
larly problematic because the majority will maintain persistent 
biochemical or structural evidence of disease despite additional 
therapies.1 Possible treatment options for structural incomplete 
response include observation, surgical intervention, RAI ther­
apy, external beam radiation therapy, focal therapies, and sys­
temic therapies. Decision making in this setting is best done in 
a multidisciplinary team setting. Indications for intervention in 
patients with a structural incomplete response should be guided 
by factors such as the size, location, rate of growth, RAI avid­
ity, FDG avidity, and underlying histology of the metastatic 
disease.
Patients with an indeterminate response are usually followed 
with additional observation with serial evaluations of the inde­
terminate biochemical or structural area of interest.1 In many 
cases, the nonspecific biochemical markers or structural find­
ings resolve spontaneously, in which case the patients can be 
reclassified as having an excellent response to therapy. In other 
cases, the indeterminate findings become more clearly abnormal, 
and the patient is then reclassified as biochemical or structural 
incomplete.

Although these response to therapy recommendations have 
been primarily based on patients who underwent total thyroidec­
tomy and RAI ablation, follow-up recommendations are essentially 
the same in patients treated either with lobectomy or with total 
thyroidectomy without RAI.426,427 By definition, these patients 
are at low risk and thus are not expected to have early recurrences 
or distant metastasis. Although the significance of a single serum 
thyroglobulin determination is uncertain in the majority of these 
patients, the trend and thyroglobulin over time can be informative 
despite being less sensitive and more nonspecific. Because of the 
lack of sensitivity in the thyroglobulin measurements or persistent 
thyroglobulin antibodies, follow-up in these patients relies more 
heavily on neck ultrasonography done every 3 to 5 years, at least 
for the first decade. 
Treatment of Local-Regional Recurrence for PTC
Patients treated with thyroidectomy should be followed with 
serial thyroglobulin levels.434 If the patient has antithyroglobu­
lin antibodies, thyroglobulin measurement analyzed using mass 
spectroscopy, rather than with immunometric assays, has been 
proposed as an alternative, but the validity of this approach 
needs further study. In such scenarios reliance on neck US to 
identify abnormal lymph nodes suggestive of cancer recur­
rence is useful. Separately, FDG-PET scanning can assist with 
full-body imaging for the detection of recurrences. Even in the 
absence of interfering thyroglobulin antibodies, a rising serum 
thyroglobulin level should lead to a neck US. If the patient’s 
tumor is radioiodine avid, then radioiodine whole-body scan­
ning is also warranted. If the patient’s tumor is non–radioio­
dine avid or is an aggressive tumor, such as PDTC or ATC, then 
a PET ([18F]FDG-PET) scan should be performed. With any 
tumor recurrence, it is advisable to have a multidisciplinary dis­
cussion regarding treatment recommendations. Locoregional 
recurrences with no distant metastases should be considered for 
surgical resection, especially if they are 1 cm in size or larger. 
However, in some instances, locoregional recurrences of <1 cm 
can be monitored with serial US evaluation and/or CT scans. 
This is increasingly favored when morbidity associated with fur­
ther surgery is considered elevated and when the small recurrent 
carcinoma is not showing signs of imminent invasion or struc­
tural concern. In selected patients, locoregional recurrences can 
also be treated with thermal ablation.
In cases where surgery is no longer a reasonable treatment 
option because of comorbidities leading to increased risk of 
operative harm, or when a patient no longer desires an operative 
option, then separate treatments such as RAI (if iodine avid), 
external beam radiation435 (if non–iodine avid and aggressive or 
invasive disease), or minimally invasive techniques such as per­
cutaneous ethanol ablation or RFA436 (if low volume of disease) 
can be considered. Each of these treatments lacks high-quality 
prospective and randomized data to confirm the full spectrum of 
risk to benefit. Thus, clinical judgment must be used to individu­
alize the optimal treatment decision that aligns with options for 
a curative or palliative approach. As a guiding principle, when 
a locoregional recurrence significantly encroaches on vital struc­
tures and is deemed to be resectable, surgical resection should 
be favored even in the presence of distant metastases. When any 
repeat neck resections are performed for removal of recurrent 
disease, preoperative flexible laryngoscopy should be performed 
to exclude the possibility of previous recurrent laryngeal nerve 
injury. 
Defining RAI-Refractory Differentiated Thyroid 
Cancer
Numerous criteria have been proposed to identify patients with 
RAI-refractory DTC.437–441 More recently, the Martinique Princi­
ples442 sought to define five clinical scenarios that suggest a patient 
may have RAI-refractory DTC. The principles note that there is no 
absolute indicator, but the following scenarios convey the likelihood 
that a tumor will potentially be refractory to additional 131I therapy:
	1.	 No 131I uptake is present on a diagnostic 131I scan.
	2.	 No 131I uptake is present on a 131I scan performed several days 
after 131I therapy.
	3.	 131I uptake is only present in some but not other tumor foci.
	4.	 DTC metastasis or metastases progress despite 131I uptake.
	5.	 DTC metastasis or metastases progress despite a cumulative 
131I activity of >22.2 GBq (600 mCi).
Imaging should be performed using appropriate nuclear medicine 
techniques and a TSH >30 mU/L, with no exogenous iodine expo­
sure, and preferably on a contemporary scanner utilizing SPECT/
CT. If pretherapy diagnostic imaging is undertaken, some prefer thy­
roid hormone withdrawal rather than stimulation with rhTSH.55
There are several caveats to these scenarios, and patients should 
be managed individually with an understanding of the likelihood 
of 131I refractoriness, the patient’s specific clinical context, and the 
risks and benefits of additional 131I therapy.442 This is particularly 
relevant in patients with disease progression despite 131I uptake 
(item 4 in previous list) or a cumulative 131I-activity of >22.2 GBq 
(600 mCi) (item 5 in previous list). Other considerations include 
age, biology of the underlying disease, duration of prior response, 
symptomatic benefit, comorbidities, and potential adverse effects. 
Furthermore, a combination approach utilizing 131I with local 
therapies (e.g., surgery, radiotherapy, thermal ablation) may be 
considered if there is one or few 131I non-avid lesions. 
Treatment of Advanced Thyroid Cancer
Systemic Therapy for RAI-Refractory DTC
The past decade has witnessed major advancements in systemic 
therapy for RAI-refractory DTC. Small-molecule inhibitors now 
offer effective treatment options for patients with progressive dis­
ease, regardless of histologic subtype.
Oncogenic driver alterations are often present in RAI-refrac­
tory DTC and include BRAF V600E mutations and RET, NTRK1, 
NTRK3, and ALK fusions.341,443,444 Thus, biomarker testing to 
identify potential oncogenic driver alterations is now considered 
essential before initiating systemic treatment in most patients with 
RAI-refractory DTC.445,446 Several tissue-based multigene panels 
for NGS are available for biomarker identification. Multigene 
panel-based NGS assays are recommended over sequential single-
gene testing because more multiple biomarker-specific therapies 
are available for patients with RAI-refractory DTC.446 In addi­
tion, actionable alterations identified by molecular testing in the 
initial diagnostic workup of thyroid nodules may be relevant to 
systemic treatment decisions later in the course of illness in select 
patients, given that these driver alterations typically remain pres­
ent in more advanced disease. 
First-Line Multikinase Inhibitor Therapy for DTC
For patients with progressive RAI-refractory DTC whose 
tumor does not harbor an actionable biomarker linked to a 
SECTION III    Thyroid
466
regulatory-approved first-line therapy, multikinase inhibitor 
(MKI) therapy with either lenvatinib or sorafenib is indicated 
in the first-line setting. Both drugs target vascular endothelial 
growth factor receptors (VEGFR) and several other kinases. The 
DECISION trial was the first randomized placebo-controlled 
clinical trial in patients with progressive RAI-refractory DTC.447 
Eligibility criteria included a requirement of structural disease 
progression within the past 14 months per Response Evaluation 
Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST). Participants were random­
ized blindly to sorafenib or placebo and were unblinded at the 
time of disease progression. Those on placebo were offered cross­
over to sorafenib at the time of disease progression. PFS was the 
study’s primary endpoint. In DECISION, the median PFS was 
significantly improved with sorafenib compared to placebo (10.8 
vs. 5.8 months; HR 0.59; 95% CI, 0.45–0.76; p <.0001). The 
objective response rate (ORR) was 12.2%. Median OS had not 
been reached for either arm by the primary analysis data cut­
off, but there was no difference in OS between the two groups. 
Of note, 71.4% of participants initially randomized to placebo 
crossed over to receive sorafenib at disease progression, which 
may have confounded the ability to detect an improvement in 
OS. The most common AEs occurring in participants randomized 
to sorafenib were hand-foot skin reaction, diarrhea, alopecia, rash 
or desquamation, fatigue, weight loss, hypertension, anorexia, 
oral mucositis, pruritus, nausea, headache, cough, and constipa­
tion. AEs were managed with supportive care, dose interruption, 
reduction, or discontinuation. Dose interruption, reduction, and 
discontinuation were necessary in 66.2%, 64.3%, and 18.8% of 
participants, respectively. Of note, benefit was seen with sorafenib 
across the various DTC histologic subtypes enrolled, as well as in 
tumors harboring BRAF and N/H/K RAS mutations.448 On the 
basis of DECISION, sorafenib was approved by the U.S. Food 
and Drug Administration (FDA) and other health authorities for 
the treatment of progressive RAI-refractory DTC.
Following DECISION, SELECT was a randomized phase 3 
trial comparing the MKI lenvatinib to placebo in patients with 
progressive RAI-refractory DTC.438 Patients with disease progres­
sion within 12 months were randomized to lenvatinib versus pla­
cebo and followed for PFS as the primary endpoint. At the time 
of disease progression, participants were unblinded, and those 
on placebo were offered crossover to lenvatinib. Median PFS was 
19.4 months with lenvatinib compared to 3.7 months with pla­
cebo (HR, 0.24; 99% CI, 0.17–0.35; p < 0.0001).449 The ORR 
with lenvatinib was 64.8%. Although the difference in median OS 
was not significant (HR = 0.73; 95% CI, 0.50–1.07; p = 0.10), 
analysis of OS was confounded by 83% of placebo participants 
crossing over to receive lenvatinib upon disease progression. The 
PFS benefit with lenvatinib held up across histologic subtype and 
BRAF and N/H/K RAS mutational status in subset analyses.450 
Treatment-related AEs with lenvatinib included hypertension, 
diarrhea, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, nausea, stomatitis, pal­
mar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, proteinuria, vomiting, headache, 
dysphonia, arthralgia, dysgeusia, and rash. An increase in TSH 
was also common with lenvatinib. Dose interruption, reduction, 
and discontinuation were needed in 82.4%, 67.8%, and 14.2% 
of participants, respectively. On the basis of SELECT, lenvatinib 
was approved by the FDA and other health authorities for the 
treatment of progressive RAI-refractory DTC. In China, a phase 
3 trial similar to SELECT was conducted in patients with progres­
sive RAI-refractory DTC.451 Median PFS was significantly longer 
with lenvatinib (23.9 vs. 3.7 months), and the ORR on lenvatinib 
was 69.9%. The safety profile in this study was similar to that in 
SELECT, apart from higher rates of hypertension and proteinuria, 
associated with more frequent dose reduction. Although there is 
no head-to-head comparison of sorafenib to lenvatinib in patients 
with progressive RAI-refractory DTC, experts generally agree that 
lenvatinib is the preferred first-line MKI, given the longer PFS 
benefit and higher ORR seen with lenvatinib.452,453
Because MKI therapy is not curative in RAI-refractory DTC 
and is associated with treatment-related AEs that can impact qual­
ity of life (QoL), and patients often have slow-growing asymp­
tomatic disease, the decision of when to initiate MKI therapy can 
be challenging. In many cases, disease monitoring alone may be 
appropriate, especially for patients without impending symptoms 
and low-volume, slow-growing disease who strongly value QoL 
over length of life and wish to avoid treatment-related AEs. On 
the other hand, patients with symptomatic disease, impending 
symptoms, and bulky or rapidly progressive disease generally can­
not wait for effective therapy to commence. In addition, patients 
who wish to be aggressive in treating their cancer and live as long 
as possible may benefit from earlier MKI initiation. When con­
sidering the timing, one important factor is if treatment improves 
OS. Both the DECISION and SELECT trials incorporated cross­
over to open-label MKI treatment for placebo patients at the time 
of disease progression, confounding the ability to detect an OS 
benefit with treatment. Nonetheless, SELECT exploratory analy­
ses demonstrated a statistically significant OS benefit with lenva­
tinib in two subsets of patients, the elderly and patients with lung 
metastases, despite the high rate of crossover.454,455 Additional 
exploratory analyses from SELECT provide further guidance 
related to timing of initiation of therapy. For example, both per­
formance status (PS) and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) 
are markers of more advanced disease in patients with cancer. In 
SELECT, patients randomized to lenvatinib had improved PFS 
when the PS was better and NLR was lower.456 Similarly, efficacy 
outcomes are improved in patients with a lower tumor burden 
compared to a higher tumor burden.457 This suggests that if the 
efficacy of treatment is the primary goal, it may be appropriate 
to initiate lenvatinib before an individual’s PS, NLR, and tumor 
burden worsen.458–460 Personalizing the decision to start MKI 
therapy and shared decision making with the patient are therefore 
essential. 
Gene-Specific Therapy for DTC
In patients with RAI-refractory DTC harboring actionable onco­
genic driver alterations involving NTRK or RET fusions, gene-
specific therapy is generally favored over MKIs in the first line. 
Larotrectinib, a potent and selective oral pan-TRK inhibitor, 
was studied in a phase 1 to 2 program involving children and 
adults with NTRK-fusion–positive cancers. In the initial study, 
55 patients with 17 types of NTRK-fusion–positive cancers were 
reported.461 The primary endpoint, ORR, was 75%. At the time 
of data cutoff, median PFS had not been reached, but the 1-year 
PFS rate was 55%. The TRK selectivity of this kinase inhibitor 
was reflected in the AE profile; clinically significant AEs were 
uncommon. Based on this study, larotrectinib received a cancer 
tissue–agnostic approval by the FDA and other health authorities 
for the treatment of NTRK-fusion–positive cancers. After further 
enrollment to the study, 29 patients with NTRK advanced thy­
roid cancer were enrolled, 2 of whom were less than 18 years of 
age.462 In the 22 patients with RAI-refractory DTC, the ORR was 
86%, whereas in 7 patients with ATC, the ORR was only 29%. In 
DTC, the duration of response was so long that the median PFS 
467
CHAPTER 12  Nontoxic Diffuse Goiter, Nodular Thyroid Disorders, and Thyroid Malignancies
was not reached. However, the PFS rate at 2 years was 69%, and 
2-year OS was 92%. In ATC, median PFS and OS were 2.2 and 
8.8 months, respectively.
A second kinase inhibitor targeting TRK, entrectinib, is also 
available. Entrectinib, which also inhibits ROS1 and ALK kinases, 
was similarly studied in a phase 1 to 2 program enrolling patients 
with multiple tumor types driven by oncogenic fusions involving 
these three kinases. Pooled analysis of the 54 adults with NTRK-
fusion–positive cancers has been reported.463 Of these partici­
pants, five had thyroid cancer. The ORR in the group was 57%, 
and median duration of response was 10 months. Responses were 
seen in all tumor types, including one of the five patients with 
thyroid cancer. The safety profile was tolerable for most patients. 
These data led to approval of entrectinib by the FDA and other 
health authorities for NTRK-fusion–positive solid tumors and 
ROS1-fusion–positive lung cancers.
In a rare tumor setting like NTRK-fusion–positive advanced 
thyroid cancer, opportunities to generate data in clinical trials are 
limited. There are no head-to-head trials comparing larotrectinib 
to entrectinib. Other than the pooled analyses detailed earlier, no 
further data to provide guidance on choosing between the two 
agents are available. Similarly, no data are available to help decide 
when to initiate gene-specific therapy, such as with larotrec­
tinib or entrectinib. Immediate treatment may not be necessary 
in all patients with NTRK-fusion–positive thyroid cancer with 
low-volume, asymptomatic, and slowly progressive disease, even 
if RAI-refractory. On the other hand, when patients have clini­
cally meaningful disease progression, the risk:benefit calculation 
involved in the initiation of treatment differs from that of MKI 
therapy, given the relatively favorable toxicity profile of larotrec­
tinib and entrectinib, and earlier initiation of treatment may make 
more sense for some patients.
Two oral drugs, selpercatinib and pralsetinib, were designed as 
specific and potent RET kinase inhibitors, with as little off-target 
activity as possible against other kinases, especially VEGFR, which 
shares a high degree of homology with RET.464 LIBRETTO-001 
was a phase 1 to 2 clinical trial enrolling adolescents and adults 
with RET-driven lung cancer, advanced thyroid cancers, and other 
solid tumors.465,466 Three thyroid cancer cohorts were enrolled: 
(1) patients with RET-mutant MTC previously treated with van­
detanib and/or cabozantinib; (2) patients with RET-mutant MTC 
who had not received prior vandetanib or cabozantinib; and (3) 
patients with RET-fusion–positive thyroid cancer. ORR was the 
primary endpoint. Nineteen patients had RET-fusion–positive 
thyroid cancer, 17 with DTC and 2 with ATC. The ORR in the 
RET-fusion–positive thyroid cancer cohort was 79%, including 
a response in one of the two patients with ATC. Responses were 
durable, with a 1-year PFS rate of 64%. Consistent with selperca­
tinib’s specificity for the RET kinase, the drug was well tolerated 
overall. Most AEs were grades 1 and 2. The most common grade 
3 or 4 treatment-related AEs were hypertension and increased ala­
nine aminotransferase. Selpercatinib’s tolerability was reflected in 
low rates of dose reduction and discontinuation, 30% and 2%, 
respectively. Results from LIBRETTO-001 led to FDA and other 
health authority approvals for the treatment of RET-driven can­
cers, regardless of prior lines of treatment.
Pralsetinib was studied in ARROW, a phase 1 to 2 trial enroll­
ing adults with RET-driven solid tumors.467,468 Three thyroid 
cancer cohorts, patients with RET-mutant MTC who previ­
ously received vandetanib and/or cabozantinib, treatment-naive 
patients with RET-mutant MTC, and patients with RET-fusion–
positive thyroid cancer, were evaluated. Of the nine patients with 
RET-fusion–positive thyroid cancer, eight responses were seen, for 
an ORR of 89%. Here, too, responses were durable; the 1-year 
PFS rate was 81%. Pralsetinib was well tolerated, with most AEs 
being grade 1 or 2. The most common grade 3 or 4 AEs were 
hypertension, neutropenia, lymphopenia, and anemia. Dose 
reduction for AEs was necessary in 46% of patients, and dose 
discontinuations occurred in 4%. Based on ARROW’s outcomes, 
pralsetinib was the second RET-specific inhibitor garnering FDA 
approval for RET-altered cancers. Given the similar outcomes of 
LIBRETTO-001 and ARROW, it is difficult to recommend either 
selpercatinib or pralsetinib over the other.
As is the case with NTRK-fusion–positive thyroid cancer, no 
data are available to help decide when to initiate gene-specific 
therapy in RET-fusion–positive thyroid cancer. But as with 
NTRK-directed therapy, the RET-specific targeted therapies are 
well tolerated. Thus, there is no strong rationale to delay the ini­
tiation of treatment in patients with RAI-refractory RET-fusion–
positive DTC with clinically meaningful disease progression. 
Second-Line Therapy for RAI-Refractory DTC
In patients with RAI-refractory DTC without an actionable driver 
alteration who have progressed on a prior VEGFR MKI, such 
as lenvatinib or sorafenib, data from COSMIC-311, a phase 3 
randomized trial, are now available and support the use of cabo­
zantinib, another oral VEGFR MKI, in the second line.469 This 
study randomized patients who experienced disease progression 
during or after treatment with one or two prior VEGFR MKIs to 
receive cabozantinib versus placebo. The dual primary endpoints 
were ORR and PFS. The ORR with cabozantinib was 15%, and 
PFS was significantly improved compared to placebo, not reached 
with cabozantinib (96% CI, 5.7 months to not estimable) versus 
1.9 months (1.8–3.6 months) with placebo (HR, 0.22; 96% CI, 
0.13–0.36; p < 0.0001). Treatment-related grade 3 or higher AEs 
included palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, hypertension, and 
fatigue. These results led to recent FDA approval for cabozantinib 
in this setting.
For patients with fusion-positive RAI-refractory DTC treated 
with gene-specific therapy, the potential clinical benefit of cabo­
zantinib or other VEGFR MKIs in the setting of disease progres­
sion is currently unknown. Acquired resistance, defined as disease 
progression after an initial response, can emerge with gene-specific 
therapy. Acquired resistance can result from the development of 
on-target drug resistance mutations in the NTRK or RET genes, 
preventing drug binding and kinase inhibition. Alternatively, 
acquired resistance can result from the development of muta­
tions and other gene alterations upregulating oncogenic bypass 
pathways such as the MAPK pathway. Studies investigating novel 
approaches to treating fusion-positive solid tumors with acquired 
resistance to gene-specific therapy are now underway. When 
disease progression occurs, tumor biopsy for NGS testing can 
be performed to search for an acquired alteration that explains 
the development of resistance and may facilitate clinical trial 
involvement.
For patients with BRAF V600E–mutation-positive RAI-
refractory DTC, BRAF-targeted therapy with dabrafenib plus tra­
metinib is now an option in the second-line setting after VEGFR 
MKI therapy. To date, large-scale trials investigating BRAF-tar­
geted therapy have not been completed in this patient population. 
Several smaller studies have, however, been conducted, includ­
ing a multicenter randomized phase 2 trial investigating dab­
rafenib with or without trametinib in progressive BRAF-mutated 
SECTION III    Thyroid
468
RAI-refractory DTC.470 Up to three prior MKIs were allowed; 
most patients had received at least one prior MKI. The ORR 
defined by RECIST v1.1 was 35% with dabrafenib alone and 
30% with combination therapy. The median PFS with monother­
apy was 10.7 months, and it was 15.1 months with dabrafenib 
plus trametinib. Grade 3 treatment-related AEs with dabrafenib 
included anemia, hyperglycemia, fever, and hypophosphatemia. 
Grade 3 treatment-related AEs with dabrafenib plus trametinib 
included hypophosphatemia. These promising data led to the 
initiation of a global randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 
study evaluating dabrafenib plus trametinib in adult patients with 
BRAF V600E–mutation-positive RAI-refractory DTC who pro­
gressed following prior VEGFR MKI therapy (NCT04940052). 
Although this phase 3 trial remains underway, dabrafenib plus 
trametinib has garnered a recent tissue-agnostic FDA approval in 
adults and children with BRAF V600E–mutation-positive solid 
tumors for whom no standard treatment is available based on 
three basket trials demonstrating ORRs of up to 80% in patients 
with BRAF V600E–mutation-positive solid tumors.471–475 With 
this approval, dabrafenib plus trametinib may be an option for 
patients with BRAF V600E–mutation-positive thyroid cancer, 
particularly in the second line. 
Systemic Therapy for Advanced ATC
Despite the major advances made over the past decade in systemic 
therapy approaches for other advanced thyroid cancers, such as 
RAI-refractory DTC and MTC, progress in systemic therapy for 
ATC has been more modest. Although new therapies have not yet 
improved outcomes for all patients with ATC, there are subgroups 
for whom effective therapies are now available.
Biomarker testing is critical for patients diagnosed with ATC 
to inform initial and, possibly, subsequent therapy.476,477 Rapid 
assessment for the presence of BRAF V600E mutation by either 
immunohistochemistry or molecular testing is indicated in all 
newly diagnosed patients who are candidates for treatment based 
on the impressive activity of dabrafenib plus trametinib in this 
patient population with very aggressive disease.471,475 In paral­
lel, comprehensive molecular testing by an NGS panel, best per­
formed on tissue obtained via core-needle biopsy or other biopsy 
providing an adequate specimen, can identify other potentially 
actionable alterations, including ALK, NTRK, and RET fusions 
and TSC2 mutations. In addition, comprehensive testing, includ­
ing markers predictive of response to immune checkpoint inhibi­
tor therapy (i.e., PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden 
[TMB], and mutations in DNA MMR genes), may identify can­
didates for immunotherapy. 
Advanced Multidisciplinary Care for ATC
The care of patients with newly diagnosed ATC frequently involves 
complex therapeutic and palliative decision making for which 
rapid multidisciplinary team coordination is necessary.477,478 For 
the small subset of patients who present with resectable T1-3a, 
N0, M0, stage IVA disease, long-term survival is possible with 
surgery followed by chemoradiotherapy administered with cura­
tive intent.451,479–481 Full-dose radiotherapy, involving at least 
60 Gy, is recommended and should be initiated within 4 to 6 
weeks postoperatively, as soon as adequate wound healing has 
been achieved.480–482 Several concurrent chemotherapy regimens 
with radiation have been investigated in ATC, but no random­
ized trial establishing the optimal regimen is available. Concurrent 
chemotherapy approaches with the most published data available 
involve a taxane (paclitaxel or docetaxel) with or without doxo­
rubicin or a platin (cisplatin or carboplatin).480,481,483 In gen­
eral, initiating cytotoxic chemotherapy postoperatively as soon as 
adequate wound healing has occurred and continuing treatment 
until the completion of radiation is recommended.477 The best 
prognostic indicator for long-term survival in patients with ATC 
remains the successful completion of intensive trimodality therapy, 
particularly in patients who have undergone an R0 or R1 resec­
tion. In these patients, locoregional disease control is achieved in 
a majority of cases, and median OS can be close to 2 years.480–483
For patients presenting with unresectable ATC without dis­
tant metastasis, neoadjuvant treatment is now available in select 
cases, particularly those harboring BRAF V600E mutations.476 An 
encouraging case series has been reported involving six patients 
presenting with unresectable ATC treated with the BRAF and 
MEK inhibitors, dabrafenib plus trametinib.484 All six patients 
experienced enough tumor shrinkage to allow for surgery, followed 
by concurrent chemoradiotherapy. In follow-up, all six patients 
remained disease-free locoregionally, whereas two patients died of 
distant metastasis. As we enter the era of gene-specific therapy for 
thyroid cancer, improvements in outcomes for many patients with 
ATC are expected.476
For patients with BRAF wild-type unresectable ATC without 
distant metastasis who wish to receive treatment and are candi­
dates for intensive chemoradiotherapy, locoregional control can 
be achieved when higher doses of radiation are administered, espe­
cially with concurrent chemotherapy, and median OS beyond 1 
year can be seen.480,482,483 
Systemic Therapy for Recurrent/Metastatic ATC
In patients with recurrent/metastatic ATC who are candidates 
for systemic therapy based on their wishes, comorbidities, disease 
burden, and PS, expeditious initiation of therapy is often neces­
sary. Now that biomarker-directed treatments are available in a 
subset of patients, biomarker testing for actionable alterations is 
indicated. If not already done, rapid assessment for the presence of 
a BRAF V600E mutation and comprehensive NGS-based testing 
should be performed.
In patients with BRAF V600E–mutation-positive disease 
identified by rapid assessment, confirmation by subsequent 
NGS-based testing may be wise. Nonetheless, treatment with 
dabrafenib plus trametinib can be initiated without delay, based 
on the breakthrough phase 2 Rare Oncology Agnostic Research 
basket trial investigating this regimen in BRAF V600E–mutant 
rare cancers.485 An updated report detailed activity in a cohort of 
36 patients with ATC with unresectable or metastatic disease.486 
The ORR was 56%, including two patients experiencing com­
plete response. Responses were durable, with a median duration 
of response (DOR) of 13.6 months. Median PFS was 6.7 months 
(95% CI, 4.7–13.8 months), and median OS was 14.5 months 
(95% CI, 6.8–23.2 months). Dabrafenib plus trametinib was 
fairly well tolerated. The most common AEs were pyrexia, anemia, 
anorexia, fatigue, and nausea. Dose reductions were required in 
47% of patients and discontinuation in 17%. This led to the first 
FDA and other health authority approval for a systemic therapy 
specifically for ATC.
NTRK, RET, and ALK fusions are seen rarely in ATC. The most 
data in targeting these fusion-positive ATCs with gene-specific 
therapy are available in a pooled analysis of NTRK-fusion–posi­
tive thyroid cancer patients enrolled in the larotrectinib phase 1/2 
469
CHAPTER 12  Nontoxic Diffuse Goiter, Nodular Thyroid Disorders, and Thyroid Malignancies
studies.462 Seven patients with ATC were enrolled, four of whom 
harbored NTRK3 fusions and three of whom harbored NTRK1 
fusions. Although four of seven patients (29%) experienced a par­
tial response (PR), the responses were short-lived. Median PFS was 
2.2 months (95% CI, 0.9 months to not estimable), and median 
OS was 8.8 months (95% CI, 2.6 months to not estimable). As of 
early 2023, we are aware of reports on only two patients with RET-
fusion–positive ATC treated with the RET-specific inhibitor selper­
catinib.466,487 Both patients were enrolled in LIBRETTO-001, and 
one of the two patients achieved a durable PR lasting longer than 18 
months. Similarly, limited information is available regarding gene-
specific targeted therapy for ALK-fusion–positive ATC, although 
several case reports point to robust activity with this approach.488–490
MKIs, particularly lenvatinib, have been studied in non–
biomarker-selected recurrent/metastatic ATC. An initial phase 2 
clinical trial conducted in Japan yielded encouraging results, with 
4 of 27 patients (24%) experiencing PR.491 Median OS was 10.6 
months. A subsequent international multicenter two-stage phase 
2 trial, however, did not confirm this degree of activity.492 Interim 
analysis revealed that only 1 of 34 patients achieved PR. Thus, the 
study was halted for futility because the minimum ORR threshold 
of 15% was not met.
Treatment of recurrent/metastatic ATC with immune checkpoint 
inhibitors has been more encouraging. The anti-PD-1 antibody 
spartalizumab was studied in an international multicenter phase 2 
trial.334 Forty-two patients were enrolled. The ORR was 19% in 
all 42 patients, whereas in the subset of 28 patients with PD-L1–
positive tumors (≥1% positive in tumor cells), the ORR was 29%. 
No responses were seen in patients harboring PD-L1–negative dis­
ease. Some of these responses were quite durable, ranging from 16.7 
weeks to 1.6 years (ongoing at data cutoff), and six of eight respond­
ing patients were still receiving treatment with ongoing responses at 
the data cutoff. AEs were consistent with the known autoimmune 
toxicity profile associated with this class of agents. Although spartal­
izumab is not approved for treatment in any setting, the anti-PD-1 
antibody pembrolizumab is FDA approved in a tissue-agnostic fash­
ion for cancers that are MMR deficient or harbor a high TMB (≥10 
mutations/Mb), both of which can be found in ATC.
This study and success with combined immune checkpoint 
inhibitor therapy plus lenvatinib in other nonthyroid tumor types 
led to investigation of pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib in ATC.493 
Early results are promising, with four of six patients experiencing 
response. A larger phase 2 trial has been reported in abstract form, 
indicating an ORR of 52%, a median PFS of 9.5 months, and 
an OS of 10.25 months.494 Of note, the regimen seems to have 
durable activity in a subset of patients, with a 2-year OS rate of 
25.9%. A second phase 2 trial investigating this approach is cur­
rently underway (NCT04171622).
The data supporting a role for cytotoxic chemotherapy in 
patients with recurrent/metastatic ATC are not robust. Bridging 
chemotherapy is suggested for patients in need of prompt treatment 
initiation while biomarker testing is underway.477 There is some evi­
dence that taxanes, namely, paclitaxel and docetaxel, yield modest 
clinical benefit in some patients.495 Published data supporting the 
use of anthracyclines and platins in the recurrent/metastatic setting 
are limited, but doxorubicin is FDA approved for use in ATC and 
may be a reasonable treatment option in select patients.496 
Systemic Therapy for Advanced MTC
As with systemic therapy for RAI-refractory DTC, the develop­
ment of multiple small-molecule inhibitors for the treatment 
of patients with advanced MTC has brought major progress to 
the field. Because approximately 60% of sporadic MTCs har­
bor somatic RET mutations, essentially all inherited cases harbor 
germline mutations, and RET gene-specific therapies are now 
available, all patients with advanced MTC who will need systemic 
therapy should have biomarker testing that includes comprehen­
sive RET gene coverage. Although patients with inherited MTC 
who have received a positive germline RET test do not require fur­
ther biomarker testing for systemic therapy decision making, all 
patients who are germline RET wild type and those who have not 
yet undergone germline RET testing should have NGS biomarker 
testing before initiating systemic therapy. Tissue-based multigene 
NGS assays are preferred at present in order to detect not just 
potentially actionable RET alterations but also H/N/K RAS muta­
tions and other alterations that may be prognostic or affect the 
identification of the optimal systemic treatment for each patient. 
Analysis of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), or “liquid biopsy,” 
has emerged as a noninvasive method for biomarker detection in 
several cancers, including colorectal, breast, and lung. In MTC, 
several small studies have explored the utility of liquid biopsy in 
patients with MTC, yielding mixed results of variable sensitiv­
ity.497–499 Although ctDNA analysis has not yet become a stan­
dard approach to biomarker testing in MTC, further optimization 
of the approach holds promise as a clinically useful biomarker in 
MTC in the future. 
Multikinase Inhibitor Therapy for MTC
In 2011, the U.S. FDA approved the RET, VEGFR, and EGFR 
MKI vandetanib as the first approved treatment for patients with 
MTC with unresectable and/or metastatic disease, based on the 
ZETA trial.500 ZETA was a randomized placebo-controlled trial 
enrolling patients with advanced MTC, with PFS as the primary 
endpoint. Participants who experienced disease progression were 
unblinded, and those on placebo were offered open-label treat­
ment with vandetanib. Median PFS was significantly prolonged 
with vandetanib (30.5 months [projected] vs. 19.3 months; HR 
0.46; 95% CI, 0.31–0.69; p <.001), and the ORR by RECIST 
was 45%. OS data were not mature by the time of study cutoff. Of 
note, a subsequent study of patients with MTC treated with van­
detanib demonstrated that approximately 25% experienced a high 
ORR of 86% and a long median PFS of 73 months.501 In ZETA, 
the most common AEs occurring in participants randomized to 
vandetanib were diarrhea, rash, nausea, hypertension, fatigue, 
headache, anorexia, and acne. Dose reduction and discontinua­
tion were necessary in 35% and 12% of participants, respectively.
Following the ZETA trial, EXAM was launched, investigating 
the MET, VEGFR2, and RET MKI cabozantinib compared to 
placebo in patients with unresectable and/or metastatic MTC.502 
Unlike ZETA, EXAM required that participants experienced dis­
ease progression according to RECIST within the prior 14 months, 
and thus a patient population with more aggressive disease was 
enrolled. In addition, this study did not allow for crossover to 
open-label cabozantinib when participants on placebo experi­
enced disease progression. The median PFS was 11.2 months for 
cabozantinib versus 4.0 months for placebo (HR, 0.28; 95% CI, 
0.19–0.40; p <0.001). The ORR with cabozantinib was 28%. 
Subsequent OS analysis of the EXAM study was conducted after 
further follow-up.503 Although a numeric increase in median OS 
with cabozantinib versus placebo was detected, 26.6 versus 21.1 
months, respectively, this difference did not reach statistical sig­
nificance (HR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.64–1.12; p = 0.24). Interestingly, 
SECTION III    Thyroid
470
exploratory analyses revealed an apparent improvement in treat­
ment effect in the RET M918T–mutation-positive subgroup, who 
did experience a statistically significant improvement in median 
OS (4.3 months vs. 18.9 months; HR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.38–0.94; 
p = 0.03).
The most frequent AEs experienced in participants on cabo­
zantinib included diarrhea, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthe­
sia, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, fatigue, dysgeusia, hair color 
changes, hypertension, stomatitis, constipation, and hemorrhage. 
Dose reduction and discontinuation were necessary in 79% and 
16% of participants on cabozantinib.502 The results of EXAM 
led to health authority approval of cabozantinib in patients with 
progressive MTC. Because of the high rate of dose reduction for 
tolerability seen in the EXAM trial that administered cabozantinib 
at a starting dose of 140 mg in capsule formulation once daily, 
a randomized, double-blind noninferiority study was conducted 
comparing this formulation of cabozantinib to a 60-mg once-
daily tablet formulation of cabozantinib in patients with pro­
gressive metastatic MTC.334 A higher incidence of AEs and dose 
modifications was seen in the 140-mg capsule arm, and median 
PFS, the primary endpoint, was similar between the 60-mg tablet 
and the 140-mg capsule arms (HR, 1.24; 95% CI, 0.90–1.70). 
Nonetheless, the primary endpoint was not met because the upper 
bound of the CI for the HR exceeded the noninferiority margin 
set at 1.58. 
RET-Specific Therapy for MTC
The two RET-specific inhibitors, selpercatinib and pralsetinib, 
have been studied in patients with advanced RET-mutant MTC. 
The phase 1 to 2 LIBRETTO-001 trial had two MTC cohorts: 
patients previously treated with vandetanib and/or cabozantinib 
and patients who had not received prior vandetanib or cabozan­
tinib.466 In the primary analysis, 55 patients were enrolled in 
the previously treated cohort, and 88 patients who were vande­
tanib and cabozantinib naive were enrolled. The ORR for the 
previously treated cohort was 69%, 9% of which were complete 
responses. The 1-year PFS rate was 82%. In the vandetanib and 
cabozantinib–naive cohort, ORR was 73%, 11% of which were 
complete responses. In this cohort, the 1-year PFS rate was 92%. 
The generally well-tolerated selpercatinib AE profile is detailed 
earlier. Results from LIBRETTO-001 led the FDA and other 
health authorities to approve selpercatinib for RET-driven can­
cers. In the United States, the approval is agnostic to prior lines 
of treatment.
In the phase 1 to 2 ARROW trial, pralsetinib was studied in 
two RET-mutant MTC cohorts: patients who previously received 
vandetanib and/or cabozantinib and treatment-naive patients.468 
Of the 55 previously treated patients with MTC treated at the 
full recommended phase 2 dose, the ORR was 60%. Complete 
responses were seen in 2%. Here, too, responses were durable; 
the 1-year PFS rate was 75%. In 21 treatment-naive patients, the 
ORR was 71%, with 5% of patients having a complete response. 
The 1-year PFS rate was 81%. Pralsetinib was well tolerated, as 
detailed earlier. Based on the outcomes in the ARROW trial, 
pralsetinib was the second RET-specific inhibitor garnering FDA 
approval for RET-altered cancers, including MTC. Given the sim­
ilar outcomes of LIBRETTO-001 and ARROW, it is difficult to 
know if selpercatinib or pralsetinib should be considered preferred 
over the other when selecting treatment for patients with RET-
mutant MTC.
In the absence of further studies, it is also difficult to know 
the optimal sequence of therapy in patients with advanced RET-
mutant MTC. Should a RET-specific treatment be given in the 
first line based on the well-tolerated AE profiles and significant 
evidence of clinical activity of these agents? Or will patients do 
better over the long term with an MKI as the initial treatment, 
followed by a RET-specific inhibitor upon disease progression? 
Currently, LIBRETTO-531, an international randomized phase 
3 trial comparing selpercatinib to cabozantinib or vandetanib in 
patients with progressive kinase inhibitor–naive, RET-mutant 
MTC, designed to answer this important question, is underway, 
and a similar trial with pralsetinib is planned (NCT04211337).

KEY POINTS
 • 
This chapter discusses mechanisms and regulation of adrenal 
steroid production, function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-
adrenal axis (HPA), and negative feedback regulation.
 • 
The chapter goes on to describe the transactivating and 
transrepressive actions of glucocorticoids.
 • 
Glucocorticoid excess and Cushing syndrome, adrenal 
insufficiency and Addison disease, and inherited disorders of 
the adrenal gland are also discussed.
 • 
Optimization of corticosteroid replacement therapies is 
addressed.
 • 
The chapter concludes with discussion of adrenal 
incidentalomas, adenomas, and carcinomas.
The Adrenal Cortex—Historical Milestones
The anatomy of the adrenal glands was described almost 450 
years ago by Bartolomeo Eustachius,1 and the zonation of the 
gland and its distinction from the medulla were elucidated 
shortly thereafter. However, a functional role for the adrenal 
glands was not accurately defined until the pioneering work of 
Thomas Addison, who described the clinical and autopsy find­
ings in 11 cases of Addison disease in his classic monograph in 
1855.2 Just a year later, Brown-Séquard demonstrated that the 
adrenal glands were “organs essential for life” by performing 
adrenalectomies in dogs, cats, and guinea pigs.3 In 1896, Wil­
liam Osler first administered adrenal extract to a patient with 
Addison disease, a feat that was repeated by others in animal and 
human studies over the next 40 years. Between 1937 and 1955, 
the adrenocorticosteroid hormones were isolated, and their 
structures were defined and synthesized.4 Notable breakthroughs 
included the discovery of cortisone and clinical evaluation of its 
antiinflammatory effect in patients with rheumatoid arthritis5 
and the isolation of aldosterone.6
The control of adrenocortical function by a pituitary factor 
was demonstrated in the 1920s, and this led to the isolation 
of sheep adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) by Li, Evans, 
and Simpson in 1943.7 Such a concept was supported through 
clinical studies, notably by Harvey Cushing in 1932, who associ­
ated his original clinical observations of 1912 (a “polyglandular 
syndrome” caused by pituitary basophilism) with adrenal hyper­
activity.8 The neural control of pituitary ACTH secretion by cor­
ticotropin-releasing factor (later renamed corticotropin-releasing 
hormone [CRH]) was defined by Harris and other workers in 
the 1940s, but CRH was not characterized and synthesized until 
1981 in the laboratory of Wylie Vale.9 Jerome Conn described 
primary aldosteronism in 1955,10 and the control of adrenal 
aldosterone secretion by angiotensin II was confirmed shortly 
afterward. Advances in radioimmunoassay, and particularly 
molecular biology, have facilitated an exponential increase in 
the understanding of adrenal physiology and pathophysiology 
(Table 13.1). 
Anatomy and Development
The cells forming the adrenal cortex originate from the inter­
mediate mesoderm. These cells derive from the urogenital ridge 
and have a common embryologic origin with the gonad and the

History of the Adrenal Cortex: Important Milestones
Year
Event
1563
Eustachius describes the adrenals (published by Lancisi in 1714).
1849
Thomas Addison, while searching for the cause of pernicious anemia, stumbles on a bronzed appearance associated with the adrenal 
glands—melasma suprarenale.
1855
Thomas Addison describes the clinical features and autopsy findings in 11 cases of diseases of the suprarenal capsules, at least 6 of which 
were tuberculous in origin.
1856
In adrenalectomy experiments, Brown-Séquard demonstrates that the adrenal glands are essential for life.
1896
William Osler prepares an oral glycerin extract derived from pig adrenals and demonstrates that it has clinical benefit in patients with 
Addison disease.
1905
Bulloch and Sequeira describe patients with congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
1929
Liquid extracts of cortical tissue are used to keep adrenalectomized cats alive indefinitely (Swingle and Pfiffner); subsequently, this extract 
was used successfully to treat a patient with Addison disease (Rowntree and Greene).
1932
Harvey Cushing associates the polyglandular syndrome of pituitary basophilism, which he first described in 1912, with hyperactivity of the 
pituitary-adrenal glands.
1936
The concept of stress and its effect on pituitary-adrenal function are described by Selye.
1937–1952
Isolation and structural characterization of adrenocortical hormones are reported by Kendall and Reichstein.
1943
Li and colleagues isolate pure adrenocorticotropic hormone from sheep pituitary.
1950
Hench, Kendall, and Reichstein share the Nobel Prize in Medicine for describing the antiinflammatory effects of cortisone in patients with 
rheumatoid arthritis.
1953

CHAPTER 13  The Adrenal Cortex
The adrenocortical primordium develops at approximately 8 
weeks of gestation and can be differentiated into two distinct lay­
ers, the inner fetal zone (FZ) and the outer definitive zone (DZ). 
At approximately 9 weeks, the adrenal blastema encapsulates, and 
the adrenal medulla develops when neural crest cells migrate into 
the adrenal gland.12 During the second trimester, the FZ enlarges, 
becomes larger than the fetal kidney, and secretes abundant 
amounts of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and dehydroepian­
drosterone sulfate (DHEAS). Concentrations of these hormones 
abruptly decline postnatally, in parallel with the postnatal involu­
tion of the FZ. The neocortex develops over the subsequent years 
into the adult adrenal gland.
In fetal life and up to 12 months of age, two distinct zones are 
evident, an inner prominent FZ and an outer DZ that differenti­
ates into the adult adrenal gland. After birth, the FZ regresses, 
and the DZ, which contains an inner zona fasciculata (ZF) and 
an outer zona glomerulosa (ZG), proliferates.13,14 The innermost 
zone, the zona reticularis (ZR), is evident after 2 years of life. The 
differentiation of the adrenal cortex into distinct zones has impor­
tant functional consequences and is thought to depend on the tem­
poral expression of transcription factors, including Pref1/ZOG, 
inner zone antigen, and SF1.15,16 In preadrenarchal children, focal 
reticular zone islets can be found, but the ZG and ZF are clearly 
differentiated.17 The occurrence of these ZR islets is consistent 
with the observation that DHEA and DHEAS synthesis gradually 
begins to rise from about 3 years of age.18 At adrenarche, the inner 
zone (ZR) thickens, corresponding with increased production 
of DHEA and DHEAS. Concurrently, changes in zone-specific 
enzyme-expression patterns, such as decreased 3β-hydroxysteroid 
dehydrogenase type 2 (3βHSD2) and increased cytochrome b5 
and sulfotransferase (SULT2A1) in the ZR, lead to increased flux 
toward DHEA. Clinically, adrenarche becomes apparent at 6 to 
8 years of age. Adrenal androgen production peaks in the third 
decade and then declines at a variable rate. Mineralocorticoids and 
glucocorticoids show a less age-specific variation.
The adult adrenal gland is a pyramidal structure, approxi­
mately 4 g in weight, 2 cm wide, 5 cm long, and 1 cm thick, 
that lies immediately above the kidney on its posteromedial sur­
face. Beneath the capsule, the ZG makes up approximately 15% 
of the cortex (depending on sodium intake) (Fig. 13.2). Cells are 
clustered in spherical nests and are small, with smaller nuclei in 
comparison with cells in other zones. The ZF makes up 75% of 
the cortex; cells are large and lipid laden and form radial cords 
within the fibrovascular radial network. The innermost ZR is 
sharply demarcated from both the ZF and the adrenal medulla. 
Cells there are irregular, with little lipid content. The maintenance 
of normal adrenal size appears to involve a progenitor cell popu­
lation lying subcapsular; cell migration and differentiation occur 
within the ZG and ZF, and senescence occurs within the ZR, but 
the factors regulating this important aspect of adrenal regenera­
tion are unknown. Fetal cells give rise to a subcapsular stem cell 
population that differentiates in a centripetal direction.19 ACTH 
administration results in glomerulosa cells adopting a fasciculata 
phenotype, and in turn, the innermost fasciculata cells adopt a 
reticularis phenotype that is reversible on withdrawal of ACTH.
The vasculature of the adrenal cortex is complex. Arterial sup­
ply is conveyed by up to 12 small arteries from the aorta and the 
inferior phrenic, renal, and intercostal arteries. These arteries 
branch to form a subcapsular arteriolar plexus, from which radial 
capillaries penetrate deeper into the cortex. In the ZR, a dense 
sinusoidal plexus is created, which empties into a central vein. The 
right adrenal vein is short, draining directly into the inferior vena 
cava, whereas the longer left adrenal vein usually drains into the 
left renal vein. 
Adrenal Steroids and Steroidogenesis
Three main types of hormones are produced by the adrenal cor­
tex—glucocorticoids (cortisol, corticosterone), mineralocorticoids 
(aldosterone, deoxycorticosterone [DOC]), androgen precur­
sors (DHEA, DHEAS, androstenedione, and 11-oxygenated, 
19-carbon steroids, or 11-oxyandrogens), and a small amount of 
testosterone. All steroid hormones are derived from the cyclopen­
tanoperhydrophenanthrene structure, that is, three cyclohexane 
rings and a single cyclopentane ring (Fig. 13.3). Steroid nomen­
clature is defined in one of two ways: by trivial names (e.g., cor­
tisol, aldosterone) or by the chemical structure as defined by the 
International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC).20 
The IUPAC classification is inappropriate for clinical use but 
does provide invaluable insight into steroid structure. The basic

structure, trivial name, and IUPAC name of some common ste­

bon atoms (C18 steroids), and androgens have 19 carbon atoms 
(C19), whereas glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and progesto­
gens are C21-steroid derivatives.
Cholesterol is the precursor for adrenal steroidogenesis. It is 
provided principally from the circulation, in the form of low-
density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol.21 Uptake is by specific cell 
surface LDL receptors present on adrenal tissue.22 LDL is then 
internalized via receptor-mediated endocytosis23; the resulting 
vesicles fuse with lysosomes and free cholesterol is produced after 
hydrolysis. However, it is clear that this cannot be the sole source 
of adrenal cholesterol because patients with abetalipoproteinemia 
who have undetectable circulating LDL and patients with defec­
tive LDL receptors in the setting of familial hypercholesterolemia 
still have normal basal adrenal steroidogenesis. Cholesterol can be 
generated de novo within the adrenal cortex from acetyl coenzyme 
A (acetyl-CoA). In addition, there is evidence that the adrenal 
gland can utilize high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol after 
uptake through the putative HDL receptor SR-B1.24
The biochemical pathways involved in adrenal steroidogen­
esis are shown in Fig. 13.4. The initial hormone-dependent, 
rate-limiting step is the transport of intracellular cholesterol from 
the outer to inner mitochondrial membrane for conversion to 
pregnenolone by cytochrome P450 (CYP) side-chain cleavage 
enzyme (CYP11A1 or P450 11A1). Naturally occurring human 
mutations have confirmed the importance of a 30-kDa protein, 
steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR), in mediating this 
effect. StAR is induced by an increase in intracellular cyclic ade­
nosine monophosphate (cAMP) after binding of ACTH to its 
cognate receptor, providing the first important rate-limiting step 
in adrenal steroidogenesis.25 Other transporters, including the 
peripheral benzodiazepine-like receptor, may be involved.26
Steroidogenesis involves the concerted action of several 
enzymes, including a series of CYP enzymes, all of which have 
been cloned and characterized (Table 13.3). CYP enzymes are 
classified into two types according to their subcellular localization 
and their specific electron shuttle system. Mitochondrial (type I) 
CYP enzymes, such as CYP11A1, 11β-hydroxylase (CYP11B1
or P450 11B1), and aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2 or P450 
11B2), rely on electron transfer facilitated by adrenodoxin and 
adrenodoxin reductase.27,28 Microsomal (type II) CYP enzymes 
localized to the endoplasmic reticulum include the steroidogenic 
enzymes 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase (CYP17A1 or P450 17A1),

21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2 or P450 21A2), and P450 aromatase 
(CYP19A1 or P450 19A1). The functions of CYP type II enzymes 
crucially depend on P450 oxidoreductase (POR), which provides 
electrons required for monooxygenase reactions catalyzed by 
the P450 enzyme.28,29 This category also includes hepatic P450 
enzymes involved in drug metabolism and enzymes involved in 
sterol and bile acid synthesis.28,29 In addition, the 17,20-lyase 
activity of P450 17A1 is dependent on a hemoprotein cytochrome 
b5, which functions as an allosteric facilitator of P450 17A1 with 
POR (Fig. 13.5; see also Fig. 13.4).30
Mutations in the genes encoding these enzymes result in human 
disease, so some understanding of the underlying pathways and 
steroid precursors is required.31 After uptake of cholesterol to the 
mitochondrion, cholesterol is cleaved by the P450 11A1 enzyme 
to form pregnenolone.32 In the cytoplasm, pregnenolone is con­
verted to progesterone by the type II isozyme of 3βHSD through 
a reaction involving dehydrogenation of the 3-hydroxyl group 
and isomerization of the double bond at C5.33 Progesterone is 
hydroxylated to 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17OHP) through the 
17α-hydroxylase activity of P450 17A1. 17α-Hydroxylation is 
an essential prerequisite for cortisol synthesis, and the ZG does 
not express 17α-hydroxylase. P450 17A1 also possesses 17,20-
lyase activity, which results in production of the C19 adrenal 
androgens DHEA and androstenedione.34 In humans, however, 
17OHP is not an efficient substrate for P450 17A1, and there is 
poor conversion of 17OHP to androstenedione. Adrenal andro­
stenedione secretion is dependent on the conversion of DHEA 
to androstenedione by 3βHSD. This enzyme also converts 
17-hydroxypregnenolone to 17OHP, but the preferred substrate 
is pregnenolone. The human adrenal gland is capable of synthesis 
of small but significant amounts of testosterone, which increases 
in clinical conditions associated with androgen excess. This con­
version is facilitated by the enzyme 17βHSD type 5 (17βHSD5), 
also called aldo-keto reductase 1C3 (AKR1C3).35 The 21-hydroxyl­
ation of either progesterone (in the ZG) or 17OHP (in the ZF) is 
carried out by the product of the CYP21A2 gene, 21-hydroxylase, 
to yield DOC or 11-deoxycortisol, respectively.36 The final step in 
cortisol biosynthesis takes place in the mitochondria and involves 
the conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol by the enzyme P450 
11B1 (11β-hydroxylase).37 In the ZG, 11β-hydroxylase may also 
convert DOC to corticosterone. The enzyme P450 11B2 (aldoste­
rone synthase) may also carry out this reaction; in addition, P450 
11B2 is required for conversion of corticosterone to aldosterone 
via the intermediate 18OH corticosterone; P450 11B1 lacks these 
two enzymatic activities.38,39 Therefore, P450 11B2 can carry 
out 11β-hydroxylation, 18-hydroxylation, and 18-methyl oxida­
tion to yield the characteristic C11-18 hemiacetyl structure of 
aldosterone.

II. As a class, adrenal androgen precursors (DHEA, DHEAS,

abundant steroids secreted from the adult adrenal gland (>20 mg/
day). In each case, secretion is facilitated through the expression of 
steroidogenic enzymes in a specific zonal manner. The ZG cannot 
synthesize cortisol because it does not express 17α-hydroxylase. 
In contrast, aldosterone secretion is confined to the outer ZG 
because of the restricted expression of P450 11B2. Although 
P450 11B1 and P450 11B2 share 95% homology, the 5′ pro­
moter sequences differ, permitting regulation of the final steps in 
glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid biosynthesis by ACTH and 
angiotensin II, respectively. In the ZR, high levels of cytochrome 
b5 confer 17,20-lyase activity on P450 17A1 and androgen pre­
cursor production. DHEA is sulfated in the ZR by the DHEA 
SULT2A1 to form DHEAS. This sulfonation reaction facilitated 
by SULT2A1 relies on the donor 3′-phosphoadenosine 5′-phos­
phosulfate (PAPS) to transfer a sulfonate group to an acceptor 
molecule. PAPS is synthesized by PAPS synthase, of which two 
isoenzymes exist (PAPSS1 and PAPSS2).40
In the fetal adrenal, steroidogenesis occurs primarily within the 
inner FZ. The FZ is a characteristic feature of higher primates, but 
the biologic role of fetal androgen production remains unclear. 
Because of a relative lack of 3βHSD and high SULT2A1 activ­
ity, the principal steroidogenic products are DHEA and DHEAS, 
which are then aromatized by placental trophoblast to estrogens. 
Therefore, the majority of maternal estrogen across pregnancy is, 
indirectly, fetally derived.41
Classic endocrine feedback loops are in place to control the 
secretion of both hormones. Cortisol inhibits the secretion of 
CRH from the hypothalamus and ACTH from the pituitary, 
and aldosterone-induced sodium retention inhibits renal renin 
secretion. 
Glucocorticoid Secretion: The Hypothalamic-
Pituitary-Adrenal Axis
Pro-Opiomelanocortin and ACTH
ACTH is the principal hormone stimulating adrenal glucocorti­
coid biosynthesis and secretion. ACTH has 39 amino acids but is 
synthesized within the anterior pituitary as part of a much larger, 
241–amino acid precursor called pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC). 
A transcription factor, TPIT, appears to be essential for differen­
tiation of POMC-expressing cells within the anterior pituitary.42 
POMC is cleaved in a tissue-specific fashion by prohormone con­
vertases to yield smaller peptide hormones. In the anterior pitu­
itary, this results in the secretion of β-lipoprotein (βLPH) and 
pro-ACTH, the latter being further cleaved to an amino-terminal 
peptide, joining peptide, and ACTH itself (Fig. 13.6).43,44 Post­
secretion cleavage of the precursor to γ-melanocyte-stimulating 
hormone (pro-γMSH) by a serine protease (AsP) expressed in 
the outer adrenal cortex is thought to mediate the trophic action 
of ACTH on the adrenal cortex.45 The first 24 amino acids of 
ACTH are common to all species, and a synthetic ACTH(1-
24), tetracosactide or cosyntropin (Synacthen, Cortrosyn), is 
available commercially for clinical testing of the HPA axis and 
assessing adrenal glucocorticoid reserve. The hormones αMSH, 
βMSH, and γMSH are also cleaved products from POMC, but

the increased pigmentation characteristic of Addison disease is 
thought to arise directly from increased ACTH concentrations

POMC is also transcribed in many extrapituitary tissues, nota­
bly brain, liver, kidney, gonad, and placenta.43,47,48 In these normal 
tissues, POMC messenger RNA (mRNA) is usually shorter (800 
nt) than the pituitary 1200-nt transcript because of lack of exons 1 
and 2 and the 5′ region of exon 3.49 Because the POMC-like pep­
tide product from this shorter transcript lacks a signal sequence 
needed to cross the endoplasmic reticulum, it is probable that it 
is neither secreted nor active in normal circumstances. However, 
in ectopic ACTH syndrome, additional POMC mRNA species 
are described that are longer than the normal pituitary POMC 
species (typically 1450 nt) as a result of the use of alternative pro­
moters in the 5′ region of the gene.50,51 This may, in part, explain 
the resistance of POMC expression to glucocorticoid feedback 
in these tumors. Other factors, including interaction with tissue-
specific transcription factors52 and lack of POMC promoter meth­
ylation,53 may explain the ectopic expression of ACTH in some 
malignant tissues. The cleavage of POMC is also tissue specific,54 
and it is possible, at least in some cases of ectopic ACTH syn­
drome, that circulating ACTH precursors (notably, pro-ACTH) 
may cross-react in current ACTH radioimmunoassays.55,56 The 
biologic activity of POMC itself on adrenal function is thought 
to be negligible.
POMC expression and processing within neurons in the hypo­
thalamus, specifically the generation of αMSH that interacts 
with melanocortin-4 receptors (MC4Rs), appears to be of crucial 
importance in appetite control and energy homeostasis (see later 
discussion).57 
Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone and Arginine 
Vasopressin
POMC secretion is tightly controlled by numerous factors, notably 
CRH and arginine vasopressin (AVP) (Fig. 13.7).58,59 Additional 
control is provided through an endogenous circadian rhythm 
and by stress and feedback inhibition by cortisol itself. CRH is a 
41–amino acid peptide that is synthesized in neurons within the 
paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus.9,60,61 Human and 
rat CRH are identical, but ovine CRH differs by seven amino 
acids62,63; ovine-sequence CRH is slightly more potent than 
human-sequence CRH in stimulating ACTH secretion and has a 
longer half-life, but both have been used diagnostically.
CRH is secreted into the hypophyseal portal blood, where it 
binds to specific type I CRH receptors on anterior pituitary cor­
ticotrophs64 to stimulate POMC transcription through a process 
that includes activation of adenylyl cyclase. It is unclear whether 
hypothalamic CRH contributes in any way to circulating levels; 
CRH is also synthesized in other tissues, and it is likely that cir­
culating CRH reflects synthesis from the testis, gastrointestinal 
tract, adrenal medulla, and particularly the placenta,65 in which 
the increased secretion across pregnancy results in a threefold 
increase in circulating CRH levels.66 In the circulation, CRH 
is bound to CRH-binding protein (CRH-BP); levels of CRH-
BP also increase during pregnancy, so cortisol secretion is not 
markedly elevated.67 CRH is the principal stimulus for ACTH 
secretion,68 but AVP is able to potentiate CRH-mediated secre­
tion.69 In this case, AVP acts through the V1b receptor to activate 
protein kinase C. The peak response of ACTH to CRH does 
not differ across the day, but it is affected by endogenous func­
tion of the HPA axis, in that responsiveness is reduced in sub­

The Stress Response and Immune-Endocrine Axis
The proinflammatory cytokines, notably interleukin 1 (IL1), 
IL6, and tumor necrosis factor-α, also increase ACTH secretion, 
either directly or by augmenting the effect of CRH.71,72 Leukemia 
inhibitory factor (LIF), a cytokine of the IL6 family, is a further 
activator of the HPA axis.73 This explains the response of the HPA 
axis to an inflammatory stimulus and is an important immune-
endocrine interaction (see Chapter 5). Physical stresses increase 
ACTH and cortisol secretion, again through central actions 
mediated via CRH and AVP. Cortisol secretion rises in response 
to fever, surgery,74 burn injury,75 hypoglycemia,76 hypotension, 
and exercise.77 In all of these cases, this increased secretion can 
be viewed as a normal counterregulatory response to the insult. 
Acute psychological stress raises cortisol levels,78 but secretion 
rates appear to be normal in patients with chronic anxiety states 
and underlying psychotic illness. However, depression is associ­
ated with high circulating cortisol concentrations, and this is an 
important consideration in the differential diagnosis of Cushing 
syndrome (see later discussion). 
Circadian Rhythm
ACTH, and hence cortisol, is secreted in a pulsatile fashion with 
a circadian rhythm; levels are highest on awakening and decline 
throughout the day, reaching nadir values in the evening (Fig. 
13.8).79 The average ACTH pulse frequency is higher in normal 
adult men compared to women (18 vs. 10 pulses/24 hours, respec­
tively). The circadian ACTH rhythm appears to be mediated prin­
cipally by an increased ACTH pulse amplitude occurring between 
5 and 9 am but also by a reduction in ACTH pulse frequency 
occurring between 6 pm and midnight.80,81 Food ingestion is a 
further stimulus to ACTH secretion. An ultradian rhythm over­
lies the circadian and appears to be driven by an oscillator created 
between the secretion of ACTH, the short delay in response at the 
adrenal, and the subsequent negative feedback by cortisol at the 
hypothalamus and pituitary.82
Circadian rhythm is dependent on both day-night83 and sleep-
wake84 patterns and is disrupted by alternating day-night shift 
work and by long-distance travel across time zones.85 It can take 
up to 2 weeks for the circadian rhythm to reset to an altered day-
night cycle. 
Negative Feedback
An important aspect of CRH and ACTH secretion is the nega­
tive feedback control exerted by glucocorticoids themselves.

Glucocorticoids inhibit POMC transcription in the anterior 
pituitary58 and CRH and AVP mRNA synthesis and secretion 
in the hypothalamus.86,87 Annexin 1 (formerly called lipocortin 
1) may also play a critical role in effecting the negative feedback 
of glucocorticoids on ACTH and CRH release.88 The negative 
feedback effect depends on the dose, potency, half-life, and dura­
tion of administration of the glucocorticoid and has important 
physiologic and diagnostic consequences. Suppression of the 
HPA axis by pharmacologic corticosteroids may persist for many 
months after cessation of therapy, and adrenocortical insuffi­
ciency should be anticipated. Diagnostically, the feedback mecha­
nism explains ACTH hypersecretion in Addison disease, as well 
as low ACTH levels in patients with a cortisol-secreting adrenal 
adenoma. Feedback inhibition is principally mediated via the glu­
cocorticoid receptor (GR); patients with glucocorticoid resistance 
resulting from mutations in the GR89 and mice lacking the GR 
gene (Nr3c1)90 have ACTH and cortisol hypersecretion due to 
perceived lack of negative feedback. 
The ACTH Receptor and ACTH Effects on the Adrenal 
Gland
ACTH binds to a G protein–coupled melanocortin-2 recep­
tor (MC2R),91 of which there are approximately 3500 on each 
adrenocortical cell. Melanocortin-2 receptor accessory pro­
tein (MRAP) is required for correct localization and signaling 
of MC2R.92 Current data suggest that MRAP might promote 
three different activities: as a chaperone assisting correct folding 
of MC2R in the endoplasmic reticulum, as an accessory pro­
tein essential for trafficking of MC2R to the plasma membrane, 
and as a coreceptor enabling MC2R to bind or to signal ACTH 
response.93 Downstream signal transduction is mediated princi­
pally through the stimulation of adenylyl cyclase and intracellular 
cAMP,94 although both extracellular and intracellular Ca2+ play a 
role.95 Other factors synergize with or inhibit the effects of ACTH 
on the adrenal cortex, including angiotensin II, activin, inhibin, 
and cytokines (tumor necrosis factor-α and leptin).96 Cell-to-cell 
communication via gap junctions is also important in mediating 
the effects of ACTH.97
ACTH produces both immediate and chronic effects on the 
adrenal gland; the end result is the stimulation of adrenal steroido­
genesis and growth. Acutely, steroidogenesis is stimulated through 
a StAR-mediated increase in cholesterol delivery to the P450 
11A1 enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane.25 Chroni­
cally (within 24–26 hours of exposure), ACTH acts to increase 
the synthesis of all steroidogenic CYP enzymes (P450 11A1, P450 
17A1, P450 21A2, P450 11B1) in addition to adrenodoxin,98,99 
the effects of which are mediated at the transcriptional level. 
ACTH increases synthesis of the LDL and HDL receptors and 
possibly also synthesis of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl (HMG)–
CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step in cholesterol biosynthesis. 
ACTH increases adrenal weight by inducing both hyperplasia and 
hypertrophy. Adrenal atrophy is a feature of ACTH deficiency. 
Mineralocorticoid Secretion: The Renin-
Angiotensin-Aldosterone Axis
Aldosterone is secreted from the ZG under the control of three 
principal secretagogues: angiotensin II, potassium, and to a lesser 
extent, ACTH (see Fig. 13.7). Other factors, notably somatosta­
tin, heparin, atrial natriuretic factor, and dopamine, can directly 
inhibit aldosterone synthesis. The secretion of aldosterone and its 
intermediary 18-hydroxylated metabolites is restricted to the ZG 
because of the zone-specific expression of P450 11B2 (aldoste­
rone synthase).100 Corticosterone and DOC, synthesized in both 
the ZF and ZG, can act as mineralocorticoids, which becomes 
significant in some clinical diseases, notably some forms of con­
genital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) and adrenal tumors. Similarly, 
it is now established that cortisol can act as a mineralocorticoid in 
the setting of impaired metabolism of cortisol to cortisone by the
