KEY POINTS
 • 
Sexual response is a motivation/incentive-based cycle 
comprising of phases of physiologic responses that 
include desire, arousal, and orgasm. These phases of the 
cycle can overlap, and their order can be variable, but this 
conceptualization of sexual response cycle has proven useful in 
classifying sexual dysfunctions.
 • 
In middle-age and older men, sexual dysfunction is often 
related to comorbid conditions, such as diabetes, coronary 
artery disease, or a hormonal problem.
 • 
Penile erection results from biochemical and hemodynamic 
events that are associated with activation of central nervous 
system sites, cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation, increased 
blood flow into cavernosal sinuses, and venous occlusion.
 • 
Corporal smooth muscle tone is regulated by transmembrane 
and intracellular calcium flux, which in turn is regulated by 
potassium channels; connexin43-derived gap junctions; and 
cholinergic, adrenergic, and nonadrenergic, noncholinergic 
mediators, including nitric oxide.
 • 
Selective phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors are safe and effective 
and have emerged as first-line therapy for men with erectile 
dysfunction.
 • 
Testosterone regulates sexual thoughts and desire, sexual 
arousal, attentiveness to erotic stimuli, and sleep-entrained 
erections. Testosterone deficiency is a treatable cause of 
hypoactive sexual desire in men. In randomized trials, 
testosterone replacement therapy has been shown to improve 
sexual desire, erectile function, and overall sexual activity in 
men with hypogonadism.
 • 
There is no normative standard for female sexual function, and 
women do not need to be partnered to be negatively affected 
by, or receive treatment for, sexual dysfunction.
 • 
For a diagnosis of female sexual dysfunction (FSD), the 
symptoms need to be episodic or persistent over a period at 
least several months and associated with clinically significant 
distress.
 • 
Hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction (HSDD) is the most 
common FSD. Other categories of sexual dysfunction in women 
include arousal and orgasm dysfunction. Sexual pain disorder is 
generally considered separately.
 • 
Any condition that causes sex hormone insufficiency may 
contribute to FSD, including ovarian insufficiency due to 
spontaneous or iatrogenic causes, adrenal insufficiency, 
hypopituitarism, and hyperprolactinemia. Other endocrine 
conditions that may be associated with FSD include diabetes, 
polycystic ovary syndrome, and thyroid disease.
 • 
The most effective hormonal therapy for HSDD in 
postmenopausal women is physiologic transdermal 
testosterone therapy.
 • 
Nonhormonal therapies for HSDD in premenopausal women 
include flibanserin and bremelanotide and, for all women, off-
label use of bupropion and buspirone.
18
Sexual Function and Dysfunction
SHALENDER BHASIN AND SUSAN R. DAVIS
Introduction
Recognizing the importance of sexual function as a determinant 
of quality of life, the World Health Organization has declared sex­
ual health a fundamental right of men and women. Sexual health 
has been defined by the World Health Organization as “a state of 
physical, emotional, mental and social well-being related to sexu­
ality.”1 This definition covers a wide spectrum of sexual well-being 
and allows for what constitutes “dysfunction” to be determined by 
each individual’s perspective.
Sexual dysfunction has assumed increasing importance in 
endocrinology for several reasons. Disorders of sexual function are 
highly prevalent in the general population, especially among men 
and women with endocrine disorders,2–5 diabetes, thyroid dis­
orders, hyperlipidemia, and testicular and ovarian disorders.6–10 
Epidemiologic surveys, such as the National Survey of Sexual 
752
SECTION V    Sexual Development and Function
Attitudes and Lifestyle, indicate that 42% of men and 51% of 
women experienced some problem with sexual response in the 
previous year causing distress in the lives of 10% to 11%.3,5 Fur­
thermore, the growing recognition that sexual dysfunction in men 
and women is commonly associated with systemic disease5–7,9,11,12 
has duly placed sexual dysfunctions in men within the purview of 
the endocrinologist and the primary care provider. Erectile dys­
function (ED) may signal asymptomatic coronary artery disease,13 
diabetes,6,7,14 or depression.15,16 Endocrine disease and its treat­
ment can frequently disturb sexual function in men and women. 
In addition, patients may believe, often incorrectly, that their sex­
ual dysfunction must necessarily be due to hormonal imbalance 
and seek management from endocrinologists.17
The most recent classification of sexual dysfunction has been 
provided by the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revi­
sion (ICD-11).18 For the most part the ICD-11 has not provided 
separate classifications for men and women as the neurologic net­
works and pathways pertaining to the stages of the sexual response 
are not sex-specific. However, as presentations are frequently sex-
specific (e.g., erectile dysfunction in men and desire dysfunction 
in women), the clinical aspects of sexual dysfunction have been 
addressed separately for men and women in this chapter. This 
chapter describes the current conceptualization of sexual response 
in men and women, the underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms 
of various types of sexual dysfunction, the sexual sequelae of vari­
ous endocrine disorders, and clinical assessment, diagnosis, and 
treatment of sexual dysfunction. Management strategies for sexual 
dysfunction stemming from hormonal and nonhormonal factors 
are also reviewed. 
The Sexual Response Cycle
William Masters and Virginia E. Johnson19 found that both men 
and women display predictable physiologic responses after sexual 
stimulation. They described the human sexual response as a lin­
ear progression from arousal to a plateau of high arousal followed 
by orgasm/ejaculation and resolution (Fig. 18.1). Subsequently 
Kaplan expanded the model to include desire resulting in a three-
stage model comprising desire, arousal, and orgasm,20 which has 
formed the basis for the classifications of sexual dysfunction. 
Whipple and Brash-McGreer then proposed a circular model of 
sexual function whereby a positive sexual experience reinforces 
desire.21 Basson added emotional intimacy, sexual stimuli, and 
relationship satisfaction as incentives for sexual activity, particu­
larly in women.22 This model has since been found to be most 
aligned to women with sexual dysfunction, but not applicable to 
women without sexual dysfunction.23 While none of these models 
are perfect, they have provided a framework for the assessment, 
diagnosis, and management of sexual function and dysfunction, 
as well as ongoing research in this field. 
Sexual Function and Dysfunction in the Male
The physiologic mechanisms that regulate various components of 
the sexual response in men and whose perturbation contributes to 
the pathophysiology of male sexual dysfunctions include neural 
input from multiple brain regions and spinal cord centers, hemo­
dynamic control of blood flow to the penis, biochemical regula­
tion of cavernosal smooth muscle tone, and veno-occlusion.
Sexual Desire and Arousal in Response to Erotic 
Cues
Sexual desire and arousal are complex processes that involve mul­
tiple brain regions and neurotransmitters.24 The hypothalamus, in 
addition to serving as the master regulator of sex hormone pro­
duction, also is important in regulating sexual behaviors.24 The 
amygdala, which is a part of the limbic system, is involved in

Physiologic Mechanisms of Penile Erection
Penile Anatomy and Blood Flow
The erectile tissue of the penis consists of two dorsally positioned 
corpora cavernosa and a ventrally placed corpus spongiosum.29,30 The 
erectile tissue of both the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum 
is composed of numerous cavernous spaces separated by trabecu­
lae.29–32 These trabeculae are composed mainly of smooth muscle 
cells that are arranged in a syncytium. Endothelial cells cover the 
surfaces of the trabeculae.32
The penile arterial blood supply is derived from pudendal arter­
ies, which are branches of the internal iliac arteries (Fig. 18.2). The 
pudendal artery divides into cavernosal, dorsal penile, and bulbo­
urethral arteries. The cavernosal arteries and their branches, the 
helicine arteries, provide blood flow to corpora cavernosa.29 
Penile Innervation
The neural input to the penis consists of sympathetic (T11–L2), 
parasympathetic (S2–S4), and somatic nerves (Table 18.1).31 
Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers converge in the inferior 
hypogastric plexus where the autonomic input to the penis is inte­
grated and communicated to the penis through cavernosal nerves. 
In man, the inferior hypogastric ganglionic plexus is located retro­
peritoneally near the rectum.31
Several brain regions, including amygdala, the median pre­
optic area (MPOA) and paraventricular nucleus of the hypo­
thalamus, and periaqueductal gray matter act coordinately to 
affect penile erections.31 The MPOA of the hypothalamus serves 
as the integration site for the central nervous system control of 
erections; it receives sensory input from the amygdala and sends 
impulses to the paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and

The parasympathetic input to the penis is proerectile, and 
sympathetic input is mainly inhibitory.31 The stimuli from the 
perineum and lower urinary tract are carried to the penis through 
the sacral reflex arc.31 
Hemodynamic Changes During Penile Erection
Penile erection results from a series of biochemical and hemody­
namic events that are associated with activation of central nervous 
system sites involved in regulation of erections, relaxation of cav­
ernosal smooth muscle, increased blood flow into the cavernosal 
sinuses, and venous occlusion resulting in penile engorgement and 
rigidity.29,32
As cavernosal smooth muscle relaxes and the blood flow to the 
penis increases, the increased pooling of blood in the cavernosal 
spaces results in penile engorgement29,32 (Fig. 18.3). The expand­
ing corpora cavernosa compress the venules against the rigid tunica 
albuginea, restricting the venous outflow from the cavernosal 
spaces.29,32 This facilitates entrapment of blood in the cavernosal 
sinuses, imparting rigidity to the erect penis. 
Biochemical Regulation of Cavernosal Smooth Muscle 
Tone
The tone of the corporal smooth muscle cells determines the erec­
tile state of the penis.29,32,33 When the cavernosal smooth muscle 
cells are relaxed, the penis is engorged with blood and erect. When 
the cavernosal smooth muscle cells are contracted, the penis is 
flaccid.33
The smooth muscle tone in the corpora cavernosa is maintained 
by the release of stored intracellular calcium into the cytoplasm 
and influx of calcium through membrane channels.34–37 The 
transmembrane influx of calcium in the cavernosal smooth mus­
cle cells is mediated mostly by L-type voltage-dependent calcium 
channels, although T-type calcium channels are also expressed in 
cavernosal smooth muscle cells.34 An increase in intracellular cal­
cium activates myosin light chain kinase resulting in phosphoryla­
tion of myosin light chain, actin-myosin interactions, and smooth 
muscle contraction.32,36
The transmembrane and intracellular calcium flux in the cav­
ernosal smooth muscle cells is regulated by a number of cellu­
lar processes that involve K+ flux through potassium channels, 
connexin43-derived gap junctions, and a number of cholinergic, 
adrenergic, and noradrenergic noncholinergic mediators (see Figs. 
18.3, 18.4, 18.5, and 18.6).38,39 The nonadrenergic noncholinergic 
mediators include vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), calcitonin 
gene–related peptide (CGRP), and nitric oxide.40
Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) binding to its cognate receptor results 
in generation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), which 
activates protein kinase A. Activated protein kinase A gates K+ 
channels, resulting in K+ efflux from the cell (see Fig. 18.3). The 
protein kinase A–mediated processes also result in a net decrease 
in intracellular calcium, favoring smooth muscle cell relaxation.
Adrenergic pathways, acting through norepinephrine and α1-
adrenergic receptors, activate phospholipase C, which generates

diacyl glycerol and inositol trisphosphate (IP3).36 Diacyl glycerol 
activates protein kinase C, which inhibits K+ channels and acti­

channels (Fig. 18.4).37 Inositol trisphosphate increases intracel­

promotes actin-myosin interactions, resulting in smooth muscle 
contraction and a flaccid penis.
Potassium Channels. At least three types of potassium chan­
nels—ATP-sensitive (KATP), voltage-gated (Kv), and calcium-
sensitive K+ channels (referred to as BKCa or maxi-K channels)—
are expressed in the cavernosal smooth muscle cells.38,39 Of these, 
the BKCa channels are the most important, as they account for 
90% of K+ efflux from the cavernosal smooth muscle cells. Agents 
that open BKCa channels have been shown to relax cavernosal 
smooth muscle cells in vitro.39 Thus, the strategies that increase 
BKCa channel expression in vivo improve erectile capacity in dia­
betic and older rodents39,41 and are being explored as therapy 
for ED. A phase 1 human gene therapy trial using this approach 
reported the feasibility of this approach, but there has not been a 
follow-up trial since then.41 A phase 2a trial using a single intra­
cavernosal injection (ICI) of hMaxi K channel was initiated in 
2016, but no data have been reported (NCT02713789). 
Nitric Oxide. Nitric oxide, derived from the nerve terminals 
innervating the corpora cavernosa, endothelial lining of penile 
arteries, and the cavernosal sinuses, is an important biochemical 
regulator of cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation. Nitric oxide 
also induces arterial dilation.42 The actions of nitric oxide on the 
cavernosal smooth muscle and the arterial blood flow are medi­
ated through the activation of guanylyl cyclase, the production 
of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), and the activation 
of cGMP-dependent protein kinase (also called protein kinase G, 
or PKG) (Fig. 18.5). cGMP causes smooth muscle relaxation by 
lowering intracellular calcium. There is some evidence that nitric 
oxide inhibits Rho kinase–induced cavernosal smooth muscle sen­
sitivity to calcium.43 
Cyclic Nucleotide Phosphodiesterases. Cyclic nucleotide 
phosphodiesterases hydrolyze cAMP and cGMP, thus reducing 
their concentrations within the cavernosal smooth muscle. Of the 
13 or more isoforms of cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases that 
have been identified, isoforms 2, 3, 4, and 5 are expressed in the 
penis.44–46 Only phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) is specific to the 
nitric oxide/cGMP pathway in the corpora cavernosa.47,48 Hydroly­
sis of cGMP by this enzyme results in reversal of the smooth muscle 
relaxation and reversal of penile erection (see Fig. 18.5). Sildenafil, 
vardenafil, tadalafil, avanafil, and udenafil are potent and selective 
inhibitors of the activity of PDE5 that prevent breakdown of cGMP 
and thereby enhance penile erection (see Fig. 18.5). 
Connexin43 Gap Junctions. The smooth muscle cells in the 
corpora cavernosa are connected by connexin43 gap junctions 
that allow the ions and some signaling molecules such as inositol 
trisphosphate to diffuse freely across smooth muscle cells49 (Fig. 
18.6), resulting in coordinate regulation of the entire corpora cav­
ernosa.49 Thus, the corpora cavernosa can be viewed functionally 
as a syncytium of interconnected smooth muscle cells.

Regulation of Sensitivity to Intracellular Calcium by Rho 
A/Rho Kinase Signaling. Sensitization to intracellular calcium is 
regulated by the balance between phosphorylation of the regula­
tory light chain of myosin II by a myosin light chain kinase and 
its dephosphorylation by a myosin light chain phosphatase (Fig. 
18.7).35,50,51 Phosphorylation of regulatory light chain of myosin 
II is necessary for activation of myosin II adenosine triphosphatases 
(ATPases) by actin, and its dephosphorylation prevents activa­
tion of myosin II ATPases.35 Rho A is a guanosine triphosphatase 
(GTPase) of approximately 20 kDa that modulates Rho kinase 
activity, myosin light chain phosphorylation, and calcium sensi­
tivity in smooth muscle cells. Rho A–GDP (guanosine diphos­
phate) complex is associated with a GDP dissociation inhibitor 
(RhoGDI) in its inactive state. A number of intracellular signals 
can promote an exchange of GDP for GTP on Rho A through 
the mediation of guanine nucleotide exchange factors.35,52 The 
Rho A–GTP interacts with its downstream effector Rho kinase, 
increasing the sensitivity of vascular smooth muscle to intracellu­
lar calcium by inhibiting the myosin light chain phosphatases. The 
activity of Rho kinase is higher in older rats than in young rats51; 
the age-related increase in Rho kinase activity has been proposed 
as one possible mechanism to explain the age-related decrease in 
erectile capacity. The inhibitors of Rho A/Rho kinase signaling 
promise to provide attractive targets for the development of thera­
pies for ED.53 
Mechanisms of Ejaculation
The ejaculatory mechanisms consist of three processes: emission, 
ejection, and orgasm.54–56 Although orgasm and seminal fluid 
ejection often occur contemporaneously, these two processes 
are regulated by separate mechanisms. Emission, the deposition 
of seminal fluid into the posterior urethra, is dependent on the 
integrity of the vasa deferentia, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, 
and the bladder neck.54,56 Ejaculation refers to the ejection of 
seminal fluid containing sperm, and the secretions of seminal 
vesicles, prostate, and bulbourethral glands from the posterior 
urethra out through the urethral meatus, and is regulated primar­
ily by the central nervous system activation of the sympathetic 
nervous system.54 This emission is ejaculated out of the urethra 
by the contractions of the bulbospongiosus and levator ani muscles, 
the closure of the bladder sphincter due to sympathetic activation, 
and synchronized opening of the external urinary sphincter.54 The 
orgasm is the sensation associated with the rhythmic contractions 
of these pelvic floor muscles.
The stria terminalis, the posteromedial amygdala, the sub­
parafascicular thalamus, the MPOA of the hypothalamus, the 
periaqueductal gray matter in the midbrain region, and the para­
gigantocellular nucleus in the pons integrate seminal fluid emis­
sion and ejection during copulatory behavior in animals54,57 (see 
Table 18.1). The paragigantocellular nucleus in the pons through 
serotonergic pathways inhibits the lumbosacral motor nuclei

onto the seminal tract.59

The Role of Testosterone in Regulating Sexual 
Function in Men (Box 18.1)
Testosterone regulates many domains of sexual function in 
men and women.9 Testosterone promotes sexual thoughts and 
desire63–65 and increases attentiveness to erotic auditory and other 
stimuli.66 Although men with testosterone deficiency can achieve 
penile erections in response to visual erotic stimuli, their over­
all sexual activity is decreased.64 Testosterone increases the fre­
quency of spontaneous but not stimulus-bound erections (Table 
18.2).64 Nocturnal penile erections are temporally related to peaks 
of nighttime testosterone secretion and are less frequent and of 
lower amplitude and duration in men with testosterone defi­
ciency; testosterone replacement therapy increases the frequency, 
magnitude, and duration of nocturnal penile tumescence.67,68 
Maximum rigidity may require a threshold circulating level of 
testosterone.69–72
Testosterone induces the expression of nitric oxide synthase 
(NOS) in the cavernosal smooth muscle71,73,74; inhibits the 
expression of rho kinase in the cavernosal smooth muscle of 
castrated rats, thereby altering its sensitivity to calcium75; exerts 
trophic effects on cavernosal smooth muscle72 and ischiocaver­
nosus and bulbospongiosus muscles; and is necessary for the veno-
occlusive response.69 Testosterone also is a potent vasodilator and 
increases the blood flow to penis through its action on calcium 
channels.76–78 Androgen-deficient men show delayed orgasm and 
low ejaculatory volume.9
Brain imaging studies suggest that processing of sexual stimuli 
may be altered in testosterone-deficient men with decreased acti­
vation in those brain areas that typically are activated in eugo­
nadal men and in testosterone-deficient men after testosterone 
replacement in response to erotic stimuli.28,79 Acting through the 
dopaminergic receptors in the medial preoptic area of the hypo­
thalamus, testosterone elicits reward-seeking behavior in male 
mammals.80 This may be the basis for testosterone’s motivational 
effects on mammalian sexual behavior.80,81 The roles of cyto­
chrome P450 19A1 (aromatase) and steroid 5α-reductase systems 
in mediating androgen effects on sexual function remain incom­
pletely understood. The aromatization of testosterone to estradiol 
is important in mediating testosterone’s effects on sexual desire82; 
studies of men with mutation of the P450 19A1 (aromatase) gene 
further corroborate this inference.83,84 However, 5α-reduction of 
testosterone to 5α-dihydrotestosterone is not essential for mediat­
ing testosterone’s effects on sexual desire or erectile function in 
eugonadal men.85 Both testosterone and estradiol are required to 
maintain sexual function.
In surveys of community-dwelling middle-age and older men, 
low libido, poor morning erections, and erectile dysfunction are 
associated with low total and free testosterone levels.86,87 In ran­
domized clinical trials in men with hypogonadism, testosterone 
has been shown to improve overall sexual activity, sexual desire, 
and erectile function.88–94 However, testosterone does not improve 
erectile response to visual erotic stimuli64 or erectile function in 
men with ED who have normal testosterone levels.95 Testoster­
one does not improve ejaculatory function in men with ejacula­
tory dysfunction and low testosterone levels.96 In male rats, in 
whom endogenous testosterone production has been suppressed 
by administration of a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) 
antagonist, testosterone restores all measures of mating behavior 
at doses that are insufficient to restore prostate and seminal vesicle 
weights.97,98 Similarly, dose-response studies in humans rendered 
testosterone deficient by the administration of a GnRH agonist, 
sexual function is restored by testosterone doses that raise serum 
testosterone levels just above the lower limit of the normal male 
range82,99,100; further increase in serum testosterone levels does 
not further improve measures of sexual function.
Testosterone deficiency and ED are two independently distrib­
uted disorders that may coexist in middle-age and older men.101,102 
Selective PDE5 inhibitors are highly effective first-line therapies 
for ED.10 However, one third of men with ED do not respond to 
PDE5 inhibitors; some of the men with ED who are PDE5 inhibi­
tor nonresponders have low testosterone levels.103 Observations that 
testosterone stimulates penile NOS, increases penile blood flow, 
and has trophic effects on cavernosal smooth muscle and bulbo­
spongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles have led to speculation 
that testosterone therapy might improve erectile response to PDE5 
inhibitors. The randomized trials in which testosterone treatment 
was added to a PDE5 inhibitor have not shown consistent improve­
ment in erectile function above that achieved with PDE5 inhibitor 
alone.104–106 Spitzer et al104 evaluated whether the addition of tes­
tosterone to sildenafil improves erectile response in men with ED 
and low testosterone. In this randomized controlled trial (RCT), 
after optimization of sildenafil dose during an initial run-in period, 
the participants were assigned randomly to 14 weeks of daily tes­
tosterone or placebo gel. Sildenafil plus testosterone was not supe­
rior to sildenafil plus placebo in improving erectile function in men 
with ED and low testosterone.104 In another placebo-controlled 
trial (TADTEST) of men with ED who were deemed tadalafil fail­
ures,105 the primary analysis of all randomized subjects also did not

The Classification and Revised Definitions of 
Sexual Dysfunction in Men
The classification and conceptualization of sexual dysfunctions in 
men have undergone substantial revisions in the Diagnostic and 
Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5),108 
as well as in ICD-11.109 The DSM is the primary diagnostic classi­
fication system developed by the American Psychiatric Association 
and is used by mental health professionals in the United States 
and a few other countries, while ICD codes are developed by the 
World Health organization and used by clinicians worldwide for 
classifying diseases and related health problems.
The updated classification and definitions of male sexual dysfunc­
tions in DSM-5108 differ from the DSM-IV in several salient ways:
	1.	 DSM-5 includes three major categories of male sexual dysfunc­
tions, as opposed to six in the DSM-IV.108 These include sexual 
desire dysfunctions, sexual arousal dysfunctions, and orgasmic 
dysfunctions. The DSM-5 also includes an additional category 
of Other Specified Sexual Dysfunction due to causes other 
than those included in the above three categories.
	2.	 The DSM-IV criteria for hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction 
required that the lack of sexual desire cause “marked distress or

Sexual Desire Dysfunctions
Male Hypoactive Sexual Desire Dysfunction
Male hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction (MHSDD) is charac­
terized by a persistent or recurrent lack or absence of sexual fan­
tasies or desire for sexual activity that causes clinically significant 
distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important 
areas of functioning and that is not better explained by another 
disorder, direct physiologic effects of a substance (medication), 
or general medical condition.111–113 A diagnosis of MHSDD is 
appropriate only if the person reports distress due to low sexual 
desire.111,112 Low sexual desire is not necessarily pathologic, as low 
sexual desire may be an appropriate adaptation to relationship and 
health-related issues.
Although DSM-5 limits a diagnosis of MHSDD to causes 
other than medication, illness (including testosterone deficiency 
and depression), and relationship and addiction problems, in clin­
ical practice, reduced or lack of sexual desire is often associated 
with multiple factors, including testosterone deficiency, prolac­
tin excess, the use of medications (SSRIs, antiandrogens, GnRH 
analogues, antihypertensives, cancer chemotherapeutic agents, 
anticonvulsants), systemic illness, and depression, as well as other 
psychological problems such as low self-esteem, fear of emotional 
intimacy, fear of loss, long-term habit of sex alone with or without 
pornography, other causes of sexual dysfunction, or relationship 
problems.5,114 Testosterone deficiency is an important, treatable 
cause of low desire in men and should be excluded by measuring 
serum total and free testosterone levels.
The incidence and prevalence of MHSDD in the general 
population are unknown. In referred patient populations, the 
prevalence has been estimated to be 5% in men.5,114 Prevalence 
increases with age.5,114 MHSDD often coexists with other sexual 
disorders, such as ED, and may develop as a consequence of other 
sexual disorders.
Appropriate evaluation and treatment of MHSDD are impor­
tant because evaluation may lead to detection of treatable disease 
including testosterone deficiency, hyperprolactinemia, or depres­
sion. Furthermore, low sexual desire may impede or reduce the 
effectiveness of treatments for other sexual disorders. 
Erectile Dysfunction
Erectile dysfunction is the inability to attain or maintain an erec­
tion or to achieve penile rigidity sufficient for satisfactory sexual 
intercourse.10,29,89,115,116 The DSM-5 requires that the inability to 
attain or maintain an erection should occur in 75% to 100% of 
encounters over a period of at least 6 months,110 although many 
professional society guidelines do not include this requirement.10 
ED profoundly adversely affects quality of life of the affected indi­
vidual117,118; it also negatively affects the sexual satisfaction and 
quality of life of the sexual partners of the affected persons.118
Prevalence 
and 
Incidence. The 
epidemiologic 
sur­
veys,2,4–6,119–123 including the Massachusetts Male Aging Study 
(MMAS)120 and the National Health and Social Life Survey 
(NHSLS)5,119 that used population-based sampling techniques, 
have revealed a high prevalence of ED. The MMAS, a cross-
sectional as well as longitudinal, community-based epidemio­
logic survey of 1709 men, 40 to 70 years of age, conducted in the 
greater Boston area between 1987 and 1989, revealed that 52% of 
men in this age range were affected by ED to some degree; 17.2% 
of surveyed men reported minimal ED, 25.2% moderate ED, 
and 9.6% complete ED.4,6,120 The NHSLS, a national probability 
survey of English-speaking persons, 18 to 59 years, living in the 
United States,5,119 also revealed a similarly high prevalence of ED 
in men; both surveys found the prevalence of ED to increase with 
increasing age.5,120 These and other studies are in agreement that 
ED is a common problem worldwide.4,120,123,124 The men suffer­
ing from other medical problems, such as hypertension, diabetes, 
cardiovascular disease (CVD), and end-stage renal disease, have a 
significantly higher prevalence of ED than healthy men.6,122
There is a paucity of longitudinal data on the incidence of ED 
in men. In the MMAS, the crude incidence of ED in White men 
in the Boston area was found to be 25.9 cases per 1000 person-
years.120 The incidence rates increased from 12.4 cases per 1000 
person-years for men 40 to 49 years of age to 29.8 cases per 1000 
person-years for men 50 to 59 years of age and 46.4 per 1000 
person-years for men 60 to 69 years of age.120 In another study, 
incidence rates were derived from a survey of men seen at a pre­
ventive medicine clinic.11 This study found the incidence rates of 
ED to be less than 3 cases per 1000 person-years among men less 
than 45 years of age and 52 cases per 1000 person-years among 
men 65 years of age or older. These studies suggest that 600,000 
to 700,000 men in the United States develop ED each year.4,11,120 
Risk Factors for Erectile Dysfunction. The risk factors for ED 
include age, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, smoking, medication 
use, depression, dyslipidemia, and CVD.6,29,122,123,125–129 Advanc­
ing age is an important risk factor for ED in men5,6,11,119,122; less 
than 10% of men below the age of 40 and over 50% of men over 
the age of 70 have ED.
Among the chronic diseases associated with ED, diabetes mel­
litus is one of the most important risk factors. In the MMAS, the 
age-adjusted risk of complete ED was three times higher in men 
with a history of treated diabetes mellitus than in those without a 
history of diabetes mellitus6; 50% of men with diabetes mellitus 
will experience ED sometime during the course of their illness. 
In the MMAS, treated heart disease, treated hypertension, and 
hyperlipidemia were associated with a significantly increased risk 
of ED.6 Among men with treated heart disease and hypertension, 
the probability of ED was more than two times greater for smokers 
than for nonsmokers.6,119 Other cardiovascular disorders, includ­
ing hypertension, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease, are all 
associated with increased risk of ED.6,119,122 Physical activity and 
exercise interventions, particularly aerobic exercise of moderate 
or high intensity, are associated with improvements in erectile 
function.130 Cigarette smoking is strongly associated with ED.131 
Chronic smoking can induce ED through multiple mechanisms, 
including endothelial dysfunction, increased oxidative stress, and 
atherosclerosis progression.131

SECTION V    Sexual Development and Function
Several reviews have emphasized the relationship of prescrip­
tion medications and the occurrence of ED. The drugs commonly 
associated with erectile dysfunction include antihypertensives 
such as β-adrenergic blockers and thiazide diuretics; antidepres­
sants such as the SSRIs and tricyclic antidepressants; antipsychotic 
drugs used to treat schizophrenia; some antihistamines such as 
diphenhydramine; and medications that inhibit testosterone 
production, such as GnRH analogues, antiandrogens, and abi­
raterone, or block androgen action, such as bicalutamide, enzalu­
tamide, darolutamide, and apalutamide.132–138 In the MMAS, the 
use of antihypertensives, cardiac medications, and oral hypoglyce­
mic drugs was associated with an increased risk of ED.6 Thiazide 
diuretics, antidepressants, and antipsychotics, because of the high 
prevalence of their use, are some of the most common drugs asso­
ciated with ED. 
Erectile Dysfunction as a Marker of Cardiovascular Disease. 
CVD and ED share common risk factors, such as diabetes mellitus, 
obesity, hypertension, smoking, and dyslipidemia.6,7,119,122,125–127 
ED precedes the symptoms of coronary artery disease by 2 to 3 
years and major adverse cardiovascular events such as myocardial 
infarction or stroke by 3 to 5 years.126,127,139,140 Men reporting 
ED are 1.3 to 1.6 times more likely to experience a cardiovas­
cular event within 10 years than men without ED.126–128,139 ED 
in men is associated with increased risk of mortality, particularly 
death due to CVD.141,142 The presence of ED is a good predictor 
of subsequent coronary artery disease, especially in younger men, 
independent of traditional coronary risk factors, although it does 
not enhance the predictive ability of models that include tradi­
tional risk factors, likely reflecting the common pathophysiologic 
mechanisms of ED and coronary artery disease.127 
Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms and Erectile Dysfunction. 
There is strong epidemiologic evidence of the association of lower 
urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) and ED,143–150 even after adjust­
ing for age and other risk factors. The Cologne Male Study and the 
Multinational Study of the Aging Male revealed that the presence 
and severity of LUTS are stronger predictors of ED, independent 
of age, when compared with all other risk factors, including dia­
betes, dyslipidemia, and hypertension143,144; these findings have 
been corroborated by other studies.145,146,148,151–153 As LUTS and 
ED are two common conditions in middle-age and older men, it is 
possible that this association reflects the coexistence of two highly 
prevalent conditions. However, there is growing evidence that the 
two conditions may be mechanistically linked, as the biochemical 
mechanisms that regulate bladder detrusor and cavernosal smooth 
muscle function share many similarities.154,155 K+ channels, espe­
cially calcium-sensitive K+ channels (BKCa channels), Rho A/Rho 
kinase signaling, L-type calcium channels, and gap junctions, are 
important mediators of both detrusor and cavernosal smooth 
muscle contractility and relaxation.154 Increased myocyte con­
tractility that characterizes both bladder detrusor dysfunction and 
ED may be mechanistically related to increased Rho kinase activ­
ity,156–158 impairments of K+ channel function,41,154 α-adrenergic 
receptor imbalance, and endothelial dysfunction.159,160 Addi­
tional proposed hypotheses include increased sympathetic activity 
and autonomic dysfunction; alterations in nitric oxide generation; 
or protein kinase G activity in the detrusor and cavernosal smooth 
muscles.
An understanding of the strong association of ED and LUTS 
in older men is important for several reasons. First, some therapies 
for ED, such as PDE5 inhibitors, may also ameliorate LUTS and 
are approved for the treatment of this condition.161–166 Second, 
there may be interactions between drugs used in the treatment of 
ED (PDE5 inhibitors) and LUTS (α-adrenergic blockers), both 
of which may lower blood pressure. Third, some types of surgi­
cal procedures and steroid 5α-reductase inhibitors may worsen 
sexual dysfunction; prostatectomy for LUTS due to benign pros­
tatic hyperplasia is associated with an increased risk of ED, and 
α-adrenergic blockers used in the treatment of LUTS can cause 
ejaculatory problems. Fourth, ED and LUTS share some common 
risk factors that may need medical attention in addition to the 
treatment of each of these disorders. 
Ejaculatory Disorders
Ejaculatory disorders include premature ejaculation, delayed ejac­
ulation, retrograde ejaculation, anejaculation, and painful ejacu­
lation.57,109 Recent surveys have highlighted the high prevalence 
and clinical importance of ejaculatory disorders.143 In a multina­
tional survey, ejaculatory problems were reported by more than 
half the men, 60 years or older, who were able to achieve erec­
tions143; in this survey, the ejaculatory dysfunction was associated 
with “bother” in 50% to 59% of affected men, independent of 
age.143 Reduced amount of ejaculation and complete absence of 
ejaculate within the previous month were reported by 46% and 
5% of respondents, respectively.
Premature ejaculation, a common form of ejaculatory dysfunc­
tion, was defined by an Ad Hoc Committee of the International 
Society for Sexual Medicine as “a male sexual dysfunction char­
acterized by (1) ejaculation that always or nearly always occurs 
before or within about 1 minute of vaginal penetration from the 
first sexual experience (lifelong PE) or a clinically significant and 
bothersome reduction in latency time, often to about 3 minutes 
or less (acquired PE); (2) the inability to delay ejaculation on all 
or nearly all vaginal penetrations; and (3) negative personal con­
sequences, such as distress, bother, frustration, and/or the avoid­
ance of sexual intimacy.”167,168 Premature ejaculation adversely 
affects sexual satisfaction, interpersonal relationship, and quality 
of life. Premature ejaculation can be lifelong or acquired later in 
life.109,167,168
This definition of premature ejaculation was informed by 
a multinational survey that found that the median intravaginal 
ejaculation latency time (IELT) among men, 18 years or older, in 
stable heterosexual relationships, was 5.6 minutes (range, 0.55–
44.1 minutes).169,170 In this survey, 2.5% of men had an IELT of 
less than 1 minute and 6% less than 2 minutes. The vast majority 
of men seeking treatment for lifelong premature ejaculation ejac­
ulate within 1 minute after penetration, and nearly all ejaculate 
within 2 minutes.171 Compared with patients with lifelong pre­
mature ejaculation, the men with acquired premature ejaculation 
are older and have a longer IELT.167,168 The acquired premature 
ejaculation is often also associated with erectile dysfunction and 
other comorbid conditions such as diabetes and cardiovascular 
disease.169,171
Some men who seek treatment for premature ejaculation do 
not meet the definition established by the International Society 
for Sexual Medicine but express distress due to their perception 
of lack of control over the timing of ejaculation and the IELT to 
be shorter than they wish. Waldinger172 has proposed the terms 
subjective premature ejaculation (SPE) and variable premature ejac­
ulation (VPE) to describe these men whose IELT is greater than 
5 minutes but who are bothered by their perceived short ejacu­
latory latency or the lack of control over the timing of ejacula­
tion. Specific duration criteria for defining premature ejaculation 
among men engaged in nonvaginal sexual activities have not been 
established.
761
CHAPTER 18  Sexual Function and Dysfunction
The prevalence of premature ejaculation is not known; pre­
vious estimates of prevalence of 20% to 25% based on older 
definitions are likely inaccurate. Although there are no recent epi­
demiologic surveys based on the International Society of Sexual 
Medicine criteria or the DSM-5 definition of premature ejacula­
tion, Waldinger has inferred from the data on the distribution of 
IELT that the prevalence is likely less than 4%.170,172
The neurobiologic mechanisms of premature ejaculation are 
not well understood. 5-HT, oxytocin, and dopamine are involved 
as neurotransmitters in the neural pathways that control ejacula­
tion.173–175 In preclinical models, 5-HT delays ejaculation, and 
dopamine and oxytocin appear to stimulate ejaculation; these 
data have led to speculation that the men with lower ejaculatory 
thresholds may either have deficient 5-HT neurotransmission or 
5-HT 2C receptor hyposensitivity.61 The “serotonin hypothesis” 
is supported by data showing that SSRIs and the tricyclic anti­
depressant clomipramine increase ejaculatory control and delay 
ejaculation in men with premature ejaculation.61,176 The earlier 
theories that premature ejaculation is largely due to psychologi­
cal factors such as anxiety or sequelae of early life sexual experi­
ences have not been supported by recent data from clinical trials 
of pharmacologic agents. Genetic studies of the polymorphisms 
in the serotonin transporter protein (5-HTTLPR) gene, oxytocin, 
and vasopressin genes, and tandem repeats of the dopamine trans­
porter gene (DAT-1) have not yielded consistent association with 
premature ejaculation.177–181 One study reported that men with 
the 5-HTTLPR S/S genotype that is associated with lower 5-HT 
levels were more likely to report premature ejaculation than those 
with L/L or L/S genotype.177 Other studies have suggested that 
polymorphisms in genes associated with oxytocin and vasopres­
sin receptors may be associated with increased risk of premature 
ejaculation.181 
Delayed Ejaculation
DSM-5 defines delayed ejaculation as a marked involuntary delay 
in ejaculation or absence of ejaculation on almost all or all occasions 
of partnered sexual activity, persisting for at least 6 months and 
causing distress to the individual.108 A timing-based definition of 
delayed ejaculation has not been established. Because the median 
intravaginal ejaculatory latency in a multinational population-
based survey was 5.4 minutes and the 97.5th percentile value was 
23 minutes,170 some experts have suggested that intravaginal ejacu­
latory latency greater than 25 or 30 minutes should be considered 
delayed ejaculation.182
Mild to moderate delay in ejaculation occurs with advancing 
age; older men with comorbid conditions are at a higher risk of 
delayed ejaculation.183,184 Epidemiologic surveys have consis­
tently found LUTS to be strongly associated with delayed ejacula­
tion even after adjusting for age.153,184,185 Ejaculatory disorders 
are common after surgical treatment of benign prostatic hyper­
plasia including transurethral resection of the prostate.186 Many 
drugs—SSRIs, highly selective α1-adrenergic blockers, steroid 
5α-reductase inhibitors—can cause delayed ejaculation.187,188 
The use of highly selective α1-adrenergic blockers such as tamsu­
losin and silodosin can lead to marked delay or inability to ejacu­
late; ejaculatory dysfunction is less common with nonselective 
α-adrenergic blockers such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, and terazo­
sin.188 The use of steroid 5α-reductase inhibitors, finasteride and 
dutasteride, is associated with increased risk of ejaculatory disor­
der.188,189 SSRIs can prolong intravaginal ejaculatory latency and 
cause delayed ejaculation in some middle-age and older men.60,190 
Excessive exposure to pornography and sexual abuse may reduce 
sexual desire, impair arousal, and lead to ejaculatory dysfunc­
tion.191 Serum testosterone levels have not been consistently asso­
ciated with delayed ejaculation.192 
Retrograde Ejaculation
Retrograde ejaculation is the failure of the semen to be ejected out 
through the urethral meatus; instead the semen is propelled back­
ward into the urinary bladder.54,57,108,193 Retrograde ejaculation 
can be the result of autonomic neuropathy associated with diabe­
tes mellitus; sympathectomy; therapy with adrenergic antagonists, 
some types of antihypertensives, antipsychotics, or antidepres­
sants; bladder neck incompetence; or urethral obstruction.194–197 
Retrograde ejaculation due to diabetes-associated autonomic neu­
ropathy is the second most prevalent ejaculatory disorder.
Retrograde ejaculation is common after transurethral resection 
of the prostate that may result in damage to the bladder neck clo­
sure mechanism.198,199 Patients may remain continent because of 
a second, more distal, continence mechanism that is present in the 
region of the membranous urethra; however, many patients who 
have undergone transurethral resection of the prostate experience 
retrograde ejaculation. Ejaculatory disorders can lead to infertility 
among men.200,201 
Endocrine Disorders and Sexual Dysfunction in 
Men
Testosterone Deficiency Syndromes
Testosterone deficiency in men is a syndrome characterized by a 
constellation of signs and symptoms associated with consistently 
and unequivocally low testosterone levels due to disorders of the 
testes, pituitary, or hypothalamus.8,9,202 Testosterone deficiency 
can occur either because of primary testicular dysfunction or as 
a result of disorders affecting the hypothalamus or the pituitary.8 
Common causes of primary testicular dysfunction include Kline­
felter syndrome, uncorrected cryptorchidism, radiation and can­
cer chemotherapy, Yq microdeletions, human immunodeficiency 
virus (HIV) infection, orchitis, trauma, and torsion.8 Secondary 
testicular dysfunction can result from systemic illness; excessive 
exercise; recreational drugs, especially opiates, anabolic steroids, 
marijuana, cocaine, and alcohol; pituitary and suprasellar tumors; 
hemochromatosis; hyperprolactinemia; and infiltrative disorders. 
After exclusion of these identifiable secondary causes of hypogo­
nadism, the clinician may arrive at a diagnosis of idiopathic hypo­
gonadotropic hypogonadism, which is a heterogeneous group of 
disorders characterized by disordered GnRH secretion.8 Opioid 
use has emerged as an important cause of testosterone deficiency 
and sexual dysfunction.203 Similarly, in many men’s health clinics 
in the United States, a substantial proportion of men receiving tes­
tosterone replacement therapy are former anabolic steroid users.204 
The testosterone levels required to maintain sexual function in 
men are close to the lower limit of the normal male range.82,99,100 
Therefore, some men with pituitary tumors may remain asymp­
tomatic until their tumor has grown substantially and testosterone 
levels have declined to a level below this threshold.
Testosterone deficiency is an important treatable cause of 
MHSDD. Therefore, men diagnosed with MHSDD should be 
evaluated for testosterone deficiency by measurement of testos­
terone levels using a reliable assay, preferably in an early morning 
fasting blood sample.8 Although ED and testosterone deficiency in 
men are separate disorders with distinct pathophysiologic mecha­
nisms, the two can coexist in the same patient. Testosterone levels 
should be measured in men presenting with any form of sexual 
762
SECTION V    Sexual Development and Function
dysfunction because testosterone deficiency is treatable; further­
more, testosterone deficiency may be a manifestation of another 
underlying disease, such as a pituitary tumor, which may require 
additional evaluation and disease-specific intervention. 
Diabetes and Sexual Dysfunction in Men
Men with diabetes mellitus are at increased risk of ED, retrograde 
ejaculation, and low testosterone levels. Peyronie disease is an 
important comorbid condition in older men with diabetes and 
ED.205,206 Men with diabetes have increased rates of several cate­
gories of sexual dysfunctions; as a group, they have lower scores for 
sexual desire, activity, arousal, and satisfaction.207–211 Diabetes also 
is associated with increased risk of low testosterone levels.212,213 In 
population studies, sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG) and 
total testosterone are more strongly associated with diabetes risk 
than free testosterone levels; these data suggest that the observed 
association of testosterone with diabetes risk may be related to fac­
tors, such as obesity and inflammation that alter SHBG.214–216
The prevalence of ED in men with diabetes increases with 
age and has been reported to be as high as 75% in some studies. 
ED in men with type 2 diabetes even without other risk factors 
for coronary artery disease may signal silent cardiac ischemia.217 
Among men with diabetes, those with ED are more likely to be 
older and smokers, and to have a longer duration of diabetes, poor 
metabolic control, untreated hypertension, neuropathy, microal­
buminuria and macroalbuminuria, retinopathy, CVD, diuretic 
treatment, low testosterone levels, and psychological vulnerabil­
ity.129,209,218–220 The risk of ED generally increases with chronic 
elevation of hemoglobin A1C.209 Increased physical activity and 
consumption of small amounts of alcohol have been found to be 
associated with lower risk of ED.
Endothelial and smooth muscle dysfunction and autonomic 
neuropathy contribute to sexual dysfunction in men with diabe­
tes.221–223 Endothelial dysfunction is evident in penile blood ves­
sels as well as in nongenital vascular beds.221 eNOS is reduced, 
possibly due to overexpression of arginase or reduced nicotin­
amide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH), an essential 
cofactor for NOS.205,224–226 Additionally, accumulation of oxy­
gen free radicals, including those from advanced glycosylation end 
products (AGEs), quench nitric oxide and attenuate the action 
of K+ channels.227 Men with long duration of diabetes may not 
be able to generate sufficient nitric oxide and cGMP within the 
cavernosal smooth muscle, and consequently, they may become 
unresponsive to PDE5 inhibitors. The reduction in NADPH is 
also associated with increased diacylglycerol and protein kinase 
C, and consequently, increased smooth muscle contractility.226 
An increased activation of the Rho A/Rho kinase pathway may 
increase the sensitivity of cavernosal smooth muscle to calcium.226
Autonomic neuropathy affecting the pelvic nerves may lead to 
ED as well as ejaculatory dysfunction.223 Retrograde ejaculation and 
partial ejaculatory incompetence affect up to one third of men with 
diabetes.223 Autonomic neuropathy in diabetes may be associated 
with dysfunction of the internal sphincter so that all or a part of the 
seminal fluid is propelled into the bladder. Partial ejaculatory incom­
petence refers to the condition in which ejaculatory emission remains 
intact but the expulsion phase is inhibited; consequently, the semen 
trickles out of the penis, and the experience of orgasm is altered in 
quality. The ejaculatory problems may be a cause of infertility. 
Hyperprolactinemia and Sexual Dysfunction
Men with hyperprolactinemia often present with decreased libido 
or ED; 75% of men with macroprolactinomas and 50% of men 
with microprolactinomas report reduced sexual desire or ED, and 
almost all have subnormal nocturnal penile erections.228–230 Hyper­
prolactinemia affects 1% to 5% of men presenting with ED230; a 
fraction of these men have prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas.
Prolactin lowers testosterone levels through its inhibitory effects 
on GnRH secretion.231 Prolactin acts on the kisspeptin–neurokinin 
B–dynorphin (KNDy) neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypo­
thalamus to suppress kisspeptin 1 expression levels.232,233 Suppres­
sion of kisspeptin results in diminished GnRH and luteinizing 
hormone (LH) secretion. Prolactin infusion in female mice sup­
presses GnRH and Kiss1 mRNA expression, while kisspeptin admin­
istration restores normal LH secretion and ovarian function.234
Most, but not all, men with sexual dysfunction and hyperpro­
lactinemia have low testosterone levels.235,236 Whether and how 
hyperprolactinemia directly affects erectile function through tar­
get organ effects is not well understood. Erectile function gen­
erally improves in hyperprolactinemic men following treatment 
with dopamine agonists.237 
Sexual Dysfunction in Patients With Thyroid Disease
Thyroid hormones regulate the circulating levels of SHBG by 
increasing SHBG transcription; thyroxine and tri-iodothyronine 
stimulate the expression levels of hepatic nuclear factor 4α and 
reduce the cellular palmitate levels in the liver and thereby regulate 
SHBG expression.238 Mendelian randomization studies using the 
United Kingdom Biobank data have reported that genetic predis­
position to hypothyroidism is associated with lower SHBG and 
total testosterone levels and genetic predisposition to hyperthy­
roidism with higher SHBG and testosterone levels.239 A major­
ity of men with hypothyroidism report hypoactive sexual desire, 
ED, and delayed ejaculation,240,241 which are corrected in most 
patients after thyroid hormone replacement. Men with hypothy­
roidism typically have lower circulating levels of SHBG, total tes­
tosterone, and total estradiol concentrations, which return toward 
normal after thyroid hormone replacement.240,242 Free testoster­
one levels are lower in hypothyroid men than in control subjects 
and become normal after thyroxine replacement.240 Serum LH 
and follicle-stimulating hormone levels are typically not elevated 
in men with primary hypothyroidism.240 Hyperprolactinemia is 
noted in only a small proportion of hypothyroid men.240
The most striking feature of hyperthyroidism is the high preva­
lence of premature ejaculation and shortened ejaculation latency 
time, which is normalized after treatment of hyperthyroidism.240 
High prevalence of delayed ejaculation in hypothyroidism and 
premature ejaculation in hyperthyroidism and normalization of 
ejaculation latency times after normalization of the thyroid hor­
mone levels suggest that thyroid hormones regulate ejaculatory 
mechanisms.240 Free testosterone levels are typically normal in 
men with hyperthyroidism, but SHBG and free estradiol levels 
are elevated, resulting in a high free estradiol to free testosterone 
ratio and gynecomastia in some hyperthyroid men.243 
Sexual Dysfunction in Men With Metabolic Syndrome
Men with metabolic syndrome have a higher prevalence of endo­
thelial dysfunction and ED than men without metabolic syn­
drome.244–247 The risk of ED is correlated with the number of 
identified components of metabolic syndrome.248 
Sexual Dysfunction Associated With Therapies for Benign 
Prostatic Hypertrophy
α1-Adrenergic receptor blockers, such as tamsulosin, are associated 
with ejaculatory dysfunction.186–188 Treatment of men with LUTS

with 5α-reductase inhibitors has been associated with increased 
risk of ejaculatory disorder, ED, and decreased libido.188,189
Several surveys have reported the development of sexual symp­
toms, including loss of libido, ED, depressive symptoms and even 
suicidality, and cognitive symptoms in a subset of young men 
who have taken finasteride for alopecia.249–252 These symptoms 
have been reported to persist even after discontinuation of fin­
asteride, and this condition has been referred to as postfinaste­
ride syndrome.250,252 Investigations of men who developed sexual 
symptoms after using finasteride and whose symptoms persisted 
even after discontinuation of finasteride have revealed that these 
men do not have evidence of testosterone deficiency, decreased 
peripheral androgen action, or persistent peripheral inhibition 
of SRD5A.253 Symptomatic finasteride users revealed depressed 
mood and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) find­
ings consistent with those observed in men with depression.253 
The causal role of finasteride and the pathophysiology of these 
symptoms remain to be established.253,254 
Evaluation of Men With Sexual Dysfunction 
(Table 18.2 and Box 18.2)
An assessment of sexual function is an important part of the 
evaluation of patients with endocrine or cardiometabolic diseases. 
Open-ended, nonjudgmental questions such as, “How is your sex 
life?” or “Many men with diabetes or high blood pressure expe­
rience changes in their erections or ejaculation—are you having 
any difficulties?” can facilitate further discussion of sexual prob­
lems. When sexual problems are identified, sensitive and respect­
ful inquiry into their nature and the sexual context is necessary. 
The use of validated questionnaires such as the Erection Hardness 
Score, the Sexual Health Inventory for Men, or the short version 
of International Index of Erectile Function can facilitate a conver­
sation about ED.10,255,256 It is important to distinguish between 
inability to achieve erection, changes in sexual desire, failure to 
achieve orgasm and ejaculation, and dissatisfaction with the sexual 
relationship, as the etiologic factors vary with the type of sexual 
dysfunction.
In circumstances in which the patient is partnered, evaluating 
both partners together as well as individually can often uncover 
problems that may not be apparent in individual interviews. A 
detailed sexual history should elicit the nature of relationships, part­
ner expectations, situational erectile failure, performance anxiety, 
and relationship discord (see Table 18.2). The suggested approach 
to a sexual history provided in Table 18.2 can also be modified for 
unpartnered patients. Establish whether self-stimulation continues 
despite lack of desire for partnered sex. With the easy accessibility 
of Internet sites, sex alone, possibly on a frequent basis, may allow 
sexual expression in spite of relationship difficulties.
General health evaluation is necessary to exclude testosterone 
deficiency, systemic illness particularly cardiometabolic disorders, 
depression, and medication use (see Table 18.2 and Box 18.2).10,29 
The presence of diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, periph­
eral vascular disease, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, stroke, 
spinal cord or back injury, a neurologic disorder, depression, and 
dementia should be verified. Information about use of recre­
ational drugs such as alcohol, opioids, marijuana, cocaine, and 
tobacco; prescription medications, particularly antihypertensives, 
antiandrogens, antidepressants, antipsychotic drugs, and opioid 
analgesics; and nonprescription over-the-counter supplements is 
important because almost one fourth of all cases of impotence can 
be attributed to medications.
A directed physical examination should focus on secondary sex 
characteristics, the presence or absence of breast enlargement, and 
testicular volume; evaluation of femoral and pedal pulses; neu­
rologic examination to determine the presence of motor weak­
ness, perineal sensation, anal sphincter tone, and bulbocavernosus 
reflex; and examination of the penis to evaluate any unusual cur­
vature, palpable plaques, or superficial lesions.10,29

Erectile Dysfunction
764
SECTION V    Sexual Development and Function
The initial laboratory workup in most men presenting with ED 
usually includes the measurement of hemoglobin, blood glucose 
and hemoglobin A1C, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, plasma 
lipids, and serum total and free testosterone levels (see Box 18.2). 
Serum total and free testosterone levels should be measured in 
the morning after an overnight fast using a reliable assay such as 
the liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry assay to 
exclude testosterone deficiency because testosterone deficiency 
is an important treatable cause of MHSDD and is observed fre­
quently in men with ED.
Further evaluation using more invasive diagnostic testing is 
limited to those men who do not respond to an empiric trial of 
oral PDE5 inhibitors; these patients should be referred to a spe­
cialist for detailed urologic evaluation.
The diagnosis of testosterone deficiency should be made only 
in men with consistent symptoms and signs and unequivocally 
low early morning serum testosterone levels that are consistently 
below the lower limit of the normal range for healthy young men.8 
Because of the diurnal, pulsatile, and interday variations in cir­
culating testosterone levels, and the known suppressive effects of 
food and glucose intake, total testosterone concentrations should 
be measured in a fasting state on two separate mornings. Serum 
testosterone levels should be measured using a reliable assay, such 
as liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/
MS) assays, which have become widely available from many 
commercial and research laboratories. Ideally, testosterone levels 
should be measured using an assay that has been certified by an 
accuracy-based standardization or quality control program (e.g., 
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC] Hormone 
Standardization Program for Testosterone [HoST]).257 The advent 
of LC-MS/MS, the availability of a testosterone calibrator from 
the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), and 
the institution of HoST have greatly improved the accuracy of 
testosterone assays and reduced interlaboratory variability among 
CDC-certified laboratories.257–259
The reference ranges for testosterone in men reported by vari­
ous laboratories vary substantially because of assay differences, 
calibrator differences, and differences in the reference popula­
tions used to generate ranges. Recently, under the auspices of the 
Endocrine Society and the Partnership for the Accurate Testing of 
Hormones, we have published harmonized reference range based 
on data from community-dwelling men from four large cohorts in 
the United States and Europe.259 The harmonized reference range 
for total testosterone in healthy, nonobese young men (age 19–39 
years) was 264 to 916 ng/dL (9.2–31.8 nmol/L).259 This reference 
range can be applied to all CDC-certified total testosterone assays.
Circulating testosterone is bound with high affinity to SHBG 
and with lower affinity to albumin, orosomucoid, and cortisol 
binding globulin; only 2% to 4% of circulating testosterone is 
unbound or free.260 The alterations in SHBG concentrations can 
alter the total testosterone concentrations; therefore, in conditions 
that alter SHBG concentrations, such as obesity, diabetes, aging, 
liver disease, hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, and intake 
of many medications, determination of free testosterone levels is 
necessary to assess androgen status.260 Testosterone’s binding to 
SHBG is a dynamic multistep process that includes heterogeneity 
in circulating isoforms of SHBG dimer, an allosteric interaction 
between the two binding sites on SHBG such that the conforma­
tion or the energetic substates of the two monomers of SHBG 
are not equivalent.261,262 The free testosterone levels computed 
using this dynamic multistep binding with allostery match closely 
the values measured directly by equilibrium dialysis.261 Free 
testosterone concentrations can be measured using the equilib­
rium dialysis assays or calculated from total testosterone, SHBG, 
and albumin concentrations.8,263 The direct tracer analogue free 
testosterone assays are used in many hospital laboratories, but they 
are inaccurate and should not be used.
In men found to be androgen deficient, measurement of LH 
levels helps distinguish between testicular (LH elevated) and 
hypothalamic-pituitary (LH low or inappropriately normal) 
defects.8 Men with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism may require 
measurement of serum prolactin, serum iron, and total iron-
binding capacity; evaluation of other pituitary hormones; and a 
pituitary MRI.
There is considerable debate about the usefulness and cost-
effectiveness of hormonal evaluation and the extent to which 
testosterone deficiency should be investigated in middle-age and 
older men presenting with ED. Only a small fraction of men with 
ED and low testosterone levels have been found to have space-
occupying lesions of the hypothalamic-pituitary region.230,235 The 
diagnostic yield of pituitary imaging to exclude pituitary tumor 
can be improved by limiting these procedures to men whose total 
testosterone level is less than 150 ng/dL or who have panhypopi­
tuitarism, persistent hyperprolactinemia, or symptoms of tumor 
mass.8
If the history, physical examination, and laboratory tests do not 
identify medical problems needing further workup, then a cost-
effective approach is to prescribe a trial of oral PDE5 inhibitor 
provided there are no contraindications (e.g., nitrate use).
Nocturnal penile tumescence recording and more specialized 
tests that evaluate the integrity of penile vasculature and blood 
flow such as ICI, penile duplex ultrasound, cavernosometry, and 
selective internal pudendal angiography264,265 are not needed in 
most patients with ED. These tests are reserved for patients with 
complex medical histories in whom the results of these tests would 
alter the management or prognosis, and they should be performed 
only by those with considerable experience with their use. For 
instance, angiography could be useful in a young man with arterial 
insufficiency associated with pelvic trauma. Similarly, suspicion 
of congenital or traumatic venous leak in a young man present­
ing with ED would justify a cavernosography. In each instance, 
confirmation of the vascular lesion might lead to consideration of 
surgery. The penile-brachial blood pressure index is a simple and 
specific, but not a sensitive, index of vascular insufficiency. It is 
rarely used today in the evaluation of ED.
Nocturnal penile tumescence testing is rarely needed for 
patients being evaluated for ED and is recommended only for a 
limited number of patients with a high clinical suspicion of psy­
chogenic ED or situational problems, to document preoperatively 
poor penile rigidity, or for medical-legal reasons. For most cases, 
a careful history of nighttime or early morning erections provides 
a reasonable correlation with nocturnal penile tumescence and 
RigiScan studies.266 
Treatment of Sexual Dysfunction in Men
Treatment of Hypoactive Sexual Desire in Men
There is need to focus on the couple when the patient has a sex­
ual partner. Treating the sexual dysfunction in the male partner 
improves the female partner’s sexual function and satisfaction. 
Comorbid depression should be treated and relationship difficul­
ties addressed. The efficacy of cognitive and behavioral therapies 
has not been evaluated systematically in men with MHSDD. 
765
CHAPTER 18  Sexual Function and Dysfunction
Testosterone therapy should be considered in men with HSDD 
who have testosterone deficiency.
There are no randomized trials of testosterone in men with 
MHSDD, and much of the information about the effects of tes­
tosterone on sexual desire has emerged from open-label trials of 
testosterone in hypogonadal men and a small number of random­
ized placebo-controlled trials of testosterone in hypogonadal men. 
Most testosterone trials recruited men based on the presence of 
low testosterone levels alone, while a small number of recent tri­
als required men to have low testosterone levels and one or more 
symptoms of testosterone deficiency. Testosterone therapy in these 
trials has been associated with significant improvements in over­
all sexual activity, sexual desire, attention to erotic cues, and the 
duration and frequency of nocturnal penile erections.67,68,88,93,94 
In the Testosterone Trials, testosterone treatment of men with tes­
tosterone deficiency and low libido improved their sexual desire 
and overall sexual activity more than placebo.88,267 Testosterone 
treatment improved most categories of sexual activity.88 The over­
all improvements in sexual desire and erectile function were mod­
est but were deemed clinically meaningful.88 A meta-analysis of 
placebo-controlled, randomized testosterone trials in hypogonadal 
men, who met the Endocrine Society’s definition of testosterone 
deficiency, confirmed that compared with placebo administration, 
testosterone treatment is associated with greater improvements 
in sexual activity, sexual desire, erectile function, and satisfaction 
with sexual experience.92
Several points should be considered when initiating testosterone 
replacement therapy. First, testosterone treatment has been shown 
to improve some but not all domains of sexual function; testoster­
one improves sexual desire and erections but has not been shown 
to improve ejaculatory disorder. Second, testosterone treatment 
has been shown to be efficacious in improving sexual function 
only in men with unequivocally low testosterone levels and low 
sexual desire; it has not been shown to improve sexual function in 
men who have normal or low-normal testosterone levels.95 Third, 
there is enormous variability in on-treatment testosterone levels, 
especially with transdermal testosterone gels; a substantial fraction 
of hypogonadal men started on the initial dose of a transdermal 
testosterone gel will not raise their on-treatment levels into the tar­
get therapeutic range, and 5% to 10% may have supraphysiologic 
levels due to substantial variations in transdermal absorption and 
plasma clearance of testosterone.268 Unsurprisingly, nearly half of 
testosterone-treated men discontinue testosterone treatment after 
3 months, and only about 25% are still on testosterone treatment 
after 12 months269; therefore, monitoring of on-treatment levels 
and dose titration are necessary to maintain testosterone levels 
in the therapeutic range. Fourth, some men with MHSDD may 
have relationship problems, which are not likely to be corrected by 
testosterone therapy. Finally, the long-term safety and efficacy of 
testosterone therapy has not been established.8 
Treatment of Erectile Dysfunction
The standard of practice today is a stepwise approach that first 
utilizes minimally invasive therapies that are easy to use and have 
fewer adverse effects and progresses to more invasive therapies that 
may require injections or surgical intervention after the first-line 
choices have been exhausted (Fig. 18.8). The physician should dis­
cuss the risks, benefits, and alternatives of all therapies with the 
couple. The selection of the therapeutic modality should be based 
on the underlying cause, patient preference, gender role and sex­
ual practices, the nature and strength of the patient’s relationship 
with their sexual partner, and the absence or presence of underly­
ing CVD and other comorbid conditions. All patients with ED 
can benefit from psychosexual counseling.10
In the execution of good medical practice, treatment of all 
associated medical disorders should be optimized. In men with 
diabetes mellitus, glycemic control should be optimized, although 
improving glycemic control may not improve sexual function. 
In men with hypertension, control of blood pressure should be 
optimized and, if possible, the therapeutic regimen may be modi­
fied to remove antihypertensive drugs that impair sexual function. 
This strategy is not always feasible, because almost all antihyper­
tensive agents have been associated with sexual dysfunction; the 
frequency of this adverse event is less with angiotensin-converting 
enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin-receptor blockers than with 
other agents.
First-Line Therapies
Psychosexual Counseling. The goals of psychosexual therapy 
are to reduce performance anxiety, develop the patient’s sexual 
skills and knowledge, modify negative sexual attitudes, improve 
communication between partners, and identify mental health dis­
orders such as major depressive disorder that may require a mental 
health consultation or separate pharmacotherapy270 (Box 18.3). 
Counseling and psychotherapy are beneficial in both psychogenic 
and organic causes of sexual dysfunction.271–273
Some individuals may focus on their sexual performance dur­
ing sexual activity rather than being fully present to enjoy the 
erotic experience270; this behavior, referred to as spectatoring, can 
contribute to anxiety and lack of pleasure, and impair erection. 
Many experts recommend a sensate focus treatment approach in 
which the couple avoids intercourse and engages in nongenital, 
nondemanding, pleasure-seeking exercises to reduce performance 
anxiety.270,274
Involving the partner in the counseling process helps to dispel 
misperceptions about the problem, decreases stress, enhances inti­
macy and the ability to talk about sex, and increases the chances 
of successful outcome.274 Counseling sessions are also helpful 
in uncovering conflicts in relationships, psychiatric problems, 
alcohol and drug abuse, and sometimes significant mispercep­
tions about sex. As many men with ED and their partners may 
harbor misinformation and unrealistic expectations about sexual 
performance and age-related changes in sexual function, cognitive 
restructuring techniques are helpful in correcting sexual myths 
and beliefs.270,274 There is a paucity of randomized trials on the 
effectiveness of psychobehavioral therapies, but meta-analyses 
have reported benefit from group psychotherapy administered in 
conjunction with PDE5 inhibitors.271 
Selective Phosphodiesterase-5 Inhibitors (Table 18.3 and 
Box 18.4). Selective PDE5 inhibitors are safe and effective and 
have become widely accepted as first-line therapy for patients 
with ED, except in men for whom these drugs are contraindi­
cated.10,275 Selective PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated in men 
using nitrates on a regular basis, in those with severe heart disease 
in whom sexual activity may not be safe, and in those with nonar­
teritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy.10,275
Mechanisms of Action. Four classes of enzymes—NOS, adeny­
lyl cyclase, guanylyl cyclase, and phosphodiesterases (PDEs)—play 
important roles in regulating the intracavernosal concentrations of 
cAMP and cGMP. Three isoforms of NOS catalyze the formation 
of nitric oxide from arginine using NADPH and oxygen as sub­
strates: neuronal NOS (nNOS or NOS1), inducible NOS (iNOS 
or NOS2), and endothelial NOS (eNOS or NOS3). Nitric oxide 
766
SECTION V    Sexual Development and Function
activates soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) to stimulate the produc­
tion of cGMP from GTP, which then activates cGMP-dependent 
protein kinases to induce myosin phosphatase, inositol 1,4,5-tri­
sphosphate receptor 1–associated protein, and some cation chan­
nels resulting in smooth muscle relaxation. PDEs hydrolyze cGMP, 
thus reducing its concentrations within the cavernosal smooth 
muscle.42,276 Although PDE isoforms 2, 3, 4, and 5 are expressed 
in the penis, only PDE5 is specific to the nitric oxide–cGMP 
pathway in the corpora cavernosa.45,277 PDE inhibitors sildenafil, 
vardenafil, tadalafil, avanafil, and udenafil are relatively selective 
inhibitors of PDE5. These drugs block the hydrolysis of cGMP, 
thus promoting cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation. The action 
of these drugs requires an intact nitric oxide response, as well as 
constitutive synthesis of cGMP by the smooth muscle cells of the 
corpora cavernosa. By selectively inhibiting cGMP catabolism in 
the cavernosal smooth muscle cells, PDE5 inhibitors restore the 
natural erectile response to sexual stimulation but do not produce 
an erection in the absence of sexual stimulation. 
Clinical Pharmacology of Selective Phosphodiesterase-5 
Inhibitors (see Table 18.3). Although the four currently available 
PDE5 inhibitors have some structural similarities, they differ in 
their selectivity and pharmacokinetics (see Table 18.3). The com­
mon adverse effects of the available PDE5 inhibitors—headache, 
visual problems, flush, and myalgias—are related to nonselective 
inhibition of PDE isoforms 6 and 11 in other organ systems45 (see 
Table 18.3). The selectivity of a PDE5 inhibitor is the ratio of its 
inhibitory potency for PDE isoforms other than type 5 relative to 
its inhibitory potency for PDE isoform 5.45 For PDE6, tadalafil is 
the most selective and sildenafil is the least selective; for PDE11, 
vardenafil is the most selective and tadalafil is the least selective.45

The retinal side effects of sildenafil are related to inhibition of 
PDE6 in the retina, whereas muscle aches experienced by a small 
fraction of men using tadalafil are related to inhibition of PDE11 
in the skeletal muscle.45
After oral administration of sildenafil, peak plasma concen­
trations are achieved within 30 to 120 minutes, after which 
plasma concentrations decline, with a half-life of 4 hours (see 
Table 18.3).44,278–281 Vardenafil achieves peak concentrations 
within 0.7 to 0.9 hour and has a half-life of 4 to 5 hours. The 
peak concentrations of tadalafil are achieved at 2 hours, and 
its half-life of 16.9 hours in young men is significantly longer 
than the half-lives of sildenafil and vardenafil. The half-life of 
tadalafil is even longer in older men (21.6 hours) than in young 
men (16.9 hours). Because of the relatively short half-lives of 
vardenafil and sildenafil, these drugs should be taken 1 to 4 
hours before the planned intercourse; in contrast, tadalafil, 
because of its longer half-life, does not have to be taken on 
demand, although it can be.279,282 The second-generation 
PDE5 inhibitors avanafil and udenafil have a more rapid onset 
of action than the first-generation PDE5 inhibitors sildenafil, 
vardenafil, and tadalafil.283–285
Food, particularly a high-fat meal and large amounts of alcohol, 
can delay and decrease the absorption of sildenafil.281 However, 
pharmacokinetic studies have not reported changes in maximum 
serum concentrations or absorption rates of vardenafil or tadalafil 
due to food or moderate alcohol ingestion.286,287 
Efficacy. The orally active, selective PDE5 inhibitors—silde­
nafil, vardenafil, avanafil, udenafil, and tadalafil—have each been 
shown to be highly effective and safe in randomized clinical tri­
als of men with ED.288 Introduced to the U.S. market in March 
1998, sildenafil citrate (Viagra, Pfizer, New York, NY) was the first 
effective oral agent for the treatment of ED. The efficacy of silde­
nafil has been demonstrated in men with organic, psychogenic, or 
mixed ED in multiple RCTs and confirmed by meta-analyses of 
randomized trials. In these trials, patients receiving sildenafil expe­
rienced greater increments in the number of successful attempts 
per month, penile rigidity, frequency of vaginal penetration, and 
maintenance of erection than those receiving placebo. Increasing 
doses of sildenafil were associated with higher mean scores for the 
frequency of penetration and maintenance of erections after sexual 
penetration. The mean scores for orgasms, intercourse satisfaction, 
and overall satisfaction were also significantly higher in the silde­
nafil group than in the placebo group. Sildenafil also is effective in 
treating ED in men with diabetes mellitus.288–290
In the vardenafil efficacy trials, 5-, 10-, and 20-mg doses of var­
denafil were all superior to placebo in improving erectile function 
domain scores; the improvements in erectile function scores were 
dose related. Vardenafil improved rates of vaginal penetration, 
penile rigidity, intercourse success, and satisfaction with sexual 
experience in men with ED from diverse causes.
Similarly, in randomized clinical trials, 2.5-, 5-, 10-, and 20-mg 
doses of tadalafil were each superior to placebo in improving
