Avanafil has a very rapid onset of action because of its rapid 
absorption, which allows it to reach maximum circulating con­
centration in about 30 to 45 minutes. Therefore, a majority of 
patients taking avanafil are able to engage in sexual activity within 
15 minutes. Udenafil also has a relatively rapid onset of action, 
with a time to maximum serum concentrations of 1.0 to 1.5 
hours. It has been approved in some other countries such as Korea, 
Russia, and the Philippines, but not in the United States.
In men treated with oral, selective PDE5 inhibitors, the rates 
of successful intercourse vary from 50% to 65%, and rates of 
improved erections vary from 70% to 75%. The selective PDE5 
inhibitors are effective in men of all ethnic groups and ages who 
have ED due to a multitude of causes, although response rates 
vary in different patient subgroups. In general, baseline sexual 
function correlates positively with response to PDE5 inhibitors, 
and patients with diabetes mellitus or previous prostate surgery 
respond less well than patients with psychogenic or vasculogenic 
ED. Because there is no baseline characteristic that predicts the 
likelihood of failure to respond to sildenafil therapy, a therapeu­
tic trial of PDE5 inhibitors should be tried in all patients except 
in those in whom it is contraindicated. The guidelines for opti­
mizing the therapeutic use of PDE5 inhibitors are provided in 
Box 18.4. 
Adverse Effects of Phosphodiesterase-5 Inhibitors (Box 18.5). 
In clinical trials, the adverse effects that have been reported with 
greater frequency in men treated with PDE5 inhibitors than in 
those treated with placebo include headaches, flushing, rhini­
tis, dyspepsia, muscle aches, and visual disturbances.291,292 The 
occurrence of headache, flushing, and rhinitis, a direct conse­
quence of nonselective PDE5 inhibition in other organ systems, 
is related to the administered dose. These drugs do not affect 
semen characteristics. No cases of priapism were noted in the 
pivotal clinical trials.
Several cases of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy 
have been reported after ingestion of oral PDE5 inhibitor use.293 
This condition is characterized by the sudden onset of monocu­
lar visual loss due to acute ischemia of the anterior portion of 
the optic nerve in the absence of demonstrable arteritis. This may 
progress to partial or complete infarction of the optic nerve head 
resulting in permanent visual loss or visual field cuts.294 Although 
a cause-and-effect relationship with PDE5 inhibitor use has not 
been established, patients with history of sudden visual loss should 
not be treated with PDE5 inhibitors without ophthalmologic 
evaluation.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has noted sev­
eral reports of sudden hearing loss with and without vestibular 
symptoms, such as tinnitus, vertigo, or dizziness, in temporal rela­
tionship to administration of sildenafil, vardenafil, and tadalafil 
in postmarketing surveillance. Hearing loss was also reported in a 
few patients in clinical trials of these drugs.295,296 Hearing loss has 
been noted in patients using sildenafil for the treatment of pul­
monary arterial hypertension. Although a causal relationship has 
not been established, the temporal relationship between the use of 
PDE5 inhibitors and the onset of sudden hearing loss prompted 
the FDA to recommend changes in the product labeling for the 
drug class. A few observational studies have reported an associa­
tion of PDE5 inhibitor use with an increased risk of melanoma

Cardiovascular and Hemodynamic Effects. In postmarket­
ing surveillance of adverse events associated with sildenafil use, 
several instances of myocardial infarction and sudden death were 
reported in men using sildenafil in temporal relation to the inges­
tion of the drug299; many of these deaths occurred in individuals 
who also were taking nitrates. Because most men presenting with 
ED also have high prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors, it is 
unclear whether these events were causally related to the inges­
tion of sildenafil, underlying heart disease, or both.299 In con­
trolled studies,300,301 oral administration of 100 mg of sildenafil 
to men with severe coronary artery disease produced only a small 
decrease in systemic blood pressure and no significant changes 
in cardiac output, heart rate, coronary blood flow, and coronary 
artery diameter. In a separate pooled analysis of five randomized, 
placebo-controlled trials of vardenafil,302 the overall frequency of 
cardiovascular events was similar in vardenafil-treated men and 
placebo-treated men. However, vardenafil treatment was associ­
ated with a mild reduction in blood pressure (4.6 mm Hg decrease 
in systolic blood pressure) and a small increase in heart rate (2 
beats per minute).303 This led the American Heart Association 
and other experts to conclude that preexistent coronary artery dis­
ease by itself does not constitute a contraindication for the use of 
PDE5 inhibitors (Box 18.6).264,304–306 
Drug-Drug Interactions. Sildenafil is metabolized mostly by 
the CYP2C9 and the CYP3A4 pathways. Cimetidine and erythro­
mycin, inhibitors of CYP3A4, increase the plasma concentrations 
of sildenafil. HIV protease inhibitors may also alter the activity of 
the CYP3A4 pathway and affect the clearance of sildenafil.307,308 
Conversely, sildenafil could potentially affect the metabolism of 
warfarin and tolbutamide. Combined administration of silde­
nafil and ritonavir results in significantly higher plasma levels of 
sildenafil than sildenafil given alone.308 There are similar inter­
actions with other drugs, including saquinavir and itraconazole. 
Therefore, the doses of PDE5 inhibitors should be reduced appro­
priately in men taking protease inhibitors or erythromycin.
Grapefruit juice can alter oral drug pharmacokinetics by differ­
ent mechanisms. Grapefruit juice given in normal amounts (e.g., 
200–300 mL) or as whole fresh fruit segments can irreversibly 
inactivate intestinal CYP3A4, thus reducing presystemic metab­
olism and increasing oral bioavailability of PDE5 inhibitors.309 
Although the magnitude of this problem in clinical practice is 
unknown, it seems prudent to warn men who are contemplat­
ing the use of PDE5 inhibitors not to ingest more than a small 
amount of grapefruit juice.
The most serious interactions of PDE5 inhibitors are with the 
nitrates and other vasodilators. The vasodilator effects of nitrates 
are augmented by PDE5 inhibitors; this also applies to inhaled 
forms of nitrates such as amyl nitrate or nitrites that are sold 
under the street name “poppers.” Concomitant administration of 
the two vasodilator drugs can cause a potentially fatal decrease in 
blood pressure.
PDE inhibitors should be used carefully in men taking 
α-adrenergic blockers. In men with congestive heart failure or 
those receiving vasodilator drugs or those who are using com­
plex regimens of antihypertensive drugs, blood pressure should 
be monitored after initial administration of PDE5 inhibitors (see 
Box 18.6).310,311 Several trials have demonstrated the safety of 
administering PDE5 inhibitors in combination with α-adrenergic 
blockers in men with ED and LUTS.310,311 
Therapeutic Regimens. Before initiating a specific pharma­
cologic or surgical therapeutic option for the treatment of ED, 
several points should be considered. First, men with ED are at 
increased risk for cardiometabolic disorders such as type 2 diabetes 
and coronary artery disease. Therefore, baseline evaluation should 
include general health evaluation and screening for diabetes and 
cardiovascular risk. Additionally, patients should be counseled for 
lifestyle modification to improve overall health and reduce cardio­
metabolic risk. Second, all men with ED can benefit from psycho­
sexual counseling. In the vast majority of patients, the counseling 
can be provided effectively by the primary care physician and 
referral to a mental health specialist is needed only if there is an 
underlying psychiatric disorder such as major depression. Third, 
PDE5 inhibitors are the first-line therapy for ED. The men who 
are prescribed PDE5 inhibitors should be counseled on their 
appropriate use guided by their clinical pharmacology because a 
substantial proportion of apparent nonresponses to PDE5 inhibi­
tors are due to inappropriate use. Fourth, due to the substantial 
variation in metabolism of PDE5 inhibitors among men, the dose 
should be titrated to the maximum tolerated dose to maximize 
efficacy while avoiding dose-related adverse effects. Fifth, many 
men with ED will have underlying CVD or LUTS, and the drugs 
used in the treatment of these disorders may have interactions 
with PDE5 inhibitors. These drug-drug interactions with other 
concomitant medications should be considered before prescribing 
PDE5 inhibitors.
In most men with ED, sildenafil is started at an initial dose 
of 50 mg. If this dose is not effective but does not produce any 
adverse effects, the dose should be titrated up to 100 mg or the 
maximum tolerated dose.10,275 The dose adjustment should be 
guided by the therapeutic response to therapy and occurrence of 
adverse effects. Vardenafil should be started at an initial dose of 
10 mg; the dose should be increased to 20 mg or maximal toler­
ated dose or decreased to 5 mg depending on the clinical response

	2.	 If the patient has stable coronary artery disease, is not taking long-

initial dose of 10 mg, with further adjustment of dose based on 
effectiveness and side effects. Tadalafil need not be taken more 
frequently than once every 48 hours. Avanafil should be started 
at an initial dose of 50 or 100 mg with further adjustment up to

Sildenafil and vardenafil are taken at least 1 to 2 hours hour 
before sexual intercourse and not more than once in any 24-hour 
period; because of its longer half-life, tadalafil need not be taken 
immediately before intercourse. Avanafil is taken 30 minutes 
before sexual intercourse.
Based on the results of randomized clinical trials,164,312,313 the 
FDA has approved 2.5 mg or 5 mg tadalafil once daily for the 
treatment of ED. In the pivotal trials, men using 2.5 mg or 5 mg 
tadalafil once daily experienced greater improvements in erectile 
function compared with those taking a placebo.164,312,313 Subse­
quent open-label extension studies indicated that once-daily 5 mg 
tadalafil for up to 2 years was effective in maintaining improve­
ments in erectile function. The adverse events associated with 
once-daily administration of tadalafil included headaches, indiges­
tion, back pain, muscle aches, nasal congestion, and flushing and 
were similar to those observed with on-demand tadalafil ingestion. 
The Use of Phosphodiesterase-5 Inhibitors in Men With 
Coronary Artery Disease. Excellent therapeutic guidelines have 
been published on this topic by expert panels from several societ­
ies.275,304,314–316 To minimize the risk of hypotension and adverse 
cardiovascular events during the use of PDE5 inhibitors, the 
American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology has 
published a list of recommendations (see Box 18.6), which should 
be followed rigorously.275
Before prescribing PDE5 inhibitors, cardiovascular risk fac­
tors should be assessed. If the patient has hypertension or symp­
tomatic coronary artery disease, the treatment of those clinical 
disorders should be addressed first.275 The use of nitrates must 
be ascertained, because PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated in 
individuals taking any form of nitrates regularly. PDE5 inhibitors 
should not be used within 24 hours of the use of nitrates or nitrate 
donors.29,275
Sexual activity can potentially induce coronary ischemia in 
men with preexisting coronary artery disease316; therefore, men 
contemplating use of ED therapies should undergo assessment of 
their exercise tolerance. In general, if the patient can safely climb 
one or two flights of stairs without angina or excessive shortness 
of breath, he can likely engage in sexual intercourse with a stable 
partner without inducing similar symptoms. Exercise testing may 
be indicated in some men with significant heart disease to assess 
the risk of inducing cardiac ischemia during sexual activity.304 
Selective PDE5 inhibitors have been shown not to impair the abil­
ity of patients with stable coronary artery disease to engage in exer­
cise at levels equivalent to that attained during sexual intercourse. 
Similarly, each of the three PDE5 inhibitors has been shown not 
to have significant adverse effects on hemodynamics and cardiac 
events in carefully selected men with ED who did not have any 
contraindication for the use of PDE5 inhibitors.301,303 None of 
the PDE5 inhibitors adversely affects total exercise time or time to 
ischemia during exercise testing in men with stable angina.301–303 
In one analysis, treatment with PDE5 inhibitors for ED after a 
first myocardial infarction was associated with a reduced mortal­
ity and hospitalization for heart failure.317 Another cohort study 
also reported reduced rates of myocardial infarction or other CVD 
events during the first 3 years after initiation of treatment with a 
PDE5 inhibitor for ED.318 
Treatment of Patients Who Do Not Respond to Phosphodi­
esterase-5 Inhibitors. Although oral PDE5 inhibitor therapy has 
revolutionized the management of ED, not all men respond to 
this treatment. The cumulative probability of intercourse suc­
cess with sildenafil citrate increases with the number of attempts, 
reaching a maximum after eight attempts319; based largely on 
these data, the failure to respond to PDE inhibitor therapy has 
been defined as the failure to achieve satisfactory response even 
after eight attempts of either the highest approved dose (e.g., 
100 mg sildenafil) or the highest tolerable dose of PDE5 inhibi­
tor, whichever is lower. Many factors may contribute to appar­
ent treatment failure, including failure to take the medication as 
recommended, suboptimal dose, dose-limiting adverse effects, 
absence of sexual stimulation, psychological issues, partner and 
relationship issues, incorrect diagnosis, and patient-specific patho­
physiologic factors.319–321 In clinical trials of PDE5 inhibitors, 
treatment failures were reported predominantly in men who had 
diabetes mellitus, non–nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy, caver­
nosal nerve damage, venous leak, and high disease severity.319–321 
In an evaluation of cavernosal smooth muscle biopsies in sildenafil 
nonresponders, Wespes et al321 found severe vascular lesions and 
cavernosal smooth muscle atrophy and fibrosis to be the underly­
ing pathologic processes.
Patients may not take the medication appropriately because 
of inadequate instructions, failure to understand the instructions, 
adverse effects, or fear of adverse effects.319,320 Oral PDE5 inhibi­
tors are taken optimally 1 to 2 hours before planned intercourse. 
The medication is unlikely to be effective if it is taken immediately 
before intercourse; a high-fat meal and large amounts of alcohol 
may further affect the maximal serum concentrations of silde­
nafil citrate. Similarly, patients may not take the appropriate dose 
because of side effects or fear of side effects. The men who have been 
misdiagnosed as having ED and whose primary sexual dysfunction 
is unresponsive to PDE5 inhibitors may be incorrectly deemed 
treatment failures. For instance, men with MHSDD, Peyronie dis­
ease, or orgasmic or ejaculatory disorder would not be expected to 
respond to PDE5 inhibitors. The anxiety associated with resump­
tion of sexual activity and unresolved relationship and partner issues 
can attenuate response to treatment. The sexual partner may not be 
willing or able to engage in sexual activity because of relationship 
issues, sexual dysfunction, or real or perceived health issues. Because 
erotic stimulation is necessary for local production of nitric oxide, 
which then stimulates the production of cGMP, PDE5 inhibitors 
do not induce spontaneous erections and may not be effective in 
inducing erections in the absence of sexual stimulation.
Patients who report lack of satisfactory response to initial 
administration of PDE5 inhibitors should be asked about the 
time of drug administration, the dose taken, and adverse effects 
experienced. Psychological and partner issues should be evaluated. 
The dose of PDE5 inhibitor should be increased gradually as tol­
erated. Some men who do not optimally respond to on-demand 
PDE5 inhibitors may respond to daily low-dose tadalafil (2.5 or 
5 mg), which is an FDA-approved regimen.322,323 Should the 
patient not respond to maximal tolerable doses of PDE5 inhibi­
tors, PDE5 inhibitors can be combined with vacuum devices or 
intraurethral therapy. Second-line therapies such as intracaverno­
sal injections should be pursued. Men who are unresponsive to 
oral PDE5 inhibitors and second-line therapies may find penile 
implant an acceptable alternative.319

Cost-Effectiveness of Phosphodiesterase-5 Inhibitor Use for 
Erectile Disorder. Cost-effectiveness analyses have shown that that 
the financial burden imposed by patients with ED on managed care 
plans is surprisingly small.324–326 Among the various therapeutic 
options for the treatment of ED, PDE5 inhibitors and vacuum 
constriction devices are the most cost-effective. In one cost-utility 
analysis, the monthly cost of providing ED-related treatment ser­
vices in a health plan with 100,000 members amounted to less 
than $0.10 per member.325 The cost-effectiveness of PDE5 inhibi­
tor therapy compares favorably with other accepted medical thera­
pies. Thus, the failure of many insurance companies to cover the 
cost of PDE5 inhibitor therapy is not informed by cost-utility 
analyses. 
Second-Line Therapies
Vacuum Devices for Inducing Erection. The vacuum devices 
typically consist of an acrylic cylinder, a vacuum pump, and an 
elastic constriction band.327–329 The negative pressure created by 
the vacuum within the cylinder draws blood into the penis, pro­
ducing an erection. An elastic band slipped around the base of 
the penis traps the blood in the penis, maintaining an erection as 
long as the rubber band is retained. The constriction band should 
not be left in place for more than 30 minutes. Also, only vacuum 
devices with a pressure-limiting mechanism should be recom­
mended to prevent injury due to high vacuum.
Limited data on the efficacy of vacuum devices from open-label 
trials indicate that these devices are safe, relatively inexpensive, and 
moderately effective.327,329 They can impair ejaculation, resulting 
in entrapment of semen. Some couples dislike the lack of sponta­
neity engendered by the use of these devices. Partner cooperation 
is important for successful use of these devices. 
Intraurethral Therapies. An intraurethral system for deliv­
ery of alprostadil, the Medicated Urethral System for Erec­
tion (MUSE, VIVUS, Menlo Park, CA) was released in 1997. 
Alprostadil is a stable, synthetic form of PGE1, which stimulates 
generation of cAMP and activation of protein kinase A. Activated 
protein kinase A stimulates K+ channels, resulting in K+ efflux 
from the cell. In addition, protein kinase A–mediated processes 
result in a net decrease in intracellular calcium, favoring smooth 
muscle cell relaxation.
Alprostadil, when applied into the urethra, is absorbed through 
the urethral mucosa into the corpus cavernosum. Alprostadil is 
available in 125-, 250-, 500-, and 1000-μg strengths. Typically, 
the initial alprostadil dose of 250 or 500 μg is applied in the cli­
nician’s office to observe changes in blood pressure or urethral 
bleeding secondary to misapplication of the device into the ure­
thra. Randomized, placebo-controlled studies reported 40% to 
60% success rates, defined as having at least one successful sexual 
intercourse during a 3-month study period.330–332 In clinical prac­
tice, only about a third of men using intraurethral alprostadil will 
respond.333
Common side effects of intraurethral alprostadil are penile pain 
and urethral burning in up to 30% of patients; its use also may 
cause dizziness, hypotension, and syncope in some users. Intraure­
thral alprostadil can cause mild burning or itching in the vagina 
of the sexual partner. Intraurethral alprostadil should not be used 
by men whose partners are pregnant or planning to get pregnant. 
Intracavernosal Injection of Vasoactive Agents (Box 18.7). 
Several different vasoactive agents—PGE1, papaverine, phentol­
amine, and atropine—have been used alone or in combination 
to treat ED since the early 1980s; among these, only alprosta­
dil is approved by the FDA. PGE1 binds to PGE1 receptors on 
the cavernosal smooth muscle cells, stimulates adenylyl cyclase, 
increases the concentrations of cAMP resulting in the activa­
tion of protein kinase A, which in turn induces K+ efflux from 
the cell and the sequestration of calcium, and smooth muscle 
relaxation. The intracavernosal injections are highly effective 
in treating ED in diverse groups of men, including those who 
have diabetes or have undergone radical prostatectomy.334,335 In 
clinical trials, 54% to100% of men using the intracavernosal 
injections report achieving an erection sufficient for successful 
intercourse, and a similar proportion report being satisfied with 
the treatment.10,89,334–338
ICI therapy is associated with higher complication rates than 
oral therapy336–339 and should be prescribed only by practitioners 
who are experienced in its use and can provide emergency medical 
support to their patients in the event of a serious adverse event, 
such as priapism. The adverse effects of intracavernosal therapy 
include penile pain, hematoma, priapism, formation of corporal 
nodules, and penile fibrosis.336,337,339 Intracavernosal injections 
should not be used in patients with sickle cell disease, multiple 
myeloma or leukemia, hypercoagulable disorder, anatomic defor­
mation of the penis, or penile implants.
Patients should be taught to inject a vasoactive agent into 
their corpora cavernosa using a 27- or 30-gauge needle before 
the planned intercourse. An in-office injection test should be 
performed to demonstrate technique and to determine the dose, 
efficacy, and safety before sending the patient home with a pre­
scription for ICI therapy.10 Erections occur typically 15 minutes 
after intracorporal injection and last 45 to 90 minutes.
Intracavernosal injections of papaverine, phentolamine, for­
skolin, and VIP have also been used, although these agents are not 
approved by the FDA.89,340 Various combinations of these drugs 
are available as “bi-mix” or tri-mix” depending on the number 
of drugs included in the formulation. Tri-mix, a combination of 
papaverine, phentolamine, and PGE1, obtained from compound­
ing pharmacies, is often used in urologic practices even though it 
is not an FDA-approved drug.
	1.	 Avoid prescribing intracavernosal therapy to men who have psychiatric 
disorders, hypercoagulable states, or sickle cell disease; those who are 
receiving anticoagulant therapy; or those who are unable to comprehend 
the risks or take appropriate action should complications occur.
	2.	 Designate a physician or a urologist to be available to handle 
emergencies related to complications of intracavernosal injections such 
as prolonged erection and priapism.
	3.	 Provide instructions to the patient in the injection technique, the risks 
of intracavernosal therapy, and the steps to be taken in the event of 
prolonged erection or priapism.
	4.	 Administer the first injection in the office and observe the blood 
pressure and heart rate response. This provides an excellent opportunity 
for educating the patient, observing adverse effects, and determining 
whether the patient will respond to intracavernosal therapy.
	5.	 Start with a low dose of alprostadil and titrate the dose based on 
the erectile response and the duration of erection. Adjust the dose of 
alprostadil to achieve an erection that is sufficient for sexual intercourse 
but that does not last more than 30 minutes.
	6.	 If the erection does not abate in 30 minutes, the patient should be 
instructed to take a tablet of pseudoephedrine or Brethine or an 
intracavernosal injection of phenylephrine. If this is not effective, the 
patient should call the designated physician or the urologist and come to 
the emergency department.

SECTION V    Sexual Development and Function
Priapism is a serious concern with the use of ICI therapy.341 In 
patients who develop a prolonged or painful erection with PGE1, 
either brethine 5 mg or pseudoephedrine 60 mg, administered 
orally, may be of benefit.341 If priapism persists longer than 4 
hours, patients should be instructed to seek medical care in which 
aspiration alone or with the injection of an α-adrenergic agent is 
used to induce detumescence. If this fails, surgical therapy may be 
needed to reverse a prolonged erection; otherwise, anoxic damage 
to the cavernosal smooth muscle cells and fibrosis can occur. 
Third-Line Therapies
Penile Prosthesis. The penile prostheses are invasive and costly, 
but they can be an effective method for restoring erectile function 
for patients with advanced organic disease who are unresponsive 
to other medical therapies, have significant structural disorders of 
the penis (e.g., Peyronie disease), or have suffered corporal loss 
from cancer or traumatic injury.342–345
There are two basic types of penile implants: hydraulic (fluid 
filled), referred to as inflatable prostheses; and malleable, semi­
rigid rods, which are bendable but always remain firm in the 
penis.343,344 Penile prostheses come in a variety of lengths and 
girths. Implantation surgery usually takes less than an hour and in 
most cases can be done as an outpatient procedure under general 
or regional anesthesia.345
Infection, perforation of the corpora during device placement, 
extrusion or migration of the device, and mechanical malfunction 
are the most common problems with penile prostheses.345 There 
are no randomized efficacy trials, but retrospective analyses have 
reported that greater than 80% of patients and 70% of partners 
are pleased with their prosthesis.345 
Testosterone Replacement in Androgen-Deficient Men 
With Erectile Dysfunction. Randomized trials have shown that 
testosterone replacement therapy improves erectile function, sex­
ual desire, overall sexual activity, and satisfaction with intercourse 
in hypogonadal men who have low sexual desire88,93,94; meta-
analyses of randomized trials have confirmed these findings.91,92 
Testosterone treatment does not improve sexual function in men 
with ED who have normal testosterone levels.95,99 It is not known 
whether testosterone replacement improves sexual function in 
men with ED and borderline serum testosterone levels. Not all 
men with ED and low testosterone levels will experience improve­
ments in their libido and overall sexual activity with testosterone 
replacement therapy; the response to testosterone therapy even in 
this group of men is variable, because of the coexistence of other 
disorders such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension, CVD, and psy­
chogenic factors.
ED in middle-age and older men is a multifactorial disorder, 
often associated with other comorbid conditions such as diabetes 
mellitus, hypertension, CVD, medications, peripheral vascular 
disease, psychogenic factors, and chronic kidney disease. There­
fore, it is not surprising that testosterone treatment alone may not 
improve sexual function in all men with hypogonadism. Testos­
terone induces NOS activity,71 has trophic effects on cavernosal 
smooth muscle and ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus mus­
cles,72 increases penile blood flow,76 and is essential for achieving 
venous occlusion.69 These observations have led to speculation 
that testosterone might improve response to PDE5 inhibitors; 
however, as discussed earlier, data from randomized trials have not 
shown the superiority of testosterone over placebo in improving 
erectile function in men with ED who have low testosterone levels 
and in whom the PDE5 inhibitor dose has been optimized.107 
However, it is possible that in men with ED who have testosterone 
deficiency, correcting testosterone deficiency first by testosterone 
replacement therapy may augment subsequent response to PDE5 
inhibitors. Also, testosterone replacement therapy in hypogonadal 
men with ED may improve libido and overall satisfaction with 
sexual experience, and may have other beneficial effects in cor­
recting anemia and improving bone mineral density and bone 
strength. 
Therapies With Either Unproven Efficacy or Limited Efficacy 
Data. There are insufficient efficacy data to support the use of tra­
zodone346 or yohimbine347 in men with ED. The literature on the 
effectiveness of herbal therapies is difficult to interpret because of 
lack of consistency in product formulations and potencies, con­
tamination of herbal products with PDE5 inhibitors, poor trial 
design, and paucity of randomized clinical trial data.348 One 
randomized trial of Korean red ginseng reported this product to 
be effective in the treatment of ED349; these data need further 
confirmation because of the variable quality and relatively small 
sizes and number of trials.350 Several other herbal products are 
advertised on the internet, but the use of these or other herbal 
therapies is not recommended because of insufficient evidence of 
their efficacy or safety. Apomorphine acts as a dopamine agonist 
centrally to initiate erection; however, there is insufficient high-
quality evidence of its efficacy. Its main adverse effects are nausea 
and dizziness. 
Gene Therapy and Erectile Disorder. The goal of gene therapy 
for ED is to introduce novel genetic material into the cavernosal 
smooth muscle cells to restore normal cellular function and pro­
duce a therapeutic effect.351 ED may be particularly amenable to 
gene therapy because of the easily accessible external location of 
the penis,351–353 which permits direct injection into the corpora 
cavernosa. A tourniquet placed around the base of the penis limits 
entry of the injected material into the systemic circulation. This 
is a distinct advantage of the gene therapy of penile diseases over 
gene therapy for other systemic diseases because introduction of 
the genetic material into the systemic circulation can potentially 
induce adverse systemic effects due to insertion of the material 
into an incorrect organ or vascular bed. Additionally, in the penis, 
only a small number of cells need to be transfected, because the 
interconnection of smooth muscle cells in the corpus cavernosum 
by gap junctions allows second messenger molecules and ions to 
be transferred to other interconnected smooth muscle cells.352,353 
The low turnover rate of the vascular smooth muscle cells of the 
penis allows the desired gene to be expressed for long periods of 
time.
The strategies of gene therapy for ED treatment have focused on 
the molecules that regulate corporal smooth muscle relaxation or 
neovascularization (Table 18.4). A number of candidate genes have 
been explored, including the maxi-K+ channel, penile-inducible 
NOS, eNOS, VIP, CGRP, vascular endothelial growth factor 
(VEGF), the brain neurotrophic factor, angiopoietin-1, neurturin 
(a member of the glial cell line–derived neurotrophic factor fam­
ily), superoxide dismutase, IGF1, protein kinase G (PKG1α), and 
Rho A/Rho kinase39,354–356 (see Table 18.4). A number of vectors 
have been used to transfer exogenous genes, including adenovi­
ruses, adeno-associated viruses, retroviruses, sindbis viruses, rep­
lication-deficient retroviruses, liposomes, naked DNA, and gold 
nanoparticles. Many preclinical studies have provided proof-of-
concept that in vivo gene transfer can be accomplished technically. 
The translation of these preclinical data into human trials has been 
slow and unsuccessful so far.
Ion Channel Innovations, Inc. has completed a phase 1 trial 
of slow K+ channel gene therapy in men with ED.41 In this trial, 
773
CHAPTER 18  Sexual Function and Dysfunction
hMaxi-K, a “naked” DNA plasmid carrying the human cDNA 
encoding for the gene for the α-subunit of the human smooth 
muscle maxi-K+ channel, was injected directly into the penises 
of 11 men with ED. Patients who received the highest dose of 
hMaxi-K reported improvement in their erectile function that 
was sustained for the 24-week duration of the trial. This trial 
demonstrated the feasibility and safety of injecting naked DNA 
into the human penis.41 Gene therapy trials using genes encoding 
VEGF, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), fibroblast growth factor 
(FGF), hypoxia-inducible factor 1-α, developmental endothelial 
locus-1, and a stromal cell–derived factor-1 (SDF1) have been 
conducted in patients with peripheral vascular disease.357 These 
trials have reported low frequencies of serious adverse effects.357 
However, these trials have not shown efficacy.357 Thus, the early 
therapeutic promise of gene therapy has yet to be realized. Suc­
cessful gene therapy may require introduction of multiple gene 
products using vectors with higher efficiency of transfection of 
a larger number of target cells and more prolonged action than 
can be realized with the current generation of vectors. Additional 
concerns about long-term safety, sustained gene expression, and 
efficiency of gene delivery and expression remain to be fully 
addressed. 
The Potential of Stem Cell Therapy for Erectile Dysfunction. 
There has been considerable interest in the transplantation of 
embryonic as well as adult stem cells derived from bone marrow, 
adipose tissue, or skeletal muscle into the corpora cavernosa.358 
Although several animal studies have reported improved erectile 
function with hMSC transplantation, few studies have shown evi­
dence of long-term stem cell survival in the cavernosal smooth 
muscle or evidence of differentiation of the transplanted stem 
cells into endothelial cells or cavernosal smooth muscle cells. The 
mechanism of the reported improvements in intracavernosal pres­
sure after stem cell injection into the corpora cavernosa remains 
unclear. The safety and efficacy of stem cell therapy in humans 
have yet to be demonstrated. It remains to be demonstrated 
whether transplanted human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) 
can differentiate into functional cavernosal smooth muscle cells 
and restore erectile capacity in men with ED. Also, the long-term 
outcomes including the tumorigenic potential of these trans­
planted progenitor cells are unknown. Stem cell therapy using 
stem cells carrying angiogenic or neurotrophic genes or proteins is 
also being explored. 
Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy for Erectile Dysfunction. 
Administration of low-intensity shock waves has been postulated 
to stimulate the growth of new blood vessels and improve blood 
flow to the penis. However, neither the efficacy nor long-term 
safety of extracorporeal shockwave therapy has yet been demon­
strated in clinical trials.10,359

Endocrinology of Sexual Function and 
Dysfunction in Women
Overview of Female Sexual Function
Expression of sexuality represents an intricate interplay between 
complex neurologic networks, peripheral tissue responsiveness, 
and personal circumstances. The latter includes factors such as 
sociocultural context and beliefs, physical health and medication 
use, psychological well-being, past experiences and expectations, 
sexual knowledge, partner status, partner’s health and relation­
ship quality, body image, and gender identity, as well as safety and 
privacy. Our knowledge of the physiology of the human sexual 
response has been informed by animal models, anatomic and 
functional human studies, and imaging studies.
Sexual desire, conscious arousal, and pleasure appear to result 
from the activation of excitatory networks in the brain related 
to desire and reward exceeding inhibitory networks related 
to satiation/sexual fulfillment, aversion, and avoidance,360 
The putative primary excitatory pathway links the hypothala­
mus and limbic regions of the brain, with dopamine exerting a 
major role on attention, desire, and arousal.360 Other excitatory 
neurotransmitters include melanocortins (desire and arousal), 
noradrenaline (arousal), and oxytocin (bonding, arousal, and 
genital blood flow).360 Inhibitory pathways opposing these effects 
involve 5-HT, which deactivates stimulatory effects of dopa­
mine and creates satiety, thus dampening desire, and the opioid-
endocannabinoids.360,361 Other brain regions identified as impor­
tant for sexual behavior include the thalamus, hypothalamus, 
amygdala, septal region, prefrontal cortex, cingulate cortex, and 
insula.361,362 A number of fMRI studies have been conducted to 
identify brain pathways involved in desire, arousal, and orgasm. 
The findings have to be interpreted with caution due to the use 
of several processing steps before data are analyzed. These steps 
include fitting individual brain shapes to a normalized template 
and then filtering out brain activity considered to be noise. These 
regions process external sexual cues as well as the body’s responses 
to sexual stimuli at an executive level and modulate sexual drive.361 
Conscious awareness and sexual imagery is believed to be regulated 
at a cortical level while brainstem structures linked to the spinal 
cord have been identified as important for genital engorgement.361
Female genital arousal involves vaginal lubrications and vascu­
lar engorgement of the clitoris. Clitoral anatomy has been delin­
eated in healthy young nulliparous women using MRI.363 MRI, 
together with anatomic studies, has shown the clitoris to be a mul­
tiplanar and highly vascular structure. As shown in Fig. 18.9, the 
glans, which is the only external part, is midline while the deeper 
erectile tissue, the corpora and the bulbs, surrounds the urethra.363 
Clitoral innervation is through pudendal neurovascular bundles, 
with the nerves supplying the densely innervated glans clitoris 
being at least 2 mm in diameter even in children.363 The intimate 
relationship between the clitoris, the urethra (which is surrounded 
by erectile tissue), and the distal vagina suggest arousal and orgasm 
are not simply due to stimulation of the glans clitoris.363 Clitoral 
engorgement and vaginal lubrication are controlled at the level 
of the spinal cord,361 with pelvic muscle contraction being spinal 
reflexes.362 Vaginal lubrication has been attributed to parasympa­
thetic pathways and orgasm to sympathetic pathways.361 
The Role of Hormones in Female Sexual Function
The primary estrogen in premenopausal women is estradiol pri­
marily produced by aromatization of testosterone in the ova­
ries.364 Following menopause, adrenal dehydroepiandrosterone 
(DHEA) and its sulfate (DHEAS) together with androstenedione 
are the obligatory precursors for the production of testosterone 
and estrogens by nongonadal tissues, with estradiol synthesized by 
aromatization from testosterone.364
As rodent adrenals do not make C19 steroids such as DHEA 
and androstenedione, oophorectomized rodents have been used as 
a model for the effects of sex hormones on sexual behavior. Estra­
diol replacement alone does not restore sexual receptivity, manifest 
as lordosis, in oophorectomized mice.365 However, in estradiol-
primed rodents lordosis can be restored either by treatment with 
progesterone365 or by microinjection of sodium nitroprusside, 
which releases nitric oxide, directly into the third ventricle.366 
Studies of the estrogen receptor (ER) knock-out mouse model 
suggest the ER-α but not the ER-β receptor is important for sex­
ual receptivity,367 although membrane-bound ERs may also play 
a role.368
Some of the highest concentrations of estradiol in the human 
brain are in the hypothalamus and the preoptic areas.369 These 
regions also have high levels of testosterone, which may be locally 
aromatized to estradiol.370 Studies also suggest that acute nonge­
nomic activation of aromatase within these brain regions can lead 
to a rapid increase in local estradiol concentrations, allowing for 
quick neurobehavioral responses to specific circumstances.371 A 
number of studies have explored the impact of the fall in estro­
gen at menopause on sexual function. Together these observa­
tional studies do not support an independent effect of estrogen 
insufficiency on sexual desire, arousal, or orgasm from that of 
menopausal vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy, and other 
estrogen insufficiency symptoms in postmenopausal women.372 
However, functional brain imaging suggests estradiol replacement 
increases brain activity in response to erotic stimuli in surgically 
menopausal women, but not to the level seen in premenopausal 
women.373
Estrogen insufficiency results in vulvovaginal atrophy (VVA), 
or thinning of the vaginal lining, and an increase in vaginal pH.374 
The increase in vaginal pH changes the vaginal microflora; lac­
tobacilli disappear, increasing vulnerability to vaginal infection. 
Symptoms of VVA include vaginal dryness, irritation, itching, 
infection, discomfort, and painful sex (dyspareunia).375,376 Estro­
gen is also important for the integrity of the lower urinary tract. 
Estrogen receptors are present throughout the distal urethra, 
bladder trigone, pelvic muscles, and ligamentum rotundum.377 
In postmenopausal women, loss of estrogen results in unwind­
ing of the urethral submucosal venous plexus and a reduction in 
vessel number,378 increased connective tissue volume,379 and a 
reduction in nerve density.380 Urogenital atrophy consequent to 
estrogen insufficiency, which includes VVA, is manifest as vaginal 
775
CHAPTER 18  Sexual Function and Dysfunction
dryness and dyspareunia, and urinary symptoms including uri­
nary frequency, urge incontinence, and recurrent urinary tract 
infections.381 Dyspareunia and urinary incontinence are both 
causes of diminished sexual desire, arousal difficulties, relation­
ship problems, and diminished physical and emotional sexual 
satisfaction.382,383
During the reproductive years, circulating testosterone is 
derived from direct ovarian secretion and peripheral production 
from adrenal DHEA, DHEAS, and androstenedione. In women 
with regular menstrual cycles, serum testosterone concentrations 
measured by LC-MS/MS increase midcycle and remain elevated 
during the luteal phase relative to the early follicular phase.384 
Median testosterone concentrations are similar to estradiol con­
centrations across the menstrual cycle.384 All C19 steroids decline 
with age during the reproductive years, with testosterone decreas­
ing in the order of 25% between the ages of 18 and 40 years.384 
In women with regular menstrual cycles, serum testosterone, mea­
sured by LC-MS/MS, is significantly positively associated with 
orgasm and sexual self-image; DHEA with sexual desire and sex­
ual pleasure; and androstenedione with sexual desire, orgasm, and 
sexual pleasure taking into account age, body mass index, cycle 
phase, smoking, parity, partner status, and psychoactive medi­
cation use.385 Testosterone has only been associated with sexual 
desire when sociodemographic factors have not been considered 
in the analysis.386 Arousal does not appear to be associated with 
serum androgens.385 Measurement of serum androgens offers no 
clinical utility in the assessment of sexual function in premeno­
pausal women as no hormone explains more than 4% of the varia­
tion in any sexual domain.385
Testosterone levels do not change acutely during the natural 
menopause transition, but decline slowly with increasing age and 
reach a nadir during the seventh decade of life, after which they 
increase to concentrations that are similar to those of premeno­
pausal women.387–389 Available evidence indicates there is no 
cutoff level for any androgen that can be used to identify post­
menopausal women with low sexual function.386,390 Functional 
brain imaging indicates that the addition of testosterone to estra­
diol therapy for oophorectomized women restores brain activation 
in response to erotic stimuli to that of premenopausal women.373 
The effect of testosterone on sexual desire in estrogenized post­
menopausal women is not blocked by aromatase inhibition, sug­
gesting that central brain effects of testosterone on desire are not 
due to its aromatization to estradiol.391
Androgen receptors (ARs) are present throughout the vaginal 
mucosa, submucosa, stroma, smooth muscle, and vascular endo­
thelium.392,393 Furthermore, both aromatase, which converts tes­
tosterone to estradiol, and 5α-reductase isotypes 1 and 2, which 
convert testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, 
colocalize to these tissues.393 AR density in these tissues lessens 
with increasing age.392,393 Testosterone has been shown to increase

systemic vasodilatory effects in postmenopausal women.396
Serum progesterone is derived from ovarian and adrenal gland 
production.397 Hence, circulating progesterone is detectable in 
postmenopausal women and in men.398 Progesterone is also pro­
duced de novo in the brain,399 and progesterone receptors A and B 
have been identified in several brain regions.400 While implicated 
by animal models as having a role in sexual receptivity,400 a simi­
lar role for progesterone in human sexual function has not been 
established.401–403
Oxytocin is a small peptide that has an important role in partu­
rition and breastfeeding. It is produced in the paraventricular and 
supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus and is released into the 
circulation by nerve terminals in the posterior pituitary. In ani­
mal models, oxytocin stimulates sexual receptivity, with the effect 
appearing dependent on the presence of sex steroids.404 Serum 
oxytocin concentrations increase with sexual stimulation of the 
breasts and genitalia and following orgasm.405,406 
Female Sexual Dysfunction
Female sexual difficulties are the patient’s subjective experience of 
symptoms. The term “sexual dysfunction” should only be applied 
when a symptom is of substantial concern to the affected woman. 
While the understanding of female sexual dysfunction (FSD) is 
primarily informed by research involving cisgender women, much 
of it is translatable to transgender women. Clinicians should be 
mindful that there is no normative standard for sexual function, 
and women do not need to be partnered to be negatively affected 
by, or receive treatment for, sexual dysfunction. There is also no 
age limit for female sexual activity or well-being, and consequently 
for the presentation of FSD.407
Sexual dysfunctions in women have been classified in relation to 
three stages of the sexual response, namely desire, arousal, and orgasm, 
each with specific definitions and diagnostic criteria (Fig. 18.10). 
These components of sexual function are interdependent and are not 
always mutually exclusive. For example, anorgasmia may be the driver 
of low desire, or these symptoms may simply coexist. Moreover, the 
classifications present sexual function and dysfunction as static, but in 
reality, the components not only overlap, such as desire and arousal, 
but the dominant component may vary over time.
The most recent classification of FSD has been provided by the 
ICD-11 (Table 18.5).18 This system was developed with extensive, 
cross-disciplinary consultation.408 It is evidence based, aligns with 
clinical presentations and specific treatment options, and provides 
outcomes for clinical trials.408 Each of the described dysfunctions,

CHAPTER 18  Sexual Function and Dysfunction
namely desire dysfunction, arousal dysfunction, and anorgasmia, 
may be lifelong or acquired, as well as generalized or situation spe­
cific. The ICD-11 recognizes sexual dysfunctions might be due to 
subjective experiences or have physiologic etiologies.18 It is note­
worthy that sexual pain disorders are classified separately to sexual 
dysfunction in the ICD-11 and exclude pain due to hormone 
insufficiency.18 The ICD-11 does not specify a time period over 
which women must have experienced symptoms, but rather states 
“Symptoms need to be episodic or persistent over a period at least 
several months, and associated with clinically significant distress.”18
There are several important differences between the ICD-11 
FSD classifications and those of the commonly referenced DSM-
5.409 A major difference is that the DSM-5 does not recognize a 
woman as having FSD if there is a concurrent attributable factor 
such as depression, medication use, or comorbidity.409 In contrast, 
the ICD-11 does not discriminate between FSD with or without 
an underlying cause. Also, low desire and arousal are combined as 
a single dysfunction in the DSM-5, but are classified separately by 
the ICD-11, in recognition of their differing etiologies and treat­
ment options.
Thus, the ICD-11 presents a real-world approach, consistent 
with a biopsychosocial model of sexual function/dysfunction.18,408 
It lists factors that might cause or contribute to FSD, but does 
not suggest that the presence of these factors should disqualify a 
woman from being treated for FSD. By not differentiating FSD as 
a condition diagnosed only when no organic cause can be identi­
fied, this allows for the treatment of women with a potentially 
attributable cause of their FSD, for example, surgical menopause 
or diabetes.
When a woman presents with low desire, arousal, or anorgasmia 
that causes her substantial concern, comprehensive history taking 
is required to identify contributing and modifiable factors. Man­
aging the psychosocial components of FSD is beyond the remit of 
most endocrinologists. Nonetheless, major as well as potentially 
modifiable contributing factors, such as relationship issues; cur­
rent or prior physical, sexual, or emotional abuse; fear; anxiety; 
and poor body image, need to be identified as part of an overall 
assessment, and followed up with appropriate referral. Similarly, 
sexually associated pain, other than dyspareunia due to estrogen 
insufficiency, generally requires gynecologic review. As the focus of 
this chapter is FSD from an endocrine perspective, management 
of the nonendocrine causes of FSD is not further addressed. 
Epidemiology of FSD
A diagnosis of sexual dysfunction requires symptoms to have 
occurred over several months.18 However, large prevalence stud­
ies have used validated sexual function questionnaires that ask 
women to report their experience over the preceding month,410,411 
combined with a distress scale, and have used cutoffs to discrimi­
nate affected from unaffected women derived from select sam­
ples. Thus, the diagnostic criteria in prevalence studies of FSD 
are less stringent than those we would apply in clinical practice 
and should be seen as a broad estimate of the true prevalence. 
Partnered and sexually active women are more likely to experi­
ence FSD.407,412 Therefore, the exclusion of sexually inactive and 
unpartnered women from study samples limits the interpretation 
of some studies.3,413–415
Hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction (HSDD) constitutes the 
absence of, or marked reduction in, the desire or motivation to 
engage in sexual activity to the extent that it causes the affected indi­
vidual distress.18 Low sexual desire increases with age,3,413,415–417 
while sexually related personal distress declines with age.415–417 
In line with this, in representative community-based samples, 
HSDD is most prevalent in women at midlife and is up to three 
times more prevalent among partnered women.416,417 An Austra­
lian lifespan study that used validated questionnaires for sexual 
desire and distress reported the lowest prevalence of HSDD to 
be among women age 18 to 24 years (12%), which increased to 
33% by age 40 years, remained constant until 64 years of age, 
after which it progressively declined to 7% by age 75 years (Fig. 
18.11).417 A similar pattern, but lower prevalences, was seen in a 
large U.S. study published over a decade earlier.416
The prevalence of HSDD was found to be lower among Austra­
lian women of Asian ethnicity.417 Using the same questionnaires, 
an Iranian study of married women age 40 to 60 years reported a 
prevalence of HSDD of 14%, compared with 40% for a matching 
sample of married Australian women.417,418 In contrast, a recent 
German study, also of a representative sample, reported similar 
prevalences of low sexual desire for women up to age 65 years as 
seen in the large Australian study,417 after which the prevalence of 
low desire declined.419 The German study reported a much lower 
prevalence of HSDD then previously reported, most likely because 
their criterion required severe distress on a single question.419
Female sexual arousal dysfunction (FSAD) describes absent or 
marked reduction in physical (genital or nongenital) or cognitive 
arousal despite desire for sexual activity with distress.18 Genital 
arousal pertains to vulvovaginal lubrication and engorgement 
and sensitivity of the genitalia, while nongenital physical arousal 
includes signs of nongenital effects such as breast nipple hardening 
and increased respiratory rate. Cognitive arousal is the feeling of 
engagement and/or being mentally turned on or aware of being 
sexually aroused.
The prevalence of FSAD is even less certain than that of 
HSDD, as most surveys have combined the different types of 
FSAD either by a single question about arousal, or in the analy­
sis. Unspecified FSAD prevalences has been reported as being in 
the order of 3% to 9% for women age 18 to 44 years,416,419,420 
5% to 7.5% for women age 45 to 64 years,416,419 and 3% to 6% 
for women age 65 or more years.416,419 Persistent genital arousal 
dysfunction (PGAD) and genitopelvic dysesthesia (GPD) com­
prise “persistent or recurrent, unwanted or intrusive, distressing 
sensations of genital arousal (e.g., feelings of being on the verge 
of orgasm and of lubrication and swelling, tingling, throbbing, 
contractions) that persist for ≥3 months and may include other 
types of GPD (e.g., buzzing, burning, twitching, itch, pain).”421 
The prevalence of this condition has been reported as ranging 
between 0.6% and 3%.421
Female orgasmic dysfunction (FOD) is marked compromise of 
orgasm frequency and/or intensity, despite a woman having sexual 
desire and adequate stimulation.18 The prevalence of orgasm dys­
function varies substantially, with many studies reporting difficul­
ties with orgasm with no measure of distress. The Global Study 
of Sexual Attitudes and Behavior reported prevalences of anorgas­
mia ranging from 10% in Northern Europe to 34% in Southeast 
Asia.422 Anorgasmia with distress has been reported as affecting 7% 
to 8% of women less than 40 years, approximately 5% to 7% of 
women at midlife, and 3% to 6% of women age 65 or older in stud­
ies conducted in Europe, Australia, and the United States.416,419,420
In summary, FSD is common, with HSDD being the most 
prevalent form. The variances in the reported prevalences of the 
subsets of FSD reflect the differences in study samples, inconsis­
tencies in the questions asked, and the severity and specificity of 
the symptoms applied to the diagnosis.

Endocrine Causes of FSD
The influence of hormone depletion and excess on female sexual 
behavior and responsiveness is not limited to sex steroids. However, 
identifying the contributions of sex steroids and other hormones to 
sexual function and FSD has many challenges. Research and clinical 
decision making are reliant on the availability of accurate and sensi­
tive assays. Immunoassays perform poorly at low sex steroid con­
centrations, with significant analytical bias compared with LC-MS/
MS,423 and LC-MS/MS assays exhibit variability in the measure­
ment of testosterone in the low female range.424 This has been a 
notable barrier in progression of the understanding of FSD.425

CHAPTER 18  Sexual Function and Dysfunction
Conditions Causing Predominantly Estrogen Insufficiency
Estrogen insufficiency can be a consequence of natural or surgical 
menopause, premature ovarian insufficiency (POI; ovarian failure 
before the age of 40 years), hypothalamic amenorrhea, hypopitu­
itarism, or antiestrogen therapy (aromatase inhibitors or selective 
estrogen receptor modulator [SERM] therapy).
Menopause is characterized by an array of estrogen deficiency 
symptoms such as vasomotor symptoms (hot flush and night 
sweats), low mood and anxiety, sleep disturbances, and arthral­
gia that adversely affect well-being, quality of life, relationships, 
and intimacy.426–428 Over 50% of postmenopausal women also 
report VVA symptoms following menopause.429 Testosterone lev­
els do not change acutely at menopause, and blood estrogen levels 
are not consistently related to sexual function in postmenopausal 
women, as described previously. In postmenopausal women fac­
tors associated with HSDD specifically include being partnered, 
having dyspareunia or pain after sexual activity, and depression or 
psychoactive medication use.412 
Endocrine Therapy for Breast Cancer
Women with hormone-sensitive breast cancer are advised to take 
endocrine therapy, such as an aromatase inhibitor or tamoxifen, 
for up to 10 years after diagnosis.430 Aromatase inhibitors cause 
systemic estrogen depletion by preventing estrogen biosynthesis, 
resulting in atrophic vaginitis. This is manifest as dryness and dys­
pareunia affecting nearly 20% of treated women.431 These symp­
toms impair sexual function, have a substantial adverse effect on 
quality of life,432 and may lead to treatment discontinuation.433 
Tamoxifen is a SERM and thus exhibits tissue-specific antagonism 
and agonism of the ERs. Like aromatase inhibitors, tamoxifen use 
is associated with vasomotor symptoms.434 However, tamoxifen is 
an estrogen agonist in the vaginal epithelium434 and is less likely to 
result in vaginal atrophy symptoms in women being treated after 
breast cancer.431 
Conditions Associated With Combined Estrogen and 
Androgen Insufficiency
Iatrogenic Menopause. Iatrogenic menopause, due to sur­
gery, chemotherapy, temporary ovarian suppression by a GnRH 
analogue, or radiotherapy, causes acute declines in ovarian estro­
gen and testosterone production. The effects of iatrogenic meno­
pause on sexual function are substantially determined by the age 
at which it occurs, the circumstances (e.g., secondary to chemo­
therapy or surgery for an ovarian abnormality), or prophylactic 
bilateral oophorectomy, as well as the individual’s relationship 
status. Thus, the effects of iatrogenic menopause on sexual func­
tion are heterogeneous and not simply consequent to hormone 
insufficiency.372 
Premature Ovarian Insufficiency. Compared with fertile con­
trols, matched for age and body mass index (BMI), women with 
POI have low testosterone as well as estrogen insufficiency.435,436 
They also have impaired sexual function compared with age-
matched controls, mainly pertaining to impaired desire and 
arousal.437 The global consensus is that women with POI should 
receive estrogen therapy at least until the average age of meno­
pause to prevent bone loss, cardiovascular disease, and premature 
death.438 But even with systemic estrogen therapy, women with 
POI continue to experience difficulty with lubrication and pain 
during intercourse.439 As women with POI live with ovarian fail­
ure for at least a decade before the average age of menopause, more 
research into the effects on sexual function and treatment options 
is sorely needed. 
Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea. Functional hypotha­
lamic amenorrhea (FHA) is hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction 
resulting in anovulation and estrogen and testosterone insuf­
ficiency. FHA is commonly a manifestation of excessive stress, 
intensive exercise, disordered eating, or other physiologic or psy­
chological conditions.440 Sexual function in affected women is at 
least in part attributable to the psychological factors underlying 
the FHA.441 
Hypopituitarism. When hypopituitarism in women results 
in hypogonadism, with or without adrenal insufficiency, both 
estrogen and androgen production are compromised.442 Sexual 
dysfunction has been reported in over 90% of women with 
hypopituitarism due to Sheehan syndrome.443 Women with 
combined ovarian and adrenal insufficiency due to hypopitu­
itarism are profoundly estrogen and androgen deplete. Replace­
ment of both estrogen and testosterone should be considered in 
affected women. 
Hyperprolactinemia. Secretion of prolactin by lactotrophs 
of the anterior pituitary is regulated by dopamine released into 
the portal hypophyseal circulation from tuberoinfundibular 
neurons. Prolactin levels in women increase following orgasm 
and may remain elevated for at least an hour.444 Dopamine 
and its agonists suppress, and dopamine antagonists stimulate, 
prolactin release. Hence, hypothalamic-pituitary stalk com­
pression, prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas, a number of 
medications, and occasionally systemic illness may cause hyper­
prolactinemia.445 Clinically significant hyperprolactinemia often 
presents as amenorrhea due to secondary hypogonadotropic 
hypogonadism in women. In two separate, small studies over 
80% of women with hypothalamic-pituitary disorders with 
hyperprolactinemia had diminished sexual desire, compared 
with less than one third of women with normal serum prolac­
tin.446,447 In an open-label study, treatment of antipsychotic-
induced hyperprolactinemia with cabergoline, a dopamine 
agonist, improved sexual function.448 In another small study, 
treatment with the dopamine agonist bromocriptine improved 
sexual function in mildly hyperprolactinemic women with no 
change in sexual function in untreated women.449 However, 
whether the observed effect was due to reducing serum prolac­
tin or an independent effect of cabergoline has not been sys­
tematically investigated. Serum prolactin should be a first-line 
investigation in woman presenting with sexual dysfunction and 
amenorrhea and/or galactorrhea. 
Oral Contraceptive Therapy. Systemic combined oral con­
traceptives (COCs) lower estrogen and testosterone blood levels 
by inducing anovulation and increasing SHBG, which in turn 
reduces free sex steroids. The significance of the latter is uncer­
tain.450 Compared with placebo, treatment with a COC con­
taining ethinylestradiol 30 μg plus levonorgestrel 150 μg was 
associated with reduced desire, arousal, and pleasure in a double-
blind randomized trial.451 No adverse effect was seen for orgasm, 
concern, responsiveness, or sexual self-image.451 The Female 
Sexual Function Index (FSFI) is a validated questionnaire used 
widely to assess female sexual function in clinical trials. The FSFI 
assumes women are heterosexual and are partnered.410 In women 
with COC-associated FSD, simply switching COCs resulted in 
significant improvements in sexual function determined by the 
total FSFI score and all of the FSFI subdomains, irrespective of 
whether the switch was to a COC containing an androgenic or 
antiandrogenic progestin.452 Thus, COCs may affect sexual func­
tion, but the effects are not specifically due to the androgenicity 
of the progestin.
