SECTION V    Sexual Development and Function
Other Potential Endocrine Causes of FSD
Adrenal Insufficiency. In premenopausal women, approxi­
mately 50% of circulating testosterone is derived from adrenal 
precursors and close to all in postmenopausal women.453 Conse­
quently, both primary and secondary hypoadrenalism are causes 
of relative testosterone insufficiency. Adrenal suppression by 
exogenous systemic glucocorticoid therapy results in low serum 
concentrations of DHEA and DHEAS, and approximately a 50% 
reduction in serum testosterone.454 The prevalence of sexual dif­
ficulties in women with primary adrenal insufficiency has been 
reported as being greater than in controls (68.2% vs. 8.7%, 
respectively) with more women with adrenal insufficiency report­
ing sexually related personal distress (45.5% vs. 8.7%).455 Adrenal 
insufficiency appears to be associated with impaired desire and 
arousal, but not orgasm or dyspareunia.455 
Diabetes Mellitus. Overall, FSD has been reported, in a meta-
analysis, as being twice as common in women with any diabetes 
compared with other women, and 2.5-fold more common in 
women with type 2 diabetes.456 High BMI was identified as the fac­
tor associated with low FSFI scores in diabetic women.456 FSD in 
diabetic women may be a result of neuropathy and impairment of 
genital sensation, vascular insufficiency, recurrent or chronic vagi­
nal candidiasis, and psychological morbidity.9 Vaginal biopsies of 
women with type 2 diabetes show increased microvessel density and 
reduced AR gene expression in the vaginal lamina propria compared 
with controls, with no difference reported in ER gene expression.457 
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome. Polycystic ovarian syndrome 
(PCOS) is characterized by ovulatory dysfunction, clinical or bio­
chemical hyperandrogenism, and/or polycystic ovaries.458 Studies 
of the impact of PCOS on sexual well-being are limited by small 
sample size and recruitment of women attending gynecology clin­
ics, often for infertility, which may bias the findings. It has been 
suggested that the psychological impact of obesity and hyperan­
drogenism in women with PCOS may contribute to sexual diffi­
culties.459,460 Studies have reported problems in specific domains 
of sexual function including arousal,461,462 desire,462,463 lubrica­
tion,464 and orgasm,465 though not all studies agree that PCOS 
affects sexual function at all.466–469 Total testosterone levels have 
been correlated positively with sexual function in some studies 
of women with PCOS461,465,470 and negatively469 or unrelated in 
others.471 A small study has implicated anovulation as a risk factor 
for impaired sexual function in PCOS, independent of BMI and 
testosterone levels.471 As women with PCOS mostly have oligo­
menorrhea, a concern is that they might be more likely to have 
unprotected sex if they believe their chance of conceiving is low. 
Thyroid Disease. The incidence of undiagnosed subclini­
cal hypothyroidism may be as high as 10% of women over 40. 
Whether subclinical hypothyroidism causes symptoms of fatigue 
and sexual complaints is unclear. Oral estrogen therapy, but not 
parenteral, may increase the thyroxine requirement by increasing 
thyroxine-binding globulin. Women with established hypothy­
roidism treated with thyroxine who are started on oral estrogen 
need to have their thyroid-stimulating hormone measured 6 
weeks after commencement to check the adequacy of their thy­
roxine replacement dose. 
Evaluation of Women With FSD
History and Examination
Women may present to an endocrinologist with sexual concerns 
with the belief they are due to a hormone deficiency. It is equally 
important for women being seen for care of an endocrine condition 
to be asked about their sexual well-being. As many women will 
not report their sexual concerns, the conversation often needs to 
be initiated by the clinician. The conversation may be initiated by 
a general comment such as, “It is not uncommon for women to 
have concerns about their sexual well-being or discomfort with 
sex; is there anything you might wish to discuss?”
Several screening tools, such as the Decreased Sexual Desire 
Screener,472 are available to assist in eliciting specific concerns. It 
is important to recognize that women do not need to be partnered 
to have sexually related concerns and that partnered women need 
the opportunity to voice possible concerns without their partner 
being present. A holistic biopsychosocial history should be taken 
in order to determine potential contributing factors and the best 
pathway of care. This should include discussion of the patient’s 
relationship if partnered, the impact of their sexual difficulty on 
the relationship, self-image, past or current sexual psychological or 
physical abuse, opportunity for privacy, personal stress, and socio­
cultural beliefs and expectations. Depressive symptoms and psy­
chotropic medication use are independently and bidirectionally 
associated with all forms of FSD.407,412,420 Along with a general 
medical history, a full gynecologic history should include men­
strual cycle irregularity in premenopausal women, symptoms of 
VVA following menopause, pelvic floor disorders such as urinary 
incontinence, fecal incontinence or prolapse, past gynecologic 
surgery, and dyspareunia and vaginismus. Identification of pre­
scription and nonprescription medication that might affect sexual 
function is important. Women should be also asked about alcohol 
consumption and other drug use.
Physical examination should be directed by the patient’s his­
tory. While a general examination mostly provides no diagnostic 
information, it may provide the opportunity to reassure the patient 
of the normality of their appearance. A breast examination should 
be performed to identify galactorrhea if hyperprolactinemia is sus­
pected, and a focused vulvar and vaginal examination is required 
for women presenting with related symptoms such as pain, loss of 
sensitivity, or discharge. 
Investigations
Biochemical and imaging investigations should be based on the 
patient’s medical history and examination findings, as there are no 
biomarkers diagnostic of FSD. Testosterone should only be mea­
sured to provide a baseline if testosterone therapy is to be initiated, 
not for a diagnostic purpose, as there is no level of testosterone 
below which a woman can be considered to be deficient.473 Mea­
surement of other hormones should not be routine but performed 
to identify a clinically suspected endocrinopathy or monitor any 
known comorbid condition. 
Management of FSD
Patient education is integral to the care of women with FSD irre­
spective of contributing factors. This includes identifying and 
responding to the patient’s concerns and relevant knowledge gaps. 
Psychosocial interventions can be instituted alone or together with 
specific medical care. Psychosocial interventions usually require 
referral to a specialized health practitioner and include sexual 
counseling, body awareness, cognitive therapy, couple counsel­
ing, and psychological therapy for potentially contributing factors 
such as anxiety or depression.
Attention should be given to potentially modifiable factors. For 
example, relief of vasomotor and VVA symptoms, and improve­
ment in sleep with systemic menopausal hormone therapy, may 
781
CHAPTER 18  Sexual Function and Dysfunction
result in substantial reduction in FSD symptoms in postmeno­
pausal women. Consideration should also be given to modifica­
tion of medications associated with FSD where possible, such as a 
change in antidepressant therapy or antiandrogen therapy. Lifestyle 
interventions, such as weight management, may also reduce sexual 
difficulties. In women with type 2 diabetes and FSD, a lifestyle 
intervention program that resulted in substantially more weight 
loss than supportive care alone resulted in improvements in sexual 
function measured by the FSFI total score and all-domain scores, 
compared with women with FSD who only received supportive 
care.474 Similarly, lifestyle intervention may improve sexual func­
tion in women with PCOS and FSD.475
When indicated, a range of directed physical therapies may be 
very beneficial. These include pelvic floor relaxation training and/
or vaginal dilator therapy for women with vaginismus,476,477 and 
clitoral devices that may improve clitoral sensation and orgasm in 
women with arousal dysfunction.478
Menopausal Hormone Therapy
Systemic menopausal hormone therapy (MHT; see Chapter 15) is 
indicated for the relief of bothersome postmenopausal-associated 
symptoms, which may include VVA symptoms.479 In contrast to 
menopause occurring in women over the age of 45 years, POI and 
early menopause (before the age of 45 years) are considered indi­
cations for MHT, even in the absence of symptoms, as untreated 
ovarian insufficiency in women younger than 45 years is associ­
ated with increased premature osteoporosis, cardiovascular mor­
bidity, and premature mortality.438
While MHT is not indicated for the treatment of FSD or VVA 
as a sole symptom, alleviation of vasomotor symptoms and sleep 
deprivation may improve sexual well-being across the spectrum 
of sexual functioning.372 MHT comprises estrogen with cyclic 
or continuous progestogen therapy, or a SERM for women with 
an intact uterus; estrogen-only therapy posthysterectomy; and 
tibolone.480 The availability of various formulations and doses 
of MHT varies between countries. In a study of early postmeno­
pausal women not selected for low sexual function, the effects of 
transdermal and oral estradiol therapy did not differ with respect 
to FSFI total scores over 4 years.481 Tibolone is a synthetic com­
pound that exhibits estrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic 
effects. In addition to alleviating vasomotor symptoms, tibo­
lone, at a dose of 2.5 mg/day, has been found to be marginally 
more effective than transdermal estradiol-progestogen therapy in 
improving sexual desire, arousal, satisfaction, and sexual respon­
siveness in postmenopausal women with HSDD.482 The benefits 
and risks of MHT vary according to each woman’s personal profile 
and indications for therapy.480 
Treatment of Vulvovaginal Atrophy
Dyspareunia due to VVA can be effectively and safely treated with 
low-dose topical vaginal estrogen therapy. Estrogen has a trophic 
effect in the vagina manifest as an increase in the proportion of 
superficial epithelial cells, mucosal thickening and revasculariza­
tion, and a reduction in the vaginal pH to premenopausal levels 
(<5.5).483 Available options include vaginal estradiol or estriol as 
a pessary and estriol cream usually applied twice a week, and a 
vaginal estradiol-releasing silicone ring, which is changed every 3 
months.484 These formulations do not require concurrent proges­
togen therapy484 and have not been associated with an increased 
risk of breast cancer.485,486 As the formulations are equally effec­
tive, mode of delivery should be according to patient preference.484 
However, unopposed vaginal conjugated estrogen preparations 
should be avoided as these have been associated with endometrial 
stimulation and bleeding.484 Although vaginal estrogen therapy 
has not been associated with a greater risk of disease recurrence or 
mortality after breast cancer,487 it is generally considered contrain­
dicated for women on aromatase inhibitor therapy.488
An intravaginal 6.5 mg DHEA pessary, renamed prasterone, has 
been approved in some countries for postmenopausal dyspareunia. 
Daily application appears to be as effective as vaginal estrogen for 
VVA symptoms.489 Although prasterone was not associated with 
increased estradiol levels in women with a history of breast cancer,490 
its safety in women who have had breast cancer has not been estab­
lished. Ospemifene is an oral SERM that is estrogenic in vaginal tis­
sues.491 At a dose of 60 mg/day, it has regulatory approval for the 
treatment of dyspareunia and/or vaginal dryness without stimulation 
of the endometrium.492 However, as a SERM it may induce vasomo­
tor symptoms in approximately 10% of treated women.492 Available 
data suggest that ospemifene has no adverse breast effects; however, 
clinical trial safety data are limited to 12 months.
There is some evidence that intravaginal testosterone may 
alleviate dyspareunia in postmenopausal women.493 Most stud­
ies have been either unblinded or have involved high-dose 
vaginal testosterone therapy.494–497 A small double-blind placebo-
controlled RCT of intravaginal testosterone, 300 mcg, three times 
a week in women with breast cancer taking an aromatase inhibitor 
showed significant reductions in vaginal dryness and dyspareunia, 
and increased sexual satisfaction with testosterone over placebo, 
with no associated changes in blood sex hormone levels.498 Fur­
ther studies are required before intravaginal testosterone can be 
considered a treatment option for VVA.493
The efficacy of vaginal erbium-YAG laser, CO2-laser, and 
temperature-controlled radiofrequency therapy for the treatment 
of postmenopausal VVA remains controversial.499 Most published 
studies have methodologic limitations, and a recent review found 
that evidence of efficacy was inversely proportional to study qual­
ity.500,501 Women offered these therapies should be advised that 
they lack regulatory approval and that efficacy remains uncertain.
A variety of vaginal moisturizers are available as nonhormonal 
options for VVA symptoms.502 While these topical therapies 
hydrate the vaginal mucosa and decrease vaginal pH, they are less 
effective than vaginal estrogen therapy for VVA symptoms.484 
Vaginal lubricants will relieve dyspareunia during sexual activ­
ity but do not alleviate other VVA symptoms, including urinary 
urgency and frequency.502 
Testosterone Therapy for HSDD
Testosterone has been prescribed for the treatment of women with 
low libido since the 1940s.503 More recent clinical trials of testos­
terone therapy for FSD have primarily focused on the treatment 
of HSDD or generalized FSD that includes HSDD. In 2019 an 
international task force was assembled to review the evidence for 
the use of testosterone in women. The task force concluded that 
the available data from RCTs demonstrate that transdermal testos­
terone therapy, which restores blood testosterone levels to approxi­
mately the levels seen in premenopausal women, is effective for the 
treatment of postmenopausal HSDD as set out in Box 18.8.473 
This is supported by a systematic review and meta-analysis, which 
found that testosterone therapy improved desire, arousal, orgasm, 
and sexual satisfaction, and reduced sexually related distress, in 
postmenopausal women with HSDD.504 The task force also con­
cluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of 
testosterone therapy for premenopausal sexual dysfunction or for 
the use of isolated arousal dysfunction or anorgasmia.473
782
SECTION V    Sexual Development and Function
Analysis of clinical trials reporting safety of nonoral testoster­
one for women found that treatment for up to 2 years was not 
associated with adverse cardiometabolic effects, altered cancer 
risk, or increased serious adverse events.504 Systemic testosterone 
therapy was associated with a small but statistically significantly 
greater likelihood of acne, increased facial or body hair growth, 
and weight gain.504 Oral testosterone therapy is not recommended 
because of potential adverse lipoprotein effects and inconsistent 
absorption.473 The task force cautioned that long-term safety 
data for testosterone therapy in women remains lacking and that 
current evidence does not support efficacy of testosterone ther­
apy for any symptoms or conditions other than postmenopausal 
HSDD.473 General guidance for prescribing testosterone is pro­
vided in Box 18.9.
There are no characteristics that predict which women are 
most likely to respond to testosterone therapy.473 Therefore, 
treatment should be considered a trial of therapy and should be 
discontinued in women who do not experience a benefit by 6 
months of treatment.473 Women who experience improvement 
in sexual function with testosterone and continue therapy need 
to be reviewed every 6 months to screen for overuse clinically 
and biochemically.473
Testosterone therapy may improve sexual function in women 
with POI and HSDD, but this has not been formally studied 
in a POI population. A 12-month RCT study of the 300 μg 
transdermal testosterone patch compared with placebo in 51 
estrogen-replete women with hypopituitarism demonstrated that 
testosterone improved mood and sexual function.505
Presently the only regulator-approved testosterone formulation 
for women is a transdermal testosterone cream, initially approved 
in Australia in 2020. The task force strongly recommended against 
the use of compounded testosterone therapy, as such formulations 
are not evaluated for absorption or their pharmacokinetic profile, 
and uncertain absorption has the potential for overdosage and 
harm.473 Hence, in countries where there is no female-specific tes­
tosterone formulation, the preferred option is a fractionated dose 
of a regulator-approved male formulation.473 
Other Hormonal Treatment Options for FSD
Systemic DHEA. There is little evidence that DHEA supple­
mentation improves any aspect of FSD. Meta-analyses have found 
no benefit of systemic DHEA as a treatment for FSD in women 
with intact adrenals506 and women with adrenal insufficiency.507 
Similarly, a small placebo-controlled study of women with hypo­
pituitarism reported no beneficial effects of systemic DHEA on 
sexual function.508 
Oxytocin. Oxytocin has been implicated as having an impor­
tant role in social and affiliative behavior.509 Intranasal oxytocin has 
not been found to improve desire, arousal, or orgasm in women.510 
Although popularized in the lay press as being important for sexual 
responsiveness, arousal, and orgasm, available data do not provide 
evidence of efficacy of oxytocin for the treatment of FSD.511,512 
Prescription Nonhormonal Treatment Options for FSD
Flibanserin is a postsynaptic serotonin receptor (5-HT1A) agonist 
and 5-HT2A antagonist with weak, partial dopamine D4 receptor 
agonist effects.513 Following studies for the treatment of HSDD 
in premenopausal and postmenopausal women,514–516 flibanse­
rin has only been approved for the treatment of premenopausal 
women with generalized, acquired HSDD in some countries.517 
It is prescribed as a daily oral dose of 100 mg taken at bedtime, 
with the warning of potentially severe hypotension and syncope 
in women who, while taking the medication, consume alcohol 
within 2 hours, are taking a moderate or strong CYP3A4 inhibi­
tor, and have liver impairment.518 Lesser side effects include som­
nolence, dizziness, nausea, fatigue, and upper respiratory tract 
infections.514–516
Bremelanotide has also been approved in the United States for 
the treatment of premenopausal, generalized, acquired HSDD. 
Bremelanotide is an analogue of the melanocortin receptor 
MC3R and MC4R agonist α–melanocyte-stimulating hormone 
(α-MSH). While bremelanotide therapy was statistically signifi­
cantly more effective than placebo for improvement in scores of 
the FSFI and a distress scale, the effect size has been noted to be 
very modest.518 It is self-administered, on an as-needed basis, by 
subcutaneous injection approximately 45 minutes before antici­
pated sexual activity. Side effects, reported by over 10% of women 
in clinical trials, include nausea, flushing, and headache.519
Bupropion and buspirone, which are approved in some coun­
tries for the treatment of depression and anxiety, respectively, 
are used off-label for the treatment of HSDD.518 Bupropion is a 
 • There is no such condition as “female androgen deficiency.”
 • Blood testosterone levels should not be used to diagnose “low 
testosterone” in women.
 • The only current evidence-based indication for testosterone therapy for 
women is for postmenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire 
dysfunction.
 • Quality clinical trials show no benefit of testosterone therapy on mood or 
psychological/general well-being.
 • Studies of the effects of testosterone on cognition and musculoskeletal 
health are limited by inconsistent reporting of outcome measures and 
short treatment durations.
 • Based on the available data, testosterone should not be used for low 
mood symptoms or cognitive symptoms or to prevent/treat bone loss or 
sarcopenia.
	 • BOX 18.8	   General Principles of Testosterone 
Therapy for Women
 1. Measurement of serum total testosterone:
 
a. Measure total testosterone, not “free” testosterone.
	
b.	 Total testosterone measurement should be used to avoid treating 
women with an unexpectedly high concentration.
	
c.	 Use total testosterone to monitor against overuse of the testosterone 
therapy by the patient.
	2.	 Where a regulator-approved testosterone formulation for women is not 
available, use a fractionated dose of an approved male transdermal 
formulation.
	3.	 Use of any testosterone preparation that results in supraphysiologic 
concentrations of testosterone, including pellets and injections, is not 
recommended.
	4.	 Explain to the patient that treatment is a trial of 3 to 6 months for 
properly diagnosed hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction.
	5.	 Check blood total testosterone at 3 to 4 weeks and reduce the dose if 
level of total testosterone is more than 50% above the upper reference 
range for premenopausal women.
	6.	 Review the patient at 3 months.
	7.	 If no benefit by 6 months stop therapy.
	8.	 Continue to monitor therapy every 6 months with blood levels and by 
clinical response to treatment and assess for signs of androgen excess.

blind RCTs, a sustained-release oral dose of 150 mg/day was 
found to improve sexual desire in premenopausal women with 
HSDD,520 whereas no effect was seen for daily doses of either 
150 mg or 300 mg in cancer survivors with HSDD.521 Buspi­

with weak affinity for 5-HT2 receptors and weak dopamine D2

are lacking; however, for women with arousal dysfunction bus­

can presently be recommended.
There is some evidence that the PDE5 inhibitor sildenafil 
improves subjective and physiologic measures of sexual response, 
notably arousal, in women following spinal cord injury523 and 
with antidepressant-associated sexual dysfunction.524 The PDE5 
inhibitors tadalafil and sildenafil have shown potential for treat­
ing genital arousal dysfunction in women with comorbid type 
1 diabetes.525,526 Commonly reported side effects include head­
ache, flushing, and dyspepsia.524 A benefit of sildenafil in healthy 
women with arousal dysfunction has not been demonstrated.527 
Summary of Current Treatment Options for FSD
Pharmacotherapies have been developed and approved for HSDD 
in premenopausal and postmenopausal women, specifically 
flibanserin and bremelanotide for premenopausal women and 
transdermal testosterone for postmenopausal women. However, 
the efficacy of these therapies is variable and their availability is 
limited to only a few countries. Specific pharmacologic treat­
ments for arousal and orgasm dysfunctions are lacking such that 
the treatment algorithms for these dysfunctions are limited to 
modifying contributing factors, counseling, and physical thera­
pies. Women with conditions associated with testosterone insuffi­
ciency and HSDD, specifically spontaneous or iatrogenic ovarian 
or adrenal insufficiency, may be very responsive to testosterone 
therapy. In such cases a trial of testosterone therapy is warranted. 
Taking a broader global perspective, FSD represents an unmet 
medical need for which satisfactory treatment options are still 
needed.

CHAPTER OUTLINE

Placental Hormone Production, 793
Endocrinology of Pregnancy and Parturition, 799
KEY POINTS
 • 
The impact of pregnancy on the endocrine system is profound 
and begins with very early production of human chorionic 
gonadotropin from the trophoblast occurring at implantation.
 • 
Changes in maternal metabolism during pregnancy prioritize 
fetal growth, including hyperinsulinemia, insulin resistance, 
increased plasma lipids, and more efficient plasma amino acid 
transport.
 • 
Increased maternal adipose stores account for a small fraction 
of maternal weight gain during pregnancy.
 • 
Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of many medications 
change during pregnancy due to increased glomerular filtration 
rates and blood volume.
 • 
The cardiac demand of pregnancy may cause hemodynamic 
destabilization in people with preexisting heart disease.
 • 
Placental sex is the same as fetal sex, and sex differences in 
placental responses to exposures translate into sex differences 
in the developmental origins of adult disease.
 • 
Universal transplacental bidirectional trafficking of maternal, 
placental, and fetal cells and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) 
occurs. Detecting cell-free fetal DNA in maternal circulation 
enables noninvasive screening for fetal aneuploidy and other 
conditions. Persistent postpartum microchimerism has been 
linked to autoimmune endocrinopathies in later life in both 
mother and offspring.
19
Endocrine Changes in Pregnancy
SARAH L. BERGA AND THADDEUS P. WATERS
Placental Development
The placenta is a robust endocrine organ comprising two cell types: 
syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts. It produces a diverse 
array of substances in support of the maternal-fetal unit. Normal 
placentation requires a coordinated series of events beginning with 
fertilization. The fertilization rate after unprotected regular inter­
course during a single menstrual cycle is 25% to 30%. However, 
in approximately one-third of conceptions there is either failure 
of implantation or clinical or subclinical spontaneous abortion.1
For the first 5 days, preimplantation development takes place 
within the fallopian tube. During this period, the zygote under­
goes cleavage division and, at least through the eight-cell stage, the 
blastomeres remain totipotential. In the 16-cell stage, differentia­
tion of the innermost cells into the inner cell mass and the sur­
rounding cells into the trophectoderm occurs. The inner cell mass 
develops into the fetus, and the trophectoderm gives rise to the 
placenta and membranes. On approximately day 5 or 6 after fertil­
ization, the blastocyst enters the uterus, but implantation does not 
occur for another 2 to 4 days with complete blastocyst incorpora­
tion into the uterine stroma by day 10. Implantation is completed 
once the zona pellucida disappears from around the embryo.2
Recent developments in embryo culture during in vitro fer­
tilization (IVF) have allowed embryos to mature to the blasto­
cyst stage, which in turn allows biopsy of the trophectoderm. The 
trophectoderm cells are then tested for euploidy or aneuploidy 
and, if a suitable probe is available, single-gene disorders.3
Implantation is a complex process that involves apposition of 
the microvilli present on the trophectoderm cells with pinocytes 
(fused microvilli) on the endometrial cells, followed by removal of 
fluid between the cells through pinocytosis by the endometrial cells, 
a process stimulated by progesterone.4 The early critical production 
SECTION VI A    Maternal-Fetal
SECTION VI       Endocrinology and the Lifespan
786
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
of progesterone synthesis by the corpus luteum is stimulated and 
sustained during this time and for the first 6 to 7 weeks of preg­
nancy by secretion of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) by the 
trophoblast cells. The hCG is first detected in the maternal serum 
6 to 9 days after conception and is essential for rescue and mainte­
nance of the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over complete 
hormone production (the luteal-placental shift) at about 9 to 10 
weeks of gestation.5 Embryo attachment is enhanced through the 
expression of a variety of adhesion molecules, including mucins, 
integrins, and trophinin, a trophoblast-specific cell membrane 
adhesion protein, as well as cytokines, growth factors, and a variety 
of transcription factors encoded by homeobox genes.4,6
Derived from advancements in IVF, there appears to be a uter­
ine “window of implantation” when the endometrium is receptive 
to implantation. During this time, it is suggested that both the 
embryo and uterus be aligned for successful implantation to occur. 
Endometrial cellular changes required for implantation are induced 
by exposure to estradiol and progesterone. Once progesterone is 
produced by the corpus luteum, synchronized changes within the 
endometrium occur with downregulation of both progesterone 
receptors (PRs) and estrogen receptors (ERs). After the trophoblast 
attaches to the endometrium during this opportunistic window 6 
to 10 days postovulation, the embryo invades the endometrium 
through a complex process involving matrix metalloproteinases and 
differentiation of the trophectoderm into cytotrophoblasts or syncy­
tiotrophoblasts. The syncytiotrophoblasts are multinucleated cells 
formed by the fusion of cytotrophoblasts. The cytotrophoblasts 
form a column of cells that invade the endometrium, form anchor­
ing villi, and enter the maternal vasculature, eventually replacing 
the endothelial layer of the endometrial and myometrial spiral 
arterioles with a layer of cytotrophoblasts (vascular trophoblasts).7 
This process converts the high-resistance, low-capacity uterine ves­
sels into low-resistance, high-volume vessels, essential for growth of 
the placenta and fetus.8 At the site of implantation, the endome­
trial cells undergo decidualization, enlarging and increasing their 
metabolic activity with enhanced production of tissue inhibitors 
or metalloproteinase, extracellular matrix proteins, cytokines, and 
growth factors that modulate the extent of trophoblast invasion 
and influence trophoblast function.4,5,9
The trophoblast cells secrete several angiogenic proteins, 
including vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), platelet-
derived growth factor (PDGF), and basic fibroblast growth fac­
tor, which stimulate blood vessel development within the villi.10 
The syncytiotrophoblasts form an outer layer of cells in the cho­
rionic villi, between the cytotrophoblast cells and the maternal 
blood space on the exterior surface. Only three tissues separate 
fetal blood from maternal blood: (1) the endothelium of the fetal 
vessels in the villi, (2) connective tissue, and (3) the trophoblasts; 
this form of placentation is referred to as hemochorial. Thus, in 
addition to hCG secretion, which is responsible for maintaining 
early pregnancy, progesterone secretion, required for continuation 
of pregnancy after the luteal-placental shift, and the synthesis and 
secretion of other hormones and growth factors (Box 19.1), the 
syncytiotrophoblasts provide the major site for transportation of 
oxygen and nutrients to and removal of waste from the fetus.
Substances are transferred across the placenta through tran­
scellular pathways that include carrier-mediated transport (e.g., 
immunoglobulin G through the Fcγ receptor) and simple extra­
cellular diffusion. The degree of transplacental passage of a hor­
mone from the mother to the fetus through diffusion depends on 
(1) the rate of placental blood flow; (2) the maternal concentration 
of the free or readily dissociable hormone; and (3) the molecular 
mass, lipid solubility, charge, and degree of placental metabolic 
degradation of the hormone. Maternal-to-fetal transfer occurs for 
hormones smaller than 700 Da, but the placenta is not permeable 
to hormones larger than 1200 Da.11
The trophoblast also anchors the placenta and fetus to the 
uterus and helps to protect the fetus, which contains paternal 
antigens, from rejection by the maternal immune system. This 
immunologic protection may be mediated by high concentra­
tions of progesterone at the trophoblast-maternal interface and

antigens.12 The mass of the trophoblast increases logarithmically 
during the first trimester, followed by a more gradual increase 
throughout the remainder of pregnancy. Trophoblastic mass 
closely correlates with maternal serum concentrations of human 
placental lactogen (hPL) and pregnancy-specific β1-glycoprotein 
throughout pregnancy and with hCG during the first trimester 
but not during the subsequent trimesters.13
Noninvasive Prenatal Testing and 
Microchimerism
Transplacental bidirectional trafficking of maternal, placental, and 
fetal cells occurs universally in pregnancy, beginning around 6 to 7 
weeks of gestation and peaking at term and with fetal and mater­
nal cells persisting indefinitely in the host postpartum.14 In addi­
tion to fetal cells, the maternal circulation also contains placental 
cell-free DNA. Cell-free DNA from the maternal circulation can 
be sequenced and is used routinely for fetal aneuploidy screening. 
This approach—termed noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT)—is 
generally highly sensitive and specific for the most common fetal 
aneuploidies but has the same drawback as trophectoderm biopsy 
in that confined placental mosaicism may render results inaccurate 
for deriving the true fetal karyotype. Nonetheless, availability of 
NIPT has resulted in a marked increase in its use in both low-risk 
and high-risk patient populations. The superior accuracy of NIPT 
compared with conventional screening methods has led to signifi­
cant decreases in the number of invasive diagnostic procedures, and 
the use of more traditional serum screening approaches for aneu­
ploidy.15,16 Although NIPT is an improvement over older methods, 
false-positive and false-negative results are encountered, and there­
fore a positive NIPT screen result requires invasive fetal testing for 
confirmation.17 As further advancements are made in the technol­
ogy with decreasing costs, NIPT may likely be used more extensively 
for fetal assessment18 including emerging uses for diagnosing single-
gene disorders and assessment of microdeletions or microinsertions.
More intriguing than the use of fetal cell-free DNA in maternal 
circulation for prenatal screening, however, is the putative contribu­
tion of persistent maternal and fetal microchimerism to the fetal 
origins of adult disease and long-term postpartum maternal health. 
Indeed, microchimerism apparently persists indefinitely, as fetal cells 
have been found in maternal circulation decades after birth and can 
be transmitted from grandmother to grandchild.19 Although both 
maternal and fetal microchimerism have been implicated as causes 
of autoimmune diseases, including autoimmune thyroid disorders 
and type 1 diabetes,20 microchimerism may also enhance tissue 
repair or rejuvenation and slow aging via transmission of stem cells. 
Microchimerism has been hypothesized to protect the host from 
development of certain types of cancer.20 Thus, acute and persis­
tent maternal and fetal microchimerism can be adverse, neutral, or 
beneficial, depending on factors such as HLA match or mismatch, 
persistence, microchimeric cell mass, and other factors as yet to be 
determined. The “discovery” of persistent microchimerism years 
after parturition adds a new dimension to our understanding of the 
endocrine changes and consequences associated with pregnancy. 
Sex Differences in the Placenta
There is now a substantial body of literature describing physiologic 
differences between men and women and how these differences 
impact numerous acute and chronic conditions and diseases. Some 
of these sex differences, such as differences in lifespan and differen­
tial risk for and outcomes related to chronic conditions such as car­
diovascular and cerebrovascular disease, have been recognized for 
decades. Ongoing investigations have revealed a burgeoning list, 
suggesting that sex differences are the norm rather than the excep­
tion. There are sex differences in frequency and manner of presen­
tation, as well as in pathophysiology and pharmacology. Examples 
of diseases and conditions that demonstrate sex differences include 
systemic lupus erythematosus, thyroid disease, osteoporosis, diabe­
tes mellitus, Alzheimer disease, and schizophrenia. Differences may 
be strictly biologic (sex) or due to sociocultural disparities (gen­
der) interacting with biologic predilections.21 For example, women 
are at an increased risk of systemic lupus erythematosus, thyroid 
disease, and osteoporosis; men are at increased risk of cardiovas­
cular disease and schizophrenia. There are also sex differences in 
responses to acute insults such as trauma, sepsis, and surgery, with 
women often responding more favorably than men.21–26
Two important determinants of pathophysiology of the con­
ditions and diseases are sex and age. We now recognize that sex 
differences begin during fetal and early neonatal life.27–32 Thus, 
sex differences interact with aging from conception. The epide­
miology surrounding the impact of these very early events is often 
referred to as the developmental origins of health and disease or fetal 
origins of adult disease. Sex differences in the fundamental processes 
mediating embryogenesis and intrauterine fetal development are 
just beginning to be understood. Insults during intrauterine life 
such as natural disasters, the death of a family member, and severe 
maternal anxiety or depression are associated with an increased 
risk of neurodevelopmental disorders (depression, anxiety, schizo­
phrenia, and autism) in the offspring.33 A classic epidemiologic 
example is the famine produced by the invasion of the Netherlands 
in 1940.34 Women in their second trimester during this time had 
male but not female offspring with an increased risk of schizo­
phrenia as adults. In most cases female offspring are more resil­
ient and male offspring more susceptible to the negative effects 
of gestational insults. Recent data suggest that sex differences in 
developmental risk are mediated by sex differences in the placental 
response to common exposures and stressors. It is often not appre­
ciated that because the placenta derives from the same cell mass as 
the embryo that the placenta has a sex. However, the placenta does 
not have a gender because gender refers to sociocultural constructs 
and behaviors related to sex-related expectations and stereotypes.
Sex chromosomes and gonadal steroids are thought to play 
a large role in mediating sex differences in placental and fetal 
responses to exposures.35 Total and free testosterone levels are 
higher in male fetuses as expected; however, so are levels of the 
female sex hormone estradiol.36 However, testosterone is a more 
potent inhibitor of cytokine production in explants from female 
compared with male placentas, suggesting female fetuses may be 
more sensitive to the effects of testosterone than male fetuses.35 
Indeed, sex-specific hormone action may be the norm and not just 
confined to sex steroids.
In addition to global sex differences described earlier, evi­
dence is accumulating that epigenetic modifications also play a 
role in gating differential sensitivity between the sexes to common 
exposures. At baseline, female placentas demonstrate increased 
expression of immune-regulating genes (JAK1, IL2RB, Clusterin, 
LTBP, CXCL1, and ILR1L1), whereas in males, placental genes 
reported to mediate graft versus host disease and inflammation 
(HLA-DQB1, HLA-DOA1, HCP5, NOS1, and FSTL3, among 
others) are more highly expressed.37 Overall, the sex differences 
788
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
in physiology appear to produce a less reactive female and more 
reactive male placental phenotype. This would better equip female 
placentas to buffer the embryo from insults during critical periods 
of development. The protection provided by a female placenta is in 
keeping with the long-known improved mortality and morbidity 
due to prematurity in female compared with male neonates.38–40
Although sex differences in gene expression profiles that drive 
placental structure and function are now well described, epigen­
etic changes also play a role. Studies using the established mouse 
model of early prenatal stress have identified DNA methyltrans­
ferases (DNMT)41 and O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase 
(OGT)42,43 as top candidates for primary roles in the epigenetic 
changes. A major function of OGT is to stabilize enhancer of zeste 
homolog 2 (EZH2), a histone H3K27 methyltransferase that 
leads to global repression of transcription. As OGT is X-linked 
and escapes X inactivation in the placenta, levels are twice as 
high in the female placenta.42,43 The lower levels of OGT in 
males would lead to a globally reactive phenotype in the placenta. 
More targeted regulation of expression may be mediated through 
DNMT1, which, in conjunction with the methyl-binding protein 
MeCP2, results in DNA methylation and repression of specific 
genes. DNMT1 is more highly expressed at baseline in the female 
placenta and is further increased with maternal stress in female but 
not in male placentas.41 Again, this would further contribute to a 
reactive male placental phenotype that could leave male fetuses at 
greater risk of complications from maternal stress. 
Maternal Adaptations to Pregnancy
To some extent, every maternal organ system is altered in preg­
nancy. The impact of pregnancy on the endocrine system is pro­
found and begins very early with the production of hCG from the 
trophoblast at implantation. The effects on many other organ sys­
tems are more gradual and may not appear until later in pregnancy. 
Although the vast majority of these changes are hormonally medi­
ated, some organ systems are also affected by the anatomic altera­
tions caused by the enlarging uterus or the physiologic increase in 
maternal blood volume. It is critically important for the clinician 
to understand these changes when caring for pregnant women, as 
many physical exam findings, laboratory values, and imaging find­
ings that would be viewed as abnormal and of great concern outside 
of pregnancy can be normal and reassuring in pregnant women.
Physiologic Adaptations
During pregnancy some amount of weight gain is expected, with 
overweight and obese individuals expected to gain less than those 
who are normal weight or underweight. Excessive gestational 
weight gain has been associated with a number of adverse neo­
natal44,45 and maternal outcomes.46–50 Given this association and 
the increasing prevalence of obesity among individuals of child­
bearing age, the Institute of Medicine (IOM) recommended an 
updated set of guidelines regarding weight gain in pregnancy 
based on the woman’s prepregnancy body mass index51 (Table 
19.1). It is also important to remember that only a small portion 
of the recommended weight gain is due to an increase in maternal 
adipose stores. For example, in a normal weight woman with a 
weight gain of 12.5 kg, 9.25 kg is due to factors other than mater­
nal adipose stores (fetus accounts for about 3.4 kg, placenta for 
0.65 kg, amniotic fluid for 0.8 kg, uterus for 1 kg, breasts for 0.4 
kg, blood for 1.5 kg, and extravascular fluid for 1.5 kg).21 Thus, 
only 3.25 kg is due to the increase in maternal adipose stores. If 
one considers the weight gain goal for overweight and obese indi­
viduals (5–9 kg) and assumes that most will be expected to gain 
9.25 kg of nonadipose weight during pregnancy, there should be 
a negligible increase and potentially a decrease in adipose stores if 
IOM guidelines are followed.
The volume of the uterine cavity increases from 10 mL in the 
nonpregnant state to an average of 5 L at term, and blood flow 
through the uteroplacental circulation reaches 450 to 650 mL/min, 
approximately a 10-fold increase.52 To maintain appropriate perfu­
sion of the mother and the fetal-placental unit, systemic blood vol­
ume increases throughout pregnancy and is 40% to 45% higher at 
term than in the nonpregnant state. The plasma volume increases 
by about 45% to 50% as a result of aldosterone-stimulated sodium 
and water retention. The red cell mass increases approximately 
20% because of increased production, resulting from a twofold 
to threefold increase in erythropoietin secretion. The net effect is 
a physiologic decrease in the hematocrit by about 15% at term.52
The increase in uterine blood flow, though essential to main­
tain the fetus and placenta during pregnancy, carries a risk of 
severe hemorrhage surrounding delivery. Regrettably, obstetric 
hemorrhage continues to be a clinical challenge and a common 
source of disparate maternal morbidity and mortality outcomes. 
Fortunately, maternal adaptations may also lessen the poten­
tial impact of the common occurrence of pregnancy-related 
blood loss and hemorrhage. For example, the physiologic drop 
in hematocrit during pregnancy leads to less red cell mass lost 
per a given volume of blood. This allows pregnant patients to 
maintain oxygen-carrying capacity after volumes of blood loss 
that would lead to advanced stages of shock in nonpregnant 
individuals.53
The renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) 
increase rapidly during pregnancy and peak during the second 
trimester, with an observed 50% increase in creatinine clearance 
and a corresponding reduction in the serum creatinine level. Atrial

part responsible for increased renal blood flow, GFR, 24-hour urine 
volume, and natriuresis.54 An alteration in the osmotic thresholds 
for the release of vasopressin and activation of the hypothalamic 
thirst centers, possibly caused by an extragonadal effect of hCG, 
lead to an approximately 4% reduction in serum osmolality (∼10 
mOsm/kg).55
It is important to consider the increase in GFR and blood volume 
when treating conditions with medications that are cleared in the 
kidney. Many medications, both prescription and over the counter, 
are cleared in this way, including aminoglycosides, β-lactams, anti­
viral agents, antifungal agents, and histamine (H1 and H2) blockers, 
among others. Some of these medications require dose adjustments 
because of the increased GFR of pregnancy. Adjustments in dose 
are particularly relevant for antiepileptic drugs, the plasma levels 
of which can become subtherapeutic if not monitored and steadily 
increased over the course of pregnancy. Although all the reasons for 
the increased drug requirement in pregnancy are unclear, it is likely 
that the increase in the volume of distribution is a contributing fac­
tor.56 This is also true of low-molecular-weight heparins, a preferred 
anticoagulant in pregnancy. Although only a small portion of the 
drug is cleared in the kidney, the increased GFR of pregnancy is 
thought to contribute to the much larger doses required in preg­
nant individuals to maintain effectiveness.57
Several hemodynamic changes are induced by the low-resis­
tance, high-capacity uteroplacental vasculature, which, in many 
respects, acts like an arteriovenous shunt. The large quantities of 
estrogens, progesterone, prostaglandins, and angiotensin present 
during pregnancy are thought to mediate these changes. Other 
changes include an increase in the heart rate by 10 to 15 beats/
min, a 30% to 50% increase in cardiac output, resulting from 
increased stroke volume in early pregnancy and heart rate during 
the third trimester, a reduction in diastolic blood pressure of 10 
to 15 mm Hg with little or no change in systolic pressure, and an 
approximately 20% reduction in peripheral vascular resistance.52
Although these increases in cardiac demand are easily met by 
most, for some, particularly those with preexisting coronary artery 
or structural heart disease, the added strain can threaten the health 
of both mother and baby. Although individuals with a history of 
myocardial infarction with normal left ventricular function tolerate 
pregnancy well, those with poor hemodynamics with significant 
left ventricular injury are discouraged from attempting pregnancy 
as maternal morbidity and mortality are markedly increased.58 In 
individuals with structural heart disease, particularly Eisenmenger 
syndrome, the increase in cardiac output and blood volume can 
overwhelm an already impaired heart leading to arrhythmia, con­
gestive heart failure, pregnancy loss, and maternal death.59
In pregnancy the pulmonary vascular resistance is reduced by 
about one-third, and pulmonary tidal volume increases by about 
30%. The latter, which results in a respiratory alkalosis that is 
compensated by increased bicarbonate excretion by the kidneys, 
increases in minute ventilatory volume by 30% to 40%. There are 
no changes in respiratory rate, maximum breathing capacity, or 
forced or timed vital capacity. However, there is an approximately 
40% reduction in the expiratory reserve because of the elevation 
of the diaphragm by the enlarged uterus.52
Although these changes do not increase the risk of pregnant 
individuals contracting respiratory infections such as influenza 
and bacterial pneumonia, their morbidity and mortality are nota­
bly increased during pregnancy. This was most recently noted 
in the COVID-19 pandemic and previously during the 2009 
H1N1 pandemic. In both pandemics, pregnant patients were 
disproportionality affected with higher morbidity and mortal­
ity than nonpregnant individuals (e.g., during H1N1 pregnant 
patients accounted for 5% of the deaths but made up only 1% of 
the population),60–62 with higher associated pregnancy complica­
tions. Pregnant patients were also more likely to be hospitalized 
with pneumonia,63 but they did not appear to be at an increased 
risk of infection compared with the general population.64
Gastrointestinal tract function is altered during pregnancy. Gas­
tric emptying time is unchanged until labor, when it becomes pro­
longed. Reduced lower esophageal sphincter tone and displacement 
of the abdominal contents by the pregnant uterus result in a marked 
increase in gastroesophageal reflux. Motility of the intestine is also 
reduced, contributing to nausea and vomiting early in pregnancy 
and constipation that is common later in pregnancy. Decreased 
motility of the gallbladder leads to an increased gallbladder volume 
and reduced emptying of bile after meals, producing a more litho­
genic bile and increasing cholelithiasis risk during pregnancy.52 
Metabolic Adaptations
Numerous changes in maternal metabolism occur in pregnancy to 
ensure that the fetus has a consistent supply of fuel during in utero 
development—many as a result of hormones controlled by the 
maternal-fetal-placental unit. These changes include hyperinsu­
linemia, insulin resistance, increased plasma lipids, relative fasting 
hypoglycemia, hypoaminoacidemia, and more efficient plasma 
amino acid transport.65 As a result of these alterations, maternal 
energy requirements are met predominately by lipolysis, allowing 
glucose and other carbohydrates to supply the energy needs of the 
fetus. This shift in maternal fuel utilization can be conceptualized 
as an accelerated starvation. Although carbohydrates are readily 
available in the maternal circulation, insulin resistance reduces 
entry of glucose into maternal cells, thereby limiting the use of 
carbohydrates for energy. To compensate, maternal cells turn 
toward lipid metabolism for energy-producing levels of ketones 
similar to that seen after prolonged fasting.66 The increased mater­
nal low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and very low-density lipopro­
tein (VLDL) that occur in pregnancy67,68 are also thought to be 
the main cholesterol supply for steroid hormone production in 
the placenta, as the placenta has very low hydroxymethylgluta­
ryl–coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase activity and thus limited 
ability to produce cholesterol from acetate in situ.69
The underlying causes of the shift in metabolic fuels during 
pregnancy are largely understood, but significant gaps in knowl­
edge persist. It is clear that the increasing levels of hPL and human 
placental growth hormone reduce insulin receptors and glucose 
transport.70 However, to what extent glucagon and cortisol, which 
demonstrate strong diabetogenic effects outside of pregnancy, 
play a role in this process has not been thoroughly investigated. 
It is evident that the placenta and pregnancy hormones are key to 
metabolic changes observed to support the fetus—a phenomenon 
largely reversed with delivery of the placenta and resolution of 
gestational diabetes shortly after birth. 
Maternal Endocrine Alterations
Pituitary Gland
The anterior pituitary gland enlarges by an average of 36% during 
pregnancy, primarily because of a 10-fold increase in lactotroph size 
and number. This enlargement increases the height and convexity 
of the pituitary that is observed on magnetic resonance imaging. 
790
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
Somatotroph and gonadotroph numbers are reduced, and there are 
no changes in corticotroph or thyrotroph numbers.71 The size of 
the posterior pituitary gland diminishes during pregnancy.72
The marked increase in estrogen levels during pregnancy 
enhances prolactin synthesis and secretion, and maternal serum 
prolactin levels increase in parallel with the enlargement of the 
lactotrophs. At term, the mean serum prolactin concentration is 
207 ng/mL (range, 35–600 ng/mL), in contrast to a mean of 10 
ng/mL in nonpregnant, premenopausal individuals.73 Prolactin 
also is present in the amniotic fluid and appears to be primarily of 
decidual origin because the decidua actively synthesizes prolactin. 
Amniotic fluid prolactin levels are 10 to 100 times higher than 
in the maternal circulation in early pregnancy. Unlike pituitary-
derived prolactin, decidual-derived prolactin is not regulated 
by dopamine or thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH). Physi­
ologically, decidual prolactin may regulate water transport in the 
amniotic space.74 Serum prolactin levels return to the baseline of 
nonpregnancy approximately 7 days after delivery in the absence 
of breastfeeding. With breastfeeding, the basal prolactin levels 
remain elevated for several months but gradually decrease; how­
ever, with suckling there is a brisk rise in prolactin levels within 
30 minutes.71
Although rare, pituitary tumors do occur in patients of child­
bearing age. Whereas most are diagnosed before pregnancy, some 
are diagnosed for the first time in pregnancy. The most common 
type of tumor is a prolactinoma, which (as the name implies) is 
due to an overgrowth of lactotrophs. Prolactinomas, and other 
pituitary tumors, are typically classified based on size, with those 
less than 10 mm in diameter designated microadenomas and those 
greater than 10 mm in diameter designated macroadenomas. The 
increase in pituitary size during pregnancy can lead to compli­
cations with prolactinomas (including visual disturbances, head­
aches, and diabetes insipidus). In cases of symptomatic tumor 
expansion in pregnancy, the dopamine agonist bromocriptine 
can be safely used and is successful in reducing tumor size and 
symptoms in the majority of cases.75 Cabergoline, a more selective 
dopamine 2 receptor agonist and the preferred treatment outside 
of pregnancy, also appears safe, but there is less experience with 
this drug in pregnancy. Transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary 
is occasionally needed if rapid tumor growth occurs or symptoms 
persist despite bromocriptine treatment.
Growth hormone (GH) levels in maternal serum remain 
unchanged throughout pregnancy, although the source of immu­
noreactive GH during gestation changes due to placental produc­
tion of the hormone. Relaxin, secreted by the corpus luteum of 
pregnancy, and estrogens stimulate GH secretion during early 
pregnancy.76
Pituitary GH is known as GH1 or hGH-N; its messenger ribo­
nucleic acid (mRNA) and GH1 secretion decrease after week 25 
of pregnancy, and beginning in the fourth month of gestation, 
the placental syncytiotrophoblasts secrete a variant of GH (called 
GH2 or hGH-V) in a nonpulsatile pattern. In concert with the 
different sources of GH during the first and second halves of preg­
nancy, the GH response to provocative stimuli differs in each half. 
Insulin hypoglycemia or arginine infusion results in an enhanced 
GH response during the first half of gestation, and during the 
second half the response is decreased compared with the response 
in nonpregnant individuals.71
Maternal serum concentrations of insulin-like growth factor 
type 1 (IGF1) are elevated during the second half of pregnancy, 
probably through the combined effect of the placental GH vari­
ant and hPL, which is evolutionarily related to GH and prolactin. 
The observed rise in placental GH- stimulated IGF1 likely sup­
presses pituitary GH during the second half of pregnancy.77 hPL 
has somatotropic biologic activity, and its serum concentration 
increases throughout pregnancy, paralleling that of IGF1.78 It 
is likely that the suppression of GH1 synthesis and secretion is 
caused by the high IGF1 concentrations, which in late pregnancy 
are five times higher than during the nonpregnant state.79
Whereas the placenta synthesizes and secretes biologically 
active gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), pituitary 
gonadotropin production decreases throughout pregnancy, as 
indicated by a marked reduction in gonadotropin immunore­
activity in the gonadotrophs beginning at 10 weeks of gestation 
and by a reduction in serum levels of luteinizing hormone and 
follicle-stimulating hormone.71 Suppression is probably mediated 
through the elevated blood levels of ovarian and placental sex ste­
roid hormones and by placental production of inhibin. Suppres­
sion is incomplete because administration of exogenous GnRH 
leads to release of gonadotropins, although the response is blunted 
compared with that of nonpregnant individuals and does not 
return to normal until a month after birth.79
The mean concentrations of human thyroid-stimulating hor­
mone (thyrotropin or hTSH) during the first trimester are sig­
nificantly lower than in the second and third trimesters or in 
the nonpregnant state.80 Much of this early decrease may be 
accounted for by the intrinsic thyrotropic activity of hCG. The 
nadir in thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in maternal serum 
corresponds to the peak concentration of hCG at 10 to 12 weeks 
after the last menstrual period, demonstrating a reciprocal rela­
tionship between the rising hCG levels and falling hTSH concen­
trations80,81 (Fig. 19.1A). Higher hCG levels are associated with 
higher T4 levels (see Fig. 19.1B). Despite the lower mean hTSH 
during early pregnancy, the hTSH response to exogenous TRH is 
normal.71
Maternal adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH, or corticotro­
pin) levels rise during pregnancy, increasing fourfold over con­
centrations in the nonpregnant state between 7 and 10 weeks of 
gestation. There is a further gradual rise to weeks 33 to 37, when 
a mean fivefold increase over prepregnancy values is found, fol­
lowed by a 50% drop just before parturition and a marked 15-fold 
increase during the stress of delivery.82 The ACTH concentration 
returns to the prepregnancy level within 24 hours of delivery. The 
pituitary gland and placenta are sources of circulating ACTH dur­
ing pregnancy, and exogenous corticotropin-releasing hormone 
(CRH) stimulates the release of ACTH from both tissues in a 
dose-dependent manner.52 Biologically active CRH is synthesized 
and secreted by the placenta and, to a lesser extent, by the decidual 
and fetal membranes, but unlike the inhibitory effect on pitu­
itary CRH, glucocorticoids stimulate the expression of placental 
CRH.83
The relationship between CRH and ACTH is altered during 
pregnancy. Although biologically active CRH would be expected 
to stimulate ACTH production, the qualitative patterns of CRH 
production, which show an exponential rise during the sixth 
month of gestation, and ACTH secretion, which demonstrates 
a more gradual rise during pregnancy, are quite different. The 
lack of a significant correlation between maternal plasma CRH 
and ACTH during pregnancy suggests that factors such as the 
elevated levels of free cortisol in the maternal serum may modu­
late the response to CRH. The circadian rhythm and the ability 
to respond to stress are maintained throughout pregnancy; how­
ever, the ACTH response to exogenous CRH during the third 
trimester is blunted, whereas the responsiveness to vasopressin is

maintained, suggesting that the elevation of CRH in the maternal 
serum downregulates the responsiveness to CRH.82
Arginine vasopressin (AVP) concentrations in the maternal 
serum are similar to those in nonpregnant individuals. During 
pregnancy, however, there is increased synthesis of AVP, which 
is offset by the increased metabolic clearance of the hormone 
through destruction by a trophoblast-derived cysteine amino­
peptidase (i.e., vasopressinase), which rises throughout preg­
nancy in parallel with the increase in trophoblastic mass.84,85 
The osmolar set-point for thirst is reduced, and the release of 
AVP is related to the 10-mOsm/kg average decrease in plasma 
osmolality during pregnancy, possibly reflecting an extrago­
nadotropic effect of hCG.53 Taking into account the reduced 
set-point, the AVP response to dehydration and water loading 
is normal.
Oxytocin levels progressively increase in the maternal blood 
and parallel the increase in maternal serum levels of estradiol 
and progesterone. The levels increase further with cervical dila­
tion and vaginal distention during labor and delivery, stimulating 
contraction of the uterine smooth muscles and enhancing fetal 
expulsion.86 Uterine oxytocin receptors also increase throughout 
pregnancy, resulting in a 100-fold increase in oxytocin binding at 
term in the myometrium.87 
Thyroid Gland
The thyroid gland enlarges by an average of 18% during preg­
nancy.80 Enlargement is associated with an increase in the size of 
the follicles with increased amounts of colloid and enhanced blood 
volume. This enlargement may be a response to the thyrotropic 
effect of hCG and asialo-hCG, which may account for some of 
the increase in serum thyroglobulin concentrations observed dur­
ing pregnancy. Although clinically contraindicated, experimental 
evidence suggests that enhanced iodine (131I) uptake by the mater­
nal thyroid gland reflects the combined effects of hCG stimula­
tion and reduction of the blood levels of iodide by increased renal 
iodide clearance.80
Rising estrogen concentrations during pregnancy induce 
increased hepatic synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) 
and enhanced sialylation of TBG, which decreases its metabolic 
clearance rate.81 The results are a twofold increase in TBG and 
increased total thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) levels in 
maternal serum throughout pregnancy,81 whereas for most of the 
gestation, the free T4 and free T3 concentrations remain normal. 
There are no significant changes in the levels of thyroxine-bind­
ing prealbumin, but albumin levels are decreased because of the 
increase in vascular volume.
Whereas hyperthyroidism is rather rare, overt hypothyroidism 
is relatively common in those of childbearing age. When manag­
ing a pregnancy complicated by hypothyroidism, it is important 
to note that the pregnant woman is the source of T4 and T3 for the 
fetus throughout the first trimester. As a result, the maternal thy­
roid hormone replacement requirements increase as early as the 
fifth week of gestation. Although requirements often plateau in 
the second trimester, they continue to increase well into the third 
trimester in many patients. Increased doses of thyroid hormone 
are needed in 50% to 85% of pregnant patients, and the total dose 
may increase as much as 50%.88,89 Thus, in those with preexist­
ing hypothyroidism, it is necessary to check thyroid function at 
the first prenatal visit to determine if additional thyroid hormone 
replacement is necessary. Alternatively, the dose can be empiri­
cally increased when pregnancy is confirmed before any labora­
tory assessment of thyroid function.90 Intermittent monitoring 
throughout pregnancy is warranted every 4 to 8 weeks to make 
certain replacement remains adequate as gestation progresses.
Subclinical maternal hypothyroidism is a commonly encoun­
tered disorder of pregnancy and affects 2% to 3% of all people 
of reproductive age, with maternal thyroid peroxidase antibodies 
(TPO-ab) identified in up to 15%. Historical interest in hypo­
thyroidism during pregnancy was related to clinical observations 
that correlated subclinical maternal hypothyroid function and 
impaired fetal neurodevelopment. These observational studies 
were further supported by the critical role thyroid hormone plays 
in normal fetal brain development.91 Subsequently, two large 
randomized trials were unable to demonstrate a benefit in neuro­
cognitive development for the offspring of patients screened and 
treated for subclinical hypothyroidism.92,93 However, limitations 
of both studies included the gestational age of enrollment and 
treatment (median gestational age of treatment after 13 weeks in 
both studies) and the absence of information related to assessment 
of an underlying autoimmune component with maternal TPO-
ab status. As the fetus is entirely dependent upon the mother for 
thyroid hormone maintenance in the first few weeks of pregnancy, 
a time period critical for optimal fetal neuronal cellular migration 
and differentiation, our understanding of potential benefits of 
treatment preconception and in the first few weeks of pregnancy

remains imperfect. Current guidance reflects these knowledge

Parathyroid Glands
During pregnancy, approximately 30 g of calcium is transferred 
from the maternal compartment to the fetus, with most of the 
transfer occurring during the last trimester. Maternal total serum 
calcium levels decrease during pregnancy, with a nadir at 28 to 
32 weeks related to the decrease in albumin levels that accom­
panies the increase in vascular volume. However, the albumin-
adjusted total calcium and the ionized calcium concentrations 
actually rise slightly above this level in the nonpregnant state.99 
The urinary calcium excretion rate increases in parallel with the 
increased GFR, and intestinal calcium absorption undergoes a 
twofold increase.99
Although some studies have suggested that parathyroid hor­
mone (PTH) levels increase during pregnancy, measurements of 
intact PTH levels by two-site immunometric assays indicate that 
they are within the normal, nonpregnancy range throughout preg­
nancy. In contrast, the circulating concentrations of PTH-related 
protein increase throughout pregnancy.100 Many normal tissues 
produce this protein, and the source of the elevated levels dur­
ing pregnancy is unclear, although the two most likely sites are 
the mammary tissue and the placenta.100 This protein is probably 
involved in placental and mammary gland calcium transport.
The serum levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D are unchanged 
during pregnancy, but the estrogen-induced rise in vitamin 
D–binding globulin results in a twofold increase in 1,25-dihy­
droxyvitamin D (1,25[OH]2D) concentrations in maternal 
serum.99 There is also a rise in the biologically active free frac­
tion of 1,25(OH)2D, which may reflect both increased maternal 
renal 1α-hydroxylase activity and the synthesis and secretion 
of 1,25(OH)2D by the placenta.99 This increase in the active 
metabolite of vitamin D may be responsible in part for the 
enhanced intestinal calcium absorption.
Although hyperparathyroidism and hypoparathyroidism are 
uncommon, they both can lead to serious complications in preg­
nancy. Pregnancy is somewhat protective for patients with hyper­
parathyroidism because calcium uptake by the fetus helps lower 
maternal calcium levels. Although patients with hypercalcemia 
in pregnancy often have mild to moderate symptoms of nausea, 
vomiting, pain, and renal colic,101 some experience more serious 
complications such as nephrolithiasis, pancreatitis, hypertension, 
bone disease, and hypercalcemic crisis.102 A crisis can be difficult 
to treat as many of the agents used in nonpregnant patients, such 
as bisphosphonates and plicamycin, are avoided because of con­
cern for the fetus. Calcitonin can potentially be used as it does not 
cross the placenta; however, its benefits and safety in pregnancy 
have not been sufficiently investigated.103
Hypoparathyroidism typically poses fewer serious risks, but 
it can lead to both maternal and fetal fractures if sufficiently 
severe.104,105 These complications can generally be prevented with 
sufficient oral calcium and vitamin D supplementation. As men­
tioned earlier, a significant amount of maternal calcium is con­
sumed by the fetus during gestation. This often requires a steady 
increase in calcium (1.0 or 1.5 g of elemental calcium per day) 
and calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D (1,25[OH]2D3; dos­
age is 0.5 to 1.0 µg/d) throughout pregnancy to maintain normal 
maternal serum calcium homeostasis.106 
Pancreas
Hyperplasia and hypertrophy of the β-cells in the islets of Lang­
erhans are probably the result of stimulation by estrogen and 
progesterone.107 During early pregnancy, the glucose require­
ments of the fetus lead to enhanced transport of glucose across 
the placenta by facilitated diffusion, and maternal fasting hypo­
glycemia may be present. Although basal insulin levels may be 
normal, there is hypersecretion of insulin in response to a meal. 
Because the half-life of insulin is not altered during pregnancy,108 
this increase represents an increase in synthesis and secretion. The 
results are enhanced glycogen storage and decreased hepatic glu­
cose production.
As pregnancy progresses, the levels of hPL rise, as do the levels of 
glucocorticoids, leading to the insulin resistance found during the last 
half of pregnancy.109 Thus, in late pregnancy, glucose ingestion results 
in higher and more sustained levels of glucose and insulin and a 
greater degree of glucagon suppression than in the nonpregnant state. 
Adrenal Glands
As a result of the hyperestrogenemia of pregnancy, hepatic pro­
duction of cortisol-binding globulin is increased. The increased 
production results in a doubling of the maternal serum levels 
of cortisol-binding globulin, which in turn results in decreased 
metabolic clearance of cortisol and a threefold rise in total plasma 
cortisol by week 26, when the levels reach a plateau until they 
rise at the onset of labor.82,110 The rate of cortisol production and 
the plasma free cortisol concentrations are also increased.105 The 
enhanced cortisol production is due to an increase in the mater­
nal plasma ACTH concentrations and hyperresponsiveness of the 
adrenal cortex to ACTH stimulation during pregnancy.82 Corti­
sol secretion follows that of ACTH, and the diurnal rhythm is 
maintained during pregnancy.110 Despite the elevated free cortisol 
levels, pregnant individuals do not develop the stigma of glucocor­
ticoid excess, possibly because of the antiglucocorticoid activities 
of the elevated concentrations of progesterone.
Levels of androstenedione and testosterone, whether they are 
of adrenal or ovarian origin, are elevated because of the estrogen-
induced increase in hepatic synthesis of sex hormone–binding 
globulin. However, the free androgen levels remain normal or low. 
The adrenal production rates of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) 
and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) are increased 
twofold, but the maternal serum concentration of DHEAS is 
reduced to one-third to one-half the nonpregnancy levels because 
of the enhanced 16-hydroxylation and placental utilization of 
16-hydroxydehydroepiandrosterone sulfate in estrogen forma­
tion. Adrenal medullary function remains normal throughout 
pregnancy. Thus, 24-hour urine catecholamine and plasma epi­
nephrine and norepinephrine levels are similar to concentrations 
in the nonpregnant state.111
Fortunately, hypercortisolism is rare in pregnancy as the disorder 
often leads to menstrual disturbance and infertility. Whereas out­
side of pregnancy hypercortisolism is most commonly caused by an 
ACTH-producing pituitary112 adenoma (Cushing disease), when 
encountered in pregnancy it is more likely due to primary adrenal 
hyperplasia (Cushing syndrome). This discrepancy may be due to 
the lower degree of menstrual disturbance in patients with primary 
adrenal hyperplasia.113 The high levels of cortisol in both conditions 
can lead to hypertension, diabetes, preeclampsia, and even mater­
nal death. Cushing syndrome in pregnancy is also associated with a 
43% risk of preterm delivery and a 6% risk of stillbirth.82

CHAPTER 19  Endocrine Changes in Pregnancy
Renin-Angiotensin System
Plasma renin substrate levels are increased as a consequence of the 
effects of estrogen on the liver. Renin levels are also increased, and 
increased renin activity results in increased levels of angiotensin 
II, which leads to an 8-fold to 10-fold increase in aldosterone 
production and serum aldosterone levels.82 The aldosterone levels 
peak in midpregnancy and are maintained until delivery.
Despite their baseline elevations, the various components of 
the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system demonstrate normal 
responses to positional changes, sodium restriction, and sodium 
loading. The elevated aldosterone levels do not lead to an increase 
in serum sodium, a decrease in serum potassium, or an increase 
in blood pressure, which again may reflect the high progesterone 
concentrations, which are capable of displacing aldosterone from 
its renal receptors. Another mineralocorticoid, 11-deoxycorti­
costerone, shows a 6-fold to 10-fold increase in concentration 
at term.114 Elevated levels of this hormone are due to estrogen-
induced extraglandular 21-hydroxylation of progesterone pro­
duced by the placenta.115
The prevalence of hypertension in individuals of childbearing 
age has steadily increased over time and is now a common prob­
lem encountered by obstetric providers. Outside of pregnancy, 
angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angioten­
sin receptor blockers (ARBs) are widely used in the treatment of 
hypertension, particularly in people with diabetes, as they have 
been shown to slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy.116 
ACE inhibitors have been linked to oligohydramnios, fetal renal 
dysplasia, and fetal calvarial hypoplasia.117 As a result, this group 
of medications is avoided in pregnancy. Although ARBs have not 
been shown to have the same adverse fetal effects, they are also 
typically avoided in pregnancy.118 Patients on these medications 
should be switched to alternative agents before or in the first tri­
mester of pregnancy. Methyldopa is the best studied antihyper­
tensive medication in pregnancy and is safe for use at any point 
in gestation.119 Although less well studied, the calcium channel 
blocker nifedipine appears to be safe for the fetus and is often 
used in pregnancy.120 β-Blockers are often used, but these medica­
tions have been associated with an increased risk of fetal growth 
restriction.121 
Placental Hormone Production
Sex Steroid Production From the Maternal-Fetal-
Placental Unit
Sex steroid production in the adult ovary has been classically 
described as a “two-cell process,” wherein the theca cells convert 
cholesterol to progesterone, testosterone, and other androgens but 
are then unable to produce estrogen as the theca cells lack the cru­
cial enzyme aromatase. This enzymatic obstacle is overcome by the 
nearby granulosa cells, which have an abundance of aromatase and 
take up androgens and rapidly convert them to estrogens.122 A 
similar strategy using multiple locations and cell types is also used 
in the massively increased sex steroid machinery of pregnancy. In 
this system, both the maternal and fetal adrenal glands interact 
with the placenta to produce very large amounts of progester­
one and estrogens. This dependence has led to the concept of the 
maternal-fetal-placental unit.123 The construct of the maternal-
fetal-placental unit is critical to the success of a healthy pregnancy 
including but not limited to its initial establishment, growth and 
development, and eventual contribution to delivery. These inter­
actions for sex steroid production are outlined in Fig. 19.2.124,125
