Our understanding of the genetic events underlying cell fate in 
the developing gonad is being advanced by newer techniques, such 
as single-cell transcriptomics. These events have been reviewed 
recently, and new data are emerging rapidly in this field.39,60,112 
These approaches are showing that the early Nr5a1+ common 
progenitor lineage first gives rise to a Sertoli cell lineage, followed 
by fetal Leydig cell lines, with a progenitor cell lineage maintained 
in the interstitium that has the capacity for a steroidogenic fate. A 
summary of these events is shown in Fig. 21.10. 
Ovarian Development. For many years, ovarian development 
was thought to be a constitutive (default) process because the gonad 
differentiates as an ovary in the absence of a Y chromosome (specifi­
cally, in the absence of SRY). However, several studies in mice and 
humans have now shown that developing ovaries and developing 
testes differentially express comparable numbers of genes at criti­
cal early stages of development.86,120 Ovarian development should 
therefore be viewed as an active process that requires expression of 
specific genes and factors both to promote ovarian differentiation 
and to prevent testicular differentiation, with considerable mutual 
antagonism between these pathways (see Fig. 21.8).
After establishment of the bipotential gonad, several key genes 
are required for supporting the early granulosa cell lineage, includ­
ing GATA4/ZFPM2, WT1, and NR5A1/SF1 (see Fig. 21.8). Sub­
sequently, WNT signaling plays a key role in promoting ovarian 
development and in repressing testis development, mostly through 
antagonism of SOX9. Loss of either WNT4, which encodes the 
signaling molecule WNT4, or RSPO1, which encodes RSPO1/R-
spondin 1, which potentiates signaling by WNT4, has been reported 
in association with XX ovotesticular DSD in humans.121,122 
RSPO1, through interaction with the LGR4/5 receptor, binds and 
sequesters the E3 ubiquitin ligases ZNRF3 and RNF43. These in 
turn inhibit WNT signaling by promoting turnover of the Frizzled 
receptor on the cell membrane. In mice lacking Znrf3, testicular 
determination is disrupted by ectopic Wnt signaling in XY gonads, 
and the resulting gonadal phenotype ranges from ovarian morphol­
ogy to dysgenetic testes.123 Disruptive variants in ZNRF3 have also 
been identified in humans with XY DSD.123
Another key factor involved in ovarian development in the 
mouse is Foxl2. Foxl2 is involved in maintaining or enforcing the 
ovarian-differentiation program and granulosa cell fate, and loss 
of Foxl2 in mice is associated with postnatal transdifferentiation 
of the ovary into a testis.124 In humans, loss of Foxl2 is associ­
ated with blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus syndrome 
(BPES). Women with BPES can have variable POI, but ovotes­
ticular DSD has not been reported.
Recent reports of ovotesticular DSD associated with specific 
variants in NR5A1/SF1 and NR2F2 suggest that both these tran­
scription factors play a role in maintaining the balance between 
ovarian and testicular differentiation, but more data regarding the 
specific mechanisms are needed,70,125 as well as data on the role 
of related estrogen receptors (see Fig. 21.8). It has been proposed 
that NR2F2 and NR5A1 may be involved in supporting theca 
cell fate in the ovary by maintaining a stromal progenitor lineage 
(similar to that in the testis that gives rise to Leydig cells), but data 
from patients suggest that the ovotestis has more profound devel­
opment of testicular structures beyond just Leydig cells.
As with testicular development, single-cell transcriptomics data 
and lineage-tracing studies are starting to map out the genetic 
events underlying development of germ cells and pregranu­
losa cells, as well as theca cell origins, in the mouse and human 
ovary.85,126 Current knowledge has been reviewed extensively 
recently, but it is likely that major new insights will emerge in the 
future in this area.39 
Phenotypic or Anatomic Sex
The developing gonad produces several steroid and peptide hor­
mones that mediate sexual differentiation and result in the phe­
notypic sex seen at birth. Alfred Jost first showed the importance 
of fetal testicular androgens in this process in 1947.127 In his clas­
sic experiments, Jost demonstrated that surgical removal of the 
gonads during embryonic development of the rabbit resulted in 
development of female reproductive characteristics, regardless of 
the chromosomal sex of the embryo.
Male Sex Differentiation
Sertoli Cells and Müllerian Regression. Sertoli cells play a 
key role in supporting germ cell survival, and they produce two 
important peptide hormones: AMH and inhibin B. AMH, a gly­
coprotein homodimer, is a member of the transforming growth 
factor-β (TGFβ) superfamily and is first secreted in humans from 
about 7 to 8 weeks after conception under the regulation of key 
transcription factors such as SOX9, SF1, WT1, and GATA4 (see 
Figs. 21.2, 21.6, and 21.10).128,129 AMH causes regression of 
müllerian structures (i.e., fallopian tubes, uterus, upper two-thirds 
of the vagina) by its paracrine action on the AMH type 2 receptor 
(AMHR2).
Müllerian structures appear to be maximally sensitive to AMH 
between 9 and 12 weeks after conception, a time when the devel­
oping testis is producing peak concentrations of AMH but before 
the onset of significant AMH production by the developing ovary. 
Boys with mutations in the AMH or AMHR2 genes can present 
with persistent müllerian duct syndrome (PMDS), which can 
present with undescended testes but otherwise typical male geni­
tal appearance. Severe forms of XY gonadal dysgenesis can also 
result in persistent müllerian structures due to impaired Sertoli 
cell development and AMH release. In some cases, a hemiuterus is 
present if AMH release is affected on only one side (the same side 
as the hemiuterus), but in these cases, virilization of the external 
genitalia is usually also impaired so that these children present 
with atypical genital appearance. In contrast, defects confined to 
Leydig cell steroidogenesis in XY DSD are not associated with 
persistent müllerian structures because Sertoli cell production of 
AMH is unaffected. In boys, a small müllerian remnant some­
times persists as a testicular appendage or as a prostatic utriculus 
or utricular remnant.
Inhibin B is also a member of the TGFβ superfamily and 
exerts negative feedback on pituitary follicle-stimulating hormone 
(FSH) secretion (but not secretion of luteinizing hormone [LH]), 
but it is unclear whether inhibin B has any local role during testis 
development. 
Fetal Leydig Cells and Steroidogenesis. Fetal Leydig cells 
develop within the interstitium of the developing testis from com­
mon precursor cells. There is a marked upregulation of steroido­
genic genes at around 53 to 57 days after conception, followed by 
androgen synthesis and secretion (see Fig. 21.2).86,130 An expan­
sion of fetal Leydig cells occurs between 12 and 16 weeks after 
conception, resulting in increased testosterone secretion at about 
16 weeks.131,132 Fetal Leydig cell steroidogenesis is stimulated by 
placental human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) during the first 
trimester of pregnancy; starting around 14 to 18 weeks after con­
ception, the developing hypothalamic-gonadotrope system begins 
856
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
to produce significant amounts of LH and becomes the primary 
driver of Leydig cell steroidogenesis.132,133
The pathways of testicular steroidogenesis are shown in Fig. 
21.11 and overlap extensively with adrenal steroidogenesis path­
ways (see Chapter 13). Individual enzymes are discussed later in 
this chapter and in several excellent reviews.134 In brief, cholesterol 
is taken up into Leydig cells by low-density lipoprotein or high-
density lipoprotein receptors or is generated de novo by choles­
terol synthesis pathways or from cholesterol ester. Stimulation of 
the LH/hCG receptor increases the ability of steroidogenic acute 
regulatory protein (StAR) to facilitate the movement of choles­
terol from the outer to the inner mitochondrial membrane.135 The 
first and rate-limiting step in steroid-hormone synthesis involves 
three distinct reactions: 20α-hydroxylation, 22-hydroxylation, 
and cleavage of the cholesterol side chain to generate pregnen­
olone and isocaproic acid. These steps are catalyzed by a single 
enzyme, P450scc (CYP11A1).
Pregnenolone is converted to progesterone by the microsomal 
enzyme 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (3βHSD2), or 
it can undergo 17α-hydroxylation by P450c17 (CYP17) to yield 
17-hydroxypregnenolone. CYP17 also has 17,20-lyase activity, 
which can cleave the C17,20 carbon bond of 17-hydroxypreg­
nenolone to generate dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). This 
17,20-lyase activity is favored by the presence of Δ5-substrates 
(e.g., 17-hydroxypregnenolone), redox partners such as P450 
oxidoreductase (POR) and cytochrome b5, and serine phos­
phorylation of CYP17. These reactions are facilitated by the rela­
tive abundance of these factors in Leydig cells in humans, and 
the main pathway to androgen production is through conversion 
of 17-hydroxypregnenolone to DHEA rather than through con­
version of 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) to androstenedi­
one.136 Subsequent testosterone production can occur through 
conversion of DHEA to androstenedione by 3βHSD2, followed 
by the 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase action of 17βHSD3 
to generate testosterone, or through the intermediate metabolite 
androstenediol (see Fig. 21.11).
Testosterone undergoes conversion to dihydrotestosterone 
(DHT) by 5α-reductase type 2 in extragonadal tissues. DHT’s 
high-affinity action on the androgen receptor (AR) results in 
virilization of the external genitalia. Studies based on the phe­
notype of patients with POR deficiency and the fetal tammar 
wallaby have proposed that an alternative pathway to DHT

Local production of testosterone stabilizes wolffian struc­
tures such as the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicle, 
whereas the potent metabolite DHT induces virilization of the 
external genitalia and urogenital sinus (Fig. 21.13). In the male, 
the urogenital sinus gives rise to the prostate and prostatic ure­
thra, the genital tubercle develops into the glans penis, the uro­
genital (urethral) folds fuse to form the shaft of the penis, and 
the urogenital (labioscrotal) swellings fuse to form the scrotum 
(Figs. 21.14 and 21.15).139
Testosterone and DHT exert their effects through the AR. 
The AR is a member of the superfamily of ligand-dependent 
nuclear receptor transcription factors encoded by a gene (AR, 
also known as NR3C4) on the X chromosome (Xq11-q12).140 
Like other nuclear receptors, it contains a highly conserved 
central DNA-binding domain (DBD) and a C-terminal ligand-
binding domain (LBD) (Fig. 21.16). In addition, the AR 
uniquely contains an extended N-terminal domain (NTD) that 
includes polyglutamine (CAG) and polyglycine (GGN) repeats 
that can vary in number; the length of these repeats can modu­
late AR activity, with a longer stretch of repeats being associated 
with decreased AR activity.
The DBD contains cysteine residues that coordinate zinc atoms 
to form two zinc fingers, the first of which contains a P-box that 
enters the major groove of DNA to form specific base-pair con­
tacts that are identical for all classic steroid receptors. The second 
zinc finger containing the D-box is involved in protein-protein 
interactions and stabilizes the unit for receptor dimerization. This 
binding requires preferential recognition of androgen response ele­
ments (AREs) composed of an inverted repeat of DNA sequences 
related to 5′-AGAACA-3′.141
The AR in the unliganded state is located in the cytoplasm and is 
complexed to heat shock proteins such as HSP70 and HSP90 and 
to co-chaperone proteins such as FKBP4 (also called FKBP52). 
Binding of ligand results in dissociation from these complexes to 
allow translocation of the AR into the nucleus, where it binds to 
DNA target sequences as a homodimer.
The crystal structure of the AR LBD bound to natural and syn­
thetic androgens is shown in Fig. 21.16B. Helix 12, in the presence 
of ligand, undergoes a conformational change to fold back on top 
of the ligand hydrophobic pocket to capture the ligand, thus slow­
ing the rate of ligand-receptor dissociation. This trapping effect by 
helix 12 enables recruitment of transcriptional coactivators.
Activation of transcription by AR involves motif activation 
function 1 (AF1) in the NTD and motif activation function 2 
(AF2) in the LBD. AF1 is ligand independent, whereas AF2 is

ligand dependent and interacts with p160 steroid receptor coacti­

unique feature of the AR is interaction between the N-terminal 
and C-terminal domains (N-C interaction). In the presence of 
its primary physiologic ligands, testosterone and DHT, the AR 
recruits diverse coregulators that cooperate in the activation 
of transcription of androgen-regulated genes (see Fig. 21.16). 
N-terminal sequences comprising amino acid residues 23 to 27 
(FQNLF) and residues 435 to 439 (WHTLF) participate in the 
AR N-C interaction to stabilize the AR and slow dissociation of 
the ligand. Further modulation of AR function occurs posttrans­
lationally by processes such as phosphorylation and sumoylation.
The action of the AR is further modulated by interaction with 
coregulatory proteins that function as coactivators or corepres­
sors.142 Agonist-induced changes in LBD organization enable 
coactivator recruitment through their LXXLL motifs.143 The 
AR exhibits a selective preference for the ARA70, ARA55, and 
ARA54 coregulators, which contain FxxLF motifs related to the 
aforementioned amino acid residues in the N-terminus.
Relatively little is known about AR targets in the developing 
wolffian structures (which are testosterone-responsive) and in the 
key target tissues, such as the developing external genitalia (which 
are DHT responsive). Studies in mice have revealed a number of 
factors that are necessary for development of the wolffian ducts 
(e.g., Gdf7, Bmps4, Bmps7, Bmps8a, Bmps8b, Hoxa10, Hoxa11) 
and for growth of the genital tubercle (e.g., Fgfs, Shh, Wnts, 
Hoxa13, Hoxd13, Bmp/noggin, ephrin signaling). Impaired 
androgen action occurs in several syndromic conditions and may 
reflect defects in genes that mediate target-tissue responsiveness 
and genital-tubercle growth (e.g., HOXA10, HOXA13). 
Testicular Descent. Testicular descent is a two-stage process that 
starts at about 8 weeks after conception and is usually complete 
by the middle of the third trimester.144 The initial transabdomi­
nal stage of testicular descent (8–15 weeks) involves contraction 
and thickening of the gubernacular ligament and degeneration of 
the craniosuspensory ligament. This stage is mediated by the testis 
itself through the secretion of factors such as insulin-like 3 (INSL3, 
a relaxin-like factor) and its G protein–coupled receptor, GREAT 
(also called LGR8 or RXFP2).145 The subsequent transinguinal 
(or inguinoscrotal) phase of testicular descent (25–35 weeks) is 
primarily driven by androgens. The genitofemoral nerve and its 
neurotransmitter, calcitonin gene–related peptide (CGRP), have 
also been implicated in this process. 
Subsequent Testicular Development. During the second and 
third trimesters, the testes show several distinct morphologic 
changes, including a reduction in fetal Leydig cell mass and 
elongation and coiling of seminiferous cords. There is no further 
significant development of germ cells during this time, and semi­
niferous cords do not canalize until later in childhood. Neverthe­
less, certain developmental insults can affect the testis at this stage. 
For example, testicular regression syndrome (previously called 
vanishing or absent testis syndrome) is most likely a late fetal event 
because boys with this condition have anorchia at birth but com­
plete or near-complete virilization and no müllerian structures, 
indicating normal testicular function in early gestation (see “Anor­
chia and Cryptorchidism”). 
Female Sex Differentiation. As noted previously, ovarian 
development and differentiation have been viewed in the past as 
a “default” or passive process, but ovarian development in fact 
involves many active processes. Studies of gene expression show 
that a specific complement of genes is implicated in ovarian devel­
opment and integrity, some of which (e.g., RSPO1, NR2F2) may 
actively antagonize testis differentiation.10,86,120,146 Even the con­
cepts of a fixed and quiescent population of ovarian germ cells at 
birth and of absence of fetal ovarian steroidogenesis have been 
challenged.147,148
In contrast to the testis, the developing ovary does not express 
FSH or LH/hCG receptors until after 16 weeks of gestation. At 
about 20 weeks of gestation, plasma concentrations of FSH reach 
a peak, and the first primary follicles are formed.133 By 25 weeks 
of gestation, the ovary has developed definitive morphologic 
characteristics. Folliculogenesis can proceed, and a few graafian 
follicles have developed by the third trimester.12 Although some 
studies have suggested that the early fetal ovary can produce ste­
roids and express aromatase, the amount of estrogen secreted by 
the developing ovary is likely to be insignificant compared with 
placental estrogen synthesis, and ovarian estrogen production does 
not seem to have significant effects on sex development until the 
time of puberty.148
In female sex differentiation, müllerian structures persist to 
form the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper portion of the vagina 
(see Fig. 21.13). Uterine development in mice occurs even in the 
absence of the ovary and requires a host of factors for uterine 
development (e.g., Pax2, Lim1, Emx2, Wnt4/Lp, Hoxa13) and 
differentiation (e.g., Wnt7a, Hoxa10, Hoxa11, Hoxa13, proges­
terone and estrogen receptors).149 The lack of local testosterone 
production leads to degeneration of wolffian structures. The uro­
genital sinus develops into the urethra and lower portion of the 
vagina, which, in the absence of testosterone, become separated

Several conditions can affect XX sex development in utero. 
Exposure of the fetus to androgens results in virilization of the 
external genitalia. If the androgens are adrenal in origin, the local 
androgen concentration is typically not sufficient to stabilize 
wolffian structures. Most frequently, virilization of the XX fetus 
results from conditions affecting adrenal steroidogenesis (e.g., 
deficiency of 21-hydroxylase [CYP21], 11β-hydroxylase, POR, 
or 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase). Rarer causes of virilization 
include aromatase deficiency (which affects both the fetus and the 
placenta), testicular and ovotesticular DSD, maternal virilizing 
tumors (e.g., luteoma of pregnancy), and possibly glucocorticoid 
resistance. Exposure to certain chemical agents in pregnancy has 
been proposed as a cause of fetal virilization, but data are limited. 
With the exception of testicular/ovotesticular DSD, these condi­
tions result in exposure to androgens but not AMH, so a uterus is 
usually present. Other developmental abnormalities of the female 
genital tract (e.g., Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser [MRKH] 
syndrome) are discussed in “XX Differences of Sex Development.” 
Psychosexual Development
Psychosexual development is traditionally viewed as having sev­
eral distinct components (see Chapter 24). Gender identity refers 
to a person’s self-identification as male, female, or a nonbinary 
gender (e.g., intermediate to male and female, combined male 
and female, agender). For some individuals, gender identity may 
be fluid. Gender-stereotypical behaviors describe behaviors that are 
generally associated with a specific gender within the individual’s 
cultural context and can include toy preferences and choices of 
activities and occupation. Sexual orientation refers to romantic 
and erotic interests (e.g., attracted to women, men, other genders/
sexes, all, or none); includes behavior, fantasies, and attractions; 
and may or may not correspond to actual sexual activity.
The past decades have seen a number of opposing theories 
about the origins of psychosexual development and debate about 
the relative contributions of chromosomes, hormones, brain

structure, and societal and family influences. Much of this work 
has focused on the study of rodents and nonhuman primate spe­
cies. For example, Young and colleagues first showed in 1959 that 
exposure of guinea pigs to testosterone during pregnancy resulted 
in altered mating behavior of female offspring.150 These effects 
may be most pronounced during a critical window of exposure 
and, in rodents and some primates, may depend in part on aro­
matization of the androgens to estrogens, receptor availability, 
and environment.151 More recently, interest has focused on the 
role of genes and chromosomes in sex behavior. For example, 
studies of differential gene-expression patterns in the develop­
ing mouse brain have shown upregulation of different X- and 
Y-chromosomal genes in early embryonic life, even before the 
onset of significant androgen secretion by the developing testis in 
males.152 Studies of XY mice in which Sry was deleted or XX mice 
in which Sry was transgenically expressed showed certain neu­
roanatomic differences between XY and XX mice, independent 
of gonadal development and endocrine status.153 These findings 
raise the possibility that sex-chromosome complement may affect 
psychosexual development through mechanisms independent of 
sex-hormone action.154
Understanding the complex issues related to psychosexual 
development in humans is even more challenging, especially 
because gender identity cannot readily be assessed in nonhuman 
species. For many years, it was thought that gender identity would 
be concordant with the sex designated at birth and that it was in 
the child’s best interest not to deviate from this sex designation 
and to offer surgical procedures and hormone therapies consis­
tent with the designated sex. This theory assumed psychosexual 
neutrality at birth, but it has been challenged by evidence for the 
influence of prenatal sex-hormone action on psychosexual devel­
opment.155,156 Direct data to assess such effects in humans are lim­
ited, but studies in women with complete androgen insensitivity 
syndrome (CAIS), who have XY sex chromosomes and whose psy­
chosexual development is female in ∼98% or more of cases, argue for 
a major role for androgen action and a lesser role for Y-chromosome 
genes alone in human psychosexual development.157 For individ­
uals with a Y chromosome and a partial degree of androgen action 
(due to conditions such as partial gonadal dysgenesis or partial 
androgen insensitivity syndrome [PAIS]), gender identity is much 
more variable and can be difficult to predict.158,159 It has been sug­
gested that the degree of virilization of the external genitalia may 
serve as a marker of in utero testosterone exposure for not only the 
genitals but also the brain. Indeed, in a study of XY individuals 
with PAIS, a greater degree of genital virilization generally cor­
related with increased scores on a composite gender index (which 
incorporated assessments of both gender identity and gender-
stereotypical behaviors), but there was wide variability for the 
genital phenotypes that were most intermediate between female 
and male appearance.160
Prenatal exposure to androgens can also influence psychosex­
ual development in XX individuals.156,161 Girls with CAH who 
have a greater degree of genital virilization are more likely to play 
more with toys stereotypically favored by boys, and preferences 
for male-stereotypical activities and professions may continue into 
adulthood.162 Prenatal androgen exposure can also be associated 
with other psychological characteristics, such as sexual orienta­
tion.163 However, the association between high prenatal androgen 
exposure and gender identity appears to be less marked, except 
perhaps in some cases of (ovo)testicular DSD and deficiencies of 
aromatase.164 Although dissatisfaction with the gender designated 
at birth is more common in individuals with DSD, more than 
90% of XX individuals with CAH who are raised as girls later 
identify as female.156,157,165 However, more XX individuals with 
CAH and raised as girls may later identify as male or have a nonbi­
nary gender identity than originally thought.166,167 Furthermore, 
there have been several case series reporting XX individuals with 
CAH and significant virilization who were raised as boys and con­
tinued to identify as men later in life.168
Social environment and gender of rearing may also play a role 
in psychosexual development. Evidence for this comes from case 
series of XY individuals with genital anatomy that was disrupted 
either developmentally (e.g., due to pelvic-wall anomalies such 
as cloacal exstrophy) or iatrogenically (e.g., penile ablation) but 
who otherwise had testosterone production and responsiveness 
that were typical for XY individuals.169,170 Historically, many of 
these individuals were raised as girls. Long-term follow-up of these 
patients has shown that many continued to identify as female, 
although a significant proportion identified as male or were 
uncomfortable with a female gender identity. Of note, of those 
raised as boys, all continued to identify as male in late adolescence 
and adulthood, and current practice favors raising XY patients 
who have isolated anatomic genital issues (i.e., that do not arise 
from underlying issues with androgen production or responsive­
ness) as boys.
Collectively, these studies show that prenatal androgen expo­
sure, and designated gender may all influence gender identity. 
However, gender identity cannot be reliably predicted from any 
of these factors. Furthermore, it is important to appreciate that 
gender identity, sex-typical behavior, and sexual orientation are 
separate components of psychosexual development and to avoid 
conflating these potentially related but distinct components.
Challenges in assessing gender identity in young children make 
it difficult to know when gender identity is established, although 
it is thought to begin between 18 and 36 months and possibly 
younger.171 Many of the effects of sex on brain structures reported 
at late childhood, puberty, or adulthood are not seen in early 
childhood and are therefore not useful for guiding gender designa­
tion.172,173 There may be some plasticity in psychosexual develop­
ment, as is evident from studies of some patients with conditions 
such as 5α-reductase deficiency and 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydro­
genase deficiency, who may experience a change in their gender 
identity in adolescence. Furthermore, some individuals with DSD 
do not fit into a binary model of gender. In several countries, 
important legal changes have taken place to acknowledge this, 
such as the option not to define gender as female or male on pass­
ports. Nevertheless, many societies and individuals still have a very 
binary view of gender, and freedom of expression remains difficult 
for many people who do not feel they fit a binary model. 
Development of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-
Gonadal Axis in the Fetus
Development of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis 
is described in detail in Chapter 20; points that are particularly 
relevant to DSD are reviewed here.
Fetal hypothalamic-gonadotrope development occurs from 6 
weeks after conception in humans, in parallel with the processes 
of sex determination and differentiation. This involves migration 
of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-producing neurons 
from the olfactory placode through the cribriform plate to the 
fetal hypothalamus, development of the hypothalamic nuclei 
(including the arcuate nucleus, which contains kisspeptin-neuro­
kinin B-dynorphin [KNDy] neurons), formation of the anterior 
862
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
pituitary from Rathke pouch, and differentiation and maturation 
of pituitary gonadotropes that are capable of releasing LH and 
FSH as part of a functional HPG axis. Defects in these systems 
can result in a range of clinical conditions, such as Kallmann 
syndrome, congenital isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, 
and gonadotropin insufficiency as part of a multiple pituitary hor­
mone deficiency; these are reviewed in Chapters 6, 20, and 23.
It is generally thought that pulsatile release of LH and FSH 
does not occur and therefore does not influence the gonads until 
about 14 to 18 weeks after conception, at which stage differentia­
tion of the external genitalia is complete.133 In typical XY fetuses, 
the main effect of gonadotropins is to stimulate testicular sex ste­
roidogenesis in the second and third trimesters of development, 
which in turn promotes elongation of the penis and testicular 
descent from the inguinal canal to the scrotum. Consequently, 
boys with congenital gonadotropin insufficiency may have a small 
penis (micropenis) and/or bilaterally undescended testes. These 
children may need monitoring for important associated features, 
such as renal agenesis in Kallmann syndrome or growth hormone 
or adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) insufficiency (which 
can cause hypoglycemia) in multiple pituitary hormone defi­
ciency. Classically, boys with hypothalamic or pituitary gonado­
tropin insufficiency do not have hypospadias because fusion of 
the urethral folds has occurred before testicular production of 
testosterone becomes dependent on gonadotropins around 18 
weeks after conception. However, hypospadias can be seen in rare 
cases of hypothalamic or pituitary disorders affecting the HPG 
axis, potentially reflecting effects at the gonadal level as well as the 
hypothalamic and/or pituitary levels.174,175 
The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis in 
Infancy and Childhood
At birth, the infant is removed from the influence of maternal and 
placental hormones and undergoes a series of distinct endocrine 
changes.
Postnatal Endocrine Changes in Typical Male 
Development
Testosterone can be detected at birth, with levels falling during 
the first few days of life. Thereafter, a reactivation of the HPG axis 
occurs and results in serum testosterone that is typically measurable 
by 1 to 2 weeks of life and peaks at midpubertal levels between 2 
and 3 months after birth (Fig. 21.17).176,177 This peak of testoster­
one is associated with an acceleration in penile growth and may be 
linked in part to early postnatal maturation of gonocytes in the tes­
tis, which may in turn be important for fertility in adulthood.177,178 
In some conditions, this “minipuberty” of infancy may be blunted 
(see “Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome” later in the chapter). The 
HPG axis then becomes relatively quiescent from around 6 months 
of age until the onset of puberty, and serum concentrations of LH, 
FSH, and the Leydig cell products testosterone and insulin-like fac­
tor 3 (INSL3) are low during this time.179
Inhibin B concentrations are similarly high at birth and in 
infancy, fall during the first 2 years of life to low but still detect­
able levels, then rise again with the onset of puberty (see Fig. 
21.17).180,181 In contrast, AMH concentrations remain high from 
birth throughout childhood and only decline with the onset of 
puberty (see Fig. 21.17).128,129 Inhibin B and especially AMH can 
therefore be useful markers of active testicular tissue (specifically, 
Sertoli cells) even when assessed between the periods of robust 
HPG activity in infancy and at puberty. 
Postnatal Endocrine Changes in Typical Female 
Development
Typical XX individuals have a discrete activation of the HPG axis 
in infancy that declines by approximately 1 year of age.179 Detect­
able concentrations of estradiol (5–20 pg/mL [20–80 pmol/L]) and 
inhibin B (50–200 pg/mL) can be measured in the first few months 
of life, and surprisingly high concentrations of FSH (with marked 
interindividual variability) can be found during infancy and early 
childhood (median, 3.8 IU/L; range, 1.2–18.8 IU/L [2.5%–97.5%] 
at 3 months of age in healthy term girls).182 Throughout childhood, 
FSH remains detectable, but LH is low. AMH is very low until 
puberty. Inhibin A, which is made exclusively by the ovary, has been 
proposed as a test of ovarian tissue in the newborn period in chil­
dren with possible ovotesticular DSD, but this hormone is below 
the limits of detection in many normal term newborn girls, and 
FSH stimulation may be needed to detect it.183 
Differences of Sex Development
DSD can have a wide range of presenting phenotypes, depend­
ing on the underlying condition and its severity. Individuals 
with these conditions can present to many different health care 
professions, including neonatologists, geneticists, urologists,

gynecologists, and internists. The classic presentation is an infant 
born with atypical genital appearance, but not all conditions are 
apparent at birth. For example, XY individuals with complete 
17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency may first present in early 
adolescence with hypertension and delayed puberty, or a young 
woman with CAIS may first present to a gynecologist with amen­
orrhea. Increasingly, DSD are being recognized due to discordance 
between sex-chromosome complement ascertained prenatally and 
genital appearance at birth.
Significant progress in understanding the molecular basis of 
gonadal development has occurred during the past 40 years. Sev­
eral single-gene disorders causing gonadal dysgenesis in humans 
have been described, and many more candidate genes are emerg­
ing. The percentage of patients with conditions affecting gonadal 
development who can be diagnosed at the molecular level is 
increasing with the use of next generation sequencing of gene 
panels or exomes (currently around 25%–40%),174,184–187 and 
molecular diagnosis of classic conditions affecting steroidogenesis 
can be reached in most situations. Defining the exact basis of a 
patient’s DSD can have important implications for advising on 
gender designation, predicting response to treatment (e.g., andro­
gen supplementation), screening for associated features (e.g., adre­
nal dysfunction), assessing the risk of tumorigenesis, determining 
potential fertility options, and providing long-term counseling for 
the individual and family. However, data from long-term outcome 
studies are incomplete for many conditions, and a fully evidence-
based approach to management is not possible in many cases.
Classification of Differences of Sex Development
DSD has been defined as “congenital conditions in which devel­
opment of chromosomal, gonadal, or anatomic sex is atypical.”1 
This definition is wide-ranging enough to cover nonendocrine 
conditions such as cloacal exstrophy but sufficiently specific not 
to encompass, for example, disorders of puberty. The consensus 
statement that introduced the term DSD further suggested a clas­
sification of DSD by karyotype (Table 21.2): sex-chromosome 
DSD (variations in sex-chromosome complement), XY DSD 
(conditions affecting testis development, androgen synthesis, 
and androgen action), and XX DSD (androgen excess and con­
ditions affecting ovarian development). Although karyotype does 
not define a person’s gender, rapid assessment of sex-chromosome 
complement can be a very useful stepping stone for focusing 
investigations and to start to counsel the patient and family about 
likely causes and outcomes. 
Sex-Chromosome Differences of Sex 
Development
Variation in the number of sex chromosomes (i.e., sex-chromo­
some aneuploidy) can be considered sex-chromosome DSD. These 
conditions include Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY and variants), 
Turner syndrome (45,X and variants), trisomy X (47,XXX and 
variants), XYY syndrome (47,XYY and variants), 45,X/46,XY 
mosaicism and its variants, and true sex-chromosome chimerism 
(46,XX/46,XY) (Table 21.3).
There can be atypical genital appearance at birth if a Y chro­
mosome or Y-chromosome fragment is present in some but not 
all cells due to sex-chromosome chimerism or mosaicism, but 
Klinefelter syndrome and classic Turner syndrome in which there 
is no Y-chromosomal material do not typically cause differences in 
genital appearance, although hypospadias may be more common 
in Klinefelter syndrome, particularly for variants in which four or 
more sex chromosomes are present. In many cases of classic sex-
chromosome aneuploidy, the diagnosis is made in childhood or 
later during evaluation of characteristic features, impaired puber­
tal development, or infertility. More detailed descriptions of the 
features and long-term management of some of these conditions 
are provided in the relevant chapters (e.g., Turner syndrome in 
Chapter 23, Klinefelter syndrome in Chapters 17 and 23).
Klinefelter Syndrome and Variants
Klinefelter syndrome and variants are the most common forms of 
sex-chromosome aneuploidy, with a reported incidence of 1 in 500 
to 1 in 1000 live male births.188 This incidence may be increas­
ing.189 The classic form of Klinefelter syndrome is associated with 
a 47,XXY karyotype and is caused by meiotic nondisjunction of 
the sex chromosomes during gametogenesis (Fig. 21.18).17 This 
abnormality occurs during spermatogenesis in approximately 
50% of patients and during oogenesis or postzygotic division in 
approximately 50%.188 Mosaic forms of Klinefelter syndrome 
(46,XY/47,XXY) likely represent mitotic nondisjunction within 
the developing zygote and are thought to occur in approximately 
10% of individuals with Klinefelter syndrome. Other variants 
with additional sex chromosomes (e.g., 48,XXXY or 48,XXYY) 
can be seen. These have more complex but overlapping 
phenotypes.
The clinical features of Klinefelter syndrome and its variants 
are summarized in Table 21.3.188 In the most obvious situations, 
a young man may be diagnosed because of small testes, gyneco­
mastia, poor virilization at puberty, eunuchoid proportions, or 
infertility. Other features, such as learning difficulties, speech and 
language delay, behavioral issues, and altered motor development, 
are common, and early support focusing on any specific areas of 
difficulty is important.190,191 It is likely that the clinical detec­
tion of Klinefelter syndrome based on postnatal karyotyping is 
biased toward detection of those individuals with a more severe 
phenotype, and it is estimated that as few as 25% of men with 
Klinefelter syndrome may be diagnosed throughout their lifespan. 
However, this pattern may change as diagnosis of Klinefelter syn­
drome on prenatal genetic testing becomes increasingly common.
The development of testes and a male genital phenotype in 
individuals with Klinefelter syndrome provides important evi­
dence for the key role of the presence of the Y chromosome (rather 
than X-chromosome number) in testis determination and subse­
quent prenatal androgen production. However, testicular func­
tion may not be completely intact; micropenis and hypospadias 
may be presenting features in some cases, and some studies report 
mildly elevated FSH concentrations during the postnatal “mini­
puberty,” together with testosterone levels in the lower half of the 
typical range.192
A more predictable elevation in gonadotropin concentrations 
(e.g., FSH, LH) occurs in the adolescent to young-adult period 
in patients with Klinefelter syndrome.193,194 By midadolescence, 
plasma concentrations of FSH are increased in 90% of patients 
with Klinefelter syndrome, and plasma concentrations of LH 
are increased in 80%. Other serum markers of testicular func­
tion (e.g., peripubertal inhibin B, midpubertal INSL3) are often 
below the typical ranges.194,195 Although puberty usually starts 
at a typical age with an appropriate rise in testosterone in classic 
Klinefelter syndrome, serum testosterone levels off around mid­
puberty (although sometimes not until later), and gonadotropins 
start to increase. In the majority of young adults, serum testoster­
one is in the lower half of the reference range.193,196 Testes usually 
864
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
remain small and firm; the median length and volume are 2.5 cm 
and 3 mL, but most are smaller than 3.5 cm (range 1–7 mL).193 
Testes typically appear inappropriately small for the degree of viril­
ization. The serum estradiol concentration is often elevated, which 
contributes to the gynecomastia observed during the adolescent 
period.
Testicular biopsy is not warranted clinically because the 
diagnosis can usually be made on karyotyping from periph­
eral blood cells. However, studies in which testicular histologic 
examination has been obtained report germ cell depletion, 
progressive hyalinization of seminiferous tubules, and Leydig 
cell hyperplasia after chronic LH stimulation.193 Testosterone 
levels need careful surveillance during puberty.194 A significant 
proportion of individuals with Klinefelter syndrome receive 
testosterone supplementation to fully induce puberty and to 
support sex characteristics, sexual desire, and bone mineral­
ization in adult life. Psychological support and educational 
support may be needed, as well as attention to potential long-
term issues such as diabetes. Men with Klinefelter syndrome have 
increased morbidity and mortality due to a range of health 
problems, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, 
and pulmonary, infectious, neurologic, and mental conditions.197 
Skewed X-inactivation or loss of X-inactivation, epigenetic 
changes, and altered gene expression, not only from the X 
chromosome but also from autosomes, seem to play a role in 
the pathophysiology and phenotypic variability of Klinefelter syn­
drome.198 Hypogonadism and reduced socioeconomic status 
may also impact long-term morbidity. Management of Kline­
felter syndrome in childhood, adolescence, and adulthood is 
described in recent guidelines199,200 and further discussed in 
Chapter 17.
Although some cases of spontaneous fertility have been reported 
for mosaic forms of Klinefelter syndrome (46,XY/47,XXY), 
the prospects for fertility in classic Klinefelter syndrome have

Turner Syndrome and Variants
Turner syndrome has an incidence of approximately 1 in 2500 live 
female births.203 The classic form of Turner syndrome is associated 
with a 45,X karyotype, which occurs in approximately one-half of 
individuals with this condition (see Fig. 21.18). Mosaic forms of 
Turner syndrome (45,X/46,XX) account for approximately one-
fourth of the patients, and the remainder have structural abnormali­
ties of the X chromosome, such as long-arm or short-arm deletions, 
isochromosomes, or ring chromosomes (see Fig. 21.18).203
A 45,X chromosomal constitution may be the consequence 
of nondisjunction or chromosome loss during gametogenesis in 
either parent that results in a sperm or ovum that lacks a sex chro­
mosome. Although errors in mitosis in normal zygotes often lead 
to mosaicism, a purely 45,X constitution may arise at the first 
cleavage division from anaphase lag with loss of a sex chromo­
some or, less often, from mitotic nondisjunction with failure of 
the complementary 47,XXX or 47,XYY cell line to survive.16 An 
estimated 2% of all zygotes have a 45,X karyotype, and approxi­
mately 7% of spontaneous abortuses have a 45,X karyotype, mak­
ing this the most frequent chromosomal anomaly in humans, but 
most zygotes do not survive to term.
The clinical features of Turner syndrome are highly variable, 
and the age at diagnosis can be similarly variable. For example, 
a prenatal diagnosis of Turner syndrome may be made inciden­
tally on prenatal genetic testing or after the detection of increased 
nuchal translucency on fetal ultrasound scanning.203 In early 
infancy, the diagnosis should be considered in females with 
lymphedema, nuchal folds, low hairline, and/or left-sided cardiac 
defects. Unexplained growth failure or characteristic somatic fea­
tures (e.g., abnormal nails, widely spaced nipples, abnormal car­
rying angle, recurrent ear infections) may point to the diagnosis 
during childhood, and Turner syndrome should be considered in 
all girls with pubertal absence or delay associated with hypergonad­
otropic hypogonadism. The clinical features of Turner syndrome 
are summarized in Table 21.3, and diagnosis and management 
are described in an international clinical practice guideline203 and 
are further discussed in Chapters 22 and 23. Growth hormone 
treatment can reduce the severity of short stature. Timely and 
appropriate introduction of estrogens is necessary in adolescence 
to ensure optimal growth, bone health, and psychosocial develop­
ment, as well as adequate breast and uterine development, thereby 
optimizing the opportunity to potentially carry a pregnancy by 
ovum donation in the future203; however, careful assessment of 
cardiovascular risk before and during pregnancy is essential (see 
later discussion).203 Women with Turner syndrome benefit from 
dedicated transition in adolescence and long-term follow-up with 
a focus on issues such as cardiovascular, bone, and reproductive 
health and hearing.203
Girls with classic Turner syndrome show ovarian dysgenesis.

recommended.203

detailed assessment and counseling before and during any poten­

45,X/46,XY Mosaicism and Variants
A mosaic 45,X/46,XY karyotype probably arises through ana­
phase lag during mitosis in the zygote, although Y-chromosomal 
abnormalities are sometimes seen, and interchromosomal rear­
rangements with loss of structurally abnormal Y material may be 
a common mechanism for variants of this condition. Although 
the classic form of this condition is associated with 45,X/46,XY 
mosaicism, 45,X/47,XYY, 45,X/46,XY/47,XYY, and other mosaic 
karyotypes can occur.
The true prevalence of this condition is unknown. Because indi­
viduals with 45,X/46,XY mosaicism are more likely to be referred 
for further assessment if they have atypical genital appearance 
most series of patients reported in the literature have probably 
reflected this bias; studies based on nonselected prenatal karyotyp­
ing have shown that most children with 45,X/46,XY mosaicism 
have typical male genital appearance.207–209
The phenotypes associated with 45,X/46,XY mosaicism are 
highly variable (see Table 21.3). The gonads can develop as dysge­
netic ovaries (ovarian-like stroma with sparse primordial follicles) 
or streak gonads (similar to those seen in Turner syndrome), nor­
mal or dysgenetic testes, or very rarely as ovotestes (with testicular 
and dysgenetic ovarian components within a single gonad).
Depending on the degree of Leydig cell activity (if any), the 
gonads may be positioned anywhere along the pathway of tes­
ticular descent, with streak gonads more likely to be intraabdomi­
nal and well-formed testes more likely to be in the inguinoscrotal 
region. Marked differences in gonadal development and histologic

gle gonad.210
All possible genital phenotypes have been reported, rang­
ing from typical female external genitalia or mild clitoromegaly 
through all stages of atypical genital appearance to hypospadias or 
typical male external genitalia.207,210–213 Asymmetry of the exter­
nal genitalia strongly suggests asymmetric gonadal development 
(i.e., mixed gonadal dysgenesis).
Müllerian structures may be present if there is absent or 
impaired AMH production by Sertoli cells, and these structures 
are also often asymmetric. The presence of a hemiuterus and fal­
lopian tube on the side of the more dysgenetic gonad in some 
cases of mixed gonadal dysgenesis provides important evidence for 
the paracrine actions of AMH on developing müllerian structures.
Somatic features associated with a 45,X/46,XY karyotype 
are also highly variable and do not always correlate well with the 
gonadal phenotype.207,210,212,213 Clinical features reminiscent 
of Turner syndrome, such as short stature, nuchal folds, low-set 
hairline, and cardiac and renal abnormalities, have been reported 
in 14% to 70% of individuals.210,214,215 Ongoing monitoring for 
features associated with Turner syndrome (e.g., thyroid function, 
hearing, and cardiac anomalies; see Chapter 23) is therefore appli­
cable for this group of individuals.203 Furthermore, many families 
benefit from the psychological support and education that can be 
linked to specialist services.
Sex designation can be difficult in individuals with 45,X/46,XY, 
and several factors should be considered, including probable gender 
identity, genital appearance and urogenital anatomy, fertility and 
reproductive options, risk of gonadal malignancy, and potential 
need for hormone replacement. Recommendation for sex designa­
tion should be handled like any other intervention, with a careful 
discussion of risks, benefits, and potential outcomes. Most infants 
with female or minimally virilized genitalia are raised as female, 
and the presence of a uterus or hemiuterus may allow the potential 
for pregnancy by ovum donation in the future, although predict­
ing future function can be difficult and, as noted above, the risk of 
cardiac complications is high. Spontaneous onset of puberty, spon­
taneous menarche, and very rarely spontaneous pregnancy have 
been reported in girls and women with 45,X/46,XY DSD and vari­
ants.216,217 As with girls with classic Turner syndrome, there may 
be risks associated with pregnancy due to cardiovascular anomalies. 
Intraabdominal streak-like (i.e., flat, scar-like gonads) and dysge­
netic gonads are thought to pose a significant risk of germ cell tumor, 
and prophylactic gonadectomy should be considered.211,213,218 
The risk of germ cell tumors (most commonly gonadoblastoma) 
in individuals with 45,X/46,XY DSD is estimated to be 15% to 
40%.214,216,219 Estrogen replacement is required to induce breast 
and uterine development in adolescence, and the addition of pro­
gestins is important to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and allows 
menstruation if a uterus is present. Growth hormone (GH) treat­
ment has been used when short stature is present, but no large trials 
have been performed to assess this group of patients. Usually there 
is a significantly reduced growth spurt during puberty, and some 
studies have suggested use of GH from earlier in childhood may 
optimize growth.212,220 Similarly, limited long-term outcome data 
on gender identity or psychosexual functioning are available.
Infants with significant virilization of the external genitalia are 
usually raised as male. Testosterone can sometimes be given to pro­
mote phallic growth in infancy, and hypospadias repair is usually 
offered as a one-stage or two-stage procedure, depending on the 
severity of the hypospadias. Attempts should be made to perform 
orchidopexy as a one-stage or two-stage procedure because there 
may be a significant risk of malignancy in these gonads.215 Gonad­
ectomy should be considered for gonads that cannot be placed in a 
palpable position; some have advocated for close monitoring, but 
imaging is not able to detect early neoplastic changes in abdomi­
nal gonads.211,213,221 Gonads that can be secured within the scro­
tum need careful monitoring by palpation/self-examination and 
imaging to detect changes suggestive of malignancy.221 At the 
time of orchidopexy and in adolescence, biopsy can be used to 
assess for premalignant changes and estimate the risk of germ cell 
cancer. Puberty should be carefully monitored to ensure adequate 
endogenous testosterone production. Most boys enter puberty 
spontaneously, but a significant number then develop andro­
gen insufficiency requiring testosterone supplementation.213,215 
Reduced final height is common, and variable response to GH has 
been reported.215,222
Designation of sex and management of a 45,X/46,XY child 
with an intermediate degree of virilization is a difficult situation 
for families and physicians, and long-term outcome data for this 
group are scant. Individuals usually have no uterus, may undergo 
gonadectomy because of tumor risk, and may undergo urogeni­
tal surgery. Folliculogenesis is rare, and spermatogenesis is often 
absent even if the gonads are intact (although focal spermatogen­
esis has been observed in gonadectomy samples in 25% of post­
pubertal patients),215 and individuals may have a significantly 
reduced height potential. There are limited data on gender iden­
tity outcomes; in one series of 11 children with mixed gonadal 
dysgenesis raised as girls, 6 later declared a male gender identity, 
but other studies have not reported gender dysphoria.223 Detailed 
assessment of each child is important, and an individualized 
approach by an experienced multidisciplinary team is important 
for long-term monitoring, management, and support. Long-term 
outcome data from larger studies may provide better guidance on 
the management of this group of individuals in the future.
A 45,X/46,XY mosaic karyotype can also be associated with 
a typical male genital phenotype and apparently normal tes­
tis development. Initial cases of typical-appearing males with a 
45,X/46,XY karyotype were described after screening of fam­
ily members as potential bone marrow transplant donors, but 
later studies of amniocentesis showed that 90% of infants with a 
45,X/46,XY karyotype have typical male genital appearance and 
apparently normal testes, and postnatally, these individuals may be 
diagnosed because of short stature or infertility.208,209,224,225 There 
seems to be variable correlation between the degree of mosaicism 
on peripheral blood sampling and gonadal or somatic phenotype. 
Monitoring of gonadal function and growth, assessment for pre­
malignant changes of the gonads, and cardiac and renal screening 
are advised in individuals with a typical male phenotype or minor 
genital anomalies because they are at risk for abnormal growth, 
Sertoli cell dysfunction, gonadal germ cell tumor, and cardiac and 
renal malformations.215,224 
Ovotesticular Differences of Sex Development
The diagnosis of ovotesticular DSD requires the presence of ovar­
ian tissue (containing follicles) and testicular tissue in the same or 
the opposite gonad (Fig. 21.19; see Table 21.3). Gonadal stroma 
arranged in whorls, similar to what is found in a typical ovary but 
lacking oocytes, is a common finding in a dysgenetic or streak 
gonad and is not considered sufficient evidence to designate the 
rudimentary gonad as an ovary or ovotestis.
Ovotesticular DSD is an uncommon condition in the United 
States and Europe, occurring in less than 5% of babies referred 
868
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
because of atypical genitalia, but is a common cause of atypical 
genitalia in southern Africa; the molecular etiology for this is 
not currently known.226 Ovotesticular DSD can occur in several 
different scenarios. The classic diagnosis is 46,XX/46,XY chime­
rism (see “Chromosomal Sex”), which is found in approximately 
20% to 30% of children with ovotestes and occurs in all ances­
tral backgrounds (Table 21.4).227,228 Somewhat more prevalent is 
ovotesticular DSD associated with an XX karyotype. In a propor­
tion of cases, this can occur due to specific variants in NR5A1/
SF1 affecting the Arg92 amino acid residue, loss of function 
of RSPO1, WNT4, or NR2F2/COUP-TFII, the presence of 
SRY, or increased expression of SOX9 or SOX3.70,71,125,229,230 
The molecular basis of these conditions is discussed later (see 
“XX Ovotesticular and XX Testicular Differences of Sex Devel­
opment”). Finally, ovotestes have rarely been reported in sev­
eral conditions associated with XY gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., 
MAP3K1, SOX9).231–233
Patients with ovotesticular DSD often have asymmetric gonadal 
development and sometimes may be subclassified according to the 
type and location of the gonads.4 Three forms are possible: lat­
eral (20%) with a testis on one side and an ovary on the other, 
bilateral (30%) with ovotestes present bilaterally, and unilateral 
cases (50%) with an ovotestis present on one side and an ovary 
or testis on the other. It has been suggested that the left gonad 
is more likely to develop as an ovary, whereas the right gonad is 
more likely to develop as a testis; the reason for this is unknown. 
An ovary is likely to be in its typical anatomic position, whereas a 
testis or ovotestis can be anywhere along the pathway of testicular 
descent and is often found in the inguinal region.
Differentiation of the external and internal genitalia and 
development of secondary sex characteristics vary in ovotesticu­
lar DSD depending on the gonadal hormones produced.234,235 
Most patients who present early have atypical genital appearance 
and/or significant hypospadias. Cryptorchidism is common, but 
often at least one gonad is palpable, usually in the labioscrotal 
fold or inguinal region, and is often associated with an inguinal 
hernia. The differentiation of the internal genital structures is 
influenced primarily by the ipsilateral gonad, and a hemiuterus 
or rudimentary uterus is often present on the side of the ovary 
or ovotestis.
Breast development at the time of puberty is common in ovo­
testicular DSD.235 Menses occur in a significant proportion of 
cases in which a uterus is present, and ovulation and pregnancy 
have been reported in a number of patients with a XX karyo­
type when an ovary is present. However, progressive virilization 
can occur in girls with testicular tissue, which can result in voice 
changes and clitoral enlargement during adolescence. Individuals 
reared as male often present with hypospadias and undescended 
testes, although bilateral scrotal ovotestes have been reported. 
These individuals can experience significant estrogenization at the 
time of puberty and may have cyclic hematuria if a uterus is pres­
ent. Spermatogenesis is rare, and interstitial fibrosis of the testis is 
common. Spermatogenesis requires Y-chromosomal genes other 
than SRY, so boys with XX ovotesticular DSD will not produce 
sperm.
Although ovotesticular DSD is rare, the diagnosis should be 
considered in all patients with atypical genital appearance. A 
46,XX/46,XY karyotype strongly suggests the diagnosis, but the 
detection of an XX or XY karyotype does not exclude the diag­
nosis, especially if there is genital asymmetry. Pelvic imaging with 
ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is useful for 
visualizing internal genitalia. The presence of testicular tissue may 
be detected by measurement of basal testosterone, AMH, and 
inhibin B in the first months of life and by measuring basal AMH 
in childhood. Ovarian tissue is more difficult to detect in early 
childhood, although estradiol, inhibin A, and follicular response 
to repeated injection of recombinant human FSH can provide 
useful information.183 Examination under anesthesia and laparos­
copy may provide the most detailed information about internal 
structures and allow a biopsy to confirm the diagnosis of ovotes­
ticular DSD when other forms of DSD have been excluded.236,237 
However, the biopsy sometimes does not sample all the tissues 
present in a gonad.237
The management of ovotesticular DSD depends on the age at 
diagnosis, genital development, internal structures, and reproduc­
tive capacity. Data on gender outcomes for ovotesticular DSD are 
scant, given the rarity of the condition, but gender outcomes for 
other DSD conditions characterized by variable degrees of action 
of gonadal androgens (partial gonadal dysgenesis, partial andro­
gen insensitivity) may be applicable, with individuals with little to 
no virilization of the external genitalia more likely to identify as 
girls/women and those with significant virilization more likely to 
identify as boys/men, but with considerable variability for those 
with intermediate degrees of virilization. Other factors to consider

in recommending gender designation include the prospects for

If an individual with ovotesticular DSD who identifies as a 
girl does not desire virilization, functional testicular tissue could 
potentially be removed before puberty, with efficacy monitored 
postoperatively by measuring serum AMH and testosterone. 
Potentially, GnRH agonists could be used to temporarily delay 
puberty if the young person needs more time to understand 
the condition and be involved in decisions about gonadectomy 
(whether complete or partial). Although still experimental, 
options for cryopreserving gonadal tissue are being explored. 
The risk of tumor in ovotesticular tissue of XX patients is not 
known but is likely to be low, given the absence of Y-chromo­
somal material and the fact that the testicular tissue is usually 
well differentiated.21
For individuals raised as boys, patients and families should be 
counseled that the presence of ovarian tissue has little to no func­
tional consequence before puberty, and removal of ovarian tissue 
(which is irreversible) should therefore be deferred at least until 
late childhood. Again, cryopreservation of gonadal tissue may 
emerge as an option but is currently experimental. When puberty 
starts, GnRH agonists or aromatase inhibitors may be considered 
on a trial basis if more time is needed to make decisions. If mülle­
rian structures are present, there is often no harm in leaving them 
intact, but in rare cases in which müllerian structures are causing 
problems with hematuria or urinary retention, these structures can 
be removed by an experienced surgeon, with extreme care not to 
disrupt the blood supply to any testicular tissue being preserved.
The capacity for gonadal sex steroidogenesis varies widely 
across individuals with ovotesticular DSD, and sex-hormone sup­
plementation may (or may not) be required for complete pubertal 
development and in adult life. 
XY Differences of Sex Development
The XY DSD can be categorized as conditions affecting testicu­
lar development, conditions affecting androgen synthesis, condi­
tions affecting androgen action, and other conditions affecting sex 
development (Table 21.5; see also Fig. 21.7).
Conditions Affecting Testicular Development
Conditions affecting testicular development can have a spectrum 
of phenotypes and presentations. Complete testicular dysgenesis, a 
condition sometimes called Swyer syndrome, is associated with a 
complete lack of virilization of the external genitalia and persistent 
müllerian structures due to low AMH production. In contrast, 
partial gonadal dysgenesis may be associated with a range of pheno­
types, ranging from clitoromegaly to atypical genital appearance 
to isolated hypospadias. A uterus or uterine remnant and vagina 
may be present. Subtle forms of testicular dysgenesis can present 
with a small penis, or male infertility in the absence of an external 
genital phenotype.
Several single-gene disorders have been described in patients 
with various degrees of testicular dysgenesis. Table 21.5 summa­
rizes these factors, and the role of many of these factors in devel­
opment has already been discussed (see “Testis Determination”). 
Some are discussed in more detail in the following subsections (in 
alphabetical order). Although associated features can sometimes 
help to direct genetic analysis, often there are no other findings, 
and a genetic diagnosis is currently reached in only about 20% to 
40% of individuals with XY testicular dysgenesis.
Single-Gene Disorders
Chromobox Homolog 2: CBX2. Chromobox homolog 2 
(CBX2) is a human homolog of the polycomb protein M33. Dele­
tion of Cbx2 causes development of the gonads as ovaries in XY 
mice.238 Loss-of-function mutations in CBX2 were described in a 
XY girl with a uterus and ovaries who was diagnosed by prenatal 
karyotyping, but CBX2 variants in humans are rare.47 CBX2 may 
stabilize the testicular pathway through the repression of genes 
involved in ovarian development.239 
Desert Hedgehog: DHH. The hedgehog signaling pathways 
play an important role in many aspects of neuronal, skeletal, and 
endocrine development. A homozygous mutation in the desert 
hedgehog gene (DHH) was originally reported in a patient with 
partial gonadal dysgenesis and minifascicular neuropathy.117 Sub­
sequently, a number of DHH changes have been found in patients 
with complete XY gonadal dysgenesis or, more often, Leydig cell 
defects, with or without apparent neurologic features.118,174 
DEAH (Asp-Glu-Ala-His)-box Helicase 37: DHX37. DHX37 
encodes an RNA helicase involved in biogenesis of ribosomes, 
which regulate transcription, splicing, translation, and degrada­
tion of RNA. It is required for maturation of the small ribosomal 
subunit, which plays a role in dissociation of the U3 small nucle­
olar RNA from preribosomal complexes. Heterozygous variants 
and one homozygous variant have recently been identified in a 
significant percentage of individuals in several cohorts with non­
syndromic XY gonadal dysgenesis (7%–14%) or testicular regres­
sion syndrome (14%–50%).240,241 These variants are found in or 
very close to highly conserved motifs in the RecA1 and RecA2 
domains that bind adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and target 
RNA sequences (Fig. 21.20). The pathophysiologic mechanism 
by which DHX37 mutations result in testicular dysgenesis is cur­
rently unclear. Because other ribosomopathies are associated with 
an increased cancer risk, it will be important to collect long-term 
follow-up data from individuals with DHX37 mutations.242 
Doublesex-Related and Mab3-Related Transcription Factor 
1: DMRT1. DMRT1, a gene with sex-specific homologs in Dro­
sophila (doublesex gene) and Caenorhabditis elegans (Mab3) that are 
expressed in early gonadal development, plays an important role 
in supporting testis development.113,243 Deletions of the region 
of chromosome 9p24-pter containing DMRT1 are associated 
with XY gonadal dysgenesis.244 A partial deletion of DMRT1 and 
a dominant-negative point mutation in DMRT1 have also been 
seen in patients with XY DSD.245,246 
Gata-Binding Protein 4: GATA4 and Friend of GATA 2 
(FOG2): ZFPM2. GATA4 is a four–zinc-finger transcription 
factor involved in early testis development and heart development. 
Haploinsufficiency of GATA4 or heterozygous loss-of-function 
changes are well established in a range of cardiac defects, such 
as atrial and ventricular septal defects. More recently, hetero­
zygous GATA4 mutations have been shown to cause testicular 
dysgenesis with or without cardiac anomalies.247 These mutations 
can be transmitted by a mother in a sex-limited dominant 
manner. Reported changes may disrupt interactions between 
GATA4 and its cofactor, friend of GATA 2 (FOG2, also known as 
ZFPM2). FOG2 is a key coregulator of GATA4, and missense 
mutations in the gene encoding FOG2 (ZFPM2) have been 
described in individuals with XY gonadal dysgenesis.174,248,249 
The point mutations affect interactions with GATA4, and 
some have been described previously in patients with cardiac 
defects, highlighting the variable penetrance of gonadal and 
cardiac phenotypes following disruption of the GATA4/FOG2 
complex.

Mastermind-Like 
Domain-Containing 
1: 
MAMLD1. 
MAMLD1 (formerly called CXORF6) is a gene on the X chromo­
some that encodes a protein expressed in the developing testes. 
Hemizygous mutations in MAMLD1 were originally described 
in boys with isolated severe hypospadias, but a range of pheno­
types has since been described, although some of the reported 
MAMLD1 variants have subsequently been found to be common 
polymorphisms rather than pathogenic variants.250 MAMLD1 
disruption results in a defect in fetal Leydig cell development and 
function. Oligogenic inheritance may be responsible for the wide 
range of phenotypes.251 
Mitogen-Activated Protein Kinase Kinase Kinase-1: MAP3K1. 
MAP3K1 is a component of one of several kinase signaling path­
ways involved in organogenesis, and heterozygous splice-site or 
point mutations in MAP3K1 have been described in individuals 
with impaired testis development.98 MAP3K1 is expressed in early 
testis cords and Sertoli cells in mice, and disruption of MAP3K1 has 
been described in diverse phenotypes ranging from 46,XY complete 
testicular dysgenesis to hypospadias and micropenis with cryptor­
chidism. Familial cases have a clear autosomal-dominant inheri­
tance. MAP3K1 mutations may be one of the more common causes 
of 46,XY DSD, and routine screening has been recommended in 
all patients with 46,XY complete or partial gonadal dysgenesis.233 
However, the pathogenicity of many variants is unclear. 
Myelin Regulatory Factor (MYRF). Myelin regulatory factor is 
a membrane protein that can autocleave to release a domain that 
acts as a transcription factor. Pathogenic variants in MYRF have 
been associated with a range of syndromic phenotypes, including 
congenital diaphragmatic hernia, cardiac defects, encephalopa­
thy, and XY DSD. The urogenital phenotype includes atypical 
external genital appearance and cryptorchidism and has also been 
described in individuals without syndromic features.252 Reduced 
levels of testosterone and AMH indicate impaired function of 
both Leydig and Sertoli cells. Anomalies/absence of the ovaries 
and uterus have been described in XX individuals.252
Steroidogenic Factor 1: NR5A1. SF1 (encoded by NR5A1) is 
a member of the nuclear receptor superfamily that regulates the 
transcription of at least 30 genes involved in gonadal develop­
ment, adrenal development, spleen development, steroidogenesis, 
and reproduction.58,253 NR5A1 mutations were first reported 
in two XY individuals with female external genitalia, persistent 
müllerian structures, and primary adrenal insufficiency.64,65 The 
first variant was a de novo heterozygous p.Gly35Glu change in 
the P-box primary DNA-binding region of SF1; the second was 
a recessively inherited homozygous p.Arg92Gln mutation in the 
A-box secondary DNA-binding region (Fig. 21.21). These changes 
resulted in impaired DNA binding. The combination of gonadal 
and adrenal phenotypes is uncommon, and it initially seemed that 
disruption of SF1 would be a rare cause of DSD in humans.
However, the past decade has seen a different picture emerging 
as an ever-increasing number of monoallelic (heterozygous) non­
sense, frameshift, and missense mutations in NR5A1 have been 
associated with a spectrum of XY DSD conditions in individuals 
with normal adrenal function (see Fig. 21.21).58,66,254,255 These 
changes usually result in haploinsufficiency of SF1. A range of phe­
notypes is seen, most commonly mild gonadal dysgenesis and sig­
nificantly impaired virilization, where alterations in SF1 are found 
in approximately 15% of cases.58 These variations usually arise de 
novo but may be inherited from the mother in a sex-limited domi­
nant fashion (i.e., the mother carries the mutation but is unaf­
fected) or even from the father and occasionally may be autosomal 
recessive.65 In XY individuals with female-appearing genitalia at 
birth, significant virilization may occur during puberty, when tes­
tosterone levels in the normal male range have been found.256 In 
some situations, there is a family history of ovarian insufficiency, 
and females in the family may be at risk of developing ovarian 
insufficiency in the future.67 Loss of SF1 function is also reported 
in some boys with severe hypospadias and undescended testes 
(∼5%), bilateral anorchia, and a small penis and in men with 
infertility (∼2%).257–259 Oligogenic effects of other genes have also 
been proposed to influence phenotype.260,261 Therefore variable 
loss of SF1 activity is associated primarily with different degrees of 
testicular or ovarian dysfunction in humans. Adrenal function may 
need to be monitored over time, but at present, adrenal insuffi­
ciency does not seem prevalent. In addition, splenic abnormalities 
have been described, ranging from asplenia to polysplenia.253,262 
Although their prevalence among patients with NR5A1 mutations 
is currently unclear, assessment of spleen anatomy and function by 
ultrasound and search for Howell-Jolly bodies in blood has been 
recommended, given the serious consequences that (functional) 
asplenia may have.262 Defining the molecular basis in different 
families can be important for counseling, especially about the

Sex-Determining Region of the Y Chromosome: SRY and 
SRY-Related Homeobox Genes 8 and 9 (SOX8 and SOX9). The 
sequence of events leading to the identification of SRY as the 
primary testis-determining gene and the actions of SRY in tes­
tis development were described earlier. SRY is a 204–amino acid 
HMG-box transcription factor that is encoded by a single exon 
on the Y chromosome (Yp11.3) (see Fig. 21.5).88 The discovery 
of inactivating mutations in SRY in patients with 46,XY gonadal 
dysgenesis confirmed the key role played by this factor in testis 
determination in humans.30
Approximately 10% of individuals with the complete form of 
46,XY gonadal dysgenesis have inactivating mutations in SRY.87 
Most of the mutations occur in the HMG-box DBD of the SRY 
protein (Fig. 21.22), a region that is involved in binding and 
bending of DNA.88 Rare mutations in the 5′ and 3′ flanking 
regions occur.263 The HMG box contains at least two nuclear 
localization signals that bind calmodulin/exportin 4 and impor­
tin B. Mutations in these nuclear localization signal domains 
in the HMG box of SRY result in failure to transport the SRY 
protein into the nucleus, and subtle alterations in nuclear import 
and export can lead to XY gonadal dysgenesis.91 Most individu­
als with SRY mutations present as girls who have no pubertal 
development (Swyer syndrome). Gonadal tumor risk in this 
group is high.
Heterozygous mutations of the autosomal SOX9 gene (17q24-
q25) cause campomelic dysplasia.100,101 Features of this condition 
include bowed long bones, hypoplastic scapulae, a deformed pel­
vis, 11 pairs of ribs, a small thoracic cage, cleft palate, macro­
cephaly, micrognathia, hypertelorism, and a variety of cardiac and 
renal defects. Death from respiratory distress often occurs in the 
neonatal period, but long-term survival has been reported.

SOX9 is an important testis-determining gene, and it is the key 
regulator of testis determination downstream of SRY (see “Testis 
Determination”). Consistent with this hypothesis, three-fourths 
of 46,XY patients with heterozygous SOX9 mutations have dys­
genetic gonads, but a wide range of genital phenotypes can 
be seen, from typical male to typical female appearance.87 Histo­
logic examination of the gonads from XY patients with atypical or 
female genital appearance shows a similarly wide range of gonadal 
phenotypes, including streak gonads, dysgenetic testes, ovotestes, 
or even ovaries.231 Müllerian structures may or may not be pres­
ent, depending on the degree of gonadal dysgenesis. XX females 
with SOX9 mutations have typical female genital appearance and 
apparently normal ovaries.
The locus for campomelic dysplasia with XY DSD was mapped 
to 17q24.3-q25.1 after studies of three patients with balanced de 
novo reciprocal translocations, and SOX9 was proposed as a candi­
date gene based on expression studies in the mouse. Subsequently, 
missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splice-junction mutations 
have been detected in SOX9 in patients with campomelic dysplasia 
with or without gonadal dysgenesis.88 These mutations are usually 
heterozygous de novo changes. In one kindred, multiple siblings 
were affected due to germline mosaicism for a SOX9 mutation in 
a parent.231 The gonadal phenotype in this kindred varied in the 
two affected XY siblings: one of them had dysgenetic gonads; the 
other was reported to have normal ovaries.
The SOX9 gene has three exons and two introns; it encodes a 
509-residue protein that contains an HMG box with 71% homol­
ogy to that of the SRY protein and a C-terminal, transactivation 
domain (see Fig. 21.22). Unlike SRY, in which most mutations 
are located within the HMG box, SOX9 mutations are located 
throughout the protein: in the HMG box, in the C-terminal 
transactivation domain, and in a region that interacts with heat 
shock proteins (e.g., HSP70), with little relation between func­
tional domains and phenotype. Chromosomal translocations that 
disrupt regulatory elements upstream of the SOX9 promoter can 
be associated with a less severe phenotype or campomelic dysplasia
