In contrast, the likelihood of finding a pathogenic AR vari­
ant in those with a PAIS phenotype is much lower, even when 
other causes of a similar phenotype (e.g., partial gonadal dysgen­
esis due to NR5A1 variants) appear to have been excluded.391 
With improved sequencing technology, deep intronic mutations 
that affect splicing have been detected in some individuals.388 The 
genital phenotype in infants with presumed PAIS but without an 
AR mutation, as based on a validated external masculinization 
score (EMS), is no different than that in infants with PAIS with 
a proven AR mutation, but gynecomastia later in life is much less 
common.381,396,397 Boys with an AR mutation are more likely to 
have multiple genital surgeries than those without a mutation.381 
Birth weight for gestational age is significantly lower in mutation-
negative patients compared with infants with PAIS who have an 
AR gene mutation.288,398 It has been suggested that this form of 
XY DSD with fetal growth restriction is a discrete category that 
as yet remains unexplained. Collectively, these findings suggest 
that individuals labeled as having PAIS in the past may actually 
have had other causes of XY DSD (e.g., gonadal dysgenesis, con­
ditions affecting androgen synthesis). The term PAIS is therefore 
best reserved for individuals with AR mutations. Although there 
is evidence that the AR can interact with more than 200 unique 
coregulator proteins, no mutations in these coregulators have been 
associated with AIS, in contrast to findings in prostate cancer.399 
Management of Androgen Insensitivity Syndromes. Female 
sex designation and gender of rearing are recommended for indi­
viduals with CAIS, although recent studies have suggested that 
around 2% of individuals with CAIS may not identify as female 
later in life.400 Inguinal hernias need repair when presenting 
in infancy. Rather than performing gonadectomy at this early 
stage, delaying a decision about gonadectomy is favored, because 
this approach enables spontaneous puberty to occur, allows the 
patient to be involved in the decision-making process and does 
not substantially increase the risk for malignancy (discussed later 
in chapter). If gonadectomy has been performed before puberty, 
hormone induction of puberty is similar to that used for girls with 
other causes of hypogonadism, typically starting around 10 to 
11 years of age; the precise timing should consider the patient’s 
wishes, family history of pubertal timing, growth and the degree 
of skeletal maturation as assessed by bone age X-ray, and whether 
gonadotropins are starting to rise.401 In the absence of a uterus, 
hormone replacement can be continuous, unopposed estrogen, 
with no need for a progestin. Some adults with CAIS report 
improved well-being when androgen replacement is also given; 
the mechanism of this androgenic effect is not understood. One 
double-blind crossover trial found increased sexual desire with tes­
tosterone compared with estradiol treatment but otherwise found 
no difference in mental health outcomes or metabolic parame­
ters.402,403 Bone mineral density of the lumbar spine in women 
with CAIS with intact gonads is lower than that in typical XX 
women, which may indicate a direct effect of androgens on bone 
mineralization or may reflect relatively low estradiol levels, and 
women who have undergone gonadectomy have lower bone min­
eral density than those with intact gonads, suggesting insufficient 
estrogen replacement may also be involved.404 Optimal estrogen 
therapy is essential, as well as adequate calcium, vitamin D, and 
physical exercise. A small increase in fractures has been reported in 
AIS, although this study did not show any difference in underly­
ing osteoporosis.405
There is an increased risk of gonadal germ cell tumors in 
AIS, but with features that are distinct from those seen with XY 
gonadal dysgenesis. Germ cell maturation is delayed in the abnor­
mal microenvironment. Some of the immature germ cells may 
subsequently mature, and although many may undergo apoptosis, 
some may retain fetal characteristics and become premalignant/
malignant. Within the testicular environment, the premalignant 
lesion is termed germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) (previously 
called carcinoma in situ [CIS] or intratubular germ cell neoplasia 
unclassified [ITGNU]). GCNIS may progress to invasive germ 
cell tumors, most commonly a seminoma. Recently, the stage 
between maturational delay and GCNIS has been termed pre-
GCNIS.406 GCNIS cells express immunohistochemical markers 
such as placenta-like alkaline phosphatase (PLAP), c-KIT (the 
receptor for the stem cell factor SCF), POU5F1 (a transcription 
factor also called OCT3/4), and NANOG. However, in individu­
als with DSD, germ cells frequently show delayed maturation and 
prolonged expression of these markers. Therefore, additional his­
tologic criteria have been developed to distinguish maturational 
delay from GCNIS (see “Tumor Risk and DSD” later in the 
chapter). In addition, SCF (or KIT ligand [KITLG]) has been 
proposed as a marker specific for germ cell neoplasia that is not 
expressed in germ cells with maturational delay.406 Nearly all cases 
of GCNIS eventually progress to invasive germ cell cancer in indi­
viduals without DSD, but it is hypothesized that this progression 
requires androgenic activity and may therefore be relatively uncom­
mon in AIS.406,407 In CAIS, the risk of developing GCNIS or a 
germ cell tumor before puberty is low (on the order of 0.8%–
2%).408,409 Hence there is a general preference to delay a decision 
about gonadectomy until young adulthood to enable spontaneous 
puberty to occur.410 The risk of pre-GCNIS or GCNIS is estimated 
to be 10% to 14% in adolescent and adult individuals with CAIS, 
but development of germ cell malignancies seems more rare.407,409 
A recent study reported that 41 women with CAIS who had 
undergone a gonadectomy indicated that gonadectomy had a 
neutral to negative effect on their life, with a median score of 2.6 
(IQR 1.1) on a scale from 1 (very negative) to 5 (very positive).411 
Individuals should be thoroughly counseled about the benefits 
and risks of undergoing or delaying a gonadectomy. Some adults 
with CAIS elect to retain the gonads for various reasons, although 
monitoring can be difficult, especially in the case of abdominal 
gonads (see “Tumor Risk and DSD”).410
Surgery to bring abdominal gonads to a more superficial 
location is a potential option; a biopsy can be taken at the time 
of surgery to assess the risk of germ cell tumor.221 GCNIS and 
seminoma usually do not secrete tumor markers such as βhCG 
and α-fetoprotein (AFP), and GCNIS cannot be detected using 
ultrasound or MRI.412 Noninvasive monitoring may potentially 
become available with the development of techniques to measure 
embryonic microRNAs in serum, but this method is also currently 
unable to detect GCNIS.413 Common findings in CAIS gonads 
on MRI include Sertoli cell adenomas and epididymal cysts.412
Surgery in CAIS is generally confined to gonadectomy. For vag­
inal hypoplasia, self-dilatation is the first-line approach.414,415 This 
technique is effective in lengthening the vagina for most women 
with CAIS but requires time; it should therefore be started only 
when a patient is thinking about sexual relations and when there is 
clear focus and motivation. A specialist nurse or gynecologist with 
experience in vaginal dilatation is important to provide support 
and guidance, and several useful written materials are becoming 
available (e.g., www.dsdteens.org). In situations in which self-
dilatation is not appropriate or possible, surgical approaches to 
893
CHAPTER 21  Differences of Sex Development
vaginal dilation or vaginoplasty may be offered.414 A recent study 
showed high satisfaction both after vaginoplasty and vaginal dila­
tion, although sexual complaints such as pain or bleeding during or 
after intercourse were more common in women who had under­
gone vaginal interventions than those who had not.411
For children with PAIS, there has been an increasing trend in 
recent decades to choose a male gender of rearing.416 A recent 
prospective study of boys with PAIS showed the value of the EMS 
at birth as a predictor of pubertal development.417 Those with an 
EMS of 5 had spontaneous virilization at puberty. Further stud­
ies on this cohort of 27 boys with PAIS involved functional anal­
ysis of the mutant ARs using reporter gene assays. In contrast 
to the EMS as a predictor, the results were not a reliable indica­
tor of whether androgens would be required to induce pubertal 
virilization. However, such assays may have a place in guiding 
the magnitude of high-dose androgens sometimes required in 
adulthood in men with PAIS. Several surgical procedures may 
be required to correct hypospadias and relocate the testes in a 
scrotal sac. Gynecomastia is an almost universal finding as boys 
with PAIS reach puberty. This raises the possibility of prevention 
by the use of antiestrogens and aromatase inhibitors, thereby 
avoiding the need for surgical reduction mammoplasty, but long-
term safety has not been established. The risk of germ cell tumor 
of the testis had previously been reported to be high in PAIS, 
but more recent reports suggest a lower risk, comparable to that 
in CAIS; the previously reported association may have been due 
to misclassification of partial gonadal dysgenesis or other condi­
tions as PAIS.381,418 When scrotal in position, testes should be 
monitored by regular self-examination and periodic imaging by 
ultrasound. It has been suggested that bilateral testicular biop­
sies should be undertaken at the time of orchidopexy and after 
puberty to screen for the presence of GCNIS.419 In view of the 
risk of malignant progression, gonadectomy is advised if GCNIS 
is discovered, although an alternative may be irradiation of bilat­
eral in situ lesions.
When an infant with PAIS is raised as a girl, gonadectomy can 
be considered before puberty if the adolescent wishes to prevent 
virilization, or alternatively, this decision can be delayed while 
suppressing sex-steroid production using a GnRH analogue. If 
gonadectomy is performed, estrogen replacement is needed to 
induce puberty and for hormone replacement thereafter. Whether 
and when to perform genitoplasty is a subject of controversy and 
is discussed in “Surgery and DSD.” In MAIS, clinical presentation 
occurs either in adolescence because of gynecomastia or in adult­
hood because of male factor infertility. Reduction mammoplasty 
may be offered for the gynecomastia. Successful fertility after 
TESE in men with MAIS has been reported.420,421 
Other Conditions Affecting XY Sex Development
Persistent Müllerian Duct Syndrome. AMH is a glycoprotein 
homodimer that is secreted by the Sertoli cells of the develop­
ing testes from approximately 7 weeks after conception. It acts 
through the AMH type 2 receptor (AMHR2) between 8 and 12 
weeks after conception to cause regression of the müllerian ducts 
(see “Development of Reproductive Systems”).128
AMH is encoded by a 2.75-kb gene containing five exons in 
the region of chromosome 19p13.3. The AMHR2 is a serine/thre­
onine kinase with a single transmembrane domain that is encoded 
by an 11-exon gene on 12q13. Exons 1 to 3 code for the signal 
sequence and the extracellular domain of the AMHR2, exon 4 
codes for the transmembrane domain, and exons 5 through 11 
code for the intracellular serine/threonine domain.
Persistent müllerian duct syndrome (PMDS) is a condition 
in which XY males have well-developed testes and normal male 
external genitalia but also have müllerian duct derivatives. The 
diagnosis is often not made until a fallopian tube and uterus are 
incidentally encountered in patients undergoing inguinal hernia 
repair, orchidopexy, or abdominal surgery. In the more prevalent 
form, a boy presents with bilaterally undescended testes, and the 
uterus, fallopian tubes, and testes are in the pelvis. In other situa­
tions, a hernia contains a partially descended or scrotal testis, and 
the ipsilateral fallopian tube and uterus are in the hernia, which 
is known as hernia uteri inguinale. In some instances, the contra­
lateral testis and tube also are present in the hernial sac, known as 
transverse testicular ectopia.
Approximately one-half of all genetically proven cases of 
PMDS result from defects in AMH, and the other half are caused 
by mutations in its receptor.422–424 AMH gene mutations are most 
commonly found in Mediterranean and North African coun­
tries,425 and most familial mutations are homozygous. In contrast, 
mutations in the gene encoding AMHR2 are more commonly 
found in Northern Europe and the Middle East. Europeans are 
often compound heterozygous, with one of the mutations involv­
ing a 27-bp deletion in exon 10.426,427 Measurement of serum 
AMH can provide a useful means for guiding genetic analysis; 
patients with PMDS caused by mutations of the AMH gene typi­
cally have low or undetectable levels of serum AMH (except for 
the p.Gln496His mutation, which is thought to affect receptor 
binding), whereas AMH concentrations are normal for age or ele­
vated in patients with mutations in AMHR2. Approximately 12% 
of patients with PMDS have an idiopathic form, with no muta­
tion in AMH or AMHR2; they often have other malformations.424
The main aim of management of PMDS is to prevent testicular 
cancer and preserve fertility, which can be difficult. An increased 
prevalence of testicular degeneration has been described, which 
probably results from torsion of the testes and/or their anatomic 
location. Anatomic abnormalities of the epididymis and the vas 
deferens are common. Infertility may result from late orchidopexy 
or from mechanical problems associated with entrapment of 
the vas deferens in the müllerian derivatives. Treatment consists 
of early orchidopexy, which often requires removal of müllerian 
structures, although it should not be attempted to remove these 
in toto because this will likely damage the genital ducts or blood 
supply. Men with high pelvic testes rarely have successful orchi­
dopexy, and many of these individuals have androgen deficiency. 
Increasing rates of testicular malignancy have been reported in 
adult men with this condition, which further complicates long-
term management of gonads that cannot undergo orchidopexy.424 
Fertility is usually impaired, but successful TESE-ICSI has been 
reported in isolated cases.424 
Hypospadias. Hypospadias is incomplete fusion of the penile 
urethra due to an arrest in development of the urethral spongio­
sum and ventral prepuce.428 The normal embryologic resolution 
of penile curvature may also be interrupted, resulting in chor­
dee. It is a common congenital anomaly with an estimated birth 
prevalence of approximately 2 cases per 1000 live births, although 
this varies considerably between geographic areas.429 Analysis of 
data from 27 surveillance programs around the world showed a 
1.6-fold increase in the rate of hypospadias between 1980 and 
2010, but there were differences in trends between programs.429 
The cause is unknown in most cases, but it is assumed that there 
is an interplay of genetic and environmental factors.430–432 Muta­
tions in candidate genes such as MAMLD1, NR5A1, HSD17B3, 
SRD5A2, and AR are found in a minority of cases.433,434 There is a 
894
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
familial clustering of cases in hypospadias, with a 7% incidence of 
one or more additional affected family members.435 Four chromo­
somal regions have been identified in familial hypospadias by fine-
mapping analysis of genes involved in steroid metabolism.436 A 
genome-wide association study involving a total of 2978 cases and 
7298 controls of European ancestry identified 18 genetic loci asso­
ciated with hypospadias at genome-wide significance.432 None of 
these loci lie near known XY DSD genes, so distinct pathways 
may underlie the susceptibility to hypospadias.
Hypospadias is associated with increased maternal age, mul­
tiple births, maternal exposure to diethylstilbestrol in utero, 
paternal subfertility, maternal vegetarian diet, maternal smoking, 
assisted reproductive techniques, paternal exposure to pesticides, 
and fetal growth restriction.437 The association with low birth 
weight is remarkably consistent across all studies of idiopathic 
hypospadias.438
Hypospadias may be the only phenotype in mild forms of XY 
DSD, but it is not entirely clear when an evaluation for DSD is 
needed in a child with isolated hypospadias. Recommendations 
have been made to conduct such an evaluation if the hypospa­
dias is severe (midshaft or more proximal) or if there are addi­
tional genital findings (e.g., unilateral or bilateral cryptorchidism, 
micropenis, anomalies of the scrotum), but some have suggested 
that genetic screening may also be beneficial in milder forms of 
isolated hypospadias.434 However, cost-effectiveness of these dif­
ferent approaches has yet to be reported.
Management is generally surgical. The urethral meatus is relo­
cated to the glans, and the penis is straightened by correcting any 
chordee to give a forward-directed urinary stream and the ability 
to have sexual intercourse. Numerous techniques are described; 
repairs may require more than one stage, usually starting at 6 to 
18 months of age or deferred until 4 years or later.439 Delaying 
surgery allows the child to be involved in decisions regarding sur­
gery, but older age at surgery has been reported to be a risk factor 
for complications.440 A course of testosterone is often given to 
induce penile growth before surgery, particularly if micropenis is 
present.439 The severity of the hypospadias may not be apparent 
until release of the chordee. Complications include fistula forma­
tion, meatal stenosis, urethral stricture, and residual chordee. Fol­
low-up studies in adulthood indicate a less satisfactory cosmetic 
appearance compared with control subjects, shorter penile length, 
and suboptimal urinary and/or sexual outcomes in approximately 
half of individuals.441–443 These problems were more common in 
severe forms of hypospadias and after multiple surgeries. 
Anorchia and Cryptorchidism. The term testicular regression 
syndrome (previously called absent testis syndrome or vanishing testis 
syndrome, but we recommend avoiding these terms because they 
can sound frivolous to families) is used to describe the pheno­
type of bilateral anorchia in a male infant with otherwise typical-
appearing genitalia. The phenotype suggests the presence of testes 
in early gestation functioning appropriately to differentiate male 
external genitalia, induce müllerian duct regression, and stabilize 
wolffian duct development. It is estimated to occur in approxi­
mately 1:20,000 boys and to be the underlying condition in 0.5% 
to 4.5% of boys with cryptorchidism.444 Surgical exploration and 
histologic findings typically show nubbins of fibrous tissue devoid 
of any testicular tissue attached to a blind-ending vas deferens. 
The cause of testicular regression syndrome is unknown in most 
cases, but an interruption of the testis blood supply by a torsion 
or vascular occlusion event in utero has been proposed. Bilateral 
anorchia with a normally differentiated but small phallus (micro­
penis) is a variant of the syndrome and may represent a form of 
testicular dysgenesis. Familial cases suggest that there may be a 
genetic cause in some cases. Indeed, mutations in DHX37 have 
been found to cause testicular regression syndrome as well as 
XY gonadal dysgenesis (see previous section on DHX37). These 
mutations account for approximately 20% of all cases of testicular 
regression syndrome.242
Diagnosis is based on a combination of biochemical tests, 
imaging studies, and/or surgical exploration. An undetectable 
serum AMH level coupled with elevated serum levels of gonad­
otropins (particularly FSH) is highly predictive of the absence 
of testes.445 If such findings are present, there may be no need 
for surgical exploration or karyotype. Androgen replacement is 
required to induce puberty at around 11 to 12 years of age. Tes­
ticular prostheses can be inserted if and when the young person 
desires. It is unclear to what extent the testicular nubbins pose a 
risk for gonadal tumors, but most studies suggest that the risk is 
low, and whether nubbins should be removed surgically remains 
a subject of debate.
Cryptorchidism (i.e., lack of testicular descent at birth) is the 
most common congenital abnormality in boys, affecting 2% to 
9% of term infants.144,446 Because testicular descent occurs late 
in gestation, undescended testes are a common finding in prema­
ture baby boys. There is epidemiologic evidence of an increasing 
prevalence of cryptorchidism in some countries.444 Longitudinal 
studies demonstrate that some boys with the expected spontane­
ous descent of the testis by early infancy experience an unexpected 
reascent of the testis to a cryptorchid position in later childhood. 
It is now recognized that there are just as many boys with acquired 
cryptorchidism as there are with congenital cryptorchidism, and 
these conditions may have a shared etiology.444,447 There is a strong 
association with low birth weight, disorders of the HPG axis, and a 
number of syndromes, but in the majority of situations, the cause 
of maldescent is unknown. Unilateral cryptorchidism does not 
require an evaluation to identify an underlying cause, but bilateral 
cryptorchidism could be a sign of hypergonadotropic hypogonad­
ism or of hypogonadotropic hypogonadotropism, which could in 
turn be a sign of combined pituitary hormone deficiency. This 
would require prompt diagnosis and treatment to avoid neurocog­
nitive deficits due to untreated central hypothyroidism and pos­
sibly hypoglycemia (due to ACTH and GH deficiency).
Bilateral nonpalpable gonads can be the presenting feature in 
rare cases of XX CAH with otherwise full genital virilization. Uni­
lateral or bilateral cryptorchidism in the context of other signs of 
undervirilization, such as hypospadias, also warrants a DSD evalu­
ation. Mutations in INSL3 and the gene for the INSL3 receptor, 
RXFP2—factors involved in the transabdominal phase of testis 
descent—were reported in a few boys with cryptorchidism.448 
Cord blood levels of INSL3 but not testosterone are decreased 
in idiopathic cryptorchidism, particularly in infants whose testes 
descended by 3 months of age.449
Congenital and acquired forms of cryptorchidism differ in 
their management. Orchidopexy is the recommended treatment 
in the former after 6 months but preferably no later than 12 to 18 
months of age, according to recent guidelines.450,451 There is no 
consensus on the role of hormonal treatment with GnRH or hCG 
due to poor-quality evidence and lack of long-term data.451 It is 
not routinely recommended because complete testicular descent 
is often not achieved, reascent is common, and most patients 
eventually require surgical orchidopexy. Both positive and nega­
tive potential effects of hormonal treatment on germ cells and 
testicular volume have been reported. The European Urology 
Association/European Society for Paediatric Urology guidelines 
895
CHAPTER 21  Differences of Sex Development
recommend offering hormonal treatment to boys with bilateral 
undescended testes to possibly improve further fertility potential, 
whereas the Canadian Urological Association–Pediatric Urologist 
of Canada guideline considers such treatment experimental.451,452 
hCG has been shown to induce descent to a lower level in the 
majority of testes, so as neoadjuvant therapy, it may improve testis 
position before surgery to increase the chances of successful orchi­
dopexy.453 Some also recommend orchidopexy for acquired crypt­
orchidism, but an alternative approach is to wait until puberty 
because in more than 50% of cases, the testes descend sponta­
neously at this time.454 There is substantial evidence to indicate 
that the relative risk of germ cell tumor development in adulthood 
associated with cryptorchidism is more than halved if orchidopexy 
is undertaken before puberty.455 Early orchidopexy is also benefi­
cial for testis development and spermatogenesis, which translates 
into improved fertility.456 
Anatomic Defects of the Pelvis and Penis. Cloacal exstrophy 
is an important developmental condition that can affect genital 
development as part of a complex anatomic anomaly involving 
the bladder, usually with associated gastrointestinal, anorectal, 
and skeletal features. Penile agenesis is a very rare isolated defect 
in penile development. In both these conditions, there is usually 
typical androgen synthesis by the testes and androgen responsive­
ness in the brain, so a male gender identity is most likely. 
Endocrine Disruptors. The proposed increase in male repro­
ductive tract disorders (testicular cancer, abnormal spermatogen­
esis, cryptorchidism, and hypospadias) led to the concept that 
testicular dysgenesis syndrome (TDS) of fetal origin might be trig­
gered by exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) dur­
ing the fetal and perinatal periods.457,458 The U.S. Environmental 
Protection Agency has defined an EDC as an exogenous agent 
that interferes with synthesis, secretion, transport, metabolism, 
binding, action, or elimination of natural blood-borne hormones 
that are present in the body and are responsible for homeosta­
sis, reproduction, and developmental processes.459 The types of 
compounds generically include detergents, pesticides, and cos­
metics with postulated modes of action comprising estrogenic 
and antiandrogenic effects. Such a broad definition and the ubiq­
uity of thousands of compounds in the environment that may 
have endocrine-disrupting effects pose an enormous challenge 
for scientific studies to prove whether EDCs cause adverse health 
effects in humans and if so, what measures can be taken for pre­
vention. Analgesics commonly used during pregnancy, such as 
paracetamol/acetaminophen and ibuprofen, have also been sug­
gested as potential endocrine disruptors interfering with testicular 
and ovarian development.460–463
Classic toxicologic methods used in animals have provided 
valuable information, but there are important differences in sex 
development between species. A number of approaches have stud­
ied effects in human cells or tissues, for example, using xenografts 
of human fetal testis tissue in animals, to complement epidemio­
logic studies.464 Application of a phenotypic marker long used 
by toxicologists testing EDCs in animals has been validated in 
humans for epidemiologic studies.465 Anogenital distance (AGD) 
is significantly reduced in individuals with isolated hypospadias 
and cryptorchidism in comparison with normative data from 
individuals without these conditions (Fig. 21.32).466 As an exam­
ple of the application of this marker in epidemiologic studies in 
reproductive development, prenatal exposure to phthalates, which 
are widely used as plasticizers in many products, was associated 
with reduced AGD in males at birth.467,468 Another epidemio­
logic approach is the study of occupational exposure, which has 
revealed evidence of increased risk of hypospadias and crypt­
orchidism in the offspring of parents working with pesticides, 
industrial chemicals, cosmetics, and several other potentially toxic 
substances.469,470
The relevance of these epidemiologic findings to the assess­
ment of an individual child with DSD remains uncertain, 
although shared clinical features between TDS and DSD suggest 
there may be common etiologic factors. There is no consensus yet 
about effects on health from exposure to a myriad of chemicals 
over the lifespan or even the optimal toxicologic methodology to 
measure exposure.471,472 An expert panel has identified compel­
ling evidence for male infertility attributable to phthalate exposure 
and has estimated the financial burden that accrues to the Euro­
pean Union from the consequences of needing additional assisted 
reproductive technology procedures.473 A similar analysis can be 
undertaken to estimate the additional cases of cryptorchidism 
requiring orchidopexy. Adopting the precautionary principle to 
reduce exposure to chemicals to as low as is reasonably practicable 
is a sensible approach in the face of so much uncertainty about the 
adverse effects of EDCs on human health. This applies particularly 
to pregnant women who may need to take an analgesic. 
XX Differences of Sex Development
XX DSD can be divided into conditions affecting steroid-hormone 
synthesis that result in androgen excess (which are the most com­
mon cause of XX DSD), conditions affecting ovarian development, 
and other rare conditions (see Table 21.2).
Conditions Affecting Steroid-Hormone Synthesis
The steroid biosynthetic disorders causing androgen excess and 
XX DSD are summarized in Table 21.5. Although 21-hydroxy­
lase (CYP21) deficiency is by far the most common cause of this 
condition, alternative diagnoses should be considered because 
approaches to counseling and management may vary.
3β-Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase Type 2 Deficiency. 
3β-HSD/Δ4,5-isomerase catalyzes the conversion of Δ5 ste­
roids (e.g., pregnenolone, 17-hydroxypregnenolone, and 
DHEA) to Δ4 steroids (e.g., progesterone, 17-hydroxyproges­
terone, and androstenedione) and is required for the genera­
tion of mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, and more potent 
androgens (e.g., testosterone, DHT) by the adrenal glands and 
gonads (see Fig. 21.11). The actions of 3βHSD and the con­
sequences of deficiency of the type 2 enzyme (3βHSD2) were 
described earlier because, in XY individuals, this deficiency 
results in variable degrees of adrenal insufficiency and andro­
gen deficiency.
Defects in 3βHSD2 can also cause a genital phenotype in XX 
individuals. Severe, recessively inherited defects in enzyme func­
tion can cause mild clitoral enlargement at birth in girls, as well 
as glucocorticoid deficiency with or without mineralocorticoid 
deficiency. This mild virilization occurs not as a direct andro­
genic effect of the excess DHEA but as a result of conversion of 
DHEA and other Δ5-3β-hydroxy-C19-steroids to testosterone by 
3βHSD1 in the placenta and in the peripheral tissues of the fetus. 
Some XX individuals may have typical female genital appearance 
but have adrenal features. Milder, nonclassic forms of 3βHSD2 
deficiency can cause premature pubarche in girls. Breast devel­
opment can occur at puberty in affected females, presumably by 
peripheral conversion of Δ5C19 steroids to Δ4C19 steroids by 
3βHSD1 expressed principally in the liver and peripheral tissues 
and by the subsequent aromatization of androgens to estrogens.
896
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
The diagnosis of 3βHSD2 deficiency can be challenging in 
nonclassic forms of this condition.318 The levels of Δ5 steroids 
(e.g., 17-hydroxypregnenolone, DHEA and its sulfate, DHEAS) 
usually are increased, and the ratio of Δ5 steroids to Δ4 steroids is 
markedly increased, especially after stimulation with ACTH. Of 
note, because of the presence of the 3βHSD type 1 enzyme in the 
liver and peripheral tissues, the ratio of 17-hydroxypregnenolone 
to cortisol is more reliable than the ratio of 17-hydroxypreg­
nenolone to 17-OHP or the ratio of DHEA to androstenedi­
one. Related to this issue, plasma concentrations of 17-OHP 
can actually be increased as a result of peripheral conversion of 
17-hydroxypregnenolone to 17-OHP. This finding may lead 
to confusion with other forms of CAH, such as 21-hydroxy­
lase (CYP21A2) deficiency or POR deficiency. The urinary 
steroid profile can also be informative because 17-ketosteroids 
and especially DHEAS and 16-hydroxy-DHEAS are elevated. 
Treatment for 3βHSD deficiency is glucocorticoid replacement, 
mineralocorticoid replacement, and salt supplementation, as 
appropriate, and estrogen replacement to induce puberty, if 
needed.319 
21-Hydroxylase Deficiency. Deficiency of 21-hydroxylase 
(CYP21A2) (see Fig. 21.11) is one of the most common causes 
of atypical genital appearance in newborns, affecting around 1 in 
15,000 children, with most XX patients presenting at birth due to 
virilization of the genitalia (see Chapter 13).474,475
An XX fetus with 21-hydroxylase deficiency can become 
androgenized to various degrees, as illustrated by the Prader clas­
sification (Fig. 21.33). High fetal concentrations of 17-OHP, 
androstenedione, and testosterone are the hallmark of CAH due 
to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. More than 75% of patients with

classic CAH, characterized by cortisol deficiency, also have miner­
alocorticoid deficiency. This is sometimes referred to as salt-wasting 
21-hydroxylase deficiency. Other children with genital viriliza­
tion do not develop such significant salt loss and are described as 
having simple virilizing 21-hydroxylase deficiency. A third form 
is nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which is characterized by 
mild subclinical mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency 
but varying degrees of excess androgen production and usually 
presents with premature pubarche, irregular menses, or hirsutism 
but may also be asymptomatic.
The high rate of mutation of the gene encoding 21-hydroxy­
lase, the CYP21A2 gene on chromosome 6p21.3, is attributable to 
the presence of a nonfunctional pseudogene, CYP21A1P, at a dis­
tance of 30 kilobases (kb). More than 90% of cases of 21-hydroxy­
lase deficiency result from a 30-kb deletion due to recombination 
with the CYP21A1P pseudogene or one of nine mutations derived 
from gene conversion with the pseudogene (Fig. 21.34). About 
5% of CYP21A2 mutations arise spontaneously.476 Worldwide, 
around 100 non–pseudogene-derived mutations are reported 
for the CYP21A2 allele. The concordance between genotype and 
phenotype for 21-hydroxylase deficiency is reasonably strong but 
exhibits some variability (see Fig. 21.34). Salt loss is usually caused 
by mutations/deletions of CYP21A2 that result in a completely 
inactive enzyme. In patients who have compound heterozygous 
mutations, the phenotype is usually determined by the milder 
allele.
The diagnosis of 21-hydroxylase deficiency in an XX newborn 
with atypical genital appearance is readily confirmed by markedly 
elevated serum 17-OHP concentrations (>300 nmol/L, >1000 ng/
dL) measured after the first 48 hours of life (to avoid confound­
ing by the surge in adrenal hormones associated with delivery). 
Sick and/or preterm infants can also have moderately increased 
adrenal steroid levels, so ACTH stimulation may be needed to 
resolve any diagnostic confusion. Affected XY individuals usually 
have no alerting clinical signs at birth; salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase 
deficiency does not result in salt-wasting crisis (decompensation 
with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and dehydration) until 5 to 
14 days after birth.475 Newborn screening programs to measure 
blood-spot 17-OHP concentrations soon after birth have been 
introduced in some countries.477 Elevated 17-OHP can also be 
seen in conditions such as 3βHSD deficiency, 11β-hydroxylase 
deficiency, and P450 oxidoreductase deficiency, although the lev­
els are usually not as high as in 21-hydroxylase deficiency. 
Treatment of 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency. Prompt diagnosis 
and treatment of 21-hydroxylase deficiency are required to replace 
adrenal steroids and to suppress adrenal androgen production. 
Details of adrenal treatment are discussed in Chapter 13, and the 
approach to diagnosis and initial management are provided later 
(see “Investigation and Management of Differences of Sex Devel­
opment”). Salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency is a potentially 
life-threatening condition, and atypical genital appearance gives 
an important sign that this diagnosis should be considered, par­
ticularly if the gonads are not palpable.

SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
dexamethasone, although this treatment is considered experi­
mental.478,479 Virilization can be prevented if dexamethasone is 
administered to the mother early enough in gestation to provide 
negative-feedback suppression of the fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-
adrenal axis. Treatment is effective if dexamethasone is started by 6 
to 7 weeks of gestation, but karyotype analysis and CYP21A2 gen­
otype analysis have traditionally not been available until weeks 9 
to 11, when chorionic villus biopsy can be performed. As a result, 
for every affected XX fetus who could benefit from treatment, 
three unaffected XX fetuses and four XY fetuses would need to be 
treated with dexamethasone during this initial period. However, 
recent advances in the detection of circulating free fetal DNA in 
the maternal serum have increased the sensitivity and specificity of 
determining fetal chromosomal sex much earlier in pregnancy.480 
Furthermore, using parental haplotype analysis by targeted mas­
sively parallel sequencing of the CYP21 locus, it has been possible 
to determine the genotype of the fetus earlier in pregnancy so that 
fewer unaffected XX individuals would be treated.481 With this 
approach, CAH can be diagnosed using a maternal blood sample 
drawn at 6 weeks of gestation, although this awaits validation in 
larger studies.482 These are all potentially promising advances to 
prevent exposure of unaffected babies to dexamethasone, if par­
ents do decide to have dexamethasone treatment in pregnancy in 
a center that offers it.
The doses of dexamethasone treatment needed for suppression 
of fetal androgen production induce features of Cushing syn­
drome in the mother. Several concerns have also been raised about 
the potential effects of dexamethasone on the developing fetus. 
Although cognitive and motor development based on question­
naires appeared not to be adversely affected by exposure to dexa­
methasone, direct examination of children who had been exposed 
to dexamethasone from gestational age 6 to 7 weeks did show 
adverse effects on verbal working memory compared with chil­
dren who did not receive such treatment.483–486 All of these stud­
ies were observational, and a meta-analysis emphasized the paucity 
of good-quality, long-term follow-up data to inform a risk-benefit 
analysis.487 Cognitive function may be more affected in girls than 
in boys.488 Limited long-term data in older children, adolescents, 
and adults have suggested that any changes may not persist.489,490 
However, this aspect should be considered when counseling fami­
lies about prenatal treatment. Clinical practice guidelines have 
suggested that prenatal therapy should only be undertaken using 
protocols approved by institutional review boards and at centers 
capable of collecting long-term outcome data as part of multi­
center studies.491,492 
P450 Oxidoreductase Deficiency. P450 oxidoreductase 
(POR) is a membrane-bound flavoprotein that plays a central 
role in electron transfer from NADPH to all microsomal P450 
enzymes, including 17α-hydroxylase (CYP17), 21-hydroxylase 
(CYP21), and aromatase (CYP19) (see Fig. 21.27). Defects in POR 
can cause apparent combined 17α-hydroxylase and 21-hydroxy­
lase deficiency, with or without a form of craniosynostosis called 
Antley-Bixler syndrome. These conditions were described earlier 
(see “Conditions affecting Androgen Synthesis”).340,342 POR 
deficiency can be associated with atypical genital appearance in 
both XX and XY infants. The virilization of XX fetuses may result 
from a defect in aromatase activity and/or may occur through a 
proposed “backdoor” pathway of DHT production that does not 
involve androstenedione or testosterone as intermediates.138 Chil­
dren with this condition usually have cortisol deficiency, but min­
eralocorticoid function is relatively preserved. Careful monitoring 
of puberty is needed because it can be delayed or disrupted.340 
11β-Hydroxylase Deficiency. 11β-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) 
deficiency can cause profound virilization in an affected XX fetus 
and accounts for approximately 5% of patients with CAH.493,494 
11β-hydroxylase deficiency typically presents with atypical genital 
appearance in the XX newborn, although in some situations the 
virilization may be so marked that the baby is thought to be a 
boy with a small penis and undescended testes.495 Subsequently 
in childhood, there can be hyperandrogenism and precocious 
puberty, with accelerated growth and skeletal maturation. Hyper­
tension occurs in two-thirds of cases because prolonged accumula­
tion of 11-deoxycorticosterone, which has some mineralocorticoid 
activity, leads to salt and fluid retention, and plasma renin is sup­
pressed. Milder changes in 11β-hydroxylase cause a nonclassic 
form of the condition, similar to nonclassic 21-hydroxylase defi­
ciency, which presents mostly with hyperandrogenism.496 The 
biochemical diagnosis can be made by urine steroid profile and 
through a pattern of reduced cortisol and elevated intermediates 
such as 11-deoxycortisol.
11β-hydroxylase is encoded by the CYP11B1 gene, which 
is located on chromosome 8q21-22 in tandem with CYP11B2, 
which encodes aldosterone synthase, the enzyme catalyzing the 
conversion of deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone and then to 
aldosterone. Of CYP11B1 mutations that cause 11β-hydroxylase 
deficiency, most are missense mutations. Arg448 appears to be 
a relative hot spot for mutations, with Arg448His possibly a 
founder mutation in the Moroccan Jewish population. Treatment 
of 11β-hydroxylase deficiency includes glucocorticoid replace­
ment to reduce ACTH drive and, in some situations, antihyper­
tensive treatment. 
Aromatase Deficiency. Aromatase (CYP19), a cytochrome 
P450 enzyme, is the only enzyme known to catalyze the conver­
sion of androgens (C19 steroids) to estrogens (C18 steroids) in 
vertebrate species and converts testosterone to estradiol and andro­
stenedione to estrone.497 Aromatase is expressed in many tissues, 
including the placenta, ovary, brain, bone, vascular endothelium, 
breast, and adipose tissue, and expression of the CYP19A1 gene 
is regulated by a number of tissue-specific enhancers. Aromatase 
plays a crucial role in the local production of estrogens and in the 
synthesis of circulating estrogens from the ovary.
Aromatase deficiency due to biallelic mutations in CYP19A1 
has been described in approximately 40 individuals with XX 
DSD. The clinical and biochemical features of this condition 
underscore the key role aromatase plays in the fetoplacental unit, 
and this condition is sometimes referred to as placental aromatase 
deficiency. Aromatase plays a critical role in protecting the fetus 
and mother from excessive androgen exposure during gestation. 
In the absence of aromatase, estrogens cannot be synthesized by 
the placenta, and large quantities of placental testosterone and 
androstenedione are transferred to the fetal and maternal circula­
tion, resulting in virilization of the female fetus and virilization of 
the mother during pregnancy.498
XX individuals with aromatase insufficiency are born with cli­
toromegaly, various degrees of posterior fusion and scrotalization 
of the labioscrotal folds, and in some infants, a urogenital sinus 
with a single perineal orifice.499–501 There is often (but not always) 
a striking history of maternal virilization after the second trimes­
ter of pregnancy (e.g., acne, hair growth, voice changes) coupled 
with elevated maternal androgen levels, which usually resolve after 
the infant is born.502,503 As expected for a steroidogenic defect, 
affected XX individuals have typical müllerian structures because 
AMH is not produced. The histologic picture of the ovaries in 
infancy is normal, but under increased FSH stimulation (due to 
899
CHAPTER 21  Differences of Sex Development
lack of negative feedback by estradiol in the absence of ovarian 
aromatase), multiple enlarged follicular cysts develop. At puberty, 
affected females have hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, typically 
fail to develop female secondary sex characteristics, and exhibit 
progressive virilization. Plasma androstenedione and testosterone 
levels are elevated, and estrone and estradiol levels are low or not 
measurable. The hypergonadotropism and the multiple ovarian 
cysts respond to estrogen replacement therapy, but in some cases, 
temporary treatment with an antiandrogen is necessary.
In addition to a role in the reproductive axis, aromatase defi­
ciency has implications for bone development, metabolism, and 
immune function, as determined by the long-term follow-up of 
the small numbers of women and men with aromatase deficiency 
and by studies of aromatase-knockout mice. Males typically pres­
ent after puberty and have tall stature, delayed bone maturation 
and delayed epiphyseal fusion, and osteopenia, demonstrating 
that estrogens are essential for normal skeletal maturation and 
proportions and for the prevention of osteoporosis in both females 
and males.504 Hyperinsulinemia and abnormal plasma lipids have 
also been reported in aromatase deficiency, which may in part 
reflect estrogen insufficiency and/or testosterone overproduction 
but may also reflect specific actions of aromatase itself. The reports 
of apparently normal psychosexual development in aromatase-
deficient individuals (and also in a man with an estrogen receptor 
defect) suggest that estrogen does not play a critical role in sex 
differentiation of the human brain, in contrast to demonstrated 
effects of estrogens on the brain in nonprimate mammals.
CYP19A1 mutations cause aromatase deficiency in females 
and males and are inherited in an autosomal-recessive fashion. 
Functional assays of aromatase activity have shown severe loss of 
enzyme function (∼0.3%) in nearly all cases associated with clas­
sic aromatase deficiency; in one case, approximately 1% activity 
was found for an Arg435Cys change in a compound heterozy­
gous state together with a null Cys437Tyr mutation.501 Partial 
aromatase deficiency has also been described; a homozygous Arg­
435Cys change has been reported in a girl who presented with 
androgenized genitalia at birth and showed some limited breast 
development during puberty, and deletion of a single phenylala­
nine residue (Phe234del) causing partial loss of aromatase activity 
was described in an androgenized XX individual who achieved sig­
nificant breast development (to Tanner stage 4) during puberty.505
Thus, a spectrum of phenotypes may be seen with aromatase 
insufficiency in humans. This important diagnosis should be con­
sidered in all androgenized XX infants when forms of CAH (e.g., 
21-hydroxylase deficiency) and ovotesticular DSD have been 
excluded. A history of maternal virilization in pregnancy should 
always be sought but may not always be present, and increased lev­
els of Δ4 androstenedione, testosterone, and DHT and low levels 
of plasma estriol, urinary estriol, and amniotic fluid estrone, estra­
diol, and estriol may be detected. The diagnosis can be difficult 
to make during childhood years, when the HPG axis is relatively 
quiescent, and genetic analysis may be needed. 
Familial Glucocorticoid Resistance. Glucocorticoid resistance 
is a rare disorder that is usually caused by sporadic heterozygous 
mutations in the glucocorticoid receptor α-isoform (GRα), which 
is encoded by the NR3C1 gene.506 Partial end-organ insensitivity 
to glucocorticoid action coupled with impaired feedback mecha­
nisms results in excess ACTH secretion and elevated circulating 
cortisol levels without the clinical features of Cushing syndrome. 
In many cases, elevated levels of mineralocorticoids cause hyper­
tension and hypokalemia, and elevated levels of adrenal andro­
gens cause hirsutism and acne. Although classic glucocorticoid 
resistance is not associated with atypical genital appearance, one 
homozygous NR3C1 mutation (Val571Ala) was reported in a Bra­
zilian girl who had a large clitoris, posterior labioscrotal fusion, 
and a urogenital sinus at birth.507 This mutation caused a marked 
reduction in GRα function without complete loss of receptor 
activity. She also harbored a heterozygous mutation in CYP21A2, 
which may have influenced the phenotype. 
Maternal Androgen Excess. Maternal sources of androgens 
that may virilize an XX fetus may be endogenous from adrenal and 
ovarian tumors or exogenous from maternal exposure to andro­
genic compounds. Danazol, a synthetic derivative of ethisterone 
with androgenic, antiestrogenic, and antiprogestogenic activities, 
is used in diverse conditions such as endometriosis, benign fibro­
cystic breast disease, and hereditary angioedema and in women 
with unexplained subfertility. It crosses the placenta and is con­
traindicated in pregnancy due to reports that an XX fetus may 
become virilized.508 Ovarian causes of virilization include primary 
malignancy and benign lesions such as luteoma, hyperreactio 
luteinalis, and hyperthecosis of pregnancy. Recurrence in subse­
quent pregnancies and maternal virilization can occur with luteo­
mas or sometimes for unclear reasons.509,510 
Conditions Affecting Ovarian Development
Conditions resulting in the presence of testicular tissue in an XX 
individual (i.e., XX testicular and ovotesticular DSD) usually 
present with atypical or typical male genital appearance at birth 
due to the action of gonadal androgens, often associated with 
absence of müllerian structures as a result of the action of AMH. 
Ovarian dysgenesis and ovarian resistance to gonadotropins usu­
ally manifest as absent puberty as a result of the absence of estro­
gen production.
XX Testicular and Ovotesticular Differences of Sex Develop­
ment. In rare situations, the developing ovary may contain testicu­
lar tissue (i.e., XX ovotesticular DSD) or may even develop as a 
functioning testis (i.e., XX testicular DSD). In XX ovotesticular 
DSD, the patient usually presents with atypical genital appearance 
at birth and progressive virilization at puberty if the testicular com­
ponent is not removed. In contrast, XX testicular DSD is usually 
associated with typical male genital appearance at birth and absence 
of müllerian structures. However, spermatogenesis is impaired in 
both situations because crucial genes on the Y chromosome are 
absent, and testicular androgen production may not be sufficient 
to support full pubertal development or may decrease with age, so 
careful monitoring is needed. In contrast, folliculogenesis may be 
possible. In some circumstances, ovotesticular DSD and testicular 
DSD may represent a spectrum of the same molecular condition.
The presentation, endocrinology, and management of ovo­
testicular DSD in XX individuals are similar to those of ovotes­
ticular DSD due to XX/XY chimerism, as described earlier (see 
“Sex-Chromosome Differences of Sex Development”), with the 
important difference that XX individuals cannot achieve sper­
matogenesis. As discussed, an XX karyotype is the most frequent 
finding in ovotesticular DSD, especially in patients from sub-
Saharan Africa.227,228 Familial cases have been described, and 
it is likely that a genetic basis exists in some situations. Indeed, 
mutations affecting a specific residue (p.Arg92Trp or p.Arg92Gln) 
of NR5A1 (SF1) have recently been identified in a number of 
individuals with ovotesticular/testicular DSD from diverse ances­
tral backgrounds (see “Gonadal Sex”) (see Fig. 21.21).70,71 These 
specific changes account for up to 10% of ovotesticular DSD. 
Disruption of another nuclear receptor, NR2F2 (COUP-TFII), 
has also been reported in ovotesticular/testicular DSD and cardiac 
900
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
defects, sometimes with additional features (e.g., diaphragmatic 
hernia, BPES).125 Homozygous mutations of the ovarian testis-
repressor genes WNT4 (encoding the signaling molecule WNT4) 
and RSPO1 (encoding R-spondin 1, which potentiates WNT sig­
naling) can cause ovotesticular/testicular DSD in the context of 
broader syndromic findings: kidney, adrenal, and lung dysgenesis 
(as part of the SERKAL [sex reversal with kidney, adrenal, and 
lung dysgenesis] syndrome) with WNT4 and eye and skin abnor­
malities and hearing impairment with RSPO1.230,511,512 Recently, 
specific heterozygous pathogenic variants in WT1 affecting the 
fourth zinc finger have been identified in individuals with XX tes­
ticular DSD.513 In vitro, this variant WT1 results in increased 
binding of β-catenin and upregulation of Sertoli cell–specific tran­
scripts in human granulosa cells.513
In contrast, individuals with XX testicular DSD often first 
present with male factor infertility, although sometimes hypospa­
dias is present. In some cases, a family history is found. Because 
different family members can have different phenotypes, it is pos­
sible that XX testicular DSD represents the most severe end of a 
spectrum of ovarian transdifferentiation phenotypes. Up to 80% 
of cases of XX testicular DSD are due to translocations of Y-chro­
mosomal material containing SRY, the testis-determining factor. 
Indeed, this finding helped considerably in mapping the SRY gene 
(see “The Y Chromosome”). Individuals with SRY translocations 
can be diagnosed by FISH analysis using a probe directed to that 
gene (see Fig. 21.3). A number of SRY-negative cases have also 
been reported. Sometimes, these arise from the same mutations 
in NR5A1, NR2F2, WT1, WNT4, and RSPO1 that can cause 
XX ovotesticular DSD. Duplication of the genetic locus contain­
ing SOX9 or of the region upstream of SOX9 that contains the 
enhancers eSR-A and eSR-B, deletions or rearrangements in dis­
tant regulatory regions that result in SOX9 overexpression,108–110 
and similar alterations in the X chromosome resulting in overex­
pression of SOX3 have also been described.514 
Ovarian Dysgenesis. Ovarian dysgenesis most often occurs as 
a result of sex-chromosome aneuploidy (e.g., Turner syndrome; 
45,X and variants) with progressive follicular apoptosis. POI can 
also result from mutations in many genes, but each gene accounts 
for only a small proportion, and often no cause of POI is identi­
fied.515 Two recent reviews provide an excellent overview of the 
various groups of genes that are involved.516–519 Some of these 
genes are important for formation of the indifferent gonad; these 
include NR5A1 and WT1, which have been discussed earlier. 
FOXL2 plays a role in early ovarian determination, and mutations 
are associated with POI, usually (but not always) as part of BPES. 
Other genes are involved in meiosis and DNA repair, such as cohes­
ins (e.g., STAG3), and various helicases (e.g., MCM8 and HFM1). 
Mutations in these genes disrupt meiotic progression of oocytes 
and result in oocyte degeneration. They form an important group 
of genes to consider in women with POI because mutations in 
some of these genes are associated with an increased risk of vari­
ous cancers. A group of genes involved in mitochondrial func­
tions causes sensorineural deafness in combination with POI, also 
known as Perrault syndrome, and other neurosensory syndromes 
(e.g., POLG). Other syndromic causes include premature aging 
syndromes (e.g., LMNA) and skeletal syndromes (e.g., BMPR1B). 
Mutations in genes involved in the formation and maturation of 
the primordial follicles, such as SOHLH1, SOHLH2, NUP107, 
FIGLA, and NOBOX, as well as those involved in the next hor­
mone-dependent step, maturation and growth from primary to 
ovulatory follicles, such as ESR1, FSHR, LHCGR, and BMP15, 
cause nonsyndromic POI. One of the most common monogenic 
causes is a premutation of FMR1, found in approximately 2% 
to 6% of women with sporadic POI. SOX8 mutations have 
recently been identified in 5% of a cohort of females with 
POI.265 Single individuals with ovarian dysgenesis have been 
described with an ESR2 variant520 and with a homozygous 
missense gain-of-function variant in MAMLD1.521 Also, twins 
with MYRF mutations have been reported to have ovarian 
insufficiency.522 
Other Conditions Affecting XX Sex Development
Several syndromic associations can cause developmental genital 
abnormalities in XX females. Complex pelvic anomalies, such as 
cloacal exstrophy, can affect both sexes and require major recon­
structive surgery for bladder and bowel function and for the lower 
genital system.
Abnormalities in uterine development can result in bicornate 
uterus (i.e., Fryns syndrome), uterine hemiagenesis or hypopla­
sia, or uterine agenesis. These conditions can be part of Mayer-
Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome, which may be associated 
with vaginal and/or ovarian agenesis as well as with renal, cardiac, 
and cervical spinal abnormalities, as in müllerian, renal, and cervi­
cal spine syndrome (MURCS).523,524 The cause of these condi­
tions is unknown for most women, although some familial cases 
have been described, and a mutation in WNT4 was reported in a 
patient with absent müllerian structures (uterus and upper vagina), 
unilateral renal agenesis, and mild hyperandrogenemia.122 Uter­
ine abnormalities have also been associated with maturity-onset 
diabetes of the young type 5 (MODY5, HNF1B) and with vagi­
nal abnormalities in patients with hand-foot-genital syndrome 
(HOXA13) and McKusick-Kaufman syndrome (MKKS; formerly 
called BBS6). Because a prominent clitoris can be associated with 
conditions such as Fraser syndrome (not to be confused with Fra­
sier syndrome) or neurofibromatosis, careful evaluation is neces­
sary before a hyperandrogenic cause is diagnosed.
Other common conditions that may be mistaken for a more 
serious underlying disorder include apparent clitoromegaly seen 
in premature or formerly premature babies and/or when little 
labial adipose tissue is present (e.g., in children born small for 
gestational age). Assessment by a surgeon or physician with expe­
rience in recognizing normal variability in clitoral size is impor­
tant. Sometimes this form of isolated clitoral prominence can 
persist into childhood.525 Labial adhesions are a common find­
ing in female infants. They often resolve spontaneously, although 
estrogen cream can be used to accelerate their resolution. Tran­
sient menstrual bleeding during the first week of life can be seen 
frequently in female infants with the withdrawal of large amounts 
of estrogens and progesterones after birth. This can be alarming 
for families but rapidly resolves, and no treatment is needed. 
Investigation and Management of 
Differences of Sex Development
DSD can present at many ages and to a wide range of different 
health professionals. Some of the most common presentations are 
shown in Table 21.6, and the range of conditions discussed in 
a European center over a 2-year period is shown in Table 21.7. 
The potential diagnosis of DSD has major implications for the 
child and the family. Most people will never have heard of DSD 
or have thought that they may be faced with, for example, a situa­
tion in which they cannot be told immediately whether their new­
born is a boy or a girl. Talking about such issues can be difficult, 
901
CHAPTER 21  Differences of Sex Development
and sensitive and positive support and education from all health 
professionals is essential to provide families with knowledge and 
confidence.526
Specialist multidisciplinary (or interdisciplinary) team 
(MDT) involvement with families, young people, and adults 
with DSD is important.1–3,370,527 The pediatric (or adult) 
endocrinologist plays a central role in the team, with support 
from psychologists, urologists, and other health professionals 
(Fig. 21.35).3,527,528 The structure and available expertise vary 
depending on the center. Specialist MDTs are usually based 
only at large centers, so effective communication between the 
team and those health professionals managing the initial pre­
sentation is crucial. Sometimes regional or national networks 
(e.g., the Scottish Differences of Sex Development Network) 
are needed to provide support where the population is scattered 
geographically or to link experts in different centers together, 
with meetings held by teleconference rather than in person.529 It 
is important to keep the primary care physician informed. It is 
also useful for families to have a clearly defined point of contact 
if they need to ask further questions.
Although there is often uncertainty at the start, a general 
diagnosis can usually be reached following a series of careful 
assessments and basic investigations. Reaching a more specific 
diagnosis can be important in some situations and may take lon­
ger and involve more detailed investigations or genetic tests (dis­
cussed later). Every person is different, and many DSD-related 
conditions can have a spectrum of presentations, so it is also 
important to take an individualized approach to the child and 
the family.
The following is a discussion of the investigation and manage­
ment of DSD at different ages. Several overarching themes are 
subsequently highlighted. More extensive details for specific con­
ditions are discussed earlier in the chapter.
Prenatal Diagnosis
Prenatal diagnosis of DSD is increasingly common as fetal ultra­
sonography improves and as more people have karyotype analysis 
or cell-free fetal DNA analysis for various reasons in pregnancy.530 
Although some prospective parents choose not to know the sex of 
their baby, many couples ask whether they are having a boy or a 
girl, and issues can arise when the genital appearance is unclear 
on the scan, when the appearance of the genitals is discordant 
with the known karyotype, or when a 45,X/46,XY karyotype (or 
other karyotype with mosaicism or chimerism of the Y chromo­
some) is detected. These situations can generate great anxiety, 
and early contact with the DSD MDT is helpful to support the 
parent(s). Sometimes prenatal genetic testing, such as a microar­
ray or gene-panel analysis, is considered, especially when multi­
ple congenital anomalies are suspected on ultrasound. However, 
prenatal genetic testing can occasionally produce inaccurate 
results that are not confirmed on karyotyping of the baby (e.g., 
due to confined placental mosaicism or rare cases of twin fetal 
demise), and confirmation of the sex-chromosome complement 
after birth is essential; this can be done from a cord blood sam­
ple or a blood sample from the infant. Also, genital appearance 
at birth can differ from that seen on prenatal scans. Given this 
potential for discrepancies between prenatal and postnatal evalu­
ation, general support to deal with this uncertainty and explana­
tions of what will happen if the baby does have atypical genital 
appearance are important, but discussion of specific diagnoses is 
often best deferred until after birth. 
The Newborn With Atypical Genital Appearance
The classic presentation of DSD is the newborn with atypical gen­
ital appearance, such that it is not possible to immediately desig­
nate the baby as a girl or a boy. Sometimes atypical genital features 
are not recognized immediately at birth but are first discovered on 
the first full newborn examination. Further investigations, such 
as a karyotype, are usually needed, and specialist review is usually 
required. It is estimated that around 1 in 2000 babies has a genital 
appearance that warrants specialist evaluation.531
Some presentations may not represent a DSD condition, such 
as labial swelling after a breech delivery or in a premature infant, 
undescended testes, or mild hypospadias, which can affect up to 
1 in 300 male infants. Placental estrogen exposure can result in 
breast development before birth, and a small episode of vaginal 
bleeding can occur several days after birth from withdrawal of 
estrogen and progesterone and may not reflect endogenous post­
natal hormonal activity. Examples of genital features that should 
trigger consideration of a DSD condition are outlined in Box 
21.12. In particular, any child with nonpalpable gonads needs 
careful review because this child could be an XX baby with severe, 
potentially life-threatening CAH.

CHAPTER 21  Differences of Sex Development
The Initial Approach to the Baby With Atypical Genitalia
A useful mnemonic for the initial approach is BASIC: bonding, 
adrenal insufficiency, sex/gender designation, imaging, and cyto­
genetics. Each of these is introduced briefly here and discussed 
more extensively elsewhere.
Bonding between the parents and the baby can be disrupted 
by the shock of the situation, which can be compounded if the 
newborn is taken away to an intensive care nursery. (A note on 
terminology: We recognize that not all children are raised by their 
biological parents. For the sake of readability, in this chapter we 
use the term parents to refer to a child’s primary caretakers, who 
may be extended family members, adoptive parents, or others.) 
It is important to allow parents time to focus on their new baby 
without undue attention to the suspected DSD. At the same time, 
the impact of the situation should not be trivialized; striking the 
right balance requires an individualized approach involving fre­
quent feedback from parents. Nursing staff can play a crucial role 
in helping families initially by engaging with them and acknowl­
edging the stress that uncertainty can bring while also addressing 
routine newborn issues such as establishing feeding, changing dia­
pers, and sleeping. Staff members themselves may feel uncomfort­
able and may also need support and guidance.
Adrenal insufficiency is associated with some causes of DSD 
and is potentially life threatening if not promptly recognized and 
treated. The most common scenario is an XX baby with 21-hydrox­
ylase deficiency, which occurs in about 15% to 20% of babies with 
atypical genitalia, more in some studies. Adrenal insufficiency can 
also occur in XY babies with conditions that affect both corti­
sol and androgen production (e.g., StAR, CYP11A, or HSD3B2 
deficiency) or both adrenal and gonadal development (e.g., bial­
lelic variants in NR5A1/SF1), but these conditions are rare. 
Monitoring for hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia 
is necessary, but the electrolyte changes usually take several days to 
manifest. During this time, the infant can be kept with the family 
if otherwise well. Micropenis and/or undescended testes may be 
caused by gonadotropin deficiency, which can be associated with 
a deficiency of other pituitary hormones, including ACTH and 
GH, which may cause hypoglycemia.
Sex/gender designation should be undertaken as soon as pos­
sible but should not be rushed. Parents sometimes have strong 
preconceptions about their baby, especially if they have been told 
prenatally to expect a boy or a girl, and/or may want a child of 
a specific sex to fit their desired family structure. However, if an 
inappropriate gender designation is made initially, it can be very 
traumatic to change the designation later, so keeping an open 
mind from the start and avoiding premature recommendations 
is critical.532 In the interim, it is advisable to use neutral terms 
such as clitorophallus rather than penis or clitoris, and to refer to 
the child as “your baby,” “your child,” or “little one” rather than 
“he” or “she.” However, some families may feel unsupported if 
the clinical team does not use the pronouns they have selected for 
their child, and open communication is essential. In most coun­
tries, there is a time limit to register the birth of a baby, but this 
can usually be deferred or, in some countries, done without des­
ignating sex.
Imaging is useful but can be operator dependent, and results 
can sometimes be deceptive. Pelvic ultrasound or MRI can show 
internal structures, but structures are not always clearly visual­
ized. Also, a utricular remnant (commonly found in boys with 
hypospadias) or a loop of bowel can be mistaken as a uterus, and 
lymph nodes can be mistaken as testes.236,533 Both parents and 
providers need to know the limitations of these tests, and confir­
mation with additional tests (e.g., measurement of serum AMH) 
is important.
Cytogenetics or some other rapid assessment of sex-chromo­
some complement is essential. Rapid karyotyping can help with 
the next stages of management and investigation, and a result is 
usually available within 2 working days. For centers that cannot 
conduct rapid karyotyping, rapid determination of sex-chromo­
some complement can be performed by FISH for X-chromosome 
and Y-chromosome markers (see Fig. 21.3), and in some centers, 
it is now being performed by quantitative fluorescent polymerase 
chain reaction (qfPCR) on DNA. The relevant laboratories should 
be informed of the urgency of the test, and samples should be 
transported quickly. An attempt to look for mosaicism should be 
made by determining the genotype in a sufficient number of cells, 
but FISH on a second tissue (e.g., a buccal smear) may be neces­
sary to detect mosaicism. 
Support for the Parents
As discussed briefly under “Bonding,” it is essential to provide 
adequate support to the child’s primary caregivers (referred to 
as parents for the sake of readability).526 Although it is entirely 
appropriate for the clinical care team to express concern for the 
child and parents, excessive expression of anxiety may exacerbate 
anxiety in the parents. On the other hand, expressing nonchalance 
may be viewed as trivializing a serious situation. It can be useful to 
share that many other parents are in a similar position each year, 
that specialists who have knowledge and experience are available, 
and that the situation will become clearer in the subsequent days. 
The staff should provide parents with information about necessary 
tests and a realistic expectation of when results will be available. 
Staff should also encourage parents to ask questions and to ask 
for clarification of any information that was unclear. Sometimes 
recording conversations can be helpful so that families have an 
opportunity to listen to information again. In addition, an infor­
mation leaflet about having a child with atypical genital appear­
ance is available.534
A potentially significant source of stress for parents can be 
repeated questions from family and friends regarding whether the 
child is a girl or a boy. There is no single strategy that suits all 
parents, but some may delay announcing the birth until the situ­
ation is clearer, asking family and friends for some private time 
and saying that they will be in touch soon with more information.

Other parents may find it helpful to discuss the situation with 
close friends or family members. This allows friends and family 
to support the parents (e.g., to help with pressure with work or 
care of other siblings). It is important to emphasize to parents that 
they need to look after not only their newborn’s needs but their 
own needs, too, and several resources have been developed to help 
support parents during this time.534 
History and Examination
A careful history is important but rarely points to an immedi­
ate diagnosis. It is important not to generate additional anxiety 
with insensitive questions, particularly questions that may be 
interpreted as laying blame on the family for the child’s condition. 
Key points to ask about include aspects of the pregnancy, such as 
growth restriction and preeclampsia, maternal acne, hair growth, 
or voice deepening during pregnancy (which could suggest aro­
matase or POR deficiency, excessive maternal androgen produc­
tion, or exogenous androgen exposure), and any prenatal tests 
or scans performed. Theoretically, certain medications and drugs 
may affect the fetus (e.g., 5α-reductase inhibitors), and assisted 
reproduction or the need for fertility treatment might indicate an 
underlying genetic cause. A careful family history should include 
any history of adrenal conditions (including known CAH) or 
infant death (which could have been due to adrenal crisis from 
salt-wasting CAH), other known DSD, hypospadias, or infertil­
ity (with attention to X-linked patterns that could suggest AIS), 
but such issues may not be known or widely discussed within 
the family. Consanguinity is associated with an increased risk of 
autosomal-recessive conditions, such as many of the steroidogenic 
enzyme deficiencies.
A careful physical examination is needed but should be done 
sensitively and only after the parents have had some time to be 
with their baby. Key features to note are the length of the clitoro­
phallus (Table 21.9), consistency of the corpora and glans, extent 
of chordee, labioscrotal transposition (extension of the labio­
scrotal folds above the clitorophallus), features of the foreskin 
(hooded, excess skin), position of the urethral opening, presence 
or absence of a separate vaginal opening, rugation (wrinkling) 
of the scrotal skin (also called scrotalization), degree of fusion 
of the labioscrotal folds (which can be expressed as the anogeni­
tal ratio; see Fig. 21.32), and size and position of any palpable 
gonads (likely to be testes if palpable). Genital appearances can 
sometimes be misleading because of chordee (bending and teth­
ering of the clitorophallus) and/or a large suprapubic fat pad, 
so palpation and inspection are important. Various scales, such 
as the external genitalia score, the Prader scale, and the Quigley 
scale, can be used to summarize findings and are particularly 
useful for research purposes, but it is also important to note and 
document individual features (Fig. 21.36).396 Asymmetry of the 
genitalia can suggest mixed gonadal dysgenesis associated with 
45,X/46,XY mosaicism and can also be seen in partial gonadal 
dysgenesis or ovotesticular DSD. Other findings such as low 
birthweight; position of the anus; skeletal, cardiac, or other 
congenital anomalies; and dysmorphic features are important to 
note. Hyperpigmentation (especially of the labioscrotal folds) 
can be a sign of primary adrenal insufficiency due to elevated 
ACTH. 
Sex/Gender Designation
As introduced earlier, designating sex/gender can be a complex 
decision. Most people wish to raise their child as either a girl or a 
boy, although in rare cases, parents raise their child without a sex/
gender designation or as gender neutral. Sufficient information 
should be gathered so that parents can be informed and educated 
to make the best decisions for their child. This should be done 
as quickly as practical but without rushing decisions. The karyo­
type per se does not determine gender identity, but it is a useful 
starting point for focusing investigations and reaching a diagno­
sis (see Table 21.2 for classification of DSD). A broad diagnosis 
is often sufficient for designating sex/gender even if more time 
is needed to reach a more specific diagnosis. Within the context 
of the karyotype and diagnosis, useful points to consider are the 
child’s future gender identity (see “Psychosexual Development” 
earlier in the chapter), functional anatomic aspects, such as likely 
urologic and sexual function, potential sex-steroid production, 
fertility options, and the risk of germ cell tumors. Many of these 
are difficult to predict, and in some situations, more investiga­
tions may be undertaken to inform the parents, but often recom­
mendations for gender designation are relatively straightforward 
based on findings from physical examination, imaging studies, 
and karyotype. Current recommendations are for XX individuals 
with CAH to be raised as girls, although some have suggested that 
those with highly virilized genitalia may be raised as boys.535–538A 
female designation is appropriate for XY individuals with CAIS 
or complete gonadal dysgenesis (Swyer syndrome) because these 
individuals are likely to identify as women in adulthood and have 
female-appearing external genitalia. A female designation is prob­
ably also appropriate for those with minimal virilization (e.g.,

Particularly challenging decisions arise in individuals with 
genitals with an appearance that is intermediate to typical female 
and typical male. A challenging decision also arises for an XY baby 
with minimal genital virilization who has 17β-hydroxysteroid
