many individuals with these conditions identify as boys starting 
around the time of puberty. In the past, there was a greater focus 
on the genitalia and a tendency to raise children with a very small 
clitorophallus as female. More recently, there has been a trend to 
raise more XY children as male and to consider other aspects of 
the child, such as likely gender identity, fertility potential, and 
endocrine function.416 Sometimes, cultural influences can be 
important for the parents.540 
Investigations for DSD
Once the sex-chromosome complement is determined, several 
investigations can be undertaken to reach a more specific diagno­
sis or to obtain a more detailed assessment of urogenital anatomy 
and future function.2,527 It is difficult to develop rigid guidelines 
for investigations because availability and affordability of tests 
vary greatly around the world.541 Details of some of the com­
monly used tests for DSD are shown in Table 21.8, and potential 
investigations based on karyotype are shown in Fig. 21.37. It is 
important to consider what the likelihood of a specific diagnosis 
might be. An overview of diagnoses considered in Europe/North 
America is shown in Table 21.7, but in areas of the world with 
greater consanguinity, the relative prevalence of recessive condi­
tions, such as various forms of CAH, is greater. There may also 
be a high prevalence of specific diagnoses in certain regions due 
to founder effects (e.g., 5α-reductase in the Dominican Repub­
lic), so knowledge of the local prevalence of certain conditions 
is important. Genetic testing is more widely available and may 
sometimes avoid the need for invasive tests or prolonged endo­
crine stimulation but may have certain drawbacks, which are 
discussed later.354 
Sex-Chromosomal DSD
In our experience, approximately 10% to 15% of newborn 
referrals have a sex-chromosomal DSD due to mosaicism or 
chimerism involving the Y chromosome (usually 45,X/46,XY 
mosaicism).3,210 These individuals require assessment of anatomy 
and gonadal function and, if monosomy X is present in some cells, 
screening for Turner syndrome–associated features (e.g., renal and 
cardiac conditions) (see Fig. 21.37). Sometimes an examination 
under anesthesia and laparoscopy (and possibly gonadal biopsy) 
are helpful to assess anatomy and to determine gonadal character­
istics and histologic features. 
XX DSD
The majority of babies with an XX DSD have 21-hydroxylase 
deficiency, although other rarer forms of CAH and ovotesticular 
and testicular DSD are seen. Clitoromegaly is sometimes not asso­
ciated with an intrinsic endocrine condition (e.g., clitoromegaly 
associated with prematurity or with maternal exposure to exoge­
nous androgens). However, any baby with atypical genital appear­
ance and nonpalpable gonads must be assumed to be at risk of 
adrenal insufficiency from salt-wasting CAH until proven other­
wise. Serial electrolytes should be monitored, and tests to confirm 
or refute the diagnosis should be undertaken according to local 
protocol and assay availability (e.g., 17-OHP, basal and stimulated 
cortisol, ACTH, plasma renin activity, and urine steroid profil­
ing). Results can be inaccurate before 3 days of age using con­
ventional immunoassays because of interfering substances; liquid 
chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS-MS) assays 
or immunoassays performed after extraction may be more use­
ful if available.542,543 Steroid replacement treatment can be started 
once the diagnosis is clear and any additional samples needed for 
diagnostic confirmation are obtained. Of note, 17-OHP can be 
mildly elevated in forms of CAH other than 21-hydroxlase defi­
ciency (e.g., deficiency of 11β-hydroxylase, 3βHSD, POR), and 
investigation of steroid intermediates (e.g., 11-deoxycortisol, 
11-deoxycorticosterone, 17-hydroxypregnenolone) and urine ste­
roid profiling can be useful in these situations.372 If all adrenal 
investigations are negative, rare diagnoses such as XX testicular 
and ovotesticular DSD and aromatase deficiency should be con­
sidered, and measurement of AMH to investigate for testicular 
tissue can be done in parallel with the adrenal evaluation.527 The 
presence of ovarian tissue can be difficult to assess in early infancy 
without laparoscopy or even biopsy. Occasionally, follicles can be 
seen on imaging, or there can be a rise in estradiol and/or inhibin 
A following recombinant FSH stimulation, but such tests are not 
commonly performed.183 
XY DSD
Children with XY DSD can have a range of conditions leading to 
reduced androgen action, including testicular dysgenesis, condi­
tions affecting androgen synthesis and action, or other diagnoses 
such as proximal hypospadias of unknown cause or a DSD-associ­
ated syndrome. In some situations, the diagnosis might influence 
decision making around gender designation. For example, most 
clinicians would recommend raising an XY individual with mini­
mal genital virilization as a girl if the underlying cause is PAIS or 
partial gonadal dysgenesis. Potential exceptions are 5α-reductase 
deficiency and 17β-HSD deficiency, and some clinicians would 
advocate raising an XY baby with minimal genital virilization due 
to these conditions as a boy and considering giving dihydrotestos­
terone cream (if available). Basic investigations in the XY baby can 
include karyotype or chromosomal microarray analysis to look for 
established chromosomal alterations (e.g., 9q deletion, 10p dele­
tion, Xp21 duplication) and basal assessment of testicular func­
tion (e.g., AMH, testosterone).2,129 Additional diagnostic tests to 
assess androgen synthesis include other androgens (DHEA, andro­
stenedione, DHT), whether unstimulated or after short-term or 
long-term stimulation with hCG.544 Basal androgens may be low 
initially and can be reassessed during minipuberty, around age 4 to 
8 weeks. The ratios of intermediates after hCG stimulation can be 
useful in diagnosing specific blocks, such as 17β-hydroxysteroid 
dehydrogenase deficiency (testosterone-to-androstenedione ratio 
often <0.8) and 5α-reductase deficiency (testosterone-to-dihy­
drotestosterone ratio often >10–30).371 However, because of the 
presence of interfering substances, these assays may not be accu­
rate in the first few days of life unless performed by LC/MS-MS or 
by immunoassay after extraction. Furthermore, diagnosing these 
conditions by androgen ratios or urine steroid profiling can be

Adrenal disorders can occur with XY DSD but are rare. Most 
children with complete blocks in steroid production (e.g., StAR, 
CYP11A1) do not present with atypical genitalia but rather pres­
ent with typical female genital appearance and salt-losing crisis, 
and the XY karyotype is only found afterward. Atypical genital 
appearance at birth can be a sign of partial defects in steroido­
genic enzymes common to both cortisol and androgen synthesis 
(e.g., partial StAR, CYP11 deficiency) or partial 17α-hydroxylase 
(CYP17A1) deficiency, as well as classic presentations of 
3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency (3βHSD2) or 
POR. Given the rarity of these conditions, it is currently unclear 
whether detailed investigations of adrenal function are justified in 
all boys with XY DSD, but an adrenal diagnosis should at least be 
considered. 
Genetic Testing and DSD
In addition to the critical role of determining the sex-chromo­
some complement, additional genetic testing is increasingly 
important in the diagnostic process.545 Genetic testing is often 
the final step in reaching a specific diagnosis, may prompt 
screening for other features associated with an identified genetic 
cause, may allow for counseling about the risk of recurrence in 
future children, and in some situations may provide guidance 
on issues such as potential gender identity, endocrine function, 
fertility, and tumor risk.353 Reaching a specific genetic diagnosis 
can also provide a sense of resolution and reduce uncertainty but 
may generate anxiety if no cause is found or if incidental genetic 
information (unrelated to the DSD) is uncovered. Parents may 
experience guilt or blame for transmitting a mutation to their 
child. Individuals and families should have a clear understanding 
of what genetic tests are being performed and what the poten­
tial benefits and disadvantages might be. Genetic testing can be 
expensive and may not be readily available or affordable, espe­
cially as a clinical service.353
Approaches to genetic testing are changing rapidly with new 
technologies for the analysis of chromosomes as well as individual 
genes. In some centers, sex-chromosome FISH is being replaced 
by qfPCR, as noted earlier, and microarray or array-based com­
parative genomic hybridization (CGH) approaches are being used 
to replace or supplement traditional karyotype analysis. These 
technologies can detect much smaller copy-number variations 
than traditional G-banded karyotypes but do not detect balanced 
translocations and, as with traditional karyotyping, may miss low 
levels of mosaicism. Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplifi­
cation (MLPA) is a method of looking for specific copy-number 
changes (deletions or duplications) in known DSD genes (e.g., 
duplication of NR0B1 or loss of exons of other genes) that are too 
small to be detected on arrays.
Analysis of single genes is also changing with the development 
of next-generation sequencing (NGS) approaches. Traditionally, 
candidate genes for a condition were amplified one by one by 
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and analyzed by Sanger sequenc­
ing. This direct-sequencing approach is still the method of choice 
when there is a clear candidate gene from biochemical analysis 
(e.g., HSD17B3, SRD5A2). Furthermore, this often remains the 
approach of choice when the presence of a pseudogene can make

NGS difficult (e.g., when sequencing CYP21A2, the gene encod­
ing 21-hydroxylase).353 However, this approach is relatively time-
consuming and expensive, particularly if there are several candidate 
genes. NGS involves massively parallel sequencing to allow simul­
taneous sequencing of a panel of genes relevant to DSD, the exome 
(all coding regions of the genome), or even the entire genome.184,546 
These methods provide high-throughput analysis but are still expen­
sive, generate large amounts of data (including incidental data for 
other genes unrelated DSD, which may or may not provide desired 
information), and are still mostly only available as research tools, 
although these approaches are increasingly used in clinical testing. 
Interpretation of identified variants in DSD genes can be challeng­
ing and may require detailed information on anatomy and endo­
crine function in the affected individual, genetic analysis in family 
members (to assess segregation of the variant with the phenotype), 
or in vitro functional studies of the variant.
Given the advances in genetics and increasing recognition that 
DSD can be a feature of many well-defined syndromes, a clinical 
geneticist can be a very valuable member of the MDT, especially 
when a child needs to be examined for additional syndromic fea­
tures or when the family needs to be counseled about genetic test­
ing and the significance of any results. 
Presentation During Childhood
DSD can occasionally present during the childhood years. 
Sometimes a parent may notice genital differences for the first 
time in childhood or notice inguinal masses that are found to be 
testes. A small proportion of inguinal hernias in girls are found 
to contain testes, most often in patients with CAIS. Sometimes, 
a feature associated with a specific cause of DSD may present for 
the first time in childhood; for example, an abdominal mass due 
to a Wilms tumor may in some cases lead to a previously unap­
preciated diagnosis of Denys-Drash syndrome (due to mutations 
in WT1). 
Presentation During Adolescence
Another common time for DSD to present is during adolescence 
in one of three well-recognized ways: (1) a girl who experiences 
spontaneous virilization at puberty, (2) a girl with absence of 
pubertal development, and (3) a girl who has primary amenorrhea 
after having normal breast development.2 Although the situation 
is not as urgent as in the newborn who may be at risk of salt-
wasting CAH, it is equally if not more important to handle the

situation with sensitivity because both the young person and the 
parents must be appropriately informed and involved in decision 
making and consent/assent.
The conditions that are typically associated with virilization at 
puberty are 5α-reductase deficiency and 17β-hydroxysteroid dehy­
drogenase deficiency. This presentation may also occur in cases in 
which previous clitoromegaly may have been overlooked in partial 
testicular dysgenesis,547 PAIS, or testicular/ovotesticular DSD. 
The diagnosis is often made based on laboratory evaluation (e.g., 
serum concentrations and ratios of androgens, blood/urine ste­
roid profiling), but results are sometimes ambiguous, and genetic 
testing may be needed to establish a diagnosis.2 It is best to avoid 
further stimulation with hCG-stimulation tests if virilization is 
undesired, and some have proposed that puberty can be blocked 
for a period with a GnRH analogue or with antiandrogens to pro­
vide time to obtain a genetic diagnosis, educate and counsel the 
young person and the family, and give them time to make manage­
ment decisions. An MDT approach is invaluable, and the input of 
an experienced psychologist or expert in gender medicine is key. 
A proportion of young people with 5α-reductase deficiency will 
choose to transition from female to male, and this has also been 
reported for some individuals with 17-HSD deficiency.158,159 
However, many girls with these conditions continue to identify as 
females and often want to have their gonads removed to prevent 
virilization; appropriate counseling about risks, benefits, and fer­
tility options is essential. If gonads are dysfunctional or removed, 
puberty will need to be induced with estrogens. Gathering and 
sharing the information and providing psychological support over 
a period of time can help ensure that the young person makes the 
best choices for the future.
Another presentation in adolescence is a girl who does not 
have any pubertal development. This situation may represent 
many diagnoses in an XX girl, including constitutional puber­
tal delay, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and congenital or 
acquired (e.g., autoimmune) POI. Absence of pubertal devel­
opment may also be the presenting feature of sex-chromosomal 
DSD (Turner syndrome) or an XY DSD (complete gonadal 
dysgenesis, 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency, or complete 
Leydig cell hypoplasia). In complete testicular dysgenesis (Swyer 
syndrome), both Leydig cell production of testosterone and Ser­
toli cell production of AMH are impaired. As a result, müllerian 
structures are typically present. However, the immature uterus 
may be difficult to see, even on MRI scan, but may become more 
easily visualized following estrogen treatment (the “clandestine” 
uterus).548 Severely dysgenetic gonads, which may appear streak-
like (i.e., flat and scar-like), have a high tumor risk even in pre­
pubertal children and have no potential for hormone production 
or gametogenesis and should therefore be removed. True streak 
gonads (i.e., gonads that consist only of fibrous tissue and lack 
germ cells and support cells) are not at risk of germ cell tumors 
(GCTs) by definition, but this can only be confirmed at histo­
logic examination. The underlying cause of complete gonadal 
dysgenesis may be a range of genetic conditions (see Table 21.5), 
but a cause is often not found. Puberty can be induced with 
estrogens.
In contrast, an XY individual with 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-
lyase deficiency has intact Sertoli cell function and AMH pro­
duction and, as a result, does not have a uterus. The block 
in adrenal steroidogenesis can be associated with hyperten­
sion and hypokalemia, which can cause arrhythmias, so this 
is a rare but important diagnosis to make. Estrogen treat­
ment is needed. The gonads are typically undescended but not 
dysgenetic, and the risk for GCT in prepubertal children is 
likely to be low, but there may be an increased risk of GCTs in 
late adolescence and adulthood. Two large studies of gonadal 
tumors in XY DSD individuals, which included 42 individu­
als with 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency, reported one 
dysgerminoma, two Sertoli cell tumors, and one Leydig cell 
tumor.549,550A decision about gonadectomy should be made 
after discussing these risks.
The third common presentation is with primary amenorrhea 
in a girl who has experienced breast development. Acquired 
hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (e.g., from a tumor in the 
pituitary/hypothalamic region) should be considered, and 
POI may also be associated with some breast development 
but absent menarche. Hormone measurements, a karyotype, 
and pelvic ultrasound are often useful initial investigations.2 
If hypogonadism has been excluded and a uterus is visualized, 
obstruction of the outflow tract is likely, such as imperforate 
hymen; this can be accompanied by cyclic abdominal pain. In 
the absence of a uterus, the diagnosis is most likely to be CAIS 
if the karyotype is XY and testosterone is in the male range or 
a form of uterine agenesis, such as MRKH syndrome, if the 
karyotype is XX. Girls with CAIS often have reduced pubic 
and axillary hair. Detailed discussion about the management of 
CAIS is provided earlier in this chapter (see “Complete Andro­
gen Insensitivity Syndrome”). 
Presentation During Adulthood
Occasionally, DSD may first present in adulthood. Examples 
include mild variants in DSD genes associated with male factor 
infertility or ovarian insufficiency (e.g., NR5A1), conditions such 
as persistent müllerian duct syndrome when a uterine-like struc­
ture is found incidentally in a man, or when a person with a more 
typical presentation of DSD presents to health professionals later 
in life, sometimes after migration from a medically underserved 
area or from one country to another. 
Sharing Information and Transitioning to Adult 
Services
Sharing information with patients is an important part of edu­
cating them about their condition and giving them insight into 
the future. In the past, there was more secrecy around DSD, 
but most research supports sharing information openly in an 
age-appropriate manner over time (Fig. 21.38).551 Sometimes 
parents have many questions and concerns, and psychological 
support is important to help them to feel confident in discussing 
these issues with their child.526,552,553 Education of a child is an 
ongoing process and must account for ongoing changes with the 
child’s cognitive development.551,554 Different families may pre­
fer different strategies, but being prepared for an open dialogue 
when opportunities arise usually works well. Sometimes a psy­
chologist or pediatric endocrinologist can provide information 
at key stages and support the family in reinforcing information 
or answering questions as they come up. It is important to dis­
cuss what terminology the child and parents prefer; most people 
prefer the use of the specific diagnosis rather than the general 
term DSD.555
During childhood, growth and development are monitored. In 
adolescence, hormone replacement therapy may be indicated in 
cases of gonadal dysfunction. In some situations, puberty may be 
blocked to prevent the progression of virilization.
910
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
Transitioning the care of young people from pediatric to 
adult services is another important and potentially challenging 
aspect of the care of DSD management.556,557 In addition to 
ensuring adolescents are fully informed about their condition as 
well as about past and present treatments, it is important to help 
adolescents acquire the skills necessary to take responsibility for 
their care, such as making appointments and filling prescriptions 
themselves, and at the same time to help parents to take a step 
back. Adolescents should have the opportunity to speak to their 
doctor without their parents being present. Often the pediatric 
endocrinologist will see the adolescent until the end of puberty 
before transfer to an adult endocrinologist, but it may be useful 
to involve the adult provider at an earlier stage, with joint con­
sultations with the pediatric and adult providers, so the young 
person can build trust with the new provider. In childhood and 
later, any genital examinations should be performed only when 
necessary and ideally by someone with experience who will be 
involved in long-term care. Photography should be avoided 
unless absolutely necessary and then only with consent.
As more young people transition into adult services, the need for 
specialist adult centers for DSD is becoming apparent. Standard­
ized follow-up has been proposed to detect and treat health prob­
lems associated with DSD in adulthood.554 The team still largely 
includes an endocrinologist, psychologist, geneticist, and surgeon 
(urologist, gynecologist), and radiologists can be important team 
members, especially when advising young people with retained 
gonads or complex anatomy. Multidisciplinary clinics in which all 
team members are available are useful for coordinating care and 
reducing the number of hospital visits and time away from work. 
The key issues in long-term management of DSD include hormone 
replacement, bone health, sexual activity and satisfaction, relation­
ship issues, genital/urinary issues, psychological well-being, fertility/
family building, and other factors that contribute to overall quality 
of life.558–560 Some data are now emerging on outcomes in adult­
hood for general medical issues and quality of life (see later). 
Support Groups and Information
Support groups can also play a very important role in providing 
additional information for children, adolescents, and adults with 
DSD and in bringing members of the community together.561 
There are well-established support groups in several countries for 
general aspects of DSD as well as for specific conditions such as 
CAH and AIS.562 Increasingly accessible information about DSD 
is becoming available through the internet, such as the biology 
of DSD,563 support for families (e.g., dsdfamilies.org),434,564 and 
information for young people about DSD (e.g., dsdteens.org).565 
It is useful to guide young people and families on how to search 
for information because general search terms such as sex can result 
in many inappropriate hits. Patients and families should also be 
counseled that there is great variability within and between DSD 
conditions, and thus some information may not be applicable. 
Tumor Risk and DSD
The gonads of individuals with DSD with Y-chromosomal mate­
rial containing the GBY region are at risk of malignant change, but 
the incidence and age range for appearance of tumors vary widely 
depending on the underlying diagnosis (Table 21.10). Data on risk 
of gonadal tumors for each diagnosis are hampered by the lack of 
a molecularly confirmed diagnosis in many studies, reporting bias, 
inconsistent criteria to define precursor lesions, and limited infor­
mation on the natural history due to the practice of early gonadec­
tomy. In general, forms of DSD with impaired or arrested gonadal 
development (gonadal dysgenesis) have a high risk of GCTs that 
can be present early in life—as early as 3 months of age—whereas 
forms of DSD with normal testis development but reduced andro­
gen synthesis or action have a lower risk, and gonadal tumors rarely 
arise before puberty.406 Severely dysgenetic, streak-like gonads (i.e., 
gonads that appear scar-like and lack endocrine function) may in 
fact contain germ cells, and these dysgenetic gonads are at high risk

of GCT. However, true streak gonads (i.e., gonads that consist of 
fibrous tissue and lack germ cells) are, by definition, not at risk of 
GCT, but this can only be concluded at histologic examination. 
Scrotal testes are thought to be at lower risk of GCT development 
than undescended testes, possibly because of a lesser degree of dys­
genesis and/or the effects of anatomic location and temperature.406
Various subtypes of germ cell cancer exist: seminomatous can­
cers, on the one hand, classified as seminoma in the testis, dysger­
minoma in the ovary and dysgenetic gonad, and germinoma when 
located extragonadally, and nonseminomatous cancers, on the other 
hand, including teratoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and 
embryonal carcinoma.406 The development of germ cell cancer is 
preceded by abnormal germ cell development. In poorly differenti­
ated gonads, germ cells may be present without the formation of 
follicles or seminiferous tubules; this is known as undifferentiated 
gonadal tissue. These germ cells may develop into a gonadoblastoma, 
which is the precursor lesion of a dysgerminoma.406 If the gonad has 
a greater degree of testicular differentiation, the germ cells are pres­
ent in seminiferous tubules, although these may remain immature 
due to impaired Sertoli cell function and/or reduced synthesis or 
action of androgens. Delayed germ cell maturation is often seen in 
DSD and is characterized by luminal gonocytes that show prolonged 
expression of markers such as POU5F1 (also known as OCT3/4) 
that are normally only expressed during early life. If, after migrat­
ing to the basal membrane, these germ cells continue to express 
POU5F1, coexpress TSPY in a heterogeneous pattern, and show 
focal expression of KITLG, they are classified as pre-GCNIS.406 
If germ cells show cytonuclear atypia with homogeneous TSPY 
expression and diffuse KITLG expression, then GCNIS is diag­
nosed.406 GCNIS, previously known as CIS, testicular intraepithelial 
neoplasia, or intratubular germ cell neoplasia, unclassified, is the pre­
cursor lesion of invasive GCT. In the general population, GCNIS 
is thought to progress to invasive GCT in the majority of cases, 
but this progression seems rare in CAIS, suggesting that androgens 
influence this progression.406,407
The risk of GCT can be estimated using information from 
clinical assessment, endocrine and genetic evaluation, and imag­
ing. Gonadal biopsy is the gold standard, although it is important

the pathologist has a high level of expertise, and one should be 
aware that a biopsy may not be representative of the entire gonad. 
Genetic predisposition to GCT development is thought to play a 
role; SNPs in candidate genes for disease development have been 
investigated as predictors of GCT risk but were found to have 
insufficient discriminatory value to use in clinical practice.418
The highest risk for early gonadoblastoma occurs for patients 
with Frasier syndrome (caused by mutations in WT1), for whom 
the risk may be as high as 60%.219
In individuals with gonadal dysgenesis due to a 45,X/XY karyotype, 
the risk of gonadoblastoma has been estimated to be 15% to 40%.219
The risk of GCT is lower in AIS407 than in gonadal dysgenesis (see 
“Conditions Affecting Androgen Action”), and again the germ cell 
tumors associated with AIS rarely arise before puberty. Other tumors, 
such as Sertoli cell adenomas, are also more common in CAIS. Fewer 
data are available on the risk in conditions affecting steroidogenesis, 
but the risk seems relatively low but not negligible.219
When counseling patients and their family members about sur­
veillance and/or treatment, the MDT should take into account the 
risk of GCT based on diagnosis, age of the individual, location of the 
gonad and results of gonadal biopsy if available, options for relocat­
ing the gonad, options for reliable surveillance, endocrine potential 
of the gonad and whether this endocrine function is desired by the 
individual, fertility potential of the gonad, risk of surgery, and need 
for hormone replacement therapy if gonadectomy is performed 
(although hormone replacement therapy may already be necessary 
if gonadal sex steroidogenesis is considerably impaired).221,406,566
Because of the high risk for early tumor development, pro­
phylactic gonadectomy in infancy or early childhood is typically 
recommended for dysgenetic gonads and streak-like gonads that 
are undescended, cannot be placed in a lower position where they 
can be monitored, and have no measurable endocrine function 
(although this may be challenging to assess if the other gonad 
has greater function). Serial monitoring with physical examina­
tion (and for older individuals, self-examination) and imaging 
(e.g., ultrasound) may be more appropriate for gonads that are 
descended or can be placed in an extraabdominal, preferably scro­
tal, position and that exhibit more robust endocrine function. In 
conditions such as CAIS with a lower risk of GCTs and where 
GCTs generally do not occur before puberty, gonadectomy should 
be deferred until after puberty; after appropriate counseling, some 
individuals may prefer to leave the gonads in situ in adulthood, 
although monitoring of abdominal gonads is difficult. GCNIS 
cannot be detected directly on ultrasound, although microlithia­
sis, especially when associated with a heterogeneous testis paren­
chyma, may be suggestive.407 Abdominal gonads may be difficult 
to visualize on ultrasound, and although MRI has been suggested 
as an alternative, this cannot reliably detect GCNIS either.407 An 
alternative may be to move abdominal gonads to a more superficial 
location221 (see “Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome”). 
Standard circulating tumor markers (e.g., α-fetoprotein, βhCG, 
lactate dehydrogenase) are of limited use in detecting GCNIS or 
seminomas. Novel serum biomarkers such as microRNAs (e.g., 
miR371-3 and miR302/367) may be useful in detecting malig­
nant lesions but currently cannot detect premalignant lesions.407 
Surgery and DSD
Surgery was once felt to be a standard part of the management of 
DSD, but there is now much more cautious consideration of the 
need for surgery and its timing.567,568
Surgery can potentially be performed on the gonads, the uro­
genital tract, and the genitals. Some procedures are functionally 
important (e.g., gonadectomy to mitigate high tumor risk), whereas 
others (e.g., clitoroplasty) may be viewed as cosmetic. The indica­
tion, timing, and choice of any potential procedure should be made 
on an individual basis and can be influenced by the underlying 
diagnosis. The MDT should inform the patient and family of all 
treatment options, including the option to refrain from treatment 
and their potential benefits and risks, and should take into account 
medical, psychological, social, and cultural aspects so that a well-
informed shared decision can be made.569 Few surgeries need to be 
performed urgently, and the family should be advised that there is 
ample time for decision making. Some countries have legal restric­
tions on genital and/or gonadal surgery in children.
Some have argued that surgery in infancy or early childhood 
may be beneficial because the child may be spared the experience of 
growing up with atypical genital appearance and because the tissues 
are easier to operate on and heal better.570 Moreover, performing 
early surgery to make the appearance of the genitalia more typical 
may (or may not) alleviate the potentially significant distress some 
parents feel due to their child’s genital appearance,571,572 but at the 
risk that the child may later regret the parents’ decisions, especially if 
surgery results in a genital appearance that proves to be inconsistent 
with the child’s identified gender, if there is impaired sexual func­
tion or sensation, or if further surgeries are required.
Others have recommended that surgery be deferred until the 
child is old enough to express gender identity, to express opin­
ions about the goals of surgery, to be part of the decision-making 
process, and/or to be part of the formal consent/assent process, 
although precisely how to define these milestones remains uncer­
tain.568,569,573,574 This approach requires strong positive parenting 
and support, and it is not well understood how well young people 
cope in these situations as they mature.
For a child born with atypical genital appearance and raised as 
a girl, the parents should be guided through a balanced discussion 
about all options. The individuals for whom clitoral surgery is most 
commonly considered are XX individuals with CAH. For babies with 
CAH, treatment to achieve adrenal suppression often results in consid­
erable reduction in the size of the clitorophallus, and the clitorophal­
lus may also become less prominent as the child grows, so a period of 
observation is appropriate before decisions about surgery are made.573 
Psychological support in dealing with worries such as diaper changing 
should be provided. Outcome studies in women with CAH who had 
undergone feminizing genital surgery have demonstrated impaired 
genital sensitivity and sexual function, but comparisons to women 
who had not undergone surgery are difficult because the practice of 
feminizing genitoplasty has been so widespread.574,575 Although sur­
gical procedures have changed, with greater emphasis on nerve spar­
ing, these data are relevant for decisions made during infancy and 
childhood on the surgical management of conditions such as CAH, 
and long-term outcome data are awaited for newer approaches. In 
centers that offer surgical options, it is generally accepted that clitoro­
plasty should be reserved for the most severe degree of clitoromegaly, 
and in many situations, vaginal surgery is deferred until after puberty. 
In adulthood, vaginal lengthening in conditions such as CAIS and 
the MRKH syndrome can often be achieved by dilator treatment 
alone, although surgery may be necessary in some cases.414
Subjects with DSD raised as boys often undergo surgery to correct 
hypospadias and/or orchidopexy for undescended testes. Hypospadias 
repair can be performed between 6 and 18 months of age or deferred 
until approximately 4 years of age or later. More than one procedure 
is often required, and complications such as stenosis, fistula, or the 
913
CHAPTER 21  Differences of Sex Development
need for redo surgery are relatively frequent. The surgeon should pro­
vide complete information on these procedures to the parents and 
ensure that their expectations are realistic.576 Many boys with severe 
hypospadias undergo surgery in early life because performing these 
approaches in adolescence may be more difficult and associated with 
a higher rate of complications, but data are lacking on optimal timing 
and outcomes.577 Open discussions with the parents and later with 
the child are needed, and boys may need more support in childhood 
and adolescence than is usually currently offered.
Gonadectomy is another issue that requires the collective 
discussion of the multidisciplinary team and may include input 
from an ethicist. One potential goal of gonadectomy is to reduce 
the risk of GCTs. As noted earlier, there is an important distinc­
tion between, on the one hand, the risk for early-onset GCT with 
gonadal dysgenesis if Y-chromosomal material is present and for 
which gonadectomy in infancy may be appropriate and, on the 
other hand, the risk for late-onset GCT in XY DSD conditions 
with typically differentiated testes (which has been best described 
for CAIS but may also exist for conditions affecting androgen syn­
thesis) and for which gonadectomy should be deferred until after 
puberty. Moreover, different causes and degrees of gonadal dys­
genesis may confer different risks for GCT, but for many causes of 
gonadal dysgenesis, the precise risk for GCT is not known.
The topic of gonadectomy before puberty in XY individuals raised 
female with the goal of preventing virilization and in others with 
DSD to avoid gonadal tumors has previously been mentioned. The 
irreversible nature of such a procedure has created uncertainty among 
professionals, particularly when the procedure is performed before the 
affected child can be engaged in discussions and in situations where 
there could be a potential for future fertility or endocrine function. 
Temporary suppression of puberty (and possibly minipuberty) using 
GnRH analogues may be used to delay a decision on gonadectomy.568
Some centers offer cryopreservation of excised gonads, but 
patients and families should not be given unrealistic expectations 
for preservation of reproductive potential, especially because cur­
rent knowledge is based primarily on fertility preservation of other­
wise normal gonads before cancer therapies.578 If tissue is preserved, 
there needs to be a clear dialogue about likely outcomes and options. 
On the other hand, germ cell number and viability may decline 
with time, so there could be a limited window of opportunity.578 
Furthermore, reproductive technologies are changing rapidly, there 
are highly publicized reports in animals of stem cell approaches, 
such as germ cell reprogramming, and successful birth following 
cryopreservation of (normal) prepubertal testis has been achieved 
in monkeys.579 Whether these technologies will eventually provide 
useful clinical approaches for patients with DSD remains to be seen. 
Fertility/Family Building
Many forms of DSD are associated with reduced fertility or infer­
tility. Successful use of assisted reproductive techniques has been 
reported in some cases, such as TESE and/or intracytoplasmic 
sperm injection (ICSI) in men with PAIS or 5α-reductase defi­
ciency,420,421,580 and a few pregnancies using donor oocytes have 
been reported in women with XY DSD who have a uterus.581,582 
Uterus transplantation has recently been shown to make preg­
nancy possible for women who do not have a uterus, resulting 
in live birth in a woman with MRKH syndrome.583 Alternative 
options to build families include the use of donor sperm, adop­
tion, or foster care. It is important to provide individuals with 
information on the possibilities in their specific situation; a recent 
study found that provision of such information is suboptimal.584 
DSD in Resource-Limited Countries
Many of our approaches to DSD are being developed within the 
context of large medical centers and experienced MDTs with 
ready access to biochemical assays such as AMH, imaging, and 
state-of-the-art genetic tests. In reality, many children and adults 
with DSD live in countries with less access to resources or with 
different social and cultural pressures.541 Each clinician needs to 
work with the tests and treatments that are available and afford­
able to optimize their ability to assess, diagnose, and treat indi­
viduals with DSD. Knowledge of the local prevalence of certain 
forms of DSD and genetic hot spots can be very important, as well 
as relevant social, cultural, and religious factors that might influ­
ence the way a child and the family view DSD. Limited education 
about DSD is available to clinicians in some countries, but tools 
such as the European Society for Paediatric Endocrinology (ESPE) 
e-learning may be valuable.585 The Paediatric Training Centres in 
Africa (PETCA), established in 2008 to provide specialist training 
in endocrinology and diabetes for qualified pediatricians, is begin­
ning to pay dividends, with more than 100 additional qualified 
specialists distributed among 13 sub-Saharan African countries.586 
Outcome Studies
There is such a wide range of conditions included under the 
umbrella of DSD that it is difficult to obtain an overarching 
assessment of the health and quality of life in adulthood for indi­
viduals who have lived with DSD from childhood. Standardizing 
longitudinal assessment in individuals with DSD across centers 
will help to facilitate future outcome studies.554
Most data regarding sexual function and quality of life come 
from women with CAH who had various genitoplasty procedures 
during their childhood.587 The debate continues regarding the 
timing of any surgery for girls with CAH and whether one-stage 
or two-stage surgery is the preferred option.588 Adult endocri­
nologists are now undertaking detailed studies of the comorbid 
conditions associated with CAH and its medical treatment (see 
also Chapter 13). The UK Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia Adult 
Study Executive (CaHASE) studies on cohorts of more than 200 
adults show poorer health status related to increased obesity, 
hypertension, insulin resistance, osteoporosis, impaired fertil­
ity, and reduced quality of life.589–591 Despite improvements in 
growth in recent years, shorter adult height was still one of the 
adverse outcomes, particularly in relation to hypertension. Similar 
findings were found in outcome studies of a Swedish population of 
adults with CAH.592 The Swedish CAH population also had lower 
educational achievement and reduced income, had increased dis­
ability allowance and sick leave, were less likely to be married, and 
had fewer children compared with control subjects.593 The comor­
bid medical conditions may result from long-standing inadequate 
control of CAH by replacement glucocorticoids, estimated to be 
the case in more than one-third of adults. Studies of modified-
release hydrocortisone preparations that more closely mimic the 
cortisol circadian rhythm are showing promising results, with a 
reduction in the total hydrocortisone daily dose required for ade­
quate adrenal androgen suppression.594
In recent years, several outcome studies for adults with other forms 
of DSD have been published. These include reports from the DSD-life 
study, a multicenter study that included 1040 individuals with various 
forms of DSD aged ≥16 years in 14 study centers in Germany, France, 
the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. In the 
DSD-life study, individuals with XY DSD were found to have good 
914
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
metabolic health status, but subjective health status was reduced.595 
Women with Turner syndrome and XY DSD were found to have a 
better physical quality of life than those with CAH, whereas psycho­
social well-being was found to be average in these three groups.596 
Across the entire DSD-life population, quality of life was similar to 
that of healthy European populations in the psychological domain, 
slightly worse in the physical-health domain, slightly better in the envi­
ronment domain, and significantly worse in the social-relationships 
domain.597 Women with Turner syndrome, CAH, or XY DSD and 
men with Klinefelter syndrome or XY DSD all reported a similar qual­
ity of life. Health status was the strongest predictor of quality of life; 
notably, 46% of participants had a chronic condition other than DSD. 
Being able to live comfortably on present income was also positively 
associated with quality of life. Having a partner was associated with 
better quality of life in the social-relationships domain.
A nationwide study of females with XY DSD in Denmark showed 
that morbidity is not increased when diagnoses directly related to 
the DSD itself were excluded.405 A Swedish study reported a higher 
rate of psychiatric morbidity in women with CAIS and complete 
gonadal dysgenesis compared with controls but similar to that in 
women with POI.598 Anxiety and depression were increased among 
individuals with Turner syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome, CAH, or 
XY DSD; more openness about the condition was associated with 
fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression.599
Quality-of-life studies have also been reported in populations of 
German, Italian, and Brazilian individuals with XX DSD and XY 
DSD and of either male or female social gender, so study cohorts are 
quite heterogeneous.600–602 In general, quality of life was satisfactory, 
there was no evidence of gender dysphoria, and psychosocial adjust­
ment was better in younger people when compared with an older 
generation of DSD individuals. Among the XY DSD group in the 
Brazilian population, those with a male social gender had a better 
quality of life than those with a female social gender (e.g., the group 
with CAIS). There were more difficulties overall in partnerships and 
sexual relationships. Another study from Germany, which included 
individuals with both XX and XY DSD, showed dissatisfaction with 
available health care services, especially in the group with XY DSD.603
In the DSD-life study, women with CAH or XY DSD were 
found to be less satisfied with their sexual life than controls.596 
Approximately two-thirds of women with Turner syndrome, 
CAH, or XY DSD had attained Tanner breast stage 5, less than in 
the general population.604 About half of the women were satisfied 
with their breasts, and breast satisfaction was associated with sex­
ual satisfaction and feelings of femininity.604 Women with Turner 
syndrome, CAH, or XY DSD were less likely to have a partner or 
to have had intimate sexual contact compared with controls.596 
In a study that compared women with either CAIS or MRKH 
syndrome, there was greater lack of sexual confidence and sexual 
satisfaction in women with CAIS, whereas those with MRKH 
syndrome, although apprehensive in sexual situations, reported 
being satisfied with their sex lives.605 Danish women with XY 
DSD had lower rates of cohabitation and motherhood compared 
with female controls, but education and income were similar to or 
higher than in controls.405 In contrast, Danish men with XX DSD 
had poorer education and reduced income in some age groups.606
As discussed, a study from 2014 of more than 400 XY subjects sub­
divided according to clinical diagnoses of PAIS, disorders of gonadal 
development (partial gonadal dysgenesis), and disorders of androgen 
synthesis (e.g., 5α-reductase deficiency) has shown an increasing trend 
for babies with atypical genitalia to be raised as boys.416 Therefore, 
outcome studies are needed for these groups of individuals. A review 
of XY DSD provided mainly anecdotal data on issues such as gender 
identity and sex redesignation, whether males were satisfied with the 
appearance of their genitalia, and the prevalence of sexual dysfunc­
tion.607 Overall, males were satisfied with their gender, and rarely did 
male-to-female gender redesignation occur in adulthood. Most males 
had some concern about the appearance of the genitalia, and many 
were dissatisfied with sexual function. Another small Dutch study 
reported poor outcomes in terms of penile size and sexual function, 
although participants’ overall body image and psychosexual function­
ing were no different from control subjects.608 Data from the DSD-
life study show that gender change had occurred in 13/81 (16%) of 
individuals with XY or 45,X/46,XY DSD raised as boys compared 
with 5/55 (9%) of individuals with partial androgenization due to XY 
or 45,X/46,XY partial gonadal dysgenesis or XX ovotesticular DSD 
raised as girls and 28/95 (14%) of individuals with XX CAH raised 
as girls.609 In CAH, the change had mainly happened before puberty 
(in 25/26), presumably shortly after birth, but in the other groups, 
approximately 40% of the gender changes had occurred after puberty. 
In individuals with partial androgenization due to XY or 45,X/46,XY 
gonadal dysgenesis or XX ovotesticular DSD, postpubertal gender 
change was more common in those raised as females (5/58, 9%) than 
in those raised as males (2/78, 3%). A gender other than female or 
male variance was reported by 4% of the entire study population 
and was associated with lower self-esteem and increased anxiety and 
depression. Clinicians should therefore be aware of the possibility that 
individuals may not identify as either male or female.
There is a paucity of information about outcomes for specific 
causes of XY DSD, such as PAIS.610,611 Often this label is applied 
without confirmation that the phenotype is due to a mutation in the 
AR gene; as a result, other diagnoses may have been included inad­
vertently. A French multicenter study reported on 15 adults with 
PAIS who had been monitored since birth.612 The external genitalia 
score (EGS) (see Fig. 21.36) was very low, and penile length was 
markedly reduced in adulthood, irrespective of additional andro­
gen treatment. All boys developed gynecomastia in adolescence, 
and sexual function was severely impaired. An international study 
of 29 males with PAIS who were at least 16 years old and a more 
recent study of 27 males with PAIS studied prospectively also con­
firmed universal development of gynecomastia.381,417 Micropenis 
was common at initial presentation but less so when assessed after 
puberty. Onset of puberty was often spontaneous, although andro­
gen treatment was sometimes required subsequently.
There has been considerable progress in many aspects of DSD 
since the previous edition of this chapter. More data are available 
on outcomes in the more common forms of DSD, but outcome 
studies in larger cohorts of individuals with rarer forms of DSD 
are needed, particularly within the XY DSD category. A major 
step toward that goal is the establishment of international regis­
tries for DSD studies (I-DSD), European Reference Networks for 
rare conditions such as DSD, and DSD Translational Research 
Network (DSD-TRN).613 Such networking should provide the 
means to gather more data on the individual, rare causes of DSD 
across the lifespan and to implement the use of clinical bench­
marking in order to improve management and outcome.

KEY POINTS
 • 
Height is an important vital sign to obtain during childhood 
because deviations from the normal linear growth pattern may 
indicate an underlying disorder.
 • 
An intact hypothalamic (growth hormone–releasing hormone 
[GHRH])/pituitary (growth hormone [GH])/insulin-like growth 
factor 1 (IGF1) axis, adequate nutrition, and absence of 
significant systemic disease are requirements for normal linear 
growth.
 • 
A comprehensive past medical, family, and social history 
with assessment of an accurate growth velocity is required 
for the initial investigation of abnormal growth. Laboratory 
and radiologic investigations include an evaluation for occult 
systemic disease and exclusion of hormonal abnormalities.
 • 
Successful treatment of the underlying disorder or correction of 
hormone deficiency(ies) improves linear growth.
 • 
Treatment of short stature with growth-promoting agents may 
improve linear growth in select patients with intact GHRH/GH/
IGF1 axis function.
22
Normal and Aberrant Growth 
in Children
SARA A. DIVALL AND SALLY RADOVICK
Normal Growth
Growth is a fundamental, intrinsic aspect of childhood health. 
It is also a complex yet tightly regulated process. An individual’s 
linear growth trajectory and adult height are predominantly 
determined by genetic composition and orchestrated by mul­
tiple hormones. Linear growth can also be affected by external 
factors, such as the quality and quantity of nutrition, and by psy­
chosocial factors. An array of membrane receptors that activate 
seemingly redundant intracellular signaling cascades is crucial to 
this process.
Whether linear growth occurs as a continuous process or with 
periodic bursts of growth and arrest1–4 has been hard to character­
ize definitively. There appears to be seasonal variations of growth, 
with slower growth in autumn and winter and greater growth in 
spring and early summer.5,6 Some normal children have a broad 
growth channel, with many showing diverse but characteristic 
growth tracks.7 Nonetheless, even though the process of growth 
is multifactorial and complex, children usually grow in a remark­
ably predictable manner. Deviation from such a normal pattern 
of growth can be the first manifestation of a wide variety of dis­
ease processes, including endocrine and nonendocrine disorders 
and involving virtually any organ system. Therefore, frequent and 
accurate assessment of growth is of primary importance in the care 
of children.
Measurement
Assessment of growth requires accurate and reproducible determi­
nations of height. Supine length is measured in children younger 
than 2 years of age, and standing height is assessed in older chil­
dren. It can be useful to measure both length and height in chil­
dren between 2 and 3 years of age to allow comparisons with prior 
length measurements and to record height measurement for future 
comparisons. The inherent inaccuracies in measuring length in 
infants are often obscured by the rapid skeletal growth during this 
period. For measurement of supine length (Fig. 22.1), it is best to 
use a firm box with an inflexible board against which the head lies 
and a movable footboard on which the feet are placed perpendicu­
lar to the plane of the supine length of the infant. Optimally, the 
child should be relaxed, the legs should be fully extended, and the 
head should be positioned in the Frankfurt plane, with the line 
connecting the outer canthus of the eyes and the external auditory 
meatus perpendicular to the long axis of the trunk.
916
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
When children are old enough (and physically capable) to 
stand erect, it is best to use a wall-mounted Harpenden stadiom­
eter like that designed by Tanner and Whitehouse for the British 
Harpenden growth study. The traditional measuring device of a 
flexible arm mounted to a weight balance should not be used as it 
does not provide accurate serial measurements.
As with length measurements in infants, positioning of the 
child in the stadiometer is critical (Fig. 22.2). The child should be 
fully erect, with the head in the Frankfurt plane; the back of the 
head, thoracic spine, buttocks, and heels should touch the vertical 
axis of the stadiometer, and the heels should be together. Every 
effort should be made to correct discrepancies related to lordosis 
or scoliosis. Ideally, serial measurements should be made at the 
same time of day because standing height may undergo diurnal 
variation.
Height determinations should be performed by a trained indi­
vidual rather than an inexperienced member of the staff. We rec­
ommend that lengths and heights be measured in triplicate with 
variation no more than 0.3 cm and recording of mean height. 
For determination of height velocity when several measurements 
are being made within a short period, the same individual should 
perform the determinations to eliminate interobserver variability. 
Even when every effort is made to obtain accurate height measure­
ments, a minimum interval of 6 months is necessary for meaning­
ful height velocity computation. Nine to 12 months of data are 
preferable so that errors of measurement are minimized and the 
seasonal variation in height velocity is assimilated into the data. 
Growth Charts
Evaluation of a child’s height must be done in the context of nor­
mal standards. Revised and updated growth charts have been avail­
able on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) 
website (https://www.cdc.gov/growthcharts) since 2000 (Figs. 
22.3–22.8).8 The data for these charts encompass measurements 
obtained in the United States between 1963 and 1995, and they 
include a broader representation of the U.S. population for all 
measures than was available in earlier charts. Growth charts based 
on the World Health Organization (WHO) data gathered from 
1997 throughout 2003 should be used to monitor the growth of 
children under 2 years of age. Although the data on length are very 
similar between the CDC and WHO curves, the CDC curves 
describe higher weight gain that, among other things, reflects the 
lower prevalence of breastfed infants in the CDC data and is not 
felt to represent optimal growth.9
These charts allow comparison of individual children with the 
3rd, 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th, and 97th percentiles of normal 
American children. There are, however, two limitations of these 
charts when applied to the individual child. First, they do not 
satisfactorily define children below the 3rd or above the 97th per­
centiles—the very children in whom it is most critical to define 
the degree to which they deviate from the normal growth centiles. 
However, the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) data 
tables (also available on the CDC website) can be used to com­
pute standard deviation scores (SDS) if not built into the elec­
tronic medical record. For example, a short child below the 3rd 
• Fig. 22.1  Technique for measuring recumbent length. (A device suitable for measurement of length of 
infants can be purchased from Raven Equipment Limited, Essex, UK.) (Photograph courtesy Noel Cam­
eron.)
• Fig. 22.2  Technique for measuring erect height using the Harpenden sta­
diometer with direct digital display of height. (Devices of this type are avail­
able from Holtain Ltd., Wales, UK, and Seritex Inc., Carlstadt, NJ.)

percentile can be described more precisely as being, for example, 
approximately 4.2 SDS below the mean for age. The height SDS 
equals the child’s height minus the mean height for children of 
the child’s age and sex, divided by the SD of the height for nor­
mal children of this age and sex. The second limitation is that 
cross-sectional data are of lesser value during adolescence than in 
infancy and childhood because differences in the timing of puber­
tal onset considerably influence normal growth rates. To address 
this issue, Tanner and Davies10 developed longitudinal growth 
charts and constructed curve shapes with centile widths obtained 
from a large cross-sectional survey, thus accounting for variability 
in the timing of puberty. Such charts are of particular value in 
assessing growth during adolescence and puberty and for plotting 
sequential growth data for any individual child.
Data from cross-sectional and longitudinal growth studies were 
used to develop height velocity standards (Figs. 22.9 and 22.10). 
Carefully documented height velocity is invaluable in assessing a 
child with abnormalities of growth. There is considerable variabil­
ity in height velocity among children at different ages; however, 
between the age of 2 years and the onset of puberty, the individual 
child grows with remarkable fidelity relative to the normal growth 
curves. Any crossing of percentile curves on the height chart dur­
ing this age period should be considered abnormal and warrants 
further evaluation. As stated earlier, height velocity is most accu­
rate when obtained at intervals of 6 months or greater.
Syndrome-specific growth curves have been developed for 
a number of clinical conditions associated with growth failure, 
such as Turner syndrome (TS),11 achondroplasia,12 and Down 
syndrome.13,14 Such growth profiles are invaluable for tracking 
the growth of children with these clinical conditions. Deviation 
of growth from the appropriate disease-related growth curve 
suggests the possibility of a second underlying cause, such as 
acquired autoimmune hypothyroidism in children with Down 
syndrome or TS. 
Body Proportions
Many abnormal growth states, including both short stature and 
excessive stature, are characterized by disproportionate growth. The 
following determinations should be made as part of the evaluation 
of short stature:
	1.	 Occipitofrontal head circumference
	2.	 Lower body segment: distance from top of pubic symphysis to 
the floor
	3.	 Upper body segment: the difference between total height and 
lower body segment (this can also be measured as the sitting 
height, subtracting the height of the chair or stool)
	4.	 Arm span
Published standards exist for these body proportion measure­
ments, which must be evaluated relative to the patient’s age.15 The

Parental Target Height
Genetic factors are important determinants of growth and height 
potential. Therefore, it is useful to assess a patient’s stature rela­
tive to that of siblings and parents. A provider should calculate a 
child’s genetic adult height potential based on the parents’ heights 
by calculating the midparental height. This is the average of the 
parents’ heights, after accounting for the average difference in 
height between adult men and women (13 cm). In other words, a 
boy’s midparental height equals the average of his parents’ heights 
plus 6.5 cm, and a girl’s midparental height equals the average of 
her parents’ heights minus 6.5 cm.
Because of regression to the mean for a particular popula­
tion,16,17 children of short parents are likely to be less short than 
their parents, and children of tall parents are likely to be less tall 
than their parents. Therefore, a child’s genetic target height range 
centers on the point that represents 80% of the difference between 
the child’s midparental height and the mean adult height for the 
child’s sex.16 For example, if a boy’s father is 168 cm tall and his 
mother is 153 cm tall, his midparental height is 167 cm, which 
is 10 cm below the mean height of adult men (177 cm). There­
fore, the boy’s target height range centers on 169 cm, which is 8 
cm below the mean adult height for men. In more than 95% of 
children, the adult height falls within 10 cm of the point thus 
calculated.16,18 In children with extremely short stature (≥3 SD), 
the father’s height may more strongly correlate with the patient’s 
height, and the mother’s height may more greatly influence birth 
length.19 
Skeletal Maturation
The growth potential in the tubular bones can be assessed by eval­
uation of the progression of ossification within the epiphyses. The 
ossification centers of the skeleton appear and progress in a pre­
dictable sequence in normal children, and this skeletal maturation 
can be compared with normal age-related standards. This forms 
the basis of the bone age or skeletal age, a quantitative determina­
tion of net somatic maturation that serves as a mirror of the tempo 
of growth and maturation. The bone age also reflects the degree 
of growth plate senescence and is therefore a useful adjunct in 
estimating growth opportunity (i.e., the ultimate adult height), as 
discussed later in this chapter.
Not all of the factors that determine the normal pattern of 
skeletal maturation have been identified, but genetic factors and 
multiple hormones, including thyroxine, growth hormone (GH), 
and gonadal steroids, are involved.20 Ultimately, growth cessa­
tion occurs after exhaustion of the proliferative capacity of the

Phases of Normal Growth
Growth occurs at differing rates during intrauterine life, early 
and middle childhood, and adolescence and then ceases after 
fusion of long bone and vertebral epiphyseal growth plates. Karl­
berg and associates resolved the normal linear growth curve into 
three additive, partially superimposable phases27,28: an “infancy” 
phase, starting in midgestation and then rapidly decelerating until 
about 3 to 4 years of age; a “childhood” phase, of slowly decel­
erating growth through early adolescence; and a sigmoid-shaped 
“puberty” phase that comprises the adolescent growth spurt. Pre­
natal growth averages 1.2 to 1.5 cm per week but varies dramati­
cally (Fig. 22.12); the midgestational length growth velocity of 2.5 
cm per week falls to almost 0.5 cm per week immediately before 
birth. Growth velocity (see Figs. 22.9 and 22.10) averages about 
15 cm/year during the first 2 years of life; it then slows to approxi­
mately 6 cm/year during middle childhood. During this time, a 
normal child’s height, plotted on a growth curve, typically remains 
within a given growth channel; that is, it does not cross percentile 
lines on the growth curve.
Prepubertal growth is similar between boys and girls. The 
height difference between men and women, an average of 13 cm, 
is accounted for by two factors. First, boys grow for an average 
of 2 years longer than girls, because girls have an earlier onset of 
puberty and, consequently, earlier cessation of growth. Therefore, 
prepubertal growth is greater for boys; they are 8 to 10 cm taller 
when their puberty starts compared with girls’ heights when their 
puberty starts.16 Second, boys achieve a greater maximal pubertal 
growth velocity than girls, giving them 3 to 5 cm greater pubertal 
growth. The time of onset of puberty varies in normal children, 
resulting in a normal variation in the timing of the pubertal growth 
spurt. The adult height is not influenced by the chronologic age at 
onset of the pubertal growth spurt because any additional time for 
prepubertal growth that occurs when puberty is late is balanced 
by the fact that pubertal growth is smaller the later it occurs (see 
Figs. 22.9 and 22.10). After puberty, chondrocyte proliferation in 
the growth plate slows and senescence occurs due to depletion of 
stem-like cells in the resting zone of the growth plate.29,30
There are two variants of normal growth whose characteristic 
patterns are such that children exhibiting these growth variants 
are often evaluated for a growth disorder. These two variants are 
crossing linear percentiles of infancy and constitutional delay of 
growth and development (CDGD). In many cases, it is difficult

Crossing Linear Percentiles of Infancy
As in postnatal growth, genetic and environmental factors are 
important determinants of fetal growth and of the size of an infant 
(weight and length) at birth. However, there are significant differ­
ences between the factors affecting birth size and those affecting 
childhood growth and adult stature. There is much less correlation 
between length at birth and ultimate adult height than between 
length at birth and height in the later years of childhood.31
Parental stature affects birth length, as it does adult stature; this 
is an indicator of the genetic influence on growth. Although mater­
nal and paternal stature contribute equally to childhood growth 
and adult stature, the effect of maternal stature may predominate 
over that of paternal stature on length at birth.32,33 However, some 
studies have found equal effects of maternal and paternal stature on 
birth size.34 Maternal nutrition and health have significant effects 
on fetal growth. Maternal weight has a positive effect and smoking 
during pregnancy has a negative effect. Maternal diabetes has a 
strong positive effect on fetal growth. It is possible for the prena­
tal determinants of growth to result, for example, in a child who 
will ultimately grow to below-average stature but is above average 
size at birth. For this reason, it is common for infants’ lengths to 
cross percentiles on the growth curve. Indeed, it is more common 
for the growth of an infant to cross percentiles than to follow a 
single percentile from birth into childhood: approximately one-
third of infants have lengths that cross percentiles moving upward 
on the growth curves, and approximately one-third have lengths

crossing percentiles do so in the first 6 to 12 months, although 
some normal infants cross percentiles after 1 year of age.
Infants who are small at birth can be divided into (1) those who 
are small only because of prematurity and are therefore of a size 
appropriate for gestational age (AGA) and (2) those who are small 
for gestational age (SGA). SGA is usually defined as a birth weight 
or length (or both) below the 3rd percentile (or, sometimes, below 
the 10th percentile) for gestational age.36 Some infants born SGA 
represent the small percentage of individuals whose genetic poten­
tial leads to small size at birth, and they can be expected to remain 
small throughout childhood and adulthood. However, many 
infants are SGA due to intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) 
and have a genetic potential expected to result in typical adult 
stature. Most infants who are born small, either premature AGA 
or SGA, have catch-up growth and achieve lengths greater than 
the 3rd percentile within the first 2 years of life. However, up to 
10% of SGA infants do not show such catch-up growth.37,38 The 
pathologic aspects of IUGR and of SGA in infants who do not 
have catch-up growth are discussed later. 
Constitutional Delay of Growth and Development
CDGD is a normal variant of growth.39 It describes the growth 
pattern of children who will experience a later than average tim­
ing of puberty. Their birth size is normal, and their final height 
is within their genetic potential. However, during most of their 
childhood, they grow at a height percentile below that expected 
based on their genetic potential. Typically, these children have a 
lower growth velocity than typical during the first years of life, 
crossing downward on the length percentile growth curves, so that 
by 2 years of age their heights are at or slightly below the 5th 
percentile. After age 3 years, their growth rate is typically nor­
mal, so that their height growth usually remains parallel to the 
5th percentile until adolescence, although the height SDS may 
gradually drift slightly lower during the middle childhood years 
in some cases.39,40 Their height diverges even further from that of 
average children during the early teen years due to the declining 
prepubertal growth velocity of these children compared with the 
accelerating growth rate of children with an average timing of the 
onset of puberty.
Ultimately, children with CDGD have a late growth spurt, 
consistent with their late puberty, and this brings their height into 
the normal adult range. Final height is often in the lower part 
of the parental target height range, and few patients exceed the 
parental target height,41–43 although this finding is probably at 
least in part the result of a selection bias of the children examined 
for such studies. There is evidence that a delayed growth spurt 
may adversely affect growth of the spine, resulting in a decrease 
in the final ratio of the upper to the lower segment and perhaps 
contributing to a limited final height.44 Studies have also reported 
that prepubertal boys with CDGD have decreased bone mineral 
density (BMD),45 although by young adulthood the majority of 
the BMD deficit is absent.46,47 
Secular Changes in Height
There are surprisingly few data concerning the stature of modern 
humans before the measurement of military recruits became cus­
tomary in the 18th century. Skeletal remains from the last ice age 
appear to indicate that adult stature 10,000 to 20,000 years ago 
was not substantially different from that of contemporary adults, 
although this record is obviously fragmentary.48 It has been sug­
gested that a reduction in stature was observed with the intro­
duction of agriculture approximately 5000 years ago, with growth 
attenuation resulting from the combined effects of nutrient defi­
ciency, population growth, and spread of infectious diseases.
Military recruits in the 18th and 19th centuries were clearly 
shorter than those of today, although it must be recognized that 
soldiers were commonly recruited from the lower socioeconomic 
classes, and poor health and nutrition would have contributed to 
both poor growth and late maturity.49 Whereas men in the 20th 
century averaged 5 to 10 cm greater in height than those in the 
18th century for whom we have records, much of this height 
gain has occurred over the past 100 years and probably reflects 
the dramatic improvement in overall nutrition and health seen in 
the Western world. This upward trend in height appears to have 
stopped in many developed countries in the early 21st century.50 
Endocrine Regulation of Growth
The Hypothalamic-Pituitary Axis: Embryogenesis 
and Anatomy
The pituitary gland is central to the regulation of mammalian 
growth. The pituitary gland develops from oral ectoderm in 
response to inductive signals from the neuroepithelium of the 
ventral diencephalon and intrinsic signaling gradients determin­
ing expression patterns of pituitary-specific transcription factors 
in the developing anterior pituitary gland.51 The primordium of 
the anterior pituitary, Rathke’s pouch, forms as an upward invagi­
nation of a single-cell-thick layer of ectoderm that contacts the 
neuroectoderm of the primordium of the ventral hypothalamus 
at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) in the mouse embryo52 and can be 
identified by the third week of pregnancy in humans.
Progenitor cells divide at the lumen of Rathke’s pouch and 
migrate ventrally, begin to differentiate, and exit from the cell 
cycle. Kinase inhibitor 1C (p57Kip2) and cyclin E are expressed 
in cells as they exit the cell cycle. Distinct developmental roles of 
cell cycle inhibitors p57Kip2 and p27Kip1 distinguish pituitary
