CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
There are cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the late 
20th century demonstrating a resurgence of a secular trend in the 
United States, including ethnic influences.183,184 The median age 
of menarche in the United States was 12.8 years according to the 
1973 U.S. National Center for Health Statistics National Health 
Education Study, and data from NHANES III (1988–1994) indi­
cate the median age at that time was 12.43 years, 0.37 years earlier 
than in 1973.185 During a 20-year period in the Bogalusa Heart 
Study, the median menarcheal age decreased by approximately 9.5 
months among Black girls compared with 2 months among White 
girls,186 leading to a 4-month difference. Between the ages of 5 
and 9 years, Black girls in the Bogalusa study had taller stature and 
greater weight, factors that were predictive of menarche before age 
11 years. Black girls have advanced secondary sexual development 
compared with White American girls of the same age during the 
first three stages of puberty, and they have an advanced bone age; 
this may be related to the higher prevalence of obesity among 
Black girls and to an ethnic-specific genetic influence.187–189
Obesity is defined as a BMI (calculated as weight in kilograms 
divided by height in meters squared) equal to or above the 95th 
percentile for age, and overweight is defined by the Centers for Dis­
ease Control and Prevention (CDC) as a BMI equal to or greater 
than the 85th percentile for age. The association between the epi­
demic of childhood obesity and overweight at age of menarche 
is well known.190 Most cross-sectional and longitudinal studies 
found an inverse relationship between menarcheal age and other 
stages of puberty and BMI or other reflections of adiposity.191–193 
Girls had a greater prevalence of overweight or obesity between 
the ages of 8 and 10 years if they were in puberty or had advanced 
breast development.194 A study of the age at onset of puberty in 
U.S. boys of various ethnic groups indicated an earlier age of onset 
between 6 months and 2 years depending on indicator and ethnic 
group.195 Except for a delay in pubertal development in boys with 
BMI below the 15th percentile there was no effect of overweight 
or obesity in male puberty as found in girls in other studies.
Longitudinal studies are limited in the United States but of 
great importance in the evaluation of a secular trend. The lon­
gitudinal National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) 
Growth and Health Study followed 1266 White and 1313 Black 
girls from 9 or 10 years of age for 10 or more years. A recent 
report of a sample of 1239 girls from the study noted that 10.4% 
of White, 23.4% of Black non-Hispanic, and 14.9% of Hispanic 
girls had attained breast stage 2 at 7 years, and 18.3%, 42.9%, 
and 30.9%, respectively, attained breast stage 2 at 8 years, younger 
than data from 10 to 30 years ago. In a sample of 1155 girls, 
the mean age of menarche among Whites was 12.7 years, and 
among Blacks, it was 12.1 years; a direct relationship was found 
between weight and BMI and the age of menarche.187 Of these 
girls, 51.6% started puberty with only one manifestation. Those 
who experienced breast development first (i.e., thelarche pattern), 
rather than the appearance of pubic hair (i.e., adrenarche pattern), 
had an earlier menarche (12.6 vs. 13.1 years); this was associated 
with a greater BMI and body weight, which was not true for those 
girls manifesting the adrenarche pattern.196 These findings sup­
port the analysis of NHANES III, in which girls with earlier breast 
development had greater BMI values at the time of menarche than 
those with adrenarche occurring first.197
During the past 40 years, menarcheal age in the White subjects 
in the Fels Longitudinal Study has remained stable even as BMI 
has increased, with no relationship shown between the two. Sub­
jects with early menarche had a tendency to increase BMI after 
menarche,51,198 suggesting that increased weight appears to be a 
consequence rather than determinant of the age at menarche and 
that secular changes in BMI and mean age at menarche may be 
independent phenomena. There was a rise in BMI; waist circum­
ference; hip circumference; and serum levels of LH, androstenedi­
one, T, and DHEAS during the years immediately after menarche 
in a shorter longitudinal study.199
International data support the effects of BMI on puberty, but 
earlier onset of pubertal growth and a tall stature in childhood do 
not lead to a taller adult height.200 Children studied longitudi­
nally in Denmark showed earlier breast development (estimated 
mean age of 9.86 years compared to 10.88 years) and menarche 
(13.42 years compared to 13.13 years) in 2006 compared to 1991, 
which could not be explained by BMI or even by a difference in 
gonadotropin values, suggesting other factors were operative.201
In countries with rapid improvement in socioeconomic condi­
tions, nutrition, and overall health status, the age of menarche 
decreases more rapidly. In a large longitudinal study that included 
almost 16,000 Indonesian girls, the age at menarche declined by 
1 year from the 1940s to 1990s.202 Where standards of living do 
not change, the age of menarche is more stable. In South America 
and Africa, some rural children fare better and have earlier puberty 
and taller stature than urban children, demonstrating a trend of 
adverse health and nutritional conditions in crowded urban cen­
ters. Malnourished individuals have a later age of menarche across 
the world.203
As a whole, these reports indicate that populations existing 
in the most difficult conditions who experience improvement in 
socioeconomic status demonstrate a greater decrease in the age of 
menarche. Once a minimum nutritional status or state of health 
is reached, the effects of socioeconomic status on the age of men­
arche are minimized or eliminated, but increased BMI can lower 
the age of menarche further. However, there are other factors,

Factors Affecting the Age of Puberty and Menarche
Diet and Puberty. The composition of diet and the number 
of calories in the diet may relate to menarche.205 The prospec­
tive, longitudinal Harvard Longitudinal Studies of Child Health 
and Development found that girls had earlier menarche if they 
were taller and consumed more animal protein and less vegetable 
protein as early as 3 to 5 years old. They had earlier peak growth 
velocity if they had higher dietary fat intake at 1 to 2 years old and 
higher animal protein intake at 6 to 8 years. Peak height velocity 
(PHV) increased, controlling for body size, if more calories and 
animal protein were consumed 2 years before peak growth. The 
correlation between higher animal protein intake and lower age of 
menarche was confirmed in Germany and Britain.37,206 Another 
longitudinal study in the United Kingdom showed that total 
energy intake in both boys and girls, and protein intake in girls, 
was associated with earlier age of puberty.207 A positive relationship 
between high fiber intake and age of menarche held true in a com­
parison of 46 countries,208 and a longitudinal study demonstrated 
a later onset of puberty and PHV in girls with higher isoflavone 
intakes, suggesting a lower risk for breast cancer with a high-fiber 
prepubertal diet.209 On the other hand, lifelong vegetarian dietary 
intake does not affect the age of menarche,210 and a low-fat diet 
in otherwise healthy prepubertal children 8 to 10 years old with 
elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol produced no 
difference in age of menarche or pubertal progression.211 Phytoes­
trogen (flavonol but not lignan) intake delays breast development, 
particularly in girls with lower BMI values.212,213 
Puberty and Maternal Factors. Another influence on the age 
of menarche is the maternal environment. Macrosomia resulting 
from maternal diabetes or obesity is associated with increased BMI 
in childhood, which itself is related to earlier puberty and men­
arche. Increased or decreased weight gain in pregnancy likewise 
decreases the age of menarche, according to data from the Nurses’ 
Health Study II.214 Heavy maternal smoking of cigarettes but not 
of marijuana leads to earlier male puberty but not female puberty 
in offspring.215 Maternal tea drinking but not coffee drinking 
was associated with a later age of menarche and puberty in their 
daughters. Daughters of mothers who were more physically active 
during pregnancy had a modest delay in menarche.216 
Stress and Puberty. Life history theories aiming to explain 
influences on the age of puberty address energetics, stress suppres­
sion, psychosocial acceleration, paternal investment, and child 
development, each of which may have various effects on the tim­
ing and progression of pubertal development.217 This approach 
acknowledges the fact that evolution optimizes allocation of 
limited resources to maximize fitness and allow reproductive 
success.218
Stress affects the age of menarche. The absence of a father or 
lower parental education increases the likelihood of early men­
arche; however, there is evidence that the exposure to paternal 
psychopathology that precedes the absence of the father might 
be causative in such situations.219 War increases the age of voice 
breaking in boys (e.g., in Bach’s choir during the War of Austrian 
Succession in 1727–1749), and the age of menarche increased 
during World War II and during more recent hostilities in the 
former Yugoslavia.220 Sexual abuse was associated with earlier 
onset of puberty and earlier menarche compared with a control 
population in a large U.S. national study, although it is dif­
ficult to eliminate the effect of family dysfunction in this situa­
tion as well.221 However, in a more recent study, when adjusted 
for these possible socioeconomic confounders, sexually abused 
girls still entered puberty approximately 1 year earlier for pubic 
hair development and 8 months earlier for breast development 
than their nonabused peers.222 Child abuse of various types was 
associated with delayed puberty and menarche in a large British 
study, and sexual abuse in this cohort led to both early and late 
menarche.223 
Genetic Determinants of Pubertal Timing. The timing of 
puberty varies widely in the general population and is influenced 
by genetic, environmental, and epigenetic factors.4 The studies of 
pubertal timing in families and twins provide evidence that 50% 
to 80% of this variation was caused by genetic factors.4–6 Recent 
genome-wide association studies (GWASs) in large populations 
shed light on the genetic determinants underlying the heritability 
of pubertal timing. By studying ∼370,000 women of European 
ancestry, Day et al224 reported ∼400 independent loci robustly 
associated with the age at menarche.224 The individual effect size 
of each locus ranges from 1 week to 1 year; however, the cumula­
tive effect of all identified genetic signals only explains 7.4% of 
population variance in age at menarche. Similar results are seen in 
GWASs on pubertal timing in males using age at voice breaking as 
a proxy for pubertal timing. A large number of the identified loci 
are implicated in BMI, height, and epigenetic regulation, consis­
tent with the critical links between energy balance, growth and 
development, and reproduction. Further, some loci implicated 
in the timing of puberty are located in imprinted regions (e.g., 
MKRN3 and DLK1) that exhibit significant effects when pater­
nally inherited.224 Notably, a few menarche loci are enriched in 
or near genes that underlie CHH (e.g., FGF8, GNRH1, KAL1, 
KISS1, NR0B1, TACR3, etc.) or CPP (MKRN3). In conclusion, 
puberty timing is a highly polygenic trait, likely involving many 
individual genetic signals. Further studies on larger cohorts with 
well-studied phenotypes are needed to uncover genetic players and 
determine the contribution of gene-environmental interactions.
Finally, there is indirect evidence relating earlier menarche 
to an increased likelihood of hepatocellular carcinoma. On the 
other hand, later age of menarche (>14 years) is associated with an 
increased risk of glioma or non-Hodgkin lymphoma.225,226 
COVID-19 and Timing of Puberty. Recent data from several 
observational studies showed that during the COVID-19 pan­
demic and associated lockdowns, the frequency of CPP in girls 
increased.227–229 In Italy, where the pandemic has raged fiercely, 
apart from the increased CPP incidence, there was also a faster rate 
of pubertal progression, as compared to previous years, in patients 
with a previous diagnosis.230 The underlying mechanism of the 
association between earlier onset of puberty in girls and COVID-
19 remains to be elucidated. Initially, the combination of lifestyle 
changes, increase in screen time, and alterations in sleeping habits 
was thought to potentially contribute to the phenomenon. How­
ever, changes in CNS mediators and an increase in catecholamines 
could also contribute as a trigger, although they are poorly studied. 
Finally, spending more time indoors has certainly exposed these 
children to specific contaminants working as endocrine-disrupt­
ing chemicals (EDCs), which could also potentially contribute. 
Future research should continue to investigate the consequences 
and the underlying mechanisms of the effects of the COVID-19 
pandemic on the timing and progression of puberty.231

CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
Other Factors. Seasonality of menarche was observed in a U.S. 
cohort of 3000 college students; those born after 1970 had an 
earlier age of menarche and a more pronounced frequency peak in 
July. Factors hypothesized to contribute to seasonality of menarche 
include stress and the photoperiod. In Peru, puberty begins at a 
later age, and pubertal development lasts longer at high altitudes 
than at low altitudes, even when nutritional status is similar. There 
is a north-to-south decrease in the age of menarche in Europe that 
may result from environmental factors or genetic influences.
Finally, the association between EDCs, a highly heterogeneous 
group of exogenous substances interfering with the endocrine sys­
tem and timing and progression of sexual maturation, has been 
investigated.232,233 In  vitro studies have shown that EDCs can 
influence the GnRH regulatory network and that they can induce 
epigenetic changes by altering methylation status. For example, the 
widely used phytoestrogen Genistein and bisphenol A (BPA) sup­
press inhibitory components of the GnRH network and activate 
stimulatory components, whereas dioxin exhibits an inhibitory 
effect at all regulatory hierarchical levels of the GnRH network.234 
Phthalates, widely used as plasticizers to make hard plastic more 
flexible, and BPA both have been shown to alter DNA methyla­
tion in genes related to pubertal onset.233,235,236 
Fetal Origins of Adult Disease
The fetal in utero environment significantly determines the risk 
for major chronic diseases, such as cardiovascular disease, stroke, 
hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and obesity later in life. This phe­
nomenon, known as the Barker hypothesis,237 also has implica­
tions for growth and puberty. As seen in longitudinal studies, 
low birth weight followed by rapid weight gain in infancy (i.e., 
catch-up growth) leads to tall childhood stature and early pubertal 
development. Poor prenatal nutrition and small-for-gestational-
age (SGA) status tend to advance the age of puberty in girls and 
the age of adrenarche238,239; a secondary effect of increased post­
natal nutrition, often leading to overweight or obesity, lowers 
the age of puberty. Fig. 23.17 describes the relationship between 
excessive adipose tissue and early puberty. A prospective study 
demonstrated that a lower expected birth-weight ratio (i.e., ratio 
of observed infant’s birth weight to median birth weight appro­
priate for maternal age, weight, height, parity, infant sex, and 
gestational age) and a higher BMI at 8 years of age led to an 
earlier age of menarche.240 Girls who are longer and lighter at 
birth and subsequently have greater BMI values at 8 years tend 
to have earlier menarche.241 Rapid weight gain in the second to 
ninth months but not thereafter correlated with a greater BMI 
at 10 years and with earlier menarche in a longitudinal study.242 
On the contrary, higher birth weight is related to a later age of 
menarche, judging from data across several countries.243 LGA 
infants tend to have an earlier age of takeoff of the pubertal 
growth spurt.244
In the Barker hypothesis, besides from prematurity, birth 
weight and rate of postnatal growth—not prematurity—are also 
inversely related to cardiovascular mortality risk and the preva­
lence of insulin-resistance syndrome (i.e., metabolic syndrome 
[MetS] or syndrome X), which consists of hypertension, impaired 
glucose tolerance, and elevated triglyceride levels, among a grow­
ing list of other findings. This outcome is attributed to fetal and 
neonatal metabolic programming, in which early adjustments to 
enhance survival in difficult intrauterine circumstances set the 
stage for later disorders. Insulin resistance, which may be the basis 
for most of these complications or may be just one feature of the 
syndrome, may spare nutrients from use in muscle, leaving them 
available for the brain. This mechanism can minimize CNS dam­
age in the fetus during periods of malnutrition.237 
Normal Pubertal Development
Physical Changes at Puberty
The timing of pubertal onset varies greatly in the general pop­
ulation, even among individuals of the same ethnicity, ranging 
roughly from 8 to 13 years in girls245 and 9 to 14 years in boys.246 
Pubertal changes follow a mostly consistent pattern that is largely 
sex dependent.
Secondary Sexual Characteristics in Females
Thelarche. A longitudinal follow-up of 432 girls age 9.5 to 15.5 
years confirmed that thelarche (i.e., breast development Tan­
ner stage 2) is the earliest clinically detectable sign of puberty in 
most White females, preceding the pubarche (i.e., appearance of 
pubic hair) by an average 4 months.247 Nevertheless, approxi­
mately 15% of girls have pubic hair as the initial manifestation 
of puberty.247 More recently, an even larger longitudinal cohort 
of >1200 girls of U.S. origin reported thelarche onset at a mean 
age of 8.8, 9.3, 9.7, and 9.7 years for Black, Hispanic, White non-
Hispanic, and Asian participants, respectively.248 The five stages of 
breast development described by Tanner are the most widely used 
staging mechanism (Fig. 23.18).249 The development of the breast 
is primarily under the control of estrogens secreted by the ovaries, 
whereas the growth of pubic and axillary hair (Fig. 23.19) is under

Secondary sexual characteristic development is completed 
approximately 1.5 years after the menarche.
Changes in the vagina, labia, and uterus also occur during 
puberty. The vaginal mucosa changes from prepubertal reddish 
to a more pink appearance. Estrogen action contributes to the 
secretion of clear or whitish discharge in the months preceding the 
menarche. The vaginal pH decreases as menarche approaches as a 
result of the increase in lactic acid produced by lactobacilli in the 
vaginal flora. The length of the vagina increases from about 8 cm 
at the onset of puberty to 11 cm at menarche. Thickening, protru­
sion, and rugation of the labia majora and minora occur. Fat is 
deposited in the area of the mons pubis, and the appearance of the 
labia majora becomes wrinkled. The clitoris enlarges slightly, and 
the urethral opening becomes more prominent.255 The uterus also 
grows until the age of 16 years under the influence of E2, proges­
terone, GH, and IGF1.256 Its shape changes considerably from an 
initial tubular corpus to a more bulbous structure, and its length 
increases from 2 to 3 cm to 5 to 8 cm, with a concomitant volume 
rise from 0.4 to 1.6 mL to 3 to 15 mL.257 
Secondary Sexual Characteristics in Males
Testicular enlargement. In boys, several prospective cohorts
195,246,258 have confirmed that testicular enlargement (volume 
≥3–4 mL) is the first detectable sign of puberty, occurring at a 
mean age of 11.5 years. Testes growth begins approximately 6 
months after the average chronologic age of breast development 
initiation in girls (see Fig. 23.16) and 6 to 12 months before penis 
growth (i.e., genital Tanner stage 3) and pubic hair development. 
Pubertal testicular enlargement is indicated when the longitu­
dinal diameter of a testis is greater than 2.5 cm (excluding the 
epididymis) or the volume is greater than 3 to 4 mL.259 TV can 
be estimated by comparing the testes with ellipsoids of known 
volume (Prader orchidometer), a measurement that correlates 
well with ultrasonographic findings260 and stages of puberty.261 A 
longitudinal study supported the validity of considering an orchi­
dometer-derived TV of 3 mL as the onset of puberty, based on 
further pubertal progression occurring within 6 months in 82% 
of boys who had reached this phase.258 In favor of the same cut­
off, serum T and calculated free testosterone (FT) levels change 
significantly at the transitions of TV between 1 and 2 mL, 2 and 
3 mL, 6 and 8 mL, and 10 and 15 mL, without any difference 
between TV of 3 to 6 mL.262 Nevertheless, another large cohort 
of 769 healthy Dutch boys age 6 months to 19 years argued that 
a TV of 4 mL, as assessed by clinical palpation, is a more specific 
threshold to define pubertal onset.263 In the same study, the lower 
reference for TV at the end of puberty was set at 15 to 18 mL by 
orchidometer and 8 to 10 mL by ultrasound scan.
Penile growth. The growth and maturation of the penis 
usually correlate closely with pubic hair development because 
both features are under androgen control. However, the stages 
of pubic hair development and genital development264 should 
be determined independently because discordant stages pro­
vide clues to potential disorders of the adrenal gland or testes 
(Figs. 23.21 and 23.22). The phallus should be measured while 
stretched and in the flaccid state because there is much variation 
among individuals in the length of the unstretched penis. Penile 
length is measured using a straight edge on the dorsal surface 
from the pubic ramus to the tip of the glans while compress­
ing the suprapubic fat pad and applying gentle traction. Mean 
stretched penile length increases sharply to approximately 9.5 
cm (±1.1 cm) by late puberty.265
Spermarche. The first histologic evidence of spermatogenesis 
appears between ages 11 and 15 years (Fig. 23.23; also see Figs. 
23.14 and 23.19). Spermaturia is an early sign of pubertal devel­
opment. Spermaturia is an intermittent event and therefore not 
a reliable indicator to assess puberty onset. Finding of spermato­
zoids in the first-morning urine specimen occurred at a median 
chronologic age of 14.1 years, with a sharp peak at pubic hair Tan­
ner stage 3, in 129 healthy German boys age 10.1 to 17.8 years.266 
Another milestone of male puberty, the age of first conscious 
ejaculation, was recently studied in 1582 boys from Bulgaria, 
with reported onset at an average age of 13.3 ± 1.1 years.267 This 
remains in agreement with historical data of a first ejaculation at a 
mean chronologic age of 13.5 years in normal boys and at a mean 
bone age of 13.5 years in boys with delayed puberty.268 Interest­
ingly, the age of spermarche decreased in China between 1995 and 
2010,269 mirroring, to a degree, the secular trend of menarche in 
girls. A strictly normal sperm count (i.e., normal sperm concentra­
tion, morphologic appearance, and motility) is not present until a 
bone age of 17 years.270
Deepening of the voice. The gender difference in voice devel­
ops during puberty. In the peripubertal period, the length of the 
vocal cords in boys and girls is about 12 to 15 mm, of which the 
membranous portion is 7 to 8 mm. In adult men, the vocal cords 
attain a length of 18 to 23 mm (membranous portion, 12–16 
mm), whereas in women, the cords enlarge only slightly (13–18 
mm).271 During puberty, the male larynx, cricothyroid cartilage, 
and laryngeal muscles enlarge, leading to the appearance of an 
Adam’s apple. Voice breaking, defined as a large change in singing 
and speaking frequencies, occurs between Tanner stages G3 and 
G4.272 Four hundred sixty-three Danish choir boys were retro­
spectively studied over a 10-year period, and the median age of 
voice break was at 14.0 years (range: 13.9–14.6 years).273 Voice

breaking is a noninvasive method to monitor pubertal develop­
ment in boys.274
Facial hair in boys is first apparent on the corners of the upper 
lip and the upper cheeks; it then spreads to the midline of the lower 
lip and finally to the sides and the lower border of the chin. The first 
stage of facial hair development usually occurs during pubic hair 
stage 3 (average age of 14.9 years in the United States), and the last 
stage occurs after pubic hair stage 5 and genital stage 5.246 
Other Physical Changes in Both Sexes
Axillary sweat glands begin to function in both sexes as the hair 
appears. The appearance of circumanal hair slightly precedes that 
of axillary hair in boys. Comedones, acne, and seborrhea of the 
scalp appear as a result of the increased secretion of gonadal and 
adrenal sex steroids. Early-onset acne correlates with the devel­
opment of severe acne later in puberty. Acne vulgaris, the most 
prevalent skin disorder in adolescence, progresses as puberty 
advances.275
Facial changes in both sexes. Facial morphologic appear­
ance changes with pubertal development, leading to the mature 
appearance. The mandible and nose enlarge more in boys, but 
the maxilla, brow, frontal sinuses, and middle and posterior fos­
sae grow in both sexes, mainly during the pubertal growth spurt. 
Accordingly, children with isosexual precocious puberty have the 
facial appearance of older children, and individuals with delayed 
puberty have faces of younger children. There is a greater change 
in various measurements of the face compared to the skull, with 
the jaw showing the largest increase.276

SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
Gonadal Maturation at Puberty
Ovarian maturation. Ovarian differentiation begins at the 10th 
week of embryonic development. Within the fetal ovaries, oocytes 
surrounded by a single layer of follicular cells (granulosa) form the 
primordial follicles, and primary follicles soon follow. The pool of 
germ cells (GCs) in the form of primordial, primary, and preantral 
follicles attains its peak by week 20 of gestation,277 and their num­
ber begins to decrease with age thereafter.278 In girls, the early stages 
of follicular growth are primarily driven by intraovarian factors.277 
Follicular growth up to the antral stage may occur (Fig. 23.24), but 
all developing follicles at this stage eventually undergo atresia.
Pubertal onset is characterized by an increase in gonadotropin 
levels that is necessary for terminal maturation of the follicles, lead­
ing to ovulation.277 GnRH-induced LH secretion stimulates the 
production of androgens by the theca cells, whereas GnRH-induced 
increased FSH is required for the recruitment of ovarian follicles 
and the aromatization of androgens to E2 by the granulosa cells.279 
During puberty, ovarian volume progressively increases (from 0.2–
1.6 mL before puberty to 2.8–10 mL at the end of puberty), and 
ultrasound scans can identify more than six follicles of at least 4 mm 
in diameter per ovary. This constellation is different from the larger 
number of developing follicles found in PCOS.279
Testicular maturation. In boys, the increase in gonadotro­
pins during early puberty leads to a second wave (after minipu­
berty) of proliferation of immature SCs and spermatogonia before

seminiferous tubule maturation. This occurs under the control of 
FSH and is indexed by a rise in serum levels of inhibin B, a marker 
of SC function.280 Progressively, GnRH-induced LH stimulates 
LC differentiation and their steroidogenic capacity to produce T. 
The concomitant stimulation of SC by FSH and the LH-induced 
intratesticular T leads to a sharp increase in TV, mainly compris­

adult, GCs predominate. While puberty progresses, the SCs cease 
to undergo mitosis and differentiate into adult-type SCs. The lat­

and inhibin B before any notable increase in testis size,281 likely 
reflecting changes in AR expression in mature versus immature 
SCs. Indeed, AR is present in only 2% to 15% of SCs until the 
age of 4 years, whereas its expression can be observed in >90% of 
SCs after the age of 8 years.282 
Hormonal Changes in Puberty
Gonadotropins
At the onset of puberty, pulsatile GnRH secretion induces a pro­
gressive increase in gonadotropin secretion, which is also episodic. 
The diurnal rhythm and pulsatile secretion of gonadotropins are 
already present before puberty, with higher levels of FSH than LH 
in both sexes.283,284 However, LH and FSH secretion begins to 
increase initially at night in prepubertal boys and girls. The ampli­
tude and frequency of both hormones increase, and night and 
daytime secretion occurs as pubertal development progresses.285
In boys, the LH levels increase more at early puberty than those 
of FSH, thanks to an increase in both pulse amplitude and fre­
quency (Fig. 23.26), whereas the FSH increase is more progres­
sive.286 In girls, FSH levels rise rapidly during the early stages of 
puberty, whereas LH levels tend to increase mainly in the later 
pubertal stages (Fig. 23.27). Qualitative changes of gonadotro­
pins also occur with puberty, in particular regarding the glyco­
sylation of their α-subunit and β-subunit, which is influenced by 
the GnRH secretion and the feedback of gonadal steroids on the 
pituitary gonadotrophs.287 
GnRH Stimulation Test
The GnRH stimulation test, also termed the luteinizing hormone–
releasing hormone (LHRH) test, consists of the administration of a 
0.1-mg intravenous (IV) bolus of synthetic GnRH (gonadorelin) 
with subsequent measurement of LH and FSH every 15 minutes 
for 1 to 2 hours. It is used when cCPP is suspected, as well as to 
differentiate constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP)

• Fig. 23.24  Schematic representation of the growth of ovarian follicles during infancy and childhood. Type 
1 (primordial follicle) and type 2 (primary follicle) are composed of a small oocyte and a few to a ring of flat 
granulosa cells. In the diplotene (nesting) stage of prophase, primary follicles are the predominant form of 
oocyte and constitute the reservoir of cells from which follicular growth occurs. Types 3 to 5 (preantral fol­
licles) are follicles that have entered the growth phase; the oocyte is enlarging and is surrounded by a zona 
pellucida, and granulosa cells increase in number and differentiate. The growth of the oocyte is complete 
by the end of the preantral stage, and the increased follicular size is caused by follicular growth and fluid 
accumulation. Types 6 to 8 represent antral follicles (graafian follicles) and contain a fully grown oocyte, a 
large number of granulosa cells, a fluid-filled cavity, and a well-developed theca external to the basement 
membrane. Large preovulatory follicles are absent (10,000–15,000 μm). Follicular growth and atresia take 
place throughout childhood. All follicles that enter the growth phase become atretic, and this can occur 
at any stage in their development but mainly involves large antral follicles. (From Peters H, Byskov AG, 
Grinsted J. Follicular growth in fetal and prepubertal ovaries of humans and other primates. Clin Endocrinol 
Metab. 1978;7:469–485.)

Gonadal Steroids
Testosterone. In males, the main source of T is the LCs of the 
testes, which also produce, in lesser amounts, androstenedione, 
α5-androstenediol, dihydrotestosterone, and E2. A small amount 
of T is derived from extraglandular conversion of androstenedione 
secreted by both the testes and adrenals. In females, extraglandular 
conversion of ovarian and adrenal androstenedione accounts for 
almost all circulating T. The widely accessible immunoassays for 
sex steroid measurement have proved to be highly inaccurate for 
T-level determination at low concentrations, arguing against their 
adequacy to assess women or children.289,290 Liquid chromatog­
raphy–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) is currently the 
gold standard for steroid quantification.291 Notably, ultrasensitive 
radioimmunoassays (RIAs) constitute a valid alternative option; 
RIAs were recently shown to be as accurate as LC-MS/MS for T 
measurement, even at the lowest ranges.292
Prepubertal boys and girls have plasma T concentrations of less 
than 0.3 nmol/L except during minipuberty in boys. Nighttime 
elevations of serum T levels are detectable in the male as early as 
5 years of age, before any physical signs of puberty, and increase 
during early puberty after the appearance of sleep-entrained secre­
tion of LH and increased pituitary sensitivity to GnRH. In the 
daytime, increases in T levels become detectable after the onset 
of puberty (TV >4 mL), with a consistent increase through­
out puberty. The steepest increment in T concentration occurs 
between pubertal stages 2 and 3 in males (see Fig. 23.26). FT, the 
unbound fraction of the steroid that more accurately reflects the 
level of biologic activity, can be directly measured by equilibrium 
dialysis or estimated using equation formulas. The best validated 
in adults is the Vermeulen equation based on serum T levels, sex 
hormone–binding globulin (SHBG), and albumin levels.293 Nev­
ertheless, validation data in pediatric populations are not avail­
able. Serum androgen bioactivity, as measured with a recombinant 
cell bioassay in 14 boys with CDGP, strongly correlated with 
serum total T concentrations and demonstrated a close concerta­
tion with pubertal development, as evidenced by progression of

pubic hair and penile development.294 The measurement of T in 
saliva is an attractive alternative to blood because of the simple 
and noninvasive sample collection. Recently, reference values 
using LC-MS/MS for salivary T levels in adolescent boys and girls 
were established.295 
Estrogens. In the female, E2 is the major secreted estro­
gen, principally (90%) by the ovary, with a small fraction of 
circulating E2 arising from the extraglandular conversion of T 
and androstenedione. In the male, approximately 75% of E2 
is derived from extraglandular aromatization of T and (indi­
rectly) androstenedione, and 25% is from direct testicular 
secretion. In the fetus and at birth, estrogen levels are high as 
a result of conversion of fetal and maternal adrenal C19 ste­
roids to estrogen by the placenta, but they drop precipitously 
during the first few days of life. Plasma E2 levels are very low 
in prepuberty, making detection by standard immunoassays 
difficult, but a rise throughout puberty and a diurnal rhythm 
are seen with highly sensitive bioassays or high-performance 
liquid chromatography (HPLC) tandem mass spectroscopy 
(HPLC-MS/MS) (Table 23.2; see Fig. 23.27). The E2 rise with 
puberty occurs earlier in girls than in boys and continues until 
the growth spurt, then decreases thereafter.296 Indeed, a sig­
nificant correlation between peak growth velocity and the peak 
in E2 concentration has been observed in both sexes.297 The 
higher E2 levels in girls may be an important factor in the more 
advanced levels of skeletal maturation in girls compared with 
boys. A human cell bioassay measuring total estrogenic bioac­
tivity in children allowed for an extremely sensitive detection 
limit (<1 pg/mL of E2 equivalents).298 
Gonadal Peptides: Inhibin, Activin, and Follistatin
Inhibin, a heterodimeric glycoprotein product mainly of the 
SCs of the testes and the ovarian granulosa cells, is composed 
of an α-subunit and one of two β-subunits, βA or βB, which, 
respectively, form inhibin A or inhibin B (INHB). The latter is 
the only detectable inhibin in adult males. INHB exerts nega­
tive feedback action on the secretion of FSH from the pitu­
itary, which in turn induces its synthesis and secretion by the 
gonads in both sexes. In women, INHB may also be an inhibi­
tor of LH release in the follicular phase.299 Inhibins are mem­
bers of the transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) superfamily 
that also includes AMH, activin A, and activin B.300 The lat­
ter antagonizes inhibin to stimulate the release of FSH from 
pituitary cells. Two distinct binding proteins for inhibin and 
activin are present in the circulation, the gonads, and other 
tissues: α2-macroglobulin, a high-capacity, low-affinity bind­
ing protein, and follistatin, a glycosylated, single-peptide chain 
that functions as a high-affinity binding protein and an inhibi­
tor of activin bioactivity (e.g., in the pituitary gland, a site of 
synthesis of activin and follistatin).
In males, following a transient rise at minipuberty, serum 
INHB levels remain detectable throughout childhood as a 
direct marker of the number and function of immature SCs.301 
In healthy boys, serum INHB increases between prepuberty 
and the first stage of puberty and between Tanner stages G1 
and G2.302 Thereafter, INHB levels are relatively constant 
during mid- and late puberty, despite a rise in the mean con­
centration of serum FSH. The rise in INHB is mirrored by a 
decrease in AMH in early puberty, reflecting SC maturation.281 
Interestingly, by Tanner stage 4, a clear negative correlation of 
serum INHB and FSH is present. Overall, dimeric INHB rises 
twice during development, reflecting the two periods of SC 
proliferation in infancy and early puberty, whereas an inverse 
relationship between INHB and FSH is seen at midpuberty 
and thereafter, attesting to the development of negative feed­
back inhibition. In early puberty, INHB is closely related to 
LH and T levels, but following its peak in Tanner stage 3, this 
relationship is lost, and INHB values become more closely 
related to FSH levels.303
In girls, serum levels of both inhibin A (INHA) and INHB 
show some moderate individual increases during the prepuber­
tal period, reflecting sporadic follicular development in the infant 
and childhood as a result of low intermittent FSH stimulation. 
Both inhibins rise early at pubertal onset, with a predominance of 
INHB and INHA in the follicular and luteal phase, respectively. 
INHA and INHB peak at Tanner stage 3 to 4,304 and INHB 
decreases thereafter. During the early stages of puberty, INHB 
values have a strong positive correlation with FSH, LH, and E2 
levels, but these relationships diminish with the progression of 
puberty.305 Although there is no significant change in activin dur­
ing female puberty, follistatin decreases from a midpuberty peak 
and thereafter, with adult levels falling below prepubertal values. 
In adult women, INHB is a marker of the number but also the 
size of antral follicles and peaks at a follicle diameter of around 
9 mm.306 In contrast to boys, AMH concentrations show only 
minor fluctuations during female puberty,307 whereas INHB pro­
gressively increases.308
Stimulation of gonadotropins by a short-term GnRH agonist 
treatment in 18 girls age 1 to 13 years and 11 boys age 9 to 15 
years led to an increase in FSH level by 30 minutes.309 Subse­
quently, an elevation of INHB was observed in girls by 8 hours 
and in boys by 20 hours. In the same study, baseline activin A con­
centrations were greater in girls and did not change with GnRH 
administration.
During the late stages of puberty, a developmental switch in 
the regulation of serum INHB occurs. More precisely, INHB 
production becomes dependent on the presence of GCs in the 
seminiferous tubules, most precisely on pachytene spermato­
cytes and early spermatids.310 Accordingly, prepubertal boys 
with SC-only (SCO) syndrome have normal INHB, whereas 
postpubertal boys and men with SCO or an early-stage sper­
matogenic arrest have undetectable or low INHB levels. Con­
versely, men with late-stage spermatogenic arrest or obstructive 
azoospermia have normal or near-normal serum INHB levels. 
The explanation for these puberty-related differences resides in 
the fact that before puberty, both the α and the βB inhibin 
subunits are expressed in SCs, whereas fully differentiated 
(matured) SCs express only the α-subunit, with the β-subunit 
being expressed in germ cells.311 A low concentration of INHB 
in men is an indicator of impaired seminiferous tubule func­
tion.312 INHB is absent in men after bilateral orchidectomy 
and can be used as a reliable marker to assess the presence of 
testes and their function (e.g., in the case of cryptorchidism) 
in prepubertal individuals.313 Further, as puberty begins, boys 
with testicular defects develop higher FSH concentrations and 
lower INHB levels. 
Anti-müllerian Hormone
AMH is a 14-kDa homodimeric glycoprotein that is structurally 
related to the subunit of inhibin and TGFβ. It is produced by the 
SCs of the fetal testis beginning at week 7 of fetal development 
and causes the regression of the müllerian ducts in the male fetus.

SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
In the female fetus, AMH production begins later in gestation 
by the granulosa cells of the fetal ovary. AMH secretion in the 
fetal testes is regulated by several transcription factors, including 
SOX9, SF1, GATA4, and WT1, until the rise of pituitary FSH, 
which becomes a strong stimulator of AMH thereafter.314 Dur­
ing minipuberty, AMH serum levels rise to achieve a peak at the 
end of the first year of life in male neonates. High secretion of 
AMH reflecting the significant activity of SCs persists throughout 
childhood despite the decrease of FSH, providing a useful marker 
to assess testicular function in this physiologically hypogonadal 
phase.301 A slow decrease of AMH levels occurs by the age of 10 
years, with a further steeper drop during puberty as SCs progres­
sively mature.281 Serum AMH levels are low in newborn females, 
with a subsequent rise at the postnatal FSH surge of minipu­
berty.108 AMH levels remain detectable during childhood in girls, 
with a moderate increase between the age of 4 and 8 years and a 
relatively constant level thereafter.307
During puberty, serum levels of AMH and INHB are inversely 
related to androgen concentrations in boys.281 Accordingly, ele­
vated serum AMH concentrations occur in androgen-insensitivity 
syndrome. AMH is slightly higher in boys with CDGP than in 
pubertal age-matched control subjects and lower in those with tes­
ticular dysgenesis associated with impaired virilization.315 Treat­
ment with recombinant FSH alone was found to further increase 
basal levels of serum AMH in men with untreated CHH.316 
Subsequent addition of hCG increased serum T levels and gener­
ated a decrease in serum AMH levels associated with SC matura­
tion and increased levels of intratesticular T. Similar to INHB, 
AMH is undetectable in boys with congenital anorchia, whereas 
it remains normal in boys with isolated cryptorchidism, facilitat­
ing the differential diagnosis during the first month after birth.317 
Serum AMH is elevated in women with PCOS, consistent with 
an increased antral follicle number.318 Recently, the critical role of 
in utero AMH excess (in pregnant women with PCOS) was high­
lighted as a mechanism of transmission to the female offspring 
with prenatal high-level AMH exposure.319 Another clinical appli­
cation of AMH is as a gonadal tumor marker, given elevated val­
ues in men with Sertoli-like tumors and in women with granulosa 
cell tumors. 
Sex Hormone–Binding Globulin
Between 97% and 99% of circulating T and E2 is reversibly bound 
to SHBG. Prepubertal levels of SHBG are approximately equal in 
boys and girls, but a significant decline occurs with sexual matu­
ration, which is more pronounced in boys as a result of down­
regulation of SHBG expression by the higher androgen levels.320 
Notably, the drop in SHBG levels has already begun at the years 
preceding pubertal onset, presumably as a result of adrenarche and 
the accompanying rise in adrenal androgens. The lower SHBG 
in pubertal males magnifies the exposure of male tissues to active 
(free) androgens. Indeed, although plasma concentration of total 
T is 20-fold higher in men than in women, the difference in FT 
is even more significant, with a 40-fold elevation in men as com­
pared to women. 
Prolactin
A specific elevation in serum prolactin levels occurs during female 
puberty321 and from Tanner stage 2 onward in particular. This rise 
of prolactin correlates with a similar change in plasma E2 levels 
throughout puberty, suggesting an estrogen-mediated stimulation 
of the lactotrope pituitary cells. In boys, prolactin levels do not 
change at puberty. 
Insulin-Like 3 Protein
Insulin-like 3 (INSL3) is a protein produced by mature LCs and 
was originally discovered as a crucial factor mediating the trans­
abdominal phase of testicular descent during development.322 
INSL3 attracted large interest as an alternative option to assess 
LC function and differentiation, given that its secretion exhib­
its minimal diurnal variation and independence from SHBG and 
other carrier protein levels. INSL3 secretion progressively rises 
during the course of puberty under the differentiating action of 
LH on LCs.323,324 A significant elevation of serum INSL3 levels 
is observed on letrozole-induced raised LH secretion in children 
with idiopathic short stature324 or after hCG stimulation therapy 
in men with CHH.325 After an initial increase in early puberty, 
INSL3 levels off in boys with Klinefelter syndrome despite persis­
tently high LH levels.324 
Prostate-Specific Antigen
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is detectable in male and female 
cord blood and in the serum of infants but becomes undetectable 
during childhood. PSA levels rise to the measurable range with the 
onset of male puberty, correlating with the pubertal stage, the size 
of the testes, and serum LH and T concentrations.326 
Growth Hormone and Growth Factors
GH secretion approximately doubles during puberty in boys and 
girls in the basal state or after stimulation but decreases after puber­
tal development. The GH elevation in girls starts at a younger age 
than in boys because of the earlier onset of puberty in the former. 
Indeed, GH secretion starts to increase concomitantly with the 
onset of breast development (Tanner stage 2) and peaks at Tanner 
stage 3 to 4 of breast development. In boys, GH rises later and 
peaks at Tanner stage 4 of genital development. GH secretion and 
IGF1 levels decrease after late puberty in both sexes. Adolescents 
of normal height have an inverse relationship between weight and 
GH levels. The increase in E2 at puberty, which in boys results 
from testicular secretion and extraglandular conversion from T 
and in girls from secretion by the ovaries, is the principal media­
tor of the pubertal increase in pulse amplitude and amount of 
GH secreted per pulse. Accordingly, administration of exogenous 
androgens in subjects with delayed puberty raises GH secretion. 
Transdermal application of T increases spontaneous GH secre­
tion.327 The effect of T is mediated mainly through its conversion 
to E2 because treatment of late pubertal boys with tamoxifen, an 
estrogen receptor (ER) blocker, causes smaller GH secretory peaks 
and fewer GH secretory episodes.328 Exogenous E2 increases the 
peak GH reached after insulin-induced hypoglycemia, exercise, 
and arginine, a priming effect that is used in clinical practice. 
Dihydrotestosterone, which is not aromatized to estrogen, does 
not increase GH secretion or IGF1 levels.329 Increased GH secre­
tion occurs in CPP, with a decrease in IGF1 levels following a drop 
in gonadal steroid levels after treatment with GnRH agonists.330 
Severe hypogonadism leads to a minimal or absent growth spurt, 
demonstrating the primary role of gonadal steroids in pubertal 
growth. Hypopituitary patients deficient in GH and gonadotro­
pins do not have an adolescent growth spurt when GH alone is 
replaced. Conversely, GH deficiency or GH resistance causes an 
attenuated pubertal growth spurt, indicating a bidirectional inter­
action between the gonadal and growth axes.
Concentrations of IGF1 rise during puberty and remain ele­
vated past the time of PHV, with a peak 1 to 2 years after the 
pubertal growth spurt (later in boys than in girls) before a sub­
sequent fall to adult levels.331 The pattern of the GH-dependent

serum levels of IGF-binding protein 3 (IGFBP3) changes dur­
ing pubertal development is similar to that of serum IGF1.332 
However, serum IGFBP3 concentrations correlate with BMI, in 
contrast to IGF1.333 Further, plasma IGF1 concentrations are 
high for chronologic age in sexual precocity and low in delayed 
puberty. Estrogens mediate the pubertal increase in IGF1 con­
centration through increased secretion of GH, as well as an 
additional effect through the gonadal steroid–induced local gen­
eration of IGF1 in cartilage and bone. Treatment with GnRH 
agonist in a 16-year-old boy with a homozygous mutation in 
the WSXWS-like motif of the human growth hormone receptor 
(GHR) causing Laron syndrome led to a further decrease in the 
already low serum levels of IGF1 and IGFBP3, which did not 
reverse with dihydrotestosterone treatment, suggesting a direct 
effect of E2 on IGF1 production.334 Accordingly, children with 
CPP treated with a GnRH agonist showed a decrease in plasma 
IGF1 concentrations, although not to prepubertal values, sup­
porting the concept that GH is the major (but not the only) fac­
tor that raises circulating IGF1 levels in puberty.330 Stressing the 
distinct role of hepatic-generated IGF1 (i.e., endocrine role) and 
locally produced IGF1 (i.e., paracrine/autocrine role), mice with 
a selective inactivation of IGF1 in the hepatocytes maintained 
normal postnatal growth despite a striking reduction (75%) in 
circulating IGF1 levels.335 
Other Hormones
Thyroid hormones have a permissive role in the pubertal 
growth spurt. A longitudinal cohort study of 323 children 
demonstrated that higher prepubertal levels of free and total 
T4 within the normal range are associated with earlier puber­
tal onset.336 Hypothyroidism affects growth indirectly through 
a decrease in GH secretion. However, thyroid hormone also 
affects growth directly through an interaction with the thyroid 
hormone receptors α1 and β, whose proteins are found in early 
proliferating chondrocytes of the human growth plate. Finally, 
thyroid hormones modify the local effects of IGF1 and GH at 
the growth plate.337 
Behavioral Changes During Puberty
Brain anatomy and function change substantially during late 
childhood and adolescence (Fig. 23.28). Puberty is the time of 
appearance of the ability to solve complex problems in a mature 
manner. An increase in cortical metabolic rate in infancy is fol­
lowed by a late-childhood decline to adult levels; this decline 
ceases by the end of the second decade. The prefrontal association 
cortex, an area of the brain that is concerned with forward plan­
ning and regulatory control of emotional behavior, continues to 
develop until the age of 20 to 25 years.338 Stress at various stages 
of development, even in early childhood, may cause psychological 
manifestations during puberty.
Behavior or psychopathology that becomes evident at this time 
has its basis in these changes and exposures dating from early life 
and the prenatal period, all interacting against a genetic back­
ground. The anatomic changes revealed by functional MRI stud­
ies of the prefrontal cortex, an area that is involved with emotional 
regulation and planning, occur during a time of physical matura­
tion and are likely to relate to many of the characteristic behavior 
changes of puberty. The volume of white matter increases linearly 
between 4 and 22 years of age owing to an increase in myelina­
tion during development.339 A reduction in cortical synaptic den­
sity and neuronal density, analogous to programmed cell death, 
occurs between 2 and 16 years of age, and this pruning of syn­
apses appears to be linked to improved memory. This change in 
gray matter follows an inverted U-shaped curve of increase from 
the age of 6 years. Longitudinal studies using dynamic mapping 
of human cortical development demonstrate that higher-order 
association cortices (e.g., those involved in executive function, 
attention, and motor coordination) mature after lower-order 
somatosensory, motor, and visual cortices mature, and those areas 
that are phylogenetically older mature before newer ones.340,341 
Intrauterine excess of androgens leads to enlargement of the amyg­
dala, and girls reach a greater mass of gray matter 2 years before 
boys during puberty, demonstrating aspects of the effects of sex 
steroids on brain growth and remodeling in human beings. Gray 
matter volume, at least in girls, appears to be related to a pubertal 
increase in E2 levels.342 Increased LH levels are related to areas of 
increased white matter density, including the cingulum, middle 
temporal gyrus, and splenium of the corpus callosum; there is a 
genetic overlay to this relationship. Brain plasticity decreases dur­
ing puberty. Examples include the inability to learn to speak a 
foreign language without an accent after puberty and recovery of 
a child from the effects of a CNS injury that might have led to 
aphasia in an older teenager or an adult. Loss of plasticity may be 
maladaptive to our rapidly changing world and extended lifespan 
compared with prehistoric times.343 Plasticity allowed develop­
mental learning before puberty, but lack of plasticity and a stan­
dard response to conditions in the adult allowed success in that 
static environment of the past.
Mania, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorders, and schizo­
phrenia are more common after puberty. They are postulated to be 
related to alterations of the normal changes in brain architecture 
and function that occur during puberty.
Sleep Patterns in Puberty
Increased sleep is characteristic of the period of growth and 
development across species. Because sleep is a time of vulner­
ability, threats leading to stress are antithetical to normal sleep, 
and a feeling of safety is thought to be necessary to allow sleep 
to proceed normally as the adolescent is preparing for indepen­
dence and increased self-care in a possibly hostile world. Increas­
ing complexity of brain function during puberty is reflected in 
increases in the amplitude and frequency of delta waves (0- to 
3-Hz electroencephalographic waves) found during deep sleep, 
which appears more related to age than to pubertal development 
or growth.344 The function of deep sleep (i.e., slow-wave or non–
rapid eye movement sleep) is thought to be restorative to learning 
and other activities of the waking state, and the most restorative 
portion is high-amplitude delta-wave sleep. During adolescence, 
the time spent in deep (stage 4) sleep declines by 40% to 50%, 
and increased (19.7%) stage 2 sleep occurs with pubertal devel­
opment. The decline of slow-wave sleep during adolescence may 
reflect developmental changes in the brain.
When an individual is allowed to “run free,” the period is 
entrained (synchronized) close to the Earth’s 24-hour light-dark 
cycle. Because human beings had little to do after dark, evolution 
favored an early bedtime, but within this schedule, developmental 
changes occur. One-year-old infants sleep an average of 11 hours 
per day, and by age 18, if circumstances permit, the mean is 8 
hours. Older people have earlier waking times and rate themselves 
as more morning-like than adolescents or young adults; because 
children are also morning-like, there is an inverted U-shaped 
curve of preferred times of awakening across the span of develop­
ment.345 This change to evening from morning alertness during

puberty appears to be related to biologic factors, in contrast to 
social factors; in the past, social factors were thought to be more 
important.
Without the pressure of work or school, adolescents would stay 
up longer and awaken hours later than a normal weekday schedule 
would dictate, a schedule far different from the one they followed 
at a younger age. Adolescents with early school start awaken earlier 
than those with later school starts, but they do not change the 
time they go to sleep, leading to great variation in the amount of 
sleep attained. Data from the Add Health study showed decreased 
self-reported sleep duration during self-reported pubertal develop­
ment, with girls reporting more problems with sleep (e.g., insom­
nia, insufficient sleep, awakening tired) as puberty progressed but 
with no such relationship seen in boys.346 There is an increase in 
daytime sleepiness during adolescence, particularly during mid­
puberty up to stage 3 to 4, even if total sleep time is held con­
stant during longitudinal multiple-year studies.347 With voluntary 
sleep deprivation (e.g., with late-night homework habits), sleepi­
ness can reach levels seen in narcolepsy and sleep apnea. Adoles­
cents adapt more poorly to changes in sleep patterns than other 
age groups; this is manifested in the difference in hours awake 
between the school week and the weekend. Adolescents are able 
to shift to a later schedule more easily than to an earlier schedule. 
When self-selected bedtimes are late during summer but have to 
be changed to allow for school attendance, the adjustment is par­
ticularly lengthy and difficult.
After a study of 27,000 individuals, it was proposed that the 
point of inflection from evening alertness during adolescence 
(after a morning-like pattern in childhood) to morning alertness 
in adulthood might be used as a marker of the end of adolescence, 
a sign that developmental remodeling of brain pathways is com­
pleted.348 The age of this inflection point is about 20.9 years in 
males and 19.5 years in females, who have an earlier change in this 
and other aspects of puberty than males. 
Psychology and Puberty
Mood and Self-Image in Puberty. Young girls at the begin­
ning of puberty frequently exhibit a negative self-image but a 
positive body image; positive peer relationships and superior 
adjustment improvement are observed with continued breast 
development. Mood in adolescence is not closely related to stage 
of puberty, but a significant curvilinear trend is seen for depressive 
affect (i.e., an increase followed by a decrease) and for impulse 
control (a decrease followed by an increase), according to the level 
of serum E2. These data suggest that hormonal changes may be 
more important than physical changes as determinants of certain 
mood and behavior patterns during adolescence. 
Behavior in Variations of the Normal Age at Onset of 
Puberty. Within the normal limits of pubertal development, 
early-maturing girls and late-maturing boys have the greatest prev­
alence of adjustment reactions in puberty and thereafter. Boys and 
girls who mature earlier are at increased risk for abuse.349
Early-developing boys are perceived to be more mature, attrac­
tive, and smart and are given more leadership roles; late-devel­
oping boys are more insecure, more susceptible to lower levels of 
self-esteem and body image, and more vulnerable to peer pressure, 
especially in working-class and minority groups. Most of these dif­
ficulties of late maturation focus on the decreased height of the 
individual rather than the lack of sexual development. Social mat­
uration lags even after androgen treatment in patients with severe 
CDP. Delayed social maturation may put boys at risk for missing 
educational opportunities.
In contrast, early-maturing girls tend to experience more dif­
ficulty, especially in the junior high school setting, where they may 
attract the attention of older, more mature boys, and they have a 
higher prevalence of internalizing symptoms and disorders. They 
are more often the target of bullying but also more often the per­
petrator of bullying than average-maturing girls.350
Early puberty may lead to negative body image in girls com­
pared with boys, in whom the effect is positive. Early maturation 
may increase a propensity toward violent behavior, which is fostered 
by living in a disadvantaged neighborhood. Early pubertal matura­
tion in girls may be related to a small intelligence quotient (IQ) 
advantage over late-maturing girls. Late-maturing girls are often 
more comfortable, remaining with the support of their families 
longer, and they are less often brought to medical attention than 
late-maturing boys. Early-maturing and late-maturing girls have a 
tendency to engage in health-risking behaviors involving strategies 
to lose weight, strategies to increase muscle, disordered eating, use 
of food supplements and steroids, and exercise dependence—ten­
dencies not found in boys at the same developmental stages. 
Risk-Taking Behavior. Adolescents who function at lower lev­
els of cognitive complexity or concrete thinking and have an early 
onset of puberty demonstrate an increase in risk-taking behavior. 
The age at onset of cigarette smoking and alcohol use is propor­
tional to the age at onset of puberty in girls: early-maturing girls 
partake earlier, and boys may follow the same pattern. 
Sexuality During Puberty. The social pressures are more 
mixed in their messages to girls, both encouraging sexuality and 
restricting it in a way more disparate than that encountered by 
boys. The earlier onset of puberty today compared with previous 
centuries has had a profound effect on societal norms of sexual 
behavior.9 For example, early onset of puberty is associated with 
earlier onset of sexual intercourse.351 In the United States, adoles­
cents become sexually active in their 17th year of life on average, 
and before the age of 20 years, more than 75% have had sex.352,353 
Sexuality appears to be correlated with T production in boys in 
some studies, but in others, it appears to be modified by the social 
effects of pubertal maturation. Religious activity may decrease the 
likelihood of sexual activity. 
Adolescent Growth
Postnatal growth follows a consistent pattern: (1) an extremely 
high growth rate just after birth, followed by a deceleration until 
the age of 3 years; (2) a slower phase of deceleration until puberty; 
and (3) the subsequent pubertal growth spurt, the second great­
est period of postnatal growth until adult height is reached. The 
pubertal growth spurt may be divided for purposes of compari­
son into three stages: (1) the pre-spurt minimal growth velocity in 
peripuberty (takeoff velocity); (2) the time of most rapid growth, 
or PHV; and (3) the stage of decreased velocity and cessation of 
growth up to the epiphyseal fusion.
Many factors influence longitudinal growth.337 The growth 
spurt in normal girls and boys is mainly driven by E2 and GH lev­
els, among other factors. Hormonal control of the pubertal growth 
spurt is complex (Fig. 23.29). GH exerts its growth-stimulating 
effect via induction of IGF1 production. Gonadal steroids have 
two effects on pubertal growth: (1) an indirect effect by inducing 
upregulation of the GH-IGF1 axis and (2) a direct effect on car­
tilage and bone through stimulation of local production of IGF1 
and other local factors.354
During puberty, boys and girls experience a growth velocity 
greater than at any postnatal age since infancy. Boys reach PHV

approximately 2 years later than girls and are taller at takeoff (Fig. 
23.30); PHV occurs during stage 3 to 4 of puberty in most boys 
(see Fig. 23.22) and is completed by stage 5 in more than 95% of 
boys. Boys achieve a PHV of 9.5 cm per year at a mean of about 
13.5 years,355 with a greater PHV in those who mature earlier 
than in those who mature later. This pubertal growth spurt in girls 
lasts approximately 2 years and accounts for the acquisition of 
roughly 20% of final height.355 The PHV in girls is approximately 
8.3 cm/year, occurring at a mean chronologic age of 11.5 years355 
between stages 2 and 3 of puberty (see Fig. 23.20). Boys grew a 
mean of 28 cm, and girls grew 25 cm, between takeoff and cessa­
tion of growth in a study in the United Kingdom.356 The overall 
average difference in adult height between women and men results 
from differences in the timing and magnitude of the growth spurt. 
More precisely, PHV occurs approximately 2 years earlier on aver­
age in girls than in boys. Thus, boys have an additional 2 years of 
prepubertal growth (at a rate of 3–8 cm per year) by the time the 
growth spurt begins. Twin studies of bone morphogenetic appear­
ance have confirmed that the difference in bone widths between 
boys and girls is also largely established before puberty.357 Based 
on the growth records of 145 healthy Swedish children followed 
longitudinally, a study introduced a mathematical model that sep­
arates the infancy, childhood, and pubertal phases of growth and 
allows prediction of final height, taking into account the variation 
in the age at onset of puberty.358 A slowly decelerating childhood 
component is the base, with a sigmoidal pubertal component 
added during secondary sexual development (see Fig. 23.30C). 
The infancy-childhood-puberty (ICP) model can detect the onset 
of the pubertal growth spurt, predict the actual magnitude of the 
pubertal growth spurt, and predict the final height by using only 
the age at onset of puberty and a single measurement of height.358 
Tanner and Davies constructed growth curves for American chil­
dren using data from the National Center for Health Statistics, and 
data calculated from theoretical growth curves can be adjusted for 
time of PHV.359 Short-term daily follow-up of growth in 10 girls 
over 128 to 150 days during their growth spurt revealed that this 
is an irregular and discontinuous process, composed of three types 
of events: stasis, steep changes, and continuous growth periods, 
with a wide individual range of daily height increments.360 Each 
girl experienced three to seven stasis events (lasting between 7 and 
22 consecutive days), one to four episodes of steep changes (with 
the sum of these steep changes accounting for 15.3%–42.9% of 
the total growth during the study period), and continuous growth 
the remainder of the time. In a large Swedish registry, faster linear 
growth during infancy and childhood was associated with earlier 
PHV during adolescence but less height gain between 8 and 18 
years.361 In the same study, greater weight and length at birth were 
associated with a later growth spurt in adolescence and an overall 
greater statural gain between the ages of 8 and 18 years.
Because girls reach PHV about 1.3 years before menarche, 
there is limited growth potential after menarche; most girls grow 
only about 2.5 cm taller after menarche, although there is a varia­
tion from 1 to 7 cm. The ages at menarche, pubertal onset, and 
PHV are not good predictors of adult height because the dura­
tion of pubertal growth is the more important determinant. Later 
onset of puberty and consequent increase in height at takeoff of 
the pubertal growth spurt can be balanced by a decrease in actual 
height achieved during PHV and result in no net change in adult 
height. However, early onset of puberty can diminish ultimate 
adult stature, as opposed to increased stature in case of prolonged 
delay of puberty.362 The age at PHV and the age at initiation of 
puberty correlate well with the rate of passage through the dif­
ferent stages of pubertal development in normal children. A boy 
or a girl is likely to have significant growth left if he or she is 
in early puberty, whereas limited growth is expected if puberty is 
advanced.
The upper-to-lower (U/L) segment ratio, defined as the length 
from the top of the pubic ramus to the top of the head divided 
by the distance from the top of the pubic ramus to the sole of the 
foot, changes markedly during the peripubertal and early pubertal 
periods because of the elongation of the extremities.363 At birth, 
the U/L ratio is about 1.7, reducing to 1.1 at age 3 years and 1.0 
at age 10 years. In this Turkish study, the nadir of the U/L seg­
ment ratio was reached age 15 years (0.922) and 13 years (0.946) 
for boys and girls, respectively. As expected, arm span was shorter 
than height in younger ages but became longer at around age 12 
in girls and boys. Unlike boys, the arm span–height difference 
did not change much after puberty in girls. In general, hypogo­
nadal patients have delayed epiphyseal fusion and lack a pubertal 
growth spurt; therefore, their extremities grow for a prolonged 
period, leading to a decreased U/L segment ratio and an increased 
arm span for height, a condition known as eunuchoid proportions. 
Eunuchoid proportions are found in subjects with defects in estro­
gen synthesis and ER deficiency,364 but normal proportions are 
observed in patients with complete androgen-insensitivity syn­
drome (CAIS),365 demonstrating the primary role of estrogen in 
mitigating these proportions.366 The distal parts of the extremi­
ties, the hands and feet, grow before the proximal parts; a rapid 
increase in shoe size is a harbinger of the pubertal growth spurt. 
The shoulders become wider in boys, and the hips enlarge more 
in girls. The female pelvic inlet widens, mainly because of growth 
of the os acetabuli. Boys with Klinefelter syndrome have long legs 
but not long arms,367 a physical feature that can assist diagnosis 
before the onset of puberty. The size of the head approaches the 
adult size by age 10 years, and the brain reaches 95% of adult size 
by the onset of puberty.

estrogens) have growth-promoting and maturational effects on

• Fig. 23.30  The infancy-childhood-puberty (ICP) model of Karlberg for mean attained height (A) and height velocity (B) for boys. The mean value for 
each component (infancy, childhood, and puberty) and their sums (combined growth [A] and combined velocity [B]) are plotted. The growth curve for an 
individual represents the additive effect of the three biologic phases of the growth process (ICP). Karlberg has provided mathematical functions for each 
component of his model. Infancy: This component starts before birth and falls off by age 3 to 4 years. It can be described by the exponential function y = a 
+ b[1 – exp(−ct)]. Average total gain in height for Swedish boys is 79 cm (44% of final height) and for girls is 76.8 cm (46.2%). Childhood: This phase begins 
at the end of the first year of life and continues to mature height. A second-degree polynomial function describes this component: y = a + bt + ct2. Average 
total gain in height for boys is 85.2 cm (47.4%) and for girls is 78.4 cm (47.3%). Puberty: The model for the pubertal growth spurt is a logistic function: 
y = a/[1 + exp(−b(t – tv))]. Average total gain in height for boys is 15.4 cm (8.6%) and for girls is 10.9 cm (6.5%); y designates attained height at time t in 
years from birth; a, b, and c are constants; tv is the age at peak height velocity. (C) A schematic male growth chart shows the features of the ICP pattern 
overlaid and illustrates the predominant endocrine mechanisms controlling each phase of growth. The first shaded area emphasizes the decreasing veloc­
ity of infantile growth as the individual leaves the rapid growth phase of fetal life. The open area is the childhood phase, which continues and magnifies 
the decreased velocity of growth into a plateau of rather constant growth during childhood. These two phases depend largely on the effects of growth 
hormone (GH) and thyroid hormone, with no or little effect derived from gonadal steroids. In the next period of the pubertal growth spurt, gonadal steroids 
exert their direct and indirect effects. Gonadal steroids exert direct effects on the bone by stimulating the generation of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) 
and other growth factors locally, and they exert indirect effects by stimulating increased GH secretion, which exerts its own effects on bone and stimulates 
the production of IGF1. In the female, the major gonadal steroid involved in the pubertal growth spurt is estradiol, whereas in the male, testosterone and 
estradiol (arising mainly from the aromatization of testosterone) are the major gonadal steroids. (D) The adolescent growth spurt in girls and boys (growth 
velocity curves). Notice the later onset of the pubertal growth spurt in boys and the approximately 2-year difference in peak height velocity and the greater 
magnitude of peak height velocity compared with girls. The timing of the effects of estradiol is indicated. Progressive epiphyseal fusion terminates the 
growth spurt and leads to final or adult height. (A and B, modified from Karlberg J. On the construction of the infancy-childhood-puberty growth standard. 
Acta Paediatr Scand Suppl. 1989;356:26–37; C and D, from Grumbach MM. Estrogen, bone, growth, and sex: a sea change in conventional wisdom. J 
Pediatr Endocrinol Metab. 2000;13:S1439–S1455.)
