chondrocytes, osteoblasts, and other bone constituents, lead­
ing eventually to epiphyseal fusion and cessation of longitudinal 
growth in both boys and girls. The report of cases with congenital 
estrogen resistance resulting from a loss-of-function homozygous 
mutation in the ERα gene or with autosomal-recessive mutations 
in the CYP19A1 gene encoding aromatase have highlighted the 
cardinal role of E2 in both sexes for the pubertal growth spurt, 
completion of epiphyseal maturation, and acquisition of nor­
mal skeletal proportions and mineralization. Affected individuals 
continue to grow, lack a pubertal growth spurt, and have open 
epiphyses and osteopenia.368,369 Estrogen treatment of affected 
men allows epiphyseal closure, cessation of growth, and a strik­
ing increase in bone mass.370,371 On the contrary, patients with 
aromatase excess, thus producing very high estrogen levels, have 
advanced skeletal maturation and rapid growth but end up with 
short final stature as a result of premature epiphyseal closure.372 
Taken together, these data establish that estrogen (not androgen) 
is the critical sex hormone in males and females for the puber­
tal growth spurt, skeletal maturation, accrual of peak bone mass, 
and maintenance of bone mass in the adult. More precisely, estro­
gen stimulates chondrogenesis in the epiphyseal growth plate via 
expression of both types of ERs (ERα and Erβ).337 On the other 
hand, histologic studies of cartilage in rabbits indicate that pro­
longed estrogen exposure accelerates several aspects of the growth 
plate senescence process, including a decline in the chondrocyte 
proliferation rate.373 This E2-induced effect of proliferative exhaus­
tion eventually culminates in epiphyseal fusion. In another clini­
cal model of interest, CAIS, where androgen signaling is absent, 
affected 46,XY females have a conserved growth spurt,365 demon­
strating the critical role of estrogen rather than androgen for the 
adolescent growth spurt. Recently, a large retrospective study in 
118 untreated Chinese patients with CAIS revealed intermediate 
heights between the average values of genotypic Chinese males 
and females.374
Bone Age
Skeletal maturation is assessed by comparing radiographs of the 
hand, knee, or elbow with reference images in a normal popula­
tion. Ossification centers appear in early life; the bones mature in 
shape and size and develop articulation of surfaces; ultimately, the 
epiphyses or growth plates fuse with their shafts in the process of 
epiphyseal fusion. Bone age, an index of physiologic maturation, 
does not have a well-defined relationship in normal children to 
the onset of puberty because it appears to be more variable than 
chronologic age.375 In addition, the radiologist interpreting the 
bone age must have experience with the method, or an erroneous 
reading may occur. However, bone age is still used for predicting 
the age of menarche and, in boys, the onset of normal, prema­
ture, and delayed puberty in a general sense. A difference between 
bone age and chronologic age must exceed 2 SD to be of biologic 
significance. Standard deviations may range from a few months 
in infancy to 1 year in later adolescence. Indeed, a 2-year varia­
tion of bone age from chronologic age is within normal limits in 
the teenage years. Overall, bone age evaluation is often imprecise 
in clinical practice and is considered a qualitative rather than a 
quantitative measure.376 Automatic computer interpretation of 
bone age scans is routinely used in Europe and has improved the 
accuracy of assessment.377 Ethnic differences in growth patterns 
also exist, with more precocious bone maturation in Asian and 
Hispanic children as compared to Black and White peers.378 These 
differences are more pronounced and clinically relevant in girls age 
10 to 13 years and boys age 11 to 15 years. Several algorithms exist 
to predict adult height based on bone age, current height, and 
chronologic age. These include the Bayley-Pinneau tables,379 the 
Roche-Wainer-Thissen algorithm,380 the Khamis-Roche algorithm 
(for healthy White children only),381 and the Tanner-Whitehouse 
techniques TW2 and TW3. When using these algorithms, the 
presence of considerable variations in height prediction between 
the methods has to be taken into consideration.382 Skeletal matu­
ration is more advanced in girls than in boys of the same chrono­
logic age in early puberty. Indeed, the bone ages of 11 years in girls 
and 13 years in boys correspond roughly to an equivalent stage of 
bone maturation. 
Bone Mass Accrual
Osteoporosis, defined as a state of increased bone fragility result­
ing from reduced bone mineral density (BMD) or deterioration 
of bone microarchitecture, is a rising adult comorbidity with a 
severe burden for patients and public health.383 It is thus not 
surprising that increasing interest has been directed to exploring 
the determinants of skeletal development in children and adoles­
cents, including the effects of age of menarche, nutrition, exercise, 
and genetics.384 Several clinical studies and animal studies have 
argued against a major role of childhood bone mass acquisition 
as a predictor of adult bone mass.385 Nevertheless, the crucial role 
of puberty has been highlighted by findings of increased fracture 
rates and microarchitectural defects in women with delayed men­
arche.386 Further, a longitudinal study of 227 girls who underwent 
a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan at a mean age 
of 12.5 years indicated that BMD at the lumbar spine is higher 
in those with an earlier onset of puberty. Conversely, a 1.9-year 
increase in mean age at menarche in young women was associated 
with lower radial areal BMD and disturbances in several high-
resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-
pQCT)-derived microarchitectural indexes without a reduction 
in cross-sectional area.387 This finding suggested that the main 
mechanism of bone impairment in the setting of late menarche is 
deficient endocortical accrual.
The annual rate of BMD accrual at the total body, lumbar spine, 
and femoral neck measured by DXA is 0.047 g/cm2 for boys and 
0.039 g/cm2 for girls. A 6-year annual DXA follow-up to measure 
BMC in healthy White adolescents indicated that boys and girls 
accumulate BMC of 407 g and 322 g per year, respectively.388 
This corresponds to a calcium accretion rate of 359 mg/day for 
boys and 284 mg/day for girls. Based on these data, 26% of adult 
calcium is laid down in the skeleton during the adolescent years 
of peak calcium accretion—14 years for boys and 12.5 years for 
girls (both mean values). BMD approaches a maximum calcium 
accretion rate by the age of 16 years in girls and 17 years in boys; 
the rate then decreases, and the bone mass reaches its peak in the 
third decade of life.389 More recently, a longitudinal study of more 
than 2000 healthy children further elucidated our understanding 
of peak bone mass acquisition. McCormack et al390 established 
that (1) only 30% to 38% of maximal observed whole BMC was 
obtained by age 7 years; (2) adolescence (2 years before and after 
PHV) accounts for 32.7% to 35.8% of the maximally observed 
BMC; (3) the peak rate of BMC acquisition was achieved at age 
12.5 years in girls and 14.0 years in boys, overall preceding the 
PHV by 0.6 to 1.2 years; and (4) a lesser part (7%–11%) of maxi­
mally observed BMC was gained after linear growth had ceased.
Abnormalities of puberty impair bone accretion in both sexes, 
mostly as a result of estrogen deficiency by decreased secretion or 
low peripheral aromatization of androgens. To dissect the indi­
vidual contribution of sex steroids to bone homeostasis, healthy

volunteers were treated with a GnRH analogue to induce hypo­
gonadism (low T and E2 levels) and were subsequently replaced 
with increasing doses of T alone or in combination with an aro­
matase inhibitor (AI) to suppress conversion of T to E2.391 Inter­
estingly, bone resorption serum markers remained elevated once 
E2 levels were lowered, even if serum T levels were restored. Cut­
offs of <10 pg/mL for plasma E2 and <200 ng/dL (6.9 nmol/L) 
for serum T (with intact aromatization) were suggested as sub­
optimal for bone health.391 Overall, the principal action of estro­
gens on the skeleton is the decrease of osteoclast formation and 
activity while increasing osteoclast apoptosis.392 Data on their 
effect on osteoblasts are less conclusive. Androgen action on the 
growth plate is also mediated via aromatization to estrogens and 
interaction with ERα. However, T also appears to have a direct 
action on the male skeleton via the AR,393 contributing to the 
maintenance of cancellous bone mass and expansion of cortical 
bone. The latter translates to greater bone size in boys as a result 
of increased periosteal apposition (which in turn enhances bone 
strength), whereas girls add bone mainly on the endocortical 
surface.394 These distinct patterns are in part explained by sex 
steroids (higher T levels promote increased bone size in boys395) 
but also by gender differences in the activity of the GH-IGF1 
axis and its synergy with the HPG axis (see Fig. 23.29), as well 
as variable mechanic sensitivity to loading.396 Lack of androgens 
is likely to produce certain bone defects that are not mediated 
by estrogens, according to evidence from women with CAIS. 
Increased prevalence of osteoporosis at the spine and the fem­
oral bone has been reported at least in women with removed 
gonads,397 although adequate estrogen supplementation gener­
ates significant bone gains.
Additional determinants of bone mass (other than sex and 
pubertal status) are as follows:
 • Ethnicity. Black children retain more calcium than White chil­
dren do, and bone structure is thicker in Black children. The 
difference between ethnic groups in trabecular bone density at 
the lumbar spine appears to develop by late puberty.398
 • Body composition. Both LBM and FM are related to skel­
etal density, although the effect of the former seems to be 
of greater magnitude and stronger in boys and regarding 
the BMC at the femoral neck.399 The mechanostat concept 
posits that developmental changes in bone strength result 
from the increasing loads imposed by larger muscle forces, 
which stimulate bone formation. In favor of this hypoth­
esis, a longitudinal study in 70 boys and 68 girls revealed 
that the maximum LBM rise precedes the peak of BMC 
acquisition.400 Further, the peak LBM velocity was inde­
pendently associated with the maximum BMC accrual in a 
multiple-regression model. The link between excess adipos­
ity and bone health is more complex, as implied by the fact 
that total FM in boys and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) in 
girls are associated with worse markers of bone strength as 
assessed by HR-pQCT.401 In obese cohorts, the thickness of 
abdominal adipose tissue is inversely associated with BMD 
levels as measured by DXA.402
 • Genetic background. Approximately 60% to 80% of variance 
in peak bone mass is attributed to genetic factors.403 In favor 
of such a link, the BMD at the beginning of puberty predicted 
62% to 92% of the bone mass variations at sexual maturity and 
seemed to effectively distinguish the subjects prone to develop 
osteoporosis as adults.404 Genetic and environmental factors 
likely interact to shape bone mass, as shown by findings of syn­
ergic action of a polymorphism (Pvull site) in the ERα gene 
and high physical activity to produce gains in weight-bearing 
skeletal sites.405
 • Physical activity. Increased physical activity is generally ben­
eficial for bone health and could in part compensate for an 
unfavorable genetic background.405 In particular, sports asso­
ciated with impact loading, such as running, produce greater 
increases in femoral BMD as compared to nonimpact sports, 
such as swimming.406 Prepubertal girls age 4 to 8 years par­
ticipating in recreational gymnastics had enhanced bone min­
eral gains over 24 months at the total body, lumbar spine, and 
forearm.407 This also extends to female adolescent athletes, 
although the effect last only as long as the activity continues. 
Studies of male athletes are less common than those of girls, 
but athletic boys age 16 to 19 years still gained more bone 
mass in the spine and femora than nonathletic control sub­
jects in a 3-year longitudinal study.408 On the contrary, high-
impact activity exceeding a certain threshold (>16 hours per 
week)409 can predispose to stress fractures, which are defined 
as skeletal defects resulting from repeated exposure to a stress 
lower than the one required for a single loading to generate a 
fracture.
 • Calcium intake. Calcium intake during puberty has been 
documented to affect bone density later in life in most stud­
ies, but the effect of increased ingestion of calcium may last 
only as long as the calcium is administered.403 The positive 
effect of calcium intake on bone mass gain seems to interact 
with the age of menarche, with more pronounced benefit in 
women with early onset of menses.410 Two cups of milk or 
other equivalent dairy intake (approximately 1000 mg of cal­
cium per day) has been shown to provide adequate calcium 
intake for normal bone accrual between the ages of 8 and 16 
years.411 Conversely, 50 children who avoided dairy products 
presented with an increased prevalence of fractures in the pre­
pubertal period, even with minor trauma.412 This is probably 
the end result of insufficient bone calcium retention in early 
pubertal girls with poor dairy intake as a result of the inability 
to adapt and compensate by increased gastrointestinal absorp­
tion or reduced excretion as older individuals do.413 A 2006 
Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis in 2859 chil­
dren without medical comorbidities who were randomized 
to receive calcium supplementation or placebo did not show 
any benefice on lumbar or femoral neck BMD.414 A small but 
significant rise in the upper limb BMD persisted after discon­
tinuation of the supplementation, but this was thought to have 
a negligible influence on the likelihood of a fracture later in 
life. However, these findings have not been explored in subjects 
with disorders of puberty, who are at the greatest risk for sub­
optimal bone accrual. Remarkably, prepubertal higher calcium 
intake is directly related to an earlier age of menarche, which 
in turn could mediate enhanced bone mass gain.410 Moreover, 
a more recent randomized trial in 220 Chinese adolescents 
age 12 to 14 years indicated that increased calcium intake at 
the beginning of puberty results in better femoral neck BMD 
acquisition in both sexes (relative difference of roughly 3% in 
girls and 4% in boys).415
 • Vitamin D status. Similar to adults, vitamin D insufficiency, 
defined as a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level <40 nmol/L, 
was very prevalent (78%) in a cohort of 193 prepubertal or 
early pubertal Finnish girls age 10 to 12 years.416 Vitamin 
D–deficient girls had secondary hyperparathyroidism, raised 
serum markers of bone resorption, and low cortical BMD at 
the distal radius and tibia.

SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
Skeletal Assessment
DXA is the standard clinical tool to assess bone mass. Although 
DXA-derived BMD is a major predictor of fracture risk,417 bone 
mass is not the sole determinant of bone strength.418 In addition, 
DXA calculates areal bone mineral density (aBMD) based on a 
two-dimensional image. Smaller bones attenuate the radiation 
beam less than larger bones, and this factor must be considered 
in the interpretation of DXA scans in children and adolescents.419 
This is particularly relevant for bone assessment of girls with 
Turner syndrome.420 Nevertheless, DXA remains the gold stan­
dard to assess bone fragility in adolescents, being readily avail­
able and with sufficient standardization and available normative 
data.421 The interpretation of the results according to the bone age 
and pubertal status is essential.
Quantitative computed tomography (QCT) and HR-pQCT 
are novel techniques to study bone health and can estimate vol­
umetric BMD (vBMD).422 The latter represents the amount of 
bone within the periosteal envelope and is of more physiologic 
importance because it does not rely on the size of the bone, which 
is constantly changing during pubertal growth. The pattern of 
growth of vBMD is region specific, with faster growth of the legs 
before puberty and of the trunk during the growth spurt.423,424 
Notably, an Australian study in 109 girls demonstrated that femo­
ral and lumbar spine BMC increased by 50% to 150% between 
the ages of 7 and 17 years, mainly attributed to an increase in 
bone size, given that vBMD went up only by 10% to 30% during 
the same period.423 Taken together, these data suggest that growth 
builds a bigger, but only moderately denser, skeleton, making the 
interpretation of DXA results in growing individuals challeng­
ing.425 In particular, HR-pQCT allows accurate visualization of 
compartment-specific bone microarchitecture at peripheral skele­
tal sites (distal radius, tibia) while simultaneously assessing vBMD 
and bone geometry.426 Normative values for HR-pQCT–derived 
measures were recently published.427 Nevertheless, these tools 
are not readily available outside a research setting, and the radia­
tion exposure is considerably higher than that of DXA, limiting 
their widespread use. Quantitative ultrasound (QUS) is another 
method for assessing bone mineral status in peripheral skeletal 
sites. It has been implemented in children and adolescents,428 pro­
viding the advantage of absent radiation exposure and the use of 
a portable device.
Bone turnover markers (BTMs) are serum markers com­
monly used in clinical practice to evaluate bone remodeling, 
especially procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (P1NP) 
and carboxy-terminal collagen crosslinks (CTX or β-CrossLaps), 
which reflect bone formation and bone resorption, respectively. 
During puberty, skeletal growth and intensified bone metabolism 
result in increased release of BTM in the circulation.429 A recent 
population-based longitudinal study in 118 peripubertal boys 
confirmed that the aforementioned classical BTM and sclerostin 
levels peak around midpuberty, driven by the growth spurt, with a 
subsequent decline toward adult values at late puberty.430 Hence, 
the association of BTM with aBMD and vBMD levels was con­
sistent but varied markedly depending on the pubertal stage and 
skeletal site. 
Metabolic Changes at Puberty
Changes in Body Composition
Changes in body composition during puberty follow sex-dependent 
patterns. GH and gonadal steroids play major roles in this process of 
sex-dependent shaping of body composition.431 Overall, the early 
pubertal increase in body mass is driven primarily by changes in 
LBM, whereas gains in adiposity are the major contributors in later 
puberty.432 Girls exhibit a higher proportion of FM gain than boys 
at all pubertal stages, with annual increases in BMI largely ascribed 
to FM gains after the age of 16 years.433 Consequently, men have 
1.5 times higher fat-free mass (composed mainly by LBM and skel­
etal mass) than women by the end of puberty, whereas women have 
a roughly double body fat percent (25% vs. 13% in men) based 
on an aggregate of different studies.434 The central distribution of 
fat in males (central fat, apple-shaped, android) develops largely 
during puberty, whereas females seem to preserve their prepubertal 
pattern of adiposity (lower body fat predominance, pear-shaped, 
gynoid).435 Some degree of ethic variation exists, with the most 
prominent changes in Asians. Puberty-related changes in body 
composition stabilize by the age of 15 to 16 years in girls and 2 
to 3 years later in boys. A strength spurt typically ensues after the 
growth spurt. As a result, boys have a greater muscle performance 
from the age of 14 years onward, as evidenced by higher cycling 
peak power accompanied by an expanded lean leg volume as com­
pared to age-matched girls.436 
Metabolic Changes
In normal male puberty, rising T concentrations increase serum 
levels of LDL cholesterol and decrease HDL cholesterol concen­
trations, accounting for a more adverse lipid ratio in men com­
pared with women.437 This is in part because androgens raise 
hepatic lipase activity, whereas estrogens exert the opposite effect. 
Insulin sensitivity also decreases during puberty. Both fasting insu­
lin concentrations and homeostatic model assessment for insulin 
resistance (HOMA-IR) levels show a two- to threefold increase 
concomitantly to PHV, and this midpuberty peak of insulin resis­
tance is in part attenuated by physical activity.438 Recently, the 
reference range for HOMA-IR, an index calculated based on fast­
ing plasma glucose and insulin, was established in a large cohort 
of 2753 White youths age 2 to 17.8 years.439 HOMA-IR levels 
peaked at age 13 and 15 years in girls and boys, respectively. Val­
ues above the 75th percentile at any pubertal stage were associated 
with cardiometabolic risk factors. The response of insulin to an 
intravenous glucose tolerance test, another index of insulin sensi­
tivity, was lower in Black than White subjects at all stages of puber­
tal development.440 This ethnic distinction reflected variations in 
total and VAT, possibly accounting for the higher incidence of 
type 2 diabetes (T2D) among Black adults. Puberty-associated 
insulin resistance has been attributed in part to increased fat oxi­
dation, which correlates with rising serum IGF1 levels and may 
be linked to the setting of statural growth (GH secretion). A typi­
cal clinical implication of this physiologic change is the increase 
in insulin requirements for adolescents with type 1 diabetes in 
order to maintain euglycemia at puberty. Blood pressure also rises 
with pubertal maturation and appears to be synchronized with the 
pubertal growth spurt, suggesting some overlap in the regulating 
mechanisms of these two processes.441
Besides physiologic changes in normal puberty, metabolic 
defects become increasingly relevant in pediatric populations 
as the prevalence of childhood obesity is rapidly rising. The 
percentage of children with a BMI equal to or above the 95th 
percentile for age and sex more than tripled to reach 17% in 
the United States from 1999 to 2021.442 Worldwide preva­
lence of childhood obesity was estimated at 5% in 2015, but 
it is increasing faster than adult obesity in most countries.443 
In healthy children, BMI is an acceptable surrogate marker to 
assess the degree of body fatness.444 More precisely, elevated 
BMI has a satisfactory sensitivity (70%–80%) and high speci­
ficity (95%) to detect fat excess in pediatric populations.445 
1043
CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
Available data do not support an added benefit for the use 
of waist circumference in addition to BMI Z-scores.446 This 
epidemic of obesity has led to the advent of MetS in youth, 
although the absence of a generally accepted pediatric defini­
tion precludes comparisons between different studies.447 MetS 
encompasses a group of cardiovascular risk factors centered 
on insulin resistance as the main underlying hallmark.448 Adi­
pose tissue distribution is a crucial predisposing factor, with 
excess VAT leading to a vicious cycle of insulin resistance and 
low-grade inflammation. In this setting, small adipocytes dem­
onstrate limited storage ability, leading to increased ectopic 
fat deposition in the muscles and the liver. Increased VAT in 
obese teenagers confers a fivefold higher likelihood of MetS 
as compared to obesity in the lowest tertile of intraabdomi­
nal fat.449 On the contrary, subcutaneous fat is associated with 
large, lipid-laden very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) par­
ticles, which are removed directly from the circulation and are 
thus less metabolically deleterious, although some conflicting 
evidence exists.450 The occurrence of MetS in childhood sub­
sequently translates into higher mortality, as demonstrated in 
a large cohort of 4857 American Indian nondiabetic children 
followed over 20 years. Childhood obesity, glucose intolerance, 
and hypertension (but not hypercholesterolemia) were strongly 
associated with increased rates of premature death in this 
study.451 Interethnic differences also affect the metabolic phe­
notype, with higher VAT and ectopic fat content in the liver 
and the muscles of obese adolescents of Hispanic origin.452
A normal individual adapts to the physiologic rise in pubertal 
insulin resistance, but an individual at genetic risk for T2D and 
an accompanying defect in pancreatic β-cell function453 may 
develop T2D during puberty, especially in the presence of addi­
tional metabolic hits, notably obesity. Currently, diabetes screening 
is recommended for overweight (>85th percentile) or obese (>95th 
percentile) children with at least one additional risk factor, such 
as: (1) positive family history of T2D in a first- or second-degree 
relative; (2) history of gestational diabetes during the child’s gesta­
tion; (3) signs of insulin resistance (e.g., acanthosis nigricans) or 
conditions associated with insulin resistance (e.g., functional ovar­
ian hyperandrogenism, hypertension, dyslipidemia); (4) high-risk 
ethnic groups (e.g., Black, Native American, Hispanic American, 
Asian American).454 The criteria for diagnosis of diabetes are similar 
to the ones used in adulthood: fasting plasma glucose level higher 
than 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or a 2-hour postprandial value 
higher than 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or a random glucose level 
higher than 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in the setting of symptoms 
such as weight loss, polyuria, or polydipsia. There are only limited 
data to support the use of glycated hemoglobin (A1C) to diagnose 
diabetes in the pediatric setting,455 but its use was nevertheless rec­
ommended by the latest American Diabetes Association (ADA) 
guidelines.454 Determination of the type of diabetes (type 1 or 2) is 
then necessary. In addition, T2D in children or adolescents should 
not be confused with the various forms of monogenetic diabetes, 
such as maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY), typically 
inherited as autosomal-dominant traits.456
Hypertension is becoming common in puberty as a comorbid 
condition of obesity. Blood pressure is related to the age, gender, 
and height of the child, and updated standards in normal-weight 
children were published in 2017.457 Blood pressure in childhood 
and adolescence is predictive of adult blood pressure (tracking). 
Notably, blood pressure begins to rise in African American chil­
dren at lower BMIs than in White children, highlighting ethnicity 
as a key prognostic factor.458 
Body Composition Assessment
MRI is currently the gold standard to assess adipose tissue distri­
bution and determine VAT and subcutaneous fat while avoiding 
computed tomography (CT)-related radiation exposure.459 How­
ever, MRI is costly and time-consuming as compared to a DXA 
scan. Recent studies in children and adolescents have shown that 
DXA-measured VAT correlates well with MRI-derived measure­
ments,460 although the agreement was weaker in the low-VAT 
range, and DXA was unable to reliably detect changes in VAT 
among obese children.460 Other validated techniques in adults to 
study body composition, such as bioimpedance analysis (BIA), 
seem to lack precision in growing youth.461 
Delayed Puberty
Delayed puberty is a common condition, occurring in approxi­
mately 2% of the general population, with more males affected 
than females.462 It is defined as a delay of pubertal onset or pro­
gression of greater than 2 SD compared to the population mean.3 
Classically, this corresponds to an absence of testicular enlarge­
ment and virilization in boys (TV <4 mL) by age 14 or the 
absence of breast development by age 13 or primary amenorrhea 
by age 15 in girls (Box 23.5).3,463 Recently, the use of a puberty 
nomogram evaluating not only the pubertal onset but also puber­
tal progression (in SD/year) led to a more accurate description 
of normal puberty and its disorders.464 Delayed puberty can be 
caused by a large group of heterogeneous disorders (Fig. 23.31). 
The first group is CDGP, the most frequent cause, which is a tran­
sient form of GnRH deficiency causing HH. The second group 
includes hypothalamo-pituitary diseases generating HH as a result 
of structural, functional, or congenital defects. Functional HH (or 
functional hypothalamic amenorrhea [FHA]) is more prevalent 
in females and could be suggested by the presence of weight loss, 
eating disorders, excessive physical activity, and/or chronic under­
lying conditions.465 The third group includes primary gonadal 
disorders such as TS or Klinefelter syndrome in girls and boys, 
respectively, leading to HH.
Standard evaluation for all cases of delayed puberty should 
include the following:
 • Complete personal and family history
Symptoms of chronic or intermittent illnesses should be 
sought. Details pertaining to growth and development will be 
elicited. Questions about the patient’s sense of smell are essential. 
Poor linear growth and poor nutritional status during the neonatal 
period and childhood may reflect long-standing abnormalities of 
development. Family history may reveal disorders of puberty or 
infertility, anosmia, or hyposmia in relatives and delay in the age 
at onset of puberty in parents or siblings. Recalled age of puber­
tal onset is relatively reliable in women but less often accurate in 
men. A history of consanguinity is important in the detection of 
autosomal-recessive disorders.
 • Thorough physical examination
Complete physical status, including the lungs, heart, kidney, 
and gastrointestinal tract, is important in the search for a chronic 
disorder that may delay puberty. In adolescents, a growth chart is 
plotted to represent growth velocity from birth. Late-onset growth 
failure with a break in the growth chart usually indicates a serious 
organic condition. Weight is plotted to determine states of malnu­
trition. BMI should be calculated and plotted by age and gender 
in this era of epidemic obesity to refine metabolic assessment. The 
upper/lower segment ratio and the arm span are measured and 
compared with the height. The signs of puberty are assessed, and 
1044
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
the stage of secondary sexual development is determined by physi­
cal examination according to the Tanner stages (see Figs. 23.18, 
23.19, and 23.21). The TV is assessed in boys using a Prader orchi­
dometer. The length and diameter of the gently stretched penis are 
also measured in boys, and the diameter of glandular breast tissue 
and areolar size are determined in girls. The presence or absence 
of galactorrhea is documented. Obese boys often appear to have 
a small penis because of excessive adipose tissue surrounding the 
phallus; only when the fat is retracted can the full extent of phallic 
development be assessed. This is among the most common causes 
of inappropriate referral for hypogonadism. The extent of pubic 
and axillary hair is assessed, as is the degree of acne or comedo­
nes. The possibility of cryptorchidism or retractile testes should be 
considered if no testes are palpated in the scrotum. The stigmata of 
gonadal dysgenesis (i.e., TS) or the small testes and gynecomastia 
of Klinefelter syndrome may suggest a chromosomal abnormal­
ity. Neurologic examination, including examination of the visual 
fields by frontal confrontation, may reveal findings suggesting the 
presence of a CNS neoplasm or a developmental defect, justify­
ing the performance of an ophthalmologic evaluation. A targeted 
physical examination to uncover CHH-associated phenotypes 
(e.g., mirror movements, ataxia) is indicated.
 • Endocrine profile and imaging studies
Laboratory studies (Box 23.6) include determination of 
plasma LH and FSH concentrations by sensitive third-genera­
tion assays in pediatric endocrine laboratories and determination

of Klinefelter syndrome (gynecomastia, developmental delay).

adolescence is made if there are no clinical signs of a systemic 
or hypothalamo-pituitary disease, if the physical examination is 
strictly normal (besides the pubertal delay), if the height is short 
for chronologic age but normal for bone age, and if a similar 
history of spontaneous resolving delayed puberty is found in 
parents or siblings. In these classic cases, MRI of the hypotha­
lamic-pituitary region may not be necessary.
Constitutional Delay in Growth and Puberty
CDGP is the most common cause of delayed puberty in both 
sexes and results from a transient state of GnRH deficiency where 
puberty eventually occurs, although with marked delay.466 There­
fore, CDGP is often considered by many as a “normal variant of 
puberty.” CDGP occurs more commonly in boys than in girls. In 
a tertiary center, CDGP represents 65% of male cases and 30% of 
female cases with delayed puberty.462 Relatively similar estimates 
(82% for boys and 56% for girls) were reported in a recent Euro­
pean study enrolling 244 patients who presented with delayed 
puberty.467
Although its pathophysiology is not fully understood, CDGP 
seems to have a clear genetic basis, as indicated by the finding of 
positive family history in 50% to 75% of patients with CDGP.468 
An autosomal-dominant pattern of inheritance is postulated in 
most familial cases.469,470 A recent GWAS for age of menarche in 
a large female cohort (n > 180,000) identified 106 genomic loci, 
some of which were also implicated in BMI, height, and epigen­
etic regulation.471 These findings further support the critical con­
nection between energy balance and reproduction. In addition, 
the reported menarche loci were enriched in or near genes that 
underlie CHH, including LEPR, GNRH1, and TACR3. Interest­
ingly, some rare and potentially deleterious variants in CHH genes

were detected in patients with CDGP with or without family his­
tory of CHH.472 Nevertheless, the hypothesis of a shared genetic 
basis between CHH and CDGP was not supported by a whole 
exome sequencing (WES) study involving 116 CHH and 72 
CDGP probands.473 Remarkably, this study identified rare vari­
ants in known CHH genes in 17% of controls but with very low 
rates of oligogenicity—2% in controls compared to 15% in CHH 
subjects—demonstrating the importance of this genetic constel­
lation. Recently, rare loss-of-function mutations in the immu­
noglobulin superfamily member 10 (IGSF10) gene were found 
in six unrelated CDGP families.474 This gene was shown to be 
important for the earliest stage of GnRH neuron migration from 
the nasal mesenchyme to the border with the telencephalon in 
mice. Interestingly, loss-of-function mutations were also identified 
in women with FHA, pointing to a role of this gene as a modifier 
of GnRH neuron function.
The major reason for seeking medical attention is the combina­
tion of both delayed growth and lack of puberty.3,462 In affected 
male adolescents, the major concerns are related to the lack of 
virilization and testicular growth. Depending on the age of refer­
ral, TV can be prepubertal (<4 mL) or may indicate some pubertal 
development (i.e., between 5 and 12 mL) yet remain below the 
normal range size for age. A recent retrospective study examined 
467 males referred for delayed puberty classified as CDGP based 
on classical criteria (G1 or TV <4 mL at ≥14 years) versus by the 
application of pubertal nomogram evaluating both pubertal onset 
and progression.464 Classical criteria detected 27% of CDGP 
cases, whereas the use of pubertal nomogram improved the detec­
tion of CDGP to 60%. Thus, pubertal nomogram appears to be 
a better tool to rationally separate normal from delayed puberty 
throughout adolescence. A delayed bone age is classically consid­
ered a clinical characteristic of CDGP, but it can also accompany 
delayed puberty resulting from chronic illness, CHH, or gonadal 
failure.3 Full sexual maturity is eventually reached in CDGP in 
a longer-than-usual process and by the age of 18 years in most 
boys. In affected female adolescents, delayed breast development 
and absent menses are the most common complaints. It is impor­
tant to note that the spectrum and natural history of females with 
CDGP has not been fully described. Indeed, studies usually focus 
on age of menarche >15 years old.463 Most patients with CDGP 
are thin, although almost 25% are overweight (>85th percentile 
of BMI for age).462 There is evidence supporting that CDGP sub­
jects have greater total energy expenditure (TEE), possibly as a 
result of an altered mitochondrial metabolism or increased non–
exercise-related thermogenesis.475 Increased energy intake was not 
found to reduce TEE.
CDGP is a diagnosis of exclusion, and other underlying 
causes of delayed puberty should be actively investigated and ruled 
out, including HH (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome or TS), permanent 
HH (e.g., CHH, tumors, infiltrative diseases), and functional HH 
(e.g., systemic illness, anorexia nervosa, excessive exercise). In par­
ticular, the differential diagnosis between CDGP and CHH in 
adolescence is particularly difficult. Unlike in KS, impaired olfac­
tion is very rare in CDGP, and undescended testes occur at the rate 
found in the general population. Plasma gonadal steroid levels are 
low at the time of presentation, but as bone age advances, the basal 
gonadotropin concentrations gradually increase, and the response 
to GnRH stimulation test begins to favor LH, reflecting the matu­
ration of the hypothalamic-pituitary system. A morning serum T 
value of >0.7 nmol/L heralds an imminent onset of phenotypic 
puberty in boys within 12 to 15 months.476 In young females, it is 
particularly challenging to ascertain CDGP and exclude FHA.465 
For this reason, excessive exercise, a subclinical eating disorder, 
and/or moderate psychological stress should be carefully assessed 
in female adolescents with delayed puberty, keeping in mind that a 
BMI within the normal range does not exclude a lack of body fat. 
The latter can be assessed by measurement of serum leptin levels 
and body composition using DXA.477–480 Management options 
for CDGP include expectant observation versus transitory sex ste­
roid replacement.3 The latter targets primarily the induction of 
secondary sexual characteristics in order to alleviate psychosocial 
distress resulting from pubertal delay and/or short stature.
CDGP is often associated with short stature because the 
growth spurt is delayed. Affected individuals are usually short (<2 
SD below the mean height value for chronologic age) at evalua­
tion, although growth velocity and height are usually appropriate 
for bone age (Fig. 23.32). Growth velocity usually increases to 
normal levels after puberty begins.481 Affected boys seem to be 
more distressed by short stature than by delay in sexual develop­
ment. GH release in the basal state and in response to growth hor­
mone–releasing hormone (GHRH) or other stimulation tests is 
moderately reduced in children with CDGP, but both parameters 
normalize in most patients after priming with sex steroids. Nev­
ertheless, patients with CDGP often do not reach their predicted 
height. This could reflect a selection bias because the patients most 
likely to be referred are those who combine familial or idiopathic 
short stature and CDGP. Adult height is lower if affected indi­
viduals already show decreased height during childhood.482,483 
Heavier individuals with CDP reach greater height than those 
who are thinner.462 There is little place for GH treatment in chil­
dren with CDGP-associated short stature, as illustrated by lim­
ited height gain in the few available clinical studies.484 Given the 
critical role of E2 in skeletal maturation, treatment with an AI to 
increase adult height by delaying skeletal maturation has attracted 
interest. A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study 
enrolled boys with CDGP who were treated with monthly T alone 
or in combination with oral letrozole, a potent fourth-generation 
AI that blocks the conversion of T to E2.485 The results revealed a 
mean increase in predicted adult height of 5.1 cm in the combina­
tion group. Subsequent studies supported these promising results, 
but data on actual final height remain scarce and inconclusive.486 
Concerns regarding suboptimal bone accrual and the occurrence 
of mild vertebral deformities when AI therapy is started in prepu­
berty or early puberty have cast doubt on the use of these agents 
in the setting of CDGP.487 A recent study comparing letrozole 
to low-dose T therapy in boys with CDGP age at least 14 years 
and having exhibited the first signs of puberty did not detect any 
vertebral deformities but noted less BMD accrual in the letrozole 
group.488 This difference disappeared after adjustment for the ver­
tebral size between the two groups. 
Congenital Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism
CHH, or idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (IHH), is 
a rare genetic disorder caused by deficiency in GnRH secretion 
or action, resulting in absent or incomplete puberty with infertil­
ity.81 Puberty fails to begin by 14 years in boys and 13 years in 
girls, or pubertal maturation is incomplete or transient. Because 
GnRH cannot be reliably measured in the serum because of a very 
short half-life, the diagnosis relies on low serum sex steroids in 
the setting of low/normal serum gonadotropin levels, otherwise 
normal pituitary function, and the absence of a hypothalamic-
pituitary lesion on MRI. When CHH is associated with anosmia, 
it is classified as KS. CHH/KS is a rare disease with an estimated 
1047
CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
prevalence of 1 in 4000 to 10,000489 and a male predominance of 
3:1. It is likely that a subsequent number of women with CHH 
with partial forms are not referred to academic centers but rather 
treated with contraceptive pills without definitive diagnosis. This 
could account for the high male/female ratio.489 The genetic 
defect involves the GnRH pulse generator or the GnRH receptor 
in the gonadotroph cells, leading to an isolated gonadotropin defi­
ciency.35 The abnormalities may affect the amplitude of GnRH 
pulses, their frequency, or both components, as evidenced in fre­
quent sampling studies of plasma LH levels (Fig. 23.33).
Clinical Presentation
CHH Males. A history of micropenis (stretched length <2 cm, 
corresponding to –2.5 SD below the mean length in newborn 
males) and/or cryptorchidism (undescended testes) at birth is a 
first hint of a fetal defect in the HPG axis (absence of midgesta­
tion peak of pituitary gonadotropins) and absent or suboptimal 
minipuberty. Undescended testes and micropenis are common in 
cases of complete CHH.490 The magnitude of the GnRH defi­
ciency correlates with the size of the testes. Males with CHH 
most frequently seek medical attention at adolescence for lack 
of virilization. The hormonal phenotype depends on the degree 
of GnRH deficiency. Although the majority of males with CHH 
exhibit absent puberty (complete CHH, i.e., no virilization and 
prepubertal testis <4 mL),491,492 approximately 25% exhibit some 
degree of pubertal development (partial CHH, TV greater than 
4 mL). This subgroup often displays detectable serum gonado­
tropin levels but with frank hypogonadism (serum T levels <1 
nmol/L).493,494 In complete CHH, concentrations of gonadal sex 
steroids and gonadotropins are low, pulsatile LH secretion is often 
virtually absent, and the LH response to GnRH or GnRH agonist 
administration is flat (Fig. 23.34). The testes are small (1–2 mL), 
and serum INHB, an estimate of seminiferous tubule function, is 
decreased (<60 pg/mL).35
In contrast to organic HH (where GH deficiency is also pres­
ent) and CDGP (in which patients are short for chronologic age), 
height is appropriate for age in most male patients with CHH 
(Fig. 23.35). Because the E2 levels are too low to cause epiphy­
seal fusion at the normal age, increased arm span for height (>5 
cm) and a decreased ratio of upper to lower body segments (i.e., 
eunuchoid body proportions) are present. The lack of increased 
sex steroids levels leads to steady linear growth490 without a 
growth spurt; however, final height is rarely affected.495 Recently, 
adult height was found to be higher in a large CHH male French 
cohort than in their siblings and the general population, as well as 
the midparental target height.362 Another study involving 41 men 
with CHH detected a positive correlation between later hormone 
replacement therapy (HRT) instauration and final adult height.496
Other physical hallmarks in some adolescents with CHH, if 
left untreated, include (1) a more female body habitus with a ten­
dency to a gynoid pattern of fat distribution; (2) the occurrence of 
mild gynecomastia as a result of a reduced T/E2 ratio in some indi­
viduals; and (3) the impairment of bone accrual, with lower bone 
density observed relative to peers and, eventually, suboptimal peak 
bone mass acquisition in most of untreated subjects. Recently, a 
large cross-sectional study performing HR-pQCT in several adult 
men with CHH/KS revealed decreased vBMD and disturbed tra­
becular microarchitecture as compared to age- and BMI-matched 
controls, despite long-term HRT.497 Adequate diagnosis of CHH/
KS at adolescence and HRT initiation before the age of 19 years 
was associated with better bone outcomes. Some specific CHH 
genetic defects may directly affect bone homeostasis (e.g., loss-of-
function mutations in FGFR1).
Although diagnosis of CHH in adolescence is more com­
mon, some patients do not seek medical attention until adult­
hood. At this point, low libido, low or absent sexual activity, and 
infertility are the most common complaints. Most patients at this 
stage exhibit prepubertal or minimal testicular growth. A subset 
of patients will present with larger TV and even preserved sper­
matogenesis despite a biochemical profile of HH in the setting 
of detectable gonadotropins. This constellation is called the fertile 
eunuch variant of CHH and is thought to be due to the presence 
of low-amplitude and/or low-frequency or sleep-entrained GnRH 
pulses only, which are sufficient to support intratesticular T but 
not enough to achieve a normal circulating T level for full viriliza­
tion.489 Recently, Patderska et al498 described six cases of men who 
were diagnosed with CHH after 50 years of age. As a result of 
the long-standing untreated hypogonadism, these patients exhib­
ited several associated complications, including osteoporosis and 
anemia.

for age); phallus is 6.0 × 1.6 cm; testes are 2.5 × 1.4 cm; and the scrotum 
showed early thinning. At a chronologic age of 15 years and 4 months, 
the bone age was 11 years, and the sella turcica was normal. The plasma 
concentration of luteinizing hormone (LH) was 0.7 ng/mL (LER-960); the 
concentration of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) was 0.5 ng/mL (LER-
869). On gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) testing, the plasma 
concentration of LH increased to 2.2 ng/mL (an increment of 1.5 ng/
mL), and the testosterone level rose from 52 to 77 ng/dL. The testes sub­
sequently spontaneously enlarged, and the patient progressed through 
puberty. For conversion to SI units, see Figs. 23.26 and 23.27. (From 
Styne DM, Grumbach MM. Puberty in the male and female: its physiology 
and disorders. In: Yen SCC, Jaffe RB, eds. Reproductive Endocrinology. 
2nd ed. Philadelphia, PA: WB Saunders; 1986:313–384.)

SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
CHH Females. The classic manifestation is primary amenor­
rhea in nearly 90% of women with CHH.499–502 The remaining 
women with CHH have some menstrual bleeding,499,501,503 which 
in most cases involves one or two episodes of bleeding during ado­
lescence (primary-secondary amenorrhea) before chronic amenor­
rhea sets in.499–502,504 The milder end of the spectrum of female 
CHH may include chronic anovulation with almost “normal” 
(although noncyclic) serum E2 and gonadotropin levels.499,505 
In these cases, E2 secretion might be sufficient for endometrial 
thickness, but there will be no ovulation, resulting in occasional 
vaginal bleeding (oligomenorrhea).505,506 Most studies conclude 
that a complete absence of breast development is observed in only 
a minority of women with CHH,499–501 with partial to full spon­
taneous breast development in the majority of them. Pubic hair 
may be absent, sparse, or even normal.499,501 This is the end result 
of varying ovarian androgen production and normal adrenal out­
put of androgen precursors (i.e., DHEA, androstenedione) that 
are converted into more active androgens in the liver and other 
extraadrenal tissues. Notably, adrenarche is normal in the majority 
of women with CHH.500,507
Linear growth and final height in women with CHH have 
been less extensively studied.508,509 The scant published data indi­
cate that the final height in these women is similar to that of the 
reference population. Dickerman et  al508 followed the growth 
of 16 females with CHH and reported unremarkable growth, 
whereas a slight mid-childhood deceleration in the growth rate of 
girls carrying FGFR1 mutations was recently reported.492 
CHH Reversal
Although CHH was previously considered a permanent condi­
tion, it is now known that a subset of patients with CHH will 
spontaneously recover HPG function after treatment with T 
or gonadotropins.510–512 Reversibility occurs in both male and 
female patients with CHH, and it appears to be more common 
(∼10%–20%) than previously thought.510–512 Patients with rever­
sal initially present have mild or severe GnRH deficiency, and 
many harbor pathogenic mutations in genes underlying CHH. 
To date, there are no clear clinical factors for predicting reversible 
CHH. An enrichment of TAC3/TACR3 mutations was observed 
in one series of patients.511,513 Importantly, recovery of reproduc­
tive axis function may not be permanent because some patients 
experience a relapse to a state of GnRH deficiency511; therefore, 
long-term monitoring is imperative. The existence of CHH rever­
sal demonstrates the plasticity of the GnRH neuronal system, 
highlighting the importance of environmental influences, such as 
sex steroid treatment, on the reproductive axis.

CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
CHH-Associated Phenotypes
CHH is associated in variable frequency with nonreproductive 
phenotypes. Anosmia (i.e., lack of sense of smell) or hyposmia 
(i.e., reduced sense of smell), resulting from agenesis or hypoplasia 
of the olfactory lobes or sulci (Fig. 23.36), is present in roughly 
half of patients with CHH,514 consistent with the diagnosis of 
KS (Fig. 23.37). The interconnected link between the GnRH 
and olfactory systems during early developmental stages, with 
the migration of the latter across the olfactory placode, explains 
this frequent co-occurrence.515 Because affected individuals often 
do not notice impaired olfaction, objective testing is necessary to 
detect partial anosmia. Other phenotypes associated with CHH 
at a lower prevalence include mirror movements (synkinesia); 
unilateral renal agenesis (or dysplasia); sensorineural hearing loss; 
midline brain defects, including absent corpus callosum; cleft lip/
palate; dental agenesis; eye movement disorders (including nystag­
mus); skeletal deformities (short metacarpals, sternum pes cavus); 
cerebellar ataxia; and cardiovascular defects.35,516 Three large stud­
ies have evaluated the prevalence of these associated phenotypes in 
CHH, although these studies were retrospective and thus without 
a systematic screening for these issues.514,516,517 The presence of 
one or more of these specific phenotypic traits can lead to the 
diagnosis of syndromic forms of CHH, such as CHARGE syn­
drome (coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, retardation of 
growth and development, genital hypoplasia, ear anomalies) and 
Waardenburg syndrome. 
Diagnostic Evaluation
Minipuberty provides a brief window of opportunity to diagnose 
CHH. For male infants, micropenis with or without cryptorchi­
dism can be suggestive of CHH. In such cases or in neonates born 
from one parent with CHH, hormone testing at 4 to 12 weeks of 
life may be used to assist in the diagnosis.44,505,518–523 Typically, 
GnRH deficiency during minipuberty is evidenced by low serum 
T, LH, and FSH levels based on comparisons with established

reference ranges.103,524 However, normative reproductive hor­
monal data from a large group of controls during minipuberty 
are lacking.
During childhood, diagnosis of CHH is very challenging 
because this period is a physiologically hypogonadal period of 
development, consistent with the relative quiescence of the GnRH 
pulse generator. Low or undetectable serum levels of gonadal pep­
tides (AMH in girls, AMH and INHB in boys) could indicate a 
reproductive defect.301 Differentiation between a primary and a 
central origin of hypogonadism at this stage is extremely difficult.
In adolescence, delayed puberty is the hallmark of a CHH 
diagnosis. Between the age of 14 and 16 years, CHH is difficult 
to differentiate from CDGP. Biochemically, both exhibit GnRH 
deficiency, attested by hypogonadal T or E2 levels and low/normal 
serum levels of gonadotropins. Absent puberty (TV <4 mL) by age 
16 is consistent with CHH.464 Similarly, incomplete puberty by

age 18 also points to the diagnosis of CHH. Once the diagnosis 
is suspected, it is crucial to assess the onset and severity of GnRH 
deficiency because these parameters will be used to tailor treat­
ment. Clinical signs such as micropenis or cryptorchidism point 
to a neonatal form of CHH (abnormal minipuberty).525 The 
absence of pubertal onset by age 16 indicates severe GnRH defi­
ciency but does not preclude the activity of the HPG axis during 
minipuberty. Evidence of initial but then stalled pubertal develop­
ment is consistent with partial CHH and thus is a less severe form 
of GnRH deficiency.
Hormonal Profile. Most men and women with CHH have 
very low circulating gonadotropin levels,493,494,500 especially 
patients with complete GnRH deficiency and absent puberty. In 
addition, this subset of CHH has apulsatile patterns of LH secre­
tion. Patients with partial puberty (i.e., some spontaneous puber­
tal development) can have low-normal circulating gonadotropin 
levels, which is inappropriate in the setting of low sex hormones 
(T or E2).499,500
Circulating E2 levels in women with CHH are usually low or 
at the lower end of the normal range during the follicular phase 
when measured by sensitive assays (certain immunoassays, gas 
chromatography–mass spectrometry [GC-MS], and liquid chro­
matography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS]) that allow detection of 
E2 concentrations below 10 pg/mL.500 In men, two studies inves­
tigated E2 levels in young men with untreated CHH. Trabado 
et al526 used a sensitive radioimmunoassay and showed a signifi­
cant decrease in serum E2 levels of 91 men with untreated CHH 
as compared to postpubertal healthy males. Using GC-MS, Giton 
et al507 confirmed the profound decrease in circulating E2 in males 
with CHH, which was largely corrected after treatment with T or 
hCG.526
The circulating T levels in patients with CHH are usually 
markedly decreased (<3 nmol/L). Patients with partial CHH and 
a larger TV also often exhibit low T levels.493 Low circulating T 
levels are reported in women with CHH despite normal circulat­
ing DHEAS concentrations.500 This relative androgen deficiency 
is likely subsequent to the inadequate stimulation of internal theca 
cells by low circulating LH.500
In men with CHH, the LH response to the GnRH stimulation 
test is highly variable and correlates with the severity of gonadotro­
pin deficiency.506 A GnRH stimulation test with complete absence 
of LH response is a strong indicator of severe GnRH deficiency. 
However, an adequate gonadotropin response can be observed in 
patients with severe GnRH deficiency (absent puberty), which 
questions the added value of this testing.503,527,528 Data on women 
with CHH and the pituitary gonadotrope response to the GnRH 
test are limited to a few case reports.506 In most affected women, 
the peak LH response to GnRH was blunted and weaker as com­
pared to controls.
Serum INHB levels have been assessed in large cohorts of males 
with CHH.316,494,529 Most patients with complete CHH (absent 
puberty as attested by prepubertal testicular volume, micropenis, 
and cryptorchidism) exhibit low serum INHB levels (<60 pg/mL). 
This is consistent with the absence of GnRH-induced FSH stimula­
tion of the seminiferous tubules during minipuberty.527,529 Higher 
serum INHB levels are encountered in a minority of patients with 
complete CHH but in the majority of patients with partial CHH, 
consistent with a preserved minipuberty in the latter. Serum INHB 
levels correlate strongly with testicular size.493 Low INHB levels are 
a negative predictor of fertility.529 Very few studies have investigated 
circulating INHB levels in females with CHH,500 with mostly low 
concentrations in the range of prepubertal girls.530
Circulating AMH levels in male patients with CHH have been 
studied during the neonatal period and in adulthood (before and 
after gonadotropin or T treatment).316,520 During minipuberty, 
infants with CHH have low AMH, which can be normalized by 
combined gonadotropin therapy.520,525 Adults with untreated 
CHH have high AMH levels, similar to the prepubertal levels in 
normal boys, indicating the immaturity of the SC population.316 
Monotherapy with recombinant FSH in previously untreated 
patients with CHH stimulates the proliferation of immature SCs 
and thus an increase in serum AMH, whereas subsequent hCG 
addition increases intratesticular T levels and dramatically low­
ers AMH levels.316 Circulating AMH concentrations were sig­
nificantly lower in women with CHH than in healthy women.500 
However, almost two-thirds of these patients had serum AMH 
levels within the normal range. The subgroup with the lowest 
antral follicular count were also those with the lowest serum FSH

and AMH levels. Thus, low AMH should not be considered a 
poor-fertility prognosis in women with CHH because an increase 
in AMH and subsequent fertility can be efficiently restored in 
these patients by both pulsatile GnRH and combined gonado­
tropin therapy.
In the evaluation of CHH, it is important to rule out other 
pituitary defects. A baseline profile that includes measurements 
of prolactin, free T4, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), morn­
ing cortisol, and IGF1 should be performed. In case of suspected 
pituitary insufficiency, appropriate dynamic challenge tests should 
be performed.531 
Radiologic Testing. Pelvic or transvaginal ultrasound (when 
appropriate) demonstrated variable uterine hypoplasia499–501,532 
in women with CHH, which correlated with the severity of E2 
deficiency532 and endometrial atrophy.533 Ovarian volume in 
females with CHH was significantly reduced compared to healthy 
adult women of similar age.499,500 The only study that assessed 
antral follicle count in women with CHH showed a significant 
decrease compared to normal, age-matched women, with reduced 
levels of AMH.500 As discussed earlier, these data should not be 
considered as a sign of poor ovarian reserve and thus an indication 
of poor-fertility prognosis in women with CHH. Indeed, both 
parameters respond favorably to pulsatile GnRH or combined 
gonadotropin therapy.
Although an orchidometer is often used in clinical practice 
to estimate testes size, testicular ultrasound has the advantage of 
being less operator dependent. A study measuring 151 testes in 
76 adults concluded that both methods were equally accurate in 
the hands of an experienced clinician.534 More recently, a study 
comparing testicular size based on ultrasound and clinical palpa­
tion (with two types of orchidometer, Prader and Rochester) in 65 
males age 7 to 24 years found a strong correlation between the two 
approaches.535 As expected, both orchidometers overestimated TV 
by approximately 6 mL in comparison to the ultrasound, likely 
because of the interference of surrounding soft tissues. However, 
the sensitivity of orchidometers was relatively low regarding their 
capacity to detect a size difference of 10% to 25% between the 
two testes. Further, ultrasound has the added value at baseline to 
allow for simultaneous assessment of the testes and the kidneys. 
Semen Analysis. Spermiogram is defined as the quantitative 
and qualitative analysis of semen in order to assess male fertil­
ity potential.536 It is indicated at baseline (when possible) and 
serially after the initiation of fertility treatment in males with 
CHH. Among the primary parameters, ejaculate volume (which 
is T dependent), sperm count, and sperm motility are the most 
critical. The latest World Health Organization (WHO) criteria 
for interpretation of semen analysis were published in 2021,537 
based on semen samples from over 3589 fertile men, and defined 
the following cutoffs for the lower-normal range (5th percentile): 
1.4 mL for semen volume, 39 million for total sperm number, 
42% for total motility, and 4% for normal morphology. Given the 
low serum T at diagnosis, most patients with CHH are unable to 
ejaculate. However, with fertility treatment, the majority of males 
with CHH will increase their ejaculate and progressively develop 
sperm in their ejaculate. Interestingly, the concentration of sperm 
needed for fertilization in patients with CHH is much lower com­
pared to the WHO guidelines, likely related to the central defect 
in GnRH in CHH and often an absence of primary testicular 
defect. 
Screening for Associated Phenotypes 
	1.	 A standardized olfactory test516,538 is especially critical because 
50% of patients with CHH who self-reported a normal sense 
of smell were in fact hyposmic or anosmic based on formal 
smell testing.538 Olfactory function is easy to test using semi­
quantitative methods such as the UPSIT score538 or the Snif­
fin Sticks539 tests, which give age- and gender-matched scores 
relative to a reference population. Alternatively, smell function 
may also be assessed using volatile-stimulated chemosensory-
evoked potentials540; however, this is less accessible in a clinical 
setting.
	2.	 A brain MRI with a dedicated KS protocol to detect aplasia/
hypoplasia of the olfactory bulbs (surrogate marker for anosmia 
in small children for whom a formal smell test is impossible), 
malformation of the corpus callosum and cerebellum,521,541 
and midline defects542
	3.	 An inner ear MRI to assess an anomaly of the semicircular 
canals. The latter is an important finding because it could indi­
cate the need for additional testing to explore the diagnosis of 
CHARGE syndrome.543
	4.	 An abdominal ultrasound to screen for renal agenesis and/or 
dysplasia.
	5.	 An audiogram in search of a congenital sensorineural hearing 
impairment, performed systematically because hearing loss is 
usually mild or unilateral, and thus patients may be unaware of 
their deficit. The prevalence of hearing loss in CHH is reported 
to be between 5% and 15%.
Such anomalies not only support the diagnosis of CHH but 
also indicate specific genetic forms of the disease (e.g., CHARGE 
syndrome) with specific clinical care and genetic counseling.505,544 
For instance, the association of CHH with hearing loss points to 
specific genetic mutations (i.e., CHD7, SOX10, IL17RD).35,517 
Differential Diagnosis of CHH
In the setting of delayed puberty, the differential diagnosis and 
diagnostic workup depend on the biological sex and serum basal 
gonadotropin levels. The principal causes and their main charac­
teristics, as well as the routine endocrine and imaging studies, are 
summarized in Table 23.3 and Box 23.6, respectively. The diagno­
sis of HH is readily established by elevation of random plasma LH 
and FSH concentrations. However, differentiating CHH from 
CDGP and other causes of HH remains challenging owing to the 
overlap in physical and laboratory findings.
CHH Versus CDGP. CDGP in more frequent than CHH, espe­
cially in boys. Currently, it remains challenging to distinguish 
adolescents with CDGP from those with CHH (specifically par­
tial forms) when the initial clinical evaluation takes place between 
the age of 14 and 16 years (Fig. 23.38). In both cases, the physi­
cal examination will reveal a prepubertal status with low levels of 
LH and FSH (Table 23.4). Differentiating CHH from CDGP 
is crucial in order to allow an early diagnosis of CHH, avoid 
delay regarding HRT instauration, and alleviate the psychologi­
cal burden associated with delayed sexual maturation.35 Herein 
follow some data on features that may assist in the differential 
diagnosis, stressing that although individual indicators may not 
provide a definitive answer, a combination of multiple factors will 
strengthen the likelihood of a particular diagnosis. Nevertheless, 
close follow-up remains crucial in all cases to ascertain an accurate 
diagnosis.
Clinical Features. Overall, lack of onset of puberty by age 
16 (<–4 SD) indicates CHH, whereas robust pubertal progres­
sion by the same age points toward CDGP. Evidence of initial 
but then stalled pubertal development is consistent with CHH. 
History of micropenis and cryptorchidism or co-occurrence of 
anosmia and other CHH-associated phenotypes constitute some 
1053
CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
red flags pointing toward a CHH diagnosis.35 More specifically, 
a medical history of micropenis and cryptorchidism may reflect 
the lack of activation of the HPG axis during minipuberty.44,525 
In a series of 174 boys referred for evaluation of delayed puberty, 
cryptorchidism was present in 36% of boys with CHH and in 
2% of boys with CDGP.495 Family history of delayed puberty is 
suggestive of CDGP (a much more frequent entity than CHH), 
although cases of CDGP have been reported in the families of 
CHH probands.469,514
TV at diagnosis is the clinical parameter with the most rele­
vance in boys with delayed puberty. In a retrospective study of 174 
boys with delayed puberty at age 14 to 15 years, a cutoff of TV at 
1.1 mL (calculated using the formula length × width2 × 0.52, with 
length and width measured with a ruler) showed a 100% sensitiv­
ity and 91% specificity in distinguishing CHH from CDGP.467 
Overall, growth is less affected in CHH than in CDGP, and a 
growth velocity of less than 3 cm per year renders more likely the 
diagnosis of the latter (or of functional hypogonadotropic hypo­
gonadism [FHH]). 
Biochemical Tests. Several basal hormones and dynamic tests 
have been proposed to discriminate between adolescents with 
CDGP and CHH, but none allows definitive diagnosis alone 
(see Table 23.4).545 Basal serum gonadotropins and particularly 
an FSH level cutoff of 1.2 IU/L were suggested to discriminate 
between these two entities in one study.546 Nevertheless, one-
fourth of CDGP patients presented with a serum FSH <1 U/L 
and a similar percentage of patients with CHH exhibited a serum 
FSH >1 IU/L in a subsequent observation.547
Gonadotropin responses to the GnRH stimulation test have 
been shown to be more robust in CDGP than CHH but with 
a significant overlap regarding LH peak values. Further, no data 
are available regarding the response to the GnRH stimulation 
test in girls. Overall, the GnRH test might be useful for identify­
ing severe cases of CHH. Indeed, CHH is highly probable when 
the GnRH-stimulated LH response is blunted. A Finnish study 
analyzing data from 19 patients with CHH and 181 patients 
with CDGP suggested a cutoff of GnRH-stimulated LH peak of 
4.3 IU/L with a sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 75% to 
detect CHH.467 Similarly, a French study with a larger number 
of patients with CHH (127 with CHH, 74 with CDGP, and 31 
healthy controls) demonstrated that all subjects with CDGP had 
a peak LH of >4.0 U/L, with 53% of subjects with CHH being 
below this cutoff.548 Patients with CHH were older at diagnosis 
than those with CDGP (25 ± 8 vs. 15 ± 1 years, respectively).
INHB, a product from SCs in the testis and granulosa cells 
in the ovary, increases sharply during normal puberty after FSH

stimulation.549 One small study identified a sensitivity and 
specificity of 100% in differentiating CHH from CDGP with a 
cutoff of 35 pg/mL.550 However, this study did not include ado­
lescent males with CHH with partial puberty, who have much 
higher INHB levels (i.e., the fertile eunuch subgroup), some­
times within the normal range.494 A serum INHB level lower 
than 60 pmol/L was proposed as a highly suggestive cutoff to 
indicate complete CHH and severe GnRH deficiency.467 A lower 
cutoff of 35 pg/mL was necessary to exclude all CDGP cases 
(but also half of CHH cases) in another study recruiting patients 
from two French tertiary centers.548 Taken together, INHB lacks 
specificity, especially in the partial forms of CHH (boys with 
TV >4 mL, girls with spontaneous breast development beyond 
Tanner stage 3). Higher AMH is suggestive of CHH, although 
there is no clear cutoff.551,552 Most patients with CHH undergo 
adrenarche at a normal age and tend to have higher DHEAS 
concentrations than those with CDGP,22 but overlap still exists. 
Other evaluated markers, such as plasma INSL3 and IGF1 lev­
els, did not improve accuracy for differential diagnosis between 
CHH and CDGP.
Genetic testing remains a promising tool; however, evidence as 
to whether CHH and CDGP exhibit common or distinct genetic 
backgrounds remains unclear. Mutations in IGSF10 have been 
reported in both families with CDGP and those with CHH.474 
A shared genetic basis is also partly supported by a previous work 
that identified pathogenic mutations of known CHH genes in 
14% of CDGP probands,472 which corresponded to a significant 
enrichment as compared to controls. GWAS studies on the age of 
menarche revealed more than 400 loci associated with the timing 
of puberty, several of which map within known CHH genes.224 
On the contrary, a recent study using WES suggested distinct 
genetic architectures,473 with CDGP resembling the control pop­
ulation in terms of both the frequency of pathogenic variants in 
known CHH genes and the presence of oligogenicity. 
Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism Due to Hypothalamo-
Pituitary Disorders. Hyperprolactinemia of any origin and struc­
tural processes affecting the hypothalamic-pituitary region may 
lead to acquired HH. These include tumors (pituitary macroade­
nomas, craniopharyngiomas, and other CNS tumors), irradiation, 
surgery, apoplexy, or infiltrative diseases (e.g., haemochromatosis, 
sarcoidosis, and histiocytosis). Less commonly, head trauma or 
subarachnoid hemorrhage can generate HH.553–555 Most patients 
with structural causes have multiple pituitary hormone deficien­
cies.554 In early adolescence, a brain MRI is indicated in patients 
with delayed puberty and biochemical HH when there is a break 
in growth, evidence of pituitary hormone deficiency, or hyperp­
rolactinemia and in the case of symptoms of mass effect (head­
ache, visual impairment, or visual field defect). If biochemical HH 
persists in late adolescence or adulthood (T <5 nmol/L), a brain 
MRI is also recommended to assess for CHH-linked changes and 
exclude secondary causes.553,554,556 
Opioid-Induced 
Hypogonadotropic 
Hypogonadism. 
Opioids use is a major cause of reversible HH in males and 
females.557,558 Endogenous opioids inhibit pulsatile GnRH 
release559 and suppress LH secretion, resulting in low sex steroid 
production.558,560–562 Opioid misuse and addiction constitute an 
ongoing and rapidly evolving public health crisis, especially in the 
United States.563 It is therefore likely that opioid-induced HH will 
become a growing diagnostic issue among adolescents and young 
people.

Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism Associated With Hemo­
chromatosis. Hemochromatosis is part of the differential diag­
nosis for CHH because it can cause HH without any additional 
pituitary deficiencies and before the appearance of cardiac and 
hepatic involvement.564 In particular, juvenile hemochromatosis 
(type 2A) can present with delayed puberty or even permanent 
hypogonadism.565,566 A hemochromatosis diagnosis is suggested 
by abnormal serum measurements of iron, ferritin, and transferrin 
saturation coefficient, especially in the setting of a positive family 
history, then confirmed by molecular diagnosis.567 It is important 
to not overlook the diagnosis of hemochromatosis because a rever­
sal of the associated HH may occur after repeated phlebotomy.568 
Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism Associated With 
Metabolic Defects. Contrary to CHH, HH associated with 
obesity and MetS is characterized by mild GnRH deficiency and 
occurs after puberty in the majority of cases.569 The physiopa­
thology of obesity-related HH is multifactorial and depends on 
the severity of the underlying metabolic defect.570 A decrease in 
SHBG is the major factor responsible for low T levels in mod­
erately obese men, whereas severely obese men (BMI >40 kg/
m2) exhibit low total T and FT and reduced GnRH-induced LH 
pulsatility.570 Increased aromatization of T to E2 in adipose tissue 
with subsequent enhanced negative feedback, insulin resistance, 
and hypothalamic inflammation have been postulated as poten­
tial causative factors.571 Notably, with the increasing incidence of 
childhood obesity, obesity-related HH is also on the rise in early 
adolescence, especially in boys, and can underlie some cases of 
delayed puberty.572–574 
Genetics of CHH
CHH is a complex and heterogeneous genetic disorder, with 
approximately 60% to 70% of cases initially appearing spo­
radic.514 In familial cases, X-linked, autosomal-dominant, and 
autosomal-recessive patterns of inheritance have been observed.

SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
The first genetic breakthrough in CHH came in 1989 with the 
identification of an Xp22.3 deletion in a fetus with KS.515 Sub­
sequent genetic studies identified mutations in ANOS1 (formerly 
known as KAL1) within the previously reported Xp22.3 dele­
tion as the first gene underlying the X-linked form of KS.575,576 
Since this initial discovery, mutations in more than 30 loci have 
been identified via cytogenetic studies, candidate gene studies, 
linkage analysis,577–579 pathway analysis,580 and next generation 
sequencing strategies.581,582 Mutations in these CHH genes act 
either alone or in combination35,583 to result in CHH with or 
without anosmia. Genes underlying CHH are classified accord­
ing to their function in the neuroendocrine control of reproduc­
tion: (1) GnRH fate specification, (2) GnRH neuron migration/
olfactory axon guidance, (3) GnRH neuron homeostasis, and (4) 
gonadotrope defects (e.g., GNRH1 and GNRHR).584 The princi­
pal causative genes are detailed in the following sections, with the 
remaining one summarized in Fig. 23.39.
ANOS1 (Anosmin 1). ANOS1 (Online Inheritance in Man 
[OMIM] 300836) encodes anosmin-1, and mutations in this gene 
are inherited in an X-linked fashion. Thus, males with a hemi­
zygous mutation in this gene are affected, whereas heterozygous 
females are nonexpressing carriers, apart from a few exceptional 
cases.499 Anosmin-1 is an extracellular matrix protein critical for 
the guidance of GnRH neurons toward the olfactory bulb during 
development.585 ANOS1 mutations are seen almost exclusively in 
patients with KS (frequency 5%–6%)580,586 and often result in 
severe GnRH deficiency. Synkinesia, unilateral renal agenesis, and 
sensorineural hearing loss are also described in patients with KS 
harboring ANOS1 mutations.514,516,587 Most mutations result in 
frameshifts and premature stop codons, although a smaller num­
ber of missense amino acid substitutions are also seen.473,588–590 
Hemizygous mutations in ANOS1 are typically highly penetrant, 
and oligogenicity involving this gene has not been reported. 
FGFR1/FGF8 (Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 1/Fibroblast 
Growth Factor 8). FGFR1 (fibroblast growth factor 1; OMIM 
136350) is the most frequently mutated gene in patients with 
CHH across multiple studies, ranging from 8% to 10% of CHH 
probands.580,586,591,592 It is inherited in a predominantly autoso­
mal-dominant fashion, may exhibit reduced penetrance, and can 
be inherited along with mutations in one or more other CHH 
genes (i.e., oligogenicity).473,580,586,593 Studies in murine models 
showed that FGFR1 is involved in GnRH neurogenesis,594 olfac­
tory bulb development,595 and GnRH neuron homeostasis.596,597
Pathogenic FGFR1 mutations have been reported in patients 
with varying degrees of GnRH deficiency. Patients harboring 
FGFR1 mutations can have a spectrum of olfactory defects (from 
normal to anosmia) and a variable frequency of CHH-associated 
phenotypes, such as cleft lip/palate, scoliosis, dental agenesis, and 
skeletal defects.527,591,598–600 Of particular interest is the associa­
tion of CHH with split hand/foot malformation (SHFM),601,602 
wherein FGFR1 mutations were detected in >80% of the 
patients.601
In 2008, FGF8, a critical ligand for FGFR1 for fate specifica­
tion of GnRH neurons, was identified through human genetics 
and murine models of CHH. Rare mutations with minor allele fre­
quencies (MAFs) of less than 1% in FGF8 (OMIM 600483) were 
described in patients with CHH with variable penetrance.603,604 
CHH-associated phenotypes similar to those seen in patients with
