mutations in FGFR1 were described in patients harboring FGF8 
mutations.
To expand the FGFR1/FGF8 pathway, genes within the tightly 
controlled “FGF8 synexpression group” (genes showing similar 
spatiotemporal expression patterns and developmental regula­
tion as FGF8) were screened in patients with CHH.580 Mutations 
in five genes within this group were identified in patients with 
CHH: FGF17 (fibroblast growth factor 17; OMIM 603725), 
IL17RD (interleukin 17 receptor D; OMIM 606807), DUSP6 
(dual-specificity phosphatase 6; OMIM 602748), SPRY4 (sprouty 
homolog 4 [Drosophila]; OMIM 607984), and FLRT3 (fibronec­
tin leucine-rich transmembrane protein 3; OMIM 604808). Het­
erozygous mutations in these genes combined with mutations in 
other genes within the FGF pathway (FGFR1, FGF8, ANOS1, 
and HS6ST1) were present in 23% of the patients with CHH.580 
Mutations were primarily found in patients with KS, consistent 
with the role of FGF8 signaling in olfactory placode development 
and GnRH neuron fate specification.603,605 Oligogenic inheri­
tance was observed, as well as reduced penetrance and variable 
expressivity.580 
FGFR1/FGF21/KLB Signaling Pathway. Recently, hetero­
zygous mutations in KLB (β-Klotho) have been described in 
patients with CHH. KLB is an obligate co-receptor with FGFR1 
for FGF21 (fibroblast growth factor 21; OMIM 609436) and 
is expressed during the postnatal period in the hypothalamus. 
Although no mutations were found for FGF21, 4% of patients 
with CHH were found to harbor mutations in KLB, with the 
majority of these patients exhibiting a variety of metabolic defects, 
including obesity, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia.597 These 
results, combined with additional murine studies, suggest that the 
FGFR1/FGF21/KLB pathway may be a link between reproduc­
tion and metabolism. Mutations in KLB exhibited incomplete 
penetrance, variable expressivity, and oligogenic involvement; 
however, autosomal-dominant inheritance was the primary mode 
of transmission.597 
CHD7 (Chromodomain Helicase DNA Binding Protein 7). 
CHD7 (OMIM 608892) encodes an important chromatin mod­
ulator and transcription regulation in stem cells of the olfactory 
placode and neural crest.606–608 Heterozygous CHD7 mutations 
occur with a prevalence of approximately 6% in patients with 
CHH.541,543,544,609–611 Mutations in CHD7 are found in both 
KS and normosmic CHH.541,543,544,609–611 Notably, CHD7 is the 
primary gene underlying CHARGE syndrome—a developmental 
disorder exhibiting both clinical and genetic overlaps with CHH. 
CHD7 mutations occur in approximately 60% of patients with 
CHARGE syndrome and are primarily de novo and protein-trun­
cating variants (i.e., frameshift or nonsense).612 In contrast, CHD7 
mutations in patients with CHH are primarily inherited missense 
mutations.543,544,609,611 A recent work investigated CHARGE-
associated features in a cohort of patients with CHH harboring 
pathogenic CHD7 mutations. Indeed, careful evaluation of these 
patients allowed the reclassification of three out of five patients as 
having CHARGE or atypical CHARGE syndrome.543 
PROK2 (Prokineticin 2) and PROKR2 (Prokineticin 
Receptor 2). PROKR2 (OMIM 607123) and PROK2 (OMIM 
607002) encode prokineticin receptor 2 and its cognate ligand 
prokineticin 2. PROK2 functions as a chemoattractant during 
GnRH neuron migration and is involved in GnRH secretion.613 
Combined, mutations in PROK2 and PROKR2 are present in 4% 
to 7% of patients with CHH528,586 and can be found in hetero­
zygous, compound heterozygous, or homozygous states.528,614,615 
More often, patients harbor heterozygous PROKR2 mutations, 
and a dominant negative effect of some of these mutations has 
been demonstrated.616,617 Incomplete penetrance and/or oligoge­
nicity is possible, given that even dominant negative effects do 
not fully account for the CHH phenotypes.615,617,618 Originally 
described only in patients with KS,619 subsequent studies have 
reported mutations in patients with normosmic CHH as well.620 
Associated phenotypes in patients with CHH harboring muta­
tions in these two genes include sensorineural hearing loss, scolio­
sis, and sleep disorders.517,619 
SOX10 (Sry [Sex-Determining Region Y]-Box 10). Heterozy­
gous mutations in SOX10 (OMIM 602229) were first described 
in Waardenburg syndrome type 4c, which is characterized by 
deafness, pigmentary abnormalities, and Hirschsprung disease.621 
SOX10 is a member of the SOX transcription factor family and 
is involved in an array of multiorgan developmental processes. 
Notably, anosmia with absent olfactory bulbs is usually present in 
patients with Waardenburg syndrome. This led to the discovery of 
heterozygous SOX10 mutations in 3% of patients with only KS.622 
Notably, in patients with KS with hearing loss, the prevalence of 
SOX10 mutations rises to 30%.622,623 Additionally, other clinical 
features may exist in patients with KS with mutations in SOX10 
that overlap with Waardenburg syndrome, specifically pigmen­
tary abnormalities (i.e., abnormal iris pigmentation and isolated 
patches of white hair).539,622,623 Reduced penetrance, oligogenic­
ity, and variable expressivity have been observed.473,539,622–625 
SEMA3A (Semaphorin 3a) and PLXNA1 (Plexin A1). A 
murine knockout model for SEMA3A (semaphorin 3A) showed 
significant defects in both olfactory bulb development and GnRH 
neuron migration626—features strikingly similar to KS in humans. 
Shortly thereafter, mutations of SEMA3A in 6% of patients with 
KS were reported, consistent with the murine model.627,628 Class 
3 semaphorins often signal through interactions with the group of 
transmembrane receptors called plexins (and specifically through 
plexin A1). Further, a mouse knockout for PLXNA1 also exhib­
ited a developmental phenotype similar to KS in humans.629 
Thus, it is not surprising that heterozygous missense mutations 
in PLXNA1 (OMIM 601055) were identified in 6% of KS pro­
bands.629 Mutations in either SEMA3A or PLXNA1 were also 
found to be involved in oligogenic inheritance. Additionally, a 
report of heterozygous mutations in SEMA3E (semaphorin 3E; 
OMIM 608166), a gene involved in GnRH neuron development, 
has been reported in two brothers with KS.630 However, confir­
mation of mutations in SEMA3E in a larger cohort of patients 
with CHH or KS has not yet been performed. Taken together, the 
biology of the semaphorin pathway combined with the reports of 
mutations in patients with KS strongly supports the importance 
of this family of genes in the pathophysiology of CHH. 
GNRH1 (Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone 1) and GNRHR 
(Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone Receptor). Homozygous and 
compound heterozygous mutations in GNRHR (OMIM 138850) 
were first reported over 30 years ago in patients with normosmic 
CHH.503,631,632 It was over a decade later before autosomal-recessive 
mutations in GNRH1 (OMIM 152760) were discovered,633,634 as 
a result of the relative rarity of patients harboring mutations in this 
gene. Combined, mutations in GNRHR and GNRH1 are present 
in approximately 3% to 5% of patients with CHH,586,635 and they 
are found exclusively in patients with normosmic CHH. Muta­
tions in GNRH1 and GNRHR are inherited almost exclusively in 
an autosomal-recessive mode and are highly penetrant.583,635 How­
ever, infrequent instances of oligogenic coupling with mutations in 
other CHH genes (primarily FGFR1) have been reported.473,580,593 
Typically, patients harboring mutations in these two genes do not 
1058
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
present with CHH-associated phenotypes. Mutations in GNRHR 
have been associated with the fertile eunuch variant of CHH. A 
homozygous p.Gln106Arg mutation in the first extracellular loop 
of the GnRH receptor at gene map locus 4q21.2 was associated 
with normal TV (17 mL) but with apulsatile, low gonadotropin val­
ues and low T levels in one subject.636 After stimulation with hCG 
alone, he developed adequate spermatogenesis to father a child, and 
after cessation of hCG treatment, he demonstrated adult T values 
and pulsatile gonadotropin secretion, an example of the reversibility 
of the syndrome. 
TAC3 (Tachykinin 3) and TACR3 (Tachykinin Receptor 3) and 
KISS1 (Kisspeptin 1) and KISS1R (Kisspeptin 1 Receptor). TAC3 
(OMIM 162330) and TACR3 (OMIM 162332) encode neu­
rokinin B and its receptor, respectively, whereas KISS1 (OMIM 
603286) and KISS1R (OMIM 604161) encode kisspeptin and 
kisspeptin receptor, respectively. Both neurokinin B and kiss­
peptin are expressed in a distinct subset of hypothalamic neurons 
called KNDy neurons (kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin 
neurons).637 KNDy neurons are upstream of GnRH neurons and 
activate and regulate the activity of GnRH neurons.637 Biallelic 
mutations in KISS1R were reported in 2003579,638 in patients with 
CHH, opening the field of exploration of the kisspeptin pathway 
in the pathogenesis of CHH. Subsequently, mutations in KISS1 
were also discovered in patients with CHH,639 confirming the 
role of this pathway in GnRH neuron regulation. Using single-
nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays in combination with 
homozygosity mapping in consanguineous families, homozygous 
mutations TAC3 and TACR3 were identified in patients with 
CHH without associated phenotypes.640 Combined mutations 
in these two receptor-ligand pairs account for approximately 2% 
to 4% of patients with CHH.579,635,641–643 Autosomal-recessive 
mutations in these genes are highly penetrant, and oligogenicity 
is seldom seen. 
NR0B1 (Nuclear Receptor Subfamily 0 Group B Member 
1)—X-Linked Congenital Adrenal Hypoplasia. A rare deletion 
or mutation in the dosage-sensitive sex reversal-A (DSS) adrenal 
hypoplasia congenital gene on the X chromosome gene 1 (NR0B1; 
formerly called DAX1; gene map locus Xp21.3-p21.2) leads to 
an X-linked recessive disorder of adrenocortical organogenesis.644 
The gene encodes an orphan receptor, a member of the nuclear 
receptor superfamily that is a putative transcriptional repressor 
mapping to the Xp21 locus. NR0B1 has an SF1 response ele­
ment in the 5′-promoter region that is another orphan member 
of the nuclear hormone receptor superfamily. The NR0B1 gene 
is expressed in the adrenal cortex, in the testes (and weakly in the 
ovary), and in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Rare mutations of 
NR0B1 are characterized by severe glucocorticoid deficiency, min­
eralocorticoid deficiency, and, at puberty, androgen deficiency.645 
The severe primary adrenal insufficiency with hyponatremia, 
hyperkalemia, acidosis, and hypoglycemia is characterized by fail­
ure to thrive, vomiting, poor feeding, dehydration, circulatory 
collapse, and increased pigmentation and is lethal if not treated 
early in life in affected boys. Adrenal insufficiency includes defi­
cient secretion of the ZR steroids, DHEA and DHEAS. The testes 
are undescended in less than one-half of affected males. Micrope­
nis is rare, but urogenital abnormalities and hearing loss occasion­
ally are present. Boys who do not present with clinical evidence of 
adrenal insufficiency in infancy often have a more insidious-onset 
course of the disease. Most commonly, signs of sexual matura­
tion at the age of puberty (e.g., pubic and axillary hair, testicular 
enlargement) are lacking, and the concentrations of serum FSH, 
LH, and T are low. The spectrum of the reproductive phenotype 
is larger than initially thought. Indeed, there is evidence of mul­
tilevel defects, including GnRH deficiency, an abnormality in the 
gonadotrophs, and even primary testicular defects.646 In some 
affected boys, the GnRH pulse generator and pituitary gonado­
tropin apparatus are intact and functional in infancy and early 
childhood, and the GnRH-gonadotroph defects do not manifest 
until later in childhood or during the peripubertal period. Azo­
ospermia unresponsive to gonadotropin treatment was detected in 
a few affected men.647 Delayed puberty is a manifestation in some 
female carriers of an NR0B1 mutation.647
A familial case including two affected boys with a hemizygous 
NR0B1 nonsense mutation and neonatal onset of adrenal insuffi­
ciency also involved a maternal aunt who was homozygous for the 
mutation and had HH (primary amenorrhea).648 This case high­
lights the complexities of the genotype-phenotype correlations, 
taking into account that the affected maternal aunt maintained 
normal adrenal function after decades of follow-up, and a mater­
nal grandfather who carried the same mutation was asymptomatic. 
PCSK1 (Prohormone Convertase 1 Gene). Biallelic mutations 
in the prohormone convertase 1 gene (PCSK1; also called PC1) 
lead to extreme childhood obesity, hypocortisolemia, defects in 
conversion of proinsulin to insulin leading to hypoglycemia, and 
isolated partial HH, allowing spontaneous pubertal development 
but primary amenorrhea in affected females.649 The HH prob­
ably results from impaired processing of GnRH or neuropeptides 
involved in its secretion. Findings in another subject extended the 
phenotypic spectrum to include a complex enteropathy with small 
intestinal dysfunction leading to malabsorption of monosaccha­
rides and fats.650 
Mutations in the Genes Encoding Gonadotropins. Isolated 
FSH or LH deficiency resulting from mutations in the genes for 
the β-subunit of FSH or LH are two extremely rare autosomal-
recessive disorders, with a dozen cases reported to date. Homozy­
gous or compound heterozygous mutations in the FSH β-subunit 
were first reported in females with delayed puberty and primary 
amenorrhea but normal adrenarche.651,652 The LH concentration 
was elevated, the serum level of E2 was low, and immunoactive 
FSH was absent. Affected women had antral follicles but no pro­
gression, demonstrating that FSH action is not necessary for fol­
licle development up to the antral stage. The phenotype in affected 
men depends on the severity of the mutation. The first reported 
case in a man was linked to a homozygous frameshift deletion 
of the second and third nucleotides (thymidine and guanine) in 
codon 61 of the gene encoding the β-subunit of FSH.653 The 
affected 18-year-old proband had azoospermia; small, soft testes 
(1–2 mL); and incomplete puberty (pubic hair Tanner stage 4). 
Biochemical profile included undetectable FSH and low INHB 
and T levels, accompanied by elevated LH. A similar constellation 
was observed in a subsequent case report of a male patient harbor­
ing a homozygous nonsense mutation.654 Selective deficiency of 
the β-subunit of LH is also extremely rare, with 10 male and 3 
female cases described to date.655 Affected men exhibit incomplete 
puberty, infertility, and disturbances of hormonal profile (low LH 
and T levels, high FSH). Spermatogenesis can be induced by hCG 
monotherapy. In women, the main clinical symptom is oligomen­
orrhea after a previously spontaneous menarche. 
Oligogenicity in CHH. Historically, CHH was originally 
thought to be a monogenic disorder; however, reports of patients 
with more than one mutation in known CHH genes challenged 
this concept.593,619 This is consistent with reduced penetrance 
and variable expressivity within and between families harboring 
identical mutations in the known CHH genes. The concept of 
1059
CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
oligogenic inheritance (a synergistic effect between mutations in 
two or more genes) was first reported for retinitis pigmentosa in 
the mid-1990s656 and Bardet-Biedl syndrome.657 The first system­
atic evaluation of oligogenicity in patients with CHH by screening 
eight genes was conducted in 2010 and identified oligogenicity 
in 2.5% of patients with CHH.586 Subsequent studies evaluating 
larger sets of CHH-related genes demonstrated even larger degrees 
of oligogenicity ranging from 7% (17 genes screened)580 to 15% 
(25 genes screened).473
It is often difficult to assess the combined effect of two mutants 
on a single patient; however, Falardeau et al603 reported a family 
with a male CHH proband and his father with CDGP. Genetic 
testing revealed digenic mutations in FGFR1 (p.R250Q) and 
FGF8 (p.K71E, de novo) in the proband, whereas only the 
FGFR1 mutation was detected in the father.603 The functional 
assay investigating the downstream mitogen-activated protein 
kinase (MAPK) FGFR1 signaling showed a synergistic effect 
of the combination of these two mutations, consistent with the 
clinical picture of this family.603 Further, the double-heterozygous 
mice (FGFR1± × FGF8±) showed a significantly larger reduction 
in the total number of GnRH neurons compared to single-hetero­
zygous FGFR1± or FGF8± mice.658 Altogether, these data suggest 
that the oligogenic mode of inheritance plays an important part 
in CHH and can partially explain the observed variable expressiv­
ity and incomplete penetrance. It is important to note, however, 
that the exact functional mechanisms or biology underlying most 
of the oligogenic mutations reported in patients473,580,619 has not 
been elucidated, despite the statistical enrichment of oligogenicity 
in the CHH population.473 
Molecular Testing and Counseling. Genetic counseling is use­
ful to inform patients about the underlying genetics of CHH and 
to counsel patients who want fertility treatment on the recurrent 
disease risk in their offspring. A detailed family history, includ­
ing questions about pubertal development, infertility, and CHH-
associated phenotypes (e.g., anosmia, cleft lip/palate, missing 
teeth, digit defects) should be performed. Approximately 30% 
of CHH probands have family members exhibiting CHH that 
extend beyond first-degree relatives. Further, isolated anosmia or 
delayed puberty within family members can be considered famil­
ial cases.514,516,659 Given the complex nature of CHH genetics, 
including oligogenic inheritance and a lack of definitive clinical 
signatures to aid in gene selection, it is valuable to minimize cost 
and maximize diagnostic yield for both diagnostic testing and 
genetic counseling. Testing for a CHH gene panel or WES is cur­
rently an accepted method and results in a 30% to 50% diagnostic 
yield.583 Notably, whole genome sequencing (WGS) is a promis­
ing technology because it allows the detection of exonic muta­
tions missed by WES, intronic or regulatory regions, and genomic 
insertions/deletions.660,661 This is a critical benefit because mul­
tiple micro-, partial-, and full-gene deletions have been reported 
in the known CHH genes.627,638,662–669
With the relative ease and low cost of identifying variants in 
CHH genes using high-throughput sequencing, the major chal­
lenge to date is the evaluation of pathogenicity for these variants. 
Variants in highly penetrant CHH genes inherited in an X-linked 
manner (ANOS1) or those primarily inherited in an autosomal-
recessive mode (GNRHR/GNRH1, TAC3/TACR3, KISS1/KISS1R) 
are evidently pathogenic. Importantly, in instances of homozy­
gous mutations in families with no evidence of consanguineous 
relations, the testing of parental DNA is critical. In the absence 
of parental DNA, deletions of one allele resulting in the appear­
ance of homozygosity cannot be ruled out by Sanger sequencing 
and therefore must be followed up with additional testing, such 
as comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) array,583,627,670,671 
multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA), or 
fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), for clarification and 
accurate genetic counseling. However, most CHH-associated vari­
ants in these genes are heterozygous, missense, and often inherited 
from asymptomatic parents.
Recently, novel standards and guidelines for evaluating DNA 
variants have been developed by the American College of Medi­
cal Genetics (ACMG),672 and these are especially useful in the 
clinical practice. The pathogenicity is determined based on 
28 criteria, which integrate data from population studies, com­
putational and predictive algorithms, functional assays, segrega­
tion analysis, and others. Of special note, the presence of de 
novo mutations and the segregation of inherited variants are 
particularly informative to both pathogenic determination and 
genetic counseling. Therefore, collection of DNA samples from 
parents and other family members is especially critical in CHH, 
even when the case appears to be sporadic. This is especially 
important in CHH because de novo mutations in CHH genes 
have been reported.473,522,541,583,623,673,674
In summary, the genetics of CHH is complex, given the large 
number of loci discovered to date, with each accounting for only a 
small proportion of patients. Further, variable expressivity, reduced 
penetrance (observed both within and across families, even those 
carrying the same mutation), and oligogenic inheritance further 
complicate the genetic counseling of individual patients. There­
fore, it is advisable to (1) employ high-throughput sequencing 
(i.e., targeted panels, or preferably whole-exome or whole-genome 
sequencing) to increase diagnostic yield, (2) collect detailed clini­
cal information on both reproductive and associated phenotypes 
in the extended family, and (3) test the proband, parents, and fam­
ily members to aid in the proper ACMG classification of detected 
variants. 
Clinical and Genetic Overlap in CHH-Associated Syn­
dromes. Progress in discovering genetic causes of disease has 
identified genetic overlaps of syndromes, and this is true for 
CHH. Several associated phenotypes have been described in 
CHH, including anosmia, defining KS. In the case of KS, the 
additional association of SHFM was found to considerably 
increase the odds of carrying an FGFR1 mutation.601 Interest­
ingly, Hartsfield syndrome has holoprosencephaly and SHFM as 
the major phenotypes, but it can often include cleft palate and 
olfactory bulb agenesis.675 Several reports identified mutations 
in FGFR1 in patients with Hartsfield syndrome.675,676 Thus, 
Hartsfield syndrome has a significant clinical overlap with KS 
that can be in a large part due to the genetic overlap. Similarly, 
reports show significant clinical and genetic overlap between KS 
and Waardenburg syndrome, with mutations in SOX10 being 
present in both disorders.622,677,678 
Treatment of CDGP and CHH
CDGP
Most of the available data on management of CDGP and CHH 
are derived from studies in men. Indeed, CDGP and CHH are 
much less common in females than males (1:4 ratio). The options 
for management of delayed puberty include expectant observation 
or HRT to induce puberty (Tables 23.5 and 23.6). The choice of 
treatment depends on both clinical judgment and the patient’s 
request. Indeed, reassurance and continued observation to ensure 
that the expected sexual maturation occurs are sufficient most of 
1060 SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
the time. However, the stigma of appearing less mature than one’s 
peers can cause psychologic stress. Some adolescents feel such 
intense social pressure and low self-esteem that only the appear­
ance of signs of puberty can reassure them and enable them to par­
ticipate in sports and social activities. Growth retardation appears 
responsible for most of the distress more often than the delay in 
pubertal development itself.
When CHH is highly suspected, such as in patients with a fam­
ily history of CHH or patients who present with CHH-associated 
phenotypes (see Fig. 23.38), pubertal induction treatment should

be started immediately. In patients without suggestive signs or 
with a family history of CDGP, low-dose hormonal treatment can 
be started for boys age 14 years or older who show no signs of 
puberty and exhibit psychosocial distress linked to the pubertal 
and/or growth delay. The most frequently used regimen for puber­
tal induction in boys is intramuscular injections of T enanthate 
50 mg per month for 3 to 6 months. A higher initial dose of 100 
mg is not advisable because it can lead to priapism in treatment-
included boys. The dose is then progressively increased by 50-mg 
increments for another 3 to 6 months if endogenous puberty has 
not advanced.3 Oral T undecanoate was found to be an alter­
native for successful pubertal induction in a large study of boys 
with CDGP, with apparently no ill effects.464 Low-dose HRT 
induces virilization and decreases psychosocial distress without 
impairing the final height.3,464 Although considered safe from a 
cardiovascular point of view, low-dose T enanthate can slightly 
raise apolipoprotein B while decreasing HDL cholesterol. Close 
follow-up is important because testicular maturation (manifested 
by an increase in TV) may occur despite exogenous T treatment, 
pointing to endogenous activation of the HPG axis consistent 
with CDGP. HRT is typically interrupted after 1 to 2 years of 
treatment to reassess the HPG axis. Rising serum T and normal 
gonadotropin levels are suggestive of CDGP and do not require 
further treatment. The combination of E2 and progestins is the 
most commonly used treatment to induce puberty in girls with 
CDGP (or CHH).679–682 Similar to boys, treatment is withdrawn 
after 1 to 2 years to evaluate whether spontaneous puberty has 
recuperated.
Most cases of CDGP are considered “cured” once puberty is 
robustly initiated. However, this practice of discharging patients 
with CDGP before the completion of puberty (TV >12 mL) raises 
the question of whether or not these patients actually do achieve 
optimal reproductive status in early adulthood. Some cases of 
partial CHH can be missed by such an approach. Additionally, 
the long-term health consequences of CDGP have not been fully 
assessed. A few studies have shown that patients with CDGP 
have an increased risk of osteopenia/osteoporosis.386,683,684 Thus, 
the notion that CDGP is a “normal variant” of puberty is under 
question. 
CHH
When puberty remains absent by age 16 (TV <4 mL in boys, 
absent breast development in girls) or stalled pubertal develop­
ment persists by age 18, CHH is diagnosed (see Fig. 23.38). In 
this case, or even in younger patients with a high likelihood of 
a CHH diagnosis (history of cryptorchidism/micropenis, posi­
tive familial history, CHH-associated phenotypes), a full pubertal 
induction over 2 to 3 years is indicated. The choice of HRT for 
patients with CHH depends on the age, the therapeutic goal, the 
timing of treatment, and the personal preference of each patient. 
It is important to note that there are no universally accepted 
treatment regimens used internationally,3,685 and data are mostly 
driven by expert recommendations.81
Available treatments for both sexes include sex steroid replace­
ment (T in boys, estrogen-progestin in girls), gonadotropin injec­
tions (twice or three times a week), or pulsatile GnRH therapy. 
The latter is administered via a subcutaneous portable pump to 
administer episodic GnRH over prolonged periods. LH and FSH 
release is elicited, which in turn stimulates the gonads to produce 
T or estrogen in patients with CHH or other hypogonadism of 
hypothalamic origin. Pulsatile GnRH therapy can induce puberty 
and promote the development of secondary sexual characteristics 
and spermatogenesis in men and ovulation in women.686 A lower 
frequency of GnRH administration favors FSH secretion, whereas 
a faster frequency favors LH secretion and has been associated with 
a PCOS-like phenotype. Available gonadotropin preparations are 
either extracted from the urine of postmenopausal women, such 
as human menopausal gonadotropin (hMG) and hCG, or are 
recombinant human pituitary LH (rLH) and FSH (rFSH). Given 
that both pulsatile GnRH and gonadotropin therapies are cum­
bersome and expensive, sex steroid replacement therapy is cur­
rently the treatment of choice for most cases of HH until fertility 
is desired.
This chapter will summarize therapeutic management in child­
hood and adolescence but will not extend the discussion to fertil­
ity management in adult patients with CHH.
Treatment of Male Infants With Presumed or Suspected 
CHH. To date, hormonal therapy in neonates with suspected 
CHH has only been applied in male patients exhibiting micro­
penis/cryptorchidism and a hormonal signature of blunted mini­
puberty.505,519,520,523,525,687 The consequences of severe GnRH 
deficiency in female neonates remain unclear, and thus no treat­
ment has been investigated for this age group.
In male infants with severe GnRH deficiency, the main goals 
of hormonal treatment are to increase the penile size and stimu­
late testicular growth and/or descent in the case of cryptorchi­
dism. The latter is an important outcome because persistent 
undescended testes confer a poor prognosis for fertility and are 
a risk factor for testicular malignancy. A standard regimen for 
micropenis consists of one or two 3-month courses of testosterone 
enanthate of 25 mg per month given intramuscularly.44 The con­
cern that the penis might not respond to androgens later in life if 
exposed to T in childhood, a pattern observed in the rat, proved 
incorrect. Early initiation of T treatment was found to be effective 
in increasing penile size and stimulating scrotal development in 
boys with either CHH or combined pituitary hormone deficiency 
(CPHD), with positive psychologic outcomes.518,687 Some reports 
have demonstrated the efficacy of hCG therapy in resolving crypt­
orchidism in neonates and prepubertal boys.688,689 A concern for 
the use of high-dose hCG treatment during infancy is its poten­
tially detrimental effect on GCs, with increased apoptosis, and 
thus negative consequences for future fertility.690 However, the 
study showing the deleterious effect of hCG did not assess men 
with congenital GnRH deficiency; all examined men had normal 
T levels at adulthood.
In 2002, Main et al519 published the first report of combined 
gonadotropin therapy (subcutaneous injections of recombinant 
LH and FSH) during the first year of life in an infant with CHH 
born with micropenis. This treatment increased penile length 
(from 1.6 to 2.4 cm) and led to a 170% increase in TV, accom­
panied by an increase in INHB levels. Subsequent reports used 
recombinant gonadotropins via subcutaneous pump for 6 months 
in neonates with CHH (including one with ANOS1 mutation) 
or CPHD.505,520 The treatment corrected the micropenis in all 
patients; induced testicular growth; and allowed for adequate 
endogenous secretion of T, INHB, and AMH. More recently, 
Lambert et  al523 reported the effect of combined recombinant 
gonadotropin infusions in a series of eight male infants with 
either CHH or CPHD and cryptorchidism or high scrotal testes. 
Besides confirming previous findings on penile length and testicu­
lar growth, the authors observed complete testicular descent in 
six out of eight cases. Similarly, daily subcutaneous injection of a 
combined preparation of recombinant LH and FSH for 3 months 
resulted in testicular descent to the scrotum in 10 male neonates 
1062
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
with cryptorchidism (either intraabdominal or inguinal), micro­
penis, and absent minipuberty at hormonal testing.691 Neverthe­
less, 2 out of 10 patients had to undergo orchidopexy—surgical 
fixation of the testes to the scrotum—as a result of recurrent ingui­
nal testicular ascent after withdrawal of hormonal therapy.
Taken together, these data suggest that combined gonado­
tropin therapy in male patients with CHH during the neonatal 
period can have a beneficial effect on both testicular endocrine 
function and genital development, although further studies are 
needed before clinical application. This treatment may be supe­
rior to androgen therapy because it stimulates SC proliferation, 
as evidenced by the marked increase in TV and serum INHB 
concentrations.525 It is possible that the normalization of penis 
size in the neonate will lead to a normal adult penis size during 
subsequent pubertal virilization with exogenous T or hCG, thus 
alleviating the psychologic burden often reported by males with 
CHH with micropenis.692 In parallel, the increase in testicular size 
could lead to better outcomes in terms of sperm output during 
fertility induction in adolescence or adulthood.525 However, the 
effect of combined gonadotropin treatment on cryptorchidism in 
infants with CHH has not been formally assessed by randomized 
controlled trials. Further, longitudinal studies are warranted to 
determine the long-term effect of this treatment on reproductive 
function. 
Pubertal Induction. In females (see Table 23.5), the thera­
peutic objectives of pubertal induction in female teenage or adult 
women include the following:
	1.	 To induce female sexual characteristics (breast development 
and external genitalia)35,693,694
	2.	 To ensure the maturity of the uterus for future pregnancy35,532
	3.	 To promote psychosexual development with respect to emo­
tional life and sexuality
	4.	 To induce a growth spurt for an optimal adult height and to 
reach a normal BMD for age35,680,685,695
There is no consensus regarding the optimal age to start puber­
tal induction.679,681 The opinions of the patients and their par­
ents need to be taken into account. Hormone therapy needs to 
be initiated when the delayed puberty is evident (delay of breast 
development greater than 2 SD) or when the CHH diagnosis 
is established or highly suspected (see earlier discussion). Most 
therapeutic regimens inducing feminization in CHH arise from 
expert opinions,35,682,685,693,696 partly because of the rarity of the 
disease and the paucity of randomized trials.679–681,693,697 In prac­
tice, regimens have often mirrored treatment of young adolescents 
with absent puberty and TS treatment,680,698–704 CPHD,705–709 
or primary ovarian failure.710,711 It is important to integrate the 
patient’s opinion in the choice of treatment while ensuring a 
favorable risk-benefit balance.
E2 therapy (oral or transdermal) is the cornerstone to induce 
feminization, but the proposed protocols in the literature vary 
widely.679,681 Currently, 17β-estradiol is preferred over ethinylestra­
diol or conjugated equine estrogen because of its better safety pro­
file. Typically, low doses of oral 17β-estradiol (i.e., 0.1 mg daily) or 
transdermal E2 (typically 0.05–0.07 μg/kg nocturnally) are started 
to treat young adolescents of 12 to 13 years of age to mimic the 
early stages of pubertal development and induce progressive femi­
nization without causing a premature epiphyseal closure.682,693,712 
A higher dose (0.08–0.12 μg/kg) is used when breast development 
is a priority, such as in older girls with CHH.680,685,713 Although 
there is interindividual variation in absorption, similar plasma 
E2 levels are achieved using 2 mg of daily oral 17β-estradiol, 2 
mg of a daily estrogen gel, and 100 mg of an estrogen patch.685 
Transdermal estrogen is associated with a better safety profile and 
reduced cardiovascular events in adult women680 because it avoids 
the first-pass hepatic effect and subsequent production of clot­
ting factors. In addition, transdermal E2 resulted in higher E2 
levels and more effective feminization compared to oral conju­
gated equine estrogen in a small randomized trial on hypogonadal 
girls with ovarian failure.697 Yet, the majority of girls with delayed 
puberty are treated with oral estrogens.680,681,714 The E2 dosage 
is then increased gradually over 12 to 24 months until sufficient 
breast development (Tanner stage 4) or until breakthrough bleed­
ing occurs.693 Subsequently, cyclic progestogen (for 10–14 days) is 
added to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and enhance artificially 
induced menses along with E2. In selected adolescents with partial 
CHH (breast development Tanner stage 3 or higher at diagno­
sis), combined estroprogestin therapy can be used directly with­
out compromising breast development. In the majority of females 
with CHH, estroprogestin therapy is effective in inducing harmo­
nious development of the breasts and genitals, contributing to a 
more satisfactory emotional and sexual life.491 Estrogen treatment 
also increases uterine size,501 and estroprogestin therapy induces 
monthly withdrawal bleeding. Finally, estrogen therapy induces a 
growth spurt and increases BMD in the majority of female ado­
lescent and older women with CHH.715 Estroprogestin replace­
ment does not restore ovulation. The pulsatile GnRH therapy (via 
a subcutaneous pump) that is used in adults to induce ovulation 
and fertility in adult women with CHH is also efficient to induce 
puberty in adolescent girls with CHH.716 This treatment, as well 
as combined gonadotropin therapy, can induce ovulation.170,717 
Both therapies are costly and intensive; therefore, they are reserved 
for women seeking fertility.718,719 After 1 to 2 years of treatment, 
we propose to discontinue HRT to assess endogenous HPG func­
tion by the appearance of spontaneous menstrual cycles (diagnosis 
of CDGP). In the absence of activity of the HPG, the diagnosis 
of CHH will be established, and HRT should be continued until 
the age of natural menopause. Case reports of CHH reversal in 
females have been described,720 and thus, as for males,35 we pro­
pose serial treatment withdrawal (every 2 years) to assess for CHH 
reversal. As part of therapeutic education, the patients and parents 
need to be informed that there is no evidence that long-term HRT 
in CHH induces breast cancer,708 especially with the use of more 
physiologic estrogens (17β-estradiol) and progestins (micronized 
progesterone, dydrogesterone).
In males (see Table 23.6), the therapeutic goals of pubertal 
induction in adolescent boys (and adult men) with CHH are also 
well defined:
	1.	 To induce virilization and normal sexual function
	2.	 To reach optimal adult height (adolescents) and promote the 
acquisition of normal bone mass and male-type body composi­
tion
	3.	 To address concerns about future reproductive capacity
	4.	 To achieve normal psychosocial development
	5.	 To promote future fertility
However, available treatment regimens may not always cover 
all of these aspects. As with girls with CHH, there is a paucity of 
literature, and only one randomized study to date has included 
several patients with CHH.721
Pubertal Induction by Exogenous Testosterone. Early treat­
ment is crucial and usually involves an injectable T ester, such 
as Tenanthate.494,685,722 Younger patients (from 12 years of age) 
typically are started on low-dose T (e.g., 50 mg of testosterone 
enanthate monthly), with a gradual increase to the full adult dose 
(250 mg every 2–4 weeks) over the course of approximately 24 
1063
CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
months to mimic physiologic puberty. For patients diagnosed in 
later adolescence or early adulthood, a higher dose of T can be 
implemented to induce virilization more rapidly (e.g., initial doses 
of 100 mg testosterone enanthate monthly with a faster pace of 
titration to adult dose). Such regimens induce secondary sexual 
characteristics while maximizing final height.464,685 Side effects 
of exogenous T treatment include erythrocytosis, premature clo­
sure of the epiphysis (if doses are too high during the first year 
of treatment), and occasional pain at the injection site. Notably, 
this therapeutic option does not stimulate testicular growth or 
spermatogenesis494,722 because very high levels of intratesticular 
T (approximately 1000-fold higher than the systemic concen­
trations) are needed to stimulate spermatogenesis. Increased tes­
ticular growth during T treatment is highly suggestive of CHH 
reversal.512
Besides testosterone enanthate, other intramuscular T esters 
are either short acting (testosterone propionate or cypionate, adult 
dose of 200–250 mg every 2–4 weeks) or long acting (testoster­
one undecanoate, 750–1000 mg every 2–5 months).723 Dermal 
preparations of T are not approved for adolescents in all coun­
tries. They consist of T patches to apply on nonsexual skin or T 
gels rubbed onto the shoulders, abdomen, or hips. The former 
(patches) may initially be given at night to re-create the diurnal 
variation of T in early puberty. A push of 10 mg of 2% T gel given 
for 6 months achieved similar effects to 50 mg monthly injec­
tions of intramuscular T in terms of height velocity.724 Another 
T gel preparation (1%) given daily to adolescents with primary 
hypogonadism raised their serum T levels to the pubertal range 
over a 6-month period of treatment.725 Nevertheless, biweekly or 
monthly injections may allow better compliance in an adolescent 
population. Additionally, contact with the skin, clothing, or tow­
els used by an adolescent treated with a T gel can cause virilization 
in young children or women.726 
Pubertal Induction and Testicular Maturation With 
Gonadotropins. Gonadotropins are used for fertility treatments 
in adult patients with CHH, but they can also be used to induce 
pubertal maturation in adolescent males with CHH. An advan­
tage of gonadotropin treatment compared to T treatment is the 
stimulation of testicular growth and spermatogenesis. Therefore, 
gonadotropin treatment may offer psychological reassurance in 
adolescents and enhance self-confidence.
Varying treatment protocols, including hCG alone or in com­
bination with FSH, have been reported.727–731 In a retrospective 
analysis of boys with CHH, Bistrizer et al727 showed a similar vir­
ilizing effect of monthly T injections and weekly hCG injections 
(5000 IU/week), but testicular growth was larger in the latter. In 
another study, a large group of adolescents with delayed puberty 
received low-dose hCG (250–500 IU twice weekly) with increas­
ing increments of 250 to 500 IU every 6 months, and rFSH was 
added once serum T moderately increased (mean level of 5.2 
nmol/L). This treatment substantially increased TV (bi-testicular 
volume: 5 ± 5 to 34 ± 3 mL) and induced spermatogenesis in 91% 
of patients.731 However, this study did not exclusively include 
patients with CHH, and the favorable outcome could in part be 
associated with a natural history of self-resolving CDGP.
Several expert groups advocate the advantage of recombinant 
FSH pretreatment alone before combined gonadotropin therapy 
for adolescent boys with CHH with severe GnRH deficiency 
(complete CHH). The crucial role of FSH in spermatogenesis 
is illustrated by the phenotype of men with biallelic inactivating 
FSHR mutations who invariably exhibit small testes and sper­
matogenesis failure.732 The rationale behind this FSH priming is 
that the mass of SCs is a strong predictor of future sperm output. 
FSH induces proliferation of immature SCs before seminifer­
ous tubule maturation by intratesticular androgens in rats733 and 
probably also in humans during minipuberty in a period in which 
the seminiferous tubules do not yet express the androgen recep­
tor.734 The rise of TV during normal minipuberty is due to the 
FSH-induced increase in the immature SC mass. Patients with 
CHH with absent puberty ± micropenis and cryptorchidism likely 
have a suboptimal SC pool as a result of a lack of minipuberty, 
as evidenced by low serum INHB levels, and could thus benefit 
from pretreatment with FSH without concomitant hCG-induced 
androgen elevation. A study of 14 gonadotropin-deficient boys 
treated with rFSH priming showed significant increases in INHB 
and TV without any change in intragonadal T production, thus 
consistent with SC proliferation.735 Following addition of hCG, 
spermatogenesis was achieved in six out of seven boys who pro­
vided semen samples (median sperm count of 8.5 million/mL).735 
In 2013, a randomized study explored the addition of recombi­
nant FSH pretreatment before GnRH pulsatile therapy in young 
adult men with CHH with severe GnRH deficiency (TV <4 mL) 
and no prior gonadotropin therapy.736 Patients with cryptorchi­
dism were excluded. After 4 months of FSH alone, serum INHB 
levels achieved the normal range in all subjects, and the TV dou­
bled in the absence of increased intratesticular T. The benefit of 
this approach was supported by histologic findings of an FSH-
induced increase in the diameter of the seminiferous tubules with­
out any sign of maturation, as well as an enhanced proliferation 
of immature SC and spermatogonia.736 Following 2 years of pul­
satile GnRH, both groups (with and without rFSH pretreatment) 
had normalized serum T levels. All patients in the pretreatment 
group developed sperm in their ejaculate (versus four out of six 
in the GnRH-only group). Despite these clear benefits, gonado­
tropin treatment (with or without FSH pretreatment) is intensive 
(frequent autoinjections) and requires close follow-up. Thus, this 
approach might not be suitable for all adolescent patients with 
CHH.
In conclusion, large prospective and certainly multicenter stud­
ies are needed to compare the clinical effect of gonadotropins in 
adolescents with CHH versus standard pubertal induction with T 
in terms of clinical satisfaction (and the psychologic effect of tes­
ticular maturation), bone and metabolic effects, and an eventual 
benefit for future fertility. Additionally, the superiority of a system­
atic pretreatment with FSH for patients with absent puberty (TV 
<4 mL) before classical androgen-increasing treatment (combined 
gonadotropins or GnRH pulsatile therapy) needs to be confirmed 
in a larger study that also recruits adolescents without excluding 
cases with cryptorchidism. 
Effect of HRT on Bone Health in CHH. Low BMD is present 
in the majority of patients with CHH. Yet, important variabil­
ity exists regarding the degree of bone involvement in CHH, as 
illustrated by a recent report of older never-treated patients with 
CHH with low to near-normal BMD and no significant differ­
ence compared with patients treated by HRT.737 Bone remodeling 
is low in CHH, as suggested by the only study that performed iliac 
crest bone biopsies in patients with CHH with low bone mass.738 
Data on bone-remodeling markers are inconclusive and do not 
always correlate with BMD.739 Evidence on fracture incidence is 
scarce, with some reports of incidental vertebral fractures but no 
comparison of the prevalence against controls.739,740 Some CHH 
genes may also have direct implications for bone health. Specific 
genetic causes that may directly affect bone include mutations in 
FGF8, FGFR1, and SEMA3A.741,742
1064
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
HRT is the first-line treatment for CHH-associated bone loss, 
with antiresorptive drugs (bisphosphonates, denosumab) as sec­
ond-line therapeutic choices.743 Given the male predominance of 
CHH, the effect of gonadal steroid replacement has been princi­
pally studied in men receiving T and/or gonadotropins. Standard 
T treatment is aromatizable and corrects low estrogen levels.526 T 
replacement increases BMD in CHH738,744 and mixed hypogo­
nadal cohorts.745–748 Increased levels of bone formation markers 
such as P1NP early in the course of treatment reflect the ana­
bolic effects of androgens.393,749 It remains unclear whether T 
replacement fully reverses the bone phenotype745 or only partially 
improves BMD.744 Recently, a large cross-sectional and case-con­
trol study revealed several microarchitectural defects as assessed by 
HR-pQCT scan in men with CHH despite long-term HRT, with 
comparatively better bone outcomes in men diagnosed before 
adulthood.497 The crucial role of age at HRT initiation was also 
supported by Finkelstein et al,738 who measured bone densities by 
CT in 21 men with CHH, of whom 15 initially had fused epiphy­
ses and 6 had open epiphyses. After normalizing T levels in all 
patients, the younger group increased both cortical and trabecular 
bone densities, whereas those with initially fused epiphyses dis­
played an increase only in cortical bone density. These data imply 
that there is a critical period of skeletal response to sex steroids, 
which would further stress the importance of timely diagnosis 
of CHH. Nevertheless, substantial bone response to HRT was 
reported by another study focusing on older patients with CHH 
with late diagnosis (median age of 56 years).498 Therapeutic adher­
ence may also explain the variability observed. Highlighting the 
importance of compliance, prolonged cessations in HRT (more 
than 5 years in total) were associated with decreased BMD at all 
measured sites in a Finnish study.739
As in other causes of secondary osteoporosis, adequate calcium 
intake (>1000 mg/day) should be ensured. Vitamin D deficiency 
is prevalent in the CHH population,740 and levels > 30 μg/L (= 
75 nmol/L) should be targeted in the presence of low BMD. A 
small retrospective study suggested that central hypogonadism 
might lead to worse bone outcomes as compared to primary hypo­
gonadism, independent of gonadal steroid levels.750 The authors 
postulated that vitamin D deficiency is more prevalent in central 
hypogonadism as a result of decreased LH-dependent vitamin D 
25-hydroxylation in the testes. Nevertheless, this was not con­
firmed in a large case-control study that did not detect a differ­
ence in serum vitamin D levels between patients with CHH and 
age- and BMI-matched controls.751 
Effect of HRT on Metabolic Health in CHH. Metabolic defects 
are prevalent in patients with CHH and are thought to be second­
ary to sex steroid deficiency.571,752 The prevalence of overweight 
and obesity in patients with CHH (40%–50%) in a recent nation­
wide Italian cohort of patients502 was found to be similar to that 
in the general Italian population.753 This finding was in contrast 
to another study of 332 young patients with CHH without prior 
androgen treatment versus 395 age- and BMI-matched con­
trols.754 Indeed, men with CHH exhibited a significantly higher 
prevalence of all components of MetS (i.e., waist circumference, 
blood pressure, fasting glucose, HOMA-IR, serum triglyceride 
levels). It is possible that genetic determinants predispose certain 
patients with CHH to metabolic disturbances. Genetic leptin 
deficiency or resistance is the classic example of CHH co-occur­
rence with severe obesity.755 Recently, the FGF21/KLB/FGFR1 
pathway was also highlighted as an important player underlying 
the link between reproduction and metabolism.597 In line with 
this, the majority of CHH probands harboring loss-of-function 
KLB mutations exhibited some degree of metabolic defect (i.e., 
overweight, insulin resistance, and/or dyslipidemia).
T therapy in CHH leads to an improvement in insulin sen­
sitivity,756,757 a reduction in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein 
levels756 and LDL cholesterol,758 and favorable changes in body 
composition.757 Accordingly, short-term withdrawal of HRT in 
men with CHH causes mild insulin resistance and a trend for 
higher glucose levels.752 Similarly, gonadotropin replacement 
raises serum T levels and is also accompanied by increased lean 
mass, reduced body fat and waist-to-hip ratio, and enhanced insu­
lin sensitivity.759
Psychological Issues. The absence of sexual hormones and 
its impact on physical appearance constitutes a major source 
of psychological distress for hypogonadal males.760 Specifi­
cally, CHH can be accompanied by anxiety and depression,761 
and these symptoms are frequently underestimated by physi­
cians.762 Low self-esteem and altered body image have also 
been reported692 and can prevent adequate psychosexual devel­
opment.763 An online survey suggested a negative perception 
of women with CHH on their health status, with a tendency 
toward depression.491 This same study suggests that care provid­
ers often do not adequately address psychosocial issues and even 
have a tendency to dismiss the psychological impact of patients’ 
poor pubertal development.491 Overall, psychologic counseling 
is beneficial to deal with the impact of a chronic visit, the risk 
of infertility, and perhaps in some individuals, a less-than-ideal 
physical development compared to peers. Further problems 
occur when patients are lost to follow-up as they make the tran­
sition to adult care.692 
Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism of Other 
Etiologies
Classic Hormonal Causes
Untreated hypothyroidism usually delays the onset of puberty or 
menarche. Levothyroxine replacement reverses this pattern, but 
there is likely to be an irreversible loss of height if the diagnosis is 
delayed. Diabetes mellitus type 1 in girls is associated with delayed 
menarche, even in the presence of good glycemic control.764 Ado­
lescents with even moderately poor control frequently manifest 
some degree of growth impairment and delayed puberty or irregu­
lar menses. Cushing disease can be associated with delayed onset 
or arrest of puberty in both sexes. Clinical signs of virilization are 
an alternative finding in affected girls resulting from excess pro­
duction of adrenal androgens stimulated by the increased plasma 
ACTH levels. 
Functional Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism
FHH (frequently termed as FHA in females) is a reversible form 
of GnRH deficiency, induced by stressors such as caloric deficits, 
psychological distress, and/or excessive exercise.465,765 Delayed 
puberty in this situation is usually a result of inadequate nutrition 
and low weight or excessive energy expenditure. When weight 
returns to normal values, puberty usually occurs spontaneously, 
although full reversal will require several months.
Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea. FHA refers to FHH 
occurring in young women. It is defined as the absence of menses 
associated with low or normal plasma gonadotropin levels due to a 
decrease in GnRH pulsatile secretion (amplitude or frequency, or 
both) in the absence of an organic abnormality.465 This condition 
can occur in women with normal weight but a decreased percent­
age of body fat, mediated by subtle dysfunction of eating patterns 
1065
CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
and altered energy expenditure. The frequency of FHA is rising in 
young women, with an estimated prevalence of 3% to 5%.766 In 
adolescents, FHA can manifest as primary amenorrhea,767 further 
complicating its distinction from CHH. Overall, the impact on 
the HPG axis range from severe inhibition and hypoestrogenemia 
to a moderate defect and anovulation or even a selective shorten­
ing of the luteal phase in milder cases. A shared genetic basis of 
CHH and FHA in women has been described.768 Indeed, genes 
involved in CHH, such as GNRHR, KAL1, and PROKR2, are 
found in heterozygous patterns in women with FHA, suggesting a 
genetic susceptibility to the condition that is unmasked by various 
types of stressors, such as psychological stress, fat tissue insuffi­
ciency, or excessive physical activity. Weight regain in women with 
low-normal BMI usually restores HPG-axis function, although 
the weight needed to restart menstrual periods and the necessary 
interval vary among individuals.769
FHA associated with competitive sports in women is a specific 
subtype of FHH. The female athlete triad (Triad) refers to the 
interrelationship between energy availability, menstrual function, 
and bone density, which may manifest as eating disorders, FHA, 
and osteoporosis.770 Indeed, extensive training (10–12 hours/
week) may negatively affect pubertal development. Athletes who 
begin strenuous training before menarche have a delay in men­
archeal age. When the strenuous physical activity is interrupted 
(e.g., by injury), puberty advances, and menarche often occurs 
within a few months in those with amenorrhea, in some cases 
before a significant change in body composition or weight. Thin­
ness and strenuous physical activity appear to act synergistically, 
but strenuous exercise training by itself may inhibit the GnRH 
pulse generator, mediated in part by endogenous opioidergic 
pathways involving β-endorphin. Further, genetic influences over­
lie changes due to weight or activity because there is a positive 
correlation between the delayed menarche in athletic girls and the 
age of menarche of their mothers. Notably, coexistence with eat­
ing disorders is often found in girls engaged in sports that empha­
size weight.771 As a typical example, teenage ballet dancers have 
less body fat and a high incidence of delayed puberty manifesting 
as primary and secondary amenorrhea. Female athletes of normal 
weight (e.g., ice skaters, swimmers) who have less fat and more 
muscle than nonathletic girls are also at risk for delayed puberty 
and amenorrhea. In contrast to runners and ballet dancers, men­
strual cycles in swimmers are irregular and anovulatory rather 
than absent, and the plasma concentrations of DHEAS and LH 
were found to be higher than normal in the setting, with normal 
plasma estrogen levels. Overall, there are conflicting data regard­
ing the endocrine repercussions of intensive sport in young girls. 
Despite several studies suggesting a meaningful pubertal delay, 
especially in rhythmic elite gymnasts,772 a literature review ordi­
nated by the Scientific Commission of the International Gymnas­
tics Federation concluded that pubertal growth, adult height, and 
body proportions are not compromised by intensive gymnastics 
training.773 The authors state that available data are inadequate 
to address the endocrine alterations generated by high-intensity 
gymnastics.
The bone status of professional adolescent female athletes 
depends on the type of sport and the degree of endocrine involve­
ment. In a small study, rhythmic gymnasts appeared to have higher 
BMD at the hip than ballet dancers, although both sport groups 
had lower bone density at the radius (nonloaded site).774 The bone 
density of female long-distance runners is greater in those with 
regular menses than in those with menstrual irregularities. Low 
bone mass persists in adult ballet dancers with amenorrhea, even 
with estrogen replacement, and nutrition therapy is likely a key 
aspect to improve management.
Although with a much rarer frequency, the male HPG axis may 
also be affected by rigorous physical training.775 Affected men 
have low T levels, decreased LH response to GnRH, and decreased 
spontaneous LH pulse frequency and amplitude. Moderation of 
physical activity leads to recovery of HH.
Stressful social situations can also inhibit growth and physical 
pubertal development in adolescence. 
Anorexia Nervosa. Anorexia nervosa is a relatively common 
cause of acquired gonadotropin deficiency in adolescence. In ado­
lescent girls, it is the third-most-common chronic disease, whereas 
it is rarer in boys. Additionally, this condition has the highest mor­
tality rate among all psychiatric disorders in adolescence.776 It is 
characterized by a distorted body image; obsessive fear of obesity; 
and food avoidance that can cause severe self-induced weight loss, 
widespread endocrine disorders, and even death. A more precise 
definition is provided in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of 
Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5) criteria of the American 
Psychiatric Association777:
	A.	Restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, lead­
ing to a significantly low body weight in the context of age, 
sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health (less than 
minimally normal/expected). Severity is based on BMI derived 
from WHO categories for thinness in adults and correspond­
ing percentiles in children and adolescents: mild, BMI greater 
than or equal to 17 kg/m2; moderate, BMI 16 to 16.99 kg/m2; 
severe, BMI 15 to 15.99 kg/m2; extreme, BMI less than 15 kg/
m2.
	B.	Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat or persistent 
behavior that interferes with weight gain.
	C.	Disturbance by one’s body weight or shape, self-worth influ­
enced by body weight or shape, or persistent lack of recogni­
tion of seriousness of low body weight.
Notably, the DSM-IV (4th ed.) criteria also encompassed the 
absence of at least three consecutive nonsynthetically induced 
menstrual cycles as an additional criterion in menstruating 
females, a feature that was dropped in the more recent DSM-5 
guidelines. Other common clinical features of anorexia nervosa 
include an onset in middle adolescence; a tendency to be overly 
active; defective thermoregulation with sensitivity to cold; the 
presence of constipation, bradycardia, and hypotension; dry skin; 
fine hypertrichosis; peripheral edema; and parotid enlargement.
The two main subtypes of anorexia nervosa are the restricting 
type and binge-eating/purging type. Purging is defined as self-
induced vomiting or misuse of laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. The 
pathogenesis is multifactorial and includes a genetic factor and a 
well-characterized psychologic component. Before the diagnosis 
of anorexia nervosa is made, organic disease accounting for the 
menses disturbances must be excluded.
Anorexia nervosa has considerable endocrine ramifications in 
adolescents.778 The onset of amenorrhea may precede the full occur­
rence of severe weight loss. The concentrations of plasma FSH, LH, 
and E2 are characteristically low. LH pulsatility may revert to an 
early puberty pattern with mostly sleep-associated increases, or the 
amplitude and frequency may be substantially diminished like in 
prepubertal subjects. Pulsatile administration of intravenous GnRH 
at intervals of 90 to 120 minutes can produce LH pulses that are 
indistinguishable from the normal pubertal pattern, attesting to 
the presence of a functional and not organic GnRH deficiency. 
Serum leptin levels are low, consistent with the strikingly decreased 
mass of adipose tissue. Other hormonal changes include increased 
1066
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
mean concentrations of plasma GH and plasma cortisol, low lev­
els of plasma IGF1 (due to hepatic resistance to GH), low levels 
of triiodothyronine (T3) with normal levels of TSH and thyroxine 
(T4) (unless presence of an euthyroid sick syndrome), and a limited 
capacity to concentrate urine. Bone age is significantly delayed in 
girls with anorexia nervosa and correlates positively with duration of 
illness and markers of nutritional status. All measures of BMD are 
lower, and the most significant predictors of bone density are LBM, 
BMI, and age at menarche. Treatment of decreased bone density 
in these individuals is accomplished with improved nutrition, 
although catch-up of bone density is rarely complete. Amenorrhea 
may persist for months after weight regain, suggesting persistent 
hypothalamic dysfunction.
Management of anorexia nervosa requires multidisciplinary 
care. Treatment of this disorder requires skillful management, 
understanding, patience, and psychiatric consultation with a team 
approach. Assisted alimentation may be indicated in resistant 
patients with severe weight loss, especially those at high mortality 
risk from infections or an electrolyte imbalance. However, refeed­
ing syndrome with attendant hypophosphatemia may occur if the 
nutritional support is handled appropriately. Overall, treatment 
of anorexia nervosa remains challenging, and an evidence-based 
approach is lacking for several aspects of management.779 
Bulimia Nervosa. Bulimia nervosa is a separated disorder from 
anorexia nervosa. According to the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria,777 
it is defined as follows:
	A.	Recurrent episodes of binge eating, characterized by both of 
the following:
	
1.	 Eating, within any 2-hour period, an amount of food that 
is definitely larger than what most individuals would eat in 
a similar period under similar circumstances.
	
2.	 A sense of lack of control over eating during the episode 
(e.g., a feeling that one cannot stop eating or control what 
or how much one is eating).
	B.	Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent 
weight gain, such as self-induced vomiting; misuse of laxatives, 
diuretics, or other medications; fasting; or excessive exercise.
	C.	The binge eating and inappropriate compensatory behaviors 
occur, on average, at least once a week for 3 months.
	D.	Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight.
	E.	The disturbance does not occur exclusively during episodes of 
anorexia nervosa.
Bulimia occurs in about 1.5% of young women. A hand lesion 
from the induced vomiting (i.e., Russell sign) and an abnormal 
level of serum electrolytes are useful clinical markers. Although 
weight loss is not frequent, amenorrhea is common. Bulimia is 
especially prevalent in high school and college female students. A 
history of childhood sexual abuse is more common than in unaf­
fected adolescents. 
Chronic Diseases. Cystic fibrosis is associated with pubertal 
delay and a late growth spurt, both of which are in part corrected 
with timely management and adequate nutritional support.780 
However, boys with cystic fibrosis almost universally develop azo­
ospermia caused by obstruction of the spermatic ducts as a result 
of the predominant expression of the cystic fibrosis transmem­
brane regulator (CFTR) in male reproductive tissues (e.g., epi­
didymis, vas deferens), leading to more viscid luminal contents. 
Normal ovaries do not express CFTR, and endometrial tissue 
expresses it only after puberty, with variable levels found in cervi­
cal epithelium and the fallopian tubes.
Sickle cell disease is also characterized by delayed pubertal 
development by about 2 years in boys and at least 6 months in girls 
(delayed menarche), even with modern treatment approaches.781 
Hypogonadism (hormonal defects and/or semen abnormalities) 
is a frequent finding in men with sickle cell anemia, associated 
with variable levels of plasma gonadotropins.782 Most studies have 
attributed these alterations to repeated vasoocclusive episodes in 
the hypothalamo-pituitary or testicular vessels secondary to sick­
ling. Thalassemia, another congenital hematologic disorder, carries 
the risk of acquired hemochromatosis resulting from transfusional 
iron deposition in the pituitary and hypothalamus. HH leading to 
pubertal delay is indeed the most common endocrine complica­
tion of the disease, occurring in approximately 40% to 80% of 
affected patients.783 Concomitant pituitary and gonadal damage 
may be present in patients with poorly controlled disease, reduc­
ing the efficacy of gonadotropin therapy for fertility induction.
Pubertal onset is significantly delayed in children with peri­
natally acquired human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection 
compared to those exposed but not affected,784 although the dif­
ference seems to diminish with rising use of combined antiretro­
viral regimens.
Chronic gastrointestinal disease (e.g., Crohn disease) is often 
accompanied by delayed puberty, and therapy to restore nutrition, 
if successful, enables puberty to begin. The pubertal growth spurt 
is compromised by active inflammatory bowel disease, especially 
if glucocorticoid therapy is necessary. Celiac disease also decreases 
the growth rate in childhood and adolescence, but with appropri­
ate dietary restrictions, adult height appears to be normal.
Chronic renal disease is associated with delayed puberty and 
growth retardation. Depending on the severity and duration of 
the renal disease, onset of puberty is often delayed by 2 to 2.5 
years in both sexes.785 Immunoreactive plasma gonadotropin 
concentrations may be elevated, presumably because of impaired 
renal clearance, but the pituitary response to GnRH is blunted 
in severe renal impairment. In addition, chronic renal failure is 
associated with elevated SHBG and thus proportionally lower FT 
levels. Successful renal transplantation usually restores gonadotro­
pin secretion and improves growth. Immune suppression and glu­
cocorticoid therapy after transplantation often result in delayed 
onset of puberty and decreased nocturnal pulsatility of both GH 
and gonadotropins. Adolescent patients also exhibit a pattern 
resembling CDGP.
Children with onset of leukemia at a younger age who achieved 
long-term remission go through puberty at an appropriate age, in 
contrast to those with manifestation of the disease in late child­
hood. Radiation treatment to the CNS may cause HH, GH defi­
ciency, or both, whereas irradiation of the abdomen or pelvis and 
certain types of chemotherapies, especially if administered during 
puberty, may lead to primary hypogonadism. Total-body irradia­
tion for bone marrow transplantation exerts the most significant 
effects, including severe GH deficiency in 50%, hypothyroidism 
in 56%, and hypogonadism in 83% of males and ovarian failure 
in 100% of women.786 Overall, 40% to 50% of childhood cancer 
survivors will develop an endocrine disorder during their lifetime, 
with the highest risk among those with radiation exposure to the 
hypothalamus, the pituitary, or the gonads.787 These endocri­
nopathies can develop several decades after the cessation of cancer 
treatment, underscoring the importance of lifelong surveillance. 
Central Nervous System Tumors and Non-Tumoral 
Disorders
Extrasellar masses may interfere with GnRH synthesis, secretion, 
or stimulation of pituitary gonadotrophs. Most patients with 
hypothalamic-pituitary tumors causing gonadotropin deficiency 
1067
CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
have one or more additional pituitary hormone deficiencies (or 
an increased serum prolactin level with prolactinomas). Those 
with GH deficiency due to a neoplasm have a late onset of growth 
failure compared with those who have idiopathic and familial 
hypopituitarism, in which growth failure starts early in life. The 
presence of anterior and posterior pituitary deficiencies in infancy 
suggests a midline developmental defect, but the development of 
this combination at a later age ominously suggests an expanding 
CNS lesion.
Craniopharyngioma. Craniopharyngioma is a rare embry­
onic malformation of nonglial origin in childhood (0.5–2 
new cases per 1 million population annually, or 1.2%–4% of 
pediatric intracranial tumors).788 It is, however, the most com­
mon brain tumor associated with hypothalamic-pituitary dys­
function and accounts for 80% to 90% of neoplasms found 
in the pituitary and up to 15% of all intracranial tumors in 
childhood.789 Overall, craniopharyngioma has a prevalence 
with a bimodal peak (childhood, late adulthood). In the youth, 
symptoms usually arise before the age of 20 years, with a peak 
incidence between the ages of 6 and 14 years (30%–50% of all 
craniopharyngioma).
Current theories on the embryologic origin of craniopharyn­
gioma are divided between development from ectodermal rem­
nants of Rathke’s pouch or from residual embryonic epithelium 
of the anterior pituitary gland and the anterior infundibulum. 
These tumors may arise from within or above the sella turcica, or 
more rarely, they may be found in the nasopharynx or the third 
ventricle. Craniopharyngioma appears to be a monoclonal tumor, 
and about 50% have cytogenetic abnormalities. The predominant 
histologic type in childhood is adamantinomatous craniopha­
ryngiomas (70%) that harbor mutations in the β-catenin gene 
(CTNNB1), thus generating a dysregulation of the Wnt path­
way.790 This is in contrast to the adult-predominant papillary type 
of craniopharyngioma that is more often accompanied by clonal 
BRAF mutations.791
As the tumor encroaches on surrounding structures, clini­
cal symptoms develop, including headache, short stature due to 
growth deficiency, diabetes insipidus, vomiting, and other symp­
toms of hypopituitarism. Visual field defects (including bitempo­
ral hemianopsia) and delayed puberty are also common features 
of craniopharyngiomas. Although most patients have decelerated 
growth at diagnosis, a long, indolent course is possible, with onset 
of symptoms several months before. Deficiencies of gonadotro­
pins, GH, thyrotropin (TSH), ACTH, and arginine vasopressin 
are common. The serum concentration of prolactin is normal or 
increased.
About 70% of patients with a craniopharyngioma have supra­
sellar or intrasellar calcifications, which are sometimes visible even 
on radiographs taken for other indications, such as orthodontia. 
An MRI scan with gadolinium contrast injection is the diagnostic 
procedure of choice and can determine whether the tumor is cys­
tic, solid, or mixed, as well as indicate the presence of hydrocepha­
lus, a common complication in children (Fig. 23.40). In unclear 
cases, a CT scan can be added to search for calcifications.
Smaller craniopharyngiomas, usually intrasellar, can be treated 
by transsphenoidal microsurgery, but larger or suprasellar masses 
usually require craniotomy, and the approach must be individu­
alized. The optimal therapeutic approach is still under debate. 
Several experts advocate in favor of a partial surgical resection in 
patients with hypothalamic lesions followed by focused stereo­
taxic radiation therapy in order to limit treatment-related hypo­
thalamic dysfunction.792 Lower rates of hypothalamic dysfunction 
without an increased rate of local progression were observed in 
children undergoing a more conservative hypothalamus-sparing 
surgery as compared to a more extensive surgical approach.793 
Nevertheless, other experts argue that with the advance of surgical
