SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
techniques, the initial operation offers the best chance for sur­
gical cure when gross total resection can be accomplished with 
low risk of neurologic injury.794 If total resection is not achieved 
with surgery, adjuvant radiosurgery or targeted radiation therapy 
is needed to prevent tumor regrowth. Alternative approaches cur­
rently under investigation include proton beam therapy or instil­
lation of radioisotopes or sclerosing substances, mainly in cystic 
craniopharyngioma.
Endocrine insufficiencies are very common in patients with 
craniopharyngioma, in part due to the extension of the primary 
tumor but also exacerbated by treatment. The rare combination of 
diabetes insipidus with impaired sense of thirst resulting from the 
hypothalamic injury constitute a complex management problem. 
Postoperative hyperphagia and rapidly progressive obesity (BMI 
>5 SD above normal) can be striking and correlate with the mag­
nitude of hypothalamic damage on initial cranial MRI. Injury to 
the hypothalamic ventromedial nuclei (associated with increased 
parasympathetic activity and hyperinsulinemia) or to the PVN 
may cause these findings, and insulin suppression may be helpful. 
There are promising preliminary data for the use of GLP1 receptor 
agonists.795 Bariatric surgery is effective to produce weight loss in 
affected patients without any difference in adverse events.796 Five-
year total weight loss was 18%, significantly less than in controls, 
yet remaining clinically relevant. Aberrant sleep patterns and even 
narcolepsy and daytime somnolence may complicate craniopha­
ryngioma surgical resection and respond to melatonin therapy.
Short-term survival rates are high, but affected patients retain 
high morbidity. A nationwide Swedish study analyzed the progno­
sis of 307 patients diagnosed with craniopharyngioma from 1987 
through 2011, of whom 106 had a childhood onset.797 After a 
mean follow-up of 9 years (range, 0–25), individuals with a child­
hood onset of craniopharyngioma had a 17-fold increased stan­
dardized mortality ratio, with a 5-fold higher rate of death from 
cerebrovascular disease. Morbidity burden was also heavy, in par­
ticular regarding type 2 diabetes, fractures, and severe infections.
A Rathke’s cleft cyst is often discovered as an incidental finding 
on MRI, but it can produce symptoms and signs indistinguishable 
from those of a craniopharyngioma, such as precocious or delayed 
puberty in 37% of pediatric cases.798 Surgical drainage and exci­
sion of the cyst wall are customary approaches. 
Germinomas. Germinomas (i.e., pinealomas, ectopic pine­
alomas, atypical teratomas, or dysgerminomas) and other GC 
tumors of the CNS are the most common extrasellar tumors 
that cause absence or delay of puberty. More precisely, germi­
nomas constitute 66% of all intracranial GC tumors (GCTs), 
which account for 3% to 11% of pediatric brain tumors. 
About 84% are found in the pineal and the neurohypophyseal 
regions. Peak incidences occur in the second decade and during 
infancy. They are found more often in males.799 Polydipsia and 
polyuria resulting from diabetes insipidus are the most com­
mon symptoms, followed by visual difficulties and abnormali­
ties of growth and puberty or movement disorders. Diagnosis 
may be delayed for months to years because the findings are 
often attributed to psychiatric disorders. Deficiencies of vaso­
pressin and GH are most common, but other anterior pituitary 
hormone deficiencies (including gonadotropin deficiency) and 
elevated serum prolactin levels are also frequent. GC tumors 
that secrete hCG cause isosexual GnRH-independent sexual 
precocity (GISP) in boys (see “Precocious Puberty”). Deter­
mination of the concentration of hCG in spinal fluid and in 
serum and assessment of α-fetoprotein levels (AFP) provide 
useful tumor markers.
Subependymal spread of GC tumors along the lining of the 
third ventricle is common, and seeding may involve the lower 
spinal cord. The first radiologic finding in MRI could be an iso­
lated enlargement of the pituitary stalk. This type of alteration 
requires close clinical and periodic MRI monitoring, especially in 
patients with diabetes insipidus.800 The size of the pituitary gland 
doubles between age 1 and 15 years, but the pineal gland does not 
normally enlarge after the first year of life. Any later enlargement 
indicates a mass lesion.
Irradiation is the preferred treatment for pure GC tumors such 
as germinomas. Surgery is rarely indicated, except for biopsy to 
establish a definitive diagnosis. Chemotherapy alone is inadequate, 
but the combination of chemotherapy and radiation therapy can 
be successful,801 and both treatment methods are recommended 
for a mixed GC tumor. Because testicular GC tumors are occa­
sionally found years after successful therapy for CNS GC tumors, 
long-term surveillance is indicated.802
Hypothalamic and optic gliomas or astrocytomas, either spo­
radic or as part of neurofibromatosis (von Recklinghausen dis­
ease), can also cause sexual infantilism. Gliomas and meningiomas 
are the most common CNS tumors to develop in childhood can­
cer survivors treated with CNS radiation, often even during the 
late teenage years. 
Pituitary Adenomas. Only 2% to 6% of all surgically treated 
pituitary tumors occur in childhood and adolescence, with an 
approximate prevalence of 1 in 1,000,000 children.789 Most func­
tional pituitary adenomas are ACTH secreting, with prolactino­
mas, GH-secreting, and nonfunctioning adenomas occurring less 
commonly. The majority of GH-secreting pituitary adenomas in 
childhood are monoclonal lesions caused by somatic mutations 
of GNAS. Adolescent onset of pituitary tumors may be the first 
manifestation of multiple endocrine neoplasia type I (MEN-I) or 
familial isolated pituitary adenoma (FIPA).803 Evaluation of secre­
tory activity of such a lesion, consideration of mass effects, and 
follow-up to monitor a change in size are important, but some 
lesions detected will remain asymptomatic and will not require 
any therapeutic intervention, especially if they were incidentally 
discovered.
The incidence of prolactinoma is low in childhood, but 20% 
of these adenomas present in late adolescence and young adult­
hood (age 15–24 years).804 A survey of 44 pediatric cases revealed 
that 61% of prolactinomas were macroadenomas (more often in 
boys, commonly associated with hypopituitarism and growth fail­
ure), and 39% were microadenomas (more often in girls, com­
monly associated with delayed puberty).805 Primary amenorrhea 
was the presenting symptom in 13 of 20 pubertal females in this 
series. The main presenting symptoms included oligomenorrhea 
and galactorrhea in the girls and headache in the boys. Galactor­
rhea may be demonstrable only by manual manipulation of the 
nipples. In the case of hyperprolactinemia without any associated 
clinical symptoms or signs, the possibility of high serum levels of 
macroprolactin, a complex of immunoglobulin G and monomeric 
prolactin with little biologic activity in vivo, which cross-react in 
commercial prolactin assays, should be considered.806
Treatment with dopamine agonists is often successful in nor­
malizing serum prolactin values and decreasing tumor size. This is 
particularly useful in the setting of large tumors for which a com­
plete surgical resection is unlikely.807 Cabergoline is the dopamine 
agonist of choice in terms of efficacy, tolerance, and ease. Trans­
sphenoidal resection of microprolactinomas in children and ado­
lescents is an effective treatment in the hands of an experienced 
pituitary neurosurgeon.

Pubertal progression and normal menstrual function in girls 
usually follow a reduction of serum prolactin levels. If treatment 
with a dopamine agonist is undertaken, withdrawal of the therapy 
can be attempted in selected cases after at least a 3-year course.808 
Patients with macroprolactinoma treated with cabergoline or 
other dopamine agonists should be warned about the risk of pitu­
itary apoplexy, tumor hemorrhage, or necrosis that can manifest 
as new-onset brutal headache or visual disturbances.809 Other 
concerns about long-term dopamine agonist therapy include the 
occurrence of cardiac valve abnormalities. Increased incidence of 
moderate tricuspid regurgitation in individuals with a high cumu­
lative dose has been reported, but all these findings were incidental 
and not associated with clinical implications.810 
Other Central Nervous System Disorders Leading to 
Delayed Puberty
Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis. Langerhans cell histiocytosis 
(LCH; also termed histiocytosis X) is a clonal proliferative disorder 
of langerin-positive (CD207+) histiocytes or their precursors. It 
is characterized by aberrant function and/or proliferation of cells 
of the mononuclear phagocyte system, leading to an inflamma­
tory infiltration with a particular affinity for the skin, the bones, 
the lungs, and the pituitary gland.811 The cause of LCH remains 
unclear to date, with the presence of features suggestive of both a 
neoplastic and a reactive immunologic disorder. Diabetes insipi­
dus, caused by infiltration of the hypothalamus and/or the pitu­
itary stalk, is the most common endocrine manifestation, followed 
by GH deficiency and delayed puberty.811 LCH has a widely vari­
able clinical course, ranging from single indolent lesions to explo­
sive multisystem disease, particularly in children. LCH lesions can 
develop in virtually all organ systems, with typical involvement 
of the lungs, the liver, the spleen, and the bones, with cyst-like 
zones in long bones and the dorsolumbar spine. Mastoid or tem­
poral bone involvement may lead to chronic otitis media. Treat­
ment with glucocorticoids, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy 
is promising in terms of survival, but more than 50% of patients 
have residual active disease and/or disease progression. The natural 
waxing and waning course of this rare disease renders adequate 
therapeutic management difficult. Recent advances in the past 
decade have redefined LCH as a disorder driven by misguided 
myeloid differentiation, with the extent of disease determined by 
the origin of the cell in which activating mitogen-activated pro­
tein kinase somatic mutations arise.811 This improved understand­
ing of the disease has not yet translated into more effective and 
personalized treatment protocols.
Inflammatory Lesions and Other Nontumoral Causes. Tuber­
culous or sarcoid granulomas of the CNS may be associated with 
delayed puberty. Hydrocephalus may also cause delayed puberty 
in some affected individuals, a disturbance that can be reversed 
with decompression. Similar findings have rarely been reported as 
a result of compressive effect of subarachnoid cysts. 
Irradiation of the Central Nervous System. Irradiation of the 
CNS for treatment of leukemia (prophylactically) or neoplasms of 
the head and face may result in the gradual onset of hypopituita­
rism.787 Although GH deficiency is the most common hormone 
disorder resulting from irradiation, gonadotropin deficiency and 
central hypothyroidism may also occur.812 Self-reported fertility 
was reported to be lower in women who received CNS radio­
therapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia before or around the 
time of menarche.813 Further, irradiation of the CNS in early life 
predisposes the patient to later onset of secondary CNS tumors, 
especially meningioma, that sometimes arise just a few years after 
the treatment of the first tumor.814 
Developmental Defect of the Midline
Septo-optic dysplasia (SOD) is a rare disorder caused by abnor­
mal development of the prosencephalon, leading to a classic triad 
of optic nerve hypoplasia, agenesis of brain midline structures 
(septum pellucidum, corpus callosum), and hypoplasia of the 
hypothalamus-pituitary axis.815 Clinical diagnosis of the disease 
can be made in the presence of two out of three of aforementioned 
manifestations. According to a report on the clinical spectrum of 
the disease, ∼30% of cases have the complete triad of manifesta­
tions, 62% harbor some degree of hypopituitarism, and 60% have 
an absent septum pellucidum.816 The prevalence is approximately 
1 in 10,000 live births. The hypothalamic defect may encompass 
GH deficiency, diabetes insipidus, and other anterior pituitary 
deficiencies. Delayed puberty may result, although precocious 
puberty has also been reported.817 A recent register multinational 
study suggested younger maternal age (20–24 years) as a risk fac­
tor for the occurrence of the disease.818 Pituitary MRI may reveal 
pituitary hypoplasia and/or an ectopic location of the posterior 
pituitary bright spot. Abnormalities of the corpus callosum and 
cerebellum are also common on MRI. Subjects with normal MRIs 
are spared from endocrine abnormalities.819 The condition is usu­
ally sporadic, but familial cases involving genes encoding tran­
scription factors such as HESX1, SOX2, SOX3, and OTX2 have 
been reported.815
Other congenital midline defects associated with hypopituita­
rism include the following:
 • The solitary median maxillary incisor syndrome, an autosomal-
dominant condition caused by mutations in the sonic hedge­
hog (SHH) gene
 • Other congenital midline defects, ranging from complete dys­
raphism and holoprosencephaly to cleft palate or lip
 • Myelomeningocele (myelodysplasia), which involves a variable 
range of hypothalamic defects and possibly CPP 
Combined Pituitary Hormone Deficiency
CPHD is a rare congenital disorder characterized by impaired 
production of pituitary hormones affecting at least two anterior 
pituitary hormone lineages with variable clinical manifestations. 
CPHD may manifest as (1) isolated pituitary hormone deficien­
cies, (2) a component of other syndromes (e.g., SOD), or (3) pitu­
itary stalk interruption syndrome with ectopic posterior pituitary 
gland.820 To differentiate CPHD from CHH, biochemical assess­
ment of pituitary function is needed, in addition to evaluating 
specific clinical manifestations of hypopituitarism. Even subtle 
indications of insufficiency for one of the pituitary hormones war­
rant further testing with appropriate dynamic challenge tests and 
brain MRI.531 The genetic basis for CPHD is complex, involving 
30 genes in a variety of syndromic and nonsyndromic presenta­
tions,821 with GLI2, HESX1, LHX3, LHX4, OTX2, POU1F1, 
PROP1, and SOX2 as the most prevalent causes. More precisely, 
biallelic PROP1 mutations cause early GH and TSH deficiency, 
as well as variable degrees of LH/FSH deficiency manifesting as 
delayed puberty or late onset of secondary hypogonadism in adult­
hood (Fig. 23.41). Notably, late ACTH deficiency can occur in 
subjects harboring mutations in this particular gene, highlighting 
the need for lifelong endocrine surveillance.822 LHX3 mutations 
are also associated with CPHD inherited in an autosomal-reces­
sive manner, which encompasses gonadotropin deficiencies and 
is often accompanied by restricted head rotation.823 LHX4 and 
GLI2 mutations follow an autosomal-dominant pattern and 
may cause isolated GH deficiency or variable degrees of CPHD, 
including gonadotropin deficiency.824 Variable expressivity and 
1070
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
incomplete penetrance have been reported. The X-linked form of 
hypopituitarism can be associated with duplication of the SOX3 
gene.825 Deficiency of SOX2, a transcription factor involved in 
early hypothalamic-pituitary embryonic development, leads to 
anterior pituitary hypoplasia. Conversely, patients with loss-of-
function heterozygous SOX2 mutations develop eye abnormali­
ties, including anophthalmia, microphthalmia, and coloboma, 
as well as pituitary hypoplasia with HH as the most common 
pituitary defect, in contrast to most other CPHD types.826 Some 
cases of CPHD may not be of genetic origin but be induced by 
hypothalamo-pituitary trauma or asphyxia in the neonatal period, 
as indicated by the relatively high incidence of idiopathic hypo­
pituitarism in infants with breech delivery and perinatal distress.
Congenital or acquired gonadotropin deficiency because of a 
lesion or surgery requires replacement therapy at an age approxi­
mating the normal age of onset of puberty (see Tables 23.5 and 
23.6). When GH deficiency coexists with gonadotropin defi­
ciency, early introduction of HRT can compromise adult height 
if advancement of bone age and epiphyseal fusion occur before 
therapy with GH achieves adequate linear growth. Interestingly, 
isolated GH-deficient patients may be associated with delayed 
onset of puberty, which is corrected with GH administration, 
sometimes with a relatively rapid pubertal course. Artificially 
delaying puberty with a GnRH analogue to attempt to achieve 
a greater final height has been attempted in isolated cases of GH 
deficiency or with normal-variant short stature, but concern over 
decreased bone density led to warnings about the use of this agent 
in GH-deficient patients.827 Patients with hypopituitarism may 
complain of sparse pubic hair growth or, in girls, total absence 
of pubic hair. This is because both gonadal (LH-dependent) and 
adrenal (ACTH-dependent) androgen production is impaired 
in panhypopituitarism. This is easily manageable in boys, whose 
pubic hair will thicken with hCG or exogenous T therapy. GH 
therapy in GH-deficient and gonadotropin-deficient males 
enhances the steroidogenic response of the testes to hCG admin­
istration. Adolescent or young adult women have also been given 
a low dose (25 mg) of intramuscular testosterone enanthate every 
4 weeks to stimulate the growth of pubic hair without virilization. 
Oral DHEAS supplementation (25 mg daily) can induce pubic 
hair growth and exert favorable psychological effects, as evidenced 
also by the findings of a randomized controlled study in 23 young 
females with hypopituitarism.828 
Miscellaneous Conditions
Prader-Willi Syndrome. Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) is an 
autosomal-dominant disorder that combines a tendency for intra­
uterine growth retardation, poor fetal activity, infantile central 
hypotonia, and lethargy, followed by early-onset childhood hyper­
phagia, pathologic obesity, and glucose intolerance.829 Physical 
signs include short stature, small hands and feet, almond-shaped 
eyes, a triangular mouth, and a narrow bifrontal diameter. Mild to 
moderate mental retardation occurs, as well as emotional instabil­
ity, including perseveration, obsessions, and compulsions. Genetic 
testing is used to confirm the clinical diagnosis of the syndrome. 
This distinct genetic disorder, with a frequency of about 1 case 
in 15,000 to 30,000 individuals, is caused by a lack of a func­
tional 15q11-q13 region of paternal origin by a variety of genetic 
mechanisms. Approximately 70% of Prader-Willi cases are caused 
by a paternal deletion of 15q11-q13 (commonly 3–5 megabase 
pairs long); 20% to 25% of cases involve maternal uniparental 
disomy (isodisomy or heterodisomy) in which both chromosomes 
15 are derived from the mother, possibly by nondisjunction dur­
ing maternal meiosis, representing a striking example of genomic 
imprinting.829 In 2% to 5% of cases, an imprinting center defect 
has been detected.
Delayed puberty and HH caused by combined hypotha­
lamic and gonadal dysfunction are characteristic features in most 
affected individuals.829 Micropenis, cryptorchidism, and scrotum 
underdevelopment are common findings in male neonates.830 
Reproductive phenotyping in a series of 37 males with PWS in 
a large age range revealed low serum T levels associated with nor­
mal LH but elevated FSH levels, thus suggesting a mixed involve­
ment with both hypothalamo-pituitary and primary testicular 
defects.831 Serum AMH levels were near the lower limits of nor­
mal, whereas INHB levels were consistently low or undetectable. 
Two adults had a more frank HH constellation with undetect­
able levels of LH and FSH, associated with frankly high AMH 
levels. A variable combination of primary gonadal defects and

hypothalamic dysfunction is also observed in female patients with 
PWS.832 In particular, female subjects exhibit underdevelopment 
of the labia majora, labia minora, or clitoris (76%). Amenorrhea 
occurs in about one-half of cases (53%), and irregular menses or 
spotting is present in the others. Weight reduction may lead to 
menarche in some females because severe obesity may play a role 
in the impaired puberty.
The role of relative GH deficiency in this disorder is uncer­
tain and controversial. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration 
(FDA) approved PWS as an indication for recombinant human 
GH treatment without a requirement for assessing GH secre­
tion. A prospective study in 54 children with PWS, including a 
controlled group (but without placebo), showed that standard-
dose GH replacement decreased body fat and increased LBM and 
linear growth at 12 months833 while possibly optimizing energy 
expenditure and improving physical strength when extended with 
a lower dose.834 However, the report of sudden deaths due to 
respiratory complications during GH treatment led to a recom­
mendation for evaluation for sleep apnea or respiratory difficulties 
before instituting GH therapy. Additionally, some more recent 
data cast doubt on the beneficial effects of GH replacement in 
these patients.835 
Bardet-Biedl Syndromes. Laurence-Moon syndrome and 
Bardet-Biedl syndrome were previously considered as separated 
autosomal-recessive ciliopathies characterized by retinitis pigmen­
tosum and hypogonadism of various types. Currently, the condi­
tions are considered as one, and the present term is Bardet-Biedl 
syndrome. The estimated incidence is 1 in 160,000 in northern 
European populations and 1 in 13,500 in some Arab popula­
tions.836 Other principal findings are developmental delay, spastic 
paraplegia, postaxial polydactyly, early onset of obesity, and renal 
dysplasia. To date, the genetically and phenotypically heteroge­
nous Bardet-Biedl syndrome is linked to mutations in more than 
16 genes, which account for 80% of cases. Although considered 
among the traditional hallmarks of the syndrome, the prevalence 
of hypogonadism was only 20% in a large cohort of 153 affected 
subjects.837 The majority of patients with low T levels had normal 
gonadotropin concentrations, consistent with a secondary hypo­
gonadism. Whether this is the consequence of obesity or a distinct 
feature of the syndrome remains unclear. 
Other. Marijuana use has been associated with gynecomastia 
and is a putative cause of pubertal delay. Untreated Gaucher dis­
ease causes delay in pubertal development, but early treatment 
with enzyme replacement allows puberty to begin on time. Girls 
with familial dysautonomia have delayed menarche and often 
have a severe premenstrual syndrome. The condition is ultimately 
compatible with pregnancy. Fröhlich syndrome or adiposodys­
genesis is a constellation of endocrine abnormalities, combining 
findings of obesity and hypogonadism due to a hypothalamic-
pituitary disorder. Mauriac syndrome is characterized by poorly 
controlled diabetes and hepatomegaly, with fatty infiltration of 
the liver. Delayed puberty in this setting is likely ascribed to poor 
nutritional status. 
Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism in Males
Klinefelter Syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome (KFS) is the most common chromosomal 
aberration in men, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 500 to 600 
live births838; it is caused by the presence of an extra X chromo­
some (47,XXY).839 KFS is a heterogeneous disease characterized 
by infertility, gynecomastia, and learning difficulties.840,841 The 
invariable clinical features include small, firm testes (usually <4 
mL with a Prader orchidometer), testicular failure with high FSH 
levels, and severely impaired spermatogenesis (Fig. 23.42). Tall 
height is a frequent finding, as well as the typical body proportions 
consisting of long legs, a decreased U/L body ratio, and a normal 
arm span. The majority of patients have hypogonadism, defined 
as the presence of symptoms and/or signs suggestive of T defi­
ciency accompanied by low serum T concentrations.842 Milder 
forms exist, given that only 25% to 40% of expected cases are 
diagnosed.838 Indeed, less than 10% of cases are diagnosed prepu­
bertally, with most diagnosis done in adolescence and some cases 
detected later in life as a result of fertility issues. With increasing 
use of karyotype determination in children with behavior prob­
lems and in pregnancy for various reasons, diagnosis earlier in life 
may increase.
Genetic Aspects. Testicular failure and other phenotypic 
traits in KFS are thought to result from a “dosage effect” of genes 
that escape X-chromosome inactivation in the setting of an XXY 
karyotype.840 Tall stature for parental heights is common in this 
disorder as a result of the disproportionate growth of the legs and 
appears to be related to multiple copies of the SHOX gene. Sev­
eral genetic mechanisms seem to be involved in the phenotypic 
variability of the disease. Notable, the AR gene encoding for the 
AR is also located on the X chromosome. This gene contains a 
highly polymorphic CAGn trinucleotide repeat zone in the cod­
ing sequence of the first exon. The length of the translated poly­
glutamate tract in the N-terminal transactivation domain of the 
resulting protein is inversely proportional to the transactivation 
activity of the receptor. Changes in this activity may aggravate the 
androgen signaling defects in men with KFS, who already exhibit 
impaired T secretion. Accordingly, CAGn repeat length has been 
reported to be inversely correlated with penile length, bone den­
sity, arm span to body height, gynecomastia, and even adult tes­
ticular volume.843 A paternal origin of the extra X chromosome 
is associated with later onset of puberty and longer CAG repeats. 
Differential gene expression is present at peripheral blood and 
the testes. This is not limited to X-linked genes but also extends 
to several genes located in autosomal chromosomes as a result of 
the preferential enrichment of the X chromosome for genes that 
encode transcriptional factors and thus influence the expression 
of genes across the whole genome. Recently, four studies reported 
extensive changes in the expression of both X-linked and auto­
somal genes in the testes of men with KFS, unraveling the com­
plex genetic signature of KFS.844–847 D’Aurora et al845 found a 
differential up- and downregulation of 303 and 747 transcripts, 
respectively, in samples from three patients with KFS with hypo­
spermatogenesis. The majority of downregulated transcripts were 
involved in spermiogenesis failure, whereas upregulated genes 
were linked to increased apoptosis. 
Natural History in Puberty. The natural history of the disease 
is complex.848 Affected infants have only a slightly increased risk 
of cryptorchidism and micropenis.849 Minipuberty, the transient 
activation of the HPG axis at infancy, is present,850 although 
serum T levels are in the low-normal range.851 Early depletion of 
GCs occurs in murine XXY models852 and in infants with KFS853 
with signs of aberrant gonocyte differentiation during fetal life.846 
Pubertal timing for patients with KFS is similar to that non-KFS 
youth,854 but the onset of puberty is characterized by accelerated 
loss of GC.855 Testes initially enlarge but their volume peaks at 
midpuberty (Tanner III), followed by a shrinkage despite rising 
levels of LH and FSH.854 Serum T levels also level off at this 
stage,856,857 whereas serum INHB gradually reaches undetectable 
1072
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
levels.858 At this stage, low T levels may lead to slow progres­
sion or arrest of pubertal changes. The majority of adults with 
KFS have only moderately decreased or low-normal serum T but 
high LH and FSH levels.856 Interestingly, KFS gives rise to a four­
fold increase in aromatase expression in the testis.859 Enhanced 
aromatization of T to E2 leads to high-normal serum E2 levels 
and altered T/E ratio as compared to controls860 and men with 
CHH.526 
Developmental Issues and Neurocognitive Phenotype. 
Neurobehavioral abnormalities, primarily in language, speech, 
learning, and frontal executive functions, are common in KFS, but 
severe retardation is uncommon.840 These problems may be severe 
enough to lead to prepubertal recognition of the syndrome. The 
prevalence of adjustment problems in adolescence is increased. 
Adults with Klinefelter syndrome have shorter education, lower 
income, earlier retirement, and increased unemployment, and 
they marry more rarely than the national average. The global IQ 
in unselected populations of patients with KFS is normal or near 
normal, but verbal IQ is usually lower (e.g., 10–20 points) than 
performance IQ. Accordingly, boys with KFS have reduced left 
hemisphere specialization for verbal tasks and enhanced right 
hemisphere specialization for nonverbal tasks. However, these 
abnormalities tend to normalize after puberty begin. There is 
ongoing controversy about the indication for T therapy of infants 
or adolescents with KFS. There are some encouraging findings 
from retrospective studies that showed significant benefits in neu­
rodevelopmental outcomes (language, intellectual, neuromotor 
skills) in young children who received a short course of andro­
gen treatment (3 injections of 25 mg of testosterone enanthate) 
in infancy.861 A randomized controlled trial of low-dose oxandro­
lone, a nonaromatized androgen, versus placebo in 84 boys with 
KFS age 4 to 12 years for 2 years resulted in improved visual-motor 
function and decreased anxiety and depression indexes without 
any improvement in cognitive functions.862 Long-term con­
trolled studies are needed. It is important to underline that data 
on the neurocognitive phenotype of KFS are prone to selection

individual’s lifetime, and patients diagnosed in childhood possibly 
represent a more severe form of the disease. These data are likely 
not generalizable to the whole KFS population. 
Metabolic Phenotype. Men with KFS have increased 
VAT,863,864 as well as a fourfold higher incidence of MetS than 
age-matched controls.865–867 Unsurprisingly, this results in an 
increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, with a hazard ratio 
of 1.6 to 2.0.868 Metabolic alterations in KFS have been attributed 
to the underlying hypogonadism.865 This assumption was ques­
tioned by findings of an unfavorable muscle/fat ratio in prepu­
bertal boys with KFS (thus before apparent hypogonadism).869 
Alternatively, the propensity to MetS may constitute an intrinsic 
feature of KFS.870 Notably, obesity can inhibit the HPG axis via 
metabolic cues and pro-inflammatory cytokines,571 as evidenced 
by decreased LH pulsatility in morbidly obese men.871 In addi­
tion, increasing insulin resistance reduces the secretory capacity of 
LCs.872 Although the hypogonadism in KFS is primary (testicular 
failure), it is possible that metabolic defects aggravate T deficiency, 
acting centrally, peripherally, or both. Three cross-sectional studies 
did not detect lower VAT or better insulin sensitivity in men with 
KFS on T replacement therapy (TRT) as compared to untreated 
patients.865,870,873 A small crossover randomized controlled trial 
of T versus placebo for 6 months showed a decrease in total body 
fat but no effect on VAT or insulin resistance.864 A retrospective 
Chinese study of 39 men with KFS found no benefit of TRT on 
metabolic outcomes,874 whereas MetS incidence was significantly 
higher in men with KFS than in men with CHH (30.8% vs. 
15%). A difference of similar magnitude between patients with 
KFS and patients with HH due to pituitary failure was found in 
an Italian study.873 
Fertility Issues. Infertility is a major issue for patients with 
KFS. The use of microdissection testicular sperm extraction 
(mTESE) has been a breakthrough, allowing the detection of focal 
areas of spermatogenesis in 40% to 45% of cases.875 Neverthe­
less, this technique results in genetic fatherhood in only 10% to 
20% of patients,875,876 highlighting the need for improved strate­
gies. Currently, there are no known predictors of mTESE success, 
with the exception of worse outcomes in men age >35 years.877 
Recent findings from testicular biopsies in patients of different 
ages elucidated the natural history of testicular degeneration in 
KFS.878 Principal alterations include (1) a progressive depletion of 
GC, (2) a pronounced hyalinization of seminiferous tubules with 
altered expression of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, and (3) 
a marked LC hyperplasia. The cause of hyalinization is unknown, 
but it has been linked to an increased number of peritubular mac­
rophages and mast cells.879 Hormonal changes during puberty 
may also play a role because hyalinization is absent in prepubertal 
samples.878 Based on prior use in men with idiopathic infertility 
and low serum T/E ratio,880 three retrospective series reported on 
the use of AIs alone881,882 or in combination with transdermal 
TRT in KFS.883 Despite high sperm retrieval rates (50%–70%), 
the absence of a control group precluded definitive conclusions, 
and AI treatment is not systematically offered before mTESE.840 
Management. TRT should be considered in adolescents when 
the LH level rises above the normal range of values but is not nec­
essary in all subjects in early puberty. In adults, T therapy should 
be initiated in all patients with frankly decreased serum T levels 
(<8 nmol/L confirmed in two morning samples. Men with bor­
derline T levels (8–12 nmol/L) and symptoms of androgen defi­
ciency can also be substituted in the absence of contraindications. 
Notably, obesity and MetS are prevalent in KFS, and weight loss 
strategies can presumably increase SHBG and improve serum T 
levels in selected cases with borderline hypogonadism.
T administration does not appear to reduce the gynecomas­
tia, but local application of a dihydrotestosterone gel may help in 
cases with mastodynia or with a recent onset of breast growth. If 
the gynecomastia does not regress within 2 years or by the end of 
puberty, reduction mammoplasty is required. 
Associated Comorbidities. Men with Klinefelter syndrome 
exhibit increased risk for several conditions, but for the major­
ity of them, the absolute risk remains low. Some of these (MetS, 
type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, fractures) are 
potentially linked to the hormonal defects. For most complica­
tions, the mechanisms are not fully elucidated. More specifically, 
patients with KFS exhibit increased risk of:
 • Venous thromboembolic events and pulmonary embolism 
(threefold to sixfold higher relative risk)
 • Breast carcinoma (approximately fourfold higher relative risk)
 • Mitral valve prolapse (variable frequency)
 • Certain hematologic malignancies
 • GC tumors in the mediastinal region or other midline local­
izations, particularly in children. With rare exceptions, these 
tumors, which may be located anywhere from the CNS to the 
pelvis, secrete hCG and induce sexual precocity.
 • Autoimmune diseases, including type 1 diabetes, multiple 
sclerosis, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syn­
drome, and systemic lupus erythematosus
 • Increased prevalence of essential tremor and osteoarthritis 
Other Forms of Primary Testicular Failure
Chemotherapy. Cancer therapy, especially irradiation of the 
gonads or the use of alkylating chemotherapeutic agents, affects 
testicular function and can lead to adult infertility.884 Delayed 
puberty and adult infertility may result in survivors of child­
hood cancer. Some courses of therapy can cause severe damage to 
GCs and seminiferous tubes without apparent effect on LCs. For 
instance, chemotherapy for childhood Hodgkin disease (cyclo­
phosphamide, mechlorethamine, vincristine, procarbazine, and 
prednisone regimen; COPP/MOPP regimen) can cause severe 
damage to Sertoli and germinal cells, but it has less effect on LCs, 
even if therapy occurred in the prepubertal period. Affected chil­
dren may produce sufficient T levels to spontaneously progress 
through puberty, but FSH concentrations will start to increase, 
mirroring a decrease in INHB concentrations during puberty. 
Lower dosing or limiting therapy to less than three courses is 
suggested to decrease these complications. The combination of 
doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine (ABVD 
regimen) can also cause GC depletion. Gonadal damage may 
not be demonstrable until the age of puberty. Chemotherapeutic 
agents used in the treatment of nephrotic syndrome or leukemia, 
such as cyclophosphamide or chlorambucil, can also damage the 
SC, LC, and GC pool in prepubertal children. These effects are 
reversible in some cases. 
Radiation Therapy. Radiation to the gonads can cause pri­
mary testicular failure, usually resulting in azoospermia, although 
T levels may be preserved in the normal range, associated with 
elevated LH (compensated LC failure) and FSH values. Direct 
radiation exposure in a dose of more than 2 Gy will likely impair 
spermatogenesis. Cumulative exposure to more than 20 Gy carries 
an 11-fold relative risk of developing frank hypogonadism requir­
ing T replacement as an adult.885 Preservation of gonadal tissue to 
allow for spermatogonial stem cell banking is being investigated 
for children with pediatric cancer, but several ethical issues persist

regarding the uncertainly of the final outcome.886 Indeed, there 
is currently a lack of any technology to differentiate these GCs 
into mature spermatozoids in vitro. Sperm banking can, however, 
be offered to affected adolescents who have started their puberty 
and are able to ejaculate, providing that ethical issues regarding 
the procedure and the cost are thoroughly presented. Informed 
consent of the affected individual and his or her legal representa­
tives is mandatory, given that it is impossible to assess to which 
degree sperm quality will be affected by the cancer treatment and 
whether increasingly implemented techniques such as mTESE 
biopsy might be able to recover functional spermatozoids in the 
future even in the presence of azoospermia. Oncofertility is a new 
field of investigation that aims to preserve fertility in children and 
teenagers subject to cancer therapy, and available tools are con­
stantly evolving. Surveys of adults who were not offered fertility 
preservation or with whom such an issue was not even discussed at 
time of diagnosis indicate that they express considerable distress. 
Steroidogenic Defects. Deficiency of 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-
lyase in 46,XY individuals resulting from biallelic mutations in 
the CYP17A1 gene leads to a disorder of sex development (DSD) 
characterized by a female phenotype and absent sexual develop­
ment.887 In particular, the enzymatic defect blocks the synthesis of 
T and adrenal androgens, impairing masculinization at all stages 
of development. Mutations generating less severe deficiencies can 
present with ambiguous genitalia due to partial virilization. Associ­
ated cortisol deficiency and increased mineralocorticoid secretion in 
this condition lead to hypertension, decreased serum potassium lev­
els, and metabolic alkalosis. Elevated serum progesterone levels and 
decreased plasma renin activity are helpful diagnostic features.888 
Glucocorticoid replacement suppresses ACTH and moderates the 
mineralocorticoid excess, correcting the electrolyte abnormali­
ties. Nevertheless, no sexual development occurs unless exogenous 
gonadal steroids are administered.
Another rare autosomal-recessive condition is deficiency of 
steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR) protein, the enzyme 
that mediates mitochondrial cholesterol import. In this disease, 
the ability to produce C21, C19, and C18 steroids is lost as a 
result of a severe impairment of the conversion of cholesterol 
to pregnenolone, an initial rate-limiting step of steroidogenesis. 
Severely affected patients have congenital lipoid CAH with large 
adrenal glands visualized on imaging.889 The massive accumu­
lation of cholesterol and cholesterol esters in the LCs and the 
cells of the adrenal cortex steroidogenesis may compress cellular 
organelles and promote oxidative damage of the tissue. Death 
often occurs in infancy if untreated because of unrecognized 
glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiencies. Affected 
individuals have a female phenotype at birth, regardless of their 
karyotype, because of the complete absence of gonadal or adre­
nal androgen production. Affected XY phenotypic females do 
not develop secondary sexual characteristics at puberty. How­
ever, ovarian steroidogenesis may be spared initially, allowing 
some development of female sex characteristics (pubic hair) or 
even spontaneous menarche in affected XX females.890 This find­
ing suggests that the ovaries express a backup system to allow 
StAR-independent cholesterol translocation to the side-chain 
cleavage system. It also reflects the fact the ovarian steroidogenic 
tissue remains dormant until the onset of puberty and is thus 
spared form the early stimulation that dooms testicular and 
adrenal cortical cells to damage from cholesterol engorgement. 
Under FSH stimulation during puberty and with recruitment 
of ovarian follicles, the ovaries undergo progressive damage and 
cyst formation related to lipid deposition. 
Luteinizing Hormone Resistance. Presumptive evidence of 
LH resistance caused by an LH receptor abnormality on the LC 
was reported in an 18-year-old boy with a male phenotype, absent 
secondary sexual development, gynecomastia, elevated plasma LH 
levels, and early pubertal plasma T levels that did not increase after 
hCG administration.891 The testes were prepubertal in size and 
histology. Plasma membrane receptor preparations from the testes 
bound only one-half as much radiolabeled hCG as control testes. 
In affected males, this autosomal-recessive disorder is caused by a 
mutation in LHCGR, the gene encoding the G protein–coupled, 
seven-transmembrane LH/hCG cell receptor. Mutations that 
cause a more severe compromise in LHCGR function are associ­
ated with 46,XY DSD. Homozygous deletion of exon 10 or the 
homozygous missense mutations p.Ser616Tyr and p.Ile625Lys of 
LHCGR are associated with micropenis (but not hypospadias) as 
a result of partial impairment of LH receptor function, leading to 
poor response to LH but a preserved response to hCG. In affected 
females, LH/hCG resistance does not affect pubertal maturation 
but does lead to amenorrhea with high serum LH levels but nor­
mal FSH and E2 concentrations. 
Cryptorchidism and Anorchia. Cryptorchidism is the condi­
tion in which one or both testes have not reached the bottom of the 
scrotum before birth. When testes are not descended, they may be 
located in high scrotal, suprascrotal, or inguinal positions, or they 
can be nonpalpable.110 Animal and human data demonstrate that 
testicular descent is influenced by both T and INSL3 in different 
stages.110 The exact numbers vary according to different studies, 
but approximately 2% to 4% of full-term and 30% of premature 
male infants are born with an undescended testis.892 Testes may 
ascend after birth, ascensus testis, which leads to a higher preva­
lence of undescended testes in prepuberty than at birth in several 
international reports, and these patients are not always included in 
cryptorchidism surveys. A population-based study on more than 
1 million Danish boys born between 1973 and 2004 showed a 
3.4% incidence of cryptorchidism, with a concordance rate that 
was higher for maternal than paternal half-brothers, as well as a 
high but similar concordance for dizygotic (24%) and monozy­
gotic (27%) twin brothers.893 Taken together, these data imply 
that the maternal intrauterine environment modulates the risk of 
cryptorchidism in addition to the expected genetic influences.
A 46,XY male without palpable testes may have intraabdomi­
nal testes (which carry an increased risk of malignant degeneration 
if left undescended); anorchia (i.e., testicular regression or “van­
ishing testes” syndrome), in which no testes are found at laparot­
omy; or retractile testes, a variation of normal. About half of cases 
with bilateral nonpalpable testes are undescended and detected 
in imaging or exploratory laparotomy/laparoscopy, whereas in the 
other half, only testicular remnants that usually do not contain 
GCs are found in the scrotum or in the abdomen. If the pheno­
type of external and internal genitalia is male, functioning testes 
capable of secreting T and AMH were present early during fetal 
life but degenerated thereafter.894 In anorchid boys, the minipu­
berty-childhood-puberty U-shaped variation of serum gonadotro­
pin levels is conserved but with higher values in all stages for both 
LH and FSH than in control boys.895 Below the age of 6 years, 
a serum FSH <2 U/L ruled out anorchia, whereas a serum LH 
>5 U/L confirmed it. Serum AMH and inhibin B are also use­
ful tools to assess the presence of viable testicular tissue because 
they are both undetectable in anorchia.896 Regarding the utility 
of imaging modalities, pelvic ultrasound does not reliably localize 
nonpalpable testes, and neither does it rule out an intraabdomi­
nal testis, according to a meta-analysis.897 Important variability in

the diagnostic accuracy of the ultrasound suggests that its value 
is probably operator dependent. The addition of MRI (combi­
nation of standard MRI with a diffusion-weighted protocol) can 
increase the diagnostic accuracy in localizing undescended testicu­
lar tissue.898 However, it is not routinely recommended by most 
experts because it does not remove the need for a confirmatory 
laparoscopy.
Discovery of unilateral cryptorchidism may represent the 
presence of an undescended testis or monorchia. Compensatory 
hypertrophy of the remaining descended testes occurs in the latter 
situation. A Japanese study demonstrated that the mean contra­
lateral testicular length and volume in the boys with monorchia 
was 22.4 mm compared with 16.6 mm in boys with a testis pres­
ent but undescended (localized by laparoscopy) and 16.6 mm in 
control subjects.899 Because this finding does not precisely pre­
dict monorchia in all cases, laparoscopy should be performed if 
ultrasound is unsuccessful or inconclusive. In the presence of a 
unilaterally undescended testis, the increased relative risk of carci­
noma in the contralateral descended testis is 1.7 (95% confidence 
interval [CI], 1.01–2.98), which is lower than in the undescended 
testes (6.3; 95% CI, 4.30–9.31).900
Most undescended testes at birth complete their descent 
within the first 3 to 4 months of life. Hormonal treatment may 
be modestly successful in promoting testicular descent, but data 
are scarce, and their interpretation is difficult owing to variation 
in treatment regimens. There is no clear superiority between the 
use of hCG injections or GnRH pulsatile therapy, both of which 
will raise the levels of intragonadal T. The T peak after an hCG 
stimulation test (single dose of 1500 U) was found to predict 
the rate of success of subsequent hormonal therapy in cryptor­
chid boys with PWS.901 A systematic review in 2012 concluded 
that hormonal therapy confers only modestly higher descent rates 
(approximately 10%) than placebo, with better outcomes when 
the testes is more distally located. Currently, several experts argue 
against the systematic use of hormonal therapy in cryptorchid 
boys, whereas other guidelines suggest a potential use to promote 
beneficial effects on fertility.902 There is no compelling evidence 
that short-term hormonal therapy is harmful, but it should not be 
allowed to significantly delay surgical therapy. Because spontane­
ous testicular descent normally occurs by 1 year of age, orchido­
pexy is recommended by most experts between 6 and 18 months 
of age. Nevertheless, histologic changes with potential prognostic 
value for future fertility may already begin at birth, which could 
constitute an argument for an earlier surgical correction between 
the age of 4 and 12 months.903
Cryptorchidism is associated with an increased risk of infertil­
ity. Two critical steps in the maturation of GCs do not occur in 
the undescended testes. First, at 2 to 3 months of age, possibly 
owing to the minipuberty surge of T, LH, and FSH, the gono­
cytes (primitive spermatogonia) in the fetal stem cell pool trans­
form into the adult dark spermatogonia, which become the adult 
stem pool. This is a very crucial step for future spermatogenesis.904 
Second, at 4 to 5 years of age, meiosis begins and primary sper­
matocytes appear. Unsurprisingly, late orchidopexy after puberty 
is associated with a greater than 85% prevalence of azoospermia 
or oligospermia. Cryptorchid testes may reflect CHH or another 
underlying disease and thus may not function properly even if 
brought into the scrotum early in life. Hormonal evaluation of the 
HPG axis (serum T, LH, FSH, INHB) between the second and 
third month of life is indicated in all cryptorchid boys to assess 
whether normal minipuberty occurs, and the results should be 
interpreted according to recently established normative ranges.850 
Normal serum gonadotropins and INHB levels correlate with a 
preserved GC number at perioperative biopsies, likely indicating 
a good fertility prognosis.905 A presumptive diagnosis of CHH 
can be made if low levels of T and gonadotropins are present, 
especially if there is a positive family history.81 Testicular dysgen­
esis will be indicated by increased gonadotropin levels, and early 
surgery may be indicated. Regarding long-term prognosis, a study 
of men with cryptorchidism reported a paternity rate of 65% for 
men with a history of bilateral cryptorchidism, compared with 
90% for the formerly unilateral cryptorchid men and 93% for 
control men.906 The reduced fertility in the bilaterally cryptor­
chid men was supported by lower concentrations and increased 
FSH levels. Nevertheless, all orchidopexies in this study were per­
formed after the age of 1 year, reflecting older recommendations. 
In a very large population-based cohort study of all liveborn boys 
in Western Australia between 1970 and 1999, subsequently fol­
lowed until 2006, the presence of undescended testes was associ­
ated with a 21% reduction in paternity and a two-times increase 
in the need for artificial reproductive therapies (ARTs).907 For 
every 6-month delay in orchidopexy, there was a 1% reduction in 
paternity and a 5% increase in risk of future ART use.
The incidence of testicular carcinoma in England rose from 2 
per 100,000 in 1909 to 4.4 per 100,000 in 1999, with a specific 
increase during puberty.908 Cryptorchidism confers a threefold-
higher risk of testicular cancer,909 with the highest risk associated 
with intraabdominal testes, underlying testicular dysgenesis and 
late or no orchidopexy.910 Undescended testes remain at a higher 
temperature and experience maturation arrest at the conversion of 
the gonocytes to spermatogonia, which appears to direct the testes 
toward malignant degeneration, a risk that seems mainly to rise 
after puberty. Periodic sonography of the testis of affected patients 
is recommended after the onset of puberty.
Retractile testes can descend into the scrotum but then reas­
cend. They are considered a normal variation, but a requirement 
for orchidopexy was reported for 22.7% in a series of 150 cases.911 
The finding of one case of testicular carcinoma in a boy with spon­
taneous descent in this series led to a suggestion of following such 
cases in the long term. 
Intrauterine Growth Restriction. Intrauterine growth restric­
tion leading to an SGA male neonate predisposes to reproduc­
tive problems. Males born SGA tend to have smaller testes, lower 
serum T, and higher LH levels, suggesting an impairment of tes­
ticular function.912 Hormonal imbalances persist in adult males 
born SGA who exhibit elevated levels of E2 and dihydrotestoster­
one, presumably as a result of higher aromatase and 5α-reductase 
activity.913 These changes can have health implications; relative 
hyperestrogenism in men has been associated with an increased 
risk of testicular cancer, as well as a tendency to MetS and type 2 
diabetes.914 
Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism in Females
The most common form of HH in the female is the syndrome of 
gonadal dysgenesis (TS and its variants), a sporadic disorder with 
an incidence of 1 per 2000 liveborn girls in which all or part of 
the second X chromosome is absent.915 The syndrome of gonadal 
dysgenesis and its variants are found in a continuum ranging from 
the typical 45,X phenotype to a normal male or female pheno­
type. About 99% of 45,X conceptions will be terminated with 
early miscarriages, accounting for roughly 1 in 15 spontaneous 
abortions. The 45,X karyotype (TS) is associated with female 
phenotype, short stature, hypogonadism, and various somatic

abnormalities. Sex chromosome mosaicism or structural abnor­
malities of an X or Y chromosome in 40% of individuals with TS 
may modify the clinical phenotype.
Turner Syndrome
Classic Genotype and Variants. Short stature and hypogonad­
ism are the two hallmarks of TS (Fig. 23.43). Half of affected 
women have a 45,X karyotype. The remaining have mosaicism 
45,X/46,XX (15%–25%), an isochromosome (20%), and ring X 
chromosomes more rarely. Additionally, 10% to 12% of women 
have differing amounts of Y chromosome material. 
Clinical Manifestations. Typical physical signs of TS include 
distinct facies with micrognathia, a fish-mouth appearance, 
high-arched palate with dental abnormalities, epicanthus, ptosis, 
low-set or deformed ears, short neck with low hairline, webbed 
neck (i.e., pterygium colli), and recurrent otitis media that often 
leads to impaired hearing.915 A broad, shield-like chest leads to the 
appearance of widely spaced nipples, with hypoplastic areolae in 
many patients. Skeletal defects include short fourth metacarpals 
and cubitus valgus (which may develop after birth), Madelung 
deformity of the wrist (∼5%–7%), genu valgum, and scoliosis. 
There are extensive pigmented nevi, a tendency to keloid forma­
tion, and hypoplastic nails. Lymphatic obstruction leads to the 
infantile puffiness of extremities and pterygium colli, as well as to 
a distinctive shape of the ears. Cardiovascular anomalies affect the 
left side of the heart and include coarctation of the aorta in about 
10% of cases, aortic stenosis, and bicuspid aortic valves. These 
individuals are at risk for an aortic dissection. Cardiovascular
