However, these methods are not infallible in differentiating the 
two conditions.
As postulated for some recurrent ovarian cysts, premature the­
larche appears to result from the ovarian response to transient 
increases in FSH levels and possibly from variations in ovarian 
sensitivity to FSH. The LH response to GnRH is prepubertal in all 
cases.1142 Plasma inhibin B and FSH levels are higher in girls with 
precocious thelarche than in control subjects, in a range similar to 
that observed in patients with precocious puberty.
Sonograms of the ovary may show one or several cysts larger 
than 0.5 cm that disappear and reappear, usually correlating with 
changes in the size of the breasts, but the volume of the ovary and 
uterus is prepubertal.1114 In clinical practice, it is rare to find a cyst 
at the time of presentation and on ultrasonic study.
Exaggerated thelarche is described as premature thelarche with 
the added findings of advanced bone age and increased growth 
rate, which are estrogen effects. The endocrine measurements 
in the basal state are in the normal prepubertal range, but after 
GnRH agonist stimulation, the level of FSH (but not of LH) rose 
higher than in control subjects or in patients with CPP. Mutation 
of GNAS1 involving Arg201His is associated with apparent pre­
mature or exaggerated thelarche and early menarche.956
Unfortunately, there are no guidelines that can determine 
which girl will undergo progression from premature thelarche to 
precocious puberty. Clinical follow-up is essential to determine 
which course will occur. 
Premature Isolated Menarche. Rarely, girls begin periodic 
vaginal bleeding at between 1 and 9 years of age without any other 
signs of secondary sexual development. The bleeding can recur for 
1 to 6 years and then cease. At the normal age of puberty (3–11 
years later), secondary sexual development and menses ensue and 
follow a normal pattern, as does stature.1143
Fertility was later demonstrated after a normal onset of puberty 
in women with this variant of pubertal development. The cause 
is uncertain, but it may be a counterpart of premature thelarche. 
There is a predominance of FSH secretion, but the gonadotropin 
secretion pattern is not characteristic of CPP.1144 Isolated men­
arche may appear before other manifestations of sexual precoc­
ity in patients with McCune-Albright syndrome and in those 
with the premature sexual maturation that can occur in juvenile 
hypothyroidism.
Before the diagnosis of premature menarche is accepted, all 
other causes of vaginal bleeding and precocious estrogen secre­
tion and of exposure to exogenous estrogens should be excluded, 
including neoplasms, granulomas, infection of the vagina or cer­
vix, and presence of a foreign body. A careful examination for 
trauma, such as that caused by sexual abuse, is indicated. Urethral 
prolapse may be misdiagnosed as vaginal bleeding. 
Premature Adrenarche. Premature adrenarche causes the pre­
cocious appearance of pubic hair (i.e., pubarche), axillary hair and 
apocrine axillary odor, comedones, and acne, without other signs 
of puberty or virilization. It is characterized by premature and 
mild adrenal hyperandrogenism.1145,1146 The term premature adre­
narche refers to the rise in serum concentrations of adrenal andro­
gens that cause the appearance of the pubic hair, which is termed 
premature pubarche. In the past, this designation was assigned 
when these clinical features appeared before age 8 years in girls 
or 9 years in boys. Although in boys the age of 9 years still seems 
appropriate as a cutoff point, the age of 8 years may no longer be 
appropriate for girls, according to the results of previously quoted 
studies showing earlier onset of puberty in recent years (mean ages 
are shown in Table 23.1). We recommend that the diagnosis of 
premature pubarche should be limited to African American girls 
younger than 6 years of age and White American girls younger 
than 7 years, which should affect the age at which laboratory stud­
ies are initiated unless there are other signs of virilization, such as 
clitoromegaly or rapid growth.
Premature adrenarche is about 10 times more common in girls 
than in boys.1147 The prevalence is increased in children with CNS 
abnormalities without a clear sex difference; the electroencephalo­
gram may be abnormal in the absence of other neurologic find­
ings. Familial transmission is uncommon. Premature adrenarche 
is commonly slowly progressive and does not have an untoward 
effect on either the onset or the normal progression of gonad­
arche or final adult height.1145 Nonetheless, there is a relation­
ship between reduced fetal growth leading to intrauterine growth 
retardation and subsequent SGA and the increased prevalence of 
premature adrenarche, and probably ovarian hyperandrogenism 
in later life, although the relationship may vary among different 
ethnic groups.1148
Plasma concentrations of DHEA, DHEAS, androstenedione, 
T, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and Δ5-17P are usually comparable 
to values normally found in pubic hair stage 2. However, some 
patients have low concentrations of adrenal androgens, indicating 
that conversion of these molecules to more active androgens or 
a rise in AR activity is as important in the development of pre­
mature pubarche as the adrenal androgen secretion itself.1145 An 
ACTH stimulation increases serum DHEA and DHEAS concen­
trations and the excretion of urinary 17-ketosteroids, but the con­
centrations of plasma 17-hydroxyprogesterone and Δ5-17P do not 
increase to the levels found in individuals with virilizing forms of 
CAH.1149 Shorter AR gene CAG number, indicative of increased 
androgen sensitivity, is reported in some girls with precocious 
adrenarche, suggesting that increased sensitivity to low androgen 
levels may be the basis rather than high androgen values per se. As 
in CAH, dexamethasone suppresses adrenal androgen and andro­
gen precursor secretion.1150
Serum gonadotropin levels in the basal state and after GnRH 
are in the prepubertal range in patients with premature adre­
narche. Premature adrenarche occurs independently of gonad­
arche and results from some unknown factor other than increased 
secretion of GnRH or ACTH. Bone age, height, and weight gain 
are slightly advanced for chronologic age, but normal adult height 
is commonly achieved, except, rarely, in some individuals with 
unusually high levels of adrenal androgens, hirsutism, acne, and a 
bone age more than 2 years advanced or 2.5 SD above the mean 
value for chronologic age.1151 In a follow-up study of 20 girls, the 
functional adrenal hyperandrogenism in premature adrenarche 
was limited to childhood.
Premature adrenarche may be considered to be a developmen­
tally regulated, normal variation in the differentiation, growth, and 
function of the ZR of the adrenal cortex, marked biochemically by 
the precocious increase in the concentration of plasma DHEAS to 
more than 40 μg/dL.11 The latter is probably related to the indepen­
dent increase of 17,20-lyase activity in the developing ZR, which 
is mediated by increased phosphorylation of serine and threonine 
residues on the CYP17 enzyme, and the increased abundance of 
cytochrome b5 and of electron-donating redox partners such as 
cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase and cytochrome b5, which are 
essential for the 17,20-lyase activity of this functional microsomal 
enzyme (see Fig. 23.4).1149 A rise in intraadrenal cortisol may inhibit 
3βHSD activity, thereby increasing DHEA according to in vitro 
evidence.1146 Nonetheless, the factors stimulating development and 
function of the ZR, independent of ACTH, remain elusive.
1118
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
The appearance of premature pubarche can be a manifesta­
tion of nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH caused by 
homozygous or compound heterozygous missense mutations in 
the CYP21 gene.1152 This condition can readily be detected by 
a plasma 17-hydroxyprogesterone above 200 ng/dL (6 nmol/L) 
in the basal state or above 2000 ng/dL or 72 nmol/L in response 
to ACTH, which is at least 10 SD above the mean value for age. 
The prevalence of nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency in children 
apparently presenting with premature adrenarche is low except in 
some ethnic groups (e.g., Hispanics, Italians, Ashkenazi Jews), in 
which the prevalence may be as high as 20% to 30%.
The cause of the observed mild deficiency in 3βHSD activity 
is unknown, but it may be multifactorial and may lead to a wide 
range in secretory capacity of the ZR. A family constellation was 
described with a dominant pattern of inheritance of elevated adre­
nal androgens and androgen precursors that manifested as prema­
ture pubarche1153; later-affected individuals developed hirsutism 
and anovulation. Several investigators joined to propose hormonal 
standards for the diagnosis of 3βHSD deficiency in cases of appar­
ent premature pubarche and stated that ACTH-stimulated Δ5-
17P values must exceed 294 nmol/L for Tanner stage 2 (17 ± 5 
nmol/L) or the ratio of Δ5-17P to cortisol (F) must be at least 
363. Studies relating genotype and hormonal analyses in basal 
and ACTH-stimulated conditions have confirmed that signifi­
cant elevations of the Δ5-17P-to-F ratio are necessary to prove 
true 3βHSD deficiency in genetically proven disease and that this 
is a rare disorder in patients presenting with putative premature 
adrenarche.1154 However, patients with a constellation of findings 
indicating PCOS may have subtler elevations of these values and 
present a picture of adrenal impairment of 3βHSD activity in the 
absence of mutations in the gene coding for the enzyme; these 
children presenting with premature pubarche are postulated to 
develop clinical PCOS at a later age.
The phenotype of premature pubarche is also associated 
with the rarer nonclassic 11β-hydroxylase deficiency. Mutation 
of HSD3B2 or HSD3B1 is an uncommon cause of premature 
pubarche, exaggerated adrenarche, and hirsutism in adolescent 
girls and women.
DHEA stimulates sebaceous gland activity,1155 and prepubertal 
acne or comedones may appear in association with elevated serum 
DHEAS concentrations in some children without the appearance 
of pubic hair, suggesting that a variant of premature adrenarche 
may manifest in this manner.275 More significant androgen effects 
(e.g., clitoral or penile enlargement, rapid growth, hirsutism, 
deepening of the voice) exclude premature adrenarche and indi­
cate a more severe form of hyperandrogenism.
Although premature adrenarche was usually considered to be a 
benign condition with no substantial long-term risk, accumulat­
ing observations indicate that girls with premature adrenarche are 
at increased risk of developing functional ovarian hyperandrogen­
ism and PCOS, hyperinsulinism, acanthosis nigricans, and dyslip­
idemia in adolescence and adult life, especially if fetal growth was 
reduced and the birth weight was low.1147 Affected girls have BMI 
values similar to those of control subjects but differing distribu­
tion of fat; they are more likely to have increased waist circumfer­
ence along with measures of insulin resistance.1156
The concept of exaggerated adrenarche was first advanced in 
relation to a postulated childhood antecedent of PCOS. It has 
been extended to include rare instances of premature adrenarche 
associated with excessive responses of Δ5-17P, DHEAS, and 
androstenedione to ACTH found in women with functional adre­
nal hyperandrogenism.
A report of a patient with premature adrenarche, advanced 
bone age, excessive acne, hyperandrogenic anovulation, very 
low DHEAS levels, and increased androgen levels demonstrated 
a mutation in PAPSS2, an enzyme that generates the sulfate 
donor 3′-phosphoadenosine-5′-phosphosulfate (PAPS), which 
is required for conversion of DHEA to DHEAS by the enzyme 
SULT2A1. Although the child was described as having prema­
ture pubarche, the androgen effects were greater than those usually 
encountered in this condition. The DHEA level was not elevated 
for age, but androstenedione was high owing to inadequate for­
mation of DHEAS that decreases the conversion of DHEA to 
androstenedione.1157 This presentation would ordinarily suggest 
an ovarian cause of the virilization, but in this index case it indi­
cates the crucial role of DHEA sulfation as a gatekeeper to human 
androgen synthesis and demonstrates that the role of DHEA sul­
fation in adrenal function is to prevent unconjugated DHEA from 
becoming available for conversion to active androgens.11 This 
monogenetic defect must be added to the differential diagnosis of 
premature adrenarche.1157 
Polycystic Ovary Disease. PCOS is the most common 
endocrine disease of reproductive-age women; it is estimated to 
affect 10% of women.1158 The hallmarks of this condition are 
hyperandrogenism, hirsutism, anovulation, amenorrhea or oli­
gomenorrhea, and insulin resistance; there is compensatory hyper­
insulinemia, with its attendant risk of major metabolic sequelae, 
including type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, an increased pro­
pensity to coronary heart disease, and, in about 50% of affected 
women, obesity. PCOS is considered equivalent to MetS in men, 
with its many manifestations in females. A 2013 review of diag­
nostic criteria supports the use of the Rotterdam criteria for diag­
nosis, noting the weakness of the method as well. Thus, diagnosis 
rests upon the presence of two of the following criteria: andro­
gen excess, ovulatory dysfunction, or polycystic ovaries.1159 Some 
prefer hyperinsulinemic androgen excess as a better indicator of the 
basis of the disorder in view of the fact that polycystic ovaries are 
not required for diagnosis.1147 Indeed, criteria for the diagnosis of 
polycystic ovary morphologic appearance may require a greater 
number of follicles (>25 on ultrasound) than recommended by 
the Rotterdam criteria, and standards may yet change.1160 The use 
of AMH in the diagnosis of PCOS is under consideration but 
remains controversial owing to differences in study criteria and in 
the assays used to report AMH values.1161 At least it can be said 
that AMH appears to correlate with polycystic appearance and 
androgen manifestations in many studies and, in the future, may 
become a diagnostic criterion.
Premature adrenarche in some populations is a risk factor for 
the later development of PCOS and functional ovarian hyperan­
drogenism in adolescent and adult women; the magnitude of this 
risk is unknown, but it appears to be rare, except in girls with a 
history of SGA.1162 However, catch-up growth after SGA may be 
as important a factor in the development of PCOS, and even pre­
maturity may be a risk. In a 770-member cohort of 8-year-olds, 
serum androstenedione and DHEAS levels were directly related 
to weight gain between 1 and 3 years and current weight and 
inversely related to birth weight.28 However, a Dutch study could 
not confirm such a relationship between the increase in premature 
adrenarche and SGA birth weight in 181 subjects born SGA com­
pared with 170 subjects born with AGA.1163
In certain ethnic groups, and especially in Black and Hispanic 
girls, there is a greater association of premature adrenarche with 
MetS (obesity, hyperinsulinism, dyslipidemia, and other factors 
that increase the risk of later coronary heart disease) and the 
1119
CHAPTER 23  Physiology and Disorders of Puberty
development of PCOS in late adolescence and early adulthood, 
especially if decreased insulin sensitivity and acanthosis nigricans 
accompany the premature adrenarche.1164
As discussed earlier, hyperinsulinism is associated with many 
metabolic and endocrine conditions and functional ovarian 
hyperandrogenism that, in some cases, is heralded by premature 
adrenarche. Lifestyle modification is the primary approach to the 
treatment of PCOS, and although success is achievable,1165 the 
failure rate is substantial. Oral contraceptives are often invoked 
but may be considered to treat the effects rather than the cause 
based on insulin resistance and excessive adiposity; nonetheless, 
the use of oral contraceptives with progestational and antian­
drogen effects can regulate menstrual periods,1148 although 
long-term studies of progestin-only contraceptives in teenagers 
with PCOS are lacking.1166 Therapeutic approaches to reduce 
insulin resistance, especially the use of insulin sensitizers, have 
been introduced into the therapy for PCOS. The most widely 
used drug is metformin because of its low prevalence of adverse 
effects and therapeutic efficacy. Substantial data support the 
safety and efficacy of its use in adolescents with insulin resis­
tance,1148 although metformin is not FDA approved for such 
use. Although flutamide in higher doses has caused hepatotoxic­
ity, low-dose flutamide (1 mg/kg) is reportedly effective in hir­
sute women,1167 but its use is not recommended by the majority 
of experts due to reported adverse hepatic effects in some studies, 
even with low dosage.
In a trial involving girls just past menarche who had a history 
of low birth weight and premature adrenarche and were therefore 
at risk for the development of PCOS, metformin prevented this 
predicted course.1162 Treatment of 8-year-old girls who had simi­
lar risk factors appeared to diminish the risk during short-term 
studies. The beneficial effects on body composition, dyslipidemia, 
insulin resistance, and other parameters were present only during 
therapy; they reverted to increased risk factors after discontinua­
tion of metformin. Weight loss is documented with the combina­
tion of metformin and oral contraceptives.1168
The Endocrine Society recommends the oral contraceptive pill 
(OCP) as the first-line treatment for PCOS. 
Adolescent Gynecomastia. Normal boys, usually in the early 
stages of puberty, may have either unilateral breast enlargement 
(∼25% of boys) or bilateral breast enlargement (∼50%–65% of 
boys to varying degrees); this commonly occurs between chrono­
logic ages 14 and 14.5 years or with pubic hair stages 3 and 4.1169 
The physical exam aims to detect glandular tissue, but because of 
the epidemic of childhood and adolescence obesity, differentiation 
of glandular tissue from adipose tissue has become more difficult. 
“Pinching” the tissue under the areole between the thumb and 
forefinger and comparing this to other areas of the chest helps in 
the determination of glandular tissue.1170 After such palpation, 
determination of serum prolactin might be misleadingly high, so 
blood samples must be taken before or well after.
In affected boys, the plasma concentrations of T and estrogen 
are normal for their stage of puberty. Some have suggested that 
the ratio of estrogen to androgen or an increase in the ratio of T to 
dihydrotestosterone is a cause. In a prospective study, adolescent 
boys with gynecomastia had a lower mean FT concentration, lower 
weight, higher plasma SHBG levels, and a tendency toward earlier 
onset of puberty and more rapid progression through puberty.1171 
In one study, a significant decrease in the concentration ratio of 
plasma androstenedione to estrone and E2 and a similarly low 
ratio of DHEAS to estrone and E2 were described in boys with 
pubertal gynecomastia who had normal ratios of plasma estrone 
and E2 to T. It was postulated that decreased adrenal production 
of androgens or (more likely) increased peripheral conversion of 
adrenal androgens to estrogens was a factor in the development of 
pubertal gynecomastia.1172
Tamoxifen, an ER antagonist, is the most extensively studied 
pharmacologic therapy for pubertal gynecomastia. It seems to be 
effective, with no significant side effects, with only a short dura­
tion of therapy of up to 6 months. However, randomized con­
trolled trials are currently missing and are warranted to confirm 
its efficacy.1173
Pubertal gynecomastia is due to ductular proliferation in 
fibrous connective tissue.1174 The condition usually resolves spon­
taneously within 1 to 2 years after onset, and reassurance and con­
tinued observation are often adequate treatment. Nevertheless, 
some boys have conspicuous gynecomastia, and if it lasts longer 
than 2 years (5%–20% in various studies), it is likely to become 
permanent. These children may have sufficient psychologic distress 
to warrant a reduction mammoplasty. Indeed, the psychologic 
stress appears unrelated to the duration or severity, and counseling 
should be considered in appropriate boys.1175 Liposuction is an 
alternative approach, but its efficacy in adolescent gynecomastia 
remains to be established. Untreated persistent gynecomastia per­
sists into adulthood. The histologic examination of physiologic 
gynecomastia tissue rarely reveals carcinoma, so routine disease 
examination may be unnecessary.1176
Gynecomastia is a component of Klinefelter syndrome, anor­
chia, primary and secondary hypogonadism, biosynthetic defects 
in T synthesis, increased aromatase activity in adipose and other 
tissues (aromatase excess syndrome),1177 SC tumors, and adven­
titious exposure to estrogens in meat or cosmetics, as well as 
variants of the androgen resistance syndromes, including Rose­
water syndrome (familial hypogonadism and gynecomastia) and 
Reifenstein syndrome (hypospadias, hypogonadism, and gyne­
comastia). These disorders usually have characteristic findings 
or environmental circumstances that allow ready differentiation 
from the normal gynecomastia of puberty. Gynecomastia has been 
described in association with the administration of drugs such as 
cimetidine, spironolactone, digitalis, atypical antipsychotics, and 
phenothiazines; with GH therapy; and with the use of marijuana. 
The aromatase excess syndrome is described earlier. 
Macroorchidism. Macroorchidism is defined as testes twice 
the normal size for age without androgenization. It is a rare mani­
festation of McCune-Albright syndrome1178 and an occasional 
finding in prepubertal boys with long-standing primary hypothy­
roidism (see discussion of Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome). This 
form of testicular enlargement appears to result from increased 
FSH secretion, independent of a pubertal increase in LH secretion 
or a pubertal LH response to GnRH. Testicular adrenal rests in 
CAH can cause bilateral macroorchidism, usually with nodules, 
as can lymphoma. In McCune-Albright syndrome, an activating 
mutation in the Gsα gene primarily expressed in the SCs can cause 
macroorchidism as a result of SC proliferation and hyperfunc­
tion with increased concentration of serum inhibin B and AMH 
but without increased T levels due to LC hyperplasia, elevated 
gonadotropins, or signs of puberty.44 Macroorchidism is a feature 
of severe aromatase deficiency in young male adults369 and in men 
with an FSH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma. Bilateral mega­
lotestis (TV, 26 mL) in adults can occur as a normal variant. One 
may speculate that some instances of bilateral macroorchidism are 
the result of a heterozygous constitutive activating mutation of 
the FSH receptor. As noted earlier, prepubertal enlargement of the 
testes was reported with a single-base-pair deletion at codon 434 
1120
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
(1301delT) of the NR0B1/DAX1 gene and led to prepubertal T 
and gonadotropin values.1042
Immunoglobulin superfamily 1 (IGSF1) gene stimulates 
transcription of the TRH receptor by decreasing activity of the 
TGFβ1-Smad signaling pathway while increasing synthesis and 
biopotency of TSH; it also downregulates the activin-Smad path­
way so that FSHB decreases. Thus, with mutations in the IGSF1 
gene, central hypothyroidism and macroorchidism develop.1179
Testes may enlarge during treatment with AIs.
Fragile X syndrome is associated with developmental delay, 
a long face and large prominent ears, and macroorchidism in 
80% of affected pubertal boys. Macroorchidism may be evident 
only after careful measurements. The enlarged testes are caused 
by increased interstitial volume and excessive connective tissue, 
including increased peritubular collagen fibers, rather than by an 
increase in the seminiferous tubules. Enlargement of the testes 
is demonstrable in the prepubertal period in most patients with 
fragile X syndrome, but the onset of true macroorchidism (>4 cm) 
occurs only in the later prepubertal period.1180
Decreased uterine size is found in patients with Turner syn­
drome,1181 childhood exposure to radiotherapy, and abnormalities 
in HOX and WNT gene expression; maternal cigarette smok­
ing can decrease uterine size at adolescence. Smaller uterine size 
is possibly associated with an increased risk of miscarriage and 
failed implantation.1182 Uterine ultrasonography measurements 
can assist the clinician in differentiating isolated premature the­
larche from true CPP. The addition of color Doppler studies may 
improve diagnostic accuracy of this test, based on findings of 
lower uterine artery impedance in girls with established CPP.1183

KEY POINTS
 • 
Transgender and gender-diverse people have gender identities 
that differ from the gender implied by their sex designated 
(assigned) at birth.
 • 
Biological, environmental, and cultural factors likely influence 
one’s gender identity.
 • 
Youth with a gender identity that is not aligned with their 
sex designated at birth seeking medical/surgical transition-
related care should undergo a comprehensive biopsychosocial 
assessment by a qualified mental health/gender specialist.
 • 
Youth deemed eligible to initiate hormone therapy generally 
start with gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists at 
Tanner stage 2 to halt further pubertal progression, and at the 
appropriate time, they start gender-affirming hormone therapy 
that is aligned with the affirmed gender.
 • 
Transfeminine adults with a gender identity that is not aligned 
with their sex designated at birth will start on a regimen of 
estrogen in combination with androgen-lowering medications.
 • 
Transmasculine adults with a gender identity that is not aligned 
with their sex designated at birth will start on testosterone 
therapy.
 • 
The presence or absence of gender-affirming hormone therapy 
can affect surgical outcomes for those who seek gender-
affirming surgeries, and hormone providers should be familiar 
with these implications.
 • 
Short-term data suggest that pubertal suppression and gender-
affirming hormone treatment are effective in improving mood 
and quality of life in transgender and gender-diverse youth. 
Longer-term data are needed to confirm that these therapies 
continue to have a positive impact through adulthood without 
adverse events.
 • 
The long-term risks of gender-affirming hormone therapy are 
relatively few when hormone levels remain in the physiologic 
range; however, monitoring of potential adverse events is still 
recommended until long-term risks can be better ascertained.
24
Transgender Endocrinology
ABBY WALCH, STEPHEN M. ROSENTHAL, JENS U. BERLI, 
AND VIN TANGPRICHA
Introduction
During the past decade there has been increasing awareness of indi­
viduals whose gender identity is not aligned with their sex designated 
at birth. Concurrently, there has been an increasing number of trans­
gender and gender-diverse (TGD)/gender-incongruent individuals 
seeking medical services to enable development of physical sex charac­
teristics consistent with their gender identity. This chapter will review 
relevant terminology/definitions, diagnosis and prevalence of gender 
dysphoria (GD), mental health comorbidities, studies that shed light 
on the biological determinants of gender identity, current treatment 
models, barriers to care, and priorities for research.
Definitions and Diagnosis of Gender Dysphoria
Terminology and definitions used in this chapter are summarized 
in Table 24.1. 
Prevalence
Based on state-level population-based surveys, a 2022 report from 
the Williams Institute of the University of California–Los Angeles 
School of Law indicated that 0.5% of U.S. adults and 1.4% of 
youth age 13 to 17 years identify as transgender.1 A 2016 inter­
national review reports transgender prevalence estimates ranging 
from 0.5% to 1.3% of birth-assigned males and from 0.4% to 
1.2% of birth-assigned females, representing an estimate of 25 
million transgender people worldwide.2 Of note, there has been 
a significant increase in the number of referrals to gender clinics 
and a striking inversion in the sex ratio of adolescents presenting 
with GD, with a predominance of birth-assigned females in recent 
years.3–8 Despite these trends, a recent study based on a biennial 
survey of high school students indicated that the sex-assigned-at-
birth ratio of TGD adolescents does not appear to favor birth-
designated females in the United States.9 
1122
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
Biological Determinants of Gender Identity
Compelling data have emerged supporting the concept that 
gender identity is not simply a psychosocial construct; rather, it 
reflects a complex interplay of biological, environmental, and cul­
tural factors.10 Studies that shed light on biological determinants 
of gender identity are derived principally from three biomedical 
disciplines: genetics, endocrinology, and neuroscience, highlights 
of which are summarized here. The intent in focusing on biologi­
cal underpinnings of gender identity is not to pathologize or to 
identify a mechanism that can be “fixed.” Instead, the purpose 
is to underscore biological variation in gender identity, which 
may in turn destigmatize gender-variant individuals and decrease 
health disparities for gender minorities.
With respect to genetics, a recent study notes heritability esti­
mates for gender identity in the range of 30% to 60%.11 A study 
in twins supporting a role for genetic factors in gender identity 
outcome demonstrated a 39.1% concordance for what was previ­
ously called gender identity disorder (based on the Diagnostic and 
Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th ed. [DSM-IV] criteria) 
in 23 monozygotic female and male twin pairs but no concor­
dance in 21 same-sex dizygotic female and male twin pairs or in 7 
opposite-sex twin pairs.12 A number of investigators have sought 
to identify polymorphisms in specific candidate genes (e.g., the 
androgen receptor, estrogen receptor, and aromatase) that may be 
more prevalent in TGD individuals in comparison to a control 
population of nontransgender individuals. Early study findings 
were inconsistent and lacked strong statistical significance.13–16 
However, more recent studies have identified certain polymor­
phisms and unique gene variants involving the androgen and 
estrogen receptors in TGD individuals. These findings support the 
hypothesis that multiple complex gene interactions influence and 
contribute to variations in gender identity.17–20
With respect to endocrine considerations, it should be noted 
that most TGD individuals do not have a disorder/difference of 
sex development (DSD). However, studies in individuals with 
DSDs have informed our understanding of the role that hor­
mones (prenatal/early neonatal androgens, in particular) may 
contribute to gender identity development. For example, in stud­
ies of 46,XX individuals raised female with virilizing congenital 
adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) caused by mutations in the CYP21A2 
gene, there was a greater degree of transgender identity (female to 
male) in comparison to what would be expected based on preva­
lence estimates in a control population.21,22 In a meta-analysis of 
250 adults with this condition raised female, although nearly 95% 
accepted a female gender identity, 5.2% reported either a male 
gender identity or GD.22 This rate is higher than what would be 
expected for a transgender prevalence of 0.5% to 1.4% in recent 
population estimates.1 A relationship between severity of disease 
and gender identity outcome was demonstrated in a study of adult 
46,XX individuals with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency: 3 of the 
42 patients (7.1%) with the salt-wasting form had GD; no GD 
Definitions of Relevant Terminology
Term
Definition
Cisgender
Gender identity and physical sex characteristics are in alignment (“congruent”).
Gender affirmation
The process during which TGD individuals change their physical, social, and/or legal characteristics consistent with their affirmed 
gender identity. Prepubertal children may choose to transition socially.
Gender-affirming 
hormone treatment
Medical therapy to reduce endogenous sex hormone levels and, subsequently, the secondary sex characteristics of the individual’s 
sex designated at birth and to replace endogenous sex hormones with exogenous sex hormones for phenotypic transition to bring 
the body into alignment with an individual’s gender identity.
Gender-affirming 
surgery
Surgeries performed to allow for phenotypic transition to bring the body into alignment with an individual’s gender identity.
Gender dysphoria
Distress and unease experienced because of gender incongruence.
Gender expression
External manifestations of gender (e.g., choice of name, pronouns, clothing, or haircut).
Gender identity
One’s internal, deeply held sense of gender. Most people have a gender identity of man or woman (or boy or girl), but gender identity 
is not always binary, nor is it visible to others.
Gender role
Behaviors, attitudes, and personality traits that a society (in a given culture and historical period) designates as masculine or 
feminine.
Nonbinary
Term to describe individuals with gender identities that are not exclusively male or female.
Sex designated at 
birth
Usually based on physical or genetic attributes (e.g., external and internal genitalia, gonads, and sex chromosomes).
Transgender/
gender diverse 
(TGD)/gender 
incongruence
This is an umbrella term used when gender identity differs from the gender implied based on the sex designated at birth. Gender 
incongruence is the term used in the International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Edition (ICD-11). Not all individuals with 
gender incongruence have gender dysphoria or seek treatment.
Transgender female
An individual designated male at birth who identifies as female.
Transgender male
An individual designated female at birth who identifies as male.

(14.4%) experienced a “gender change,” 25 of whom experienced 
this before puberty.24 This gender change was actually a sex reas­

and predating the child’s awareness of their gender identity.10,24 A 
role for prenatal/early natal androgens in gender identity develop­
ment is also supported by studies in a variety of other hormonal 
and nonhormonal DSDs, as recently reviewed.10
With respect to brain and gender identity, some studies in 
transgender individuals carried out before treatment with gender-
affirming hormone therapy have demonstrated that some sexually 
dimorphic structures (both gray and white matter) are more closely 
aligned with a person’s gender identity than with their physical sex 
characteristics.25–27 A more recent study analyzing structural MRI 
data found that transgender persons have a unique brain phenotype 
that differs significantly compared to cisgender persons rather than 
being shifted toward either end of the binary gender spectrum.28 
In addition, some functional studies (e.g., analysis of hypothalamic 
blood flow in response to smelling odorous compounds or brain-
imaging studies carried out during mental rotation tasks) have dem­
onstrated that patterns typically observed to be sexually dimorphic 
were more closely aligned with gender identity than with physical 
sex characteristics, even before cross-sex hormone treatment in both 
transgender adults and adolescents.29–32 
Mental Health Considerations and Care of 
Transgender Youth
TGD youth are at increased risk for internalizing disorders, 
including an increased prevalence of anxiety, depression, 
and suicidal ideation, and are at increased risk for suicide 
attempts.10,33–39 Notably, early-pubertal TGD youth present­
ing for gender-affirming medical care had better baseline mental 
health compared to those presenting at later stages of puberty, 
pointing to the potential benefits of accessing gender-affirming 
care earlier in life.40,41 With respect to the impact of family sup­
port, TGD youth had greater positive self-esteem and life satis­
faction, as well as lesser anxiety and fewer suicide attempts, in 
comparison to those individuals whose parents were not sup­
portive.42 Such studies support the concept that many of the 
mental health challenges faced by TGD youth are not intrinsic 
to being transgender but rather are largely a consequence of lack 
of societal acceptance.10
GD that either worsens or emerges with onset of physical 
puberty implies a high likelihood of a transgender identity dur­
ing adulthood.43 Given the complexity of GD—and of ado­
lescence itself—it is essential that youth with GD undergo a 
thorough evaluation by a qualified mental health/gender spe­
cialist. A comprehensive biopsychosocial evaluation is impor­
tant not only to determine the presence or absence of GD, 
incongruence, and diversity but also to assess for the presence 
of other mental health concerns that may co-occur.44 There is 
an association between gender incongruence and autism spec­
trum disorder.43,45–49 For these reasons, it is recommended 
that TGD adolescents maintain an ongoing relationship with 
a mental health/gender specialist to support their decision 
making about whether gender-affirming medical therapies or 
surgeries are appropriate and remain indicated throughout the 
course of treatment.44 Although the involvement of relevant 
disciplines throughout this entire process is recommended, a 
lack of availability to certain disciplines should not preclude 
timely initiation of medically necessary care.44
Based on pioneering work from the Netherlands, gender-
affirming medical care of TGD youth has been primarily 
informed by a clinical practice guideline (CPG) from the Endo­
crine Society (ES) and cosponsoring organizations and by stan­
dards of care (SOCs) from the World Professional Association 
for Transgender Health (WPATH).44,50 Not all TGD youth 
desire or require medical or surgical interventions for gender 
affirmation; however, some TGD youth may require medi­
cally necessary gender-affirming hormone therapies to achieve 
changes consistent with their gender identity, embodiment 
goals, or both.44 The approach to gender-affirming medical care 
of TGD adolescents should be tailored to meet the individual’s 
needs and dependent on their development stage and treatment 
goals while striving to minimize any potential adverse impacts of 
treatment (as discussed later in the chapter).44 The ES CPG and 
WPATH SOCs endorse the use of pubertal suppression in TGD 
adolescents who meet the criteria for GD using gonadotropin-
releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists at Tanner stage 2 of puber­
tal development (testicular volume ≥4 mL for assigned males 
at birth; initial stage of breast budding for assigned females at 
birth). Considered fully reversible treatments, GnRH agonists, 
by pausing puberty in this clinical setting, provide additional 
time for gender identity exploration without the pressure of 
continued pubertal progression and prevent irreversible develop­
ment of secondary sex characteristics associated with a puberty 
that is not aligned with the person’s gender identity.44,50 Such 
undesired physical changes include a prominent Adam’s apple, 
lowered voice, male bone configuration, and potentially tall stat­
ure in designated males at birth and, conversely, breast devel­
opment, female body habitus, and potentially short stature in 
designated females at birth.50 TGD adolescents typically expe­
rience a regression of one Tanner stage following initiation of 
GnRH agonist treatment; Tanner stage 2 breast and testicular 
development typically fully regresses.44 A recommended baseline 
and follow-up protocol for physical examination and laboratory 
monitoring during pubertal suppression is outlined in Box 24.1. 
Although GnRH agonists are the preferred option for puber­
tal suppression, this treatment is costly and often inaccessible. 
Other options for pubertal suppression include depot and oral 
progestins, which inhibit GnRH activity when given at higher 
doses.10,50,51 Table 24.2 provides select progestogens available in 
the United States.51
Adolescents who continue to meet the criteria for GD may 
request phenotypic transition with gender-affirming sex hormone 
(GAH) therapy. Although age-specific recommendations for the 
initiation of GAH therapy in adolescents with GD are not delin­
eated in the WPATH SOCs, the most recent version of the ES 
CPG recommends initiating treatment “using a gradually increas­
ing dose schedule after a multidisciplinary team of medical and 
mental health professionals has confirmed the persistence of GD/
gender incongruence and sufficient mental health capacity to give 
informed consent, which most individuals have by age 16 years.”50

Box 24.2 provides a protocol for induction of puberty, and Box 
24.3 provides recommendations for baseline and follow-up physi­
cal examination and laboratory evaluation during induction of 
puberty in such TGD adolescents who were previously treated 
with GnRH agonists for pubertal suppression.
An important change in the current ES CPG is the acknowl­
edgment that there may be compelling reasons to start GAH treat­
ment before the age of 16 years in some adolescents with GD.50 
Delaying sex hormone treatment until age 16 years in an ado­
lescent whose puberty was blocked at Tanner stage 2 could not 
only be detrimental to bone health, but also keeping someone 
suspended in an early pubertal state until this age could isolate 
the individual further from age-matched peers, with potentially 
negative consequences for emotional well-being.50
When puberty is initiated with gradually increasing doses 
of sex hormones, the initial levels will not be sufficient to sup­
press endogenous sex hormones. In individuals designated 
male at birth and treated with estrogen therapy, it is therefore 
recommended that GnRH analog treatment (or an alterna­
tive antiandrogen) be continued until gonadectomy, if such 
surgery is pursued.50 Because some transgender young adults 
may opt not to have gonadectomy, long-term studies are neces­
sary to examine the potential risks of prolonged GnRH ana­
log treatment. In individuals designated female at birth and 
treated with testosterone, GnRH analog treatment can typi­
cally be discontinued once adult testosterone levels have been 
reached.50 If uterine bleeding occurs, a progestin can be added, 
as outlined in Table 24.2.50,51
Some TGD adolescents first come to medical attention when 
they are already in the later stages of puberty or are postpubertal. 
These adolescents are treated using protocols like those used in 
TGD adults (see later discussion on hormone therapy in TGD 
adults). For some, GnRH agonists may be prescribed without 
concomitant sex steroid hormone replacement if they are unsure 
about or do not wish to begin GAH therapy.44 Certain physical 
changes, such as facial hair in TGD adolescents with functioning 
testes and breast development in TGD adolescents with func­
tioning ovaries, will not regress completely; however, any further

estradiol is associated with an increased risk for venous thromboem­
bolic disease and death from cardiovascular causes in adult studies (see 
later discussion on hormone therapy in TGD adults).
Outcomes of Current Treatment Models for TGD 
Youth and Potential Adverse Effects
Mental Health Outcomes
Increasing outcomes data support the ES CPG and WPATH SOCs 
for care of TGD youth. A study from the Netherlands evaluated the 
mental health of 55 transgender adolescents/young adults at three 
time points: before the start of GnRH agonist treatment (average 
age 13.6 years), at the start of cross-sex hormone treatment (aver­
age age 16.7 years), and 1 year after gender-reassignment surgery 
(average age 20.7 years).52 After the completion of this three-stage 
approach to care, GD was resolved, general psychological func­
tioning steadily improved, and a sense of well-being based on stan­
dardized survey results was noted to be equal to or greater than 
that seen in age-matched controls from the general population; 
none of the study participants regretted treatment.52 Several other 
studies have demonstrated that access to gender-affirming medical 
care during adolescence, including GnRH agonists for pubertal 
suppression and GAH therapy, is associated with improvement 
in body image, quality of life, anxiety, depression, and suicidal 
ideation.53–57 The largest observational study of TGD adolescents 
and young adults in the United States (n = 315, age 12–20 years) 
assessing the mental health impact of gender-affirming medical 
care demonstrated significant improvements in psychosocial func­
tioning, with decreases in depression and anxiety and increases 
in appearance congruence (the degree to which physical charac­
teristics align with gender identity), positive affect, and life sat­
isfaction.58 Those who access care at earlier pubertal stages and 
younger ages have better mental health outcomes compared to 
those who access care at older ages or not at all.56,57 
Potential Adverse Effects of Gender-Affirming Medical 
Care in Transgender Youth
There are potential adverse effects of pubertal suppression with 
GnRH agonists in TGD youth. The primary risks include 
impaired bone mineral density (BMD), impaired growth, com­
promised fertility, and unclear effects on brain development and 
physiologic and metabolic parameters.10,59

tal suppression without gender-affirming hormone therapy is

associated with a risk of compromised BMD.10 A 6-year lon­
gitudinal study assessed BMD in 34 transgender adolescents 
(15 transgender females, 19 transgender males) at the start of 
GnRH agonist treatment, at the start of cross-sex hormone 
treatment, and at age 22 years, following gonadectomy at a 
minimum age of 18 years (at which time GnRH agonist was 
stopped and cross-sex hormone treatment was continued). 
During the study period, there was a significant decrease in 
lumbar spine area BMD Z-scores (relative to sex designated at 
birth) in the transgender females, with a similar trend in the 
transgender males, suggesting either a delay in attainment of 
peak bone mass or an attenuation of peak bone mass itself.60 
The authors acknowledged potential study limitations, includ­
ing a relatively small number of participants, use of relatively 
low doses of gender-affirming hormones during the initial 
period of that phase of treatment, and a lack of information 
regarding vitamin D levels, dietary calcium intake, and weight-
bearing exercise, all of which can influence BMD.60
Subsequent studies have evaluated BMD in TGD adolescents 
before and after initiating pubertal suppression. At least four stud­
ies have demonstrated that TGD adolescents have BMD Z-scores 
below reference standards for sex designated at birth before ini­
tiation of GnRH agonist therapy, most notably transgender 
females.61–64 Suboptimal calcium intake, vitamin D deficiency, 
and decreased physical activity may explain, in part, the lower 
baseline BMD Z-scores.61,62 Treatment with GnRH agonist ther­
apy in TGD adolescents is associated with significant decreases in 
BMD Z-scores.62,64–66
Addition of GAH therapy in TGD adolescents treated with 
pubertal suppression results, in some cases, in an increase in BMD 
Z-scores.64,66 In one study, BMD Z-scores normalized following 
3 years of combined GnRH agonist and GAH therapy in trans­
gender males but remained below zero in transgender females.64
A 22-year follow-up study of the first described adolescent with 
GD, treated initially with GnRH agonist and subsequently with 
GAH, found that BMD was in the normal range for both sexes 
when evaluated at 35 years of age.67 Given previous study results, 
particularly during GnRH agonist treatment, it would seem impor­
tant to ensure adequate intake of calcium and vitamin D, to encour­
age weight-bearing exercise, and to routinely monitor 25(OH)D 
levels, with a goal of maintaining levels of ≥30 ng/mL.68 
Growth. Several studies have examined the impact of GnRH 
agonist and GAH on growth in transgender adolescents.69–71 In 
a retrospective cohort study of transgender female adolescents, 
height velocity decreased during treatment with GnRH agonist 
and increased during treatment with GAH.69 Although stan­
dard oral estradiol treatment (2 mg/day) resulted in adult height 
that was close to target height, high-dose oral estradiol (6 mg/
day) or ethinyl estradiol (100–200 mcg/day) reduced adult height 
by 0.9 cm (95% confidence interval [CI], –0.9 to 2.8 cm) and 
3.0 cm (95% CI, 0.2–5.8 cm), respectively.69 In a study of trans­
gender male adolescents, for those with a bone age of ≤14 years, 
height velocity decreased following GnRH agonist treatment and 
increased with GAH treatment.70 Adult height was 3.0 ± 3.6 cm 
above predicted adult height at the start of GnRH agonist treat­
ment.70 A separate study examining growth in transgender youth 
in the first year of GnRH agonist treatment demonstrated that 
those who were Tanner stage 2 or 3 at initiation of pubertal sup­
pression demonstrated a height velocity that was similar to that 
of prepubertal children.71 Transgender youth who started GnRH 
agonist treatment later in puberty (Tanner 4), however, had a 
height velocity below the prepubertal range.71 
Fertility. It is essential that an informed consent process and a 
discussion about implications for fertility precede any treatment 
of TGD youth with pubertal suppression and/or GAH. TGD 
adolescents may wish to preserve fertility, which may be compro­
mised if puberty is suppressed at an early stage and the patient 
subsequently pursues physical transition with GAH. In vitro mat­
uration of human germ cells has not yet been achieved; however, 
some families choose to freeze a section of early-pubertal gonadal 
tissue for possible future use.10 A recent study analyzed orchiec­
tomy specimens from transgender women treated with a com­
bination of estrogens and testosterone-suppressing therapy who 
underwent genital gender-affirming surgery and found immature 
germ cells present in 100% of those who initiated treatment in 
Tanner stage 2 or 3, some previously treated with GnRH agonist 
therapy, if applicable.72 This is the first study to report the pos­
sibility of retrieval and cryopreservation of testicular tissue con­
taining spermatogonial stem cells at orchiectomy in TGD people 
who initiated gender-affirming medical therapy in early puberty.72 
However, there is still no currently available technology to allow 
for in  vitro maturation of spermatogonial germ cells. The first 
successful in vivo maturation, retrieval, and cryopreservation of 
oocytes in a transgender male adolescent who initiated GnRH 
agonist therapy in early puberty and continued therapy through­
out the entire process was recently described.73 The gonadal stim­
ulation process did cause a transient period of distressing physical 
changes, including vaginal bleeding and breast development with 
depressed mood and brief passive suicidal ideation, in response.73 
Fertility preservation (through in  vivo oocyte maturation) may 
now be possible for TGD adolescents designated female at birth 
and treated with GnRH agonists starting in early puberty without 
disruption in therapy and the resulting long-term development of 
undesired physical changes associated with endogenous sex hor­
mones; more research is needed for TGD individuals designated 
male at birth in this setting.10
Late pubertal and fully pubertal adolescents have the option 
of cryopreservation of mature sperm or eggs before initiation of 
hormone therapy. More recent reports have described the poten­
tial for successful fertility in individuals designated female at 
birth treated with testosterone therapy.74 Despite advancements 
in fertility preservation techniques, use among TGD adolescents 
remains low due to cost, invasiveness of procedures, and desire not 
to delay gender-affirming medical therapies.75–77 
Brain. Few studies have thus far investigated potential adverse 
effects of GnRH agonists on the brain in TGD adolescents. 
A cross-sectional study in adolescents with GD treated with 
GnRH agonist, in comparison to untreated adolescents with 
GD, showed no significant compromise of executive function­
ing, a developmental milestone thought to reflect prefrontal 
brain activation and to be typically achieved during puberty.78 
A 28-month longitudinal study in a single pubertal transgen­
der adolescent undergoing GnRH agonist treatment reported 
a lack of significant variation in brain white matter fractional 
anisotropy, thought to be a measure of brain maturation, and 
a 9-point drop in operational memory testing after 22 months 
of pubertal suppression.79 A recent study found that the asso­
ciation between IQ pretreatment and educational achievement 
posttreatment in transgender adolescents treated with pubertal 
suppression appears to be similar to the general population.80 A 
systematic review and meta-analysis found no adverse impacts 
of hormone therapy on cognitive function in transgender young 
adults treated with hormone therapy.81 Additional longitudinal 
studies are needed to determine the impact of GnRH agonist 
1127

and GAH treatment on brain development and function in 
TGD adolescents. 
Physiologic and Metabolic Parameters. The impact of 
GnRH agonist treatment of TGD adolescents on physiologic 
and metabolic parameters has also been studied. Although vari­
able results have been reported with respect to body mass index 
(BMI), a decrease in lean body mass percentage and an increase 
in fat percentage were reported after 1 year of treatment with 
GnRH agonist in TGD adolescents.60,62,82 In an earlier study, 1 
of 27 adolescents treated with GnRH agonist developed signifi­
cant weight gain, although BMI was above the 85th percentile 
before treatment.83 A recent study demonstrated that TGD youth 
on GnRH agonist therapy have lower estimated insulin sensitiv­
ity, higher glycemic markers, and higher body fat compared to 
cisgender controls.84
Some studies have evaluated potential adverse effects of GAH 
therapy in TGD adolescents. A 2020 study found that in TGD 
youth designated male at birth, mean high-density lipoprotein 
(HDL) cholesterol levels increased after 6 months of estradiol 
treatment but decreased in TGD youth designated female at birth 
and treated with testosterone therapy; obesity attenuated the 
benefit and exacerbated the decrease in HDL levels with estra­
diol and testosterone treatments, respectively.85 Another study 
found that transmasculine adolescents treated with testosterone 
had more atherogenic lipoprotein profiles with higher low-density 
lipoprotein (LDL) and lower HDL cholesterol levels compared 
to cisgender females.86 A cross-sectional study of TGD adoles­
cents treated with GAH therapy found significant differences in 
body composition compared with cisgender controls, with TGD 
adolescents having a body composition intermediate between 
BMI-matched cisgender males and cisgender females.87 A 7-year 
follow-up study of TGD young adults treated sequentially with 
a GnRH agonist and GAH demonstrated an increased preva­
lence of obesity but was otherwise safe regarding cardiovascular 
risk.88 Aside from an increase in hemoglobin and hematocrit and 
a decrease in HDL cholesterol in TGD adolescents treated with 
testosterone, several other short-term studies in TGD adolescents 
demonstrated no clinically significant adverse effects associated 
with GAH treatment on a variety of physiologic and metabolic 
parameters.10,59,89–96 
Care of Transgender Adults
Because adults can articulate their gender identity more clearly 
than children and most adults have a gender identity that is fixed, 
any physician with the appropriate knowledge and expertise can 
manage and prescribe GAH therapy to TGD adults. Endocrinolo­
gists and other physicians with expertise should evaluate individu­
als with TGD identities for eligibility and readiness for hormone 
therapy and should serve as a liaison between mental health pro­
viders and surgeons. Endocrinologists should follow updated 
national/international guidelines on how to initiate and moni­
tor hormone therapy in TGD individuals and serve as a resource 
for medical professionals in the community. In some instances, 
co-management with an endocrinologist along with another hor­
mone prescriber may be necessary if there are other coexisting 
mental health or medical comorbidities.
The initial encounter with a TGD adult should include a his­
tory of the duration and severity of the GD (if present) and a 
careful review of chronic medical issues that can be exacerbated 
by hormone therapy. An assessment of the individual’s family and 
social support structure is important to determine if the timing 
of hormone therapy is appropriate (especially if not currently liv­
ing in the affirmed gender role) or if additional social support is 
needed before starting hormone therapy. It is important to dis­
cuss any history of depression and to assess suicide risk because 
TGD individuals are at increased risk.97,98 The prescription of an 
antidepressant medication or urgent referral to a mental health 
provider may be necessary. Finally, the endocrinologist should 
carefully review the past medical history and referral letters from 
the individual’s primary care or mental health provider to deter­
mine if any other medical risk assessments are required. It is not a 
requirement to have a mental health referral in adults as stated in 
the ES CPG50; however, in cases where the severity and duration 
of GD are not quite clear and where there may be other mental 
health concerns that affect the gender transition, a mental health 
referral may be helpful.
Follow-up visits with the endocrinologist should focus on the 
response to the GAH therapy in terms of the individual’s mood, 
GD, and embodiment goals. The endocrinologist should continue 
to assess the individual’s social support structure and environ­
ment. The endocrinologist should also assist in any legal matters 
that arise, such as providing medical statements to support gen­
der or name change and referral to surgical specialists for gender-
affirming surgery when the timing is appropriate.
Hormone therapy protocols have been developed to mimic 
the sex steroid (testosterone and estradiol) concentrations in the 
expected reference laboratory range for males and females. Many 
centers around the world have used different preparations and 
delivery methods of sex steroid hormones and adjunctive treat­
ments to achieve this goal. Over time, these protocols have been 
refined and adopted by other clinics around the world. These pro­
tocols involve careful titration of hormone doses according to the 
blood concentrations of sex steroid hormones until a steady-state 
concentration is achieved. The ES CPG recommends several dif­
ferent hormone regimens that can be used for TGD adults (Table 
24.3) and a protocol for monitoring for potential adverse events 
(Box 24.4). In general, when hormone therapy is taken under 
medical supervision, the risks of adverse events are low, likely due 
to the careful attention not to exceed supraphysiologic concentra­
tions.99 However, it is important to note that self-treatment with 
hormone therapy still remains common in countries where hor­
mones can be obtained without prescription, particularly in the 
developing world.100
Transfeminine Hormone Therapy
Estrogen
Several formations of estrogen have been used in the past, including 
synthetic estrogens (e.g., diethylstilbestrol, ethinyl estradiol), con­
jugated estrogens (Premarin), or estradiol. Estrogens can be given 
by several routes of administration, including orally, transder­
mally, or intramuscularly/subcutaneously (see Table 24.3). More 
recent studies have determined that estradiol tablets taken sublin­
gually can also be effective in raising serum estradiol levels into the 
target range.101 Studies have demonstrated that conjugated estro­
gens and synthetic estrogens are associated with increased risks of 
thromboembolism and thus are no longer recommended for use 
by the ES CPG.50 Another issue with conjugated estrogens and 
synthetic estrogens is the inability of physicians to measure these 
drugs in blood and/or estimate equivalent estradiol levels, which 
impairs efforts to avoid supraphysiologic exposure to estrogen.
Oral estradiol is the most prescribed route of administration 
of estrogen due to its convenience, cost, and relatively good safety 
1128
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
profile. The dose of oral estradiol is titrated to a serum estradiol 
range of 100 to 200 pg/mL.50,102 Liang et  al103 reported that 
oral estradiol doses in the range of 2 to 7.5 mg daily in combina­
tion with spironolactone resulted in serum estradiol concentra­
tions between 50 and 200 pg/mL in transwomen followed in the 
United States for over 3 years. Chantrapanichkul et al104 reported 
that an oral dose of estradiol between 4 to 5 mg increased serum 
estradiol concentrations to the target range of 100 to 200 pg/mL 
in transgender women followed in the United States. In trans­
women followed in the European Network for the Investigation 
of Gender Incongruence (ENIGI), oral estrogen is prescribed to 
those under age 40 at 4 mg daily in combination with cyproterone 
acetate; estradiol levels reach 100 to 200 pg/mL.105
Transdermal estrogen, presumed to be less stimulatory of 
prothrombotic proteins, is preferred in transgender women 
over the age of 40 due to the increased risk of thromboem­
bolic disease.106 In the Netherlands, all transgender women 
are switched to transdermal estrogen after age 40.107 In an 
academic endocrinology practice in Austria, 162 transwomen 
were prescribed primarily transdermal 17β-estradiol. They 
found no cases of thromboembolism after a mean follow-up 
time of 64 months.108 However, in 676 transgender women 
prescribed oral estradiol followed in the United States, only 
one person developed a thromboembolism after a mean follow-
up time of 1.9 years.109 Therefore, it is unclear at this point if 
oral or transdermal formulations are equally as safe for use in 
transgender women. There have been no head-to-head studies 
investigating these two methods of administration. However, a 
recent case-control study conducted in the UK of women with 
a diagnosis of venous thromboembolism matched to women 
without a thromboembolism found that transdermal estrogen 
preparations are associated with a lower risk of thromboembo­
lism compared to oral estrogen preparations.110 
Testosterone-Lowering Agents
Most published transfeminine hormone regimens involve the use of 
a testosterone-lowering agent in combination with estrogen therapy 
(see Table 24.3). Testosterone-lowering agents allow for estrogen 
therapy to induce secondary sex characteristics unopposed from the 
actions of testosterone, and thus a lower dose of estrogen might be 
sufficient. There are three commonly prescribed testosterone-lowering 
agents: spironolactone, cyproterone acetate, and GnRH agonists.
Spironolactone is often used in the United States for its wide­
spread availability and ease of administration. It is taken orally 
once or twice a day in doses ranging from 100 to 300 mg total 
daily (see Table 24.3). Spironolactone was developed for its antago­
nism of the mineralocorticoid receptor and as a potassium-sparing 
diuretic. Less is known about the precise mechanism by which 
spironolactone lowers testosterone, but it is widely appreciated in 
cisgender men to cause gynecomastia, likely due to antagonism 
of the androgen receptors, increased clearance of testosterone, 
increased conversion of testosterone to estradiol, and direct inhibi­
tion of testosterone production.111,112 Largely retrospective studies 
based in the United States on the effectiveness of spironolactone in 
lowering testosterone concentrations in transgender women report

mixed results.103,113 Unfortunately, no prospective randomized 
controlled trial has been conducted to examine estrogen regimens 
with or without spironolactone.
In Europe and parts of Asia, cyproterone acetate has been 
commonly used as the testosterone-lowering agent. Cyproterone 
acetate is taken orally, between 10 and 25 mg daily. Cyproter­
one has progestin-like activity and lowers testosterone by lower­
ing gonadotropin levels. A recent study in transgender girls found 
that cyproterone acetate monotherapy resulted in lower gonado­
tropins and lower total and free testosterone, which were asso­
ciated with favorable physical changes, including less facial hair 
and increased breast growth.114 A randomized controlled trial of 
cyproterone acetate 25 mg daily versus spironolactone 100 mg 
daily, both in combination with estradiol 4 mg daily, found that 
cyproterone was more effective in lowering serum testosterone 
concentrations.115 However, there have been some recent con­
cerns associated with cyproterone acetate that are not seen with 
spironolactone, including increased incidence of hyperprolac­
tinemia and meningiomas.116–118 Given these potential adverse 
events from cyproterone, some centers propose using the lowest 
effective dose of cyproterone of 10 mg daily, which was found to 
be equally effective in suppressing serum testosterone levels in a 
longitudinal study.119
In the United Kingdom, GnRH agonists are primarily used to 
lower testosterone in transgender women.120 These medications 
are highly effective in lowering levels of gonadotropins and lower­
ing testosterone to nearly undetectable levels. Some of the limita­
tions of GnRH agonists are the high cost of therapy and the lack 
of long-term data with this approach. 
5α-Reductase Inhibitors
5α-Reductase inhibitors, such as finasteride or dutasteride, have 
not been routinely recommended for use in transgender women 
because they do not lower serum concentrations of testosterone, 
and they have a higher cost. In addition, there have been concerns 
regarding an increased risk of sexual dysfunction and depression, 
as reported in cisgender men.121–123 Because there is already an 
increased rate of depression and suicide in the transgender pop­
ulation,97,98 these medications should not be used as first-line 
therapies. However, 5α-reductase inhibitors may have a role in 
transgender women who have androgenic alopecia and who do 
not achieve an adequate response to spironolactone.124 
Progestins
Many transgender women request progesterone as part of their 
GAH regimen despite the lack of any high-quality data to support 
its use.125 Several websites and forums have suggested that pro­
gesterone may enhance breast development and areolar darkening 
based on anecdotal reports. A population-based survey of more 
than 100 transgender women living in New York City revealed 
that 17% of transgender women were taking progesterone.126 The 
ES CPG does not make a recommendation for the use of proges­
terone as part of a gender-affirming hormone regimen. The Guide­
lines for the Primary and Gender-Affirming Care of Transgender 
and Gender Nonbinary People by the University of California–
San Francisco (UCSF) Center of Excellence for Transgender 
Health mention the use of progesterone as a treatment option, 
with the caveat that there are limited high-quality data supporting 
its effectiveness.127 Concerns raised about the use of progester­
one include data from cisgender postmenopausal women indicat­
ing increased risk of stroke when medroxyprogesterone acetate 
is taken in combination with conjugated estrogens.125,128 There 
currently is insufficient evidence to support the use of progester­
one for transgender women.125 Physicians and other clinicians 
should discuss the known risks of progesterone with transgender 
women who ask for progesterone therapy and make a shared deci­
sion of whether a trial of progesterone is indicated. 
Transmasculine Hormone Therapy
The main hormone used for transgender men for GAH therapy 
is testosterone. Testosterone esters (cypionate or enanthate) can 
be given intramuscularly every 1 to 2 weeks or subcutaneously 
weekly (see Table 24.3).129 In a small retrospective study of 22 
transgender men who received both intramuscular and subcuta­
neous testosterone at some point during their gender transition, 
all preferred testosterone administration subcutaneously.129 Tes­
tosterone undecanoate is a longer-acting testosterone that can be 
given by intramuscular injection every 12 weeks and is also well 
tolerated among transgender men, as reported by a prospective 
study of 17 transgender men in Europe.130 Transdermal prepa­
rations of testosterone as gels or patches are also an option for 
treatment of transgender men.131 In Europe, and more recently 
in the United States, testosterone is available orally as testosterone 
undecanoate, which is not commonly prescribed because of its 
short half-life, which requires dosing two to four times daily.
The goal of the testosterone therapy is to reach serum testoster­
one concentrations in the range expected for cisgender men and 
to induce male secondary sex characteristics, including increased 
body and facial hair, deeper voice, increased muscle mass, and ces­
sation of menses (see Box 24.4). Testosterone will also reduce GD, 
improve mood, and induce physical changes that better align with 
the individual’s gender identity. 
Potential Adverse Effects of Gender-Affirming 
Sex Hormones in Transgender Adults
In general, GAH therapy is safe when prescribed under medi­
cal supervision with monitoring of circulating hormone levels 
to ensure that these values remain in the physiologic range (Box 
24.5; see also Box 24.4).99 However, there have not been any head-
to-head studies on which hormone preparations are the safest to 
use in this population, and increased risks of several conditions 
associated with GAH therapy have been identified and should be 
considered. 
Potential Risks Associated With Transfeminine 
Hormone Therapy
Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism
Thromboembolism is the most well-studied and most serious 
complication resulting from transfeminine hormone therapy, pri­
marily from estrogen. Earliest reports found a 45-fold increase 
in the expected incidence of venous thrombosis and/or pulmo­
nary embolism in Dutch transgender women taking primarily 
ethinyl estradiol and cyproterone acetate.106 After changing the 
route from oral to transdermal estrogen in transgender women 
above the age of 40, the risks of thromboembolism declined to 
20-fold.107 A more recent review of 10 cohort studies based in 
Europe and Canada found a low incidence of thromboembolism 
in transgender women on oral estradiol in the range of 2 to 4 mg 
daily or transdermal estradiol 0.1 to 0.2 mg/day.132 A cohort study 
from Austria found no thromboembolic events in 162 transgender 
women followed for a mean of 5 years exclusively treated with 
1130
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
transdermal estradiol, cyproterone acetate, and finasteride, sug­
gesting improved safety with transdermal formulations of estro­
gen.108 In a systematic review of 23 studies representing 3231 
subjects, venous thromboembolism (VTE) was found in 56 sub­
jects and had a prevalence between 0% and 5% in the individual 
studies.133 The study subjects ranged between 19 and 44 years of 
age and were followed for between 3 months and 41 years. In a 
European cohort of 214 transgender women, the cases of VTE 
before and after initiating GAH therapy increased from 9.2 cases 
to 60.7 cases per 1000.133 In a large cohort based in the United 
States of more than 7000 transgender women followed in a man­
aged health care system, the rates of VTE increased starting after 
5 years following the initiation of estrogen therapy compared to a 
reference group of cisgender men and women.134
Estrogen is likely the cause for the increased incidence of 
thromboembolism, given its known mechanism for promoting 
prothrombotic factors and evidence from clinical trials of cisgen­
der women on estrogen therapy. However, there are other factors 
that increase the risk of thromboembolism in transgender women, 
including the formulation of estrogen, the route of administration, 
postoperative state (especially following gender-affirming surgery 
and with inadequate deep vein thrombosis [DVT] prophylaxis), 
and age.132 The ES CPG recommends the use of estrogen com­
pounds that can be measured in blood and against synthetic or 
conjugated estrogens, which make monitoring blood levels diffi­
cult.50 Some authors have suggested that transgender women hold 
their estrogen therapy for a period of time before gender-affirm­
ing surgery, typically 2 to 3 weeks.132 However, Kozato et al135 
completed a single-center retrospective chart review of over 400 
transgender women who underwent primarily vaginoplasty, with 
approximately half of the cohort suspending estrogen therapy and 
the other half continuing estrogen therapy before surgery. They 
reported only one VTE in the group suspending estrogen therapy 
compared to no cases of VTE in the group continuing estrogen 
therapy to the time of surgery. Therefore, transgender women who 
receive adequate VTE prophylaxis peri- and postoperatively using 
conventional therapies such as subcutaneous heparin and lower 
extremity compression devices may not need to discontinue estro­
gen therapy. The referring physician should discuss with the gen­
der surgeon what VTE prophylaxis plans are in place to determine 
if suspending estrogen therapy outweighs the risk of continuing 
estrogen therapy. 
Myocardial Infarction and Cerebrovascular Accidents
Most cohort studies in transgender women show low rates of 
myocardial infarction (MI) or cerebrovascular accidents (CVAs). 
In the Maraka et al systematic review,133 they found only 14 MIs 
and 8 CVAs among 3231 subjects. However, in the European 
ENIGI cohort,134 the cases of MI and CVA found in transgender 
women initiating GAH therapy increased from 4.7 to 18.7 and 
23.4 per 1000, respectively. In a cohort of over 7000 transgender 
women followed in the United States, the risks of CVA appear to 
increase after 7 years following the initiation of hormone therapy, 
whereas in contrast, there does not appear to be an increase in MI 
compared to cisgender women and men. The ES CPG recom­
mends that clinicians evaluate for risk of cardiovascular disease, 
but there are no current recommendations on prevention or treat­
ment in transgender women who have risk factors.50 
Hypertriglyceridemia
In a systematic review of 29 studies, GAH therapy with estrogen 
in transgender women was associated with increased levels of tri­
glycerides by 31.9 mg/dL (95% CI, 3.9–59.9) at 24 months with 
no significant increase in LDL or HDL cholesterol for up to 24 
months.133 It is not known whether the changes in triglycerides seen 
in adult transgender women are clinically meaningful and/or result 
in an increased risk of cardiovascular disease in the long term. 
Hyperprolactinemia
Early reports of prolactinomas occurring in transgender women 
and animal studies suggesting that estrogen may induce the growth 
of lactotroph cells prompted the ES to recommend screening for 
hyperprolactinemia in transgender women.136,137 However, in the 
majority of these cases, the transgender women were also taking the 
antiandrogen cyproterone acetate. Defreyne et al117 demonstrated 
that prolactin levels declined significantly after discontinuation of 
cyproterone acetate therapy following orchiectomy. Furthermore, 
in a study conducted in Canada, transgender women who were 
prescribed cyproterone acetate had much higher increases in pro­
lactin compared to transgender women prescribed spironolactone 
as the antiandrogen drug.138 These studies suggest that cyproter­
one has a more stimulatory impact on prolactin secretion than 
estrogen. In fact, a recent study in the United States, where trans­
gender women were treated with estrogen and spironolactone,

A systematic review commissioned by WPATH suggested that
