Osteoporosis
Adequate estrogen therapy is protective against bone loss in trans­
gender women. In an early study of 20 transgender women, lower 
luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) 
concentrations (markers of estrogen adequacy) were associated with a 
lower rate of decline in bone mineral density at the lumbar spine.140 In 
a cohort of 231 transgender women, 1 year of GAH therapy resulted 
in a significant increase in BMD at the lumbar spine and hip.141 A 
recent systematic review of 13 studies representing 392 transgender 
women found that GAH therapy was associated with increased lum­
bar BMD at 12 and 24 months.142 However, despite the positive 
effects of GAH therapy on bone density, transgender women have 
been reported to have lower expected BMD before the initiation of 
hormone therapy.143 A cohort study of over 2000 transgender men 
and women and their cisgender age-matched controls found that 
fracture rates of the transgender men and women were similar to the 
rates of matched controls of the individual’s affirmed gender.144 The 
International Society for Clinical Densitometry recommends obtain­
ing baseline screening BMD testing only for transgender women who 
have risk factors for osteoporosis.145 
Breast Cancer
Transgender women have been reported to develop breast cancer 
in a few case series, raising the concern that GAH therapy may be 
associated with an increased risk of breast cancer.146 Data from the 
North American Association of Central Cancer Registries report 
increased proportional incidence ratios (PIRs) of breast cancer 
compared to cisgender men (PIR 20.7: 95% CI, 15.0–27.9) but 
lower PIRs of breast cancer compared to cisgender women (PIR 
0.2: 95% CI, 0.1–0.2). Similarly, in a large cohort of U.S. trans­
gender women followed at Kaiser Permanente, the risk of breast 
cancer was increased compared to cisgender men but the same 
compared to cisgender women.147 
Liver Dysfunction
Early reports from Dutch transgender women found elevations in 
liver enzymes in 10% (88 of 816) of the cohort initiated on GAH 
therapy. However, a third of these cases were related to hepatitis B 
infection and alcohol, and another quarter were only transient eleva­
tions lasting less than 6 months. The ES CPG initially recommended 
routine measurement of liver enzymes in transgender women, but 
subsequent reports showed that most changes in liver function due 
to GAH therapy were transient and did not result in any permanent 
liver abnormalities. A subsequent larger cohort study in the United 
States of over 9000 TGD men and women initiating GAH therapy 
did not find clinically meaningful changes in liver transaminases ala­
nine transaminase (ALT) and aspartate transaminase (AST).148 Thus, 
the recommendation for routine monitoring of liver enzymes was 
removed in the 2017 guidelines update.50,90,149,150 
Potential Risks Associated With Transmasculine 
Hormone Therapy
Erythrocytosis
GAH therapy with testosterone in transgender men is commonly 
associated with increases in red blood cell mass and hematocrit 
due to stimulation of erythropoietin.151 Several cohort studies of 
transgender men report significant increases in hemoglobin and 
hematocrit, but very few studies have demonstrated serious con­
sequences from these increases.152–155 The ES CPG recommends 
maintaining hematocrit below 55% to avoid adverse events aris­
ing from increased red cell mass.50 Some clinics have advocated 
reduction of red cell mass with phlebotomy, but there are no trials 
examining this approach in terms of improving safety.113 
Hyperlipidemia
A recent systematic review found that testosterone therapy in 
transgender men results in lowered HDL cholesterol, higher LDL 
cholesterol, and higher triglycerides.133 However, there are insuf­
ficient data to determine if this adverse pattern of lipids results in 
long-term cardiovascular events. Data from a cohort of transmas­
culine adults indicate that the risks of MI are not increased.134 
Routine pharmacologic therapy to improve lipid parameters is not 
indicated, given the available evidence in low-risk individuals. 
Uterine and Cervical Cancer
The risk of cancers of the reproductive tract in transgender men 
appears to be comparable to the risk of cisgender women; there­
fore, the ES CPG recommends screening based on remaining 
organs as recommended for the general population. Among trans­
masculine adults receiving care in the Kaiser Permanente system 
in the United States, the risk of cervical cancer was not increased 
compared to matched cisgender women.147 There were no cases of 
uterine cancer reported.
Gender-Affirming Surgery
Gender-affirming care with the goal of alleviating gender incon­
gruence is, in many cases, a multidisciplinary endeavor with hor­
mone providers, mental health professionals, and gender surgeons 
working with the patient to alleviate GD. GAH therapy signifi­
cantly alters fat composition and distribution, muscle, sebaceous 
excretions, hair cycle, and hypertrophy or hypotrophy of second­
ary sex characteristics, thereby directly affecting surgical desires, 
feasibility, and goals. Endocrinologists and other hormone provid­
ers therefore need to be familiar with the impact that endogenous 
and exogenous sex hormones, as well as potential treatment with 
pubertal suppression, may have on decisions realted to gender-
affirming surgery (GAS). 
Facial Gender-Affirming Surgery
Transmasculine individuals usually respond sufficiently to exog­
enous testosterone with facial hair growth, deeper vocal pitch, skin 
changes, and male-pattern hair loss. The structural components 
of the face, however, will not be affected, and individuals may 
rarely seek autologous or alloplastic augmentation of structural 
facial components (e.g., jaw, chin). Facial feminization surgery to 
mitigate the effects of endogenous hormonal exposure is, however, 
a frequent request. If a patient desires exogenous hormones, it is 
prudent, albeit not required, to wait until the facial fat distribution 
and connective tissue changes have taken effect.156 Osseous and 
cartilaginous reduction and repositioning allow, in combination 
with skin and fat resection, for a reduction in the most affected 
facial structures. The importance of electrolysis/laser hair removal 
cannot be understated in reducing masculine facial characteristics. 
Gender-Affirming Chest Surgery
For transfeminine patients, exogenous estrogen supplementation 
frequently is not sufficient to reach a Tanner stage 4 or 5 with full 
1132
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
development of the lower breast pole. Further, shoulder width, 
sternal width, and overall chest dimensions are not proportional to 
the mammary growth. Breast augmentation by means of lipofill­
ing or alloplastic implant placement therefore serves both to shape 
an adult breast and align overall proportions of the chest.157 With­
out exogenous hormone supplementation, breast augmentation is 
unlikely to yield an aesthetic result, and a minimum of 1 year of 
hormonal supplementation is required before surgery. Compared 
to implants in the cisgender population, gender-affirming chest 
surgery requires implants with a wider base width and volume.158
In transmasculine individuals seeking mastectomy or breast-
reductive procedures, exogenous hormonal supplementation is 
not a prerequisite. Preoperative screening for breast cancer follows 
regional/national screening guidelines. In the case of a positive 
genetic predisposition, involvement of the surgical oncologist is 
prudent. If someone is on exogenous hormones, hypertrophy of 
chest muscles and hypotrophy of glandular breast tissue can affect 
the choice of surgical technique. Although not a requirement, it 
is best to provide surgery when an individual’s body habitus is 
stable to ensure longevity of the results. Surgically, three domains 
are addressed: skin/fat, glandular tissue, and nipple-areolar com­
plex (NAC). In someone with minimal glandular tissue and good 
skin quality and NAC position, minimal scar techniques around 
the areola (periarolar, circumareolar, extended circumareolar) can 
be offered. For a majority of individuals, a formal skin excision 
with the mastectomy is required to adequately masculinize the 
chest (double incision ± nipple graft or buttonhole technique).159 
Gender-affirming mastectomy differs from oncologic resection in 
that breast capsule and/or pectoralis fascia are partially retained. 
Currently, there are no agreed-upon long-term cancer screening 
guidelines for individuals after gender-affirming mastectomy. In 
the setting of breast-reductive techniques, they follow the cisgen­
der female guidelines. 
Gender-Affirming Genital Surgery
Transfeminine individuals may seek vulvoplasty or vaginoplasty as 
part of their transition. The most frequently performed technique 
for individuals who do want a vaginal canal is the penile-inversion 
technique. The vaginal and introital lining is created using penile and 
scrotal skin flaps and grafts.160 Hair removal of the surgical flap is a 
preoperative requirement. Other variations include the use of perito­
neum for vaginal lining or, in rare cases, colonic conduits. Peritoneal 
lining and/or distant skin grafts can be used for individuals who have 
inadequate penoscrotal skin (e.g., treatment with pubertal suppres­
sion at an early stage of puberty, as discussed subsequently). Patients 
who have a vaginal canal will require lifelong dilation to maintain 
patency of the canal.161 Medical providers need to maintain aware­
ness of the presence of the prostate for routine screening.162
Transmasculine individuals seeking gender-affirming genital 
surgery have a variety of options beyond the scope of this chapter. 
There are four broad categories: metoidioplasty with or without 
urethral lengthening (use of locoregional tissue to lengthen the 
clitoral shaft and bringing the urethra up to the glans of the clito­
ris) and phalloplasty with or without urethral lengthening (use of 
distant tissue to create a phallus of adult dimensions and length­
ening the native urethra up to the phallus and connecting it to a 
neo-urethra inside the phallus). A metoidioplasty is a lower-risk 
surgery but requires a patient having sufficient clitoromegaly after 
exogenous testosterone use and/or topical dihydrotestosterone 
gel.163 For phalloplasty, exogenous testosterone is beneficial in 
providing growth of the clitoral tissue, including the urethral plate 
for urethral lengthening. Phalloplasty often requires two to four 
stages for completion and may include an erectile device place­
ment for sexual function.
Effects of Pubertal Suppression on Need for GAS 
and Effects on GAS
Suppression of pubertal hormones has tremendous benefits from 
a phenotypical alignment with gender identity.164 This can be 
particularly valuable for individuals assigned male at birth who, 
with pubertal suppression, forgo the effects that testosterone 
has on facial features, minimizing or preventing the desire for 
gender-affirming facial surgery in the future. However, pubertal 
suppression at an early stage of puberty also leads to underde­
velopment of the penoscrotal tissue, which can have an impact 
on gender-affirming genital surgery.165 Providers, patients, and 
families therefore need to be aware that future genital surgery 
may require additional tissue for vaginal lining, either through 
the use of peritoneum, distant skin grafts, or rarely, intestinal 
conduits. In individuals assigned female at birth, pubertal sup­
pression can prevent development of glandular breast tissue and 
thus the need for gender-affirming mastectomy later in life. 
Barriers to Care and Priorities for Research 
for Transgender Youth and Adults
Although there have been significant advances in our understand­
ing and management of TGD youth and adults, many questions 
remain. There are limited long-term efficacy and safety data regard­
ing current treatment models, with additional studies needed on 
the use of GnRH agonists in TGD youth younger than 12 years 
of age, GAH therapy in adolescents younger than 16 years of age, 
tailored protocols for nonbinary individuals, and long-term risks 
(>10 years) of cardiovascular disease and cancer. Questions also 
arise regarding the dose and choice of hormone therapy in elderly 
transgender adults. Furthermore, GnRH agonists and gender-
affirming sex hormones are off-label for TGD youth and adults, 
can be expensive (GnRH agonists and transdermal preparations of 
hormones, in particular), and are often denied by insurance com­
panies. In addition, although new clinical programs for the care 
of TGD youth have emerged in many parts of the world in recent 
years, there are still relatively few such programs, and patients are 
often required to travel long distances to receive care. Access to 
GAS has increased over the past decade. Evidence as to the ben­
efits of GAS in treating both GD and associated mental health 
comorbidities is rising, albeit long-term longitudinal studies using 
validated patient-reported outcome questionnaires are still lack­
ing. Formal training for medical providers is not universally avail­
able, and there is often prejudice and misunderstanding. Finally, 
myriad attempts to ban and criminalize gender-affirming medi­
cal care add further barriers to care access and will require ongo­
ing advocacy efforts.166 Further training and prospective studies 
focused on long-term safety and efficacy are needed to optimize 
health care for TGD youth and adults.

CHAPTER OUTLINE
Effect of Athletic Performance on Hormonal Systems, 1133
Performance Enhancing (Ab)use of Hormones, 1139
Transgender Persons and Sport Participation, 1145
KEY POINTS
 • 
Physical activity exerts an important influence on the 
endocrine system, modulating synthesis and secretion of 
several hormones. Almost every organ and system in the body 
is affected by physical activity and exercise, mainly mediated 
through the endocrine and neuroendocrine systems.
 • 
Exercise mode, intensity and duration, age, gender, individual 
fitness level, and environmental and psychological factors may 
affect endocrine responses to physical activity.
 • 
Several hormones influence physical performance and body 
composition, with a bidirectional interrelationship between 
exercise and hormones.
 • 
Hormone abuse has become a widespread habit among 
professional and recreational athletes. Anabolic androgenic 
steroids, growth hormone and growth hormone secretagogues, 
insulin-like growth factor 1, insulin, erythropoietin, and 
glucocorticosteroid properties are used and misused in sports. 
Specific methods to detect hormone abuse are described.
 • 
Professionals involved in sports medicine and in endocrinology 
are presented with an elucidation of the complex interactions 
between physical activity and the endocrine system. Hormone 
abuse in competitive and recreational sports exerts negative 
consequences for long-term health.
25
Hormones and Athletic Performance
FABIO LANFRANCO, EZIO GHIGO, AND CHRISTIAN J. STRASBURGER
Effect of Athletic Performance on Hormonal 
Systems
Catecholamines
Norepinephrine and epinephrine are closely coupled in their actions 
and respond rapidly to exercise to redistribute blood flow and meet 
metabolic demands. Norepinephrine increases from a resting level 
of 1.2 to 3.0 nmol/L to levels as high as 12.0 nmol/L at maximal 
exercise. Resting concentrations of epinephrine are 380 to 655 
pmol/L. With maximal exercise, epinephrine concentrations can 
increase up to 3300 pmol/L. Both these hormones progressively 
increase as workload increases.1,2 After exercise, plasma levels of cat­
echolamines return to resting levels in a matter of minutes.
Mild exercise produces little or no response in catechol­
amines, whereas at moderate exercise levels norepinephrine 
significantly increases with minimal change in circulating 
epinephrine. At intense or prolonged exercise levels both hor­
mones increase significantly. Acute, short duration maximal 
exercise can significantly increase norepinephrine and epi­
nephrine levels. This rapid response suggests that the levels are 
primarily regulated via neural release mediated by activation of 
the sympathetic nervous system. Spillover from active muscle 
during exercise appears to be the primary contributor, but the 
kidneys are a possible other source.1 Moreover, alteration in the 
ratio of norepinephrine to epinephrine, with a greater increase 
in the release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla dur­
ing exercise, suggests a possible hypothalamic mediation in the 
response to exercise.
Graded exercise produces a lower catecholamine response than 
continuous prolonged exercise. The responses are directly related 
to workload and oxygen uptake and are greater with small muscle 
groups than with large muscle groups.
Higher adrenaline response to exercise occurs in endur­
ance-trained compared with untrained subjects in response to 
intense exercise at the same relative intensity as all-out exercise. 
This higher capacity to secrete adrenaline was observed both in 
response to physical exercise and to hypoglycemia and hypoxia.3 
This phenomenon partly explains the higher physical perfor­
mance observed in trained compared with untrained subjects.
The combination of mental and physical challenges can elicit 
exacerbated catecholamine responses above that of a single chal­
lenge alone. Acute mental challenges and physical stress together 
elicit a greater catecholamine and cardiorespiratory response than 
SECTION VI C     Adulthood
1134
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
a single challenge, and this response is affected by fitness level (i.e., 
higher in individuals with higher fitness).4
Studies in women are scarce; the results are more conflicting 
than in men, and the type of physical training (aerobic or anaero­
bic) effects on catecholamine response are as yet unclear.
Epinephrine and norepinephrine are responsible for adapta­
tions both at rest and during exercise, including cardiovascular 
and respiratory adjustments and substrate mobilization and uti­
lization. Redistribution of circulation to working muscles and to 
the skin for heat loss and sweating is mediated through changes 
in catecholamines directly or indirectly via other intermediate 
hormones. Moreover, catecholamines may improve mental per­
formance that occurs through exercise.3,5 
Fluid Homeostasis–Vasopressin–Renin-
Angiotensin-Aldosterone System
The maintenance of fluid and electrolyte homeostasis during phys­
ical exercise depends on the action of arginine vasopressin (AVP), 
natriuretic peptides, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (RAA) 
axis, and catecholamines. These hormonal systems are modified 
in response to exercise, with different patterns depending on the 
amount of relative work performed, the duration of exercise, and 
the training status. Other factors influencing the response of hor­
mones to exercise include the mode of exercise, environmental 
factors, age and gender of the subjects, and several medical/physi­
ologic conditions.1,6
AVP concentrations increase during exercise up to 24 pg/mL, 
and this elevation persists for over 60 minutes following maxi­
mal exercise. The stimulus is the increase in plasma osmolality and 
reduction in blood volume. Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) and 
brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), which may be altered by exer­
cise,1 also elicit a natriuretic effect.
ANP is increased with exercise in a linear response. With pro­
longed exercise, ANP undergoes an initial increase, a subsequent 
fall, and then a reelevation of levels, persisting until completion 
of the exercise. The increase in ANP with exercise appears to be 
related to atrial stretching due to volume changes, neurologic 
inputs, and sodium intake.1
BNP response to exercise is modulated by sodium intake, 
hydration status, and hypoxia.1,7 BNP is not consistently altered 
in normal subjects in response to acute exercise except under con­
ditions of high altitude/hypoxia, whereas it increases with long-
duration exercise such as a 100-km ultramarathon.7
The RAA system responds to acute exercise with a significant 
increase of activity, and increased plasma renin activity (PRA) 
occurs following maximal exercise.1 With the increase in PRA, 
there is a concomitant elevation in angiotensin II (A-II), which 
partially mediates increased circulating aldosterone concentra­
tions up to 250 to 3300 pmol/L. Elevated levels of aldosterone 
may persist for days after the end of exercise, depending on water 
and sodium intake. The primary activator of the RAA system 
during exercise is the sympathetic nervous system. Stimulation 
of renin release is modulated by changes in renal sympathetic 
nerve activity resulting in increased local norepinephrine. The 
increase in aldosterone with exercise is assumed to be mediated 
by the increase in A-II in response to activation of the RAA sys­
tem. Other factors include sodium intake, potassium balance, 
and levels of ACTH.
In contrast with acute exercise, PRA is reduced after exercise 
training, whereas no effect is observed on serum aldosterone or 
A-II. Significant reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure 
following exercise training have been observed with no relation 
between PRA changes and changes in blood pressure.6 
Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Adrenal Axis
Glucocorticoids
Exercise of an appropriate intensity is a potent stimulus for cor­
tisol secretion.8 Glucocorticoids exert many beneficial effects in 
exercising humans, increasing the availability of metabolic sub­
strates for the need of energy of muscles, maintaining normal vas­
cular integrity and responsiveness, and protecting the organism 
from an overreaction of the immune system in the face of exercise-
induced muscle damage.9
During acute exercise, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal 
(HPA) axis responds to numerous stimuli demonstrating the regu­
latory and integrative functions of the HPA axis: neuronal homeo­
static signals (chemoreceptor, baroreceptor, and osmoreceptor 
stimulation), circulating homeostatic signals (glucose, leptin, and 
ANP), and inflammatory signals (interleukin 1, interleukin 6, and 
tumor necrosis factor α).10
In humans, repeated brachial blood samplings have shown 
that the dynamics of HPA axis activation during exercise associ­
ate stimulation of hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone 
(CRH) and AVP secretion (with a prominent role of CRH), syn­
thesis, and release of ACTH from pituitary corticotroph cells pre­
ceding the increase of cortisol.11
Response to Endurance Exercise. Two major factors modu­
late the HPA axis response to endurance exercise: the intensity 
and the duration of exercise.9,11 The minimum intensity of exer­
cise necessary to produce a cortisol response from the HPA axis is 
60% of maximal oxygen uptake ( ˙Vo2 max), with a linear increase 
between the intensity of exercise and the increase in plasma cor­
tisol concentrations for exercise above 60% ˙Vo2 max.11 Below 
this intensity threshold, such as during light and prolonged exer­
cise (<60% ˙Vo2 max), ACTH and cortisol concentration may 
increase, with a duration threshold around 90 minutes of exercise 
at 40% ˙Vo2 max. These thresholds are independent of training.
A number of other factors modify the response of the HPA 
axis to physical activity. The cortisol response to exercise is modu­
lated by hypohydration, meals, and time of day. Independently 
of external thermal stress, hypohydration (up to 4.8% body mass 
loss) greatly amplifies the exercise-induced responses to cortisol to 
exercise. This enhancement probably results from increased core 
temperature and cardiovascular demand consecutive to decreased 
plasma volume.12 Meals also affect cortisol release in humans. 
Exercise performed immediately after food ingestion results in 
a blunted cortisol response to the exercise stimulus. Finally, the 
cortisol response to exercise is significantly modulated by time of 
day, which influences the incremental response (greater increase 
in the evening than in the morning), but not the peak response 
to exercise.11
Endurance training has been compared to chronic stress in 
humans. When the HPA axis is repeatedly challenged by exercise, 
humans demonstrate modifications in HPA axis activity, suggest­
ing an adapting process to endurance training. In endurance-
trained subjects, the HPA axis activity in resting conditions is 
similar to that of healthy sedentary subjects. Accordingly, 0800-
hour plasma cortisol, nycthemeral cortisol rhythm, overnight and 
24-hour urinary free cortisol, seasonal rhythmicity of cortisol 
excretion, and cortisol response to dexamethasone suppression 
test in resting endurance-trained subjects are similar to those of 
age-matched untrained subjects.11,13
1135
CHAPTER 25  Hormones and Athletic Performance
However, when the HPA axis is challenged, endurance-trained 
subjects demonstrate a decreased pituitary sensitivity to the nega­
tive feedback of glucocorticoids, which explains their capacity to 
successfully achieve a second bout of exercise separated by a short 
rest period. Different mechanisms can be involved in this adapta­
tion. At the central nervous system level, neuropeptides and cor­
ticosteroid receptors (glucocorticoid receptors, mineralocorticoid 
receptors) in the brain and anterior pituitary play a major role in 
the regulation of circulating cortisol levels. At the peripheral level, 
tissue sensitivity to glucocorticoids may also be different between 
endurance-trained and sedentary subjects.14 These adaptation 
processes function to protect the body from severe metabolic and 
immune consequences of increased cortisol levels. 
Response to Resistance Exercise. Resistance (strength) exer­
cise is also a potent stimulus to the HPA axis. In humans, a bout 
of resistance exercise acutely increases cortisol secretion and then 
plasma cortisol concentrations.15
Two major factors modulate the HPA axis response to resis­
tance exercise: the intensity and volume (sets × repetitions × inten­
sity) of the exercise performed. Resistance protocols of moderate 
to high intensity, high in volume, stressing large muscle mass, and 
using short rest intervals produce the greatest acute hormonal 
elevations (ACTH and cortisol).15
The role of cortisol during resistance exercise is multiple: meet­
ing the greater metabolic demand of resistance training, remodel­
ing of muscle in response to a bout of exercise, as cortisol regulates 
muscle protein content by inhibiting muscle protein synthesis, 
and stimulating protein degradation, likely via activation of the 
ubiquitin pathway.11 Moreover, cortisol can also influence neuro­
muscular function (i.e., neuronal activity, intracellular signaling, 
muscle force) through various rapid or short-term mechanisms. 
Mineralocorticoids
The RAA system is closely coupled and responds to acute exercise. 
PRA values increase following maximal exercise.1 Progressively 
higher increases in aldosterone levels have been observed with 
increasing degrees of exertion. Elevated levels of aldosterone may 
persist for days after the end of exercise, depending on water and 
sodium intake.1
The interaction of regulating factors involved in mediating 
the response of aldosterone include the sympathetic nervous sys­
tem, renin activity, A-II, sodium intake, potassium balance, blood 
volume reductions, and levels of ACTH.1 In contrast with acute 
exercise, PRA is reduced after endurance training, whereas serum 
aldosterone and A-II are unaltered.6 
Endorphins
Exercise influences release of β-endorphins depending on inten­
sity and duration of the physical activity. If a threshold intensity 
is exceeded, endogenous opiate levels start to increase. Incremen­
tal graded exercise tests elevate β-endorphin levels 1.5- to 7-fold. 
Circulating β-endorphins increase with an appropriate minimal 
intensity of exercise (>60% ˙Vo2 max), but this is not always the 
case.16 Instead of a critical intensity related to aerobic capacity, 
other studies associated increased β-endorphins to the lactate 
threshold.16 Moreover, other factors such as diet and immune 
function can influence β-endorphin response.
Interestingly, the psychological and physiologic stress related 
to competitive practice has been proposed to stimulate secretion 
of endorphins to counter negative effects of competitive stress.17 
A physiologic purpose of endogenous opiate increase in athletes 
could be modulation of pain and mood improvement. Overall, 
the action of endogenous opiates can be described as a reward 
system that encourages the athlete to continue physical activity. 
Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis
Female Gonadal Axis
The endocrine equilibrium that regulates reproductive function 
in women can be affected by physical and psychological factors. 
In females, short-term consequences of physical exercise on the 
hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis have not been as 
widely studied as in males. A few studies have demonstrated 
increases in total testosterone after acute bouts of resistance 
and endurance training in women.18,19 Studies evaluating acute 
changes in estradiol are challenging given that estradiol levels 
change widely during a typical menstrual cycle. Nevertheless, 
multiple investigations have found an acute increase in estradiol 
immediately after exercise.20,21 This increase in estradiol seems to 
be responsible for greater lipid and less carbohydrate oxidation 
compared to men during exercise and seems to be protective for 
muscle during the stress of exercise.22
The long-term impact of exercise and training on hormone lev­
els has been more widely studied in females, particularly in the 
setting of decreased energy availability. Women who engage in 
regular high-intensity exercise may be at risk of developing men­
strual disturbances such as delayed menarche, oligomenorrhea, 
amenorrhea, and luteal phase defects.23
Although factors such as physical and/or psychological stress 
of competition have been postulated to underlie exercise-induced 
reproductive disorders, evidence accumulated to date indicates 
that negative energy balance is the primary cause of the impair­
ment of normal reproductive function commonly observed in 
female athletes.24 The energy availability hypothesis is supported 
by endocrine observations of athletes. Amenorrheic athletes 
display low 24-hour blood glucose, low 24-hour insulin, high 
24-hour insulin-like growth factor binding protein 1 (IGFBP1),25 
loss of the leptin diurnal rhythm,26 and low T3 levels in the morn­
ing.27 Loucks et al28 found that low-energy availability reduced 
luteinizing hormone (LH) pulse frequency and increased LH 
pulse amplitude, and that exercise stress had no suppressive effect 
on LH pulsatility beyond the impact of the energy cost of exercise 
on energy availability. LH pulsatility was disrupted regardless of 
whether energy availability was reduced by extreme energy restric­
tion alone, by extreme exercise energy expenditure alone, or by a 
combination of moderate dietary energy restriction and moderate 
exercise energy expenditure. Dietary supplementation prevented 
the suppression of LH pulsatility by exercise energy expenditure.
In female athletes, low energy availability is a component of 
the female athlete triad, a term used to describe the interrelation­
ship of decreased energy availability, subsequent HPG axis inhibi­
tion leading to menstrual irregularity, and decreased bone mineral 
density.29 The triad was first described by the American College 
of Sports Medicine (ACSM) in the 1990s. In 2007, the ACSM 
published a revised position stand on the female athlete triad, 
correcting the former misunderstanding of the triad as a narrow 
syndrome consisting of disordered eating, amenorrhea, and osteo­
porosis by describing the triad more broadly as the harmful effects 
of low energy availability on menstrual function and bone mineral 
density.30 More recently, the International Olympic Committee 
(IOC) has proposed an expansion of the concept of the female 
athlete triad to include males and has coined the term relative 
energy deficiency in sport.31 This had three main purposes: (1) to 
draw awareness to the fact that energy restriction can have negative 
1136
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
consequences in men in addition to women; (2) to highlight other 
potential negative health and performance consequences of low 
energy availability in athletes besides bone problems; and (3) to 
encourage expansive research into the potential myriad effects of 
low energy availability in various populations, including Paralym­
pic athletes.
The discovery of leptin in 1994 was fundamental in clarifying 
the relationship between negative energy balance and reproductive 
dysfunction. Leptin may serve as a signal to the central nervous 
system with information on the critical amount of adipose tis­
sue stores that is necessary for gonadotropin-releasing hormone 
(GnRH) secretion and pubertal activation of the HPG axis. 
Several unfavorable metabolic situations are associated with low 
plasma leptin, increased secretion of hypothalamic neuropeptide 
Y (NPY), and hypogonadism, and a causal relationship has been 
evoked. Severe dietary restriction in juvenile female rats is asso­
ciated with low plasma leptin and sexual immaturity. Cessation 
of food restriction leads to immediate increase in plasma leptin 
followed by sexual maturation.32 Leptin administration for the 
relative leptin deficiency in women with hypothalamic amenor­
rhea improves reproductive, thyroid, and growth hormone axes 
and markers of bone formation, confirming that leptin is required 
for normal reproductive and neuroendocrine functions,33 and can 
restore ovulatory cycles.34
Impaired production of gonadotropins, which leads to luteal 
phase deficiency and anovulation, is a common hormonal finding 
with exercise-induced menstrual disturbances, but several other 
hormones may show significant alterations.
The HPA axis activation may be involved in the gonadal axis 
functional disruption during physical exercise.24
Involvement of endogenous opioid peptides and catecholestro­
gens in provoking menstrual irregularities in women athletes has 
been suggested.35
Hyperandrogenism represents a possible alternative mecha­
nism underlying oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea in some female 
athletes with menstrual disturbances.36,37 Sports that emphasize 
strength over leanness, such as swimming and rowing, are not asso­
ciated with low weight and restrictive eating patterns, yet athletes 
engaged in these sports are vulnerable to menstrual irregularities 
as well. The endocrine profile of athletes engaged in these sports 
is characterized by mildly elevated LH levels, elevated LH/follicle-
stimulating hormone ratios, and mild hyperandrogenism rather 
than hypoestrogenism. Interestingly, hyperandrogenic female ath­
letes have a more anabolic body composition and higher ˙Vo2 max 
and performance values in comparison to female athletes with 
menstrual disturbances but normal androgen concentrations.36 
Male Gonadal Axis
The effects of physical activity on the HPG axis in males vary 
with the intensity and duration of the activity, the fitness level of 
the individual, and nutritional-metabolic status. Relatively short, 
intense exercise usually increases serum testosterone levels, while 
more prolonged exercise usually decreases serum testosterone lev­
els.38,39 Increased serum testosterone levels have been reported 
during relatively strenuous free and treadmill running, weight 
training, rock climbing, and ergometer cycling.40
The testosterone response increases with increased exercise 
load.41 Similar workloads produce similar responses, regardless of 
whether the load is aerobic or anaerobic.42 Increased and decreased 
ambient temperature, altitude, and dehydration have no effect on 
testosterone response to intense exercise.43 Acute exercise-induced 
testosterone increments are also seen in older men, although the 
magnitude of elevation is smaller than that of younger men per­
forming the same exercise (i.e., ∼1 nmol/L−1 in young vs. ∼0.1 
nmol/L–1 in older men).44,45
The relationship between exercise and testosterone responses 
has been extensively reviewed in young men,39 with most studies 
suggesting that acute transient elevations in testosterone likely 
drive hormonal adaptations associated with muscle growth. For 
example, immediately following resistance exercise, serum tes­
tosterone levels peak (from 13 nmol/L−1 [resting levels] to 38 
nmol/L−1 [at ∼30 minutes]), with a concomitant upregulation 
of androgen receptor mRNA and protein content within the 
muscle.46,47 High-intensity resistance exercise seems to stimu­
late basophilic cells of the anterior pituitary to release LH from 
gonadotrophs in the anterior pituitary, which then acts as the 
primary regulator of testosterone secretion from the Leydig cells 
of the testes.48 However, early increased circulating testosterone 
levels during resistance exercise are also LH-independent and 
may be directly stimulated via increases in lactate levels induced 
by an increase in the production of cAMP in testicular tissues.49 
Other possible mechanisms responsible for the acute testoster­
one increase include hemoconcentration, reduced clearance, 
and/or increased testosterone synthesis.40 However, since the 
timing of testosterone response differs from that of other cir­
culating steroids (e.g., androstenedione and dehydroepiandros­
terone increase simultaneously with cortisol), specific testicular 
mechanisms may be involved.50 These mechanisms may include 
activation of the sympathetic system, which stimulates testicular 
testosterone production during exercise via a direct neural path­
way in some species.
Whereas the acute testosterone response returns to baseline 
rapidly after exercise and is not elevated chronically following 
repeated bouts of resistance exercise,47 acute upregulation of 
androgen receptor (AR) mRNA and protein content can last up 
to 1 to 2 days after exercise,51 thus increasing testosterone uptake 
into muscle and potentiating anabolic effects of testosterone over 
longer periods.39 The combined effects of acute testosterone eleva­
tion after exercise and sustained AR upregulation in the muscle 
may thus represent an additional mechanism through which resis­
tance exercise might regulate muscle growth.
In contrast to short-term testosterone increases, a suppression 
of serum testosterone levels occurs during and subsequent to more 
prolonged exercise, and to some extent in the hours following 
intense short-term exercise.22
A variety of systems could influence decreased testosterone 
synthesis during and subsequent to prolonged exercise. A lack 
of significant elevation in basal LH in correspondence with the 
reduced testosterone concentration has been reported, reflecting 
hypogonadotrophic-hypogonadism characteristics.52,53 Moreover, 
altered basal prolactin has been described in response to prolonged 
exercise.52,54
Leptin and ghrelin levels, which may be influenced by physical 
exercise, have been suggested to be altered in exercise-hypogonadal 
men. Acute and chronic exercise can reduce leptin concentrations, 
independent of changes in body adiposity.55,56
Ghrelin may function as a metabolic modulator of the HPG 
axis, with predominantly inhibitory effects in line with its role 
as signal of energy deficit.57 Acute and chronic exercise has been 
shown to increase ghrelin concentration levels.55
Another potential disruptive hormone to the HPG axis is 
cortisol. Direct infusion of cortisol in men results in concurrent 
declines in testosterone levels.58 However, in the hormonal profile 
1137
CHAPTER 25  Hormones and Athletic Performance
studies reporting the existence of low testosterone in trained men, 
none have reported elevated resting cortisol levels.40
Reductions in testosterone levels, if extensive and prolonged, 
can compromise health status. Relative to athletes, these reduc­
tions can negatively affect adaptation processes associated with 
skeletal muscle (i.e., myoplasticity) fundamental to exercise train­
ing progression and improved performance.59
Hormonal changes involved in overtraining and/or decreased 
energy availability can decrease testosterone production. Par­
ticipation in sports where leanness is considered a competitive 
advantage, such as running, cycling, lightweight rowing, and gym­
nastics, has been linked to lower body mass index (BMI), eating 
disorders, and low energy availability.22,29
Research in exercising men demonstrates the existence of a 
select group who, through chronic exposure to endurance exer­
cise training, have developed altered reproductive hormonal 
profiles (i.e., persistently low basal resting testosterone concen­
trations).52 In particular, most of these men exhibit clinically 
“normal” testosterone concentrations, but these concentrations 
are at the low end of normal range or even reach subclinical 
status. The health consequences of such hormonal changes are 
increased risk of abnormal spermatogenesis, male infertility, and 
compromised bone mineralization. The prevalence of such disor­
ders seems low, but studies examining this condition and its con­
sequences are few in number.52 The specific terminology used to 
refer to this condition has not been universally agreed on, and 
the phrase “the exercise-hypogonadal male” has been proposed as 
a label for this condition.60
The effects of intense training on male fertility are controver­
sial. Some studies have found changes in semen from exercise, not­
ing decreases in sperm motility, quality, and number,61,62 whereas 
others have not found such alterations.63,64 Several studies, how­
ever, did not control for energy availability. Thus, like much of 
the work in female athletes, research in male athletes will be more 
easily interpretable in the future if energy availability is accurately 
quantified and factored into the analysis.22 
Prolactin
Blood prolactin levels increase during exercise, and this response 
appears proportional to the exercise intensity.54 It is unclear 
whether a specific intensity threshold is required to induce a hor­
monal response, but most exercise above the anaerobic threshold 
initiates substantial and rapid prolactin elevations.65 Provided 
the intensity is adequate, the increase in prolactin is quite rapid. 
Nonetheless, short-term, graded exercise may result in a peak hor­
monal response after the exercise ends.
In a prolonged exercise session, the prolactin response is pro­
portional to the intensity at which it is performed. However, 
extending the duration of exercise can augment the magnitude of 
the prolactin response.54
Mechanisms underlying prolactin increase with exercise are 
unclear. Prolactin levels may increase when the anaerobic thresh­
old is reached, perhaps concomitantly with a growth hormone 
(GH) increase.66 In some situations, such as competitive sports, 
excessive emotional stress can cause an anticipatory increase in 
prolactin even before the initiation of exercise.65 Moreover, the 
prolactin increase may be related to changes in body temperature 
and dehydration, is reduced with habituation and hypoxia, and is 
unresponsive to metabolic events.67
Vigorous, high-intensity anaerobic exercise results in greater 
prolactin response than typically seen in submaximal steady-state 
aerobic exercise.42 The effect of intermittent resistance exercise on 
prolactin has not been extensively studied.
Chronic effects of exercise training on basal, resting prolactin 
levels are yet unclear. Some studies have found increases in resting 
levels, whereas others have found decreased levels.54 These con­
tradictions seem to be related to differences in training protocols 
(intensity, frequency, and duration of training sessions). 
Growth Hormone/Insulin-Like Growth 
Factor 1 Axis
In 1963, Roth et  al68 demonstrated that plasma levels of GH 
increase during exercise, and it was later shown that exercise is 
the most potent physiologic stimulus to GH release.69 Most cur­
rent knowledge regarding the GH response to exercise is based on 
studies of the effect of aerobic-type exercise.
The GH response to exercise is dependent on the duration 
and intensity of the exercise bout, the fitness level of the exer­
cising subject, the refractoriness of pituitary somatotroph cells to 
the exercise stimuli, and other environmental factors.70 Lactate 
and nitric oxide are suggested to be afferent stimulation for the 
exercise-induced GH response.71 A linear dose-response relation­
ship between exercise intensity and the GH secretory response was 
demonstrated, with escalating GH release across the range of exer­
cise intensities (25%–175% of lactate threshold).
Exercise duration should be at least 10 minutes, because 
shorter duration both below and above the lactate threshold was 
not accompanied by increases in circulating GH levels.70 GH 
begins to rise 10 to 20 minutes after commencing exercise and 
peaks at the end of it, returning to baseline values around 60 min­
utes after exercise,39 corresponding to approximately 4 half-lives 
of GH in circulation. Exercise increases the amplitude of each GH 
pulse rather than the frequency.
The nature of the exercise may also influence the GH response. 
Although continuous exercise protocols may be comparable to 
competition events, endurance-type training undertaken by many 
athletes involves intermittent or interval exertion. Comparing 
exercise at equivalent total workloads, GH levels are lower with 
continuous (40%–45% ˙Vo2 max) as opposed to interval pro­
tocols with twice the work rate for half the time, reflecting the 
greater metabolic stress and lactate levels in the latter.72 With 
resistance exercise, incremental GH responses have also been 
described.73 The important determinants appear to be the rela­
tionship between load and frequency of individual repetitions. 
Greater GH increments have been reported following “hypertro­
phy” protocols (moderate loads, high number of repetitions) than 
“strength” protocols (heavy loads, low repetitions) in both men 
and women.74
The exact mechanisms of exercise-induced GH release remain 
ill-defined but are likely driven by higher exercise intensities 
directly stimulating the anterior pituitary, facilitated via increases 
in circulating catecholamines, lactate, and nitric oxide and via 
changes in acid-base balance.71 Mechanisms involving choliner­
gic, serotoninergic, α-adrenergic, dopaminergic, and opioidergic 
pathways have also been proposed.75 The GH response to exercise 
is greater in women than in men, as is the unstimulated GH out­
put over time, and declines with aging.75
Environmental and nutritional factors, as well as some patho­
logic states, may interfere with the GH response to exercise. A 
high-fat meal inhibited the magnitude of GH response to exer­
cise, the inhibition of the exercise-induced GH response being 
correlated with circulating levels of somatostatin.76 High ambient 
1138
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
temperature may in itself increase circulating GH levels,77 whereas 
low temperature attenuates GH release.78 Obesity and polycystic 
ovarian syndrome are characterized by attenuated GH response 
to exercise.79
Exercise exerts acute effects on other components of the growth 
hormone/insulin-like growth factor 1 (GH/IGF1) axis. The effect 
of exercise on circulating IGF1 has been examined by several 
investigators with differing results depending on the intensity, 
duration, and type of exercise performed. IGF1 levels are rap­
idly increased in humans in response to exercise from ∼45 nM 
(resting levels) to 65 nM (immediately after exercise) and return 
to baseline levels ∼30 minutes after exercise, which may play an 
important role for exercise-induced hypertrophy, neurogenesis, 
and improved muscle strength with exercise training.39,80
There remains much to discover about the roles of systemic 
versus locally produced IGF1 in mediating the outcomes of resis­
tance exercise.81 It appears that local IGF1 is consistently upregu­
lated with both acute and chronic exercises, whereas in certain 
situations, circulating IGF1 may actually decrease, increase, or not 
change.81 Studies showing no change in circulating IGF1 can vary 
due to the temporal frame of measurement following stimulation 
with GH.18
Few studies have investigated the response of insulin-like 
growth factor binding proteins (IGFBPs) to exercise. IGFBP1 
levels have been shown not to change during 30 minutes of mod­
erate exercise,74 but to increase transiently after acute exercise.82 
The physiologic role of the postexercise increase in IGFBP1, given 
IGFBP1 inhibition of IGF1 metabolic actions, may be to prevent 
late hypoglycemia.
IGFBP3 levels increased with both low- and high-intensity 
exercise, and high-intensity exercise increased IGFBP3 proteoly­
sis.80 A transient increase in IGFBP3 levels in response to acute 
exercise has been confirmed by Wallace et al82 who described an 
acute increase of all components of the ternary complex, IGF1, 
IGFBP3, and the acid-labile subunit.
Functional and structural indices of fitness were correlated 
with mean overnight GH levels, growth hormone binding pro­
tein (GHBP), and serum IGF1 levels in late pubertal adolescent 
girls. Moreover, thigh muscle volume was inversely correlated with 
IGFBP2 and IGFBP4.83
The acute increase in serum GHBP in response to acute exer­
cise has been described82; because GHBP at rest acts as a damper 
on GH oscillation, postexercise GHBP increase may prolong the 
GH signal for postexercise protein synthesis, tissue repair, and 
muscle glycogen replenishment. Increased serum GHBP concen­
tration may represent either increased synthesis from the liver or 
reduced clearance.82 
Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Thyroid Axis
Exercise has effects on thyroid function, which can be viewed as 
an adaptive mechanism associated with enhanced performance, 
possibly serving to provide a better balance between energy con­
sumption and expenditure.84 Short-term incremental exercise 
(≤20 minutes) increases blood thyroid-stimulating hormone 
(TSH) levels, with a critical intensity threshold of approximately 
≥60% of ˙Vo2 max necessary to induce significant changes.54 
Even though TSH is elevated, most research involving short-
term exercise indicates that total and free T4 and T3 are not 
immediately affected.54 On the other hand, total T4 and T3 lev­
els can increase following such exercise, although these findings 
appear primarily due to exercise-induced hemoconcentration.85
The influence of more prolonged submaximal exercise 
(approaching 60 minutes) on thyroid hormones is controversial. 
Some investigations report no effect on blood TSH levels, whereas 
others have found TSH and/or free T3 to increase progressively 
with high-intensity steady-state workloads.54 These divergent 
findings are difficult to interpret due to the highly variable exercise 
sessions (i.e., different durations and intensities of exercise) and 
the varying blood sampling protocols employed.
Energy balance plays an important role in the body thyroid 
hormone response to exercise. Loucks and Heath86 found a 
decrease in T3 and free T3 along with an increase in reverse T3 
in healthy women undergoing aerobic exercise testing with low 
caloric intake. This “low T3 syndrome” was not seen in individuals 
receiving a higher caloric diet. An increase in reverse T3 concen­
trations is one of the more consistent findings, particularly when 
caloric energy deficiency is associated with exercise.84 
Insulin and Glucose Metabolism
Physical activity affects the metabolism of glucose and other 
intermediate substrates in normal subjects and in subjects with 
diabetes. The effects of exercise on carbohydrate metabolism are 
complex and involve type, intensity, and duration of exercise; 
changes in body composition; alterations in other behaviors, such 
as food intake; degree of insulin deficiency; and a complex time 
course of the glucose-insulin response.87
In normal individuals, no major alterations in blood glucose 
levels are usually seen during exercise, despite the increase in 
glucose utilization by skeletal muscle. With the onset of activity, 
activation of the α-adrenergic system results in inhibition of insu­
lin release from the pancreas. This results in increased peripheral 
lipolysis and stimulation of hepatic glucose output. As glucose lev­
els begin to fall, glucagon levels rise, further stimulating hepatic 
glucose output. Finally, as plasma glucose drops toward hypogly­
cemic levels, epinephrine is released, further stimulating hepatic 
glucose production and increasing lipolysis in the periphery. 
Increased availability of free fatty acid (FFA) for muscle metabo­
lism helps restrain the rate of glucose utilization. When one of 
these mechanisms fails, the others largely compensate, avoiding 
hypoglycemia.87
Training induces a reduction in basal insulin levels and in the 
exercise-associated changes in glucagon and insulin, increases 
insulin sensitivity at rest and in response to a glucose load, and 
reduces insulin decline during acute exercise.88 Regular exercise 
has become an integral part of the treatment recommendations 
for patients with type 2 diabetes, because it improves insulin sen­
sitivity and reduces average blood glucose concentrations.89,90 
Physical training increases insulin-stimulated glucose disposal and 
improves glucose control in type 2 diabetes. However, increased 
insulin sensitivity is rapidly lost if exercise is not performed on a 
regular basis. Exercise may also be effective in delaying or prevent­
ing development of type 2 diabetes.90,91 
Erythropoietin
Plasma erythropoietin (EPO) levels are not usually affected by 
single bouts of strenuous exercise at sea level. The lack of major 
effects of normoxic exercise on EPO production is plausible, 
because the O2 sensor in control of EPO synthesis is not located 
in the skeletal muscle or the heart but in the kidneys.92 Generally, 
there are no major differences in basal red blood cell (RBC) count, 
hematocrit (Hct), blood hemoglobin (Hb) concentration, and 
1139
CHAPTER 25  Hormones and Athletic Performance
mean corpuscular Hb concentration (MCHC) values in athletes 
compared with nonathletes. Hemoglobin mass has been described 
to be increased in elite endurance athletes.93 However, sportsmen, 
particularly in endurance sports, may present with relatively low 
Hb concentrations and Hct values. This “sports anemia” is usu­
ally a pseudoanemia due to an enlarged plasma volume. If intra­
vascular hemolysis is increased by compression, RBC lifespan is 
reduced.92 
Performance Enhancing (Ab)use of 
Hormones
Androgenic Steroids
The use of ergogenic substances by athletes continues to be a 
growing problem, and androgens are among the most frequently 
abused drugs.94 Not only classical sport disciplines are involved; 
the phenomenon is similarly widespread among bodybuilders, so 
that the drugs used have been collectively classified as “appearance 
and performance-enhancing drugs” (APEDs). The best available 
epidemiologic study of androgen abuse is a meta-analysis of 271 
studies involving 2.8 million participants. This study reported that 
men were the predominant users (6.4% vs. 1.6% in females) with 
the prevalence of androgen abuse highest among nonelite sports 
(18.4%), well ahead of athletes (13.4%), prisoners (12.4%), drug 
users (8.0%), and high school students (2.3%), compared with 
the general nonathlete population (1.0%).95
Although doping has been practiced since ancient times, often 
with placebo or toxic effects, truly effective APEDs only became 
available with the rise of modern pharmacology, and in particular, 
following the isolation and synthesis of testosterone and andro­
genic steroids (ASs). Testosterone came into clinical use shortly 
after its synthesis in 1935,96 and its first documented use for dop­
ing was by German rowers in 1952 (to maintain their marital 
duties during exhausting training) and by Russian weightlifters in 
1954 to enhance their power.
The IOC introduced antidoping regulations for the first time 
in 1967 and performed the first antidoping testing in the 1972 
Munich Olympics. In 1976, androgens were placed on the IOC 
doping list.97
Interestingly, an early and comprehensive review of previous 
results concluded that there was little evidence for supraphysi­
ologic doses of testosterone or synthetic ASs having any appre­
ciable effect on muscle size or strength in healthy men.98 However, 
many of the studies reviewed had a lack of adequate control and 
standardization. Conclusions from other reviews suggested that 
the administration of ASs could consistently result in significant 
increases in strength if male athletes satisfied certain criteria, 
including the timing of doses and dietary factors.99,100 In 1996, 
Bhasin et al101 demonstrated that administration of supraphysi­
ologic doses of testosterone in combination with exercise in male 
weightlifters induces a greater increase in muscle size and strength 
compared to exercise alone or testosterone treatment alone (i.e., 
the effects of combining supraphysiologic doses of testosterone 
with exercise are additive). Subsequent work showed that increases 
in fat-free mass and muscle size, strength, and power are highly 
dose-dependent and correlated with serum testosterone concen­
trations.102,103 In fact, significant increases in muscle strength 
occur only with doses of 300 mg per week and higher.102 The 
increase in muscle size is due to a hypertrophy that results from an 
increase in cross-sectional areas of both type I and type II muscle 
fibers and an increase in myonuclear number.104
Anabolic effects of androgens are primarily mediated through 
androgen receptor (AR) signaling. ARs are widespread in human 
tissues and organs. There are three main action mechanisms: (1) 
direct binding to AR; (2) via dihydrotestosterone (DHT) pro­
duced by the action of 5α-reductase; and (3) via estrogen recep­
tors by means of estradiol produced by CYP19 aromatase.105 ARs 
are expressed in the satellite cells and other stemlike cells in the 
interstitium of the skeletal muscle fibers.106 A growing body of 
evidence supports the hypothesis that testosterone and DHT 
promote myogenic differentiation of mesenchymal, multipotent 
stem cells and inhibit their differentiation into the adipogenic 
lineage.107,108 At normal physiologic levels of testosterone ARs 
are saturated and the ASs’ effects may be a consequence of other 
mechanisms rather than AR activation. High testosterone levels 
may have an antagonist effect on glucocorticoid receptors, leading 
to inhibition of glucose synthesis and protein catabolism. High 
AS doses may displace glucocorticoids from their receptors and 
decrease protein breakdown in muscles, leading to an increase in 
muscle mass and muscle strength. The inhibition of glucocorti­
coid action is also due to the stimulation of GH and the IGF1 
axis. In this regard, ASs induce androgen-mediated stimulation of 
GH and hepatic synthesis of IGF1, leading to muscle protein for­
mation and anabolic effects.105 Moreover, high doses of ASs exert 
an antiestrogenic effect due to downregulation of ARs and com­
petition with estrogens with their receptors. Overall, AS effects 
are the results of the amplification of testosterone and estrogen 
physiologic consequences.105
ASs used for nontherapeutic purposes include endogenous 
androgens (e.g., androstenedione, DHEA); 17β-esters of tes­
tosterone (e.g., cypionate, enanthate, heptylate, propionate, 
undecanoate, bucyclate); 17α-alkyl derivatives of testoster­
one (e.g., methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone, oxandrolone, 
stanozolol); 19-nortestosterone (nandrolone); 17β-esters of 
19-nortestosterone (e.g., decanoate, phenpropionate); 19-noran­
drostenedione and 19-norandrostenediol; and tetrahydrogestri­
none. More than 100 different ASs have been developed, most 
being used illegally, synthesized in clandestine laboratories, com­
mercialized without medical prescription or safety controls, and 
sometimes unknown to the scientific world (Box 25.1).109 An 
updated list of ASs is available at https://www.wada-ama.org/en/
content/what-is-prohibited.110
Intramuscular injections are used far more frequently than oral 
formulations. The dose of ASs used by athletes varies considerably

and is often thought to exceed 10 to 40 times the recommended 
therapeutic dose. Also, combinations of androgens are used more 
frequently than single agents. Multiple androgens may be com­
bined in a practice known as stacking, in which two or more 
androgens are added in progressively increasing doses over a 
period of several weeks. Athletes also often use a practice called 
cycling, in which weeks of androgen use are followed by periods 
of drug holiday; this routine is based on the unproven premise 
that cycling prevents desensitization to massive doses of androgen. 
Building a pyramid refers to the progressive increase in the doses 
of androgens during a cycle. Toward the end of a cycle, athletes 
may reduce the doses of androgens or switch to other drugs, such 
as human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) or aromatase inhibitors 
or estrogen antagonists, that they believe will reduce the likelihood 
of testicular suppression. In most surveys, the duration of steroid 
administration or steroid cycle lasts between 4 and 12 weeks.111
Adverse Effects. The side effects associated with AS use 
are numerous and involve multiple organ systems (Box 
25.2).94,105,112,113 Data from large observational studies suggest 
that the majority (88%–96%) of AS users experience at least one 
minor subjective side effect, including acne (40%–54%), testicu­
lar atrophy (40%–51%), gynecomastia (10%–34%), cutaneous 
striae (34%), and injection site pain (36%).114
AS-induced hypogonadism (ASIH) is common among for­
mer AS abusers and usually presents as hypogonadotropic hypo­
gonadism due to abrupt decreases in plasma androgen levels 
following AS cessation.115 Scientific data on ASIH are limited, 
but the condition is characterized by symptoms and signs of 
hypogonadism, such as testicular atrophy, low plasma testos­
terone levels, impaired spermatogenesis, erectile dysfunction, 
fatigue, decreased libido, and depressive symptoms, and is con­
sidered to resolve spontaneously within 6 to 12 months.112,113 
However, studies investigating the recovery phases of young men 
with ASIH are scanty. AS use may induce dyslipidemia, cardio­
vascular disease, insulin resistance, glucose intolerance, diabetes 
mellitus, and liver disease.105,116
AS use may also influence platelet aggregation and the myo­
cardium, although the relationship between these effects and 
cardiovascular disease is unclear. One autopsy series found that 
cardiovascular disease was widespread in AS-related deaths.117 
Another series showed that all cases had the same findings: absence 
of asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy, coronary atherosclero­
sis causing significant luminal narrowing, pulmonary thrombo­
embolism, coronary and endocavitary thrombi, and inflammatory 
infiltrates.118
Arrhythmic events following long-term administration of ASs 
were reported. Atrial fibrillation is the most frequent event, but 
ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death were described 
in the literature. The hypothesized mechanisms are proarrhyth­
mic effects of ASs, induction of myocardial ischemia, structural 
changes, and repolarization impairment.119
Liver disease is a well-documented side effect of most, but 
not all, C17α-alkylated anabolic-androgenic steroids, the excep­
tion being oxandrolone. In contrast, most non–C17α-alkylated 
steroids exert minimal hepatotoxicity. The 17α-alkyl substitution 
creates oral bioavailability but causes class-specific hepatotoxicity, 
including hepatic tumors (adenoma, carcinoma, cholangiosar­
coma, angiosarcoma), peliosis hepatis, and drug hepatotoxicity 
(usually cholestasis).94,105 Peliosis hepatis, a benign pattern of 
focal hepatic necrosis causing vascular cysts, causes hepatic and/or 
splenic enlargement and serious, even fatal, bleeding either spon­
taneously or after liver biopsy.94
Potential effects on the reproductive system include infertility 
and testicular atrophy in men, and menstrual and genital tract 
alterations and infertility in women.94,112,113 Although all ASs 
suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to some extent, result­
ing male infertility is generally reversible.120 The recovery of sper­
matogenic function has been shown to occur within 1 to 2 years 
of discontinuation of chronic AS abuse. However, there appears 
to be a delay in spermatogenic recovery with longer duration of 
androgen abuse and longer-acting formulations of androgens.121

The effects of AS use on fertility in women are unknown.112 Men­
struation is either diminished or absent in steroid users, but ovula­
tion may occur.122
Balding is common in those who use ASs that undergo 5α 
reduction to potent androgens. In some male steroid users, gyne­
comastia may be caused by increased circulating estrogen associ­
ated with the use of aromatizable androgens and/or hCG, with 
decreased clearance of circulating estrogens as a result of impaired 
hepatic function, and/or with a temporary state of hypotestostero­
nemia following AS withdrawal.116 Gynecomastia may become 
evident during or even soon after stopping androgen abuse but 
usually regresses spontaneously as testicular function recovers.94
Androgen-induced acne in adults is typically truncal but rarely 
facial, the reverse of adolescent acne. Hence, adult-onset truncal 
acne is almost pathognomonic for androgen abuse.94
Several studies have suggested that AS use may lead to sig­
nificant psychological morbidity. Anxiety, psychosis, irritability, 
increased aggression, and antisocial and violent behavior have 
been described to be associated with ASs. In addition, depen­
dence, withdrawal symptoms, and depression may accompany or 
follow the nonmedical use of ASs.94,105
Finally, there are concerns about potential effects of androgens 
on the risk of prostate disease, although long-term effects of sup­
raphysiologic doses of androgens on the risk of prostate cancer, 
benign prostatic hypertrophy, and lower urinary tract symptoms 
are still unknown.112 
Detection. Known ASs can be detected via urinalysis for a 
period of time following the last dose. Detection of the misuse 
of exogenous substances is preferably done using gas chromatog­
raphy/mass spectrometry (GC-MS).123 To improve the selectiv­
ity and sensitivity, traditional GC-MS methods are accompanied 
by high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) and/or MS/MS 
techniques.124
Endogenous androgens and their metabolites occur naturally 
in the human body, and thus specific indicators for the detection 
of the exogenous administration of these steroids are required.124 
For screening purposes, a set of urinary concentrations of several 
endogenous steroids or metabolites is determined by the GC-MS 
method used for the detection of steroid abuse. The method of 
steroid profiling was first introduced into routine doping control 
in 1983 (testosterone to epitestosterone [T/E] ratio). The most 
important steroid profile parameters in doping control are the 
ratios of T/E, androsterone/etiocholanolone, androstane/testos­
terone, and the 5α/5β forms of androstane-3,17-diol. Admin­
istration of steroids such as testosterone or its precursors (e.g., 
androstenediol, androstenedione, or DHEA) or metabolites 
(e.g., dihydrotestosterone or epitestosterone) alters one or more 
parameters of the urinary steroid profile,125 enabling screening for 
potential misuse. 
Growth Hormone
Growth hormone (GH) has been used as a drug of abuse in sport 
since the early 1980s, although the first scientific studies demon­
strating a clear-cut physiologic role for GH in adults were only 
published in the peer-reviewed medical literature in 1989.126,127
Human GH (hGH) misuse in sport predates its use in adult 
endocrinology by 10 years, although cadaveric GH had been used 
in children from the 1950s. This practice was stopped by clini­
cians (but not athletes) when cases of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease 
were discovered in patients who had previously received hGH 
for treatment of short stature. The clinical use of GH resumed 
following US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of 
the first synthetic recombinant hGH in 1985. Other formulations 
subsequently followed.128
In patients with growth hormone deficiency (GHD), multiple 
studies have demonstrated that treatment with exogenous GH 
increases lean body mass and decreases total body fat. Aerobic 
exercise capacity also improves with GH replacement in deficient 
adults.129,130 The benefits of GH replacement in deficient patients 
do not necessarily extend to healthy adults. A systematic review 
analyzed 44 randomized trials comparing GH treatment with no 
treatment to evaluate the effects of GH administration to healthy 
adults.131 Although GH increased lean body mass, strength was 
not increased. Exercise capacity may actually worsen, and adverse 
events, such as edema and fatigue, were more common with the 
use of exogenous GH.
On the other hand, a very well-controlled study showed an 
effect on strength and peak power output in a group of well-defined 
abstinent steroid abusers using recombinant hGH (rhGH).132
Interestingly, GH administration modifies protein metabolism 
in untrained individuals but is unlikely to induce a major anabolic 
effect in highly trained athletes.133 Importantly, in healthy adults, 
GH does not increase aerobic exercise capacity or muscle strength 
but improves anaerobic exercise capacity.134
Because GH is a banned substance, the doses that athletes use 
are difficult to evaluate. It has been suggested that athletes abusing 
GH take rhGH three to four times per week at a dose of 10 to 
25 IU/day (1 IU = 0.333 mg) to increase their lean body mass.135
GH abuse extends beyond professional sports and is also pres­
ent among adolescents engaged in sports in schools. This wide­
spread use presents a public health problem because GH use is 
accompanied by adverse effects, and long-term use can lead to 
serious morbidity.136
Adverse Effects. The side effects of GH treatment in GH-defi­
cient adults are well documented and include edema, arthralgias, 
myalgias, sweating, fatigue, and dizziness.128 Athletes typically 
take pharmacologic doses that are likely 10 or more times greater 
than typical replacement doses. Although the long-term adverse 
effects of these megadoses are not known at present, some insight 
may be obtained from patients with acromegaly. Acromegalic 
patients have an increased risk of insulin resistance and diabe­
tes, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, and certain forms of cancer 
(colorectal, thyroid, breast, and prostate).130,133
Finally, the risk of infections such as HIV/AIDS or hepatitis 
due to the use of nonsterile or contaminated syringes,135 as well as 
the availability on the black market of GH derived from extracts 
of human pituitary glands (a source for Creutzfeldt-Jacob disease), 
must be taken into account. 
Detection. Two different strategies have been proposed to 
detect GH doping in sports.137 For the marker method “pharma­
codynamic endpoints of GH use,” the GH-2000 and GH-2004 
consortiums identified biochemical parameters of the IGF system 
such as IGF1, IGFBP3, and the acid-labile subunit as suitable 
markers of GH use in combination with procollagen cleavage 
products that also show a clear-cut increase following GH use. 
The combination of IGF1 and the procollagen III N-terminal 
extension peptide (PIIIP) is proposed to provide a set of markers 
that allow the detection of GH abuse in athletes for up to 2 weeks 
after the last application.
The “GH-isoform method” exploits the difference in isoform 
composition between recombinant growth hormone consisting 
mostly of monomeric 22-kDa hGH while the pituitary secretes 
a variety of GH isoforms including a 20-kDa form lacking 14 
1142
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
amino acids, as well as amidated and acylated isoforms, and 
dimers, oligomers, and fragments of GH. After peripheral injec­
tion of recombinant 22-kDa hGH, the pituitary’s production of 
GH isoforms is reduced by negative feedback via IGF1. Subject­
ing serum samples to two immunoassay analyses—one of which 
is specific for 22-kDa monomeric hGH, whereas the other recog­
nizes the majority of isoforms released from the pituitary—allows 
the calculation of an isoform ratio (Fig. 25.1).
The isoform test is an excellent strategy to detect GH doping, 
provided it is administered shortly after the last GH dose (within 
24–36 hours, depending on the dose),138 realistically probably 
within 12 to 24 hours.136 Due to this short window of oppor­
tunity the test is not well suited for in-competition testing. Its 
use in unannounced out-of-competition testing, however, should 
be more successful in identifying GH abusers, and recently it has 
been used mostly in that setting.136 
GH Secretagogues
GH secretagogues act at the ghrelin receptor (also called growth 
hormone secretagogue receptor) in the hypothalamus to promote 
GH release. GH secretagogues are not intrinsically growth pro­
moting; many result in the ultimate increased production or secre­
tion of IGF1, which acts at target tissues to promote growth and 
anabolism.139
There is evidence that GH secretagogues are being used by 
athletes as an indirect method for GH doping. Secretagogues 
include GHRH and its analogues, ghrelin analogues (known 
as GH-releasing peptides) or GHS (GH secretagogues in a nar­
rower sense), and amino acids (e.g., arginine or ornithine). GH 
secretagogues have short-lived effects and provide a relatively weak 
boost in GH exposure compared with what can be achieved by 
direct GH administration.136 Nevertheless, GH secretagogues 
may be attractive to athletes who want to avoid detection because 
the GH released is endogenous and therefore not detectable by the 
GH isoform test.136
There are currently no published studies of the effects of GH 
secretagogues on performance, but investigations have shown that 
they increase GH secretion and potentially could improve athleti­
cism through this mechanism.128 
Insulin-Like Growth Factor 1
Recombinant human IGF1 (rhIGF1) is used in clinical practice, 
but a variety of IGF1 compounds and IGF1 analogues are also 
advertised on the internet, and many have been available on the 
black market for several years.140 The rationale for using rhIGF1 
as an ergogenic aid differs little from that of rhGH. The potential 
benefits include increased muscle protein synthesis, increased gly­
cogen synthesis, and FFA availability,141 but in contrast to GH, 
IGF1 is not lipolytic.
Abuse of IGF1 is more recent than that of rhGH. In fact, 
until recently, IGF1 was only available in limited supply, partly 
because there is no natural source for this hormone and partly 
because there were no pharmaceutical preparations. This situation 
changed with development of two compounds, mecasermin and 
mecasermin rinfabate. Both preparations were approved for treat­
ment of growth failure in children with severe primary IGF1 defi­
ciency or with GH gene deletion who have developed neutralizing 
GH antibodies.142
