CHAPTER 25  Hormones and Athletic Performance
IGF1 is now extensively discussed on internet bodybuilding 
forums. The list of purported benefits includes increases in muscle 
size and strength, improvements in energy and endurance, ben­
efits to the immune system, and increased bone density.140
Very few studies have been undertaken to examine effects 
of IGF1 on performance. Studies have shown a 9% increase in 
˙Vo2 max in recreational athletes following 28 days’ administra­
tion of rhIGF1/rhIGFBP3 despite no change in body composi­
tion.143 The mechanism underlying this change is unknown, but 
previous studies have shown that intravenous administration of 
rhIGF1 increased cardiac output, heart rate, and stroke volume 
in healthy adults.144 IGF1 may have a role in regulation of vas­
cular tone through alterations in nitric oxide synthesis, allowing 
improved intramuscular blood flow. Serum IGF1 correlates posi­
tively with hemoglobin concentration, which may enhance oxy­
gen delivery to exercising muscle. Finally, an anabolic effect on 
respiratory muscle strength may improve inspiratory effort.128
Adverse Effects. The adverse effects reported with mecasermin 
include hypoglycemia, jaw pain, headache, myalgias, and fluid 
retention.145 The most common adverse effects observed so far 
with the use of mecasermin rinfabate include local injection site 
erythema and lipohypertrophy, and headaches, increased liver 
and kidney size, and altered liver function tests have also been 
reported.142
It also seems reasonable to hypothesize that IGF1 could result 
in adverse effects that are similar to acromegaly.141 
Detection. At present there is no specific test to detect IGF1 
abuse, and detection of this form of doping poses many challenges. 
IGF1 is excreted in urine at low concentrations, and methods for 
measuring urinary IGF1 are complex and time-consuming. Sev­
eral factors contribute to renal clearance of IGF1: a significant 
increase in urinary IGF1 concentration is observed as part of 
the proteinuria that occurs in response to exercise. Blood sample 
collection, rather than urine, is thus required for IGF1 doping 
tests.140
The GH-2004 research group has been investigating methods 
for detection of IGF1 misuse, and a test is being developed on the 
basis of the principles of the successful GH-2000 marker method. 
Commercial immunoassays for these markers have been validated 
for antidoping purposes, but new methods, including IGF1 mea­
surement by use of mass spectrometry, are hoped to improve per­
formance of the tests and to help identify athletes who are doping 
with these peptide hormones.140,146 
Insulin
Insulin stimulates uptake of glucose into muscle and fat by 
making available an increased number of glucose transporters 
(Glut-4) at the cell membrane. However, its main effect is inhib­
itory to lipolysis, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis, and 
proteolysis.147
Insulin regulates hepatic glucose output by inhibiting gluco­
neogenesis and promoting glycogen storage. Similarly, in muscle 
cells, insulin-mediated glucose uptake enables glycogen to be syn­
thesized and stored, and for carbohydrates, rather than fatty acids 
or amino acids, to be utilized as the immediately available energy 
source for muscle contraction. Although insulin stimulates cell 
uptake of amino acids and promotes protein synthesis in a range 
of tissues at high concentrations, the major action of insulin is to 
inhibit proteolysis, which occurs at lower concentrations.141
The theoretical performance benefits of insulin are mediated 
by an increase in muscle glycogen storage and the inhibition of 
proteolysis, but these have not been demonstrated in clinical or 
scientific trials.141 Insulin has been misused to improve perfor­
mance and muscle strength, and synthetic analogues were the 
subject of several studies describing beneficial effects of biotech­
nologically modified insulins.148
Adverse Effects. The most common and serious adverse effect 
of insulin use is hypoglycemia. Most athletes who abuse insulin 
usually balance ingestion of carbohydrate when injecting rapidly 
acting insulin analogues. Another problem associated with insulin 
is weight gain, although most competitive athletes are accustomed 
to diet and follow training regimens that allow strict control over 
weight gain.141,142 
Detection. Regular and some short-acting insulins are very dif­
ficult to measure, because of the very short time one can detect a 
high concentration of insulin (half-life ∼4 minutes). A high ratio 
of insulin to C-peptide may distinguish subcutaneous regular 
insulin use from insulin-stimulating medications such as the sul­
fonylureas. These agents drive endogenous secretion of proinsulin, 
an equimolar compound composed of insulin and its connecting 
C-peptide. Both analytes may be detected in the circulation with 
commercially available immunoassays.141
Only sophisticated procedures including immunoaffinity puri­
fication followed by liquid chromatography and tandem mass 
spectrometry have enabled detection of synthetic insulins in dop­
ing control blood or urine samples.149 Insulin analogues have been 
designed to alter their pharmacokinetics by genetic substitutions 
of one or two amino acids from human insulin. These small dif­
ferences can be utilized to differentiate between native and exog­
enous insulin.142 
Erythropoietin and the Erythropoietin System
Erythropoietin (EPO) is an essential growth factor for bone mar­
row erythrocytic progenitors. Tissue hypoxia is the physiologic 
stimulus for EPO expression and erythropoiesis. EPO stimulates 
hemoglobin increase and the oxygen-carrying capacity of the 
blood.92
Successful cloning of the human EPO gene allowed for the pro­
duction of recombinant human erythropoietin (rhEPO) and later 
the approval to treat patients with anemia. More recently, several 
newer generations of EPO analogues have been produced.150
Because hemoglobin mass correlates with aerobic capacity, 
some athletes seek to increase erythropoiesis by pharmacologic 
means. Treatment with rhEPO may enhance performance by 
raising Hb concentration. When rhEPO is applied to healthy 
volunteers in low dosages, ˙Vo2 max is increased by 6% to 12% 
when Hct is raised to approximately 0.50. In addition, the time to 
exhaustion (in the laboratory) is increased by up to 50% at a given 
level of ˙Vo2 max.151 When rhEPO is discontinued, ˙Vo2 max 
remains elevated for at least 3 weeks.92
A recent systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to clar­
ify the relationship of varying treatment periods and dosages of 
rhEPO with multiple parameters of performance enhancement 
to determine the validity of its ban from competition.152 The 
authors concluded that there is low to moderate quality evidence 
suggesting that low, medium, and high doses of rhEPO may be 
more beneficial than placebo in enhancing hematologic param­
eters, pulmonary measures, and athletic performance. These ergo­
genic effects, however, are almost exclusively seen during maximal 
exercise intensities. Athletic performance mostly appears similar 
between placebo and intervention groups during submaximal 
exercise conditions, which may be more relevant to performance 
in sporting competitions, especially in endurance sports. As a 
result of its prohibited nature, there is a lack of current research 
1144
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
on effects of rhEPO in professionally trained athletes in condi­
tions that mirror actual competition.152
Several other erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) have 
been developed. Darbepoetin alfa is an rhEPO glycosylation 
analogue that was approved for use in 2002–2003 in the Euro­
pean Union and the United States. It has the same mechanism of 
action as rhEPO, binding and activating the EPO receptor, but 
it has a longer serum half-life and an increased in vivo potency. 
Another long-acting ESA is methoxy polyethylene glycol-epoe­
tin beta (methoxy PEG-epoetin beta). The half-life of methoxy 
PEG-epoetin beta amounts to 130 to 140 hours on intramuscular 
injection. The prolonged in vivo survival of darbepoetin alfa and 
methoxy PEG-epoetin beta is in part due to a reduced EPO-R 
binding affinity.153
EPO mimetic peptides (EMPs) are synthetic cyclic peptides of 
about 20 amino acids that signal through the EPO-R but show no 
sequence homology to EPO. The clinically most advanced product 
was peginesatide, a pegylated homodimer of two EMPs, initially 
approved in the United States for treatment of anemic patients 
with chronic renal failure but subsequently recalled after lethal 
acute hypersensitivity reactions occurred in several patients.153
Sotatercept (ACE-011) is a recombinant erythropoietic protein 
that increased blood Hb levels, RBC numbers, and Hct.154 How­
ever, the mechanisms underlying the effect of sotatercept or of 
analogue compounds on erythropoiesis are poorly understood.92
Expression of the EPO gene (chromosome 7q22) is under the 
control of several transcription factors, including GATA-2, which 
inhibits EPO expression. GATA antagonists are organic small 
molecule compounds that prevent GATA-2 from suppressing 
the EPO promoter. GATA antagonists may be misused in sports, 
because they have been shown to increase EPO concentrations, 
Hb levels, and endurance performance in mice, although human 
studies have not yet been reported.92,155
Hypoxia-inducible 
factor 
(HIF) 
stabilizers, 
such 
as 
α-ketoglutarate competitors, stimulate erythropoiesis by increas­
ing EPO gene expression in the kidneys and at extrarenal sites. 
Advantages of the HIF stabilizers relative to recombinant proteins 
include the oral route of administration. However, the HIFs can 
activate >1000 genes apart from EPO, including genes for proteins 
involved in tumor growth, such as vascular endothelial growth fac­
tor (VEGF). On the other hand, some of the HIF-activated genes 
encode proteins that may increase physical performance indepen­
dent from the stimulation of erythropoiesis.92 Although none of 
the HIF stabilizers have FDA approval, some are in clinical trials. 
The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) added HIF stabilizers 
to the list of banned substances in 2011, suggesting that they have 
been available on the black market for some time. The first athlete 
to test positive for an HIF stabilizer was reported in 2016.156
Synthetic oxygen carriers are a class of therapeutic agents that 
utilize modified forms of hemoglobin to circumvent free hemoglo­
bin toxicities with the aim of improving oxygen delivery in ane­
mic patients. Hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs) have 
not been demonstrated to increase athletic performance. Perfluo­
rocarbon emulsions (PFCs) seem only of benefit in the presence 
of supplemental oxygen, thus limiting their utility in endurance 
sports. Both HBOCs and PFCs have been banned by the WADA, 
and tests for their detection have been available since 2004.156
In vivo allogeneic EPO gene transfer can cause immune reac­
tions. Furthermore, antidoping research has provided techniques 
to specifically amplify intronless DNA sequences, allowing detec­
tion of small amounts of circulating transgenic DNA.157 Ex vivo 
EPO gene transfer is performed by the use of transfected autologous 
or allogeneic cells transferred from in vitro cultures into the indi­
vidual.158 However, the method has made little progress beyond 
the clinical trial phase. Taken together, for technical difficulties 
gene doping with EPO is probably not applied in sports.92
Adverse Effects. Artificially raising hemoglobin levels can 
have dangerous consequences. In contrast to the effect of 
endurance training, which results in increased plasma volume, 
administration of rhEPO produces a selective increase in red 
cell mass. If Hct exceeds 0.50, blood viscosity and cardiac 
afterload increase significantly. The main risks of erythrocyto­
sis with Hct >0.55 include heart failure, myocardial infarction, 
seizures, peripheral thromboembolic events, and pulmonary 
embolism.159 Moreover, EPO withdrawal may be implicated in 
neocytolysis, that is, hemolysis of young RBCs in the presence 
of increased Hct.160 
Detection. The authorities of sports forbade the use of EPO in 
1990, and now any analogue or mimetic is also included in the list 
of prohibited substances of the WADA. The challenge of detecting 
EPO misuse has given strength to several proposed strategies.161 
The marker methods rely on measurement of hematologic and 
serum parameters and their comparison with populational or 
individual limit values.162 An indirect test based on measurement 
of five blood parameters (reticulocyte Hct, serum EPO, Hct, 
soluble transferrin receptor, and the percentage macrocytes) was 
developed.163 The “on” model used all parameters to detect recent 
use of EPO. The “off” model used three parameters to detect EPO 
use with more retrospectivity.162 An advantage of indirect meth­
ods to detect rhEPO is its universal coverage of increasingly used 
different types of analogues and mimetics.
The most powerful way to directly discriminate between 
endogenous and rhEPO is based on glycosylation differences 
between both molecules.164 A method able to separate both 
types of molecules in blood and urine is reliable, because it 
allows clear identification of the presence of rhEPO in urine and 
blood.165 However, the proposed method is valid only as long as 
the biologic samples are collected within 24 hours after the last 
rhEPO injection.
In June 2000, a few weeks before the Sydney Olympic games, 
an innovative test based on the isoelectric separation of urinary 
EPO isoforms on a polyacrylamide gel followed by a double blot­
ting process was proposed.166,167 This test has since been adapted 
to several recombinant EPO forms, such as darbepoetin-α, whose 
isoforms are located in the most acidic part of the gel, epoetin-δ, 
or, more recently, generic (biosimilar) or “copy” EPOs. 
Glucocorticoids
Glucocorticoids (GCs) were first purified and manufactured in 
the 1930s and 1940s following the discovery of their potent anti­
inflammatory actions.168 GCs are widely used in medicine and 
have shown remarkable therapeutic potential in several chronic 
inflammatory and other diseases.
GCs are also widely used in sports medicine for treatment of 
conditions such as asthma and acute injuries. Nevertheless, their 
beneficial effect in certain conditions in sports, where inflamma­
tion is only a secondary reaction, remains to be validated.169
In addition to their therapeutic uses, some claim that GCs 
may improve athletic performance.170–172 GCs may increase the 
availability of substances that supply energy to muscles, such as 
through increasing lipolysis, plasma free fatty acids, and glycogen 
synthesis. Moreover, their immunosuppressive and antiinflamma­
tory effects may attenuate feelings of fatigue or muscle pain during 
exercise.
1145
CHAPTER 25  Hormones and Athletic Performance
This potential to provide athletes with an unfair advantage may 
explain their current status as banned substances on WADA’s list 
of prohibited substances under the category “S9.”110 However, the 
evidence surrounding the ergogenicity of glucocorticoids has yet 
to be fully elucidated.173
The first use of GCs as performance-enhancing drugs was 
described in the 1960s.168 The most interesting systemic effect of 
the GCs in athletes is energy production. A possible increase in 
cardiovascular performance is a matter of debate as there is no 
evidence for such effects. As a consequence, systemic GCs have 
been misused to enhance performance, and represented the most 
commonly used sport doping substances.169
A recent systematic review and meta-analysis indicates low 
to moderate evidence suggesting that GC administration may 
be more beneficial than placebo in enhancing athletic perfor­
mance.172 These ergogenic effects may differ depending on the 
specific type of drug, dose, and administration time frame, and 
the interpretation was also limited by small sample sizes. There­
fore, there is a need for large, high-quality randomized controlled 
trials to determine the true ergogenic properties of GCs because 
this may influence future doping policy and the care of athletes 
requiring glucocorticoids for medical conditions.
Adverse Effects. GCs have pleiotropic effects, causing several 
adverse effects, especially when administered at higher doses and 
for long periods. These include osteoporosis, insulin resistance, 
and cardiovascular effects (hypertension and atherosclerosis).173,174 
Importantly, the etiology of these symptoms may be unrecognized 
by the athlete and medical personnel, particularly in a sporting 
context, where athletes train at high intensity and symptoms can 
masquerade as fatigue related to overtraining. Importantly, an ath­
lete who suffers trauma or serious injury may be at increased risk 
for adrenal crisis due to hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal suppres­
sion from prior GC use.173 
Detection. All GCs are prohibited when administered by 
any injectable, oral (including oromucosal), or rectal route dur­
ing the in-competition period. Examples of injectable routes of 
administration include intravenous, intramuscular, periarticular, 
intraarticular, peritendinous, intratendinous, epidural, intrathe­
cal, intrabursal, intralesional (e.g., intrakeloid), intradermal, and 
subcutaneous. Other routes of administration (including topical, 
inhaled, intranasal, ophthalmologic, perianal, and dermal) are not 
prohibited when used within the manufacturer’s licensed doses 
and therapeutic indications.110
A presumptive adverse analytical finding is reported by WADA-
accredited laboratories when the urinary levels of in-competition 
samples exceed a 30 ng/mL reporting level. Pharmacokinetics 
of GCs is complex and influenced by the formulation, type of 
esterification and salt, administration route, site, and method of 
administration. Accordingly, although the laboratory reporting 
limit may demonstrate the presence of a GC, it cannot necessarily 
indicate if the administration was in-competition or out of com­
petition or likely to have a pharmacologic or ergogenic effect.173 
Detection of administered GCs is complicated by the fact that 
these steroid hormones are produced naturally. Several groups 
have described protocols and screening methods for analysis of 
endogenous GC urinary metabolites using liquid chromatog­
raphy/mass spectrometry. Some methods allow for analysis of a 
large number of analytes from most of the classes in the WADA 
Prohibited List, including anabolic agents, β2-agonists, hormone 
antagonists and modulators, diuretics, stimulants, narcotics, glu­
cocorticoids, and β-blockers, and do so while meeting WADA 
sensitivity requirements.175 
Transgender Persons and Sport Participation
Transgender persons are those who experience incongruence 
between the gender that they were assigned at birth (based on 
the appearance of their genitals) and their gender identity/expe­
rienced gender. Whether transgender individuals should be able 
to compete in sport in accordance with their gender identity is a 
widely contested question within the literature and among sport 
organizations, fellow competitors, and spectators.
Performance disparities based on “assigned sex at birth” vary 
across sports; they are lowest for swimming and highest for track 
and field events.176,177 These differences in athletic performance 
appear after puberty and most likely are due to increased circulat­
ing testosterone levels in the “male” assigned sex at birth athletes 
compared to the “female” assigned sex at birth athletes.178 How­
ever, there is a general lack of data showing whether higher tes­
tosterone levels correlate with improved athletic performance.179
Owing to concerns surrounding transgender persons (espe­
cially transgender female individuals) having an athletic advan­
tage, several sport organizations place restrictions on transgender 
competitors.180
Hormone therapies are currently employed by transgender 
women to suppress testosterone levels to those more similar to cis­
gender women to comply with competition regulations. A maxi­
mum testosterone level has been introduced that must be met by 
individuals born with XY chromosomes and initially assigned a 
female gender due to a mutation in the fetal 5α-reductase enzyme 
but not in the promoter driving 5α-reductase from puberty 
onward and then leading to overt masculinization. Interestingly, 
the muscular advantage of transgender women over cisgender 
women is only minimally reduced after testosterone suppres­
sion.181 Transgender men are not thought to possess an athletic 
advantage, despite being injected with testosterone if they chose 
to medically transition with cross-sex hormones.180
In transgender athletes, the transition process may vary con­
siderably depending on the medical community, the diagnostic 
criteria, and the law in the respective country, also considering the 
fluidity of gender and implications for the biology of inclusion for 
transgender and intersex athletes.182–184 Transgender athletes may 
be granted a therapeutic use exemption (TUE) once their eligibil­
ity and gender have been established by respective sport federation 
criteria, as documented in the TUE application.184
In transgender male athletes, testosterone is the administered 
prohibited substance. In transgender female athletes, the antian­
drogen spironolactone is the prohibited substance often used for 
therapeutic reasons. Notably, estrogen preparations and cyproter­
one acetate are not prohibited substances.
Transgender female athletes eligible to participate as females in 
their sport do not require a TUE for GnRH analogues, because 
they are prohibited substances only in males. If a transgender ath­
lete is in the process of feminizing their body while still partici­
pating as a male in their sport, then a TUE for GnRH analogues 
should be requested.183,184
A fundamental issue regarding the current sports policies on 
transgender athletes is that the governing bodies of different ath­
letic organizations have different policies for these athletes to fol­
low to be included in sports competitions.
In November 2021, after a 2-year consultation process with 
more than 250 athletes and concerned stakeholders, the IOC 
released the “IOC Framework on Fairness, Inclusion and Non-
Discrimination on the Basis of Gender Identity and Sex Varia­
tions.” The Framework recognizes both the need to ensure that 
1146
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
everyone, irrespective of gender identity or sex variations, can 
practice sport in a safe, harassment-free environment that recog­
nizes and respects their needs and identities, and the interest of 
everyone—particularly elite athletes—to participate in fair com­
petitions where no participant has an unfair and disproportionate 
advantage over others.185

KEY POINTS
 • 
Interactions between the endocrine system and aging 
include age-related changes in the secretion and actions of 
hormones, as well as the evolutionarily conserved influence of 
hormonal signaling on the biologic process of aging. A clearer 
understanding of the physiologic meaning of the age-related 
endocrine changes is needed to establish the role of hormone 
manipulations to delay or reverse aging.
 • 
The most dramatic age-related endocrine change is represented 
in menopause, defined as the permanent cessation of 
menstruation resulting from the loss of ovarian follicular 
function. The subject of menopause is covered comprehensively 
in Chapter 15.
 • 
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) rises during normal 
aging, and many older adults with isolated TSH elevations are 
misclassified as subclinically hypothyroid, despite having age-
appropriate TSH levels. Thyroid hormone replacement in older 
adults with isolated TSH elevation should be reserved for those 
with TSH levels persistently above 7 mIU/L, and in the oldest-
old, above 10 mIU/L, due to lack of benefits of restoring TSH to 
youthful levels and substantial risks of overtreatment.
 • 
Aging is associated with a phase advance in the circadian 
cortisol secretion and possibly with increased activity of the 
hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. A greater diurnal decline in 
cortisol and lower 24-hour average cortisol secretion have been 
associated with reduced risks for functional decline, morbidity, 
and mortality in older individuals.
 • 
Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), a precursor for androgen and 
estrogen production in target tissues, declines with aging. Oral 
DHEA replacement modestly improves bone mineral density in 
postmenopausal women, and intravaginal DHEA administration 
may ameliorate genitourinary syndrome of menopause. 
Despite being widely used as a dietary supplement to prevent 
physiologic consequences of aging, no compelling benefits in 
older men and women have been consistently demonstrated, 
and the safety of increases in sex steroids associated with oral 
DHEA replacement is unknown.
 • 
Aging men experience a decline in testosterone, which is 
accelerated by obesity and metabolic dysfunction. In such men, 
weight loss may normalize testosterone levels. Testosterone 
replacement in older men improves anemia, bone mineral 
density, and sexual symptoms. Given that the long-term risks of 
testosterone replacement in older men without clear gonadal 
axis pathology are unresolved, testosterone replacement 
should be considered in carefully selected older men with clear 
hypogonadal symptoms.
 • 
During the aging process, growth hormone–insulin-like 
growth factor 1 (GH-IGF1) activity declines, but it is unclear 
if this attenuation is causal for age-related changes in body 
composition and functional capacity. GH replacement in older 
adults with physiologic decline in GH-IGF1 activity improves 
body composition but does not benefit overall functional 
capacity, and it is associated with adverse effects and uncertain 
long-term safety.
 • 
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels rise with age, likely as a 
result of reduced expression of vitamin D receptor and 1,25 
dihydroxyvitamin D in the parathyroid gland. It is unknown 
whether age-related elevation in PTH is pathologic or benign.
 • 
The possibility of slowing down or reversing aging by 
manipulating endocrine function remains to be explored, but 
currently appears to have no place in clinical practice.

Endocrine Function and Aging
SANDRA ALEKSIC, ANDRZEJ BARTKE, STEVEN W. J. LAMBERTS, 
AND SOFIYA MILMAN
1148
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
Introduction
The function of the endocrine glands and the biologic process of 
aging are intricately related. Resembling age-related changes in 
other organ systems, aging is associated with reduced activity of 
hormone-producing cells, leading to decreased circulating levels 
of their products, including gonadal steroids, pituitary growth 
hormone (GH), and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) derived 
from the adrenal cortex. Accompanying these changes, the preci­
sion of the regulation of hormone release and the amplitude of 
diurnal fluctuations of circulating hormone levels tend to decline 
with age.1–4 There is also accumulating evidence that hormonal 
signaling is one of the key regulators of aging and longevity. Evo­
lutionarily conserved cellular processes, including insulin/insulin-
like growth factor signaling (IIS) and downstream mechanistic 
target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 activity, have been linked 
to the rate of aging and to lifespan in organisms ranging from uni­
cellular yeast and microscopic worms to insects and vertebrates, 
including mammals.5–9 Not surprisingly, the same mechanisms 
may be involved in human aging.10–12
In mammals, GH has an important role in the regulation of 
the aging process, acting via multiple mechanisms, including 
IIS and mTOR.13–16 Genetic, pharmacologic, or environmen­
tal suppression of these nutrient-dependent pathways (GH, IIS, 
and mTOR) can produce remarkable extension of longevity.13–16 
Importantly, increases of average and/or maximal lifespan are 
typically (although not universally) associated with extension of 
“healthspan,” that is, the period of life free of frailty, disability, and 
disease.13–16 In humans, reduced somatotroph (GH and IGF1) 
signaling has been linked to familial longevity,10,12,17 likelihood 
of attaining exceptionally old age,10,12,17 and resistance to chronic 
age-related diseases such as cancer, atherosclerosis, and diabe­
tes.18–20 Intriguingly, activity of the somatotroph axis appears to 
have a role in mediating the trade-offs between growth, matu­
ration, fecundity, and aging. These are likely causally associated 
with the differences in longevity both within and among different 
mammalian species.13
Because of the complexity of bidirectional relationships 
between endocrine functions and aging, the biologic significance 
of age-related changes in circulating hormone levels is open to 
various, often seemingly opposing, interpretations. For example, 
the pronounced decline in plasma GH levels with aging can 
be viewed as a symptom (a “biomarker”) of aging, likely reflect­
ing reduced stimulatory input of hypothalamic GH-releasing 
hormone (GHRH) on GH biosynthesis and release,21,22 as a 
mechanism of aging, or at least of some age-associated alterations 
in body composition (such as increased adiposity and reduced 
muscle mass) and physiologic functions,23 or as an evolutionary-
developed protective process that ameliorates the risk of cancer and 
diabetes by reducing IGF1 signaling and preserving insulin sen­
sitivity.24–26 The complexity of the underlying molecular, cellular, 
and regulatory mechanisms suggests that these interpretations are 
not mutually exclusive, and each may be at least partially correct. 
At first glance, these considerations may appear to be distant from 
practical clinical considerations. However, a clearer understanding 
of the physiologic meaning of the changes in endocrine function 
that accompany aging is needed to determine risk:benefit ratio 
for administration of hormone replacement to the elderly. Such 
therapy can potentially be beneficial, futile, or harmful, depend­
ing on the symptoms, desired goals, and characteristics of the indi­
vidual patient.
Understanding the complex interplay between hormonal sig­
naling and aging acquires increasing significance in the context 
of major ongoing changes in the age composition (age profiles) of 
the human population. Global life expectancy at birth is currently 
69.1 years for men and 73.8 years for women.27 Twenty-nine 
countries have an average life expectancy of 80 years or higher. By 
2030, average global life expectancy at birth is predicted to further 
increase by 4 years.27 Between 1950 and 2050, the number of 
people in the world aged over 80 years is expected to increase from 
14.5 million to 394.7 million.28 The obvious consequences of 
these demographic changes include a major, progressive increase 
in the number of individuals experiencing age-related changes in 
endocrine function who may be considered for some forms of hor­
monal replacement therapy. 
The Endocrinology of Aging
The most pronounced age-related changes in the function of the 
endocrine system include reduced secretion of estrogens by the 
ovary, DHEA by the adrenal cortex, and GH by the pituitary, 
along with the changes in the dynamics of insulin secretion by 
the pancreatic islets and in the sensitivity of peripheral tissues to 
insulin.
Menopause is the best-recognized endocrine consequence of 
aging. It is defined as the permanent cessation of menstruation 
resulting from the loss of ovarian follicular function and is diag­
nosed retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhea. Hypoes­
trogenemia causes many women to experience vasomotor and 
genitourinary symptoms, whereas prolonged estrogen loss leads 
to a decline in bone mass. Although estrogen replacement was a 
widely recommended treatment for postmenopausal women until 
the early 2000s, findings from the landmark Women’s Health Ini­
tiative (WHI) study led to a paradigm shift after it demonstrated 
that, compared to placebo, combined estrogen and progesterone 
replacement increased the risk for invasive breast cancer, coronary 
heart disease, stroke, venous thromboembolism,29 and probable 
dementia.30 Estrogen alone was also associated with a greater risk 
for stroke and venous thromboembolism.31 However, estrogen 
and a combination of estrogen-progesterone were found to be 
protective against osteoporotic fractures. Based on these findings, 
hormone replacement is currently recommended for short-term 
treatment of vasomotor symptoms, but not for the prevention of 
age-related diseases. The availability of potent pharmacologic ther­
apies specific for osteoporosis obviates the need to use estrogen 
for osteoporosis treatment. The topics of menopause, its conse­
quences, and recommended treatments are covered comprehen­
sively in Chapter 15.
Prevalence of impaired glucose tolerance and diabetes increases 
with age. Prevalence of diabetes among individuals age 65 and 
older is estimated at 19.2% globally and 29.2% in the United 
States. In the United States, another 48.8% of people age 65 and 
older are estimated to have prediabetes.32,33 These adults are at 
risk for development of secondary, mainly macrovascular, com­
plications at an accelerated rate. Pancreatic, insulin receptor, and 
postreceptor changes associated with aging are critical compo­
nents of the endocrinology of aging. Apart from decreased (rela­
tive) insulin secretion by the β-cells, peripheral insulin resistance 
related to poor diet, physical inactivity, increased abdominal fat 
mass, and decreased lean body mass contribute to the deterio­
ration of glucose metabolism.34 Dietary management, exercise, 
hypoglycemic agents, and insulin are the four components of 
1149
CHAPTER 26  Endocrine Function and Aging
treatment for these patients, whose medical care is costly and 
intensive (see Chapter 25). 
Thyroid Axis in Aging
The development of ultrasensitive thyroid-stimulating hormone 
(TSH) assays35 allowed investigation of changes in thyroid axis 
function that occur with aging. Although circadian modula­
tion of TSH secretion appears to be preserved until advanced 
age,36 several studies reported that both basal and thyrotropin-
releasing hormone–stimulated TSH secretion are lower in older 
individuals.37,38 In contrast to these cross-sectional findings, 
which included relatively small numbers of selected male sub­
jects, larger epidemiologic cross-sectional and longitudinal stud­
ies in iodine-replete populations have demonstrated that levels 
of TSH increase with age,39–42 especially in women.43 Examina­
tion of data from the National Health and Nutrition Examina­
tion Survey (NHANES), a cross-sectional cohort representative 
of the U.S. population, found that in the absence of thyroid 
disease, thyroid antibodies, or medications with a major impact 
on thyroid parameters, the TSH population distribution curve 
shifted toward higher values with advancing age (Fig. 26.1).39 
Median and the 97.5th percentile TSH values, respectively, 
shift from 1.26 and 3.56 mIU/L between the ages of 20 and 
29 years to 1.90 and 7.49 mIU/L in those 80 years of age and 
above. Longitudinal studies confirmed that in iodine-sufficient 
individuals free of thyroid disease and thyroid antibodies, TSH 
increases with age, associated with stable or modestly rising free 
thyroxine (T4) and declining triiodothyronine (T3).41,42 Given 
that these changes were independent from the presence of thy­
roid antibodies and that individuals with the highest baseline 
TSH demonstrated the smallest TSH increase,41 they cannot be 
attributed to increased prevalence of subclinical autoimmune 
hypothyroidism with age. Furthermore, although obesity has 
been associated with higher TSH levels, age-associated increase 
in TSH occurs independently from change in body mass index 
(BMI).41 Proposed mechanisms for the observed changes in thy­
roid function in aging populations include alteration in TSH 
set-point due to reduced sensitivity of thyrotrophs to negative 
feedback by thyroid hormones, decrease in TSH bioactivity, 
reduced response of the thyroid gland to TSH, and altered T4 
deiodination into T3.39,41
To what extent the observed age-related changes in the thyroid 
axis result from aging vs. comorbidities and/or pharmacotherapies 
that are more prevalent in older individuals is unresolved.44 How­
ever, higher levels of TSH and lower levels of T4 may be advan­
tageous for healthy aging and longevity, because in longitudinal 
studies, age-associated rise in TSH was found to be neutral42 or 
associated with longer survival,45 whereas rise in free T4 was asso­
ciated with higher mortality.42,45 These findings were independent 
of declining T3 levels, suggesting that greater mortality could not 
be explained by a higher prevalence of nonthyroidal illness result­
ing in low T3 syndrome.42,45 Studies from individuals with excep­
tional longevity and their offspring support the notion that mild 
TSH elevations are not detrimental in aging individuals and are, 
in fact, compatible with healthy aging. A study in a large group 
of centenarians in good general health found higher levels of TSH 
with similar free T4 compared to older adults without exceptional 
longevity.46 Offspring of parents with exceptional longevity, who 
similarly to their parents have delayed onset of age-related disease 
and mortality, have higher levels of TSH with similar levels of free 
T4 and free T3 and similar in vitro TSH activity compared to con­
trols.47 These findings have been attributed to decreased sensitivity 
of thyrocytes to TSH,48 which may at least in part be explained by 
genetic polymorphisms in TSH receptors, as such polymorphisms 
were found in offspring of parents with exceptional longevity.49 
Intriguingly, in naked mole rats and dwarf mice, lower thyroid 
function is associated with longevity,50,51 possibly via reducing 
the growth, development, and production of reactive oxygen spe­
cies.52 Moreover, experimental induction of hypothyroidism and

the lifespan of laboratory rats.53
The observed age-related shift toward higher TSH values can 
have a significant clinical impact on classifying TSH values as 
“normal” or “abnormal.” Seventy percent of older adults classified 
as having subclinical hypothyroidism based on non–age-specific 
TSH ranges (i.e., with TSH levels above 4.5 mIU/L, or the 97.5th 
percentile in the NHANES III54) would be reclassified to “nor­
mal” if age-specific reference ranges were used.39 In another study, 
prevalence of subclinical hypothyroidism in individuals residing 
in iodine-excess areas was reduced from approximately 30% to 
3% with the application of age-specific TSH reference ranges.40 
Other concerns favoring the use of age-specific TSH reference 
ranges to classify older individuals as euthyroid vs. subclinically 
hypothyroid include absence of clear benefit from thyroid hor­
mone therapy55–57 and high risk for overtreatment58 in older 
adults with mildly elevated TSH levels.
The decision to prescribe thyroid hormones to older adults 
(i.e., those older than 65–70 years) with subclinical hypothyroid­
ism needs to be individualized while taking into consideration sev­
eral variables, including the following: (1) TSH levels and trends 
over time, (2) likelihood that elevated TSH levels are a result of 
normal aging vs. thyroid disease, (3) use of medications and sup­
plements known to affect parameters of thyroid function,44 (4) 
symptoms and signs of hypothyroidism, (5) comorbidities, (6) 
polypharmacy, (7) risks due to overtreatment, (8) patient prefer­
ence, (9) life expectancy, and (10) cost and burden for the patient 
and the health care system. In general, treatment should not be 
commenced based on a single elevated TSH level, because more 
than 60% of individuals with subclinical hypothyroidism and 
TSH values <10 mIU/L will revert to euthyroid range with repeat 
testing.59 With regard to older adults with TSH levels that are 
persistently above the upper limit of the reference range for the 
general population, most experts agree that levothyroxine replace­
ment should not be prescribed to individuals with TSH levels 
in the range of 4.5 to 6.9 mIU/L, whereas it should be consid­
ered in most of those with TSH ≥10.0 mIU/L.60–62 TSH levels 
of 4.5 to 6.9 mIU/L fall within the age-specific reference range 
for older adults.39 Thus, it may not be surprising that observa­
tional studies did not identify negative health outcomes in older 
adults who have subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH levels in 
the range 4.5 to 6.9 mIU/L,63–65 and the few available random­
ized controlled trials (RCTs) in such patients did not show clini­
cal benefit of levothyroxine treatment.55,63,66 On the other hand, 
persistently elevated TSH of ≥10.0 mIU/L is less likely to result 
from normal aging and has been associated in observational stud­
ies with a higher risk for metabolic syndrome,67 heart failure,63 
coronary heart disease, and mortality.65 In the absence of history 
of hemithyroidectomy, goiter, or dyslipidemia, observation with­
out treatment is likely appropriate in most older adults with inter­
mediate TSH levels (i.e., 7.0–9.9 mIU/L), especially in those age 
85 years and older.60,61 One possible exception are those with a 
history of heart failure, because several prospective observational 
studies and a meta-analysis have shown that subclinical hypothy­
roidism is associated with higher risk for hospitalization, cardiac 
death, and all-cause mortality in individuals over the age of 65 
years with preexisting heart failure, although these studies did not 
stratify analysis by TSH levels.68,69 Presence of thyroid autoanti­
bodies and thyroid ultrasound findings of thyroiditis, goiter, or 
atrophy may identify individuals with ongoing autoimmune thy­
roid disease who are at risk for progression to overt hypothyroid­
ism.70 Although signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism should 
be included in treatment decisions, they are frequently nonspecific 
(e.g., fatigue, constipation) and prevalent in the older population. 
Treatment with levothyroxine is not likely to improve symptoms 
of hypothyroidism in older individuals with subclinical hypothy­
roidism and TSH level <10.0 mIU/L.55,57 In summary, benefits 
of levothyroxine treatment need to be balanced against risks of 
overtreatment, polypharmacy, and increasing complexity of health 
care in older adults. Well-powered RCTs studying long-term 
effects of thyroid hormone replacement on morbidity and mor­
tality in older adults with subclinical hypothyroidism are needed 
because most of the recommendations in the literature are guided 
by observational data. If a decision is made to treat, initial dos­
ing should be low (e.g., 0.3–0.4 μg/kg/day of levothyroxine), with 
careful adjustments to target TSH levels at or above the upper 
limit of reference range for the general population.71,72
Conclusions
In iodine-sufficient individuals, free of thyroid disease and thyroid 
antibodies, TSH levels increase with age. Although TSH levels are 
affected by comorbidities and use of medications that are preva­
lent in older adults, a rise in TSH in an otherwise healthy aging 
individual does not appear to be pathologic and might even be 
associated with healthy longevity. Use of non–age-specific TSH 
reference ranges results in misclassification of many older adults 
as subclinically hypothyroid, despite them having age-appropriate 
TSH and thyroid hormone levels. Restoring TSH to youthful lev­
els with thyroid hormone replacement in such individuals does 
not confer clinical benefit and is associated with substantial risks 
due to overtreatment. Thyroid hormone replacement in older 
persons with isolated TSH elevation should be individualized 
and reserved for those with TSH levels persistently higher than 7 
mIU/L, and in the oldest-old, higher than 10 mIU/L. 
Adrenal Axis in Aging
Overlap among many characteristics of aging with signs and symp­
toms of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hyperactivity 
(including increase in visceral adiposity, decrease in muscle mass 
and strength, decline in cognitive function, increase in insulin 
resistance, and rise in blood pressure) has prompted investigations 
into hypercortisolemia as a contributing pathophysiologic factor 
to age-related diseases and loss of function. Age-related changes in 
the HPA axis have been studied extensively, albeit frequently with 
inconsistent results, attributed to both methodologic differences 
between studies and biologic differences between studied popula­
tions.73 The complexity of HPA axis regulation, which is affected 
by stress, sleep, illness, and energy balance, and modulated by sex 
and age, creates challenges for studies that aim to delineate changes 
that occur due to aging per se vs. impairments that are a result 
of age-related pathologies. Most reports agree that aged individu­
als display alterations in cortisol circadian rhythm, such that early 
morning maximum and evening nadir occur 1 to 2 hours earlier 
(phase advance) than in younger subjects.74–76 Evening cortisol 
nadir is higher with aging,76,77 resulting in relative flattening of the 
diurnal cortisol curve.78,79 Whether these circadian alterations in 
cortisol are a cause or an effect of circadian impairments observed 
in aging (e.g., sleep disruption) is presently unresolved.
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and cortisol response 
to physiologic and pharmacologic stimuli are largely preserved in 
aging, as demonstrated by appropriate responses to insulin-induced 
hypoglycemia,77 surgery,80 and corticotropin-releasing hormone 
1151
CHAPTER 26  Endocrine Function and Aging
(CRH)81 and ACTH stimulation,77 although the cortisol response 
in older individuals may be reduced when low doses of ACTH are 
used.82 Whether aging results in hyperactivity of the HPA axis, in 
terms of an enhanced response to stimulation and/or dampened 
response to suppression, has been less clear; however, the consensus 
appears to be shifting toward the notion that aging is associated 
with HPA axis hyperactivity. Although individual studies, mostly 
cross-sectional and relatively small, reported conflicting results, 
more often than not they found greater HPA axis activity in aging, 
especially in women.73 A meta-analysis of 45 cross-sectional stud­
ies, which included more than 1200 young and older nonhospital­
ized subjects, reported that age was associated with higher cortisol 
levels in response to challenges, defined as either stronger response 
to physiologic or pharmacologic stimulation (including psychoso­
cial stress, insulin-induced hypoglycemia, CRH, ACTH, or opioid 
antagonists, among others) or reduced inhibition after a suppres­
sion test with agents such as dexamethasone or prednisolone.83 The 
association of age with enhanced cortisol response was significantly 
greater in women.83 Several epidemiologic studies investigated 
effects of age on unstimulated 24-hour cortisol secretion, fre­
quently with opposing findings between cross-sectional and longi­
tudinal studies76,84 and among different longitudinal studies. The 
discrepant results could be attributed to differences in methodolo­
gies employed for the assessment of 24-hour cortisol secretion (e.g., 
repeated venous blood sampling vs. 24-hour urine free cortisol), 
variation in studied populations (some studies included hospital­
ized77 or nursing home74 populations), and different participant 
ages. In fact, the relationship between cortisol secretion and age 
may be nonlinear as suggested by a recent longitudinal study that 
included the largest number of subjects to date with a wide age 
range between 20 and 90 years.85 This study found a U-shaped 
association between 24-hour urinary free cortisol excretion and 
age, with a decline in cortisol excretion between the ages of 20 
and 30 (attributed to developing of physiologic and psychological 
stress-coping mechanisms), stable levels between the ages of 40 and 
60, and increase after 60 years of age85 (Fig. 26.2). This study also 
highlighted a large inter- and intraindividual variability in 24-hour 
cortisol excretion, which is not unexpected given that both chronic 
and acute alterations in health and nutritional status affect cortisol 
secretion. Experimental data in humans suggest that age-associated 
alterations in HPA function stem from the suprapituitary level, 
and it has been postulated that HPA axis hyperactivity results from 
reduced feedback inhibition at the level of the hippocampus, which 
normally downregulates HPA axis activity.82,83
Several studies have investigated associations between param­
eters of the HPA axis and functional performance, morbidity, and 
mortality in older individuals. These studies frequently reported 
inconsistent findings that may be explained by heterogeneity in the 
HPA axis parameters selected for investigation (e.g., diurnal profiles 
of salivary cortisol, single morning salivary or serum cortisol, 12- or 
24-hour urine cortisol measurement) that have variable intervisit 
reliability,86 studying institutionalized or hospitalized individu­
als, and variations in clinical outcome definitions. Because many 
of these studies were cross-sectional, the question remains to what 
degree altered HPA axis reflects or causes aging-associated changes 
in functional ability, cognition, depression, and various age-related 
diseases. In cross-sectional studies conducted later in life, a more 
dynamic activity of the HPA axis, characterized by a greater diurnal 
decline, has been associated with better physical performance,87–89 
longer sleep duration and less sleep disturbance,79 and lower preva­
lence of osteoporotic fractures90 and type 2 diabetes (T2D).91 In 
longitudinal studies, a more dynamic HPA axis was associated with 
lower mortality, predominantly due to cardiovascular causes,92 
whereas it was not predictive of cognitive decline.93 In a study 
that longitudinally measured 24-hour urinary cortisol excretion, 
higher mean levels and higher variability over time in urinary free 
cortisol predicted incidence of Alzheimer disease.94 The associa­
tions between diurnal HPA axis dynamics and total diurnal cor­
tisol secretion with clinical outcomes may be modified by sex. For 
instance, higher nighttime salivary cortisol was associated with 
progression of aortic wall stiffness95 and increased mortality in 
women,96 whereas these associations were not significant in men, 
in whom higher morning salivary cortisol levels predicted increased 
mortality.96 It is unknown whether diurnal cortisol measures are 
relevant and which measures are reliable and feasible in identifying 
those who might benefit from preventive interventions.
Conclusions
Aging is associated with phase advance in the circadian cortisol 
secretion such that morning maximum and evening nadir occur 
1 to 2 hours earlier in older vs. young individuals. Increasing 
evidence also suggests that aged individuals display hyperactiv­
ity of the HPA axis, defined as greater cortisol response to chal­
lenge, reduced inhibition in suppression tests, and greater average 
24-hour cortisol secretion. A more dynamic activity of the HPA 
axis, characterized by a greater diurnal decline in cortisol, and 
lower average 24-hour cortisol secretion have been associated with 
enhanced functional performance and protection from morbid­
ity and mortality in older individuals. However, given the obser­
vational nature and methodologic challenges of available studies, 
measures of HPA axis activity that are feasible and reliable in iden­
tifying those who might benefit from interventions that modulate 
HPA axis function remain unknown. 
Dehydroepiandrosterone in Aging
Humans are unique among primates and rodents because the 
human adrenal cortex secretes large amounts of the steroid precur­
sor DHEA and its sulfate derivative, DHEAS.97 Serum DHEAS

concentrations in adult men and women are 100 to 500 times 
higher than those of testosterone and 1000 to 10,000 times higher 
than those of estradiol. In healthy individuals, serum concentra­
tions of DHEA and its sulfate are highest in the third decade of 
life, after which the concentrations of both gradually decrease as a 
result of atrophy of zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex,98 so that 
by age 70 to 80 years, the values are about 20% of peak values in 
men and 30% of peak values in women99 (Fig. 26.3).
DHEA and DHEAS seem to be inactive precursors that are 
converted into androgens or estrogens, or both.97 The term “intra­
crinology” was coined to describe the process of active steroid syn­
thesis in the same cells where targeted hormonal action is exerted, 
without release of the hormones into extracellular space or gen­
eral circulation. In postmenopausal women, nearly 100% of sex 
steroids are synthesized in peripheral tissues from precursors of 
adrenal origin, except for a small contribution from ovarian or 
adrenal testosterone and androstenedione. Thus, in postmeno­
pausal women, virtually all active sex steroids are produced in tar­
get tissues by an intracrine mechanism. In older men, intracrine 
production of androgens is also important; less than 50% of the 
tissue androgen supply is derived from testicular production.97
The high secretion of adrenal precursor sex steroids in men and 
women differs from that in laboratory animals, in which secre­
tion of sex steroids occurs exclusively in the gonads. In rats and 
mice, long-term administration of DHEA prevented obesity, dia­
betes mellitus, cancer, and heart disease, and enhanced immune 
function.100–102 These experimental animal data have been used 
to argue that DHEA administration in adult or elderly individuals 
prolongs lifespan and might be an “elixir of youth.” Supportive 
data in humans are few, however, and highly controversial.
Epidemiologic studies do suggest a mild cardioprotective effect 
of higher DHEA and DHEAS levels in both men and women.,103 
In one study, DHEA and DHEAS concentrations were inversely 
associated with the risk of diabetes.104 Functional parameters of 
activities of daily living in men older than 90 years were lowest 
in those with the lowest serum DHEAS concentrations,99 and in 
healthy elderly individuals there was an association between the 
ratio of cortisol to DHEAS levels and cognitive impairment.105 
Nonetheless, a recent longitudinal study in 1800 men from the 
European Male Aging Study (EMAS) cohort found no associa­
tion between either baseline or longitudinal levels of DHEAS and 
cognitive aging,106 and the English Aging Study, which followed 
over 5000 older men and women, found no association between 
baseline DHEAS levels and cognitive decline.107 Lower baseline 
DHEAS levels predicted worsening frailty over 4.3 years of fol­
low-up in the EMAS, but only in men who were older than 70 
years at baseline.108
DHEA Replacement Therapy
Several double-blinded randomized placebo-controlled trials, with 
follow-up ranging from a few weeks to 2 years, studied effects of 
pharmacologic restoration of DHEA to youthful levels on health 
outcomes in older adults.109,110 In a number of studies, partici­
pants were selected to participate if they had low DHEAS levels; 
however, the definition of low DHEAS varied between stud­
ies.111–113 DHEA was mostly administered orally at a dose of 50 
mg/day (in women) to 75 to 100 mg/day (in men).114,122 At these 
doses, DHEA administration in older adults restores DHEAS to 
young adult levels; increases serum testosterone, free testoster­
one, estrone, estradiol, and IGF1 concentrations; and lowers sex 
hormone–binding globulin (SHBG) levels.114–116
In most studies, administration of DHEA in older men and 
women with low serum DHEAS levels did not significantly 
improve metabolic parameters, including insulin secretion and 
sensitivity, glucose tolerance, lipid metabolism,112,114,117–119 or 
body composition.111,114,117 Modest improvements in glucose 
tolerance and body weight were observed in a few studies involv­
ing older adults with metabolic dysfunction (glucose intolerance 
and obesity), but the DHEA dose used for female participants 
was supraphysiologic (100 mg/day) and the sustainability of the 
observed effects is unclear due to short follow-up in these stud­
ies.120,121 Furthermore, a meta-analysis of 25 RCTs, including 
1300 elderly men with a mean follow-up of 36 weeks, showed 
that DHEA supplementation (50–100 mg/day) was associated 
with a reduction in fat mass, but statistical significance was lost 
after adjustment for increases in testosterone and estradiol, and no 
effect was observed on lipid and glucose metabolism.122

Administration of DHEA in healthy older men and women 
in the absence of a structured exercise program did not improve 
muscle strength or physical performance,115,116,123 whereas in the 
setting of an exercise training program some,124 but not all,125 
studies suggested that DHEA supplementation may potenti­
ate beneficial effects of exercise on muscle strength and volume. 
In terms of cognition, several small and relatively short studies 
reported either no effect in older men and women126 or even harm 
in postmenopausal women,127 and a larger study with longer fol­
low-up reported no significant effects on cognition with restoring 
DHEAS to the youthful levels in older men and women.128
Oral DHEA administration has been reported to increase 
libido in postmenopausal women,129 whereas no effect on sexual 
function or quality of life was found in a meta-analysis of RCTs 
performed in older men.122 Daily intravaginal administration of 
DHEA was shown to improve signs and symptoms of genitouri­
nary syndrome of menopause, including vaginal dryness and pain 
with sexual activity,130 and has been approved by the U.S. Food 
and Drug Administration for treatment of moderate to severe 
dyspareunia due to menopause.131 During the 12-week course of 
daily intravaginal administration of 6.5 mg of DHEA, a modest 
increase was observed in serum DHEA and other sex steroid lev­
els, but these hormones remained within the corresponding ranges 
observed in untreated postmenopausal women, supporting the 
intracrine action of DHEA in the vulvovaginal tissues.132
A beneficial effect of oral DHEA administration has been 
constantly reported for increase in bone mineral density (BMD) 
in postmenopausal women,114,116,123,129 possibly mediated by 
increases in serum estrogens.116 These positive effects, how­
ever, were modest, equating to approximately half of the ben­
efit observed with use of approved osteoporosis therapies, such 
as bisphosphonates.133 Furthermore, none of the available RCTs 
were adequately powered to establish effects of DHEA administra­
tion on fracture risk. A recent observational study applied Men­
delian randomization to investigate causal relationship among 
endogenous DHEAS levels, BMD, and fracture risk in more than 
230,000 women of white ancestry in the UK Biobank.134 This 
study found that genetically predicted higher levels of DHEAS 
were associated with higher BMD in the lumbar spine and lower 
risk for forearm fracture, but had no effect on femoral neck BMD 
or hip fractures.134 In older men, a pooled analysis of four RCTs 
involving 290 men and a meta-analysis of eight RCTs involving 
640 men found no improvement in lumbar or femoral BMD 
or markers of bone turnover after DHEA administration for 1 
year.122,135 
Conclusions
DHEAS is a universal precursor for the peripheral local pro­
duction and action of estrogens and androgens in target tissues, 
including brain, bone, skin, and adipose tissue. However, the 
importance of these pathways remains undefined, particularly in 
men, who have relatively higher levels of testosterone of gonadal 
origin. DHEA administration in older adults increases sex steroids 
and IGF1 and lowers SHBG levels.114–116 It is not known whether 
this increase in sex steroid levels induced by DHEA administra­
tion is safe with regard to risk for development or growth of ovar­
ian, breast, prostate, or other types of steroid-depended cancers. 
The addition of DHEA (50 mg/day) to the existing large pool of 
DHEA and DHEAS in elderly individuals, even if they have been 
selected on the basis of low circulating levels of these steroids, has 
very limited, if any, clinically meaningful effects. DHEA, which is 
currently available as a dietary supplement, is widely used within 
the United States as an unapproved preventive treatment against 
aging. There is no convincing evidence at present to recommend 
the use of DHEA for delaying or preventing the physiologic con­
sequences of aging, and its safety is unknown.136,137 
Male Gonadal Axis in Aging
Changes in the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-
Testicular Axis During Aging
Endocrine activity of the male hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular 
(HPT) axis, as reflected by circulating levels of total and free tes­
tosterone, reaches its peak soon after sexual maturation and begins 
to decline in early adulthood1,3,138 (Fig. 26.4). Longitudinal stud­
ies demonstrate that the decline in total testosterone levels acceler­
ates from 0.85%/year in men age 24 to 46 years139 to 1.6%/year 
in men age 40 to 70 years,140 and up to 2.6%/year in men older 
than 70 years.141 Age-related decline in testosterone production 
is associated with increases in the levels of SHBG, also known 
as testosterone-binding globulin or testosterone-estradiol binding 
globulin. Therefore, an even steeper decline with age is observed 
in free testosterone levels.142 The amplitude of diurnal (day/night) 
fluctuations in plasma testosterone levels is also reduced with 
age along with changes in the feedforward and feedback regula­
tory mechanisms of testosterone secretion.1,3 A detailed analysis 
of the temporal changes in serum levels of luteinizing hormone 
(LH) and testosterone in samples collected at 10-minute intervals 
revealed age-related impairment of both feedforward and feedback 
relationships between the release of these hormones, as well as a 
decline in the amount of LH released in a secretory burst.1,3,143
Etiology of age-related changes in the HPT axis is multifacto­
rial. Aging is associated with functional alterations in the testes, 
including a decrease in Leydig cell numbers,144 leading to reduced 
testicular steroidogenesis. Aging is also associated with alterations 
in hypothalamic, gonadotropin-releasing hormone–mediated 
“drive” of pituitary function, including a compensatory increase 
in gonadotropin release in response to reduced negative feedback 
of testicular steroids.143 Obesity, metabolic syndrome, and comor­
bidities interfere with hypothalamic control of the pituitary, lead­
ing to hypogonadotropic (secondary) hypogonadism. By contrast, 
men with exceptional longevity, who are considered a model of 
healthy aging, preserve hypothalamic-pituitary regulation of the 
gonadal axis such that they have markedly lower prevalence of 
secondary hypogonadism.145,146 Alterations in regulation of LH 
release are most evident in men in whom decline in testosterone 
levels is related to obesity or diabetes, whereas effects of aging 
itself appear to be exerted primarily at the testicular level.146–150 
The association of obesity with hypogonadism is almost certainly 
causal, because in overweight or obese men with low testosterone 
levels, weight loss leads to increase of testosterone,151 although the 
mechanistic underpinnings of this relationship remain unclear.
In other species, including commonly used strains of labora­
tory rats and mice, age-related changes in the biosynthesis and 
release of testicular sex hormones primarily are due to the reduced 
hypothalamic stimulation of LH and follicle-stimulating hor­
mone release from the pituitary.22 Thus, if relative testosterone 
deficiency develops at old age in these animals, it represents sec­
ondary, rather than primary, hypogonadism. However, in some 
strains of the same species, most notably the Brown Norway (BN) 
rat, aging does lead to primary hypogonadism, providing a very 
1154
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
useful model system for studying mechanisms that are likely to 
be involved in human testicular aging.152,153 Studies in BN rats 
indicate that testosterone production declines with age due to 
accumulation of reactive oxygen species, the resulting oxidative 
damage, and increase in inflammatory processes.154–157 These 
changes lead to reduced responsiveness of the Leydig cells to the 
stimulation of LH receptors, defects in cholesterol transport to 
the mitochondria, and reduced steroidogenesis.154,157 Studies in 
mice genetically predisposed to accelerated aging or to delayed 
and slower aging indicated that extended longevity confers antiin­
flammatory and antioxidant capacity to the testis.155
Although a gradual decline in circulating testosterone levels 
in men is strongly associated with chronologic age, the onset, 
magnitude, and exact time course of this decline is affected by 
general health, diet, and body composition, with obesity having 
clear detrimental effects (see Fig. 26.4).147 Some studies have chal­
lenged the view that testosterone decline in aging men is inevi­
table, because total testosterone levels may be preserved in selected 
groups of aging men with low burden of obesity and other comor­
bidities at least until the age of 70.158,159 Nonetheless, decline in 
testosterone production appears to be inevitable in advanced old 
age; in one study, more than two-thirds of men older than 90 years 
were shown to exhibit testicular hypofunction.145
Concomitant declines in muscle mass and strength, libido, 
erections, and fertility, along with the evidence for a key role of 
androgens in development and maintenance of these features of 
male phenotype, imply that the decline in testosterone production 
is not only a biomarker of aging, but also a causative factor in age-
related changes in body composition, muscle strength, and repro­
ductive functions. However, reduced testosterone levels can also be 
a marker of obesity and/or poor health.142,147,160 Viewed against 
this background, it is probably not surprising that the effects of 
age-related decline in testosterone levels on cardiovascular func­
tion, heart attacks (myocardial infarction), strokes, atrial fibrilla­
tion, and death from cardiovascular events or from all causes have 
been very difficult to establish. Both beneficial and detrimental

Androgen Deficiency in the Aging Male: 
Definition and Clinical Relevance
Existence of age-related male hypogonadism as an identifiable 
clinical syndrome and a legitimate indication for testosterone 
replacement therapy has been vigorously debated166–168 and 
remains controversial.169 Nevertheless, there is a general consensus 
that some older men experience clinically relevant symptoms of 
androgen deficiency associated with, and almost certainly due to, 
severe reduction in circulating levels of total and/or free testoster­
one. Many authors referred to this condition as partial androgen 
deficiency in the aging male (PADAM),138 and more recently as 
late-onset hypogonadism (LOH).152 A recently proposed term, 
functional hypogonadism (FH),170 denotes absence of clinically 
obvious anatomic or genetic causes for testosterone decline in 
aging men; focuses on the role of age-related comorbidities, rather 
than aging itself, in testosterone decline; and is consistent with the 
observed reversibility of hypogonadism with treatment of under­
lying comorbidities.151,170,171
Much information on age-related changes in male endocrine 
function was derived from the European Male Aging Study 
(EMAS), which involved over 3000 community-dwelling men 
from eight European countries, age 40 to 79 years, and followed 
for up to 4.3 years.160 The EMAS investigators proposed mini­
mal diagnostic criteria for LOH, consisting of the “syndromic” 
simultaneous presence of three sexual symptoms (i.e., poor morn­
ing erections, decreased sexual interest, and erectile dysfunction), 
together with a serum total testosterone level less than 11 nmol/L 
(320 ng/dL), and free testosterone levels less than 0.22 nmol/L 
(6.4 ng/dL) (Fig. 26.5).172 Men fulfilling these criteria with serum 
total testosterone levels less than 8 nmol/L (230 ng/dL) are con­
sidered to have severe LOH. The prevalence of such defined LOH 
in the EMAS population was 2.1%, and it increased with chrono­
logic age, BMI, and number of comorbidities, reaching 5.1% in 
men 70 to 79 years old.172 Men with LOH had lower hemoglo­
bin, muscle, and bone mass and poorer physical performance and 
general health compared to their peers. Men with low testosterone 
only, irrespective of sexual symptoms, showed considerably lesser 
magnitude of associations with the same endpoints.173 These 
results suggest that the implications of low testosterone levels for 
health in middle-age and older men need to be considered in the 
context of associated sexual symptoms, because decline in testos­
terone in the absence of sexual symptoms does not seem to be 
associated with poor health to the same extent as syndromic pres­
ence of low testosterone with sexual symptoms.
In the EMAS, severe LOH was associated with increased car­
diovascular and all-cause mortality rates, which were indepen­
dently related to both the level of testosterone and the presence 
of sexual symptoms.160 In men from this population, the risk of 
developing metabolic syndrome was related to low levels of tes­
tosterone, but not 17β-estradiol (E2), and was independent of the 
levels of SHBG, BMI, and insulin resistance. There was also an 
indication that a lower E2/testosterone ratio may be protective in 
this regard.174 Symptoms of androgen deficiency were related to 
calculated levels of free testosterone, even if total testosterone lev­
els were in normal range.175 This is consistent with the well-doc­
umented importance of testosterone that is not bound to SHBG, 
and thus is present in circulation in a free form, or is bound with 
low affinity to other blood components and is biologically avail­
able for interacting with androgen receptors. It also provides addi­
tional evidence that the age-related increase in SHBG levels may 
amplify the consequences of reduced androgen production by the 
testes. Indeed, men with normal total testosterone, but low calcu­
lated free testosterone, had higher levels of SHBG and also higher 
levels of LH, indicative of reduced negative androgen feedback 
on the hypothalamic pituitary system. Follow-up studies in obese 
men, in whom SHBG is typically decreased, showed that symp­
toms of androgen deficiency developed only in those in whom 
both total and free testosterone were reduced.176 Other prospec­
tive studies in men enrolled in EMAS identified an increase of 
LH despite normal testosterone levels as a marker of deteriorating 
health.177 Diabetes, low physical activity, and chronic pain pre­
dicted development of these endocrine features along with erectile 
dysfunction and increased risk of various comorbidities.177 Wors­
ening of frailty in the entire EMAS cohort and in specific age 
groups of men in this study was related to the levels of androgens 
and other anabolic hormones.108,178
Observational studies analyzing relationships among levels of 
testosterone, cardiovascular events, and mortality in aging men 
have reported both beneficial179,180 and detrimental,181 as well 
as null, associations.182–184 More recently, a study that included 
150,000 men age 40 to 69 years from the UK Biobank who were 
followed over a median of 11 years reported that lower total tes­
tosterone and calculated free testosterone levels at baseline were 
associated with higher all-cause and cancer-related mortality, but 
not cardiovascular mortality.185 A meta-analysis of eight longitu­
dinal studies, including 20,000 middle-age and older men, did 
not find an association between total testosterone levels at base­
line and either all-cause or cardiovascular mortality.158 In another 
study involving 210,000 men from the UK Biobank who were 
followed for 9 years, baseline total testosterone levels were not 
associated with incident myocardial infarction, stroke, or major 
cardiovascular events (MACE). Intriguingly, lower calculated free 
testosterone was associated with reduced risk for MACE.186 These 
observational studies, conducted in a large and well-characterized 
UK Biobank cohort, adjusted for many more potential confound­
ers than prior studies and may settle some of the controversies 
regarding epidemiologic associations between endogenous testos­
terone levels and long-term outcomes in aging men. These studies 
show that total testosterone levels are not associated with cardio­
vascular events or cardiovascular mortality, whereas they may be 
protective for all-cause and cancer-related mortality in middle-age 
and older men. However, these observational data in predomi­
nantly Caucasian men may not be representative for other popu­
lations, and their findings should not be extrapolated toward the 
effects of pharmacologic testosterone replacement on long-term 
outcomes in aging men.
The relationship among testosterone, obesity, metabolic syn­
drome, and risk for T2D, is particularly complex. Low total tes­
tosterone has been associated with increased risk for metabolic 
syndrome and T2D, independently from BMI, in some obser­
vational studies.187,188 As reviewed,189 obesity and metabolic 
syndrome, prevalent in aging men, predispose them to both low 
testosterone (through hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction) and to 
T2D. Presence of low testosterone may act synergistically with 
obesity to potentiate the risk for T2D, possibly through indepen­
dent detrimental effects of low testosterone on body composition 
and insulin sensitivity. In a multicenter RCT that included 1000 
men age 50 to 74 years with impaired glucose tolerance or newly 
1156

ment to lifestyle intervention for 2 years reduced the proportion 
of men with T2D, compared with placebo.190 Although these 
results support the mechanistic role of testosterone in glucose 
metabolism, they do not automatically apply to older men with 
androgen deficiency, given that the men in the said study were 
selected for low-normal testosterone levels (≤14 nmol/L or 404 
ng/dL) and were not hypogonadal.190 Of note, 22% of men in
