Androgen Deficiency in the Aging Male: 
Testosterone Replacement Therapy
Chronologic age is not an approved indication for testosterone 
therapy.191 Nevertheless, testosterone use in the United States 
continues to increase at a rate that outpaces the gradual changes 
in the age distributions of the population.165,192 This reflects 
increasing interest by men in receiving this therapy and increas­
ing willingness of physicians to prescribe it. Both of these trends 
are undoubtedly related to development of new products (patches 
and gels for transdermal treatment and long-acting testosterone 
esters), as well as intense advertising to both prospective consum­
ers and health care professionals. The increasing popularity of 
treatment of men without clear pathology of the HPT axis reig­
nites the long-standing discussion of the risks and benefits of this 
therapy.191–196 This subject has long been debated, and consensus 
appears to have been reached on a few points, but many ques­
tions remained unanswered and controversial. Concerning the 
benefits, there is clear evidence that testosterone therapy can mod­
estly increase skeletal muscle mass and strength, enhance libido, 
improve erectile function, reduce anemia, and increase BMD. 
Testosterone therapy is also likely to reduce visceral adiposity and 
improve some measures of mood.192–195 However, these benefits 
may be less pronounced or absent in men with testosterone levels 
that are not reduced below the normal range.197 The normal range 
of total testosterone levels is usually considered to be between 300 
and 1100 mg/dL,138 but lower levels should probably be regarded 
as “normal” for men over age 70 years,167 and different authors 
have used the thresholds of <200, <250, or <300 ng/dL as indica­
tive of hypogonadism in older men.146,168 The effect of testoster­
one therapy on other clinical outcomes, including cardiovascular 
disease (CVD), metabolic syndrome, diabetes, osteoporosis, and, 
most important, all-cause mortality, remains debated, with many 
studies ongoing, and is generally considered as having no proven 
benefit.177,198,199 Documented risks of testosterone therapy in 
middle-age and older men without HPT axis pathology include 
acne, polycythemia, and progression of preexisting carcinoma of 
the prostate.200 Although increased risk of developing prostate 
cancer is invariably mentioned in this context, it remains a theo­
retic risk that has yet to be conclusively proven.198 Recent analysis 
of data from nearly 150,000 men indicated that testosterone treat­
ment of men with low testosterone levels did not increase the risk 
of aggressive or any cancer of the prostate.201 Paradoxically, thera­
peutic regimens that include high doses of testosterone have been 
used in treatment of advanced prostate cancer.202,203
There are many reasons for conflicting information and contro­
versies concerning risks and benefits of testosterone therapy. Many 
of the studies included a fairly small number of subjects, often 
undergoing relatively brief periods of treatment and follow-up; 
thus, these were underpowered for detecting meaningful changes 
in the incidence of relatively rare events. In some studies, it is dif­
ficult to determine whether individuals given testosterone therapy 
were similar to individuals not given testosterone, in respect to 
levels of plasma testosterone, etiology of reduced testosterone 
levels (testicular hypofunction vs. hypothalamic-pituitary dys­
function), and incidence and severity of comorbidities, including 
obesity. Other difficulties in deriving clear conclusions from the 
available data include use of different doses and formulations of 
testosterone, different duration of treatment, lack of data concern­
ing restoration of normal plasma testosterone levels, and different 
criteria for recruitment and inclusion of subjects into the studies. 
It is hoped that results of the ongoing RCT studies, including the 
TRAVERSE Trial,204 will bring some clarity on the controversial 
and highly contested issues related to safety and effectiveness of 
testosterone therapy in middle-age and older men with testoster­
one decline due to FH, who are otherwise free of HPT disease. 
Which Older Men Should Be Treated With 
Testosterone?
According to practice guidelines,168,191,205 testosterone treatment 
might be considered for the diagnosis of androgen deficiency in 
older men, which should be based on the concurrent presence of 
unequivocally low serum (free) testosterone and consistent symp­
toms of hypogonadism.
The biochemical diagnosis consists of measuring morning 
serum total testosterone levels, or calculating serum free tes­
tosterone concentration based on measures of morning serum 
total testosterone and SHBG levels, in men who are suspected 
of having an abnormal SHBG level.191 Testosterone should be 
measured in the morning, under fasting conditions (to avoid 
reduction in testosterone levels due to circadian fluctuation and 
prandial suppression), and should be unequivocally low on two 
separate days to establish the biochemical part of the diagnosis of 
androgen deficiency.191 To ensure optimal sensitivity, specificity, 
and precision, it is recommended to measure total testosterone 
with a liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-
MS) assay, which has been verified by an external quality-control 
program, such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 
(CDC) Hormone Standardization (HoSt) Program in the United 
States.191 Selection of reference ranges for testosterone in older 
men presents unique challenges, and recommendation on the 
threshold for “unequivocally low” level of total testosterone differs 
between different clinical practice guidelines. For instance, if total 
testosterone is measured with LC-MS assays that have been certi­
fied by the CDC-HoSt program, the Endocrine Society suggests 
to use levels below estimated 2.5th percentile (264 ng/dL) or 5th 
percentile (303 ng/dL) of total testosterone levels for young, non­
obese men to diagnose androgen deficiency in older men.191,206 
Guidelines by the European Academy of Andrology, which have 
been endorsed by European Society of Endocrinology, suggest 
that the lower limit of normal total testosterone concentrations are 
in the range of 231 to 350 ng/dL, which has been derived based 
on the prevalence of sexual symptoms and benefits for sexual func­
tion with testosterone replacement in RCTs. In men with total 
testosterone below 231 ng/dL, diagnosis of androgen deficiency 
can likely be established with confidence; for in those in the “bor­
derline” 231 to 350 ng/dL range, it is suggested that determina­
tion of free testosterone can aid in the diagnosis.207 When total 
testosterone lower reference limit is defined at <300 ng/dL, as in 
EMAS, close to 14% of men age 40 to 79 years meet biochemi­
cal criterion for androgen deficiency.146 These challenges raise 
the question of whether and how age-specific reference ranges 
for testosterone should be established in aging men and, more 
broadly, how normal aging of the HPT axis should be defined. 
One approach is to apply the reference ranges established in young 
men to aging men191; however, this approach fails to capture the 
gradual decline in testosterone levels that might occur with aging, 
even in the absence of appreciable comorbidities.140 Excluding 
1158
SECTION VI    Endocrinology and the Lifespan
older men with comorbidities would result in reference ranges 
that reflect the effects of the aging process per se on the HPT axis 
function. However, given the increasing prevalence of obesity,208 
diabetes,209 and other comorbidities210 as men enter middle age, 
this approach may not be feasible or clinically applicable to the 
majority of men. An alternative approach would be to set refer­
ences based on the risk of adverse health outcomes associated with 
different levels of circulating testosterone and the underlying eti­
ology of low testosterone defined by either primary or secondary 
hypogonadism. The latter approach may be optimal, because it 
would allow creation of reference ranges for sex hormones that 
will have clinical prognostic value.
Another important challenge with a biochemical approach to 
the diagnosis of LOH/FH in elderly men is that men with low tes­
tosterone may not exhibit clinically significant symptomatology, 
raising the possibility that large numbers of men, simply by virtue 
of falling below an arbitrary biochemical threshold, are diagnosed 
as needing testosterone replacement therapy. Indeed, the clinical 
diagnosis of androgen deficiency of the aging male has impor­
tant drawbacks.211 Most symptoms and signs of androgen defi­
ciency are nonspecific and readily accounted for or modified by 
comorbidities and medications. Lethargy, reduced concentration, 
sleep disturbance, irritability, and depressed mood may relate to 
physical illness (and side effects of treatment), obesity and/or lack 
of physical exercise, and other lifestyle issues (such as alcohol or 
drug use), relationship difficulties, and occupational or financial 
stresses. Sexual complaints, including reduced libido, decreased 
spontaneous erections, and erectile dysfunction, have been more 
frequently associated with low testosterone concentrations than 
physical/psychological symptoms, and are therefore considered 
more specific for androgen deficiency in older men.207,212 Indeed, 
existing screening tools for androgen deficiency lack adequate 
specificity and sensitivity to be reliably employed directing clinical 
diagnosis and treatment. 
Randomized Controlled Trials of Testosterone 
Replacement Therapy in Older Men
Many reports in the literature indicate that testosterone replace­
ment in men of all ages (young, middle-age, and old), with clear 
clinical and severe biochemical hypogonadism, quickly reverses 
vasomotor activity (flushes and sweats), improves libido, sex­
ual activity, and mood, increases muscle mass, strength, and 
bone mineralization, decreases fat mass, and decreases fatigue 
and poor concentration.213–215 Also, treatment of adult men 
who do not have low testosterone levels with supraphysiologic 
doses of testosterone, especially when combined with resistance 
exercise training, increases fat-free mass and muscle size and 
strength.216
Most studies reporting results of androgen therapy in older 
men were small, short-term, noncontrolled, and without uniform 
endpoints. The results of one of the first RCTs with longer follow-
up in healthy older men seem representative of the effects expected 
from androgen therapy.217,218 Ninety-six men, mean age 73 years, 
wore a testosterone patch on the scrotum (6 mg of testosterone 
per 24 hours) or a placebo patch for 36 months. Mean serum total 
testosterone concentrations in the men treated with testosterone 
increased from 12.7 ± 2.9 nmol/L (367 ± 7.9 ng/dL) before treat­
ment to 21.7 ± 8.6 nmol/L (625 ± 249 ng/dL; p <0.001) at 6 
months of treatment and remained at that level for the duration of 
the study. The decrease in fat mass (−3.0 ± 0.5 kg) and the increase 
in lean mass (1.9 ± 0.3 kg) in the testosterone-treated men were 
significantly different from the changes observed in the placebo-
treated men (−0.7 ± 0.5 kg and 0.2 ± 0.2 kg, respectively, both p 
<0.001) (Fig. 26.6). However, changes in parameters of muscle 
strength and physical function were not significantly different 
between the groups. The subjective perception of physical func­
tioning decreased significantly during the 36 months of treatment

Bone mineral density in the lumbar spine increased in both the 
testosterone-treated (4.2% ± 0.8%) and placebo-treated (2.5% ± 
0.6%) groups, but mean changes did not differ between groups 
(see Fig. 26.6). However, the effects of testosterone treatment on 
lumbar spine bone density after 36 months were greater in those 
with lower pretreatment serum testosterone concentrations. A 
minimal effect (0.9 ± 1.0%) of testosterone treatment on BMD 
was observed in men with a pretreatment serum testosterone con­

2.2% was found in men with a pretreatment testosterone concen­
tration of 6.9 nmol/L (200 ng/dL).
To determine definitively whether testosterone treatment in 
older men with low testosterone is efficacious in improving symp­
toms and objective measures of age-associated conditions, a coor­
dinated set of seven clinical trials, the Testosterone Trials (TTrials), 
was designed. The TTrials included 788 men with measurements 
of physical function, sexual function, vitality, cognitive function, 
anemia, and cardiovascular and bone parameters.219 These trials 
reported that in men age >65 years with testosterone levels below 
9.5 nmol/L (275 ng/dL), a 12-month treatment with a transder­
mal testosterone gel, with dose adjustments to maintain testoster­
one levels in the midnormal range of young men, led to greater 
improvement in self-reported sexual function compared with pla­
cebo treatment.220 The effect sizes of the observed improvements 
in sexual function were small to moderate.220 Improvement in 
erectile dysfunction was less than that previously reported with 
phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, but the number of men who 
reported improvement in sexual desire was greater in those treated 
with testosterone than placebo, which was considered a clinically 
relevant outcome.220 There was a small difference between the 
testosterone group and the placebo group in the percentage of 
men whose 6-minute walking distance increased by at least 50 m, 
which was not statistically significant when only men from the 
Physical Function Trial arm were analyzed, but reached statisti­
cal significance in the analysis including all men enrolled in the 
TTrials131,220 (Fig. 26.7). Further, testosterone treatment showed 
no significant benefit over placebo with respect to vitality, as deter­
mined by an increase of at least 4 points in the FACIT–Fatigue 
score220 (Fig. 26.8). With respect to mood and depressive symp­
toms, testosterone therapy resulted in small, but statistically sig­
nificant, improvements.131,220 In the Bone Trial, which included 
211 men, treatment with testosterone significantly increased volu­
metric BMD and the mean estimated strength of the spine and hip 
trabecular and peripheral bone.221 Testosterone treatment also sig­
nificantly improved anemia due to unknown cause.222 Cognitive 
function was longitudinally evaluated at baseline, 6 months, and 
12 months in all of the TTrials participants; however, testosterone 
therapy did not improve memory or other cognitive functions.223
Other RCTs investigating testosterone replacement in older 
men with FH were smaller and narrower in scope compared to 
the TTrials. One placebo-controlled RCT in 129 healthy men age 
60 years and older with low or low-normal total testosterone levels 
(100–400 mg/dL) showed that 3 years of testosterone replacement 
attenuated age-related decrease in aerobic capacity, but the effect 
was modest and mediated by an increase in hemoglobin.224 Sev­
eral RCTs have investigated effects of testosterone replacement in 
subpopulations of older men with obesity. In a placebo-controlled 
study of 80 obese hypogonadal men age 65 and older with mild or 
moderate frailty, addition of testosterone to lifestyle intervention 
for 6 months resulted in similar weight loss, but with attenuated

loss of lean mass and greater improvement in aerobic capacity; 
however, there was no difference in muscle strength or physical 
function.196 In another RCT in obese men with total testosterone 
<12 nmol/L (<346 ng/dL) who underwent caloric restriction, 56 
weeks of testosterone therapy enhanced fat mass reduction and 
attenuated lean mass loss.225 However, in the 82-week post-RCT 
follow-up, these beneficial effects were not sustained and, in fact, 
the participants who had received testosterone demonstrated an 
accelerated lean mass loss.226 In respect to bone health, testos­
terone replacement did have beneficial effects on the markers of 
bone turnover in obese older men,227 but the effects on BMD 
varied.227,228
With regard to the potential adverse effects of testosterone 
treatment in healthy older men, RCTs218,220 reported a small 
but statistically significant increase in the mean serum prostate-
specific antigen (PSA) concentration in the testosterone-treated 
group compared to placebo. Three cases of prostate cancer were 
observed in the testosterone-treated group versus one in the pla­
cebo group. The urine flow rate and postvoid urinary residual 
in the bladder were similar in the two groups. Hemoglobin and 
hematocrit did not change in the placebo-treated group, but both 
increased significantly in the testosterone-treated group. Seven 
men treated with testosterone developed persistent erythrocytosis 
(hemoglobin >17.5 g/dL; hematocrit >52%) during treatment.220
There have been no RCTs that were sufficiently large or of 
long enough duration to determine effects of testosterone-
replacement therapy on major adverse cardiovascular events. A 
meta-analysis suggested that testosterone therapy increases car­
diovascular-related events among men. The risk of testosterone 
therapy was particularly marked in trials that were not funded 
by the pharmaceutical industry.162 The TTrials investigated the 
effects of testosterone therapy in older men on cardiovascular-
related parameters. In the TTrials, testosterone treatment resulted 
in modest reductions in total, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), 
and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, fasting insulin, and 
homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), 
but had no effect on glucose levels or markers of inflammation, 
fibrinolysis, or troponin levels compared with placebo.163 On 
the other hand, in a subset of 73 men testosterone treatment 
was associated with a significantly greater increase in coronary 
artery noncalcified plaque volume compared to placebo.164 In 
addition, in the Testosterone Effects on Atherosclerosis in Aging 
Men Trial, a placebo-controlled, randomized, double-blind trial 
of 308 community-dwelling men >60 years of age, insulin sensi­
tivity did not improve in a subset of 134 nondiabetic men treated 
with testosterone for 36 months.229 One study of 53 obese older 
men with low or low-normal total testosterone found that testos­
terone replacement increased 24-hour blood pressure, primarily 
when combined with exercise, and it attenuated exercise-induced 
reduction in diastolic blood pressure, suggesting that blood 
pressure should be carefully monitored when testosterone is 
prescribed to middle-age and older men, particularly if also 
engaging in an exercise program.230 An updated meta-analysis 
including individual-participant data from 17 RCTs, involving 
approximately 1700 older men per testosterone/placebo treat­
ment groups, with a testosterone treatment mean duration of 
9.5 months, found no difference in cardiovascular events or all-
cause mortality between the groups.231 Although these findings 
are reassuring, long-term safety of testosterone replacement, par­
ticularly in men with high cardiovascular risk, is still unknown; 
an ongoing TRAVERSE study may help resolve this.204 
Conclusions
Aging is associated with altered dynamic regulation and decline in 
HPT function, which is biochemically evident by reduced levels 
of circulating testosterone. This decline is accelerated in the setting 
of unhealthy aging, primarily obesity and metabolic dysfunction.

CHAPTER 26  Endocrine Function and Aging
Although maintaining good health may alleviate or even prevent 
testosterone decline in middle-age and older men, limited data 
from men with exceptional longevity suggest that most men will 
ultimately experience significant reductions in testosterone con­
centrations if they reach advanced old age. Nonetheless, the syn­
drome of male sex hormone deficiency, unlike female menopause, 
has not been clearly defined. In many older men, a low testos­
terone level is a marker of poor health, and it is unclear whether 
the benefits of testosterone replacement outweigh the still largely 
unknown risks in these men.
The decline in testosterone levels attributed to aging, rather 
than to identifiable anatomic or genetic disorders of the HPT axis, 
has been referred to as “functional hypogonadism,” and is poten­
tially reversible.232 Lifestyle modifications, in particular weight 
loss (because obesity is the strongest risk factor for low testoster­
one levels in older men), can increase testosterone levels.151
The current recommendation191 is not to treat asymptomatic 
older men with age-related decline in testosterone levels. The 
guidelines suggest that clinicians consider offering testosterone 
therapy on an individualized basis to older men with low testos­
terone levels measured on more than one occasion, and clinically 
significant symptoms of androgen deficiency, after exclusion of 
clinical HPT axis pathology and explicit discussion of uncertainty 
about the risks and benefits of testosterone therapy. Among experts 
there is disagreement on serum levels below which testosterone 
therapy should be offered to older men with symptoms. At pres­
ent, the recommended duration of testosterone administration is 
uncertain. Monitoring of prostate size, PSA levels, and hematocrit 
is mandatory. The identification of older men who might benefit 
most from testosterone treatment remains uncertain, and stud­
ies are underway to establish long-term safety to the prostate and 
cardiovascular system. 
Somatotropic Axis in Aging
The activity of the somatotropic axis, clinically characterized by 
GH and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) levels, progressively 
declines with age. Mean GH pulses are lower in amplitude and 
shorter in duration in healthy older men and women compared 
with younger people1,2,233 (Fig. 26.9). Although the frequency of 
GH pulses does not decrease with aging, the observed changes in 
characteristics of GH pulses result in lower levels of GH secreted 
per 24-hour period.233 In parallel, a progressive drop in circulating 
IGF1 levels occurs in both sexes with advanced age, but most data 
on age-related changes are derived from cross-sectional studies, 
and there is significant degree of overlap in IGF1 levels between 
age groups234–236 (Fig. 26.10). The decline in somatotropic hor­
mones is attributed to alterations in hypothalamic signaling 
because treatment with GH-releasing peptides restores production 
of GH by pituitary somatotrophs, even in octogenarians237,238 
(Fig. 26.11). Similarly, GHRH and GH administration restore 
circulating IGF1 levels, indicating that the response to GH is 
maintained with age.238 Despite substantial increase in GH levels 
in elderly individuals in response to GHRH and GH-stimulating 
peptides, the levels have not consistently achieved youthful ranges 
in all studies.237,239 The attenuated response of GH to GHRH was 
reversed with coadministration of arginine, a somatostatin inhibi­
tor, suggesting that increased somatostatin tone with age may also 
contribute to a reduction in GH production.239
Physiologic changes that result from stress or chronic illness, 
weight gain, and decline in sex steroids, all commonly observed 
with aging, also contribute to a reduction in GH secretion. Stress 
and illness can attenuate somatotropic signaling mediated by 
changes in GH pulsatility and GH resistance,240 thereby shifting 
resources away from growth and anabolic processes toward tissue

maintenance. GH and IGF1 levels are inversely proportional to 
body weight and BMI at all ages, but the combined effect of both 
age and BMI results in lowest IGF1 levels among the oldest adults 
with the highest BMI234 (Fig. 26.12). Obese individuals are less 
responsive to GHRH stimulation, although moderate weight loss 
of an average 5.8% of body weight results in partial restoration 
of GH secretion.241 Reduction in sex steroids that accompanies 
aging is another cause for the decrease in GH levels.242 Estrogen 
and testosterone are potent stimulators of GH secretion, and 
their decline with age further contribute to decrease in GH levels. 
Administration of estrogen to postmenopausal women or testos­
terone to middle-age men augments GH pulsatile secretion, with 
the effect in men partially mediated by estradiol formed by aroma­
tization of testosterone.243,244 Whereas both oral and transdermal 
estrogens enhance GH release in response to administration of 
GHRH in postmenopausal women, only oral estrogen activates 
spontaneous nocturnal GH secretion and reduces circulating 
IGF1 levels via induced GH resistance at the liver.245 However, in 
healthy women, the decline in IGF1 leads to a compensatory rise 
in GH, resulting in restoration of IGF1 levels.242 Nonetheless, it 
is important to note that even after accounting for differences in 
BMI and sex steroid levels, the inverse association between GH 
and age persists, indicating that the effect of aging on the somato­
troph axis occurs independently of other factors.233
Role of Growth Hormone and Insulin-like Growth

Although age-related GH and IGF1 decline is well recognized, 
whether this change has adverse or beneficial effects is extensively 
debated.246 In invertebrates and rodents, attenuation of the insu­
lin/IGF signaling pathway has led to an extension of lifespan.6 In 
laboratory stocks of mice, genetic GH deficiency or GH resistance

and the resulting suppression of circulating IGF1 levels are associ­
ated with a remarkable extension of longevity.51,247,248 In humans, 
genetic defects in the somatotroph axis leading to decreased IGF1 
signaling are associated with reduced risk of age-related chronic 
disease, retention of some youthful characteristics, and, in some 
populations, also a suggestion of increased survival.19,20,249,250 
Similarly, nonagenarians and centenarians with lower circulat­
ing IGF1 levels or IGF1 bioavailability exhibit extended survival, 
preserved cognition, and better daily functional status.246,251–253 
Familial longevity has also been associated with lower GH secre­
tion.254 However, in the general population, low IGF1 concentra­
tions have not been consistently associated with beneficial clinical 
outcomes.246
Most of our current understanding of the role of GH/IGF1 
in age-related diseases and mortality is derived from cross-sec­
tional and prospective epidemiologic studies that rely on associa­
tions. Clinical trials to date are invariably of short duration and 
are insufficient to draw conclusions about disease incidence and 
mortality. Because accurate measurements of pulsatile GH secre­
tion are challenging to conduct in large population-based studies, 
most investigators rely on measures of circulating IGF1 levels that 
serve as a read-out of integrated GH action. Epidemiologic stud­
ies of cardiovascular outcomes demonstrate inconclusive results 
for associations between IGF1 and risk for congestive heart fail­
ure, myocardial infarction, and stroke, with some studies showing 
positive association, some showing negative association, and some 
showing total lack of association.255–259 Results for cardiovascular 
mortality have been similarly indeterminate, with a number of 
population studies demonstrating 1.5 to 2 times increased risk 
for cardiovascular mortality in association with low IGF1 lev­
els,260–262 whereas in the NHANES III cohort association was not 
found.263 Of note, a number of studies have reported a U-shaped 
relationship between IGF1 and risk of CVD and CVD-related 
mortality, indicating that both low and high IGF1 levels are likely 
associated with increased risk.235,264,265
The relationship between IGF1, cognitive function, and 
dementia has been similarly shrouded in controversy,266 but the 
largest study to date did demonstrate a U-shaped association 
between IGF1 and incident dementia.235 Higher IGF1 levels have 
also been associated with protection from incident osteoporotic 
fractures in men267 and women268,269; however, these results have 
not been consistently replicated in men.269
Higher IGF1 was associated with a reduced risk of develop­
ing impaired glucose tolerance or T2D in one study of middle-
age adults,270 but these results were not confirmed in subsequent 
studies.259,271 A recent study, on the other hand, demonstrated a 
U-shaped relationship between serum IGF1 levels and incidence 
of T2D.235 Interestingly, an Ecuadorian population with Laron 
syndrome, who have extremely low circulating IGF1 levels caused 
by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the GH 
receptor (GHR) gene, are protected from T2D, despite the pres­
ence of obesity.20 Protection from diabetes, however, has not been 
consistently observed in an Israeli cohort with Laron syndrome, 
with the divergence hypothesized to result from differences in 
specific GHR mutations, environmental exposures, or variance in 
population genetic makeup.272,273
The evidence linking higher IGF1 levels to an increased risk 
of developing malignant disease is more robust, specifically for 
breast and prostate cancers.274–276 IGF1 is a mitogenic factor that 
promotes cell proliferation and growth via the IRS/Akt/MAPK 
pathway,277 whereas GH impairs repair of DNA damage in 
epithelial cells.278 Moreover, recent evidence indicates that age-
associated DNA damage in colon cells and fibroblasts induces 
local production of GH, which in turn suppresses p53 and DNA 
damage response.279 These mechanisms may contribute to and 
promote neoplasia in older individuals who may have already 
accumulated an increased number of DNA mutations with age 
from endogenous replication errors and environmental exposures. 
A U-shaped relationship between IGF1 and cancer mortality 
was also noted in men.264,280 The complex relationship between 
somatotroph signaling, aging, and cancer includes the roles of 
both systemic and local paracrine/autocrine GH and IGF1 lev­
els and production of growth factors, including IGF1, by some 
tumors.278,279,281–284 It is noteworthy that both Ecuadorian and 
Israeli populations with Laron syndrome exhibit remarkable pro­
tection from cancer.20,273,285
A large number of studies have sought associations between 
IGF1 levels and mortality risk. Some have found no associa­
tion,255,263,284,286 other studies have found that lower levels of 
serum IGF1 were associated with greater all-cause mortal­
ity,262,265,287,288 and still others found that low IGF1 levels or 
serum IGF1 bioavailability were predictive of extended sur­
vival.252,259,289 One study showed that higher IGF1 levels were 
associated with a higher mortality risk,290 and three studies found 
an elevated risk of mortality in individuals with both high and low 
IGF1 levels.265,291 Two meta-analyses confirmed that both high 
and low IGF1 concentrations are associated with increased all-
cause mortality, and another one also confirmed it for cancer and 
cardiovascular-related mortality in the general population.264,292
These conflicting results have been contextualized by a recent 
study that included over 440,000 participants from the UK Bio­
bank,235 which confirmed that both high and low IGF1 levels 
were associated with an increased hazard of developing vascu­
lar disease, T2D, dementia, and osteoporosis. However, the risk 
was not uniform across all age groups. Notably, over an average 
follow-up time of 11 years, the risk conferred by low IGF1 for 
the above diseases and mortality was much lower for older adults

(baseline age 63–74 years) than for younger individuals (baseline 
age 37–50 years)235 (Fig. 26.13). These differences translated into 
approximately 20%, 50%, 10%, 6%, and 20% reduced hazard 
for mortality, dementia, diabetes, vascular disease, and osteoporo­
sis, respectively, for older people compared with younger people 
with low IGF1. On the other hand, a high IGF1 level was associ­
ated with greater risk of dementia, vascular disease, and diabetes 
in older people than in younger individuals, and accounted for 
about 25%, 18%, and 10% increased hazard, respectively, in older 
adults. The mortality risk associated with high IGF1 was similarly 
elevated across all age groups, averaging 3% to 9%. This under­
scores the importance of considering the impact of hormonal 
changes in the context of age and aging. A number of prior studies 
that have not identified associations may have been underpowered 
or have not accounted for age-specific effects.257,263,293 The fact 
that low IGF1 is associated with a greater hazard in younger indi­
viduals also deserves attention. Low IGF1 levels in young people 
may result from stress, illness, and obesity, or may be a marker of 
premature aging that manifests as a more rapid decline in soma­
tropic hormones. All of these would be expected to increase an 
individual’s risk for morbidity and mortality. In older people, on 
the other hand, age-appropriate decline in GH and IGF1 may be 
an adaptive response that promotes maintenance over prolifera­
tion and growth; thus, persistence of higher somatotropic levels 
may be detrimental for older adults.246
The actions of IGF1 can be modulated by IGF-binding pro­
teins (IGFBPs). IGFBP1, IGFBP2, and IGFBP3 are most exten­
sively studied. IGFBP3 is the most abundant in circulation and 
binds up to 80% of IGF1.294 The production of IGFBP3 is regu­
lated by GH, and its levels correlate highly with IGF1. The molar 
ratio of IGF1 to IGFBP3 is an estimate for free or unbound IGF1 
available to bind to the IGF1 receptor. Higher IGFBP3 levels are 
associated with reduced all-cause mortality,259,262,263 although 
not in all studies.295 IGFBP3 is also associated with increased risk 
of incident T2D in older women but not in men.271,296 A low 
IGFBP3 level, on the other hand, is associated with an increased 
risk for coronary disease.257 IGFBP2 is the second most abundant 
IGFBP in the circulation, and it increases with age and decreases 
with higher BMI.297,298 A strong association between low IGFBP2 
levels, metabolic syndrome, and low insulin sensitivity has been 
identified.298–301 Surprisingly, although higher IGFBP2 was asso­
ciated with favorable risk factors, including lower fasting glucose 
and lower fasting insulin, two studies found a strong association 
between higher IGFBP2 and mortality in older adults.298,302 
Hepatic production of IGFBP1 is negatively regulated with insu­
lin and is stimulated by starvation and stress.294 Levels of IGFBP1 
are inversely correlated with IGF1, and low IGFBP1 levels are 
associated with obesity,303 high fasting insulin, impaired glucose 
tolerance, and increased incidence of T2D.259,271,304 Paradoxically, 
high IGFBP1 levels are consistently associated with increased all-
cause, cancer, and cardiovascular mortality,293,299,305 as well as 
difficulties in performing activities of daily living in older popu­
lations.295 These observations suggest that IGFBP1 may not be 
universally protective, and its effects should be interpreted in the 
context of an individual’s overall health status. 
Growth Hormone Replacement Therapy in Aging
The age-associated decline in GH and IGF1 that often parallels 
reductions in vigor, lean body mass, bone density, skin turgor, cog­
nitive function, and glucose tolerance led to investigations of GH/
IGF1 supplementation in older adults. The results of a landmark 
RCT of GH treatment in 21 healthy men, age 61 to 81 years, with 
serum IGF1 concentrations in the lower third for their age, were 
reported by Rudman and colleagues in 1990.306 This trial showed 
that treatment with biosynthetic GH at a dose of approximately 
0.03 mg/kg three times weekly for 6 months restored the men’s 
IGF1 levels into the youthful range. In the treatment group, lean 
body mass rose by 8.8%, skin thickness increased by 7.1%, lumbar 
vertebral density increased by 1.6%, and adipose mass decreased 
by 14.4%. The magnitude of these initial changes was equivalent 
to a reversal of the age-related changes by 10 to 20 years. How­
ever, during the treatment period, systolic blood pressure also rose 
by an average of 8 mm Hg and fasting glucose increased by an 
average of 7.2 mg/dL, causing some participants to cross into the 
prediabetes range.
In the subsequent years, it became clear that GH administration 
in healthy older individuals frequently caused acute adverse effects 
such as carpal tunnel syndrome, gynecomastia, fluid retention, 
arthralgias, and hyperglycemia, which were severe enough for an 
appreciable number of individuals to drop out of these studies.307 
For example, in one placebo-controlled study in healthy women 
(n = 57) and men (n = 74) age 65 to 88 years,308 subcutaneous 
administration of GH at an initial dose of 0.03 mg/kg, three times 
per week and subsequently at a dose of 0.02 mg/kg for 26 weeks, 
was associated with carpal tunnel syndrome in 38% of women 
and 24% of men treated with GH compared to 7% of women 
and 0% of men on placebo. Edema developed in 39% and 30% 
of treated women and men, respectively, compared to 0% and 
12% of women and men on placebo. Similarly, arthralgias were 
reported in 46% and 41% of women and men, respectively, tak­
ing GH, and in only 7% and 0% of women and men on placebo. 
Additional concerning findings included that 18 men treated with 
GH developed glucose intolerance or diabetes compared with 7 
men in the nontreatment group.308
Moreover, despite increased lean muscle mass in response to 
GH treatment, no positive effects of GH administration were 
observed on muscle strength, maximal oxygen consumption, or 
functional capacity. When GH was administered in combination

with resistance exercise training, effect on muscle mass and muscle 
strength did not differ from those seen with placebo treatment, 
which suggests that GH does not add to the beneficial effects of 
exercise.309–311 In a systematic review of 31 articles describing 18 
unique well-defined study populations, the safety and efficacy of 
GH in the healthy elderly were included.307 A total of 220 par­
ticipants who received GH for 107 person-years completed the 
studies. Their mean age was 69 years and they were overweight 
(mean BMI 28 kg/m2). Initial daily GH dose (mean 14 μg/kg 
body weight) and treatment duration (mean 27 weeks) varied. 
Overall fat mass decreased by 2.1 kg and lean body mass increased 
by 2.1 kg in those treated with GH, and total cholesterol levels 
decreased by 0.29 mmol/L. Similar to individual trials, no con­
sistent changes in muscle strength, physical activity, or psycho­
social outcomes were observed. In an RCT the synergistic effects 
of a combination of GH and sex steroids was studied in healthy 
older women and men.308 A slight increase in lean body mass and 
muscle strength was observed in men treated with GH and tes­
tosterone, but not in women who received GH and estrogen. In 
another study in healthy older men, coadministration of low-dose 
GH with testosterone also resulted in slightly beneficial changes 
(muscle strength, quality of life) compared to GH or testosterone 
alone.312 A systematic review of pharmacologic interventions that 
increased GH or IGF1 levels did not find conclusive evidence for 
benefit for muscle strength or physical performance in individuals 
over age 65 years.313
Sustained GH benefits have also been elusive in respect to 
other aging conditions. In a placebo-controlled trial in patients 
with mild to moderate Alzheimer disease, 12 months of treat­
ment with a GH secretagogue did not result in improvement 
on cognitive tests despite increase in IGF1 levels by more than 
70%.314 In a placebo-controlled trial in 131 healthy older men 
and women, mean age 72, administration of recombinant human 
(rh) GH alone or in combination with testosterone or estrogen, 
respectively, for 6 months reduced LDL cholesterol but increased 
triglyceride levels.315 However, an 18-month placebo-controlled 
GH treatment trial in middle-age men with GH deficiency found 
that despite initial decline, the LDL levels returned to baseline 
after 6 months, and by the end of the trial were not significantly 
different compared to the placebo-treated group.316 The same 
study also demonstrated that glucose and Lipoprotein(a) eleva­
tions persisted throughout the trial period.
Other biologic effects of GH/IGF1 on the aging body also 
should be considered. Both GH and IGF1 are anabolic hormones 
that play important roles in development, growth, and injury 
repair. However, these processes also result in the generation of 
reactive oxygen species, diminished stress resistance, and cellu­
lar proliferation that may be harmful to an aging organism (Fig. 
26.14). On the other hand, reduction of somatotropic hormones 
stimulates autophagy, a process that promotes cellular homeo­
stasis by eliminating cellular debris, and contributes to reduced 
inflammation. Moreover, reduced GH signaling promotes DNA 
repair.278,317 The latter actions likely contribute to maintenance 
and repair, which are expected to be beneficial in aging. Thus, in 
weighing the risks and benefits of GH replacement therapy in the 
elderly, special consideration must be given to the impact of this 
hormone on the biologic process of aging. 
Conclusions
During the aging process, GH-IGF1 axis activity declines. It is 
unclear whether changes in body composition and functional 
capacity are directly related to these changes. Administration of 
GH in older adults causes an increase in lean body mass and an 
appreciable loss of fat mass. However, GH treatment does not 
improve muscle strength and functional capacity in older people, 
despite restoration of circulating IGF1 concentrations to young 
adult levels. Furthermore, most dose regimens of GH cause appre­
ciable adverse effects, and long-term safety with regard to tumor 
development and progression remains uncertain. Age-related GH 
and IGF1 decline is not considered pathologic, and, at present, 
there is no evidence to recommend medical or other intervention 
in the GH-IGF1 axis as an antiaging effort or to prolong life.318 
In the United States, chronologic age is not included among 
approved indications for GH therapy, and use of GH in healthy 
older individuals as antiaging therapy is expressly forbidden.319 
Parathyroid Hormone in Aging
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) mediates plasma calcium and phos­
phate homeostasis. It maintains ionized calcium levels in a narrow 
range by regulating renal calcium reabsorption and bone resorp­
tion. Physiologic rise in circulating PTH is observed in response 
to low ionized calcium, reduced vitamin D levels, and elevated 
phosphate. Gastrointestinal malabsorption, excess urinary cal­
cium excretion, and renal insufficiency, as well as environmental 
factors, including certain medications, reduced dietary intake of 
calcium, or lack of sun exposure, may result in secondary rise of 
PTH. A number of studies have also noted that PTH rises with 
age, independent of other factors.320–322
The age-associated increase in PTH levels was described in 
two large studies conducted on blood samples left over from 
stored samples at clinical laboratories.320,322 In one study of over 
15,000 patients, after careful exclusion of individuals with a his­
tory of osteoporosis or known parathyroid disease, abnormal 
ionized calcium or phosphate levels, estimated glomerular filtra­
tion rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73m2, or 25-hydroxyvitamin D 
of <50 nmol/L, it was found that each 10-year increase in age 
above age 20 was associated with a 5% to 6% increase in PTH 
concentrations.320 Similarly, in a study of over 33,000 patients 
with normal total calcium levels and eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73m2, 
an increase in PTH concentrations was noted with each age 
decade at all levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D322 (Fig. 26.15). This

with 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations of greater than 75 
nmol/L.322 In addition, using a single PTH reference range for all 
age groups, rather than age-specific references ranges, resulted in 
misclassification of approximately 11% of adults age 70 and older 
as having abnormally elevated PTH.322 It is important to note 
that both studies were cross-sectional and were limited by not hav­
ing measurements of 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D concentrations or 
access to comprehensive medical and medication patient histories. 
Nonetheless, given the large number of samples and exclusion of 
most confounders, the results are compelling for an age-related 
rise in PTH.
Elevated intact PTH levels in older men persist throughout 
the 24-hour day cycle, even though the men maintain normal 
diurnal variation in ionized calcium and PTH, with a PTH nadir 
observed at noon and a broad PTH peak between midnight and 
3:00 am321 (Fig. 26.16A). In fact, in healthy older men an average 
of 74 years of age and in whom secondary causes for elevated PTH 
were excluded, PTH was two times higher compared to younger 
men with a mean age of 39 years, despite having the same lev­
els of ionized calcium, 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D, and 24-hour 
urinary calcium and phosphate321 (see Fig. 26.16B). Intravenous 
infusion of calcium gluconate that raised ionized calcium concen­
tration into the upper physiologic range did not suppress PTH 
levels in older men to the same degree as it did in the younger 
men, whereas infusion of Na EDTA that reduced ionized calcium 
concentrations to the lower physiologic range resulted in 20% 
greater elevation in PTH among older men compared to younger 
men.321 These results suggested that aging alters the steady-state 
relationship between calcium and PTH, such that at any concen­
tration of ionized calcium the PTH level is increased, with the 
PTH curve shifted to the right (Fig. 26.17). PTH in older men is 
likely functional because higher PTH levels were associated with 
greater renal fractional excretion of phosphate and renal cAMP.321 
Similarly, older women exhibited persistently higher PTH levels 
compared to younger women during dynamic calcium testing, 
but in older women, a shift in the PTH curve was not observed.323 
The differences observed between men and women may reflect 
sex-specific effects or result from variations in experimental condi­
tions. Interestingly, PTH levels in older women decreased after 
treatment with calcitriol 1 μg at bedtime for 8 days.323
The cause for age-associated PTH elevation has not been con­
clusively identified. One study histologically examined 70 para­
thyroid specimens incidentally removed during thyroid surgery 
from patients without known parathyroid or mineral metabolic 
disease, ranging in age from 10 to 70 years.324 Age was inversely 
correlated with expression levels of vitamin D receptor (VDR), 
vitamin D 1α-hydroxylase enzyme, and 24-hydroxylase enzyme 
in the parathyroid glands. On the other hand, there was a positive 
correlation between age and PTH expression in the parathyroid 
tissue (Fig. 26.18). These results suggest that reduction in VDR 
and 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D in parathyroid tissue with aging

Although the age-related increase in PTH is well documented, 
it remains unknown whether this rise is a normal manifestation 
of aging or is pathologic. Numerous studies explored the relation­
ship between PTH and age-related diseases, physical function, 
and mortality.326–331 The studies were heterogeneous and did not 
consistently account for age-specific PTH levels or confounding 
causes for PTH elevation, thus limiting the conclusions that can 
be drawn from them. Before implementation of age-specific refer­
ence ranges for PTH can be recommended, additional research 
is needed to determine whether the observed age-related eleva­
tions in PTH are benign or are associated with adverse clinical 
outcomes.
Conclusions
PTH levels rise with age, independently of ionized calcium con­
centrations, vitamin D levels, or other potential confounders. 
Reduced VDR and 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D expression in the 
parathyroid gland with older age may be a cause for age-associated 
elevation in PTH levels. Insufficient evidence exists to conclude 
whether age-related elevation in PTH is pathologic or benign. 
Additional research and longitudinal studies are needed to deter­
mine the etiology and effects of rising PTH with age. 
The Concept of Successful Aging
There is considerable variation in the effects of aging on healthy 
individuals, with some exhibiting greater, and others evidencing 
few or no, altered physiologic age-related functions. It has been 
suggested that it might be useful to distinguish between usual and 
successful (or “healthy”) patterns of aging.332 Thus, biologic age 
may differ, sometimes quite substantially, from the chronologic 
age. There is considerable evidence that genetic factors, lifestyle, 
and access to health care, as well as societal investments in a safe 
and healthful environment, have an important impact on the 
chances of achieving successful aging.333
This contrasts with the traditional view that the aging process, 
including development of physical frailty toward the end of life, 
is physiologic (normal) and unavoidable. Indeed, it is increasingly 
evident that it might not be necessary to accept the grim stereotype 
of aging as an unalterable process of decline and loss.332 Decades of 
research have produced compelling evidence that the rate of aging 
can be slowed and that both lifespan and “healthspan” (period 
of life free of disability and disease) can be extended. In animal 
models, this can be achieved by calorie restriction, changes in diet 
composition, exercise, and a variety of genetic and pharmacologic 
interventions. As human life expectancy continues to increase, 
there is an emerging consensus that the overarching goal should be

“an increase in years of healthy life with a full range of functional 
capacity at each stage of life.”334 Reducing the incidence and/or 
delaying the onset of age-related chronic disease and the result­
ing reduction of early mortality without major changes in maxi­
mal longevity is referred to as compression of morbidity or squaring 
of the survival curve. These highly desirable outcomes are in part 
promoted by lifestyle measures. However, this does not diminish 
the interest in developing antiaging interventions or the poten­
tial significance of treatments targeting mechanisms or symptoms 
associated with aging. Age-related changes in the endocrine sys­
tem invite interest in developing medical interventions involving 
long-term replacement therapy with one or more hormones to 
extend healthspan or perhaps also increase the chances for longer 
survival.335 However, evidence available to date indicates that hor­
monal interventions with sex steroids, thyroid hormone, DHEA, 
and/or GH have very limited effects on physical capacity in elderly 
individuals, whereas adverse effects are often considerable. Antiag­
ing or rejuvenating effects of hormonal or hormone-related prod­
ucts advertised directly to consumers are generally poorly or not 
at all supported by data, are grossly exaggerated, are often unsafe, 
and sometimes are preposterous.
The possibility of rejuvenation (i.e., reversal of the aging pro­
cess) has excited human imagination for centuries. Although in 
modern times this concept has been largely discredited and aban­
doned, it continues to represent an exciting possibility. Recent 
studies provided evidence that cellular senescence contributes to 
age-related deficits and diseases of the endocrine system. Acquisi­
tion of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) by 
a subset of pancreatic β-cells has been related to development of 
both type 1 and type 2 diabetes, presumably via impact of cyto­
kines secreted by senescent cells on the surrounding tissue.336,337 
In these and other preclinical studies, reducing the burden of 
senescent cells by pharmacologic senolytic agents or by trans­
genic senolysis produced major metabolic benefits, including 
prevention of diabetes.336–339 In addition to its role in metabolic 
syndrome and diabetes, cellular senescence affects endocrine 
control of bone metabolism and reproductive functions in both 
sexes.340 Well-established antiaging effects of senolytic drugs sug­
gest potential utility of these compounds in the prevention and 
treatment of a variety of chronic endocrine-related diseases and 
conditions associated with aging, including osteoporosis and 
diabetes.340,341

Studies of cardiovascular function in individuals voluntarily 
practicing long-term calorie restriction indicate that with regard to 
some clinically relevant characteristics of this system, it may indeed 
be possible to “turn back the clock.”342,343 Intriguing results of recent

currently appears to have no place in clinical practice.

KEY POINTS
 • 
Interactive hormonal homeostatic mechanisms maintain the 
concentrations of calcium and phosphate in the blood within 
narrow limits.
 • 
These mechanisms include prevailing extracellular calcium 
and phosphate concentrations and the hormones parathyroid 
hormone (PTH), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and fibroblast growth 
factor 23 (FGF23).
 • 
Adaptation of calcium and phosphate metabolism during 
physiologic challenges depends on alterations of absorption in 
the gut, excretion through the kidney, and buffering properties 
of bone.
 • 
Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause of 
hypercalcemia.
 • 
The most common cause of hypercalcemia that is not 
dependent on PTH is hypercalcemia of malignancy. Many other 
etiologies are included in this category of PTH-independent 
hypercalcemia, but they are uncommon.
 • 
Hypoparathyroidism is a rare disorder characterized 
by hypocalcemia and an inadequate or undetectable 
concentration of parathyroid hormone.

DAVID GOLTZMAN, AND MICHAEL MANNSTADT
Basic Biology of Mineral Metabolism: Roles 
of the Mineral Ions
Calcium (Ca) and phosphorus (P) are the major constituents 
of bone and comprise approximately 65% of its weight. Fur­
thermore, virtually all of the Ca and P in the body are found in 
bone, as well as more than 50% of magnesium. Nevertheless, 
the relatively small quantities of these ions located outside bone 
(i.e., 1–2 mmol/L) serve critical physiologic functions, both 
with cells and with each other, that are critical for bone miner­
alization, neuromuscular function, and mineral ion homeostasis 
(Fig. 27.1).
Calcium
The skeleton, the gut, and the kidney each play a major role in 
maintaining Ca homeostasis. Overall, in a typical individual, if 
1000 mg of Ca are ingested in the diet per day, approximately 
200 mg will be absorbed. Ordinarily, in individuals with bal­
anced bone turnover, approximately 500 mg of Ca is released 
from bone per day, and the equivalent amount is accreted per day 
(see Fig. 27.1). Approximately 10 g of Ca will be filtered daily 
through the kidney, and most will be reabsorbed, with about 200 
mg being excreted in the urine. The normal 24-hour excretion of 
Ca may, however, vary between 100 and 300 mg/day (2.5–7.5 
mmol/day).
SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
1172
SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
In adults, the body contains approximately 1 kg of Ca, of 
which 99% is located in the mineral phase of bone as the hydroxy­
apatite crystal [Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2]. The crystal plays a key role in 
the mechanical weight-bearing properties of bone and serves as 
a mobilizable source of Ca to support a variety of Ca-dependent 
biological systems and to maintain blood ionized Ca within the 
normal range. The remaining 1% of total-body Ca is located in 
the blood, extracellular fluid (ECF), and intracellular fluid of soft 
tissues.
In serum, total Ca concentration is approximately 10–3 M. 
Of the total Ca in blood, 45% is bound mainly to albumin in a 
pH-dependent manner and, to a lesser extent, to globulins; the 
remaining 10% exists as a complex with anions, including phos­
phate (PO4) and citrate (1). The free or ionized fraction (45%) 
is the biologically functional component of total Ca, is tightly 
regulated by hormonal mechanisms, and can be measured clini­
cally. Although only the ionized Ca is available to enter cells and 
activate cellular processes, most clinical laboratories report total 
serum Ca concentrations. Concentrations of total Ca in normal 
serum generally range between 8.5 and 10.5 mg/dL (2.12–2.62 
mM), and levels above this are considered to be hypercalcemic. 
The reference range for ionized Ca is 4.65 to 5.25 mg/dL (1.16–
1.31 mM). When protein concentrations, and especially albumin 
concentrations, fluctuate, total Ca levels may vary, whereas the 
ionized Ca may remain relatively stable. Dehydration or hemo­
concentration during venipuncture may elevate serum albumin 
and falsely elevate total serum Ca. Such elevations in total Ca, 
when albumin levels are increased, can be “corrected” by subtract­
ing 0.8 mg/dL from the total Ca for every 1.0 g/dL by which the 
serum albumin concentration is >4 g/dL. Conversely, when albu­
min levels are low, total Ca can be corrected by adding 0.8 mg/dL 
for every 1.0 g/dL by which the albumin is <4 g/dL. Even in the 
presence of a normal serum albumin, changes in blood pH can 
alter the equilibrium constant of the albumin-Ca2+ complex, with 
acidosis reducing the binding and alkalosis enhancing it. Con­
sequently, a major shift in serum protein or pH requires direct 
measurement of the ionized Ca level to determine the physiologic 
serum calcium level.
In addition to being the major substrate for the mineralization 
of cartilage and bone, extracellular calcium is tightly maintained 
within a rather narrow range because of the importance of the 
Ca ion to numerous cellular functions, including cell division, 
cell adhesion and plasma membrane integrity, protein secretion, 
muscle contraction, neuronal excitability, glycogen metabolism, 
and coagulation.
A very large chemical gradient (i.e., 10,000:1), augmented by 
a large negative electrical potential, favors calcium entry into cells 
via calcium channels, where the intracellular free calcium concen­
trations are only approximately 100 nM. This gradient is main­
tained by the limited conductance of resting calcium channels and 
by the energy-dependent extrusion of calcium into the extracel­
lular fluid via high-affinity Ca2+-adenosine triphosphatases and 
H+-adenosine triphosphatases (ATPases) and low-affinity sodium-
calcium (Na+-Ca2+) exchangers.
More than 99% of intracellular calcium exists in the form of 
complexes within membrane-bound compartments, including 
mitochondria, the inner plasma membrane, and the inner mem­
branes of the endoplasmic reticulum, as well as other compart­
ments. Calcium release from membrane-bound compartments 
transduces cellular signals and is tightly regulated. The mechanisms 
responsible for translocations of intracellular calcium between the 
cytosol and these sequestered regions involve specific receptors for 
calciotropic signaling molecules, including inositol triphosphate 
(IP3) receptor and ryanodine receptors.

CHAPTER 27  Hormones and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
Phosphate
Approximately 85% of phosphate is located in the mineral phase 
of bone, whereas the remainder is found in inorganic or organic 
form throughout the extracellular and intracellular compartments. 
In human serum, the concentration of inorganic phosphate is 
approximately 1 mmol/L and exists almost entirely in an ionized 
form as either H2PO4– or HPO42–. Only about 12% of serum 
phosphate is protein bound, whereas approximately 3% is loosely 
complexed with calcium, magnesium, and other cations. Con­
centrations of intracellular free phosphate are generally similar 
to extracellular fluid concentrations (i.e., 1–2 mmol/L); however, 
the negative electrical potential inside the cell requires significant 
energy for translocation of phosphate into cells. Phosphate trans­
location is generally accomplished via sodium-phosphate cotrans­
port driven by the transmembrane sodium gradient. A number of 
sodium-phosphate cotransporters have been identified, and vari­
ous cells and tissues use different species of such transporters with 
distinctive regulatory characteristics.
Although phosphate acts with calcium to regulate bone min­
eralization outside cells, few if any of the intracellular actions of 
phosphate involve actions of intracellular calcium. Organic phos­
phate is an integral component of nucleic acids, phospholipids, 
complex carbohydrates, glycolytic intermediates, structural, sig­
naling, and enzymatic phosphoproteins, as well as nucleotide 
cofactors for enzymes and G proteins. Thus, phosphate is a major 
constituent of virtually all types of structural, informational, and 
effector molecules that are critical for normal genetic, develop­
mental, and physiologic processes. The need for the large amounts 
of phosphate incorporated into cellular constituents during cell 
proliferation explains why phosphate levels in the blood are 
regulated by growth factors, such as insulin-like growth factor 1 
(IGF1), in addition to regulation by hormones of bone mineral­
ization. Of particular importance are the high-energy phosphate 
ester bonds present in molecules such as adenosine triphosphate 
(ATP), diphosphoglycerate, and creatine phosphate that store 
chemical energy. Phosphate plays a particularly prominent role 
as the key substrate or recognition site in numerous kinase and 
phosphatase regulatory cascades. Cytosolic phosphate per se also 
directly regulates a number of crucial intracellular reactions, 
including those involved in glucose transport, lactate production, 
and synthesis of ATP. In view of this broad spectrum of actions of 
phosphate, disorders of phosphate homeostasis leading to severe 
depletion of intracellular concentrations result in profound and 
widespread impairment of organ function. 
Magnesium
Magnesium is the fourth most abundant cation in the body. 
Approximately 50% of magnesium is found in bone and 50% 
in muscle and other soft tissues. As much as half of the magne­
sium in bone is not sequestered in the mineral phase but is freely 
exchangeable with the extracellular fluid and therefore may serve 
as a buffer against changes in extracellular magnesium concentra­
tion. Less than 1% of magnesium is present in the extracellular 
fluid, where the magnesium concentration is approximately 0.5 
mmol/L. The concentration of magnesium in serum is normally 
0.7 to 1 mmol/L, of which roughly one-third is protein bound, 
15% is complexed with phosphate or other anions, and 55% cir­
culates as the free ion. Over 95% of intracellular magnesium, the 
concentration of which is approximately 5 mmol/L, is bound to 
other molecules, most notably ATP. The intracellular cytosolic 
free magnesium concentration is approximately 0.5 mmol/L (i.e., 
1000-fold higher than that of calcium) and is maintained by an 
active sodium-magnesium antiporter. The mechanism(s) whereby 
magnesium enters cells continues to be explored.1,2
Intracellular magnesium, like phosphate, is necessary for a 
wide range of cellular functions. It is an essential cofactor in enzy­
matic reactions, including most of the same glycolytic, kinase, and 
phosphatase pathways that also involve phosphate. Magnesium 
serves to directly stabilize the structures of a variety of macromol­
ecules and complexes, including deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), 
ribonucleic acid (RNA), and ribosomes; is a key activator of the 
many ATPase-coupled ion transporters; and plays a direct role in 
mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. Consequently, magnesium 
is critical for energy metabolism and the maintenance of a nor­
mal intracellular environment. Extracellular magnesium is crucial 
for normal neuromuscular excitability and nerve conduction, and 
many of the clinical consequences of magnesium deficiency or 
excess reflect abnormalities in this area.
The levels of extracellular calcium and phosphate are regu­
lated in a coordinated way that reflects the roles of calcium and 
phosphate in mineralization of bone. The concentrations of these 
ions in body fluids are together close to the concentrations that 
could lead to spontaneous precipitation in soft tissues. In fact, 
elaborate mechanisms, most poorly understood, have evolved to 
prevent calcium phosphate precipitation in tissues and yet allow 
the controlled deposition of calcium and phosphate in bone.3,4 
The importance of the mineral ions for normal cellular physiology 
as well as skeletal integrity is reflected in the important endocrine 
control mechanisms that have evolved to maintain their extracel­
lular concentrations within relatively narrow limits.
Hormonal Regulation of Calcium and Phosphate 
Homeostasis
Extracellular fluid calcium concentrations are tightly regulated, 
largely by the action of the hormones PTH and 1,25 dihydroxyvi­
tamin D (1α,25[OH2D], the active form of vitamin D, also known 
as calcitriol). The hormones fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) 
and calcitonin may also participate in calcium homeostasis. In 
addition, the extracellular calcium, via the calcium-sensing recep­
tor (CaSR), itself modulates calcium homeostasis and therefore, in 
this respect, acts as an endocrine factor.5 Thus, when the extracel­
lular calcium declines, as in severe calcium deprivation (Fig. 27.2), 
this alteration is sensed by the CaSR in the parathyroid glands, 
leading to decreased suppression of PTH synthesis and secretion 
and therefore to increased PTH exocytotic release from the para­
thyroid glands. The decreased ECF Ca can itself promote calcium 
reabsorption by its reduced action on CaSR in the cortical thick 
ascending loop (TAL), in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT), 
and in the collecting duct to diminish renal calcium loss.6
Once PTH is secreted, the NH2-terminal domain of the 
increased circulating PTH binds to the PTH/PTH–related pro­
tein (PTHrP) receptor (PTHR1), a G protein–coupled receptor 
(GPCR),7 in the osteoblasts of bone, increasing intracellular cyclic 
adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) production and thus enhanc­
ing the release of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-related cytokine 
receptor activator of nuclear factor κβ (RANKL) and decreasing 
the release of the RANKL antagonist osteoprotegerin (OPG). 
RANKL binds to the RANK receptor in cells of the osteoclast lin­
eage, increasing osteoclast production and action and augmenting 
bone resorption.8 The calcium liberated from bone now increases 
Ca in the extracellular fluid. PTH, when released intermittently 
rather than continuously, can also enhance bone formation by its 
1174
SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
actions on osteoblastic cells.9 This action is partly mediated by 
effects on Wnt signaling and reductions in sclerostin expression 
in osteocytes.10
Increased PTH also augments calcium reabsorption in the kid­
ney by its action in the distal renal tubule, including the cortical 
TAL of the loop of Henle and DCT. In the TAL, PTH binds to 
PTHR1, increasing Na/K/2Cl-transporter activity and enhancing 
the reabsorption of calcium, sodium, chloride, and magnesium.11 
This leads to decreased renal excretion of calcium. In addition, 
PTH can act via the PTHR1 in the proximal renal tubule to 
increase the activity of CYP27B1, the renal 1α(OH)ase, and thus 
enhance the conversion of the precursor 25-hydroxyvitamin D 
[25(OH)D] to the active form, 1α,25(OH)2D.12
The increased 1α,25(OH)2D produced can then act on its 
nuclear receptor, the vitamin D receptor (VDR), in the intestine 
to facilitate calcium reabsorption.13 This may occur by facili­
tating active calcium reabsorption in the small intestine, where 
transcellular absorption occurs via the luminal transient receptor 
potential vanilloid family member 6 (TRPV6), followed by intra­
cellular calcium transport by calbindin-D9k and, subsequently, 
basolateral calcium extrusion via an Na/Ca exchanger 1 (NCX) 
and plasma membrane Ca ATPase 1b (PMCA1b). This sequence 
and other mechanisms are likely enhanced by 1α,25(OH)2D.14 
1,25(OH)2D also regulates claudin 2 and claudin 12, which form 
paracellular calcium channels and can reroute Ca through these 
paracellular epithelial cell junctions and render them more Ca 
permeable.15 Renal tubular calcium reabsorption by increased 
PTH and reduced CaSR stimulation may also be enhanced by 
increased 1,25(OH)2D-stimulated expression of calbindin-D28K 
in the distal tubules
In addition, in the presence of reduced ECF Ca, the increased 
1α,25(OH)2D can bind to the VDR in osteoclasts and enhance 
bone resorption, thus increasing calcium release into the ECF. 
Augmented 1α,25(OH)2D can also stimulate release of FGF23 
from cells of the osteoblast/osteocyte lineage. FGF23 can in turn 
inhibit renal 1α,25(OH)2D production, thus closing a negative 
feedback loop. FGF23 may also inhibit PTH release.
Thus, increased PTH-induced bone resorption and renal reab­
sorption of Ca, and increased 1α,25(OH)2D synthesis leading to 
augmented gut absorption of Ca, as well as a reduced ECF Ca per 
se, acting via CaSR, and resulting in diminished renal Ca reab­
sorption, all contribute toward restoring ECF Ca to normal. Once 
ECF Ca is restored to the normal range, the signals for further 
hormonal release and action are diminished.
The opposite sequence of events occurs in the face of an elevated 
ECF Ca, leading to the restoration of ECF Ca concentrations into 
the normal range. Additionally, at least in other mammals, sus­
tained elevated ECF Ca can lead to release of the hormone calci­
tonin from thyroidal C cells, which in turn can inhibit osteoclastic 
bone resorption and contribute to Ca lowering into the normal 
range. The role of calcitonin in regulating calcium homeostasis 
in humans is less clear, however, because states of hypercalce­
mia rarely result in accompanying hypercalcitoninemia, and the 
absence of calcitonin, as in post–total thyroidectomy states, rarely 
leads to hypercalcemia. Furthermore, states of calcitonin excess, 
such as occur with elevated calcitonin release by medullary thyroid 
carcinoma, rarely result in hypocalcemia.
Calcium balance in the body must also adapt to changes due 
to growth, pregnancy, lactation, menopause, and aging, and other 
hormones may also play a role in maintaining calcium homeostasis 
during these various stages. Thus, PTHrP, which may be ectopi­
cally secreted by malignant tumors, causing paraneoplastic hyper­
calcemia, shares homology with PTH at its NH2-terminal domain 
and binds to PTHR1.16 However, PTHrP also plays an important 
physiologic role in pregnancy, during which it is secreted by the 
placenta to regulate maternal-to-fetal calcium transport and thus 
ensure sufficient calcium availability for fetal bone development, 
and is also produced in breast tissue during lactation.17 PTHrP is 
also expressed in many tissues, where it acts as a paracrine regula­
tor regulating growth of bone and other organs in fetal and early 
life.18
Several other hormones, such as sex steroids, glucocorticoids, 
and growth and thyroid hormones, as well as changes in ion con­
centrations and pH, also affect calcium balance. Thus, increased

increases the affinity of albumin for calcium, decreasing the con­
centration of ionized ECF Ca, whereas acidosis decreases calcium 
binding to albumin and increases ionized ECF Ca concentrations. 
Systemic acidosis can also increase urinary calcium loss and acti­

for the maintenance of normal ECF calcium concentration.
Elevated FGF23 release by osteoblasts/osteocytes may occur 
in response to elevated 1α,25(OH)2D. Although 1α,25(OH)2D 
may have a modest effect on augmenting PO4 absorption from 
the intestine, FGF23 is a very potent regulator of PO4 transport 
in the kidney, inhibiting the Na/P cotransporters, NaPT2a and 
NaPT2c, on the luminal surface of the proximal tubule cell and 
thus inhibiting PO4 reabsorption and facilitating phosphaturia.19 
FGF23 appears to act in this regard by binding to FGF receptor 
1 (FGFR1) in heterotrimeric association with the protein Klotho. 
PTH also decreases renal proximal tubule PO4 reabsorption by 
inhibiting the NaPT2a and NaPT2c cotransporters and promot­
ing renal PO4 wasting. However, in contrast to PTH, FGF23 
inhibits renal 1α,25(OH)2D synthesis. Consequently, the hypo­
phosphatemic effect of FGF23 appears to exceed that of PTH. 
Elevated circulating PO4 per se has also been implicated as a direct 
stimulator of FGF23 release; however, a basal level of ECF Ca 
appears necessary for this effect.20 FGF23 has also been reported 
to inhibit PTH release, an effect that may also limit its phospha­
turic action. Overall, therefore, both calcium and phosphate initi­
ate complex hormonal mechanisms to maintain homeostasis, with 
several hormonal factors contributing to these mechanisms.
The following sections describe the structures, secretory con­
trols, detailed actions, and interactions of PTH, calcitonin, 
1,25[OH]2D (calcitriol), and FGF23—the major hormones 
involved in mineral ion homeostasis. Subsequent sections cover 
the spectrum of clinical disorders that accompany abnormalities 
in this hormonal network. 
Parathyroid Hormone
PTH is the peptide hormone that controls the minute-to-minute 
level of the ionized calcium concentration in the blood and ECF. 
PTH binds to cell surface receptors in bone and kidney, thereby 
triggering responses that increase blood calcium (Fig. 27.3). These 
include (1) stimulation of bone resorption, which delivers cal­
cium and phosphorus into the circulation, (2) stimulation of renal 
tubular calcium reabsorption, and (3) an increase in the renal syn­
thesis of 1,25(OH)2D3, the hormonally active form of vitamin 
D, which then acts on the intestine to augment absorption of 
dietary calcium. The resulting increase in blood calcium [and in 
1,25(OH)2D3] feeds back on the parathyroid glands to decrease 
the secretion of PTH. The parathyroid glands, bones, kidney, and 
gastrointestinal tract are thus the key organs that participate in 
PTH-mediated calcium homeostasis.
Parathyroid Gland Biology
Parathyroid glands first appeared in evolutionary history with the 
exit of amphibians from the sea and a switch from dependence 
on gills to sole dependence on bone, intestine, and kidney to 
maintain extracellular calcium homeostasis. Reptiles, birds, and 
mammals all have parathyroid glands that develop as epithelial 
specializations from the endoderm of the pharyngeal pouches. 
Although fish have no discrete parathyroid glands, they do have 
several PTH-related genes, including two or more that can influ­
ence calcium homeostasis.21
Parathyroid chief cells have three properties vital to their 
homeostatic function: First, they rapidly secrete PTH in response 
to changes in blood calcium. Second, they can synthesize, process, 
and store large amounts of PTH in a regulated manner. Third, 
parathyroid cells replicate when chronically stimulated. These 
functional attributes allow for short-, intermediate-, and long-
term adaptation, respectively, to changes in calcium availability.
Parathyroid Hormone Biosynthesis
PTH, a protein of 84 amino acids in mammals, is synthesized as 
a larger precursor, pre-proparathyroid hormone (pre-pro-PTH) of 
115 amino acids. These pre-pro-PTH sequences share a 25-resi­
due “pre” or signal sequence and a 6-residue “pro” sequence. The 
signal sequence acts as a “zip code” to direct the protein into the 
secretory pathway, and the pro-sequence may allow for efficient 
and accurate cleavage of the precursor.22 Pre- and pro-sequences 
are cleaved off during transit across the endoplasmic reticulum. 
The importance of the signal sequence for normal secretion of 
PTH and the cleavage of the pro-sequence is illustrated by the 
hypoparathyroidism inherited in families carrying mutations in 
the signal sequence of pre-pro-PTH or a mutation at the first 
amino acid of the mature PTH, respectively.23–25
After cleavage of the pro-sequence, the mature PTH(1-84) 
is concentrated in secretory vesicles and granules, where it co-
localizes with cathepsin B and H proteases. A portion of PTH is 
secreted from parathyroid glands as carboxy-terminal PTH frag­
ments, which are inactive on the PTH1 receptor; they may even 
block bone resorption.26 The intracellular degradation of newly 
synthesized PTH to these carboxy-terminal fragments thus may 
provide an important regulatory mechanism. Under conditions 
of hypercalcemia, the secretion of PTH is markedly reduced, and 
most of what is secreted consists of carboxy-terminal fragments.27 
Parathyroid Hormone Secretion
The major regulator of PTH secretion is the concentration of 
ionized calcium in blood. An increase in serum ionized calcium
