concentration leads to a decrease in PTH secretion through the 
activation of the CaSR on the surface of parathyroid cells. The 
physiologic relationship between extracellular calcium concen­
trations and PTH secretion is an inverse sigmoidal curve (Fig. 
27.4). The level of calcium at the midpoint of this curve deter­
mines the set-point of serum calcium levels. The steepness of the 
curve reflects the large changes in PTH induced by relatively small 
changes in serum calcium, ensuring the tight regulation of serum 
calcium within a relatively narrow range.
The sigmoid curve reveals several important physiologic prop­
erties of the parathyroid gland. The minimal secretory rate is low 
but not zero. The maximal secretory rate represents the reserve of 
the parathyroid’s capacity to respond to hypocalcemia. Because 
values from normal persons in the steady state are located in the 
lower portion of the sigmoid curve, the system seems designed to 
respond more dramatically to hypocalcemia than to hypercalcemia.
Physiologic studies in humans have revealed that the parathy­
roid cell responds both to the absolute level of blood calcium and 
to the rate of fall of calcium level, offering additional protection 
against sudden hypocalcemia.
The extracellular calcium is sensed by the CaSR on the sur­
face of the parathyroid cells, a member of the class C GPCRs28 
(Fig. 27.5). The CaSR functions as an obligate homodimer and 
binds a number of small ligands, including amino acids, calcium, 
phosphate, and other cations. The structure of the near-full-length 
human CaSR has been solved by cryogenic electron microscopy 
(cryo-EM), and binding sites for calcium, phosphate, and other 
ligands have been identified.29 The activated receptor couples to 
several G proteins, including Gq/11, which leads to increases in 
phospholipase C (PLC) and Gi, which causes decreases in cAMP 
production to block PTH secretion.
Mutations in the CaSR gene cause characteristic human dis­
eases. Inactivating mutations cause familial hypocalciuric hyper­
calcemia (FHH), a disease of defective calcium sensing,30 whereas 
activating mutations cause autosomal-dominant hypocalcemia 
type 1.31,32 Engineered mice with a loss of a copy of the CaSR gene 
or with activating point mutations mirror the respective human 
phenotypes.33 Of importance, calcimimetic compounds that 
activate the CaSR have been shown to inhibit PTH secretion in 
humans and are useful in the treatment of certain hyperparathy­
roid states.34,35 Despite the enormous increase in the understand­
ing of how extracellular calcium activates the parathyroid CaSR, 
the mechanism whereby this activation leads to a decrease in PTH 
secretion is poorly understood.
The expression of the CaSR in the renal tubules contributes 
to calcium homeostasis by modifying renal calcium excretion. 
However, the CaSR is expressed widely and has functions besides 
calcium homeostasis. These other functions are being discov­
ered. For example, knockout of the CaSR in osteoblasts of mice 
shows that this receptor regulates osteoblast differentiation and 
mineralization.36 
Regulation of the Parathyroid Hormone Gene
The minute-to-minute regulation of PTH blood levels can be 
explained by two mechanisms already discussed—regulation of 
PTH secretion by the CaSR and amplification of this regulation 
by varying amounts of intracellular degradation of stored hor­
mone. Over a longer time frame, the parathyroid cell regulates the 
expression of the PTH gene as well.
Although 1,25(OH)2D3—the active form of vitamin D—
has no direct effect on PTH secretion, it dramatically suppresses 
PTH gene transcription.37 This suppression of transcription does 
not occur when 1,25(OH)2D3 is administered to chronically 
hypocalcemic animals, however, perhaps because hypocalcemia 
leads to a fall in parathyroid cell VDRs or because hypocalcemia 
increases the expression of calreticulin in the parathyroid.38 The 
capability of hypocalcemia to override the effects of high levels of 
1,25(OH)2D3 represents an important defense because it provides 
a way for the parathyroid cell to synthesize large amounts of PTH 
and 1,25(OH)2D3 at the same time when both are needed.
Calcium also regulates the biosynthesis of PTH. Studies in 
rats show that acute hypocalcemia leads to an increase in PTH 
messenger RNA (mRNA) within an hour. In contrast, hypercal­
cemia leads to little or no change in PTH mRNA. Thus, under 
normal conditions, the inhibition by calcium of PTH biosynthe­
sis is already nearly maximal, just as it is for PTH secretion. The 
parathyroid gland is poised to respond to a fall in calcium much 
more readily than to its rise. The mechanism for the increase in 
PTH mRNA in response to hypocalcemia may involve gene tran­
scription, mRNA translation, and mRNA stability. The posttran­
scriptional mechanism is the one best understood at the molecular 
level.39 In the parathyroid cell, specific proteins bind to the 3′UTR 
of the PTH mRNA to change the mRNA stability. K-homology 
splicing regulator protein (KSRP) destabilizes PTH mRNA, and 
AU-rich binding factor 1 (AUF1) increases PTH mRNA stability, 
and their activities are regulated by changes in serum calcium and 
by chronic kidney disease (CKD).40,41
For decades, it has been known that increases in phosphate 
stimulate PTH secretion, largely by lowering blood calcium 
and 1,25(OH)2D3 levels. But a series of studies in vitro42,43 and

FGF23, an important phosphate-regulating hormone (see

els are elevated. This paradoxical observation (given the role of 
FGF23 in suppressing PTH secretion) may be explained by the 
downregulation of parathyroid cell FGF receptor 1 and Klotho in 
renal failure.49,50 
Regulation of Parathyroid Cell Number
Parathyroid cells divide during the growth of young animals but 
replicate little in adulthood.51 Parathyroid cell number can dra­
matically increase, however, in the setting of hypocalcemia, low 
levels of 1,25(OH)2D3, hyperphosphatemia, or uremia, or during 
neoplastic growth.
Calcium, acting through the parathyroid CaSR, restrains 
parathyroid proliferation. The behavior of the parathyroids in 
patients who lack both copies of the CaSR gene is consistent 
with this hypothesis. These neonates exhibit severe primary 
hyperparathyroidism with large, diffusely hyperplastic glands 
that presumably have developed because of insufficient activation 
of the parathyroid CaSR by extracellular calcium. Furthermore, 
administration of the calcimimetic compound NPS R-568, which 
activates the CaSR directly, prevents parathyroid cell proliferation 
in experimental uremia.52
1,25(OH)2D3 can dramatically suppress parathyroid cell num­
ber, which been shown in vivo in many settings. This effect might 
be indirect through a transient increase in serum calcium. Cal­
cium alone can prevent parathyroid cell hyperplasia in mice engi­
neered to lack VDRs.53 An effect independent of blood calcium 
was suggested by the observation that 1,25(OH)2D3 suppresses 
the proliferation of cultured parathyroid cells in vitro.54 Hypocal­
cemia and experimental renal failure activate the mTORC1 com­
plex, and this increased signaling by mTOR is required for the 
parathyroid cell proliferation observed.55
Although the ability to increase parathyroid cell number in 
response to physiologic challenge represents an important defense 
against hypocalcemia, it is a slow response that is not easily revers­
ible. When the need for an increased number of parathyroid cells 
disappears (e.g., after renal transplantation for uremia), persis­
tent hyperparathyroidism can cause vexing clinical problems for 
months and years thereafter. The mechanisms for decreasing para­
thyroid cell number are poorly understood.

development may have broad clinical implications. Although the 
genetic mechanisms used to generate parathyroid chief cells dur­
ing development are largely unknown, the importance of several 
specific transcription factors has become clear. Studies of gene 
knockout mice have shown that the Hoxa3,57 Pax1,58 Pax9,59 
and Eya160 transcription factors are needed to form parathyroid 
glands. Tbx1 is also essential for parathyroid cell development, 
and haploinsufficiency for this transcription factor is likely to be 
the cause of hypoparathyroidism in the 22q11.2 deletion syn­
drome.61 The parathyroid-specific transcription factor GCM2 is 
needed for the continued survival of parathyroid cells.62 Mice 
or humans63 missing the GCM2 genes have hypoparathyroid­
ism and no discernible parathyroid glands. Deletion of one 
copy of the gene encoding MafB in the mouse leads to ectopic 
parathyroid glands and, in adulthood, suppression of secondary 
hyperparathyroidism in a renal failure model.64,65 Humans with 
X-linked hypoparathyroidism manifest a deletion-insertion near 
the end of the SOX3 gene, a finding that suggests an important 
role for Sox3 in parathyroid development.66 Individuals with 
mutations in the gene encoding the transcription factor GATA3 
exhibit a syndrome of hypoparathyroidism, sensorineural deaf­
ness, and renal anomalies (HDR) when only one copy of the 
gene is mutated.67 GATA3 synergizes with GCMB and MafB in 
stimulating PTH gene expression.68 
Metabolism of Parathyroid Hormone
As noted previously, both PTH(1-84) and carboxy-terminal frag­
ments of PTH are secreted by the parathyroid gland; the ratio 
of inactive PTH to active PTH secretion increases with increas­
ing blood calcium.69 Secreted intact PTH(1-84) is extensively 
metabolized by the liver (70%) and kidney (20%) and disappears 
from the circulation, with a half-life of approximately 2 minutes. 
This rapid peripheral metabolism of PTH is unaffected by widely 
varying levels of blood calcium or 1,25(OH)2D3. These features 
of PTH metabolism ensure that the blood level of PTH is deter­
mined principally by the activity of the parathyroid glands and 
that the PTH level can respond rapidly to small changes in the 
rate of secretion of the hormone.
Carboxy-terminal fragments are also cleared efficiently by 
glomerular filtration. In fact, the kidney is the only known site 
of clearance of carboxy-terminal PTH fragments. These frag­
ments thus accumulate dramatically when the glomerular fil­
tration rate (GFR) falls. Even in the presence of normal renal 
function, the half-life of carboxy-terminal fragments of PTH 
exceeds that of PTH(1-84) by several-fold. Consequently, the 
concentration of carboxy-terminal fragments in the circulation 
exceeds that of intact PTH, reaching about 80% in normocal­
cemic subjects with intact renal function, even though intact 
PTH is usually the major form of PTH secreted from the para­
thyroid gland.
High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and 
immunologic methods have revealed PTH fragments that are 
missing only a few N-terminal amino acids that are predicted 
to be unable to stimulate the PTH1R.70 Nevertheless, the pos­
sible biologic activity of these and other PTH fragments, perhaps 
through novel receptors, remains an area of active investigation. 
Experiments with PTH(7-84) suggest that such extended car­
boxy-terminal fragments may exert potent effects in vivo, oppos­
ing those of intact PTH.26,71,72 
Actions of Parathyroid Hormone
Actions of Parathyroid Hormone on the Kidney
Stimulation of Calcium Reabsorption. Almost all of the cal­
cium in the initial glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal 
tubules. Sixty-five percent or more is reabsorbed by the proxi­
mal convoluted and straight tubules via a passive, paracellular 
route.73 Changes in the transepithelial voltage gradient, deter­
mined largely by the rate of sodium reabsorption, control the 
rate of calcium transport in the proximal tubule, and PTH does 
little to affect calcium flux in this region. The remaining calcium 
is largely reabsorbed more distally—20% of the initial filtrate in 
the cortical thick ascending limb (cTAL) of Henle loop and 10% 
in the distal convoluted and connecting tubules. In the cTAL, 
calcium reabsorption is also mainly passive and paracellular, 
although some transcellular, active calcium transport may occur 
as well. Efficient paracellular calcium and magnesium movement 
requires expression of a unique tight-junction protein, paracel­
lin-1, also called claudin-16; mutant paracellin-1 genes underlie 
a rare renal calcium-wasting and magnesium-wasting disorder.74 
Because paracellular cation transport in the cTAL is driven by the 
lumen-positive transepithelial voltage gradient that is established 
by active Na-K-Cl2 reabsorption, calcium reabsorption there 
is strongly inhibited by loop diuretics such as furosemide. The 
CaSR, initially characterized in the parathyroid, is also expressed 
in the cTAL. When activated by high blood calcium or magne­
sium, this receptor inhibits Na-K-Cl2 reabsorption in the cTAL 
and, thereby, paracellular calcium reabsorption as well. This pro­
vides a parathyroid-independent mechanism for controlling renal 
calcium handling in direct response to changes in blood calcium 
concentration.
Although PTH modestly stimulates paracellular calcium reab­
sorption in the cTAL, the primary site for hormonal regulation of 
renal calcium reabsorption is the distal nephron, which normally 
reabsorbs nearly all of the remaining 10% of filtered calcium by 
a unique transcellular active transport mechanism. As depicted in 
Fig. 27.1, the intracellular level of calcium is extremely low, about 
150 nM, compared with the millimolar levels in the glomerular 
filtrate and the blood. Calcium enters distal tubular cells from the 
tubular lumen down a highly favorable electrochemical gradient 
via selective channels (TRPV5 and TRPV6) present on the apical 
membrane of cells in the DCT and connecting tubule (CNT). 
Intracellular calcium inhibits the activity of these channels, but 
this is minimized by the avid binding of calcium to calbindin-
D28K, which effectively buffers cytosolic calcium and transports 
it to the basolateral membrane. There, calcium is ejected via active 
processes involving mainly the sodium-calcium exchanger NCX1 
and an ATP-driven calcium pump (PMCA).58 PTH stimulates 
DCT and CNT active calcium transport by upregulating several 
of these components, including TRPV5, calbindin-D28K, and 
NCX1, both directly and indirectly, via increased synthesis of 
1,25(OH)2D.75 PTH acutely increases the flux of calcium through 
TRPV5 by leading to protein kinase A (PKA) phosphorylation of 
a residue of TRPV5 that otherwise would bind calmodulin and 
thereby close the channel.76
The amount of calcium present in urine also depends crucially 
on the initial filtered load of calcium, which is a direct function of 
the serum calcium level. This is best illustrated in states of primary 
PTH excess and hypercalcemia. In this setting, the total amount 
of calcium in urine is likely to be high because of the high initial 
filtered load, even though the rate of distal tubular calcium reab­
sorption is increased by PTH. 
1179
CHAPTER 27  Hormones and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
Inhibition of Phosphate Transport. Phosphate reabsorption 
occurs mainly in the proximal renal tubules, which reclaim roughly 
80% of the filtered load. Some additional phosphate (8%–10%) 
is reabsorbed in the distal tubule (but not in Henle loop), leaving 
about 10% to 12% for excretion in the urine. The normal overall 
fractional tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TRP), therefore, is 
about 90%, although a more reliable measure of renal phosphate 
handling is the phosphate threshold (TmP/GFR), which can be 
derived from the TRP through the use of a nomogram (Fig. 27.6) 
based on studies of experimental phosphate infusions in healthy 
persons and in patients with a variety of diseases that affect phos­
phate excretion.77
Phosphate reabsorption in both proximal and distal tubules 
is strongly inhibited by PTH, although the proximal effect is 
quantitatively most important. Phosphate reabsorption in the 
parathyroid is mediated by the sodium-phosphate (NaPi) cotrans­
porters NaPi-IIa (encoded by SLC34A1) and NaPi-IIc (encoded by 
SLC34A3).78 In response to PTH, the maximum velocity (Vmax) 
for sodium-phosphate cotransport decreases because both NaPi 
cotransporters are rapidly (within 15 minutes) removed from the 
apical membrane and sequestered within subapical endocytic vesi­
cles, after which they are delivered to lysosomes and undergo pro­
teolysis.79 cAMP and PKA mediate the rapid decrease in phosphate 
transport in response to PTH, although PLC activation by the 
PTH receptor is also required for prolonged suppression of phos­
phate transport by PTH.80 This response to PTH is dependent on 
Na+/H+ exchange regulatory factors (NHERFs), which physically 
interact with both the PTH1R and the NaPi-II transporters and 
control the pattern of PTH receptor signaling.81,82 Conversely, in 
hypoparathyroidism, expression of NaPi protein and mRNA is 
strongly upregulated, leading to hyperphosphatemia.
Dietary intake of phosphate also reciprocally regulates the 
expression and activity of NaPi cotransporters and thus the proxi­
mal tubular absorption of phosphate by a mechanism that is inde­
pendent of PTH. Dietary deprivation of phosphate, for example, 
leads to a stimulation of phosphate reabsorption that can override 
the effects of PTH on the proximal tubule. It is likely that this 
dietary regulation of NaPi expression is mediated by FGF23 (see 
later discussion).83 
Other Renal Effects of Parathyroid Hormone. PTH stimu­
lates the synthesis of 1,25(OH)2D in the proximal tubule by rap­
idly inducing transcription of the 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25[OH]
D) 1α-hydroxylase gene (CYP27B1) and inhibition of the metab­
olizing enzyme 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1), both through the 
inhibition of salt-inducible kinase (SIK). This was recently shown 
to be mediated by SIKs downstream of the PTH1R.84 (See dis­
cussion under “Metabolism of Vitamin D.”) PTH inhibits proxi­
mal tubular sodium, water, and bicarbonate reabsorption, mainly 
via inhibition of the apical Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3) and the 
basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase. PTH also stimulates proximal tubu­
lar gluconeogenesis and acts directly on glomerular podocytes to 
decrease both single nephron and whole kidney GFR. 
Actions of Parathyroid Hormone on Bone
PTH acts directly on osteoblasts and osteocytes that express the 
PTH1R. In addition, through the activation of osteoblasts and 
the RANKL/RANK/OPG system, PTH indirectly stimulates the 
activation of osteoclasts that do not express the PTH1R. There­
fore, PTH leads to an increase in bone formation and bone resorp­
tion. Which action dominates depends on the dose of PTH and 
the route of administration. When PTH is administered continu­
ously, the effect of PTH on bone resorption dominates, and the 
net result is a release of calcium from bone and a decrease in bone 
mass. This action of PTH thus contributes to the increase in blood 
calcium seen in primary hyperparathyroidism (Fig. 27.7).

active amino-terminal fragments of PTH by once-daily subcuta­
neous injection leads to a net increase in bone mass, with only

transient effects on blood calcium. Mechanisms for these diver­
gent effects of PTH are incompletely understood but certainly 
reflect the variety of cell types in bone that respond directly to 
PTH, the varying time courses of these responses, and the indirect 
effects of PTH caused by autocrine and paracrine responses to 
PTH.85
Fig. 27.8 illustrates the cells of the osteoblast lineage. Osteo­
blasts are probably derived from pluripotent mesenchymal stem 
cells that can differentiate into chondrocytes, adipocytes, osteo­
blasts, and other cell types.86,87 Perivascular cells within human 
bone can reconstitute bone that supports hematopoiesis after 
subcutaneous transplantation in mice88; these cells may well 
represent one of probably several groups of osteoblast stem cells 
in vivo. Within the osteoblast lineage, committed osteoprogeni­
tor cells divide, become preosteoblastic stromal cells (which can 
divide further), and then become osteoblasts. Osteoblasts no 
longer divide and are cuboidal cells found on the bone surface 
actively laying down new bone. These cells can surround them­
selves with newly formed bone matrix and extend large num­
bers of dendritic processes, becoming osteocytes. Alternatively, 
osteoblasts can stop synthesizing matrix and remain on the bone 
surface as bone lining cells. Not all preosteoblasts and osteoblasts 
mature; a variable number die by apoptotic, programmed cell 
death.89
PTH administration in vivo, whether administered continu­
ously or intermittently, increases osteoblast surface and number 
and bone formation rate. Several mechanisms have been revealed 
that lead to the increase in osteoblast numbers. PTH adminis­
tration increases the number and rate of differentiation of early 
osteoblast precursors in a murine lineage-tracing model.74 Stud­
ies using genetically marked mice show that PTH converts bone 
lining cells to active osteoblasts.76 Further, the decreased rate of 
osteoblast apoptosis after intermittent PTH administration leads 
to an increase in the number of osteoblasts.89
In addition to changing osteoblast numbers, PTH changes 
the activity of mature osteoblasts by a variety of mechanisms. 
PTH stimulation of osteoblastic cells leads to release of growth 
factors such as IGF1, FGF2, and amphiregulin from these cells.90 
PTH also decreases the synthesis of dickkopf-191 and scleros­
tin (synthesized by osteocytes),92 inhibitors of Wnt signaling.93 
These latter actions are expected to increase the anabolic actions 
of Wnt proteins on osteoblasts. Further, because bone matrix 
is a rich source of osteoblast growth factors, the release of these 
growth factors from this matrix following PTH-induced bone 
resorption may increase bone formation and deliver osteoblastic 
cells to sites of bone formation.94 Thus a variety of both direct 
and indirect actions of PTH can lead to the increased produc­
tion of bone. 
PTH Increases Bone Resorption. Surprisingly, osteoclasts, the 
bone-resorbing cells derived from hematopoietic precursors, have 
no PTH receptors on their surfaces. Instead, cells of the osteo­
blast lineage, including preosteoblasts, osteoblasts, and osteocytes, 
signal to osteoclast precursors to cause them to fuse and form 
mature osteoclasts. This signaling also serves to stimulate mature 
osteoclasts to resorb bone and to avoid apoptosis (see Fig. 27.7). 
Two cell surface proteins, macrophage colony-stimulating factor 
(M-CSF) and RANKL, are essential for stimulation of osteoclas­
togenesis,95 and RANKL is essential for the activation of mature 
osteoclasts. The growth factor M-CSF (or CSF1) is expressed both 
as a secreted protein and as a cell surface protein. The production 
of both forms is stimulated by PTH.96 RANKL is a membrane-
bound member of the TNF family. Its synthesis is also increased 
by PTH. RANKL binds to its receptor, RANK, a member of the 
TNF receptor family. RANK is found both on osteoclast precur­
sors and on mature osteoclasts. The binding of RANKL to RANK 
can be blocked by osteoprotegerin (OPG), another member of 
the TNF receptor family. OPG circulates and is also secreted by 
cells of the osteoblastic lineage. PTH decreases the synthesis and 
secretion of OPG from these cells. Thus, PTH, by increasing 
RANK and decreasing OPG locally in bone, serves to increase 
bone resorption.
Activation of PTH receptors also causes release of calcium from 
bone by a less understood mechanism called osteocytic osteolysis. 
Osteocytes can directly release mineral from the matrix immedi­
ately surrounding them. These cells produce proteins associated 
with bone resorption by osteoclasts, including carbonic anhydrase 
2, cathepsin K, and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase.97 For 
example, during lactation in mice, lacunae surrounding osteocytes 
release calcium; this release depends on those osteocytes express­
ing PTH1Rs.98 Little is known about the quantitative importance 
of osteocytic osteolysis versus osteoclastic bone resorption in vari­
ous settings. 
Molecular Basis of Parathyroid Hormone Action
PTH binds to its receptor, a class B GPCR, expressed on the sur­
face of target cells. The resulting conformational changes in the 
receptor activate G proteins and second messengers, eventually 
leading to the physiologic responses of bone and kidney cells.
Parathyroid Hormone and Parathyroid Hormone–Related 
Protein Receptors. DNA encoding a PTH1R has been isolated 
from tissues of many species, including rat, opossum, human, 
pig, Xenopus (toad), zebrafish,99 and even some insects.100 It is a 
member of the family B GPCRs, which include receptors for the 
secretin family of peptides (secretin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, 
glucagon, etc.), corticotropin-releasing hormone, calcitonin, and 
others.

The PTH1R is unique because it transmits extracellular stimuli 
from two distinct native peptide agonists, PTH and PTHrP. The 
cloned PTH1R binds amino-terminal fragments of PTH and 
PTHrP with equal affinity. In contrast to the calciotropic endo­
crine hormone PTH, PTHrP is a paracrine-acting factor that is 
expressed in many tissues and exerts multiple physiologic roles, 
including bone, skin, and breast development. The receptor is 
expressed at high levels in the kidney and in osteoblasts of bone 
but is also expressed in a wide variety of tissues, such as smooth 
muscle, brain, and a variety of fetal tissues, which are thought to 
be targets more for PTHrP than for PTH. PTH1R knockout mice 
show defects both in calcium homeostasis and in local actions of 
PTHrP on the growth plates of bone, for example.101 Mutations 
in the receptor found in humans are also consistent with this idea 
(see upcoming discussion). It is unlikely that all of the actions of 
PTH can be explained by interactions with the identified PTH1R: 
fragments of PTH that seem not to bind the receptor may be bio­
logically active.102 Furthermore, the carboxy-terminal portion of 
PTH(1-84) binds a cell surface protein distinct from the PTH1R.
A second PTH receptor (PTHR), which can be activated by 
PTH but not by PTHrP, called the PTH2 receptor (PTH2R), has 
been cloned. This receptor is expressed in many tissues, including 
brain, vascular endothelium and smooth muscle, gastrointestinal 
cells, and sperm. Expression is not seen in osteoblasts or renal 
tubules, however. A ligand called TIP39 (tubero-infundibular 
peptide of 39 residues) has been characterized and shown to be 
a potent activator of PTH2R. TIP39 bears only a weak resem­
blance to PTH or PTHrP and is likely to be a physiologically 
relevant activator of the PTH2. The functional role of the PTH2R 
is unknown, but it appears to mediate many actions of TIP39 in 
the brain and testis; studies of knockout mice implicate TIP39 in 
regulation of responses to stress103 and germ cell development.104 
Functional Implications of Parathyroid Hormone Structure. 
The PTHR engages peptide agonists through a two-step mecha­
nism. The carboxy-terminal part of the ligand initially binds to the 
extracellular domain of the receptor (contributing to the binding 
affinity and kinetics), and then the amino terminus of the ligand 
engages the transmembrane domain (TMD) region of the recep­
tor (determining the signaling profile), leading to the activation 
of the receptor.
Cryo-EM structural analyses of the PTHR in its active state 
bound to Gsa and long-acting PTH, PTHrP, and abalopara­
tide105–107 have been successfully accomplished. These studies 
revealed unprecedented details of the atomic structure of the 
PTHR, the precise location of ligand-binding sites, and specifics of 
the activation mechanism. The ligand agonist forms an extended 
helix with its amino terminus dipping deeply into the receptor’s 
TMD pocket, forming extensive interactions. This changes the 
conformation of the sixth TMD, allowing the activated recep­
tor to couple with G proteins. Recently, the binding pocket of a 
small molecule agonist to the PTH1R was resolved.107a It binds 
an intracellular pocket of the receptor and rearranges the receptor’s 
intracellular portion into the active state without changes in the 
extracellular binding pockets of the native ligand. These discover­
ies will allow a structure-based design of small molecule agonists 
to the PTH1R.
Amino-terminal fragments of PTH as short as PTH(1-34) have 
potency at least as great as that of the full-length PTH(1-84).99 
The first several residues of PTH are particularly important for 
triggering the conformational change in the receptor that results 
in activation of Gs and adenylate cyclase. Sequences responsible 
for transmembrane activation of Gs make up most of the first 13 
residues of PTH; these are the residues that are highly conserved 
between PTH and PTHrP. At high concentrations, PTH(1-14) by 
itself can activate the PTH1R.
The PTH1R appears to have two pharmacologically distin­
guishable high-affinity conformations. A G protein–indepen­
dent conformation called R0, for which binding is insensitive to 
GTPγS, a GTP analogue that dissociates a GPCR from G pro­
teins, and a conformation called RG that is G protein dependent 
and sensitive to GTPγS. Ligands binding to the RG receptor 
conformation appear to activate the receptor on the cell surface. 
When the receptor is internalized, signaling is terminated. How­
ever, ligands bound to the R0 conformation of the PTH1R ini­
tially also signal from the cell surface; the ligand-bound receptor 
also gets internalized but continues to signal from within intracel­
lular compartments, leading to a prolonged signaling response. 
Ligands with preferential binding to the RG conformation, such 
as PTHrP or abaloparatide, lead to transient responses and are 
therefore more likely to work as an anabolic therapy for osteopo­
rosis. R0 selective ligands, such as PTH or long-acting PTH (LA-
PTH), are more likely helpful when prolonged calcemic effects are 
desired, for example, in treating hypoparathyroidism. However, 
when PTH(1-34) is used in low doses and intermittently, it also 
seems to bind preferentially to the RG conformation and thus is 
an effective therapy for osteoporosis.108–111 
Activation of Second Messengers. Precisely how binding of 
PTH to the extracellular domains of the PTH1R leads to activa­
tion of G proteins is not understood. The crystal structures of 
the transmembrane portions of other family B receptors resemble 
those of the more extensively studied rhodopsin family A recep­
tors but differ in that the potential pocket expected to bind the 
peptide ligands is larger, forming a V when seen from the side, 
with TMDs 1, 6, and 7 forming one arm of the V and TMDs 2 to 
5 forming the other. This proposed structure, with TMD 1 adja­
cent to TMDs 6 and 7, is consistent with the behavior of certain 
mutant PTH1Rs.112,113 Presumably, binding of PTH to several 
different regions of the receptor changes the relationships of the 
transmembrane domains114 such that the receptor’s three intracel­
lular loops and carboxy-terminal tail interact with G proteins in 
an altered way.
Receptors with certain point mutations in the second, sixth, 
and seventh TMDs can activate Gs even without stimulation by 
hormone. These mutant receptors were discovered by analyzing 
the PTH1Rs in patients with Jansen metaphyseal chondrodys­
trophy.115 Patients with this disorder have signs of parathyroid 
overactivity (hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and high levels 
of 1,25[OH]2D3 and urinary cAMP) but low PTH and PTHrP 
levels. These patients have growth abnormalities, presumably 
reflecting inappropriately vigorous PTHrP-like actions on growth 
cartilage. The mutations, all near the bottom of the predicted 
V-shaped structure of the TMDs,116 must change the confor­
mation of the intracellular portion of the receptor in a way that 
resembles the effect of binding of PTH to the normal receptor. 
The observation that inappropriate activation of the PTH1R in 
Jansen chondrodystrophy leads to all of the metabolic abnormali­
ties found in primary hyperparathyroidism is one of the most 
persuasive pieces of evidence that the cloned PTH1R does, in 
fact, mediate the actions of PTH in bone and kidney in humans 
in vivo.
PTH and PTHrP can both bind to and activate the PTH1R 
on the surface of target cells. The fate of the ligand-receptor com­
plexes differs dramatically subsequently, however.117–119 PTH, but 
not PTHrP, is internalized in vesicles, along with the PTH1R, 
1182
SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
β-arrestin, Gαs, and adenylate cyclase. Remarkably, within these 
vesicles, PTH can signal for longer than PTHrP, which loses its 
signaling properties when it is internalized. Certain PTH ana­
logues can signal for hours because of their intracellular stabiliza­
tion and signaling. The tight and acid-resistant binding of PTH to 
its receptor probably explains the differing properties of PTH and 
PTHrP, but this distinction and its full functional significance are 
current topics of active investigation. 
Second Messengers and Distal Effects of Parathyroid Hor­
mone. The activation of the PTH1Rs leads to signaling through 
multiple G proteins. The major signaling pathways are through 
Gas, which activates the cAMP/PKA pathway, and Gaq/11, which 
activates the PLC/Ca++/PKC pathway. The importance of cAMP 
as a mediator of the physiologic actions of PTH has been demon­
strated by studies in vivo and in vitro.120,121 Furthermore, patients 
with pseudohypoparathyroidism type I, who cannot increase uri­
nary cAMP levels in response to PTH, show clear renal resistance 
to PTH (see later). Recent studied highlighted the importance 
of the PKA-dependent inactivation of SIKs, which are key in the 
skeletal response to PTH and in PTH-dependent stimulation of 
the renal 25(OH)D 1α-hydroxylase.
Activation of PLC, with concomitant activation of protein 
kinase C and synthesis of IP3, may contribute to physiologic 
actions of PTH as well, such as inhibition of sodium-phosphate 
cotransport.122 Mice with mutant PTH1Rs that cannot activate 
PLC have a mild delay in bone development123; growth plate 
abnormalities manifest when Gs is also defective in the growth 
plates,124 and abnormalities of phosphate handling by the kid­
ney occur when challenged with a low-calcium diet.125 When 
these mutant mice are challenged with prolonged infusions of 
PTH peptides, a defect in phosphate handling occurs.80 When 
these same mutant mice are infused with high levels of PTH, they 
also exhibit a defect in generation of the expected accumulation 
of stromal cells in the marrow (osteitis fibrosa) that normal mice 
exhibit after prolonged PTH infusion.126 Internalization of recep­
tor is stimulated by PTH binding, which leads to phosphoryla­
tion of specific serines found in the receptor’s cytoplasmic tail and 
subsequent internalization directed by binding of β-arrestin to the 
receptor.127,128 Thus the actions of PTH on bone and kidney that 
require PLC activation are most clearly seen with high levels of 
PTH sustained for some time. 
Parathyroid Hormone–Related Protein
PTHrP (or parathyroid-like hormone [PTHLH]) was discovered 
because the secretion of PTHrP by a wide variety of tumors con­
tributes to the humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy. For this rea­
son, the initial studies of PTHrP in humans and animals stressed 
the PTH-like structure and properties of the molecule. Subse­
quent studies soon showed, however, that PTHrP, unlike PTH, is 
synthesized by a wide variety of tissues, in which it acts locally in 
ways that may have little relevance to the control of blood calcium.
Gene and Protein Structure
PTHrP sequences in several species, ranging from fish to humans, 
have been identified.129,130 (Fig. 27.9). In humans, alternative 
RNA splicing yields transcripts that encode three distinct proteins 
of 139, 141, and 173 residues that differ only after residue 139.
Inspection of these sequences suggests that PTHrP has several 
functionally distinct domains. Eight or nine of the first 13 resi­
dues of PTHrP are identical to those in known mammalian PTH 
sequences. These sequences encompass the known “activation” 
domain of PTH that interacts with the receptor’s TMD region 
(see earlier) and are instrumental in the ability of PTHrP to acti­
vate PTH1Rs.
The sequences in PTHrP(14-34) are also highly conserved. 
Although these sequences little resemble the corresponding region 
of PTH, they can displace PTH from the PTH1R and, in the 
crystal structure of the amino-terminal domain of the PTH1R, 
bind to overlapping but distinct contact sites.111
The remaining portion of the PTHrP molecule bears no 
resemblance to corresponding sequences in PTH. Nevertheless, 
residues 35 to 111 of PTHrP are strikingly well conserved, with 
only nine residues differing between mammalian and chicken 
PTHrP sequences. This sequence conservation is considerably 
greater than that found in the carboxy-terminal portion of PTH, 
suggesting that this region of PTHrP has unique and important 
functions. This region also includes a nuclear localization signal 
that has been demonstrated to be functional in cultured cells.131 
After residue 111, the PTHrP sequences vary considerably from 
species to species.
Interspersed within the PTHrP sequences are multiple sites 
containing one or several basic residues that might serve as post­
translational cleavage sites (see Fig. 27.9). Extensive analysis of 
PTHrP fragments in tumors, cell lines, and transfected cells has 
shown that several of these sites are, in fact, functional cleavage sig­
nals. PTHrP is cleaved after the arginine at residue 37; this cleav­
age, followed by carboxypeptidase cleavage, generates a PTH-like 
PTHrP(1-36) fragment, as well as the fragments PTHrP(38-94) 
amide, PTHrP(38-95), and PTHrP(38-101).132 More carboxy-
terminal fragments of PTHrP have been detected in cells as well. 
Fragments such as PTHrP(107-139) and PTHrP(107-111) can

trigger intracellular kinase cascades and affect bone mass in vivo,133 
although the physiologic roles of any of the carboxy-terminal frag­

In the blood of patients with humoral hypercalcemia of malig­

found that may well correspond to the fragments of PTHrP in 
cells and tissue culture media, although precise characterization 
of these various immunoreactive species is incomplete (see later). 
Full-length PTHrP may well not circulate because an amino-
terminal–specific immunoaffinity column was unable to extract 
carboxy-terminal immunoreactivity from the serum of patients 
with malignant hypercalcemia.134 
Functions of Parathyroid Hormone–Related Protein
The first actions of PTHrP to be defined were the PTH-like actions 
associated with the humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy. In this 
pathologic entity, PTHrP acts as a hormone; it is secreted from 
the tumor into the bloodstream and then acts on bone and kidney 
to raise the calcium level.135 Whether or not PTHrP circulates 
at high enough levels in normal adults to contribute to normal 
calcium homeostasis is an unanswered question. With metasta­
ses of breast cancer to bone, locally produced PTHrP can raise 
serum calcium without necessarily raising blood levels of PTHrP. 
PTHrP expression by tumors also contributes to the cachexia seen 
in cancer patients and stimulates the “browning” of adipocytes in 
tumor models.136
PTHrP acts as a calciotropic hormone during fetal life and 
in lactation. Fetal mice missing the PTHrP gene transport cal­
cium-45 (45Ca) across the placenta inefficiently. This action of 
PTHrP requires only the midregion of PTHrP and probably 
involves a receptor distinct from the PTH1R. Amino-terminal 
portions of PTHrP and PTH may also be able to increase placen­
tal calcium transport because PTH(1-84) can also increase placen­
tal calcium transport in mice missing the PTH gene.137
The second setting for humoral actions of PTHrP is lactation. 
In mice, secretion of PTHrP from the breast into the bloodstream 
leads to an increase in bone resorption.138 Calcium then activates 
the CaSR in breast tissue, increases the movement of calcium into 
milk, and downregulates expression of PTHrP in the breast.139 
PTHrP therefore probably contributes to the dramatic but largely 
reversible bone loss during lactation in humans, which is only 
minimally affected by calcium supplementation.140 The bone loss 
is caused by both an increase in osteoclastic bone resorption and 
activities of osteocytes to resorb the matrix that surrounds them 
that require activation of the PTH1R (osteocytic osteolysis).98 An 
exaggeration of this lactational role of PTHrP may explain the 
rare presentation of hypercalcemia and high PTHrP levels in preg­
nant and lactating women.141 Large amounts of PTHrP are also 
secreted into breast milk, although the role of PTHrP in milk is 
unknown.
Most of the physiologic actions of PTHrP are likely to be para­
crine or autocrine, with broad roles in cell differentiation and pro­
liferation.142 PTHrP is synthesized at one time or another during 
fetal life in virtually every tissue. For example, its role in the devel­
opment of fetal bone has been demonstrated through the striking 
abnormalities found in genetically engineered mice missing the 
PTHrP gene. These abnormalities suggest that PTHrP normally 
keeps chondrocytes proliferating in orderly columns, thereby 
delaying chondrocyte differentiation.143,144
PTHrP is synthesized by many adult tissues, including skin, 
breast, neurons, and muscles. It is expressed in smooth muscle in 
response to stretch and appears to promote muscle relaxation.145 
Many of the actions of PTHrP are mediated by the PTH1R. 
Increasing evidence suggests that some actions of PTHrP involve 
direct nuclear actions of PTHrP.146 Thus both PTH and PTHrP 
are likely to use multiple mechanisms to stimulate cells. 
Calcitonin
Calcitonin has an important role in regulating blood calcium in 
fish and a demonstrable role in rodents; however, the importance 
of calcitonin in human calcium homeostasis remains uncertain.
Calcitonin was first discovered as a hypocalcemic hormone 
in dogs and was initially thought to be produced by parathyroid 
glands; it was named calcitonin because of its ability to regulate 
the “tone” or level of calcium.147 It was subsequently found to 
be synthesized in the C cells (parafollicular cells) of the thyroid 
gland, which are derived from the neural crest.148 In fish, calcito­
nin was subsequently isolated from discrete organs containing C 
cells called the ultimobranchial bodies.
Synthesis and Secretion
Calcitonin is a 32–amino acid polypeptide with an intrachain 
disulfide bond formed by cysteines at positions 1 and 7149 (Fig. 
27.10). These two cysteine residues, along with a carboxy-terminal 
proline amide and six additional residues, are the only amino acids 
conserved among the calcitonins isolated from various species. 
The disulfide linkage and proline amide residues are important 
for the function of the molecule, although biologically active ana­
logues lacking disulfide bonds have been developed. The mature 
peptide is derived from the middle of a 136–amino acid precursor. 
The human calcitonin gene, located on the short arm of chromo­
some 11, contains six exons, which are alternatively spliced in a 
tissue-specific manner to yield the mRNAs encoding calcitonin or 
calcitonin gene–related peptide (CGRP) (see Fig. 27.10).
The mRNA encoding calcitonin is derived by splicing together 
the first four exons150 and represents over 95% of mature tran­
scripts in the thyroid C cells. The splicing of the first three exons to 
exons 5 and 6 results in an mRNA that encodes the 37–amino acid 
αCGRP molecule. The mRNA encoding αCGRP is expressed in 
multiple tissues and is the only mature transcript of the calcitonin 
gene detected in neural tissue. A second CGRP gene encodes the 
closely related βCGRP. In humans, the predicted sequence of the 
mature peptide differs from that of αCGRP by only three amino 
acids (see Fig. 27.10). The βCGRP gene is also found on chromo­
some 11; its tissue distribution is the same as that of αCGRP. 
Regulation of Synthesis and Secretion
The synthesis and secretion of calcitonin are tightly regulated. 
Studies in a porcine model reveal a linear relationship between 
the secretion of calcitonin and ambient calcium levels.151 Cell cul­
ture studies with calcium ionophores and calcium channel block­
ers demonstrated that the calcium ion concentration within the 
C cell determines this secretion rate.152 The CaSR expressed in 
parathyroid cells is also expressed in C cells and contributes to 
the regulation of calcitonin secretion.153 Other calcitonin secre­
tagogues include glucagon, CGRP, glucocorticoids, β-adrenergic 
agents, enteroglucagon, gastrin, pentagastrin, and pancreozy­
min.154 The physiologic role of the gastrointestinal hormones in 
regulating calcitonin remains unclear; however, in rodents, calci­
tonin has been shown to play a role in modulating postprandial 
hypercalcemia.155,156 The secretion of calcitonin is inhibited by 
1184
SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
somatostatin, which is also secreted by thyroid C cells. In vivo156,157 
and in vitro157,158 studies have demonstrated that 1,25(OH)2D3 
decreases calcitonin mRNA levels by transcriptional regulation.
Many of the effects of calcitonin are mediated by a G protein–
coupled cell surface receptor in the PTH/secretin receptor fam­
ily.156,159–161 The mRNA encoding this receptor has been found 
in multiple tissues, including kidney, brain, and osteoclasts. The 
coupling of this receptor to different G proteins results in the acti­
vation of either adenylate cyclase or PLC; in some settings, this is 
cell cycle dependent.160
Calcitonin, when administered acutely, decreases tubular 
resorption of calcium158,162,163 and, by directly suppressing osteo­
clasts,159,164 impairs bone resorption and the skeletal response to 
lactation.160,165 Interestingly, fish calcitonin is more potent in 
mammals than is the mammalian hormone, and salmon calcitonin 
is the form that has been used therapeutically in humans. Stud­
ies in calcitonin knockout mice reveal a doubling of bone forma­
tion rate in the absence of hormone, accompanied by resistance to 
ovariectomy-induced bone loss.163,166 An increase in bone forma­
tion is also found in mice heterozygous164,167 or homozygous for 
calcitonin receptor ablation.165,168 This increase in bone forma­
tion is thought to be due to absence of calcitonin-mediated osteo­
clastic bone resorption and secretion of sphingosine-1-phosphate, 
which induces bone formation.165,168
The physiologic role of calcitonin in humans, however, remains 
unclear. The effect of calcitonin on bone density was examined in 
patients with long-term hypercalcitoninemia secondary to med­
ullary carcinoma of the thyroid (MCT) and in patients with sub­
total thyroidectomy resulting in lack of calcitonin secretory rese
rve.161,162,166,167 The abnormal calcitonin levels had no influence 
on the bone density at the lumbar spine and distal radius. Addition­
ally, after total thyroidectomy in humans, hypercalcemia secondary 
to endogenous calcitonin deficiency is rarely, if ever, seen; as well, in 
medullary thyroid carcinoma in humans, associated with elevated 
endogenous calcitonin levels, hypocalcemia is rarely, if ever, observed.

the calcitonin receptor, with RAMP1 results in a CGRP receptor, 
whereas RAMP2 and RAMP3 interactions with the same CLR 
generate adrenomedullin receptors. CGRP receptors have been 
shown to exhibit ligand-dependent and RAMP-dependent signal­
ing bias among the Gαs, Gαi, and Gαq/11 pathways.172
CGRP is thought to act as a neurotransmitter and vasodilator 
rather than as a hormone. In support of this hypothesis, inhibi­
tion of CGRP receptor signaling using monoclonal antibodies 
decreases the frequency of migraines in predisposed individu­
als,173,174 and mice lacking αCGRP have been shown to have an 
increase in mean arterial pressure.175 Immunohistochemical stud­
ies of CGRP in the brain and peripheral nervous system suggest 
that this neuropeptide also plays an important role in sensory and 
integrative motor functions.
Three structurally related peptides have been isolated from por­
cine brain (see Fig. 27.10). These calcitonin receptor–stimulating 
peptides (CRSPs) are also expressed in the thyroid gland. CRSP1, 
which is 60% homologous to αCGRP at the amino acid level, 
binds to the calcitonin receptor, dose-dependently stimulates 
cAMP production, and inhibits osteoclastogenesis.176 Consistent 
with this observation, administration of CRSP1, like that of cal­
citonin, results in a decrease in serum calcium. The receptors for 
CRSP2 and CRSP3 have not been identified.177
Amylin is highly homologous to CGRP and calcitonin (see Fig. 
27.10). Although amylin has been shown to have skeletal actions, 
the presence of amylin in the pancreas of patients with type 2 diabe­
tes mellitus may suggest an etiologic role for this peptide in this dis­
order.178 Because amylin slows gastric emptying, promoting satiety 
and attenuating the postprandial rise in glucagon, analogues of this 
peptide are currently being used as therapeutic agents for type 2 dia­
betes and are being investigated for the treatment of obesity. Amy­
lin administration inhibits bone loss associated with ovariectomy 
and streptozotocin-induced diabetes mellitus in rats.179,180 Targeted 
ablation of amylin in mice results in low bone mass as a result of an 
increase in bone resorption.152,155 Amylin has also been shown to 
decrease food intake and inhibit gastric acid secretion, protecting 
against ulcer development in numerous models.181
Adrenomedullin (see Fig. 27.10) has vasodilatory effects similar 
to those of CGRP. In addition to activating CGRP receptors, adre­
nomedullin binds to specific receptors in the vascular system.182 
Mice lacking adrenomedullin die in midgestation.183 Haploinsuf­
ficiency of RAMP2, which regulates binding of adrenomedullin 
to the calcitonin receptor, results in hyperprolactinemia, delayed 
bone development, and decreased bone mineral density.184 Unlike 
other family members, adrenomedullin does not inhibit osteoclast 
activity or formation.176 The physiologic role of adrenomedullin 
in the skeleton remains to be clarified.
Adrenomedullin-2, also called intermedin, the newest member 
of this family (see Fig. 27.10), was identified by homology screen­
ing of expressed sequence tags. It is expressed primarily in the pitu­
itary and the gastrointestinal tract. Adrenomedullin-2(Intermedin) 
is able to signal through CGRP receptors and competes with CGRP 
for receptor binding.185 However, unlike CGRP, adrenomedullin-2 
is a nonselective agonist for the RAMP coreceptors. 
Calcitonin in Human Disease
Calcitonin is secreted by several endocrine malignancies and 
therefore can serve as a tumor marker.186 Basal and pentagastrin-
stimulated calcitonin levels have been used to identify and follow 
those at risk for, or affected by, both familial and sporadic medul­
lary thyroid carcinoma187 (see Chapter 42), although abnormal 
basal and stimulated levels may be observed in patients on chronic 
hemodialysis.187 Calcitonin may also be ectopically secreted by 
other tumors, including insulinomas, VIPomas, and lung can­
cers. Severely ill patients, including those with burn inhalation 
injury,188 toxic shock syndrome,189 and pancreatitis,190 may also 
have elevated calcitonin levels. 
Therapeutic Uses
The observation that calcitonin inhibits osteoclastic bone resorp­
tion has led to its therapeutic use for the treatment of several 
disorders associated with excess bone resorption, including

rapid decrease in serum calcium is required, and until more specific 
treatment of the underlying disease can be accomplished. It may 
also be added to existing therapeutic regimens for acute hypercal­
cemia, such as intravenous fluids and furosemide, or other agents. 
Its utility, however, is limited to acute situations and short-term 
treatment because of the rapid development of tachyphylaxis. 
Vitamin D
Vitamin D Metabolism
Vitamin D is not a true vitamin in that oral intake is not 
required for people with adequate sun exposure.194 When skin is 
exposed to ultraviolet-B radiation (UVB; wavelength 280–315 
nm), the cutaneous precursor of vitamin D3, 7-dehydrocholes­
terol, undergoes photochemical cleavage of the bond between 
carbons 9 and 10 of the steroid ring (Fig. 27.12). The resul­
tant product, previtamin D3, is thermally labile and, over ∼48 
hours, undergoes temperature-dependent molecular rearrange­
ment resulting in production of vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol).195 
Upon prolonged cutaneous UVB exposure, most of this previta­
min D3 undergoes further photochemical changes, one of which 
leads to production of lumisterol3, a stereoisomer of 7DHC, 
and another to tachysterol3. This alternative photoisomerization 
prevents production of excessive amounts of vitamin D3 with 
prolonged sun exposure in that lumisterol3 has historically been 
felt to be inactive. However, more recent study finds that lumis­
terol3 can be hydroxylated by CYP11A1. Some of these metab­
olites are detectable in circulation and have biological activity 
in vitro.196 The degree of skin pigmentation also regulates con­
version of 7-dehydrocholesterol to vitamin D3 because greater 
amounts of melanin absorb and scatter more UVB, leading to 
less conversion of 7DHC to previtamin D3.197
In addition to skin production, vitamin D may be obtained 
orally from food or supplementation. Indeed, some individuals 
(e.g., older institutionalized adults and those living far from the 
equator) likely obtain most of their vitamin D orally. Moreover, 
with increasing sun exposure avoidance by many individuals, 
ensuring adequate oral vitamin D intake assumes greater impor­
tance for the population at large.198 The major dietary sources 
of vitamin D are fortified dairy products, although the lack of 
monitoring of this supplementation has potential to produce sub­
stantial variation in the amount of vitamin D provided and thus 
potential for vitamin D toxicity.199,200 Food sources of vitamin 
D include egg yolks, fish oils, and fortified cereal products. Vita­
min D from plant sources is generally vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol), 
whereas that provided by animal sources is in the form of vita­
min D3 (see Fig. 27.12). Ergocalciferol exists in nature, primar­
ily in plants and fungi, and low circulating levels of 25(OH)D2 
are present in free-ranging nonhuman primates and in human 
population studies.201,202 The two forms of vitamin D (i.e., cho­
lecalciferol and ergocalciferol) may be used interchangeably for 
supplementation or treatment of vitamin D deficiency. Indeed, 
historically, vitamins D2 and D3 were considered equally effec­
tive in treating rickets.203 Consistent with this, some guidelines 
consider vitamins D2 and D3 as being interchangeable.200 Subse­
quently, however, multiple studies and meta-analyses comparing 
the effect of supplementing with D2 or D3 on circulating 25(OH)
D concentration find cholecalciferol to be superior.204–207
Cholecalciferol and ergocalciferol are fat soluble and, although 
data are somewhat limited, have historically been felt to be 
absorbed into intestinal enterocytes by a passive process. However, 
there is some evidence that vitamin D is also actively transported 
through the enterocyte membranes via cholesterol transporters. 
To generalize, ∼80% of oral vitamin D is absorbed, but there can 
be substantial variation in absorption.208 From the enterocytes, 
vitamin D is exported in chylomicrons by the lymphatic route.209 
Subsequently, vitamin D enters the circulation bound primarily to 
vitamin D–binding protein (VDBP), although a fraction of vita­
min D circulates bound to albumin. Human VDBP is a 52-KDa 
α-globulin synthesized in the liver.210 The protein has a high affin­
ity for 25(OH)D but also binds vitamin D and 1,25(OH)2D.

Approximately 88% of 25(OH)D circulates bound to the VDBP, 
0.03% is free, and the rest circulates bound to albumin.211 In con­
trast, 85% of the circulating 1,25(OH)2D3 binds to the VDBP, 
0.4% is free, and the rest binds to albumin. Mice lacking VDBP 
have increased susceptibility to 1,25(OH)2D3 toxicity, as well as 
to dietary vitamin D deficiency.212 VDBP polymorphisms have 
been postulated to be the basis for difference in 25(OH)D lev­
els in several groups, including African Americans and Finns.213 
Measurements of free 25(OH) vitamin D across multiple popu­
lations, however, suggest that the monoclonal antibody used in 
the former study can bring misleading results.214,215 The “free 
hormone hypothesis” holds that bound vitamin D does not have 
biologic activity, and thus free 25(OH)D measurement may 
improve assessment of an individual’s vitamin D status. Assays for 
free 25(OH)D have been limited, but standardization efforts have 
begun,216 and the development of liquid chromatography–tan­
dem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) methodologies has recently 
been reported.217
In the liver, vitamin D undergoes 25-hydroxylation by 
CYP2R1, located in the microsomal P450 fraction of hepato­
cytes.194 The 25-hydroxylation of vitamin D is not tightly regu­
lated; therefore, the blood levels of 25(OH)D reflect the amount 
of substrate (i.e., vitamin D3 or D2) entering the circulation. 
When levels of VDBP are low, such as in nephrotic syndrome, 
circulating levels of 25(OH)D are also reduced. The half-life of 
circulating 25(OH)D is approximately 2 to 3 weeks.218
The final step in the production of the active hormone is 
1α-hydroxylation of 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH)2D3 by CYP27B1.194 
The half-life of this hormone is approximately 5 to 10 hours.219 
Like the 25-hydroxylase, the 1α-hydroxylase in the proximal con­
voluted tubule is a cytochrome P450–like mixed function oxidase, 
but unlike the 25-hydroxylase, the 1α-hydroxylase is tightly regu­
lated. PTH and hypophosphatemia are the major inducers of this 
microsomal enzyme, whereas calcium, 1,25(OH)2D, and FGF23 
repress it.220,221 Analogous to mice lacking FGF23, mice with 
inactivating mutations of the FGF23 coreceptor, α-Klotho, a type 
I membrane protein with homology to β-glycosidases, develop 
hypercalcemia as a result of increased levels of 1,25(OH)2D3. 
Like the FGF23 null mice, Klotho null mice have increased lev­
els of the 1α-hydroxylase,222 and their phenotype is ameliorated 
by impairment of 1,25(OH)2D3 action. In animal models and 
in  vitro studies, other hormones such as estrogen, calcitonin, 
growth hormone, and prolactin increase 1α-hydroxylase activity; 
however, the clinical importance of these observations is unclear.
The 1α-hydroxylase enzyme is also expressed in keratinocytes; 
the trophoblastic layer of the placenta; and granulomas, including 
sarcoid granulomas, among many other tissues. In granulomatous 
tissue, the 1α-hydroxylase gene that is expressed is identical to that 
expressed in the kidney but is not regulated by PTH, phosphate, 
calcium, or vitamin D metabolites in these cells. Activation of 
macrophages with interferon-γ223 or with ligands that activate the 
heterodimer of toll-like receptors 1 and 2,224 however, increases 
the expression of the 1α-hydroxylase in macrophages, whereas 
treatment of sarcoidosis-associated hypercalcemia with gluco­
corticoids, ketoconazole,225 or chloroquine226 has been shown 
to lower serum 1,25(OH)2D3 levels. Activation of the VDR in 
human macrophages induces the antimicrobial peptide cathelici­
din and increases killing of intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculo­
sis.224 Thus the pathologic excess of 1,25(OH)2D3 in sarcoidosis 
may represent an exaggeration of a healthy paracrine response 
of tissue macrophages. This action can be viewed as a paradigm 
for many other actions of vitamin D that are likely mediated 
by local production of 1,25(OH)2D3 rather than by circulating 
1,25(OH)2D3.
25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D3 are hydroxylated by vitamin 
D 24-hydroxylase, CYP24A1, which is present in most tissues, 
including kidney, cartilage, and intestine.194 1,25(OH)2D3 
increases the activity of the 24-hydroxylase, thereby inducing its 
own metabolism. The 24-hydroxylated vitamin D metabolites, 
24,25(OH)2D3 and 1,24,25(OH)3D3, are not thought to play 
major biologic roles other than inactivation of 1,25(OH)2D3. 
Mice and humans with nonfunctional 24-hydroxylase genes dem­
onstrate hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, and nephrocalcinosis due 
to vitamin D toxicity.227,228
1,25(OH)2D3 is also metabolized to several inactive products 
by 23-hydroxylation or 26-hydroxylation and side-chain oxida­
tion and cleavage. This latter side-chain cleavage, resulting in 
the formation of calcitroic acid, occurs in the liver and intestine, 
whereas inactivation of 1,25(OH)2D3 in a wide variety of target 
tissues occurs by 24-hydroxylation. In addition, polar metabolites 
of 1,25(OH)2D3 are excreted in the bile. Some of these metab­
olites are deconjugated in the intestine and reabsorbed into the 
enterohepatic circulation. The role, if any, of the multitude of 
vitamin D metabolites in producing a systemic vitamin D effect 
remains to be clarified.229
Actions of Vitamin D
Vitamin D Receptors. 1,25(OH)2D3 exerts its biologic func­
tions by binding to a nuclear receptor, which then regulates tran­
scription of DNA into RNA. The VDR closely resembles the 
retinoic acid, triiodothyronine, and retinoid X receptors (RXRs). 
The receptor affinity for 1,25(OH)2D3 is approximately three 
orders of magnitude higher than that for other vitamin D metabo­
lites (Fig. 27.13). Although 25(OH)D3 is less potent on a molar 
basis, its concentration in the serum is approximately three orders 
of magnitude higher than that of 1,25(OH)2D. However, its free 
concentration is only two orders of magnitude greater than that 
of 1,25(OH)2D3. Therefore, although 25(OH)D3 does have bio­
logic activity, it likely does not contribute importantly to calcium 
homeostasis. Because the affinity of the VDBP for 25(OH)D3 is 
greater than for 1,25(OH)2D3, in states of vitamin D intoxica­
tion (with its associated high levels of 25[OH]D3), the free lev­
els of 1,25(OH)2D3 increase because 25(OH)D displaces it from 
the VDBP. 25(OH)D3 may therefore play a role in the clinical 
syndrome of vitamin D intoxication both by its direct biologic 
effects, when present at toxic levels, and by increasing free levels of 
1,25(OH)2D3. Local activation of 25(OH)D may contribute to 
nonclassical vitamin D effects.230
1,25(OH)2D3 has biologic effects that occur too rapidly for 
transcriptional mechanisms to be implicated.231 These so-called 
nongenomic actions, including a rapid increase in intracellu­
lar calcium, activation of phospholipase C, and opening of cal­
cium channels, are observed in several cell types within minutes 
of exposure to 1,25(OH)2D3. The physiologic importance of the 
nongenomic actions of vitamin D metabolites232 has not yet been 
established.
The VDR is expressed in most tissues and has been shown to 
regulate cellular differentiation and function in many cell types. 
Nevertheless, the most dramatic physiologic effects of vitamin 
D, acting through the VDR, involve regulation of intestinal cal­
cium transport. This is most clearly demonstrated by the pheno­
type of patients and mice with mutant VDRs (hereditary vitamin 
D–resistant rickets)233,234: Dramatic abnormalities in bone min­
eralization can be reversed by bypassing the defect in intestinal 
calcium absorption.235,236 
1188
SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
Intestinal Calcium Absorption. Under normal dietary con­
ditions, calcium intake is in the range of 700 to 900 mg daily. 
Approximately 30% to 35% of this calcium is absorbed; how­
ever, losses from intestinal secretion of calcium lead to a net daily 
uptake of approximately 200 mg. Although vitamin D is the 
major hormonal determinant of intestinal calcium absorption, 
the bioavailability of mineral ions in the intestinal lumen may 
be affected by a number of local factors and dietary constituents. 
Absorption of calcium and magnesium is impaired by bile salt 
deficiency, unabsorbed free fatty acids in steatorrheic states, and 
high dietary content of fiber or phytate. Gastric acid is needed 
to promote dissociation of calcium from anionic components of 
food or therapeutic preparations of calcium salts. Administration 
of calcium salts with meals, especially in achlorhydrics, and use 
of divided doses or more soluble salts, such as calcium citrate, are 
commonly used strategies to increase calcium bioavailability.
Calcium is thought to be absorbed by two pathways: a saturable 
transcellular pathway and a nonsaturable paracellular route. The 
transcellular pathway is dependent on 1,25(OH)2D3. Although 
the necessity of vitamin D for paracellular calcium absorption 
remains controversial, substantial evidence exists that the hor­
mone enhances this pathway as well.237 Notably, 1,25(OH)2D3 
induces the expression of claudin-2 and claudin-12, which con­
tribute to intestinal calcium absorption and are thought to form 
paracellular channels between neighboring cells.238
The most extensively studied mechanism of intestinal cal­
cium absorption involves the transcellular route. This pathway is 
thought to involve three steps: entry of calcium into the entero­
cyte (which is the rate-limiting step), transport across the cell, and 
extrusion across the basolateral membrane.239 
Entry Into the Enterocyte. 1,25(OH)2D3 induces synthesis of 
a number of brush border proteins, including the intestinal mem­
brane calcium-binding protein, brush border alkaline phosphatase, 
and low-affinity Ca2+/Mg2+-ATPase. The activity of these proteins 
correlates with active calcium transport; however, a causal rela­
tionship remains to be established. Two calcium channels, TRPV5 
and TRPV6, members of the transient receptor potential vanilloid 
receptor subfamily containing six membrane-spanning domains, 
are expressed in the duodenum, the jejunum, and the kidney, as 
well as in other tissues. TRPV6 is thought to play a critical role 
in intestinal calcium absorption, and 1,25(OH)2D3 increases its 
expression, as well as that of TRP5.240 Studies in mice lacking 
TRPV5 demonstrate that this channel is primarily responsible 
for renal calcium reabsorption because mice lacking TRPV5 have 
enhanced, rather than impaired, intestinal calcium absorption due 
to their high circulating levels of 1,25(OH)2D.241 Upon entering 
the enterocyte, calcium binds to components of the brush bor­
der complex subjacent to the plasma membrane. Calmodulin is 
redistributed to the brush border in response to 1,25(OH)2D3 
and may play a role in this process, as may the 1,25(OH)2D3-
inducible calcium-binding protein, calbindin-9K. 
Transcellular Transport. The best-studied effect of vitamin D 
on the enterocyte is the induction of synthesis of the intestinal 
calcium-binding protein, calbindin-9K. This protein has an EF-
hand structure that permits the binding of two calcium ions per 
molecule. The affinity of calbindin for calcium is approximately 
four times that of the brush border calcium-binding components, 
so calcium is preferentially transferred to calbindin. Calbindin 
serves to buffer the intracellular free calcium concentration during 
calcium absorption. It associates with microtubules and may play 
a role in the transport of calcium across the enterocyte. However, 
studies in mice lacking both TRPV6 and calbindin-D9k main­
tain 40% of normal 1,25(OH)2D3-mediated calcium transport, 
demonstrating that other hormone-responsive genes may play 
a significant or compensatory role.242 Organelles such as the

mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, and endoplasmic reticulum also 
serve as repositories for intracellular calcium. 
Exit From the Enterocyte. The transport of calcium across the 
antiluminal surface of the enterocyte, the final process involved 
in intestinal calcium absorption, is dependent on 1,25(OH)2D3. 
The main mechanism of calcium extrusion is the 1,25(OH)2D3-
inducible ATP-dependent Ca2+ pump (PMCA1b). The affinity of 
the pump for calcium is approximately 2.5 times that of calbin­
din. With high calcium intake, a 1,25(OH)2D3-independent Na+/
Ca2+ exchanger may play a role in the transfer of calcium across 
the basolateral membrane as well.
Actions on Bone. 1,25(OH)2D3 has important effects on bone: 
it is a major regulator of the two most abundant bone matrix pro­
teins repressing synthesis of type I collagen and induces osteo­
calcin. Additionally, 1,25(OH)2D3 promotes differentiation 
of osteoclasts from monocyte-macrophage stem cell precursors 
in vitro and increases osteoclastic bone resorption in high doses 
in vivo by stimulating osteoblast RANKL production.243 Notably, 
osteoblast-specific knockout of the VDR leads to increased bone 
mass associated with impaired bone resorption due to decreased 
RANKL expression.244 Consistent with this, and despite the mul­
tiple effects of 1,25(OH)2D3 on in vitro bone biology, in vivo 
studies in 1,25(OH)2D3-deficient rats and in mice lacking func­
tional vitamin D receptors233,245 suggest that the major osseous 
consequences of hormone and receptor deficiency can be reversed 
when mineral ion homeostasis is normalized. Additionally, paren­
teral calcium infusions heal the osteomalacic lesions in children 
with mutant VDRs.52 The effects of 1,25(OH)2D3 on phosphate 
transport are less well studied but promote the already efficient 
intestinal phosphate absorption and induce expression of the 
phosphaturic hormone FGF23.246
These observations indicate that the major role of vitamin D in 
bone is to provide the proper microenvironment for bone miner­
alization through stimulation of intestinal calcium and phosphate 
absorption. 
Other Actions of Vitamin D. Profound vitamin D deficiency 
leads to myopathy with severe muscle weakness and immobil­
ity.247–249 Although some studies demonstrate VDR expression in 
skeletal myofibers,250–252 both the expression and the role of this 
receptor in muscle remain controversial and suggest that the effect 
of vitamin D on muscle is either indirect or does not occur via 
the known receptor.253 Regardless, vitamin D repletion of severely 
deficient adults improves muscle strength, which is associated with 
an increase in mitochondrial function assessed by 31-phosphate 
nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.254 Studies in 
vitamin D–deficient rats demonstrate that maintenance of nor­
mal mineral ion levels precludes the development of myopathy.255 
Vitamin D deficiency has also been implicated in statin-induced 
myopathy.256 
Vitamin D: Clinical Assessment and Utility. As noted earlier, 
vitamin D inadequacy may lead to inadequate bone mineraliza­
tion (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults) and also adversely 
affect bone via the development of secondary hyperparathyroid­
ism, with resultant bone loss leading to osteopenia/osteopo­
rosis.257,258 Moreover, because vitamin D may either reduce or 
increase risk of falls (with resultant fracture), clinical assessment of 
vitamin D status, and often supplementation to improve/optimize 
bone health and reduce fracture risk, is routine in the evaluation of 
people with metabolic bone disease.
Serum total 25(OH)D (the sum of circulating 25[OH]D2 and 
25[OH]D3 concentration) is widely accepted as the best measure 
of an individual’s vitamin D status and is used to define vitamin 
D insufficiency/deficiency.259–262 Assays for 25(OH)D were ini­
tially devised in the 1970s. Subsequently, many total 25(OH)
D assays (primarily immunoassays) have been developed for 
use clinically and in research. Recently a trend toward measur­
ing 25(OH)D by LC-MS/MS in research and in some clinical 
settings has emerged.263 Despite proliferation of available assays 
and methodologies, it has long been appreciated that a 25(OH)
D value from a single sample may vary substantially based on 
the assay used. This recognition led to the creation of the Vita­
min D External Quality Assessment Scheme (DEQAS) in 1989, 
whose objective is to ensure analytical reliability of 25(OH)D and 
1,25(OH)2D assays.264 In 2010 the Vitamin D Standardization 
Program (VDSP) was begun under the umbrella of the National 
Institutes of Health (NIH) to coordinate efforts to standardize 
25(OH)D measurement.265 Guidance for both prospective and 
retrospective 25(OH)D standardization have been published by 
the VDSP.266,267 Despite these efforts, substantial between- and 
within-assay variability persists (Fig. 27.14). This variability has, 
and continues, to make it challenging, if not impossible, to pool 
“25(OH)D” data from different studies and subsequently conduct 
meaningful meta-analyses of such data as part of clinical and pub­
lic health guideline development. In fact, a moratorium on such 
meta-analyses has been proposed266 but generally ignored.
An additional consideration regarding 25(OH)D measure­
ment is that acute illness/inflammation appears to rapidly lower 
measured 25(OH)D concentration.268 Indeed, various condi­
tions associated with inflammatory events demonstrate a lower 
25(OH)D.269 A particularly compelling, albeit small, study found 
administration of lipopolysaccharide derived from Escherichia 
coli to reduce circulating 25(OH)D by over 20% within 2 to 3 
hours.270 The mechanism(s) underlying, and indeed importance 
of, this reduction in 25(OH)D remain to be determined. How­
ever, this phenomenon raises the possibility that many reports of 
low 25(OH)D with various acute illnesses (e.g., COVID infec­
tion) may be due to reverse causality; that is, it may be that the 
acute illness lowers 25(OH)D rather than low vitamin D status 
contributing in a causal manner to the disease being considered. 
It is possible that this phenomenon contributes to the associations 
reported between vitamin D status and a multitude of acute and 
chronic inflammatory conditions.
The previously noted assay variability has contributed to differ­
ences in definitions of low vitamin D status and recommendations 
for daily intake. Indeed, many studies used in guideline develop­
ment did not utilize standardized 25(OH)D data.271 Additionally, 
but of major importance, many of the large vitamin D supple­
mentation randomized controlled trials (RCTs) recruited primar­
ily vitamin D–replete subjects272; in such individuals, one would 
not expect any benefit of providing additional vitamin D. Indeed, 
once an individual has “enough” of any nutrient (in this case vita­
min D), provision of more could be expected only to potentially 
produce toxicity.273,274 Inclusion of such RCTs (which are preor­
dained to obtain negative results) in meta-analyses compromises 
the ability to identify potential relationships with diseases poten­
tially related to vitamin D deficiency.
A number of large vitamin D supplementation RCTs of vary­
ing study design and duration have recently been reported; given 
their high profile, they are briefly noted here. The VITAL study 
evaluated daily vitamin D3 2000 IU versus placebo in 25,871 par­
ticipants, with a median follow-up of 5.3 years.275 The primary 
endpoints were cancer and cardiovascular disease, upon which no 
effect was observed. Importantly, the mean (standard deviation 
[SD]) 25(OH)D at baseline was 30.8 (10) ng/mL. In a subsequent 
1190
SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
analysis from this study, no effect of vitamin D supplementation 
on fractures was seen.276 The Vitamin D Assessment (ViDA) study 
evaluated a 200,000-IU vitamin D3 bolus followed by 100,000 IU 
monthly versus placebo in 5110 adults, with a median follow-up 
of 3.3 years.277 No effect was observed on incident cancer, frac­
ture, cardiovascular disease, or falls. In this study, the mean (SD) 
baseline 25(OH)D was 27 (9) ng/mL. The D2D study evalu­
ated 2423 individuals at risk for diabetes mellitus who randomly 
received 4000 IU D3 daily or placebo for a median follow-up 
of 2.5 years. No effect on risk of diabetes was observed. Mean 
25(OH)D at baseline was 28.0 ng/mL. The DO-HEALTH study 
randomized 2157 adults age ≥70 years to intervention groups 
that included vitamin D3, 2000 IU daily, omega-3, or strength 
training.278 No effect on blood pressure, cognitive performance, 
infection rate, nonvertebral fracture, or physical performance was 
observed. Mean (SD) serum 25(OH)D was 22 (8) ng/mL. Finally, 
in a much smaller but important study of 311 adults who received 
either 400, 4000, or 10,000 IU of vitamin D3 daily for 3 years, 
radius volumetric bone mineral density (BMD) was reduced by 
both the 4000- and 10,000-IU doses.279 In this study, the mean 
baseline 25(OH)D was ∼31 ng/mL; thus, this may be an example 
showing that provision of more vitamin D to replete individuals 
will not be of benefit and will only cause toxicity.
Given these challenges, it is unsurprising that quite variable 
recommendations exist in the >40 vitamin D guidelines identified 
in two recent systematic reviews.271,280 The previously described 
issues explain the wide variations in recommended values for 
serum 25(OH)D spanning from 20 to 40 ng/mL and in recom­
mended daily vitamin D intake (Table 27.1).271 Given the prior 
and ongoing guideline challenges,281 it has been suggested that 
the 25(OH)D concentration of highly sun-exposed individuals be 
used to define normal vitamin D status.282 The mean 25(OH)D 
concentration in such individuals is ∼40 ng/mL.283
When vitamin D supplementation is used, as a generalization, 
1000 IU daily will increase circulating 25(OH)D concentration 
by ∼7 ng/mL.284 Given the ∼2- to 3-week half-life of 25(OH)
D, a new steady state will be attained at approximately 3 months. 
To generalize, a greater increment in 25(OH)D is observed at a 
lower starting level, but it is important to appreciate that substan­
tial variation in 25(OH)D response occurs.285 Additionally, daily 
dosing is preferred because intermittent high-dose (i.e., “bolus”) 
dosing may increase vitamin D degradation (i.e., 24-hydroxy­
lase activity) and, as such, may be counterproductive.286 Finally, 
because some 25(OH)D assays may not accurately measure both 
25(OH)D2 and 25(OH)D3, use of ergocalciferol, particularly in 
high doses (e.g., 50,000 IU), is not recommended.287,288

multiple systematic reviews/meta-analyses, reporting discordant 
conclusions.289,290 From such analyses, discordant recommenda­

challenges noted earlier, such as lack of standardized 25(OH)D 
reporting and inclusion of vitamin D–replete individuals, there 
remains a lack of clarity regarding the effect of vitamin D on

fracture, the population(s) most or least likely to benefit, and the
