into the variable results of systematic reviews, an umbrella review 
of RCT meta-analyses of vitamin D was recently performed.97 
This assessment evaluated 13 systematic reviews of vitamin D 
with calcium and 19 on vitamin D alone and found as a general­
ization that studies of vitamin D with calcium reduced hip frac­
ture and any fractures, whereas vitamin D alone did not. Further, 
no fracture risk reduction was noted in studies of community-
dwelling individuals. Importantly, this work also reported that 
the majority of these systematic reviews were of low, or critically 
low, quality. At this time, it seems a reasonable conclusion that 
vitamin D supplementation benefits high-risk individuals, such as 
those who are older, those with low 25(OH)D, and those who are 
institutionalized.290 
Vitamin D and Falls. Prevention of falls is a public health pri­
ority because 1% to 2% of falls lead to hip fractures, falls are inde­
pendent determinants of functional decline, and falls lead to 40% 
of all nursing home admissions.291 Moreover, falls are a substantial 
and increasing cause of mortality in the very old.292
In contrast to the aforementioned studies that suggest a ben­
eficial effect of vitamin D on muscle function, clinical trials of 
vitamin D supplementation with muscle function or falls as the 
primary endpoint are mixed. Two meta-analyses published in 
2009 and 2011 found that vitamin D supplementation had a 
modest beneficial effect on fall risk in older adults.293,294 One of 
these articles suggested that fall risk reduction with supplementa­
tion may be more effective in individuals with low 25(OH)D lev­
els.293 A meta-analysis concluded that vitamin D with or without 
calcium did not alter falls relative risk.295 However, a later meta-
analysis found vitamin D to be more effective in elders with low 
25(OH)D levels.296 Recently, the ViDA study found no effect of 
treatment for 3.4 years with 100,000 IU of vitamin D3 per month 
on fall risk in older adults with a mean serum 25(OH)D level of 
25 ng/mL.297 In contrast, among postmenopausal women with 
a low mean 25(OH)D level of 15 ng/mL, treatment with 1000 
IU of vitamin D3 per day for 9 months reduced fall risk by about 
50%.298 Importantly, some studies find that vitamin D supple­
mentation increases falls/fractures. Notably, Sanders et al299 found 
that a large annual oral dose of 500,000 IU of vitamin D increased 
the risk of falls (and fractures) in elders. An increase in fall risk was 
also seen in a trial administering an oral dose of 60,000 IU of vita­
min D3 monthly.300 In long-term care residents, treatment with 
100,000 IU of vitamin D3 per month, when compared with stan­
dard dosing, significantly increased fall risk (secondary endpoint) 
while significantly lowering risk of developing an acute respiratory 
infection (primary outcome).301 A common feature of these trials 
is that they employed high intermittent doses of vitamin D. These 
studies provide additional support for daily, rather than intermit­
tent, vitamin D dosing being preferred. Further confounding the

“fall” is not an easily captured endpoint; as an example, diary col­

In summary, the relationship of vitamin D with falls remains 
unclear. In part, this reflects challenges in identification/data col­
lection of falls and accurate measurement of 25(OH)D, as noted 
earlier. However, proximal muscle weakness clearly can occur with 
severe vitamin D deficiency, and this should lead to increased falls 
risk. Indeed, existing data find that older adults with low 25(OH)
D levels are most likely to benefit from vitamin D supplementa­
tion, and the degree of fall risk reduction may be proportional to 
the degree of insufficiency. It is to be expected that studies provid­
ing additional vitamin D to replete individuals show no benefit. 
The mechanism(s) by which high-dose and intermittent dosing 
increase falls risk remain to be clarified. 
Laboratory Assessment of Mineral Metabolism
Vitamin D Metabolites. As noted earlier, the 25-hydroxylation 
of vitamin D is not tightly regulated, and as such 25(OH)D con­
centration is currently recommended to assess an individual’s vita­
min D status. Importantly, measurement of 1,25(OH)2D3 is not 
indicated to assess vitamin D status and indeed should be reserved 
for individuals in which excessive or impaired 1α-hydroxylation 
is suspect. High 1,25(OH)2D3 levels can be seen in sarcoidosis, 
lymphomas, and intoxication with 1α-hydroxylated metabo­
lites. Impaired 1α-hydroxylation can contribute to hypocalcemia 
observed in those with CKD, oncogenic osteomalacia, and inher­
ited disorders of vitamin D metabolism.
Although measurement of total 25(OH)D concentration has 
been and remains the standard approach to defining vitamin D 
status, it is important to recognize that multiple other vitamin D 
metabolites exist, some of which may have physiologic “vitamin D” 
activity. This recognition has led to increased interest in the so-called 
vitamin D metabolome.3 Such vitamin D metabolites include, but 
are not limited to, cholecalciferol, 24,25(OH)2D, 3 epi-25(OH)
D, 22(OH)D, various conjugated metabolites (e.g., 25[OH]D 
sulfate), and various hydroxylumisterols. Additionally, both the 
24,25(OH)2D/25(OH)D ratio and measurement of free 25(OH)
D may have clinical utility. It is plausible that a combination of such 
measurements may better define an individual’s vitamin D status. 
Parathyroid Hormone. The major challenges in the measure­
ment of blood PTH have been the low levels of circulating PTH 
and the presence of inactive PTH fragments in far greater abun­
dance than for the intact, biologically active PTH molecule. The 
measurement of inactive fragments would not be a concern if 
the ratio of inactive to active PTH molecules remained constant. 
However, this ratio does change in response to changes in GFR 
and in parathyroid gland secretory activity (see earlier discus­
sions under “Parathyroid Hormone Secretion” and “Metabolism 
of Parathyroid Hormone”). Consequently, radioimmunoassays of 
PTH have suffered from lack of sensitivity and from the inability 
to measure the biologically active hormone directly.
For these reasons, two-site assays that require the presence of 
amino-terminal and carboxy-terminal sequences of full-length 
PTH(1-84) on the same molecule have replaced older radioim­
munoassays.303 The assays are sensitive enough to detect PTH in 
all normal persons. The assays have demonstrated modest circadian 
variation in PTH levels and some pulsatility in PTH secretion, but 
these variations have not interfered with the diagnostic usefulness of 
randomly drawn PTH measurements. Some studies have reported 
modest increases in PTH levels with age, although others have not. 
Unlike older radioimmunoassays, the two-site assays demonstrate 
virtually no overlap in PTH levels between patients with primary 
hyperparathyroidism and those with nonparathyroid hypercalcemia 
(Fig. 27.15). Because this distinction represents the most important 
challenge in the clinical setting, the use of the two-site assay has 
dramatically facilitated the clinician’s task.
This straightforward picture has been complicated by the real­
ization that most two-site assays detect small amounts of PTH 
fragments that are large but do not extend to the hormone’s amino 
terminus.304 These fragments accumulate in significant amounts 
in patients with renal failure. These observations have prompted 
the development of two-site PTH assays that use antibodies spe­
cific for the first four amino acids of PTH and thus do not detect 
large fragments of PTH. Although it seems plausible that such 
assays might prove particularly useful in some clinical situations, 
their role is presently unclear. They offer no advantage over older 
two-site assays, for example, in diagnosing primary hyperparathy­
roidism.305 These assays do detect a minor peak of PTH immu­
noreactivity that is also recognized by antibodies directed to the 
carboxy-terminus of PTH and yet is not recognized by the usual 
“intact” PTH assays, perhaps because of a posttranslational modi­
fication of PTH in the PTH(15-20) region.306 Perhaps because of 
detection of this unusual form of PTH, the PTH immunoreactiv­
ity recognized using the antibody to PTH(1-4) is particularly high 
in patients with parathyroid cancer when compared with patients 
with benign primary hyperparathyroidism.307

(PTH-dependent hypercalcemia) and (2) that which occurs despite 
appropriate suppression of parathyroid hormone (PTH-indepen­
dent hypercalcemia). This distinction is particularly useful clinically 
because it can be readily determined which category that patient is 
in by simply measuring the level of circulating PTH. If the PTH 
level is suppressed, the etiologies are not related to parathyroid 
gland dysfunction. If the PTH level is elevated or detectable within 
the normal range, the hypercalcemia is due to abnormal parathy­
roid gland function. The predominant cause of PTH-dependent 
hypercalcemia is primary hyperparathyroidism. Rarely, FHH can 
be the etiology. Other etiologies of PTH-dependent hypercalcemia 
relate to the use of lithium or thiazide diuretics. Ectopic production 
of authentic PTH from a malignancy is rare (see later).
Primary Hyperparathyroidism
In primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT), one or more of the 
four parathyroid glands oversecrete PTH. Patients with PHPT 
typically have hypercalcemia, but in the newest variant of this 
disease, normocalcemic primary hyperparathyroidism, the serum 
calcium is normal. In this setting, it is important to distinguish 
between this form of PHPT and secondary hyperparathyroidism. 
In secondary hyperparathyroidism, the driving force for increased 
PTH secretion does not consist of abnormal parathyroid gland(s) 
but rather is due to another stimulus for PTH secretion, such as 
vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, or renal insufficiency. In 
PHPT, the excessive secretion of PTH leads to actions on PTH’s 
two major target organs: bone and kidney. In bone, excessive 
bone resorption leads to characteristic reductions in bone density, 
primarily at cortical sites. In the kidney, despite the physiologic 
actions of PTH to conserve filtered calcium at sites along the 
nephron, hypercalciuria is common because the filtered load of 
calcium can be high. Phosphaturia often leads to low or low-nor­
mal serum phosphorus concentrations. 1,25(OH)2D synthesis is 
enhanced by PTH’s action on the renal 1α-hydroxylase, and thus 
levels of active vitamin D can be above normal. These actions 
of PTH produce the characteristic phenotype of the disease: 
hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, loss of cortical bone (distal 
1/3 radius), and hypercalciuria. Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcino­
sis, and/or reduced renal function form another aspect of this 
classical phenotype. In PHPT, a single benign adenoma is seen 
most often (75%–80%), but four-gland parathyroid hyperplasia 
can be seen in about 20% of patients. Four-gland parathyroid 
hyperplasia is more likely to be discovered in younger individuals 
and in those with a familial syndrome, such as multiple endo­
crine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) or type 2 (MEN2). Very rarely, 
parathyroid carcinoma may be found (<1%). The clinical presen­
tation of parathyroid cancer is usually markedly different from 
the much more common benign form, with the malignant form 
presenting with marked hypercalcemia, very high levels of PTH, 
and overt kidney and skeletal involvement.308,309
Classic Primary Hyperparathyroidism. The radiographic 
depiction of skeletal disease in PHPT, “osteitis fibrosa cystica,” 
was described first by von Recklinghausen in 1891, but the etio­
logic link between this disease and a parathyroid gland disorder 
was not established until 1925, when Mandl observed clinical 
improvement following removal of a parathyroid adenoma from a 
young man with severe bone disease. In early clinical descriptions 
of PHPT, the disease emerged as a distinctly uncommon disorder 
with significant morbidity and mortality rates, in which nearly all 
affected patients manifested radiographically significant or symp­
tomatic skeletal or renal involvement or both. It was considered 
to be a rare disease.
Skeletal involvement in classic PHPT reflects a striking and 
generalized increase in osteoclastic bone resorption, which is 
accompanied by fibrovascular marrow replacement and increased 
osteoblastic activity. The radiographic appearance (Fig. 27.16) is 
characterized by generalized demineralization of bone, with coars­
ening of the trabecular pattern (due to osteoclastic resorption of 
the smaller trabeculae); characteristic subperiosteal resorption, often 
most evident in the phalanges of the hands, which gives an irreg­
ular, serrated appearance to the outer, subperiosteal cortex and 
may progress to extensive cortical resorption; bone cysts, usually 
multiple, which contain a brownish serous or mucoid fluid and 
tend to occur in the central medullary portions of the shafts of 
the metacarpals, ribs, or pelvis and may expand into and disrupt 
the overlying cortex; osteoclastomas, or brown tumors, composed of 
numerous multinucleated osteoclasts (“giant cells”) admixed with 
stromal cells and matrix, which are found most often in trabecular 
portions of the jaw, long bones, and ribs; and pathologic fractures.
The skull may exhibit a finely mottled, “salt-and-pepper” radio­
graphic appearance, with loss of definition of the inner and outer 
cortices. Dental radiographs may show erosion or disappearance 
of the lamina dura as a result of subperiosteal resorption, often 
with extension into the adjacent mandibular bone. The erosion 
and demineralization of cortical bone may lead to radiographic 
disappearance of some bones, most notably the tufts of the distal 
phalanges of the hands, the inferolateral cortex of the distal third 
of the clavicles, the distal ulna, the inferior margin of the femoral 
neck and pubis, and the medial aspect of the proximal tibia. The 
clinical correlates of these changes may include aching bone pain 
and tenderness, “bowing” of the shoulders, kyphosis and loss of 
• Fig. 27.16  Radiograph of the hand of a patient with severe primary hyper­
parathyroidism. Note the dramatic remodeling associated with the intense 
region of high bone turnover in the third metacarpal, in addition to widespread 
evidence of subperiosteal, endosteal, and trabecular resorption. (Courtesy 
Fuller Albright Collection, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston.)

SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
height, and collapse of lateral ribs and pelvis with “pigeon breast” 
and triradiate deformities, respectively.
The renal manifestations of classic severe PHPT include recur­
rent calcium nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, and renal func­
tional abnormalities that range from impaired concentrating 
ability to end-stage renal failure. Associated signs and symptoms 
include recurrent flank pain, polyuria, and polydipsia. The stone 
disease may be recurrent and severe, and in some patients, the 
stones may be composed entirely of calcium phosphate instead 
of the pure oxalate or mixtures of oxalate and phosphate more 
commonly encountered in other disorders. In patients diagnosed 
before 1965, the frequency with which nephrolithiasis compli­
cated PHPT was as high as 60% to 80% (the frequency is cur­
rently <25%).
Other clinical features reported in association with classic 
severe PHPT are conjunctival calcifications, band keratopathy, 
hypertension, gastrointestinal signs and symptoms (anorexia, 
nausea, vomiting, constipation, or abdominal pain), peptic ulcer 
disease, and acute or chronic pancreatitis.
Signs and symptoms in PHPT may result from the involve­
ment of bone (fractures, bone pain) or kidneys (renal colic, renal 
failure), peptic ulcer disease, pancreatitis, or hypercalcemia per 
se (weakness, apathy, depression, polyuria, constipation, altered 
mental status). The presence and severity of neuropsychiatric 
symptoms, in particular, correlate poorly with the serum calcium 
concentration, although few patients with severe hypercalcemia 
are entirely asymptomatic. Classic presentations of PHPT include 
a neuromuscular syndrome, first described in 1949, typified by 
symmetric proximal weakness and gait disturbance, with muscle 
atrophy, characteristic electromyographic abnormalities, gen­
eralized hyperreflexia, and tongue fasciculations.310 As will be 
described, the more modern phenotypes of PHPT do not feature 
this neuromuscular syndrome. 
Other Phenotypic Presentations of PHPT. The peak inci­
dence of PHPT occurs in the sixth decade of life, but it can occur 
in any decade even, although rarely, in those younger than 15. It 
is three to four times more common in women, who are slightly 
older at diagnosis than are men. The aforementioned description 
of classical PHPT changed markedly in the early 1970s with the 
introduction of routine multichannel biochemical screening. The 
widespread use of biochemical screening that included serum cal­
cium as a component of this screening methodology led to the dis­
covery of patients with “asymptomatic” PHPT. The terminology 
asymptomatic was applied to these individuals because they were 
discovered incidentally in the course of having laboratory evalua­
tions for other reasons. In Rochester, Minnesota, for example, the 
annual incidence of the disease increased abruptly from 0.15 to 
1.12 per 1000 persons between the prescreening era (1965–1974) 
and 1975, the year after routine screening was introduced.311 Sub­
sequently, the incidence of PHPT fell.312 More recent studies have 
suggested another increase beginning in 1998, which may relate to 
widespread measurement of PTH in individuals diagnosed with 
osteoporosis.313,314
Such screening, several decades later, led to the recognition 
of a “normocalcemic variant” in which serum calcium levels are 
normal but PTH levels are persistently elevated.315 When serum 
calcium and PTH were measured in a large population of Swed­
ish women undergoing routine mammographic screening, the 
prevalence of unsuspected PHPT, defined by criteria that included 
the combination of high-normal serum calcium plus elevated or 
high-normal early intact PTH (iPTH), was 2.1%.316 Two-thirds 
of these women (72/109) were normocalcemic (10–10.4 mg/dL), 
yet bone density was reduced in the group as a whole, and the 
disease was confirmed histologically in 98% of the 61 who had 
surgery. Many of these normocalcemic patients became hypercal­
cemic during follow-up.
For the decades between 1970 and 2000, this form of PHPT, 
known as asymptomatic PHPT, was the dominant one. The severe 
phenotype that was characteristic before the onset of multichan­
nel screening continued to be seen but not necessarily more or 
less than before. Once the asymptomatic variant dominated this 
clinical landscape after multichannel screening, the much more 
rare severe phenotype seemed to have disappeared, but it was 
always present, probably with the same rarity as it used to be. The 
Swedish experience described earlier in which patients with nor­
mal serum calcium levels and elevated PTH concentrations were 
first attributed to PHPT presaged the subsequent more definitive 
description of the third phenotype of PHPT, namely, normocal­
cemic PHPT. This form of PHPT, characterized by consistently 
normal levels of serum calcium but consistently elevated levels of 
PTH, became evident first in medical centers that routinely mea­
sured the PTH in patients with or suspected of having low bone 
density. After secondary causes of elevated PTH levels are ruled 
out (e.g., vitamin insufficiency, malabsorption, renal failure), the 
diagnosis becomes more certain. 
Etiology and Pathogenesis. Parathyroid adenomas are caused 
by mutations in the DNA of parathyroid cells; these mutations 
confer a proliferative or survival advantage for affected cells over 
their normal neighbors.317,318 As a consequence of this advantage, 
the descendants of one particular parathyroid cell, a clone of cells, 
undergo clonal expansion to produce an adenoma. Multiple chro­
mosomal regions are missing in the parathyroid cells of individual 
parathyroid adenomas. These genetic deletions probably reflect 
the deletion of tumor-suppressor genes. These chromosomal loci 
include portions of chromosome 1p–pter (in 40% of adenomas), 
6q (in 32% of adenomas), 15q (in 30% of adenomas), and 11q 
(in 25%–30% of adenomas). Many of the 11q deletions are asso­
ciated, in the undeleted chromosome 11, with mutations in the 
gene encoding the transcription factor menin, the gene mutated 
in MEN1. This gene is also commonly involved in somatic muta­
tions in patients with sporadic parathyroid adenomas. Somatic 
mutations have also been found in the mitochondrial genomes 
of a fraction of chief cell adenomas and have been found even 
more frequently in so-called oxyphil adenomas, known to exhibit 
mitochondria with abnormal morphologic appearance.319 The 
widespread presence of somatic mutations in sporadic parathyroid 
adenomas, which are detectable only because large numbers of 
cells in any one tumor contain the same deletion, constitutes the 
strongest evidence that parathyroid adenomas are clonal expan­
sions of mutant cells.
Cyclin D1, initially called PRAD1, was the first noted recur­
rent parathyroid proto-oncogene.320 This gene was discovered 
at the breakpoint of an inversion on chromosome 11 in a para­
thyroid adenoma. This inversion led to the juxtaposition of the 
PTH gene’s regulatory region and the DNA encoding cyclin D1. 
As a consequence, the cyclin D1 gene was overexpressed. Cyclin 
D1 is an important regulator of the transition from the G1 phase 
of the cell cycle (which follows mitosis) to the S phase (associ­
ated with DNA synthesis) and is mutated or amplified in a wide 
variety of malignancies. Cyclin D1 is overexpressed in about 20% 
of parathyroid adenomas, although cyclin D1 gene rearrange­
ments have been documented in only 5% of adenomas. Over­
expression of cyclin D1 in the parathyroids of transgenic mice 
leads to formation of parathyroid adenomas and hypercalcemia 
1195
CHAPTER 27  Hormones and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
over many months.321 The phenotype of these mice demonstrates 
that cyclin D1 overexpression can cause primary hyperparathy­
roidism. Cyclin D1 enables the functions of cyclin-dependent 
protein kinases. More recently, inhibitors of cyclin-dependent 
protein kinases (encoding the proteins p21, p15, and p18) have 
been found mutated in the germline and somatically in sporadic 
parathyroid adenomas, in a pattern that suggests these genes act 
as tumor suppressors.322 The gene mutated in MEN1 (encoding 
menin) is also mutated only in the tumors of a substantial fraction 
of sporadic parathyroid tumors.323
Improvements in DNA sequencing technology have allowed 
the sequencing of virtually all the exons in the human genome, 
and this sort of whole exome sequencing has been performed by 
three groups.324–326 The most striking finding of these studies 
(sequencing 43 tumors between them) was that these tumors aver­
aged roughly 5 exome mutations per tumor (with the exception 
of one tumor with 110 mutations in association with a mutation 
in the protection of telomeres 1 gene [POT1] known to increase 
genetic instability). This number is considerably lower than the 
number of mutations typically found in cancers or even benign 
tumors that have been sequenced. In both studies, 35% of the 
tumors harbored mutations in the MEN1 gene, usually in asso­
ciation with deletion of the second MEN1 gene. No other gene 
was mutated frequently in these series, although mutation in a 
known oncogene, an activating mutation in EZH2, was found a 
second time when a larger series of tumors was tested for that 
mutation.324 A recent whole exome sequencing study of 24 para­
thyroid cancers demonstrated that these tumors harbor a much 
higher frequency of mutations than do parathyroid adenomas; the 
genes mutated in parathyroid cancer, so far, appear distinct from 
the genes mutated in parathyroid adenomas.327
As expected for a disease caused by mutations in DNA, parathy­
roid adenomas occur more frequently in patients who underwent 
external neck irradiation decades earlier, with greater radiation 
exposure leading to higher risk. However, most patients have no 
definite history of exposure to specific mutagens. An intriguing 
clue that abnormalities of vitamin D physiology may predispose 
to PHPT has come from the observation that patients with para­
thyroid adenomas are more likely than others to inherit a par­
ticular allele of the VDR gene.328 These patients have tumors with 
particularly low levels of mRNA encoding the VDR. Nevertheless, 
no mutations in the coding regions of the gene encoding the VDR 
have been found in parathyroid adenomas.329
The cause of sporadic primary PHPT due to multiple hyper­
plastic parathyroid glands is unknown. The known stimulus for 
parathyroid cell proliferation—low levels of blood calcium or 
1,25(OH)2D3—is not present in this disease. Presumably, some 
other stimulus outside the parathyroid glands or a genetic abnor­
mality present in all four parathyroid glands leads to inappropriate 
cell proliferation. Such abnormalities have been found in several 
inherited forms of parathyroid hyperplasia (see later), but most 
cases of parathyroid hyperplasia are not found in familial clusters.
The theoretic distinction between adenoma as a clonal pro­
liferation and hyperplasia as a polyclonal growth is clear-cut. In 
some settings, however, clonal expansion can occur in the con­
text of preexisting nonclonal proliferation. The clearest example 
of this complication has been found in the large glands associated 
with severe renal failure. In many such glands removed surgically 
because of hypercalcemia or severe parathyroid-dependent bone 
disease, evidence for clonal proliferation complicating secondary 
hyperplasia has been found. Interestingly, the pattern of chro­
mosomal abnormalities in these clonal tumors differs from that 
found in parathyroid adenomas in the absence of renal failure.330 
Analogous mechanisms may be operative in a number of settings 
associated with stimuli to parathyroid cell proliferation, such as 
X-linked hypophosphatemia and long-term lithium therapy. Fur­
thermore, just as clonal tumors can arise in the setting of secondary 
parathyroid hyperplasia, they can also arise in the setting of spo­
radic primary parathyroid hyperplasia331 and in MEN1.332
The distinction between adenoma and hyperplasia is clini­
cally important because removal of the one abnormal gland can 
be expected to cure a parathyroid adenoma, whereas removal of 
multiple glands is required to successfully treat parathyroid hyper­
plasia. Unfortunately, differentiating adenoma from hyperplasia 
from normal parathyroid tissue at pathologic examination is not 
straightforward. Pathologists distinguish normal from abnormal 
parathyroid glands by the increase in size and the paucity of fat 
in abnormal glands. Attempts have been made to distinguish an 
adenoma from an individual hyperplastic gland on the basis of 
morphologic features, but no criteria have proved completely reli­
able.309,333 The formation of clonal neoplasms in originally hyper­
plastic tumors may explain some of the difficulty in pathologic 
diagnosis.
An increase in cell number is not the only abnormality in 
PHPT. The ability of the normal parathyroid cell to suppress 
PTH secretion in response to hypercalcemia might be expected to 
protect the individual from sustained hypercalcemia, even if the 
number of parathyroid cells increased moderately. Unfortunately, 
parathyroid cells in parathyroid adenomas usually demonstrate 
abnormalities in their responsiveness to calcium, with a shift in 
set-point to the right (Fig. 27.17). This set-point shift, combined 
with the nonsuppressible component of PTH secretion, leads to a 
new steady state in which both the PTH level and the blood cal­
cium level are higher than normal. The molecular underpinning 
of the abnormal parathyroid cell responsiveness is beginning to be 
understood. Parathyroid cells from adenomas respond to changes 
in extracellular calcium with smaller-than-normal increases in 
intracellular calcium, and the amount of CaSR protein on the cell 
surface is reduced.334 Perhaps surprisingly, no mutations in the 
gene encoding the CaSR have been found in parathyroid adeno­
mas. In the experimental model in which overexpression of cyclin 
D1 results in primary hyperparathyroidism,321 reduced expression 
of the CaSR occurs only after cell proliferation has been increased 
for some time. Thus, the decreased expression of the CaSR in 
parathyroid adenomas is likely to be a secondary response that 
occurs during tumor formation. One demonstrated regulator of 
expression of the CaSR gene in parathyroid cells is the develop­
mental regulator gcm2.335 
Inherited Primary Hyperparathyroidism. Although uncom­
mon, inherited forms of PHPT are clinically important for sev­
eral reasons. The management of the parathyroid tumors found in 
familial parathyroid syndromes often differs from that of sporadic 
PHPT. Furthermore, extraparathyroidal manifestations of inher­
ited syndromes may need treatment, and awareness of familial 
clustering should prompt systematic family screening.
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (See Also Chapter 42). 
MEN1 is caused by inactivating mutations in the tumor-suppres­
sor gene encoding menin.336 Menin is a ubiquitously expressed 
transcription factor that is part of a complex that targets histone 
H3 for methylation337 and thereby leads to expression of cell cycle 
inhibitors in pancreatic islets and other tissues.338 Menin interacts 
with many nuclear proteins, and it is not known which interac­
tions are central to the pathogenesis of MEN1. Rarely, mutations 
in genes encoding cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, such as p27, 
1196
SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
are found in patients with MEN1 without menin mutations339; 
some have termed this variant, which presents primarily with 
parathyroid and pituitary tumors, MEN4.340 These patients can 
also harbor pancreatic neuroendocrine, gonadal, adrenal, renal, 
and thyroid tumors.341,342 Although MEN1 includes tumors of 
the parathyroid, anterior pituitary, and pancreatic islets, the para­
thyroid tumors are far more prevalent than the others; 95% of 
affected patients eventually develop hyperparathyroidism. Most 
of the parathyroid tumors harbor mutations in both copies of the 
menin gene; one mutation is inherited, and the second occurs in 
the parathyroid cell whose progeny forms the tumor.
The onset of hypercalcemia occurs in the second and third 
decades of life, although occasional patients present in the first 
decade. Hypercalcemia never presents at birth or in infancy. The 
disease involves all four parathyroid glands, although the involve­
ment can be asymmetric and apparently asynchronous. Apart 
from the earlier age at diagnosis, the presenting clinical picture 
generally resembles that of sporadic primary hyperparathyroid­
ism, perhaps with somewhat greater loss of bone density.343 One 
common complicating feature is that hypercalcemia can dramati­
cally increase the gastrin levels and symptomatology of patients 
who also have gastrinomas. Treatment of the parathyroid disease 
in this setting can greatly simplify the management of the gas­
tric hyperacidity. After parathyroid surgery, hypoparathyroidism 
and recurrent hyperparathyroidism are more common than in 
other forms of hyperparathyroidism.344 The timing and type of 
surgery are therefore more complicated issues than in sporadic 
primary hyperparathyroidism. Most authorities agree that para­
thyroid disease recurs eventually, particularly if fewer than three 
glands are removed. Some surgeons prefer subtotal parathyroidec­
tomy, whereas others prefer total parathyroidectomy with forearm 
implantation of a small amount of parathyroid tissue. 
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2a (See Also Chapter 42). 
Parathyroid disease is a usually late and infrequent (5%–20%) 
occurrence in MEN2a, a disease defined by the clustering of MCT, 
pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism. The parathyroid 
disease is typically mild and can be asymptomatic.342–344 In some 
families, hyperparathyroidism is more common; however, these 
families have the same mutations in the RET gene as are found 
in families without frequent hyperparathyroidism. Both parathy­
roid hyperplasia and adenoma have been noted at surgery. Because 
asymptomatic parathyroid hyperplasia has been noted at the time 
of thyroid surgery, a progression from hyperplasia to adenoma 
in MEN2a has been suggested. The approach to diagnosis and 
treatment of hyperparathyroidism is similar to that in sporadic 
primary hyperparathyroidism, but hyperplasia is more frequently 
the underlying disorder. The pathogenesis of the hyperparathy­
roidism is uncertain, but the RET gene, mutated in virtually all 
cases of MEN2a, is expressed in parathyroid cells,345 so abnormal 
RET expression in parathyroid cells may directly cause parathy­
roid tumor formation. Hyperparathyroidism does not occur in 
MEN2b, the variant associated with mucosal neuromas. 
Hyperparathyroidism–Jaw Tumor Syndrome. Patients with 
hereditary hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor syndrome309,346,347 
present with parathyroid adenomas that can be multiple and that 
are usually cystic. These tumors are often but not invariably associ­
ated with fibrous jaw tumors that are unrelated to the hyperpara­
thyroidism. Importantly, the parathyroid tumors are frequently 
malignant, in contrast to the findings in MEN1 and MEN2. Wilms 
tumor and polycystic renal disease also have occurred in affected 
families. The gene mutated in this syndrome, called CDC73 or 
HRPT2, encodes the nuclear protein parafibromin.347 Parafibro­
min is part of the evolutionarily highly conserved PAF complex 
that binds RNA polymerase II, regulates chromatin structure, and 
regulates gene expression.348–350 Parafibromin binds β-catenin 
and can mediate Wnt-pathway signaling and notch signaling, 
although whether these properties of parafibromin are related to 
its tumor-suppressor function is unknown.351 Inactivating muta­
tions in parafibromin are found in a high number of patients 
with apparently sporadic parathyroid cancer.352 In a whole exome 
sequencing study of sporadic parathyroid cancer, 8 of 17 patients 
harbored mutations in CDC73; half of the patients with CDC73 
mutations also manifested germline mutations, even though they 
presented as patients with apparently sporadic disease.309,327,328 
These findings suggest that all patients with parathyroid cancer 
should be screened for germline mutations in CDC73. 
Clinical Presentation. Given that PHPT is usually now diag­
nosed incidentally, few patients have overt signs or symptoms of 
the classic disease and thus are considered to be asymptomatic. 
For example, only 2% of patients with PHPT residing in Olm­
sted County, Minnesota, and only 17% of 121 patients studied at 
an academic referral center in New York City had classic disease 
symptoms.311,353 Many patients regarded as having asymptom­
atic PHPT with minimally elevated serum calcium suffer from

various neuropsychiatric or other symptoms that may or may not 
improve after curative surgery.354,355 These symptoms, however, 
which include fatigability, weakness, forgetfulness, depression, 
and somatization, are common in otherwise normal persons. In 
the small randomized studies of surgery for PHPT (see later), the 
effects of surgery on measures of quality of life (QoL) have been 
conflicting.356–359 Throughout this chapter, asymptomatic PHPT 
refers to patients who lack signs or symptoms of the classic dis­
ease, whether or not they experience any of the subtle symptoms 
mentioned earlier. A more proactive approach to the evaluation 
of asymptomatic PHPT has led to recognition that many of these 
patients need to be reclassified as either asymptomatic PHPT 
without target organ involvement or asymptomatic PHPT with tar­
get organ involvement. This distinction is based on a more detailed 
evaluation of the skeleton and the kidney, now recommended for 
all patients with PHPT.360,361
Abnormalities of bone in modern, mild PHPT are far more 
subtle than those associated with the classic disease. Histologi­
cally, the rate at which new bone remodeling cycles are activated 
is increased. Because the phase of restorative bone formation at 
each remodeling site takes much more time than does the initial 
resorptive phase, such an increase in remodeling rate inevitably 
increases the ambient volume of the remodeling space and thus 
the porosity of bone. Depending on the rate and extent of the 
accompanying increase in osteoblastic activity and the resulting 
local balance between net bone formation and resorption, miner­
alized bone volume may decrease further, remain stable, or even 
increase (despite an increased remodeling space). For reasons not 
yet understood, the balance achieved between increased resorption 
and formation of bone in PHPT depends not only on the severity 
of the hyperparathyroidism but also on skeletal location. Thus, net 
resorption of endosteal bone may predominate in cortical sites, 
whereas net apposition of mineral may occur in trabecular bone 
when measured by iliac crest biopsy362,363 (Fig. 27.18). Thus, pref­
erential reduction in BMD may be seen at sites of predominantly 
cortical bone, such as the one-third radius. To this point, stud­
ies using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) demonstrate 
relative preservation of vertebral bone mass in PHPT.364 Despite 
this evidence of preserved trabecular bone mass in PHPT, the 
incidence of vertebral fracture is increased.365,366 The explanation 
for this paradox appears to relate to abnormalities in trabecular 
(and cortical) microarchitecture that can be detected using newer 
technologies. High-resolution peripheral quantitative computed 
tomography (HRpQCT) and measurement of the Trabecular 
Bone Score (TBS) during DXA measurements both indicate that 
trabecular indices are deteriorated.367,368 These abnormalities 
weaken trabecular bone and presumably account for the elevated 
risk of vertebral fracture. These defects are improved after success­
ful parathyroidectomy.369 Thus, the paradox presented by appar­
ently preserved trabecular bone by DXA in PHPT associated with 
increased risk of vertebral fractures is resolved by appreciating that 
both cortical and trabecular microstructure are abnormal in this 
disease.370
Kidney stones are reported now in only 10% to 25% of 
patients with PHPT, although some degree of renal dysfunction, 
either a significant reduction in creatinine clearance or impaired 
concentrating or acidifying ability, may be found in up to one-
third of those with asymptomatic disease. These renal abnormali­
ties are not progressive in the majority of affected patients.353,371 
In patients with the modern form of PHPT, no parameters of dis­
ease severity predict a lower estimated GFR.372 The association of 
kidney stones with PHPT generally is viewed as an indication for 
parathyroidectomy because successful surgery usually prevents fur­
ther symptomatic stone disease.353,354 On the other hand, it is not

possible at present to confidently predict, from biochemical mea­
surements in blood or urine, which asymptomatic patients with 
PHPT will proceed to develop new stone disease. Stone-formers 
are more likely to be hypercalciuric than not, but less than one-
third of hypercalciuric patients with hyperparathyroidism actually 
develop stones. Recently, hypomagnesuria has been identified as 
another independent risk factor for kidney stones in PHPT.373
Although kidney stones continue to be the most common 
overt complication of PHPT and are an acknowledged indication 
for surgery, it should be recognized that there may not be an etio­
logic link between these two common disorders in every patient. 
Common diseases can be coincidentally found. Nevertheless, it 
seems reasonable to conclude a possible relationship and accept 
kidney stones as an indication for parathyroid surgery.
Nonclassical Manifestations in Patients With Asymptomatic 
PHPT. Nonclassical manifestations of PHPT are apparent associ­
ated aspects that involve organ systems other than the skeleton 
and kidney. These include cardiovascular, neuropsychological, gas­
trointestinal, and rheumatic effects. Although gastrointestinal and 
rheumatic symptomatology were features of classical PHPT, they 
are not part of the modern presentation of PHPT. In contrast, 
neuropsychological symptoms such as altered mood and cogni­
tion, as well as cardiovascular disease, have been associated with 
the mild “asymptomatic” form of PHPT seen today, but the rela­
tionship is controversial and not clearly causal.360,361
Excess risk of mortality, mainly from cardiovascular disease, has 
been observed during extended follow-up of postsurgical patients 
with hyperparathyroidism.354 Increased cardiovascular mortality 
risk may, however, only pertain to severe PHPT.374–379 In a study 
of patients with mild hypercalcemia in Olmsted County, Min­
nesota, increased mortality was only present in those within the 
highest quartile of serum calcium. The study otherwise showed 
an overall decreased risk of death.378 Similarly, a randomized 
10-year clinical trial of parathyroidectomy versus observation in 
191 patients with mild PHPT indicated no benefit of surgery on 
mortality compared with observation.380 On the other hand, a 
very large observational study in 16,374 patients with PHPT and 
163,740 controls indicated those with PHPT had a higher risk of 
death that was reduced by parathyroidectomy. Because biochemi­
cal indices were not reported, it was not possible to assign a rela­
tionship of this outcome index to disease severity.381 Thus, there 
remains significant controversy regarding the effect of the disease 
on mortality.
Associations of hypertension, increased vascular stiffness, left 
ventricular hypertrophy, vascular calcifications, and other indi­
cators of subclinical cardiovascular disease, as well as glucose 
intolerance, have been implicated, together with hypercalcemia, 
as contributors to elevated cardiovascular mortality in patients 
with PHPT.382,383 Some but not all observational studies sug­
gest reversibility after parathyroidectomy.384 Randomized studies 
assessing the impact of parathyroidectomy compared with obser­
vation on subclinical cardiovascular indices have, however, not 
shown a benefit.385–388
Neuropsychiatric symptoms such as depression, anxiety, 
fatigue, decreased QoL, sleep disturbance, and cognitive dysfunc­
tion are reported by many patients.356,358,389–411 Whether neu­
ropsychological symptoms are specifically attributable to PHPT 
and reversible after parathyroidectomy is controversial, and results 
from both observational studies and randomized trials have been 
conflicting.356,358,401,412 Three short-term (1- to 2-year) RCTs 
have investigated the reversibility of reduced QoL and psychiat­
ric symptoms.356,358,401 Despite being of similar design and using 
similar assessment tools, all three RCTs came to different conclu­
sions; one RCT suggested parathyroidectomy prevents worsen­
ing of QoL, another indicated no benefit, and a third indicated 
improvement.356,358,401 The results of 10 years of follow-up after 
randomization to parathyroidectomy or observation suggest no 
consistent long-term improvement in QoL.413 
Normocalcemic PHPT. The appearance of this third phenotype 
of PHPT occurred chronologically after decades of a singular pre­
sentation, namely, classic symptomatic PHPT, and then decades 
of asymptomatic PHPT. This normocalcemic form of PHPT was 
first described in detail in the early 2000s.315 Normocalcemic 
PHPT was first found among patients in medical centers that spe­
cialized in metabolic bone diseases and then more widely there­
after. The ready availability and measurement of PTH in these 
patients, even when the serum calcium was normal, led to the 
recognition of this phenotype. Normocalcemic hyperparathyroid­
ism (NPHPT) is characterized by persistently normal albumin-
adjusted total calcium and normal ionized serum calcium levels, 
on at least two consecutive measurements at least a week apart 
over a 3- to 6-month-period, along with consistently elevated lev­
els of PTH. When these patients are encountered, it is important 
to consider secondary causes for an elevated PTH, such as vitamin 
D insufficiency (e.g., 25[OH]D <75 nmol/L or 30 ng/mL), CKD 
(estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] <60 mL/min/1.73 
m2), renal calcium loss (idiopathic hypercalciuria and loop diuret­
ics), or any gastrointestinal tract disease that can affect calcium 
absorption (inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, bariatric 
surgery). It is also important to recognize certain medications that 
can be associated with elevated levels of PTH, such as lithium, 
anticonvulsants, bisphosphonates, and denosumab.414,415
It is unclear how common this disease is because many pub­
lished reports have not adequately considered all secondary causes 
for an increased level of PTH. Thus, prevalence estimates in the 
general population vary widely between 0.1% and 8.9%.416 The 
simple statement that the adjusted serum calcium is normal and 
the PTH is elevated has been refined recently by using nomograms 
that relate the adjusted serum calcium to the PTH level.417,418 
Even albumin-adjusted calcium-to-phosphate ratios have been 
proposed.419 Complicating this discussion are other factors, such 
as the intrinsic variability of albumin-adjusted calcium values and 
age-related increases in PTH independent of vitamin D status or 
renal function.420–422 To a certain extent, measuring the ionized 
calcium may reduce this variability.423
As is the case for the hypercalcemic form of PHPT, the patho­
physiology of NPHPT may be due to an increase in the calcium 
set-point for PTH release. Genetic factors such as calcium sen­
sor receptor polymorphisms might also be a relevant pathophysi­
ologic point.424 Although the definition of NPHPT requires 
consistently normal adjusted total calcium and normal ionized 
calcium, longitudinal follow-up of these patients has shown, in 
some but not all reports, progression to hypercalcemia.425–429 
Although it is clear that some of these individuals will progress to 
hypercalcemic PHPT, the natural history of the disorder is unclear 
in part because studies have not always used consistent definitions 
for NPHPT, nor has regular follow-up been consistent at defined 
time points.
Clinical features of NPHPT can be similar to those described 
in PHPT (skeletal and renal complications). Studies from refer­
ral centers have shown that the frequency of skeletal compli­
cations, osteoporosis, and fractures is similar to PHPT in 
some430–432 but not all studies.426,433 The data on kidney stones 
and nephrolithiasis are also inconclusive.434 By ultrasound, one 
1199
CHAPTER 27  Hormones and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism
study reported a prevalence of nephrolithiasis to be as high as 
20%.435 As is the case for asymptomatic hypercalcemic PHPT, 
off-target features in NPHPT related to glucose metabolism, 
hypertension, and QoL are inconsistent. Given the existence of 
NPHPT, it is apparent that there are symptomatic and asymp­
tomatic forms. Among those with asymptomatic NPHPT, one 
can further classify them, after evaluation, as with or without 
target organ involvement.
The description of three phenotypes of PHPT has followed a 
chronology with classic symptomatic disease followed by asymp­
tomatic PHPT followed by NPHPT. It is important to recog­
nize, however, that all three forms of PHPT coexist in the world 
today. Whether one form is more likely to be seen over another 
will depend, in part, on demographic, nutritional, and practice 
patterns. For example, in countries where multichannel screen­
ing is not routinely performed and in which vitamin D deficiency 
is endemic, symptomatic PHPT is common. In countries where 
multichannel screening is routine, asymptomatic PHPT is more 
likely to be seen. In medical centers where PTH levels are routinely 
measured in anyone with or suspected of having a metabolic bone 
disease, NPHPT will surface as a common variant. Not only do 
all three forms of PHPT coexist in the world today, but one might 
speculate also that these three forms have always been present. 
Management of PHPT. The strategy for management of PHPT 
has evolved in parallel with more recently recognized clinical 
aspects of the disease, as well as with greater mechanistic insights 
into skeletal and renal aspects of the disease. Although our man­
agement strategies have followed in step with these advances, one 
constant remains: the only cure for this disease is successful para­
thyroidectomy. When PHPT was virtually always a symptomatic 
disease, surgery was always the approach. It is still the treatment 
of choice in those who do not have a medical contraindication to 
parathyroid surgery.
The management dilemma relates to those with asymptomatic 
PHPT. For the past 50 years, experts have been wrestling with the 
question of surgery versus medical management. This dilemma 
has become more complex in the context of NPHPT. In favor of 
surgery are its consequences, namely, restoration of normal serum 
calcium and PTH levels. Improved calcium balance often leads to 
substantial improvements in BMD at all sites. By inference, frac­
ture risk should be reduced.436 The development of effective mini­
mally invasive surgical procedures (see later) is also an argument 
in favor of parathyroid surgery. Those who favor an observational 
approach emphasize lack of disease progression in most asymp­
tomatic patients; the small but finite risk of surgical failure and 
postoperative complications; the probability that excess mortality 
in patients with relatively severe disease may not apply to those 
with mild, asymptomatic PHPT; the difficulty in assigning vague 
neuropsychiatric symptoms to the parathyroid disorder; the lack 
of evidence (or negative evidence) that hypertension, fracture, or 
cardiovascular mortality, even if present, are improved by success­
ful parathyroidectomy; and the availability of sensitive techniques 
for monitoring disease status in patients who are observed.353 
Unfortunately, no large prospective studies adequately powered to 
compare clinical outcomes in patients with asymptomatic PHPT 
randomly assigned to surgery versus medical management have 
been conducted. Nevertheless, several valuable smaller RCTs of 
surgery versus observation have been conducted that allow some 
conclusions to be made.356–358 Referencing these clinical tri­
als, increases in bone density in the spine and hip in the surgical 
group were similar to those seen in the context of bisphospho­
nate therapy (see later). As useful as these studies have been, their 
limitations have forced the field to refer to observational studies 
that are necessarily limited.
Recommendations have emanated from a series of conferences: 
an NIH-sponsored Consensus Conference held in 1990, followed 
by International Conferences on the Management of Asymp­
tomatic Primary Hyperparathyroidism in 2002, 2008, 2014, and 
2021.104 The most recent guidelines reiterate that although sur­
gery is indicated for symptomatic hyperparathyroidism and is an 
appropriate option in asymptomatic PHPT, many with asymp­
tomatic disease can be safely monitored without surgery.
The most recent guidelines recommend parathyroidectomy if 
any one of the following criteria is met and there are no medical 
contraindications361:
	1.	 Serum calcium >1.0 mg/dL above the upper normal limit
	2.	 DXA T-score < −2.5 at the spine, hip, or distal 1/3 radius
	3.	 Presence of a vertebral fracture on imaging
	4.	 Creatinine clearance <60 cc/min
	5.	 24-hour urine calcium >250 mg/day in women (or >300 mg/
day in men)
	6.	 Increased stone risk by biochemical stone risk analysis
	7.	 Presence of nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis on imaging
	8.	 Age <50 years
The expert panel did not make recommendations for surgery 
in NPHPT because it was felt that the data were not sufficiently 
conclusive. However, these recommendations for asymptomatic 
hypercalcemic PHPT seem reasonable if the diagnosis of NPHPT 
is unequivocally established (authors’ opinion).
These recommendations lead logically to revised recommenda­
tions for evaluation of PHPT361:
	1.	 Biochemical
	
a.	 Adjusted total serum calcium (ionized if NPHPT is a con­
sideration)
	
b.	 Intact PTH
	
c.	 25-hydroxyvitamin D
	
d.	 Phosphorus
	
e.	 Creatinine
	2.	 Skeletal
	
a.	 Three-site DXA (lumbar spine, hip, distal 1/3 radius)
	
b.	 Imaging for vertebral fractures (vertebral fracture assess­
ment [VFA] or vertebral x-rays; the TBS can be helpful if 
available)
	3.	 Renal
	
a.	 eGFR or, preferably, creatinine clearance
	
b.	 Full 24-hour urinary calcium
	
c.	 Abdominal imaging for nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis
	
d.	 In those with hypercalciuria, a stone risk profile is recom­
mended.
	
e.	 In those with stones, a stone risk profile is recommended 
whether or not the patient has hypercalciuria.
The expert panel did not recommend surgery for the so-called 
off-target aspects of PHPT, although it was recognized that symp­
toms such as fatigue, lethargy, weakness (without objective muscle 
weakness), and depression could be due, at least in part, to PHPT. 
Similarly, the panel did not opine on whether surgery might be 
indicated for those with cardiovascular disease. Most clinicians 
do not routinely recommend parathyroidectomy on the basis of 
such symptoms alone, although dramatic responses to surgery are 
occasionally seen. With the availability of improved, minimally 
invasive surgical approaches, the threshold for considering sur­
gery in patients who are significantly disabled by such symptoms 
clearly is lower now than in the past. The most recent guidelines 
from the 5th International Workshop on the Management of

Asymptomatic Primary Hyperparathyroidism do not recommend 
surgery for neuropsychiatric symptoms or cardiovascular disease 
because of the lack of robust evidence indicating improvement 
after parathyroidectomy.361 Guidelines from some others differ in 
this regard but do note weak evidence.437
Surgical Treatment of PHPT. Parathyroidectomy is a safe and 
highly effective approach to definitive treatment of PHPT.438 The 
most serious potential complications of parathyroid surgery—
vocal cord paralysis and permanent hypoparathyroidism—occur 
after fewer than 1% and 4%,438,439 respectively, of procedures 
performed by highly skilled surgeons, although these rates can be 
much higher in less experienced hands. Such complications occur 
most often in patients who require subtotal parathyroid resec­
tions for hyperplasia or resection of carcinoma. The surgical cure 
rate for primary hyperparathyroidism in the best hands is at least 
95%.440,441 Apart from operator inexperience, the usual cause of 
initial surgical failure (“persistent disease”) is the presence of either 
unrecognized (often very asymmetric) parathyroid hyperplasia or 
ectopic parathyroid tissue (i.e., intrathyroidal, undescended, ret­
roesophageal, or mediastinal glands) (Fig. 27.19).442 Up to one in 
five parathyroid glands may be located ectopically, and this is espe­
cially true of supernumerary glands. Recurrent disease, defined 
as that occurring after an interval of at least 6 to 12 months of 
normocalcemia, varies in incidence from 2% to 16%. Recurrent 
hyperparathyroidism usually arises in unresected hyperplastic 
glands, but rarely, it may be due to parathyroid carcinoma, to a 
second adenoma, or to a multicentric or miliary “parathyromato­
sis” engendered by inadvertent local seeding of parathyroid tissue 
(usually hyperplastic) into the neck during previous parathyroid 
surgery.443
In the past, there was broad agreement that the best approach 
is a bilateral neck exploration in which all four parathyroids are 
identified and all enlarged glands removed.
With the advent of preoperative 99mTc sestamibi scanning and, 
more recently, ultrasound and high-resolution CT with dynamic 
contrast administration (four-dimensional CT [4D-CT]),444 uni­
lateral explorations and minimally invasive surgical approaches 
have gained traction. 99mTc-sestamibi scanning, the traditional 
imaging modality for localizing hyperfunctioning parathyroids, 
identifies 80% to 90% of single adenomas. Sestamibi does localize 
to thyroid nodules, which may accompany parathyroid disease in 
20% to 40% of patients, although it tends to wash out of thyroid 
tissue much more rapidly than from parathyroids. 99mTc-sesta­
mibi can be combined with 123I scanning to improve distinction 
of parathyroids from thyroid nodules or with single-photon emis­
sion CT (SPECT) imaging to achieve accuracy in localization not 
possible with planar imaging (Fig. 27.20). Sestamibi scanning may 
fail to reveal small glands (uptake is related to gland size and PTH 
levels).445 It can also detect the occasional mediastinal adenoma 
and thereby allow the avoidance of an unnecessary neck explora­
tion. On the other hand, the sensitivity and positive predictive 
value of sestamibi scanning are poor (<50%) in the presence of 
multiglandular disease (hyperplasia or double adenomas), and 
thus the test may frequently miss the presence of bilateral disease. 
The choice of preoperative imaging test depends, however, on 
local expertise because sensitivity and specificity may vary widely. 
Rapid intraoperative PTH assays have been developed to verify 
successful excision when minimally invasive surgical approaches 
are used.446 Because the half-life of intact PTH in blood is very 
short (<2 minutes), a decline of 50% or more from baseline within 
10 minutes or so, into the normal range, can signal successful

removal of all hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue. Minimally 
invasive approaches reduce operative and recovery-room time, 
minimize the number of frozen sections required, and are associ­
ated with significantly fewer postoperative complications.447
At present, preoperative imaging enables consideration of a 
minimally invasive unilateral parathyroidectomy in approximately 
70% of those patients thought preoperatively to have sporadic 
primary hyperparathyroidism due to a solitary adenoma. Surgi­
cal cure rates in appropriately selected patients are comparable 
to those after bilateral neck exploration (i.e., 95%–97%).438,440 
Patients known or suspected to have multiglandular disease, such 
as those with MEN1 and those younger than 30 years of age, 
should undergo bilateral neck exploration.116 Options for patients 
with hyperplasia include resection limited to visibly abnormal 
glands, subtotal parathyroidectomy with cryopreservation of tis­
sue, and total parathyroidectomy with immediate autotransplan­
tation (i.e., in the forearm) of some excised tissue. In patients with 
MEN1, considerations of recurrence rates (30%–50% or higher 
with long-term follow-up) and the timing thereof versus the 
potential morbidity of surgical hypoparathyroidism tend to favor 
subtotal parathyroidectomy as the preferred approach at present.
The incidence of parathyroid carcinoma in PHPT is less than 
1%,448,449 but this possibility should be strongly considered in 
patients with unusually severe hyperparathyroidism, a palpable 
neck mass, hoarseness, evidence of local invasion at surgery, or 
recurrent hypercalcemia. Even so, parathyroid carcinoma rarely is 
suspected preoperatively and often eludes diagnosis at the time of 
initial surgery. When the disease is recognized, vigorous attempts 
should be made to remove the tumor en bloc. The incidence of 
local recurrence approaches 50%, however, and distant metasta­
ses, particularly to the lung, may be heralded by recurrent, severe 
hyperparathyroidism. Because apparently sporadic and isolated 
parathyroid cancer can occur in families with parafibromin muta­
tions, a search for such mutations in all patients with parathyroid 
cancer can facilitate family counseling.352
The immediate postoperative management of parathyroidec­
tomy focuses on establishing the success of the surgery and moni­
toring the patient closely for symptomatic hypocalcemia and for 
uncommon but potentially serious acute complications such as 
bleeding, vocal cord paralysis, or laryngospasm. After successful 
resection of a parathyroid adenoma, serum intact PTH and cal­
cium levels normalize rapidly. “Hungry bone” syndrome, associ­
ated with hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and low urinary 
calcium excretion, was common in the past but is rarely seen today.
Many surgeons recommend oral calcium supplements rou­
tinely to prevent hypocalcemia. Moderate doses of 1,25(OH)2D 
(0.5–1 μg daily) may be added for those with large adenomas and 
severe hyperparathyroidism or for those in whom alkaline phos­
phatase had been elevated preoperatively in whom an impressive 
calcium requirement can be anticipated, often for many weeks 
postoperatively, as they remineralize their skeletons.
The approach to patients with persistent or recurrent hyper­
parathyroidism is informed by the recognition that parathyroid 
hyperplasia or carcinoma, ectopic or supernumerary parathyroid 
tissue, and postoperative hypoparathyroidism and other compli­
cations of further surgery all are more common in this popula­
tion.442 The first issue to address is whether surgery is indicated. 
When a presumed adenoma had not been identified initially, the 
original indications for surgery generally still exist, although some 
patients may not be suitable candidates for more extensive surgery, 
such as a median sternotomy, because of concurrent medical ill­
ness. Patients with parathyroid hyperplasia may have experienced 
significant clinical improvement, even after incomplete parathy­
roidectomy, although those with MEN1 are very likely to experi­
ence further progression of their disease.
Preoperative localization studies are recommended for patients 
with persistent or recurrent disease after a first operation, and 
some surgeons require two concordant studies to proceed with 
reoperation. Use of 4D-CT with synchronous contrast-enhanced 
multiplanar anatomic reconstruction has been shown to provide 
sensitivity superior to sestamibi scanning alone for localizing func­
tioning parathyroid tissue in candidates for reoperation.450
More invasive techniques have been used as well, including 
angiography and selective venous sampling, for measurement of 
PTH.451,452 Ultrasound-guided or CT-guided fine-needle aspira­
tion of suspected parathyroid tissue may be used to obtain cytologic 
or immunochemical confirmation before surgery, and intraop­
erative ultrasonography has been useful in some cases to locate 
cervical or intrathyroidal glands.453 Success with video-assisted 
thoracoscopic resection of documented mediastinal lesions454 
offers a less invasive alternative to median sternotomy for this rela­
tively common cause of persistent hyperparathyroidism.
After successful surgery for PHPT, observational studies show 
robust improvement in bone mass by as much as 5% to 10% in 
the first year at sites rich in trabecular bone (spine, femoral neck), 
whereas improvement at cortical sites (distal radius) is less pre­
dictable.353,455 Increases at trabecular sites may continue for sev­
eral years, to as much as 12% to 15% after 10 years, although 
normal BMD may not be achieved. This improvement, which is 
most apparent in those with the greatest preoperative reductions 
in bone mass, may be related in part to rapid remineralization of 
the previously enlarged bone remodeling volume,456 but the con­
tinued improvement over years suggests a more sustained increase 
in net bone formation and total bone volume as well.353 Random­
ized trials of surgery versus observation confirm gains in BMD 
observed in observational studies, although the magnitude of such 
gains tends to be lower.357,358,457 A decline in the risk of fracture 
has been harder to show. Observational studies suggest fracture 
risk decreases after parathyroidectomy.381,458,459 A randomized 
clinical trial demonstrated that the risk of vertebral fracture was 
reduced after parathyroidectomy, but the decline was of border­
line statistical significance.457 Patients who do not meet criteria for 
surgery experience the same postsurgical increase in bone density 
as those who do.353,456
New data using HRpQCT indicate improved volumetric 
BMD, bone microarchitecture, and strength at the distal radius 
and tibia, although there are conflicting results regarding whether 
TBS changes after parathyroidectomy.369,460–462 
Nonsurgical Management of PHPT
The natural history of untreated asymptomatic PHPT, as cur­
rently detected, indicates that few patients seem to experience 
progression of disease, as measured by further elevations of serum 
or urinary calcium, appearance of renal dysfunction or nephro­
calcinosis, or worsening osteopenia with observation, in the short 
term.353 On the other hand, late cortical bone loss observed at the 
femoral neck and distal radius in a small number of patients fol­
lowed without surgery for 15 years points to the potential impor­
tance of continued monitoring in such patients.463 Ultimately, 
when patients are followed for 15 years, close to 40% develop dis­
ease progression, defined as meeting a new criterion for surgery.463
Patients not treated surgically should be followed carefully, 
with annual measurement of serum calcium and calculated creati­
nine clearance and serial determination of BMD at intervals of 1 
1202
SECTION VII    Mineral Metabolism
to 2 years.361 Symptoms suggestive of nephrolithiasis or vertebral 
fracture should prompt investigation with appropriate studies.
Patients undergoing nonoperative medical management must 
be cautioned to maintain adequate hydration, avoid diuretics and 
prolonged immobilization, and seek prompt medical attention in 
the event of illnesses accompanied by significant vomiting or diar­
rhea. Dietary calcium should not be restricted.
Medical therapy can address osteoporosis and serum calcium 
levels within the range that may cause symptoms. Small random­
ized clinical trials indicate that alendronate and hormone replace­
ment therapy increase BMD compared with placebo at multiple 
skeletal sites in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism, but 
most show no meaningful change in serum calcium.361,440,441 Intra­
venous bisphosphonates have been used successfully in the urgent 
therapy of hypercalcemia due to primary hyperparathyroidism.
Cinacalcet, a type-2 calcimimetic, binds to the CaSR and 
increases its sensitivity. Cinacalcet reduces serum calcium in pri­
mary hyperparathyroidism and maintains long-term normocalce­
mia across a wide spectrum of disease severity.440,441 Cinacalcet 
was approved for PHPT by the U.S. Food and Drug Administra­
tion (FDA) in 2011 for the “treatment of severe hypercalcemia in 
patients with PHPT who are unable to undergo parathyroidec­
tomy.” It is not indicated for those with mild or moderate hyper­
calcemia. Neither BMD nor urinary calcium excretion improves 
with treatment. Further, there are no data regarding nephrolithia­
sis risk reduction. 
Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia
FHH, also appropriately called familial benign hypercalcemia, is, 
in most families, a disorder of autosomal-dominant inheritance 
caused most often by mutations of the CaSR gene. The mutations, 
which cause complete or partial loss of function of the CaSR, 
lead to a shift in the parathyroid cell’s set-point for calcium.464 
As a consequence, higher-than-normal levels of blood calcium 
are needed to suppress PTH secretion. Furthermore, abnormal 
function of the CaSR in the renal thick ascending limb leads to 
increased PTH-independent calcium reabsorption and conse­
quent hypocalciuria. In a minority of patients, mutations in two 
other genes in the signaling pathway activated by the CaSR have 
been found. One encodes the α-subunit of the G11 heterotrimeric 
G protein465 known to participate in responding to the activation 
of the CaSR, and the other is in the AP2S1 gene that encodes 
the α-subunit of adapter protein complex 2, a scaffolding protein 
needed for formation of clathrin-coated pits needed to internalize 
the CaSR.466 Mutations in AP2S1 are considerably more com­
mon than mutations in Gα11 in FHH467,468; patients with AP2S1 
mutations have particularly severe hypercalcemia and can present 
with developmental delay and cognitive dysfunction.467
The presence of one normal CaSR gene with the abnormal one 
usually leads to a very mild clinical disorder, although the recep­
tor functions as a dimer, and certain mutations can worsen the 
function of the normal allele. Rare patients who inherit mutant 
CaSR genes from both parents present at birth with severe, life-
threatening hypercalcemia and almost always require immediate 
parathyroid surgery.
FHH is manifested at birth by hypercalcemia. Although 
some controversy exists, most observers note that the condition 
associated with CaSR mutations is usually asymptomatic and 
that apparent symptoms represent ascertainment bias. Possible 
exceptions include the occurrence of chondrocalcinosis and per­
haps pancreatitis. The blood calcium level is usually less than 12 
mg/dL but can be higher. Phosphate measurements are low, as 
in PHPT. Serum magnesium levels are high-normal or slightly 
elevated. PTH levels are inappropriately normal for the degree of 
hypercalcemia and are occasionally modestly elevated. Urine cal­
cium is usually low, although one novel mutation in the receptor’s 
intracellular tail has been associated with hypercalciuria, possibly 
because of only mild dysfunction in the kidney.469
When patients present as adults, the distinction from mild 
PHPT can be difficult. The distinction between FHH and PHPT 
is a crucial one, however. Young patients with PHPT are usually 
treated surgically and cured. In contrast, hypercalcemia always 
recurs after surgery for FHH, unless the patient is rendered hypo­
parathyroid. Therefore, surgery is contraindicated as therapy for 
FHH, except in the very rare patient with severe, symptomatic 
hypercalcemia. No blood or urine measurements are completely 
reliable for distinguishing between the two conditions, although 
the ratio of calcium clearance to creatinine clearance distinguishes 
most patients with FHH from those with PHPT.470 Fig. 27.21 
shows, however, that this ratio separates the two groups, with 
modest overlap between the groups. However, because PHPT is 
much more common than FHH, most patients with values near 
the cutoff value of 0.01 for the ratio of calcium clearance to cre­
atinine clearance will have PHPT and not FHH. Consequently, a 
case can be made471 that many such patients, particularly before 
parathyroid surgery, should undergo genetic testing. The most 
helpful diagnostic information is the presence of hypercalcemia 
in an infant relative. Furthermore, a past history of clearly normal 
blood calcium, considerably lower than current measurements, 
makes FHH unlikely if no other reason, such as severe vitamin 
D deficiency, for a change in blood calcium exists. A final point 
to make with regard to the differential diagnosis of FHH versus
