C. RONALD KAHN, HEATHER A. FERRIS, AND BRIAN T. O’NEILL
Epidemiology
Type 2 diabetes mellitus is the predominant form of diabetes 
worldwide, accounting for 90% to 95% of cases globally. An epi­
demic of T2D is underway in both developed and developing 
countries. The International Diabetes Federation estimated in 
2021 that 537 million adults age 20 to 79 years have diabetes 
worldwide and that by 2045 this number will rise to 738 million. 
Of those with diabetes currently, most live in higher-income coun­
tries, but the largest growth of new cases of diabetes is expected 
in low- to middle-income countries, which have larger population 
growth.1 In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control 
and Prevention (CDC) estimated in 2022 that 37.3 million peo­
ple, or 11.3% of the population, had diabetes and that 8.5 million 
of them (23.0%) were undiagnosed. Based on fasting glucose or 
hemoglobin A1c levels, they also estimated that 96 million people 
(38% of adults over age 20) had prediabetes and thus are at high 
risk of developing diabetes.2
The economic burden of diabetes is enormous. The Interna­
tional Diabetes Federation estimated that in 2021 diabetes-related 
health expenditures amounted to 966 billion US dollars (USD).1 
The American Diabetes Association estimated that in the United 
States alone in 2017 diabetes accounted for 237 billion USD in 
direct health care expenditures and an additional 90 billion USD 
in lost productivity. Average expenditures per person, adjusted for 
age and gender, were 2.3-fold higher compared to the nondiabetic 
U.S. population. The increased spending was driven by both the 
increased prevalence of the disease and the costs associated with 
care.3 In addition, the high cost of diabetes medications, including 
insulin, leaves many patients in the United States unable to afford 
1327
CHAPTER 33  Pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
the medications they are prescribed, leading to increased diabetes-
related complications and additional individual and cost burdens.
Considerable information is available on the factors that are 
responsible for the development of T2D, and these determi­
nants are summarized in Box 33.1.4,5 T2D is thought to occur 
in genetically predisposed persons who are exposed to a series of 
environmental influences that precipitate the onset of clinical 
disease. Although T2D is strongly associated with high body mass 
index (BMI), there are clear differences in fat distribution and the 
degree of excess fat that is required to drive susceptibility to T2D.6 
For example, individuals with high levels of visceral fat (central 
obesity) are generally more insulin resistant and at higher risk for 
T2D than those with high levels of peripheral, mainly subcutane­
ous fat. Individuals with central obesity also have more ectopic 
fat accumulation in liver and muscle, which likely contributes to 
increased insulin resistance.7 Likewise, individuals from Southeast 
Asia are at high risk of developing T2D at lower BMIs than other 
ethnicities, in part due to greater visceral adipose stores, leading 
to recommendations to increase screening for T2D in people of 
Asian descent if the BMI is above 23 kg/m2.8 Historically, when 
ethnicities prone to developing T2D at lower BMIs migrate to the 
United States they see weight gain and a rapid rise in the rate of 
T2D with the change to a Western diet.9,10 Not surprisingly, as 
many in Asia adopt a more Western diet, the rates of T2D increase 
even within those countries with previously low incidence rates, 
and there is no longer a migration effect as the diet has already 
changed.11 In the United States the prevalence of T2D varies by 
race and ethnicity, with Native American populations having twice 
the rate of diabetes at 14.5% than non-Hispanic White patients 
at 7.4% (Fig. 33.1).2
Although the prevalence of T2D increases with age, over the 
past decade the prevalence of obesity and T2D in children has 
risen dramatically. Thus, in the past, the overwhelming majority 
of children with diabetes had type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D), with 
only 1% to 2% of diabetic children considered to have T2D or 
other rare forms of diabetes. Recent reports suggest almost 30% of 
children in the United States with newly diagnosed diabetes have 
T2D. Thus, the estimated prevalence of T2D (per 10,000 youths

Pathogenesis
The pathogenesis of T2D is complex and involves the interac­
tion of genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors. A number 
of environmental factors have been shown to play a critical role 
in the development of the disease, particularly excessive caloric 
intake leading to obesity and a sedentary lifestyle (Fig. 33.2). 
Other environmental factors that affect obesity and T2D devel­
opment, including medications, inflammation, circadian rhythm 
disruptions, and the microbiome, also need to be considered. The 
clinical presentation of T2D is heterogeneous, with a wide range 
in age at onset, severity of associated hyperglycemia, and degree of 
obesity. From a pathophysiologic standpoint, persons with T2D 
consistently demonstrate four cardinal abnormalities:
 • Resistance to the action of insulin in peripheral tissues, par­
ticularly muscle, fat, and liver (the classical tissues of insulin 
action).
 • Defective insulin secretion, particularly in response to a glu­
cose stimulus, although absolute levels may be high, low, or 
normal.
 • Decreased glucose uptake in muscle in response to insulin lead­
ing to postprandial hyperglycemia.
 • Increased glucose production by the liver leading to hypergly­
cemia in the fasting state.
In addition, people with T2D may have hyperglucagonemia, 
alterations in incretin secretion or action, accelerated lipolysis in 
the fat cell, increased renal tubular reabsorption, and abnormali­
ties in central nervous system regulation of metabolism.14
From a pathophysiologic standpoint in the development of 
T2D, there is still debate as to which is more important: insu­
lin resistance or the inability of the pancreatic β cell to adapt to 
the insulin resistance. What is clear is that the earliest detectable 
abnormality in those predisposed to T2D is insulin resistance. 
Indeed, insulin resistance may precede T2D by more than 20 
years.15 Many common factors further increase insulin resistance 
and place an increased secretory burden on the β cell: puberty, 
pregnancy, a sedentary lifestyle, and weight gain all add to 
increased T2D risk. Although many polymorphisms identified 
by genome-wide association studies (GWASs) linked to T2D 
suggest an underlying genetic predisposition to β-cell failure, no 
single genetic alternation or single diagnostic test has been identi­
fied to predict this outcome.
Genetic Factors in the Development of Type 2 
Diabetes Mellitus
The precise way in which genetic, environmental, and pathophysi­
ologic factors interact to lead to the clinical onset of T2D is com­
plex and may vary from individual to individual. The common 
forms of T2D are polygenic in nature and are caused by an inter­
action between these genes and multiple environmental factors 
(known and unknown), as well as epigenetic factors. Therefore, 
it is not surprising that the individual genes involved in the com­
mon polygenic forms of T2D have been difficult to identify and 
their contribution to disease development modest. The mono­
genic forms, although relatively uncommon, are important to rec­
ognize because they have led to important insights about normal 
physiology; if identified early, they may be important in selecting 
appropriate therapy (see Chapter 37). Several genes involved in 
monogenic forms have been identified and characterized.
Monogenic Forms of Diabetes Associated With Insulin 
Resistance
In the monogenic forms of diabetes, the gene involved is both 
necessary and sufficient to cause disease. In other words, envi­
ronmental factors play little or no role in determining whether 
a genetically predisposed person develops clinical diabetes, 
although there is often considerable variation in penetrance of dis­
ease among individuals with the same genetic defect. Monogenic 
forms of diabetes are usually diagnosed in younger patients, often 
in the first 2 to 3 decades of life; however, if only mild, asymptom­
atic elevations in blood glucose occur, the diagnosis may be missed 
until later in life. Indeed, in a recent study of individuals with 
presumed T1D for 50 years or more, genotyping revealed that 
almost 8% had a mutation consistent with a monogenic form of 
diabetes.16 Monogenic forms of diabetes can be divided into those 
in which the mechanism is a defect in insulin secretion and those 
that involve defective responses to insulin or insulin resistance. 
In this chapter, we will discuss the forms associated with insulin 
resistance.
Mutations in the Insulin Receptor. Numerous mutations have 
been identified in the insulin receptor gene. Although there is a spec­
trum of disorders, at least three distinct clinical syndromes caused 
by mutations in the insulin receptor gene have been described. Type 
A insulin resistance is defined by the presence of insulin resistance, 
acanthosis nigricans, and hyperandrogenism. Most often these 
patients are identified as adolescents or young adults, often based on 
the acanthosis nigricans and/or signs of hyperandrogenism, rather 
than by their disturbances in glucose metabolism, even though 
insulin resistance can be very severe and accompanied by marked 
hyperinsulinemia.17 Patients with Donohue syndrome (formerly 
called leprechaunism), on the other hand, have multiple early abnor­
malities, including severe intrauterine growth retardation, abnor­
mal facies leading to the name leprechaunism, and death within the 
first 1 to 2 years of life.18–20 Interestingly, these patients may also 
have episodes of fasting hypoglycemia despite their severe insulin 
resistance due to the very elevated insulin levels. The third variant,

Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome, is associated with short stature, pro­
tuberant abdomen, abnormalities of teeth and nails, and, in some 
patients, pineal hyperplasia.21
These mutations impair receptor function by different mecha­
nisms. The majority of mutations associated with type A insulin 
resistance are in the intracellular tyrosine kinase domain, whereas 
in Donohue and Rabson-Mendenhall syndromes the mutations 
are more frequently found in the extracellular domain, causing 
impairment in ligand binding, or the FnIII domains, which are 
key for receptor folding.22 As noted, the insulin resistance asso­
ciated with these insulin receptor mutations is usually severe, 
manifesting in the neonatal period (e.g., Donohue and Rabson-
Mendenhall syndromes), or it can occur in a milder form in 
adulthood, and is often easily detected biochemically by marked 
hyperinsulinemia and clinically by acanthosis nigricans often 
in the absence of obesity. Some individuals with insulin recep­
tor mutations are able to remain normoglycemic due to massive 
elevations of endogenous insulin secretion, whereas others have 
presented with hyperglycemia, which fails to respond to insulin 
therapy, sometimes in doses exceeding 10,000 U/day.17 
Lipodystrophic Diabetes. Lipodystrophic diabetes syn­
dromes can either be genetic or acquired, and they are character­
ized by severe insulin resistance associated with lipoatrophy (loss 
of fat) and/or lipodystrophy (loss and maldistribution of fat). 
Clinically, these patients present with decreases in subcutane­
ous fat, insulin resistance, and hypertriglyceridemia. The genetic 
forms can be divided into generalized lipodystrophies or partial 
lipodystrophies, but within each of these categories, mutations 
in many different genes have been identified. The gene muta­
tions that cause lipodystrophy control a variety of functions, 
including insulin signaling (AKT2, PIK3R1), caveolins (CAV1, 
PTRF), phospholipid biosynthesis (AGPAT2, PCYT1A), lipid 
droplet morphology (LMNA, BSCL2, ZMPSTE24), adipogen­
esis (CIDEC, PPARG), and lipolysis (LIPE, PLIN1).23 Depend­
ing on the gene mutation and the particular mutation within the 
gene, the associated syndrome may be confined to loss of fat and 
the associated metabolic abnormalities or may cause a syndrome 
with a wider array of phenotypes. For example, mutation in the 
lamin A gene (LMNA) can cause either the face-sparing famil­
ial partial lipodystrophy, commonly referred to as Dunningan 
syndrome, or, through a different mutation in the same gene, 
mandibuloacral dysplasia syndrome with partial lipodystrophy 
accompanied by postnatal growth retardation and craniofacial 
and skeletal malformations.24,25 The generalized lipodystro­
phies are quite rare but easily diagnosed by the marked loss of 
subcutaneous fat throughout the entire body. These syndromes 
cause severe metabolic abnormalities, including severe fatty liver 
disease, sometimes leading to ascites and esophageal varices. 
Generalized lipodystrophy is also associated with very low levels 
of the adipose tissue–derived hormones leptin and adiponec­
tin.26 Leptin-replacement therapy improves glycemic control, 
decreases fatty liver disease, and decreases circulating triglycer­
ide levels in patients with generalized lipodystrophy and leptin 
deficiency.27
In contrast, the partial lipodystrophies are frequently missed 
on routine examination, and thus the true incidence is unknown. 
The phenotypes of the partial lipodystrophies vary significantly by 
mutation and gender. Leptin levels may be in the normal range 
or slightly below the normal range.28 Diagnosis is made by clini­
cal phenotype, with genetic testing generally only performed in 
research settings. The majority of these patients do not respond to 
leptin-replacement therapy.23
Acquired generalized lipodystrophy (also known Seip-Lawrence 
syndrome) is a rare condition that may appear during childhood, 
adolescence, or young adulthood and is characterized by fat loss 
affecting large areas of the body, initially usually the face, arms, 
and legs. Acquired generalized lipodystrophy is thought to be an 
autoimmune disorder with secondary destruction of the adipose 
organ, but definitive proof of autoimmunity is lacking. 
Genetics of the Polygenic Forms of Type 2 Diabetes 
Mellitus
The common polygenic form of T2D has complex pathophysiol­
ogy, with genetic and environmental factors playing major roles. 
The phenotypic manifestations of the disease are also complex 
and include resistance to the action of insulin in muscle, fat, and 
liver and defects in insulin secretory responses from pancreatic β 
cells. Together these lead to reduced glucose uptake and increased 
hepatic glucose production. Although in many individuals there 
is a strong family history for T2D, the primary defect or defects 
responsible for the development of the syndrome remain elusive. 
Indeed, with over 700 genes linked to T2D,29 the role of these 
genes and the nature of the gene-environment interactions that 
are ultimately responsible for development of the disorder in pre­
disposed persons remain unknown.
Insulin resistance is present in persons predisposed to T2D 
long before the onset of hyperglycemia,30 suggesting that insulin 
resistance is at least one of the primary abnormalities in the devel­
opment of T2D. It has been argued that because some patients 
with severe insulin resistance can mount extreme hyperinsulin­
emic responses, it seems likely that an individual with develop­
ing T2D and less profound insulin resistance should also be able 
to do so, implying that defective β-cell function is also present 
before the onset of T2D, although the normal range of β-cell 
response to insulin resistance is difficult to define. Altered insu­
lin secretion has been reported in first-degree relatives of persons 
with T2D who have normal plasma glucose concentrations,15 
suggesting there may be an underlying β-cell defect in addition 
to insulin resistance, even in the prediabetic state.29 Therefore, 
although there is still controversy about whether insulin resistance 
or abnormal insulin secretion represents “the” primary defect in 
T2D, there is general consensus that both defects are present in 
most subjects with the disorder at clinical presentation.
Over the past decade, there have been dramatic advances in 
understanding the role of genes in T2D. Earlier genetic studies 
relied either on the candidate gene approach, in which the search 
for diabetes genes is dictated by the prevailing understanding of 
the pathways involved in glucose regulation, or on linkage stud­
ies, which involve identifying regions of chromosomal DNA that 
are shared to excess by affected family members. Although these 
approaches did allow identification of important diabetes genes, 
especially in monogenic forms of the disease, as discussed earlier, 
more recent studies have focused on the application of GWASs. 
These GWASs use an unbiased interrogation of the entire genome 
comparing cases and controls to determine which single-nucleotide 
polymorphisms (SNPs) are associated with disease. The location 
of the SNP can suggest associated genes in the region, but most 
SNPs are in noncoding intragenic regions, making the causative 
gene unclear. Some of the genes that have been implicated in the 
pathogenesis of T2D are depicted in Fig. 33.3. The following 
sections provide a brief summary of some of the genes that have 
strong evidence in the pathogenesis of T2D.
Insulin Receptor Substrate 1 Gene. The first polymorphism 
identified for T2D was Gly972Arg in insulin receptor substrate

1 (IRS-1), a key protein in the canonical insulin signaling path­
way. This common polymorphism was detected by direct sequenc­
ing of 86 patients with T2D and 76 controls, with three times as 
many cases present in cases than controls.31 Subsequent studies 
demonstrated that this polymorphism results in impaired insulin-
stimulated phosphatidylinositol 3–kinase signaling.32 As genomic 
information expanded, it became clear that this polymorphism 
plays a relatively minor role in overall T2D risk; however, this 
initial finding provided the first evidence of the genetic association 
with T2D. 
Transcription Factor 7–Like 2 Gene. Grant and colleagues33 
genotyped 228 microsatellite markers in Icelandic patients with 
T2D and in control subjects. A microsatellite, DG10S478, in 
intron 3 of the transcription factor 7–like 2 gene (TCF7L2; for­
merly TCF4) was associated with T2D. This was replicated in a 
Danish cohort and in a U.S. cohort. Compared with noncarri­
ers, heterozygous and homozygous carriers of the at-risk alleles 
(38% and 7% of the population, respectively) have relative risks 
of 1.45 and 2.41 for development of T2D. Follow-up studies 
showed that specific polymorphisms in TCF7L2 increase the risk 
of progression from impaired glucose tolerance to T2D, and 
this effect is associated with a reduction of glucose-stimulated 
insulin secretion.34 The TCF7L2 gene product is a high-mobility 
group box containing transcription factor previously implicated 
in colon cancer. In T2D it has been suggested to act through 
regulation of adipogenesis and proglucagon gene expression in 
enteroendocrine cells by affecting the Wnt signaling pathway.35 
Of the common variants that determine diabetes risk, variants 
at the TCF7L2 locus have the greatest impact, although, as with 
most GWAS-associated genes, the polymorphism is intronic, and 
how or if this affects expression or function of the TCF7L2 pro­
tein remains unknown. 
KATP Channel Genes: KCNJ11 and ABCC8. The β-cell KATP 
channel is composed of two subunits, Kir6.2 (KCNJ11) and 
SUR1 (ABCC8). Kir6.2 is the pore-forming component of the 
potassium channel, and SUR1 is the sulfonylurea receptor, which 
regulates opening of the channel. Opening of the channel results 
in potassium efflux from the β-cell, causing insulin secretion. 
Mutations in these genes are the most common cause of neona­
tal diabetes. Identification of these patients is important, because 
these forms of neonatal diabetes are generally treatable with sulfo­
nylureas rather than insulin.36 The two genes are located adjacent 
to each other on chromosome 11, and SNPs within both genes 
are associated with an increased risk of diabetes.37 A missense 
mutation Glu23Lys (E23K) in KCNJ11 has also been associated 
with increased risk of typical adult-onset T2D by an average 
of 13%, and the KK homozygote is at greatest risk (relative risk, 
1.28).38 One study suggests that, like neonatal diabetes caused by

Peroxisome Proliferator–Activated Receptor γ Gene. 
Peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ (PPARγ) is a member 
of the PPAR subfamily of nuclear receptors. It is an important 
regulator of lipid and glucose homeostasis and cellular differentia­
tion. Although PPARγ is most abundantly expressed in adipose 
tissue, it is also expressed in muscle and in the pancreatic β cell. 
Targeted elimination of PPARγ in muscle alters muscle fatty acid 
oxidation,40 and knockout in the β cell leads to a blunting of the 
normal increase in β-cell mass that occurs on a high-fat diet.41 
Meta-analyses show that a relatively common missense muta­
tion Pro12Ala (P12A) in PPARG (the gene encoding PPARγ2) 
is associated with decreased risk for T2D (estimated risk ratio 
for the alanine allele, 0.79).42 People homozygous for the non­
variant Pro12 allele are more insulin resistant and have a 1.25-
fold increased risk of diabetes than those with one Ala12 allele. 
A second polymorphism, C161 → T, has been linked to insulin 
resistance in Hispanic and non-Hispanic White women.43 Loss-
of-function mutations in PPARγ cause familial partial lipodys­
trophy type 3 (FPLD3), and these patients may show dramatic 
improvement when treated with the thiazolidinedione PPAR 
agonists.44 
Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor 4α Gene. Despite its name, hepa­
tocyte nuclear factor 4α (HNF4A) was the first discovered maturity-
onset diabetes of the young (MODY) gene, where it leads to 
abnormalities in insulin secretion.45 HNF4α is also active in the 
liver, where it is upregulated by an alternative promoter from 
the pancreas and is important for gluconeogenesis. Patients with 
the risk alleles have increased hepatic glucose production, not 
impaired insulin secretion, confirming the liver-specific impact of 
the polymorphisms in the alternative hepatic promoter.46 Several 
clinical studies have demonstrated that genetic variation in this 
liver-specific promoter for the HNF4A gene is associated with 
increased risk of T2D.46–49 
Kruppel-Like Factor 14 (KLF14). Kruppel-like factor 14 
(KLF14) is a maternally imprinted transcription factor. Non­
coding polymorphisms in the KLF14 gene are associated with 
increased fasting insulin, waist-to-hip ratio, and T2D.50,51 
Regulatory variants of KLF14 appear to influence T2D risk by 
causing a redistribution of fat from gynoid to visceral depots and 
increasing adipocyte size.50 Accompanying in vitro experiments 
demonstrated that these changes are mediated, in part, by an 
increase in preadipocyte proliferation, but impairment in lipogen­
esis. Due to maternal imprinting, these effects occur only when 
the polymorphism is inherited from mother to daughter. 
Diabetes Genes Identified by Genome-Wide Association 
Studies
GWASs continue to identify variants that determine genetic risk 
of T2D and to define the genetic architecture of the disease. Fig. 
33.3 depicts the intersection between loci associated at genome-
wide significance with T2D and five metabolic traits strongly 
associated with T2D (BMI, waist circumference, waist-to-hip 
ratio, fasting insulin, and fasting glucose). Note that there is sub­
stantial, but not complete, overlap in the loci significantly associ­
ated with these traits. For example, a variant in the gene CREBRF, 
found almost exclusively in the Samoan population, is associated 
with a large (1.4 kg/m2) increase in BMI per risk allele, while also 
associated with a paradoxical decrease in odds ratio of 0.6 for the 
development of T2D.52 The mechanisms driving the increase in 
BMI yet protection from T2D are still to be elucidated but sug­
gest that the increase in adipose tissue is confined to metabolically 
healthy subcutaneous tissues rather than proinflammatory visceral 
adipose tissue.
Based on these advances, the following general comments can 
be made regarding the genetics of T2D:
	1.	 The genes identified to date individually lead to a modest 
increase in the risk of diabetes. Persons with these individual 
polymorphisms have odds ratios between 1.10 and 1.45 when 
compared with individuals who do not have the at-risk poly­
morphisms.
	2.	 The presence of multiple at-risk polymorphisms in a single 
individual substantially increases the risk of developing diabe­
tes and has led to development of genetic risk scores that are 
composed of multiple gene variants.
	3.	 Although early GWASs suggested a substantial proportion of 
the genetic variants associated with increased risk for diabetes 
were in genes that might alter insulin secretion, in more recent 
studies the number of SNPs associated with decreased insulin 
sensitivity have increased, and at least some of these effects on 
insulin sensitivity appear to be independent of obesity.50,53,54
	4.	 The majority of the SNPs associated with risk of T2D appear 
to reside in noncoding regions of DNA. Some of these allelic 
variations exist in open chromatin regions alternatively called 
stretch enhancers,55 which appear to be bound by proteins. 
Stretch enhancers across the genome are cell type specific and 
are located near and associated with increased expression of 
genes involved in cell specification, as opposed to housekeep­
ing processes.
	5.	 A large number of genes are associated with increased suscep­
tibility to this disease. Whereas the total number of loci linked 
to T2D is large, they account for a small proportion (estimated 
at no more than 10%) of the total heritable risk for diabetes 
in the population. In the search for this missing heritability 
increasing attention is being given to the rare variant hypoth­
esis, which states that common diseases are due to multiple, 
but rare, variants with large effects. Alternatively, there is new 
evidence that T2D can be divided into multiple phenotypic 
subgroups with distinct genetic signatures that were difficult 
to identify when all of these subtypes were grouped together in 
previous studies.56,57 Finally, the high familial risk of T2D may 
be due to some element of shared environment or epigenetic 
effects (see the following discussion) or perhaps to some aspect 
of these polygenes that affects genetic architecture. 
Epigenetic Risk of Diabetes
In addition to variations in the sequence of genes conferring risk of 
T2D, epigenetic marks, which influence the expression of genes, 
can also influence disease risk. Detrimental epigenetic marks can 
be created in the developing fetus by both overnutrition and 
undernutrition.58,59 The idea that perinatal nutrition could influ­
ence the risk for obesity in offspring came from the observation of 
children born of pregnancies during the Dutch Hunger Winter, 
a period of starvation in the Netherlands during World War II. 
During this period, all Dutch citizens, including pregnant moth­
ers, were restricted to as little as 400 to 800 calories per day. It was 
subsequently noted that the offspring of these pregnancies were 
more likely to become obese than same-sex siblings conceived dur­
ing normal food availability. This is attributed to epigenetic marks 
that persisted 60 years beyond the neonatal exposure.60 Evidence 
of the same phenomenon has been documented following several 
1332
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
other famines around the world. These human observations have 
since been replicated in mouse models of undernutrition, which 
not only demonstrate the passage of obesity risk from mother 
to offspring but that risk can be perpetuated for an additional 
generation by male offspring of undernourished mothers due to 
epigenetic changes to primordial sperm.61 Similar to undernutri­
tion, evidence also exists that overnutrition during pregnancy can 
cause epigenetic changes that predispose offspring to obesity and 
T2D for multiple generations.62,63 Recent studies indicate that 
the effects of environmental exposure may also be passed from 
fathers to their offspring.64 Exactly how these affect T2D and the 
exact mechanisms involved are still unknown but are active areas 
of investigation. 
Insulin Signaling
Insulin signaling is initiated through binding and activation of 
its tyrosine kinase cell surface receptor. This initiates a cascade 
of phosphorylation and dephosphorylation events, generation of 
second messengers, and protein-protein interactions that result in 
diverse metabolic events in almost every tissue. Insulin receptors 
are ubiquitously expressed, yet insulin action is highly tissue spe­
cific due to the varied composition of downstream targets of insu­
lin signaling. The insulin receptor consists of two insulin-binding 
α-subunits and two catalytically active β-subunits. Like insulin 
itself, the α- and β-subunits are derived from a single chain precur­
sor or prereceptor. Once the subunits are formed, they are linked 
via disulfide bonds into an α2β2 heterotetrameric complex. Insulin 
binds to the extracellular α-subunits, activating the intracellular 
tyrosine kinase domains of the β-subunits that then phosphorylate 
intracellular partners on specific tyrosine residues.65 Cryoelectron 
microscopy images of insulin receptors reveal a conformational 
change of the extracellular domain from an inverted V shape to a 
T shape after ligand binding.66–68 This brings the transmembrane 
and intracellular tyrosine kinase domains of the receptor closer 
together, allowing for transphosphorylation and receptor activa­
tion (Fig 33.4). On phosphorylation of the receptor, multiple 
classes of adapter proteins, including insulin receptor substrates 
(IRSs), Src homology 2 domain containing (Shc), growth factor 
receptor–bound protein (Grb), and others,69 can associate with 
the receptor and propagate the downstream signal resulting in 
modulation of cellular metabolism, stimulation of mitogenesis,70 
and receptor internalization.71
Downstream Events After Insulin Receptor 
Phosphorylation
Insulin receptor substrates (IRSs), phosphoinositide 3-kinase 
(PI3K), and AKT (also known as protein kinase B) represent three 
critical nodes of insulin signaling that regulate a majority of the 
metabolic and transcriptional effects downstream of insulin acti­
vation (see Fig. 33.4). The IRS proteins serve as both substrates 
and adaptor proteins that mediate many of the key metabolic 
actions of insulin across multiple tissues. IRS proteins have 
multiple functional domains—including pleckstrin homology 
(PH), phosphotyrosine binding (PTB), and Src homology (SH) 
domains that allow for interaction with phosphorylated tyrosine 
residues on the insulin receptor and the closely related insulin-
like growth factor 1 (IGF1) receptor and multiple tyrosine phos­
phorylation sites allowing for docking with downstream effectors, 
such as PI3K.72 There are four IRS isoforms (IRS1–IRS4), with 
IRS1 and IRS2 being ubiquitously expressed. Although there is 
evidence for functional overlap, IRS1 and IRS2 do display unique 
roles in growth and metabolism across tissues. Disruption of IRS1 
in mice results in mild insulin resistance and growth retardation, 
whereas disruption of IRS2 results in β-cell failure and secondary 
insulin resistance.73
Phosphorylated IRS proteins then bind to and activate PI3K, 
which in turn generates phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-triphosphate 
(PIP3) that activates several PIP3-dependent serine-threonine 
kinases, such as PI-dependent protein kinases 1 and 2 (PDPK1 
and PDPK2), which in turn activate AKT isoforms, atypical 
PKCs, wortmannin-sensitive and insulin-stimulated serine kinase, 
and others.
AKT kinase exists as three distinct isoforms.74,75 Full activa­
tion of AKT requires phosphorylation on specific threonine and 
serine residues, including PDPK1-directed phosphorylation at 
threonine 308 (T308) in the kinase domain (KD) followed by 
phosphorylation at serine 473 (S473) in the hydrophobic motif 
(HM) of AKT by the rictor-containing complex, mTOR complex 
2 (mTORC2).75 Activated AKT has the ability to phosphorylate 
proteins that regulate lipid synthesis, glycogen synthesis, protein 
synthesis, and apoptosis. Disruption of AKT1 results in growth 
retardation,76 whereas disruption of AKT2 results in insulin resis­
tance and diabetes in mice.77 Several investigators have examined 
the role of PI3K and AKT in persons with insulin resistance. Stud­
ies have shown a decrease in IRS-associated PI3K78 and AKT79 
activity in insulin-resistant skeletal muscle; however, in some 
patients with reduced PI3K activity, there was normal activation 
of AKT.80
Forkhead box O (FOXO) transcription factors are targets of 
AKT that have emerged as critical regulators of insulin action in 
metabolic tissues. AKT phosphorylates three sites on FOXOs, 
leading to nuclear exclusion and thus reduces its action on gene 
transcription.81–84 In the liver, FOXOs contribute to glucose pro­
duction by transcriptional upregulation of glucose-6 phosphory­
lase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK),85 and also 
bind with corepressor Sin3a to repress glycogen synthase kinase.86 
In muscle, FOXO deletion rescues the muscle atrophy from strep­
tozotocin diabetes and from combined deletion of insulin recep­
tors/IGF1 receptors.87 As a result, deletion of FOXOs in metabolic 
tissues fully or partially rescues many of the detrimental effects of 
insulin deficiency in T1D and T2D.88–91 
Tissue-Specific Actions of Insulin
Mechanisms of Insulin-Mediated Glucose Uptake in 
Muscle and Fat
A primary effect of insulin in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue is 
to stimulate glucose uptake by translocation of glucose transporter 
type 4 (GLUT4) from an intracellular pool to the surface of cells 
(Fig 33.5A).92 Indeed, disruption of GLUT4 in muscle or adipose 
tissue causes an insulin resistant phenotype.93,94 AKT substrate 
of 160 kDa (AS160, also known as TBC1D4) and TBC1D1 are 
paralog Rab family guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase)–activating 
(Rab GAP) proteins that have been proposed to inhibit the trans­
location of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane through interaction 
with insulin-responsive aminopeptidase (IRAP).95 AS160 activity 
is suppressed by AKT phosphorylation in response to insulin stim­
ulation and mediates translocation of GLUT4-containing vesicles 
to the plasma membrane to increase glucose uptake in muscle and 
adipose tissue.95,96 TBC1D1, however, is also phosphorylated by 
adenosine monophosphate–activated kinase (AMPK), and that 
appears to play a key role in exercise-regulated increases in muscle 
1333
CHAPTER 33  Pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
glucose uptake, which remain intact in patients with T2D.97–99 
Upon phosphorylation of the Rab GAPs, the inhibition of 
GLUT4 translocation by AS160 and/or TBC1D1 is relieved, 
contributing to the increased glucose uptake. Although the com­
position and signaling pathways that converge on the intracellular 
GLUT4-containing vesicles to cause GLUT4 translocation are 
still not fully understood, it appears that the number of glucose 
transporters in skeletal muscle of insulin-resistant persons is not 
changed, but the ability of insulin to effect GLUT4 translocation 
is disrupted.100–102 In adipose tissue, PI3K-independent mecha­
nisms also mediate glucose uptake. Insulin receptors can associate 
with Cbl-associated protein (CAP) and the E3 ubiquitin-protein 
ligase Cbl to activate TC10, an actin remodeling enzyme,103 con­
tributing to GLUT4 vesicle translocation. A similar mechanism of 
actin remodeling to regulate GLUT4 trafficking occurs in skeletal 
muscle, but this is via Rac proteins.104 
Proteostasis
In addition to its regulation of glucose metabolism, insulin also 
has profound effects on protein homeostasis (proteostasis).105 
In muscle, insulin promotes hypertrophy by both enhancing 
protein synthesis and suppressing protein degradation pathways 
including proteasome and autophagy (see Fig 33.5A). Insulin, 
via Akt, activates mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) to promote 
protein synthesis and cellular growth.106 At the same time, 
insulin suppresses activation of FoxO transcription factors, key 
regulators of protein degradation pathways.105,107 Mouse models 
with muscle-specific deletion of insulin receptor, or both insulin 
receptor and IGF1 receptor, show profound muscle atrophy,108 
but this atrophy is completely rescued by deletion of FOXOs.87 
This increased protein degradation is also seen in rodent mod­
els of T1D109 and in patients with T1D when insulin is with­
drawn for as little as 8 hours.110,111 Thus, insulin coordinates

Insulin Regulation of Lipolysis and Lipogenesis
Insulin plays a critical role in regulating lipid storage. The liver is 
the primary site for de novo lipogenesis of fatty acids and triglyc­
erides, whereas adipose tissue serves as the primary storage depot 
for triglycerides. Insulin signaling enhances lipid storage in adipose 
by both stimulating triglyceride synthesis and suppressing lipolytic 
triglyceride breakdown (Fig 33.5B). Insulin stimulates rapid and 
potent increases in adipose tissue glucose uptake, which is then con­
verted into glycerol-3-phosphate and used to synthesize triglycerides 
from fatty acids. Fatty acid transport into adipose is also increased 
by insulin, which involves translocation of fatty acid transporters, 
including FATP1 and cluster of differentiation 36 (CD36),112 and/
or increases in lipoprotein lipase expression and activity.113–115 In 
addition to providing substrates for triglyceride synthesis, glucose 
also activates carbohydrate response element–binding proteins to 
upregulate glycolytic and lipogenic genes in adipocytes.116 This 
pathway to enhance lipid storage is critical for metabolic homeosta­
sis, as overexpression of GLUT4 in adipose protects against insulin 
resistance caused by diet-induced obesity, but deletion of carbohy­
drate response element–binding protein prevents this effect.116,117
Insulin potently suppresses adipose tissue lipolysis, which, when 
combined with the enhanced lipid uptake in adipose, can signifi­
cantly reduce circulating fatty acid content.118 Insulin regulates 
lipolysis at multiple levels (see Fig 33.5B). β-Adrenergic signaling 
enhances cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)–induced pro­
tein kinase A activation, which in turn activates two of the prin­
cipal lipases in fat cells: adipose tissue triglyceride lipase (ATGL) 
and hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL). Insulin activates phospho­
diesterase 3B, which reduces cAMP levels and inhibits protein 
kinase A–mediated activation of ATGL and hormone-sensitive 
lipase.119,120 Two further mechanisms by which insulin suppresses 
lipolysis are by decreases in ATGL mRNA and by increased expres­
sion of fat-specific protein 27 (FSP27), a lipid droplet stabilizing 
protein.121–123 These actions of insulin to suppress lipolysis are 
clinically important in T1D, because individuals with uncon­
trolled T1D have unsuppressed lipolysis and oxidation of free 
fatty acids resulting in increased ketone body production, whereas 
newly diagnosed and treated T1D patients show a rapid gain of fat 
during the first year of insulin therapy.124,125
Regulation of fat distribution by insulin is also important in 
metabolic health. GWASs have found strong associations between 
reduced adiposity in peripheral compartments, severe insulin 
resistance, and SNPs in 53 genes, among which insulin receptor 
(INSR), IRS1, and a regulatory subunit of PI3K (PIK3R1) were 
identified.126 The 53 genes also correlated highly with familial 
partial lipodystrophy type 1 (FPLD1). These studies are consistent 
with data from rodent models that indicate deletion of insulin 
receptors in adipocytes leads to rapid decreases in adipose tissue 
mass, redistribution of body fat to liver, and lipodystrophic dia­
betes.127–129 Thus, insulin regulation of lipolysis and lipogenesis 
in adipose plays a critical role in storage of lipids, maintaining 
whole-body insulin sensitivity, and preventing metabolic disease.
Insulin also regulates hepatic lipogenesis, the primary site of 
de novo lipogenesis in the body.118 Sterol regulatory element-
binding protein (SREBP) transcription factors are master regula­
tors of lipogenic genes including fatty acid synthase, lipoprotein 
lipase, acetyl coenzyme A carboxylase (ACC), and stearoyl coen­
zyme A (CoA) desaturase isoforms, and are regulated by insulin 
at multiple levels in liver (see Fig. 33.5C). Through activation of 
atypical PKC isoforms λ/ζ (aPKC), expression of sterol regulatory 
element–binding transcription factor 1c (SREBP1-c) is increased 
by insulin in liver.130,131 Furthermore, SREBP1-c requires pro­
teolytic cleavage to enter the nucleus and activate transcription 
of lipogenic genes. This processing of SREBP1-c is regulated by 
mTORC1 signaling downstream of the IRS-PI3K-Akt path­
way,132 and mTORC1 activation can also promote mRNA stabil­
ity of SREBP1 target genes.133 Studies in mice and humans with 
insulin receptor mutations show that reduced insulin signaling in 
liver protects against hepatic steatosis.134,135 However, patients 
with T2D and metabolic syndrome, who have muscle and adi­
pose insulin resistance, have a paradoxical upregulation of hepatic 
lipogenesis and dyslipidemia, which is occurring in the context of 
altered central nervous system signaling to the liver and increased 
nutrient supply. Although the exact mechanisms have not been 
elucidated, the upregulation of hepatic lipogenesis in insulin resis­
tant states is likely due to pathway selective postreceptor insulin 
resistance134–136 and/or a combination of insulin resistance with 
altered substrate supply and extrahepatic signaling.137–139 
Insulin Regulation of Hepatic Carbohydrate Metabolism
The production of glucose by the liver is regulated primarily by 
a balance between the actions of insulin to suppress glucose pro­
duction and glucagon to activate glucose production, with insulin 
being dominant over glucagon (see Fig. 33.5C). The sympathetic 
nervous system140 and glucose autoregulation also play roles in 
hepatic glucose production, but are probably less important.141 
The ability of insulin to reduce hepatic glucose output is an 
important mechanism for maintaining normal fasting blood glu­
cose and normal glucose tolerance.142,143 Insulin also suppresses 
glucose release from the liver by inhibiting glycogenolysis.144 As 
with gluconeogenesis, the effect of insulin to suppress hepatic 
glycogenolysis is dominant over glucagon.145 Glucagon increases 
glycogenolysis by activation of the protein kinase A cascade with 
increases in cAMP and also increases in gluconeogenesis, in part 
by increasing transcription of PEPCK by means of cAMP response 
element–binding protein (CREB).143,146
The regulatory mechanisms triggered by cAMP are complex, 
with the CREB transcriptional coactivator, TORC2, playing 
an important role. TORC2 is specifically dephosphorylated in 
response to cAMP; this results in translocation of the TORC2 pro­
tein to the nucleus, allowing activation of CREB-dependent tran­
scription of gluconeogenic enzymes.147 In addition, CREB may 
increase transcription of PPARγ coactivator 1α (PGC1A), which 
serves as a critical coactivator of the transcription factor forkhead 
box protein O1 (FOXO1). FOXO1 plays a role in the transcrip­
tional activation of various genes associated with gluconeogenesis, 
including PEPCK and glucose-6-phosphorylase.146 Indeed, dele­
tion of FOXO isoforms in liver can restore glucose levels to nor­
mal in mice with insulin receptor knockout.88,148 Deacetylation of 
transcription factors and coactivators can also regulate gluconeo­
genesis. The sirtuin, SIRT1, deacetylates PGC1A149 and histone 
deacetylases and sirtuins can deacetylate FOXOs,150,151 increas­
ing their nuclear localization and interaction with HNF4A. The 
PGC1A/FOXO1/HNF4A complex is a potent activator of gluco­
neogenic gene transcription.146
Insulin decreases endogenous glucose production by direct and 
indirect mechanisms.152 In its direct action, portal insulin sup­
presses glucose production by inhibiting glycogenolysis and glu­
coneogenesis by insulin receptor activation (see Fig. 33.5C). The 
indirect or peripheral effect of insulin in controlling glucose pro­
duction by the liver is twofold. First, insulin profoundly decreases 
1336
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
glucagon secretion by pancreatic alpha cells through systemic 
and paracrine effects.153,154 The decrease in glucagon secretion 
decreases the activation of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. 
The second important peripheral action of insulin is to decrease 
substrates for gluconeogenesis, such as alanine from muscle pro­
tein degradation,105 and glycerol and free fatty acid levels by sup­
pressing lipolysis in adipose tissue155 (see Fig. 33.5A,B). When the 
reduction in plasma fatty acids during a hyperinsulinemic clamp 
is prevented by infusion of triglyceride emulsions with heparin 
(which produces increased fatty acid levels through activation 
of lipoprotein lipase), insulin-mediated suppression of hepatic 
glucose output is reduced.156 The suppression of glucagon secre­
tion and the decrease in gluconeogenic substrate delivery to the 
liver are additive in reducing liver glucose production.157
Clinically, hepatic insulin resistance plays a very important 
role in the fasting hyperglycemia of T2D,158,159 and the impaired 
suppression of hepatic glucose output appears to be quantita­
tively similar to, or even larger than, the defect in stimulation of 
peripheral glucose disposal.160 Defects in the direct effect of insu­
lin to suppress hepatic glucose production in humans appear to 
be caused by a large rightward shift in the steep dose-response 
curve for insulin’s inhibition of glycogenolysis.161 There is a direct 
relationship between increased hepatic glucose output and fast­
ing hyperglycemia162 (Fig. 33.6). Insulin-mediated suppression of 
hepatic glucose output is impaired at both low and high plasma 
insulin levels in T2D160,163; hepatic glucose production is elevated 
early in the course of the disease,164,165 but may be normal in 
leaner, relatively insulin-sensitive T2D.166 Treatment of patients 
with metformin, which suppresses hepatic glucose production, 
results in improved glucose tolerance.165 
Expanding Collection of Insulin-Sensitive Tissues
Although much of our understanding of insulin action on metab­
olism involves the insulin-sensitive metabolic tissues of muscle, 
liver, and adipose, insulin receptors are ubiquitously expressed, 
and insulin action on other “nonclassic” tissues plays an impor­
tant role in health (Fig. 33.7). Insulin signaling in β cells is critical 
for adaptive survival and proliferation of these cells. Insulin secre­
tion and β-cell mass both increase in response to chronic mild 
hyperglycemia, and the ability to upregulate β-cell mass influences 
the development of T2D. Interestingly, when insulin receptors 
are deleted from β cells, first-phase insulin secretion is lost and 
compensatory growth of β cells is impaired in response to diet-
induced obesity and hepatic insulin resistance,167,168 indicating 
an unexpected autocrine loop. Furthermore, FOXO transcription

factors, which are downstream targets of insulin action, are impor­

appear to de-differentiate when FOXOs are deleted.170 Evidence 
that β-cell de-differentiation occurs in insulin resistant states and 
T2D in humans is emerging,171 but the degree to which this phe­
nomenon accounts for β-cell failure in T2D and whether this 
process can be intervened upon is still under investigation. The 
fact that the β cell is insulin responsive also raises the question 
as to how much the insulin resistance of T2D may itself directly 
affect β-cell function.
Insulin action on glucagon-producing α cells suppresses glu­
cagon secretion and maintains glucose homeostasis. This was 
demonstrated by deletion of insulin receptors on α cells of mice, 
which leads to mild glucose intolerance, increased glucagon secre­
tion, and progressive hyperinsulinemia,154 all of which are features 
of metabolic syndrome and T2D. Thus, insulin signaling on α 
and β cells in islets is important for metabolic health and glucose 
homeostasis.
Vascular complications are a major contributor to morbid­
ity and mortality in diabetes. Although originally thought to be 
insulin insensitive, it is now clear that vascular endothelium and 
cardiomyocytes are indeed insulin responsive. In endothelial cells, 
insulin action promotes vasodilation via nitric oxide production, 
which is impaired in insulin resistant states.172–174 Endothelial 
insulin sensitivity is also important for transendothelial transport 
of insulin, at least to some peripheral tissues,175,176 although how 
important this mechanism is in different tissues, such as skeletal 
muscle,177 liver, and different brain regions,178,179 may vary con­
siderably depending both on the density of insulin receptors and 
the extent of capillary fenestration. The relative permeability of 
the endothelial barrier in various tissues plays an important role in 
timing of insulin action in those tissues after a bolus of insulin.180 
Endothelial insulin signaling also plays a major role in the devel­
opment of atherosclerosis. Insulin receptor knockout in endothe­
lial cells caused a twofold to threefold increase in atherosclerotic 
lesions in an atherogenic mouse model.181 Conversely, enhancing 
downstream activation of insulin signaling by either overexpres­
sion of IRS or inhibition of FOXOs improves vascular endothelial 
function and can prevent atherosclerosis.182,183 In cardiomyo­
cytes, the insulin signaling cascade controls growth and metab­
olism in both physiologic and pathologic conditions.184,185 The 
heart has a remarkable ability to use a wide variety of substrates for 
energy production, but under fasted states, fatty acids are prefer­
entially metabolized. Upon insulin stimulation, glucose oxidation 
is increased and fatty acid oxidation is suppressed, but in insu­
lin resistant or diabetic states, this metabolic flexibility is lost.186 
Insulin also plays an important role in postnatal cardiac growth by 
suppression of autophagy.187 These signals in the cardiovascular 
system integrate with insulin action in other tissues and metabolic 
flux to coordinate cardiovascular health. Disruption of the tissue 
crosstalk during obesity and insulin resistance results in features 
of the metabolic syndrome, which increase cardiovascular risk.188
Insulin can also affect cardiovascular risk by its action on 
immune cells, particularly macrophages. Macrophages play an 
important role in the development of atherosclerosis by formation 
of foam cells within atherosclerotic plaques, enhanced inflamma­
tion, and apoptosis leading to a necrotic core that is susceptible to 
rupture.189 Mouse models with loss of insulin signaling in mac­
rophages show mild protective effects on atherosclerotic lesion 
size190 but also show worsening of the necrotic core, likely due 
to enhanced macrophage apoptosis from endoplasmic reticulum 
(ER) stress.191 This observation also extends to obesity and aging 
models of atherosclerosis,192,193 indicating that insulin resistance 
in macrophages contributes to plaque progression in the context 
of metabolic syndrome.194
Insulin Signaling in the Central Nervous System. Although 
previously considered insulin independent, it is now clear that the 
brain is an important site for insulin signaling. Although insulin 
action is not required for glucose uptake in most regions of the 
brain, because it predominantly expresses the insulin-independent 
glucose transporters GLUT1 and GLUT3, the insulin receptor is 
expressed throughout the brain. Brain-specific knockout of the 
receptor in mice results in a variety of abnormalities, including 
increased body weight, hypothalamic hypogonadism, increased 
hepatic glucose production, and a depression-like phenotype.195 
In clinical studies, brain insulin resistance correlates with visceral 
adipose tissue, and those with less brain insulin resistance have 
better responses to lifestyle interventions.196 The impact of insu­
lin signaling in the brain is cell-type specific. Although neuronal 
insulin receptor appears to be key for regulation of hepatic glucose 
production,197 astrocyte insulin receptor signaling, which plays 
an important role in ATP secretion, is vital for insulin-mediated 
effects on mood.198 Activation of the brain insulin receptor can 
lead to improved synaptic transmission through cholesterol syn­
thesis; proliferation through mitogen-activated protein kinase; 
axon growth and neuroplasticity through glycogen synthase kinase 
3β (GSK3B); gene transcription and neuronal polarity through 
FOXO; and autophagy, protein synthesis, and neuronal plastic­
ity through mTORC1.199,200 Insulin entry into the brain shows 
regional differences and in some areas is dependent on a receptor-
mediated transcytosis process.180,201 In the hypothalamus, insu­
lin receptors in specialized cells called tanycytes appears to gate 
hypothalamic insulin uptake and regulation of agouti-related 
protein (AgRP) neuron activity and appetite.202 Systemic insulin 
resistance results in lower than expected cerebrospinal fluid insulin 
levels due to decreased transport across the blood-brain barrier.203 
Brain-specific resistance to both insulin and IGF1 signaling in 
humans is associated with Alzheimer disease, but the significance 
of these findings to disease progression is still uncertain.204
The insulin receptor has two isoforms: IR-A is missing exon 11, 
whereas IR-B includes exon 11. Isoform A has a higher affinity for 
insulin-like growth factor 2 binding than isoform B. In contrast to 
most other tissues in the body, the brain predominantly expresses 
isoform A. Other unique aspects of brain insulin signaling include 
a unique glycosylation pattern of the brain IR and the propensity 
for IR to form heterodimers with the more abundant insulin-like 
growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R), which appears to favor IGF1 
signaling over insulin signaling.205 Greater understanding of the 
relative impacts of insulin and IGF1 signaling on the various cell 
types of the brain may prove critical as clinical trials are underway 
testing the efficacy of insulin delivered to the brain intranasally to 
treat such diverse disorders as Alzheimer disease, depression, and 
obesity.206 
Insulin Resistance and the Risk of Type 2 
Diabetes Mellitus
Insulin Resistance
The term insulin resistance indicates the presence of an impaired 
biologic response to either exogenously administered or endog­
enously secreted insulin. Insulin resistance is primarily manifested 
by decreased insulin-stimulated glucose transport and metabolism 
1338
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
in skeletal muscle, impaired insulin suppression of adipocyte 
lipolysis, and impaired ability of insulin to suppress hepatic glu­
cose output. However, given the pleiotropic actions of insulin, it 
is clear that insulin resistance could lead to disorders of multiple 
organ systems and metabolic pathways involving amino acids, glu­
cose, and lipid metabolism.
Insulin resistance can be measured using a variety of tech­
niques. The gold standard for determining insulin sensitivity/resis­
tance in an individual is a hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp. 
In this technique, a patient is given a constant infusion of insulin 
to produce hyperinsulinemia. A second infusion containing glu­
cose is given concurrently and adjusted to produce euglycemia. 
Because the individual is in steady state, the glucose infusion rate 
represents the rate of glucose uptake/disposal into muscle, fat, 
and other tissues under hyperinsulinemic conditions—that is, the 
insulin sensitivity of the patient.207 When conducted with tracers, 
one can also measure the hepatic glucose production rate, as a 
measure of liver insulin sensitivity. Because this technique is costly, 
somewhat invasive, and time consuming, alternative approaches 
have been developed to estimate insulin resistance, such as the 
steady-state plasma glucose (SSPG) method of Reaven208 or the 
Bergman minimal model of glucose disposal assessed using a fre­
quently sampled intravenous glucose tolerance test.209 When cou­
pled with insulin levels, one can also obtain the Disposition Index, 
which is a combined measure of insulin sensitivity and insulin 
secretion.210,211 For large cohort studies or a simple measure in an 
outpatient setting, homeostatic model assessment of insulin resis­
tance (HOMA-IR) can be calculated using just fasting glucose 
and insulin levels. HOMA-IR correlates favorably with insulin 
resistance estimated from the hyperinsulinemic euglycemic clamp 
with an Rs of 0.88.212 Others favor the use of the quantitative 
insulin sensitivity check index (QUICKI) as an alternative math­
ematical model, but associations are similar albeit inverse as it is 
based on the reciprocal of the logarithm of HOMA-IR.213
Insulin sensitivity is influenced by a large number of factors, 
including age, weight, ethnicity, body fat (especially intraabdomi­
nal obesity), physical activity, dietary intake, gut microbiota, and 
medications. Substantial data indicate that insulin resistance plays 
a major role in the development of impaired glucose tolerance 
and diabetes. Insulin resistance is a consistent finding in patients 
with T2D, and resistance is present years before the onset of dia­
betes.214–217 Prospective studies have shown that insulin resistance 
precedes and predicts the onset of diabetes.215,216 There is also 
a strong influence of environmental factors on the genetic pre­
disposition to insulin resistance and therefore to diabetes.218,219 
Although there is a general correlation between the level of insulin 
resistance and obesity, it is important to note that the range of 
variation is very large, such that even in individuals with BMI 
above 25 or 30 kg/m2, some individuals remain insulin sensitive, 
while more are insulin resistant.
The molecular mechanisms of insulin resistance are initi­
ated by various pathophysiologic processes that feed back on the 
insulin receptor and its adapter proteins (Fig. 33.8). The insulin 
receptor β-subunit has been shown to undergo serine/threonine 
phosphorylation, which might decrease the ability of the recep­
tor to autophosphorylate. The activities of a number of serine/
threonine protein kinases that catalyze inhibitory phosphoryla­
tion of the insulin receptor or IRS proteins are elevated in animal 
models of insulin resistance and in insulin-resistant humans.220,221 
Interventions that decrease serine phosphorylation (inhibitory sig­
nal) of the insulin receptor result in increased insulin signaling.222 
Furthermore, enhanced tyrosine dephosphorylation by protein 
tyrosine phosphatases can attenuate insulin signaling. Two protein 
tyrosine phosphatases that have been shown to negatively regu­
late insulin signaling, protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) 
and leukocyte antigen–related (LAR), have been reported to be 
elevated in insulin-resistant patients.223,224 Conversely, disruption 
of PTP1B in mice results in a marked increase in insulin sensitiv­
ity and resistance to diet-induced obesity.225 Recent studies using 
iPS cells of patients with T2D differentiated in vitro to mus­
cle have multiple alterations in insulin signaling, indicating cell 
autonomous as well as extrinsic factors in the insulin resistance 
of T2D.226
As mentioned previously, mutations in the insulin receptor are 
associated with rare forms of insulin resistance. In addition, indi­
viduals may develop autoantibodies to the insulin receptor, which 
induce severe insulin resistance often requiring thousands of units 
of insulin per day (type B insulin resistance and acanthosis nigri­
cans).17,227 The latter can sometimes be treated successfully with 
combined immunotherapy.228 
Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
The association of obesity with T2D has been recognized for 
decades (Fig. 33.9). Central (also referred to as intraabdominal or 
visceral) adiposity is more strongly linked to insulin resistance and 
to a number of important metabolic variables, including increased 
ectopic fat in liver and muscle, elevated plasma glucose, insu­
lin, total plasma cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations, and 
decreased plasma high-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentra­
tion, than is total adiposity.229–235 Indeed, some studies suggest 
subcutaneous fat may actually be protective against insulin resis­
tance.236 As a result, the association between abdominal fat and 
glucose tolerance is independent of total adiposity.237,238 The rea­
son for the relationship between intraabdominal fat and abnormal 
metabolism is not clearly defined, but a number of hypotheses have 
been proposed and may interact in this association. Abdominal fat 
is more lipolytically active than subcutaneous fat, perhaps because 
of its greater complement of adrenergic receptors.239 In addition, 
the abdominal adipose store is resistant to the antilipolytic effects 
of insulin,240 including alterations in lipoprotein lipase activity; 
this leads to increased lipase activity and a greater flux of fatty 
acids into the circulation, with the portal circulation receiving the 
greatest fatty acid load. Conversely, subcutaneous fat makes and 
releases more adiponectin, a beneficial adipokine. Finally, the high 
levels of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (HSD11B1) 
in intraabdominal fat could result in enhanced conversion of inac­
tive cortisone to active cortisol, resulting in increased local cortisol 
production. This might change adipocytes to increase lipolysis and 
alter the production of adipokines, which may directly modulate 
glucose metabolism. Adipose tissue has also been shown to secrete 
extracellular vesicles called exosomes, which may be taken up and 
regulate gene expression in other tissues, also contributing to insu­
lin resistance.241 
Hyperinsulinemia and Insulin Resistance
Hyperinsulinemia itself can cause insulin resistance. Elevated 
concentrations of insulin downregulate insulin receptors and 
desensitize postreceptor pathways.242 Del Prato and associates 
showed that 24 and 72 hours of sustained physiologic hyperin­
sulinemia in normal persons specifically inhibited the ability of 
insulin to increase nonoxidative glucose disposal in association 
with an impaired ability of insulin to stimulate glycogen synthase 
1339
CHAPTER 33  Pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
activity.243 Suppression of insulin secretion in obese, insulin-resis­
tant persons results in increased insulin sensitivity.244,245
In cell systems, serine phosphorylation of IRS proteins inhib­
its insulin signaling and is mediated by a variety of kinases (see 
Fig. 33.8), including mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR)/
S6 kinase (S6K), which is downstream of the PI3K-Akt pathway. 
Feedback serine phosphorylation of IRSs on appropriate residues 
might increase ubiquitination and degradation IRS isoforms, 
which would result in decreased insulin signaling.246 However, the 
mechanisms appear much more complex in vivo, because a mouse 
model with a serine to alanine mutation at 302 on IRS1, the prime 
target of mTOR-induced disruption of IRS signaling, did not pre­
vent insulin resistance from mTOR activation in the liver.247 Sig­
naling via mTOR can also increase growth factor receptor–bound 
protein 10 (GRB10) levels by phosphorylation.248 GRB10 and 
GRB14 are negative regulators of insulin signaling, which act in 
key metabolic tissues, including muscle and adipose,249 and con­
tain polymorphisms in humans that are linked to development 
of T2D.250 Extracellular-signal–regulated kinase (ERK) has also 
been shown to feed back and inhibit IRS function and is down­
stream of insulin-mediated mitogen-activated protein kinase acti­
vation. Last, FOXO transcription factors regulate transcription of

Nutrient Overload and Insulin Resistance
Cells have developed a number of ways to sense incoming nutri­
ents, including direct and indirect activation of transcription fac­
tors and protein kinases. Amino acids stimulate growth by direct 
activation of mTOR complex 1.106 Fatty acids are sensed by sev­
eral mechanisms, including cell surface receptors such as toll-like 
receptors (TLRs), and by transcription factors, including PPARα 
and PPARγ.252 Glucose itself can be converted to O-Linked 
β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAC) posttranslational modifica­
tions that modify enzymes on Ser/Thr residues, acting similar to 
or opposing phosphorylation.253 Many of these signals provide 
feedback inhibition on the insulin receptor cascade through Ser/
Thr kinase activation (including S6K), c-Jun N-terminal kinase 
(JNK), and inhibitor of κB kinase (IKK).246,254–256 However, 
chronic overnutrition can alter these normal cellular signals, caus­
ing insulin resistance (see Fig. 33.8). In a sense, the reaction of 
different tissues to obesity may be a relatively normal physiologic 
response to excess nutrient delivery, with prolonged activation 
leading to unintended and pathologic states that result in insulin 
resistance, inflammation, and even cell death. 
Adipose Tissue and Insulin Resistance
To maintain metabolic homeostasis when nutrient intake exceeds 
energy expenditure, the excess calories must be used to increase 
cellular mass or it must be stored. Most excess nutrients, whether 
carbohydrate, protein, or lipid, are ultimately stored as triglyceride 
in white adipose tissue. If the storage capacity of adipose tissue 
is exceeded, lipids and other nutrients enter nonstorage tissues. 
This ectopic lipid accumulation occurs in myocytes, hepatocytes, 
vascular cells, and β cells, and can produce toxic lipid metabolites 
(e.g., diacylglycerols or ceramides) that trigger activation of PKC 
isoforms among other adaptive and maladaptive cellular responses 
that lead to insulin resistance.257 Indeed, some data suggest the 
inability to expand fat mass in response to overeating may be an 
important factor in the development of insulin resistance.258
Adipocytes are more than storage cells. They regulate the 
uptake and release of fatty acids; participate in the glycerol–fatty 
acid cycle; release leptin and other hormones that signal the energy 
status of the body; and secrete an ever-expanding number of cyto­
kines that have hormonal, paracrine, and autocrine actions.259 The 
adipocyte itself can be adversely affected by accumulation of excess 
nutrients, leading to events that can have adverse consequences on 
the body. As adipocyte surface area increases in obesity, there is
