with heart failure, a cardiovascular complication of diabetes that 
is increasingly common.258,260 The mechanisms underlying these 
cardiovascular and renal effects are not well understood. At present 
it seems likely that several factors contribute, including improve­
ment of glycemic control, blood pressure, and weight control, 
together with improved regulation of fluid balance, attenuation 
of sympathetic nervous system activity, increased availability of 
ketones as fuel for injured cardiac tissues, and more.261
These agents have now been proven effective for heart failure 
in those without diabetes as well, supporting the contribution of 
the non–glucose-lowering mechanisms. Dapagliflozin and empa­
gliflozin are currently FDA approved for heart failure in those 
with or without diabetes and recommended for such use by the 
American College of Cardiology.262 Canagliflozin is approved for 
heart failure only in those with diabetes.
In addition to the consistency of benefits on heart failure, this 
class of agents has shown benefits for kidney protection in patients 
with and without cardiac disease as well as with or without dia­
betes.263–266 It appears that SGLT2 inhibitors will ultimately play 
a larger role in heart failure and chronic kidney disease than in 
glucose control but will be a mainstay in T2D care.
The ratio of benefits to adverse effects of this class of drugs 
appears highly favorable, but there are distinctive symptomatic 
side effects.265 The most common of these are related to glycosuria 
and include urinary frequency, genital infections, and relatively 
rare episodes of lower urinary tract infections as well as dehydra­
tion and its consequences. Genital infections are usually related 
to yeast, occur in at least 10% to 15% of women (about a five­
fold higher risk), and may recur.267,268 Genital mycotic infections 
are much less common in men and predominantly are found in 
those who have not been circumcised. A cardiovascular outcome 
trial found increased lower extremity amputations with cana­
gliflozin.248 There is still uncertainty about this risk and whether it 
could involve other agents in the class, but it does require consider­
ation of risk factors such as previous amputations.254,255,265,269,270 
Theoretical questions related to bone metabolism have been 
raised, but an increased risk of fractures has not been found in 
most completed clinical trials.241,265,271
Good renal function is essential for full glycemic efficacy of 
SGLT inhibitors. Initiation for glucose control is not recom­
mended when eGFR is below 45 mL/min/1.73 m2. However, 
lower eGFR levels are associated with continued cardiac and renal 
protection. Although acute renal insufficiency has been reported, 
presumably due to changes in renal perfusion, this class of medica­
tions clearly has demonstrated long-term renal protection.272–274 
An unexplained imbalance in bladder cancer without a change in 
total cancer or cancer fatality was reported in early development 
of dapagliflozin.275,276 Dapagliflozin is the only agent in the class 
with a warning against use of the drug in patients with bladder 
cancer.
As a final concern, there is good evidence of diabetic ketoacido­
sis occurring without markedly elevated glucose levels (euglycemic 
diabetic ketoacidosis) during treatment of presumed T2D with an 
SGLT inhibitor.277,278 The mechanisms underlying this adverse 
effect are only partly understood, but may include a tendency 
toward dehydration, elevation of circulating glucagon levels, 
and accelerated gluconeogenesis due to glucosuria during fast­
ing.241,277–279 Some proposed risk factors deserving consideration 
include metabolic stress and low carbohydrate intake, and there 
seems to be higher risk with older patients. Any patient treated 
with an SGLT inhibitor who experiences persistent or recur­
rent nausea, vomiting, or malaise, or who develops a metabolic 
acidosis, should be evaluated for the presence of urine and serum 
ketones, even if glucose levels are near normal.280 
Colesevelam
Colesevelam is a second-generation bile acid sequestrant. It was 
observed to mediate modest reductions in glucose during the clin­
ical development program. An expanded program in patients with 
T2D resulted in approval for marketing of this drug as an adjunct 
for the treatment of diabetes. It provides an HbA1c reduction of 
about 0.5% in addition to approximately 15% improvement in 
LDL.281 HDL changes tend to be trivial. Triglycerides can increase 
by 5% to 20%, so use should be avoided in those with underlying 
high triglyceride levels. Gastrointestinal side effects affect 10% or 
more of patients but seldom lead to withdrawals. The mechanisms 
for the glycemic effects are not definitively known.282 
Bromocriptine
A quick-release formulation of bromocriptine administered 
within 2 hours of rising in the morning has been developed and is 
approved for marketing in the United States. Creating a circadian 
peak in central dopaminergic tone is suggested to improve insulin 
sensitivity. Nausea is the most common adverse effect, occurring 
in about 30% of patients and leading to discontinuation in about 
10% at highest doses. Lower doses are better tolerated. HbA1c 
reductions are generally modest but have been reported to be as 
high as 1.2%. In a 1-year safety study, broad cardiovascular out­
comes were improved 40% compared with placebo.283 Studies 
suggest substantial efficacy in the setting of inadequate glycemic 
control on high-dose insulin therapy.284,285 However, this agent is 
seldom used for T2D now. 
Glucose-Lowering Agents Administered by 
Injection
In addition to the glucose-lowering therapies that are orally 
administered small molecules, there is a group of relatively larger 
peptide agents that must be administered by other means. At pres­
ent, these are mostly delivered by subcutaneous injection, but 
delivery by inhalation, sublingual absorption, nasal spray, or other 
means may become more common in the future (e.g., oral sema­
glutide; discussed later). At present, one formulation of inhal­
able insulin is available for use, and other products that can be 
delivered by means other than injection are under study. Because 
injected therapies require more active participation by the patient, 
or the assistance of others, more education and support in their 
use is needed than with oral therapies. However, pen devices, very 
small needles, and many long-acting medications have improved 
convenience and acceptability.
Insulins
Insulin has been commercially available since the early 1920s 
and is arguably the best-studied form of therapy for diabetes. It 
is essential for all patients with T1D and a mainstay of treatment 
for T2D. Subcutaneous injection of insulin can be used to supple­
ment endogenous production of insulin both in the basal state, 
to modulate hepatic glucose production, and in the postprandial 
state, in which a surge in insulin release normally further sup­
presses hepatic glucose production and facilitates glucose uptake 
by muscle and fat. Almost all insulins currently used worldwide 
are human insulins synthesized by recombinant technology or 
synthetic analogues of the human molecule.286,287 The various 
formulations differ largely in their pharmacokinetics, as shown in 
1370
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Table 34.11. As patents on insulin analogues expire, equivalent 
products that are manufactured by different companies are becom­
ing available. These “biosimilar” insulins appear to have effects 
very similar to those of the originally patented versions.288–290 
The FDA has designated biosimilar insulins as “interchangeable” 
if they have adequate switch trials as evidence. Interchangeable 
biosimilar insulins such as glargine-yfgn can be substituted by the 
pharmacist.289
Insulins are grouped into shorter- versus longer-acting for­
mulations. This distinction has practical importance, as these 
two categories of insulin are used quite differently. Both short-
acting and long-acting insulins have profiles of action that vary 
by the size of the dose injected. With higher doses the onset and 
time to peak effect become more delayed and the total duration 
longer.
Long-Acting Insulins. Long-acting insulins are usually ini­
tiated before short-acting ones. In the past, formulations of 
human insulin were modified to prolong its action by slow­
ing absorption. The most widely used formulations were ultra­
lente insulin and protamine zinc insulin (PZI), both of which 
were very long acting, and lente insulin and neutral protamine 
Hagedorn (NPH), both considered intermediate acting. Ultra­
lente, lente, and PZI are no longer available, but NPH human 
insulin is still commonly used. The time to onset, peak effect, 
and full duration of action of NPH are about twofold greater 
than those of regular human insulin, with an onset in 1 to 2 
hours, a peak usually at 4 to 8 hours, and a duration of 12 to 
16 hours. NPH is usually given as a single injection at bed­
time or twice daily, before breakfast and at bedtime. Insulin 
detemir is a long-acting analogue in which a fatty-acid side 
chain is covalently bound to the insulin molecule, resulting in 
slowing of both absorption from subcutaneous tissue and clear­
ance from circulation. Detemir’s duration of action is a little 
longer than that of NPH, and more consistent from injection 
to injection.291 To reliably provide a sustained between-meal 
and overnight (basal) effect, detemir, like NPH, must be taken 
twice daily, usually before breakfast and either before dinner or 
at bedtime. However, for patients with T2D who add detemir 
as basal insulin while continuing noninsulin agents to cover 
the day, once-daily dosing can be sufficient for at least 40% of 
the patients.82
U-100 insulin glargine is a long-acting analogue that is soluble 
at acid pH but precipitates when neutralized in tissues after injec­
tion. The resulting gradual absorption leads to a duration of action 
that, at doses commonly needed in T2D, usually provides more 
than 24 hours of basal insulin effect with relatively little peak-to-
trough variation. This action profile results in consistently less risk 
of hypoglycemia than occurs with NPH insulin and has led to use 
of insulin glargine taken once daily, either before breakfast or at 
bedtime, as a reliable way to initiate insulin therapy.

CHAPTER 34  Therapeutics of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
The newest long-acting analogues, degludec and the U-300 
formulation of glargine, are taken once daily. Prolongation of the 
action of degludec is due both to slower absorption after injection 
and to delayed clearance, whereas that of U-300 glargine results 
entirely from effect on absorption. Both offer a modest further 
reduction of risk of hypoglycemia compared with U-100 glargine, 
especially for patients using lower doses and those with prior dif­
ficulties with hypoglycemia.292–294 There is evidence that hypo­
glycemia during initiation of basal insulin is associated with lower 
adherence and higher costs of care.295
Insulin icodec, which is in development but not yet FDA 
approved, is considered ultra long acting, with a 1-week half-life 
and once-weekly dosing, and may provide advantages over daily 
injection for some patients.296,297 
Short-Acting Insulins. Regular human insulin and the rapid-
acting analogues (insulins lispro, aspart, and glulisine) are all 
administered by injection with meals to assist in control of post­
prandial hyperglycemia.286,287 Regular insulin has an onset of 
action about 30 minutes after injection, a peak at 2 to 4 hours, 
and duration of 6 to 8 hours or longer at high doses. The three 
standard rapid-acting analogues all have an onset in 5 to 15 
minutes, peak activity in approximately 1 hour, and duration of 
approximately 4 hours. More rapidly absorbed formulations of 
insulin aspart and lispro are now available. Faster-acting aspart is 
formulated with nicotinamide to help facilitate insulin absorp­
tion. Ultrarapid lispro is formulated with a prostaglandin ana­
logue, treprostinil, along with citrate. Both formulations speed 
up absorption, resulting in measurable reduction in postpran­
dial glucose, but have not shown an improvement in HbA1c in 
T2D.298–300 Other very rapid-acting insulin formulations and 
delivery technologies are being developed. Regular human insu­
lin administered intravenously is immediately effective, with a 
half-life on the order of 10 minutes. Lispro, aspart, and gluli­
sine are approved in the United States for intravenous use but 
offer no advantage over regular insulin for this purpose and cost 
much more.
U-500 regular insulin has been available for decades, but its 
use has increased in the setting of severe insulin resistance.301 
This concentrated insulin has a delayed and prolonged action 
profile compared to U-100 regular.302 It has been administered 
twice daily, three times daily, and by insulin pump with good 
efficacy.303 Pen devices are now available for ease and safety. To 
some degree its use has been attenuated by the availability of 
highly effective GLP1 agonists that reduce weight and insulin 
requirements.
One inhaled formulation of human insulin is available.304,305 
The device by which it is delivered is quite convenient to carry 
and use. The insulin-loaded microparticles produce rapid onset 
of effect with peak activity in 30 minutes (the tmax is about 10 
minutes), much earlier than with lispro.306 The time to peak is 
extended with higher doses and the duration also varies from 90 
minutes at lower doses to 180 minutes with 12 units. Inhaled 
insulin may be preferred by patients who are very averse to tak­
ing injections, and some patients prefer its more rapid action to 
help with postprandial glucose control. Its onset of action makes 
it the fastest among available insulins, but the shorter duration 
can be problematic. The current formulation requires spirome­
try before initiation, at 6 months, and annually thereafter. This 
preparation is contraindicated in patients with asthma or chronic 
obstructive pulmonary disease, and there are advisory precautions 
for patients with active lung cancer and patients who smoke. Its 
use is associated with cough or throat irritation in addition to the 
usual hypoglycemic risk. Doses are limited to 4-, 8-, and 12-unit 
equivalent doses resulting in limitations of dose adjustments. 
Premixed Insulins. Premixed insulin formulations provide 
greater convenience and accuracy of dosing than mixing of two 
formulations in a syringe by the patient at the time of administra­
tion, but at the expense of reduced flexibility of dosing. Premixed 
formulations available in the United States are 70/30 and 50/50 
mixtures of NPH and regular insulin, a 75/25 and a 50/50 mix­
ture of lispro insulin in its NPH-like formulation with insulin 
lispro, and a 70/30 mixture of insulin aspart with its NPH-like 
congener. Premixed insulins provide a single-peak action at about 
4 to 6 hours after each injection, as expected from summation of 
the activities of their components. In a very instructive study, use 
of 70/30 insulin in T2D showed greater improvement in glucose 
control but at the cost of significantly more hypoglycemia com­
pared to basal insulin.307 
Human Versus Analogue Insulins. Insulin analogues are clearly 
helpful in managing T1D, which requires complete replacement of 
endogenous insulin and accurate matching of the profile of action 
to daily needs. The degree to which both long-acting and rapid-
acting analogues offer advantages over NPH and regular human 
insulin for T2D is less well established, and a focus of debate. 
Among the issues is that both the list price and the direct cost 
to patients can be much higher for the analogues.46,308,309 Both 
long-acting and rapid-acting insulin analogues have been shown 
in large studies to cause less frequent hypoglycemia than human 
insulins, but for some patients little difference may be found. The 
absolute risk of severe hypoglycemia in patients with T2D is rela­
tively small, approximately one-third to one-tenth as high as in 
similarly treated patients with T1D. However, it is possible that 
nocturnal hypoglycemia in particular might be unrecognized and 
have dire consequences. Elderly patients are likely at greatest risk. 
Risk can be minimized with appropriate education of patients 
and expectant monitoring of glucose at times when hypoglycemia 
is most likely to occur, such as at night or during unplanned or 
strenuous activity. Also, blinded professional CGM might identify 
unrecognized hypoglycemia and personal CGM is of benefit to 
those with T2D treated with basal-bolus insulin regimens to guide 
dosing and alert the patient and family to hypoglycemia. Allergies 
to currently available insulins are rare, as are chronic skin reac­
tions, which include lipoatrophy and lipohypertrophy. 
Insulin Delivery Devices
Newer insulin needles cause less discomfort than those previously 
available because of a finer gauge, shorter length, sharper points, 
and smoother surfaces. Improved insulin pen design has made 
teaching a patient to take insulin much easier and provides greater 
convenience and accuracy of dosing. Pen injectors capable of 
injecting larger doses, up to 160 units, are now available for U-300 
glargine and U-200 degludec. Insulin pump therapy has been used 
in patients with T2D but is not widely accepted as cost-effective 
in routine practice.310–312 Insulin pump delivery of U-500 regular 
insulin has been proposed for highly insulin-resistant T2D. Stud­
ies have shown more HbA1c reduction and lower daily insulin use 
with pump therapy versus three daily injections of U-500 insulin, 
but no change in hypoglycemia and no difference in weight. At the 
present time pump therapy of T2D is relatively uncommon.301,313 
Durable insulin pen devices using replaceable insulin cartridges 
offer more precise insulin dose administration compared to the 
patient drawing the insulin from the vial into a syringe, and are 
more convenient for the patient. For patients with intensive insu­
lin therapy, the use of smart pens that help calculate doses and 
1372
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
track therapy may be helpful. Pen caps that identify when the last 
dose was given may help reduce missed doses or second doses.314 
GLP1 Receptor Agonists
GLP1 receptor agonists are homologs or analogues of human 
GLP1 that have substantially changed the landscape of T2D 
therapy.229,315–317 Like GLP1 itself, these agents potentiate insu­
lin secretion in response to rising glucose levels, suppress post­
prandial glucagon secretion, delay gastric emptying, and promote 
satiety. As with insulins, GLP1 agonists divide logically into two 
groups: those that are short acting and those with longer duration 
of effects. Important features of the available agents in this class 
are shown in Table 34.12.
Short-Acting GLP1 Receptor Agonists. The first GLP1 recep­
tor agonist to be developed was exendin-4, a short-acting homolog 
of GLP1. It is a naturally occurring component of the saliva of the 
Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum) and shares 53% sequence iden­
tity with GLP1, but is relatively resistant to degradation by DPP4. 
Exenatide is synthetic exendin-4 and was the first GLP1-based thera­
peutic agent to be approved for human use.318,319 When injected 
subcutaneously, it has a peak of action at about 2 hours and total 
duration of no more than 6 hours. There is some indication that dos­
ing three times daily with meals may be an option for post-prandial 
control with basal insulin but this has not been adequately studied 
and is unlikely to gain popularity due to the availability of long-act­
ing agents.320 With twice-daily injection before breakfast and before 
dinner it produces a reduction in HbA1c of approximately 1.0%, 
largely through a reduction of postprandial glucose along with mod­
est 2 to 4 kg weight loss. With prolonged use, these effects are associ­
ated with modest improvements in blood pressure and lipids. The 
most common adverse effect is nausea, which occurs in up to 50% 
of patients, is usually mild to moderate in intensity, occurs early in 
the course of therapy, and typically wanes over time. Nausea leads to 
withdrawal of therapy in about 5% of patients. Use of the standard 
short-acting exenatide has decreased dramatically, and there is no 
biosimilar product available at this point to reduce cost.
Lixisenatide is another agent that has properties similar to those 
of exenatide except for a slightly longer duration of action.321 It 
has been approved for administration once daily before breakfast. 
It reduces postprandial increments of glucose during the daytime 
but has much less effect overnight. Both exenatide and lixisenatide 
are recommended to be started at the lower available dose and 
advanced to full dosage after several weeks in order to limit side 
effects on initiating therapy. 
Long-Acting GLP1 Receptor Agonists. Newer, longer-acting 
GLP1 receptor agonists include liraglutide, an extended-release 
formulation of exenatide, dulaglutide, and semaglutide.229,316,322 
Albiglutide is a long-acting GLP1 receptor agonist not marketed 
in the United States. Efpeglenatide is another long-acting GLP1 
receptor agonist in development that is not yet FDA approved but 
has published results indicating comparable glycemic efficacy and 
a potential for cardiovascular and renal benefits.323,324
Liraglutide is administered once daily without any restriction 
as to timing or relation to meals. The other long-acting agents 
are to be given once weekly. In general, they are associated with 
greater HbA1c-lowering efficacy than short-acting exenatide and 
lixisenatide, providing greater effects on overnight fasting glucose 
levels.229,316 However, they have much less effect on postprandial 
increments of glucose than the short-acting agents. They also are 
associated with a lower frequency of gastrointestinal side effects. All 
the various long-acting agents appear to be quite effective in lower­
ing HbA1c, although some differences are shown in head-to-head 
trials as well as systematic reviews.177,325–327 Semaglutide may cause 
superior but marginally different reduction in HbA1c from dulaglu­
tide.326,328 Both medications are now approved at higher doses than 
used in the comparative studies (semaglutide 2.0 mg and dulaglu­
tide 3.0 and 4.5). Direct head-to-head trials have not been reported, 
but an indirect comparison suggests the semaglutide 2.0 mg dose 
would still have marginal added efficacy compare to dulaglutide 3.0 
mg or 4.5 mg for glucose control and weight loss.329 Studies under 
conditions of clinical practice have shown some differences from 
randomized clinical trials, suggesting that results of treatment can 
be influenced by differences in adherence to therapy.330 There are 
some differences in the pen injectors used for delivering doses of the 
various agents that may affect preferences as well.
Weight loss is consistently seen with the various GLP1 recep­
tor agonists, although the magnitude of weight loss varies with the 
agents, and only liraglutide (3.0 mg) and semaglutide (2.4 mg) are 
currently approved for weight loss indications in patients with or 
without diabetes. Semaglutide appears to cause slightly more weight 
loss when used at doses approved for diabetes in the United States.
Large randomized trials examining cardiovascular safety of 
liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide, and albiglutide have shown 
cardiovascular benefit in populations selected for having high car­
diovascular risk, although the populations studied and the exact 
findings demonstrate some heterogeneity.331–335 Details of these 
studies are shown in Table 34.13. The Liraglutide Effect and 
Action in Diabetes: Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcome Results 
(LEADER) was the first GLP1 receptor agonist CVOT reported. 
The study followed patients randomized to treatment with lira­
glutide or placebo for a median of more than 3 years. Significant 
reductions of risk were found for the primary composite cardio­
vascular endpoint (13%), cardiovascular death (22%), all-cause 
mortality (15%), and progression of albuminuria (26%).332 The 
Trial to Evaluate Cardiovascular and Other Long-term Outcomes 
with Semaglutide in Subjects with Type 2 Diabetes (SUSTAIN-6) 
had a generally similar design but studied patients starting with 
somewhat worse glycemic control who received randomized treat­
ment for about 2 years.331 This study demonstrated somewhat 
greater reduction of risk for its primary cardiovascular compos­
ite endpoint (26%) compared with LEADER, and also showed a 
reduction of renal endpoints. However, no reduction of mortality 
was found. Neither LEADER nor SUSTAIN-6 showed a reduc­
tion of hospitalizations for heart failure. Table 34.13 shows find­
ings from the CVOT studies with the various long-acting GLP1 
receptor agents. Up to now, these favorable outcomes have not 
been found with short-acting GLP1 receptor agonists, and there 
has been inconsistency in the specific benefits seen in trials of the 
other long-acting agents. Many of the variations could relate to 
the study designs and populations selected in those trials.
Nausea and diarrhea are the most common side effects attributed 
to GLP1 receptor agonists. Relative to the HbA1c reduction, the fre­
quency of nausea is greater with short-acting agents and the gastroin­
testinal side effects tend to be dose related with the long-acting agents.
Hypoglycemia is not a direct effect of GLP1 receptor agonists 
but can occur when they are added to other agents. When one is 
added to prior therapy with a secretagogue, it is prudent to reduce to 
the minimum dose of secretagogue, at least initially. When a GLP1 
receptor agonist is added to insulin, a 20% reduction of insulin dos­
age is advised unless HbA1c is greater than 8% (63.9 mmol/mol).
Concern about pancreatitis has emerged from postmarketing 
reports of GLP1 receptor agonists. A direct causal link has not 
been proved, although passage of gallstones accompanying weight 
loss remains a possible mechanism. Meta-analyses from CVOTs 
1373
CHAPTER 34  Therapeutics of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
failed to show increased risk of acute pancreatitis with GLP1 ago­
nists, although DPP4 inhibitors did show risk.336,337 Nevertheless, 
it is recommended that drugs in this class be avoided in patients 
with a history of pancreatitis.
Exenatide is renally cleared and is contraindicated in the setting 
of advanced kidney disease (eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2). 
The other GLP1 receptor agonists do not share this feature with 
exenatide and have been shown to be safe and effective at various 
levels of kidney dysfunction.338 Overall, the CVOTs have also sug­
gested benefit of GLP1 agents in patients’ renal protection.338,339 
Nevertheless, cases of acute renal failure have been reported in 
association with GLP1 receptor agonist therapy, usually in patients 
with chronic renal insufficiency who develop superimposed prer­
enal azotemia in the context of prolonged anorexia, nausea, and 
vomiting. To mitigate the risk of pancreatitis and renal failure, it is 
prudent to instruct patients treated with GLP1 receptor agonists to 
stop their medication if they develop nausea, vomiting, or abdomi­
nal pain of more than a few hours’ duration and to seek medical 
attention if they are unable to keep down fluids after 4 hours.
Although most trials did not carefully follow retinopathy pro­
gression during treatment, the SUSTAIN-6 trial with semaglu­
tide raised the question of diabetic retinopathy in treated patients. 
Subsequent meta-analyses have indicated increased progression of 
retinopathy, though it appears this is a temporary effect related to 
rapid rate and degree of HbA1c reduction.340,341
Another safety concern is medullary thyroid cancer. No signal 
exists for this problem with GLP1-based therapy in humans, but 
a clear increase in the incidence of these tumors was observed in 
preclinical testing in rodents, although not in other animal mod­
els. It is suggested that these agents be avoided in those with a 
personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer. 
The GLP1 Oral Exception. GLP1 receptor agonist peptides are 
subject to degradation by gastric acid and are poorly absorbed 
through the intestinal wall; therefore they have been admin­
istered as injectable agents since their introduction to the U.S. 
market in 2004. However, semaglutide formulated with sodium 
N-(8-[2-hydroxybenzoyl] amino) caprylate to enhance absorp­
tion is stable when administered orally and gained FDA approval 
in 2019. Oral semaglutide is available as 3-, 7-, and 14-mg tablets 
that are to be taken at least 30 minutes before eating or taking 
other medications and with no more than 4 oz of water.342 Many 
patients prefer oral therapy; however, once-weekly injections of 
the injectable semaglutide with a very small needle and injection 
pen are convenient and generally well accepted. Although incom­
plete absorption requires larger doses, the efficacy of oral sema­
glutide for glucose reduction and weight loss has been equal to or

A Step Beyond GLP1 Receptor Agonists: GIP/GLP1 Dual 
Receptor Agonist. Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypep­
tide (GIP) was identified early in the study of incretins for effects 
on glucose metabolism. GIP is a 42-amino-acid peptide produced 
primarily in the small intestine by K cells in response to carbohy­
drate and lipid intake. It increases insulin synthesis and secretion, 
glucose sensing, glucagon secretion, and cell proliferation.345,346 
GIP tends to decrease food intake but has some beneficial effect 
to reduce nausea. However, early studies failed to demonstrate sig­
nificant clinical effects compared to GLP1 receptor agonists.
Recently, the development of tirzepatide, a single molecule 
that binds to the GLP1 as well as the GIP receptor, has provided 
new possibilities for diabetes and weight management. Tirzepatide 
was approved by the FDA in 2022 after multiple trials demon­
strated benefits over available agents. Of particular note, a study 
comparing tirzepatide 5, 10, and 15 mg versus 1 mg semaglutide 
demonstrated superior HbA1c reduction with all three doses of tirz­
epatide. With the tirzepatide 15 mg weekly dose HbA1c decreased 
2.3% from a baseline of 8.3% (67.0 mmol/mol), with 46% of the 
treatment group reaching an HbA1c of 5.7% (38.8 mmol/mol). 
Additionally, the 15 mg dose resulted in weight loss of greater than 
10% in 57% of the participants compared to 24% with semaglu­
tide. Side effects were similar in type and frequency.347
Beyond an anticipated high price, another relevant limitation 
is lack of cardiovascular and renal outcome studies for tirzepatide, 
although cardiac biomarkers have been positively affected.346,348 
This dual gut-peptide receptor agonist, which seems likely to have 
an important role in T2D in the near future, also serves as a proof-
of-concept agent for other dual agonist agents in the future. 
Amylin Receptor Agonists
Amylin is a neuroendocrine hormone that is co-secreted with 
insulin by pancreatic β-cells. A deficiency of amylin is therefore 
evident in patients with T1D or T2D, in parallel with insulin defi­
ciency. Amylin and insulin have complementary actions in regu­
lating plasma glucose. Amylin binds to brain nuclei and promotes 
satiety and reduces appetite. Through efferent neural pathways 
it mediates a decrease in the rate of gastric emptying and limits 
inappropriate glucagon secretion in a glucose-dependent fashion. 
By these means it regulates the rate of plasma glucose appearance 
from the gastrointestinal tract and the liver. Insulin concurrently 
regulates the rate of glucose appearance from the liver and stimu­
lates glucose uptake in muscle and fat.
Amylin is relatively insoluble in aqueous solution and aggre­
gates on plastic and glass. Pramlintide is a soluble, nonaggregating 
amylin analogue, with similar clinical effects, that is administered 
by injection before meals. It is approved for use by patients with 
T1D or T2D requiring both basal and mealtime insulin.349 Most

increments, with little effect on overnight control. When pram­

a sulfonylurea in T2D, HbA1c can be reduced by about 0.5 to 0.7

an increase to the full 120 μg dose over 1 to 2 weeks as toler­

in patients with T1D and can be limited by reducing dosage of 
mealtime insulin by about 50% when initiating therapy, with the 
option of subsequently returning to higher doses as needed.349 Oral 
medications that require rapid absorption for effectiveness should 
be administered either 1 hour before or 2 hours after injection of 
pramlintide. Coformulations of pramlintide with regular human 
insulin are being evaluated, as are combination therapies for weight 
management given the effects on gastric emptying and appetite. 
Practical Aspects of Treatment
A Team Approach
Considering the wide array of interventions available, and the 
need to adapt to differences between patients as well as changing 
needs over time, it is obvious that many treatment decisions will 
be needed for every patient. It is also clear that various kinds of 
providers with differing training and experience can contribute 
to making and implementing these decisions. No one provider 
can do it all, and the concept of a team approach to manage­
ment of diabetes is well established. Teams may include nurses, 
nutritionists, pharmacists, educators, and physicians, all with spe­
cific interest and experience in diabetes. Although the previous 
discussion of DSMES describes in detail the services and processes 
required for care, it does not define specifically the kinds of pro­
viders needed. This is because different health systems use differ­
ent models for providing DSMES, with different configurations 
of providers. However, in each setting a locally available group of 
providers should be identified who can function as a team with 
each individual patient. Providers specialized in other aspects of 
care commonly needed by people with T2D—such as cardiology, 
nephrology, ophthalmology, and podiatry—also can contribute to 
the team effort. The overall goal of this collaboration is to ensure 
optimal management of overall metabolic control, other risk fac­
tors for complications of diabetes, and the complications them­
selves. Making the team concept a reality is a major challenge for 
health systems today.
The specialized team can assist at various points in the natu­
ral history of T2D. As noted in Fig. 34.1 and Table 34.6, these 
include the time of diagnosis, a later time when injected therapies 
or use of devices such as CGM systems are needed, or whenever 
diabetes-related problems such as severe hypoglycemia, ketoacido­
sis, or repeated hospitalization occur or recur.111,351 
Identifying Pathophysiologic Subgroups
The time of diagnosis of diabetes presents an opportunity to favor­
ably influence the entire future experience of the patient. It is typi­
cally a “teachable moment” at which the patient can be introduced 
to DSMES and develop a long-term plan of management. It is 
also an opportunity to identify those individuals who do not have 
the most typical form of T2D, and adjust the plan accordingly. 
Several of the more common atypical subgroups are discussed in 
this section and should be considered as treatments may vary.
Latent Autoimmune Diabetes of Adulthood
The largest subgroup of diabetes presenting in adulthood is that of 
autoimmune origin, commonly called latent autoimmune diabetes 
of adulthood (LADA) or adult-onset T1D. This group comprises 
up to 12% of patients diagnosed with diabetes after age 20. There is 
heterogeneity in rate of progression of hyperglycemia and the need 
for advanced insulin regimens. Often the relatively slow progres­
sion of β-cell loss will lead to uncertainty about diagnosis.352–354
T1D patients with LADA frequently are not obese, and they may 
have other autoimmune disorders or a family history of these. 
Laboratory support can be provided by detection of antibodies 
to glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) or islet-cell antibod­
ies, although lack of antibodies does not exclude an autoimmune 
process. Both family history and genetic markers are likely to be 
more consistent with T1D.355,356 Insulin has been considered the 
main therapy from the outset, but other therapies may be possible 
in those with slow progression and individualization is important. 
Early use of insulin may prolong β-cell function, as well as pre­
venting a period of sustained hyperglycemia that could initiate 
chronic complications. An evolving question is whether SGLT2 
inhibitors or GLP1 receptor agonists should be considered for 
their cardiovascular and renal benefits in LADA.357 The concern 
here would be diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitors, par­
ticularly in cases where β-cell loss is advanced. 
Pancreatic Diabetes
Another relatively common subgroup comprises patients with 
other disorders affecting the pancreas. Pancreatic diabetes has been 
referred to as type 3c diabetes and is likely underdiagnosed.358,359 
The leading causes include acute or chronic pancreatitis, pancre­
atectomy for cancer or pancreatitis, hemochromatosis, and cystic 
fibrosis. Despite widely differing pathogenesis, patients with pan­
creatic diabetes share a tendency to have significant deficiency of 
insulin secretion and prominent postprandial hyperglycemia, and 
may respond less well than expected to oral therapies.359 In addi­
tion to insulin deficiency, there is significantly decreased glucagon 
and pancreatic polypeptide, and also decreased incretin responses. 
As in the case of LADA, patients in this subgroup commonly need 
insulin at or relatively soon after diagnosis, and quite frequently 
require both basal and prandial insulin. In some cases, due to the 
multihormonal loss, there is more glucose variability than is seen 
in T2D and potentially even more than in those with T1D.360,361 
Monogenic Diabetes
A smaller but increasingly recognized subgroup is that with mono­
genic diabetes (see Chapter 37). This is a heterogeneous group of 
heritable disorders, which are often diagnosed in childhood but 
sometimes present as diabetes diagnosed in adulthood.362–364 A 
subset of this group of disorders has been commonly described 
as maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY). The propor­
tion of newly diagnosed adults with one of these conditions is 
estimated to be between 1% and 2%. The diagnosis should be 
considered in atypical cases that might otherwise be diagnosed 
as T1D or T2D. A strong family history consistent with auto­
somal dominant inheritance with high penetrance is typical but 
not always present. A definitive diagnosis depends on genetic test­
ing that can identify specific subtypes and thus assist in planning 
treatment. This approach to monogenic diabetes is one of the best 
present-day examples of precision medicine.365,366
1376
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Two of these disorders deserve specific comment. One is a heri­
table deficiency of glucokinase (GCK-MODY) that alters glucose 
sensing in the β-cell.367 It presents typically in youth as mild fast­
ing hyperglycemia (e.g., 100–140 mg/dL [5.6–7.8 mmol/L]) that 
is not progressive and causes little or no tissue damage over time. 
The HbA1c may range from 5.6% to 7.8% (37.7–61.7 mmol/
mol). In many cases this disorder is not recognized until routine 
chemistry tests indicate elevated fasting glucose levels typical of 
prediabetes. It is often recognized earlier in women during testing 
for gestational diabetes. Recognition of GCK-MODY is impor­
tant mainly to avoid unnecessary treatment of the patient and 
other identified members of the family. Current evidence indi­
cates that those with a GCK mutation will not develop chronic 
complications of diabetes, and treatment is not likely to render 
significant changes in glucose control. However, longer follow-up 
of larger numbers of individuals with this disorder will be needed 
to be certain.368
In contrast, the most common form of monogenic diabetes, 
hepatic nucleocyte factor 1A (HNF1A), has direct clinical rele­
vance.369 It can present in adulthood with progressive hypergly­
cemia, more postprandial than fasting, that responds very well 
to sulfonylureas. Other monogenic forms of diabetes, such as 
HNF4-α mutations, may also respond to sulfonylureas, which 
bind to the molecular complex on the surface of β-cells that is 
genetically affected. Successful responses to sulfonylureas may per­
sist for extended periods of time. The possibility of sulfonylurea-
responsive monogenic diabetes can be suspected when there is a 
prominent history of adult-onset but quite stable and slowly pro­
gressive diabetes on one side of the patient’s family, often in the 
absence of obesity. Laboratory screening for these disorders is now 
more available than in the past but not always covered by insur­
ance. Identification of affected families can avoid unnecessary or 
inappropriate therapy for many family members. There is signifi­
cant heterogeneity in the age of diagnosis and rate of progression 
in these patients. 
Standardized Versus Personalized Tactics
The remaining majority of patients with diabetes newly diagnosed 
in adulthood can be considered to have T2D. Although some 
progress is being made in identifying subgroups based on clinical 
characteristics,370 at the present time it is simplest to begin with 
relatively standardized, algorithmic approaches (described later). 
Moreover, even after separation of subgroups T2D remains physi­
ologically heterogeneous, and patients also differ markedly in their 
daily habits, preferences, and capacities for self-management. The 
metabolic defects leading to diabetes also tend to worsen, and the 
burden of diabetes-related and other infirmities increases over 
time. For all these reasons, whatever approach is first used will 
need to be “personalized” eventually. This expectation can from 
the start be shared with the patient, who should be enlisted to par­
ticipate actively in making decisions beyond any initial algorithm.
Recommendations from professional societies continue to 
evolve as new agents are added to the therapeutic arsenal, espe­
cially in the case of the GLP1 receptor agonists and SGLT inhibi­
tors. Evidence comparing their glucose-lowering effectiveness 
versus risks, and especially their potential for important nonglyce­
mic benefits, has led to important changes in guidance from the 
ADA and EASD. Notably, these agents were developed for their 
glucose-lowering effects, but their favorable effects on the cardio­
vascular and renal systems have moved them toward use sooner 
after diagnosis and involving larger numbers of individuals than 
was originally expected (Fig. 34.3). However, these changes do 
not entirely replace experience with regimens based on the older 
agents. 
A Standardized Initial Therapeutic Approach
The most critical part of long-term glycemic management is ongo­
ing reassessment of glucose patterns and HbA1c values to guide 
refinement of interventions. The goal is to maintain optimal con­
trol with the simplest regimens including the lowest doses of the 
fewest medications. Lifestyle intervention and support continues 
to be essential. In general, drug therapy should also be considered 
from the time of diagnosis, along with lifestyle intervention. By 5 
years after diagnosis most patients require two or more drugs to 
maintain selected targets. Early in therapy it is usually desirable 
to add additional agents to prior therapies, rather than replacing 
one agent with another. Data from randomized trials, when avail­
able, should guide selecting among therapeutic choices. A general 
approach to be considered in the absence of any patient-specific 
factors is suggested here.46,48,49
Metformin
Metformin is generally considered the choice for initial drug ther­
apy for T2D in patients with adequate renal function. Used in 
combination with diet, exercise, and a DSMES program, metfor­
min can usually provide impressive glucose lowering with essen­
tially no risk of hypoglycemia.371 It has been shown to reduce 
rates of progression from prediabetes to overt diabetes, so it can be 
started early and continued if HbA1c is lowered below 6.5% (47.5 
mmol/L).192 There appears to be some cardiovascular benefit, 
although it may not be recognized in the early years of therapy, 
similar to SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP1 receptor agonists.372 There 
have been valid discussions of whether these latter agents should 
be first-line therapies when atherosclerotic cardiovascular or renal 
disease is evident,373 but a large number of individuals do not 
have evidence of these complications at or soon after the time of 
diagnosis. If metformin is contraindicated or poorly tolerated, or 
when the response to it is inadequate after a trial of 3 to 6 months, 
various agents can be substituted or added. There are multiple 
recommended second-line therapies: beside the GLP1 receptor 
agonists and SGLT inhibitors, these include sulfonylureas, TZDs, 
DPP4 inhibitors, and basal insulins. Tirzepatide is likely to be 
added to this group. Each has advantages and disadvantages. They 
have all been used successfully in combination therapy with met­
formin.177,374 Two-agent therapy including metformin and any of 
these other classes is likely to be successful in attaining glycemic 
targets for 5 to 10 years from diagnosis. Last, although metformin 
has been proposed to have potential benefits for cognition, cancer 
prevention, and cancer therapy as indications, these have not been 
established in prospective studies. 
Stepwise Combination Therapy With Oral Agents or Basal 
Insulin
With more than 60 years of clinical experience, widespread current 
use, and clear evidence of benefit relative to risk from long-term 
randomized interventional studies, sulfonylureas and basal insu­
lins remain appropriate considerations for second-line therapy. 
Each class of therapeutic agents acts through distinct cellular and 
molecular mechanisms, and glycemic effects are usually additive. 
Moreover, combining agents generally allows greater glucose-low­
ering effects without increased side effects. In the case of metfor­
min and the preferred sulfonylureas (glimepiride and long-acting 
glipizide and gliclazide), more than half the maximal therapeutic

effect can be obtained at half-maximal dosage of each agent. At 
the same time, the leading side effects—gastrointestinal symptoms 
with metformin and hypoglycemia with sulfonylureas—are less 
likely at the lower doses. As a specific example, combining met­
formin 500 mg twice daily with glimepiride 1 mg daily is likely to 
provide greater therapeutic power and fewer side effects than full 
dosage of either alone. However, if metformin has previously been 
titrated to the maximally effective dose of 2000 mg daily and is 
well tolerated, there is no reason to decrease the metformin dose 
when adding a second agent, including sulfonylureas, unless renal 
function is impaired. Continuing metformin and a sulfonylurea 
when basal insulin is added may allow continuation of good glyce­
mic control while keeping insulin dosage and risk of hypoglycemia 
at an acceptable level. Although increased cardiovascular risk with 
sulfonylureas has long been suspected, recent evidence strongly 
supports safety, but even so cardiovascular implications of hypo­
glycemia must be considered, particularly in older patients.197,199
The glycemic effectiveness of combination-therapy approaches 
using these agents in the Outcome Reduction with an Initial 
Glargine Intervention (ORIGIN) trial is shown in Fig. 34.4.375 
This trial enrolled participants who had either dysglycemia 
(impaired glucose tolerance and/or impaired fasting glucose) or 
T2D treated with diet and no more than one oral agent. Partici­
pants were selected for having high cardiovascular risk. They were 
randomly assigned to one of two regimens, each seeking fasting 
glucose no higher than 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L). One regimen 
was based on glargine as basal insulin with continuation of any 
prior oral therapy, the other on conventional stepwise use of oral 
therapies with insulin added only if necessary. Participants were 
followed an average of 5 years. Both regimens maintained HbA1c 
levels close to 6.5% (47.5 mmol/L) during the study, which for 
those with T2D at entry was up to approximately 10 years from 
time of diagnosis.376 Most participants in both randomized arms 
used only combinations of metformin, a sulfonylurea, or basal 
insulin, confirming the ability of these older agents to provide 
good glycemic control for many patients up to 10 years after diag­
nosis. No differences in medical outcomes between the two arms 
of the trial were observed other than more hypoglycemia in the 
group assigned to initial glargine therapy, and also less progression 
from dysglycemia to overt diabetes in that group.
The only large randomized controlled comparative effectiveness 
trial of single agents added to metformin is the recently completed 
Glycemia Reduction Approaches in Type 2 Diabetes: A Compara­
tive Effectiveness (GRADE) study. This study of 5047 subjects, 
nearly 20% Black and nearly 20% Hispanic or Latinx, had HbA1c 
values at baseline ranging from 6.8% to 8.5% (50.8–69.4 mmol/
mol). The subjects were randomized to have one of four classes of 
medications added to the metformin: sulfonylurea (glimepiride), 
basal insulin (glargine), DPP4 inhibitor (sitagliptin), and GLP1 
agonist (liraglutide). The primary outcome was time to eleva­
tion of HbA1c to ≥7.0%. All four medications decreased HbA1c, 
but liraglutide and glargine were moderately more effective than 
glimepiride or sitagliptin in reducing and maintaining the value 
<7.0%.377 Sitagliptin appeared to be the least effective, particu­
larly with baseline HbA1c values ≥7.8% (61.75 mmol/mol). Lira­
glutide was associated with significantly more gastrointestinal side 
effects, but overall adverse events were similar for all four medica­
tions. Severe hypoglycemia was rare but did occur significantly 
more often with glimepiride than the other agents. Weight gain 
was greater with glimepiride and glargine. In this study of sub­
jects with early diabetes, there was no significant difference in 
microvascular outcomes among the four medication groups.378 
The differences between the agents in this study were informative 
but not definitive in directing therapy after metformin. Unfortu­
nately, SGLT2 inhibitors were not FDA approved at study initia­
tion and therefore were not included in the study. 
Considerations in Personalizing Therapy
As noted, personalizing drug therapy beyond traditional use of 
metformin, sulfonylureas, and basal insulin is increasingly com­
mon and appropriate. Any of the classes of agents may be favored 
as second-line therapy when there are specific reasons to do 
so.46,48,177,379 The rationale for the choice of therapy should be 
discussed with the patient, especially in the case of the newest 
agents. This is where the details of personalized therapy become 
important.
Oral Agents Beyond Sulfonylureas and Injected 
Therapies Other Than Insulin
The DPP4 inhibitors, the TZD pioglitazone, and long-acting 
GLP1 agonists are often used in combination with metformin. 
The glucose-lowering effect of DPP4 inhibitors is less than that 
of sulfonylureas, but they are unlikely to cause hypoglycemia and 
have few symptomatic side effects.178,377,380 Pioglitazone is vari­
ably effective in controlling glucose and often causes weight gain 
and edema, among other side effects, but it improves peripheral 
insulin sensitivity and can reduce hepatic fat content in patients 
with NASH.381,382 It is most often prescribed in lower doses now

and the NASH studies have been performed with the 45 mg full 
dose. Fixed-dose combination formulations of metformin with a 
DPP4 inhibitor or pioglitazone can facilitate dosing.
The injectable GLP1 receptor agonists have proven to be 
equally effective as or more effective than basal insulin. In the 
GRADE study liraglutide had similar efficacy to basal insulin 
when added to metformin, but it is now recognized that the once-
weekly GLP1 agonists are generally more effective than liraglu­
tide.317,327,377 GLP1 receptor agonists are also associated with 
significant weight loss rather than weight gain and low rates of 
hypoglycemia. There is no dispute that in a patient known to have 
high cardiovascular risk, a GLP1 receptor agonist would be pre­
ferred over insulin (if there are no contraindications) because of 
the cardiovascular protection shown in multiple cardiovascular 
outcome trials.335,383 However, they often cause gastrointestinal 
symptoms. Use of the long-acting GLP1 receptor agonist agents 
with once-weekly dosing improves convenience and may improve 
long-term adherence. Oral semaglutide is an option to GLP1 
receptor agonist injections but is not better in terms of glucose 
lowering or tolerance profile. Although separate CVOTs for the 
oral product are not available, it is expected that this agent would 
yield similar cardiovascular protection.
Fixed-dose combinations of basal insulin with GLP1 recep­
tor agonists have been proposed as initial injectable therapy, and 
while they are reliably effective in reducing glucose the selection 
of proper doses and the titration process itself require specialized 
skills.384,385 Because the mechanism of action of GLP1 agonists is 
similar to that of DPP4 inhibitors, the latter should be discontin­
ued when an injected GLP1 receptor agonist is started.
Following the studies showing cardiovascular benefits with 
empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and canagliflozin, early use of an 
SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended for patients with established 
cardiovascular disease, especially when heart failure has been diag­
nosed or suspected. However, the glucose-lowering effect of these 
agents is only moderate.257,386,387
Basal Insulin
Uniquely among the classes of glucose-lowering therapies, use 
of insulin must always be personalized. The need to personalize 
dosing of insulin is driven by both physiologic and behavioral 
factors. The strategy of adding and optimizing basal insulin after 
failure of agents other than insulin, before progressing to basal-
bolus insulin, is well established.388 Some practitioners prefer 
to stop oral glucose-lowering agents when insulin is started, 
especially when using twice-daily premixed insulin, but most 
continue oral therapy while adding NPH or a long-acting ana­
logue as basal insulin. Delays in the initiation of basal insulin 
as well as its appropriate titration over time and the progression 
beyond basal insulin have all been characterized as clinical iner­
tia, though the phenomenon is not necessarily unique to advanc­
ing to insulin therapy.390,391
Personalization of basal insulin applies particularly to the dose 
required. The necessary daily dosage ranges between 10 and 200 
units, and a given patient’s requirement must be determined by 
titrating to a fasting glucose target. Treatment can be started either 
with a fixed daily dose of 10 units or with a dose calculated as 
0.1 to 0.2 units per kilogram body weight.46,48 Dosage should be 
increased at regular intervals, guided by SMBG or CGM before 
breakfast. Various titration schemes can be used with equal suc­
cess.392 Once-weekly titration by 2 to 4 units is commonly used, 
as is daily titration by a single unit every day until a target level 
of fasting glucose is attained. For patients continuing metformin 
alone or with one additional oral agent, a typical dose of basal 
insulin required to approach the fasting glucose target is 0.4 to 0.5 
units per kilogram, but with wide variation between patients. In 
many clinical trials the titration target has been set at 100 mg/dL 
(5.5 mmol/L) or less, and early in the natural history of T2D this 
is often attainable with little or no risk of hypoglycemia. However, 
when insulin is started after HbA1c levels have increased to above 
8% (63.9 mmol/mol), an initial target of less than 120 mg/dL 
(6.7 mmol/L) is safer and more realistic. The glucose goals and 
the importance of titration must be emphasized at each visit as it 
has been shown that patients often do not remember the initial 
instructions in basal insulin dosing.393 In most cases a patient-
directed titration is safe and effective, even to fasting goals below 
100 mg/dL.394 Fig. 34.5 illustrates the responses of fasting glucose 
and HbA1c to this approach to starting basal insulin with use of 
human NPH versus insulin glargine when one or two oral agents 
are insufficient.81 A stable level of fasting glucose can often be 
attained after 12 weeks of careful titration, with HbA1c levels lag­
ging slightly behind as expected. Failure to maintain HbA1c at 
the individualized target despite use of a regimen that includes 
properly titrated basal insulin calls for attention to postprandial 
hyperglycemia. 
Treating Postprandial Hyperglycemia
Hyperglycemic exposure in untreated T2D is quantitatively due 
more to overnight and between-meal (basal) hyperglycemia than 
to postprandial elevations. The predominance of basal hyper­
glycemia is more pronounced when overall control is poor and 
HbA1c is above 8.0% (63.9 mmol/mol).395 Fortunately, most 
glucose-lowering therapies are more effective in controlling basal 
hyperglycemia than limiting postprandial increments. Specifi­
cally, metformin, the long-acting secretagogues, basal insulin, 
DPP4 inhibitors, long-acting GLP1 agonists, and SGLT inhibi­
tors have greater basal than postprandial effects. After initial 
therapy with one or several of these agents, most of the residual 
glycemic exposure is postprandial.396 As β-cell function declines 
over time, postprandial hyperglycemia becomes more prominent 
and maintaining HbA1c in a target range becomes more difficult. 
After therapy of basal glucose has been optimized, the postpran­
dial glucose excursion is generally highest after breakfast and the 
highest postprandial glucose is after dinner.397 At this stage of 
T2D, which commonly is reached by 10 years from diagnosis, 
further therapy targeting postprandial control is needed, and 
always requires an individualized approach. Use of prandial 
therapies demands consideration of the patient’s eating habits, 
and these can differ markedly between individuals and in each 
patient from day to day.
In addition to dietary strategies—more frequent but smaller 
meals and selection of foods that are absorbed less rapidly and 
have less tendency to increase glucose—several drugs can be help­
ful. The short-acting secretagogues modestly limit postprandial 
increments of glucose when taken at low dosage two or three times 
a day with meals.209,398 The AGIs reduce postprandial hypergly­
cemia significantly and have favorable effects on weight, but their 
use is often limited by gastrointestinal side effects.
Short-acting insulins are more effective and are the most widely 
used approach. Adding a single injection of short-acting insulin 
(at the morning meal or at the largest meal) is just as effective as 
basal-bolus therapy at this stage, and less likely to cause weight 
gain or hypoglycemia.399–401 Initial dosage for the first prandial 
injection can be 4 units or 10% of the daily basal dose, with 
1380
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
systematic titration upward by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% twice 
weekly, aiming for glucose before the next meal (or at bedtime if 
the dose is before dinner) approaching 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L; 
target range 80–130 mg/dL, 4.4–7.2 mmol/L).46 When pran­
dial insulin is added to basal insulin with continuation of one or 
more oral agents, optimal control often requires total daily insulin 
doses greater than 1 unit per kilogram of body weight daily. In the 
typical patient with insulin-resistant T2D, there is usually little 
advantage to splitting basal insulin into two injections. As with 
basal-bolus insulin therapy in T1D, close monitoring and effec­
tive DSMES are needed. CGM is appropriate for those on three 
or more injections per day.
While adding prandial insulin remains a common practice 
when basal insulin is not adequately effective in T2D, adding 
a GLP1 receptor agonist while continuing basal insulin is pre­
ferred if one is not already in use. The shorter-acting drugs in this 
class have the greater postprandial effect, but the longer-acting 
ones—despite having less ability to control postprandial glucose 
excursions—may improve overall control sufficiently to equal 
the effect of added prandial insulin. Compared with addition of 
prandial insulin, addition of a GLP1 receptor agonist has essen­
tially the same advantages as previously mentioned when deciding 
between basal insulin and a GLP1 agonist: less glucose monitor­
ing is required, hypoglycemia is less likely, and weight gain will be 
avoided.402 It is important to remember that patients can be “over­
basalized” with titration of long-acting insulin, especially when a 
GLP1 receptor agonist or prandial insulin is added. The resulting 
tendency for glucose to drop overnight is a problem that can be 
exposed when the additional agent is started, leading to nocturnal 
hypoglycemia. It may be prudent to reduce the basal insulin dose 
if the HbA1c is below 8.0% (63.9 mmol/mol) when another agent 
is added. 
Examples of Personalized Choices of Therapy
Table 34.6 illustrates specific ways in which personalized choices 
of therapy may be applied.
Minimizing Cardiovascular Risks
Evidence supporting cardiovascular risk reduction established 
metformin as the fundamental therapy for T2D, although car­
diovascular benefit may take many years to manifest.38,403 The 
FDA requirement starting in 2008 for cardiovascular outcome 
trials in order to show safety has led to clear findings of cardio­
vascular benefit for GLP1 receptor agonists and SGLT inhibitors 
in patients with known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or 
very high risk.335,404 Although there has been some variability of 
specific outcomes in the different trials, the overall benefits have 
been reasonably consistent leading to strong expert recommenda­
tions for use of these agents (see Tables 34.10 and 34.13).46,259 For 
patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease without heart 
failure either class is recommended. However, the GLP1 receptor 
agonists have greater efficacy for HbA1c reduction and may have 
some unique benefit for stroke prevention and possibly major 
adverse limb events.335,405,406
In patients with heart failure, SGLT2 inhibitors have dem­
onstrated superiority over GLP1 receptor agonists and are now 
the preferred agents.46,48,262 It is still uncertain whether ben­
efits of these two classes of drugs for these conditions can be 
extrapolated to all drugs in each class, and whether primary 
protection against cardiovascular or renal events will be found 
in the larger numbers of T2D patients with relatively low car­
diovascular risk. In the GRADE study, liraglutide treatment was 
associated with a statistically significant 30% lower rate of any 
cardiovascular events compared to the other three agents studied 
in a population with low levels of known cardiovascular disease 
at baseline.378 However, the event rates were low and this is not 
sufficient support for a recommendation to use GLP1 receptor 
agonists in primary prevention.
Sulfonylureas and insulin have been suspected of increasing 
cardiovascular risk. Although direct evidence supporting this 
contention is weak, the availability of other agents providing gly­
cemic control allows these classes to be moved down the priority 
list for patients with known cardiovascular disease. It seems espe­
cially desirable to avoid use of prandial insulin, which is much 
more likely to cause weight gain and hypoglycemia than basal 
insulin. Pioglitazone could be considered a third-line option 
in those with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. It increases 
the risk of heart failure in susceptible patients but it has shown 
some benefit for prevention of myocardial infarction and isch­
emic stroke and has a place in therapy of those with diabetes
