Reducing Progression of Kidney Disease
Chronic kidney disease affects 30% to 40% of individuals with 
T2D. The incidence of diabetes-related ESRD is increasing glob­
ally while other complications seem to be decreasing.11,266 Angio­
tensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin-receptor 
blockers have been a mainstay of renal protection aimed at reducing 
progression of the disease. Finerenone is a recently approved min­
eralocorticoid receptor blocker that is useful in slowing the decline 
of kidney function. However, CVOTs helped bring to light the 
renal benefits of medications initially developed to reduce glucose 
in T2D. The greatest benefit is seen with SGLT2 inhibitors where 
improvement in secondary renal endpoints such as albuminuria, 
doubling of serum creatinine, or a composite of 40% decline in 
eGFR, ESRD, and death were observed.266,408 This benefit has 
subsequently been shown in diabetes patients without cardiovas­
cular disease and also in those with chronic kidney disease but 
without diabetes. Various renal endpoints have been evaluated in 
multiple trials and 30% to 50% improvements in kidney measure 
versus comparators are consistently observed.264,266 Although the 
glucose-lowering ability of SGLT2 inhibitors is diminished with 
lower eGFRs, the benefits for chronic kidney disease and cardio­
vascular protection are seen across a wide range of baseline eGFR 
values. SGLT2 inhibitors are therefore strongly recommended for 
those with diabetes and chronic kidney disease. GLP1 receptor 
agonists have also been shown to have renal benefits in those with 
diabetes and chronic kidney disease, but the degree of improve­
ment is not as significant as seen with SGLT2 inhibitors.335,339,409 
Minimizing Hypoglycemia
Hypoglycemia is of concern for reasons beyond its possible contri­
bution to cardiovascular events. Older patients with a long dura­
tion of diabetes, especially those who have cognitive impairment 
or nephropathy, have greater risk of hypoglycemia-related falls or 
other injuries.203,410,411 Fear of hypoglycemia can limit attain­
ment of even conservative glycemic treatment goals, either due 
to therapeutic inertia on the part of the provider or incomplete 
adherence by the patient. A prior history of hypoglycemia requir­
ing assistance by another person is a strong risk factor for future 
hypoglycemia. When these considerations apply, therapeutic tac­
tics should be adjusted to avoid hypoglycemia. Metformin does 
not cause hypoglycemia when used alone, and drug choices after 
metformin with little or no additional risk include DPP4 inhibi­
tors, GLP1 receptor agonists, SGLT inhibitors, GLP1/GIP dual 
agonists, and TZDs.46,49,412,413 Combination therapy using these 
agents could provide considerable glucose lowering with little risk 
of hypoglycemia. Should insulin eventually become necessary, the 
newer long-acting insulins will cause the lowest risk of hypogly­
cemia. Finally, prior occurrence of severe hypoglycemia may be 
sufficient reason to increase the HbA1c target range from 7% to 
8% (from 53.0 to 63.9 mmol/mol) or even higher. 
Minimizing Weight Gain
Weight gain associated with the treatment of diabetes is of con­
cern to most clinicians and is often an overriding issue for some 
patients. A strategy to minimize weight gain emphasizes diet and 
exercise and employs metformin as initial therapy. The GLP1 
receptor agonists, GIP/GLP1 dual agonist, and SGLT inhibi­
tors are all options as second-line therapy when weight is a major 
consideration. Tirzepatide, the GIP/GLP1 dual agonist, may have 
the greatest weight loss potential at this time followed by long-
acting GLP1 receptor agonists, especially semaglutide. Surgical 
procedures that lead to both weight loss and improved glycemic 
control are beyond the scope of this chapter (see Chapter 40), but 
are highly effective treatments that appear to have greater benefit 
than medical therapy.45,414,415 Because of their tendency to cause 
weight gain, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, and prandial insulin are 
less desirable. Basal insulin is less likely to cause weight gain than 
prandial insulin and can be included in the regimen when neces­
sary to maintain glucose control.
Minimizing Costs
For many patients, including large populations in developing 
countries and individuals with inadequate insurance coverage in 
developed countries, the cost of drugs limits management of dia­
betes. Despite the effectiveness of newer agents in clinical trials 
where they are provided free of charge, no therapy is successful 
when it is unaffordable. Fortunately, diet and exercise can be effec­
tive and are almost cost free. The least expensive drugs for the 
treatment of diabetes are metformin, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, 
AGIs, and human insulin. There can be marked differences in 
price between regions and between pharmacies, and websites are 
available to find the best prices.416 In the case of insulin, there 
is a name brand of human regular, NPH, and 70/30 premixed 
human insulin (ReliOn) that is generally available in the United 
States for approximately 10% of the list price of analogue insu­
lins. Human insulin remains an effective option for treatment of 
T2D, although its use may require twice-daily dosing of NPH, 
more consistent timing of meals, and slightly higher HbA1c targets 
(e.g., 7.5%–8.0%, 58.5–63.9 mmol/mol) to limit hypoglycemia. 
A statement by the World Health Organization has endorsed these 
considerations for treatment of T2D in low-resource settings.417 
Special Situations in Clinical Management
In addition to the principles of treatment described for most T2D 
patients in the usual ambulatory setting, some specific therapeutic 
challenges deserve further comment.
Severe Hyperglycemia at Diagnosis
Some patients have very poor glycemic control when first diag­
nosed with T2D, and may even have ketoacidosis.418 Those who 
are especially ill, with serious dehydration, acidosis, impaired 
mental status, or serious concomitant illness, will need hospital­
ization to receive intravenous fluids and insulin. Some will recover 
remarkably after in-hospital treatment, with substantial recovery 
of insulin secretion and tissue responsiveness to insulin. Those 
with the best metabolic recovery may maintain good glycemic 
control with lifestyle management and little or no oral therapy. 
How such patients differ from those who continue to need routine 
oral therapy or insulin is not entirely clear, but they have been 
described as having ketosis-prone diabetes.419
Many other patients will be diagnosed when they have poor 
glycemic control, with HbA1c above 10% (85.8 mmol/mol) and 
random glucose values over 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L) or with 
catabolic symptoms of weight loss, weakness, and severe fatigue 
but without acidosis. It is always important to look for the occa­
sional patient who has been drinking large amounts of sugar-
sweetened beverages where cessation of that practice can make a 
dramatic difference. However, for most patients presenting with 
1382
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
these very high glucose levels, most experts recommend initial 
insulin therapy.46 Intensive glycemic management in this setting 
may also lead to remission of diabetes by reversal of gluco-lipotox­
icity in a number of patients.420,421 After 2 to 4 weeks of treatment 
with oral combination therapy, basal insulin, or basal plus pran­
dial insulin aiming for nearly normal glucose levels, HbA1c levels 
below 6.5% or 7.0% (47.5 or 53.0 mmol/mol) may persist for 
up to a year, even if pharmacotherapy is completely withdrawn. 
These proof-of-principle studies have not led to recommendations 
for this approach routinely in newly diagnosed T2D, but they do 
suggest that temporary use of insulin to attain excellent glycemic 
control soon after diagnosis is appropriate for some patients. It 
has also been proposed that those with very high HbA1c at diag­
nosis, especially if accompanied by symptoms, could also be 
treated immediately with dual or triple therapy that may include 
basal insulin.49 Multiple-drug combinations without insulin may 
reduce HbA1c to target levels more consistently than the single-
agent approach and may have greater durability than the usual 
single-step approach.422–424 Surprisingly, even initial treatment 
with a sulfonylurea alone or in combination with basal insulin can 
have good efficacy in newly diagnosed patients presenting to an 
emergency department.425,426 Although GLP1 receptor agonists 
could be very effective in some patients with very high glucose 
levels at diagnosis, the very long action and need to titrate the 
doses slowly due to gastrointestinal side effects limit their desir­
ability as initial treatment in the setting of marked hyperglycemia. 
However, independent of the regimen used, rapid reduction of 
HbA1c in patients who have had many months of poor control 
has potential risks. Aside from the risk of hypoglycemia from use 
of insulin by relatively inexperienced patients, there is potential 
for worsening of retinopathy or neuropathy accompanying overly 
rapid reduction of glucose. As a general rule, patients diagnosed 
with HbA1c above 9% (74.9 mmol/mol) who are found to have 
retinopathy should seek a gradual improvement of control with 
HbA1c below 7.0% (53.0 mmol/mol) within 6 months, with con­
tinuation of at least metformin after that. 
Type 2 Diabetes in Youth
The worldwide increase of obesity has led to diagnosis of T2D in 
susceptible individuals at earlier ages than in the past. One con­
sequence of this is an alarming increase of onset below age 20 
years, particularly in racial and ethnic minority groups.13,427 In 
some regions, the incidence of T2D in children is approaching 
that of T1D. Studies of T2D in adolescence demonstrate severe 
insulin resistance and initially high levels of insulin secretion, but 
a relatively rapid decline of β-cell function that is not slowed by 
metformin therapy.428,429 At present there is still limited evidence 
how youths with T2D can be best managed, but it is clear that sig­
nificant effort to improve dietary and exercise patterns is needed 
for both prevention and treatment.430 Attention must be given to 
age and cultural considerations in dietary recommendations, and 
family involvement is crucial. For most, a reasonable treatment 
goal is to attain an HbA1c below 7.0% (53 mmol/mol), but there 
are exceptions. As in adults, treatment of T2D in young patients 
may begin with metformin. However, if blood glucose measure­
ments are over 250 mg/dL (19.4 mmol/L) fasting or HbA1c is 
over 8.5% (69.4 mmol/mol), it is most reasonable to start with 
basal insulin as well as metformin. If the child is acidotic or highly 
symptomatic, it is usually appropriate to start with basal bolus 
insulin therapy.431,432 Liraglutide is approved for children over age 
10 years and has proven effective as add-on therapy.433 While the 
ability of weekly GLP1 receptor agonists to conveniently control 
both glucose and weight suggests these agents may become an 
important option, their use in this setting is at present off-label. 
In those with youth-onset T2D there is high risk of complications 
early in adulthood and initial attention to preventive approaches 
for complications is critical. 
Pregnancy
Management of diabetes during pregnancy is beyond the scope 
of this chapter. However, because it is centrally important in the 
natural history of T2D some important features must be men­
tioned. Women with risk factors for diabetes often first develop 
overt hyperglycemia during pregnancy, otherwise known as ges­
tational diabetes mellitus (GD). After delivery, some continue to 
have sufficient hyperglycemia to justify the diagnosis of T2D, but 
more revert to having normal glucose levels. For the latter group, 
the risk of reappearance of hyperglycemia consistent with the 
diagnosis of T2D in the absence of pregnancy is 50% to 70% after 
15 to 25 years, a risk that is increased 10- to 18-fold.434,435 Con­
sequently, periodic follow-up with testing of glucose or HbA1c 
is indicated every 1 to 3 years to allow early detection. In addi­
tion to signaling a high risk of future development of diabetes, 
GD poses more immediate risks to both mother and child. The 
likelihood of complicated delivery or neonatal complications is 
greatly increased by GD. Furthermore, children with exposure to 
hyperglycemia in utero have increased risk of later obesity and/
or T2D.436 This risk appears to be attenuated by good maternal 
glycemic control during gestation. Preconception counseling of 
women at high risk, routine screening for GDM during preg­
nancy, careful management of hyperglycemia during pregnancy, 
and systematic follow-up after delivery should be part of routine 
clinical practice. For women of childbearing age who already have 
diabetes, preconception planning and gestational management are 
even more urgently needed, especially to limit the risk of fetal 
malformations resulting from poor glycemic control in the first 
10 weeks of pregnancy. Glucose targets during gestation are lower 
than advised in routine management of T2D. The recommended 
target ranges are <95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L) for fasting glucose, 
<140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) for 1-hour postprandial glucose, and 
<120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L) for 2-hour postprandial glucose and 
an HbA1c under 6.0% (42.1 mmol/mol).437 Careful nutritional 
therapy is essential, and additional treatment with insulin is often 
needed. Metformin and the sulfonylurea glyburide are sometimes 
used instead of insulin, but there are concerns about their safety, 
particularly with sulfonylureas.438 For women with preexisting 
T2D, insulin therapy is generally recommended during gestation. 
Whenever possible, an experienced specialized team should assist 
in management of diabetes during pregnancy. 
Preventing Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
The possibility that T2D can be prevented in high-risk persons 
has been formally tested in a series of clinical trials reviewed else­
where. Lifestyle intervention can provide a 30% to 60% reduction 
in progression to diabetes over a 3- to 5-year time frame. This ben­
efit is sustained and correlates with weight loss. However, the aver­
age sustained weight loss in these trials was modest, on the order 
of 5%.439–441 Intervention with metformin was associated with a 
somewhat smaller reduction in progression to diabetes, although 
the benefit was similar to that of lifestyle in persons younger than 
60 years of age, those with BMI greater than 35 kg/m2, those 
1383
CHAPTER 34  Therapeutics of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
with a FPG level greater than 110 mg/dL (6.1 mmol/L) or an 
HbA1c ≥6.0%, and those with previous gestational diabetes.191,192 
Metformin had less effect in patients older than 60 years of age, 
those with a BMI of less than 30 kg/m2, and those with a FPG of 
less than 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L). Metformin’s ability to reduce 
progression to diabetes has been shown to be durable and cost 
effective.442
Acarbose has also been shown to reduce progression to diabetes, 
without evidence of diminished efficacy in different subgroups. 
The TZDs provide sustained improvement of insulin sensitivity 
and can delay onset of diabetes. However, concern regarding pos­
sible long-term effects on weight, heart, and bones has limited 
the use of this class for prevention. GLP1 receptor agonists have 
also shown promise, but the expense and initial adverse effects 
preclude their promotion for this indication at present. Bariatric 
surgery has also been shown to reduce incident diabetes in more 
severely obese patients.
The success of the lifestyle interventions is impressive, showing 
that by using various techniques at-risk individuals can achieve 
physiologically relevant changes in body weight. It is unknown 
whether lifestyle plus medications provides even greater benefit. 
It seems reasonable to screen on the basis of the recommenda­
tions outlined earlier, while recognizing that patients with pre­
diabetes (HbA1c >5.7% and particularly ≥6%, FPG ≥100 mg/
dL [5.6 mmol/L] and particularly ≥110 mg/dL [6.1 mmol/L], or 
impaired glucose tolerance) are the best candidates for preventive 
strategies.443 High-risk persons should be counseled about nutri­
tional approaches to weight loss, instructed to increase physical 
activity, and monitored for progression of dysglycemia. Transla­
tion of the evidence found in the Diabetes Prevention Program 
(DPP) study to practical expansion across the United States has 
been evolving through the CDC’s National Diabetes Prevention 
Program. The program includes a structured curriculum of 22 ses­
sions over a year in a group setting or online programs delivered 
through a diverse group of public and private organizations. Each 
local program is certified through the CDC’s Diabetes Prevention 
Recognition Program to maintain standards, promote utilization, 
and document outcomes. Providers must increase identification 
of those with prediabetes or other high-risk characteristics and 
direct patients to the programs available in the community.444,445 
The status of drug therapy, notably with metformin, is less clear, 
in part because significant diabetes complications are unlikely 
to develop in the relatively short window of time during which 
fasting glucose levels increase from 100 to 126 mg/dL (5.6–7.0 
mmol/L). On the other hand, metformin therapy brings little risk 
and offers substantial benefit for some individuals, notably those 
with BMI ≥35 kg/m2, those under age 60 years, and women with 
previous gestational diabetes.52 On balance, therefore, consider­
ation of metformin therapy is recommended in patients who are 
at particularly high risk. 
Future Directions
Present-day management of T2D is significantly more effective 
and easier for patients than in the past. In addition to a better 
understanding of nutritional principles and various approaches to 
prevention of complications, glucose-lowering medications have 
become available that reduce weight, require less frequent dosing, 
avoid hypoglycemia, and directly reduce complications such as 
major cardiac events and kidney disease.
Development of new drugs with new mechanisms of action 
continues with expectations of expanded efficacy, safety, and 
nonglycemic benefits, including reduction of microvascular and 
macrovascular complications and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. 
Dozens of novel compounds are in early-phase studies. These med­
ications include categories that offer improved glucose-dependent 
insulin secretion from the β-cell, alteration of the incretin axis, 
modulation of hepatic glucose production, and enhanced insu­
lin sensitivity.446 Detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this 
chapter. Some agents may not make it from discovery to clinical 
use. For example, glucokinase is an active enzyme in both the liver 
and β-cells. Glucokinase activators have shown increased insulin 
secretion but may cause liver toxicity in addition to relatively fre­
quent hypoglycemia. Lower doses are being explored, and efforts 
are underway to get more β-cell specificity with this class. The 
potential for incretin variations is demonstrated with the arrival of 
tirzepatide, a GIP/GLP1 dual agonist. It is likely that other dual 
and triple agonists will be developed such as GLP1-glucagon dual 
receptor agonists or GLP1-GIP-glucagon triple agonists. Oxynto­
modulin is a peptide secreted by enteroendocrine cells of the small 
intestine and can activate both GLP1 and glucagon receptors, 
providing another method of dual hormone action. Adiponectin 
is secreted by adipocytes and improves insulin sensitivity in liver 
and muscle, presenting a pathway for drug development. Imegli­
min has shown an ability to both increase insulin secretion and 
enhance insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle. Finally, develop­
ment of glucose-responsive insulin products covering both basal 
and prandial requirements with a single injection continues to 
progress.312,447 These are but a few of the possible future advances 
in pharmacologic therapy of T2D and add to the present tools 
that advance precision therapy as parallel advances in biomarker 
identification, phenotyping, and pharmacogenetics occur.446,448
Additionally, smart devices for tracking glucose levels and 
lifestyle measures as well as methods of medication delivery 
that make therapy more convenient will evolve. Evaluating 
impact and integrating new tools will be a challenge. Notable 
unmet needs remain, such as controlling glucose after meals and 
maintaining metabolic control during acute illness and hospi­
talization. However, it can be argued that the main limitation 
of therapy at present is not a lack of tools and treatments, but 
a variety of economic, psychological, and organizational barri­
ers to using them to full advantage.449 Practical, cost-effective 
public health approaches are needed to slow the increase in 
incidence and prevalence of T2D. Screening for diabetes or 
prediabetes may be cost-saving and should be made more effi­
cient. Globally, there continues to be inequality in access to 
medical care for all conditions, including diabetes. Although 
the prognosis for people with diabetes has never been better, 
the greatest challenges they face relate to the complexity and 
cost of care. If both the means of managing diabetes and the 
organizational structure of health systems are improved simul­
taneously, the morbidity and mortality of T2D may be greatly 
reduced in the near future.

KEY POINTS
 • 
Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D) is a disorder resulting from islet 
dysfunction and chronic autoimmune destruction of the insulin-
producing pancreatic β-cells.
 • 
Worldwide, the incidence of T1D is increasing by 2% to 5% per 
year, especially in underdeveloped nations.
 • 
More than half of genetic disease susceptibility for T1D is 
provided by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), yet 
the disorder is clearly polygenic; these genes/loci have been 
combined into a “genetic risk score” (GRS) to identify a given 
individual’s genetic predisposition to this disease.
 • 
The risk for the disease can be ascertained through a 
combination of immunologic, genetic, and metabolic markers 
of disease, with the natural history now defined by a series of 
“stages.”
 • 
There is a growing appreciation that T1D, rather than being 
a singular disease, may be a heterogeneous disorder with a 
common phenotype at clinical presentation/diagnosis.
 • 
The pancreas of T1D patients possesses an islet immune 
infiltrate derived from a variety of immunologic phenotypes, 
is smaller in size and of lower weight, and also has reduced 
exocrine function.
 • 
Diagnosis of T1D is a medical emergency, both for the 
avoidance of adverse outcomes (diabetic ketoacidosis [DKA] 
being all too often present at diagnosis, with morbidity and 
mortality, particularly in the young) and to allow participation 
of people with newly diagnosed T1D in research-based 
interventions to protect remaining β-cells.
 • 
Care for people with T1D builds on integrated approaches 
by multidisciplinary teams, where structured diabetes 
education, provided by certified educators, elevates the 
person living with T1D to an integral member of the disease 
management team. Exercise guidance and nutritional and 
psychological support should be offered to all living with 
T1D.
 • 
Significant advances in terms of disease management, afforded 
by technologic innovations related to insulin analogues, 
advanced diabetes technologies, and more, set the foundation 
for marked reductions in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), enhanced 
diabetes care, and improved biomedical and psychosocial 
outcomes. This said, those with T1D still have a reduced life 
expectancy of about 10 years, especially when diagnosed at a 
young age.
 • 
Although there have been many advances in the 
management of T1D, this disease remains associated with 
many lifestyle changes, in addition to acute and chronic 
complications, affecting quality of life and even life 
expectancy.
 • 
Recent advances in immunotherapies and cellular therapeutics 
(both immune and metabolic) are poised to dramatically impact 
treatment of this disease.

CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
Introduction
Where to begin to tell the story of the disorder we now refer to 
as type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D) represents somewhat of a liter­
ary challenge. Does one begin with the earliest writings scripted 
thousands of years ago conveying the disease’s symptoms, or is it 
more fitting to describe exciting works performed in the 1800s 
and early 1900s that defined both the anatomy of and physiologic 
roles for the pancreas and insulin-secreting β-cells?1 Other pieces 
of literature initiate their narrative on T1D by sharing an account 
of the fast-paced and ultimately Nobel Prize–winning efforts in 
the 1920s by Banting and Best,2 when the ability to purify insulin 
from animal pancreata brought forward a means to sustain life to 
those who, in the absence of such an intervention, met an early 
demise. Indeed, in 2021, a series of articles highlighted a centen­
nial of efforts in diabetes care that built on this discovery.3–7
We have elected to begin this chapter by building on the story 
of a German pathologist named Martin Schmidt,8 who, in 1902, 
noted a small peri-islet cellular infiltrate on microscopic evalua­
tion of the pancreas obtained at autopsy from a 10-year-old child 
with diabetes. This effort represented a key early investigation 
seeking to better define the pathogenesis of the disorder, a pro­
cess that was continued by many over the ensuing century. Works 
shortly thereafter by Shields Warren9 in the 1920s drew attention 
to the relationship between this infiltrate and the age of diabe­
tes onset. The term used to define this pancreatic feature, insu­
litis, was coined in 1940 by yet another pathologist, Hanns von 
Meyenburg.10 Studies of pancreatic disease over ensuing decades 
taught us much regarding this inflammatory lesion, including its 
relative infrequency in older individuals diagnosed with diabetes, 
its association with reduction in β-cell mass, the identification of 
pseudoatrophic islets (i.e., islets devoid of insulin-containing cells), 
a preferential targeting of insulitis for β-cells containing insulin, 
and many other findings eventually deemed seminal.11,12 These 
conditions, when joined together with immunologic and genetic 
studies of living patients in the 1970s noting the presence of self-
reactive antibodies (i.e., autoantibodies) against islet cells in per­
sons with T1D and that disease susceptibility was associated with 
major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules known to 
influence immune system functions, formed three lines of evi­
dence pointing to an autoimmune basis for T1D.13 Built on this 
foundation, this chapter will share current views on the natural 
history and pathogenesis of T1D; emerging views on genetics, dis­
ease biomarkers, and epidemiology; increased information on the 
contribution of β-cells, potentially α-cells, and the exocrine pan­
creas to the disease; continuing challenges of disease-associated 
complications; emerging methods of disease management; and 
importantly, how advances in research are poised to change the 
way T1D is treated and perhaps even prevented. 
Natural History of Type 1 Diabetes
Perhaps the most helpful and beneficial guide to studies pertaining 
to the natural history of T1D was the model put forward in 1986 
by a previous author of this chapter, the late Dr. George Eisen­
barth.14 In this model (Fig. 35.1), persons destined to develop 
T1D were assumed to begin life with a full cadre of β-cells. A 
triggering insult, likely environmental, was proposed to initiate 
a process involving recruitment of antigen-presenting cells. The 
antigen-presenting cells would sequester self-antigens released by 
injured β-cells, followed by their transport to pancreatic lymph 
nodes, where they are subsequently presented to autoreactive

T cells. These T cells, rogue constituents brought to life because 
of genetically driven failures of thymic deletion (i.e., central toler­
ance), combined with defects in mechanisms designed to induce 
peripheral immune tolerance, would come into play.15 This toxic 
duo imparting lack of tolerance formation, again in the context 
of genetic susceptibility, would allow for migration of self-reactive 
T cells to islets, mediating β-cell killing and promoting further 
inflammation.16 Symptoms of the disease were thought to appear 
when 85% to 90% of pancreatic β-cells had met their demise. In 
the final stage of the model, the autoimmune process ends with 
the complete elimination of β-cells. Although this model faith­
fully served as a guide for multiple decades, and certainly, the 
majority of its aspects hold true to this day, some constituents are 
under states of correction (e.g., the aforementioned notion that 
C-peptide production is lost in T1D at onset, as demonstrated 
using newer C-peptide assays with accurate lower levels of detec­
tion) or are still subject to intense investigation—facets that will 
be discussed throughout this chapter. 
Epidemiology
Disease Incidence and Prevalence
The highest known incidence of T1D is observed in Finland and 
Sardinia. Finland now has an annual incidence approaching 60 per 
100,000 children.17 Since the 1950s, the incidence has increased 
almost fivefold, suggesting a dramatic environmental change 
(either an increase of causative factors or a decrease of protective 
factors), and it is doubling in many Western countries, including 
the United States, every 10 to 15 years (Fig. 35.2). Of note, the 
increased T1D incidence in many countries has not been linear 
but rather fluctuating over the past several decades. In contrast, 
the disorder is quite uncommon in China, India, and Venezuela 
(∼0.1 per 100,000 per year).
In the United States, the risk of childhood diabetes is approxi­
mately 1 in 300.18 This risk is 15 times lower than the diabetes 
risk for a first-degree relative of a patient with T1D (Table 35.1), 
which, in turn, is 150 times lower than the risk for a monozygotic 
twin of a patient with T1D.19 Although the risk of diabetes is much 
greater for relatives of patients with T1D, it is important to real­
ize that most persons (>85%) in whom T1D develops do not have 
a first-degree relative with the disease. The incidence of sporadic 
cases results, in part, because almost 40% of persons in the general 
population carry high-risk human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles 
for T1D (see “The Major Histocompatibility Complex” section).

Studies From Long-Term Family and Population Studies
Many major longitudinal clinical epidemiologic studies of T1D 
were initiated between 1989 and 2004, including BABYDIAB in 
Germany20; T1D Prediction and Prevention (DIPP) in Finland21; 
Diabetes Autoimmunity Study in the Young (DAISY) in Den­
ver, Colorado22; the Environmental Determinants of Diabetes in 
the Young (TEDDY) with U.S. sites in the states of Colorado, 
Georgia, Florida, and Washington, as well as European sites in 
Germany, Sweden, and Finland23; T1D TrialNet Pathway to Pre­
vention, with more than 200 locations across the United States, 
Europe, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand24; and the Search 
for Diabetes in Youth (SEARCH), with study centers in South 
Carolina, Ohio, Colorado, California, and Washington.25 More 
recently, driven by the European Innovative Medicines Initia­
tive, the INNODIA consortium initiated a natural history study 
of people newly diagnosed with T1D as well as unaffected fam­
ily members (www.innodia.eu).26 These efforts, together with 
cross-sectional investigation of human pancreas tissues obtained 
through biobanks, such as the Network for Pancreatic Organ 
donors with Diabetes (nPOD),27 have reshaped our understand­
ing of the natural history of T1D and human pancreas pathology, 
with some of the seminal findings reviewed in Table 35.2.
Although many concepts arising from these efforts could be 
noted, one pivotal discovery was made from combined analysis 
of data generated in the BABYDIAB, DAISY, and DIPP studies.

Namely, once two or more anti-islet autoantibodies are present in a 
given individual, the individual’s 10-year risk for developing diabetes 
ranges from 60% in older seroconverters (>3 years) to 75% in those 
who seroconvert before 3 years of age.28 Beyond this, recent and 
ongoing analyses of longitudinal data generated from the DIPP and 
TEDDY cohorts have unveiled a series of potential environmental 
influences (e.g., birth by cesarean section, gut microbiome, dietary 
fiber, early introduction of cow’s milk or gluten to an infant’s diet, 
vitamin D, antibiotic use in early life, vaccination, infections)29–35 
that may contribute to disease risk, as well as the identification of 
novel biomarkers (e.g., gut microbiome, metabolomics, lipidomic 
and proteomic profiles)36,37 indicative for eventual T1D progres­
sion (see the “Emerging Biomarkers of T1D Natural History and 
Diagnosis” section)38 that might ultimately enable identification of 
the disease early in its pathogenesis. Importantly, with such find­
ings, the hope is that prevention or delay of T1D onset may one day 
be possible through tailored intervention. 
Stages in the Natural History of Type 1 Diabetes
Whereas the etiology and precise mechanisms leading to T1D 
remain somewhat elusive, studies over the past 3 to 4 decades have 
generated, without question, a wealth of information—immu­
nologic, serologic, metabolic, or genetics based—regarding the 
natural history of early stages of T1D through the time of formal 
diagnosis.39 One example, as noted earlier, is that anti-islet auto­
immunity in the form of anti-islet autoantibodies, in the context 
of genetic susceptibility and metabolic assessments, is a predictive 
tool for progression to overt disease.28 Large international cohorts 
(e.g., TEDDY, Diabetes Prevention Trial Type 1 [DPT-1], DAISY, 
BabyDiab, INNODIA) in both relatives of patients with T1D and 
in the general population who are at high genetic risk have been 
studied26,40–43 to better understand the disease, reduce rates of 
diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) at diagnosis, decrease mortality, and 
set the stage for research efforts seeking T1D prevention. Indeed, 
these natural history studies often lead to earlier diagnosis of T1D 
and a reduced frequency of DKA at onset in those followed pro­
spectively.44 Several recent studies have also demonstrated long-
term glycemic benefits for those patients who did not experience 
the severe metabolic derangement of DKA at formal diagnosis.45
Although the diagnosis of diabetes has traditionally been based 
on American Diabetes Association (ADA) criteria,46 it is increas­
ingly clear that the actual onset of the disease per se generally

occurs months to years before the appearance of symptoms. Thus, 
T1D is a unique physiologic state where autoimmunity is pres­
ent, where progression to metabolic derangement and clinical 
onset can be predicted, especially in younger children and adoles­
cents. As such, the ADA, Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation 
(JDRF), and Endocrine Society released a joint position statement 
calling for the staging of pre-T1D47 (Fig. 35.3). Stage 1 is defined 
by the presence of two or more anti-islet autoantibodies with nor­
moglycemia (normal glucose tolerance on 2-hour oral glucose tol­
erance test [OGTT]). Stage 2 shows progression to dysglycemia 
(impaired glucose tolerance) in the setting of two or more anti-
islet autoantibodies. Stage 3 occurs when a patient meets ADA 
criteria for the diagnosis of diabetes.
Data collated from multiple large prospective natural his­
tory studies support screening for islet autoantibodies at 2 and 
7 years of age in children with high genetic risk for T1D as a 
public health measure40; this is based on long-standing research 
efforts addressing the feasibility and benefit of islet autoantibody 
screening in children and adolescents from the general popula­
tion.41–43 However, the risk of progressing to T1D varies widely 
according to age, autoantibody type, and the recently described 
Index60 value (calculated using C-peptide and glucose values 
at 60 minutes in the OGTT), factors that, among many, reflect 
fasting and stimulated C-peptide production as well as blood 
glucose levels48 (discussed in the “Emerging Biomarkers of 
T1D” section). Moreover, diagnosis of stage 3 T1D can occur 
in individuals with a single autoantibody, an observation that is 
typically associated with older age, greater capacity for C-pep­
tide production, higher homeostatic model assessment for insu­
lin resistance (HOMA-IR), and lower Index60,49 highlighting 
the heterogeneity of this disease (discussed in the “Heterogene­
ity” section).
To be clear, at present, there are no evidence-based recom­
mendations for practitioners caring for anti-islet autoantibody–
positive patients or for performing formal “T1D staging,” other 
than to encourage enrollment in research studies. Nonetheless, 
close monitoring of high-risk patients in natural history studies 
markedly reduces DKA rates at diagnosis,45 and when combined 
with the notion that partaking in research is critical to finding a 
means of preventing T1D, research participation in family mem­
bers of those with T1D should be encouraged. Yet only when 
an effective preventative strategy for T1D is identified will the 
notion of universal risk screening and T1D staging for all chil­
dren be considered justifiable. 
Type 1 Diabetes Genetic and Immunologic 
Heterogeneity by Age of Onset
T1D can develop at any age, from the neonatal period to the 
last decades of life.50,51 Those diagnosed at under 1 year of age 
should be screened for monogenetic causes of diabetes because 
treatments may differ (see Chapter 37, “Monogenetic Diabetes”). 
Given that identical twins can become concordant more than 40 
years after the first twin develops T1D, not all age heterogeneity 
can be ascribed to different genetic syndromes.52 Nevertheless, 
there is an overall correlation between the age at which diabetes 
develops in one twin or sibling and the age of development of 
diabetes in his or her relative. Children in whom T1D develops 
at an early age more often are DR3/4-DQ2/8 heterozygotes (see 
“The Major Histocompatibility Complex” section). In addition,

there is evidence that class I HLA alleles (or other non–class II 
genes within the HLA region) can influence the age at diabetes 
onset; an example is the A24 allele.53 At the other end of the 
age spectrum, there is evidence that the protective HLA allele 
DQA1*01:02-DQB1*06:02 is not as protective for young adults 
as it is for children.54
The most characteristic difference related to age at diabetes 
onset is the presence of higher levels of insulin autoantibodies 
(IAAs) in children who develop the disease at an early age (e.g., 
less than 5 years of age). The high levels and frequent positiv­
ity of IAA make measurement of these autoantibodies the best 
single marker for diabetes development in young children.55 In 
those children in whom autoantibodies arise during the first 3 
years of life, IAAs often (but not exclusively) appear first. In con­
trast, glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 autoantibodies (GADAs) 
are more often positive in adults who develop T1D, and again, in 
young children, they appear after IAAs. Beyond HLA-DR3 and 
GADA positivity, elevated body mass index (BMI) and HOMA-
IR are associated with disease progression in older individuals. 
Seroconversion to IAA or GADA as the first anti-islet autoanti­
body has also been linked to HLA.56 The correlation of levels of 
IAA and age at diabetes onset may be related to faster progres­
sion to diabetes in children with higher levels. However, such 
rapid progression occurs only if IAAs are present with another 
anti-islet autoantibody (discussed in the “Stages in the Natural 
History of T1D” section). 
Endotypes
Although initially considered controversial, increasing awareness 
of heterogeneous disease progression, presentation, and develop­
ment of complications has given rise to the notion of T1D “endo­
types.”57,58 This area remains subject to intense investigation and 
debate, with the majority of efforts focused on identifying observ­
able phenotypes (e.g., age at onset, HLA type) corresponding to 
distinct biological mechanisms that can be targeted therapeuti­
cally in an endotype-specific manner (i.e., personalized medicine) 
to delay or prevent progression of the disease. For this reason, 
extensive efforts are being directed at biomarker identification to 
guide personalized therapies targeting immune and/or β-cells in 
T1D stages 1 to 359 (discussed in the “Emerging Biomarkers of 
T1D” section). 
Pathophysiology
Histopathology
As noted earlier, T1D in humans is characterized by selective 
destruction of β-cells within the pancreatic islets (Fig. 35.4).7 
Although certain exceptions exist, an overall assimilation of the 
literature supports that patients with T1D with a disease onset 
at age 0 to 14 years and within 1 year of diagnosis show more 
inflamed islets (68%) and fewer islets with residual β-cells (39%) 
than in patients with onset at 15 to 39 years of age.60 This finding 
suggests that a more vigorous autoimmune response occurs when 
disease develops in young children.
The immunotype of insulitic lesions shows a predominance of 
CD8+ T lymphocytes and macrophages, but cells of other pheno­
types are also observed (e.g., CD4+, CD20+, and CD68+).61 More 
recent studies have evaluated immunotype as a function of age, 
with younger age of onset associated with higher levels of CD20+ 
B cells, CD45+ cells, and CD8+ T cells in insulitis lesions, along­
side fewer insulin-positive islets.60,62 With this, tertiary lymphoid 
organs (TLOs), which are structurally and functionally similar to 
antigen-priming sites in secondary lymphoid organs, have been 
identified within human pancreas samples examined from organ 
donors with T1D, and TLOs were present more commonly in 
young donors.63 Conversely, infiltrates with fewer CD20+ cells are 
observed in patients with T1D who are older at onset and associ­
ated with lower levels of CD45+ cells and CD8+ T cells, as well 
as more insulin-positive islets. These studies and others also show 
that islet CD8+ T cells express T-cell receptors that bind MHC 
class I tetramers loaded with the β-cell autoantigens islet-specific 
glucose 6 phosphatase catalytic subunit related protein (IGRP), 
preproinsulin, and other target peptides in patients with recent-
onset T1D.64 These findings are also in agreement with recent 
findings that the T cells invading pancreatic islets and even the 
exocrine pancreas tissue are, in fact, directed at β-cell antigens.65,66 
In contrast to long-standing dogma, the presence of insulitis in 
human T1D is quantitatively limited, with an expert panel estab­
lishing a standardized definition for this lesion of three islets con­
taining more than 15 CD45+ cells in a pancreas.11
Somewhat surprisingly, inflammation is also present in pan­
creatic exocrine tissue in T1D. Specifically, chronic inflammation, 
including enhanced CD8+ T-cell infiltration (and to a lesser degree, 
CD4+ and CD11c+ cells), is present in the exocrine pancreas in

neutrophil invasion of the pancreas (along with decreased periph­

for inflammation/pancreatitis induced by multiple factors (e.g., 
hypertriglyceridemia, virus infection, drugs) could be a result of 
susceptibility genes that affect tissue-based inflammation or other 
facets that have, in the past, been considered “leakiness.” Impor­
tantly, the inflammatory process in the exocrine pancreas appears 
to be subclinical because most patients with new-onset T1D do 
not present with symptoms of pancreatic inflammation (discussed 
in the “Pancreatic Exocrine Abnormalities in T1D” section).
As described earlier, recent studies assessing the persistence of 
insulin production in patients with long-standing T1D (i.e., stim­
ulated C-peptide production) using ultrasensitive assays have over­
turned the long-standing dogma that residual C-peptide secretion 
is rare.69 Emerging histopathologic evidence supports this notion 
through identification of insulin-positive islets, albeit extremely 
limited in number, in patients with long-standing T1D.58,70 
The non–insulin-producing cells of the islets (i.e., alpha, delta, 
pancreatic polypeptide; see Chapter 33) persist in patients with 
long-standing T1D, and these remaining islets, lacking insulitis 
and β-cells, are termed pseudoatrophic.11 This information sets the 
stage for another remarkable feature of the pancreas of patients 
with new-onset T1D, namely, heterogeneity of islet lesions. His­
topathologic examination of the same section of pancreas showed 
that a normal islet with no immune infiltrate can coexist with 
an islet containing β-cells with intense infiltration, as well as a 
pseudoatrophic islet that has no infiltrate (Fig. 35.5). This spot­
tiness of the pathologic process is reminiscent of the destruction 
of areas of the skin in patients with vitiligo, in which melanocytes 
are destroyed in patches. Such heterogeneity of lesions may under­
lie the variable natural history of T1D, in which the time period 
between initial β-cell autoimmunity and overt symptoms can be 
one of months, years, or even many decades. Additionally, pancre­
ata from non-T1D but autoantibody-positive organ donors often 
show limited to no insulitis but have distinct histologic abnor­
malities, such as an increased ratio of proinsulin to insulin area,71 
that match functional alterations. Such information has been con­
sidered to support the notion that T1D is a relapsing/remitting 
disease,70 with waves of immunologic destruction.
Finally, reduced pancreatic weight has been demonstrated at 
autopsy or in organ donors with recent-onset T1D, as well as in 
those with long-standing disease.72 Reduced pancreatic volume 
has also been shown in living patients with T1D through noninva­
sive imaging techniques.73 Mechanisms underlying loss of pancre­
atic size or weight in T1D are not well understood but have largely 
been hypothesized to result from loss of insulinotropic effects on 
the exocrine pancreas because islets constitute a small minority of 
pancreatic volume (see the “Pancreatic Exocrine Abnormalities in 
T1D” section). 
β-Cell Mass Is Not Equal in All Individuals
Most historical models of T1D have assumed a normal β-cell mass 
at birth that declines once the autoimmune attack occurs (see Fig. 
35.1). However, recent studies of cadaveric pancreata have shown 
that β-cell mass in normal, nondiabetic humans varies threefold 
to fivefold, independent of adult age or BMI, with β-cell mass 
likely mostly determined in the first 2 decades of life.74 This has 
important implications when one considers the starting point for

might be affected because endocrine islet cells and exocrine cells 
share a common embryologic heritage. Together, these structural 
changes emphasize the need to better understand the timeline and 
determinants of human β-cell mass. 
β-Cell Dysfunction and β-Cell Death in Type 1 
Diabetes
First proposed by Dr. Gian Franco Bottazzo in 1986, the notion of 
β-cell participation in T1D pathogenesis is not a new one,75,76 yet 
over the ensuing decades, a vast majority of research was directed 
at exploring the autoimmune facets of this disease. Through large 
clinical studies of T1D natural history as well as access to rare 
transplant-quality human pancreas from donors with and at risk 
for T1D, an abundance of recent evidence has emerged suggesting 
that β-cell stress and dysfunction may potentiate the disease pro­
gression, at least in a subset of individuals. Specifically, evidence 
of endoplasmic reticulum stress, expression of integrated stress 
response genes, altered prohormone processing and secretion, and 
production of neoantigens have been reported in human pancreas 
from donors with T1D.70,65,77–80 Interestingly, there appears to 
be an imbalance between β-cell mass and β-cell function in both 
recent-onset and long-standing disease, and downregulation of 
characteristic β-cell markers has been suggested to represent an 
attempt to evade recognition by autoreactive immune cells.81 In 
living individuals, impaired insulin sensitivity, β-cell responsive­
ness, and insulin clearance are present in stage 1 T1D, more than 
5 years before the onset of stage 3 disease.82,83
The mechanism(s) by which β-cells die in T1D remains con­
troversial. A majority of studies support necrotic cell death, medi­
ated by cytotoxic T cells in response to self-antigens, as one likely 
mechanism. Evidence from studies of human T1D pancreas not­
ing the presence of CD8+ T cells and macrophages is consistent 
with this concept.12 T cells can induce necrosis after the release of 
cytolytic granules containing granzymes and perforin, which act 
on the β-cell membrane. Ischemia resulting from impaired vas­
cularity, a process that may result from hyperexpression of extra­
cellular matrix materials (e.g., hyaluronan, hyaluronan-binding 
proteins), may also lead to necrotic cell death.84 Additional media­
tors of necrotic cell death finding support in T1D studies include 
reactive oxygen species, which are capable of inducing mitochon­
drial injury and loss of cell membrane integrity through oxidative 
DNA damage, lipid peroxidation, and protein damage.85 Finally, 
necrosis of β-cells may release factors, including posttranslation­
ally modified antigenic peptides80 or modifications of “normal” 
antigens (i.e., hybrid peptides86), that further stimulate the 
immune response and thereby perpetuate β-cell death by necrosis.
Beyond necrosis, apoptosis has also been implicated for its role 
in β-cell death in T1D through activities largely linked to the janus 
kinases (JAK1, JAK2) and nonreceptor tyrosine-protein kinase 
(TYK2) pathways.87 Immunity finds a link here, with apoptosis 
likely driven by cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor (TNF), 
that activate Fas/FasL, TNFR1, and TNFR2. Apoptosis can also 
be initiated through the B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2) pathway via 
cytokine deprivation or endoplasmic reticulum stress, leading to 
caspase activation. Apoptosis due to the activity of caspases leads 
to apoptotic cell morphology, nuclear fragmentation, and chroma­
tin condensation—facets that have been observed in human T1D 
pancreas. The notion of the so-called unfolded protein response 
(i.e., how a cell responds to the accumulation of misfolded pro­
teins in the endoplasmic reticulum) and how it may modulate 
β-cell inflammation and death in T1D is also gaining interest in 
type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) research.88
In reality, both necrosis and apoptosis likely contribute to 
β-cell death in T1D. The dynamic glycemic fluctuations, includ­
ing modest to overt hyperglycemia seen in the period of stage 
2 to stage 3 disease (see the “Stages in the Natural History of 
T1D” section), support ever-increasing functional changes in the 
β-cells, possibly as a result of immunologic stressors coupled with 
increased metabolic demand for residual β-cells. 
α-Cell Dysfunction in T1D
α-Cells within islets isolated from T1D- or GADA-positive donors 
may also exhibit an altered functional and transcriptional pheno­
type.89 Notably, islets isolated from nondiabetic GADA-positive 
donors demonstrate impaired glucose suppression of glucagon 
secretion and transcriptomic evidence of α-cell dysfunction90 
before overt T1D onset. In line with this, one study demonstrates 
that responses to both hyper- and hypoglycemia are improved in 
patients with T1D with high levels of residual C-peptide,91 imply­
ing a potential link between α- and β-cell function. 
Pancreatic Exocrine Abnormalities in Type 1 
Diabetes
Autopsy studies first revealed reduced pancreas weights in deceased 
persons with T1D. More recently, studies of higher-quality organ 
donor tissues reveal this phenomenon affects not only people with 
long-standing T1D but also those with recent-onset T1D and 
nondiabetic persons with anti-islet autoantibodies.72 Noninva­
sive imaging methods permit studies of pancreas volume in living 
subjects, which confirm that the pancreas is generally smaller in 
patients with T1D than in those without disease.73 Islets consti­
tute only 1% to 2% of the entire pancreatic volume; hence, β-cell 
loss alone cannot account for the reduction in total pancreas size. 
Insulinopenic effects were initially thought to cause loss of pan­
creatic size or weight after T1D diagnosis. However, detection of 
low pancreas weight at T1D onset and in anti-islet autoantibody–
positive organ donors without diabetes,72,73 together with cer­
tain histopathologic findings in the T1D exocrine pancreas (e.g., 
invasion of exocrine pancreatic tissue by CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T 
cells, CD11c+ dendritic cells, neutrophils,67,68 and C4d comple­
ment deposition92), suggest early loss of pancreas mass before 
diagnosis. Moreover, exocrine pancreas enzyme levels (i.e., tryp­
sinogen, amylase, and lipase in serum, as well as fecal elastase-1), 
which are indicative of exocrine pancreas function, are reduced 
in patients with long-standing T1D, in those with recent-onset 
T1D, and in nondiabetic individuals with anti-islet autoantibod­
ies,93,94 implying that disease-related effects within the exocrine 
pancreas may be present before T1D diagnosis. Interestingly, 
serum levels of trypsinogen and lipase closely reflect pancreatic 
volume measured by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).94 In 
addition, fecal elastase-1 concentration was observed to decline 
in islet autoantibody–positive children who progressed to T1D, 
1393
CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
supporting exocrine pancreas enzymes as minimally invasive dis­
ease biomarkers.95 
Genetics
It has long been recognized that diabetes is a heterogeneous group 
of metabolic disorders, with hyperglycemia representing a com­
mon feature. More recently, it has become apparent that T1D is 
also heterogeneous as a disease entity. This conclusion is based on 
a series of observations, including the age at disease onset, form 
of symptomatic presentation (i.e., rapid and ketotic versus mild 
without ketosis), pancreatic pathologic changes, type and number 
of autoantibodies, and certainly, genetics.
Genetic factors influence not only the development of diabetes 
but also the expression of anti-islet autoantibodies. For identical 
twins, the expression of anti-islet autoantibodies is tightly linked 
to the eventual progression to overt diabetes, and true to form, 
monozygotic twins have a highly concordant prevalence for the 
presence or absence of anti-islet autoantibodies. Dizygotic twins 
much less often exhibit concordant positivity for anti-islet autoan­
tibodies, and the prevalence is similar to that of nontwin siblings.52
Indeed, there are likely many genetic forms of T1D, influenced 
to a major degree by the presence of specific forms of HLA class 
II molecules.96 Beyond HLA, the form of T1D is also influenced 
by the presence of abnormalities (immunologic, β-cell, etc.) fos­
tered by the quantity and combinations of genes that influence 
these aberrancies. The number of specific genes that contribute to 
T1D remains in flux, to some degree, as studies of loci validation 
in varying global populations are conducted. However, current 
estimates provided by genome-wide association studies (GWASs) 
support that more than 150 such loci exist, with the majority 
thought to influence immune responses.97 Many of the HLA 
and non-HLA genes underlying T1D susceptibility are similar in 
diverse countries, although specific alleles of those genes differ in 
their frequency. It is generally thought that specific combinations 
of HLA and non-HLA genes contribute to a loss of tolerance to 
self-antigens in β-cells, ultimately resulting in T1D.
Beyond the polymorphisms seen in these HLA and non-
HLA genes identified by GWASs, genetics studies have also been 
extremely helpful in identification and characterization of several 
monogenic forms of T1D. Although these disorders often clini­
cally continue to be classified as T1D, such diseases should strictly 
be identified as monogenic diabetes (discussed in Chapter 37). 
Genetic risk scores (GRSs) accounting for HLA and non-HLA 
risk alleles can discriminate T1D from other forms of diabetes, 
including monogenic diabetes and T2D98–100 (see the “Genetic 
Risk Scores” section).
Twin Studies
Twin studies have contributed impressively to our understanding 
of T1D. The study of monozygotic twins of patients with diabe­
tes by Barnett and coworkers101 contributed to the recognition 
of distinct forms of diabetes, initially termed juvenile onset and 
adult onset, later insulin dependent and non–insulin dependent, and 
now T1D and T2D. The concordance rates for monozygotic and 
dizygotic twins provide important information regarding genetic 
factors contributing to a given disease because monozygotic twins 
share all germline-inherited polymorphisms or mutations, whereas 
dizygotic twins are similar to nontwin siblings of patients with a 
disease and have only half of their genes in common. For a locus 
that contributes to disease in a recessive manner, only one-quarter 
of dizygotic twins would be homozygous to a sibling with diabetes 
at that locus, but all monozygotic twins would be homozygous for 
all recessive loci of the diabetic twin. Because overall concordance 
rates of monozygotic twins for T1D vary across studies, it is likely 
that T1D is heterogeneous and that different pairs of monozygotic 
twins have different genetic causes for their diabetes. With such 
genetic heterogeneity, one would expect different concordance 
rates for different genetic causes.
Redondo and coworkers102 analyzed prospective follow-up 
data from a large series of initially discordant monozygotic twins 
from the United Kingdom combined with a series from the United 
States. Progression to diabetes was identical for both series of 
twins. There was no length of time of discordance beyond which 
a monozygotic twin of a patient with T1D did not have a risk of 
developing the disease. Nevertheless, the hazard rate for develop­
ment of diabetes decreased as the period of discordance increased. 
There was also a marked variation in the risk of diabetes relative to 
the age at which the disorder developed in the index twin. With 
long-term follow-up, the overall rate of concordance for mono­
zygotic twins exceeds 50%.19 However, if T1D developed in the 
index twin after age 25 years, the concordance rate by life table 
analysis in the study of Redondo and coworkers102 was less than 
10%. If diabetes developed in the index twin before age 5 years, 
the concordance rate was 70% after 40 years of follow-up. There­
fore, environmental factors, random factors, and non–germline-
inherited variations (e.g., epigenetic imprinting, T-cell–receptor 
polymorphisms, somatic mutations) likely contribute to lifetime 
diabetes risk. Interestingly, studies of dizygotic twins suggest that 
their risk of diabetes may not differ from that of nontwin siblings 
or, at most, may be increased by a factor of 2 as compared with the 
10-fold increase for monozygotic twins.103 
The Major Histocompatibility Complex
The function of HLA molecules is to present peptides to T lym­
phocytes. Each HLA molecule is made up of two chains, and each 
chain is encoded by a separate gene. These molecules are extremely 
polymorphic in amino acid sequence. The most important loci 
determining the risk of T1D reside within the MHC on chromo­
some 6p21 and, in particular, the HLA class II molecules (DR, 
DQ, and DP).96 The major determinants of T1D susceptibility 
are DR and DQ molecules, and specific alleles of both HLA-DR 
and HLA-DQ can either increase or decrease the risk of diabetes. 
Table 35.3 summarizes the diabetes risk associated with several 
DR and DQ haplotypes.104 In addition, HLA class I loci (HLA-
A, HLA-B, and HLA-C) influence disease, and it is likely that 
additional loci within or linked to the MHC influence immune 
function and contribute to risk.105 The nomenclature for alleles of 
this region is somewhat daunting, but with definitions of several 
terms and a description of the basis for classification, it is compre­
hensible and quite important to understand.
Each polymorphic variant of each chain is designated with a 
gene locus name (e.g., HLA-DRB1) followed by an asterisk (*), 
followed by two digits referring to the serologic specificity (from 
the time in diagnostic history when typing was performed with 
antibodies), followed by two digits for the specific allele (now 
determined with DNA-based typing), followed by a single digit 
to distinguish silent-nucleotide polymorphisms (nucleotide dif­
ferences that do not change the amino acid sequence). For exam­
ple, the designated allele HLA-DRB1*04:05 has DR4 serologic 
specificity and is associated with high T1D risk. There are hun­
dreds of known alleles of HLA-DRB1. Each person inherits two 
1394
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
HLA-DRB1 alleles, one from each parent. For HLA-DR alleles, 
usually only the DRB chain is specified because the DRA chain 
is not polymorphic. Likewise, for the class I molecules (A, B, and 
C), only a single chain is specified because the other chain, β2-
microglobulin, is minimally polymorphic.
Because HLA gene loci are in close proximity to each other 
on the sixth chromosome, a group of alleles is usually inher­
ited as a unit, which is termed a haplotype. For example, the 
alleles HLA-A*01:01, HLA-B*08:01, and HLA-DRB1*0301-
DQA1*0501-DQB1*0201 constitute a common haplotype 
associated with diabetes risk, probably related to the presence of 
HLA-DRB1*0301. When specific alleles of different genes are 
nonrandomly associated with each other on a haplotype (e.g., 
A1, B8, and DR3), the alleles are said to be in linkage disequilib­
rium. Linkage disequilibrium is not the same as linkage, although 
to have linkage disequilibrium, genes must be linked. Genes are 
linked when they are close together on the same chromosome and 
thus transmitted from parent to child as a haplotype group. If 
alleles of linked genes are nonrandomly associated with each other 
in a population, they are in linkage disequilibrium.
Two MHC haplotypes, one inherited from each parent, consti­
tute an individual’s MHC genotype. This genotype ultimately deter­
mines the MHC-encoded risk of T1D. For HLA-DQ molecules, 
both of the chains (DQA and DQB) are polymorphic. This adds an 
important level of diversity in that the protein chains encoded by 
the alleles of one haplotype can combine with the chains encoded 
by the other haplotype. For example, persons with the highest-
risk genotype, HLA-DRB1*03:01-DQA1*05:01-DQB1*02:01 
and HLA-DRB1*04:05-DQA1*03:01-DQB1*03:02, can pro­
duce four different DQ molecules: the expected DQA1*05:01-
DQB1*02:01 
and 
DQA1*03:01-DQB1*03:02 
but 
also 
DQA1*05:01-DQB1*03:02 and DQA1*03:01-DQB1*02:01. 
Studies suggest that the DQA1*05:01-DQB1*03:02 combination 
determines enhanced diabetes risk for DR3/4 individuals. The 
DQ molecule DQA1*05:01-DQB1*02:01 is also called DQ2, 
and DQA1*03:01-DQB1*03:02 is called DQ8.
A common DQ molecule, HLA-DQA1*01:02-DQB1*06:02, 
provides dominant protection from T1D and is termed DQ6. A 
DR allele, HLA-DRB1*14:01, also appears to provide dominant 
protection.106 The protective haplotype HLA-DRB1*15:01-
DQA1*01:02-DQB1*06:02 is present in 20% of the general 
population and in fewer than 3% of patients with T1D.
In several studies, children from the general population or 
relatives of patients with T1D have been HLA typed.107,108 
In the United States, 2.4% of newborns have the highest-risk 
HLA-DR-DQ genotype for T1D, namely, DR3-DQ2 with 
DR4-DQ8 (DR3/4-DQ2/8 heterozygotes). Fifty percent of 
children younger than 10 years and approximately 30% of older 
children who develop T1D have this highest-risk genotype. 
Approximately 1 of 16 children with the highest-risk HLA geno­
type from the general population progresses to T1D (compared 
with a population risk of 1 per 300). Alternatively, 15 of 16 
children from the general population who are DQ2/DQ8 het­
erozygotes do not develop T1D. Studies indicate that newborn 
siblings of patients with T1D who have DQ2 and DQ8 have a 
risk of expressing islet autoantibodies exceeding 40% by age 6 
years, and 50% of these newborns will develop diabetes by age 
10 years. Ninety-five percent of persons who develop T1D have 
either DR3-DQ2 or DR4-DQ8, as does approximately 40% of 
the general population.
There are additional high-risk haplotypes that are not com­
mon, such as HLA-DQA1*04:01-DQB1*04:02. It has been pro­
posed as a simple rule that the presence of aspartic acid at position 
57 of the DQβ chain and arginine at DQα 52 is associated with 
T1D risk.109 There are many exceptions to this rule, and knowl­
edge of the complete sequences (allele) rather than dependence on 
this rule is essential. 
Other Genetic Loci
Although much of the attention toward T1D genetics has resided 
on HLA, other loci have drawn interest for their potential contri­
butions to disease risk, including those related to insulin. In 1984, 
Bell and colleagues110 published their discovery that variations in 
the number of nucleotide repeat elements located upstream (also 
known as 5′) of the insulin gene were associated with the develop­
ment of T1D. The longest group of repeats was associated with 
decreased diabetes risk.111 In a mechanism potentially related 
to the role of autoimmune regulator (AIRE) in the thymus, the 
protective insulin gene polymorphism is associated with greater 
insulin messenger RNA expression within the thymus.112 Indeed, 
for both the AIRE mutation of autoimmune polyendocrine syn­
drome type 1 (APS1) and the effect of insulin gene mutations, the 
level of expression of insulin in the thymus may be critical.
Additionally, PTPN22, a gene encoding a lymphoid-specific 
phosphatase that influences T-cell–receptor signaling, is the third 
confirmed gene (vs. mere loci) influencing T1D risk.113 The poly­
morphism associated with T1D (Trp for Arg) blocks binding to 
a signaling kinase molecule, C-terminal Src kinase (CSK). Nev­
ertheless, the relative risk associated with this polymorphism for 
T1D and other autoimmune disorders, such as rheumatoid arthri­
tis, is only 1.7. The variant associated with disease risk is debated 
as to whether it results in a gain or loss of phosphatase function 
that in turn modulates T-cell–receptor signaling.114
