In impressive collaborative form, more than a decade of inter­
national GWAS efforts have defined many loci that contribute 
generally small but varying degrees toward the development of 
T1D.115 For example, polymorphisms of the cytotoxic T-lym­
phocyte–associated protein 4 (CTLA4) gene contribute to Graves 
disease and to T1D in some but not all populations, with relative 
risks of less than 1.3.116 A locus associated with the interleukin 
(IL)2 receptor has a statistical association based on analysis of 
thousands of persons.117 Sequencing in one region has also iden­
tified rare mutations of a gene influencing interferon-α induc­
tion.118 A curated list of T1D risk loci can be found at https://
genetics.opentargets.org/immunobase. 
Genetic Risk Scores
A recent advance in the ability to stratify patients with high risk 
for developing T1D has occurred through construction of cumu­
lative genetic risk models using logistic regression algorithms that 
incorporate HLA and non-HLA alleles associated with T1D.98–
100Although HLA predominates risk, the inclusion of non-HLA 
loci increases model accuracy for classifying individuals as patients 
with T1D versus those at low risk. Genetic risk models enable pre­
diction of T1D progression,119 differentiation of T1D from T2D 
and monogenic forms of diabetes,98,99 and determination of T1D 
onset prevalence in individuals older than 30 years, and in the 
prospective TEDDY study, a GRS model improved the ability to 
identify infants with a high risk of developing anti-islet autoanti­
bodies by 6 years of age.120 Although not currently used in stan­
dard clinical care, the GRS is being applied in research to improve 
subject selection and stratification. One caveat is due to inherent 
biases resulting from the predominance of GWASs and genotype/
phenotype studies being conducted in majority populations with 
Western European ancestry. The need for studies characterizing 
the T1D genetic risk profile across diverse populations repre­
sented a clear limitation to the initial GRS model, now termed 
GRS1.103 Importantly, through the development of GRS2121 and 
African ancestry-specific GRS models,122 progress is being made 
to address this shortcoming. Importantly, a combined risk score, 
which includes GRS2, islet autoantibody status, and family his­
tory of T1D, provides marked improvement on autoantibodies 
alone for the prediction of T1D in young children.123 
Environmental Factors
Environmental factors have long been considered to influence the 
pathogenesis of T1D. Regional differences in disease rates based 
on geography, seasonality in its diagnosis, rising incidence trends, 
and variance among twins are consistent with this conclusion. 
However, despite decades of research, no single environmental 
agent has been identified that would universally explain these 
observations. Identification of any such agent is especially difficult 
because of facets of the disorder’s pathogenesis (e.g., the long pro­
dromal/prediabetic phase that often precedes T1D, that 85% of 
new cases arise from the general population rather than having a 
family history of T1D, the limited disease frequency of 1 in 300).
The fivefold increase in T1D rates over the past half century 
has been considered strong evidence that environmental factors 
related to diabetes risk have changed since the 1960s. Factors that 
increase diabetes risk may be increasing, or just as likely, factors 
that suppress the development of T1D may be decreasing. It is 
interesting that the rising incidence as a function of age at onset 
is occurring globally at different rates. The increase in Finland 
is highest for children in whom the disease develops before age 
5 years, yet in the United States, the recent Search for Diabe­
tes in Youth Study (SEARCH) showed the most rapid rise in 
teenagers.25,124
Models to Explain the Influence of Environment
Although the mechanisms by which environment influences T1D 
are not known, numerous hypothetical models have been pro­
posed. The accelerator and overload hypotheses suggest that child­
hood obesity increases insulin demand, overloading the islet cells 
and accelerating β-cell autoimmune damage.125,126 In the Copen­
hagen model, β-cell destruction is proposed to result from interac­
tions between the environment, immune system, and the β-cells 
themselves in genetically susceptible individuals.127 The hygiene 
hypothesis attributes the rising incidence of autoimmune disor­
ders to the decline in infections with reduced stimulation of the 
immune system.83 Conversely, the fertile field hypothesis proposes 
that microbial infection induces a temporary state in which other 
antigens can more easily react to yield autoreactive T cells.128 Also 
implicating the gut, the old friends hypothesis implicates dietary 
exposure as a possible direct regulator of the immune system and 
of self-tolerance by altering gut microbiota and intestinal perme­
ability.129 Finally, the threshold hypothesis suggests that the etio­
logic influences of genetics and environment, when evaluated as 
intersecting and reciprocal odds-ratio–based trend lines, result in 
a method to define the attributable risk for T1D.130
A popular model of T1D involves an environmental “trigger” 
presumed to initiate disease. Although it is true that the underly­
ing genetic susceptibility to T1D might allow for a triggering of 
anti–β-cell immunity by an environmental event, it is increasingly 
accepted that environmental agents may contribute far beyond 
an initial triggering and, rather, act throughout the natural his­
tory of T1D development, such as by modulating the ongoing 
autoimmune process (e.g., genes controlling immune regulation). 
There is no shortage of potential environmental candidates (e.g., 
antibiotics, infant and childhood diet, viruses) that, either alone 
or in combination, may contribute to the disorder’s pathogenesis. 
However, most fall into the groups involving infection (particu­
larly viruses), vaccination, and diet. 
Candidate Environmental Factors
Infection
The best evidence, if not the only strong evidence, for a specific 
environmental agent to contribute to T1D pathogenesis involves 
congenital rubella infection, which, in contrast to noncongeni­
tal infection, greatly increases risk for development of T1D.131 
The mechanism(s) by which congenital rubella increases diabetes 
development is currently unknown, with hypotheses ranging from 
molecular mimicry to long-term alteration in T-cell function sec­
ondary to the congenital insult.
Enteroviruses are the most often discussed viruses associated 
with T1D. Enteroviruses are small RNA viruses that frequently 
infect young children. Coxsackie virus (a form of enterovirus) 
infections were implicated after anecdotal reports involving chil­
dren who had severe infections and died at T1D onset. These case 
studies preceded the recognition that T1D is not an acute disease 
but one involving a chronic prediabetic period of autoimmunity. 
It has been reported that at the time of presentation with dia­
betes, almost all children have a rising elevation in hemoglobin 
A1c (HbA1c), reflecting what is likely months of hyperglycemia 
1396
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
preceding diagnosis.132 Meanwhile, searches for viral particles and 
viral RNA within islets of patients with new-onset diabetes have 
largely been unrewarding. Thus, it is likely that viral infection at 
the onset of T1D is most often incidental, although the potential 
relationship between viruses and acute T1D onset remains contro­
versial, as discussed later.
The potential importance of enteroviral infection was evalu­
ated in studies from Scandinavia, with enteroviral infection 
(detected by changes in antiviral antibodies or detection of 
enteroviral RNA by molecular techniques) assessed during preg­
nancy and in infancy.133 Some studies report an increased inci­
dence of enteroviral infection during pregnancy among mothers 
whose children later developed T1D, but others have not.133,134 
It is possible to prospectively analyze the expression of entero­
virus RNA in infants with a genetic risk for development of 
diabetes who are followed from birth in epidemiologic studies. 
Enteroviral infections have been associated with appearance of 
anti-islet autoantibodies in some regions (Finland)133 but not in 
others (Colorado),134 a finding that may be related to differing 
frequency and/or timing of enteroviral infections in these two 
populations. Longitudinal data collected through the TEDDY 
study demonstrate that prolonged, but not short-duration, 
enteroviral shedding is associated with islet autoimmunity in 
genetically at-risk children, suggesting that in some cases, persis­
tent enterovirus infection may influence T1D progression before 
autoantibody seroconversion.35
Rotavirus infection, another virus that commonly infects 
young children, has been associated with increased anti-islet auto­
antibodies in one study from Australia,135 but an increase in rota­
virus infection was not found in children with T1D compared 
with controls. Other viruses are also being evaluated for associa­
tion with the triggering of autoimmunity.
An emerging area of intense research interest surrounds 
the potential link between T1D and coronavirus disease 2019 
(COVID-19), caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coro­
navirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. Like many other viruses, 
COVID-19 can cause hyperglycemia in individuals with or with­
out a prior diagnosis of diabetes.136,137 Beyond this, however, 
multiple studies have reported increased incidence of T1D during 
the COVID-19 pandemic era as compared to the years imme­
diately prior.138–141 Moreover, in a large-scale study of the U.S. 
Department of Veteran affairs database, risk of diabetes onset was 
markedly increased during the year following acute COVID-19, 
although diabetes type (i.e., T1D or T2D) was not distinguish­
able in this report.142 The mechanisms underlying this potential 
association remain unclear as to whether SARS-CoV-2 may infect 
β-cells directly, kill islet cells indirectly through microvascular 
thrombosis, or enhance preexisting autoimmunity in at-risk indi­
viduals, and research is ongoing to address these questions.143–150 
Vaccines
A series of studies have been performed addressing the concern that 
childhood vaccine timing might influence development of T1D, yet 
none has provided any evidence that childhood vaccinations influ­
ence the development of diabetes.151 This is an important health 
concern if parents alter their family’s childhood vaccination sched­
ule because of concern about development of T1D. 
Dietary Factors
Dietary factors as environmental T1D triggers have also been 
extensively investigated. Early introduction of bovine milk in 
the form of infant formula has been hypothesized to increase 
T1D, based primarily on retrospective studies associating early 
or increased bovine milk ingestion (or less breastfeeding) with an 
increased risk of disease. Prospective studies in which infants were 
observed until the development of anti-islet autoantibodies failed 
to find any association or found only a weak association with 
either reduced breastfeeding duration or increased bovine milk 
ingestion.152–154 Pilot studies of an infant formula lacking bovine 
milk proteins were initiated in Finland and suggest weaning to 
insulin-free cow’s milk formula might reduce the development of 
anti-islet autoantibodies in the first 3 years of life.155 In contrast, 
the TEDDY study found no association between choice of first 
infant formula and risk of developing anti-islet autoantibodies.156 
In line with this, hydrolyzed infant formula did not increase the 
development of islet autoimmunity in genetically at-risk infants 
as compared to conventional cow’s milk formula in a prospective 
clinical trial.157
Early (younger than 3 months) introduction of cereals has been 
suggested to increase development of islet autoimmunity.158 Both 
low vitamin D and ω-3 fatty acids, which can influence immune 
function, have also been associated with risk of T1D.159 To date, 
dietary interventions with these factors have not been shown to 
be therapeutic. 
The β-Cell–Immune Cell Dialogue
The specific means by which the immune system destroys 
β-cells is not known. The islets of T1D and T1D autoantibody-
positive nondiabetic patients overexpress class I HLA antigens, 
interferon-α, and potentially Fas molecules.160 Molecules such as 
Fas may be important because T cells expressing Fas ligand can 
induce apoptosis of β-cells. This said, more enthusiasm surrounds 
the notion that cytokines (e.g., IL1) and CD8+ cytotoxic T lym­
phocytes are likely to be major contributors to β-cell destruction. 
With respect to what might induce these features, reduced blood 
vessel diameter and innervation within pancreatic islets, impaired 
integrity of basement membrane and extracellular matrix, and 
hyaluronan accumulation have been suggested to collectively 
contribute toward islet cell dysfunction and facilitate immune cell 
infiltration.161 Indeed, there is growing support for the hypothesis 
that β-cells and immune cells together contribute toward T1D 
pathogenesis.162 In line with this notion, type 1 interferon expres­
sion and endoplasmic reticulum stress in β-cells have each been 
shown to increase β-cell recognition and killing by CD8+ T cells 
in vitro.163–165 However, newer technologies and concepts should 
facilitate additional studies, and it is likely that there will be het­
erogeneity among patients. 
Mouse Models of Type 1 Diabetes
Although studies of nonhuman primate, porcine, and canine 
models have proven valuable toward the advancement of under­
standing diabetes, metabolism, and islet cell function over recent 
decades,166,167 none offers the benefits of a spontaneous model 
of T1D. To that end, the nonobese diabetic (NOD) mouse has, 
without question, served as the most intensively studied animal 
model for spontaneous T1D.168 Unlike human T1D, which has a 
relatively equal prevalence among genders, incident disease has a 
strong female bias in the NOD mice. However, the frequency of 
diabetes among different colonies169 ranges from 30% to 100% 
among female NOD mice, suggesting that housing conditions 
(i.e., environment) represent an important variable, as they do in 
people. As with T1D of humans, diabetes in the NOD mouse 
1397
CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
is polygenic, with specific MHC class I and II molecules being 
central for disease pathogenesis169 and many other genetic loci 
bearing relatively small contributions neither necessary nor suffi­
cient for disease.170 NOD mice, like humans, produce IAA before 
developing diabetes, although T cells, not autoantibodies, appear 
to mediate the β-cell destruction. The insulitis lesion, the hallmark 
feature of T1D, appears more intense and quantitatively obvious 
in NOD mice as compared with humans, with a relative abun­
dance of T cells bearing a receptor specific for the β-cell antigen, 
insulin.171 Studies of islet β-cell mass indicate that both destruc­
tion and replication/regeneration are present months before the 
onset of T1D, with an acceleration of β-cell destruction at disease 
onset.172 A seeming plethora of published studies highlight the 
therapeutic potential of β-cell replication/regeneration in NOD 
mice or other rodent strains.172–174 However, recent convincing 
evidence suggests that in terms of β-cell replication, rodent mod­
els differ dramatically from human physiology, with β-cell repli­
cation being a rare event in humans from adolescence through 
adulthood.175 One of the primary concerns for the NOD mouse 
relates to the relative ease with which the disease can be prevented 
or reversed.168 One can observe clear therapeutic benefits in the 
NOD mouse (e.g., preserved C-peptide secretion), yet only a very 
limited number of these approaches have been effectively trans­
lated to humans (see the “Prevention and Reversal of T1D” sec­
tion). Animal models (unfortunately) represent somewhat of an 
idealized situation characterized by features that are not reflective 
of the sociologic and lifestyle settings in humans, such as limited 
genetic diversity through selective inbreeding, housing in highly 
controlled environments devoid of pathogens, uniform diets, and 
several other facets. It remains unclear which of these or other dif­
ferences underlie the generally disappointing translation. 
Diagnosis
With these emerging definitions of disease, T1D presents in three 
stages, as described previously (see “Stages in the Natural History 
of T1D” section). Most patients present during stage 3, the clas­
sical definition of T1D onset, when significant β-cell destruction 
has taken place to afford symptomatic disease. During the latter 
stage, the clinical diagnosis of T1D relies mainly on the need for 
insulin to control hyperglycemia, low C-peptide levels, and pres­
ence of β-cell–directed autoantibodies.
Symptoms
T1D can occur at any age, but the peak age for presentation of 
T1D is at or during puberty (age 10–14 years), with a smaller peak 
in children between 5 and 7 years of age.176 Yet, as noted earlier, 
emerging evidence suggests that up to 50% of cases occur during 
adulthood, perhaps because more years are spent in adulthood than 
in childhood, providing more time for the disease to manifest in 
those at risk.50 The symptoms and signs of this disease are classical 
and relate to the presence of hyperglycemia and the resulting effects 
on fluid and electrolyte balance, which include polyuria, polydipsia, 
polyphagia, weight loss, and blurred vision.46 These symptoms are 
often present several weeks before diagnosis. Because infection may 
have preceded or precipitated the initial presentation, symptoms of 
infection may also be present, such as fever, sore throat, cough, or 
dysuria. Particularly in children, the onset of symptoms can occur 
over a brief period, and families may be able to date the onset with 
considerable accuracy. In older persons with T1D, the onset of 
symptoms may be insidious over months, and many are mistakenly 
diagnosed as having T2D by screening during this asymptomatic 
period. If onset of T1D is associated with DKA (discussed later in 
the chapter), which occurs in a third of children at diagnosis, addi­
tional symptoms related to this acute metabolic complication of 
diabetes are also present. These symptoms can include abdominal 
pain, nausea, and vomiting. Variable effects on mental status may be 
seen, ranging from slight drowsiness to profound lethargy and even 
coma if the condition has been untreated for a significant period. 
Laboratory Findings
Glucose
For all types of diabetes, the diagnostic criteria are the same, 
including an elevated fasting blood glucose level (≥126 mg/dL, 7.0 
mmol/L), any glucose value higher than 200 mg/dL (11 mmol/L) 
with symptoms of hyperglycemia (≥126 mg/dL, 7.0 mmol/L), 
or an abnormal 2-hour OGTT (≥200 mg/dL, 11.1 mmol/L).46 
Abnormal glycemia must be present on two different occasions if 
symptoms are absent. ADA guidelines for the diagnosis of diabe­
tes were modified in 2009 to include an HbA1c value of greater 
than 6.5%.177
The diagnosis of T1D usually relies on the presence of fasting 
hyperglycemia, but with prospective evaluation, many persons have 
diabetes determined by OGTT according to the 2-hour criterion, 
with a nondiagnostic fasting glucose level. Impaired fasting glucose 
(100–125 mg/dL, 5.6–6.9 mmol/L) or impaired glucose tolerance 
(glucose at 2 hours on OGTT, 140–199 mg/dL, 7.8–11.0 mmol/L) 
is usually present within 6 months before the onset of overt T1D.
Plasma glucose concentrations at presentation of T1D are 
often in the range of 300 to 500 mg/dL (16.7–27.8 mmol/L). If 
the presentation is uncomplicated, the remainder of the fluid and 
electrolyte measurements may be completely normal. However, 
if DKA is present, the measurements will reflect the presence of 
acidosis, as well as more severe dehydration. 
C-peptide
C-peptide in serum can be used to assess remaining β-cell func­
tion while on exogenous insulin because C-peptide is released 
from the β-cell in equimolar concentrations with insulin but does 
not undergo hepatic extraction and has a longer half-life in circu­
lation. C-peptide levels are usually measured in the fasting state, 
after intravenous glucagon, with an OGTT or a standard liquid 
meal or during the hyperglycemic clamp test. Abnormalities in 
C-peptide secretion can be detected years before hyperglycemia 
develops or clinical symptoms occur. At clinical presentation, 
C-peptide levels are generally in the low-normal range and decline 
further over time. Age influences the rate of C-peptide decrease, 
and many people have rapid C-peptide changes during a window 
of around 6 months on either side of clinical diagnosis.178 Despite 
these rapid changes around diagnosis, residual C-peptide may 
be detected throughout the natural history of diabetes. A small 
amount of remaining C-peptide is associated with reduced glu­
cose variability and improved metabolic control, as shown in the 
Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT).179 C-peptide 
measurements are therefore also of importance for trials of thera­
pies to alleviate loss of insulin secretion after diagnosis. Determi­
nation of the C-peptide concentration provides the best current 
measure for assessing the impact of these new therapies. 
Autoantibodies
At present, the best criterion for distinguishing T1D from other 
forms of diabetes resides in laboratory identification of any one of a 
1398
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
number of islet cell autoantibodies (also known as T1D-associated 
autoantibodies; i.e., anti-insulin [IA], anti–glutamic acid decar­
boxylase [GADA], anti–insulinoma-associated antigen 2 [IA2A], 
or anti-zinc-transporter 8 [ZnT8A]). Literally hundreds of stud­
ies over the past 3 decades have suggested that the presence of 
these autoantibodies provides high sensitivity for diagnosing per­
sons with T1D.28 Indeed, approximately 90% of White children 
presenting with diabetes express at least one of these four T1D-
associated autoantibodies180; however, this frequency is subject to 
variation based on the ethnicity and country analyzed. In terms 
of disease specificity, T1D-associated autoantibodies are typically 
positive in less than 1% to 2% of unaffected (i.e., non-T1D) indi­
viduals, further validating their diagnostic utility. Some issues are 
related to using antibody positivity to diagnose T1D. First, most 
commercial laboratories do not provide either the full spectrum of 
assays or equivalently sensitive or specific assays, resulting in both 
false-negative and, on rare occasion, false-positive results, mainly 
in adult populations. Second, antibodies may be less prevalent in 
certain ethnicities.181 Among Black and Hispanic children and 
adolescents in the United States diagnosed with diabetes, almost 
one-half lack any T1D-associated autoantibody. Third, antibody 
titers diminish over time, so some White children and even more 
adults (up to 10%) are devoid of a T1D-associated autoantibody 
at disease diagnosis (i.e., time of hyperglycemic onset). This raises 
questions as to whether such persons lost their autoantibody 
expression (or at least the ability to detect it with laboratory test­
ing) by the time of diagnosis or whether a diagnosis of T1D is 
accurate. The notion of autoantibody loss versus the presence of a 
different form of diabetes (discussed further in this chapter) is also 
difficult to ascertain because many have HLA alleles associated 
with susceptibility for T1D; are not insulin resistant; present with 
DKA; and, with time, lose their C-peptide secretion. With appro­
priate laboratory testing, notation of such persons as patients 
with T1D negative for T1D-associated autoantibodies can be an 
appropriate diagnosis. This said, advances in understanding the 
heretofore underappreciated disease classifications of monogenic 
diabetes (see Chapter 37), including those of maturity onset of 
diabetes in youth, warrant genetic testing of diabetes cases diag­
nosed in the very young (i.e., under 1 year of age).182
The most characteristic difference related to age at diabe­
tes onset is the presence of higher levels of IAA in children who 
develop the disease at an early age (e.g., below 5 years of age). The 
high levels and frequent positivity of IAA make measurement of 
these autoantibodies the best single marker for diabetes develop­
ment in young children.183 In those children in whom autoanti­
bodies arise during the first 3 years of life, IAAs often appear first. 
In contrast, GADAs are more often positive in adults who develop 
T1D. Seroconversion to IAA or GADA as the first anti-islet auto­
antibody has also been linked to HLA.56 The correlation of levels 
of IAA and age at diabetes onset may be related to faster pro­
gression to diabetes in children with higher levels. However, such 
rapid progression occurs only if IAAs are present with another 
anti-islet autoantibody (discussed in the “Stages in the Natural 
History of T1D” section). 
Emerging Biomarkers of Type 1 Diabetes
As mentioned throughout this chapter, seroconversion to anti-islet 
autoantibody positivity is the most reliable predictive biomarker of 
T1D identified to date,28 but as noted, as many as 10% of patients 
with T1D are negative for anti-islet autoantibodies at the time 
of diagnosis.184 Early diagnosis and treatment with exogenous 
insulin have been associated with improved disease management 
and fewer complications.185 Moreover, there are notions that early 
intervention before the first signs of autoimmunity might offer 
the greatest chance to successfully prevent T1D progression and 
onset in high-risk individuals. Hence, a substantial effort has been 
directed at the discovery and characterization of new biomarkers 
to improve our understanding of the disease pathogenesis, as well 
as our ability to predict and stage disease progression, facilitating 
early diagnosis.
The majority of biomarkers identified signify metabolic defects 
across T1D progression. Specifically, proinsulin/C-peptide ratio 
and the Index60186 monitor the decline in functional β-cell mass 
related to autoimmune pathology and/or β-cell stress in T1D. 
An elevated serum proinsulin/C-peptide ratio measured under 
fasting conditions or after a mixed meal tolerance test implies 
impaired processing of proinsulin to insulin and C-peptide within 
the β-cell, suggesting duress related to metabolic, oxidative, or 
immunologic stress.187 After T1D diagnosis, proinsulin/C-pep­
tide ratios continue to climb, with stimulated proinsulin secre­
tion persisting even in individuals with long-standing disease 
and undetectable C-peptide.188,189 These findings, supported by 
histopathologic observations in human pancreas from the nPOD 
repository,58,70 suggest that small numbers of β-cells survive, albeit 
with progressive endoplasmic reticulum stress and defective pro­
insulin processing. Proinsulin/C-peptide assays are expected to 
have the greatest utility in the research setting, but the ability 
to evaluate changes in β-cell dysfunction in real time represents 
a massive step forward. Similarly, delayed time to peak glucose 
and peak C-peptide during a 2-hour OGTT is associated with a 
higher risk of T1D progression in at-risk individuals.190 Likewise, 
a mixed model known as M120, which includes sex, age, BMI, 
HbA1c, islet antigen 2 (IA-2) autoantibody status, glucose, and 
C-peptide area under the curve (AUC) determined from a single 
blood draw at 2 hours after OGTT, has a high capacity to predict 
T1D progression in persons with stage 1 or 2 disease.191 Mean­
while, the Index60 has been introduced as a clinical/diagnostic 
biomarker measuring functional β-cell mass. The test requires an 
OGTT with calculations incorporating the log-adjusted fasting 
C-peptide level, 1-hour C-peptide level, and 1-hour blood glucose 
level.192 An Index60 value greater than 2 in an individual with 
anti-islet autoantibodies is considered indicative of T1D onset.193 
Additionally, Index60 has been shown to identify a high risk of 
progression to stage 3 T1D in autoantibody-positive individu­
als.186,194 However, the need for standard clinical C-peptide assays 
has limited its widespread implementation.
Alterations to the microbiome have been suggested as yet 
another biomarker of T1D. Although less conclusive than the 
metabolic markers discussed previously, prospective studies of 
infants and children with high genetic risk for T1D have revealed 
the gut microbiome as an early indicator of disease progression, 
even before seroconversion. Extensive profiling of the gut micro­
bial community is generally accomplished by sequencing the 
microbial 16S ribosomal RNA gene from fecal samples. Overall, a 
high Bacteroides-to-Firmicutes ratio has been associated with anti-
islet autoimmunity, whereas the presence of butyrate-producing 
bacteria may protect against T1D by promoting the synthesis of 
mucin and reducing intestinal leakiness.195 In addition, low diver­
sity and poor stability of the gut microbial community are asso­
ciated with T1D,196 although a cause-and-effect relationship has 
not been determined, and T1D-related microbiome biomarkers 
have geographically distinct patterns, with the relative abundance 
of the most prominent strains and overall microbial diversity dif­
fering across geographical regions.29 At present, it is unknown 
1399
CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
what factors contribute toward these shifts in stage 1 or 2 T1D 
gut microbiome, but they have been hypothesized to include diet, 
antibiotics, infections, and/or household environment (e.g., expo­
sure to pets, allergens, pollutants).
The TEDDY study also identified altered lipid metabolism, 
accumulation of intracellular reactive oxygen species, and a pro­
inflammatory immune signature in the months before islet auto­
antibody seroconversion.36 Additionally, bulk RNA sequencing 
of blood samples from children enrolled in TEDDY identified 
a unique gene-expression signature in those who progressed to 
T1D.37 Finally, there are extensive efforts underway seeking to 
identify cellular biomarkers of T1D. For example, functional 
T-cell assays, T-cell phenotyping, and T-cell–receptor repertoire 
profiling are potential candidates to identify overall risk of disease 
progression, as well as to define distinct endotypes and guide clini­
cal trial enrollment for treatment with immunotherapies currently 
in development.197–199 
Differential Diagnosis
Transient Hyperglycemia
Significant numbers of children are evaluated by endocrinologists 
for transient hyperglycemia. The usual history is one of severe 
stress associated with hyperglycemia that resolves within days to 1 
month. Such children may be in the honeymoon phase of T1D, or 
they may truly have a transient episode of hyperglycemia. Rarely, 
diabetes in children is misdiagnosed. Children without severe 
stress who have transient hyperglycemia or who have a relative 
with T1D are more likely to have early T1D. Absence of anti-islet 
autoantibodies and normal first-phase insulin secretion during 
an intravenous glucose tolerance test strongly indicate transient 
hyperglycemia and not T1D. It is not known whether children 
with transient hyperglycemia are at increased risk for T2D later 
in life. 
Monogenetic Forms of Diabetes
The most common forms of diabetes, T1D and T2D, are poly­
genic, meaning that the risk of developing these disorders is 
related to multiple genes. Environmental factors (discussed ear­
lier) also play a part in the development of polygenic forms of 
diabetes. However, additional and rare forms of diabetes, termed 
monogenic, result from mutations in a single gene. Monogenic 
forms of diabetes account for about 1% to 5% of all cases of dia­
betes in young individuals. So far, more than 20 genes have been 
linked to monogenic diabetes. In most cases of monogenic dia­
betes, the gene mutation is inherited; in the remaining cases, the 
gene mutation develops spontaneously. Neonatal diabetes (ND) 
and maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) are the two 
main forms of monogenic diabetes (Table 35.4), with ND far less 
common than MODY.
Genetic testing can diagnose most forms of monogenic dia­
betes. If genetic testing is not performed, people with mono­
genic diabetes may appear to have one of the polygenic forms 
of diabetes (i.e., T1D or T2D). When hyperglycemia is first 
detected in adulthood, monogenic diabetes is often misdiag­
nosed as general T2D or antibody-negative T1D. Importantly, 
some monogenic forms of diabetes can be treated with oral dia­
betes medications, whereas other forms require insulin injec­
tions. A correct diagnosis that allows the proper treatment to 
be selected should lead to better glucose control and improved 
health in the long term. Monogenic forms are discussed in 
more detail in Chapter 37. 
Type 2 Diabetes
Under certain settings (e.g., obesity, racial status other than White) 
and particularly among adults, the diagnosis of T1D versus T2D can 
prove quite challenging. At present, the best criterion for separating 
the two disorders resides in laboratory identification of any one of 
a number of islet cell autoantibodies. Efforts to differentiate adult-
onset T1D from T2D (Table 35.5) have also resulted in a series of 
proposed new disease classifications, most notably ketosis-prone dia­
betes and latent autoimmune disease of adults.200 The lack of firm 
diagnostic criteria dampens enthusiasm for adopting these presumed 
new disease entities as novel categories for diabetes. It is also impor­
tant to note that patients with T1D can manifest insulin resistance, 
a feature most often associated with T2D. Specifically, patients with 
T1D (including those who are autoantibody positive) may present 
with diabetes characterized by high serum levels of fasting insulin 
or C-peptide but loss of stimulated insulin secretion. Many patients 
from ethnic minorities in the United States present clinically as if they 
have early-onset T2D (e.g., mild ketosis, slow symptomatic onset), 
some have attendant risk factors such as obesity, and many lack HLA 
alleles associated with T1D. Increasingly diverse genetic admixtures, 
due to geographic migration and social changes (e.g., multiracial off­
spring), further contribute to diagnostic complexity.
The measurement and presence of T1D-associated autoan­
tibodies have also fueled much debate regarding the percentage 
of T1D cases that are errantly misclassified as T2D. Indeed, it is 
conceivable that 5% to 15% of adults diagnosed with T2D may 
have T1D, given the frequency of T1D-associated autoantibodies 
in populations diagnosed with T2D.201 This is, in effect, a prob­
lem in health care provider recognition of the potential for T1D 
disease in adult populations combined with a lack of widespread 
screening for such autoantibodies in settings in which screening 
would seem warranted. If this assertion is correct, given the vastly 
greater number of persons diagnosed with T2D (relative to that 
of T1D), the number of actual T1D cases in a given population 
may be massively underestimated. This is therapeutically unfortu­
nate because an accurate diagnosis of T1D is vital; persons misdi­
agnosed as having T2D when they indeed have T1D experience 
higher HbA1c, have a risk of DKA from the use of noninsulin 
therapies, and have accelerated progression toward micro- and 
macrovascular complications. 
Monogenic and Polygenic Autoimmune 
Endocrinopathy
T1D and thyroid disease are the most common endocrine diseases 
resulting from autoimmunity. Several autoimmune endocrine and 
nonendocrine diseases can cluster as a result of monogenic mutations 
or polygenic predisposition. Monogenic syndromes have an earlier 
onset on average than polygenic syndromes and are characterized by 
specific hallmark features that should lead to further genetic testing 
because a correct diagnosis is essential for familial counseling, therapy, 
and prognosis. Here, we give a short overview of the most frequent 
syndromes that can present with T1D. For an in-depth description of 
immunoendocrinopathies, refer to Chapter 44.

early in childhood (median age 3.3 years) and is characterized by 
the main components of mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypopara­

disorders almost always have mutations (usually autosomal reces­

in maintaining self-tolerance and may influence the expression of 
what immunologists term peripheral antigens (e.g., insulin) in the 
thymus. This notion is relevant because it has been hypothesized 
that greater thymic expression of insulin and other tissue-specific 
antigens leads to T-cell tolerance and disease suppression. At the 
same time, the influence on insulin is not specific because damage 
to the adrenal glands, parathyroid glands, and other organs under­
lies the major features of APS1 and is why candidiasis infections 
predominate. 
X-Linked Polyendocrinopathy, Immune Dysfunction, and 
Diarrhea (Scurfy Gene)
The syndrome of X-linked polyendocrinopathy, immune dysfunc­
tion, and diarrhea (XPID; also termed IPEX) is associated with 
overwhelming neonatal autoimmunity, and most children die 
in the first few days of life or in infancy.202 In this syndrome, 
lymphocytes invade multiple organs. It is associated with protein-
losing enteropathy caused by lymphocytic intestinal inflammation 
with flattened villi. T1D, as a consequence of insulitis and β-cell 
destruction, usually follows in the first 6 months of life. Other 
components are dermatitis and increased risk of infections. It is 
inherited as an X-linked recessive disease affecting only boys, with 
a frequent clinical history of lack of male births. The disease results 
from mutations of the gene encoding forkhead box P3 (FOXP3), 
which functions as a transcription factor and master switch for 
regulatory (suppressor) CD4+CD25+CD127–/low T lympho­
cytes.101 Lack of such regulatory T cells leads to overwhelming 
autoimmunity. This is an important syndrome to recognize early 
because bone marrow transplantation, affording restoration of 
functional T-regulatory cells (even with partial chimerism), has 
proved to be therapeutic. 
Other Monogenic Polyendocrinopathies
Other monogenic polyendocrinopathies that might present with 
T1D are immunodeficiency 41 with lymphoproliferation and 
autoimmunity, multisystem autoimmune disease with facial dys­
morphism, common variable immunodeficiency 8 with autoim­
munity, immunodeficiency 31C and infancy-onset multisystem 
autoimmune disease (see Chapter 44).

Disorders Associated With Immunity to Insulin
Insulin Autoimmune Syndrome
The insulin autoimmune syndrome, also termed Hirata syndrome, 
is rare and is typically associated with hypoglycemia.204 These 
patients have extremely high concentrations of autoantibodies 
reacting with human insulin in the absence of exogenous insu­
lin therapy. It is thought that inappropriate (i.e., nonregulated 
by the overall blood glucose level) release of autoantibody-bound 
insulin produces the hypoglycemia. Interestingly, and for reasons 
unknown, the disease occurs most commonly in persons of Asian 
descent.205 Among 50 Japanese patients with the syndrome and 
possessing the typical polyclonal anti-IAA, 96% had an HLA-
DR4 allele, and 84% possessed a DRB1*04:06 allele. In contrast, 
patients with monoclonal anti-IAA do not possess such a pro­
found and specific HLA association.206 Most patients with this 
disorder develop the disease in association with treatment with 
sulfhydryl-containing medications, particularly methimazole, as 
well as α-lipoic acid.207 Treatment usually consists of stopping 
these medications, and for more than 75% of the patients, the 
disease remits. 
Associated Autoimmunity
Common Comorbid Autoimmune Disease
There is a higher prevalence of additional autoimmune conditions 
among persons with T1D compared with the general popula­
tion. In an analysis of more than 25,000 participants in the T1D 
Exchange Registry, 27% of children and adults with T1D were 
diagnosed with one or more additional autoimmune diseases, 
and prevalence was higher in those of older age, female sex, and 
non-Hispanic White race.208 The most common comorbidities 
are autoimmune thyroid dysfunction (15%–30% of people with 
T1D) and celiac disease (2%–16%), but autoimmune primary 
adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease; 0.5%), autoimmune gastri­
tis and/or pernicious anemia (5%–10%), vitiligo (2%–10%), and 
others (i.e., inflammatory bowel disease, collagen vascular disease) 
can occur as well. Regular assessment for signs and symptoms of 
other autoimmune diseases and periodic screening in asymptom­
atic individuals are thus recommended. Here, we discuss thyroid 
and celiac disease. 
Thyroid Disease
Approximately 15% to 30% of individuals with T1D have hypo­
thyroidism or hyperthyroidism, making thyroid disease the most 
common autoimmune disorder associated with T1D.208–211 The 
ADA and International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Dia­
betes (ISPAD) recommend measuring thyroid antibodies and 
thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels soon after diagnosis of 
T1D.212,213 Thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO) and/or thyro­
globulin (TG) autoantibodies are expressed by 20% to 30% of the 
population with T1D and show greater expression in females and 
people with long T1D duration.214–216 Up to 80% of individu­
als with T1D with TPO antibodies will develop hypothyroidism 
during life.217 Thyroid function tests may be slightly abnormal at 
the time of T1D diagnosis as a result of sick euthyroid syndrome; 
if this is the case, thyroid function tests should be reassessed once 
glycemic control improves. If antibodies are negative and TSH 
levels are normal soon after diagnosis, regular measurement of 
TSH concentrations is recommended every 1 to 2 years, sooner 
if the patient develops any new symptoms or signs concerning 
for thyroid dysfunction, including thyromegaly, abnormal growth 
pattern, or unexplained fluctuations in blood glucose level. There 
is evidence that autoimmune thyroid disease affects diabetes con­
trol, weight, and menstrual cycle and is associated with decreased 
growth velocity in children.218 
Celiac Disease
Celiac disease (CD) is the second most common coexistent auto­
immune disorder in patients with T1D, is diagnosed in 2% to 
16% of people with T1D, and is more prevalent in those who 
were younger at T1D diagnosis and those of White race.208,213,219 
Of people with T1D, 5% to 10% have tissue transglutaminase 
(TTG) antibodies.213,220,221 Introduction of gluten-containing 
foods between 4 and 6 months of age (compared with introduc­
tion in the first 3 months of life or in the 7th month or later) 
in infants at increased risk for CD and T1D appears to mitigate 
the risk of CD.222 Classical gastrointestinal symptoms of CD 
include mild abdominal pain and bloating. Individuals with T1D 
and CD may experience increased glycemic variability, iron and 
vitamin D deficiency, osteoporosis, infertility, growth failure, 
and unexplained hypoglycemia.218,223–228 The ADA and ISPAD 
recommend screening for CD in children and adults with T1D 
soon after diagnosis and at regular intervals after diagnosis (ADA: 
rescreen within 2 years and again after 5 years; ISPAD: screen 
every 1–2 years).212,213 Screening labs include immunoglobulin 
(Ig) A tissue transglutaminase antibodies, with documentation of 
normal total serum IgA levels; if an individual is found to be IgA 
deficient, IgG-specific antibody tests should be performed. More 
frequent screening may be necessary if symptoms develop or in 
people who have a first-degree relative with CD. If screening tests 
are positive, referral to gastroenterology is recommended before 
prescribing a gluten-free diet. Typically, a biopsy is done to con­
firm the diagnosis of CD, especially in asymptomatic children.229 
In symptomatic individuals with high antibody titers, some pro­
viders may prescribe dietary changes without a confirmatory 
biopsy. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, people with CD should 
be placed on a gluten-free diet and be referred to a dietitian experi­
enced in managing both diabetes and CD because the nutritional 
management of a person with both T1D and CD can be complex 
and burdensome. A gluten-free diet may reduce gastrointestinal 
complaints, metabolic symptoms, and hypoglycemia.230 
Chronic Complications of Type 1 Diabetes
One hundred years ago, the discovery of insulin—or rather, the 
possibility of using insulin as therapy for people with T1D—
changed the face of T1D from a (sub)acutely lethal disease to a 
chronic disease.4 This chronic disease is demanding on the peo­
ple living with it and their families and affects quality of life, in 
particular, the complications of T1D arising in many after years, 
characterized by micro- and macrovascular complications. These 
typically include retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and 
1404
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
cardiovascular disease.231,232 We refer to Chapter 38 for detailed 
discussion of the complications of diabetes. The complications 
arising in T1D are common to those in people with other forms of 
diabetes, but microvascular complications remain prevalent.233,234 
Tight glycemic control has been shown to prevent or delay the 
onset of microvascular complications, and a multifactorial 
approach, including tight glycemic control and lipid and blood 
pressure management, reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease in 
those living with T1D.231,232,235
In addition to the chronic complications, arising years after 
onset of T1D, people living with T1D are also exposed to acute 
complications. DKA is a complex metabolic situation, typically 
characterized by hyperglycemia, acidosis (pH below 7.3), and the 
presence of ketone bodies; its presentation and how to prevent and 
treat it are discussed later in the chapter. The most frequent acute 
complication of T1D is hypoglycemia, a situation where the blood 
glucose levels drop as a result of an imbalance between admin­
istered insulin and insulin needs. Hypoglycemia is discussed in 
more detail in Chapter 39. Briefly, the ADA defines different lev­
els of hypoglycemia. Level 1 hypoglycemia is defined as a situa­
tion with blood glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), typically 
accompanied by symptoms, such as trembling, sweating, and a 
feeling of hunger. It is frequent in people with T1D who strive for 
tight glycemic control. Clinically important hypoglycemia (level 
2, <54 mg/dL [3.0 mmol/L]), particularly level 3 hypoglycemia 
(any hypoglycemia characterized by altered mental state and/or 
physical status needing the intervention of a third party for recov­
ery), should be avoided. Severe hypoglycemia (level 3) is associ­
ated with morbidity and mortality and is particularly common 
in those with longer duration of diabetes, older age, a history of 
recent severe hypoglycemia, alcohol ingestion, exercise, chronic 
kidney disease, and socially vulnerable profiles (lower education, 
lower income).236–240
Diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES) 
focusing on how to adapt insulin doses to exercise, food intake, 
or other circumstances (e.g., illness) is crucial in helping people 
living with T1D limit the risk of hypoglycemia and react appro­
priately when a hypoglycemic event does occur.241 Use of insulin 
analogues has also been shown to reduce risk of (in particular, 
severe) hypoglycemia.241 Both randomized controlled trials and 
real-world evidence demonstrate that the use of continuous glu­
cose monitoring (CGM), in particular systems with alarms that 
warn people with T1D when glucose levels are falling and near­
ing hypoglycemic values, is valuable in reducing the risk of severe 
hypoglycemic attacks.242,243 A head-to-head study comparing a 
sensor with alarms to a sensor without alarms showed an improve­
ment in overall glycemic control (HbA1c, time in range [TIR]), 
reduced risk of (severe) hypoglycemia, and improved quality of 
life.244 A Belgian real-world study evaluating the impact of intro­
duction of real-time CGM in people with T1D on continuous 
subcutaneous insulin infusions (CSIIs) via insulin pump showed 
reductions in risk of acute complications (DKA and hospitaliza­
tion for severe hypoglycemia) and improvements in quality of 
life.245,246 Furthermore, the use of CSII linked to sensors and 
hybrid closed-loop systems has proven to be even more efficacious 
in preventing severe hypoglycemia in people with T1D and in all 
age groups.247–253
When measuring quality of life in people with T1D, it is 
mainly the presence of acute and chronic complications that affect 
quality of life.253–255 Complications such as blindness, amputa­
tions, and chronic kidney disease reduce quality of life, as do acute 
complications such as DKA or severe hypoglycemia. Moreover, 
T1D affects longevity.256,257 A recent study demonstrated that 
T1D leads to a reduction in life years of 14.2 years (95% confi­
dence interval [CI], 12.1–18.2 years) in men and 17.7 years (95% 
CI, 14.5–20.4 years) in women diagnosed before the age of 10 
years.258 These life years lost are due to complications of T1D, 
with ample evidence available that tight glucose control prevents 
chronic complications. 
Management
Principles of Type 1 Diabetes Management
Despite advances in understanding the autoimmune nature of 
T1D, this disease remains incurable yet manageable. Central in 
therapy remains the replacement of all functions of the β-cells 
under attack in T1D, which involves more than just administra­
tion of insulin. T1D treatment consists of an integrated approach 
that includes insulin replacement, mimicking the physiologic 
insulin profiles of the body’s own β-cells as closely as possible, 
assisted by intensive monitoring of blood glucose levels and 
health-promoting behavior by the person living with T1D. The 
person living with T1D is at the center of the treatment and deter­
mines, to a large extent, the day-to-day basis of the treatment him­
self or herself. Support systems should be diverse, ranging from 
the health care team, consisting of doctors, diabetes educators, 
dietitians, and others, to the person’s family and the whole social 
network around the person living with T1D.212,237
Management requires orchestrated efforts on the part of the 
person with diabetes, family members, and the multidisciplinary 
health care team. Important stakeholders may vary, depending on 
the age of onset of the disease, comorbid conditions, and stages of 
transition throughout the lifespan, from early childhood through 
adolescence and young adulthood to adulthood and the middle-
age years, then finally culminating in the advancing years of the 
geriatric population. Although diabetes diagnosed in childhood 
is predominantly due to T1D, half of those living with T1D are 
diagnosed in adulthood.259,260 Loss of functional β-cell mass is 
most rapid in those diagnosed at a young age, making their treat­
ment most challenging.261 Nonetheless, a diagnosis of T1D at any 
age requires exogenous insulin therapy given by injection or CSII; 
careful attention to dietary intake, especially with regard to carbo­
hydrates, the major contributor to glycemic excursions; frequent 
or continuous monitoring of glucose levels with a blood glucose 
meter or CGM, respectively; and an exercise program that is as 
much therapeutic as recreational in nature. These management 
activities require constant vigilance, with attention to treatment 
needs 24 hours per day, 7 days a week, every week of the year.
Such a management program requires input of a multidisci­
plinary treatment team composed of an endocrinologist or phy­
sician with specific training and interest in diabetes, a certified 
diabetes educator, a dietitian, and a mental health professional 
(either a social worker or psychologist) with diabetes behavioral 
health expertise. Other team members can include an exercise 
physiologist, an ophthalmologist or optometrist with diabetes 
expertise, a podiatrist, a nephrologist, a gynecologist in case of 
pregnancy (planning), and other specialists as indicated. Most 
importantly, persons with T1D of all ages require continuous 
access to a health care provider through an emergency contact 
number in case of emergence of acute complications, such as 
severe hypoglycemia or DKA.
Visit frequency for diabetes care depends on the age at diag­
nosis, duration of disease, and presence of comorbidities. At T1D 
1405
CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
diagnosis, initiation of insulin therapy is amenable to outpatient 
management when electrolytes are stable and in the absence of 
acidosis, but in many countries, inpatient structured educational 
programs spanning 4 to 5 days are preferred at diagnosis (see fol­
lowing discussion).237 When in an outpatient setting, initial visits 
usually entail 2 to 3 sequential days of multidisciplinary visits, 
followed by visits in 2 to 3 weeks, then 1 to 2 months later. There­
after, diabetes follow-up care generally occurs quarterly, especially 
in childhood, when there is a need to monitor growth and devel­
opment. Both weight and height, along with vital signs, should be 
obtained at every quarterly visit, and Tanner staging should be per­
formed at least annually for pediatric patients, along with timely 
screening for complications and cardiovascular risk factors.237
In early childhood, initial management education is directed 
to the parents/guardians, whereas a family-based approach to 
care continues throughout later childhood and adolescence.212 As 
children get older, diabetes management tasks and the delivery of 
medical care gradually shift to the person with diabetes, although 
T1D at any age is not a do-it-yourself condition, given the many 
daily treatment demands and nuances of advanced diabetes tech­
nologies. In adulthood, following the visit frequency required for 
all persons newly diagnosed with T1D, follow-up visits may occur 
every 3 to 6 months, depending on the achievement of glycemic 
goals and the presence of comorbidities.237,262
Diabetes education for all stakeholders occurs in a develop­
mentally appropriate manner, geared to ensure comprehension of 
all involved in care. Fundamental aspects of diabetes care include 
promoting healthy behaviors through medical nutrition therapy 
(MNT), physical activity, and psychological support, as well as 
the growing issue of weight management in T1D as needed. This 
should be delivered in the context of DSMES, which is critical to 
an integrated, holistic, person-centered approach in T1D263–265 
and is as important to the management plan as insulin replace­
ment itself.
DSMES should be offered on an ongoing basis to all people 
with T1D throughout their life, should be provided by trained 
educators, and can be delivered using multiple approaches and in 
a variety of settings.37,264 Four critical times where DSMES is par­
ticularly important occur (1) at diagnosis, (2) when not meeting 
targets, (3) when transitions occur, and (4) when complications 
develop.264,266
Diabetes management should be tailored to the needs and 
desires of the person with diabetes, creating an individualized care 
approach. Management approaches must be reassessed during the 
various developmental stages, especially during puberty, when 
physiologic insulin resistance coupled with psychosocial turmoil 
can lead to increased insulin needs and deteriorating glycemic 
control.267,268 Similarly, adult needs change and require equal 
attention by the provider tailored to the individual’s preferences. 
In particular, more and more people with T1D now reach older 
ages, with newly emerging special needs when confronted with 
cognitive impairment or incapacity for self-care.269
Furthermore, it should be acknowledged that social determi­
nants of health (SDOH) contribute to medical and psychosocial 
outcomes and must be addressed to improve health outcomes. 
SDOH are often out of the individual’s direct control and poten­
tially represent lifelong risk. Specific SDOH areas have been 
identified to influence outcomes in people with T1D, including 
socioeconomic status (education, income, and occupation), living 
and working conditions, multisector domains (e.g., housing, edu­
cation, criminal justice system), sociocultural context (e.g., shared 
cultural values, practices, experiences), and sociopolitical context 
(e.g., societal and political norms that are root-cause ideologies 
and policies underlying health disparities).270 It is especially 
important to address these SDOH in children and families living 
with T1D, and additional members may have to be added to the 
multidisciplinary health care team accompanying the person liv­
ing with T1D. The types of professional needed may vary during 
the lifespan of the person with T1D.
Finally, specific attention needs to be paid to “key” moments 
in life, like the transition to adulthood. At the age of 18 years, in 
most centers throughout the world, people with T1D will tran­
sition from pediatric teams to teams accompanying adults with 
T1D. Care should be taken to allow smooth transitions, reas­
suring the people with T1D who have been used to the care by 
teams of people who have known them for many years that the 
care in the new setting will be of similar standards and quality. At 
the moment of transition, introduction to the whole team, medi­
cal and paramedical, should happen, reassuring the person with 
T1D. Adult clinics should take care to give appropriate attention 
to those living with T1D and not let these people with special 
needs disappear in the pool of people living with T2D, who often 
outnumber those with T1D and have different needs. In prepara­
tion to transition, growing teens should begin to learn about the 
process of transition to adult health care starting in early to mid-
adolescence from the pediatric diabetes health care team. In the 
final year of pediatric care, the young adult should receive names 
and contact information of adult diabetes care providers. Then, 
both the pediatric and adult providers can help support the trans­
fer and ensure the appropriate transmission of important diabetes 
medical information.271,272 Numerous online resources have been 
developed to assist in the transition process.273 Finally, although 
the topic of transition from pediatric to adult care continues to 
generate substantial clinical and research interest, another tran­
sition period, specifically the one from adulthood to a more 
mature older adult group, also requires ongoing attention. This 
is especially important given that there are substantial numbers of 
persons with T1D living many decades with diabetes and surviv­
ing well into the geriatric years, indicating a need to reassess the 
cognitive abilities and hypoglycemia risk in the older person with 
diabetes.274,275 Many people with T1D are now at advanced ages, 
and data on effectiveness and safety of novel technologies in this 
age group are as convincing as in those at younger ages, including 
use of the most complex hybrid closed-loop systems.275 A grow­
ing problem, however, is the care for people with T1D living in 
nursing homes, where experience with T2D is mostly present but 
experience with the specific characteristics of T1D therapy, in par­
ticular, use of novel technologies, such as CGM, CSII, or hybrid 
closed-loop systems, is mostly limited.275 
Insulin Therapy
Background
The cornerstone of T1D therapy remains insulin replacement, 
mimicking the physiologic insulin secretion by the destroyed 
β-cells. This is challenging because insulin demands vary accord­
ing to meals, exercise, and many other factors, such as stress or 
even stages of life (e.g., puberty or pregnancy). Therefore, insulin 
replacement needs to be embedded in an individualized treatment 
approach that includes DSMES and self-monitoring of glucose 
(see later discussion).237
Normal physiologic insulin secretion results in low levels of 
insulin in the fasting and overnight periods and rapid increases in 
1406
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
insulin after food intake, stress, and certain medications. Low basal 
insulin secretion is necessary for covering fasting metabolic needs, 
suppressing lipolysis, and balancing glucose utilization by organs 
such as the brain with hepatic glucose production.276 Increases in 
insulin in response to rising blood glucose levels facilitate cellular 
glucose uptake and suppress hepatic glucose production. Nor­
mally, this response to glucose is achieved through a substantial 
initial first-phase release, followed by an extended second-phase 
secretion into the portal circulation.
The goal of insulin therapy in persons with T1D is to mirror 
pancreatic insulin patterns, and this biphasic insulin release is par­
ticularly difficult to replicate. Fortunately, improvements in the 
pharmacology and delivery of insulin have made it increasingly 
possible to achieve closer mimicking of the physiologic insulin 
profiles in many living with T1D.277
Many changes in the way insulin has been used in people 
with T1D have occurred since its first clinical use in 1922. 
The discovery and initial isolation of animal insulin in 1921 
first made it possible to treat persons with T1D, changing this 
acutely lethal disease into a chronic condition. In the late 1940s, 
regular animal insulin was combined with protamine (neutral 
protamine Hagedorn insulin [NPH]) to delay absorption and 
increase duration of action.4 In 1977, recombinant DNA tech­
nology allowed purification of insulin and production of syn­
thetic “human” insulin. This major breakthrough generated the 
production of large amounts of insulin and also resulted in a 
reduction of insulin antibodies and insulin allergies. This devel­
opment was followed by the biochemical modification of the 
insulin molecule to vary insulin action, giving rise to the so-
called insulin analogues.278
The treatment of diabetes was further improved by subsequent 
development of rapid-acting insulin analogues in the 1990s and 
long-acting (basal) insulin analogues in the early 2000s, which has 
led to lower rates of hypoglycemia, along with less weight gain and 
improved glycemic control in persons with T1D.279
In parallel to the availability of novel insulin preparations, 
novel tools for insulin administration became available, with the 
evolution from glass syringes to plastic ones in the 1970s and the 
arrival of insulin pens and user-friendly insulin pumps for CSII 
in the 1980s and 1990s. In the 21st century, technology for T1D 
treatment really evolved, with the arrival of hybrid closed-loop 
pump systems, connected insulin pens, and all kinds of educa­
tional apps and decision-making systems supporting people living 
with T1D (see following discussion and Chapter 36).280 
Insulin Preparations
Examples of commercially available insulin preparations are shown in 
Table 35.6 and vary in time to onset, peak, and duration of action.

U-200), and U-500 regular human insulin (Lilly Humulin). These 
concentrated insulin preparations are most commonly used in per­
sons with T2D, but they are beneficial for some individuals with 
T1D who have significant insulin resistance and high insulin require­
ments.281 In very young children requiring small doses of insulin 
(e.g., less than 0.5 unit bolus doses), rapid-acting insulin diluted to a 
tenth of the usual concentration (10 units/mL, often called U-10) or

Considering the results from the DCCT, intensive insulin 
therapy has become the standard of care for treatment of T1D 
and can be achieved with multiple daily injections (MDIs) basal-
bolus therapy or insulin pump therapy. In both MDIs and pump 
therapy, rapid-acting insulin is given as a bolus at meals and snacks 
and periodically to correct hyperglycemia (no more frequently 
than every 2–3 hours). Basal insulin is given once or twice a day 
with long-acting insulin (for MDIs) or as a basal rate (for insulin 
pumps). 
Initial Management in People With Newly 
Diagnosed Type 1 Diabetes
Despite growing numbers of initiatives for screening for T1D risk 
in families with T1D or even in the general population, people, 
in particular children, still often present in DKA (see later discus­
sion) at diagnosis, which is unfortunately still a life-threatening 
situation and has long-term implications.283–285
In people with newly diagnosed T1D, initial management often 
includes resuscitation with oral or intravenous fluids to rehydrate 
and correct electrolyte imbalances, administration of insulin to 
halt lipolysis and reverse hepatic gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis, 
and commencement of diabetes education. Depending on factors 
such as the age of the individual and severity of his or her clini­
cal presentation, family factors, and availability of diabetes-related 
resources, initial management may occur in an intensive care unit, 
inpatient hospital setting, or outpatient unit.237,286 People with 
newly diagnosed T1D should also be informed of the many clini­
cal trials aiming to arrest further β-cell destruction and the pos­
sibility of screening family members for their risk of developing 
T1D themselves.24,26,287 
Initiation of Insulin Therapy
For those individuals who do not initially present in DKA, treat­
ment with subcutaneous insulin should be started at diagnosis of 
diabetes. For those who present in DKA, subcutaneous insulin 
should begin with resolution of DKA and normalization of the 
anion gap, in conjunction with the first meal being eaten post-
DKA. Determination of the appropriate starting insulin dose 
must consider the person’s weight, age, pubertal status, and his­
tory of DKA. For young children and postpubertal adults who are 
not obese and do not present in DKA, a typical starting dose is 0.3 
to 0.5 units/kg per day. Higher doses will be needed for individu­
als who are obese, children in puberty, or after presentation with 
DKA, such that a pubertal child with obesity and resolved DKA 
may receive a starting dose of 1 unit/kg per day. This total daily 
dose (TDD) of insulin is typically given in a divided program of 
MDIs, with about 50% of the TDD delivered as a once-daily dose 
of basal insulin and 50% given as boluses.288
In MDIs, basal insulin is initiated mostly as insulin analogues 
once daily, typically at bedtime, preferentially at the same time 
every day. However, with the newer, longer-acting insulin ana­
logues (e.g., insulin degludec and U-300 glargine), more flexible 
timing of administration is possible.4,237
For assessing bolus doses, a combination of premeal glucose 
levels and carbohydrate content of the meal will guide the person 
with T1D or their caretakers. With the help of dietitians, people 
with newly diagnosed T1D are assisted in learning to assess the 
carbohydrate content of their meals. Depending on the abilities 
and preferences of the person affected by T1D and their families, 
fixed boluses (when eating relatively stable amounts of carbohy­
drates at meals) or, more often, carb-counting can be used.7 When 
deciding on carb-counting, weighing of foods, and deduction of 
carbohydrate content, use of educational materials and, more often 
now, apps will guide the person and their caretakers to assess the 
carbohydrate content of each meal.289 The medical team will then 
provide guidance on insulin doses by offering a schedule of how 
many grams of carbohydrate will require 1 unit of fast-acting insu­
lin. When the person or the family prefers not to or is not able to 
weigh foods, the team can propose use of carbohydrate equivalents, 
where a specific number of units of insulin per estimated carbohy­
drate unit (15 g of carbohydrate) is prescribed at every meal.290,291 
Insulin Dose Adjustments
Treatment with MDIs or CSII requires calculation of the appro­
priate insulin bolus at each meal and snack based on the premeal 
blood glucose level and the planned carbohydrate intake.
To calculate the bolus, the person will first calculate the proper 
carbohydrate coverage for the meal using his or her individualized 
insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio. The carbohydrate ratio is the number 
of grams of carbohydrate covered by 1 unit of insulin (roughly 450 
divided by the TDD). Most patients do these calculations by hand, 
with mental math or calculators, or with the help of apps or pump 
or smart pen bolus wizards, but some patients and families require 
sliding scales or charts for determination of bolus dosing.290,291 
Rapid-acting insulin boluses using insulin analogues (lispro, aspart, 
glulisine) should be given 10 to 15 minutes before the start of a 
meal or snack because onset of action is about 15 minutes. The 
newer generations of analogues (faster-acting insulin aspart, ultra-
rapid insulin lispro) have an even faster onset of glucose-lowering 
action and allow for shortening the time between injection and start 
of meal, without compromising on glucose control.7 In cases where 
food intake is less predictable (e.g., very young children, gastroen­
teritis), the more rapid onset of action of the novel rapid-acting insu­
lins allows safe and effective postmeal bolus administration.292,293 
Because rapid-acting insulin has a 2- to 3-hour action time, a cor­
rection bolus is usually not given any more frequently than every 2 
to 3 hours to avoid hypoglycemia from “stacking” of insulin action. 
Physical activity (i.e., recent or planned exercise) should factor into 
insulin bolus calculations, with less insulin required before, during, 
or after certain types of exercise. Additionally, a blood glucose trend 
based on continuous glucose monitor arrows may also factor into 
the insulin bolus calculation at mealtime.294
With MDIs, the basal insulin component is kept stable from 
day to day, with dose adaptations by the person with T1D, in 
shared decision making with the health care team, every week 
based on fasting glycemia (titration to the individualized insulin 
target) in the absence of nocturnal hypoglycemia. Again in shared 
decision making with the team, adaptations of basal insulin can be 
done on a more frequent basis, for instance, in periods of exercise, 
intercurrent illness, or other disruptors of daily life.237 Basal insu­
lin rates in people using CSII vary depending on the systems used 
(see later discussion and Chapter 36). 
Principles of Insulin Pump Use
For a detailed description of the use of insulin pumps and 
advanced CSII technology, we refer to Chapter 36. Briefly, CSII 
1408
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
is a form of insulin delivery that enables intensive insulin therapy 
through a continuous infusion of rapid-acting insulin subcutane­
ously using an insulin pump. Insulin pumps are gaining in popu­
larity, thanks to their growing user-friendliness and, in particular, 
their combination with glucose-sensing systems and algorithms, 
elevating them to more intelligent systems that will adapt the flow 
of insulin depending on sensor-measured glucose levels, rapidly 
approaching the concept of an “artificial pancreas.” As is discussed 
in more detail in Chapter 36, several CSII systems are available to 
people with T1D, with different features, sizes, and technology to 
support their individual needs and requirements.295–297
One of the advantages of the use of CSII, even in its simplest 
format, as its name implies, is its ability to continuously deliver 
insulin and allow users to respond more rapidly to any changes 
in their physiologic insulin requirements. Second, most modern 
CSII pumps enable the user to program and modify key param­
eters that affect insulin delivery, such as (1) the basal rate profile, 
in which several basal rates with multiple insulin segments can be 
entered to address changes in insulin requirements between work­
days and weekends, active days or sick days, and more; (2) the 
storing of multiple sensitivity factors, as well as carbohydrate-to-
insulin ratio; (3) alerts and alarms; and (4) bolus calculators and 
insulin-on-board estimators, to prevent overstacking of insulin.
CSII therapy in itself has been associated with improved glycemic 
control, decreased hypoglycemia, and better quality of life.298–301 
Still, there are several disadvantages of this delivery route. Using 
CSII means that the user is attached to an external device, which 
may be inconvenient in daily life. Classic insulin pumps deliver 
insulin under the skin through a catheter and an infusion set. 
Although catheters allowing use for up to 7 days are reaching the 
clinic, for most catheters, it is recommended to change the infu­
sion set every 3 days to reduce problems with site irritation and 
irregularity in insulin delivery caused by blocked catheters, insulin 
leakage, or cannula dislodgement.302–305 A failure of the infusion 
site can lead to hyperglycemia—and potentially DKA if the prob­
lem is not detected in time.
In recent years, patch pumps, where the device is attached 
directly to the skin and infusion happens without the need for 
catheters linking the pump to an infusion set, have become 
popular.297
The largest advantage of pump technology is the availability of 
smarter devices that integrate CGM functionality, as well as algo­
rithms that enable insulin suspension based on a fixed threshold or 
predictive design, to minimize hypoglycemia and improve glyce­
mic outcomes. The latest leap forward in pump technology is the 
development of hybrid closed-loop insulin delivery devices that 
build on the current small and smart devices and add a control 
algorithm that is tasked with calculating the safe dose of insulin 
and adapting the basal rate to glucose levels and trends in these 
levels, as well as desired glucose targets in an individual person, 
taking into account exercise and other features of daily life. These 
devices are available as commercial packages combining pump, 
algorithm, and sensor, or they can be a “do-it-yourself” composed 
system (see Chapter 36).306–309
Use of CSII, from its simplest to its most complex, integrated 
format, requires specific education that should be embedded in 
the individualized DSMES program of the patient and their fam­
ily, as well as accompaniment of the person using the devices and 
their family members, to fully capture the benefits of the system. 
Specific technical education should be provided, but education on 
nutrition and exercise should also be refreshed when switching to 
pump systems.237 
Decision Support Systems
An emerging field in diabetes care is decision support that uses 
connected care devices such as CGM, smart insulin pens, self-
monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG), and insulin pumps to 
provide guidance and advice to people with T1D via smart apps 
or cloud-based algorithms (see following discussion).310–312 This 
evolving field can improve care of both MDI and CSII users 
by providing tools to adjust basal insulin doses, as well as meal 
and correction boluses, based on glucose input and peoples’ 
lifestyles. These tools can provide additional insight for the 
clinical team with enhanced visualization and advice on insulin 
management.313 
Other Insulin Regimen Options
In individualizing each person’s insulin regimen, clinicians must 
consider the frequency of blood glucose monitoring (BGM), 
the number of daily injections, the need for flexibility in meal 
planning, and the work/family schedule. In a minority of people 
living with T1D, treatment with intensive insulin therapy and 
mealtime bolus calculations may not be feasible or appropriate. 
In these cases, other regimens, including human insulin and, in 
rare circumstances, even premixed insulins (70/30, 75/25, 50/50 
mixtures) can be used. To avoid hypoglycemia in such regimens, 
meals are typically fixed with regard to timing and amount of car­
bohydrates consumed. 
Insulin Allergy
In contrast to the problematic formation of antibodies against 
animal insulins used in the early days, the advent of human insu­
lins or analogues has significantly reduced issues with reactivity 
against injected insulin. Mild immune reactivity against exog­
enously administered insulin is, however, frequent in all with 
T1D after initiation of exogenous insulin. Indeed, essentially all 
patients treated with recombinant human insulin or analogues 
produce anti-insulin antibodies.314 The levels of these antibodies 
are relatively low, and they do not appear to interfere with insu­
lin therapy for the majority of individuals. Most studies show no 
relationship between the presence of anti-insulin antibodies and 
complications associated with T1D (e.g., retinopathy, neuropa­
thy).314 With the introduction of recombinant human insulin 
replacing animal insulins, symptomatic immune responses to 
insulin, such as immediate hypersensitivity, delayed hypersen­
sitivity, and lipoatrophy, have decreased. However, repetitive 
injection of insulin in the same area of the body continues to 
induce lipohypertrophy, which can interfere with the stability of 
insulin resorption.315 Avoidance of lipohypertrophy is a topic of 
diabetes education, and providers should evaluate injection sites 
for its occurrence during physical examination of patients using 
insulin.316
Allergic reactions can occur with insulin analogues, modifica­
tions of recombinant human insulin, although this is uncommon. 
More common features include allergies to affiliated lubricants; 
preservatives; and plastics in bottles, stoppers, syringes, and 
needles. The usual mode of therapy for such situations consists 
of substituting the type or formulation of insulin and adminis­
tration of oral antihistamines or topical mast cell stabilizers for 
IgE-mediated local reactions, followed by insulin desensitization 
or addition of small amounts of glucocorticoids to the insulin 
injected for local delayed hypersensitivity reactions.317
