CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
Health Behavior Management: Nutrition and 
Exercise
Health behavior management is a major component of the care of 
persons with T1D. Attention to both nutrition and exercise is fun­
damental in glycemic management (avoidance of insulin-induced 
hypoglycemia and weight gain), as well as for overall health and 
cardiovascular disease prevention. There is a need to provide edu­
cation on these health behavior issues to the persons with T1D 
and to the family members of young children and adolescents 
with T1D, especially given the global epidemic of childhood and 
adult overweight/obesity.237 Overall, all diet and physical activ­
ity recommendations are individualized to meet the patient’s and 
family’s needs. These knowledge areas should be addressed in a 
structured way, using DSMES programs, and should begin at 
diagnosis and progress as disease duration increases and the needs 
of the person with T1D change.264,318
Nutrition Therapy
MNT addresses diabetes-specific issues, such as those related 
to the carbohydrate content of foods to limit postprandial gly­
cemic excursions, as well as ways to maintain normal growth in 
the pediatric population and avoid excessive weight gain across 
the lifespan.237 Nutrition education, generally provided by a reg­
istered dietitian annually after the initial education at diagnosis, 
includes both personal and family dietary choices, food prefer­
ence changes over time, challenges regarding access to food, meal 
schedules, patterns of exercise, growth and development, weight 
status, cardiovascular risk factors, and consideration of disordered 
eating behaviors.
For the growing child with diabetes, provision of adequate cal­
ories to maintain normal growth and development is fundamen­
tal.319 Underweight is a rare occurrence today in youth with T1D. 
In fact, one-third of pediatric patients with T1D are overweight 
or obese.320,321 Diet prescriptions for adults with T1D should also 
account for weight status, given the rise in overweight and obesity 
among those with T1D and the association of increased weight 
with cardiovascular risk in T1D.322,323
Nutrition education addresses the way foods affect glu­
cose excursions, how diet can help achieve glycemic goals, and 
dietary approaches to avoid hypo- and hyperglycemia with exer­
cise. Nutrition education addresses numeracy, literacy, and self-
management abilities of those with diabetes and their family 
members.324–326
Principles of general nutrition include a focus on whole foods 
and the standard composition of macronutrients, with approxi­
mately 50% of energy intake as carbohydrates, 20% as protein, 
and 30% as fat. Fat intake should include less than 10% of energy 
intake as saturated fat, less than 10% as polyunsaturated fat, and 
greater than 10% as monounsaturated fat. One should try to eat 
five portions of fruits and vegetables daily. Often, young persons 
with diabetes, with the support of their parents, may choose to eat 
less healthy food choices, such as prepackaged foods that include 
the carbohydrate content on the label, instead of fruits or veg­
etables. Nutrition education should follow published guidelines 
by professional organizations, such as the ADA, the European 
Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD), and ISPAD.237,327 
Very low carbohydrates should be avoided because such diets can 
lead to elevations in lipid levels, and there can be a risk for ketosis, 
especially with insulin dose reductions, disordered eating behav­
iors, or use of the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) class 
of oral agents, currently not approved for use in persons with T1D 
(see later discussion of adjunctive therapies).
The major focus of nutrition education is on carbohydrate 
counting because carbohydrates have the largest impact on gly­
cemic excursions. So-called carbohydrate counting can provide 
flexible diet management by allowing for a wide range of food 
choices. It can also offer a way to select insulin doses based on 
food intake.328 When numeracy skills are deficient, experienced 
estimation of carbohydrate intake suffices. In fact, previous studies 
have shown that exactitude in carbohydrate counting is unneces­
sary because under- or overestimating the carbohydrate content 
by 5 to 7 g, or by +/–15%, does not produce significant hypo- or 
hyperglycemia, respectively.329 Furthermore, it is more important 
to be consistent rather than exact with carbohydrate counting 
because the former is associated with better glycemic control.330
Additional studies have addressed the need to consider pro­
tein and fat intake on glycemic excursions.331,332 After one has 
mastered carbohydrate counting, additional advanced nutrition 
education can include issues related to meal composition, car­
bohydrate quality (the glycemic index), and the contributions of 
protein and fat to glycemic excursions. Considering that meals 
containing substantial protein and fat can delay gastric empty­
ing and the subsequent postprandial glycemic excursion, nutrition 
education can address advanced approaches to insulin bolusing. 
For example, one can use a square-wave (or extended-wave) bolus 
or a dual-wave (or combination-wave) bolus with CSII, or one 
can divide the injected bolus doses into two separate injections 
separated in time by 60 to 90 minutes.
Specific diets are not advised in people with T1D, but many 
will discover the advantage of somewhat cutting carbohydrates in 
their meals for stabilization of postprandial glucose excursions.333 
Reduction of carbohydrate intake is acceptable, but extreme 
“ketosis-prone” diets where all carbohydrates are cut should be 
avoided, in particular in those on CSII, to avoid DKA risk.334 
In cases where families or persons living with T1D want to fol­
low these ketogenic diets, specific educational interventions are 
needed.335 
Physical Activity and Exercise
Physical activity is important for persons with and without dia­
betes. Exercise offers physical fitness, strength building, weight 
management, socialization, enhancement of self-esteem, and car­
diovascular risk factor management.336,337 Exercise is a key com­
ponent of diabetes management. Recommendations for youth 
include 60 minutes or more of daily physical activity, which 
should include muscle- and bone-strengthening activities on 3 
or more days each week.338 Recommendations for adults include 
at least two to three sessions per week of resistance exercise on 
nonconsecutive days, 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic 
activity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity each 
week, decreasing the amount of time spent in daily sedentary 
behavior, and flexibility training and balance training two to three 
times per week for older adults with diabetes.339
Adults with diabetes, and occasionally pediatric patients with 
diabetes, should receive medical clearance before embarking on an 
exercise program to evaluate the presence of any comorbid condi­
tions or diabetes complications that could limit exercise partici­
pation, such as previously undiagnosed coronary heart disease or 
proliferative retinopathy.
It is important to recognize how exercise affects glyce­
mic excursions because exercise can lead to both hypoglycemia 
1410
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
and hyperglycemia. Exercise affects fuel metabolism through 
the recruitment of various hormones (insulin, glucagon, cat­
echolamines, and glucocorticoids), and the impact of exercise 
on metabolism varies by the type, intensity, and duration of the 
activity.340,341 With intact islet cells, including fully functioning 
β-cells, the body maintains euglycemia during exercise by balanc­
ing glucose uptake with hepatic glucose production. In T1D, it is 
not possible to reduce insulin production after the administration 
of an insulin dose; therefore, the circulating insulin can lead to 
hypoglycemia by both inhibiting hepatic glucose production and 
promoting exercise-related glucose uptake. Alternatively, in T1D, 
high-intensity activities, such as sprints or resistance training, can 
lead to hyperglycemia when there is not enough circulating insu­
lin because of the intense exercise’s stimulation of counterregula­
tory hormone release, which in turn will increase hepatic glucose 
production and inhibit glucose uptake into skeletal muscle.
Even though the positive effects of regular physical activity 
are well described, only 40% to 50% of individuals with T1D 
achieve a physically active lifestyle as assessed by questionnaires 
and motion sensors.342,343 Glucose fluctuations during and after 
physical activity are related to several factors, such as type (aero­
bic vs. anaerobic), intensity, timing, and duration of the planned 
or unplanned physical activity, as well as the person’s insulin 
regimen and physical fitness.340,341,344 In general, most persons 
with T1D, as well as their family members, worry more about 
exercise-induced hypoglycemia. Further, they are often frustrated 
and puzzled by the appearance of hyperglycemia with exercise. 
Hypoglycemia can occur during and immediately after the activ­
ity, then again 7 to 11 hours after the exercise, corresponding to 
the so-called lag effect of exercise. The latter phenomenon was 
shown in insulin clamp studies345 and likely results from enhanced 
insulin sensitivity, blunted counterregulatory hormone release, 
and increased glucose uptake by the liver and skeletal muscles to 
replenish glycogen stores after exercise. The late risk of hypogly­
cemia often occurs overnight when persons with diabetes exer­
cise in the late afternoon or evening, causing particular concern 
for patients and family members. For some persons with T1D, 
there can be additional impairment of counterregulatory hormone 
responses as a result of blunting during sleep, antecedent hypo­
glycemia, and autonomic failure.346–348 Thus, exercise-related 
hypoglycemia, along with fear of hypoglycemia, can curtail exer­
cise participation. Fortunately, there are ways to limit the risk of 
exercise-related hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia while managing 
glycemia with exercise. Management approaches follow; for more 
in-depth discussion, there are recently published exercise manage­
ment guidelines.340,341,344,349
To prevent glycemic excursions, people with T1D should first 
take into account five important parameters that affect glucose 
during exercise: (1) type, intensity, and duration of the exercise; 
(2) actual glucose values and trends (preferably by CGM); (3) 
timing of exercise (i.e., fasting or postmeal); (4) actual insulin on 
board; and (5) carbs needed during exercise (Fig. 35.6A). A recent 
position statement reports on the evidence-based efficacy of glu­
cose sensing around exercise and adaptations in the use of inter­
mittently scanned CGM (isCGM) and real-time CGM (rtCGM) 
to improve glucose control by providing guidance for exercise in 
children, adolescents, and adults with T1D (Box 35.1).344 To pre­
vent hypoglycemia, one should begin exercise with a glucose of 
at least 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) or higher and plan to ingest 
carbohydrates during and/or after the exercise according to its 
duration and intensity. One can consider providing 0.25 g to up 
to 1.00 g of carbohydrate per minute of exercise when the activity 
lasts 40 minutes or longer, individualized based on the person’s 
size (i.e., toddler or child), his or her needs, and past experi­
ence. The additional carbohydrates can be provided by increasing 
food intake. Additionally, one can reduce bolus insulin doses, by 
approximately 25% to 75% as a starting point, for any meal or 
snack within 2 hours of the planned activity, which may be prefer­
able to increasing carbohydrate ingestion for weight management 
(see Fig. 35.6B). For those receiving CSII, basal rates can also be 
lowered by approximately 50% or even suspended for periods of 1 
to 2 hours for exercise based on the patient’s needs.350 To manage 
the lag effect or late hypoglycemia risk after exercise, basal rates 
can be reduced by approximately 20% for up to 6 hours at bed­
time for those treated with CSII, or long-acting insulin doses can 
be reduced by approximately 20% at bedtime.351 Despite these 
insulin-dosing strategies, it remains important to have carbohy­
drates available for ingestion and to ensure continuous or frequent 
glucose monitoring for safe exercise.
To prevent significant hyperglycemia with exercise and induc­
tion of ketosis, it is important not to exercise when one is in an 
insulin-deficient state. The person with diabetes should exer­
cise only when feeling well and in the absence of significant 
ketosis, defined as more than small urinary ketones or a blood 
β-hydroxybutyrate level of 1.5 mmol/L or more.340,341,344,349 One 
should also postpone intense exercise with significant hyperglyce­
mia, defined as a glucose level of 350 mg/dL (19.4 mmol/L) or 
more, until corrected with insulin. Exercise education can help 
limit the hypo- and hyperglycemic effects of exercise. When avail­
able, an exercise physiologist can add training with respect to 
exercise management, which can be especially important for the 
competitive athlete.
These strategies to avoid physical activity–induced hypo- and 
hyperglycemia, although helpful, are often not sufficient. People 
with T1D have to plan their physical activity in advance to adjust 
insulin injections or pump infusion rates and are often required to 
consume extra carbs, which can lead to excess caloric intake, more 
complex weight management, and exercise-related hyperglycemia. 
As described in short earlier and in detail in Chapter 36, closed-
loop systems are increasingly used by patients with T1D. Differ­
ent strategies are advised for the management of exercise while on 
closed-loop systems, but none is able to completely avoid exercise-
related glucose fluctuations. Several reasons exist, such as insuffi­
cient adaptations of the algorithm to physical activity and a delay 
in subcutaneous insulin absorption that reduces the effectiveness 
of its suspension. In a recent trial,352 a single-hormone closed-loop 
system (insulin alone) was compared to a dual-hormone closed-
loop system (insulin plus glucagon) during exercise in adults 
with T1D. The results suggest that using a dual-hormone system 
with exercise announcement 20 minutes in advance but without 
extra carb intake may reduce exercise-induced hypoglycemia and 
improve TIR during both continuous and interval exercise. 
Glucose Measurement
Self-Monitoring of Blood Glucose
Self-management of diabetes requires the routine monitoring of 
glucose levels to select and adjust insulin doses, to understand the 
impact of various foods on glycemic excursions, to reduce the risk 
of exercise-related hypo- or hyperglycemia, and to react to periods 
of illness or stress that can lead to increased glucose variability 
and hyperglycemia with ketosis, along with risk for ketoacidosis. 
In some situations (toddlers, very old people, incapacitated or 
hospitalized persons), glucose monitoring is performed by a third 
1411
CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
person, such as teachers and childcare or health care providers. 
In order to perform a glucose measurement, a drop of blood is 
obtained from the fingertip with the help of an automated spring-
loaded puncturing device and applied on a glucose strip that is 
inserted into a glucose meter. There are numerous glucose meters 
available that use a small volume of blood (0.3–1 μL), provide 
results in less than 5 seconds, offer alternative site use beyond 
fingertips, and meet recent standards of accuracy. Adequate edu­
cation on the proper use of glucose meters (e.g., avoid unclean fin­
gers, no milking of fingertip) and possible interfering substances 
(e.g., acetaminophen, ascorbic and uric acid, xylose, galactose, 
or L-dopa) is essential to avoid inaccurate measurements. Accu­
racy standards include the need for at least 95% of blood glucose 
meter results to fall within ±15 mg/dL (0.8 mmol/L) for blood 
glucose <100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) and within ±15% for blood 
glucose ≥100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) performed with a reference 
method,353 with recommendations allowing for ongoing assess­
ment of meter performance.354 Each year, the ADA provides an 
update of available meters, along with a cataloging of their vari­
ous features.355 Although there may be substantial choice in the 
selection of glucose meters, one must mainly consider insurance 
coverage and the need to link the meter with a pump for CSII.
Daily BGM frequency has been repeatedly linked to lower 
HbA1c levels and lower rates of acute complications in children 
and adults.356–358 For persons with T1D, BGM is generally rec­
ommended at least 4 times daily and up to 10 to 12 times daily.

Timing and frequency should be individualized based on the goals 
and needs of the person. Monitoring generally occurs before meals/
snacks and at bedtime (target 80–130 mg/dL; 4.4–7.2 mmol/L), 
with monitoring at other salient times, such as postprandially (tar­
get <180 mg/dL [10 mmol/L] or <140 mg/dL [7.8 mmol/L]), 
overnight, before/during/after exercise, when low glucose is sus­
pected, and during periods of illness or stress. More frequent 
monitoring is often recommended for persons with hypoglycemic 
unawareness (i.e., before driving), during pregnancy, and for those 
unable to communicate symptoms, such as the very young or the 
elderly. It is important to download the glucose meter data at rou­
tine appointments to review glycemic patterns with patients and 
families and to utilize the data to encourage self-management for 
insulin dose adjustments. Modern CGM technologies, especially 
those with nonadjunctive claims for insulin management, have 
supplanted the need for frequent BGM (see the next section). 
Continuous Glucose Monitoring
CGM is increasingly used for routine diabetes care in adults, chil­
dren, and adolescents with T1D. The benefits of CGM devices 
have accrued with improved performance of the devices over 
time.359–361 CGM devices have alerts and alarms for both low and 
high glucose concentrations, as well as trend arrows to fine-tune 
insulin bolus doses at mealtimes in pediatric and adult patients to 
avoid extreme postprandial glucose excursions, especially given the 
recognition that the glucose trajectory and the magnitude of the 
glucose level affect the response to the insulin bolus and ingested 
meal.362,363 CGM is discussed in more detail in Chapter 36. 
Goals of Glucose Control
The ultimate goal in the treatment of T1D is the optimalization of 
the quality of life of the person living with T1D, mostly through 
the prevention of acute and chronic complications.237 Central to 
achieving this goal is achieving glycemic targets through an indi­
vidualized approach, tailored to the profile of each individual per­
son. Considering the overwhelming evidence on the relationship 
between tight glycemic control and prevention of chronic compli­
cations, in all people with T1D, glycemic targets will be set such 
as to achieve the tightest possible glycemic control with the lowest 
risk of hypoglycemia.237
Hemoglobin A1c
Glycemic targets are often based on HbA1c levels, especially given 
that the explanation for complication risk in the DCCT and Epi­
demiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) 
studies was attributable to glycemia.364 The DCCT was the ran­
domized clinical trial that laid the foundation of intensive insulin 
therapy as the standard of care.231 In the DCCT, intensive insulin 
was compared with conventional insulin therapy in 1441 persons, 
13 to 39 years old, with established T1D. Intensive insulin ther­
apy consisted of physiologic insulin replacement with either basal-
bolus therapy or CSII; conventional therapy included one to two 
injections of insulin daily. Intensive insulin therapy yielded supe­
rior glycemic control to conventional insulin therapy, with HbA1c 
levels that were approximately 2% lower in the intensively treated 
group than in the conventionally treated group, with medians of 
7% and 9%, respectively.231 The intensively treated group experi­
enced a 35% to 76% reduction in the occurrence of microvascular 
complications, including retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropa­
thy, compared with the conventionally treated group. The cost of 
intensive management was, however, a two- to threefold increase 
in the rates of severe hypoglycemia, as well as weight gain. More 
than 30 years later, these data need to be put in context, realizing 
that the participants of the DCCT were using human insulins, 
syringes, and older CSII systems to deliver insulin, as well as fin­
gerstick capillary blood glucose measurements as SMBG. During 
the subsequent 20 to 25 years of the DCCT observational follow-
up study, the EDIC study, the intensively treated group compared 
with the conventionally treated group continued to demonstrate a 
reduced risk of both micro- and macrovascular complications and 
overall mortality, mainly attributable to the difference in glycemic 
control during the DCCT.364–370 These findings help derive the 
glycemic targets used in practice today.236
Various national and international professional organizations 
have created HbA1c goals. The ADA recommends HbA1c levels of 
less than 7% for adults and less than 7.5% for younger children 
and adolescents; additionally, HbA1c levels should be routinely 
monitored quarterly.181,212,236 Before 2014, the ADA’s pediatric 
HbA1c goals were higher for younger children, at less than 8.5% 
for those younger than 6 years and less than 8% for those 6 to 
12 years old, whereas the goal was less than 7.5% for those 13 to 
19 years old, due to previous concerns regarding neurocognitive 
Before Exercise
 • Know type, intensity, and duration of exercise.
 • Consider timing of exercise.
 • Know how much insulin is on board.
 • Target a sensor glucose range based on exercise routine and risk of 
hypoglycemia, accompanied by adequate trend arrow. 
During Exercise
 • Target sensor glucose ranges should be between 7.0 and 10.0 mmol/L 
(126–180 mg/dL) and slightly higher for those with an increased risk of 
hypoglycemia.
 • At a glycemic threshold of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) accompanied 
by a horizontal trend arrow, 10 to 15 g of carbohydrates should 
be consumed; 15 to 25 g of carbohydrates should be consumed 
immediately if accompanied by a slightly downward trend arrow; 20 
to 35 g of carbohydrates should be consumed if accompanied by a 
downward trend arrow.
 • If sensor glucose levels are elevated (>15.0 mmol/L [>270 mg/dL]), 
monitor blood ketone levels, and an insulin correction may be performed 
(50% of individual’s regular correction factor).
 • Exercise should be suspended in adults if the sensor glucose level 
reaches <3.9 mmol/L (<70 mg/dL), and if below 3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/
dL), then exercise should not be restarted. 
After Exercise
 • During the first 90 min after exercise, a sensor glucose range of 4.4 
to 10.0 mmol/L (80–180 mg/dL) might be targeted, and 10 to 15 g of 
carbohydrates should be consumed at the lower glucose limit based on 
the trend arrow.
 • If an insulin correction is applied because of high sensor glucose levels, 
then the regular correction factor might be reduced by up to 50%. CGM 
alarm should set at 4.4 mmol/L (80 mg/dL), and those using an isCGM 
system should perform at least one scan during the nighttime period.

In consideration of emerging data on risk of hyperglycemia 
for the central nervous system, along with available manage­
ment tools to minimize risk of hypoglycemia in young persons 
with T1D, HbA1c targets have been lowered by some professional 
organizations, including the ISPAD and the National Institute for 
Health and Clinical Excellence Guidelines in the United King­
dom. ISPAD now recommends HbA1c targets of less than 7%, 
and the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence rec­
ommends targets HbA1c of 6.5% or less.381 Similarly, for adults, 
the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists recom­
mends an HbA1c target of 6.5% or less.382
Although HbA1c target recommendations may have become 
more rigorous over recent years, the ADA and other organizations 
emphasize that glycemic targets need to be individualized. The 
target HbA1c goal for any single person with diabetes needs to 
reflect his or her risk of severe hypoglycemia, as well as hyperglyce­
mia, considering the presence of comorbidities that may interfere 
with survival. For example, the ADA now offers higher HbA1c 
goals of less than 8% for persons with a history of severe hypo­
glycemia, limited life expectancy, or advanced complications, as 
well as more stringent HbA1c goals of less than 6.5% for those 
without hypoglycemia risk.236 ISPAD also considers less stringent 
goals for regions of the world where advanced diabetes thera­
pies and technologies may be unavailable to reduce risk of severe 
hypoglycemia.381 Thus, personalized glycemic goals are tailored to 
individual needs and taking into consideration the risk of severe 
hypoglycemia (see Chapter 38). 
Outcomes Beyond HbA1c
With the advent of novel technologies allowing continuous mea­
surement of glucose levels (CGM), novel measures expressing 
the time an individual spends in a specific glycemic range have 
arisen.383 As such, new standards for expressing glycemic control 
are more commonly used. Evidence is growing on the relation­
ship between the time that glucose is within a specific target range 
(TIR; 70–180 mg/dL; 3.9-10.0 mmol/L) and long-term compli­
cations.383–385 Thus, more and more organizations are adopting 
TIR as a novel metric when setting glycemic targets for people 
living with T1D. An international consensus group proposed that 
for most people living with T1D, an appropriate target is 70% 
TIR (between 70 and 180 mg/dL; 3.9-10.0 mmol/L), with less 
than 4% time below range (TBR; <70 mg/dL; 3.9 mmol/L), of 
which <1% should be <54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L) and less than 
25% in time above range (TAR) (>180 mg/dL; 10.0 mmol/L) and 
less than 5% >250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L).383 In specific stages of 
life, more (e.g., pregnancy) or less (e.g., older age) stringent mea­
sures are proposed.383 Graphic illustrations of the concept of TIR 
are now available for most CGM readout systems, allowing open 
conversations with people living with T1D on their individualized 
targets and ways to achieve them.386 DSMES sessions specifically 
focusing on the interpretation of TIR can be introduced, elevating 
the TIR concept to an important educational tool.387
Several RCTs comparing the use of CGM with capillary blood 
glucose measurements showed that isCGM and rtCGM have a 
beneficial effect on glycemic outcomes and quality of life in peo­
ple with T1D treated with MDIs or insulin pump therapy.388–393 
Consistent CGM use of 6 or more days per week has been associ­
ated with improvements in glycemic control, reflected in lower 
HbA1c levels, more patients achieving HbA1c targets, and reduc­
tion in time in the hypoglycemic range of less than 70 mg/dL 
(<3.9 mmol/L) or less than 54 mg/dL (3 mmol/L).394–397 Simi­
larly, more frequent scanning of the Freestyle Libre has also been 
associated with improved glycemic control, noted by an increase 
of glucose TIR, with reductions of time in hypoglycemia and 
hyperglycemia; mean scanning frequency was about 16 times per 
day in one study.398 In a study comparing first-generation isCGM 
without alerts with rtCGM with alerts, it was shown that 6-month 
use of rtCGM with alert functionality improved TIR and reduced 
time in hyperglycemia >10.0 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) and time in 
hypoglycemia <3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL). This resulted in more 
people achieving the consensus target of >70% TIR and HbA1c 
of <7%.244
Finally, it needs to be acknowledged that although of great 
value to most living with T1D, the novel technology of CGM may 
be beyond affordability for many. Thus, capillary BGM remains of 
great value in the management of T1D and can help people with 
T1D achieve HbA1c goals. 
Glycemic Variability
Glycemic variability is most often defined as fluctuations of glu­
cose values, either measured within or between days (short-term 
variability) or over a longer period (long-term variability). Sev­
eral studies suggest that glycemic variability is an independent 
risk factor for diabetes complications such as cardiovascular dis­
ease and that it relates to the risk of hypoglycemia, cognitive 
function, and quality of life.399,400 Fluctuations can be charac­
terized by their frequency, duration, and amplitude. Currently, 
no consensus exists on the best way to quantify glucose vari­
ability, so several indices are used in clinical care and for research 
purposes. The coefficient of variation for glucose (%CV) is cal­
culated as the standard deviation around the 24-h mean glucose 
divided by 24-h mean glucose expressed as a percentage. It is 
currently integrated into CGM reports (together with standard 
deviation [SD] and TIR) and most often used for quantifying 
daily glucose fluctuations. Per consensus, stable glucose control 
is defined as a CV of <36%, whereas unstable glucose control is 
defined as a CV of >36%.401,402 
Patient-Reported Outcomes
In addition to glycemic metrics beyond HbA1c, there are numer­
ous patient-reported outcomes that warrant attention. These 
include quality of life, well-being, fear of hypoglycemia, diabetes 
distress or burden, treatment satisfaction, self-efficacy, disordered 
eating behaviors, anxiety, depression, diabetes family conflict, 
sleep deprivation, and others, many of which have been discussed 
in a recent position statement by the ADA.403 Several validated 
surveys to assess such patient-reported outcomes are catalogued 
in this publication. With the continued development of adjunc­
tive therapies and advanced diabetes technologies, there will be a 
continued need to consider the patient- and family-reported out­
comes in addition to metrics of glycemic control. In two studies 
from Belgium, for instance, use of rtCGM and isCGM was associ­
ated with significantly higher treatment satisfaction and less work 
absenteeism than SMBG.245,404

Acute Diabetic Emergencies
Hypoglycemia
Hypoglycemia is the main side effect of insulin therapy in people 
with T1D. For detailed coverage, we refer to Chapter 39. With 
the present insulin therapy modalities, level 1 hypoglycemia (glu­
cose levels < 70 mg/dL; 3.9 mmol/L), typically accompanied by 
symptoms such as trembling, sweating, and a feeling of hunger, is 
frequent in people with T1D who strive for tight glycemic con­
trol. Use of insulin analogues, CSII, CGM, and in particular, CSII 
systems connected to CGM with integrated algorithms contrib­
utes to decreasing the risk for hypoglycemia.279 Clinically impor­
tant hypoglycemia (level 2, <54 mg/dL; 3.0 mmol/L), particularly 
level 3 hypoglycemia (any hypoglycemia characterized by altered 
mental state and/or physical status needing the intervention of a 
third party for recovery), should be avoided. Severe hypoglycemia 
(level 3) is associated with morbidity and mortality and is particu­
larly common in those with longer duration of diabetes, older age, 
a history of recent severe hypoglycemia, alcohol ingestion, exer­
cise, chronic kidney disease, and socially vulnerable profiles (lower 
education, lower income).236–240 With duration of T1D (and 
development of autonomic neuropathy) or repetitive episodes of 
severe hypoglycemia, individuals with T1D can lose their ability 
to detect hypoglycemia alarm signs (hypoglycemia unawareness). 
This dangerous situation can be reverted partly through educa­
tion and relaxation of glucose control (avoiding repetitive hypo­
glycemia), but in particular, the availability of CGM systems with 
alarms and educational programs on how to use them have helped 
individuals suffering from hypoglycemia unawareness.241,244,405 
Education on how to avoid these hypoglycemic attacks and how 
to resolve them should be an integral part of the DSMES offered 
to those living with T1D and their families.406,407
An acute hypoglycemic attack needs to be dealt with swiftly by 
taking glucose (15 g) in cases where the person is conscious. Mon­
itoring of recuperation of glucose levels will guide the necessity of 
repeating the intake of glucose, but persons using CGM should 
be aware of the lag time between restoration of glucose levels in 
the blood and those in subcutaneous tissue. In the case of hypo­
glycemia, capillary blood glucose control is advised to avoid over­
substitution. Those using CSII, in particular, hybrid closed-loop 
systems, may require less glucose for correction because they can 
switch off the basal insulin delivery. In cases of loss of conscious­
ness, intravenous (IV) glucose or parenteral glucagon should be 
administered.236 Recently, soluble glucagon and intranasal prepa­
rations have become available, improving the user-friendliness 
and effectiveness of this rescue therapy.408 After correction of the 
acute symptoms, relapse can be avoided by intake of longer-acting 
carbohydrates (20 g).
Review of hypoglycemia attacks and prospective insulin dose/
regimen adaptation should be an integral part of every consulta­
tion with the medical team.212,236 
Diabetic Ketoacidosis
DKA is a possibly lethal and potentially avoidable acute compli­
cation of T1D. Emerging evidence shows an adverse impact of 
DKA at onset of T1D on subsequent metabolic control and even 
complications of diabetes in later life.409–411
Pathophysiology of Diabetic Ketoacidosis
DKA is defined by hyperglycemia (blood glucose over 200–250 
mg/dL, 11–13.9 mmol/L), ketonemia (blood β-hydroxybutyrate 
≥3 mmol/L or moderate/large urine ketones), and acidosis (venous 
pH below 7.3 or serum bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L).283 DKA 
results from relative or absolute insulin deficiency, causing an 
increase in glucagon concentrations and accompanying increases 
in epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol, and growth hormone 
levels. These hormone changes lead to a catabolic state in the 
periphery, mobilizing substrates that the liver then uses to increase 
production of glucose and ketone bodies. When serum glucose 
concentrations exceed the renal threshold of approximately 180 
mg/dL (10 mmol/L), osmotic diuresis leads to dehydration and 
loss of electrolytes. Vomiting, which commonly occurs with severe 
ketosis, can further contribute to dehydration and electrolyte 
abnormalities. The vicious cycle continues with additional stress 
hormones production, which leads to worsening insulin resis­
tance, hyperglycemia, and ketosis.283 
Epidemiology and Risk Factors for Diabetic Ketoacidosis
DKA is a common presentation in new-onset T1D. The estimated 
proportion of children with new-onset T1D who present with 
DKA ranges from 15% to 70% in different studies and in differ­
ent countries.412–415 Preschool children, adolescents, and children 
from ethnic minority groups were found to have the highest risk 
of DKA at diabetes diagnosis in most countries.415 Screening pro­
grams for presence of autoantibodies to detect people at risk for 
T1D reduce the risk for DKA at presentation through education 
of those identified to be at risk.41,416
However, most cases of DKA occur in those with established dia­
betes, where the risk of DKA is between 1 and 10 per 100 person-
years. Risk is higher in patients with poor metabolic control and/or 
a history of insulin omission; a history of a prior episode of DKA; 
gastrointestinal illness; psychiatric disorders, including eating disor­
ders; low socioeconomic status; and for unclear reasons, females in 
adolescence.283,417,418 Insulin pump failure is an important cause 
of hyperglycemia, ketonemia, and DKA, but pump use does not 
increase overall risk of DKA, with some studies showing decreased 
risk.419,420 Special attention needs to be paid to those on sodium-
glucose cotransporter (SGLT) inhibitors, who have a higher risk of 
DKA and may present without the typically elevated glucose levels 
in the blood (see later discussion).421 
Treatment of Diabetic Ketoacidosis
Detailed guidelines for the treatment of DKA are avail­
able.283,422–424 Immediate treatment of DKA begins with fluid 
replacement, typically with one to two intravenous fluid boluses 
with normal saline, 10 mL/kg each. Rehydration should begin 
before starting insulin therapy. Initial fluid resuscitation is then 
followed by continued cautious rehydration with the goal of 
replacing the estimated fluid deficit over the first 24 to 48 hours. 
Initiation of an insulin drip at a rate of 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg per 
hour, without an insulin bolus, should begin at least 1 hour after 
fluid replacement is started. Different infusion rates may be used 
depending on the clinical presentation of the patient, but evi­
dence of the effect of different infusion rates of fluids on neu­
rologic outcomes is lacking.425 Patients must be monitored very 
closely for clinical and biochemical responses to treatment. Fluid 
content and rate, and occasionally insulin rate, should be titrated 
so that blood glucose falls gradually at a rate of 50 to 75 mg/dL 
per hour (2.8–4.2 mmol/L per hour). Fluid should typically con­
tain saline with potassium, phosphate, and acetate. Bicarbonate is 
not typically recommended in the treatment of DKA, except in 
unusual circumstances related to severe acidosis or hyperkalemia. 
Potassium replacement is usually required as a result of total-body 
1415
CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
potassium depletion, but potassium supplementation should be 
deferred until urine output is documented.283,426
The Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network 
(PECARN) Fluid Therapies Under Investigation in DKA 
(FLUID) study was a multisite prospective randomized factorial 
trial examining long- and short-term neurologic outcomes associ­
ated with the rate of IV fluid administration (rapid or slow) and 
the sodium chloride content of IV fluids (0.9% or 0.45%).425 In 
the 1389 episodes of DKA reported in 1255 children, the primary 
outcome of a decline in mental status (two consecutive Glasgow 
Coma Scale scores of <14; possible scores range from 3 to 15) 
was met in 48 episodes of DKA (3.5%) and was not associated 
with either the rate of fluid administration or the sodium chloride 
content of the fluids. Secondary neurologic outcomes, including 
clinically apparent brain injury during treatment for DKA, short-
term memory, and memory and IQ, measured 2 to 6 months after 
recovery from DKA were also not associated with fluid adminis­
tration rate or content. Recent data show that acute kidney injury 
may occur more frequently in children with greater acidosis and 
circulatory volume depletion during DKA.427
One important cause of morbidity and mortality in DKA is 
cerebral edema. Risk factors for cerebral edema include young age 
(<5 years), new-onset T1D, longer duration of symptoms, lower 
initial pH, higher initial blood urea nitrogen, treatment with 
bicarbonate, and increasing serum sodium concentrations dur­
ing initial treatment of DKA. In patients at high risk of cerebral 
edema or suspected of having cerebral edema, timely intervention 
with mannitol or hypertonic saline is important, as is swift correc­
tion of acidosis.428–430 
Prevention of Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Sick Day 
Management
The ADA recommends yearly education on sick day management 
and DKA prevention for persons with T1D and their caregivers, 
including the importance of insulin administration, as well as glu­
cose and ketone monitoring.212 Appropriate management of sick 
days can usually be achieved in the outpatient setting with ongoing 
education and support. Guidelines are available for management 
of sick days in children and adolescents with diabetes.431 Adapta­
tions of insulin doses on days of sickness are an important way to 
prevent development of DKA. The degree of hyperglycemia and 
ketosis, along with the rate of change of these parameters, helps 
guide insulin dose adjustments. Supplemental rapid-acting insulin 
boluses (correction doses, or 5%–20% of the TDD) should be 
given every 2 to 3 hours while ketones persist; see Table 35.7 for 
bolus dosing suggestions. For ketones with hypoglycemia, con­
sider reducing basal insulin for a short period of time. For ketones, 
hypoglycemia, and decreased oral intake over a prolonged period, 
consider reducing the basal insulin dose (i.e., glargine or other 
long-acting insulin) for patients on MDIs and basal rates for those 
on insulin pumps.
The prevention of progression from ketonemia to DKA and 
avoidance of hypoglycemia rely on modifying doses of but never 
omitting insulin, frequent monitoring of blood glucose and 
ketone levels every 1 to 3 hours, preventing/treating dehydration 
and hypoglycemia, treating the underlying illness, and maintain­
ing frequent contact with the diabetes team when not in the clinic 
or hospital setting. Monitoring of ketones using blood ketone 
meters that measure β-hydroxybutyrate is preferred over moni­
toring of urine ketone strips for easier sampling, lower rates of 
hospitalization/emergency department visits, and the potential for 
earlier and more accurate identification of clinical worsening or 
improvement.431–433
Persons with T1D and ketonemia require extra fluid because of 
the risk of dehydration. A reasonable target oral fluid intake is 0.5 
to 1.0 oz per year of age per hour (maximum of 8 ounces/hour). 
The type of drink should be adjusted according to blood glucose 
levels such that when blood glucose is 250 mg/dL (∼14 mmol/L) 
or less, rehydrate with sugar-containing clear liquids (e.g., sports 
drinks, soda, popsicles, oral electrolyte solution), and when blood 
glucose is greater than 250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L), give sugar-free 
clear liquids (e.g., water, diet soda, seltzer, diet juices). Patients 
and families should be aware that they should seek immediate 
medical attention for signs of dehydration, prolonged vomiting 
for more than a few hours, persistent hyperglycemia (>250–300 
mg/dL, >14–16.7 mmol/L), ketones that do not improve after 12 
hours, or symptoms of DKA (abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, 
fruity-smelling breath, hyperventilation, or altered mental status).
Several guidelines and protocols to prevent DKA in people on 
SGLT inhibitors have been published.421,434 In short, these include 
stopping SGLT inhibitors in the case of symptoms suggestive for 
DKA (e.g., lethargy, nausea); frequent ketone testing, preferen­
tially using blood ketone meters that measure β-hydroxybutyrate; 
increased fluid and carbohydrate intake; and administration of 
supplemental insulin together with the carbohydrates. Caution 
should be exerted with low-carb diets, alcohol, extreme exercise,

Use of Adjunctive Drugs in T1D
Advances in treatment for T1D have primarily targeted the devel­
opment of insulin analogues and devices that optimize insulin 
delivery and mimic normal physiologic serum insulin levels, as 
well as improvements in glucose monitoring. Even with these 
advances, insulin therapy has been associated with hypoglycemia 
and weight gain. To offset some of these side effects of insulin 
therapy, several drugs that are currently used in T2D have been 
investigated for adjunctive use in T1D to assess potential benefits 
related to improved glycemic control, less hypoglycemia, reduced 
glucose variability, and less weight gain.435–439
For specific classes of agents, such as SGLT2 inhibitors and 
glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP1) receptor agonists, additional ben­
efits of organ protection, analogous to the cardiorenal protection 
observed in those with T2D or even people without diabetes, are 
anticipated, but to date, data are lacking.436,440
Currently, pramlintide is the only drug that is approved by the 
U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for adjunctive use 
in adults with T1D; no adjunctive treatments have been FDA 
approved for use in children with T1D. In Europe, the European 
Medicines Agency (EMA) has approved the use of low-dose SGLT 
inhibitors (dapagliflozin and sotagliflozin) for adults with T1D 
and a BMI over 27 kg/m2, but the manufacturers chose to with­
draw the indication for dapagliflozin.
In considering the addition of adjunctive drugs in a person 
with T1D, any potential benefits must be carefully weighed 
against risks and costs of the medications. Information about ben­
efits and side effects needs to be discussed with those planning 
to use them, and intensive education programs on how to adapt 
insulin doses and mitigate side effects should be installed.421,438,439 
Here, we give an overview of the most commonly used adjunct 
therapies in T1D; however, only pramlintide is approved for use 
in adults with T1D by the FDA; sotagliflozin is approved for use 
in adults (BMI over 27 kg/m2) by the EMA.
Pramlintide
Pramlintide, an injectable amylin analogue, slows gastric empty­
ing, suppresses postprandial glucagon secretion, and enhances 
satiety. Addition of pramlintide to insulin at mealtime in adults 
with T1D improves glycemic control, including modest reduc­
tions in HbA1c by 0.3% to 0.6%, and decreases postprandial 
glucose excursions.441–443 Pramlintide is also associated with 
modest weight loss (mean, 0.4–1.3 kg) and reduced insulin dose; 
nausea is the most frequent side effect. Pramlintide is approved 
by the FDA for adjunctive use in adults with T1D but not in 
children. Pramlintide is not approved for use in people with 
T1D by the EMA. 
Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter Inhibitors
Oral SGLT2 or mixed SGLT1/2 inhibitors reduce hyperglycemia 
by reducing glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule 
(SGLT2) and, in some agents, decreasing and slowing intestinal 
glucose absorption (SGLT1).444 In those with T2D, they improve 
glycemic control, promote weight loss and blood pressure reduc­
tion, lower rates of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in those 
at high cardiovascular risk, and are renal protective, giving them 
a prominent place in the treatment of people with T2D.445–449 
Beneficial effects on cardiovascular and renal endpoints were also 
observed in people without diabetes.450,451
Studies show that use of SGLT2 (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, 
less for canagliflozin) or SGLT1/2 (sotagliflozin) inhibitors as 
adjunct therapies in people living with T1D on intensive insulin 
therapy (MDIs or CSII) reduces HbA1c, increases TIR by more 
than 2 hours, and reduces weight by 2 to 4 kg after 6 to 12 months 
of therapy and does so without an increased risk of hypoglyce­
mia.435,452–455 Unfortunately, those treated with SGLT inhibi­
tors also had higher rates of genital mycotic infections and DKA 
(two- to fourfold increase).421 Interestingly, in one study, small 
doses of empagliflozin (2.5 mg) showed a more limited effect on 
HbA1c and weight but also a smaller risk for DKA.456,457 A recent 
real-world study from Belgium and Spain confirmed these trial 
observations when SGLT inhibitors are used in the real world.458
SGLT inhibitors are not FDA approved for use in T1D, and 
although the EMA had given a label for dapagliflozin and sota­
gliflozin in low doses in people with T1D on intensive insulin 
therapy and a BMI over 27 kg/m2, this label was given up by the 
manufacturer of dapagliflozin, thus limiting possibilities of per-
label use of these agents. 
Metformin
Several clinical trials have studied the addition of metformin to 
target insulin resistance, particularly in individuals with T1D who 
are obese and during puberty. Clinical trials have failed to demon­
strate improvement in HbA1c with adjunctive use of metformin, 
although some studies in youth have shown decreases in weight 
and insulin requirement.459–461 In a recent RCT of adjunctive 
metformin in adults with T1D at risk for cardiovascular disease, 
the metformin group exhibited improvements in body weight, 
low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and estimated glomerular fil­
tration rate, but metformin did not significantly improve carotid 
artery intima-media thickness (the primary study outcome) or 
glycemic control.462 Metformin is not FDA or EMA approved for 
treatment of T1D. 
Incretin-Based Therapies
With the growing problem of overweight and obesity also occur­
ring in people with T1D,322 attention has turned to incretin-
based therapies, in particular GLP1 receptor agonists, for use 
as adjunct therapies in people with T1D. GLP1 is an incretin 
hormone produced in the gut that has been shown to boost glu­
cose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress glucagon secretion, 
delay gastric emptying, and promote satiety. Individuals with 
T1D appear to have normal GLP1 production but dysregulation 
between the pancreas and the gut, leading to ineffective gluca­
gon suppression.463 Several studies, in particular in overweight 
adults with T1D, have shown improved HbA1c and weight loss, 
without an increased risk in DKA.437,464–467 However, in the 
Efficacy and Safety of Liraglutide as Adjunct Therapy to Insulin 
in the Treatment of Type 1 Diabetes (ADJUNCT) program, an 
increase in hypoglycemia risk was observed.468–470 To date, no 
GLP1–based therapy is approved for use in T1D by either the 
FDA or EMA.

CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
β-Cell–Replacing Therapies
Treatment options of intensive insulin therapy and, more specifi­
cally, closed-loop systems offer promise to improve glucose con­
trol to such an extent that acute (i.e., severe hypoglycemia and 
DKA) and chronic complications can be avoided in a majority 
of people with T1D. This will almost certainly raise the bar for 
consideration of the risks and benefits of both islet and pancreatic 
transplantation. However, a subgroup of patients will still develop 
chronic complications (such as end-stage renal disease) or be dis­
abled by refractory hypoglycemia despite using the most advanced 
insulin delivery systems available. Furthermore, although closed-
loop systems resemble more and more a true artificial pancreas, 
they do not constitute a cure for type 1 diabetes. A cure will only 
be reached when all the islet functions lost during the autoim­
mune destruction can be replaced, such as continuous and pul­
satile secretion of insulin and precise crosstalk between β-cells, 
other endocrine cells such as α- and δ-cells, and vascular cells.471 
Pancreas and islet transplantation have long been considered as an 
alternative treatment for T1D and a possible cure. Transplantation 
of insulin-secreting cells is indeed attractive because it leads to 
the (partial) restoration of the population of insulin-secreting cells 
(β-cells) that were once lost. By implantation of a metabolic ade­
quate number of β-cells, functional β-cell mass can be restored, 
and insulin secretion might again be adjusted to the metabolic 
needs so that full metabolic homeostasis is restored.
Pancreas Transplantation
At this moment, a pancreas can be transplanted in combination 
with a kidney transplant, either simultaneously (simultaneous 
pancreas-kidney [SPK]), afterward (pancreas after kidney [PAK]), 
or alone (pancreas transplant alone [PTA]). There is considerable 
debate concerning PTA (i.e., without transplantation of a kidney). 
Several studies suggest that improved results for pancreatic trans­
plantation occur in the setting of SPK versus PTA.472 Patients 
with a kidney transplant receive immunosuppressive drugs that, 
given the nature of clinical monitoring for renal transplant rejec­
tion (e.g., creatinine, albumin), allow for careful (i.e., tailored) 
drug delivery for optimal care. With a successful pancreas trans­
plant, hyperglycemia is immediately reversed for most, and there 
is growing evidence of improved long-term outcomes. Pancreatic 
transplantation for people with T1D requiring a kidney transplant 
has therefore become the preferred clinical procedure but one that, 
for a variety of reasons, particularly the shortage of organ donors, 
remains relatively rare. Nevertheless, the surgery is extensive, 
and there are many potential complications associated with the 
transplant and the long-term intake of immunosuppressive drugs. 
Perhaps for these reasons, along with improvements in diabetes 
management (and thus a reduction in long-term complications, 
including kidney failure), it appears that the procedure peaked in 
the mid- to late 2000s, with declines in the number of procedures 
performed in the United States thereafter.473
Most currently performed procedures use enteric drainage of 
pancreatic secretions, preventing most complications associated 
with bladder drainage.474 A possible complication associated with 
enteric drainage is the occurrence of a leak at the site of duodenal 
anastomosis. In contrast, bladder drainage remains the preferred 
option in PTA because amylasuria is used as a surrogate of pancre­
atic endocrine function.475,476 The vascular drainage of the pancreas 
transplant may be performed with comparable outcome either into 
the systemic venous system or into the portal venous system.477
In a 30-year follow-up study from the Netherlands, the sur­
vival time of SPK transplants was found to be a median of 16.5 
years, with a 10-year cumulative patient survival rate of 77% for 
recipients transplanted between 2000 and 2015.478 These results 
are comparable to UK and U.S. data479 and have been achieved 
as a result of accumulated experience and adaptation and stan­
dardization of the surgical techniques. A surviving graft offers 
many benefits, not only the fact of being off insulin. Indeed, exog­
enous insulin can frequently be stopped while the normal gluca­
gon response to hypoglycemia is restored so that hypoglycemic 
episodes are rare. Another major benefit is that long-term tight 
glycemic control is frequently achieved, reducing HbA1c levels to 
near-normal ranges, and fasting blood glycemia in patients with 
surviving grafts is comparable to that of nondiabetic patients. Sev­
eral studies showed that this long-term glycemic control prevents 
or delays chronic micro- and macrovascular complications480 
and improves quality of life.481,482 Beyond therapeutic interest 
in pancreatic transplantation, additional research has focused on 
the mechanisms of pancreas rejection for what they might reveal 
regarding the immunologic mechanisms of T1D. In that regard, 
in patients with T1D provided with a pancreatic transplant, dia­
betes (i.e., a repeated need for exogenous insulin replacement 
therapy) can recur as a result of mechanisms considered attribut­
able to either recurrent autoimmunity (as typified by the recur­
rence of T1D-associated autoantibodies once lost) or, more often, 
allograft rejection.483 Even with pancreas biopsies, it is difficult to 
monitor and determine which of these two forms of islet destruc­
tion might be occurring with the development of hyperglycemia, 
and currently, there are no specific means in terms of treatment 
that would separate the two. 
β-Cell Transplantation From Islet Isolation
With respect to islet β-cell transplantation, therapeutic hopes for 
this procedure have been high since the late 1960s when early pio­
neering approaches were developed for islet isolation from whole 
pancreata. It was not until the early 2000s that a group from 
Edmonton, Canada, used meticulous islet isolation techniques for 
transplantation of islets from multiple pancreata, avoided the use 
of steroids, and utilized an immunosuppressive regimen involving 
the drug rapamycin, resulting in improved outcomes for patients 
with T1D.484 The so-called Edmonton protocol has subsequently 
been tested in a series of specialized centers throughout North 
America and Europe.485
The islet isolation procedure can differ somewhat but is gen­
erally similar in different islet transplant centers.485,486 After 
procurement by a surgical team, organs are transported to a 
β-cell facility for preparation of β-cell suspensions, and pancre­
ases are perfused and cold-preserved during the transport. After 
reaching the laboratory, 4 to 6 hours is required for complete 
processing and quality assessment of the cell preparations. The 
pancreas is initially digested using an enzyme targeting the col­
lagen structure (i.e., collagenase), which is infused in the pan­
creatic duct in order to separate islets from exocrine and ductal 
tissues, most frequently using a Ricordi chamber as a semiau­
tomated method. After digestion, the tissue is submitted to 
Ficoll density-gradient centrifugation so that an islet-enriched 
interphase can be harvested. Centers can either use this freshly 
harvested material for transplantation in their patients, or the 
tissue is washed and cultured at 37°C under serum-free condi­
tions for up to 4 weeks, allowing preferential survival of β-cells 
and analysis of the islet-enriched fractions for their β-cell 
1418
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
number and purity. Fractions from more than one donor can 
be used for each islet β-cell graft, but by using selected donor 
criteria, fractions from only one donor are often sufficient.487 
The implantation is done via injection in the portal vein by 
percutaneous transhepatic approach using a Seldinger tech­
nique under general or local anaesthesia.488
In most clinical studies, the most frequently reported ben­
eficial effect is more stable glucose control, indicated by lower 
variation of glycemia, lower HbA1c, and a decrease in hypogly­
cemic episodes.489,490 In general, it is clear that in many centers, 
albeit with varying degrees of success, islet β-cell transplant can 
prove effective (i.e., about 60% insulin independent at 1 year), 
especially for patients with severe hypoglycemia when the goal 
is long-term prevention of severe hypoglycemic episodes. One 
of the main limitations is that transplants from a single donor 
are often insufficient to reach optimal graft function as recently 
defined.491 Frequently, two, three, or more donor infusions are 
required for each recipient.486,489,490,492 But even then, for most 
of the patients who achieve optimal graft function after one or 
more implantations, a decrease in graft function is often seen 
within 2 years, and by 5 years, the benefits of the form of therapy 
wane. This deterioration of graft function can be attributed to 
a combination of several mechanisms.493 First, there is the pos­
sibility that the grafted β-cell mass is marginally low from the 
beginning and therefore susceptible to becoming insufficient. 
Second, local inflammatory reactions around the implant in the 
liver may acutely destroy a major part of the graft already in the 
first hours after transplantation. Third, at variance with most 
other transplantations, implantation of β-cells may reactivate an 
autoimmune destructive process, being the target of the origi­
nal autoimmune disease. A fourth reason might be progressive 
destruction by acute and chronic rejection as in other forms of 
transplantation. Fifth, a number of arguments point to β-cell 
damage and/or insulin resistance by the immune-suppressive 
agents. Therefore, currently, the toxicities of the drugs used to 
prevent rejection probably exceed the level of benefit achieved in 
the long term, except for those most subject to disease-associated 
complications (e.g., severe, recurrent hypoglycemia) or patients 
having to take immunosuppressive drugs for another organ (e.g., 
islet after kidney). Further research to achieve tolerance without 
long-term immunosuppression is therefore essential.
Several groups investigated alternative implantation sites such 
as the omentum,494,495 but better outcomes than the intraportal 
site have not been demonstrated, although glucose-responsive 
islet function495 or even insulin independence using a biodegrad­
able thrombin scaffold was demonstrated.496 Less predictable 
outcomes and a decline in islet function were seen, probably as 
a consequence of postimplantation ischemia and inflammatory 
destruction. 
β-Cell Transplantation Using Other Cell Sources
Another key remaining issue that needs to be tackled before islet 
transplantation can be considered a cure for T1D is that the num­
ber of islets available from cadaveric donors for transplantation is 
very limited. Numerous research efforts have been extended over 
the past decade toward the development of sustainable sources of 
“surrogate” insulin-producing cells (e.g., induced pluripotent stem 
cells, fetal stem cells, and xenogeneic islets) alongside additional 
methodologic investigations, all designed to improve therapeutic 
outcomes with the use of such cells (e.g., genetic modification, 
encapsulation).
Stem Cell Transplantation
A first possible unlimited source of islet β-cells is surrogate β-like 
cells (i.e., insulin producing, glucose responsive) produced from 
stem cells, either embryonic or induced from pluripotent cells 
originating from a variety of tissues. Stem cell therapy–based 
efforts as a therapy for T1D largely arose from a strategy designed 
in laboratory-based settings to recapitulate the islet cell develop­
mental pathway while generating single-hormone-positive β-cells 
capable of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.497 Although the 
future of stem cells as a clinical therapy is promising, some con­
cerns/limitations remain. First, β-cells in their natural setting do 
not exist in isolation (i.e., β-cells alone) but rather exist in a het­
erogenous, three-dimensional structure composed of the islets of 
Langerhans. Hence, the notion of generating a cell therapy in the 
absence of a full complement of islet cells (i.e., alpha, beta, delta, 
pancreatic polypeptide; see Chapter 33) must be considered mov­
ing forward, especially in the context of hormonal counterregula­
tion. In addition, strong consideration must continue to be given 
toward averting what likely would be an assault on the target tis­
sue—both autoimmune and alloimmune, depending on the set­
ting. To this end, effort for any so-called protective devices should 
encompass a need to (1) provide biocompatibility; (2) see ample 
blood supply to sustain cellular survival and functional β-cell 
mass capable of imparting normoglycemia; (3) prevent sensitiza­
tion and be immune protective; (4) trap potentially oncogenic 
cells; and (5) allow for rapid response of insulin, in terms of both 
activating and suppressing insulin secretion, to changing glucose 
concentrations.498
Despite these challenges, progress has been remarkable in recent 
years, with human clinical trials already running involving the use 
of stem cell–derived pancreatic progenitors capable of develop­
ing into functional β-cells and islet cells. In a first-in-man phase 
1/2 clinical trial, human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived 
pancreatic progenitor cells were encapsulated in a semiperme­
able device and implanted under the skin.499 Data presented at 
a conference (no full publication) showed some evidence of insu­
lin-immunoreactive cells at 2 years after implantation, but graft 
survival was limited, probably as a result of hypoxia exacerbated 
by a foreign body response to the encapsulation device. In order 
to avoid cell death from fibrosis, a second phase 1/2 clinical trial 
was performed with hPSC-derived pancreatic progenitor cells in a 
non-immunoprotective device that allows vascularization. People 
were to take systemic antiinflammatory and immunosuppression 
treatment to avoid alloimmune and inflammatory responses. Data 
showed that these cells have a mature β-cell phenotype and are 
able to survive and secrete insulin in a glucose-responsive way, 
although currently, without relevant clinical effect.500,501 Next to 
this, another source of β-cells derived from hPSCs is under inves­
tigation, with the FDA granting approval for a phase 1/2 trial of 
an investigational stem cell–derived, fully differentiated pancreatic 
islet cell therapy in combination with systemic immunosuppres­
sion in T1D complicated by severe hypoglycemia. A press release 
on the first patient caused enthusiasm in the scientific and diabe­
tes communities, but further data will have to show if this ther­
apy constitutes a predictable, reproducible, and long-term β-cell 
replacement therapy. 
Xenogeneic β-Cell Transplantation
A second possible unlimited source of islet cells is xenogeneic 
islets. The pig is the animal most likely to be used for xenotrans­
plantation, especially because porcine insulin only differs by one 
1419
CHAPTER 35  Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
amino acid from human insulin and has been used for many years 
in the treatment of patients with diabetes. The major barrier for 
xenotransplantation from pigs to humans is the very severe xeno-
rejection by the immune system, requiring heavy and sustained 
immune suppression. One way to avoid this phenomenon is to 
use genetically engineered cells that do not express xenogenic 
surface antigens, such as those developed in transgenic pigs or in 
humanized animals, as shown for heart xenotransplantation.502,503 
Another way to avoid severe xeno-rejection and the need for heavy 
immune suppression is to use macroencapsulation devices504 or 
microcapsules on an alginate base to prevent hyperacute rejection 
through direct exposure of xenogeneic cells, as tested in several 
non-human primate studies.505
The risk of infection with porcine endogenous retrovirus 
(PERV) has been extensively debated. PERV is integrated into 
the porcine genome, from where it can infect cells from other 
organisms.506 Until now, studies did not provide evidence of 
PERV infection in patients who were in contact with organs or 
living tissue of porcine origin.507 To reduce the risks of trans­
mission, the International Xenotransplant Ethics Committee 
recommended that source animals should be obtained from 
closed colonies from which known and potential pathogens 
have been excluded. Furthermore, the possibility of trans­
mission of microorganisms that have not yet been identified 
requires careful consideration whenever a clinical trial is pro­
posed. Because of these and other technical challenges, as well 
as remaining concerns about safety, xenogeneic cells are cur­
rently less favored than stem cells, although they are still a 
potential therapeutic option.508 
Prevention and Reversal of Type 1 Diabetes
The intersection of two independent events in the 1970s—the 
generalized acknowledgment that T1D represents an autoim­
mune disease, alongside the development of immunosuppressive 
agents—led to decades of efforts directed toward immunotherapy 
as a means to either prevent T1D (i.e., avert symptomatic onset) 
or, once diagnosed, reverse it (commonly termed intervention). To 
be clear, studies attempting to prevent the development of T1D 
involve treatment of persons at varying stages of disease risk based 
on a combination of genetic susceptibility, the number of T1D-
associated autoantibodies, and the degree to which glucose levels 
are elevated.113 Although the populations subject to such proce­
dures would differ, the common goal is to prevent further loss of 
β-cell function.
At present, in a setting of either disease prevention or inter­
vention, there is no proven safe and effective immunotherapy for 
use in a general public health care setting that prevents T1D or 
reverses the disease, as judged by preservation of C-peptide. How­
ever, in research settings, potentially promising candidates do exist 
for delaying disease onset (e.g., anti-CD3, GAD vaccine) and for 
intervention (e.g., anti-CD3, low-dose antithymocyte globulin 
[ATG], anti-TNF, CTLA4-Ig).509–515 Indeed, dozens of clinical 
trials, ranging from small to large, have been completed in both 
settings; a limited number are discussed later based on their pro­
posed method of action (Fig. 35.7).
Immunosuppression39
The earliest studies of therapies to prevent β-cell destruction used 
immunosuppressive agents. Large intervention trials of cyclospo­
rine indicated that this agent prevented further loss of C-peptide 
secretion and improved metabolic function when it was admin­
istered in recent-onset T1D cases. Cyclosporine therapy did not, 
however, maintain a nondiabetic state when therapy was insti­
tuted after the onset of diabetes, and with discontinuation of the 
drug, patients rapidly lost C-peptide reserve. The combination of 
inability to cure diabetes and toxicities associated with cyclospo­
rine (particularly nephrotoxicity and concern about increased risk 
of malignancy) ruled out its acceptance for use. Other immuno­
suppressive agents used in subsequent studies, such as prednisone 
and azathioprine, demonstrated relatively little effect in disease 
intervention. In the time since, a litany of agents (e.g., anti-CD20, 
ATG, mycophenolate plus anti-IL2 receptor α-monoclonal anti­
body) thought to act at least in part via immune depletion, a form 
of immune suppression, have demonstrated mixed results in T1D 
intervention efforts (see Fig. 35.7A). Some provide no therapeu­
tic benefit (i.e., preservation of C-peptide, reduced insulin needs, 
reduction in hypoglycemic events), whereas others have achieved 
at least one of these beneficial parameters, usually C-peptide pres­
ervation. However, even when efficacious, for most subjects, the 
beneficial effect was not durable (i.e., 6 months to 2 years of ben­
efit).513 It is possible that the treatment effect may persist for a 
longer term with repeat dosing, although this approach has not 
been tested. Therefore, at present, although T1D is an immune-
mediated disorder, it is not treated with immunotherapeutic 
agents in clinical practice. This is not to say that hope is lost for 
such being the case in the future. Indeed, in recent times (e.g., 
year 2000 to the present), studies related to two forms of modified 
antibodies against the CD3 molecule have, without question, gen­
erated the most research interest and offer some degree of eventual 
optimism.
Throughout several phase 1 and phase 2 intervention studies, a 
single course of anti-CD3 therapy decreased the loss of C-peptide 
secretion over a 12- to 24-month period in patients with new-
onset T1D.116 Concerns related to the activation of Epstein-Barr 
virus infection, the degree of therapeutic benefit in phase 3 trials, 
the duration of C-peptide preservation, and the protocol by which 
the drugs are administered initially disrupted their development 
and commercialization. However, a recent study demonstrated 
that a short course of the anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody tepli­
zumab delayed progression to clinical T1D by approximately 3 
years in high-risk patients.510 Teplizumab binds the CD3 com­
ponent of the T-cell–receptor complex and thereby modulates the 
T-cell compartment. Most notably, treatment with teplizumab has 
been reported to reduce the frequency of CD4+ effector memory T 
cells, increase the frequency of CD8+ central memory T cells, and 
promote an exhausted phenotype in CD8+ T cells in blood516,517; 
however, the exact mechanism by which teplizumab delays 
T1D progression remains unclear. In November 2022, the FDA 
approved teplizumab as the first disease-modifying therapy in type 1 
diabetes (https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/
fda-approves-first-drug-can-delay-onset-type-1-diabetes). 
Immunologic Vaccination
In animal models (especially the NOD mouse), it is relatively easy 
to prevent T1D. Indeed, although somewhat dated, a widely rec­
ognized effort notes more than 200 such means.518 Yet animal 
models have permitted development of the most exciting potential 
prevention or intervention modality of immunologic vaccination. 
Excitement is derived from the specificity and the relatively low 
risk of these therapies compared with immunosuppression. The 
basic concept behind immunologic vaccination is the induction 
1420
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
of regulatory T lymphocytes that target a given β-cell antigen and, 
on encountering the target antigen (e.g., insulin, GAD) in the 
context of the vaccine formula or route of administration, produce 
cytokines and cell-mediated effects that suppress autoimmunity 
and tissue destruction.519
Induction of a protective immune response may depend on the 
route of administration of the given antigen (e.g., oral, nasal, intra­
dermal) or on the use of an altered antigen (e.g., altered peptide 
ligands). For example, insulin given either orally or by subcutane­
ous injection prevents diabetes in NOD mice.520,521 Intact insulin

In terms of translation, the Diabetes Prevention Trial—Type 1 
Diabetes (DPT-1) studied both oral insulin and parenteral injec­
tions of low doses of insulin (see Fig. 35.7B). The results of the 
parenteral trial did not demonstrate a reduction in the risk of devel­
oping diabetes. The oral trial did not document an overall ben­
efit of insulin, but in the subgroup with higher levels of IAA at 
entry, a statistically significant delay in progression to diabetes was 
observed.523 Although the National Institutes of Health T1D Trial­
Net conducted a follow-up study testing the efficacy of oral insulin 
in preventing T1D in those having certain criteria related to age and 
IAA level, no benefit of oral insulin for delay or prevention of T1D 
was seen.524 Nevertheless, a pilot trial (Pre-POINT) led by investi­
gators in Germany involving the administration of high-dose oral 
insulin in children at high genetic risk for T1D with a family his­
tory of the disease reported that this form of therapy was capable of 
altering the anti-insulin immune response without inducing hypo­
glycemia.525 Thus, potential value of oral insulin remains uncertain.
An alternate approach to autoantigen vaccination involves 
intra-lymphatic treatment with GAD-alum. Specifically, in a 
small pilot study of GAD-alum injection into an inguinal lymph 
node combined with oral vitamin D supplementation, both meta­
bolic and immunologic outcomes supported the potential benefit 
of this therapy in recent-onset T1D.511 However, larger studies 
will be necessary to expand on these preliminary findings. 
Therapeutic Targeting for Mechanisms of β-Cell 
Death
As noted, the most prominent immune cell found in human islets 
in settings of T1D is the CD8+ T cell, which likely participates in 
cytotoxic β-cell killing because of its ability to recognize targets via 
antigen in the context of MHC class I, which is elevated in many 
islets in those with the disease.526 Therapeutically, lymphocytes 
and memory lymphocytes of the adaptive immune response can 
be targeted by anti–T-cell drugs directed at CD3 (teplizumab), 
CD2 (LFA3-Ig), and certain co-stimulatory blockers.527–529 
Indeed, the partial success of such compounds in recently diag­
nosed T1D, defined by preservation of C-peptide production 
over several months to years, speaks toward an important role for 
such autoreactive lymphocytes in β-cell destruction, at least late in 
the pathogenesis of this disease. Inflammatory cytokines are also 
known to harm islets, and therefore antiinflammatory therapies 
targeting cytokines may hold promise, as observed in a trial that 
involved blocking TNF.530

With the growing concept that multiple mechanisms 
likely contribute to the pathogenesis of T1D, enthusiasm has 
increased for utilizing combination therapies to prevent or 
reverse the disease. Examples of combinations with respect to 
immune intervention would include an induction component 
using drugs targeting inflammation and T- and B-lymphocyte 
memory and a maintenance component that could involve anti­
gens to induce tolerance to β-cells. At the same time, emerg­
ing data support an increasing role for β-cell stress and loss 
of function as potential contributing factors for T1D develop­
ment; therefore, combination therapy involving the addition 
of drugs that stabilize and maintain β-cell survival and func­
tion should be considered.531 As but one example, the calcium 
channel blocker verapamil, which promotes β-cell survival, 
demonstrated partial preservation of C-peptide in adults with 
recent-onset T1D enrolled in a phase 2 trial.532 As noted ear­
lier, because of the disease’s heterogeneity, a precision-medicine 
approach may be key to the ultimate success of combination 
therapies for T1D.

KEY POINTS
 • 
The use of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is 
transformative for diabetes management, improving glycemia, 
reducing acute complications, and improving quality of life.
 • 
All individuals with diabetes, regardless of the diabetes type, 
therapy modality, or stage of the disease, benefit from the use 
of CGM.
 • 
The use of CGM-derived metrics such as time in range (TIR), time 
below range (TBR), and time above range (TAR) facilitates day-to-
day diabetes management, glycemic outcomes, and quality of life.
 • 
Artificial intelligence decision-support systems (advisers) can 
facilitate the day-to-day use of CGM.
 • 
Connected insulin pens (smart pens) can further facilitate 
treatment with multiple daily injections and improve glycemic 
outcomes.
 • 
Insulin delivery with continuous subcutaneous insulin 
infusion (CSII, insulin pump) improves glycemia, reduces acute 
complications, and improves quality of life.
 • 
Advanced hybrid closed-loop systems for automated insulin 
delivery (AID) currently represent the most successful treatment 
modality for individuals treated with insulin.
 • 
Special considerations are important for different user 
populations, age groups, sick-day management, regular sport 
activities, and in-hospital and intensive care treatment.
 • 
Better access to diabetes technologies for all individuals with 
diabetes is paramount.
 • 
Further technologic developments may improve user-
friendliness, additionally increase automation, and improve 
long-term user experience and satisfaction.
