mitochondria, inhibiting mitochondrial biogenesis and func­
tion.150 The resultant decrease in maximal respiration suggests 
that oxidative damage to enzymes of the TCA cycle, the electron 
transport chain (ETC), or inner mitochondrial membrane lipids 
has occurred.151,152 Knockout of NOX4 increases mitochondrial 
biogenesis and maximal respiratory capacity dramatically, which 
would reduce substrate-driven increased mitochondrial ROS 
production.150 Mitochondrial ROS cause activation of other 
NOX isoforms.153 Although NOX4 has been implicated in the 
pathogenesis of diabetic nephropathy in mice, clinical trials of 
NOX4 inhibitors were disappointing. Recently, overexpression 
of a NOX5 construct in NOX4-deleted mice was shown to 
increase renal damage, and NOX5 expression was increased in 
human diabetic kidney disease in proportion to HbA1c.154 There 
are multiple splice variants of NOX5 and multiple intronic and 
exonic SNPs, and NOX5 binds to numerous cytosolic proteins 
important for its activity, however.
NOX5 activation is dependent on intracellular calcium signal­
ing. Normal activity of PKM2 suppresses intracellular calcium 
release and signaling.155 This may contribute to the observed pro­
tection against diabetic nephropathy in patients with long-dura­
tion T1D by normal PKM2 activity.142
The initiating role of mitochondrial ROS is supported by the 
observation that cells lacking mitochondrial ETC function (ρ0 
cells)46 fail to increase ROS production in response to high glucose.
Dugan and associates156 suggested diabetic nephropathy is 
caused by reduced, rather than increased, mitochondrial ROS 
production, based on the observation that AMP-activated protein 
kinase (AMPK) activity is decreased in diabetic kidney. Metformin 
acts through both AMPK-dependent and AMPK-independent 
mechanisms.157 Protein levels of the master regulator of mitochon­
drial biogenesis and function, peroxisome proliferator-activated 
receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC1α), and mitochon­
drial density were also decreased. These authors proposed a model 
in which these observations reflect a feed-forward cycle initiated 
and maintained by decreased mitochondrial ROS. However, in 
human endothelial cells, silencing of AMPK causes increased, not 
decreased, ROS.158
An alternate model of a feed-forward cycle involving decreased 
AMPK activity and decreased mitochondrial biogenesis caused 
by increased mitochondrial ROS is more consistent with these 
and other observations. In this model, increased mitochondrial 
superoxide causes release of Fe++ from ferritin and iron-sulfur 
cluster–containing proteins. Interaction of this released free iron 
in the nucleus with mitochondrial superoxide–derived hydro­
gen peroxide forms hydroxyl radicals, the only ROS capable of 
cleaving bonds in macromolecules (Fig. 38.12).159 This results in 
ROS-mediated DNA double-strand breaks in the nucleus. DNA 
double-strand breaks activate DNA repair mechanisms, includ­
ing the enzyme poly-ADP-ribose polymerase 1 (PARP1). Activa­
tion of PARP1 inhibits the key glycolytic enzyme glyceraldehyde 
3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) by poly-ADP-ribosylation 
and depletes intracellular NAD+ by degrading it to synthesize 
ADP-ribose. Inhibition of GAPDH activity causes upstream accu­
mulation of early glycolytic intermediates, which are diverted into 
pathogenic signaling pathways.46 Diversion of glucose increases 
polyol pathway flux, whereas diversion of fructose-6-phosphate 
increases hexosamine pathway activity. Diversion of glyceralde­
hyde-3-phosphate to α-glycerol phosphate activates PKC, and 
reduced activity of GAPDH diverts accumulated triose phos­
phates toward methylglyoxal formation. Methylglyoxal increases 
expression of the RAGE and its activating ligand S100A8/9. 
Hyperglycemia-induced ROS reduce intracellular NAD+ content 
by 50%.160 Reduced content of NAD+ inhibits activity of the 
NAD+-dependent protein SIRT1, which normally deacetylates 
and activates both the master regulator of mitochondrial bio­
genesis, PGC1α, and of liver kinase B1 (LKB1), the kinase that 
activates AMPK. Thus, decreased SIRT1 activity would decrease 
activity of LKB1, PGC1α, and AMPK, as observed by Nishikawa 
and coworkers, but would result in increased, not decreased, mito­
chondrial ROS production.161
SIRT1 also deacetylates and thereby inactivates the p65 sub­
unit of NFκB and skews macrophages to their reparative polar­
ity.162 Consistent with this model, diabetic db/db mice with a 
conditional deletion of SIRT1 in podocytes developed more pro­
teinuria and kidney injury compared to db/db control mice,163 
and PGC1α knockout diabetic mice developed a more severe neu­
ropathy, with mitochondrial degeneration and an increase in oxi­
dative modification of intracellular proteins.164 Recently, real-time 
in vivo studies using a mitochondrial matrix localized GFP-based 
redox biosensor in db/db mice confirmed increased mitochondrial 
ROS production in diabetic nephropathy.165
Together, these metabolic diversions and pathway activations 
lead to cellular dysfunction, inflammation, apoptosis, and fibrosis 
in cells exposed to high intracellular glucose. The central impor­
tance of ROS in initiating each of these processes is illustrated by 
the fact that each can be prevented when hyperglycemia-­mediated 
ROS generation is curtailed by transgenic expression of the 
enzymes superoxide dismutase or catalase.
Intracellular formation of ROS also upregulates soluble epoxide 
hydrolase messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) and protein in mouse 
endothelial cells.166 Essential mitochondrial genes are downregu­
lated in glomeruli of the diabetic nephropathy–susceptible mouse 
strain DBA/2J but not in the diabetic nephropathy–resistant strain 
C57BL/6J. Diabetic nephropathy–susceptible DBA/2J mice had 
increased tissue levels and urinary excretion of 8-oxo-deoxyguanosine, 
a major product of DNA oxidation. In humans with diabetic kidney 
disease, biopsies showed increased mitochondrial DNA damage and 
increased urinary 8-oxo-­deoxyguanosine.167 Glomerular podocyte-
specific knockout of PKM2 in diabetic nephropathy–susceptible 
mice had reduced expression of PGC1α, reduced mitochondrial 
mass, increased mitochondrial fission, and increased ROS. Increased 
ROS caused DNA strand breaks, increased activated PKCδ, and 
increased methylglyoxal levels. Activities of PARP and GAPDH were 
not reported. These changes were associated with accelerated podocyte 
apoptosis and glomerular pathology. Analysis of cellular respiration 
using Seahorse Extracellular Flux (XF) analyzers showed that high 
glucose decreased mitochondrial maximal respiration by about 36%, 
suggesting oxidative damage to enzymes of the TCA cycle, the ETC, 
or the inner mitochondrial membrane lipids had occurred.151,152 In 
cultured podocytes and in diabetic mice, activation of PKM2 with 
a small-molecular-weight activator increased mitochondrial biogen­
esis, normalized mitochondrial maximal respiration, prevented high 
glucose–induced elevated ROS, and restored levels of PKCδ and 
methylglyoxal to low glucose levels. These effects are consistent with 
increased shunting of glucose to lactate, thereby reducing nonproduc­
tive increased flux through the mitochondrial ETC. 
Insulin Resistance Increases Fatty Acid 
Oxidation, Causing Mitochondrial 
Overproduction of ROS
Insulin resistance occurs in most patients with T2D. To isolate 
effects of insulin resistance from those of hyperglycemia and 
1479
CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
diabetes, insulin resistance was evaluated in persons without 
diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance.17 Those in the highest 
quintile of insulin resistance had a 2.5-fold increase in CVD risk 
compared to those in the lowest quintile. Additional adjustment 
for LDL, triglyceride (TG), high-density lipoprotein (HDL), 
systolic blood pressure, smoking, alcohol consumption, exercise, 
and waist circumference only modestly reduced the magnitude 
of these associations (P for trend 0.02; quintile 5 vs. quintile 1, 
odds ratio [OR], 1.94, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.05–3.59). 
Furthermore, there were no significant interactions between 
Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance (HOMA-
IR) and ethnicity, sex, hypertension, dyslipidemia, glucose toler­
ance (impaired glucose tolerance versus normal glucose tolerance), 
or obesity. This observation suggests insulin resistance itself is a 
major cause of CVD in T2D.
Patients with T1D are also insulin resistant, with insulin sen­
sitivity reduced by about 50% compared to healthy volunteers. 
Patients with T1D have significant insulin resistance in adipose 
tissue, as well as in liver and skeletal muscle.168,169 In patients with 
T1D, insulin resistance predicts the extent of coronary artery cal­
cification and likely contributes to their increased risk of CVD.170 
The role of insulin itself remains controversial. In mice fed a 
high-fat diet, genetically induced reduction of hyperinsulinemia 
decreased adipose tissue inflammation and increased insulin 
responsiveness.171
Adipocyte insulin resistance increases lipolysis and circulating 
free fatty acids (FFAs). Current data support a causal role for TG-
rich lipoproteins (TGRLs) in atherosclerosis, and TGRL concen­
trations correlate better with inflammation than does LDL itself.172

did not reduce MACEs compared to placebo in the Pemafibrate 
to Reduce Cardiovascular Outcomes by Reducing Triglycerides

Ectopic storage of fatty acids in liver and muscle eventually causes 
impaired insulin signaling and insulin resistance in these tissues. 
This leads to impaired insulin stimulation of hepatic glycogen syn­
thesis and impaired transcriptional downregulation of gluconeo­
genic genes. Skeletal muscle insulin resistance caused by increases 
in intramyocellular ectopic lipid impairs insulin-stimulated glu­

Insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia increases mitochondrial 
fatty acid oxidation in arterial endothelial cells, macrophages, 
and cardiomyocytes, causing excessive ROS production. The 
major site of electron leakage from increased fatty acid oxidation 
is electron transfer flavoprotein, which receives electrons from 
FADH2 formed during the first oxidation step of β-oxidation 
(Fig. 38.13).176 These fatty acid oxidation–derived ROS induce 
expression of the noncoding RNA growth arrest- and DNA dam­
age-inducible gene 7 (gadd7), which is activated by DNA dam­
age. ROS produced by electron leakage from the electron transfer 
protein during fatty acid oxidation amplify oxidative stress and 
induction of the ER stress response in a feed-forward loop.177 
In two insulin-resistant nondiabetic animal models, inhibition 
of either FFA release from adipocytes or FFA oxidation in arte­
rial endothelium prevented increased production of ROS and its 
damaging effects.178 In human arterial endothelial cells, this FFA-
induced increase in ROS activates the same damaging pathways 
seen with high glucose. FFA-induced overproduction of superox­
ide also inactivates two important antiatherogenic enzymes: pros­
tacyclin synthase and eNOS.178
In vitro studies suggest insulin has both antiatherogenic and 
proatherogenic effects at the level of the vessel wall (Fig. 38.14).179 
One major antiatherogenic effect is stimulation of endothelial 
NO production. NO released from endothelial cells is a potent 
inhibitor of platelet aggregation and adhesion to the vascular 
wall. Endothelial NO also controls expression of genes involved 
in atherogenesis. It decreases expression of monocyte chemoat­
tractant protein 1 (MCP1) and of surface adhesion molecules 
such as CD11/CD18, P-selectin, vascular cell adhesion molecule 
1 (VCAM1), and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1). 
Endothelial cell NO also reduces vascular permeability and 
decreases the rate of oxidation of LDL to its more proatherogenic 
form. Finally, endothelial cell NO inhibits proliferation of vascular 
smooth muscle cells (VSMCs).180 However, in insulin resistance,

overproduction of ROSs leads to oxidation of tetrahydrobiopterin 
(BH4), the essential cofactor of eNOS. Decreased BH4 uncouples 
oxygen reduction from NO synthesis, thereby converting eNOS 
to a superoxide-producing enzyme.181 Although this important 
antiatherogenic effect of insulin is blocked by insulin resistance–
induced ROS, two major proatherogenic effects of insulin are not. 
Insulin both potentiates PDGF-induced VSMC proliferation and 
stimulates endothelial and VSMC production of the thrombolysis-­
inhibitor plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 (PAI1).182–184
Macrophages are a central participant in atherogenesis. 
Although most atherosclerotic lesions are stable, insulin resistance 
increases macrophage ROS, which drives progression to unstable, 
rupture-prone lesions. These plaques have a greater inflammatory 
infiltrate, a larger prothrombotic necrotic core, and increased pro­
duction of matrix metalloproteinases that weaken the fibrous cap. 
Insulin resistance in macrophages induces mitochondrial ROS 
production by activating the CHOP branch of the stress unfolded 
protein response (UPR).185,186 Plaque necrosis is caused by a 
combination of increased macrophage apoptosis and decreased 
phagocytic clearance of the apoptotic macrophages by a process 
called efferocytosis, which results in post–apoptotic necrosis of 
apoptotic cells and inflammation. Both of these processes are pro­
moted by macrophage insulin resistance.187 Apoptotic cells can 
inappropriately express the ROS-TNFα-NFκB–inducible “don’t 
eat me” cell surface signal CD47,188 and efferocyte receptors on 
phagocytes such as Mer tyrosine kinase (MerTK) can be cleaved 
and inactivated by the mitochondrial ROS-activated protease 
ADAM17 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase).189 Blocking anti­
bodies to CD47 prevents progression of established lesions, pro­
tects against plaque rupture, and induces regression of the necrotic 
core in several mouse models.136,188,190,191
Fatty acid oxidation appears to be the source of mitochondrial 
ROS production in macrophages, directly or indirectly via altered 
mitochondrial cardiolipin fatty acid composition.192,193 When 
fatty acids are oxidized instead of glucose, the ratio of NADH to 
FADH2 changes from 5:1 to 2:1. This causes an overreduction of 
the mitochondrial ETC coenzyme Q (CoQ) pool and an increase 
in reverse electron transport (RET) and ROS production by com­
plex I. ROS from mitochondrial ETC complex I cause a high per­
centage of irreversible overoxidation of cysteine thiols.44,45 RET to 
complex I, driven by increased complex II oxidation of the TCA 
cycle intermediate succinate, drives the polarization of macro­
phages to a proinflammatory phenotype.194
In diabetic heart, increased myocardial ROS production occurs 
early, before accumulation of TGs and subsequent synthesis of 
C16:0 ceramides are evident.195,196 This likely reflects increased 
fatty acid oxidation and resultant oxidative damage to mitochon­
drial cardiolipin,197 the specific phospholipid of mitochondrial 
membranes. Cardiolipin is important for efficient electron flux, 
adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis, and reduced ROS for­
mation. In addition, cardiolipin is involved in mitochondrial-­
mediated apoptosis and plays a critical role in regulating 
mitochondrial fission and fusion.198–200 In nondiabetic heart, the 
major species of cardiolipin contains four linoleic acids (tetra 18:2 
cardiolipin). This unique acyl composition is not derived from de 
novo synthesis of cardiolipin but rather from a remodeling process 
that involves phospholipases and acyltransferase-transacylases. In 
diabetic myocardium from murine models with insulin resistance 
(ob/ob, db/db, and high-fat diet) and in models of severely insulin-
deficient T1D, the fatty acyl content of the more saturated 18:2 
cardiolipin is dramatically reduced, whereas the content of 
longer-chain, more unsaturated fatty acyl cardiolipin, such as 
20:4, is substantially increased.201 Because of this increase in 
highly unsaturated side chains, diabetic heart cardiolipin is 
more vulnerable to oxidative damage. Cardiac overexpression of 
cardiolipin synthase increases tetra 18:2 cardiolipin in diabetic 
mice and prevents diabetes-induced changes in cardiolipin lipid 
remodeling. The cardiolipin deficiency and profound remodel­
ing caused by diabetes and insulin resistance are caused by ROS-
induced transcription of acyl-CoA:lysocardiolipin acyltransferase 
1 (ALCAT1) (see Fig. 38.13). ALCAT1 catalyzes the transfer of

deficiency increased levels of tetra 18:2 cardiolipin in mouse heart

Diabetes Reduces Activity of Nuclear Erythroid–Related 
Factor 2, the Master Regulator of Antioxidant Gene 
Expression
The number of recognized ROS-regulating enzymes has increased 
substantially over the past 15 years.43 Examples include super­
oxide dismutases, catalases, glutathione peroxidases, glutathione 
reductase, thioredoxins, thioredoxin reductases, methionine sulf­
oxide reductases, and peroxiredoxins. Activity of these enzymes 
is largely determined by ROS-induced changes in their tran­
scription. Increased transcription of many of these antioxidant 
enzymes is mediated by the transcription factor nuclear ery­
throid–related factor 2 (Nrf2), a member of the cap ‘n’ collar sub­
family of basic region leucine zipper transcription factors.206 By 
regulating oxidant levels and oxidant signaling, Nrf2 participates 
in control of the UPR, apoptosis, mitochondrial biogenesis, and 
stem cell regulation. Nrf2 also increases transcription of GLO1, 
the rate-limiting enzyme of the glyoxalase system, which prevents 
posttranslational modification of proteins and histones by methyl­
glyoxal, the major AGE precursor.207,208 It also increases transcrip­
tion of the rate-controlling enzyme in the nonoxidative branch 
of the pentose phosphate pathway, transketolase. Activation of 
transketolase inhibits three of the major hyperglycemia-driven 
pathways implicated in the pathogenesis of diabetic vascular dam­
age (the diacylglycerol-PKC pathway, the methylglyoxal-AGE 
formation pathway, and the hexosamine pathway) and inhibits 
hyperglycemia-induced NFκB activation.63 Preclinical studies 
using Nrf2 activators or Nrf2-deficient diabetic mice established 
that Nrf2 is a crucial endogenous modulator of ROS and protects 
from experimental diabetic nephropathy.209–211 In kidneys of db/
db mice, treatment with the tetracycline antibiotic minocycline 
increased Nrf2 protein levels, reduced glomerular oxidative stress 
markers, and ameliorated diabetic nephropathy.212
Nrf2 is expressed constitutively, and its intranuclear levels are 
controlled posttranslationally. In the absence of inducers, Nrf2 
associates with the redox-sensitive protein Kelch-like erythroid 
cell–derived protein with cap ‘n’ collar homology–associated pro­
tein 1 (Keap1), where it is rapidly polyubiquinated by Keap1-asso­
ciated cullin-3–RING E2 ubiquitin ligase proteins and degraded 
by proteasomes. Nrf2 bound to Keap1 is released by ROS oxida­
tion of critical cysteine thiols of Keap1 or by reaction of these 
thiols with ROS-generated electrophiles such as glycolysis-derived 
methylglyoxal and unsaturated fatty acid peroxidation-derived 
4-hydroxynonenal. Phosphorylation of Nrf2 by protein kinases 
such as casein kinase 2 (CK2) may help target Nrf2 to the nucleus. 
After forming heterodimers with small Maf proteins, Nrf2 binds 
to the antioxidant response element (ARE) to induce transcription 
of its target genes. Export of Nrf2 from the nucleus is controlled 
by phosphorylation. Src family members, such as Fyn, phosphory­
late Nrf2 at Tyr568, causing export from the nucleus and degrada­
tion.213 Reduction of Nrf2 protein in the cytosolic compartment 
is mediated by β-transducin repeat–containing protein, a substrate 
adaptor for the S-phase kinase-associated protein 1−Cul1−F-box 
protein E3 ubiquitin ligase, which targets GSK3β-phosphorylated 
Nrf2 to the proteosome214 Hyperglycemia-induced mitochon­
drial overproduction of ROS has been shown to increase glycogen 
synthase kinase 3 beta (GSK3β) activity by inhibiting Akt1-­
dependent phosphorylation of GSK3β at serine 9 (Fig. 38.15).159
Modification of critical Keap1 cysteine thiols by sulfora­
phane, a dietary isothiocyanate found in cruciferous vegetables, 
also releases Nrf2.215 In endothelial cells, sulforaphane prevented 
hyperglycemia-induced activation of the hexosamine and PKC 
pathways and prevented increased cellular accumulation and 
excretion of the major AGE precursor methylglyoxal.216 In aor­
tae of diabetic mice, sulforaphane treatment restored aortic lev­
els of Nrf2 and Nrf2-dependent antioxidant gene expression, 
preventing diabetes-induced increases in wall thickness, fibrosis, 
inflammation (tumor necrosis factor-α [TNFα] and vascular cell 
adhesion molecule-1 expression), apoptosis, and increased cell 
proliferation.217 Diabetic cardiomyopathy was also prevented in 
mouse models by sulforaphane treatment.215 Normalized Nrf2 
activity also prevented diabetes-associated cardiac inflammation, 
fibrosis, lipid accumulation, and impaired autophagy. In hearts 
from patients with diabetes, Nrf2 protein is significantly reduced. 
In mice, cardiac Nrf2 protein was similarly reduced after 5 months 
of diabetes mellitus.218 
Diabetes Activates the NLR Family Pyrin Domain 
Containing 3 Inflammasome
Dysregulated NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) 
inflammasome activity underlies many chronic inflammatory 
states. The NLRP3 inflammasome is formed by oligomerization 
of inactive NLRP3, associated with apoptosis-associated speck–
like protein (ASC), and procaspase-1. This complex, in turn, cata­
lyzes conversion of procaspase-1 to caspase-1, which contributes 
to production and secretion of mature proinflammatory IL1β and 
IL18.219 Activation requires two steps. The first, called priming, 
activates the transcription factor NFκB, which promotes tran­
scription of NLRP3, pro-IL1β, and pro-IL18.220 In mononuclear 
cells from patients with diabetes and in vascular endothelial cells 
from diabetic rats, NFκB is chronically active,221 likely resulting 
from TLR4 or TLR4/RAGE heterodimer signaling stimulated 
by binding of ROS-induced S100A8/9 calgranulins. A second 
signal activates the NLRP3 inflammasome by facilitating oligo­
merization of inactive NLRP3, ASC, and procaspase-1. Although 
diverse molecular cues can trigger this step, several studies suggest 
these might all act through a mitochondrial pathway associated 
with high levels of mitochondrial ROS. Blocking ROS genera­
tion by mitochondria has been shown to abolish NLRP3 inflam­
masome activation, whereas artificial induction of mitochondrial 
ROS can spontaneously induce NLRP3-mediated IL1β secre­
tion.222,223 Mitochondrial ROS stimulate calcium influx via the 
channel transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M 
member 2 (TRPM2), and macrophages deficient in TRPM2 have 
drastically impaired NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL1β 
secretion.224 Synthesis and oxidation of mitochondrial DNA also 
drive this activation step. TLR4 signaling increases levels of the 
human mitochondrial cytidine/uridine monophosphate kinase 2 
(CMPK2) enzyme, which increases nucleotide cytidine triphos­
phate, causing synthesis of mitochondrial DNA. Oxidized DNA 
fragments then exit the mitochondria, bind to the NLRP3 inflam­
masome, and activate it (Fig. 38.16).
Increased expression of the NLRP3 inflammasome components 
Nlrp3 and ASC and increased inflammasome activation are found

Diabetes Activates the Nuclear Factor of Activated T Cells 
(NFAT) Transcription Factor
The transcription factor NFAT contributes to development of 
DR, nephropathy, atherosclerosis, and cardiomyopathy. In rest­
ing cells, NFAT proteins are phosphorylated and are located in 
the cytoplasm. In diabetes, intracellular calcium is increased by 
increased ROS. Increased intracellular calcium then activates 
NFATc1-c4 by increasing NFAT dephosphorylation by the Ca2+/
calmodulin-dependent serine/threonine phosphatase calcineurin, 
which facilitates NFAT translocation into the nucleus. Once in 
the nucleus, NFAT interacts with coregulators to achieve optimal 
NFAT activation.233 In the nucleus, ADP-ribosylation mediated 
by PARP1 acts as a molecular switch to positively regulate NFAT-
dependent cytokine gene transcription (Fig. 38.17).234 In dia­
betes, nuclear PARP1 is activated by intracellular ROS-induced 
DNA strand breaks (see Fig. 38.12).
In DR, upregulation of proinflammatory cytokines such as 
TNF­α and upregulation of retinal microvascular endothelial cell 
adhesion proteins are important components of chronic inflam­
mation.235 In human retinal microvascular endothelial cells, 
TNF­α activates NFAT signaling. Activated NFAT specifically 
upregulated expression of the adhesion protein VCAM1, which 
increases adhesion of lymphocytes and macrophages to endo­
thelium, the inflammatory cytokine CX3CL1 (C-X3-C motif 
chemokine ligand 1), which promotes leukocyte adhesion, the 
neutrophil chemotactic cytokine CXCL6, and the activated T-cell 
chemotactic cytokine CXC11.236 In human renal glomerular 
podocytes exposed to sera from patients with diabetic kidney 
disease, increased TNF­α production caused NFATc1-mediated 
repression of the cholesterol efflux regulator ATP-binding cas­
sette transporter A1 (ABCA1), and reduced activity of sterol-O-
acyltransferase 1 (SOAT1), resulting in free cholesterol-mediated 
podocyte injury.237
In arteries of diabetic mice, activated NFATc3 induces arte­
rial smooth muscle cell expression of the proinflammatory 
matrix protein osteopontin, a cytokine that promotes atheroscle­
rosis and diabetic vascular disease. NFAT inhibition effectively 
reduces arterial wall osteopontin, IL6, MCP1, intercellular 
adhesion molecule-1, CD68, and tissue factor expression and 
lowers plasma IL6 in diabetic mice.238 In diabetic ApoE−/−mice, 
inhibition of NFAT signaling completely suppressed a 2.2-fold 
increase in atherosclerotic plaque area. Inhibition of NFAT also 
reduced lipid content in plaque of diabetic mice independent 
of plasma glucose and lipid levels.239 NFATc3 activated by 
increased mitochondrial ROS production also increases arterial

Diabetes Increases Neutrophil Extracellular Traps
In atherosclerotic plaques, neutrophils prime macrophages for 
proinflammatory responses.245 This priming is mediated by 
extracellular webs of DNA bound to cytotoxic histones, which 
are released by activated neutrophils, called neutrophil extra­
cellular traps (NETs).246 This process follows a coordinated 
multistep process: histone citrullination, chromatin deconden­
sation, migration of elastase and other granule enzymes into the 
nucleus, disintegration of the nuclear membrane, and release 
of DNA, histones, and granule proteins into the extracellular 
space.247 The release of NETs primes macrophages to produce 
pro-IL01β, which is cleaved to mature proinflammatory IL01β 
by caspase-1. Caspase-1, in turn, is secreted by macrophages 
in response to activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.245 
Both ROS and increased intracellular Ca2+ activate NET for­
mation (Fig. 38.18).248 Atherosclerosis-prone ApoE−/− mice 
with deletions of two serine proteases that localize to NETs 
form dramatically smaller atherosclerotic lesions compared to 
ApoE−/− control animals, despite similar lipid concentrations 
and leukocyte counts in blood. These triple-mutant mice had 
no NETs, lower systemic IL1β concentration, and fewer lesional 
IL17–producing T cells.249 Quenching mitochondrial ROS in a 
mouse model of atherosclerosis (aged myeloid cell mCAT→LDL 
receptor null [Ldlr−/−] chimeric mice) decreased lesional NETs 
compared to age-matched Ldlr−/− mice and also decreased total 
macrophage content in atherosclerotic lesions.250 Oxidized LDL 
(oxLDL) and 7-keto-cholesterol, the most abundant oxysterol 
in human oxLDL, induced mitochondrial ROS production and 
highly proinflammatory oxidized mitochondrial DNA-bound 
NETs.251 Neutrophils from humans with both T1D and T2D 
have elevated expression of peptidyl arginine deiminase 4, the 
enzyme critical for histone citrullination-mediated chromatin 
decondensation and NET formation.252

SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Nonresolving Inflammation in Metabolic Syndrome, 
Diabetes, and Atherosclerosis
Chronic low-grade inflammation is associated with metabolic syn­
drome, diabetes, and atherosclerosis.253–258 In normal physiology, 
inflammation has two temporal phases: an initiation phase of acute 
inflammation and a resolution phase. The initiation phase involves 
recruitment of neutrophils followed by monocytes, which differ­
entiate into proinflammatory macrophages. These cells engulf the 
inflammatory stimulus and remove damaged tissue debris. Resolu­
tion of inflammation is an active process involving a switch from 
synthesis of arachidonic acid–derived proinflammatory prostaglan­
dins and LTs to synthesis of at least four families of SPMs. These 
SPM families are arachidonic acid–derived lipoxins and omega-3 
polyunsaturated fatty acid–derived resolvins, protectins, and mares­
ins.134 SPMs decrease further recruitment of PMNs, stimulate mac­
rophage uptake and clearance of apoptotic cells (efferocytosis), shift 
macrophage phenotype from proinflammatory to proresolution, 
and initiate tissue repair processes. Obesity and diabetes delay PMN 
apoptosis and impair macrophage efferocytosis. In human arteries, 
high levels of resolvin D1 and low levels of the proinflammatory 
leukotriene B4 are associated with plaques having less necrosis and 
thicker fibrous caps. In contrast, high levels of leukotriene B4 and 
low levels of resolvin D1 are associated with plaques having large 
necrotic cores and thin fibrous caps.259
Current evidence suggests diabetes causes defective SPM 
biosynthesis downstream of their fatty acid precursors.256,257 In 
macrophages from patients with acute ischemic stroke who have 
diabetes compared to those do not have diabetes, the ratios of 
resolvin D1 and D2 to leukotriene B4 (LTB4) were decreased, 
accompanied by reduced expression of the synthesis enzyme, 
15-lipoxygenase-1. Levels of proinflammatory pathway mark­
ers were increased, and macrophages were skewed to the pro­
inflammatory M1 polarization. In diabetic animals with acute 
ischemic stroke, treatment with resolvin D2 ameliorated stroke-
induced brain injury, neurologic dysfunction, and inflammatory 
response.260 Diabetes-induced defective SPM biosynthesis causes 
nonresolving inflammation, with continuous leukocyte influx 
into atherosclerotic lesions, inflammatory macrophage polariza­
tion, and defective efferocytosis. Together, these drive progression 
of atherosclerosis toward development of clinically dangerous 
lesions with large necrotic, procoagulant cores and thin fibrous 
caps. SPMs limit plaque progression by suppressing inflam­
mation, enhancing efferocytosis, and promoting an increase in 
thickness of the fibrous cap (Fig. 38.19). Enhanced efferocyto­
sis promotes macrophage production of several SPMs, including 
lipoxin A4, resolvin E1, and protectin D1. Lipoxins also recruit 
macrophages, which further enhance efferocytosis in resolving 
lesions. Efferocytosis requires specific phagocytotic receptors 
that bind to apoptotic cells. Deletion of one of these receptors, 
MerTK, causes impaired efferocytosis, accumulation of apoptotic 
cells, and large necrotic cores in murine atherosclerotic lesions. 
It also causes impaired SPM production by macrophages because 
MerTK signaling decreases proinflammatory leukotriene synthesis 
and increases synthesis of proresolving lipoxin A4.257

Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential and 
Diabetic Cardiovascular Disease
Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminant potential (CHIP) is an 
age-related increase in the growth of a single clone of hemato­
poietic stem cells without other associated hematologic abnor­
malities. It arises from a somatic mutation in a single stem cell 
that causes a proliferative advantage. CHIP is associated with a 
substantially higher risk for myocardial infarction and stroke, 
independent from traditional risk factors, accounting for a 40% 
increase in mortality.263,264 The most widely studied CHIP gene 
in atherosclerosis is TET2, an enzyme that catalyzes conversion of 
5-methylcytosine to 5 hydroxymethylcytosine. Both catalytic and 
noncatalytic domains of TET2 play a key role in DNA demethyl­
ation and hematopoietic stem cell maintenance. Diabetes is linked 
to a loss of TET2 function. People with diabetes have decreased 
levels of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine as a result of reduced activity of 
AMPK. Metformin treatment of cells from these patients restored 
TET2 activity.265 Reduced activity of the NAD-dependent SIRT1 
also reduces TET2 activity. Increased mitochondrial production 
of ROS could account for reduced AMPK and SIRT1 activities 
(see Fig. 38.3). 
Diabetes Alters Mitochondrial Dynamics
Mitochondria dynamics are continuous processes of mitochon­
drial fusion, fission, biogenesis, and mitophagy, which together 
maintain optimal cellular bioenergetics and ROS homeostasis.266 
Mitochondrial dynamics influence and often orchestrate not only 
metabolism but also complex cell signaling events, such as those 
involved in regulating cell pluripotency, division, differentiation, 
senescence, and cell death. Reciprocally, mitochondrial membrane 
dynamics are extensively regulated by posttranslational modifica­
tions of mitochondrial machinery and by formation of membrane 
contact sites between mitochondria and other organelles, both of 
which have the capacity to integrate inputs from various path­
ways.267 In normal physiology, fission helps facilitate mitophagy, 
which degrades and recycles damaged mitochondria and mito­
chondrial fragments, although fission also increases ROS produc­
tion as a result of incomplete transfer of electrons through the 
ETC. Mitochondrial fission is a critical process that enables mac­
rophages to clear multiple apoptotic cells. When fission is disabled, 
phagosome formation around secondarily encountered apoptotic 
cells is impaired.268 The primary regulators of outer mitochondrial 
fusion are dynamin-related guanosine triphosphate hydrolases

coronary endothelial cells, where levels of the fusion protein Opa1 
are decreased and Drp1 levels are increased.273 Persistent increased 
fission is also associated with myocardial dysfunction in humans 
with T2D, due in part to decreased expression of the fusion pro­
tein mitofusin 1.274 Drp1 recruitment to mitochondria is regu­
lated by its phosphorylation at serine 616 by either CaMKII or 
ROCK1. In diabetic heart and kidney, ROS can activate both of 
these kinases.119,271 
Genetic Determinants of Susceptibility to Microvascular 
Complications
Clinicians have long observed that different patients with simi­
lar duration and degree of hyperglycemia differ markedly in their 
susceptibility to microvascular complications. Such observations 
suggest genetic differences exist that affect the multiple molecular 
pathways by which hyperglycemia damages microvascular cells. 
The leveling of risk of overt proteinuria after 30 years’ duration 
of T1D at 27% is evidence that only a subset of patients are sus­
ceptible to the development of diabetic nephropathy.275 A role for 
genetic determinants of susceptibility to diabetic nephropathy is 
more directly supported by familial clustering, with an estimated 
heritability of at least 40%. In two studies of families in which two 
or more siblings had T1D, the risk of nephropathy in a diabetic 
sibling was 72% to 83% if the proband sibling with diabetes had 
advanced diabetic nephropathy, but only 17% to 22% if the index 
patient did not (Fig. 38.21).276,277 Familial clustering for risk of 
severe DR was also reported by the DCCT. Likewise, familial 
aggregation of coronary artery calcification occurs in families with 
T2D.278 Numerous associations have been made between various 
candidate gene polymorphisms and risk of diabetic complications. 
However, in a meta-analysis of three large cohorts from the Genet­
ics of Nephropathy—an International Effort (GENIE), no asso­
ciations remained significant after correction for multiple testing 
or application of stringent significance thresholds.279
Although genome-wide association studies (GWASs) per­
formed in large, well-characterized study populations have identi­
fied a few susceptibility loci for DR, nephropathy, and CVD,280 
the cumulative effects of disease-associated SNPs have failed to 
account for the majority of complex-trait heritability for a large

number of diseases, including diabetes and its complications (the 
“missing heritability” conundrum). Early research aimed at iden­
tifying genetic determinants of diabetic complications relied on 
underpowered GWASs limited by sample size. Availability of new 
genomic data sets from biobanks and aggregation of worldwide 
cohorts has increased detection of common genetic variants, and 
development of more sequencing data sets will help identify rare 
variants. Improved phenotyping will also help isolate genetic vari­
ants specific for diabetic complications from variants contributing 
to risk factors such as hypertension.281
DNA methylation, a key component of the epigenome, can 
regulate gene expression by altering transcription factor binding 
strength or recruiting proteins involved in gene expression. Heri­
tability analysis reveals that methylation variation explains a larger 
fraction of heritability of diabetic kidney disease than gene expres­
sion, and most of these variants are located on proximal tubule-
specific open chromatin areas. More severe diabetic kidney disease 
(higher fibrosis and worse kidney function) is associated with 
higher methylation and lower expression of solute carrier family 
47 member 1 (SLC47A1)/MATE1, a multidrug and toxin extru­
sion transporter. Loss of SLC47A1 was associated with activation 
of necroptosis, a regulated cell death pathway that plays an impor­
tant role in progression of acute kidney injury (AKI) to CKD.282 
Necroptosis occurs in response to mitochondrial or nuclear DNA 
damage that results in DNA appearance in the cytosol. This acti­
vates the receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 
(RIPK1), which then activates receptor-interacting serine/threo­
nine-protein kinase 3 (RIPK3). RIPK3, in turn, phosphorylates 
the mixed-lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL), leading to 
a change in its conformation, translocation to the plasma mem­
brane, and subsequent cell membrane disruption and death.283
Ultimately, the central unanswered question is: How is coor­
dinated gene-expression regulatory information conveyed—
the information that determines when, where, at what level, in 
what combinations, and for how long genes are expressed? With 
more than 90% of identified kidney function GWAS variants 
occurring in noncoding regions of the genome, research is cur­
rently focused on genetic-epigenetic interactions, noncoding 
RNAs, and long-range chromatin three-dimensional looping 
architecture.284,285 
Noncoding RNAs and Diabetic Complications
Although piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs), endogenous small 
interfering RNAs (siRNAs), intron-derived microRNAs (miR­
NAs), and a host of long noncoding RNAs all have regulatory 
roles, the best understood noncoding RNAs with respect to dia­
betic complications are the miRNAs, which regulate several key 
biologic pathways and cellular functions involved in diabetic com­
plications. Most individual miRNAs target hundreds of specific 
mRNAs,286 thereby coordinately regulating complex gene net­
works. In retina, diabetes increases levels of microRNA mediators 
of inflammation (miR155 and miR132)287 while decreasing levels 
of the antiinflammation mediator miR146a. Levels of miR146a 
are also reduced in the sciatic nerve of db/db mice. Treatment with 
a miR146a mimetic reduced macrophage activation and improved 
nerve conduction velocity, intraepidermal nerve fiber density, and 
axonal degeneration. miR146a is also decreased in kidneys and 
hearts of type 1 and type 2 diabetic animals.288 Various miRNAs 
are downregulated in diabetic kidney disease, including the miR-
30 family and miR-146a, which protect against inflammation 
and fibrosis. miRNAs upregulated or downregulated during the 
course of diabetic kidney disease in rodents and humans have been 
reported to have protective or deleterious effects. miRNAs have 
direct or indirect effects on targets with roles in processes includ­
ing epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), glomerular hyper­
trophy, fibrosis, and inflammation (Fig. 38.22).
miR33 regulates cellular functions associated with coronary 
artery disease. It increases macrophage activation, inhibits mito­
chondrial biogenesis, and represses autophagy.289 In mice placed 
on an atherogenic diet for 16 weeks and then made diabetic by 
streptozotocin injection, anti-miR33 treatment decreased ath­
erosclerotic plaque macrophage content and inflammatory gene 
expression. The decreased macrophage content in anti-miR33–
treated diabetic mice was associated with a blunting of hypergly­
cemia-induced monocytosis and reduced monocyte recruitment 
to the plaque.290 Diabetes increases circulating numbers of neu­
trophils and monocytes through an ROS-mediated mechanism 
and impairs regression of early atherosclerosis by increasing mac­
rophage entry into the lesion in mouse models.291,292
MicroRNAs may also play a role in the pathogenesis of diabetic 
cardiomyopathy. miR499, miR133a, and miR373 are downregu­
lated in diabetic cardiomyocytes.293 Downregulation of miR133a 
in a normal adult genetic background was sufficient to induce 
cardiac hypertrophy, and its downregulation is a prerequisite for 
development of apoptosis, fibrosis, and prolongation of the QT 
interval in animal models.294 The protective capacity of cardiac 
progenitor cells after myocardial infarction is also enhanced by 
miR133a.295
Emerging data suggest altered long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) 
expression may play an important role in the pathogenesis of dia­
betic complications.296 LncRNAs are >200 nucleotides in length 
and have many features similar to protein-coding genes. They are 
widely expressed and have key roles in gene regulation. Recent 
studies have begun to unravel how the biogenesis of lncRNAs is 
distinct from that of mRNAs and how lncRNA function is linked 
with their specific subcellular localizations.297 LncRNA may pro­
vide novel therapeutic targets. Levels of the lncRNA myocardial 
infarction associated transcript (MIAT) are upregulated in cardiac 
tissues from patients with diabetic cardiomyopathy and in reti­
nal tissues from humans with diabetes. Knockdown of MIAT in

Molecular Basis for Metabolic Memory
The phenomena of metabolic memory and the legacy effect are 
described at the beginning of this chapter in the Clinical Over­
view section. Here, current thinking about the molecular basis for 
these is presented. Stable cellular phenotypes are maintained by a 
multitude of interconnected multilevel positive and negative feed­
back loops,301,302 interacting with combinatorial extracellular sig­
nals from adjacent cells, from receptor ligands secreted by cells in 
other tissues, and from changes in metabolite flux and concentra­
tion. Familiar examples of stable alterations in cellular phenotype 
are the induction of pluripotency in terminally differentiated cells 
and the differentiation of these induced pluripotent stem (iPS) 
cells into a variety of cell types.303 In preclinical models of T1D 
and T2D, diabetes irreversibly depletes two bone marrow–derived 
mesenchymal progenitor subpopulations having provasculogenic 
expression profiles, and this deficit in vascular progenitor cells 
is not correctable by restoring glucose homeostasis in  vitro or 
in vivo.304 These data suggest diabetes causes permanent modi­
fications in subpopulations of mesenchymal progenitor cells that 
are passed to daughter cells with each division.
Similarly, when fibroblasts from patients with T1D for more 
than 50 years with complications were used to make iPS cells, 
the miR200 family was upregulated in fibroblasts from patients 
with complications, in the reprogrammed iPS cells from these 
fibroblasts, and in neurons differentiated from iPS cells from the 
cohort with complications. These neurons had increased suscep­
tibility to genotoxic stressors, including exposure to high glucose 
and various sources of increased ROS. The miR200 family tar­
get transcripts encoding DNA damage checkpoint proteins, and 
there was a concomitant loss of DNA damage checkpoint proteins 
and an increase in the DNA damage mark γH2AX phosphoryla­
tion (pH2AX).47 These findings were confirmed in aortic tissue 
from patients with complications and were reversed in fibroblasts 
and iPS cells by knockdown of miR200 (Fig. 38.23). In fibro­
blasts from patients with complications, there was also a striking 
impairment in reprogramming efficiency, and iPCs had impaired 
cellular growth and differentiation. Impaired reprogramming 
efficiency and impaired cellular growth and differentiation of 
iPCs have been linked to impaired mitochondrial dynamics.305 
In tissue from patients with complications, there was increased 
inflammation as a result of macrophage infiltration. There was also

Taken together, the observations from both these studies could 
reflect underlying genetic or epigenetic causes. However, because 
the DCCT and UKPDS study patients were randomly assigned 
to one of two different treatment groups, treatment-related epi­

metabolic memory observed subsequently in the EDIC and the

Epigenetic causes are those that change DNA or RNA struc­
ture and function but do not change DNA-RNA sequence. Along 
with the activities of microRNAs and other noncoding RNAs, a 
variety of enzymes modify chromatin by adding and removing 
chemical groups to DNA (primarily cytosine methylation) and to 
the protruding N-terminal tails of nucleosome histone proteins 
(monomethylation, dimethylation, and trimethylation of lysine 
and arginine residues, acetylation of lysine residues, and modifica­
tion of arginines by methylglyoxal and of serines and threonines 
by O-GlcNAc).208,307 In conjunction with remodeling complexes, 
these modifications mediate the availability or nonavailability of 
DNA sequences for transcription (Fig. 38.24). Increased ROS 
modulate several epigenetic mechanisms in different cell types and 
contexts.308–310
DNA methylation can repress or activate transcription, 
depending on its location. DNA methylation levels at repetitive 
elements and CpG-dense regions around promoters do not vary 
much between different cell types. In contrast, patterns of meth­
ylation at regions that regulate gene expression, such as enhancers, 
are very cell-type specific and essential for maintenance of cellular 
phenotype, and the formation and erasure of DNA methylation 
patterns is tightly linked to cellular metabolism. DNA methyl­
transferase 1 activity maintains these patterns during successive 
rounds of cell division. Demethylation of these is mediated by 
TET2, a ten-eleven translocation dioxygenase. Both catalytic and 
noncatalytic domains of TET2 play a key role in DNA demeth­
ylation and hematopoietic stem cell maintenance.311 Diabetes 
is linked to a loss of TET2 function, as discussed earlier under 
“Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential and Diabetic 
Cardiovascular Disease.”
Histone proteins are subject to a wide range of posttransla­
tional modifications that shape functional chromatin states. The 
regulation and function of these are determined by three classes

of proteins: (1) enzymes that catalyze the covalent modification 
of specific amino acid residues, called writers, examples include 
histone acetyltransferases (HATs), (2) enzymes that remove these 
modifications, called erasers, examples include histone deacety­
lases (HDACs) and NAD+-dependent sirtuins, and (3) proteins 
that bind to specifically modified histones, called readers, exam­
ples include bromodomain proteins, YEATS domain proteins, 
and double PHD finger domain proteins.312 In endothelial cells, 
proinflammatory activation of NFκB leads to rapid recruitment 
of NFκB to newly formed superenhancers and rapid, large-scale 
redistribution of the epigenetic reader bromodomain and extra­
terminal domain 4 (abbreviated BET4 or BRD4) from decom­
missioned preexisting basal enhancers to the newly formed 
superenhancers.313 This recruitment causes increased levels of 
H3K27ac and immediate transcription of inflammatory genes. 
Blocking the association of BRD4 with acetylated lysines in LDL 
receptor–deficient hypercholesterolemic mice attenuated both 
early and late atherosclerosis development. BRD4 and other 
members of the BET family are also critical effectors of pathologic 
cardiac remodeling and heart failure via their ability to coactivate 
multiple master transcription factors known to initiate and pro­
mote heart failure, including NFκB and NFAT.314 BET inhibi­
tion suppresses pathologic cardiac gene-expression programs and 
arrests pathologic hypertrophy and heart failure in vivo. BRD4 
(most potently, its splice isoform BRD4B) also functions as an 
endogenous inhibitor of DNA damage response signaling, which 
enhances radiation ROS-induced cell death. In contrast, knock­
down of this isoform caused rapid cell-cycle checkpoint recovery 
and enhanced cell survival.315
The metabolic state of the cell regulates histone lysine acetyla­
tion by acting on writers and erasers. Eight types of metabolite-
derived histone lysine modifications affect signal-dependent gene 
activation, tissue injury, and metabolic stress: propionylation, 
butyrylation, 2-hydroxyisobutyrlation, succinylation, malonyl­
ation, glutarylation, crotonylation, and β-hydroxybutyrlation.312 
Methylation of histone tails can repress or activate transcription, 
depending on the position of the modified residue in a specific 
histone tail, degree of methylation, and context of other histone 
modifications.

found in genes related to complications, including binding sites 
for the C/EBP transcription factor and in enhancer/transcription 
regions of hematopoietic stem cells. The most enriched sites were

The most significant associated site is in the TXNIP 3′ untrans­
lated region. Several associated methylation sites together explain 
as much as 70% to 85% of the association between mean DCCT 
HbA1c and risk of complications during EDIC. Because these 
data show that DNA methylation changes can occur in enhancer 
regions of HSCs, metabolic memory may arise from hyperglyce­
mia-induced epigenetic changes in stem cells, probably through 
modifying enhancer activity, which may persist in differentiated 
cells.
In the DCCT conventionally treated group, the effect size at 
specific DNA methylation sites was larger than in the DCCT 
intensively treated group. Mean DCCT HbA1c values were sig­
nificantly higher in the conventional than in the intensively 
treated group, suggesting that changes in DNA methylation 
at some HbA1c-associated sites are triggered only when HbA1c 
is above some threshold and maintained for a certain time 
period.316
Gene regulation requires dynamic coordination of hundreds of 
regulatory factors at precise genomic and RNA targets. Recently, 
functionally related DNA, RNA, and proteins have been shown 
to spatially concentrate within precise three-dimensional nuclear 
compartments. High concentrations of functionally related 
molecules lead to nonstoichiometric molecular interactions and 
nonlinear regulatory behaviors that quantitatively control gene 
regulation. This spatial organization can also play an important 
role in establishing epigenetic memory.317
Much has been learned since the original clinical description 
of metabolic memory, but much more research remains to be 
done before the molecular basis for metabolic memory is clearly 
understood. 
Diabetic Retinopathy and Other Ocular 
Complications of Diabetes
Diabetic retinopathy is a well-characterized sight-threatening 
chronic microvascular complication that eventually afflicts virtu­
ally all patients with diabetes mellitus.318–321 DR is characterized 
by gradually progressive alterations in the retinal microvascula­
ture, leading to areas of retinal nonperfusion, increased vascular 
permeability, and pathologic intraocular proliferation of retinal 
vessels. The complications associated with retinal neovasculariza­
tion, termed proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), and increased 
vascular permeability, termed diabetic macular edema (DME), can 
result in severe and permanent vision loss.
Early-stage DR eventually occurs in nearly all patients, 
although early intensive treatment of hyperglycemia delays its 
onset and progression in T1D. In selected patients with T2D, sys­
temic treatment with fenofibrate, angiotensin-converting enzyme 
inhibitors (ACEis), and angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs) 
may affect the development and progression of DR. Multiple 
phase 3 clinical trials over the past 5 years have now established 
intravitreous injections of anti-VEGF therapy as the standard of 
care for most eyes with visual impairment from center-involved 
DME (ciDME).322,323 In eyes with ciDME and only mild visual 
impairment (20/32 to 20/40), visual outcomes were similar with 
treatment with aflibercept, bevacizumab, or ranibizumab. In eyes 
with ciDME and moderate visual impairment (20/50 or worse), 
aflibercept provided visual gains superior to those achieved with 
bevacizumab at 1 and 2 years, and vision outcomes were superior 
to ranibizumab at 1 year but not 2 years. However, a subsequent 
study revealed that in these eyes with moderate or worse visual 
impairment from ciDME, using a step therapy approach of beva­
cizumab first, with a switch to aflibercept treatment for eyes with 
suboptimal response, provides similar visual outcomes to afliber­
cept monotherapy. Additional agents that are commercially avail­
able, including brolucizumab and faricimab, have been shown to 
be noninferior to aflibercept in treatment for DME. However, 
cases of occlusive vasculitis associated with brolucizumab treat­
ment have led to limited use of this medication clinically.
Currently, more than 90% of severe vision loss resulting from 
PDR can be prevented, and approximately 50% of eyes with 
visual loss from DME can resolve their retinal thickening and/
or recover vision of 20/20 or better with appropriate medical and 
ophthalmologic care.324,325 Although poor baseline visual acuity is 
one of the predictors of worse outcome, patients with poor visual 
acuity may fully recover to their baseline vision. Thus, the pri­
mary clinical care emphasis for the prevention of vision loss in 
the patient with diabetes is on early identification, accurate clas­
sification, and timely treatment of retinopathy through lifelong 
routine ophthalmologic follow-up appointments and optimized 
treatment of hyperglycemia, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.
Epidemiology and Impact of Proliferative 
Diabetic Retinopathy and Diabetic Macular 
Edema
There is a higher risk of more frequent and severe ocular complica­
tions in T1D than T2D.326 Approximately 25% of patients with 
T1D have retinopathy after 5 years, and this figure increases to 
60% and 80% after 10 and 15 years, respectively. The most visu­
ally threatening form of retinopathy (PDR) is present in about 
67% of patients with T1D who have had diabetes for 35 years.327 
However, because T2D accounts for 90% to 95% of the diabetic 
population in the United States, type 2 disease accounts for a 
higher fraction of patients with vision loss. Increasing duration of 
diabetes is one of the strongest predictors for onset and progres­
sion of retinopathy.
In the United States, an estimated 700,000 people have PDR, 
130,000 of whom have high-risk PDR. Among people with 
diabetes, 500,000 have macular edema, of whom 325,000 have 
clinically significant macular edema (CSME).328–332 An estimated 
63,000 cases of PDR, 29,000 cases of high-risk PDR, 80,000 
cases of macular edema, 56,000 cases of CSME, and 12,000 to 
24,000 new cases of legal blindness occur each year as a result of 
DR.328,329,333 In 2020, the number of adults worldwide with DR, 
vision-threatening DR, and CSME was estimated to be 103.12 
1494
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
million, 28.54 million, and 18.83 million, respectively; by 2045, 
the numbers are projected to increase to 160.50 million, 44.82 
million, and 28.61 million, respectively.334 Globally, the preva­
lence of DR was highest in Africa (35.90%) and North Amer­
ica and the Caribbean (33.30%) and was lowest in South and 
Central America (13.37%). Blindness is estimated to be 25 times 
more common in persons with diabetes than in those without the 
disease.335,336 Rates of progression to PDR or severe visual loss 
have declined over the past 4 decades in developed countries as 
a result of improvements in medical management, earlier iden­
tification, and treatment of DR with laser photocoagulation.337 
However, given the dramatically increasing prevalence of diabetes 
worldwide, with 783 million individuals expected to be affected 
by diabetes by the year 2045,338 a proportionally larger number 
of individuals will be at risk for vision loss from diabetic eye com­
plications over the next few decades. Threefold increases in vision-
threatening DR will affect 3.4 million Americans age 40 and older 
by 2050, as estimated by the Centers for Disease Control and 
Prevention (CDC).339,340
Many individuals with diabetes and vision-threatening DR are 
not aware of the presence or the severity of their disease. The 2010 
National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey revealed that 
only 45% of Americans with DME were aware that diabetes had 
affected their eyes, and nearly 60% of these individuals had not 
had a dilated eye examination within the past year. These findings 
reflect both a lack of awareness among patients at risk for vision 
loss from diabetic eye complications and insufficient evaluation 
for many patients with vision-threatening retinopathy.340 
Pathophysiology of Diabetic Retinopathy
A detailed discussion of the pathophysiologic mechanisms under­
lying DR and other diabetes-related complications has been 
presented earlier in this chapter. The earliest histologic effects of 
diabetes mellitus in the eye include loss of retinal vascular peri­
cytes (supporting cells for retinal endothelial cells), thickening of 
the vascular endothelium basement membrane, and alterations in 
retinal blood flow (Fig. 38.25).341–344 With increasing loss of reti­
nal pericytes, the retinal vessel wall develops outpouchings (micro­
aneurysms) and becomes fragile.
Clinically, microaneurysms and small retinal hemorrhages 
might not always be readily distinguishable from each other and 
are usually evaluated together as “hemorrhages and microaneu­
rysms” (Fig. 38.26A). Rheologic changes occur in DR and result 
from increased platelet aggregation, integrin-mediated leuko­
cyte adhesion, and endothelial damage.345–347 Disruption of the 
blood-retina barrier can ensue, characterized by increased vascular 
permeability.348,349 Subsequent leakage of blood and serum from 
the retinal vessels results in retinal hemorrhages, retinal edema, 
and hard exudates (see Fig. 38.26A and C). Vision loss can follow 
if the fovea is affected by the leakage.350
With time, increasing sclerosis and endothelial cell loss lead to 
narrowing of the retinal vessels, which decreases vascular perfusion 
and can ultimately lead to obliteration of the capillaries and small 
vessels (see Fig. 38.26B). The resulting retinal ischemia is a potent 
inducer of angiogenic growth factors. Several angiogenic growth 
factors have been isolated from eyes with DR, including insulin-
like growth factors, basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), and 
VEGF.351,352 These factors promote the development of new vessel 
growth and retinal vascular permeability.353,354 Indeed, inhibition 
of angiogenic molecules such as VEGF and their signaling path­
ways can suppress the development of retinal neovascularization 
and retinal vascular permeability.355,356 VEGF-independent 
endogenous inhibitors of angiogenesis and vascular permeability 
such as pigment epithelial-derived factor (PEDF), plasma kalli­
krein, and erythropoietin have also been found in the eye.357,358
New vessels tend to grow in regions of strong vitreous adhe­
sion to the retina, such as at the optic disc and major vascular 
arcades (see Fig. 38.26D and E). The posterior vitreous face also 
serves as a scaffold for pathologic neovascularization, and the 
new vessels commonly arise at the junctions between perfused 
and nonperfused retina. When the retina is severely ischemic, the 
concentration of angiogenic growth factors can reach sufficient 
concentration in the anterior chamber to cause abnormal new ves­
sel proliferation on the iris and the anterior chamber angle.352,359 
Uncontrolled anterior segment neovascularization can result in 
neovascular glaucoma because the fibrovascular proliferation in 
the angle of the eye causes blockage of aqueous outflow through 
the trabecular meshwork.360
Proliferating new vessels in DR are fragile and have a tendency 
to bleed, which results in preretinal and vitreous hemorrhages (see 
Fig. 38.26E and F). Although the presence of a large amount of 
blood in the preretinal space or vitreous cavity is not damaging to 
the retina, these intraocular hemorrhages often cause vision loss 
by blocking the visual axis. Vitreous hemorrhage can clear spon­
taneously without intervention, but eyes in which hemorrhage is 
nonclearing may need vitrectomy surgery to restore vision. Vit­
reous hemorrhage can also decrease the ability to visualize the 
retina and thereby limit the ability to adequately diagnose and 
treat other retinal disease. Membranes on the retinal surface can 
be induced by blood and result in wrinkling and traction on the 
retina. Although all retinal neovascularization, given sufficient 
time, eventually becomes quiescent, as with most scarring pro­
cesses, there is progressive fibrosis of the new vessel complexes that 
is associated with contraction. In the eye, such forces can exert 
traction on the retina, leading to tractional retinal detachment and 
retinal tears that can cause severe and permanent vision loss if left 
untreated (see Fig. 38.26G and H).
In short, causes of vision loss from complications of diabetes 
mellitus include retinal ischemia involving the fovea, macular 
edema at or near the fovea, preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage, reti­
nal detachment, and neovascular glaucoma. Vision loss can also 
result from more indirect effects of vasculopathy in patients with 
diabetes, such as retinal vessel occlusion, accelerated atheroscle­
rotic disease, and embolic phenomena. 
Clinical Features of Diabetic Retinopathy
Risk Factors for Diabetic Retinopathy
Duration of diabetes is closely associated with the onset and sever­
ity of DR. Nearly all patients with T1D develop some degree of 
retinopathy after 20 years.326,329,361 In the United States, approxi­
mately 20% of patients with newly diagnosed T2D have retinopa­
thy at the time of diagnosis,361 and more than 60% develop some 
degree of retinopathy over subsequent decades. In the UKPDS 
study of T2D, 35% of female subjects and 39% of male subjects 
had some level of DR at the time of diabetes diagnosis.362 As 
shown in the studies cited earlier, the incidence of retinopathy 
increases with increasing diabetes duration.
Age of onset of diabetes is another risk factor. DR is rare in pre­
pubescent patients with T1D.92 In the Wisconsin Epidemiologic 
Study of Diabetic Retinopathy, approximately 4% of patients 
younger than 30 years of age at diagnosis and nearly 2% of patients 
older than 30 years of age at diagnosis were legally blind. In the 
1495
CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
younger-onset group, 86% of blindness was attributable to DR. 
More severe retinopathy at baseline was associated with a greater 
likelihood of visual impairment over the subsequent 25 years, even 
when adjusting for diabetes duration.363 In the older-onset group, 
in which other eye diseases such as age-related macular degenera­
tion were also common, 33% of the cases of legal blindness were 
a result of DR.327,361,364
Lack of appropriate glycemic control is the most significant 
known risk factor for the onset and progression of DR. The 
DCCT demonstrated a clear relationship between hyperglycemia 
and a higher risk of diabetic microvascular complications, includ­
ing retinopathy, in 1441 patients with T1D.9,365,366 Intensive 
insulin therapy reduced or prevented the development of reti­
nopathy by 27% as compared to conventional therapy in patients 
monitored for 4 to 9 years in the DCCT. Additionally, intensive 
insulin therapy reduced the progression of DR by 34%, to 76%, 
and had a substantial beneficial effect over the entire range of reti­
nopathy severity. These results underscore the fact that although 
intensive therapy instituted early after diagnosis might not prevent 
retinopathy completely, it reduces the risk of retinopathy onset 
and progression.

from 9.1% for conventional treatment to 7.3% for intensive treat­

in mean HbA1c levels of the two former randomized treatment 
groups was only 0.4% at 1 year (p <0.001), continued to nar­

to increased expression of a protein tyrosine phosphatase called Src

pericyte apoptosis. Inhibition of SHP-1 is being investigated as a pos­

with active PDR compared to other retinopathies.380 Proteomic and

and vitreous of patients protected from advanced DR despite diabetes 
durations of over 50 years. Early work on retinal cell–based assays and 
rodent models has shown that elevation of RBP3 can prevent or stop 
neural and capillary changes induced by diabetes.381 Mechanistically, 
RBP3 may have a role in protection against the progression of DR 
by decreasing expression of inflammatory cytokines and VEGF and 
inhibiting glucose uptake into retinal cells via glucose transporter 1 
(GLUT1), thereby mitigating adverse effects of chronic hyperglyce­
mia. Data from plasma and vitreous samples from the Joslin 50-Year 
Medalist Study have shown that higher vitreous RBP3 concentrations 
are associated with less severe DR and slower rates of progression to 
PDR, supporting its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic agent 
for preventing worsening of DR, possibly by lowering retinal VEGF 
and inflammatory cytokines.382 Recent studies have established that 
other protective factors are also important in modulating the develop­
ment severity of diabetic complications.382a 
Clinical Findings in Diabetic Retinopathy
Clinical findings associated with early and progressing DR 
include microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard 
exudates, and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, along 
with venous abnormalities such as venous loops, venous tortu­
osity, and venous beading (see Fig. 38.26A and C). Microan­
eurysms are outpouchings of the capillary walls that can leak 
fluid and result in intraretinal edema and hemorrhages. The 
intraretinal hemorrhages can be flame-shaped or dot-blot–like 
in appearance, reflecting the architecture of the retinal layer in 
which they occur. Flame-shaped hemorrhages occur in the inner 
retina closer to the vitreous, and dot-blot hemorrhages occur 
deeper in the retina. Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities 
are either new vessel growth within the retinal tissue itself or 
shunt vessels through areas of poor vascular perfusion. It is com­
mon for intraretinal microvascular abnormalities to be located 
adjacent to cotton-wool spots. Cotton-wool spots are caused by 
microinfarcts in the nerve fiber layer of the retina. Venous caliber 
abnormalities, also known as venous beading, are generally a sign 
of severe retinal hypoxia. In some cases of extensive vascular loss, 
however, the retina may actually appear free of nonproliferative 
lesions on clinical examination. Such areas are termed featureless 
retina and are a sign of severe retinal hypoxia.
Vision loss from DR generally results from persistent non­
clearing vitreous hemorrhage, traction retinal detachment, retinal 
nonperfusion, or DME (see Figs. 38.25 and 38.26). Neovascular­
ization with fibrous tissue contraction can distort the retina and 
lead to traction retinal detachment. The new vessels can bleed, 
causing preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage. The most common 
causes of vision loss from diabetes, however, are macular disease 
and macular edema. Macular edema is more likely to occur in 
patients with T2D. In diabetic macular disease, macular edema 
involving the fovea or nonperfusion of the capillaries in the central 
macula is responsible for the loss of vision. 
Classification Systems of Diabetic Retinopathy
DR is broadly classified into the NPDR and PDR categories.383,384 
Macular edema can be present in eyes with nonproliferative or 
proliferative disease and is not used in the classification of level 
of retinopathy. The historic terms background retinopathy and 
preproliferative DR have been replaced to reflect the specific char­
acteristics and risk stratification of the prognostically important 
subgroups in NPDR (Table 38.1).
Generally, DR progresses from no retinopathy through mild, 
moderate, severe, and very severe NPDR and eventually to PDR. 
The level of NPDR is determined by the extent and location of 
clinical manifestations of retinopathy. Mild NPDR is character­
ized by limited microvascular abnormalities such as hemorrhages 
or microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, and increased vascular 
permeability. Moderate and severe NPDR are characterized by 
increasing severity of hemorrhages or microaneurysms, venous 
caliber abnormalities, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, 
and vascular closure. The level of NPDR establishes the risk of 
progression to sight-threatening retinopathy and dictates appro­
priate clinical management and follow-up.
PDR is characterized by vasoproliferation of the retina and its 
complications, including new vessels on the optic disc (NVD), 
new vessels elsewhere on the retina (NVE), preretinal hemorrhage 
(PRH), vitreous hemorrhage, and fibrous tissue proliferation 
(FP). On the basis of the extent and location of these lesions, PDR 
is classified as early PDR or high-risk PDR. Larger areas of these 
lesions and new vessels that are near the optic disc are associated 
with greater risks of vision loss. 
Classification of Diabetic Macular Edema. DME can be 
present at any severity of DR. However, the incidence of DME 
increases with increasing DR severity. Historically, eyes with 
DME were categorized as having nonclinically significant or clini­
cally significant macular edema (CSME). The term CSME was 
first introduced in the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy 
Study (ETDRS) to indicate an increased risk for moderate visual 
loss and was used as a threshold to determine the need for laser 
treatment. CSME exists if there is retinal thickening at or within 
500 μm of the fovea, hard exudates at or within 500 μm of the 
fovea with adjacent retinal thickening, or an area or areas of retinal 
thickening of one disc area or more in size, any part of which is 
within 1500 μm of the fovea.383,385,386 CSME is a clinical diag­
nosis that is not dependent on visual acuity or results of ancillary 
testing such as fluorescein angiography and can be present even 
when vision is 20/20 or better.
In the recent era, with the advent of ocular coherence tomog­
raphy (OCT) and its objective quantitative measurement of 
retinal thickness, clinical care and clinical trial endpoints have 
shifted to evaluating whether the center of the macula is involved 
or not. Data from the ETDRS evaluating eyes with macular 
edema have shown the presence or absence of thickening involv­
ing the center of the macula, now termed center-involved DME, 
which is highly associated with short- and long-term visual acu­
ity outcomes. In the ETDRS, eyes with center-involved DME 
had nearly a 10-fold greater risk for developing moderate visual 
loss compared to eyes without center involvement. The identifi­
cation of center-involved DME is critical because it will gener­
ally indicate how likely the DME is to cause visual impairment 
and is a key criterion for determining the need for treatment. 
Non–center-involved DME does not typically cause visual loss 
1498
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
or symptoms and frequently does not progress to center-involved 
DME. Thus, if the center of the macula is not involved, there is 
often not a compelling reason to treat. As a result, recent clinical 
studies and guidelines for clinical care have generally used the 
presence or absence of thickening of the central 1-mm diameter 
of retina and visual status as the defining criteria to consider 
initiation of treatment for eyes with DME. 
International Classification of Diabetic Retinopathy and 
Diabetic Macular Edema. The American Academy of Ophthal­
mology initiated a project to establish a consensus International 
Classification of Diabetic Retinopathy and Diabetic Macular 
Edema in an effort to simplify classification and standardize com­
munication among diabetes health care providers.387,388 This 
international classification describes five clinical levels of DR: no

Term
Definition
Antivascular endothelial growth factor 
(anti-VEGF) therapies; VEGF inhibitors
For the purposes of this chapter, these refer to VEGF inhibitors (including aflibercept, bevacizumab, and 
ranibizumab) that are given intravitreously for the treatment of diabetic macular edema and proliferative 
diabetic retinopathy.
Background diabetic retinopathy (BDR)
An outdated term referring to some stages of NPDR; not closely associated with disease progression; replaced 
by the various levels of NPDR.
Center-involved (or central-involved) 
diabetic macular edema (ciDME)
Abnormal thickening of the central retina (usually 1 mm in diameter central retinal subfield) due to increased 
vascular permeability. Because central involvement is more likely to cause visual impairment, it is commonly 
used as a threshold for treatment.
Clinically significant macular edema (CSME)
Thickening of the retina in the macular region of sufficient extent and location to threaten central visual function.
Cotton-wool spot
A gray or white area lesion in the nerve fiber layer of the retina resulting from stasis of axoplasmic flow caused 
by microinfarcts of the retinal nerve fiber layer.
Diabetes Control and Complications Trial 
(DCCT)
A multicenter, randomized clinical trial designed to address whether intensive insulin therapy could prevent or 
slow the progression of systemic complications of diabetes mellitus.
Diabetic retinopathy (DR)
Retinal damage related to the underlying systemic disease of diabetes mellitus.
Diabetic Retinopathy Study (DRS)
The first multicenter, randomized clinical trial to demonstrate the value of scatter (panretinal) photocoagulation in 
reducing the risk of vision loss among patients with all levels of diabetic retinopathy.
Diabetic Retinopathy Vitrectomy Study 
(DRVS)
A multicenter clinical trial evaluating early vitrectomy for patients with very advanced diabetic retinopathy or 
nonresolving vitreous hemorrhage.
Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy 
Study (ETDRS)
A multicenter, randomized clinical trial that addressed at what stage of retinopathy scatter (panretinal) 
photocoagulation was indicated, whether focal photocoagulation was effective for preventing moderate 
vision loss due to clinically significant macular edema and whether aspirin therapy altered the progression of 
diabetic retinopathy.
Focal or grid laser photocoagulation
A type of laser treatment whose main goal is to reduce vascular leakage, either by focal treatment of leaking 
retinal microaneurysms or by application of therapy in a grid-like pattern for patients with clinically significant 
macular edema.
Hard exudate
Lipid accumulation within the retina as a result of increased vasopermeability.
High-risk characteristic proliferative 
diabetic retinopathy (HRC-PDR)
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy of defined extent, location, or clinical findings that is particularly associated 
with severe vision loss.
Microaneurysm
An early vascular abnormality consisting of an outpouching of the retinal microvasculature.
Neovascular glaucoma (NVG)
Elevation of intraocular pressure caused by the development of neovascularization in the anterior segment of the eye.
Neovascularization at the disc (NVD)
Retinal neovascularization occurring at or within 1500 μm of the optic disc.
Neovascularization elsewhere (NVE)
Retinal neovascularization that is located more than 1500 μm away from the optic disc.
Neovascularization of the iris (NVI)
Neovascularization occurring on the iris (rubeosis iridis), usually as a result of extensive retinal ischemia.
No light perception (NLP)
The inability to perceive light.
Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)
Severities (mild, moderate, severe) of clinically evident diabetic retinopathy that precede the development of PDR.
Preproliferative diabetic retinopathy 
(PPDR)
An outdated term referring to more advanced levels of NPDR; not closely associated with disease progression; 
replaced by the various levels of NPDR.
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)
An advanced level of diabetic retinopathy in which proliferation of new vessels or fibrous tissue occurs on or 
within the retina.
Rubeosis iridis
Neovascularization of the iris.

ETDRS grading system. However, because of this simplification, 
the International Classification of Diabetic Retinopathy and Dia­
