Advances in Retinal Markers for Diabetic Retinal Disease 
Activity and Progression. The ETDRS standardized grading 
scale is based on 30o retinal images from seven standard defined 
retinal fields and characterizes the extent of specific retinal lesions 
located in the posterior pole that are predictive of the risk of DR 
progression. However, multiple independent groups have demon­
strated that retinal lesions can appear or develop outside of the 
seven-standard-field ETDRS photography.389–392 Ultrawide-field 
imaging has demonstrated DR lesions outside the ETDRS seven 
standard fields, and the retina is categorized as having predomi­
nantly peripheral lesions (PPLs) when these lesions are greater 
in extent or severity outside as compared to within the ETDRS 
standard fields. Eyes with PPLs identified on ultrawide fluores­
cein angiography have increased retinal nonperfusion compared 
to eyes without.393 The cause of PPLs is currently unknown but 
may involve loss of autoregulation in retinal arterioles or micro­
vascular degeneration causing capillary nonperfusion and retinal 
ischemia.394 PPLs identified on ultrawide angiography are present 
in about 50% of eyes with DR, and in approximately 10% of eyes, 
PPLs identify a more severe level as compared to that obtained 
from findings only within the ETDRS fields.395 Moreover, the 
baseline presence of angiographic PPLs in an eye suggests an over 
1.7-fold increased risk of future worsening and the development 
of advanced, sight-threatening retinopathy over the subsequent 
4 years.396,397 At this time, fluorescein angiography (FA) is typi­
cally used clinically to identify or confirm the presence of dia­
betic retinal neovascularization, vascular leakage, or nonperfusion. 
However, the results from Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research 
(DRCR) Protocol AA suggest that future use of ultrawide-field 
FA-determined PPLs and nonperfusion may improve prediction 
of retinopathy outcomes beyond what can be predicted from stan­
dard color photographs. These are consistent with the hypothesis 
that ultrawide-field angiographically identified PPLs and nonper­
fusion may be retinal markers for more severe underlying retinal 
vascular disease than is evident on color photography or clinical 
examination alone. 
Other Ocular Manifestations of Diabetes
All structures of the eye are susceptible to complications of dia­
betes. The consequence of these changes can range from being 
unnoticed by both patient and physician to symptomatic but not 
sight threatening to requiring evaluation to rule out potentially 
life-threatening underlying causes other than diabetes.
Mononeuropathies of the third, fourth, or sixth cranial nerves 
can arise in association with diabetes; mononeuropathy of the 
fourth cranial nerve is least likely associated with diabetes and

warrants workup for other causes.398–400 Nerve palsies present a 
significant diagnostic challenge because misdiagnosis can result in 
a life-threatening lesion remaining untreated. The percentage of 
all extraocular muscle palsies attributable to diabetes mellitus is 
estimated at 4.5% to 6%.400 This finding underscores the danger 
of routinely attributing mononeuropathies to the diabetic con­
dition itself without carefully ruling out other potential causes. 
Mononeuropathies may be the initial presenting sign of new-
onset diabetes, and diabetes should therefore be considered in 
the differential diagnosis of any mononeuropathy affecting the 
extraocular muscles, even in patients who do not have a known 
history of diabetes. Diabetes-induced third-nerve, fourth-nerve, 
and sixth-nerve palsies are usually self-limited and should resolve 
spontaneously in 2 to 6 months. Palsies can recur or subsequently 
develop in the contralateral eye.
The optic disc can be affected by diabetes in a variety of ways 
other than vasoproliferation. Diabetic papillopathy is a diagno­
sis of exclusion and must be distinguished from other causes of 
disc swelling, including true papilledema from increased intracra­
nial pressure, pseudopapilledema such as optic nerve head dru­
sen, toxic optic neuropathies, neoplasms of the optic nerve, and 
hypertension.401 Optic disc pallor can occur after spontaneous 
remission of proliferative retinopathy or remission following scat­
ter (panretinal) laser photocoagulation (see Fig. 38.26I). Because 
diabetes poses an increased risk for developing open-angle glau­
coma, the disc pallor following remission of retinopathy or laser 
photocoagulation must be considered when evaluating the optic 
nerve head for glaucoma.
A diabetic ocular complication with potentially serious con­
sequences is neovascularization of the iris. Neovascularization of 
the iris occurs in 4% to 7% of diabetic eyes and may be present 
in 40% to 60% of eyes with proliferative retinopathy. New iris 
vessels are usually first observed at the pupillary border, followed 
by a fine network of vessels over the iris tissue progressing into the 
filtration angle of the eye. Closure of the angle by the fibrovascular 
network results in neovascular glaucoma, which can lead to irre­
versible optic nerve damage and vision loss as a result of the rise 
in intraocular pressure.402–404 Neovascular glaucoma is difficult to 
manage and requires aggressive treatment. Diabetes is the second-
leading cause of neovascular glaucoma, accounting for 32% of 
cases.405 When possible, scatter (panretinal) laser photocoagula­
tion is the primary therapy for neovascular glaucoma and provides 
durable regression of neovascularization of the iris and angle for 
most eyes. Other approaches, such as goniophotocoagulation, top­
ical or systemic antiglaucoma medications, and antiglaucomatous 
filtration surgery, are available when needed.406–408 Intravitreal 
administration of VEGF inhibitors is now frequently used in eyes 
with acute neovascular glaucoma and results in remarkably rapid 
regression of the neovascularization with resulting normalization 
of the intraocular pressure.409 However, the effects of anti-VEGF 
agents are often transient, and there is frequently recurrence of 
neovascularization unless injections are given on a monthly basis. 
Thus, a more durable therapy such as scatter laser photocoagula­
tion is often performed.
The cornea of the person with diabetes is more susceptible to 
injury and slower to heal after injury than is the nondiabetic cor­
nea.410,411 The diabetic cornea is also more prone to infectious 
corneal ulcers, which can lead to rapid loss of vision, need for 
corneal transplant, or loss of the eye if it is not treated aggressively. 
Consequently, patients with diabetes using contact lenses should 
exercise caution to avoid contact lens overwear and to maintain 
careful monitoring.
Open-angle glaucoma is 1.4 times more common in the dia­
betic population than in the nondiabetic population.412,413
Diabetes effects on the crystalline lens can result in transient 
refractive changes, alterations in accommodative ability,414 and 
cataracts. Refractive change can be significant and is related to 
fluctuation of blood glucose levels with osmotic lens swelling.415 
Cataracts can occur earlier in life and progress more rapidly in 
the presence of diabetes.415,416 Cataracts are 1.6 times more com­
mon in people with diabetes than in those without diabetes.415,416 
In patients with earlier-onset diabetes, duration of diabetes, reti­
nopathy status, diuretic use, and HbA1c levels are risk factors.417 
In patients with later-onset diabetes, age of the patient, lower 
intraocular pressure, smoking, and lower diastolic blood pres­
sure may be additional risk factors.418,419 Patients with diabetes 
undergoing simultaneous kidney and pancreas transplantation are 
at an increased risk of developing all types of cataracts, indepen­
dent of the use of corticosteroids after transplantation.420 Both 
phacoemulsification and extracapsular cataract extraction with 
intraocular lens implantation are appropriate surgical therapies. 
The principal determinant of postoperative vision and progression 
of retinopathy is related to the preoperative presence of DME and 
the severity of DR.421,422
Other findings with higher incidence among patients with 
diabetes include xanthelasma,398 microaneurysms of the bulbar 
conjunctiva,423 posterior vitreous detachment,424 and the rare 
but often fatal orbital fungal infection with Mucorales phycomyco­
sis.402,403 Prompt diagnosis and treatment of phycomycosis caused 
by Mucor species are crucial, although the survival rate remains at 
only 57%.403,425 
Monitoring and Treatment of Diabetic 
Retinopathy
Appropriate clinical management of DR has been defined by 
the results of major randomized, multicenter clinical trials (Fig. 
38.27): the Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research Network 
Protocols I, S, and T,322,323,426 the Diabetic Retinopathy Study 
(DRS),427 ETDRS,350 Diabetic Retinopathy Vitrectomy Study 
(DRVS),428 DCCT,429 and UKPDS.430 These studies have elu­
cidated the progression rates of each level of DR, guided follow-
up intervals, and demonstrated the proper delivery, timing, and 
resulting effectiveness of glycemic control, laser photocoagulation, 
and intravitreous anti-VEGF therapy (Figs. 38.28–38.31). They 
have also established recommendations for vitrectomy surgery for 
diabetic eye complications.
Comprehensive Eye Examination
An accurate ocular examination detailing the extent and location 
of retinopathy-associated findings is critical for determining mon­
itoring and treatment decisions in patients with DR. As detailed 
later, most of the blindness associated with advanced stages of reti­
nopathy can be averted with appropriate and timely diagnosis and 
therapy. Unfortunately, many patients with diabetes do not receive 
adequate eye care at an appropriate stage of their disease.431,432 In 
fact, 11% of patients with T1D and 7% of patients with T2D 
with high-risk PDR necessitating prompt treatment had not been 
examined by an ophthalmologist within the past 2 years.432 In one 
study, 55% of patients with high-risk PDR or CSME had never 
had laser photocoagulation.431
The comprehensive eye examination is the mainstay of such 
evaluation and is necessary on a repetitive, lifelong basis for 
patients with diabetes.383,433 Such an evaluation has four major 
1501
CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
components: history, examination, diagnosis, and treatment as 
needed. Annual retinal evaluation to assess the presence and level 
of DR and DME is essential to guide patient care. The funda­
mentals of a comprehensive eye examination for the nondiabetic 
patient have been detailed by the American Academy of Oph­
thalmology433 and the American Optometric Association.434 The 
examination of the patient with diabetes should be similar, with 
additional emphasis on portions of the examination that relate to 
problems particularly relevant to diabetes.
Dilated ophthalmic examination is superior to undilated evalu­
ation because only 50% of eyes are correctly classified as to the pres­
ence and severity of retinopathy through undilated pupils.435,436 
Appropriate ophthalmic evaluation entails pupillary dilation, slit-
lamp biomicroscopy, examination of the retinal periphery with 
indirect ophthalmoscopy or mirrored contact lens, and sometimes 
gonioscopy.433,434 Because of the complexities of the diagnosis and 
treatment of PDR and CSME, ophthalmologists with specialized 
knowledge and experience in the management of DR are required 
to determine and provide appropriate surgical intervention.437 
Thus, it is recommended that all patients with diabetes should 
have dilated ocular examinations by an experienced eye care pro­
vider (ophthalmologist or optometrist), and patients with diabetes 
should be under the direct or consulting care of an ophthalmolo­
gist experienced in the management of DR at least by the time 
moderate DR or DME is present. Validated methods of retinal 
imaging (typically color fundus photography) that have demon­
strated equivalency to dilated retinal fundus examination or the 
accepted standard of ETDRS seven-standard-field stereoscopic 
retinal imaging when interpreted by a trained eye care provider 
can also be appropriate for retinal evaluation.438,439 Furthermore, 
ocular telehealth programs for DR that use validated means of ret­
inal imaging have the potential to expand access to highly effective

Initial Ophthalmic Evaluation
The recommendation for initial ocular examination in persons 
with diabetes is based on the prevalence rates of retinopathy and 
the incidence of subsequent vision-threatening diabetic eye com­
plications (see Fig. 38.28). Approximately 80% of patients with 
T1D have retinopathy after 15 years of disease, but only about 
25% have any retinopathy after 5 years of diabetes.436 The preva­
lence of PDR is less than 2% at 5 years and 25% by 15 years. For 
T2D, the onset date of diabetes is usually unknown, and severe 
retinal disease can be observed even at the time of diabetes diag­
nosis. Up to 3% of patients whose diabetes is first diagnosed after 
age 30 years (T2D) have CSME or high-risk PDR at the time of 
initial diagnosis of diabetes.441 Thus, in patients older than 10 
years, initial ophthalmic examination is recommended beginning 
5 years after the diagnosis of T1D and immediately after diagnosis 
of T2D (see Fig. 38.28).383,442
Puberty and pregnancy can accelerate retinopathy progres­
sion. The onset of vision-threatening retinopathy is rare in chil­
dren before puberty, regardless of the duration of diabetes442,443; 
however, significant retinopathy can arise within 6 years of disease 
if diabetes is diagnosed between the ages of 10 and 30 years.328 DR 
can become particularly aggressive during pregnancy in patients 
with diabetes.444,445 In the past, the prognosis for pregnancy in 
the patient with diabetes with microvascular complications was 
so poor that pregnant patients with diabetes were commonly 
advised to avoid or terminate pregnancies.446 With recognition 
of the importance of glycemic control, patients with diabetes in 
the childbearing age range can now experience safe pregnancy and 
childbirth with minimal risk to both the mother and the baby.447
Ideally, patients with diabetes who are planning pregnancy 
should have a comprehensive eye examination within 1 year 
before conception (see Fig. 38.30). Treatment may be indicated 
before conception for patients who are at risk for vision loss if 
their DR were to worsen during pregnancy. Patients who become 
pregnant should have a comprehensive eye examination in the first 
trimester of pregnancy. Close follow-up throughout pregnancy is 
indicated, with subsequent examinations determined by the find­
ings present at the first-trimester examination.383 This recommen­
dation does not apply to women who develop gestational diabetes 
later in their pregnancy because they are not at increased risk of 
developing DR.

Follow-Up Ophthalmic Examination
Follow-up ocular examination is determined from the risk of dis­
ease progression at any particular retinopathy severity (see Fig. 
38.29). NPDR is clinically categorized into four levels of severity 
based on clinical findings compared to stereo fundus photographic 
standards: mild, moderate, severe, and very severe.448 Progression 
of nonproliferative retinopathy to the visually threatening level of 
high-risk PDR is closely correlated with baseline NPDR sever­
ity (Table 38.4). Progression rates from each individual NPDR 
level to any other retinopathy level are also known. These are used 
to define standard minimal follow-up intervals as detailed in Fig. 
38.29 and Table 38.5. Because significant sight-threatening reti­
nopathy can initially occur with no or minimal visual symptoms, 
patients with no clinically evident DR and no known ocular prob­
lems still require annual comprehensive ophthalmic examinations 
even if they are totally asymptomatic. 
Teleretinal Screening for Diabetic Retinal Disease
In recent years, there has been broader adoption of teleretinal 
examinations for DR. Approaches include integration in pri­
mary care settings, prison or penal populations, remote areas 
with limited health care facilities, underserved populations, and 
hospital-based or tertiary care facilities. These teleretinal programs 
function in a variety of roles, from providing access in areas where 
eye care is limited to established tertiary health care settings that 
further improve patient outcomes. The teleretinal model for dia­
betic retinal disease relies on remotely acquired retinal images that 
are evaluated centrally, either with human graders or with a vali­
dated artificial intelligence platform. The findings identified are 
communicated to the remote site in a store-and-forward manner 
(asynchronous collection of clinical information and electronic 
transmittal for evaluation) or in real time. The use of telemedicine 
has been shown to overcome patient resistance to eye examina­
tions through the use of nonmydriatic imaging and by locating 
imaging services at the point of diabetes care.449 Data from the 
United Kingdom have shown that combined with current diabe­
tes and eye treatments, telemedicine for diabetes may reduce the 
incidence of diabetes-related blindness by as much as 95%.450 
Evaluation and Treatment of Proliferative Diabetic 
Retinopathy
The extent and location of neovascularization determine the level 
of PDR.451,452 PDR is best evaluated by dilated fundus exami­
nation using slit-lamp biomicroscopy combined with indirect 
ophthalmoscopy or stereo fundus photography. FA and optical 
coherence tomography angiography can also aid in identifying 
small, subtle patches of retinal neovascularization. However, these 
imaging modalities are usually not required for the diagnosis of 
PDR because these findings are clinically evident in most cases 
(Fig. 38.32).

The presence of PDR in an eye substantially increases the risk 
for severe vision loss. Severe vision loss is defined as best corrected 
acuity of 5/200 or worse on two consecutive visits 4 months apart. 
This represents vision loss substantially worse than the 20/200 or 
worse limit defined as legal blindness. Without treatment, eyes 
with high-risk PDR have a 28% risk of severe vision loss within 2 
years. This risk compares with a 7% risk of severe vision loss after 
2 years for eyes with PDR but without high-risk characteristics.451
In the past, scatter (panretinal) laser photocoagulation was the 
sole therapy shown to be effective against PDR. The DRS dem­
onstrated that panretinal laser photocoagulation was effective in 
reducing the risk of severe vision loss from PDR by 50% or more. 
The ETDRS further demonstrated that panretinal laser photoco­
agulation applied when an eye approaches or just reaches high-risk 
PDR reduces the risk of severe vision loss to less than 4%. Based 
on these results, prompt scatter photocoagulation is considered 
appropriate for all patients with high-risk PDR, is usually appro­
priate for patients with PDR less than high risk, and may be advis­
able for patients with severe or very severe NPDR, especially in the 
setting of T2D (see Fig. 38.29).350,451–454
Recent progression of eye disease, status of the fellow eye, com­
pliance with follow-up, concurrent health concerns such as hyper­
tension or kidney disease, and other factors must be considered in 
determining if laser surgery should be performed in these patients. 
In particular, patients with T2D should be considered for scatter 
photocoagulation before high-risk PDR develops because the risk 
of severe vision loss and the need for pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) 
can be reduced by 50% in these patients, especially when macular 
edema is present.454
In scatter photocoagulation, 1200 to 1800 laser burns are 
applied to the peripheral retinal tissue, actually focally destroy­
ing the outer photoreceptor and retinal pigment epithelium of 
the retina (see Fig. 38.26I). Large vessels are avoided, as are areas 
of preretinal hemorrhage. The treatment is thought to exert its 
effect by increasing oxygen delivery to the inner retina, decreasing 
viable hypoxic growth factor–producing cells, and increasing the 
relative perfusion per area of viable retina. The total treatment is

The response to scatter photocoagulation varies. The most 
desirable effect is to see a regression of the new vessels, although 
stabilization of the neovascularization with no further growth can 
result. This latter situation requires careful clinical monitoring. In 
some cases, new vessels continue to proliferate, requiring addi­
tional scatter photocoagulation or adjuvant treatment with intra­
vitreous anti-VEGF agents (see Fig. 38.31).
Studies from the DRCR Retina Network (formerly the Dia­
betic Retinopathy Clinical Research Network) have shown that 
anti-VEGF treatment with aflibercept or ranibizumab is an effec­
tive first-line alternative to scatter photocoagulation in carefully 
selected patients with PDR.426,455,456 Neovascular processes are 
exquisitely sensitive to anti-VEGF agents, and eyes with severe 
neovascularization of the retina or anterior segment have dra­
matic and rapid improvement with anti-VEGF therapy.356,457 The 
DRCR Retina Network Protocol S demonstrated that visual acu­
ity outcomes at 2 and 5 years were noninferior in eyes treated with 
intravitreal ranibizumab to those obtained with scatter photoco­
agulation. Anti-VEGF treatment with ranibizumab was associated 
with several advantages over laser therapy. There was greater aver­
age visual gain over the course of the first 2 years, reduced rates of 
visual impairment from DME onset, less loss of peripheral visual 
field, and decreased need for vitrectomy surgery at both 2 and 5 
years in the ranibizumab group.
When delivered by a standardized retreatment algorithm such 
as that developed for Protocol S (Fig. 38.33), anti-VEGF therapy 
is highly effective in reducing retinal neovascularization. In Pro­
tocol S, 38% of the eyes treated with ranibizumab were eligible 
to defer monthly injections as a result of sustained stability of 
neovascularization at least once over the first 2 years of follow-up, 
and retinal neovascularization was completely resolved at 44% of 
visits through 2 years.458 Nonetheless, eyes randomized to ranibi­
zumab treatment in Protocol S continued to need a median of 
three injections per year through 2 to 5 years to maintain stability 
or regression of neovascularization. It should also be realized that 
patients with PDR often have systemic comorbidities that may 
contribute to missed or rescheduled office visits. Thus, patient 
compliance with follow-up and treatment recommendations is a 
critical aspect of ensuring successful outcomes with anti-VEGF 
therapy for PDR. If compliance is expected to be a problem for 
a specific patient, then treatment with laser panretinal photoco­
agulation alone, or in combination with a VEGF inhibitor, is the 
preferred therapeutic approach.
Surgical intervention with PPV is usually reserved for eyes with 
nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage or traction detachment from 
PDR. The DRVS, completed in 1989, demonstrated that early 
PPV in persons with severe fibrovascular proliferation was more 
likely to result in better vision and less likely to result in poor 
vision, particularly in patients with T1D.428 PPV aims primarily 
to remove abnormal fibrovascular tissue, alleviate retinal traction, 
allow the retina to obtain a more anatomically normal position, 
and remove vitreous opacities such as vitreous hemorrhage. The 
actual outcome data from this study are not entirely applicable 
today due to dramatic advances in surgical techniques and the 
advent of laser endophotocoagulation that have occurred in the 
intervening years. Nevertheless, it is clear that PPV can save and 
restore vision in many cases of severe retinal disease that are not 
amenable or not responsive to laser photocoagulation.

have demonstrated beneficial effects of these medications on dia­
betic retinopathy severity and rates of progression to PDR-related 
complications such as vitreous hemorrhage and need for vitrec­
tomy. Nearly 40% of eyes achieve a regression of DR severity of 
two or more steps after 3 years of monthly continuous anti-VEGF 
therapy for DME.459–461 Decreased rates of PDR onset and need 
for PDR treatment are also observed after ranibizumab therapy 
as compared to sham treatment.460 After an average of 4.4 injec­
tions of aflibercept over 6 months, 58% of eyes experienced an 
improvement in DR severity of two or more steps as compared 
to 6% of sham-treated eyes.461 Two randomized clinical trials 
of early treatment using the anti-VEGF agent aflibercept versus 
sham injections in eyes with NPDR demonstrated reductions 
in vision-threatening complications such as PDR and center-
involved DME with vision loss over 2 years.462,463 However, there 
was no superiority in visual acuity outcomes in the aflibercept ver­
sus sham group in either of these studies at 2 years.
Steroid therapy, which is typically used as a second-line treat­
ment for DME in patients who are not responsive to anti-VEGF 
or are not good candidates for anti-VEGF therapy, whether deliv­
ered by the peribulbar or intravitreal route, also resulted in a 
decreased risk of worsening DR. Over 2 years, intravitreal steroid 
administration resulted in a 32% relative risk reduction for reti­
nopathy progression as compared to sham treatment.460 Although 
these results are promising, there is no treatment mandate at this 
time for eyes with NPDR because long-term visual outcomes have 
not been definitively shown to be superior after treatment with 
any of these intraocular therapeutic approaches versus medical 
care alone. 
Treatment of Diabetic Macular Edema
Untreated CSME is associated with an approximately 25% chance 
of moderate vision loss after 3 years (defined as at least doubling 
the visual angle; e.g., 20/40 reduced to 20/80).350 Macular edema 
is best evaluated clinically by dilated examination using slit-
lamp biomicroscopy or stereo fundus photography. The newer 
diagnostic ophthalmic imaging technique of optical coherence 
tomography has provided a means to objectively quantify reti­
nal thickening and is currently the objective method of choice. 
When used in conjunction with visual acuity measurement, opti­
cal coherence tomography has been used to monitor response to 
treatment and help determine timing of intervention.464,465 As 
discussed earlier, the current standard for macular edema evalu­
ation focuses on determining the presence or absence of edema 
involving the center of the macula.
Current first-line therapy for most eyes with center-involved 
DME and DME-related visual impairment of 20/32 or worse is 
intravitreous injections of VEGF inhibitors following a defined 
protocol such as that described by the DRCR Network (Fig. 
38.34).323 Typically, injections are performed monthly with a 
loading dose of at least four to six injections. On average, eight to 
nine injections are performed in the first year of treatment. The 
average number of injections required to maintain the beneficial 
visual acuity gains declines substantially to three or four in the 
second year, one or two in the third year, and zero to one in years 
4 and 5.
Results from an initial multicenter randomized controlled 
clinical trial evaluating intravitreal administration of ranibi­
zumab either with immediate laser or with deferred laser show a 
marked benefit of the anti-VEGF agent compared to laser alone. 
After 1 year, ranibizumab, as applied in the trial, resulted in a 
nine-letter mean gain (p <0.001) when combined either with 
prompt laser or deferral of laser for at least 24 weeks. This was 
more effective than prompt laser alone (three-letter gain) for the 
treatment of center-involving DME in eyes with central thicken­
ing and vision reduced to 20/32 to 20/320. The number of eyes 
gaining two or more lines of vision almost doubled in the anti-
VEGF groups as compared to laser alone. Conversely, eyes losing 
two or more lines of vision were about one-third as many in the 
anti-VEGF groups as compared to laser alone. Results were sus­
tained over 5 years despite a substantially decreased number of 
injections throughout years 2 to 5.466,467 No increased systemic 
events or serious ocular adverse events were attributed to the 
treatment other than the known small risk of endophthalmitis 
(1 per 1000 injections) associated with intravitreal injections 
themselves.
A head-to-head comparative effectiveness trial demonstrated 
overall efficacy of all three currently commercially available intra­
ocular VEGF inhibitors (aflibercept, bevacizumab, and ranibi­
zumab) in improving visual acuity and reducing retinal thickening 
in eyes with center-involved DME.323 Eyes with only mild visual 
impairment from DME and baseline vision of 20/32 to 20/40 
had similar visual acuity outcomes on average regardless of thera­
peutic group assignment. However, in eyes with baseline vision of 
20/50 or worse, aflibercept provided visual gains superior to those 
achieved with bevacizumab at 1 and 2 years, and vision outcomes 
were superior to ranibizumab at 1 but not 2 years. A subsequent 
study revealed that in these eyes with moderate or worse visual 
impairment from center-involved DME, using a step therapy 
approach of bevacizumab first, with a switch to aflibercept treat­
ment for eyes with suboptimal response, provides similar visual 
outcomes to aflibercept monotherapy.468

SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Although VEGF inhibitors are highly successful in many eyes, 
approximately 40% to 50% of eyes still have persistent DME 
or visual impairment despite chronic monthly therapy. Thus, 
there is a continued unmet need for novel therapies that address 
VEGF-independent mechanisms for DME onset, persistence, and 
worsening.
Focal laser photocoagulation may still be indicated for some 
patients with DME (see Figs. 38.26C and 38.29) without center 
involvement or in eyes with good vision or in patients who cannot 
tolerate a regimen of intravitreal injections. The ETDRS demon­
strated that focal laser photocoagulation for CSME reduced the 
5-year risk of moderate vision loss by 50%, but 15% of patients 
continue to experience vision loss.386 In focal laser photocoagula­
tion, lesions from 500 to 3000 μm from the center of the macula 
that are contributing to thickening of the macular area are gener­
ally directly photocoagulated. These lesions are identified clini­
cally or by FA and consist primarily of leaking microaneurysms. 
When leakage is diffuse or microaneurysms are extensive, photo­
coagulation may be applied to the macula in a grid configuration, 
avoiding the fovea region.
If macular laser is planned, FA can be a useful test for guiding 
the focal treatment of microaneurysms that are leaking fluid into 
the retina and identifying areas of macular capillary nonperfu­
sion that might benefit from grid laser treatment (see Fig. 38.32). 
Because there are risks associated with FA, including nausea, urti­
caria, hives, or severe medical sequelae (1 in 2000 patients) and 
rarely death (1 in 222,000 patients),469–471 FA is not otherwise 
part of the routine examination of a patient with diabetes without 
DR, and the procedure is usually contraindicated in patients with 
known allergy to fluorescein dye or during pregnancy.
Follow-up evaluation after focal laser treatment generally 
occurs after 3 months (see Fig. 38.29). In cases in which mac­
ular edema persists, further treatment may be necessary. In the 
presence of macular edema, patients with PDR or severe NPDR 
should be considered for anti-VEGF or laser treatment of macu­
lar edema whether or not the macular edema is center involved 
because they are likely to require scatter laser photocoagulation 
in the near future and because scatter photocoagulation, although 
beneficial for PDR, can exacerbate existing macular edema.
The timely evaluation and identification of patients with cen­
ter-involving DME treatment is critical for preserving vision and 
preventing visual loss. Data from the DRCR Retina Network have 
shown that patients with center-involving DME and good vision 
can confidently be managed by observation alone, with only 34% 
requiring anti-VEGF injections due to later visual deterioration. 
However, it is essential that these eyes be monitored closely with 
retinal examination that includes visual acuity measurements and 
optical coherence tomography scans to identify eyes at risk for 
visual loss that would require treatment. Over a 2-year period, an 
estimated 66% of patients with center-involving DME and good 
vision will not require anti-VEGF treatment but should undergo 
retinal examinations at least every 16 weeks.472
The ophthalmic use of corticosteroids administered either 
through the periocular or intravitreal routes for the treatment of 
DME gained widespread use because of early case reports and 
uncontrolled clinical trials documenting its rapid and often dra­
matic effect on retinal thickening. Two multicenter randomized 
prospective clinical trials were undertaken to address both the 
effectiveness and safety of both routes of steroid administration. 
In the first, peribulbar steroid injections were found to have no 
significant benefit for the treatment of DME.473 The 3-year results 
of a second multicenter randomized controlled trial comparing 
intravitreal steroids to focal laser therapy have shown that despite 
an initial rapid reduction in retinal thickness and improvement 
in vision with the intravitreal steroid injection, by 1 year, the 
results were no better than laser photocoagulation, and at 2 years 
through 3 years, steroid was inferior to the laser treatment in both 
visual outcome and retinal thickness improvement.474,475 Intra­
vitreal steroid injections were associated with an approximately 
fourfold increase in the rate of intraocular pressure complications 
and a fourfold increase in need for cataract surgery compared to 
laser treatment. The development of cataract was likely a large 
contributor to declining visual acuity in the steroid-treated group 
after the first 6 months. This hypothesis is supported by the fact 
that patients who had already undergone cataract surgery before 
initiating intravitreal steroid treatment demonstrated vision 
improvement comparable to that seen in the anti-VEGF–treated 
group.426
Intravitreous steroid therapy has also been investigated as a 
potential additive therapy to intravitreous VEGF inhibitors in 
patients who have persistent retinal thickening and visual impair­
ment despite at least six injections of anti-VEGF. Although retinal 
thickening is significantly reduced in eyes after combined steroid 
and anti-VEGF therapy compared to those receiving anti-VEGF 
treatment alone, visual acuity outcomes do not appear to be 
improved.476 Thus, currently, intravitreal steroid alone is not the 
preferred primary therapy for DME or a recommended adjuvant 
therapy in eyes that have not responded successfully to anti-VEGF 
therapy. Intraocular steroid treatment may have a role, however, 
for treatment of patients with DME who cannot receive anti-
VEGF agents or who are pseudophakic before treatment because 
steroid use substantially increases the risk of developing visually 
significant cataracts.
The pathogenesis of DME is highly complex, and a variable 
response to treatment modalities has been observed in many 
patients. Investigations of varying drug dosages to identify the 
optimal treatment concentration and development of sustained 
drug delivery devices to limit risks, costs, and inconvenience asso­
ciated with repeated intraocular injections are underway. Multiple 
potential therapeutics are also being tested in clinical trials for the 
treatment of DME, including a bispecific antibody against VEGF 
and angiotensin II, plasma kallikrein inhibition, photobiomodu­
lation therapy, and other novel approaches. 
Control of Systemic Disorders and Effect of Systemic 
Medications
In addition to the importance of intensive glycemic control in 
reducing the onset and progression of DR, as discussed earlier, it is 
critical for the optimal ocular health of patients with diabetes that 
several other systemic considerations be optimized.
Elevated blood pressure exacerbates development and progres­
sion of DR. Concomitant hypertension is common in diabetes. 
Patients with T1D have a 17% prevalence of hypertension at base­
line and a 25% incidence after 10 years.477 There is a 38% to 68% 
prevalence in T2D.478–480 In most studies, hypertension correlates 
with other retinopathy risk factors, including duration of diabetes, 
higher HbA1c level, presence of proteinuria, and male gender. The 
risk of PDR is associated with the presence of hypertension at the 
baseline visit, higher HbA1c levels, and presence of more severe 
levels of retinopathy at the initial visit.481 Patients with hyper­
tension are more likely to develop retinopathy, DME, and more 
severe levels of retinopathy482–484 and have more rapid progression 
of retinopathy when compared to patients with diabetes who do 
not have hypertension.484–486
1509
CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
The large randomized, prospective UKPDS in 1148 patients 
with T2D demonstrated a 34% (p = 0.0004) and 47% (p <0.004) 
reduction in risk of DR progression and moderate visual acuity 
loss, respectively, in patients assigned to intensive blood control.487 
Effects were independent of glycemic control, and risk reductions 
were similar regardless of whether the hypertension was controlled 
with an ACEi (captopril) or a β-blocker (atenolol). Overall, hyper­
tension appears to be a significant risk factor in the development 
and progression of DR and should be rigorously controlled. Until 
the results of specific trials investigating the blood pressure levels 
required to minimize end-organ damage in patients with diabetes 
are known,488 target blood pressure should most likely be main­
tained as low as safely possible.
Associations between renal and retinal angiopathy are numer­
ous. Both microalbuminuria and macroalbuminuria (urine 
albumin excretion rate [AER] >300 mg/d) are associated with 
retinopathy.489–492 The presence and severity of DR are indi­
cators of the risk of macroalbuminuria,493,494 and conversely, 
macroalbuminuria predicts PDR.490,495,496 Half of all patients 
with T1D with PDR and 10 or more years of diabetes have 
concomitant macroalbuminuria.489 In T1D, the prevalence of 
PDR increases from 7% at onset of microalbuminuria to 29% 
4 years after onset of albuminuria, compared to 3% and 8%, 
respectively, in patients without persistent microalbuminuria.497 
The Appropriate Blood Pressure Control in Diabetes (ABCD) 
trial found that both the severity and progression of retinopathy 
were associated with overt albuminuria.498–500 The presence of 
macroalbuminuria at baseline is associated with a 95% increased 
risk of developing macular edema among patients with T1D,481 
and dialysis can improve macular edema in patients with diabetes 
with renal failure.
Despite these associations, a causal relationship between dia­
betic kidney disease and DR has not been established. The fre­
quent coexistence of retinal and renal microangiopathies with 
factors that affect both complications, such as associated hyper­
tension and disease duration, make it difficult to establish.501 
Overall, it is important to carefully consider the renal status of 
any patient with diabetes and ensure that the patient is receiv­
ing optimal care in this regard. In addition, rapidly progressive 
retinopathy, especially in a patient with a long history of diabetes 
where retinopathy previously has been stable, should suggest the 
need for renal evaluation.
Both hematocrit and hemoglobin levels have been associated 
with the presence of DR. Low hematocrit was an independent risk 
factor in the ETDRS analysis of baseline risk factors for develop­
ment of high-risk PDR and severe vision loss.502 A cross-sectional 
study involving 1691 patients revealed a twofold increased risk of 
any retinopathy in patients with a hemoglobin level of less than 
12 g/dL compared to those with a higher hemoglobin concentra­
tion, using multivariate analyses controlling for serum creatinine, 
proteinuria, and other factors.503 In patients with retinopathy, 
those with low hemoglobin levels have a fivefold increased risk 
of severe retinopathy compared to those with higher hemoglobin 
levels. There have been limited reports of resolution of macular 
edema and hard exudate with improvement or stabilization of 
visual acuity in erythropoietin-treated patients after an increase in 
mean hematocrit.504 In view of the potential associations between 
low hematocrit, low hemoglobin, and DR, it is important to 
ensure that patients with DR and anemia are receiving appropri­
ate management.
In summary, diabetes is clearly a multisystem disease requir­
ing a comprehensive medical team approach. Even with regard to 
ocular health, this necessitates the involvement of multiple health 
care specialists for optimal patient care. 
Diabetic Nephropathy
Diabetic nephropathy is a substantial public health problem 
and remains a major cause of morbidity and death for per­
sons with either T1D or T2D. In 2021, 10% of the global 
population (about 537 million adults) was living with diabetes; 
up to 40% of these individuals will ultimately develop CKD 
with impaired kidney function or kidney damage with albu­
minuria.505 Globally, CKD remains an important, common 
complication of diabetes despite improvements in therapy, and 
diabetes is the leading cause of kidney failure. Kidney failure, 
or end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), is devastating to the indi­
vidual and has enormous financial and social consequences to 
society. Of all people treated for kidney failure in 2018, the 
proportion of individuals commencing kidney replacement 
therapy because of diabetes varied greatly in different coun­
tries, ranging from 13% of kidney failure cases in China to 
66% in Singapore.506 In the United States, incidence rates of 
kidney failure in diabetes increased by 50% between 1996 and 
2006 but have stabilized since then, and in 2018, the rate was 
∼180 per million per year.506 The incidence of kidney failure 
in T1D remained stable or declined over the past decade but 
increased in T2D.507–510 Most people with diabetes on kidney 
replacement therapy have T2D, although the rates have been 
higher in T1D compared to T2D because of the much larger 
number of persons with T2D.
Importantly, kidney disease is accompanied by an increased 
cardiovascular risk, and for every 20 patients with diabetes and 
CKD, less than 1 will survive to end-stage renal disease, suc­
cumbing instead to atherosclerotic CVD, heart failure, or infec­
tion. Management of kidney disease in diabetes, therefore, has to 
include control of cardiovascular risk factors in addition to pre­
vention of loss of kidney function. 
Definitions in Diabetic Nephropathy
Diabetic nephropathy refers to the chronic condition developing 
over many years that is characterized by gradually increasing 
urinary albumin excretion, blood pressure and cardiovascular 
risk, declining GFR, and eventual kidney failure. The clini­
cal syndrome is associated with characteristic histopathologic 
features.511 A small proportion of individuals with T1D,512,513 
and approximately 50% of those with T2D,514 with progres­
sively declining GFR have no or minimal albuminuria. This 
may reflect a more heterogenous background for CKD in 
T2D related to a higher prevalence of hypertension, dyslip­
idemia, and older age. Whereas the term diabetic nephropathy 
has classically been used for this phenotype with increasing 
albuminuria, characteristic pathologic lesions, and linkage 
to hyperglycemia, the broader term CKD in diabetes is often 
used now. CKD refers to kidney disease of any etiology lasting 
more than 3 months, including non–diabetes-related causes 
and impaired kidney function with normal urinary albumin 
excretion, as well as albuminuria (kidney damage) with normal 
kidney function. The term diabetic kidney disease is sometimes 
used and refers to both classical (albuminuric) and nonclassi­
cal (normoalbuminuric) diabetic nephropathy; unfortunately, 
there is no clear consensus on the nomenclature except for 
CKD.515

SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Screening for and Classification of Chronic 
Kidney Disease
Guidelines suggest systematic screening, as part of the annual 
clinical review, from diagnosis in T2D and at least 5 years after 
diagnosis in T1D.516 Albuminuria and GFR should be measured, 
allowing identification of proteinuric and nonproteinuric disease. 
Screening should be performed when the person is free from acute 
illness and in stable glucose control because many acute illnesses 
and acute hyperglycemia increase albuminuria temporarily.
Because albuminuria may increase in the upright posture and 
with exercise, measurements are best made in an early-morning 
urine sample where day-to-day variability is less; however, a spot 
urine sample is acceptable if there is no alternative. Both urine 
albumin and creatinine are measured, and the urinary albumin-
to-creatinine ratio (UACR) is calculated. Because of the high day-
to-day variation in the UACR (up to 30%), if the first sample is 
positive, additional samples should be obtained, ideally within 3 
months. At least two out of three measurements should be abnor­
mal before a diagnosis of elevated albuminuria is made.
Serum creatinine should be measured annually using an 
accredited assay standardized to the recommended isotope dilu­
tion mass spectrometry reference method. Many laboratories cal­
culate the estimated GFR (eGFR) using the CKD-EPI equation 
using serum creatinine, age, sex, and ethnicity, which estimates 
measured GFR more accurately than previous equations, par­
ticularly at higher levels of GFR.517 The CKD-EPI equation also 
categorizes risk of mortality and kidney failure more accurately 
than the previous Modification of Diet in Renal Disease Study 
(MDRD) equation in a wide range of populations, including 
those with diabetes.518,519 Recently, the CKD-EPI equation was 
updated in order to exclude ethnicity, and this new equation 
has been recommended particularly in the United States.520 
The most precise eGFR equation includes serum cystatin C in 
addition to creatinine and is recommended when precision is 
important.520 The 2020 Kidney Disease Improving Global Out­
comes (KDIGO) Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation 
and Management of CKD advocates that screening status should 
indicate both the GFR and albuminuria status (Tables 38.6 and 
38.7).521 The term moderately increased albuminuria has replaced 
microalbuminuria, and severely increased albuminuria replaced 
macroalbuminuria. The information can then be used as a mea­
sure of risk of progression to kidney failure, and this classifier is 
also a good indicator of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality 
(Fig. 38.35).515,522
The importance of regular screening begun shortly after dia­
betes diagnosis in order to be able to initiate therapy as early as 
possible was recently reinforced.523
KDIGO guidelines previously recommended calculating cys­
tatin-based eGFR in adults whose creatinine-based eGFR is 45 to 
59 mL/min/1.73 m2 without other markers of kidney disease.515 
Use of cystatin C has gained more interest and is now more widely 
recommended with the ethnicity-free equation, but it is gener­
ally more expensive than creatinine. Cystatin C is not affected by 
change in muscle mass, but whether its use is a superior predic­
tor of cardiovascular events has not been firmly established. If 
more precision on GFR is requested, an exogenous tracer such 
as iothalamate, inulin, or110 Tc-diethylenetriamine pentaacetate 
should be used for the assessment. In relation to imaging with 
computed tomography (CT), caution should generally be taken 
in persons with impaired kidney function when intravenous con­
trast media are used because they may cause contrast nephropathy, 
and iodine-based contrast media should be avoided if possible or 
patients should be well hydrated. For magnetic resonance imaging 
(MRI), caution in selecting agents with the lowest risk for neph­
rogenic systemic fibrosis should be selected.524 
Diagnosis of Diabetic Nephropathy
CKD is diagnosed when two eGFR measurements, at least 3 
months apart, are below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 and/or 2 out of 
3 albuminuria measurements are abnormal (UACR ≥30 mg/g 
creatinine). Diagnosis should be made in the absence of an acute 
serious illness.525 Persistent albuminuria (above 300 mg/24 hour 
in a 24-hour collection or UACR above 300 mg/g creatinine) is 
the hallmark of diabetic nephropathy, which can be diagnosed 
clinically if the following additional criteria are fulfilled: pres­
ence of DR and absence of clinical or laboratory evidence of 
other kidney or renal tract disease. This clinical definition of dia­
betic nephropathy is valid in both T1D and T2D.526 Previously, 
urinary albumin measures between 30 and 300 mg/g creatinine 
were considered microalbuminuria, and concentrations above 
300 mg/g creatinine were considered macroalbuminuria; these 
terms have been replaced with moderate albuminuria and severe 
albuminuria, respectively. 
Monitoring Kidney Disease
Once urinary albumin excretion is severely increased, the 
UACR should be measured every 3 months and the eGFR 
every 3 to 6 months, depending on the CKD stage and rate of 
progression of the disease. The rate of decline in eGFR varies 
between patients, partly depending on risk factor management 
and intervention, and often the slope is fairly linear. Episodes 
of intercurrent illness may lead to AKI as a complication of the 
CKD and make it difficult to predict the future course of the 
disease. 
Excluding Nondiabetes Chronic Kidney Disease
Excluding other causes of kidney disease is especially important 
among patients who do not follow the usual course of diabetic 
nephropathy disease progression. Diabetic nephropathy is usu­
ally a slowly evolving condition; thus, if acute decline in GFR is 
present (>10 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year), other causes should be

extremely low among patients with T1D without CKD530,531 and 
in Pima Indians with T2D.532 
Natural History and Histopathology
Classical Diabetic Nephropathy
Gradually increasing urinary albumin excretion over many 
years is the hallmark of classical diabetic nephropathy (Fig. 
38.36). At presentation of T1D, increased albuminuria may 
be present. As glycemia is controlled, albuminuria returns to 
normal. In those who will never develop nephropathy, urinary 
albumin excretion remains normal, except during periods of 
particularly poor glucose control or during acute intercurrent 
illness, when a transient increase in urinary albumin excretion 
may occur. In those who will develop diabetic nephropathy, 
urinary albumin excretion increases gradually, with moderately 
elevated albuminuria (microalbuminuria) usually appearing 
within 5 to 15 years of diabetes. Untreated, the mean increase 
in urinary albumin excretion is 20% per year. In people with 
T1D, approximately 1.5% to 2.5% per annum develop mod­
erately elevated albuminuria,533,534 and 50% develop persistent 
moderately elevated albuminuria (microalbuminuria) at some

point.535,536 Approximately one-third with moderately elevated 
albuminuria progress gradually over a further 5 to 15 years to 
severely increased albuminuria (macroalbuminuria), one-third 
will remain at moderately elevated albuminuria, and one-third 
will revert to normoalbuminuria.537,538 In the short term, 
reversion from moderately elevated albuminuria to normoal­
buminuria appears common, with one study reporting regres­
sion in 58% of participants over 6 years.539 Short-duration 
moderately elevated albuminuria and lower HbA1c, systolic 
blood pressure, total cholesterol, and TGs were all indepen­
dently associated with regression. In other studies, regression 
was rarely spontaneous and usually treatment induced.540 The 
development of kidney failure without albuminuria was rare 
in a large population-based study in persons with T1D.541 The 
eventual outcome in those who regress, or who do not initially 
progress, remains unclear. However, they probably remain at 
increased risk of nephropathy compared to individuals who 
have never had elevated albuminuria.
Most people with T1D and severely increased albuminuria 
eventually progress to kidney failure. The use of eGFR rather than 
serum creatinine has unmasked a decline in eGFR within the nor­
mal range of creatinine in individuals with moderately increased 
albuminuria (microalbuminuria), but eGFR below 60 mL/
min/1.73 m2 is rare at this stage. However, in severely increased 
albuminuria (macroalbuminuria), the mean annual rate of decline 
of GFR is 10 to 12 mL/min/1.73 m2 untreated.542
In addition to this classical trajectory, in some with T1D, the 
GFR falls before the onset of albuminuria.513 Using serial esti­
mates of eGFR derived from serum creatinine and cystatin C, a 
median annual decline in eGFR of 1.5% per year was reported 
in individuals with normoalbuminuria and 2.2% in those with 
moderately increased albuminuria. The authors argued that 
albuminuria is therefore not a universally good guide to diabetic 
nephropathy.543 Alternative explanations are suppression of albu­
minuria by the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors or that 
kidney disease with and without albuminuria are different patho­
logic processes, as discussed later. In addition, a subset of individ­
uals with T1D will have a very fast, almost malignant decline in 
kidney function and should be identified with novel biomarkers. 
Although many have been suggested, including tumor necrosis 
factor receptor 1+2,544 no biomarkers are recommended in cur­
rent guidelines.545
The natural history of diabetic nephropathy is generally simi­
lar in T2D. Moderately or severely increased albuminuria may be 
present at diagnosis and may persist in individuals who have had 
undiagnosed diabetes for some years. GFR is usually above 60 
mL/min/1.73 m2 at the onset of moderately elevated albuminuria, 
only declining to CKD stage 3 or more when severely increased 
albuminuria develops.546,547 
Structural Kidney Lesions in Diabetic 
Nephropathy
In patients with T1D, glomerular lesions can be demonstrated 
after diabetes has been present for a few years, whereas in T2D, 
they can be present at diagnosis, probably reflecting delayed diag­
nosis, often occurring years after onset of disease. The changes in 
kidney structure caused by diabetes are specific, creating a pattern 
not seen in any other kidney disease. The severity of these diabetic 
lesions correlates with functional abnormalities (decreased GFR 
and albuminuria)530,548,549 and is also related to diabetes dura­
tion, glycemic control, and genetic factors. These later relation­
ships are not precise and are in line with the marked variability in 
diabetic nephropathy susceptibility among patients with diabetes 
(see “Relationships Between Kidney Structure and Function” sec­
tion later in the chapter).
Light Microscopy of the Diabetic Kidney
Renal hypertrophy, the earliest renal structural change in T1D, 
is not reflected in any specific light microscopy findings. In some 
patients, glomerular structure may remain normal or near nor­
mal for many decades, whereas others develop progressive disease. 
Early changes often include arteriolar hyalinosis, thickening of the 
glomerular basement membrane (GBM), and diffuse mesangial 
expansion.530,548,549 In about 40% to 50% of patients develop­
ing proteinuria, areas of extreme mesangial expansion called 
Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules or nodular mesangial expansion can 
be observed. Although Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are diag­
nostic of diabetic nephropathy, they are not necessary for severe 
renal dysfunction to develop. Global glomerulosclerosis can also 
be observed, especially with progressive disease (Fig. 38.37). Atu­
bular glomeruli and glomerulotubular junction abnormalities can 
also be present in proteinuric patients with T1D.550,551 Tubular 
atrophy and interstitial fibrosis, common to most chronic renal 
disorders, can be present at later stages. 
Electron Microscopy of the Diabetic Kidney
Using morphometric techniques, the first measurable diabetic 
nephropathy change is thickening of the GBM, which can be 
detected as early as 1 to 2 years after onset of T1D.549,552–555 
Tubular basement membrane thickening can also be detected, 
and it parallels GBM thickening.556 An increase in the rela­
tive area of the mesangium becomes measurable by 4 to 5 
years.530,549,553 Immunohistochemical studies indicate that these 
changes in mesangium, GBM, and tubular basement membrane 
represent expansion of the intrinsic extracellular matrix compo­
nents at these sites, likely including types IV and VI collagen, 
laminin, and fibronectin. Foot processes (podocyte) changes can 
be observed by electron microscopy, and the severity of these 
abnormalities has been associated with kidney function.557,558 
Changes in fenestrated endothelium have also been described 
in diabetes.558 Interstitial expansion is common to many kidney 
diseases. Early on in diabetes, interstitial expansion is associated 
with cellular alterations, whereas later in the disease process, 
when GFR is already reduced, there is increased fibrillar collagen 
in the interstitium.559

Although about 30% of patients with T2D and microalbumin­
uria who have had a kidney biopsy performed for research rather 
than clinical reasons had the classical diabetic nephropathy lesions 
described earlier, 41% had disproportionally severe interstitial 
fibrosis and tubular atrophy, and the remaining 29% had minimal 
lesions with normal or near normal glomerular structure.560 The 
presence of retinopathy supports that the underlying lesion is dia­
betic nephropathy.561 
Relationship Between Kidney Structure and 
Function
In T1D, the associations between kidney structure and function 
are strong.548,562,563 Mesangial fractional volume and GBM 
width are inversely correlated with GFR and directly correlated 
with albuminuria548,563 and blood pressure.563,564 Importantly, 
GBM width is a strong independent predictor of progression to 
clinically advanced kidney disease among normoalbuminuric 
patients with T1D.565 Among these patients, global glomeru­
lar sclerosis565,566 and interstitial expansion565,567 are present 
and are additional independent predictors of GFR loss.565 
Although increases in podocyte foot process width also cor­
relate with albuminuria increases in T1D,568–570 our studies in 
patients with T1D who had no clinical manifestations of CKD 
at time of their research kidney biopsies indicate that podocyte 
parameters do not predict long-term progression to clinical 
CKD.571 In T2D, the correlation between glomerular struc­
ture and renal function is less strong, which may be related 
to the more complex patterns of renal injury seen in patients 
with T2D.565 These considerations are relevant to prognosis, 
in that the patients with more typical diabetic glomerulopathy 
morphometric findings of mesangial expansion on electron 
microscopy were more likely to have progressive loss of GFR 
over the next years of follow-up.562,567 The novel Kidney Pre­
cision Medicine Project in the United States will go beyond 
the use of biopsies as a tool to study histology—the project 
aims to obtain kidney biopsies from participants with CKD or 
AKI, create a reference kidney atlas, and characterize disease 
subgroups to stratify patients based on molecular features of 
disease, clinical characteristics, and associated outcomes. An 
additional aim is to identify critical cells, pathways, and targets 
for novel therapies and preventive strategies.572 
Nonclassical Diabetic Kidney Disease
Some 7% to 22% of individuals with T1D573,574 and 50% of 
those with T2D514,575,576 who develop progressive CKD do not 
have preceding albuminuria. Identification of people with non­
diabetic kidney changes on the basis of clinical features, including 
the absence of DR,577 is difficult. Individuals with T2D and CKD 
stage 3 or more plus moderately or severely increased albuminuria 
are very likely to have histologic features of diabetic glomeruloscle­
rosis, whereas those with normoalbuminuria are much more likely 
to have arteriosclerosis.578 The underlying disease process in non­
classical diabetic CKD probably reflects a combination of aging, 
hypertension, and atherosclerotic vascular disease in addition to 
diabetes. Obesity, with ectopic lipid accumulation in the kidney, 
may also be important579 and may be a target for intervention.580
The rate of progression of CKD in the absence of significant 
albuminuria is slower than in those with albuminuria in both 
T1D513 and T2D, but kidney failure remains a risk, in addition to 
the CVD risk.581,582

Epidemiology of Diabetic Nephropathy
Diabetic nephropathy is characterized by a gradual increase in uri­
nary albumin excretion, blood pressure levels, and impaired GFR. 
As mentioned, approximately 25% to 50% of individuals with 
T1D573,583 and 45% to 57% of those with T2D514,575,576,584,585 
have progressively declining GFR with no or minimal albumin­
uria. Nonalbuminuric renal impairment is the predominant phe­
notype among youth with T1D and short duration586 and also 
among patients with T2D,587 and it is a strong predictor of mor­
tality.588 Comparing nonalbuminuric to albuminuric patients 
with T1D, those with nonalbuminuric CKD are generally older 
at evaluation and at T1D onset589; are more often female583,589; 
have lower HbA1c, total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein 
cholesterol (LDL-c), TG levels, and serum uric acid levels; have 
higher eGFR; are less often hypertensive; and are less likely to 
have retinopathy or to smoke583,589 than patients with albumin­
uric CKD.587,588,590,591 HbA1c and blood pressure levels are higher 
and HDL-cholesterol levels are lower among nonalbuminuric 
youth with T1D and CKD than in nonalbuminuric youth with 
CKD who do not have T1D.586 T2D patients with nonalbumin­
uric CKD are also generally older and more often are nonsmokers, 
are White or Asian, have shorter diabetes duration584; have lower 
HbA1c, total cholesterol, LDL-c, TGs, and systolic blood pressure 
levels; have higher eGFR, and less often have retinopathy or a 
history of CVD576,584,585,592 compared to patients with T2D with 
albuminuric CKD.
Diabetic Nephropathy in Type 1 Diabetes
Data suggest that in T1D, moderately and severely increased albu­
minuria and kidney failure may be less common than previously, 
at least in some countries, probably reflecting better care and 
improved risk factors such as less smoking.593,594
Older studies suggested a lifetime risk of developing moder­
ately elevated albuminuria of about 50%, generally appearing 
between 10 and 20 years’ duration of T1D. In the DCCT/EDIC 
cohort, the cumulative incidence of persistent moderately elevated 
albuminuria (microalbuminuria) was 38% after 30 years in the 
conventional group and 25% in the intensive group.595 The inci­
dence appeared to plateau in both groups after 25 to 30 years. 
Moderately increased albuminuria developed most frequently in 
the second decade of diabetes in the conventional group, with the 
incidence being blunted particularly during this time in the inten­
sive group.
Older data suggest that the cumulative incidence of severely 
increased albuminuria is about 40% after 40 years’ duration of 
T1D. In the DCCT, 25% of the conventional group and 9% of 
the intensively managed group had severely increased albumin­
uria after 30 years’ T1D duration.596 Several Scandinavian studies 
also reported rates as low as 13% after 20 to 25 years’ T1D dura­
tion.597,598 In contrast, in the Pittsburgh cohort, the incidence has 
remained relatively steady at 32% after 25 years.599
Several European countries report a current prevalence of kid­
ney failure in T1D of 2.5% to 7.8% after 30 years of diabetes.600,601 
The Pittsburgh Epidemiology of Diabetes Complications Study602 
and the Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopa­
thy (WESDR) cohort603 suggested a declining incidence in those 
diagnosed after 1970. Survival with kidney failure may also have 
improved.
In the United Kingdom, in the Golden Years cohort of individ­
uals with a duration of T1D above 50 years, 36% had moderately 
or severely increased albuminuria.604 In a similar cohort in the 
United States, the prevalence of albuminuria, defined using a 
higher cutoff than in the UK cohort, was 13.1%.605 Thus, the 
observed decline in incidence of nephropathy may represent delay 
rather than true prevention. 
Diabetic Nephropathy in Type 2 Diabetes
A widely varying prevalence of moderately elevated albumin­
uria, from 10% to 42%, has been reported. Longitudinal 
studies suggested the rate of progression from normo- to mod­
erately elevated albuminuria grade is 3% to 4% per annum. 
One older study demonstrated an equivalent cumulative inci­
dence of severely increased albuminuria in T1D and T2D with 
25 years’ duration of diabetes.606 In Pima Indians, the inci­
dence of kidney failure has declined since 1990.607 National 
U.S. survey data reported a prevalence of CKD (eGFR <60 
mL/min/1.73 m2 or urinary albumin excretion >30 mg/g) of 
43.5% in the overall T2D population and 61.0% in those age 
≥65 years.608 In the United Kingdom, using a similar defini­
tion, the prevalence was remarkably similar at 42.3%.609 The 
increasing number of individuals with diabetes commenc­
ing kidney replacement therapy in many countries is mainly 
attributable to persons with T2D506 and is accounted for in 
part by an increased acceptance of older, sicker individuals and 
improved cardiovascular survival.
CKD in people with diabetes can be the result of diabetic 
nephropathy, other associated conditions, such as hypertensive 
renal disease and obesity-related glomerulopathy, or other renal 
diseases, such as IgA nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulo­
sclerosis, and acute tubular necrosis, membranous nephropa­
thy, among others.517–519 The frequency of other renal diseases 
depends on the prevalence of these conditions in the background 
population (see “Excluding Other Causes of Kidney Disease” later 
in the chapter). 
Risk Factors and Markers for Chronic Kidney 
Disease in Diabetes
Many factors are associated with CKD in diabetes. Associations 
may be with both albuminuria and GFR or with one measure­
ment only. Factors that influence the initial development of kid­
ney disease may not be the same as factors influencing progression. 
Putative progression promotors are seen in Fig. 38.38.
Glucose in Diabetic Nephropathy
Dysregulated glucose is an important risk factor for the devel­
opment and progression of diabetic nephropathy. The mecha­
nisms relating poor glycemic control to the development of 
complications were outlined earlier in this chapter. Data from 
multiple observational and intervention studies in both T1D 
and T2D support the importance of glycemia.610 There is a 
strong positive association between HbA1c and incident CKD 
(eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2), independent of other risk fac­
tors and present even in the absence of albuminuria.611 Not 
only mean values but also greater variability in HbA1c are inde­
pendently associated with albuminuria and diabetic nephropa­
thy,612–614 and variability in blood glucose levels as detected by 
continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has also been associ­
ated with complications. 
1515
CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
Blood Pressure in Diabetic Nephropathy
Elevated blood pressure is critical in the development and progres­
sion of diabetic nephropathy. Compared to the general popula­
tion, the excess prevalence of hypertension in T1D is confined to 
those with nephropathy.615 In T2D, the link between hyperten­
sion and kidney disease is less striking, perhaps because hyperten­
sion is very common among these patients, present in 70% to 
80% of the patients with T2D at the time of diagnosis. In young 
people with moderately elevated albuminuria, changes in blood 
pressure are subtle, perhaps manifesting only as reduced noctur­
nal diastolic blood pressure dipping.616 The nondipping type is 
associated with mortality and progression of CKD in both T1D 
and T2D.617,618 Once severely increased albuminuria is present, 
overt hypertension is present in 80% of patients and is almost 
universal in later stages of CKD (stage 4 and above). In addition 
to the mean blood pressure, variability in systolic and diastolic 
blood pressure independently predicts progression of CKD.612,619 
Hyperfiltration in Diabetic Nephropathy
Hyperfiltration is common at onset of T1D, particularly with 
elevated glucose levels, and it is also present in some individu­
als at T2D diagnosis. Kidney function usually returns to normal 
values as glucose is controlled but may remain elevated in some 
individuals. Whether individuals with persistent hyperfiltration 
are at increased risk for later development of diabetic nephropa­
thy risk remains controversial.620–623 SGLT2is were introduced to 
lower glucose in T2D, but in addition, they were found to reduce 
the progression of kidney disease with or without diabetes (see 
later discussion), although the mechanisms behind this are still 
debated. Whereas there was no effect on normal kidney function, 
a marked effect was seen on hyperfiltration in T1D with SGLT2i, 
and it was suggested to reflect lowering of intraglomerular hyper­
tension and to support lowering of hyperfiltration as an important 
kidney-protective measure.624 More recently, results in T2D were 
less clear.625 
Kidney Function and Kidney Damage
Albuminuria and kidney function (eGFR) independently influ­
ence the development and rate of progression of CKD.626,627 The 
level of baseline albuminuria is a strong predictor of kidney fail­
ure.628 Higher levels of albuminuria, even within the normoalbu­
minuric range (10–30 mg/g),629,630 and lower eGFR631 predict 
a faster decline in eGFR. Conversely, a short-term reduction in 
albuminuria with intervention in randomized controlled studies 
or in observational studies is associated with reduced progression 
of kidney and cardiovascular complications.632–634 The reductions 
in albuminuria usually reflect hemodynamic changes with reduced 
intraglomerular pressure but could alternatively reflect metabolic, 
antiinflammatory, or antifibrotic effects or a combination thereof. 
The hemodynamic changes have been most important for cur­
rently approved agents (see later discussion). A 30% reduction in 
UACR has been identified as a treatment target in the American 
Diabetes Association Standards of Care.516 
Other Metabolic Factors in Diabetic 
Nephropathy
Blood lipids, including cholesterol and TGs,604,635 are associated 
with the development and progression of nephropathy, although 
the lipid phenotype alters as nephropathy progresses.636–638 
Obesity has also been linked to CKD in general and to diabetic 
kidney disease more specifically.639 Obesity is potentially linked 
to CKD through intrarenal lipid accumulation, which may be 
important for the progression of nephropathy in humans similar 
to that seen in diabetic and nondiabetic experimental models of 
CKD.580,640,641 In these models, a defective cholesterol metabo­
lism primarily linked to reduced ATP-binding cassette transporter 
A1 (ABCA1) expression is closely associated with the pathogen­
esis and progression of CKD, including diabetic kidney disease 
and Alport syndrome.642 Whether this contributes to the progres­
sion of kidney disease and could be a target for intervention in 
humans, as in animal models, is under investigation (EUDRACT 
2020-001155-40).
Although insulin resistance is typically a feature associated with 
T2D, it is also seen in T1D, particularly as obesity is becoming 
more prevalent in general. As in T2D, it has been identified as a 
risk factor for CKD in T1D and a potential target for reducing 
the progression of albuminuria.643–645 Insulin resistance increases 
the risk of albuminuria and rapid eGFR decline in patients with 
T1D646 and of albuminuria in those with T2D.647 Individuals 
with T1D or T2D and CKD are more likely to have the meta­
bolic syndrome.648,649 Uric acid predicts the development of 
severely increased albuminuria650 and a decline in GFR, as well 
as cardiovascular events.651 Despite this association, which was 
demonstrated in many cohorts, it may not be causal because a 
reduction in uric acid by treatment with allopurinol could not 
slow GFR decline in patients with T1D.590 A more aggressive uric 
acid–lowering intervention in T2D showed a reduction in albu­
minuria.652 In addition to the metabolic factors discussed earlier, 
current smoking predicts development of albuminuria. 
Genetic Factors in Diabetic Nephropathy
Genetic factors influence susceptibility to diabetic nephropathy. 
Although recent GWASs have found several significant genetic 
associations, they are of limited impact on an individual level.653–656 
Early studies demonstrated that if one sibling with T1D had 
nephropathy, the risk for the second sibling was increased four- to 
eightfold compared to siblings where neither have nephropathy, 
suggesting strong inheritance.657 The clustering of conventional 
cardiovascular risk factors and CVD in people with diabetic
