the genetic susceptibility to nephropathy also influences the asso­
ciated CVD. Research kidney biopsies in siblings with T1D also 
demonstrated heritability in the severity and patterns of renal 
lesions.660 Sodium-hydrogen antiport activity661 and mRNA 
expression of catalase, an antioxidant enzyme associated with dia­
betic nephropathy risk,662 were also found to be, at least in part, 
genetically regulated in siblings concordant for T1D. It is likely 
that multiple genes are associated with diabetic nephropathy, and 
they can be either protective or deleterious. Moreover, different 
loci may influence albuminuria and GFR.663 Epigenetic modifica­
tions discussed in detail in the first section of this chapter show 
that heritability analysis of DNA methylation variation explains a 
larger fraction of heritability of diabetic kidney disease than does 
gene expression.664,665 
Ethnicity in Diabetic Nephropathy
In the United States, the prevalence of early CKD (defined as 
moderately elevated albuminuria or greater and eGFR <60 mL/
min/1.73 m2) is higher in Latino and Black individuals than White 
people.666 A similar pattern is seen in Europe, where United King­
dom Afro-Caribbean and South Asian individuals more often 
have albuminuria and advanced CKD (stages 4–5) than White 
European individuals.667,668 Albuminuria and CKD are also more 
common in Pima Indians669 and in Māoris and Pacific Island­
ers670,671 than White Europeans. Of the 15 countries or regions 
globally with the highest incidence of treated kidney failure in 
2018, 7 were in Asia (Taiwan, Thailand, Singapore, South Korea, 
Japan, Malaysia, Indonesia). Perhaps more ominously, of the 10 
countries or regions with the highest percentage increase in the 
incidence of treated end-stage renal disease between 2009 to 2010 
and 2017 to 2018, 7 were in Asia (Bangladesh, Thailand, South 
Korea, Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, and Saudi Arabia), driven 
by an increase in prevalence of diabetes. The findings suggest that 
as countries around the world continue to develop economically 
and improve access to health care, the incidence and prevalence of 
treated kidney failure are poised to grow substantially.506 Reasons 
for this varying prevalence of kidney complications may, in addi­
tion, include differing genetic influences on disease progression, a 
tendency to higher visceral adiposity at a given body mass index 
(BMI) in South Asians, and/or altered response to or poorer access 
to treatments for diabetes. 
Type 2 Diabetes in Youth and Diabetic Kidney 
Disease
Individuals who develop T2D in youth have a high prevalence 
of hypertension and moderately elevated albuminuria.672 Kidney 
failure and death are particularly common in young people from 
ethnic minorities.673–675 However, in some of these populations, 
there is a high prevalence of nondiabetic kidney disease.676 With 
increasing obesity in youth and early onset of T2D, there is con­
cern that CKD in young individuals with T2D may be a particu­
lar issue in the future. 
Other Risk Markers for Diabetic Nephropathy
Risk factors or markers for nephropathy include preeclampsia,677 
inflammatory markers (soluble urokinase plasminogen activator 
receptor, tumor necrosis factor receptor 1+2, interleukin recep­
tor α subunit [IL15RA]; IL17F),678,679 cytokines (IL1, IL6, IL16, 
and IL18) and growth factors (transforming growth factor 1β, 
CTGF),680,681 periodontitis,682 and serum bilirubin levels (inves­
tigated as a potent antioxidant but also inversely associated with 
nonalcoholic fatty liver disease).683,684 Obstructive sleep apnea685 
and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease are both independently associ­
ated with diabetic nephropathy.686,687 Circulating levels of TNF­α 
receptor 1 are independently associated with the cumulative risk 
of kidney failure in T1D and T2D.688–690
The use of “omics” is increasing in research areas looking to 
identify biomarkers or early preclinical signs of disease or to 
increase understanding of complex pathologic processes that 
determine prognosis of the disease. Diabetic nephropathy is no 
exception, and multiomics data are needed for further improve­
ment of mechanistic understanding, prognosis prediction, and 
treatment optimization.691 In addition, the current concept 
of precision medicine uses molecular profiling, such as pro­
teomics,678,692 lipidomics,638 metabolomics,693,694 and epigenom­
ics, in addition to transcriptomics and genetics, to identify drug 
targets that can help individualize therapy. Increasing numbers 
of cohort studies using these techniques are published, but only 
a few have been validated in external cohorts or even replicated 
by other groups. Prospective validation is needed for such results 
to have clinical impact. This was done using urinary proteomics 
and CKD 273, a urinary proteomics–based classifier including 
273 peptides, which was developed to detect CKD irrespective 
of the underlying etiology in the Proteomic Prediction and Renin 
Angiotensin Aldosterone System Inhibition Prevention of Early 
Diabetic Nephropathy in Type 2 Diabetic Participants With 
Normoalbuminuria (PRIORITY) study.692 Such techniques are 
promising, but much more information must be acquired and 
then validated in clinical trials. 
Comorbidities and Associated Complications
The prognosis for people with diabetes and CKD is worse than 
that for those without CKD. Both albuminuria and eGFR <60 
mL/min/1.73 m2 (Fig. 38.39) contribute independently and syn­
ergistically to the increased risk for all-cause and cardiovascular 
mortality.582,695–698
Association of Diabetic Kidney Disease With 
Cardiovascular Disease In Type 1 Diabetes
In T1D, the relative risk of premature mortality is 2- to 3-fold 
higher in patients with moderately elevated albuminuria, 9-fold 
higher in severely increased albuminuria, and 18-fold higher 
in kidney failure compared to the nondiabetic population.699 
Individuals with T1D and normoalbuminuria did not have a 
higher risk of premature death in some studies.699,700 How­
ever, more recent and complete studies suggest that there is an 
increased risk for CVD events even in normoalbuminuria with 
normal kidney function. Standardized incidence rates are 3.5 
for coronary artery disease and 1.6 for stroke compared to the 
background population.701 CVD is 1.2-fold more common in 
T1D with moderately increased albuminuria.702 In a study fol­
lowing 5148 persons with T1D, there was an adjusted 10-fold-
higher risk for any CVD in those with severely increased 
albuminuria (event rate by the age of 40 years: 43%) compared 
to those with T1D and normoalbuminuria (7%).703 In kidney 
failure, the risk of CVD is even higher, and the median sur­
vival on kidney replacement therapy is 3.8 years.704 Different 
risk engines have been proposed to describe the risk, and a few 
include CKD.705 
1517
CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
In Type 2 Diabetes
In T2D, CVD risk is increased with risk factors such as hyper­
glycemia, smoking, elevated blood pressure and lipids, and 
albuminuria.706 For kidney damage, the risk increases two- to 
fourfold with moderately increased albuminuria707 and ninefold 
in severely increased albuminuria.708 Once serum creatinine is 
outside the normal range, cardiovascular risk increases exponen­
tially.709 Risk factors for CVD (hypertension, dyslipidemia, obe­
sity, and smoking) tend to cluster in people with diabetes and 
CKD, and the more risk factors, the higher the CVD risk.710 
Median survival from initiation of kidney replacement therapy 
is 2.2 years.704 
Microvascular Complications
Patients with diabetic nephropathy often have other microvascu­
lar complications. Significant retinopathy is almost always pres­
ent in people with T1D and moderately elevated albuminuria. 
Progression of retinopathy and development of nephropathy each 
increase the risk for the other, supporting the notion of a common 
etiology.711 In people with T2D, the relationship is less strong.712 
Those with classical nephropathy and progressively increasing 
albuminuria usually have significant retinopathy, and indeed, 
moderately elevated albuminuria predicts the development and 
progression of retinopathy in T2D.713–715 In those with nonclassi­
cal disease, retinopathy may be absent.
Peripheral neuropathy is also more common in diabetic 
nephropathy and associated with both albuminuria and declining 
GFR.715 Autonomic neuropathy, diagnosed by loss of nocturnal 
blood pressure dipping, occurs frequently716,717 and predicts kid­
ney function decline.718 
Prevention and Management of Diabetic 
Nephropathy
Prevention of diabetic nephropathy is particularly obtained by 
achievement and maintenance of good blood glucose and blood 
pressure control.719 Although multiple strategies are now available 
to slow diabetic nephropathy progression, prevention of kidney 
disease remains crucial. Glycemic management early after diabe­
tes diagnosis and early risk factor intervention are more likely to 
prevent or delay kidney failure. Health economic analysis also sug­
gests that implementation of new organ-protective interventions 
with, for example, SGLT2is, is cost saving because preventing or 
delaying dialysis is a major cost driver.720,721
To evaluate the current evidence and support implementa­
tion of the many recent positive developments in management, a 
guideline on management of diabetes in CKD from KDIGO was 
developed and emphasizes management of lifestyle factors (diet, 
exercise, and smoking cessation) and cardiorenal risk factors, such

Glucose Control
Glucose Control in Type 1 Diabetes
Among the participants in the DCCT who initially had normo­
albuminuria, the intensively treated glycemia group had a relative 
risk reduction of 39% for developing moderately elevated albumin­
uria and a relative risk reduction of 54% for developing severely 
increased albuminuria (macroalbuminuria) compared to those in 
the conventionally managed group over the 6.5-year study.723 Mean 
achieved HbA1c was 7.0% and 9.1%, respectively. There was no 
HbA1c threshold below which risk was not reduced.724
In the open follow-up of the DCCT cohort, the EDIC study, 
HbA1c in the previously intensive and conventional treatment 
groups became similar, at about 8.0%. Despite this, the incidence 
of moderately and severely increased albuminuria grades,725 eGFR 
<60 mL/min/1.73 m2, and kidney failure725 were significantly 
reduced in those who had previously received intensive manage­
ment, as summarized in Table 38.8. These results are supported by 
an observational study of individuals with T1D and CKD stages 1 
to 3 with severely increased albuminuria at baseline.726 The cumu­
lative risk of kidney failure after 15 years was significantly lower 
in those whose HbA1c improved compared to those whose HbA1c 
remained stable or deteriorated. Hence, improving glucose con­
trol significantly reduces the risk of development and progression 
of all stages of diabetic nephropathy in T1D. The beneficial effects 
extend far beyond the actual period of good glucose control, a 
phenomenon termed metabolic memory, as previously discussed. 
The reversibility of diabetic nephropathy remains controversial. 
In the advanced diabetic nephropathy modeled by the leptin-
deficient BTBR ob/ob mouse, replacing leptin reversed both 
structural (mesangial matrix expansion, mesangiolysis, basement 
membrane thickening, podocyte loss) and functional (proteinuria, 
accumulation of ROS) effects.727 It has been suggested that not 
only mean glycemic level, as reflected by HbA1c, but also time in 
the target glycemic range are important for the development of 
renal complications.728 There is limited information on this so far, 
although the increased use of CGM will provide opportunities to 
investigate this in more detail. Insulin pump therapy was associ­
ated with less variability compared to multiple daily insulin injec­
tions in a small study, and the reduced variability and improved 
glucose time in range contributed to a decline in albuminuria in 
participants with T1D and increased albuminuria, beyond the 
change in HbA1c. After 1 year, the mean change in UACR was 
13% with sensor-augmented pump therapy versus a mean change 
in the control group of 30% (adjusted for HbA1c, p = 0.04).729,730

Glucose Control in Type 2 Diabetes
In the UKPDS, improved glucose control also affected progression 
of kidney disease. The mean achieved HbA1c in the intensively man­
aged group was 7.0% compared to 7.9% in the less strictly managed 
group, which translated to a 30% reduction in the relative risk of 
developing moderately or severely increased albuminuria after 9 to 12 
years.731 Again, no threshold of HbA1c and risk was observed, suggest­
ing that the lower the HbA1c, the lower the risk of nephropathy.732 
In the open follow-up of the UKPDS cohort, HbA1c was similar in 
the previously intensively and conventionally managed groups after 1 
year.733 Despite this, microvascular risk in T2D remained lower, con­
firming the “metabolic memory” as seen in the DCCT/EDIC study 
in T1D. In the Action in Diabetes and Vascular Disease: Preterax and 
Diamicron Modified Release Controlled Evaluation (ADVANCE) 
study, the HbA1c achieved in the intensively managed group was 
6.5%, compared to 7.3% in the standard-care group.734 In the inten­
sive group, there was a 9% relative risk reduction in new-onset mod­
erately elevated albuminuria, a 30% reduction in the development 
of severely increased albuminuria, and a 65% reduction in kidney 
failure over 5 years.735 Also, the Action to Control Cardiovascular 
Risk in Diabetes (ACCORD) study demonstrated significant reduc­
tions in new-onset moderately and severely increased albuminuria 
and kidney failure with intensive glucose management.736 Progres­
sion of albuminuria was reduced, and regression of albuminuria 
increased. In the subjects randomized to intensive control, there 
was an inverse association between hypoglycemic events and mor­
tality, which was not seen in the standard-care group.737 However, 
in those with CKD at baseline, the risk of all-cause and cardiovas­
cular mortality was significantly increased in the intensive glucose 
management group.738 Hence, the kidney benefits of extremely 
tight glucose control were outweighed by the excess mortality. 
A less intensive HbA1c target in individuals with T2D and a duration 
of 10 years or more seems sensible. 
Glucose Control in Kidney Failure
Most739–741 but not all742 observational studies demonstrate 
increasing all-cause and cardiovascular mortality with increasing 
HbA1c in people with diabetes on kidney replacement therapy.

Glucose-Lowering Medications With Organ Protection
SGLT2 Inhibitors. For over 20 years, RAS blockade was the only 
treatment slowing the progression of diabetic nephropathy. After 
many unsuccessful attempts to develop new therapies, SGLT2is 
became the first medication class to show reduced progression of 
kidney disease in diabetic nephropathy and, later, in nondiabetic 
kidney disease. When initially tested for safety in cardiovascular 
outcome trials in participants with T2D and high CVD risk, the 
SGLT2i empagliflozin showed not only a benefit on the primary 
endpoint of MACEs745 but also a significant benefit on hospitaliza­
tion for heart failure. In addition, a reduction in the incidence or 
worsening of nephropathy occurred (hazard ratio [HR], 0.61; 95% 
CI, 0.53–0.70).746 These findings were confirmed in cardiovascular 
outcome trials with canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and ertugliflozin.747 
The effects on hospitalization for heart failure were seen very quickly, 
as were effects on albuminuria, probably reflecting diuretic effects 
and effects on intraglomerular pressure. Importantly, the benefits on 
kidney outcomes are independent of baseline eGFR from 20 mL/
min/1.73 m2 to >90 mL/min/1.73 m2,722 and they are also indepen­
dent of UACR of <30 mg/g, 30 to 300, or >300 mg/g.748 The first 
study with hard renal endpoints (ESKD or significant loss of renal 
function) as a primary endpoint using an SGLT2i was Canagliflozin 
and Renal Events in Diabetes With Established Nephropathy Clini­
cal Evaluation (CREDENCE), which showed a major benefit on 
kidney outcome and also on heart failure and MACEs in people with 
T2D, urine albumin creatinine ratio over 300 mg/g, and eGFR of 30 
to 90 mL/min/1.73 m2.749 The primary outcome was a composite of 
kidney failure, a doubling of the serum creatinine level, or death from 
kidney or cardiovascular causes. The study was stopped early because 
of positive effects, showing a benefit of canagliflozin (HR 0.70; 95% 
CI, 0.59–0.82). These data were confirmed and extended by the 
Dapagliflozin and Prevention of Adverse Outcomes in Chronic Kid­
ney Disease (DAPA-CKD) study, which included subjects with CKD 
with or without diabetes (Fig. 38.44).750 In the DAPA-CKD study, 
the benefit for progression of kidney disease was independent of the 
presence of diabetes, prediabetes, or normal glycemia at baseline.751 
Although SGLT2is were introduced to treat hyperglycemia in people 
with preserved kidney function, they also provide organ protection in 
diabetes with eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73 m2. Dapagliflozin and empa­
gliflozin are also able to reduce heart failure hospitalization in people 
with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction752 and subsequently 
in people with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, with sim­
ilar benefit in those with and without diabetes.624,753,754 The DAPA-
CKD study also demonstrated that dapagliflozin was able to reduce 
progression of CKD, hospitalization for heart failure, and mortality 
in people with CKD with T2D and in people with nondiabetic CKD 
(Table 38.9).750
Similar benefits were demonstrated in the Study of Heart and 
Kidney Protection with Empagliflozin (EMPA-KIDNEY).754a 
The study enrolled 6609 participants with a broad range of CKD 
including eGFR 20-45 mL/min/1.73 m2 regardless of albuminuria 
and eGFR 45-90 with UACR>200 mg/g with CKD with or with­
out diabetes. The primary outcome was a composite of progression 
of kidney disease (defined as end-stage kidney disease, a sustained 
decrease in eGFR to <10 mL/min/1.73 m2, a sustained decrease in 
eGFR of ≥40% from baseline, or death from renal causes) or death 
from cardiovascular causes, which was reduced HR 0.72 (95% CI 
0.64 to 0.82). The primary endpoint was not reduced in the group 
with normal albumin excretion rate, but rate of decline in eGFR 
from month 2 was significantly reduced also in this group, with an 
annual difference in slope of 0.78 (0.32, 1.23) mL/min.
The explanation for the kidney and cardiac benefits is not 
clear, but multiple mechanisms have been suggested. Glucose 
reduction is probably not very important, given similar benefit in 
those without diabetes. The inhibition of SGLT2 in the proximal 
tubule leads to blockade of glucose and sodium reabsorption, thus 
increasing distal tubular sodium delivery, which, via macula densa

and tubulo-glomerular feedback, reduces intraglomerular pressure 
through constriction of the afferent glomerular arterioles. This is 
reflected clinically in the small dip in GFR when starting SGLT2i 
treatment, and this has been suggested as the key mechanism 
behind the kidney-protective effects. Reduction in blood pressure 
and body weight, increased uric acid excretion, and change in fuel 
metabolites have also been suggested to contribute.673 Blocking 
uptake of sodium in the proximal tubule has also been suggested 
to reduce oxygen consumption, thereby reducing hypoxia, leading 
to less inflammation and fibrosis in experimental studies. Acute 
studies in humans with T1D demonstrated improved renal oxy­
gen availability after treatment with an SGLT2i.755 Interestingly, 
abnormalities in the urinary proteome related to extracellular 
matrix proteins also trended toward normal with an SGLT2i.756
In T2D, metformin has been recommended as the first glucose-
lowering agent after lifestyle improvements, and this also holds 
for T2D with CKD, as long as the need to reduce the dose with 
severely impaired kidney function is taken into consideration. 
Now SGLT2is are also recommended as first-line agents, inde­
pendent of HbA1c, for their organ-protective effect, particularly 
in patients with albuminuria or heart failure (Fig. 38.45).757,758
In T1D, the risk for euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis is 
increased with SGLT2is, and they are currently not approved for 
use in T1D. There are no studies of the kidney benefit in dia­
betic nephropathy in T1D, but a post hoc analysis of a study 
with the SGLT1 and SGLT2 inhibitor sotagliflozin suggested a 
potential benefit in T1D,759 and simulation studies also indicated 
benefit.760 However, dedicated randomized controlled studies are 
required to clarify potential cardiovascular and kidney benefits 
and risks with SGLT inhibition in T1D. 
Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists. Glucagon-like 
peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) were introduced 
as glucose- and weight-lowering medications. Cardiovascular out­
come trials for some long-acting forms of GLP-1RAs (liraglutide, 
semaglutide, dulaglutide, and efpeglenatide) in T2D demonstrated 
cardiovascular benefits in subjects with existing atherosclerotic 
CVD.758,761 The benefit on CVD outcomes was also demonstrated 
in CKD populations, and thus GLP-1RAs are recommended in the 
treatment of T2D with diabetic nephropathy when metformin and 
SGLT2 inhibition cannot control glucose (see Fig. 38.44).722 Stud­
ies also demonstrated positive kidney effects as secondary endpoints, 
mostly driven by reductions in albuminuria, but also some potential 
effects on eGFR. Post hoc studies suggested benefits for decline in 
kidney function in those with CKD and T2D.762 A kidney benefit 
was supported by the “A Study Comparing Dulaglutide With Insulin 
Glargine on Glycemic Control in Participants With Type 2 Diabetes 
(T2D) and Moderate or Severe Chronic Kidney Disease” (AWARD 
7) study with dulaglutide in T2D with CKD, although the primary 
endpoint was glycemic control.763 Semaglutide is being tested in the 
Effect of Semaglutide Versus Placebo on the Progression of Renal 
Impairment in Subjects With Type 2 Diabetes and Chronic Kid­
ney Disease (FLOW) study, the first primary kidney outcome study 
with a GLP-1RA (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03819153). The study will 
determine whether it will confer benefits on hard renal and cardio­
vascular outcomes among participants with T2D when compared 
to placebo; the study was stopped in October 2023 at an interim 
analysis because of a beneficial outcome. The mechanism of action 
for potential kidney and CVD benefit with GLP-1RA is not clear, 
although glucose control, weight loss, blood pressure reduction, anti­
inflammatory effects, and natriuretic effects may all contribute.764,765

Management of Diabetic Nephropathy
Rigorous blood pressure control dramatically improves the prog­
nosis in diabetic nephropathy. Conservative estimates suggest 
good blood pressure management doubles the time from first 
appearance of severely increased albuminuria to need for kidney

management in moderately elevated albuminuria may prevent 
progression and promote regression to normoalbuminuria. Blood 
pressure– and blood glucose–lowering effects are independent of 
one another but have synergistic effects.766,767 In contrast to glu­
cose “metabolic memory,” the benefits of blood pressure reduction 
are lost rapidly when blood pressure control deteriorates.766
Blood Pressure in Type 1 Diabetes
It has been suggested all patients with T1D should be treated with 
RAS inhibitors to prevent nephropathy, but RAS inhibitors do 
not prevent moderately elevated albuminuria in normotensive 
people with T1D.531,768,769 There is also no evidence that con­
trol of hypertension in T1D with normoalbuminuria prevents 
progression of albuminuria and decline in kidney function. Thus, 
treatment of normoalbuminuric patients to prevent CKD is not 
recommended, although in hypertension, RAS inhibitors are 
often used.
Once moderately or severely increased albuminuria is present, 
inhibition of the RAS is the backbone of management of kidney 
disease because it reduces intraglomerular pressure. A meta-­
analysis summarized the effects of ACEis in people with T1D 
with moderately elevated albuminuria.770 The OR for progression 
to severely increased albuminuria was reduced by angiotensin-­
converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition to 0.35, and the likelihood 
for regression to normoalbuminuria increased to 3.07, compared 
to placebo treatment. After 2 years of treatment, the mean reduc­
tion in albumin excretion was 50.5% with ACE inhibition, and 
it was greatest in those with highest baseline levels. However, the 
response to treatment plateaued with time, suggesting that treat­
ment delays, rather than prevents, progression. Furthermore, 
when the ACE inhibition is stopped, the albuminuria promptly 
returns to its former levels.
Addition of an ACEi to non-ACEi antihypertensive therapy 
reduces the risk of a doubling of the serum creatinine by 48% 
and the composite endpoint of death, need for dialysis or kid­
ney transplantation, by 50% in people with T1D and with 
severely increased albuminuria and hypertension.771 Both benefits 
appear independent of blood pressure. In short-term studies, the 
effects of ARBs on blood pressure and urinary albumin excretion 
were similar to those of ACEis in T1D with severely increased 
albuminuria.772
For a similar reduction in blood pressure, there is a greater 
reduction in protein excretion using ACEis (or ARBs) compared 
to other classes of antihypertensive agents.773 This may be ben­
eficial because the passage of protein across the glomerular filtra­
tion barrier may accelerate the progression of nephropathy.774 
Animal data show that this is a result of a preferential reduction 
in intraglomerular pressure with ACEis due to a dilatation of the 
efferent vessels.775 An effect on the filtration barrier has also been 
suggested.776
Treatment guidelines therefore recommend RAS inhibitors to 
all individuals with T1D and albuminuria, particularly if blood 
pressure is increased. The dose should be titrated up to the maxi­
mum recommended or tolerated to obtain maximal antiprotein­
uric effect. If blood pressure remains above 125/75 mm Hg on 
maximum dose of RAS inhibitor, antihypertensive therapy should 
be intensified. Lower blood pressure reduces the rate of decline of 
GFR from 10 to 12 mL/min/year untreated to below 5 mL/min/
year.777 Regression from severely to moderately increased albu­
minuria can be achieved, with the fall in GFR reduced to below 1 
mL/min/year.635 The choice of additional agents should be made 
on an individual basis because there is no evidence in T1D that 
any one add-on agent is better than others. Often, multiple agents 
are needed in CKD stage 3 and beyond, including diuretics (often 
needed for fluid overload), calcium channel blockers, and perhaps 
β-blockers or aldosterone antagonists. 
Blood Pressure in Type 2 Diabetes
Control of hypertension reduces the risk of developing moder­
ately or severely increased albuminuria.778–781 There is a particular 
benefit of RAS inhibition in prevention of nephropathy,782–784 
but lowering blood pressure sufficiently is the key. Achieved blood 
pressure in these studies was generally about 140/80 mm Hg, but 
most guidelines now suggest a blood pressure target of 130/80 
mm Hg in T2D.

SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
As with T1D, there is good evidence in T2D that inhibition 
of the RAS should be the standard of care if albuminuria is ele­
vated. RAS blockade reduces progression of moderately elevated 
albuminuria to severely increased albuminuria779,785 and increases 
regression to normoalbuminuria.785 The benefits are at least partly 
independent of blood pressure lowering. In more advanced dia­
betic nephropathy, RAS inhibition with an ARB reduces progres­
sion, defined as doubling of serum creatinine, kidney failure, or 
death, by 50%.786,787 Hence, people with T2D and moderately 
or severely increased albuminuria should be prescribed an RAS 
inhibitor, titrated to the maximum tolerated dose.788 Hyperkale­
mia is common in individuals with T2D and nephropathy taking 
RAS blocking agents and is associated with increased risk of kid­
ney failure.789 General steps to lower potassium, such as dietary 
advice, additional or increased dose of diuretics, discontinuation 
of other medications or dietary supplements that might be increas­
ing potassium levels, and potassium binders, should be considered 
before stopping RAS blockade.757 Initiation of therapy with an 
RAS inhibitor often leads to an acute decline in GFR, which then 
stabilizes. Individuals with the greatest initial fall in GFR have the 
slowest subsequent decline in kidney function.790 As mentioned 
earlier, a reduction of albuminuria of at least 30% after onset of 
therapy has become a new treatment target because this is associ­
ated with beneficial long-term outcome.516
Most people with T2D and albuminuria will require additional 
antihypertensive therapy. The choice of additional agents should 
be made on an individual basis, with diuretics and calcium channel 
blockers often being appropriate. In resistant hypertension with 
preserved renal function (eGFR >45 mL/min/1.73 m2), MRAs 
may be useful, although long-term outcome studies are lacking.791
It is debated whether there is a lower threshold for blood pres­
sure when treatment is initiated. In the UKPDS, there was no 
blood pressure level below which the risk of developing moderately 
elevated albuminuria or beyond increased (i.e., no “J” shape).792 
The ADVANCE study explored the effects of reduction of blood 
pressure below the currently recommended targets of 130/80 mm 
Hg in individuals with normal or moderately increased albumin­
uria and 125/75 mm Hg in those with severely increased albu­
minuria.793 Over 4 years, the risk of kidney events was reduced 
by 21%, mainly because of reduced risk of developing moderately 
or severely elevated albuminuria. However, an achieved systolic 
blood pressure below 120 to 130 mm Hg was associated with 
increased mortality and kidney failure.794 Therefore, extremely 
tight blood pressure control should be avoided. 
Dual Blockade of the Renin-Angiotensin System
Addition of an ARB to an ACEi795,796 or of the direct renin inhib­
itor aliskiren to an ARB reduces blood pressure and albuminuria 
more than each agent individually. However, in the longer term, 
dual blockade increases the risk of hyperkalemia, hypotension, 
and acute irreversible kidney failure.797–800 Hence, dual blockade 
is not recommended. 
Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonism
Prevention of incident diabetic nephropathy in T2D with normoalbu­
minuria was evaluated in the PRIORITY trial. A high risk for progres­
sion to CKD/moderately elevated albuminuria was identified using a 
urinary proteomic–based risk score (CKD-273). High-risk individuals 
were randomized to spironolactone or placebo. Spironolactone failed 
to reduce progression compared to placebo over 3 years.692
Short-term studies in established diabetic nephropathy 
revealed an approximate 30% reduction in albuminuria with the 
steroidal MRAs spironolactone or eplerenone.801 Preventing over­
activation of the mineralocorticoid receptor reduces inflammation 
and fibrosis, but because of hyperkalemia, diabetes with kidney 
disease became a contraindication for these agents. Nonsteroidal 
MRAs have been developed and are interesting because there are 
fewer potassium issues. The nonsteroidal MRAs esaxerenone and 
finerenone reduced moderately elevated albuminuria in T2D in 
short-term studies, with a good safety profile and very little hyper­
kalemia.802,803 This led to two large studies testing finerenone in 
T2D with CKD. The Finerenone in Reducing Kidney Failure 
and Disease Progression in Diabetic Kidney Disease (FIDELIO-
DKD) trial tested finerenone on a background of RAS blockade 
and included 5734 subjects with relatively advanced CKD and 
T2D (UACR ≥3 to ≤5000 mg/g, eGFR ≥25 to <75 mL/min/1.73 
m2). The primary endpoint (kidney failure, sustained decrease of 
eGFR of ≥40%, or kidney death) was reduced (HR, 0.82; 95% 
CI, 0.73–0.93, p = 0.001). The key secondary outcome (cardio­
vascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or hospitalization for 
heart failure) was also reduced (HR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75–0.99; p 
= 0.03). The incidence of hyperkalemia-related treatment discon­
tinuation was infrequent but higher with finerenone than placebo 
(2.3% and 0.9%, respectively).804
The Efficacy and Safety of Finerenone in Subjects With Type 2 
Diabetes Mellitus and the Clinical Diagnosis of Diabetic Kidney 
Disease (FIGARO-DKD) trial also tested finerenone but included 
patients with T2D with less advanced CKD, including a greater 
number of patients with albuminuria in the range of 30 to 300 
and impaired eGFR or albuminuria >300 with normal eGFR. 
FIGARO-DKD was a randomized, double-blind, phase 3 study 
of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, and the primary end­
point was time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfa­
tal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for 
heart failure. The key secondary composite outcome was time to 
kidney failure, sustained ≥40% decrease in eGFR from baseline, 
or renal death.805 The study randomized 7437 patients, and the 
results demonstrated a significant reduction in the primary car­
diovascular composite endpoint with finerenone compared to pla­
cebo (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.76–0.98; p = 0.03). The effect on the 
kidney composite endpoint (kidney failure, sustained decrease of 
eGFR ≥40%, or kidney death) was not significant with finere­
none versus placebo (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.76–1.01; p = 0.07).805 
However, the standard kidney composite endpoint with a ≥57% 
decline in eGFR (equivalent to doubling of serum creatinine) 
instead of the ≥40% decline in eGFR was significantly reduced 
with finerenone compared to placebo (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.60–
0.99; p = 0.04).805 A subgroup analysis from the finerenone stud­
ies suggests that finerenone is just as efficient when added on top 
of SGLT2i as a placebo, which could suggest that the beneficial 
effects of SGLT2 inhibition and finerenone were additive. The 
combination lowers the risk of hyperkalemia.806 Similar indepen­
dent effects were seen with GLP-1RA and finerenone.807 Current 
guidelines recommend nonsteroidal MRAs with proven effect 
for people with T2D and UACR >30 mg/g despite standard of 
care,516,808 as shown in Fig. 38.45. 
Sodium Intake
Short-term dietary sodium restriction (target sodium intake 50 mmol 
or 1150 mg Na+ per day), added to RAS blockade, reduces albumin­
uria.809 The treatment effects of ARBs are greater in patients with 
1525
CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
lower rather than higher dietary sodium intake.810 Hence, dietary 
counseling to reduce sodium intake is essential, and an intake of less 
than 2 g of sodium per day (or <90 mmol or 2070 mg of sodium per 
day, or under 5 g of sodium chloride per day) is recommended.757 
Chronic Kidney Disease With Normoalbuminuria
There is no specific evidence for the use of RAS inhibition in indi­
viduals without albuminuria. However, control of blood pressure 
remains crucial to slow progression of CKD. The EMPA-KIDNEY 
study is investigating the effect of the SGLT2i empagliflozin on 
CKD in people with or without diabetes, including participants 
with low eGFR (20–45 mL/min/1.73 m2) but normal urinary 
albumin excretion.811 Post hoc analyses from the cardiovascular 
outcome studies with SGLTis suggested benefit on progression of 
CKD independent of baseline albuminuria, and SGLTi use is there­
fore recommended for CKD in diabetes with or without albumin­
uria, although the risk for progression to kidney failure and benefit 
of intervention increases with increasing albuminuria.772,812 
Endothelin Receptor Antagonists
Atrasentan is an endothelin receptor A antagonist with a demon­
strated ability to lower proteinuria without significant edema.813 
Previously, edema had been a concern with this class of agents.814 
The Study of Diabetic Nephropathy with Atrasentan (SONAR) 
evaluated atrasentan in T2D with severely increased albuminuria, 
with progression of kidney disease, kidney failure, and mortality 
as the primary outcome.815,816 Although the study was stopped 
early for concern of futility, it eventually showed a kidney benefit 
of the same magnitude as with SGLT2is but without effect on 
MACEs and with a tendency to increase the risk of heart failure. 
The primary endpoint was a composite of doubling of serum cre­
atinine (sustained for ≥30 days) or ESKD (eGFR <15 mL/min 
per 1.73 m2 sustained for ≥90 days, chronic dialysis for ≥90 days, 
kidney transplantation, or death from kidney failure). The HR for 
atrasentan compared to placebo was 0.65 (95% CI, 0.49–0.88; p 
= 0.0047). The mode of action may relate to an effect on inflam­
mation, but an effect on podocytes, endothelium, and glycoca­
lyx has been proposed from experimental data.816 Given that the 
side effect of other endothelin receptor A antagonists was fluid 
retention, it has been suggested that combination with SGLT2 
inhibition could improve outcomes because SGLT2is have dem­
onstrated benefits in heart failure and have diuretic effects. How­
ever, the benefit of the combination has not yet been proven. 
Low-Protein Diet
A meta-analysis concluded that a low-protein diet significantly 
improves GFR but not albuminuria across all subtypes of diabetes 
and stages of nephropathy.817 A randomized trial of 82 patients with 
T1D, severely increased proteinuria, and progressive loss of kidney 
function demonstrated reduced mortality and kidney failure (RR, 
0.23; 95% CI, 0.07–0.72) for patients assigned to a low-protein diet 
targeting 0.8 g protein/kg body weight/day compared to usual diet.818 
Protein intake should not be restricted to less than 0.7 g protein/kg 
body weight/day because of concerns about malnutrition in kidney 
failure. In line with recommendations for the general population, a 
protein intake of 0.8 g protein/kg body weight/day is recommended 
for diabetes and CKD, except for people on peritoneal dialysis, where 
a higher intake (1.0–1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day) is recom­
mended because peritoneal dialysis is a catabolic state.757 
Obesity and Lipids
In diabetic nephropathy, lipid-lowering medications are recom­
mended to reduce the risk for CVD. There is some evidence that 
lipid-lowering agents are beneficial to the kidney. In a post hoc 
analysis of the Collaborative Atorvastatin Diabetes Study, the rate 
of decline of eGFR was significantly less in those individuals taking 
atorvastatin 10 mg daily compared to placebo. Fibrates also reduce 
albuminuria, although they reversibly increase serum creatinine.819
In a trial comparing intensive lifestyle intervention with diabetes 
support and education in T2D, individuals randomized to inten­
sive lifestyle modification were less likely to develop CKD over 8 
years.820 The effect was partly attributable to reductions in body 
weight, HbA1c, and systolic blood pressure. Low-­carbohydrate, 
Mediterranean, and low-fat diets have similar beneficial effects on 
change in eGFR and albuminuria over 2 years.821 In individu­
als with T2D who have undergone bariatric surgery, moderately 
and severely increased albuminuria can regress to normoalbu­
minuria.822 Similar benefits were described in a 5-year study in 
severely obese adolescents with and without T2D.823 Weight loss 
could be part of the benefit of GLP-1RA and could suggest ben­
efits also with the dual agonist tirzepatide.824 
Other Factors
Smoking increases the likelihood of the development of diabetic 
nephropathy, as discussed earlier. There have been no good trials 
of smoking cessation. However, smoking cessation should clearly 
be encouraged. There are no studies in diabetic kidney disease with 
aspirin evaluating long-term benefits, although short-term studies 
suggest no effect on urinary albumin excretion or GFR.825 In many 
individuals with established CVD or high risk for CVD, aspirin 
should be considered for prevention of cardiovascular events. There 
is an increased risk for atrial fibrillation in diabetes and in CKD, in 
addition to higher morbidity and mortality associated with throm­
boembolic events, including stroke in diabetes with atrial fibrilla­
tion.826 In diabetes with atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation is often 
recommended, and direct oral anticoagulants are usually preferred 
compared to vitamin K antagonists. In addition to a reduced risk 
for bleeding and similar or better effects on reducing the risk for 
thrombosis, observational studies suggest a reduction in the pro­
gression of CKD. Thus, a recent study using a health claim database 
included patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and diabetes 
who initiated rivaroxaban (N = 10,017) or warfarin (N = 11,665).826 
Patients were matched using propensity scores. In comparison to 
warfarin, rivaroxaban was associated with lower risks of AKI events 
(HR, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.74–0.92) and development of stage 5 CKD 
or need for hemodialysis (HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.70–0.96).826 The 
mechanism could be reduced vascular calcification but needs to be 
confirmed in randomized controlled trials.
A flow diagram for integrated management of CKD in diabetes 
is provided in Fig. 38.46.

In progressive CKD from stage 3 onward, bone chemistry, full 
blood count, and iron stores should be assessed every 3 to 6

Monitoring Glucose Control
Red blood cell and protein turnover are abnormal in CKD, mak­
ing the interpretation of HbA1c, glycated albumin, and fructos­
amine results difficult, particularly in subjects with CKD 4+. 
Thus, more reliance should be placed on self-monitoring of 
blood glucose and CGM, particularly if treatment can cause 
hypoglycemia.757
With declining kidney function, it is important to be aware 
of the increased risk for hypoglycemia. The glycemic target 
may have to be increased to avoid hypoglycemic episodes,827 
and glucose-lowering agents may have to be changed or have 
their dose adjusted. There are several explanations for this: (1) 
the kidney is important for the metabolism of many glucose-
lowering medications, including insulin, and this function 
is impaired in advanced CKD; (2) the kidney accounts for 
approximately 30% of total endogenous glucose production, 
which declines with loss of kidney function; (3) in advanced 
CKD, acidosis affects the liver’s ability to produce glucose and 
compensate for failing kidney gluconeogenesis, and malnutri­
tion and muscle wasting contribute to the risk for hypoglyce­
mia; and (4) people with diabetic nephropathy are often older, 
have longer diabetes duration, and more frequently suffer from 
comorbidities, especially CVD, and are thus more likely to be 
on multiple medications that can have potential interactions 
with glucose-lowering medications.827,828
Metformin and its metabolites are excreted mainly by the kid­
ney. In kidney failure, they accumulate and inhibit lactate oxida­
tion. Metformin should therefore be used cautiously in those with 
eGFR of <45 mL/min/1.73 m2 and stopped completely when 
eGFR is <30 mL/min/1.73 m2.829
The sulfonylureas glibenclamide, gliclazide, and tolbutamide 
are excreted predominantly by the kidneys and accumulate in 
CKD. Their dose, and indeed the dose of any sulfonylurea, may 
need to be reduced as CKD progresses. Only ∼10% of the meg­
litinides repaglinide and nateglinide are excreted by the kidneys, 
making them suitable alternative agents. The thiazolidinediones, 
rosiglitazone and pioglitazone, are predominantly metabolized in 
the liver. However, their use in kidney failure may be limited by 
fluid retention.
Insulin is also degraded by the kidney, so reduced dosage, and 
perhaps a switch to shorter-acting preparations, may be required.
The dose of some but not all dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-
4) inhibitors and GLP-1RAs may need to be reduced as

Anemia
Anemia is common in people with diabetes and CKD stage 3 or 
poorer.830 Full investigation of iron-deficiency anemia may be 
needed to exclude a nonkidney cause. Those with anemia have a 
higher mortality, higher rates of hospital admission with heart fail­
ure, and poorer quality of life. Iron stores should be repleted with 
oral or parenteral iron as necessary, and erythropoietin replace­
ment should be commenced if indicated. Anemia is a risk factor 
for progression of CKD and CVD. The Trial to Reduce Cardio­
vascular Events With Aranesp Therapy (TREAT) investigated 
whether treatment of anemia in T2D with CKD with darbepoetin 
alfa would improve renal or cardiovascular outcome, but the trial 
showed no benefit.831 
Referral to Nephrology
Patients who begin dialysis as an emergency do less well than those 
in whom treatment is planned.832 Referral to nephrology should be 
made when eGFR is declining rapidly (>5 mL/min/1.73 m2/year 
or when eGFR is <30–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). This allows struc­
tured physical and psychological preparation for kidney replace­
ment therapy. Earlier referral may be necessary in some situations 
but also depends on local agreements (Box 38.1). The need for 
kidney replacement therapy should be discussed with all patients, 
and those who wish it should have access. A person with diabetes 
and kidney failure has several options for renal replacement ther­
apy: (1) transplantation (kidney only, pancreas plus kidney simul­
taneously, pancreas after kidney), (2) hemodialysis (center, limited 
care, self-care, or home dialysis), and (3) peritoneal dialysis. There 
is consensus that medical rehabilitation and survival are best after 
transplantation,833 particularly after transplantation of pancreas 
plus kidney, where the risk for recurrence of the diabetes kidney 
disease in the transplanted kidney is reduced.834,835 The results 
of peritoneal dialysis and hemodialysis are inferior to transplanta­
tion but comparable between peritoneal dialysis and hemodialy­
sis. Increased frequency or duration of dialysis improves clearance 
of uremic solutes and was associated with favorable results with 
respect to composite outcomes of death, change in left ventricular 
mass and death, or change in a physical health composite score 
but prompted more frequent interventions related to vascular 
access.836 People without significant comorbidities will usually be 
offered transplantation, but shortage of organs is a limitation and 
often delays transplantation. Full cardiovascular assessment and 
treatment are essential before transplantation. 
Organization of Care in the Patient With Diabetic 
Nephropathy
Structured care, delivered by trained specialists working with 
clear protocols with specific, multiple treatment goals for all the 
variables described earlier, reduces the incidence of moderately 
elevated albuminuria837,838 and provides greater kidney and car­
diovascular benefits than routine care for individuals with T2D 
and CKD.757,839,840 Progression to kidney failure or death, need 
for laser therapy for management of retinopathy, and cardiovascu­
lar endpoints, including stroke and heart failure, are all reduced by 
such multifactorial interventions.841–844 When structured inten­
sive multifactorial intervention targeting lifestyle factors (diet, 
exercise, smoking) and heart and kidney risk factors (blood glu­
cose, blood pressure, lipid management) compared to usual care 
was started in T2D with moderately elevated albuminuria, long-
term follow-up of the Steno-2 study demonstrated that 8 years of 
intervention translated into almost 8 years of extended median 
survival841 and reduced development of kidney failure or death 
(HR, 0.53).845 
Diabetic Neuropathies
Diabetic neuropathies are a group of clinical syndromes with dis­
tinct presentations secondary to different underlying pathogenetic 
mechanisms. These syndromes are most commonly classified into 
two broad groups: diffuse versus focal neuropathies. Among the 
diffuse diabetic neuropathies, distal symmetric polyneuropathy 
(DSPN) is the most common, followed by the family of auto­
nomic neuropathies, including cardiac autonomic neuropathy 
(CAN), and autonomic neuropathy of the gastrointestinal, uro­
genital, and sudomotor systems. Focal neuropathies are much less 
common than diffuse neuropathies and include isolated mono­
neuropathies of one or more peripheral nerves; even rarer are focal 
neuropathies of one or more nerve roots, classified as radiculopa­
thy or polyradiculopathy, respectively (Box 38.2 and Table 38.10).
Epidemiology and Impact of Diabetic 
Neuropathies
Diabetic neuropathies are the most common complications of 
T1D and T2D. DSPN represents the most commonly diagnosed 
and highly morbid of the diabetic neuropathies. Although prev­
alence estimates vary depending on how the diagnosis is made, 
DSPN occurs in at least half, if not more, of all patients with 
diabetes over time.846 Prevalence was approximately 45% after 25 
years of diabetes, as determined by clinical examination, in the 
classic study by Pirat following a cohort of 4400 patients with dia­
betes between 1947 and 1973.847 Studies completed since 2017 
reveal varying prevalence, depending on the sensitivity of the mea­
sures used and the examined population (Table 38.11). When the 
most sensitive measures are used, such as quantitative sensory test­
ing or nerve conduction studies, as part of the diagnostic criteria, 
the prevalence of DSPN increases to 60%848 or even greater than 
75%.849 Quantitative sensory testing for both large- and small-
fiber neuropathy is used for cold, heat, and vibration. These are 
not precise because they depend on the patient’s cooperation, so 
they are generally not used in differential diagnosis or for confirm­
ing a particular aspect of DSPN.
DSPN also occurs in patients with prediabetes and the meta­
bolic syndrome,850–852 a finding that is now well established in 
multiple cohorts from multiple countries (Table 38.12). Although

DSPN prevalence rates are higher in those metabolic syndrome

levels, DSPN can also occur independent of glycemic status852 
and is strongly associated with central obesity.853,854 With the 
alarming rise of the metabolic syndrome, prediabetes, and T2D, 
20 million to 35 million individuals in the United States are esti­
mated to be living with DSPN.846
DSPN leads to a poor quality of life, limiting a patient’s func­
tion, especially when DSPN is associated with pain.855 Up to 70% 
of patients with DSPN experience some form of disrupted sleep, 
depression, anxiety, and poor work productivity.856 Impairment 
of physical functioning in DSPN is associated with a 15-fold 
increase in the likelihood of falling and fractures, particularly in 
older individuals with diabetes, who also experience increased 
bone fragility and sarcopenia.857,858 Foot ulceration leading 
to amputation is one of the most serious and adverse effects of 
DSPN,859 with an overall amputation rate of 3.3% to 42.8% in 
diabetics with foot ulcers. The strongest predictors of amputation 
included DSPN, male sex, older age, peripheral arterial disease, 
and osteomyelitis.860 Foot ulcers are also a strong predictor of 
early mortality in patients with diabetes.861 Of patients with new 
foot ulcers, 5% die within 1 year of their first ulcer, and 42.2% 
of people with existing ulcers die within 5 years.862 Even higher 
mortality rates of 13.6% and 50.6% at 1 and 5 years are seen in 
patients requiring an amputation.863 Worldwide, DSPN accounts 
for more hospitalizations than all the other diabetic complications 
combined and is the root cause of 50% to 75% of nontraumatic 
amputations in North America.864,865 The rates of lower extrem­
ity amputation among Medicare-enrolled individuals with dia­
betes decreased by 28.8% between 2000 and 2010,866 although 
there was no change in the cost of caring for DSPN complications 
because of delay in diagnosis.867 Unfortunately, rates of amputa­
tion are now on the rise, particularly in men between the ages 
of 18 and 64 years, with a 62% increase in minor lower extrem­
ity amputations and a 29% increase in major lower extremity 
amputations.868
Like DSPN, autonomic neuropathies adversely affect patients 
with T1D and T2D, affecting a wide variety of organ systems, 
including cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, urogenital, and sudo­
motor/thermoregulatory systems. Of these, CAN is the best stud­
ied, with early mortality and sudden death reported in up to 56% 
over a 10-year period.869 One-third of patients with autonomic 
neuropathy have impaired quality of life,870 with erectile dys­
function predicting not only poor quality of life in the affected 
patient871 but also in the patient’s sexual partner.872
Although fiscal estimates vary, the total annual cost of DSPN 
is estimated to be over $25 billion,873 with total annual medical 
costs for a patient with diabetes with painless DSPN estimated at 
$12,492 compared to $6632 for a patient with diabetes without 
DSPN. Direct costs are even greater with painful DSPN, rang­
ing from $27,931 up to $30,755 per patient, depending on the 
severity of the pain873 and the use of generic versus nongeneric 
medications.874 Importantly, little money is spent in the United 
States on patient education or preventive foot care, an investment 
that has been proven to be effective in decreasing the incidence of 
DSPN complications.875

Pathophysiology of Diabetic Neuropathies
Although the pathophysiology of microvascular complications has 
been discussed earlier in this chapter, an understanding of nerve 
structure (Fig. 38.47) provides additional insight into neuropathy 
pathogenesis and clinical presentation. In the peripheral nervous 
system, afferent axons from sensory receptors send information 
to the dorsal root ganglia of the central nervous system (CNS), 
whereas efferent axons relay CNS signals to muscles and joints. 
Schwann cells envelope and myelinate large and midsize sensory 
axons, known as large fibers. In contrast, the cytoplasm from one 
Schwann cell can envelope 30 or more unmyelinated small axons, 
known as small fibers. These large and small fibers carry specific 
information: large fibers relay vibratory, proprioception, and tac­
tile sensation; small fibers relay thermal sensation and pain, and 
they also regulate microvascular blood flow. Small-fiber damage 
usually precedes large-fiber damage in diabetes876 and frequently 
presents as burning pain, although patients also report tingling 
and prickly sensations.877 With time, large-fiber involvement 
occurs, with corresponding numbness and poor position sense.
How diabetes changes the interaction between Schwann cells 
and axons is an active source of investigation, and it remains 
unclear if the primary insult in DSPN lies in the sensory neu­
ron, axon, or Schwann cell. It is likely that all three components 
are adversely affected in both distinct and overlapping ways, and 
the unifying theme is one of bioenergetic failure, with a focus on 
the mitochondria. For normal nerve function, mitochondria must 
traffic long distances along axons to meet axonal energy demands 
(Fig. 38.48A). In the diabetic microenvironment, glycolytic inter­
mediates are depleted in Schwann cells,878 whereas fatty acid 
oxidation is increased,879 producing a state of mitochondrial and 
cellular oxidative stress, excess cytosolic bioactive lipids,880 and a 
lack of normal transfer of energy substrates from the Schwann cell 
to the axon, a process known as metabolic coupling. Disrupted met­
abolic coupling, in turn, disrupts normal mitochondrial traffick­
ing881,882 along energy-starved axons, producing a loss of function 
in a distal-to-proximal fashion and the well-known stocking-glove 
signs and symptoms of DSPN. Metabolic coupling can occur via 
myelinic channels or monocarboxylate transporters at the node of 
Ranvier (see Fig. 38.48B).883–885 The concept of crosstalk between 
Schwann cells and axons is further supported by a recent finding 
that delivery of exosomes from Schwann cells cultured in HG to 
sciatic nerves of mice resulted in murine DSPN.886
Clinical trials have yielded insights into potential differences 
underlying the pathogenesis of DSPN in T1D and T2D. Glucose 
control has a significant effect on DSPN onset and progression in 
T1D but no effect or a modest 3% to 5% effect at best on DSPN 
in T2D.887 The idea that DSPN is actually two distinct disorders, 
DSPN T1D and DSPN T2D, is a source of active investigation,11 
with the emerging concept that Schwann cells and neurons can 
develop insulin resistance888 that contributes to DSPN in T2D 
(see Fig. 38.48B).889

CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
Clinical Features of Diabetic Distal Symmetric 
Polyneuropathy
Clinical Symptoms
DSPN is the most common and widely recognized form of dia­
betic neuropathy. An international consensus meeting defined 
DSPN as “the presence of symptoms and/or signs of peripheral 
nerve dysfunction in people with diabetes after the exclusion 
of other causes.”890,891 The onset of DSPN is usually insidious 
but can be acute, as discussed later. DSPN is primarily a sensory 
neuropathy and can involve small fibers, large fibers, or both.892 
Motor involvement is only seen late in the disease, if at all.
Symptoms of DSPN secondary to diabetes depend on the 
affected fiber types. Early in the course of the disease, small fibers 
are preferentially involved, leading to symptoms of pain, hyper­
algesia, and allodynia in the lower limbs, followed over time by 
a loss of thermal sensitivity and pain perception.877 These same 
early symptoms of DSPN are also the main constellation of pre­
senting symptoms in prediabetic neuropathy.851 Symptoms often 
are exacerbated at night and are manifested in the feet more than 
the hands. Spontaneous episodes of pain can be severely disabling. 
The pain varies in intensity and character and has been variably 
described by patients as lancinating, stabbing, or sharp. Paresthe­
sias or episodes of distorted sensation, such as pins and needles, 
tingling, coldness, numbness, or burning, often accompany the 
pain.892 These multiple symptoms are classified as positive symp­
toms because the affected patient with diabetes actively experi­
ences discomfort.
In contrast, the symptoms of large-fiber neuropathy are com­
monly denoted as negative symptoms, with the patient presenting 
with a numb, insensate foot. Patients with diabetes with large-
fiber–predominant DSPN are frequently unaware of their neu­
ropathy and are surprised when a physical examination reveals 
absent sensation in their feet. Because large fibers mediate posi­
tion sense, poor balance with frank falling is a common presenting 
symptom in patients with diabetes with a large-fiber–predominant 
DSPN. Although less common, these patients can also experience 
a deep-seated, dull, toothache-like sensation in their feet and, in 
very severe cases, will experience symptoms of distal weakness 
of the toes and ankles, secondary to late-onset large motor fiber 
involvement.846
Although the distinction is classically made between small- 
and large-fiber–predominant DSPN, a common presentation of 
DSPN in patients with diabetes is a combination of symptoms 
from both fiber types. 
Clinical Signs of Diabetic Neuropathy
A simple examination can distinguish between small- and large-
fiber impairment. Inspection of the skin is an essential first part 
of the clinical examination because small fibers also subserve 
sudomotor function (Box 38.3). The foot is inspected for dry 
skin, fissures, and calluses (see “The Diabetic Foot” later in this 
chapter). Small-fiber function is then assessed using a simple dis­
posable safety pin or cotton wisp or by assessing the ability of a 
patient to distinguish temperatures between a proximal location 
(the face) and a distal location (the dorsum of the great toe).

• Fig. 38.47  The peripheral nervous system (PNS). The PNS is composed of both neurons and Schwann 
cells (SCs), and the structure, location, and interaction of these components have important implications 
for PNS function. Efferent axons of motor neurons, whose cell bodies are located in the ventral horn of the 
spinal cord, carry signals from the central nervous system (CNS) to muscles and glands, whereas afferent 
axons of sensory neurons, whose cell bodies are located in the dorsal root ganglia, relay information from 
peripheral sensory receptors to the CNS. Thin and unmyelinated sensory axons, also known as C fibers 
or small fibers, are associated with nonmyelinating SCs and are grouped as Remak bundles. These rep­
resent a large portion of the PNS neurons. Myelinated sensory axons, on the other hand, are surrounded 
by myelin sheaths made by SCs that form distinct nodal domains important for saltatory conduction. They 
also form a tubular network of myelinic channels that connect the SC cytoplasm with the periaxonal space, 
providing substrate for energy generation to the axonal compartment. (Redrawn from Feldman EL, Nave 
KA, Jensen TS, et al. New horizons in diabetic neuropathy: mechanisms, bioenergetics, and pain. Neuron.

• Fig. 38.48  Anatomy and pathophysiology of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. (A) Peripheral neuron cell bodies are only microns in width, but axons are up to 
several feet in length. For nerve function, neurons traffic mitochondria from the cell body along the axons to areas of high energy demand. Failure to traffic mito­
chondria results in energy failure at axon termini followed by distal-to-proximal (pink to blue) nerve injury, which underlies the stocking-glove pattern of clinical 
signs and symptoms. (B) Homoeostatic conditions, healthy nerve (blue): axons take up glucose in an insulin-independent manner through glucose transporter 
3 (GLUT3; green transporter), which is metabolized to pyruvate in the cytoplasm and further to adenosine triphosphate (ATP) in mitochondria. Schwann cells 
take up glucose in an insulin-dependent manner through GLUT1 (blue transporter); some glucose is metabolized for energy use by Schwann cells, and some 
is metabolized to pyruvate and then lactate for transport to axons through the monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1; gray, on Schwann cells), then MCT2 
(purple, on axons). Schwann cells take up fatty acids using fatty acid transporters, translocases, or binding proteins, primarily for myelin production. Mito­
chondria are trafficked in anterograde or retrograde direction to areas of high energy demand. Mitochondria generate a mitochondrial membrane potential 
for ATP production, powering Na+/K+ ATPase channel activity (pink; purple spheres represent cations). Mitochondrial biogenesis can replenish dysfunctional 
mitochondria, which are eliminated by mitophagy. In pathologic conditions, in a peripheral nerve (pink), hyperglycemia increases glucose flux into axons 
through GLUT3; excess glucose that is not metabolized by glycolysis can activate other pathways (e.g., polyol, AGEs, and PKC pathways). Downstream, this 
activation triggers inflammation and disrupts Na+/K+ ATPase channel activity (no cations pumped, stop sign). Insulin resistance impairs insulin-dependent 
GLUT1-facilitated glucose uptake by Schwann cells, disrupting MCT-mediated fuel transport to axons and possibly the balance with lipid metabolism and 
myelin production. Hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia also enhance oxidative stress and apoptosis in Schwann cells. Hyperlipidemia disrupts mitochondrial 
biogenesis and trafficking in the axon, lowering the proportion and velocity of motile mitochondria. Palmitate also depolarizes axonal mitochondria and 
reduces their ability to dissipate mitochondrial membrane potential to meet physiologic energy demands. Mitophagy is also impaired. AGE, advanced glyca­

protein kinase C; PYR, pyruvate; ROS, reactive oxygen species. (The figure was created by use of BioRender.com. From Elafros MA, Andersen H, Bennett

A simple bedside approach is to determine if the patient can 
differentiate between the sharp and dull end of the safety pin 
on the dorsum of the toe and if he or she can perceive a cotton 
wisp in the same anatomic location. To assess temperature in the 
simplest manner, a cool tuning fork is placed on the patient’s 
cheek, the same instrument is then placed on the great toe, and 
the patient is asked to report whether the same cool temperature 
is perceived in both anatomic locations or not. Large-fiber func­
tion is initially assessed by measuring the time in seconds that 
a patient can perceive vibration sensation on the great toe after 
a health care provider places a 128-Hz vibrating tuning fork on 
the dorsum of the patient’s great toe. Proprioception is assessed 
by minor movements of the first metatarsophalangeal joint of 
the great toe. Ankle reflexes are an essential part of assessing 
large-fiber function and are best produced with the examiner 
mildly dorsiflexing the patient’s foot and striking the Achilles 
tendon with a reflex hammer.
The Semmes-Weinstein 10-g filament as an assessment of 
touch pressure, a large-fiber function, can be used as a screening 
tool for DSPN.893 The filament is bent to a C-shape, applying 
pressure to the plantar surface of the great toe. Because of the vari­
ability in the sensitivity and specificity of the 10-g filament,894 it is 
recommended that a three-site test be done involving the plantar 
aspects of the great toe, the third metatarsal, and the fifth metatar­
sal. The ability to sense the 10-g filament on the soles of the feet is 
also frequently used by podiatrists as a screening tool for DSPN, 
although it is generally held that this is not sufficiently sensitive to 
diagnose DSPN.893
Diagnostic methods in routine clinical use
Clinical history
Diabetes is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy. Long diabetes 
duration, uncontrolled diabetes (high levels of hemoglobin A1c), obesity, 
dyslipidemia, hypertension, and age are risk factors for DPN. 
Clinical presentation
Positive symptoms (e.g., tingling, burning, and lancinating pain) and negative 
sensations, such as numbness, usually occur in a symmetric, distal-to-proximal 
formation, starting in the feet up to the calves and then progressing to the 
fingers. 
Physical examination
Temperature or pinprick sensation tests assess small-fiber neuropathy. Vibration 
tests assess large-fiber neuropathy. Monofilament tests assess ulcer risk. 
Small-fiber neuropathy usually precedes large-fiber neuropathy. Isolated small- 
and large-fiber neuropathy can also occur. 
Methods for clinical diagnosis of atypical presentations or in 
research settings
Nerve conduction studies
Electrodiagnostic measures of nerve conduction velocities in sensory (sural, 
peroneal, tibial) and motor (peroneal, tibial) nerves using surface or needle 
electrodes. Nerve conduction velocities and amplitudes drop with progressive 
large-fiber neuropathy. Abnormality (velocity or amplitude) in the sural nerve 
with at least one other nerve conduction abnormality signifies large-fiber 
neuropathy. Alternatively, a composite Z-score summation from multiple nerves 
is compared to normative values. 
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density is the gold standard for small-fiber 
neuropathy.44 Immunohistochemical tests can be done on skin punch biopsy, 
generally on the distal leg. Stained small fibers are counted and compared to 
normative values. Intraepidermal nerve fiber density drops with progressive 
small-fiber neuropathy. Morphologic (e.g., fiber length, branching, axonal 
swellings) and molecular (e.g., substance P, calcitonin gene–related peptide, 
and growth-associated protein 43) changes can be assessed. 
Diagnostic criteria
Hierarchical classification schemes rate the degree of certainty in the diagnosis, 
ranging from possible to probable to definite, using a combination of signs and 
symptoms (e.g., the Toronto Consensus Panel). 
Diagnostic methods in research settings
Corneal confocal microscopy
Noninvasive imaging of corneal fibers, which are counted and compared to 
normative values. Corneal confocal microscopy can also assess fiber length 
and branching. Studies suggest that decline in nerve fiber density can correlate 
with DPN progression. Sensitivity is 60.0% to 91.0%, and specificity is 40.0% 
to 87.0%. 
Hand-held electrodiagnostic device
A handheld point-of-care device is able to measure sural nerve conduction 
velocity and response amplitude in a few minutes. Sensitivity is 84.3% to 
90.5%, and specificity ranges from 68.3% to 86.1%. 
Sticker sweat detector
A sticker affixed to the plantar surface of the foot measures moisture (sweat) 
by turning from blue to pink. Sensitivity ranges from 65.1% to 100.0%, and 
specificity ranges from 32.0% to 78.5%. 
Instrument sweat detector
Measures conductance of chloride ions from sweat released from hands 
and soles of the feet after electrical stimulation of sweat glands. Measures 
sudomotor function in a few minutes. Sensitivity is 87.5%, and specificity is 
76.2%. 
Diagnostic methods for painful DPN in research settings
Quantitative sensory testing
Standardized protocols can measure the response to well-defined sensory 
stimuli. Parameters include thermal and mechanical detection; pain, vibration, 
and pressure pain thresholds; dynamic mechanical allodynia; and wind-up 
ratio, which assesses function in all fiber types (Aβ large myelinated, Aδ thinly 
myelinated, and C unmyelinated). 
Microneurography
A needle electrode measures spontaneous activity and stimulus-evoked 
activity of unmyelinated C fibers in peripheral nerves, usually peroneal. 
Irregular so-called saw-tooth baselines in abnormal nerves have been 
observed. This is a labor-intensive technique that requires cross-laboratory 
validation. 
Hoffman-Reflex rate-dependent depression
Differentiates pain of spinal disinhibition origin from pain of peripheral origin by 
measuring the deep tendon reflex response neural pathways. 
Functional brain imaging (fMRI)
fMRI uses different protocols, including the blood oxygen level–dependent 
(BOLD) response, arterial spin labeling, and connectivity analysis. This type of 
imaging relates these changes to both spontaneous and evoked pain states, 
illustrating the distributed cortical network involved in the discriminative 
and affective pain components, as well as the descending pain modulatory 
system.

Given that the glove-and-stocking distribution of the DSPN 
reflects nerve fiber length, when sensory loss reaches the midcalves, 
patients begin to perceive symmetric sensory loss of the fingertips. 
Examination of the upper extremity is commonly performed as 
outlined earlier for the lower extremity, except the dorsum of the 
index finger is used by the examiner.
In advanced cases of DSPN, examination will reveal wasting of 
the small muscles of the feet, with hammertoes and weakness of 
toe extension; in extreme cases, there is weakness of the anterior 
tibialis and the intrinsic hand muscles. 
Differential Diagnosis of Diabetic Neuropathy
The American Academy of Neurology suggests checking a 
serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, a B12 
level, and thyroid function tests in all patients suspected of 
having DSPN to exclude a paraproteinemia, B12 deficiency, or 
hypothyroidism as the underlying etiologies. If these are nor­
mal, and there are no atypical signs, the most likely diagnosis 
is prediabetic neuropathy or DSPN.890 The importance of per­
forming these screening tests was confirmed in the Rochester 
Diabetic Neuropathy Study, in which up to 10% of peripheral 
neuropathy in patients with diabetes was determined not to be 
secondary to diabetes.895
Importantly, a few clinical “pearls” can assist the clinician in 
identifying symptoms that are atypical for DSPN secondary to 
diabetes. Symptoms and signs of DSPN are sensory and symmet­
ric, and any convincing asymmetry evidence of motor greater than 
sensory involvement, or a rapid and aggressive clinical course, 
should lead the clinician to suspect an alternative etiology for the 
patient’s clinical presentation. In these atypical cases, it is essential 
to exclude other causes of neuropathy in patients with diabetes 
(Table 38.13).896

	3.	 Confirmed DSPN. The presence of an abnormality of nerve 
conduction and a symptom(s) or sign(s) of neuropathy con­

the ankle and/or abnormal thermal thresholds at the foot (both 
of the latter provide class 1 evidence). 
Graded Scores for the Classification of Distal Symmetric 
Polyneuropathy
Although DSPN is diagnosed at the bedside, several scores provide 
structure to the bedside examination and range from simple assess­
ments of large and small fibers to more complex assessments requir­
ing quantitative thermal testing, electrophysiology, or skin biopsies. 
These scores include the Neuropathy Impairment Score (NIS),898 
Michigan Neuropathy Screening Instrument Examination (MNSI-
E),899 Modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score (mTCNS),900 
Total Neuropathy Score (TNS),901 Utah Early Neuropathy Score 
(UENS),902 and Diabetic Neuropathy Examination Score, a modi­
fication of the Neuropathy Disability Score (NDS).903 A descrip­
tion of these scores is presented in Box 38.4, and the sensitivities 
and specificities are listed in Table 38.14. Questionnaire-based 
screening tools are also used, including the Douleur Neuropathique 
en 4 Questions,904 the Leeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symp­
toms and Signs,905 and the MNSI-Questionnaire899 (see Box 38.4). 
Electrophysiologic testing or nerve conduction studies, along with a 
referral to a neurologist, are normally not needed unless the patient 
has either atypical symptoms or signs.
The importance of the skin biopsy as a diagnostic tool for 
DSPN is increasingly recognized when no clear objective evi­
dence of small- or large-fiber dysfunction is present on examina­
tion.877 This technique quantitates small intraepidermal nerve 
fibers through antibody staining of the neuronal antigen protein 
gene product (PGP) 9.5. Prediabetic neuropathy and DSPN are 
accompanied by a loss of these small fibers in a distal-to-proximal 
gradient. It is minimally invasive (3-mm-diameter punch biop­
sies) but enables direct study of small fibers that cannot be evalu­
ated by standard nerve conduction studies. 
Treatment of Distal Symmetric Polyneuropathy
Treatment of DSPN is commonly divided into either direct dis­
ease-modifying therapies or treatment of pain, a common occur­
rence in patients with DSPN. Accumulating evidence supports 
the idea that disease-modifying therapies are distinct for DSPN 
in patients with T1D and T2D.906 In contrast, treatment of pain 
is not personalized to the type of diabetes, although emerging 
research indicates there may be differences in the pain phenotypes 
among the different types of diabetes.883
Clinical scales
These scales measure a combination of signs and symptoms and are used to 
screen for and monitor DPN progression.
Diabetic Neuropathy Examination Score
Eight-item examination tool that consists of muscle strength; muscle jerk reflex 
at the triceps; pinprick in the index finger and great toe; and vibration, joint 
position, and touch in the great toe. 
Michigan Neuropathy Screening Instrument Examination (MNSI-E)
A physical exam consisting of great toe vibration with a 128-Hz tuning fork, 
muscle jerk reflex at the ankle joint, monofilament testing, and foot exam 
(appearance, ulcerations). 
Modified Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score (mTCNS)
Includes six questions regarding impact of symptoms on daily living and 
examination of the loss of sensation to five modalities (touch, pinprick, 
temperature, vibration, and proprioception) in lower extremities. The mTCNS is a 
modification of the Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score, which included ankle and 
knee jerk reflexes and did not include gradation of symptom impact or severity 
of sensory loss. 
Neuropathy Impairment Score (NIS)
Examination-based measure that includes muscle strength in 24 muscle 
groups; jerk reflexes at the biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, quadriceps, and 
ankle; and sensation to touch, vibration, and joint position in the index finger 
and great toe. The NIS-LL is a condensed measure focused on the lower 
extremities. The NIS-LL+7 was developed specifically to measure impairment in 
DPN and includes nerve conduction studies of sural, tibial, and peroneal nerves, 
vibratory threshold at the great toe using quantitative sensory testing, and heart 
rate response to deep breathing. 
Total Neuropathy Score
Multimodality measure that includes history of sensory, motor, and autonomic 
symptoms; strength at major muscle groups; muscle jerk reflex at the ankle 
joint; vibratory threshold at the great toes bilaterally and right index finger using 
quantitative sensory testing; and nerve conduction studies of the bilateral sural 
nerves, right common peroneal, and bilateral posterior tibial nerves. 
Utah Early Neuropathy Score
Examination-based measure that includes muscle strength at the great toes; 
extent of sensory loss to pinprick and vibration in the lower extremities; 
proprioception at the great toes; muscle jerk reflexes at the ankle joints; and 
presence of allodynia in the toes or foot. 
Screening and assessment scales
Douleur Neuropathique en 4 Questions
Includes questions related to history of seven types of pain, loss of sensation to 
touch and pinprick, and hyperesthesia. 
Leeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs Pain Scale
Includes five questions related to type of pain and associated signs and 
examination of decreased sensation to pinprick and hyperesthesia. 
Michigan Neuropathy Screening Instrument Questionnaire (MNSI-Q)
Includes 15 questions related to history and neuropathy symptoms.50
