SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Disease-Modifying Therapy in Distal Symmetric Poly­
neuropathy. There are no U.S. Food and Drug Administration 
(FDA)-approved therapies that directly address DSPN as a dis­
ease entity. In the absence of pharmaceuticals, dietary and lifestyle 
interventions are recommended to modify the course of the illness. 
Glucose control has only modest effects, if any at all, on DSPN in 
T2D, whereas it is an important factor in determining the onset 
and progression of DSPN in T1D.906 Collectively, components 
of the metabolic syndrome are drivers of neuropathy in both pre­
diabetes and T2D. Thus, modification of factors beyond glucose 
control alone, including dyslipidemia, hypertension, obesity, and 
high waist:hip ratios, are required to effect a clinically meaningful 
change in neuropathy in both of these patient groups. Of interest, 
normoglycemic obese patients with the metabolic syndrome also 
have neuropathy, further confirming that glucose control alone 
is insufficient to address neuropathy pathogenesis in the patient 
with prediabetes or T2D.851
The 2017 American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommen­
dations are outlined in Box 38.5.907 
Treatment of Painful Neuropathy. Pain is a common pre­
sentation of prediabetic and diabetic neuropathy and is present 
in approximately 20% of patients with DSPN.908 There are no 
compelling studies to show glucose control is helpful in the treat­
ment of pain. In contrast, aggressive glucose control over a short 
period of time can result in debilitating pain syndromes in both 
patients with T1D and those with T2D.909 These pain syndromes 
are known as treatment-induced neuropathies, and the degree of a 
patient’s impairment correlates with the rate of change in HbA1c 
(Fig. 38.49),910 cautioning the clinician against achieving glyce­
mic control at a rate above 1% (about 8.6 mmol/mol) per month 
HbA1c.910 This observation is similar to the rapid acceleration in 
retinopathy observed with rapid correction of hyperglycemia and 
suggests a unifying microvascular component to neuropathy.
There are three FDA-approved drugs for the treatment of pain­
ful DSPN, pregabapentin, duloxetine, and tapentadol, with better 
evidence for duloxetine and pregabalin than the opioid tapent­
adol. In light of the current opioid epidemic in both North Amer­
ica and worldwide, opioid use is discouraged in the treatment of 
painful DSPN.
Both the American Academy of Neurology (AAN) and the 
European Federation of Neurological Societies (EFNS) have 
reviewed class 1 and 2 studies for the treatment of painful DSPN, 
including non–FDA-approved approaches (Table 38.15). In gen­
eral, three classes of therapies appear effective in the treatment 
of painful DSPN: the voltage-gated α2δ ligands (pregabalin, 
gabapentin), the serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors 
(duloxetine, venlafaxine), and the secondary amine tricyclic anti­
depressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, desipramine). Fig. 38.50 
provides a potential management algorithm for the patient with 
painful DSPN; Table 38.16 outlines the commonly used doses 
and range of side effects, noting that not all drugs are FDA 
approved for the treatment of painful DSPN. A simple rule is to 
begin with one drug from one of the three classes and maximize 
the dose of this drug to either side effects or known therapeutic 
dosage; if there is some clinical benefit, although not complete, 
then a second agent from a different drug class should be added 
for more symptom relief. This agent is again titrated slowly to 
either side effects or maximal known therapeutic dose. Although 
figures vary, this approach generally provides relief for at least 
two-thirds of patients.874 There is also emerging literature that 
coupling pain treatment with an exercise regimen provides even 
greater symptom relief.911 This approach to pain is recommended 
in the 2017 ADA position statement and the more recent 2022 
AAN guidelines.912
Addition of selected therapies may be considered for patients 
who do not achieve pain control with metabolic control, combi­
nation therapy, and exercise, as discussed in the older 2011 AAN

guidelines.913 Alpha-lipoic acid is an antioxidant that is used in 
Europe at a dose of 600 mg per day as an adjunct to the treat­
ment of painful DSPN.914,915 Capsaicin is a natural substance that 
locally depletes substance P, resulting in a loss of small fibers. Cap­

studies,917 although a Cochrane systematic review found no role 
for lidocaine in the treatment of painful neuropathy.918 Studies 
on the use of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) 
units are limited for painful DSPN but do support its use as an 
adjuvant therapy in treatment-resistant patients.919–921
The current clinical opinion, despite the approval of tapentadol 
for painful DSPN, is that there is no role for opioids in the treat­
ment of chronic painful DSPN and limited use, if at all, in acute 
painful DSPN, except possibly for the pain experienced with acute 
glycemic treatment–induced neuropathy. If pain management is 
not achieved without opioids, then referral to a pain clinic for the 
patient is recommended in the AAN guidelines on the treatment 
of painful neuropathy.912 
Other Diabetic Somatic Neuropathies: Clinical 
Features and Treatment Paradigms
Additional forms of diabetic neuropathies are presented in Box 
38.2. Cranial mononeuropathies occur primarily in the older 
population. Onset is usually acute and associated with pain, 
and the course is self-limited, resolving within 6 to 8 weeks. It 
is generally believed these neuropathies are secondary to vascular 
insufficiency.922 The most common cranial mononeuropathy sec­
ondary to diabetes is a mononeuropathy of the third cranial nerve, 
presenting as a complete third-nerve palsy with pupillary sparing. 
Less common are mononeuropathies of cranial nerves 4, 6, and 7. 
Because it is essential to distinguish these mononeuropathies from 
a more serious central etiology, including cranial aneurysms and 
stroke, neuroimaging is frequently required to confirm that the 
symptoms and signs are due solely to diabetes.
Mononeuropathies must be distinguished from entrapment 
syndromes, which start slowly, progress, and persist without inter­
vention (see Table 38.10). The most common entrapment site 
in patients with diabetes is the median nerve, although patients 
also experience ulnar, lateral cutaneous femoral, and peroneal 
nerve entrapment. Median nerve entrapment, commonly known 
as carpal tunnel syndrome, occurs three times more frequently in 
persons with diabetes than in the healthy population,923,924 and 
its increased prevalence in diabetes may be related to diabetic 
cheiroarthropathy,925 repeated undetected trauma (resulting from 
repetitive use of the hands), metabolic changes, or accumulation 
of fluid or edema within the confined space of the carpal tun­
nel.926 Diagnosis can be confirmed by nerve conduction studies or 
ultrasound.927 The mainstays of nonsurgical treatment are resting 
of the wrist, aided by the placement of a wrist splint in a neutral 
position for day and night use, and the addition of antiinflam­
matory medications. Surgical treatment consists of sectioning the 
volar carpal ligament.928 The decision to proceed with surgery 
should be based on several considerations, including severity of 
symptoms, appearance of motor weakness, and failure of nonsur­
gical treatment.929
Another distinct class of diabetic neuropathies includes the dia­
betic polyradiculoneuropathies. This disorder is known by many 
other names, including proximal motor neuropathy, diabetic

Clinical Features of Diabetic Autonomic 
Neuropathy
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy is secondary to dysfunction in the 
sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. The pathogen­
esis underlying diabetic autonomic neuropathy is generally con­
sidered to be similar to that of DSPN, with a distal-to-proximal 
dying back of axons due to multiple metabolic insults.933 Because 
of the widespread innervation pattern of the autonomic nervous 
system to critical organs, the symptoms and signs of autonomic 
dysfunction are varied, depending on the organ system. These are 
summarized in Table 38.17.907
CAN is clinically the most important of the autonomic neu­
ropathies because of its association with early cardiac arrhythmia, 
silent myocardial infarctions, and early mortality.934 CAN may 
present as lightheadedness upon standing, palpitations, frank syn­
cope, and a generalized sense of weakness. In very early stages, 
CAN may be asymptomatic and only identified by abnormal 
heart rate variability, either with deep breathing or upon standing. 
Later signs include resting tachycardia with a heart rate above 100 
beats per minute and orthostatic hypotension, defined as a reduc­
tion of more than 20 mm Hg in systolic or 10 mm Hg in diastolic 
pressure when going from a lying to a standing position.
Screening for CAN is recommended in all patients with dia­
betes with DSPN or other microvascular complications of diabe­
tes (Box 38.6).907 As with DSPN, there are no disease-modifying 
therapies, and patients with T1D are instructed to monitor glu­
cose control, whereas patients with T2D are instructed to focus

Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can involve the gastrointes­
tinal tract, resulting in esophageal dysmotility, delayed gastric 
emptying, and both constipation and diarrhea with frank fecal 
incontinence. Among these disorders, the best studied is diabetic-
mediated delayed gastric emptying, also known as gastroparesis. 
Although estimates vary, the disorder is more prevalent in T1D 
than T2D, with a prevalence of approximately 5% in patients 
with T2D.935 The 2017 ADA recommendations for the screening 
and diagnosis of gastroparesis are presented in Box 38.8.907 Treat­
ment of gastroparesis is multifaceted. Patients are instructed to eat 
multiple small meals with lower fat and fiber content and to dis­
continue any drugs that decrease gastric motility, such as tricyclic 
antidepressants or opioids. If these interventions do not provide 
sufficient symptomatic relief, patients can begin metoclopramide, 
the only FDA-approved drug for the treatment of gastroparesis. 
Patients should not take metoclopramide for more than 5 con­
secutive days, secondary to the risk of developing extrapyramidal 
symptoms, and even this short regimen should only be undertaken 
when all other interventions have failed.907 The risk of tardive dys­
kinesia increases with the duration of treatment and cumulative 
dose and may be higher in the elderly, in women, and in diabetes.
Sexual and bladder function are also under the control of the 
autonomic nervous system. Erectile dysfunction is common in 
men and may occur in up to 50% of men over the age of 40. Men 
with either T1D or T2D are more likely to experience erectile dys­
function than those without, with an increase in dysfunction with 
a longer duration of diabetes. Erectile dysfunction is further exacer­
bated by obesity, smoking, and hypertension, along with excessive 
alcohol use and selected medications.936 Although there is likely a 
component of autonomic dysfunction in most affected individu­
als, it is essential to address the modifiable risk factors, as outlined

earlier. The phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors provide a first line 
of therapy for erectile dysfunction; these drugs include sildenafil, 
tadalafil, and vardenafil.937 Additional therapeutic approaches 
include intracavernosal injections, vacuum devices, psychosexual

Bladder and lower urinary tract dysfunction can occur in men 
and women with diabetes. Symptoms include frequent urination 
with urinary urgency, nocturia, and a weak urinary stream. In 
older men, these symptoms can be attributed to benign prostatic 
hyperplasia but are frequently exacerbated by diabetes. Although 
estimates vary, studies suggest up to a twofold increase in lower 
urinary tract symptoms in men with diabetes.938 Urinary incon­
tinence occurs in 50% of middle-age women with diabetes; in 
several studies, the presence of diabetes is reported to significantly 
increase the risk of female urinary incontinence.938 This can be 
multifactorial and may result from multiple pregnancies, obesity, 
and medications, in addition to diabetes. The studies that directly 
link bladder and lower urinary tract dysfunction to autonomic 
neuropathy are listed in Table 38.18938 and suggest an association 
with bladder and lower urinary tract dysfunction with both CAN 
and DSPN. In both men and women, bladder and lower urinary 
tract dysfunction increase the risk of urinary tract infections.939 
As with all forms of diabetic autonomic neuropathy, patients are 
counseled to achieve glucose control and address other comor­
bidities, including obesity, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, that 
may contribute to the disorder.940
Hypoglycemic unawareness is another form of diabetic auto­
nomic neuropathy with significant patient morbidity (see Chap­
ter 39). Hypoglycemia is defined as a plasma glucose level of 
less than 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) without autonomic warning 
signs.941,942 In most patients, two categories of symptoms occur 
with hypoglycemia: neuroglycopenic and autonomic symptoms. 
Neuroglycopenic symptoms are directly correlated with a lack 
of available glucose for brain function, including hunger, altered 
mental status, confusion, perioral paresthesias, difficulty speak­
ing, diffuse weakness, and syncope. In more severe cases, patients 
develop seizures, become comatose, and (in extreme cases) die. 
Autonomic symptoms occur concomitantly and include diapho­
resis, tremulousness, pallor, palpitations, and generalized anxiety. 
Hypoglycemic unawareness is defined as the presence of neurogly­
copenic symptoms before or in the absence of autonomic warning 
symptoms.943
Counterregulatory responses under the control of the auto­
nomic nervous system are required to restore normal glycemia 
in response to hypoglycemia. These essential responses include 
stimulation of catecholamines (both norepinephrine and epineph­
rine), glucagon, cortisol, and growth hormone while inhibiting 
insulin secretion.944 These counterregulatory responses stimulate 
hepatic glucose production while decreasing glucose utilization 
in the periphery and collectively restore euglycemia (Fig. 38.51). 
Recurrent hypoglycemic episodes decrease the plasma glucose 
level that serves as the setpoint for activating the counterregula­
tory response in both patients with T1D and those with T2D.944

T2D on insulin therapy as 97.4% and 95.3%, respectively, with 
approximately 6.9 events per month in patients with T1D and 2.4 
events in patients with T2D.947
Regardless of the exact percentages, hypoglycemic unaware­
ness is common and a source of significant patient morbidity. 
There is a strong association between recurrent hypoglycemia 
and an increase in fatal cardiac arrhythmias.948 An analysis of

Pharmacologic treatment options begin with optimizing insu­

Levels of Excess Cardiovascular Risk Vary by Age

Cardiovascular Risk Associated With Prediabetes and 
Type 2 Diabetes
T2D in high-income countries is associated with an approxi­
mate doubling in cardiovascular risk compared to those without 
diabetes after adjusting for traditional risk factors, such as age, 
sex, smoking, adiposity, blood pressure, and basic lipids levels.965 
However, absolute risk in people with T2D is much higher than 
in those without because the development of T2D is also associ­
ated with the development of multiple other vascular risk factors 
beyond hyperglycemia. This concept is nicely demonstrated in 
a study of the UK Biobank where HbA1c levels across the non­
diabetes and diabetes range were related to future cardiovascular 
outcomes (Fig. 38.52). Here, the unadjusted risk in diabetes was 
nearly fourfold higher but reduced to around twofold higher after 
adjustment for traditional cardiovascular risk factors and BMI. 
This twofold adjusted excess risk thereby approximates the vascu­
lar risk imparted by hyperglycemia and other associated features of 
T2D not captured by the usual risk factors. Other meta-analyses 
have confirmed an adjusted cardiovascular risk of approximately 
twofold higher in T2D, with this risk being somewhat greater for 
fatal versus nonfatal vascular events.965

39.6–47 mmol/L), broadly equal to the prediabetes categoriza­

the Emerging Risk Factor Collaboration meta-analysis, which 
reported that fasting glucose levels between 110 and 124 mg/dL 
(6.1–6.9 mmol/L) are associated with a very modest HR of 1.1 
for incident cardiovascular events, whereas frank diabetes is asso­
ciated with a twofold higher risk.965 Collectively, these findings 
demonstrate that excess vascular risk in people with prediabetes 
is driven largely by factors other than hyperglycemia. In line with 
this, UK Biobank data showed that people with prediabetes were 
on average 3 years older, had a BMI that was 3 units higher (∼20 
lb [9 kg]), had systolic blood pressure that was 6 mm Hg higher, 
and a higher ratio of total cholesterol to HDL-c relative to their 
normoglycemia counterparts.966 They were also more likely to be 
smokers and live in less affluent communities. It is these character­
istics, therefore, that mainly explain the higher cardiovascular risk 
in prediabetes rather than the higher HbA1c per se. These reflec­
tions further imply that to meaningfully lower cardiovascular risk 
in people with diabetes, addressing several risk factors is required 
rather than just focusing on hyperglycemia. 
Age of Onset of Type 2 Diabetes, Excess Weight, and 
Cardiovascular Risk
As the obesity epidemic has expanded, increasing numbers of 
younger people have developed T2D, which is noticeable in many 
diabetes clinics. This is a concern because emerging research shows 
the age of diabetes onset to be a major determinant of life years 
lost from diabetes, attributable in large part to premature CVD.967 
Life years lost from diabetes are projected to be greater than a 
decade when T2D develops at under 20 years of age but around 
5 to 6 years when diagnosed in middle age, tapering to minimal 
difference when first diagnosed above the age of 70 years, as shown 
in a study from Sweden (Fig. 38.53).967 Similarly, a Chinese study 
suggested a near doubling of the risk for nonfatal cardiovascular 
events in those with early- (<40 years) versus later-onset diabe­
tes,968 and work from the Emerging Risk Factor Collaboration 
from 96 cohorts reported that every decade earlier diagnosis of 
diabetes (in mainly white populations) was associated with about 
3-4 years of lower life expectancy.969 This pattern of higher relative 
and lifetime risks in younger-onset T2D is thus consistent across 
several studies, races and ethnicities, and geographical areas.
A less well-known factor for higher lifetime risks in younger-
onset T2D is the greater difference in weight and thus the need for 
greater weight gain to develop T2D at younger ages compared to 
differences later in life, in keeping with greater insulin resistance/
ectopic fat. In a UK study, men with T2D between the ages of 20 
and 39 years were around 33 lb (15 kg) heavier than their age- 
and sex-similar counterparts without diabetes, and women with 
T2D were 53 lb (24 kg) heavier than their counterparts. However, 
in both sexes, weight differentials between T2D and nondiabe­
tes counterparts tapered the older people were when diagnosed 
with T2D for both men and women (Fig. 38.54). The need for a 
higher weight at younger ages of T2D diagnoses, in turn, drives a 
greater difference in systolic blood pressure and TG levels relative 
to age- and sex-matched counterparts without T2D.970 Younger 
onset of T2D is also accompanied by faster glycemic deterioration 
compared to those who develop it much later in life.971,972 These 
findings suggest young-onset T2D is a more toxic condition than 
T2D onset later in life. 
Ectopic Fat as an “Upstream” Driver of Excess 
Cardiovascular Risk in T2D
New research over the last 5 to 10 years demonstrates that patients 
with T2D can achieve disease remission.973 This introduces sev­
eral important concepts. Most people with T2D have excess liver 
fat, a change reported to be causally linked to T2D. It is thought 
that adipocyte insulin resistance and resultant increased lipolysis 
contribute to liver fat in the face of systemic hyperinsulinemia 
and continued caloric excess. Increased circulating fatty acids

accumulate in tissues such as the liver, where mitochondrial fatty 
oxidation capacity is overwhelmed. Excess liver fat, in turn, pro­
motes excess production and delivery of pro-atherogenic TGRLs 
into the peripheral circulation (Fig. 38.55).974,975 As a result, high 
TG levels are also a common feature of T2D and can be consid­
ered as another manifestation of ectopic fat in many individuals, 
as recently argued.976 Higher TG concentrations also drive lower 
HDL-c, in part via enhanced neutral lipid exchange, although 
recent human genetic studies and the failure of several different 
HDL-raising drugs to reduce myocardial infarction rates have 
called into question epidemiologic-based assumptions for a pro­
tective effect of high HDL levels. Furthermore, high TG levels 
contribute to a greater number of apo-B carrying particles (both 
VLDL and smaller LDL particles), notable because a recently 
reviewed series of genetic studies977 confirms it is the number of 
apo-B carrying particles that best explains lipid-associated car­
diovascular risk. Indeed, with the exceptions of the abnormal 
chylomicron remnants in type III hyperlipoproteinemia and lipo­
protein (a), all apo-B particles are likely equally atherogenic.977
Among other mechanisms, excess adiposity is also linked 
to ectopic fat in other areas (e.g., perivascular fat978), as well as 
hemodynamic perturbances (a rise in total and central blood vol­
ume979) that collectively contribute to an increase in blood pres­
sure levels and cardiac output in people with T2D or obesity (see 
Fig. 38.55). There is now ample evidence that weight loss reduces 
systolic blood pressure, with conventional evidence suggesting a 
decline of 1 mm Hg per 2.2-lb (1-kg) weight loss.980 In those 
not on antihypertensives at baseline, the DiRECT diabetes remis­
sion trial9 reported a rapid decline in systolic blood pressure after 
commencement of a low-calorie diet, too fast to be attributable 
only to a reduction in fat or muscle mass, and thus hemodynamic 
changes were likely relevant.981 Systolic blood pressure reductions 
were also seen in those who discontinued antihypertensives. Other 
pathways linking weight excess to risk of heart failure but inde­
pendent of systolic blood pressure are also emerging and discussed 
further in the following section. 
The Relevance of Other Commonly Discussed Risk Factors 
for Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease in T2D
Other than age of onset, several other factors contribute to the 
heterogeneity in cardiovascular risks in T2D. All are relevant to 
assessment of future cardiovascular risks. 
T2D Duration
The greater the duration of diabetes, the greater the cardiovas­
cular risk because hyperglycemia is causally related to excess risk 
in a manner consistent with cumulative exposure. In the British 
Regional Heart Study,982 men without prior myocardial infarction 
and with diabetes of mean duration of 16.7 years had subsequent 
coronary heart disease risks approaching those with prior myocar­
dial infarction but without diabetes, whereas men of the same age 
but with short mean diabetes duration (mean 1.9 years) had much 
lower risks. Of course, those with longer duration also had to have 
had earlier onset of diabetes, so it is often difficult to tease out the 
independent effects of duration from earlier onset of disease, but 
both are independently relevant. 
Presence of Microvascular Disease
The presence of microvascular diabetes complications signals excess 
vascular risk better than differences in usual risk factors measured 
at the same time, as demonstrated in the UK Clinical Practice 
Research Datalink.983 Furthermore, cardiovascular risks are even 
higher with the presence of two or three such complications.984 Of 
course, microvascular disease is also linked to longer diabetes dura­
tion and thus longer-term exposure to hyperglycemia and other 
risk factors, including, in particular, dyslipidemia and hyperten­
sion. That noted, the presence of end-organ disease, whether it is 
in the eyes, kidneys, or legs, may capture the cumulative exposure 
of many other risk factors that are also predictive of CVD but never 
fully accounted for by the measurement of distinct risk factors.
In recent guidelines, the presence of severe target organ damage 
has been listed to be equivalent in outcome risks as having a prior 
cardiovascular event. For example, the recent European Society of 
Cardiology (ESC) cardiovascular prevention guidelines985 defined 
severe target organ damage as at least one of the following:
 • eGFR of <45 mL/min/1.73 m2, irrespective of the presence or 
absence of albuminuria
 • eGFR of 46 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m2 and microalbuminuria 
(albumin-to-creatinine ratio [ACR] of 30–300 mg/g or 3–30 
mg/mmol)
 • Proteinuria (ACR of >300 mg/g or >30 mg/mmol)
 • Presence of microvascular disease in at least three different sites 
(e.g., microalbuminuria plus retinopathy plus neuropathy)
Prior epidemiologic studies confirm such features as strongly 
predictive of future outcomes.

Sex
This is a topic of great interest because considerable evidence 
supports that the relative risk of CVD increases more as women 
move from nondiabetes to diabetes than for men. Indeed, a 
recent meta-analysis suggested that after controlling for major 
vascular risk factors, diabetes roughly doubles occlusive vascular 
mortality risk among men while tripling risk among women.986 
However, relative risks should not be confused with absolute 
risks. Although relative risks often increase more in women with 
diabetes (relative to their nondiabetes counterparts), absolute 
risks in women with diabetes are not higher than in their male 
counterparts. Rather, the presence of diabetes appears to nar­
row or (in some studies) abolish the sex gap in absolute vascu­
lar risks.986 That noted, in other recent high-quality studies,987 
although relative risk increased more in women who had T2D 
versus non-T2D (because of a lower starting risk level), the abso­
lute gains in risk appear similar to those seen in men. Therefore, 
men with T2D continue to have greater absolute risks than do 
women with T2D.
Some researchers have proposed that any excess vascular risk 
imposed by T2D in women may be due to women requiring 
greater weight gain than men to develop T2D; women start 
from a point of lower T2D risk.988 This is likely because women 
have an ability to store more fat in gluteofemoral peripheral fat 
depots—or subcutaneous fat—whereas men store more fat in 
visceral fat depots. As a consequence, women require greater 
weight gain to start to spill fat into ectopic fat stores, includ­
ing the liver, compared to men. Accordingly, women without 
diabetes have lower liver fat levels than men and are more insulin 
sensitive. In a recent study, it was noted that in women, greater 
weight increase and hepatic fat accumulation are necessary for 
diabetes development than for men.989 By the time diabetes 
develops, liver fat levels have increased to equally high levels in 
men and women.
These latter observations may explain why other changes in 
risk factors relative to nondiabetes (in particular blood pres­
sure) are, on average, greater in women who develop diabetes 
than their male counterparts.970,990 The need for less weight 
gain in men to develop diabetes also explains why a higher 
prevalence of diabetes in middle-age men exists compared to 
women, a finding that seems true for multiple ethnicities.991 
Of course, men without diabetes have higher cardiovascular 
risks than age-similar women, and the location and pattern of 
excess body fat stores (more adverse in men) and related risk 
factors may in part explain excess cardiovascular risk in males, 
as recently reviewed.992 The summary of this latter review is 
that men and women with T2D deserve equal attention in risk 
mitigation. 
Ethnicity
For South Asian and Black patients, the median age of T2D diag­
nosis is around a decade or so earlier than that for White patients 
(Fig. 38.56).970
The reasons for this are not fully understood and are likely dif­
ferent in different ethnicities. In South Asians, ectopic fat levels 
in the liver are higher at lower body weight than in Whites993 in 
the nondiabetes state, suggesting greater adipocyte hypertrophy 
and inflammation and less adipocyte proliferation,994 in keep­
ing with greater waist-to-hip ratios in South Asians even at lower 
weight. South Asians therefore increase ectopic fat levels faster 
for a given weight gain, and there is also some evidence they 
have poorer β-cell function.995 In terms of cardiovascular risk, 
the evidence indicates greater coronary artery disease in South 
Asians with diabetes in high-income countries,996 which may 
be a result of a decade or more of hepatic insulin resistance and 
β-cell dysfunction, and consequent hyperglycemia, which also 
rises more rapidly in South Asians relative to their White coun­
terparts. In this way, the weighting of hyperglycemia for CVD 
is likely greater in South Asians with diabetes than their White 
counterparts (as greater overall exposure but less weight). How­
ever, such excess cardiovascular risks in South Asians with diabe­
tes compared to their White counterparts appear to be reducing 
over time, as recently reviewed.996 The reasons for this favorable 
trend are not fully established, but earlier diabetes diagnosis also 
means earlier prescriptions of statins and antihypertensives in 
this higher-risk group, at least in high-income countries, a pat­
tern that may be attenuating excess cardiovascular risks, even if 
glycemia levels remain less well controlled. Even so, more work

Diabetes as a Comorbid Condition to Preexisting Vascular 
Disease and Life Years Lost
Diabetes in the context of established vascular disease increases 
the risk of premature mortality. In an individual participant meta-
analysis, the presence of diabetes together with premature myo­
cardial infarction or stroke at the age of 40 years led to a near 
doubling of life years lost compared to having only diabetes, 
whereas when all three conditions coexisted, over 20 years of life 
were lost.997 Although life years lost were less when such diseases 
coexisted later in life, having diabetes plus myocardial infarction 
or stroke at 65 years of age led to a loss of nearly 10 years of 
life compared to a loss of 5 years in those with diabetes alone. 
These considerations, combined with evidence for significant car­
diovascular and total mortality benefits for some newer diabetes 
drugs (discussed later in the chapter), mean that it is important 
to check for undiagnosed diabetes in patients with existing vascu­
lar disease. Here, HbA1c testing, which can easily be done at any 
time, including during acute illness, should substantially increase 
opportunities for diabetes diagnosis in those with existing vascular 
disease. Relevant guidelines have ratified use of HbA1c in such 
scenarios.998 
Which Glycemia Measure Best Associates With 
Cardiovascular Risk?
The precise contribution of hyperglycemia per se as being a causal 
role in cardiovascular risk versus being a marker for insulin resis­
tance and residual factors not otherwise captured in people with 
T2D remains incompletely understood. However, hyperglycemia 
is a causal risk factor for vascular disease, as shown in T1D, and 
therefore continues to be an informative biomarker associated 
with increased cardiovascular risk in those with T2D, raising 
the question of which glycemic measure best captures this risk. 
This question has been debated in many cardiometabolic forums, 
and some uncertainty exists in current guidelines. For example, 
in the 2013 ESC Guidelines on diabetes, prediabetes, and CVD 
developed in collaboration with the European Association for the 
Study of Diabetes (EASD), HbA1c was included as diagnostic, but 
its measurement had to be accompanied by the measurement of 
fasting glucose998 or oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) if there 
was any doubt based on the results of HbA1c and fasting glucose 
because a number of factors, such as severe anemia, can meaning­
fully alter HbA1c results.999
The inclusion of HbA1c in diagnostic algorithms followed 
improvements in assay performances, but the need for paral­
lel fasting glucose and OGTT negated some of the advantages 
of HbA1c, in that it can be accurately conducted at any time 
of the day. Nevertheless, most cardiologists are now comfort­
able with testing for diabetes using HbA1c alone in most clinical 
circumstances.
A follow-up of patients in the Whitehall study, in which 
civil servants had repeated HbA1c and OGTTs performed, has 
added important new information that supports the primacy 
of HbA1c.1000 In their analyses, the authors noted that patients 
diagnosed with diabetes with OGTT but where HbA1c was not 
in the diabetes range had future cardiovascular and CKD risks 
that were not different from those of their nondiabetes coun­
terparts. By contrast, those with a positive OGTT confirmed 
by a diagnostic HbA1c did have a higher future risk for cardio­
vascular and CKD outcomes (Fig. 38.57). These data suggest 
HbA1c-based diabetes diagnosis is better aligned to future hard 
cardiorenal outcomes, and hence, HbA1c should be the preferred 
test in most circumstances. HbA1c superiority to OGTT may 
reflect its better representation of long-term glycemia or intra­
cellular metabolic processes. Of course, where patients have

Lowering Cardiovascular Risk in T2D: Role of 
Established Risk Factors and the Importance of 
Multifactorial Risk Reduction
Type 2 Diabetes Is Much More Than Hyperglycemia, So 
Multifactorial Risk Reduction Is Essential
As noted previously, although T2D is a disease diagnosed by gly­
cemic cutoffs, many other risk factors (many in turn linked to 
excess adiposity) are perturbed well in advance. These include dys­
lipidemia, hypertension, and hypercoagulability, all risk pathways 
variably linked to ectopic fat and greater insulin resistance. Such 
factors add to the cardiovascular risk in T2D and do so well before 
frank diabetes ensues. Hence, multifactorial risk management is 
required. 
Impact of Intensive Glucose Per Se on Cardiovascular 
Outcomes
Four landmark intensive glucose-lowering trials have been pub­
lished, UKPDS, ADVANCE, ACCORD, and the Veterans Affairs 
Diabetes Trial (VADT), all conducted before 2008. Their details 
are described in a prospectively planned meta-analysis published 
in 2009.1001 Overall, the aggregated results from these four tri­
als, which had variable inclusion criteria, suggest that intensive 
glucose control does not lower overall mortality relative to less 
intensive glucose control, and in some trials, mortality was higher. 
However, the meta-analysis does suggest that lowering HbA1c by 
an average of 0.9% lowers major cardiovascular events by a mod­
est 9% (1%–16%) and myocardial infarction by 15% (Fig. 38.58) 
(95% CI, 6%–24%), but with no evidence of benefit on stroke, 
heart failure, or cardiovascular mortality.
These trials used mostly more established diabetes drugs, such 
as metformin, sulfonylureas, and insulin (minor glitazone use in 
some), to improve glucose control, and understandably, hypogly­
cemia rates were higher by almost a factor of 2.5-fold in the more 
versus less intensive glucose-lowering arms. Given these classes of 
drugs have quite diverse actions, with only glucose lowering as 
common, they suggest that targeting glucose levels per se in peo­
ple with T2D only modestly affects cardiovascular risk in the short 
to medium term, with little evidence of mortality benefit over the 
same time course. Collectively, these data imply that although 
hyperglycemia is important to cardiovascular risk, glucose lower­
ing per se has at best a “slow burn” and modest benefit on nonfa­
tal myocardial infarction in T2D, findings that again reiterate the 
importance of multifactorial risk management. However, because 
hypoglycemia has adverse effects, increased rates of these events 
with older agents could offset the benefits of overall glucose lower­
ing. Multiple mechanisms have been proposed for why hypogly­
cemia may enhance cardiovascular risk, such as a proinflammatory 
effect.1002 That noted, a definitive link between hypoglycemia and 
cardiovascular risk remains elusive. 
Impact and Choice of Low-Density Lipoprotein 
Cholesterol–Reducing Drugs in Diabetes
Although LDL-c is often not elevated in patients with T2D, the 
number of atherogenic lipid particles (captured by apo-B levels) 
is. Multiple statin trials have been published in patients with and 
without diabetes. The seminal Cholesterol Treatment Trialists’ 
(CTT) Collaboration report in 2008 looked at the efficiency of 
cholesterol-lowering therapy in nearly 19,000 participants with 
diabetes in 14 randomized trials,1003 establishing that people 
with diabetes had similar benefits in all outcomes examined as 
their nondiabetes counterparts. Specifically, a significant 21% 
proportional reduction in major vascular events per mmol/L 
reduction in LDL-c was noted for people with diabetes (RR, 
0.79; 95% CI, 0.72–0.86), an identical point estimate in non­
diabetes. Looking at specific outcomes showed a 22% reduction 
in myocardial infarction or coronary death, a 25% reduction in 
coronary revascularization, and a 21% reduction in stroke per 
mmol/L LDL-c reduction in people with diabetes. The findings 
translated into 42 (95% CI, 30–55) fewer people with diabetes 
having a major vascular event per 1000 allocated statin therapy 
over 5 years (Table 38.19). An identical point estimate of 0.79 
was seen for the cardiovascular benefit of statins in patients with 
T1D, even though this was not nominally significant because 
of fewer patients with T1D and thus wider confidence intervals 
(0.62–1.01).1003
Statins are the mainstay of lipid reduction in T2D, and in 
many countries, statins are recommended to be commenced 
at diagnosis of T2D in those over 40 years of age. Over time, 
LDL-c targets have been pushed progressively lower based on 
trial evidence from high-intensity statins showing that even 
lower achieved LDL-c levels reduce cardiovascular outcomes 
further.1004 This means additional lipid-lowering therapy 
beyond statins is not uncommonly required in T2D, and here, 
ezetimibe has emerged as a very useful add-on therapy. Statin 
use has, however, been beset with multiple concerns over side 
effects, particularly muscle-related effects. A recent CTT Col­
laboration specifically evaluating this issue using individual 
participant data from all randomized trials has provided reas­
suring data because it suggests most (over 90%) of all reports of 
muscle symptoms by participants allocated statin therapy were 
not attributable to the statin.1005
Statins have also been reported to increase risk of new-
onset T2D,1006 perhaps in part as a result of minor increases in 
weight.1007 However, the cardiovascular benefits substantially 
outweigh any small impacts of glycemic deterioration imposed 
by statins. Even so, this minor effect of statins should be used to 
motivate patients to take lifestyle changes more seriously.
Ezetimibe is a non-statin that works to lower reabsorption 
of cholesterol in the small intestine and can reduce LDL-c lev­
els by around 20% to 25% on top of statins. In the Improved 
Reduction of Outcomes: Vytorin Efficacy International Trial 
(IMPROVE) trial,1008 conducted in over 18,000 participants 
hospitalized for an acute coronary syndrome within the pre­
ceding 10 days and with an LDL-c level of 50 to 100 mg/
dL (1.3–2.6 mmol/L), the group randomized to simvastatin-­
ezetimibe had a median time-weighted average LDL-c of 54 
mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) versus 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) in the 
simvastatin-monotherapy group. Overall, relative risk reduc­
tion was 0.94 (95% CI, 0.89–0.99) for the primary endpoint 
of a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial 
infarction, unstable angina requiring rehospitalization, coro­
nary revascularization (≥30 days after randomization), or 
nonfatal stroke in those randomized to simvastatin-ezetimibe. 
Absolute risk reduction was 2%, giving a number needed 
to treat (NNT) of 50. However, the benefits appeared more 
marked in the diabetes subgroup. Here, simvastatin-ezetimibe 
reduced the 7-year Kaplan-Meier primary endpoint event rate 
by 5.5% absolute (HR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.78–0.94) relative to

very few side effects and can be given at any time of the day, it 
is an excellent add-on to statins where the maximal statin dose 
is not reached as a result of apparent side effects of statins or 
where more LDL-c lowering is desired. A useful way to con­
sider ezetimibe’s benefit on LDL-c is to understand that its 
addition is equivalent to more than tripling the dose of a statin.
Finally, proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 
(PCSK9) inhibitors have emerged as a new class of injectable 
drugs to lower LDL-c in patients at elevated cardiovascular 
risk. Currently licensed drugs include monoclonal antibodies 
(and more recently, small [PCSK9]-interfering mRNA) that 
inhibit PCSK9, a molecule that normally functions to degrade 
intracellular LDL-c receptors in the liver. These drugs increase 
expression of hepatic LDL-c receptors and reduce LDL-c by 
around 50% to 60%. They work well in patients with T2D 
regardless of differing baseline characteristics1009 and have been 
shown to lower vascular events—a composite of cardiovascu­
lar death, myocardial infarction, stroke, hospital admission for 
unstable angina, or coronary revascularization—by 17% (95% 
CI, 7%–25%) for evolocumab in T2D in FOURIER.1010 In 
the Odyssey trial, the PCSK9 inhibitor alirocumab resulted in 
a 16% (3%–26%) risk reduction in the primary endpoint—
a composite of death from coronary heart disease, nonfatal 
myocardial infarction, fatal or nonfatal ischemic stroke, or 
unstable angina requiring hospital admission—in people with 
T2D, similar to the effect of alirocumab in patients with nor­
moglycemia.1011 However, because patients with diabetes had 
a greater absolute risk, they had near twice the absolute risk 
reduction (2.3%, 95% CI, 0.4–4.2) than in those with predia­
betes (1.2%, 0.0–2.4) or normoglycemia (1.2%, −0.3 to 2.7; 
absolute risk reduction pinteraction = 0.0019). Unlike statins, 
neither evolocumab nor alirocumab increased the risk of new-
onset diabetes.
In most guidelines, many patients above 40 years of age with 
T2D, irrespective of measured risk, are recommended for a mod­
est-dose statin. This more aggressive use of statins in patients with 
T2D reflects their higher atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease 
(ASCVD) risk for a given LDL-c compared to those without T2D. 
Also, in most guidelines, more intensive statins are recommended 
in T2D when residual cardiovascular risk remains elevated or in 
the presence of severe target organ damage or established CVD. 
Presently, PCSK9 inhibitors are indicated only in a minority of 
patients with diabetes and established CVD, usually when the 
maximal statin dose is not achievable or because of complete statin 
intolerance. 
Impact of Systolic Blood Pressure Reduction
Over 4.2 years of median follow-up, a reduction of 5 mm Hg 
in systolic blood pressure decreases the risk of major cardio­
vascular events in those with and without T2D, as shown in a 
recent comprehensive meta-analysis of data collated from 51 
randomized clinical trials published between 1981 and 2014 
and involving 358,533 participants (58% men), among whom 
103,325 (29%) had known T2D at baseline.1012 The relative 
treatment effect is weaker in those with T2D (HR, 0.94; 95% 
CI, 0.91–0.98) compared to those without (HR, 0.89; 95% 
CI, 0.87–0.92; pinteraction = 0.0013). However, because of the 
higher absolute cardiovascular risk among participants with 
T2D, absolute risk reductions did not differ substantially 
between people with and without diabetes (Fig. 38.59). There 
was also no reliable evidence for heterogeneity of treatment 
effects by baseline systolic blood pressure in either group. These 
findings do not support adoption of differential blood pres­
sure thresholds, intensities of blood pressure lowering, or drug 
classes to be used in people with and without T2D, at least in 
terms of preventing major cardiovascular events. This is a fun­
damental change to prior thinking and should help improve 
care going forward. That noted, ACEis or ARBs are preferred 
first-line agents in T2D for their protective effects against kid­
ney damage, although recent guidelines suggest starting with 
combined blood pressure treatment with two agents at a lower 
dose rather than one agent at a higher dose.

Comparing Impact of Intensive Glucose Lowering Versus 
Targeting Low-Density Lipoprotein or Systolic Blood 
Pressure Based on Meta-analyses
The relative benefits of the three main pharmacologic risk-
reducing modalities—glucose, LDL-c, or systolic blood pres­
sure—for cardiovascular risk reduction were assessed in a 2009 
meta-analysis of intensive glucose-lowering trials.1013 Their 
results, shown in Fig. 38.60, nicely illustrate the importance of 
systolic blood pressure and LDL-c control, being demonstrably 
more powerful than intensive glucose control in lowering car­
diovascular risk in people with T2D in trials done at different 
times. However, because all three interventions reduced risks 
and glycemia reductions also benefit microvascular complica­
tions, the need for multifactorial risk reduction is once again 
advanced in T2D. 
Multifactorial Risk Reduction—A Randomized 
Trial
The high clinical value of treating multiple cardiovascular risk 
factors simultaneously was demonstrated by a 53% (95% CI, 
27%–76%) lower risk of cardiovascular events over 7.8 years of 
follow-up in the intensive multifactorial risk therapy arm com­
pared to conventional treatment in the Steno-2 study of 160 ran­
domized patients with T2D and albuminuria.1014 The patients in 
the intensive arm achieved a systolic blood pressure that was 11 
mm Hg lower and a reduction in LDL-c of nearly 39 mg/dL (1 
mmol/L) but only a 0.7% relative reduction in HbA1c compared 
to the conventional therapy arm. The intensive therapy group also 
reported greater improvement in some lifestyle behaviors, and 
more were prescribed aspirin. Although the study was modest in

Trends in Cardiovascular Risks and Causes of 
Death in T2D in High-Income Countries
Cardiovascular Risks Had Been Declining From the Late 
1990s Onward
The progressive increase in statin and blood pressure therapy use 
in people with T2D from the late 1990s onward, combined with 
earlier diagnosis, has driven down cardiovascular event rates in 
this disease. If one considers data from the United States, a pat­
tern of substantially lowering rates for myocardial infarction and 
stroke in patients with diabetes has been noted over the past 2 
decades,1015 although such events still remain far in excess of those 
seen in individuals without diabetes (Fig. 38.61A,B). Similar data 
are found in European countries. For example, a Swedish study 
with data covering the period between 1998 and 2013 demon­
strated a greater (44% vs. 29%) relative risk reduction for hospi­
talizations for CVD in patients with T2D than their nondiabetes 
counterparts (see Fig. 38.61C,D).1016
The reductions in cardiovascular event rates and cardiovas­
cular deaths have been so marked over the past few decades 
that cancer is now reported as the leading contributor to 
diabetes-related deaths in the United Kingdom.1017 Similarly, as 
cardiovascular mortality has declined in Sweden, cancer deaths 
are predicted to become the largest cause of death in T2D by 
2030.1018 That said, a recent report from the United States 
noted that vascular deaths have declined in both individuals 
with diabetes and in those without. In this study, the percent­
age of total deaths in the United States attributable to vascular 
causes declined from around 48% to 34% in people with dia­
betes and from 45% to 31% in those without from 1988 to 
2015.1019 The percentage of deaths attributable to cancer was 
stable in both groups, and thus proportionately more deaths are 
now also attributable to nonvascular and noncancer causes.1019 
The consequence of such changes is a substantial rise in life 
expectancy for people with diabetes, and it is this, more than 
changes in incidence, that has increased diabetes prevalence in 
high-income countries. 
Diversification of Outcomes
In general, as cardiovascular events and deaths have declined, there 
has also been a diversification in the types of vascular outcomes 
occurring in people with diabetes in high-income countries. Indeed, 
heart failure (14.1%) and peripheral arterial disease (16.2%) out­
comes are now the most common first “vascular” outcomes in 
patients with T2D, with myocardial infarction and stroke1020 being 
progressively less frequent, as shown in a recent analysis of data from 
the United Kingdom (Fig. 38.62). Thus, the advent of increasingly 
greater multifactorial risk reduction in people with T2D has led 
not only to lower vascular deaths but also to meaningful changes 
in the profile of vascular outcomes seen in high-income countries. 
Additionally, people with diabetes are now living sufficient lifespans 
to have other chronic complications related to aging, such as heart 
failure, osteoporosis and cognitive decline. 
Recent Stagnation in Cardiovascular Gains and a 
Potential for Reversal?
There are several cautionary notes to consider when evaluating the 
epidemiologic data on CVD in patients with T2D. First, reduc­
tions in mortality in T2D may have been far less in people with 
younger onset of diabetes,1019 emphasizing the need for more 
aggressive risk management in this group, a group notably expe­
riencing greater socioeconomic challenges and often neglected for 
multifactorial risk reduction. Secondly, recent evidence from the 
United States suggests a slight deterioration in glycemic and blood 
pressure control in people with diabetes when comparing 2015 to 
2018 to the 2007 to 2010 period, whereas lipid control has leveled 
off.1021 These data suggest cardiovascular risk reductions may have 
stagnated over the past decade or may even have worsened in the 
United States. In a preliminary analysis of data from the CDC, 
the authors of a viewpoint1022 suggested there may be a resurgence 
in diabetes-related complications, including cardiovascular out­
comes, perhaps most evident in younger people with T2D, and 
that better surveillance is needed to monitor and determine the 
reasons for such trends. 
Heart Failure in Type 2 Diabetes Has Come to the Fore
Although there have been clear gains in the prevention of athero­
sclerotic disease in T2D in high-income countries, there is now 
better recognition of heart failure risks in T2D,1023 in part because 
of the results of recent outcome trials in which sizeable reductions 
in the risk of heart failure hospitalization have been seen, as dis­
cussed further in this section.
Overall, risks for heart failure are around two- to threefold 
higher in people with T2D than in the general population, and 
there is a greater weighting for excess adiposity and kidney disease 
in the prediction of heart failure than for general CVD. Going 
forward, guidelines are likely to recommend that health care 
providers more often consider heart failure signs (ankle swelling, 
raised jugular venous pressure [JVP]) and ask about the symp­
toms of heart failure in their patients with T2D. If any clinical 
suspicions are aroused, then measurement of N-terminal prohor­
mone of brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) as a screening 
test, and additional workup as needed, is appropriate.1024 Routine 
testing of NT-proBNP in all patients with T2D is generally unaf­
fordable in most health care systems. Heart failure with preserved 
ejection fraction and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction 
are both more common in T2D. SGLT2is lower the risks of heart 
failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death across the spec­
trum of ejection fractions1025–1027 and are becoming the standard 
of care in addition to other established heart failure treatments for

Pandemic-Related Issues
Finally, the recent COVID-19 pandemic, which adversely affected 
people with diabetes particularly hard (greater mortality and mor­
bidity for reasons not fully understood),1028 could have further 
impaired or reversed recent cardiovascular gains in diabetes. This 
could be a result of both direct effects of the virus or COVID-19 
in survivors or pandemic-related treatment and surveillance per­
turbances. However, it will be several years before we fully under­
stand such impacts because longer-term epidemiologic data are 
needed to robustly dissect such trends. 
Impact of Drugs for Diabetes on Cardiovascular 
Outcomes: Old and New
For many years, the three main classes of drugs available to treat 
hyperglycemia were metformin, sulfonylurea, and insulin. Several 
new classes of drugs are now licensed for the treatment of patients 
with diabetes. From a cardiovascular perspective, SGLT2i and the 
GLP-1RAs have accumulated considerable evidence for roles in 
reducing adverse cardiovascular outcomes. The relevant data and 
potential mechanisms underpinning their benefits are discussed 
here. However, a summary of the cardiovascular risks associated 
with other diabetes drugs is first usefully discussed.
Metformin
Metformin remains the first-line diabetes drug in many parts 
of the world. It has a long track record of safety and is inex­
pensive. It is an excellent glucose-lowering agent that does not 
cause weight gain (and may cause weight loss) or potentiate 
hypoglycemia. The UKPDS trial identified a cardiovascular 
benefit for metformin, but this evidence stemmed from a sub­
group analysis and involved very low numbers of patients and 
events,1029 such that the medical community remains skeptical 
about the certainty of the observation. Moreover, subsequent 
meta-analyses of all randomized trials using metformin have 
not added additional support for a metformin-associated car­
diovascular benefit.1030 
Sulfonylureas
In a recent large, randomized trial (Study of Linagliptin vs. 
Glimepiride in Type 2 Diabetes [CAROLINA]),1031 there was 
no clear benefit of the DPP-4 inhibitor linagliptin versus the 
sulfonylurea glimepiride: the primary outcome occurred in 
356 of 3023 participants (11.8%) in the linagliptin group and 
362 of 3010 (12.0%) in the glimepiride group (HR, 0.98; 
95.47% CI, 0.84–1.14). Because DPP-4 inhibitors have not 
been shown to lower ASCVD risk compared to placebo (see 
later discussion), by extension, glimepiride is unlikely to do 
so either. However, because DPP-4 inhibitors, including lina­
gliptin,1032 are largely safe with respect to CVD (as discussed 
later), glimepiride must be safe and should be the preferred 
sulfonylurea.

CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
Insulin
The Outcome Reduction With an Initial Glargine Intervention 
(ORIGIN) trial (n = 12,537 people) showed that basal insulin 
did not lower cardiovascular risk compared to standard care when 
given in early diabetes or prediabetes.1033 Incident cardiovascu­
lar outcomes rates were 2.94 and 2.85 per 100 person-years in 
the insulin-glargine and standard-care groups, respectively, for the 
first coprimary cardiovascular outcomes of nonfatal myocardial 
infarction, nonfatal stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes 
and these events plus revascularization or hospitalization for heart 
failure (HR, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.94–1.11; p = 0.63). 
Dipeptidyl Peptidase 4 (DPP-4) Inhibitors
This class of drugs interferes with the breakdown of the incretin, 
GLP-1. However, they reduce glucose relatively modestly. Four 
DPP-4 inhibitor outcome trials testing alogliptin, saxagliptin, 
sitagliptin, and lingagliptin1032,1034–1036 failed to demonstrate any 
superiority compared to placebo in patients with T2D and high 
cardiovascular risk. In addition, there was an unexpected higher 
risk of hospitalization for heart failure with saxagliptin in the Saxa­
gliptin Assessment of Vascular Outcomes Recorded in Patients with 
Diabetes Mellitus (SAVOR)–Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarc­
tion 53 (SAVOR-TIMI-53) trial, which remains incompletely 
understood but has not been seen with other DPP-4 inhibitors.1035 
Pioglitazone
In the Prospective Pioglitazone Clinical Trial in Macrovascular 
Events (PROACTIVE) trial, pioglitazone (a thiazolidinedione or 
peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor [PPAR]-gamma activa­
tor) reduced the secondary outcome composite of all-cause mor­
tality, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and stroke in patients with 
T2D who had a high risk of cardiovascular events.1037 Heart fail­
ure risk increased significantly even if the absolute risk escalation 
was relatively low. In a subsequent pioglitazone trial called Insulin 
Resistance Intervention after Stroke (IRIS), pioglitazone lowered 
stroke and myocardial infarction risks in patients with prediabetes 
and insulin resistance.1038
Pioglitazone is, however, less commonly used compared to 
alternatives now available because of its side effects. Pioglitazone 
causes weight gain; even though this occurs by increasing meta­
bolically favorable subcutaneous fat stores and reducing ectopic 
fat, which may be one of the main mechanisms for its atheroscle­
rotic benefit, most patients do not like to gain more weight. Piogl­
itazone also increases fracture risks and heart failure risks in people 
with diabetes, the latter thought to be a result of the increase in 
total body water.
Even so, pioglitazone is still used in some patients, and these 
trials have also helped advance the idea that some drugs can have 
differential effects on atherosclerosis, on the one hand, and heart 
failure, on the other, suggesting that the pathophysiologic pro­
cesses underpinning these outcomes can be differentially influ­
enced, depending on the mode of action of specific drugs. 
Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 Inhibitors (SGLT2is)
SGLT2is increase glucose and sodium loss in the kidneys via 
inhibition of relevant channels, as their name implies.1039 The 
trials of these agents have had a profound effect on cardiometa­
bolic disease thinking and management. A recent meta-analysis 
of five SGLT2i outcome trials in patients with T2D reported that 
this class lowers MACE rates modestly (around 10%), signifi­
cant in those with prior atherosclerotic CVD (at 11%) but not 
those without (Fig. 38.63A). However, the results showed a far 
greater SGLT2i-induced reduction in the risk of incident heart 
failure hospitalization in those with (by 30%) and without (by 
37%) prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular events (see Fig. 38.63B). 
In addition, these drugs also improve CKD outcomes and slow 
decline in the eGFR over time, suggesting meaningful renal-
protective properties, subsequently confirmed in CKD-dedicated 
trials.1040,1041 They have also been shown to reduce the primary 
outcomes of heart failure or cardiovascular death in people with 
heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)1042,1043 and 
preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)1025,1026 in recent trials that 
have established SGLT2is as foundational in the treatment of such 
patients, with and without T2D.
The SGLT2i drugs with the best benefit-to-safety ratio appear 
to be empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, although canagliflozin is 
also licensed for some indications. Based on these results, and the 
fact that SGLT2is are given orally once a day and help to lower 
weight, blood pressure, and glucose levels and do not cause hypo­
glycemia in the absence of insulin provisional therapy, they are 
progressively being used earlier in the life course of diabetes, com­
monly second or third line, but even first line in some countries. 
They do, however, increase the risks of genital infections (often 
easily treated and preventable by good urinary hygiene) and of 
euglycemia diabetic ketoacidosis by around twofold. The latter is 
more of a concern, but better education of patients with advice 
to temporarily stop drugs when unable to eat or drink normally 
when ill (so-called sick-day rules) can help reduce such outcomes. 
SGLT2i Trial Findings Forced a Relook at Mechanisms 
Linking T2D to Cardiorenal Complications
The benefits of SGLT2is on cardiorenal outcomes were not widely 
predicted, especially the sizeable reductions in heart failure and 
renal outcomes, as well as notable reductions in cardiovascular 
deaths. Trial analyses also showed such benefits did not depend on 
baseline HbA1c values or their reduction but rather correlated best 
to increases in hematocrit. Although association does not prove 
causation, such findings initially suggested hemoconcentration 
secondary to fluid loss might be somewhat relevant to the car­
diorenal benefits of this class. These data, allied to opposite find­
ings for pioglitazone on heart failure risks (a drug that has been 
reported to increase total body water1044,1045) collectively suggest 
patients with diabetes are exquisitely sensitive to changes in body 
fluid. Consequently, hemodynamic pathways have gained more 
consideration as risk pathways for cardiorenal risk disease in T2D, 
as recently argued by Sattar and McGuire (Fig. 38.64). There may 
be other favorable hemodynamic and metabolic effects of this class 
of drugs, discussed in recent excellent reviews1046,1047 and further 
later in this chapter.
At the same time, the role of obesity in the development of heart 
failure and CKD complications in diabetes, and more broadly, 
has also come more into focus. In a recent epidemiologic analy­
sis, although HbA1c levels were similarly associated with incident 
myocardial infarction and heart failure rates in Swedish patients 
with diabetes, higher BMI levels were much more strongly linked 
to incident heart failure than to incident myocardial infarction 
(Fig. 38.65).1048 Genetic mendelian randomization analyses also 
suggest BMI to be more strongly linked to incident heart failure 
than to myocardial infarction. 
Summarizing Current State of Knowledge of Actions of 
SGTL2is—Hemodynamic Effects
It has also been established that SGLT2i benefits on cardiore­
nal outcomes are also seen in patients without diabetes. Hence, 
1560
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
multiple other actions must operate, and chief among these may 
be early hemodynamic effects secondary to loss of fluid from 
interstitial and/or extracellular compartments, in turn contribut­
ing to lessening of glomerular hyperfiltration and adverse cardiac 
remodeling.1049–1051 Randomized trials have also now variably 
shown reductions in extracellular fluid volume in myocardial1052 
and renal tissues,1053 both estimated by MRI, as well as surrogate 
evidence of reduced renal perfusion. Although these studies are 
not definitive, they are generally consistent. 
SGLT2is—Mimicking Starvation and Hypoxia to Effect 
Positive Cellular Health
More recently, cellular changes arising from SGLT2i actions on 
nutrient fluxes have been proposed to play a key role in their car­
diovascular benefits (Fig. 38.66). It seems SGLT2is may, in part 
via their enhancement of glucose loss even in patients without dia­
betes, stimulate a nutrient-deprivation signal that leads to upregu­
lation of energy-deprivation sensors SIRT1 and AMPK. These two 
molecular changes, in turn, drive multiple downstream effects, 
the net effect promoting cellular repair mechanisms, including 
autophagy and proteostasis. These changes, in turn, reverse meta­
bolic harm and inflammation. Cardiac and renal disease appear 
to evoke a state of perceived nutrient overabundance, contribut­
ing to disease progression.1054,1055 It follows that SGLT2is lower 
such risks by correcting some of these “nutrient overabundance” 
signals.
Because T2D is also a state of overnutrition—with excess adi­
posity being upstream and causally linked to dysglycemia and 
many other T2D perturbances1056—some of the same malfunc­
tioning cellular processes noted in cardiac and renal disease may 
link diabetes to its cardiorenal complications. In this regard, it is 
notable that the benefits of SGLT2is on hospitalization for heart 
failure and CKD outcomes appear similar in relative terms in 
patients with diabetes whether or not they have prevalent athero­
sclerotic CVD, prevalent heart failure, or CKD.1057

together. It suggests that although a traditional focus on target­
ing glycemia, lipids, and blood pressure has been very helpful in

the profound and rapid cardiorenal benefits of SGLT2is or their 
benefits in people without diabetes. 
Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists (GLP-1RAs)
GLP-1RAs are novel antidiabetic agents that imitate the 
actions of the incretin hormone GLP-1. GLP-1 is a small pep­
tide hormone released from gastrointestinal L-cells after food 
intake. It binds to the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R), leading to an 
incretin effect that enhances glucose-dependent insulin secre­
tion from pancreatic β-cells and inhibits glucagon release from 
pancreatic α-cells. GLP-1 also slows gastric emptying and, by 
stimulating GLP-1Rs in the brain, induces satiety. Differing 
penetration of the blood-brain barrier may underlie different 
weight loss properties of the various agents in this drug class. 
The net effect of GLP-1RAs is a reduction in blood glucose 
and in weight.
The vast majority of GLP-1RAs are delivered by subcutaneous 
injection, but the development of an orally available GLP-1RA 
has been made possible with the co-formulation of semaglutide 
and the absorption enhancer sodium N-(8-[2-hydroxybenzoyl] 
amino) caprylate (SNAC). Other oral GLP-1RAs are set to 
follow.
Eight cardiovascular outcome trials of GLP-1RAs in diabetes 
have now been reported. Their characteristics and effects on major 
adverse cardiovascular outcomes have been summarized in a recent 
meta-analysis.1058 Fig. 38.67 presents the findings in that meta-
analysis when one of the trials, called the Evaluation of Lixisena­
tide in Acute Coronary Syndrome (ELIXA), was excluded. ELIXA 
tested the short-acting lixisenatide (half-life of 2–3 hours), a weak 
GLP-1RA, and it is generally agreed that the once-daily dosing used 
in the trial was insufficient to have had a meaningful clinical benefit, 
in line with ELIXA’s uniformly null results.
In the seven other trials, GLP-1RAs reduced MACEs by 15%, 
cardiovascular death by 15%, fatal or nonfatal myocardial infarc­
tion by 12%, and fatal or nonfatal stroke by 19%. There were like­
wise modest improvements in the reduction of all-cause mortality 
and hospital admission for heart failure.1058
Other key observations from this meta-analysis and relevant 
trial data include the following:
 • No formal statistical heterogeneity between the effect of a GLP-
1RA in at-risk “primary prevention” patients (those without estab­
lished CVD) and those with CVD at baseline: HR 0.94 (95% CI, 
0.83–1.06) and 0.85 (0.78–0.92), respectively, p for interaction = 
0.18. However, the absolute and lifetime benefits of GLP-1RA 
are likely far less in those without prior atherosclerotic CVD, as 
recently reported in a post hoc analysis of the Trial to Evaluate 
Cardiovascular and Other Long-term Outcomes With Semaglu­
tide in Subjects With Type 2 Diabetes (SUSTAIN-6) and Peptide 
Innovation for Early Diabetes Treatment (PIONEER) trial.1059 
Therefore, most guidelines prioritize GLP-1RA in secondary 
prevention patients and recommend restricting GLP-1RA for the 
primary prevention to those at elevated cardiovascular risk (i.e., 
those with multiple risk factors, evidence of atherosclerotic disease 
on imaging, or elevated calculated cardiovascular risk).
 • There is no heterogeneity by type of GLP-1RA used—human 
versus exendin-4.
 • GLP-1RA benefits may occur on top of SGLT2is. The Effect 
of Efpeglenatide on Cardiovascular Outcomes (AMPLITUDE-
O) trial1060 recruited by far the most patients on prior SGLT2i 
(15%), and the cardiovascular benefits of efplegenatide (the GLP-
1RA tested in this trial) were found to be broadly similar whether 
or not patients were on baseline SGLT2i, with very similar point 
estimates for the primary outcome, as well as a number of sec­
ondary outcomes.1061 Pharmacoepidemiologic studies, although 
not alternatives to randomized trials, also seem to suggest that

an additive benefit of SGLT2is and GLP-1RAs is likely.1062 This

ferent molecular mechanisms of action, and both lower weight 
and blood pressure by variable amounts.1063 There is also prelim­
inary evidence that higher doses of GLP-1RAs1064 (or the dual

MACE and other outcome risks more than lower doses, which is 
of major interest because several ongoing trials are testing the car­

(Table 38.20), which also lead to far greater weight loss.
 • GLP-1RAs seem to have more consistent benefits in reduc­

an outcome not reduced by SGLT2is.1057 This finding implies 
that GLP-1RAs are potentially more antiatherosclerotic in their 
actions, whereas SGLT2is are more cardiorenal. Ongoing trials 
are testing the value of both drugs combined on outcomes, and 
an increasing number of patients with considerably elevated 
risk of future cardiovascular events are being prescribed both.
The agents with the best evidence include liraglutide, dulaglu­
tide, albiglutide, efpeglenatide and semaglutide, although albig­
lutide and efpeglenatide have not been licensed for use. There is 
some evidence that these drugs may lessen incident heart fail­
ure hospitalizations (HFH) but far more modestly (11%–12% 
reduction) than seen with SGLT2is.1058 
GLP-1RA Mechanisms of Action
As noted earlier, GLP-1RAs lower glucose and weight, but they 
also improve blood pressure and lipids, albeit modestly. These 
effects, in combination, may not account for all the antiathero­
sclerotic benefits of GLP-1RAs, and several other direct and indi­
rect vascular and myocardial effects have been proposed. The list 
of reported benefits derived from a range of preclinical and clinical 
models includes improving plaque stability and endothelial func­
tion, decreasing vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, cardio­
myocyte apoptosis, and myocardial fibrosis and oxidative stress,

guidelines1068 recommend their use after metformin is first prescribed 
in drug-naive patients, whereas the 2019 ESC guidelines1069 recom­
mend their use regardless of metformin in those with established 
CVD or with evidence of severe target organ damage. There is also 
consistent evidence for the use of SGLT2is in patients with heart 
failure or CKD, whereas GLP-1RAs are also mentioned in guide­
lines relating to the prevention of stroke.1070 Based on such guide­
lines, rates of SGLT2i prescriptions by cardiologists have progressively 
increased,1071 with the use of GLP-1RAs lagging somewhat behind.
The more recent 2022 ADA/EASD recommendations1072 (Fig. 
38.69) have gone further and now recommend either SGLT2is or 
GLP-1RAs in patients with existing ASCVD and T2D with no need 
to start metformin or consider HbA1c levels first. They also suggest 
the need to prioritize SGLT2is in those with prevalent heart failure 
or CKD, in line with the plentiful trial evidence summarized earlier.
Taking all guidelines into consideration, in those without prior 
myocardial infarction or stroke, GLP-1RAs are to be prioritized in 
patients with either multiple risk factors, evidence of some athero­
sclerotic disease on imaging, or elevated calculated cardiovascular 
risk score. Different countries or health authorities will make indi­
vidualized treatment decisions, taking into consideration costs and 
benefits of GLP-1RAs. For patients with T2D but no established 
CVD, early use may be appropriate. The GLP-1RA liraglutide 
demonstrated fewer cardiovascular events when added to metfor­
min in a randomized trial compared to a sulfonylurea, basal insu­
lin, or DPP-4 inhibitor in the Glycemia Reduction Approaches in 
Diabetes: A Comparative Effectiveness (GRADE) study, although 
there were too few events to draw firm conclusions.1073
Because SGLT2is do not lower the risk of MACEs in those 
without prior CVD but do lower incident heart failure hospital­
ization and incident CKD, their use in those without prior car­
diovascular events could be debated. Some organizations, such as 
the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in 
the United Kingdom, have, however, proposed basing the deci­
sion to start an SGLT2i on the use of a cardiovascular risk score. 
Those with a high risk for cardiovascular events should be recom­
mended to start an SGLT2i with proven benefits soon after start­
ing metformin.1074
As SGLT2is and GLP-1RAs come down in cost, they are likely 
to be used more often and earlier in the diabetes life course, given 
their cardiovascular benefits and benefits on weight, glycemia, and 
other risk factors.

SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Ongoing Trials of Interest and What the Future 
May Hold
One of the big unknowns in diabetes is whether its prevention with 
modest weight loss or its remission with larger-magnitude weight 
loss973 can lower future cardiovascular event risks. Given the pre­
ceding discussions, substantial weight loss should not only improve 
glycemia (which it does considerably, given the importance of 
ectopic fat1056) but also lower blood pressure, improve lipids, and 
improve many other less well-studied risk pathways implicated in 
the pathogenesis of cardiovascular complications. The findings bear 
out expectations, as perhaps best illustrated by the 10-year follow-
up of a trial comparing the outcomes of patients with long-stand­
ing diabetes randomized to either two forms of bariatric surgery 
versus medial therapy or intensive lifestyle.1075 Fig. 38.70A and B 
reports substantial differences in glycemic control and weight over 
the course of 10 years (by greater than 44 lb [20 kg]) between the 
medical and surgical arms and, linked to this, major improvements 
in glycemia, particularly marked in those randomized to biliopan­
creatic diversion, where the average HbA1c remained below 6.5% 
(48 mmol/mol) for the entire 10 years of follow-up
When the authors returned to look at outcomes, they noticed 
that whereas 11% of patients randomized to the lifestyle arm had 
macrovascular complications, none did in the surgical arms, and 
microvascular complications were also dramatically lower when 
comparing the lifestyle and surgery arms (61% vs. 5%) (see Fig. 
38.70C). Of course, the small number of events means this trial is 
interesting but far from definitive, and further outcome data are 
needed to prove the benefits of weight loss.
The importance of weight loss to lower cardiovascular out­
comes in diabetes had been weakened by the results of the Look 
AHEAD trial, which did not show that intensive lifestyle inter­
ventions improved outcomes in mostly women with diabetes with 
very controlled risk factors.1076 However, a post hoc analysis of 
those who had lost at least 10% of their body weight in the first 
year of the study had a 21% (95% CI, 2%–36%) lower risk of 
the primary outcome, a composite of death from cardiovascular 
causes, nonfatal acute myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or 
admission to hospital for angina.1077 These two studies, combined 
with plentiful evidence for benefits of weight loss on a range of risk 
factors and supportive evidence from Mendelian randomization 
studies on BMI and CVD,1078 do suggest large-scale weight loss 
should lower cardiovascular outcomes in the context of diabetes. 
Ongoing and Recent Trials of Interest to Advance 
Knowledge on Impact of Large-Scale Weight 
Loss in Diabetes on Cardiovascular Outcomes
Two trials are of particular interest. The first is Semaglutide Effects 
on Heart Disease and Stroke in Patients With Overweight or Obe­
sity Trial (SELECT),1079 which, although excluding patients with 
diabetes, does include many patients with prediabetes and prior 
CVD. This trial is randomizing patients with high BMI and prior 
CVD to high-dose semaglutide or placebo on top of standard of 
care. This trial recently reported out and demonstrated a 20% reduc­
tion in major adverse cardiovascular events with a rapid separation 
of Kaplan-Meier curves. There were also nominally significant ben­
efits for all-cause mortality and heart failure composite endpoint 
but these were not able to be claimed as such due to hierarchical 
testing. These results occurred with a 8.5% greater weight loss and 
in context of lower serious adverse events in the semaglutide group. 
The results thereby provided the first evidence that a weight loss 
drug can lower cardiovascular outcomes, though to what extent the 
direct effects of the drugs versus its weight loss effects explain ben­
efits remains debated. The second trial of note is A Study of Tirzepa­
tide Compared With Dulaglutide on Major Cardiovascular Events 
in Participants With Type 2 Diabetes (SURPASS-CVOT),1080 
which is comparing the effect of high-dose tirzepatide (15 mg), a
