a GLP-1RA per se on cardiovascular outcomes, a question now set 
up nicely by SELECT.
Looking to the Future in Type 2 Diabetes and 
Cardiovascular Disease
The last 20 to 30 years have witnessed a remarkable reduction in 
cardiovascular outcomes in people with diabetes in high-income 
countries, especially myocardial infarction and stroke, leading to 
relatively more heart failure and peripheral arterial disease. Impor­
tant goals for the future include the following:
	1.	 Maintain gains accrued over the past 2 to 3 decades in lower­
ing of lipid levels and blood pressure in high-income countries, 
along with better glycemic control, rather than slipping back, 
as some recent data suggest.
	2.	 Increase the use of diabetes drugs that lower cardiovascular 
outcomes, as and when recommended by relevant guidelines.
	3.	 Continue to study the relevance of large-scale weight loss on 
cardiovascular outcomes in people with T2D, which is now 
more achievable via a range of interventions (lifestyle, newer 
diabetes drugs, and surgery), and implement those that prove 
cost-effective in the longer term.
	4.	 Continue to determine novel mechanisms linking diabetes to 
cardiorenal outcomes, as revealed by SGLT2i trials, because 
this new knowledge may help the development of newer classes 
of drugs that more efficiently lower cardiovascular risks.
	5.	 Determine whether and to what extent the recent pandemic 
may have accelerated cardiovascular harm in people with T2D.
Fortunately, more tools are available to prevent cardiovascular 
complications in diabetes in terms of novel drugs that lower car­
diovascular risks, plus newer agents to lower lipids. There is also 
potential to help patients lose more weight with novel agents or 
more intensive lifestyle changes, although costs inevitably escalate.
At the same time, industrialization is leading to adverse lifestyles 
and to more diabetes and related cardiovascular events in people in 
low- and middle-income countries. To lower outcome risks in these 
countries requires the sustainable availability of at least cheap met­
formin, statins, and blood pressure drugs, along with better diagno­
sis of diabetes closer to true onset. Such changes, which need not 
be too costly or difficult, can lead to remarkable improvements in 
risk factors, as recently reported in Mexico.1082 Preventing obesity 
in low- and middle- income countries is essential to prevent rising 
long-term chronic conditions including diabetes. 
Cardiovascular Risks in Type 1 Diabetes
Although much more research has been done on cardiovascular 
risks in T2D, considerable evidence exists documenting excess risks 
in T1D. Dysglycemia is the strongest risk factor for CVD in people 
living with T1D, and because the median age of onset is around 
14 to 15 years of age, many with T1D will have accrued 3 to 4 
decades of hyperglycemia by the time they reach 50 to 60 years of 
life (the median age of onset of T2D). Thus, in those with T1D in 
whom glycemic control has been poorer, vascular damage leading 
to nephropathy or frank CVD is more likely to have occurred by 
middle age than in patients where control has been excellent.
An increased risk of CVD in T1D was first observed over 30 
years ago.1083 A contemporary large study in Scotland observed 
a relative risk of CVD of 2.3 in men and 3 in women.1084 The 
risk of CVD was highest among those with diabetic nephropathy 
(evaluated in this study by eGFR, linked in turn to poorer glyce­
mic control over many years, as well as other risk factors, such as 
higher blood pressure, excess weight, lifestyle, and family history of 
premature heart disease). As discussed earlier in the “Genetic Deter­
minants of Susceptibility to Microvascular Complications” section, 
the level of risk of overt proteinuria after 30 years’ duration of T1D 
at 27% is evidence that only a subset of patients are susceptible to 
the development of diabetic nephropathy. A role for genetic deter­
minants of susceptibility to diabetic nephropathy is more directly 
supported by familial clustering, with an estimated heritability of at 
least 40%. More recently, QRISK3, which included coronary heart 
disease, ischemic stroke, or transient ischemic attack as outcomes, 
demonstrated that men with T1D have a 3.4-fold-higher risk and 
women with T1D have a 5.6-fold-higher risk of CVD independent 
of other usual and novel risk factors.1085 However, this risk score 
does not consider diabetes-specific factors such as diabetes duration, 
glycemia levels, or albuminuria. Other work from Sweden suggests 
relative hazards and life years lost are greatest in those who develop 
T1D in younger life, such that development of T1D before 10 years 
of age resulted in a loss of 17.7 life years (95% CI, 14.5–20.4) for 
women and 14.2 life years (12.1–18.2) for men.1086 Life years lost 
were far less in those who developed diabetes in later life.
A risk score to help physicians determine 10-year CVD risk 
and thus potentially guide statin prescriptions was recently devel­
oped by researchers in Scotland and Sweden and includes both 
usual risk factors and diabetes-specific ones (https://diabepi.shin­
yapps.io/cvdrisk/).1087 This application also gives some indication 
of the likely benefits achieved with improvement in risk factors.
People living with T1D also experience around threefold-
higher risk for heart failure than the general population.1088 
Moreover, their 30-day mortality after admission for heart failure 
is greater than that for the general population or those with T2D. 
These observations mean health care providers should more read­
ily ask about heart failure symptoms and signs, especially in those 
with other risk factors for heart failure.
Treatment Approaches
Glycemic Control. Intensive glycemic control reduces the 
development and progression of microvascular disease in T1D 
and reduces the risk of long-term cardiovascular outcomes, as 
shown in the seminal DCCT/EDIC trial.1089
Glycemic control, achieving and maintaining an HbA1c of 6.5% 
to 7.5% (48 to 58 mmol/L), should be the goal for long-term care 
in T1D. This is feasible with structured education to effect best self-
management (in order to minimize the risk of hypoglycemia), access 
to regular specialist review, and use of intensive insulin regimens 
(including access to CGM and insulin infusion treatment and other 
novel technologies) (see Chapter 35). Tight glycemic control during 
the first decade of T1D is considered especially important, with evi­
dence of a longer-lasting legacy effect of sustained benefit. In reality, 
however, the majority of patients with T1D have suboptimal con­
trol. For example, in the United Kingdom, the median HbA1c levels 
were around 8.8% to 9.1% (73–76 mmol/mol), among the worst in 
Europe as reported in 2015,1090 whereas in the United States, only 
approximately 20% of patients with T1D had HbA1c below 7% (53 
mmol/mol) in a study of 31,430 patients from 2014 to 2016.1091
There is currently no proven role for adjunctive glycemic ther­
apy in T1D to lower ASCVD or its surrogates. Metformin is not 
uncommonly used in people with T1D who are also living with 
1568
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
excess weight, but although it helps modestly lower weight, no 
effect was observed on glucose control or the primary surrogate 
cardiovascular endpoint in a recent international trial.1092 
Lipid-Lowering Therapy
In a meta-analysis demonstrating the benefit of cholesterol-­
lowering therapy in diabetes, 1466 people with T1D were treated 
out of almost 19,000 patients with diabetes in the analysis.1003 
These data suggest that cardiovascular benefits in T1D are identi­
cal to those in T2D, with a 21% reduction in cardiovascular risk 
per mmol/L reduction in LDL-c.1003 Thus, LDL-c reduction is as 
important in people with T1D as in those with T2D.
Currently, there is no basis to support routine initiation of 
statins in patients with T1D age <18 years or in newly diagnosed 
cases age ≤30 years without any risk factors. People with T1D 
who have existing ASCVD or evidence of target organ damage, 
such as macroalbuminuria or CKD, should be offered statins 
with the option of intensifying treatment. Some guidelines take 
the view that all patients with T1D above the age of 40 or 50 
should be offered a statin, but this approach ignores the fact some 
people living with T1D at that age have no other risk factors, so 
such guidelines are not rigorously adhered to in clinical practice. 
An alternative to this approach would be to use a risk score to 
determine when to commence a statin. Also, lipid-lowering agents 
other than statins should be used in people living with T1D in the 
same way as they are in patients with T2D. In particular, ezetimibe 
should be used to reach LDL-c goals in diabetes in general on the 
supportive post hoc evidence from the Improved Reduction of 
Outcomes: Vytorin Efficacy International Trial (IMPROVE-IT), 
which noted a significant benefit in people with diabetes whether 
or not they had prior ASCVD.1093 
Weight Excess in T1D, an Emerging Issue
As weight levels rise in populations, some people living with 
T1D are also now considerably overweight, and this is leading to 
additional issues. For example, patients with T1D in the highest 
quartile of excess weight gain in the DCCT study had associated 
sustained increases in central obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipid­
emia, and blood pressure, as well as more extensive atherosclerosis, 
during EDIC.1094 The Coronary Artery Calcification in Type 1 
Diabetes (CACTI) study showed that people with T1D are also 
insulin resistant compared to nondiabetic subjects, and the degree 
of resistance is not related to current glycemic control, BMI, vis­
ceral fat area, waist circumference, or waist:hip ratio. Insulin resis­
tance predicts the extent of coronary artery calcification and may 
contribute to the increased risk of CVD in patients with T1D and 
individuals without diabetes.1095 It has been suggested that when 
coronary artery calcium (CAC) scores are above 100 Angstrom 
units, the risk is high enough to warrant a statin, but data support­
ing this are lacking. Whether adjunctive GLP-1RAs can be used in 
people with T1D to help mitigate weight excess and improve gly­
cemia is the subject of ongoing trials. If they do prove useful and 
are safe, the hope is these drugs may also offset the high ASCVD 
and CKD risks in people with T1D. 
Antihypertensive Therapy
Antihypertensive therapy aimed at a target blood pressure of 120/80 
mm Hg is established practice in T1D, with evidence of benefit 
from therapies that modify the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone 
system (RAAS) on the early development and later progression 
of microvascular disease in younger patients with T1D.1096–1098
Summary for Type 1 Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease
Chronic glycemia, measured as HbA1c, and age are the strongest risk 
factors for CVD in T1D. In addition, genetic factors assessed using 
polygenic risk scores are associated with the risk of subsequent CVD 
in T1D above and beyond the effect of established risk factors, such 
as glycemia, age, blood pressure, and lipids. Coronary artery disease 
polygenic risk scores are more strongly associated with CVD risk 
than LDL-c.1099 Rates of CVD are higher in patients with T1D 
with advanced DR, kidney disease, or CAN than in those without 
microvascular disease.1100 Weight gain in the intensive treatment 
group of the DCCT/EDIC study affected CVD outcomes only in 
the highest quartile of weight gain and started 14 years after the 
DCCT ended.1101 Intensive treatment of hyperglycemia to achieve 
HbA1c levels of 6.5% to 7.5% (48–58 mmol/mol) is recommended 
and is now possible for many patients using CGM technology. 
Antihypertensive treatment with therapies modifying the RAAS is 
recommended, with a target blood pressure of below 130/80. Lipid-
lowering therapy is also recommended. In the United States, statins 
are recommended for people with T1D with LDL-c above 160 mg/
dL (4.1 mmol/L) or LDL-c above 130 mg/dL (3.4 mmol/L) and 
one or more CVD risk factors. Because of the potential teratogenic 
effects, females should receive reproductive counseling, and statins 
should be avoided in females of childbearing age who are not using 
reliable contraception.1102
In the United Kingdom, statins are used in people with T1D 
who have existing atherosclerotic CVD or evidence of target organ 
damage, such as albuminuria or decreased eGFR. However, risk 
scores for assessing cardiovascular risk in T1D are now emerging 
and could be used to guide the need for lipid-lowering or other 
therapies in those without prevalent cardiovascular or kidney dis­
ease. Further work in this area is needed. 
The Diabetic Foot
Foot complications of diabetes, including ulceration and amputation, 
are associated with high mortality, yet diabetic foot ulcers are the most 
preventable late adverse outcome of diabetes.1103–1106 Elliott Joslin 
correctly noted in 1934, “diabetic gangrene is not heaven-sent, but 
earth-born.” The neuropathic foot does not spontaneously ulcerate; 
insensitivity, deformity, and unperceived trauma (e.g., inappropriate 
footwear) promote skin breakdown. Most amputations are preceded 
by foot ulcers. Increased appreciation of the complex pathogenesis of 
foot ulcers permits the design of screening programs for risk identifi­
cation, preventive education, and the design of multidisciplinary foot 
care programs. Much progress has been made, but suboptimal adher­
ence to current professional guidelines has prevented translation into 
a universal decline in amputation rates.
Epidemiology of Diabetic Foot Ulceration
Foot ulceration is common in both T1D and T2D. The annual 
incidence of foot ulceration is about 2% to 2.5% in Western 
countries.1107 Higher rates are found in select diabetes popula­
tions, including U.S. Medicare recipients (6%) and U.S. veterans 
(5%), and in the global diabetes population (6.3%).1107 Approxi­
mately 5% to 10% of patients with diabetes have had past or pres­
ent foot ulceration, and 1% have undergone amputation.1103 The 
overall incidence of foot ulceration was 7.8 per 1000 person-years 
for first ulcers and 11.2 for any ulcers in a recent population-based 
1569
CHAPTER 38  Complications of Diabetes Mellitus
study using data from the National Diabetes Register in Scot­
land.1108 The lifetime risk for development of a foot ulcer in a 
patient with diabetes is estimated to be 25% or higher.1103,1104,1107 
Multiple factors likely contribute to different rates of foot ulcer­
ation, including diabetes duration, smoking, dialysis, and other 
neurologic and cardiovascular risk factors. In experienced dia­
betic foot clinics, more than 50% of patients with new foot ulcers 
give a past ulcer history. Thus, foot ulceration is most common 
in patients with a prior similar complication. Patients with other 
complications of diabetes, including retinopathy and renal dys­
function, are also at increased risk for foot ulceration. Patients on 
dialysis are among those with the highest risk for ulceration and 
amputation.1109
Diabetes is the most frequent cause of nontraumatic lower 
limb amputation in the United States, and rates are 15 times 
greater than those in the nondiabetic population. More than 80% 
of amputations are preceded by foot ulcers, and reduced amputa­
tion rates occur after implementation of foot screening and edu­
cation programs.1110,1111 Implementation of strategies to reduce 
ulceration and amputation are necessary, and patients benefit 
from additional education on behavioral aspects of diabetic foot 
care, including awareness of ulceration risk, compliance with daily 
foot inspection, and the importance of non–weight-bearing with 
early foot infections.1112 Treatments to reduce cardiovascular and 
renal risk likely further reduce amputation rates, but this has been 
less clearly established.
Although a reduction in multiple diabetes-related complica­
tions was reported in the United States between 1990 and 2010, 
more recent data suggest the previously observed decrease in lower 
extremity amputations has now been reversed.1113 The importance 
of lower limb complications of diabetes is emphasized as a top 10 
condition on the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global 
Burden of Disability.1114 Furthermore, the annual costs of diabe­
tes foot ulcers are more expensive in terms of direct costs than the 
five most costly cancers in the United States.1107,1115 
Pathogenesis of Foot Ulceration
Foot ulceration results from multiple interacting component 
causes, none of which alone is sufficient to cause ulceration but, 
when combined, may lead to skin breakdown. A combination 
of two or more risk factors promotes diabetic foot ulceration, 
and the triad of component causes—neuropathy, deformity, and 
trauma—is present in 63% of incident ulcers. Edema and isch­
emia are also common component causes, as demonstrated in a 
North American/United Kingdom collaborative study of more 
than 150 consecutive foot ulcer cases.1116
Diabetic Neuropathy and the Foot Ulcer
All three components of neuropathy—sensory, motor, and auto­
nomic—can contribute to foot ulceration. The risk of foot ulcer­
ation in patients with neuropathy is sevenfold higher than in those 
without.1104,1107 Chronic sensorimotor neuropathy is common, 
affecting at least one-third of older patients with diabetes in West­
ern countries. Its onset is gradual and insidious, and symptoms 
may be so minimal that they go unnoticed. Although uncomfort­
able, painful, and paresthetic symptoms predominate in most 
patients, some never experience symptoms. Clinical examination 
usually reveals a sensory deficit in a glove-and-stocking distribu­
tion, with signs of motor dysfunction such as small muscle wasting 
in the feet and absent ankle reflexes. Although a history of typi­
cal symptoms strongly suggests a diagnosis of neuropathy, absence 
of symptoms does not exclude the diagnosis and must never be 
equated with a lack of foot ulcer risk. Therefore, assessment of foot 
ulcer risk must always include a careful foot examination, includ­
ing assessment of proprioception (i.e., pressure perception using 
a 10-g monofilament), regardless of history. Loss of sensation and 
proprioception reduce capillary perfusion and increase ischemia at 
sites of increased pressure load.
Sympathetic autonomic neuropathy affecting the lower limbs 
results in reduced sweating, dry skin, and development of cracks 
and fissures. In the absence of large-vessel arterial disease, there 
may be increased blood flow to the foot, with arteriovenous shunt­
ing leading to the warm but at-risk foot. 
Callus, Deformity, and High Foot Pressures
Motor neuropathy, with imbalance of the flexor and extensor 
muscles in the foot, commonly results in foot deformity, with 
prominent metatarsal heads and clawing of the toes (Fig. 38.71). 
The combination of proprioceptive loss resulting from sensory 
neuropathy and the prominence of metatarsal heads leads to 
increased pressures and loads under the diabetic foot. High pres­
sures, together with dry skin, often result in the formation of cal­
lus under weight-bearing areas of the metatarsal heads, resulting in 
a further rise in foot pressure. Presence of plantar callus is a highly 
significant marker for foot ulcer risk. Conversely, removal of plan­
tar callus is associated with reduced foot pressures and thereby a 
reduced foot ulcer risk.1104,1107 
Peripheral Arterial Disease, Diabetic Foot Ulcers, and 
Amputation Risk
Peripheral arterial disease in isolation rarely causes ulceration. 
However, the common combination of vascular disease with 
minor trauma can lead to ulceration. Minor injury and subse­
quent infection increase the demand for blood supply beyond 
the circulatory capacity, and ischemic ulceration and risk of 
amputation develop. Early identification of patients at risk for 
peripheral arterial disease is essential; however, typical symptoms 
of peripheral artery disease, such as intermittent claudication, 
may be absent in patients with significant neuropathy. Presence 
or absence of a dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pulse may be 
the simplest and most reliable indicator of significant ischemia 
that can be elicited at the bedside.1117 However, Doppler-derived 
ankle pressure can be misleadingly high in patients with long-
standing diabetes, so the use of the toe-brachial index together 
with Doppler waveforms of distal arteries can be useful in decid­
ing which patients need further diagnostic intervention.1118 
Urgent vascular imaging and revascularization should be consid­
ered in a patient with a diabetic foot ulcer and a toe pressure of 
<30 mm Hg or a transcutaneous oxygen pressure (TcPO2) of <25 
mm Hg.1119
Appropriate investigation involving noninvasive Doppler stud­
ies, together with arteriography, often leads to revascularization 
procedures to improve lower extremity blood flow. Distal bypass 
surgery or endovascular interventions have good short-term but 
mixed long-term results in terms of limb salvage.1105,1117 Advances 
in techniques and devices for both distal arterial bypass surgery 
and endovascular interventions have been made, and it is unclear 
which approach is preferred. A systematic review was unable to 
conclude any particular method was superior to any other.1105 
However, a more recent study in all patients with diabetic foot 
ulcers demonstrated that prompt vascular evaluation and revas­
cularization within 2 weeks reduced the rate of amputations to 
the rate of those without diabetes with peripheral artery disease, 
1570
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
supporting a substantial change in clinical disease management 
with early revascularization; thus, early referral to a vascular ser­
vice is recommended.1119,1120 
Prevention of Foot Ulceration and Amputation
Relatively simple interventions can reduce amputations by up to 
80%.1110,1111 Because foot ulcers precede most amputations, are 
among the most common causes of hospital admission for patients 
with diabetes, and account for much morbidity and even fatal­
ity, the widespread application of preventive foot care strategies is 
urgently required, including strategies for early identification of 
patients at potential risk for ulceration and education programs 
that can be adapted for widespread use.
Patients with any type of diabetes require regular foot exami­
nation for evidence of risk factors for ulceration, irrespective of 
disease duration. Neuropathy, vascular disease, and even foot 
ulceration may be the presenting feature of T2D, so there can 
be no exception to the rule of screening (Fig. 38.72). At a min­
imum, such screening should be carried out annually. In high-
risk patients, screening should be done at every visit. Of all the 
long-term complications of diabetes, foot problems and their risk 
factors are probably the easiest to detect. No expensive equip­
ment is required, and feet can be examined for evidence of neu­
ropathic and vascular deficits in the office setting using simple 
equipment.1104,1105
In 2008, a task force of the ADA published a report on the 
examination components that should be included in the annual 
Comprehensive Diabetic Foot Examination (CDFE); this 
approach to screening remains the recommendation of the 2022 
ADA clinical practice guidelines (Box 38.9).1119,1121 The most 
important message is for practitioners to have patients remove 
shoes and socks to examine feet for the presence of callus, defor­
mity, muscle wasting, and dry skin, all of which are clearly visible 
on inspection. A simple neurologic examination includes assess­
ment of pressure perception using a 10-g monofilament. Sensory 
neuropathy with clinical evidence of peripheral arterial disease is 
the strongest predictor of future foot ulceration. Absence of the 
ability to perceive pressure from a 10-g monofilament, inability 
to perceive a vibrating 128-Hz tuning fork over the hallux, and 
absent ankle reflexes all have been shown to be predictors of foot 
ulceration.1104,1107 Patients with evidence of sensory loss, prior 
ulceration, or amputation should have their feet inspected at 
every visit. 
The Diabetic Foot Care Team
Patients identified as being at high risk for foot ulceration should 
be managed by a team of specialists with expertise in the diabetic 
foot. The podiatrist usually takes responsibility for care of the skin 
and nails and, together with the specialist nurse or diabetes educa­
tor, provides foot care education. The orthotist, or shoe fitter, is 
invaluable to advise about and sometimes design footwear to pro­
tect high-risk feet. Team members should work closely with the 
diabetologist and the vascular and orthopedic surgeons. Patients 
with risk factors for ulceration require preventive foot care educa­
tion, including self–foot care at home, frequent review by a foot 
surgeon or podiatrist, good footwear with orthotics when indi­
cated, and avoidance of potentially dangerous over-the-counter 
foot products.1104,1111

Classification of Foot Ulcers
There are multiple classification systems for grading diabetic 
foot ulcers.1104,1107 One developed by Wagner1122 (Table 
38.21) was previously widely used. An alternative classifica­
tion system that, in addition to ulcer depth (as in the Wag­
ner system), accounts for the presence or absence of infection 
and ischemia was developed by the University of Texas (UT) 
group (Table 38.22). The UT scheme is a better predictor of 
outcome than the older Wagner system, as shown in a prospec­
tive study comparing the two approaches.1122 Although the UT 
scheme is still widely used in the United States, most recently, 
the Wound Ischemia and Foot Infection (WIFI) system has 
been introduced, and internationally, the Site Ischemia Neu­
ropathy Bacterial Infection and Depth (SINBAD) system has 
been recommended for use1123 by the International Working 
Group on the Diabetic Foot. The WIFI system,1124 also widely 
used in the United States, has been developed and validated as 
a method to accurately assess limb threat; it asks the clinician 
to grade degrees of tissue loss, ischemia, and foot infection as 
“none, mild, moderate or severe.” It prompts the clinician to 
identify the dominant conditions to better organize rapid team 
care.1125 The WIFI staging (Table 38.23) is highly predictive for 
limb loss and morbidity and can be used to determine the need 
for revascularization.1124
Management of Diabetic Foot Ulcers
Basic principles of wound healing apply equally to diabetic foot 
ulcers as to wounds in any other site or condition. In general, a 
diabetic foot ulcer has a high likelihood of healing if the following 
three conditions are satisfied:
 • Arterial inflow is adequate.
 • Infection is treated appropriately.
 • Pressure is removed from the wound and the immediate sur­
rounding area.
Although this approach appears simplistic, failure of diabetic 
foot ulcers to heal is usually a result of failure to pay sufficient 
attention to one or more contributing conditions, including 
pressure on the wound, infection, ischemia, and inadequate 
debridement.
The most common cause of nonhealing neuropathic foot ulcers 
is failure to remove pressure from the wound and immediate sur­
rounding area. Patients who are advised not to put pressure over 
an ulcer find it especially difficult to adhere to such advice when 
peripheral sensation is lost or reduced. Pain results in protection

of an injured area; the lack of pain permits pressure to be put 
directly onto the ulcer and results in nonhealing. A patient with 
normal sensation and a foot wound will limp to avoid putting 
pressure on the wound because doing so is painful. A patient who 
walks on a plantar wound without limping must have neuropathy.
The effect of pressure relief on the histopathologic features of 
neuropathic ulcers was assessed in a randomized study,1126 with 
biopsy either at presentation or after 20 days of off-loading in a 
total-contact cast (TCC). Histologic features of chronic inflam­
mation, with mononuclear infiltration, cellular debris, and scarce 
evidence of angiogenesis or granulation, were seen in patients who 
underwent biopsy at presentation, whereas granulation, neoangio­
genesis, and a predominance of fibroblasts were seen in patients 
treated with TCC before biopsy. These important observations 
support that repetitive pressure on a neuropathic wound contrib­
utes to the chronicity of the wound, whereas pressure relief results 
in a reparative phase.
The next most common error is inappropriate management 
of infection. Topical applications are usually unhelpful, and if 
clinical infection is present, then it must be treated urgently with 
antibiotics. Most infections are polymicrobial, with gram-positive 
cocci, gram-negative rods, and anaerobes, with or without multi­
drug-resistant organisms (see later discussion).
Another common management error is failure to appreciate 
ischemic symptoms that are atypical because of altered pain sensa­
tion as a result of neuropathy. The most difficult ulcer to heal is the 
neuroischemic ulcer. Symptoms and even signs of ischemia may 
be altered in the diabetic state. Therefore, appropriate noninvasive 
investigation and arteriography are indicated for patients with a 
nonhealing diabetic foot ulcer if there is any question about the 
vascular status.
Insufficient wound debridement contributes to slow healing 
or nonhealing of a diabetic foot ulcer. Appropriate debridement 
and removal of all callous, dead, and macerated tissue is essential 
local treatment of a diabetic foot ulcer, which results in more rapid 
healing compared to inadequately debrided wounds.
The principles of management of neuropathic and neuroisch­
emic foot ulcers are considered in the following sections, referenc­
ing both the UT and the Wagner grading systems. 
Neuropathic Foot Ulcer Without Osteomyelitis (Wagner 
Grades 1, 2; University of Texas Grades 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b)
Provision of adequate pressure relief is the most important feature 
in the management of neuropathic foot ulcers that occur under 
weight-bearing areas such as the metatarsal heads and great toe. 
This is usually achieved by a TCC, a regular below-knee cast, or a 
removable cast walker (RCW).1103,1106
The TCC has long been recognized as the gold standard for 
off-loading a foot wound because it was associated with the short­
est healing time in a randomized controlled trial comparing three 
off-loading techniques, total-contact casts, removable cast walkers, 
and half-shoes (Fig. 38.73).1127 When any cast device is used, reg­
ular removal of the cast is essential because regular debridement of 
the wound by a specialist is essential, and any casting device could 
injure insensitive skin, especially over bony prominences. Because 
the TCC requires a specially trained casting technician to apply 
it, and frequent removal is required for wound assessment, recent 
research has focused on alternative reusable devices that can only 
be removed in the specialist’s office.
The RCW resulted in slower healing than the TCC,1127 even 
though prior gait laboratory studies suggested they are equally 
efficacious at off-loading. The reason for this disparity may be 
explained by the observation that although patients were instructed 
to wear the RCW at all times, patients used these devices for only 
28% of all footsteps during a 24-hour period. To overcome this 
limitation, the RCW, which can be applied by any clinic personnel 
and does not require specialist training, can be rendered irremov­
able by wrapping it in casting material. A controlled trial showed 
the irremovable RCW was as effective at healing neuropathic foot 
wounds as the TCC.1128
Theoretically, complete healing of all superficial and neuro­
pathic ulcers should be possible without the need for amputa­
tion. In the treatment of neuropathic ulcers with good peripheral 
circulation, antibiotics are not indicated unless there are clear 
clinical signs of infection, including prominent discharge, local 
erythema, and cellulitis. The presence of any infective features in 
Wagner grade 1 or 2 ulcers would warrant reclassification in the 
UT system from 1a or 2a to 1b or 2b. In such cases, deep wound 
specimens should be taken, and broad-spectrum oral antibiotic 
treatment should be started with, for example, either an amoxi­
cillin–clavulanic acid combination (Augmentin) or clindamy­
cin. The antibiotic may need to be altered after sensitivity results 
become available.1129 
Neuroischemic Ulcers (Wagner Grades 1, 2; University of 
Texas Grades 1c, 1d)
The principles of management of neuroischemic Wagner grade 
1 and 2 ulcers are similar to those for neuropathic ulcers, with 
the following important differences. TCCs are not usually rec­
ommended for management of neuroischemic ulcers, although 
removable casts and pneumatic cast boots (Aircast) may be used 
in cases without infection. Antibiotic therapy is required for most 
neuroischemic ulcers. Urgent investigation of the circulation 
is indicated, including noninvasive assessment and, if required,

Osteomyelitis (Wagner Grade 3; University of Texas 
Grades 3b, 3d)
Wagner or UT grade 3 ulcers are deeper and involve underlying 
bone, often with abscess formation. Osteomyelitis is a serious 
complication of foot ulceration and may be present in as many 
as 50% of patients with diabetes with moderate to severe foot 
infections.1104,1129 If the physician can probe down to bone in 
a deep ulcer or there is sausage-shaped distension of a toe, the 
presence of osteomyelitis is strongly suggested. Plain radiographs 
are indicated for any nonhealing foot ulcer and are most useful in 
the diagnosis of osteomyelitis in more than two-thirds of patients, 
although radiologic changes may be delayed. In difficult cases, fur­
ther investigation, such as MRI, bone scans, or an indium-111 
(111In)–labeled white blood cell scan can be useful in diagnosing 
bone infection.1129,1130
Although osteomyelitis treatment is traditionally surgical and 
involves resection of the infected bone, there is increasing evi­
dence that antibiotic therapy may be just as effective in osteomy­
elitis, particularly restricted to a small area of the foot, such as a toe 
or metatarsal head region.1129 Antibiotic therapy for 90 days was 
equally efficacious when compared to local surgery for diabetic 
foot osteomyelitis in a randomized trial.1131 There has always been 
controversy as to whether antibiotic treatment of osteomyelitis 
should be delivered intravenously or orally. The recent Oral Vs 
IntraVenous Antibiotics (OVIVA) trial showed that oral therapy is 
equally efficacious as intravenous therapy.1132 Thus, in most cases, 
oral antibiotics (often starting with broad-spectrum coverage, 
such as clindamycin together with ciprofloxacin) for 6 to 8 weeks 
may be successful in the treatment of osteomyelitis.1129 
Gangrene (Wagner Grades 4, 5)
The presence of gangrene is always a serious sign in the diabetic 
foot. However, localized areas of gangrene, especially in the toes, 
that are without cellulitis, spreading infection, or discharge can 
occasionally be left to spontaneously auto-amputate. The presence 
of more extensive gangrene requires urgent hospital admission; 
treatment of infection, often with multiple antibiotics; glycemic 
control, usually with intravenous insulin; and detailed vascular 
assessment. It is in this situation that the team approach is most 
important, with close collaboration among the diabetes specialist, 
the vascular surgeon, and the radiologist.

SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Charcot Neuroarthropathy
Charcot neuroarthropathy is a disabling condition of progressive 
degeneration of the weight-bearing joints and bones of the foot. 
Although Charcot neuroarthropathy is rare, it should be suspected 
in any patient with unexplained swelling and heat in a neuropathic 
foot. It is much more frequent (10%–13%) in high-risk patients 
with diabetes. In the Western world, diabetes is the most common 
cause of a Charcot foot, and increased awareness of this condi­
tion can enable earlier diagnosis and treatment. Early intervention 
with immobilization may halt progression that, in the untreated 
state, can lead to marked foot deformity and disability and require 
local or major amputations.
The pathogenesis of the Charcot process remains poorly under­
stood. Permissive features include the presence of severe periph­
eral neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction, with increased blood 
flow to the foot reflecting the autonomic dysfunction. The periph­
eral circulation is usually intact. The foot is vulnerable to trauma, 
which the patient may not recall. Repetitive trauma results in 
increased blood flow through the bone, increased osteoclastic 
activity, and bone remodeling. In some cases, patients walk on a 
fracture, which leads to continuing bone and joint destruction in 
that area. Evidence suggests that acute Charcot neuroarthropathy 
may be triggered in the susceptible (i.e., neuropathic) individual 
by any event that leads to localized inflammation in the affected 
foot, triggering a vicious cycle in which there is increasing inflam­
mation, increasing expression of receptor activator of nuclear 
factor-κΒ ligand (RANKL), a member of the tumor necrosis fac­
tor superfamily, and increasing bone breakdown.1133 Targeting 
activation of the RANKL/osteoprotegerin pathway might lead to 
novel future treatments.
Charcot neuroarthropathy can be difficult to distinguish from 
osteomyelitis or an inflammatory arthropathy.1130 A unilateral 
swollen, hot foot without an ulcer in a patient with neuropathy 
must be considered to be a Charcot foot until proven otherwise. 
Charcot neuroarthropathy can be diagnosed in most patients by 
plain radiography and a high index of suspicion (Fig. 38.74). 
Radiographs reveal bone and joint destruction, fragmentation, 
and remodeling, although radiographic findings may be normal 
early in disease. In such cases, three-phase bisphosphonate bone 
scans show increased bone uptake, whereas 111In-labeled bone 
scans will be negative in the absence of infection. In patients where 
osteomyelitis is suspected, 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emis­
sion tomography–computed tomography (FDG-PET-CT) has 
the highest sensitivity for distinguishing Charcot neuroarthropa­
thy from osteomyelitis.
After diagnosis, management of the acute phase involves 
immobilization, usually in a TCC.1134 There is little evidence at 
this time to support use of any pharmacologic treatment in the 
management of this condition. 
Adjunctive Treatments for Foot Ulcers
In recent years, there has been a renaissance in diabetic foot 
care, with new evidence-based treatments that include topical 
agents, oxygen therapies, and negative-pressure wound therapy 
(NPWT).1135
Topical Treatments
	1.	 Leucopatch or 3-C Patch (Reapplix, Birkerod, Denmark). This 
treatment comprises a disc of autologous leucocyte, platelet, 
and fiber multilayered material derived from patients’ centri­
fuged venous blood. This has been shown in a randomized trial 
to speed healing in hard-to-heal diabetic foot ulcers.1135,1136
	2.	 Sucrose octasulfate. A novel dressing has been developed that 
incorporates sucrose octasulfate into a nonadherent dress­
ing (UrgoStart, Urgo company, Paris, France). The dressing

Oxygen Therapy for Diabetic Foot Ulcers
For many years, hyperbaric oxygen has been used empirically for 
the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers that failed to respond to stan­
dard of care. However, the data supporting hyperbaric oxygen are 
of poor quality, and there have been a number of negative tri­
als.1138 Thus, the use of hyperbaric oxygen is not recommended 
in several guidelines for the treatment of chronic diabetic foot 
ulcers. In contrast, there is increasing evidence to support use 
of topical oxygen therapies with a multimodality approach that 
applies cyclically pressurized oxygen within a disposable extremity 
chamber.1135 The strongest evidence comes from a well-designed 
randomized controlled trial using cyclically pressurized topical 
oxygen therapy for healing recalcitrant diabetic foot ulcers; the 
trial was sham-controlled and reported in 2020. Efficacy was so 
strong that at the first a priori planned interim analysis, active 
therapy was found to be superior to sham, and this form of ther­
apy is now widely used in the United States.1139 
Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy
NPWT, also known as vacuum-assisted closure, is increasingly used 
to treat large and complex diabetic foot wounds. It is also useful 
in localized postoperative wounds in the diabetic foot. The system 
consists of an electronically controlled pump and a foam dressing. 
The treatment drains the wound and may stimulate development 
of granulation tissue, including in previously nonhealing wounds. 
NPWT can be helpful in the postoperative management of dia­
betic foot wounds, as supported by randomized controlled trials 
in complex nonhealing diabetic foot ulcers and postoperative 
cases.1134
The choice between these newer adjunctive therapies will 
depend on a number of considerations, and they would nor­
mally only be used after a lack of response to standard of care. 
For example, NPWT is commonly used in larger postoperative 
wounds to promote granulation, and topical oxygen is used for 
nonhealing neuroischemic wounds; similarly, sucrose octasul­
fate dressings can help accelerate the healing of neuroischemic 
wounds and can be used with topical oxygen therapy. Oxygen 
therapy can be used with any of the adjunctive therapies except 
NPWT.1134 
Final Conclusions for the Diabetic Foot
Diagnosis and management of the diabetic foot are “coming of 
age” at long last. There has been a renaissance in new treatments 
for diabetic foot ulcers with a strong evidence base, which has 
been summarized in this section. The use of telemedicine has 
been advanced during the COVID-19 pandemic, and many stud­
ies are now ongoing to evaluate the efficacy of self-monitoring of 
risk of foot problems, such as those using technologies for tem­
perature and pressure monitoring. It is hoped that in addition to 
patient education, the ability of patients to monitor their risk of 
foot ulcers through modern technology will lead to a reduction of 
ulcers, amputation, and even premature death in the forthcoming 
decades.

atrogenic hypoglycemia is the limiting factor in the glycemic 
management of diabetes mellitus with insulin provisional 
therapies: insulin, a sulfonylurea, or a glinide.1 On the other 
hand, hypoglycemia is a distinctly uncommon clinical disorder in 
persons who do not have diabetes.2
Glucose is an obligate metabolic fuel for the brain under physi­
ologic conditions.3 Because the brain cannot synthesize glucose, 
store more than a few minutes’ supply as glycogen, or use physio­
logic concentrations of other circulating fuels, normal brain func­
tion requires a virtually continuous supply of glucose from the 
circulation. Blood-to-brain glucose transport is a direct function 
of the arterial plasma glucose concentration and requires mainte­
nance of the plasma glucose concentration within, or above, the 
physiologic range. Hypoglycemia causes functional brain failure, 
KEY POINTS
 • 
Hypoglycemia—a plasma glucose concentration low enough 
to cause symptoms or signs—is a rare occurrence in individuals 
without diabetes but is common in insulin-, sulfonylurea-, or 
glinide-treated diabetes or in children with some metabolic 
conditions.
 • 
The plasma glucose concentration is normally maintained in a 
relative narrow range: 70 to 140 mg/dL (3.9–7.9 mmol/L). This 
results from a fine balance between glucose influx (exogenous 
glucose absorption and endogenous glucose production) and 
glucose efflux (glucose utilization by insulin-sensitive tissues 
such as the skeletal muscle and insulin-insensitive tissues, 
particularly the brain).
 • 
Hypoglycemia results from an imbalance between glucose 
influx and glucose efflux due to either excessive glucose 
removal from the circulation, deficient glucose delivery into the 
circulation, or both.
 • 
Hypoglycemia in diabetes is typically the result of the interplay 
of therapeutic hyperinsulinemia and compromised defenses 
against falling glucose levels including failure to increase 
glucagon and development of an attenuated sympathoadrenal 
response that lead to defective glucose counterregulation and 
impaired awareness of hypoglycemia.
 • 
An attenuated sympathoadrenal response to falling glucose 
levels, the key feature of hypoglycemia-associated autonomic 
failure (HAAF), is induced by recent antecedent hypoglycemia, 
sleep, or prior exercise, and may be reversible through 
scrupulous avoidance of hypoglycemia.
 • 
Iatrogenic hypoglycemia is associated with both morbidity and 
mortality in type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
 • 
The practice of hypoglycemic risk reduction in persons with 
diabetes includes addressing the issue, considering the 
conventional risk factors and those indicative of HAAF, and 
applying the principles for achieving glycemic control targets.
 • 
In the absence of diabetes, hypoglycemia in ill or medicated 
individuals can be caused by many drugs, critical illnesses, 
endocrine deficiencies, or non–islet cell tumors; in 
seemingly well individuals it may be caused by endogenous 
hyperinsulinism or by various accidental, surreptitious, or 
malicious mechanisms. In children, it may also be the result 
of abnormalities in enzyme deficiencies that are key for 
the metabolism of fuel substrates that will contribute to 
abnormalities in glucose production and utilization.
 • 
The decision to evaluate a given nondiabetic person 
systematically—seeking evidence of a metabolic disorder 
or an endogenous insulin excess during hypoglycemia—is 
recommended only for persons in whom Whipple triad (signs, 
symptoms, or both consistent with hypoglycemia; a low reliably 
measured plasma glucose concentration; and resolution of 
those symptoms or signs after the glucose concentrations is 
raised) can be documented.
 • 
Short-term treatment of hypoglycemia includes oral 
carbohydrates, parenteral glucagon or glucose, or intranasal 
glucagon; long-term treatment requires correction of the 
hypoglycemic mechanism.

rected after the plasma glucose concentration is raised. If pro­
found and prolonged, however, hypoglycemia leads to permanent 
brain damage or death. Severe hypoglycemia can also cause fatal 
cardiac arrhythmia.
Given the survival requirement to maintain the plasma glucose 
concentration, it is not surprising that physiologic and behavioral 
mechanisms that prevent or rapidly correct hypoglycemia have 
evolved.3 These mechanisms are so effective that hypoglycemia is 
an uncommon clinical event except in persons who use drugs that 
lower the plasma glucose concentration, such as insulin, sulfonyl­
ureas, glinides, or alcohol.
Glucoregulatory failure resulting in hyperglycemia (diabetes 
mellitus) is discussed in Chapters 32 through 38; that resulting in 
hypoglycemia is discussed in the paragraphs that follow.
Physiology of Defense Against 
Hypoglycemia
Glucose Metabolism
Glucose is derived from three sources: intestinal absorption after 
digestion of dietary carbohydrates; glycogenolysis, which is the 
breakdown of glycogen, the polymerized storage form of glucose; 
and gluconeogenesis, which is the formation of glucose from pre­
cursors including lactate (and pyruvate), amino acids (especially 
alanine and glutamine), and to a lesser extent, glycerol. There are 
multiple fates of glucose transported into cells (external losses are 
normally negligible) (Fig. 39.1). Glucose may be stored as glyco­
gen or may undergo glycolysis to pyruvate, which can be reduced 
to lactate, transaminated to form alanine, or converted to acetyl

coenzyme A (CoA). Acetyl CoA in turn may be oxidized to carbon 
dioxide and water through the tricarboxylic acid cycle, converted 
to fatty acids that can be incorporated into triglycerides, or utilized 
for synthesis of ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate) 
or cholesterol. Finally, glucose may be released into the circula­
tion. Only the liver and kidneys express glucose-6-phosphatase, 
the enzyme necessary for release of glucose into the circulation, 
at levels sufficient to permit substantial endogenous contributions 
to the systemic glucose pool. Many tissues express the enzymes 
required to synthesize and hydrolyze glycogen (glycogen syn­
thase and phosphorylase, respectively). The liver and kidneys also 
express the enzymes necessary for gluconeogenesis, including the 
critical gluconeogenic enzymes pyruvate carboxylase, phospho­
enolpyruvate carboxykinase, and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
The liver is the major source of net endogenous glucose produc­
tion (through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis). Conversely, 
the liver can be an organ of net glucose uptake and glycogen syn­
thesis. The kidneys also produce glucose (through gluconeogen­
esis) and utilize glucose.
Muscle can take up and store glucose as glycogen, or it can 
metabolize glucose (through glycolysis) to pyruvate, which, 
among other fates, can be reduced to lactate or transaminated to 
form alanine. Lactate (and pyruvate) released from muscle can be 
transported to the liver and the kidneys to serve as a gluconeo­
genic precursor (the Cori or glucose-lactate cycle). Alanine, glu­
tamine, and other amino acids can also flow from muscle to liver 
and kidneys, where they also serve as gluconeogenic precursors. 
These constitute the glucose-alanine and glucose-glutamine cycles, 
in which new glucose formation is from precursors (e.g., amino 
acids) where the carbons are not derived from glucose via these 
cycles. Although quantitatively less important than muscle, fat can 
also take up and metabolize glucose.
Glucose is essentially the sole metabolic fuel for the brain 
under physiologic conditions.3 Glucose largely undergoes termi­
nal oxidation in the brain. Although the adult human brain con­
stitutes only about 2.5% of body weight, its oxidative metabolism 
accounts for approximately 25% of the basal metabolic rate and 
more than 50% of whole-body glucose utilization. In general, the 
human brain does not utilize alternative fuels circulating at physi­
ologic concentrations.4,5 However, the brain can oxidize alterna­
tive fuels if their circulating plasma levels rise high enough for 
them to enter the brain in quantity. For example, during extended 
fasting, markedly elevated circulating ketone levels can support 
the majority of the energy needs of the brain and reduce its utiliza­
tion of glucose. Nonetheless, that is not a physiologic condition, 
and ketogenesis is suppressed during episodes of insulin-mediated 
hypoglycemia. 
Systemic Glucose Balance
Although obligatory glucose utilization, largely by the brain, is 
continuous, the delivery of exogenous glucose from dietary car­
bohydrates is intermittent. However, the systemic glucose balance 
(Table 39.1) of endogenous glucose influx into the circulation and 
those of glucose efflux out of the circulation into tissues other than 
the brain, is normally maintained, and hypoglycemia and hyper­
glycemia are prevented, largely by a dynamic, minute-to-minute 
regulation of endogenous glucose production from the liver and 
kidneys and of glucose utilization by tissues outside the cen­
tral nervous system (CNS), such as muscle.1,3 This regulation is 
exerted primarily by the plasma glucose-lowering (regulatory) hor­
mone insulin and the plasma glucose-raising (counterregulatory) 
hormones glucagon and epinephrine1–3 (Fig. 39.2; see also Table 
39.2), although an array of hormones, neurotransmitters, and 
substrates are also involved.6 This balance is accomplished despite 
wide variations in exogenous glucose influx (e.g., after meals ver­
sus during fasting) and in glucose efflux (e.g., during exercise ver­
sus rest).
In healthy adults, the physiologic postabsorptive (fasting) 
plasma glucose concentration ranges from approximately 70 mg/
dL (3.9 mmol/L) to 110 mg/dL (6.1 mmol/L), with a mean of 
about 90 mg/dL (5.0 mmol/L).3 In the postabsorptive steady 
state, rates of glucose production and utilization average approxi­
mately 2.2 mg/kg per minute (12 μmol/kg per minute), with a 
range of 1.8 to 2.6 mg/kg per minute (10 to 14 μmol/kg per min­
ute). These rates are as much as threefold higher in infants, at least 
in part because of their greater brain mass relative to body weight.
The liver is the predominant source of endogenous glucose 
production in the postabsorptive state; the kidneys, which both 
utilize and produce glucose, contribute little to net glucose pro­
duction. However, as in the liver, glucose production in the kidney 
is regulated; it is suppressed by insulin and stimulated by epineph­
rine but not by glucagon. As a result, net renal glucose production 
occurs under some conditions, including hypoglycemia.7 There­
fore, endogenous glucose production cannot be equated solely 
with hepatic glucose production.
Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis are important for mainte­
nance of the plasma glucose concentration.8 The glucose pool—
namely, free glucose in the extracellular fluids and in the cells 
of certain tissues (primarily the liver)—is only about 15 to 20 g

(83–111 mmol). Glycogen that can be mobilized to provide circu­
lating glucose (e.g., hepatic glycogen) contains approximately 70 g 
(390 mmol) of glucose, with a range of about 25 to 130 g (135–722 
mmol). Therefore, in an adult of average size, preformed glucose can 
provide less than an 8-hour supply of energy, even at the diminished 
rate of glucose utilization that occurs in the postabsorptive state.
If fasting is prolonged to 24 to 48 hours, the plasma glucose 
concentration declines and then stabilizes; hepatic glycogen content 
falls to less than 10 g (55 mmol), and gluconeogenesis becomes the 
sole source of glucose production. Because amino acids are the main 
gluconeogenic precursors that result in net glucose formation, mus­
cle protein is degraded. Glucose utilization by muscle and fat virtu­
ally ceases. As lipolysis and ketogenesis accelerate and circulating 
ketone levels rise, ketones become a major fuel for the brain. Glu­
cose utilization by the brain declines by about half, which reduces 
the rate of gluconeogenesis required to maintain the plasma glucose 
concentration and hence decreases protein wasting.
After a meal, glucose absorption into the circulation increases to 
more than twice the rate of postabsorptive endogenous glucose pro­
duction, depending on the carbohydrate content of the meal, the 
rate of gastric transit, and the rate of digestion and absorption. As 
glucose is absorbed, endogenous glucose production is suppressed, 
and glucose utilization by muscle, fat, and liver accelerates. The 
exogenous glucose is assimilated, and, after a small rise, the plasma 
glucose concentration returns to the postabsorptive level.
Exercise increases glucose utilization (by muscle) to rates that 
can be several times greater than those of the postabsorptive state. 
Endogenous glucose production normally accelerates to match 
use so that the plasma glucose concentration is maintained.
In summary, the plasma glucose concentration is normally 
maintained within a relatively narrow range despite wide varia­
tion in glucose fluxes that maintains systemic glucose balance. 
This remarkable homeostatic feat is accomplished by an array of 
hormonal, neural, and substrate glucoregulatory factors. 
Physiology of Glucose Counterregulation: 
Responses to Hypoglycemia
Hypoglycemia occurs when rates of glucose appearance in the cir­
culation (the sum of endogenous glucose production and exog­
enous glucose absorption) fail to keep pace with rates of glucose 
disappearance from the circulation (the sum of ongoing glucose 
metabolism largely by the brain and of variable glucose utilization 
by tissues including muscle, fat, liver, and kidneys).
Falling plasma glucose concentrations cause a sequence of 
key physiologic and behavioral responses, with defined glycemic 
thresholds, in healthy individuals: (1) a decrease in insulin, (2) 
an increase in glucagon, and, in the absence of the latter, (3) an 
increase in epinephrine.3 The behavioral defense is carbohydrate 
ingestion prompted by autonomic symptoms that are largely sym­
pathetic neural in origin (see Table 39.2 and Fig. 39.2).1,3,9–13
The first physiologic defense against hypoglycemia is a decrease 
in insulin secretion by the pancreatic islet β-cells. Signaled pri­
marily by declining glucose concentrations sensed at the level of 
the pancreatic islet β-cells, this response occurs as plasma glucose 
concentrations decline within the physiologic range3 (see Table 
39.2) and favors increased hepatic and renal glucose produc­
tion with virtual cessation of glucose utilization by insulin-sen­
sitive tissues such as muscle (see Fig. 39.2). The β-cell response 
to decrease insulin secretion is coupled to the second physiologic 
defense against hypoglycemia, an increase in glucagon secretion 
by pancreatic islet α-cells via paracrine communication within the 
pancreatic islet. The α-cell response to increase glucagon secre­
tion is signaled primarily by the decrease in intraislet insulin, 
perhaps among other β-cell secretory products, in the setting of 
low α-cell glucose concentration (see Fig. 39.2)14–18 and other 
paracrine signals that may include a decrease in somatostatin 
among other as yet to be determined mechanisms14–18 and only 
secondarily by increased autonomic nervous system (sympathetic, 
parasympathetic, adrenomedullary) inputs.19 This increase in glu­
cagon occurs as the plasma glucose concentration approaches the 
lower limit of the physiologic range (see Table 39.2) and normally 
prevents glucose from declining to <70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) by 
stimulating hepatic glucose production, largely by stimulating gly­
cogenolysis (see Fig. 39.2).
Further lowering of the plasma glucose concentration causes 
the third physiologic defense against hypoglycemia, an intense 
autonomic nervous system (sympathetic neural, adrenomedul­
lary, and parasympathetic) response and symptoms. This becomes 
critical when glucagon is deficient. Falling glucose levels sensed in 
the periphery and in the CNS, acting through a putative cerebral 
network that may modulate the hypothalamic response, signal an 
increase in autonomic nervous system activity that results in an 
increase in adrenomedullary epinephrine secretion and in auto­
nomic (or neurogenic) symptoms, the latter largely resulting from 
increased sympathetic neural activity1–3 (see Table 39.2). This 
autonomic response raises plasma glucose concentrations largely 
by epinephrine-mediated β2-adrenergic stimulation of hepatic 
and renal glucose production (see Fig. 39.2). However, the plasma 
glucose-raising actions of epinephrine also involve limitation of 
glucose clearance by insulin-sensitive tissues, mobilization of glu­
coneogenic precursors such as lactate and amino acids from mus­
cle and glycerol from fat, and α2-adrenergic limitation of insulin 
secretion (Fig. 39.3).20 Circulating epinephrine is derived almost 
exclusively from the adrenal medulla in adults.9 Whereas circu­
lating norepinephrine is derived largely from sympathetic nerve 
terminals under resting conditions and in many stimulated states 
(e.g., exercise), the plasma norepinephrine response to hypoglyce­
mia is derived largely from the adrenal medulla.9

CHAPTER 39  Hypoglycemia
These physiologic defenses against hypoglycemia typically 
abort episodes of declining plasma glucose concentrations and 
prevent clinical (i.e., symptomatic) hypoglycemia. If they do not, 
the lower plasma glucose concentration causes a more intense 
autonomic response, resulting in the generation of symptoms 
(see Table 39.2).1,3 These symptoms, particularly the neurogenic 
symptoms, cause awareness of hypoglycemia that prompts the 
behavioral defense against hypoglycemia, ingestion of carbohy­
drates (see Fig. 39.2).3 Symptoms are the last defense as even lower 
glucose levels cause cognitive dysfunction and additional manifes­
tations of functional brain failure including seizure or coma. 
Clinical Hypoglycemia
Clinical Manifestations of Hypoglycemia
The symptoms and signs of hypoglycemia are nonspecific.13 
Clinical hypoglycemia—that sufficient to cause symptoms and 
signs2—is most convincingly documented by Whipple triad: (1) 
symptoms, signs, or both consistent with hypoglycemia; (2) a low 
reliably measured plasma glucose concentration; and (3) resolu­
tion of those symptoms and signs after the plasma glucose concen­
tration is raised (Box 39.1).
Neuroglycopenic symptoms are a direct result of brain glu­
cose deprivation. They include cognitive impairments, behavioral 
changes, psychomotor abnormalities, and at lower glucose levels, 
seizure, and coma.1,13 Neurogenic (or autonomic) symptoms are 
largely the result of the perception of physiologic changes caused 
by the sympathoadrenal (particularly the sympathetic neural9) dis­
charge triggered by hypoglycemia. They include adrenergic (cate­
cholamine-mediated) symptoms such as palpitations, tremor, and 
anxiety/arousal and cholinergic (acetylcholine-mediated) symp­
toms such as sweating, hunger, and paresthesias. Central mecha­
nisms may also be involved in the generation of some of these 
symptoms (e.g., hunger).21 Subjective awareness of hypoglycemia 
is largely the result of the perception of neurogenic symptoms 
(Fig. 39.4).13
The mechanism(s) of the signaling of the glucose regulatory 
and counterregulatory hormone and autonomic nervous sys­
tem responses to hypoglycemia are not known. However, those 
responses are not mediated by a decrease in brain glucose metabo­
lism because the glycemic threshold for a decrease in the cerebral 
metabolic role of glucose, measured with [11C]glucose positron 
emission tomography, is at a lower plasma glucose concentration 
than the glycemic thresholds for the hormonal and autonomic 
responses (see Table 39.2).22
Signs of hypoglycemia include pallor and diaphoresis, which 
result from sympathetic adrenergic cutaneous vasoconstriction 
and cholinergic activation of sweat glands, respectively.2,3 Heart 
rates and systolic blood pressures are raised, but often not greatly, 
as there is simultaneous activation of the parasympathetic nervous 
system.13 Neuroglycopenic manifestations are often observable. 
Clinical Classification of Hypoglycemia
Causes of hypoglycemia2 are outlined in Box 39.2. Drugs are, by 
far, the most common cause of hypoglycemia. Such drugs include 
insulin and insulin secretagogues (e.g., a sulfonylurea or a glinide) 
used to treat diabetes. Although persons with diabetes can suffer 
from the same hypoglycemic disorders as those without diabetes, 
their hypoglycemic episodes are usually the result of treatment of 
their diabetes. Furthermore, the pathophysiology of hypoglyce­
mia in diabetes is unique, and the diagnostic and management 
approaches are different from those for individuals without diabe­
tes. Therefore, hypoglycemia in persons with diabetes and hypo­
glycemia in those without diabetes are discussed separately in this 
chapter. 
Hypoglycemia in Persons With Diabetes
The Clinical Problem of Hypoglycemia in 
Diabetes
Iatrogenic hypoglycemia is the limiting factor in the glycemic 
management of diabetes with insulin, a sulfonylurea, or a glinide.1

SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
It causes recurrent physical and psychosocial morbidity in most 
persons with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1D) and in many of those 
with advanced type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D), and it is some­
times fatal. The barrier of hypoglycemia generally precludes main­
tenance of normoglycemia over a lifetime of diabetes and thus 
full realization of the vascular benefits of glycemic control. Fur­
thermore, hypoglycemia compromises physiologic and behavioral 
defenses against subsequent falling plasma glucose concentrations, 
resulting in a vicious cycle of recurrent hypoglycemia.
Hypoglycemia in diabetes is caused by pharmacokinetically 
imperfect treatment with insulin or an insulin secretagogue (such 
as a sulfonylurea or a glinide) that results in episodes of thera­
peutic hyperinsulinemia. Thus, it is fundamentally iatrogenic. 
Exposure to substantial absolute therapeutic hyperinsulinemia 
can cause isolated episodes of severe hypoglycemia. Furthermore, 
hypoglycemia often causes functional brain failure that is typically 
reversed after the plasma glucose concentration is raised. How­
ever, as developed later in this chapter, recurrent hypoglycemia in 
diabetes is typically the result of the interplay of relative or mild 
to moderate absolute therapeutic hyperinsulinemia and compro­
mised physiologic and behavioral defenses against falling plasma 
glucose concentrations.1,2
Frequency of Hypoglycemia in Diabetes
Hypoglycemia is unfortunately a fact of life for people with 
T1D.23–25 The average patient suffers untold numbers of epi­
sodes of asymptomatic hypoglycemia (which are not benign 
because they impair defenses against subsequent hypoglycemia), 
approximately two episodes of symptomatic hypoglycemia per 
week (thousands of such episodes over a lifetime of diabetes), 
and roughly one episode per year of severe, of at least tempo­
rarily disabling hypoglycemia, often with seizure or coma. This 
problem has not abated since it was highlighted by the report 
of the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) 
in 1993.23 After approximately 30 years of follow-up in the 
DCCT/Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complica­
tions (EDIC) cohort, severe hypoglycemia persisted at a rate of 
about 39 episodes per 100 patient-years, similar in those ini­
tially assigned to intensive insulin therapy and affecting approxi­
mately 50% of participants from both the previously intensive 
and conventional groups.26 In clinical practice, incidence rates 
of severe hypoglycemia are much higher. For example, a preva­
lence of severe hypoglycemia of 22% and an incidence of 110 
episodes per 100 patient-years among patients who had T1D 
for less than 5 years, and these figures rose to 46% prevalence 
and 320 episodes per 100 patient-years among those with T1D 
for more than 15 years, was reported by the United Kingdom 
Hypoglycaemia Study Group (UKHSG).27
The overall incidence of hypoglycemia in T2D during treat­
ment with an insulin secretagogue, or even with insulin, is lower 
than that in patients with T1D.25,27–34 Furthermore, the time 
course to develop hypoglycemia differs in T2D from T1D. In 
T1D β-cell failure and loss of both insulin and glucagon responses 
result in compromised defenses against hypoglycemia from disease 
onset,35 whereas in T2D defenses against hypoglycemia are intact 
early in the disease course but become compromised over time1,36 
as patients approach the absolute endogenous insulin-deficient 
state.27,29,30 In advanced T2D (i.e., with absolute deficient endog­
enous insulin), insulin and glucagon responses to falling plasma 
glucose concentrations are lost and sympathoadrenal responses to 
hypoglycemia are reduced by recent antecedent hypoglycemia, as 
is observed in T1D.36
The temporal pattern of compromised glycemic defenses 
explains why iatrogenic hypoglycemia becomes progressively 
more frequent as patients approach the insulin-deficient end 
of the spectrum of T2D.27 The UKHSG found a prevalence of 
severe hypoglycemia of 7% and an incidence of 10 episodes per 
100 patient-years among patients with T2D treated with insu­
lin for less than 2 years; among those treated for longer than 5 
years, these figures rose to 25% prevalence and 70 episodes per 
100 patient-years.27 The patterns for self-treated hypoglycemia 
were similar. Therefore, at least with current, less than euglyce­
mic treatment goals, the frequency of iatrogenic hypoglycemia is 
relatively low during the first few years of treatment of T2D with 
insulin but increases substantially in advanced T2D, approach­
ing the frequency among patients with T1D. As discussed later 
in this chapter, new technologies, particularly continuous glucose 
monitoring (CGM) and drugs for the treatment of T2D that do 
not cause hypoglycemia, reduce the frequency of hypoglycemia 
for those who are able to use them (see Chapter 35).
The incidence and prevalence rates of hypoglycemia in diabetes 
are generally underestimated because of the challenge of ascertain­
ment.1,2 Asymptomatic episodes will be missed unless they are 
incidentally detected by self-monitoring of blood glucose or by 
CGM. Symptomatic episodes may not be recognized to be the 
result of hypoglycemia because the symptoms of hypoglycemia are 
nonspecific. Even if they are recognized, they may not be remem­
bered37,38 and reported at periodic patient contacts. Severe hypo­
glycemic events (those requiring the assistance of another person) 
are dramatic and more likely to be reported (by the patient or 
an associate); therefore, frequency estimates are more reliable,

although they represent only a small fraction of the total hypogly­
cemic burden. Prospective, population-based studies with a focus 
on hypoglycemia provide the most reliable data.
The overall incidences of any episode of hypoglycemia and of 
severe hypoglycemia in insulin-treated T2D are about one third 
of those in T1D, based on data from a prospective, population-
based study.25 The incidence of severe hypoglycemia requiring 
emergency treatment in insulin-treated T2D ranges from 40%31 
to 100%32 of that in T1D in two other population-based studies. 
Taken together, and considering that the prevalence of T2D is 
approximately 20-fold greater than that of T1D and that most 
patients with T2D ultimately require treatment with insulin, 
data suggest most episodes of iatrogenic hypoglycemia, including 
severe hypoglycemia, occur in persons with T2D. 
Impact of Hypoglycemia in Diabetes
Episodes of symptomatic hypoglycemia can impair judgment, 
behavior, and performance of physical tasks such as driving, 
and can progress to causing a seizure or loss of consciousness. 
Transient focal neurologic deficits sometimes occur mimicking 
a cerebrovascular accident, but permanent neurologic damage 
is rare. Systematic long-term follow-up of the DCCT patients 
suggests recurrent iatrogenic hypoglycemia does not cause 
chronic cognitive impairments in young adults,39 but the pos­
sibility remains that it does so in young children40,41 and older 
adults.42,43 Rarely, severe episodes of hypoglycemia cause sud­
den death, presumably the result of cardiac arrhythmia, or, if it 
is profound and prolonged, permanent brain dysfunction and 
death. Among other psychological disorders, fear of hypoglyce­
mia can be a barrier to glycemic control.44
That hypoglycemia can be lethal has been known since the 
discovery of insulin.45 There are epidemiologic associations of 
hypoglycemia with death,46 reports of excessive mortality rates 
during intensive glycemic therapy in randomized controlled trials 
of patients with T2D46,47 and intensive care unit patients,48,49 and 
reports of hypoglycemia mortality rates in series of patients with 
diabetes.43,50–54 Early reports indicated that 2% to 4% of patients 
with T1D died of hypoglycemia.50–52 More recent reports indi­
cate that 4%,52,53 7%,54 8%,55,56 and 10% or greater57 of deaths 
of persons with T1D are caused by hypoglycemia. Indeed, hypo­
glycemia at the time of death has been documented by CGM.58 
Death rates of up to 10% of patients who suffer severe sulfonyl­
urea-induced hypoglycemia have been reported.59 The finding 
of Currie and colleagues60 that lower glycosylated hemoglobin 
(HbA1c) levels are associated with increased mortality in patients 
with T2D at higher risk of hypoglycemia is entirely consistent 
with this body of evidence that iatrogenic hypoglycemia is a risk 
factor for death in diabetes. Thus, there are iatrogenic mortality 
rates in both T1D and T2D.
Although prolonged, profound hypoglycemia can cause brain 
death, most sudden hypoglycemic deaths are thought to result 
from cardiac arrhythmias based on increasing evidence that 
hypoglycemia is proarrhythmogenic.61–63 Simultaneous Holter 
monitoring and CGM during episodes of iatrogenic hypogly­
cemia in persons with diabetes has detected cardiac arrhythmias 
ranging from repolarization abnormalities,63 to bradycardia,62 to 
ventricular tachycardia.61 Thus, fatal cardiac arrhythmias almost 
assuredly underlie hypoglycemic cardiovascular mortality in 
diabetes.
Cardiac arrhythmias are triggered by the intense sympatho­
adrenal response to hypoglycemia47,64,65 and mediated through 
β-adrenergic receptors.65 Sudden death has been associated with 
QT interval prolongation and reduced baroreflex sensitivity in 
patients with classic diabetic autonomic neuropathy.66–68 Like­
wise, recent antecedent hypoglycemia causes reduced baroreflex 
sensitivity the following day in nondiabetic individuals.69 The 
induction of functional sympathetic failure by recent antecedent 
hypoglycemia as an additional, potentially fatal, feature of the 
concept of hypoglycemia associated autonomic failure (HAAF) in 
diabetes1 is discussed later in this chapter. 
Clinical Definition and Classification of Hypoglycemia in 
Diabetes
The American Diabetes Association (ADA)/Endocrine Society 
(ES) Workgroup on Hypoglycemia70 define hypoglycemia in 
diabetes as “all episodes of abnormally low plasma glucose con­
centration that expose the individual to potential harm.” That is 
broader than the recommended definition of clinical hypogly­
cemia in persons without diabetes (i.e., a plasma glucose con­
centration low enough to cause symptoms or signs1,2) because 
it includes asymptomatic episodes. The latter are not benign in 
persons with diabetes; they compromise defenses against subse­
quent hypoglycemia,1,2 and they identify increased risk of immi­
nent severe iatrogenic hypoglycemia.71 The glycemic thresholds 
for counterregulatory responses and consequently the symptoms 
and signs of hypoglycemia are dynamic; for example, they shift 
to lower plasma glucose concentrations in patients with recur­
rent hypoglycemia72–74 and to higher concentrations in those 
with poorly controlled diabetes.20,72 As one considers these gly­
cemic thresholds, it is also important to recognize that glucose 
concentrations measured in whole blood are approximately 15% 
lower than those in plasma and may be further reduced if the 
hematocrit is high.
The ADA/ES Workgroup recommends people with diabetes 
(implicitly those treated with an insulin secretagogue or insulin) 
become concerned about the possibility of developing hypogly­
cemia at a self-monitored plasma glucose concentration of 70 
mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or less.70 Within the error of self-mon­
itoring (or CGM), that conservative alert value approximates 
the lower limit of the nondiabetic postabsorptive plasma glucose 
range1,2 and the normal glycemic thresholds for activation of 
physiologic glucose counterregulatory systems1,2 (see Box 39.2); 
it is low enough to reduce glycemic defenses against subsequent 
hypoglycemia in nondiabetic persons. Therefore, the recom­
mended glucose alert level of 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or less 
is data driven; it usually gives the patient time to take action to 
prevent a clinical hypoglycemic episode, and it provides some 
margin for the limited accuracy of glucose monitoring devices 
at low plasma glucose concentrations. It has been implicitly 
endorsed by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the 
European Medicines Agency.
The recommended alert value does not, of course, mean that 
persons with diabetes should always self-treat with carbohydrate 
ingestion for hypoglycemia at an estimated plasma glucose con­
centration of 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) or less. Rather, they should 
consider actions ranging from repeating the measurement in the 
near term, through behavioral actions such as avoiding exercise or 
driving until the glucose level is raised, to proceeding with carbo­
hydrate ingestion and subsequent adjustments of the therapeutic 
regimen.
The International Hypoglycaemia Study Group75 proposes 
three levels of iatrogenic hypoglycemia in diabetes (Table 
39.3). Level 1 is a glucose alert value less than 70 mg/dL (3.9 
mmol/L), which is less than the physiologic lower limit of
