normal in the postabsorptive state. Level 2 is a glucose level 
less than 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L), which is sufficiently low to 
indicate serious clinically important hypoglycemia. Level 3 is 
severe hypoglycemia as defined by the ADA. These levels are 
endorsed by the ADA and the European Association for the 
Study of Diabetes.75
It has been suggested76 that the classification of severe hypo­
glycemia (see Table 39.3) be expanded to include a distinctly low 
plasma glucose concentration, perhaps less than 50 mg/dL (2.8 
mmol/L) or less than 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L),75 detected by 
self-monitoring of plasma glucose, CGM, or a laboratory deter­
mination. A distinctly low glucose concentration in the absence 
of symptoms at the time of the detection documents impaired 
awareness of hypoglycemia, a potentially treatable condition. 
Pathophysiology of Glucose Counterregulation 
in Diabetes
The pathophysiology of glucose counterregulation and its rela­
tionship to clinical hypoglycemia in diabetes1,2 are summarized 
below (see earlier discussion and Figs. 39.2 and 39.3). Again, the 
key physiologic defenses against falling plasma glucose concentra­
tions are a decrease in insulin, an increase in glucagon, and in the 
absence of the latter, an increase in epinephrine. The behavioral 
defense is carbohydrate ingestion prompted by symptoms13 that 
are largely sympathetic neural in origin.9 However, people with 
diabetes and β-cell failure may have episodes of insulin excess and 
these physiologic and behavioral defenses are compromised, lead­
ing to the syndrome of hypoglycemia-associated autonomic fail­
ure and thus a vicious cycle of recurrent hypoglycemia.
Episodes of therapeutic hyperinsulinemia, produced by treat­
ment with insulin or with an insulin secretagogue (a sulfonylurea 
or a glinide), are a prerequisite for the development of iatrogenic 
hypoglycemia. Marked absolute insulin excess can cause isolated 
episodes of hypoglycemia. However, iatrogenic hypoglycemia is 
typically the result of the interplay of relative or mild to moderate 
absolute therapeutic hyperinsulinemia and compromised physi­
ologic and behavioral defenses against falling plasma glucose con­
centrations (Fig. 39.5).1,2
Importantly, after insulin administration circulating (exog­
enous) insulin concentrations do not decrease as plasma glu­
cose concentrations fall. The effect is exaggerated in the setting 
of absolute β-cell failure when there is no longer any compensa­
tion through regulated endogenous insulin secretion. Therefore, 
the first physiologic defense against hypoglycemia3 is lost. Fur­
thermore, despite the presence of functional α-cells, there is no 
increase in glucagon secretion (Fig. 39.6).1,2,18 That, too, is largely 
the result of β-cell failure14–18 and loss of the decrement in insu­
lin that normally signals an increase in α-cell glucagon secretion 
during hypoglycemia (see Figs. 39.2 and 39.5).1,18 Therefore, the 
second physiologic defense against the development of clinically 
important hypoglycemia3 is also lost.
In addition, the increase in epinephrine secretion, the third 
physiologic defense against hypoglycemia,3 becomes attenuated 
by recurrent exposure to even nonserious hypoglycemia (see Fig. 
39.6).1,2,77 In the setting of absent insulin and glucagon responses, 
the attenuated epinephrine response causes the clinical syndrome 
of defective glucose counterregulation (see Fig. 39.5),77–79 which 
is associated with a 25-fold79 or greater80 increased risk of severe 
hypoglycemia in T1D. The attenuated epinephrine response is a 
marker of attenuation of the sympathoadrenal response (including 
the sympathetic neural response) that normally causes autonomic 
or neurogenic symptoms that largely prompt the behavioral 
response leading to carbohydrate ingestion (see Figs. 39.2 and 
39.7). This attenuated response (largely the reduced sympathetic 
neural response) causes the clinical syndrome of impaired aware­
ness of hypoglycemia (see Fig. 39.5),1,2 which is associated with a 
sixfold increase of severe iatrogenic hypoglycemia, and in cases of 
hypoglycemia unawareness, 20-fold increased risk of severe hypo­
glycemia in T1D.81,82
Although the term hypoglycemia unawareness is used widely, 
“impaired awareness of hypoglycemia”81 is more precise because 
there is a spectrum ranging from partial to complete loss of symp­
toms. Attenuated sympathoadrenal responses to falling plasma

include gender, race, age, socioeconomic status, duration of dis­

a minority of episodes.90 A history of severe hypoglycemia is an 
important risk factor for experiencing a future event, especially in 
the presence of HAAF (including both defective glucose counter­
regulation and impaired awareness of hypoglycemia).1 
Hypoglycemia-Associated Autonomic Failure in 
Diabetes
The concept of HAAF1,2,77,78,91 in diabetes posits that in patients 
with absolute endogenous insulin deficiency (T1D or advanced 
T2D), necessarily imperfect insulin replacement results in falling 
plasma glucose concentrations but no decrease in insulin secre­
tion and no increase in glucagon secretion, and, thus, recurrent 
episodes of hypoglycemia. Those episodes83 (as well as sleep85,86 
or prior exercise84) attenuate adrenomedullary epinephrine secre­
tion and sympathetic neural activation in response to subsequent 
hypoglycemia. The resulting recurrent hypoglycemia further 
attenuates the sympathoadrenal response to falling plasma glu­
cose concentrations (see Fig. 39.5). The mechanisms77 and back­
ground78,91 of HAAF have been reviewed in detail.
Recent antecedent hypoglycemia, even asymptomatic noc­
turnal hypoglycemia, reduces epinephrine and autonomic 
symptom responses to a given level of subsequent hypogly­
cemia,92 reduces detection of hypoglycemia in the clinical 
setting,93 and reduces glycemic defense against hyperinsu­
linemia87 in T1D and in advanced T2D.36 Perhaps the most 
compelling support for the clinical relevance of HAAF is the 
finding, originally from three independent laboratories,94–97 
that 3 or more weeks of scrupulous avoidance of hypoglycemia 
can reverse impaired awareness of hypoglycemia, although may 
not improve the attenuated epinephrine component of defec­
tive glucose counterregulation in individuals with longer (>10 
years) diabetes duration (Fig. 39.8).
There are three recognized causes of reversibly attenuated 
sympathoadrenal response to hypoglycemia and, therefore, three 
forms of HAAF,1,2 including antecedent hypoglycemia–related 
HAAF.83,87 Exercise, in particular aerobic, is itself associated 
with the development of hypoglycemia,98 and exercise-related 
HAAF84 is exemplified by late postexercise hypoglycemia, which 
typically occurs 6 to 15 hours after strenuous exercise and is often

nocturnal.99,100 Sleep-related HAAF85,86 is the result of further 
attenuation of the sympathoadrenal response to hypoglycemia 
during sleep. Sleeping patients with T1D are much less likely to be 
awakened by hypoglycemia than nondiabetic individuals,86 prob­
ably because of their attenuated sympathoadrenal responses. There 
may well be additional, unrecognized causes of HAAF, and there 
may also be a structural (neuropathic) component.1,2
Notably, HAAF is a functional form of autonomic failure, 
distinct from classic diabetic autonomic neuropathy.101 Whereas 
early studies suggested a relationship between diabetic autonomic 
neuropathy and impaired epinephrine and neurogenic symp­
tom responses to hypoglycemia in T1D,102 subsequent work has 
shown no causal relationship.103 Nevertheless, HAAF has car­
diovascular implications because, like autonomic neuropathy, it 
reduces baroreflex sensitivity69 and may predispose patients to 
cardiac arrhythmias.
The integrated pathophysiologic mechanisms of HAAF and 
the CNS are illustrated in Fig. 39.9. Loss of insulin and gluca­
gon responses to falling plasma glucose concentrations caused 
by therapeutic hyperinsulinemia result from β-cell failure in 
T1D and advanced T2D.1,2,77 Neither can be attributed to loss 
of islet autonomic innervation, because low glucose concentra­
tions decrease insulin secretion and increase glucagon secretion in 
patients with a transplanted (i.e., denervated) pancreas,104 in dogs 
with a denervated pancreas,105 and in isolated perfused pancreas 
and perifused islets. The mechanism of the attenuated sympatho­
adrenal response is not known, but it must involve the brain or the 
afferent or efferent components of the sympathoadrenal system.77 
Proposed mechanisms include the systemic mediator, alternative 
brain fuel transport, brain glucose metabolism and cerebral net­
work hypotheses,106–110 as well as a reduced secretory capacity of 
adrenal chromaffin cells.111
The potential mechanism of changes in brain metabolism 
with an increase in cerebral glucose consumption (CMRglu) or 
increased glycogen production have not been well supported. 
However, the potential mechanism of an alternative brain fuel 
may be more promising. Increased blood-to-brain acetate trans­
port has been reported in patients with diabetes.112 The effect 
of lactate on brain metabolism has been studied.113–115 Lactate 
concentrations rise during insulin-mediated glucose disposal, 
including during hypoglycemia; therefore, the possibility that 
increased blood-to-brain transport of other monocarboxylates, 
such as lactate, into the brain might serve in a very limited 
capacity as an alternative fuel substrate, and maybe involved 
in the pathogenesis of HAAF. Interestingly, [3-13C]lactate 
NMR spectroscopy data in rats indicate that hypoglycemia per 
se increases brain neuronal lactate consumption, and that the 
increase is greater after recurrent hypoglycemia.114 Furthermore, 
it includes evidence of reduced glutamate release within the ven­
tromedial nucleus of the rat hypothalamus.116 A component of 
the impaired counterregulatory response involving suppressed 
activity at the level of the adrenal medulla111 may explain the 
dissociation between the development of and recovery from 
impaired epinephrine (seen first before impaired symptom 
awareness117) and autonomic symptom (recovers ahead of epi­
nephrine118) responses to hypoglycemia.
Much of the fundamental research into the mechanism of 
HAAF has focused on the hypothalamus, the central integrator 
of the sympathoadrenal response to hypoglycemia. It is conceiv­
able, however, that the changes in the hypothalamic/sympathoad­
renal response reflect modulation by higher brain centers.77,108–110 
For example, measurements of regional cerebral blood flow using 
oxygen-15–labeled water and positron emission tomography indi­
cate that hypoglycemia increases synaptic activity in widespread 
but interconnected brain regions in humans108 and that recent 
antecedent hypoglycemia both reduces sympathoadrenal and 
symptomatic responses (a model of HAAF) and increases synaptic 
activation in the dorsal midline thalamus (and only in that brain 
region) during subsequent hypoglycemia.109,110 Therefore, it has 
been suggested that there may be a cerebral network that results in 
thalamic inhibition of hypothalamic activity in HAAF.109,110 Such 
a putative cerebral network is included in Fig. 39.9, although it 
remains theoretical.
Risk Factors for HAAF
The risk factors for HAAF89,119–124 (see Box 39.3) include the 
following:
	1.	 Absolute endogenous insulin deficiency (C-peptide negative 
[<0.5 ng/mL]),1,89,119–123 usually with long (>10 years) diabe­
tes duration
	2.	 A history of severe iatrogenic hypoglycemia, impaired aware­
ness of hypoglycemia, or both and recent antecedent hypogly­
cemia, particularly frequent asymptomatic hypoglycemia (as 
may occur with sleep), or prior exercise89,120–122,125
	3.	 Aggressive glycemic therapy per se (i.e., lower HbA1c levels, 
lower glycemic goals, or both)89,120–124
	4.	 Excessive glucose variability126–129

CHAPTER 39  Hypoglycemia
As discussed earlier, the degree of β-cell failure determines the 
extent to which insulin levels will not decrease and glucagon lev­
els will not increase as glucose levels fall in response to therapeutic 
hyperinsulinemia. The importance of loss of a decrease in insulin as 
glucose levels decline in response to therapeutic hyperinsulinemia 
is underscored by the fact that patients with T1D and some degree 
of preserved insulin secretion have a lower incidence of hypogly­
cemia.130 A history of severe hypoglycemia indicates (and that of 
impaired awareness of hypoglycemia implies) recent antecedent 
hypoglycemia. Like prior exercise or sleep, recent antecedent hypo­
glycemia causes attenuated sympathoadrenal and symptomatic 
responses to subsequent hypoglycemia, the key feature of HAAF. 
Aggressive glycemic therapy and excessive glucose variability are 
additional risk factors for hypoglycemia. That does not mean, how­
ever, that one cannot both improve glycemic control and minimize 
the risk of hypoglycemia in many patients89 (see later discussion). 
Prevention of Hypoglycemia in Diabetes
Hypoglycemia risk factor reduction (Box 39.4)89,131 is an empiric 
approach to minimizing the risk of iatrogenic hypoglycemia while 
maintaining or improving glycemic control in persons with dia­
betes. It involves four steps: (1) acknowledge the problem, (2) 
consider the conventional risk factors, (3) consider the risk fac­
tors for HAAF, and (4) apply the principles of aggressive glycemic 
therapy89 (see Box 39.3).
Acknowledge the Problem
The problem of hypoglycemia should be addressed, at least in per­
sons treated with insulin or with an insulin secretagogue, in every 
patient contact. Acknowledging the issue allows the caregiver to 
move on, if hypoglycemia is not a problem, or to deal with it and 
keep it in perspective, if hypoglycemia is a problem. Some patients 
are reluctant to raise the issue, but their concerns about the real­
ity, or even the possibility, of hypoglycemia can be a barrier to 
glycemic control.132–134 If possible, close associates of the patient 
should be asked whether they have observed clues to episodes 
not recognized by the patient. Even if no concerns are expressed, 
review of the record of self-monitoring of blood glucose or CGM 
data may disclose that hypoglycemia is a problem. 
Consider the Conventional Risk Factors
The conventional risk factors are those that result in relative, as 
well as absolute, insulin excess (see Box 39.3). In addition to insu­
lin and insulin secretagogue doses, timing, and type, they include 
conditions in which exogenous glucose delivery or endogenous 
glucose production is decreased, glucose utilization or sensitivity 
to insulin is increased, or insulin clearance is decreased. 
Consider the Risk Factors for HAAF
The risk factors indicative of HAAF (see Box 39.3) are those that 
lead to impaired awareness of hypoglycemia and attenuated coun­
terregulatory responses.120–122 In a patient with impaired aware­
ness of hypoglycemia, patient reeducation135–137 and an at least 
3-week period of scrupulous avoidance of hypoglycemia is advis­
able and may help to restore awareness.94–97 This approach usually 
requires somewhat higher glycemic goals in the short term, and 
usually requires a change in insulin regimen or delivery approach. 
A history of late postexercise hypoglycemia, nocturnal hypoglyce­
mia, or both should prompt appropriately timed regimen adjust­
ments to provide more carbohydrate intake, less insulin action, 
or both. 
Apply the Principles of Aggressive Glycemic Therapy
These principles131 include diabetes self-management by a well-
informed patient, frequent self-monitoring of blood glucose lev­
els and/or CGM, flexible and appropriate insulin and other drug 
regimens, individualized glycemic goals, and ongoing professional 
guidance and support (see Box 39.4).
As the therapeutic regimen becomes progressively more com­
plex—early in T1D and later in T2D—successful glycemic man­
agement becomes progressively more dependent on the many 
decisions and the skills of a well-informed person with diabetes. 
Therefore, patient education and empowerment are fundamen­
tally important. Patients treated with insulin or insulin secreta­
gogues need to know the common symptoms of hypoglycemia, 
their individual most meaningful symptoms, and how to treat 
(and not overtreat) an episode. They need to know the relevant 
conventional risk factors for hypoglycemia, including the temporal 
patterns of the glucose-lowering actions of their individual insulin 
preparations or secretagogues and the effects of missed meals, the 
overnight fast, exercise, and alcohol ingestion. They also need to 
know that increasing episodes of hypoglycemia signal an increased 
likelihood of future, often more severe, hypoglycemia.120–122,125 
Close associates also need to know how to recognize hypoglyce­
mia, to understand why a neuroglycopenic patient may become 
uncooperative, and to know when and how to administer gluca­
gon (see later discussion). Finally, patients need to learn to apply 
the data from their self-monitoring of blood glucose concentra­
tions or from CGM toward the goal of minimizing hypoglyce­
mia (as well as hyperglycemia). Structured education focused on 
avoidance of hypoglycemia can improve awareness of hypoglyce­
mia, reduce glucose variability, and reduce the incidence of severe 
hypoglycemia without deterioration of glycemic control.135–138
Frequent self-monitoring and/or CGM becomes vital to dia­
betes self-management as the therapeutic regimen becomes more 
complex, early in T1D and later in T2D (see Chapter 35). Ideally, 
patients should monitor their glucose level whenever they suspect 
hypoglycemia. That would confirm or refute an episode and help 
the patients learn their individual key symptoms and might lead 
to regimen adjustments. It is important for patients with impaired 
awareness of hypoglycemia to monitor glucose levels before per­
forming critical tasks such as driving. Unfortunately, conventional 
blood glucose monitoring, in which a measurement is obtained at 
one point in time, does not indicate whether the glucose level is 
falling, stable, or rising. That shortcoming is addressed by using 
technologies for CGM.139,140

Real-time CGM enables identification of falling (and rising) 
glucose values and the use of alerts (vibration) and alarms to indi­
cate when glucose levels are declining (or increasing) rapidly, or 
cross user set thresholds for hypoglycemia (and hyperglycemia) 
(Fig. 39.10). Earlier identification of incipient or actual hypo­
glycemia allows for an individual to ingest carbohydrate and/
or decrease or suspend insulin delivery to prevent or correct low 
blood glucose sooner, especially for those with impaired awareness 
of hypoglycemia, and helps to limit exposure to and severity of 
hypoglycemia. In patients with T1D and impaired awareness of 
hypoglycemia, high adherence to the use of CGM over at least 
a 4-month period reduces hypoglycemia frequency and severity 
without deterioration in glycemic control140–143 that is associated 
with improvement in hypoglycemia awareness140 and reduction in 
glucose variability142,143 in some but not all studies. Consequently, 
near-complete adherence to use appears necessary for CGM to 
reduce clinically significant hypoglycemia in clinical practice144 
and persistence of impaired awareness of hypoglycemia is com­
mon among CGM users.145 Incomplete avoidance of time spent 
with hypoglycemia on CGM, which is dependent on the patient 
to respond appropriately to device alerts and alarms and especially 
challenging during sleep, likely accounts for documented persis­
tent impairment in the epinephrine response to hypoglycemia and 
consequently ongoing defects in glucose counterregulation.140
Despite considerable enthusiasm for continuous subcutane­
ous insulin infusion (CSII) over multiple daily injections (MDI) 
of insulin,146 one meta-analysis147 disclosed no significant differ­
ence in minor or severe hypoglycemia events with CSII or MDI, 
and a randomized trial148 that specifically included structured 
patient education in both groups revealed no difference in severe 
hypoglycemia with CSII or MDI. In another study where par­
ticipants using MDI were first assigned to CGM, subsequent

with glucose in the target range 70 to 180 mg/dL with CSII vs. 
MDI, but also with more time spent with hypoglycemia and no 
difference in HbA1c.149
There is convincing evidence that insulin analogues reduce the 
incidence of severe hypoglycemia when compared to regular insu­
lin preparations in patients with diabetes who are at high risk for 
hypoglycemia150 that includes both rapid acting prandial insulins 
(lispro, aspart) and the long-acting basal insulins degludec151 and 
glargine U300,152 both compared with glargine U100 once daily. 
Nevertheless, insulin analogues still cause hypoglycemia.153,154
There is increasing evidence that automated insulin delivery 
systems, specifically those that temporarily suspend insulin infu­
sion when a low glucose concentration is predicted using inte­
grated CGM, reduces hypoglycemia in T1D155 (see Fig. 39.10). In 
patients with T1D and either impaired awareness of hypoglycemia 
or a recent severe hypoglycemia event, use of automated insulin 
suspension compared to standard CSII and CGM reduced time 
spent with hypoglycemia by >50% that was especially effective 
during the nocturnal period and associated with a reduction in 
severe hypoglycemia events.156 Whether closed loop systems that 
also automate increased insulin infusion when an elevated glucose 
concentration is predicted may better address excessive glucose 
variability and further reduce clinically important hypoglycemia 
is an area of active investigation. Nevertheless, automated suspen­
sion of insulin infusion remains limited by the subcutaneous (SC) 
route of delivery that may not lower circulating insulin concen­
trations fast enough to correct a rapidly declining glucose result­
ing from excessive insulin bolus administration or the increased 
glucose utilization that accompanies exercise. The recent develop­
ment of soluble preparations of glucagon provides the future pos­
sibility for either automated or patient-directed administration of 
micro- or “mini”-dose glucagon to prevent or correct low blood 
glucose.157
Whole pancreas and isolated pancreatic islet transplantation, 
which replace islet cell function to decrease β-cell insulin secretion 
and consequently increase α-cell glucagon secretion in defense 
against the development of low blood glucose, are the only inter­
ventions that have been shown to restore both glucose counterreg­
ulation and hypoglycemia symptom recognition in patients with 
T1D and impaired awareness of hypoglycemia.158,159 Pancreatic 
islet transplantation prevents hypoglycemia as long as the trans­
plant is functional, even if low-dose insulin therapy is required 
to maintain normoglycemia. CGM measures demonstrate sig­
nificant reductions in mean glucose (and HbA1c), glucose vari­
ability, and time spent with clinically significant hypoglycemia in 
both insulin-independent and insulin-requiring islet transplant 
recipients.160–162 The glycemic thresholds for activation of coun­
terregulatory glucagon and epinephrine secretion in response to 
hypoglycemia are normal in individuals studied 6 months post­
transplant relative to marked impairment in matched control 
subjects with T1D.163 Longitudinal follow-up of islet transplant 
recipients spending essentially no time with hypoglycemia (CGM 
time < 70 mg/dL ∼1%) showed normalization of hypoglycemia 
symptom recognition with partial improvement in the magnitude 
of the epinephrine response to hypoglycemia at 6 months and 
complete normalization of epinephrine secretion by 18 months.164 
Thus, complete recovery from HAAF in patients with T1D and 
impaired awareness of hypoglycemia is possible, but may require 
near-complete avoidance of hypoglycemia together with signifi­
cant reduction in glucose variability maintained for more than a 
6-month period.
Therapeutic hyperinsulinemia, a prerequisite for iatrogenic 
hypoglycemia, can occur during treatment with an insulin or 
with an insulin secretagogue (such as a sulfonylurea or a glinide). 
Early in its course, T2D may respond to drugs that do not raise 
insulin levels at normal or low plasma glucose concentrations 
and therefore should not, and probably do not,1,165 cause hypo­
glycemia. Such drugs include the biguanide metformin, SGLT2 
(sodium-glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, 
α-glucosidase inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP1) recep­
tor agonists, and dipeptidyl peptidase (DPP-IV) inhibitors. All 
of these drugs require endogenous insulin secretion to lower 
plasma glucose concentrations, and insulin secretion declines 
appropriately as glucose levels fall into the normal range. That is 
true even for the GLP1 receptor agonists and DPP-IV inhibitors, 
which enhance glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (among other 
actions). Nonetheless, all six categories of drugs increase the risk 
of hypoglycemia if used with insulin or with an insulin secreta­
gogue. Among the commonly prescribed insulin secretagogues, 
hypoglycemia is more often associated with the longer-acting sul­
fonylurea glyburide (glibenclamide) than with the shorter-acting 
glimepiride166 or the short-acting glinides.
Given the premise that glycemic goals in diabetes are a trade-
off between glycemic control and iatrogenic hypoglycemia,167 it 
has been suggested that a reasonable individualized glycemic goal 
is the lowest HbA1c that does not cause severe hypoglycemia and 
preserves awareness of hypoglycemia, preferably with little or no 
symptomatic or even asymptomatic hypoglycemia, at a given stage 
in the evolution of the individual’s diabetes. Parenthetically, the 
substantial relationship between a lower HbA1c level and a higher 
incidence of severe hypoglycemia has been consistently docu­
mented in randomized controlled clinical trials in both T1D26,28 
and T2D.6,46,55,168,169 In these trials when patients with diabetes 
were randomly assigned to intensive glycemic therapy, largely with 
insulin, and shown to have lower HbA1c levels or to more conven­
tional glycemic goals and shown to have higher HbA1c levels, the 
incidence of severe hypoglycemia was two- to threefold higher in 
each of the groups with the lower HbA1c levels. The frequency of 
hypoglycemia was inversely related to the HbA1c level in both the 
original DCCT and in follow-up EDIC phase,26,28 although the 
slope was less steep in the EDIC phase. The extent to which the 
latter is the result of insulin analogues, improved insulin delivery 
systems, CGM, patient education, patient or caregiver skill, or 
some other fact is not known. For patients with T1D receiving 
care at specialty diabetes clinics in the United States, 7% to 8% 
reported experiencing a severe hypoglycemia resulting in seizure 
or loss-of-consciousness in the prior 3 months regardless of HbA1c 
level (<7%, 7% to <8%, and ≥8%).170 Thus, simply recommend­
ing a higher HbA1c target for patients with clinically significant 
hypoglycemia or impaired awareness of hypoglycemia is unlikely 
to impact the current burden of severe hypoglycemia and may not 
be acceptable to patients striving to avoid or mitigate the devel­
opment of micro- and macrovascular complications.171 Instead, 
using CGM targeted reduction in time-spent with hypoglycemia 
and glucose variability may more directly mitigate risk for experi­
encing future severe hypoglycemia.172
Clearly, one should strive to balance benefits and harms in the 
selection of a glycemic goal for a person with diabetes. Many per­
sons with diabetes—those with HAAF, a history of severe hypo­
glycemia, chronic kidney disease, a long duration of diabetes, or 
malnutrition—are at risk of harm from iatrogenic hypoglycemia. 
Those with chronic vascular complications, serious comorbidities, 
or a short life expectancy have little likelihood of benefit. In both 
1592
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
of these groups, a less stringent glycemic goal is indicated,173 per­
haps a HbA1c less than 7.5% to 8.5% (69 mmol/mol),174 and 
instead of targeting CGM time in the normal glucose range 70 to 
180 mg/dL at >70% and allowing time-below-range <70 mg/dL 
at <4%, time-in-range may be targeted to >50% to 60%, whereas 
time-below-range is kept <1%.175
Finally, because the glycemic management of diabetes is 
empiric, caregivers should work with each patient to find the most 
effective and safest regimen at a given point in the course of that 
patient’s diabetes. 
Treatment of Hypoglycemia in Diabetes
Most episodes of symptomatic or asymptomatic hypoglycemia 
detected by self-monitoring or CGM are effectively self-treated 
by ingestion of glucose tablets, glucose gel, or other fast-acting 
carbohydrates.1 A reasonable dose is 15 to 20 g of glucose.1 A 
meta-analysis indicated that glucose tablets result in a higher rate 
of relief of symptomatic hypoglycemia than dietary sugar.176 Clin­
ical improvement should occur in 15 to 20 minutes. The tempta­
tion to overtreat is understandable but should be avoided. With 
ongoing hyperinsulinemia, the glycemic response to oral glucose 
is transient, typically lasting less than 2 hours. Therefore, ingestion 
of a snack or meal shortly after the glucose level is raised is usually 
advisable after correcting symptomatic or serious hypoglycemia 
but may not be desirable when correcting asymptomatic mild or 
predicted hypoglycemia as long as a stable glucose >70 to 90 mg/
dL is achieved.
In a patient who is unable or unwilling (because of neuroglyco­
penia) to take carbohydrate orally, glucagon therapy is necessary. 
Glucagon, now available in several preparations,157 can be injected 
subcutaneously or intramuscularly, or for a dry powder prepara­
tion delivered intranasally,177 by an associate of the patient. Glu­
cagon should be readily accessible to all patients with diabetes 
treated with insulin or an insulin secretagogue. Administration of 
glucagon can be lifesaving, but it often causes substantial, albeit 
transient, hyperglycemia (Fig. 39.11), and it can cause nausea and 
even vomiting, and with intranasal delivery headache. Whereas 
standard glucagon forms fibrils in aqueous solution and so has been 
manufactured as a lyophilized powder requiring reconstitution in 
sterile water immediately before injection, there is now a glucagon 
stable in nonaqueous solution and a glucagon analogue stable in 
solution that retain rapid plasma glucose-raising action and are 
available for emergency use by auto injection. Both intranasal and 
auto injection of stable liquid glucagon preparations represent 
major improvements for simplifying the treatment of severe hypo­
glycemia. Intramuscular (IM) glucagon is given at a dose of 0.5 
mg for children <25 kg and at 1 mg for patients >25 kg. A single 
3-mg dose of nasal glucagon is an alternative to IM glucagon for 
patients ≥4 years of age and provides increased ease of administra­
tion. Dasiglucagon, a stable glucagon analogue, available as 0.6 
mg ready-to-use pen SC can also be used for severe hypoglycemia 
in patients ≥6 years old. In addition, smaller doses of stable liquid 
glucagon, repeated if necessary, have been found to be effective for 
correcting nonsevere hypoglycemia with fewer side effects,178,179 
for preventing exercise-associated hypoglycemia,180 or in children 
with hypoglycemia and gastrointestinal illness and/or poor oral 
carbohydrate intake. The dose is administered subcutaneously and 
is age based; 2 units (20 μg) for children <2 years and 1 unit/year 
for children >3 to 15 years (with a maximum dose of 150 μg or 
15 units). If blood glucose failed to rise over the first 30 minutes, 
a repeat injection was given using twice the initial dose. The mini­
dose glucagon regimen resulted in an increase of 3.3 to 5 mmol/L 
of glucose (60–90 mg/dL) within 30 minutes of administration 
with an average increase of 4.7 mmol/L.181 If blood glucose failed 
to rise over the first 30 minutes, a repeat injection was given using 
twice the initial dose. These small doses may also be infused along­
side of insulin in bihormonal artificial pancreas systems currently 
under development.182
Because it acts by stimulating glycogenolysis, glucagon is inef­
fective in glycogen-depleted individuals (e.g., after a binge of alco­
hol ingestion). Although it is not an issue in T1D or advanced 
T2D, glucagon stimulates insulin secretion. Indeed, glucagon has 
been reported to cause hypoglycemia in nondiabetic individuals 
(see later discussion). Glucagon can be administered intravenously 
by medical personnel, but in that setting intravenous (IV) glucose 
(dextrose) is the standard parenteral therapy. A common initial 
dose is 25 g, but lower doses are generally advisable to avoid post­
hypoglycemic hyperglycemia.6
The glycemic response to IV glucose is transient in the setting 
of ongoing hyperinsulinemia. Therefore, IV glucose administra­
tion often needs to be followed by glucose infusion and, once it is 
practical, by carbohydrate feeding.
The duration of an episode of severe hypoglycemia is a function 
of its cause. An episode caused by a rapid-acting insulin analogue 
or insulin secretagogue will be relatively brief. That caused by a 
long-acting insulin analogue or insulin secretagogue can result in 
prolonged hypoglycemia requiring hospitalization.

Hypoglycemia in Persons Without Diabetes
The Decision to Evaluate for Hypoglycemia
Although hypoglycemia is common in persons with diabetes,1 it is 
a distinctly uncommon clinical event in persons who do not have 
diabetes2,184 because of the effectiveness of the normal physiologic 
and behavioral defenses against falling plasma glucose concentra­
tions. Therefore, in the absence of diabetes, a thorough evalua­
tion for hypoglycemia is recommended only for patients in whom

Whipple triad (see Box 39.1) (symptoms, signs, or both consistent 
with hypoglycemia; a low, reliably measured plasma glucose con­
centration; and resolution of those symptoms or signs after the 
plasma glucose concentration is raised) can be documented. In the 
absence of such documentation, evaluation for hypoglycemia may 
expose the patient to unnecessary evaluation, costs, and potential 
harm without expectation of benefit.2
Plasma glucose concentrations used to document Whipple 
triad must be measured with a reliable laboratory method and 
not with a blood glucose self-monitor. A low, reliably measured 
plasma glucose concentration obtained in the absence of recog­
nized symptoms or signs should not be ignored. However, such a 
finding raises the possibility of “pseudohypoglycemia,” an artifact 
of continued glucose metabolism by the formed elements of the 
blood after the blood sample is drawn.2 This may occur if the 
sample is collected in a container that does not include an inhibi­
tor of glycolysis, such as NaF-EDTA-citrate (EDTA: ethylene­
diaminetetraacetic acid), and separation of the plasma or serum 
from the formed elements is delayed, particularly in the setting of 
erythrocytosis, leukocytosis, or thrombocytosis.
Venous sampling is standard in the clinical setting, but it is the 
arterial plasma glucose concentration that fuels the brain. Arterio­
venous plasma glucose concentration differences are negligible in 
the postabsorptive state, but antecubital venous glucose levels are 
as much as one third lower than arterial glucose levels when insulin 
secretion is increased (e.g., after an oral glucose load) stimulating 
glucose extraction across the forearm.185 Because of the provision 
of alternative fuels (specifically ketones) to the brain, plasma glu­
cose concentrations lower than the overnight fasted physiologic 
range occur in healthy individuals, especially women and chil­
dren, during extended fasting.3 Finally, the glycemic thresholds 
of responses to hypoglycemia shift to lower plasma glucose con­
centrations in patients with recurrent hypoglycemia.72,73 For all of 
these reasons, it is important to document Whipple triad before 
concluding that a hypoglycemic disorder exists in a person with­
out diabetes.2 On the other hand, a reliably measured, unequivo­
cally normal plasma glucose concentration (e.g., >70 mg/dL [3.9 
mmol/L]) during a symptomatic episode provides strong evidence 
that the symptoms were not the result of hypoglycemia.2 
Clinical Classification of Hypoglycemic Disorders
The traditional classification of hypoglycemic disorders in non­
diabetic persons, as either postabsorptive (fasting) or postprandial 
hypoglycemia, has been supplanted by a clinical categorization. 
This distinguishes a patient who has a relevant disease or treat­
ment from a patient who is otherwise seemingly well (see Box 
39.2).2,186 The presence of postprandial symptoms without Whip­
ple triad, previously called “reactive hypoglycemia,” is now con­
sidered a functional disorder in which symptoms are not due to 
hypoglycemia and for which oral glucose tolerance testing should 
not be performed.2
Ill or Medicated Individual
Drugs are the most common cause of hypoglycemia.187–193 In 
addition to insulin and insulin secretagogues (discussed ear­
lier), offending drugs include alcohol among many others (Box 
39.5).188–192 Drugs, often in the setting of critical illnesses includ­
ing renal failure, are the most common cause of hypoglycemia in 
hospitals.187 Again, insulin or insulin secretagogues are common 
offending drugs,187,194 particularly if they are administered when 
enteral or parenteral nutrition is interrupted. Offending drugs 
can be discontinued or their dosage reduced to prevent further 
hypoglycemia.
Ethanol inhibits gluconeogenesis. Clinical alcohol-induced 
hypoglycemia typically follows a binge of alcohol consumption 
during which the person eats little food (i.e., in the setting of gly­
cogen depletion).189 Alcohol-induced hypoglycemia can be fatal, 
but with restoration of euglycemia and supportive care, recovery 
is the rule. Ethanol is usually measurable in blood at the time of 
presentation.
Hypoglycemia sometimes occurs in patients with critical ill­
nesses (see Box 39.1).2 Hepatogenous hypoglycemia occurs most 
commonly when destruction of the liver is rapid and massive (e.g., 
in toxic hepatitis). It is unusual in common forms of cirrhosis or 
hepatitis, although glucose metabolism is measurably altered in 
uncomplicated viral hepatitis.195 Hypoglycemia is also unusual in 
metastatic liver disease despite extensive hepatic replacement.196 
The pathogenesis of hypoglycemia in some patients with renal 
failure is unknown and likely multifactorial; it has been attributed 
to drugs, sepsis, or inanition.187,197–199 Reduced renal clearance 
of insulin and reduced renal glucose production are contributing 
factors.200 However, renal transplantation may not correct hypo­
glycemia in patients with glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency.201
The pathogenesis of the hypoglycemia occasionally seen in 
patients with severe cardiac failure is also not understood. The

finding of elevated blood lactate levels associated with hypogly­
cemia202 raises the possibility of inhibited gluconeogenesis, per­
haps as a consequence of hepatic congestion and altered glycogen 
turnover.
Sepsis is a relatively common cause of hypoglycemia.187,188,203 
Increased glucose utilization (by skeletal muscle and by macro­
phage-rich tissues such as liver, spleen, and lung), which is thought 
to be cytokine mediated and is matched initially by increased 
glucose production, characterizes experimental sepsis.204–206 The 
later decline in glucose production, which in the setting of per­
sistently high glucose utilization results in hypoglycemia, is not 
the result of glucose counterregulatory failure; rather, it is caused 
by decreased responsiveness to appropriate glucose counterregu­
latory signals (i.e., low insulin and high glucagon and epineph­
rine levels).207 A similar mechanism explains hypoglycemia that 
can presents as a manifestation of a large malignant tumor bur­
den (hyper-Warburgism) and may respond to chemotherapy.208 
Hypoglycemia can be caused by inanition.209 A plausible sugges­
tion is that glucose becomes the sole oxidative fuel in the setting 
of total body fat depletion, and the resulting high rates of glucose 
utilization exceed the capacity to produce glucose because of a 
limited supply of gluconeogenic precursors (e.g., amino acids). 
Postabsorptive hypoglycemia (with low circulating alanine con­
centrations) has been reported in patients with profound muscle 
atrophy210,211; hypoglycemia is presumably the result of substrate 
limitation of gluconeogenesis in such patients.
With the notable exception of HAAF in patients with T1D 
and advanced T2D (discussed earlier), hormone deficiencies 
resulting in hypoglycemia are not common. Postabsorptive hypo­
glycemia, typically after a period of caloric deprivation caused by 
an intercurrent illness, can occur in patients with deficient secre­
tion of cortisol, growth hormone, or both, particularly infants 
and young children.212–214 Glycemic intolerance of fasting is 
largely corrected by glucocorticoid replacement; growth hormone 
replacement has a lesser effect,213,214 and isolated growth hormone 
deficiency does not cause hypoglycemia in adults.215 Because 
cortisol normally supports gluconeogenesis by increasing gluco­
neogenic enzyme activities and mobilizing gluconeogenic precur­
sors,213,216 the hypoglycemic mechanism is thought to be reduced 
glucose production in the setting of glycogen deficiency. Primary 
autoimmune adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) should be 
considered in T1D presenting with worsening hypoglycemia and 
additional signs of primary adrenal insufficiency (hyperpigmenta­
tion, salt craving, orthostasis, hyponatremia). Hypoglycemia has 
been reported in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-deficient 
adults when glucose utilization or loss was increased (as during 
exercise or pregnancy, respectively)217 or when glucose production 
is impaired (as after alcohol ingestion).218
Non–islet cell tumor hypoglycemia (NICTH) is rare. The 
tumors are usually, but not invariably large, clinically apparent, 
and mesenchymal in origin. NICTH is often the result of over­
production of incompletely processed pro–insulin-like growth 
factor 2 (pro-IGF2),219–222 but hypoglycemia attributed to over­
production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) has also been 
reported.223 The pro-IGF2 binds poorly to its binding proteins 
and therefore more freely enters tissue spaces, where its insulin-
like actions cause hypoglycemia. Concentrations of plasma free 
IGF2 (or IGF1223) are elevated.220 Because of suppression of 
growth hormone secretion and the resulting low IGF1 levels, the 
ratio of plasma IGF2 to IGF1 is elevated in pro-IGF2–mediated 
hypoglycemia. Plasma total IGF2 levels may be within the nor­
mal range, but the ratio of pro-IGF2 to IGF2 may be elevated.221 
Endogenous insulin secretion is suppressed appropriately during 
hypoglycemia in NICTH. Reduction of NICTH with surgery, 
irradiation, or chemotherapy may alleviate hypoglycemia even if 
the tumor cannot be cured. Treatment with a glucocorticoid may 
be effective. Prevention of ongoing or recurrent hypoglycemia 
requires treatment that corrects or circumvents the hypoglycemic 
mechanism.2 Obviously, treatment should be tailored to the spe­
cific hypoglycemic disorder identified. 
Seemingly Well Individual
In seemingly well individuals with no evidence of drug, critical 
illness, hormone deficiency, or non–islet cell tumor as a cause of 
their hypoglycemia, the differential diagnosis narrows to two cat­
egories: accidental, surreptitious, or even malicious hypoglycemia 
and endogenous hyperinsulinism (see Box 39.2).2,184,186,224–226 
Consideration of the former possibility should precede a sys­
tematic assessment of the latter. Medical, pharmacy, and hospi­
tal errors can result in hypoglycemia and do occur. Surreptitious 
hypoglycemia224–228 is more common in people with knowledge 
of, and access to, glucose-lowering medications. Malicious hypo­
glycemia224,225 can be accomplished by administration of insulin 
or an insulin secretagogue.
Insulinomas (insulin-secreting pancreatic β-cell tumors) are 
the prototypical, but not the only, cause of endogenous hyperin­
sulinemic hypoglycemia.2,184,229–233 Patients with an insulinoma 
typically present with a history of episodes of neuroglycopenia 
occurring in the postabsorptive (fasting) state. However, an appre­
ciable subset of patients (6% in one series229) report symptoms 
exclusively in the postprandial state. Insulinoma is also typically 
associated with weight gain. Insulinomas are rare; an incidence of 
1 in 250,000 patient-years has been reported. Fewer than 10% of 
the patients have malignant insulinomas, multiple insulinomas, 
or the multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) syndrome.233 
Interestingly, a missense MAFA mutation leading to familial insu­
linomas or diabetes mellitus has been identified in two families.234 
Insulinomas often exhibit impaired proinsulin processing, and 
some may predominantly produce and secrete proinsulin.235 Sur­
gical resection of a benign insulinoma is typically curative, and 
long-term survival is the rule after successful operation.233 Deb­
ulking malignant insulinoma by surgical resection, chemoemboli­
zation of hepatic metastases,236 and/or radiolabeled somatostatin 
analogue therapy237 may help to control hypoglycemia and pro­
long time to progression and survival. In unresectable disease, 
empirical treatments (diet, glucocorticoids, diazoxide, octreotide) 
can be tried. Octreotide may block the glucose raising action of 
diazoxide238 and so should generally be trialed first. A minority of 
insulinomas fail to express type 2 or type 5 somatostatin recep­
tors, and so octreotide may cause paradoxical worsening of hypo­
glycemia by inhibiting counterregulatory glucagon and growth 
hormone secretion without suppressing insulin secretion from 
somatostatin receptor negative tumors;239 candidates for long-act­
ing IM octreotide may be selected by positive somatostatin recep­
tor scintigraphy (see below) and/or response to a monitored trial 
of IV or SC octreotide.240 Inhibitors of the mammalian target of 
rapamycin may also be useful for controlling hypoglycemia and 
delaying tumor progression.241–243
Some patients (4% of one series233) with fasting endogenous 
hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia do not have an insulinoma but 
have diffuse islet involvement with islet hypertrophy, some­
times with hyperplasia, and enlarged and hyperchromatic β-cell 
nuclei. This condition is often termed nesidioblastosis, although 
the histologic finding of islets budding from pancreatic ducts 
1595
CHAPTER 39  Hypoglycemia
is not invariably present. Such patients are clinically indistin­
guishable from those with an insulinoma.244–248 Other patients 
with predominantly postprandial endogenous hyperinsulinemic 
hypoglycemia may have the noninsulinoma pancreatogenous 
hypoglycemia syndrome (NIPHS)248–251 or post–gastric bypass 
hypoglycemia.252–256
NIPHS248–251 is characterized by spells of neuroglycopenia 
caused by endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia occur­
ring typically, but not invariably, after a meal. NIPHS is less 
common than insulinoma.2,184 Because the syndrome is dif­
fuse, anatomic tumor imaging studies are uniformly negative. 
Given documented postprandial hyperinsulinemic hypoglyce­
mia, documentation of diffuse β-cell hyperfunction depends on 
a positive selective arterial calcium stimulation test. The findings 
from that test can be used to guide partial pancreatectomy if 
empiric medical therapy (e.g., diet including frequent feedings, 
an α-glucosidase inhibitor, diazoxide, octreotide) fails. In one 
relatively large surgical series, most patients improved but recur­
rence of symptoms was the rule, and some patients were not 
helped after partial pancreatectomy.250
Post–gastric bypass hypoglycemia is a form of alimentary 
hypoglycemia where gastric bypass and Roux-en-Y gastrointesti­
nal reconstruction may result in “late dumping syndrome” where 
altered nutrient transit with accelerated delivery to the distal small 
intestine leads to more rapid glucose absorption and exaggerated 
GLP1 and insulin responses257,258 that with dysregulated islet 
function in some individuals results in postprandial hypoglyce­
mia typically occurring 2 to 4 hours after meals252–255,259,260 (see 
Chapter 40). This form of alimentary hypoglycemia usually pres­
ents more than 6 to 12 months postoperatively.252–256,260,261 Ali­
mentary hypoglycemia can also occur after gastrectomy,262 total 
pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation that involves Roux-
en-Y gastrointestinal reconstruction,263,264 and fundoplication 
and sleeve gastrectomy that accelerate gastric emptying.265 GLP1 
receptor blockade prevents postprandial hypoglycemia in affected 
individuals that is associated with greater reduction in postpran­
dial insulin secretion than that observed in postsurgical controls 
without alimentary hypoglycemia, although this remains experi­
mental.261,266 Counterregulatory responses to defend against the 
development of hypoglycemia are also impaired after gastric bypass 
surgery, including marked reductions in glucagon and epineph­
rine secretion in response to insulin-induced hypoglycemia267 evi­
dencing induction of HAAF by presumably frequent exposure to 
even mild postprandial hypoglycemia that may contribute to the 
long-term development of more severe hypoglycemia. Initial man­
agement involves dietary modification emphasizing controlled 
portions of low glycemic index complex carbohydrates ingested 
together with protein and fat to slow the rate of glucose absorp­
tion. Treatment may also include an α-glucosidase inhibitor to 
further slow carbohydrate absorption and minimize postpran­
dial glycemia and thus reduce the stimulus for insulin secretion. 
Additional interventions may include diazoxide or octreotide to 
suppress insulin secretion.260 Emergency treatment includes glu­
cagon (discussed earlier), and one of the new stable liquid formu­
lations delivered by automated pump rescue dosing informed by 
CGM has been shown to reduce severe hypoglycemia in individu­
als affected by post–gastric bypass hypoglycemia.268 Altering the 
route of nutrient delivery through gastrotomy tube placement269 
and deconstruction of the Roux-en-Y gastric bypass270 have been 
tried with varying short-term success. Partial pancreatectomy may 
lead to improvement, but recurrence of hyperinsulinemic hypo­
glycemia can occur.253
Autoimmune hypoglycemia caused by an antibody to insulin 
is rare.271,272 Affected individuals often have a history of other 
autoimmune disorders. Higher rates are reported among Asians 
that may be explained by higher prevalence of the HLA-DR4 
allele.273 Hypoglycemia occurs in the late postprandial period as 
insulin, which is secreted in response to the meal, and then bound 
to the circulating antibody, spontaneously dissociates from the 
antibody in an unregulated fashion.274 A clue to the diagnosis is 
the finding of very high measured plasma insulin levels during 
hypoglycemia with a molar ratio of insulin-to-C-peptide >1.275 
The diagnosis is made by the finding of high-titer serum insulin 
antibodies. Most patients enter remission within 3 to 6 months 
spontaneously or with treatment of an underlying autoimmune 
condition. Strategies described above for decreasing postprandial 
insulin secretion may help. Glucocorticoids may lower the anti­
body titer and should be considered. Refractory cases may require 
plasmapheresis276 or rituximab.277,278 Failing these treatments, 
frequent feedings during the day and bedtime administration of 
large doses of uncooked cornstarch or even overnight intragastric 
glucose infusion may be necessary. A similar disorder has been 
reported in patients with a high-capacity insulin-binding mono­
clonal paraprotein.279
Accidental or surreptitious ingestion of an insulin secretagogue 
causes endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia indistinguish­
able from that caused by an insulinoma aside from the presence 
of a measurable oral hypoglycemic agent in the circulation at the 
time of hypoglycemia.2,184
Very rare causes of insulin-related hypoglycemia have been 
linked to a mutation of the insulin receptor,280 to exercise-induced 
hyperinsulinemia,281 or to an agonist antibody to the insulin 
receptor.282 In the latter case, endogenous insulin secretion is 
suppressed appropriately, and inappropriately high insulin levels 
are thought to result from blockade of receptor-mediated insulin 
clearance by the antibody. Finally, although seemingly convincing 
cases of ectopic insulin secretion have been reported (e.g., by Seckl 
and colleagues283), the condition must be extraordinarily rare. 
Diagnostic Approach
Patients with a hypoglycemic disorder may present in a number 
of different ways including with a history of symptomatic epi­
sodes compatible with hypoglycemia, a serendipitously measured 
low plasma glucose concentration, or a familial syndrome that 
includes a hypoglycemic disorder (e.g., MEN1).2,186,224 A care­
ful history of any spells—including the specific symptoms, their 
timing in relation to meals, their duration, and any factors that 
aggravate or alleviate them—is important for the formulation 
of a diagnostic plan. A history that includes neuroglycopenia is 
particularly compelling.2 Again, documentation of Whipple triad 
establishes that a hypoglycemic disorder exists.2 The diagnostic 
strategy recommended in the Endocrine Society clinical practice 
guideline2 is described here.
First, review the history, physical findings, and all available 
laboratory data seeking clues to specific disorders such as drugs, 
critical illnesses, hormone deficiencies, or non–islet cell tumors 
(see Box 39.2) and pursue those.2 This approach will identify the 
cause of hypoglycemia in most instances. Again, drugs2 are, by far, 
the most common cause of hypoglycemia (see Box 39.5).
If the cause of a hypoglycemic disorder is not evident (i.e., in 
a seemingly healthy individual), measure plasma glucose, insu­
lin, C-peptide, proinsulin, and β-hydroxybutyrate concentra­
tions and screen for oral hypoglycemic agents during an episode 
1596
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
of spontaneous hypoglycemia, and observe the plasma glucose 
response to IV injection of 1.0 mg of glucagon.2 Also, measure 
insulin antibodies.2
Failure of insulin secretion to fall to very low rates as plasma 
glucose concentrations fall to hypoglycemic levels is the key 
pathophysiologic feature of endogenous hyperinsulinism. Hypo­
glycemia is the result of low rates of glucose production rather 
than high rates of glucose utilization.284 Plasma insulin, C-pep­
tide, and proinsulin concentrations may not always be high rela­
tive to normal values obtained under euglycemic conditions, but 
they are essentially always inappropriately high for the low plasma 
glucose concentrations.2,186,224 The traditional critical diagnostic 
criteria (assuming Whipple triad is documented) are plasma insu­
lin concentrations equal to or greater than 3 μU/mL (18 pmol/L), 
plasma C-peptide concentrations of 0.6 ng/mL (0.2 nmol/L) 
or higher, and plasma proinsulin concentrations of 5.0 pmol/L 
or higher when plasma glucose concentrations are less than 55 
mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L) (Table 39.4). These data, first published in 
1995,186 reassessed in 2009,229 and incorporated into the Endo­
crine Society clinical practice guideline on adult hypoglycemic 
disorders,2 were independently reassessed in 2013.232 Notably, 
however, the extent to which the unaffected subjects in the latter 
study had low plasma glucose concentrations at the time of insu­
lin, C-peptide, and proinsulin sampling is not made clear.232 The 
insulin criterion of 3 μU/mL (18 pmol/L) or higher was generally 
supported: 93% sensitivity with 95% to 100% specificity229 and 
98% sensitivity with 60% specificity.232 The C-peptide criterion 
of 0.6 ng/mL (0.2 nmol/L) or higher was not: sensitivity at 100% 
or lower with specificity of 60% to 78%229 versus sensitivity at 
100% but specificity only 10%232; raising the criterion to 2.3 ng/
mL (0.8 nmol/L) or higher lowered sensitivity to 84% but raised 
specificity to 76%.232 The proinsulin criterion of 5 pmol/L or 
higher provided 100% sensitivity in both series but with speci­
ficity of 68% to 78%229 and 41%;232 raising the criterion to 27 
pmol/L or higher still provided 100% sensitivity but with 100% 
specificity.232 Plasma β-hydroxybutyrate concentrations of 2.7 
mmol/L or lower, and an increase in the plasma glucose concen­
tration of more than 25 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) over the low value 
30 minutes after glucagon injection provide evidence of biologic 
actions of inappropriately high insulin (or IGF) levels, with sup­
pression of lipolysis and ketogenesis and preservation of hepatic 
glycogen stores, respectively. Finding an elevated insulin level dur­
ing hypoglycemia without elevation of C-peptide or proinsulin 
concentrations supports surreptitious or malicious administration 
of exogenous insulin, which may potentially be confirmed using 
an insulin-analogue specific immunoassay. The patterns of find­
ings in patients with a hypoglycemic disorder and in those with 
hyperinsulinemic (or IGF-mediated) hypoglycemia are summa­
rized in Table 39.4. Occasionally, a patient with an insulinoma 
may not fulfill these criteria even during a 72-hour fast,2,285 and a 
few have plasma insulin levels lower than 3 μU/mL (18 pmol/L) 
during hypoglycemia that may be attributable to impaired proin­
sulin processing, but at least in some series plasma C-peptide and 
proinsulin levels are elevated in such patients.286
If Whipple triad has not been documented and the mea­
surements described have not been obtained during an episode 
of spontaneous hypoglycemia, an attempt should be made to 
recreate the circumstances in which symptomatic hypoglycemia 
is likely to occur2 (see Box 39.1). This can be accomplished by 
withholding food in a patient with a history suggestive of fast­
ing hypoglycemia or by providing a mixed meal likely to cause 
a symptomatic episode in a patient with a history suggestive of

procedures, a patient with a history suggestive of fasting hypo­

fast should be continued until Whipple triad is documented 
(or until a plasma glucose concentration of less than 55 mg/dL

with a history suggestive of postprandial hypoglycemia should 
undergo a mixed meal test conducted over 5 hours (Box 39.7). 
Standards for interpretation of the findings of the mixed meal test 
have not been established; current usage2 is to apply the criteria 
developed under fasting conditions;186 however, the postprandial 
dynamics of glucose and β-cell peptide levels should be carefully 
interpreted because the peripheral concentrations represent the 
net sum of secretion and clearance at a given timepoint. Detailed 
suggestions for performance of a prolonged supervised fast and of 
a mixed meal test have been published (see Boxes 39.6 and 39.7).2 
For the hospitalized patient requiring continuous IV glucose to 
prevent hypoglycemia, diagnostic results can be obtained by serial 
sampling under close supervision after temporary discontinuation 
of glucose infusion.
A patient with documented Whipple triad; inappropriately high 
levels of insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin and no detectable cir­
culating oral hypoglycemic agent; suppressed β-hydroxybutyrate 
levels; a brisk glycemic response to IV glucagon during fasting 
(or even postprandial229) hypoglycemia; and no circulating insulin 
antibody may well have an insulinoma. However, as noted earlier, 
there are other causes of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (see Box 
39.2 and Table 39.4). Therefore, the next step is to attempt to 
localize an insulinoma.2
Computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging 
(MRI), and transabdominal ultrasonography detect approxi­
mately 75% of insulinomas.229,287,288 They also detect metastases 
in the minority of patients who have a malignant insulinoma. 
Older somatostatin receptor scintigraphy with planar imaging 
is somewhat less sensitive.289 Endoscopic pancreatic ultraso­
nography (EUS), with the option of fine-needle aspiration of a 
detected tumor, has a sensitivity of greater than 90%.289,290 With 
the combination of noninvasive imaging and, if necessary, EUS, 
preoperative localization of insulinomas has become the rule.229 
More sensitive single photon emission CT using radiotracers 
such as 111Indium DOTA-exendin-4291 and 68Gallium DOTA-
(Tyr3)-octreotate292 combined with CT (SPECT/CT) can iden­
tify most insulinomas and their metastases, making noninvasive 
localization of insulinomas increasingly possible. Given the high 
expression of GLP1 receptors in insulinomas and normal GLP1 
receptor expression in pancreatic tissue,293,294 the use of radio­
labeled GLP1 analogues have shown promising results for the 
diagnosis of insulinomas.291,293,295,296 However, there is lack of 
widespread available onsite radiopharmaceutical synthesis. 6-[18F]
Fluoro-3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (with or without CT

catecholamine-secreting tumors and more recently in the detec­

 • Date the onset of the fast as the time of the last food intake. Discontinue all 
nonessential medications.
 • Allow the patient to drink calorie-free beverages. Ensure that the patient is 
active during waking hours.
 • Collect samples for plasma glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, and 
β-hydroxybutyrate every 6 h until the plasma glucose concentration is <60 
mg/dL (<3.3 mmol/L); at that point the frequency of sampling should be 
increased to every 1–2 h.
 • Analysis of samples for plasma insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin may be 
limited to those in which the plasma glucose concentration is <60 mg/dL 
(<3.3 mmol/L).
 • End the fast when the plasma glucose concentration is <45 mg/dL (<2.5 
mmol/L) and the patient has symptoms and/or signs of hypoglycemia (or if 
72 h have elapsed without symptoms). The decision to end the fast before 
72 h should not be based on a low plasma glucose concentration alone, 
in the absence of symptoms or signs, because some healthy individuals, 
especially women and children, have low glucose levels during prolonged 
fasting. Alternatively, the fast can be ended when the plasma glucose 
concentration is <55 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L) without symptoms or signs if 
Whipple triad was documented unequivocally on a prior occasion or if the 
plasma β-hydroxybutyrate concentration is unequivocally elevated.
 • The decision to end the fast should be based on laboratory-measured 
plasma glucose concentrations, not those estimated with a point-of-
care blood glucose monitor. Serum is acceptable in place of plasma 
when processed immediately for analysis. If it is judged necessary to 
treat urgently because of severe symptoms, obtain samples for all of the 
following before administering carbohydrates:
 • At the end of the fast, collect samples for plasma glucose, insulin, 
C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate, and oral hypoglycemia agents, 
and then inject 1.0 mg of glucagon intravenously and measure plasma 
glucose 10, 20, and 30 min later. The glycemic response to glucagon may 
be assessed using a blood glucose monitor as the incremental rather than 
absolute glucose concentration is used to assess the response. (Insulin 
antibodies should be measured, but not necessarily during hypoglycemia.)

Hypoglycemia in Infancy and Childhood
Normal Glucose Metabolism in the Fetus, Term 
Neonates, and Children
Glucose is the main energy source for fetal development. Glucose 
homeostasis during fetal life depends primarily on a continuous 
supply of glucose from the maternal circulation across the placenta 
to meet a substantial proportion of its energy needs, and its glucose 
levels are mostly reflective of the maternal glycemic level. There is 
no hepatic glucose production and gluconeogenesis during fetal 
life, due to the absence or very low activity of pyruvate carboxyl­
ase, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, glucose-6-phosphatase, 
and fructose-1,6-diphosphatase.306 These rate-limiting enzymes 
of gluconeogenesis rapidly increase within the first few hours of 
life. Typically, the fetal metabolic milieu is characterized by high 
plasma insulin levels and low plasma glucagon levels. Though 
insulin in the blood can be detected after 13 weeks of gestation 
and the fetal pancreas can start producing insulin in response to 
glucose and amino acids after the 20th week of pregnancy, insulin 
is inactive until the start of glucocorticoid action in the second 
trimester. At that time, glucocorticoids induce the expression of 
enzymes needed for lipid and glycogen synthesis, as well as glyco­
genolysis; therefore, hepatic glycogen stores do not increase much 
until the third trimester, accounting for about 5% of the total liver 
weight at birth. In addition, insulin enhances fatty acid synthesis 
in the liver and glucose uptake in adipose tissue leading to triglyc­
eride synthesis and fat storage in adipose tissue during the third 
trimester.307 Thus, at birth, in the term infant, glycogen and fat 
constitute stores available for metabolic homeostasis.308
Plasma glucose concentrations decline after birth as placental 
blood flow is interrupted by cutting the umbilical cord. They reach 
their nadir usually in the first 2 hours of life.309 This is accompa­
nied by a decrease in insulin and activation of glucose counter­
regulatory systems such as an increase in plasma catecholamines, 
glucagon, and cortisol, that activate adenyl cyclase and promote 
not only mobilization of glycogen stores and gluconeogenesis, but 
also lipolysis and eventually ketogenesis in the neonate. Because 
mobilizable glycogen stores are limited and quickly depleted, 
and feeding is intermittent, the newborn is forced to increase its 
endogenous glucose production and thus become largely depen­
dent on gluconeogenesis initially. In most infants, the plasma glu­
cose concentration is usually steady or is increasing by 4 to 6 hours 
of life. As feedings are spaced and the fasting period is prolonged, 
lipolysis and ketogenesis increase and ketones become a significant 
fuel source, particularly for the brain.
The brain relies almost exclusively on a constant supply of glu­
cose to meet its metabolic demands and to fuel brain growth and 
key maturational changes. The brain cannot support gluconeogen­
esis or use free fatty acids (FFA) because they are not transported 
across the blood-brain barrier. However, under special circum­
stances it can use ketone bodies (β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoace­
tate) or lactate as transient surrogate fuels if levels rise significantly 
enough. In the first years of life, the human brain accounts for 
nearly 50% of the body’s glucose consumption due to the pro­
portionally larger brain-to-body mass ratio.306,310 Overall, the 
rates of glucose flux (production and utilization) are nearly three 
times higher in infants and children than in adults, with the peak 
of CMRglu occurring during middle childhood (∼5–10 years 
old).311 Likewise, this metabolic peak is mirrored by increases in 
synaptic density and synaptic pruning, which occurs well beyond 
the periods of greatest linear brain growth and differs across brain 
regions (Fig. 39.12).312 Thus, if energy demands during this 
period are unmet due to hypoglycemia, key neurodevelopmental 
processes could be irreversibly compromised leading to life-alter­
ing deficits, increased risk for health problems, and lower intelli­
gence quotient. The extent of brain injury seems to be influenced 
by multiple factors, such as duration and degree of hypoglycemia 
or inherited to the underlying mechanism.
Diagnosing Hypoglycemia in Infants and Children
As in adults,2 the diagnosis of clinical hypoglycemia should be 
considered in pediatric patients that have a Whipple triad: (1) 
signs, symptoms, or both consistent with hypoglycemia; (2) a 
documented low, reliably measured plasma glucose concentra­
tion; and (3) resolution of those symptoms and signs after the 
plasma glucose concentration is raised (see Box 39.1). Signs and 
symptoms of hypoglycemia are nonspecific in a neonate or chil­
dren and may be difficult to recognize. Some of these may include 
jitteriness/tremors, hypotonia, changes in the level of conscious­
ness, apnea/bradycardia, cyanosis, tachypnea, poor suck or feed­
ing, hypothermia, and/or seizures. In addition, as in adults, it is 
not possible to state a single low plasma glucose concentration 
that categorically defines hypoglycemia in infants and children;

CHAPTER 39  Hypoglycemia
its precise definition continues to be controversial. This is because 
(1) normal distributions of glucose values will vary depending 
on age, (2) glucose values will vary depending on conditions of 
feeding and fasting, (3) there are potential artifacts that may lead 
to inaccuracies in glucose determination, (4) the thresholds for 
specific responses to hypoglycemia can be altered by recent ante­
cedent hypoglycemia, and (5) there is lack of outcome data, as 
there is not a single glucose value that has been associated with 
brain injury.313–315 However, most clinical guidelines propose 
arbitrary glucose thresholds to provide guidance on when to initi­
ate a workup to identify children with an underlying disorder and 
when to initiate an intervention to reduce potential harm from 
hypoglycemia and minimize possible overtreatment.
The American Academy of Pediatrics in 2011, followed by the 
Pediatric Endocrine Society (PES) in 2015, wrote clinical reports 
and guidelines on screening and subsequent management of neo­
natal hypoglycemia.315,316 Though these guidelines do not align 
on the glycemic thresholds for the diagnosis of hypoglycemia, 
they both endorse that hypoglycemia persisting beyond 48 hours 
is not likely to be transitional and they emphasize the need of 
early identification of the infant at risk for severe hypoglycemia 
during the first 48 hours after delivery and for persistent hypogly­
cemia beyond 48 hours of life to determine the need for screen­
ing. These include the infant of a mother with diabetes with poor 
glycemic control, as well as the child with a family history of a 
genetic form of hypoglycemia or a congenital syndrome associated 
with hypoglycemia, such as congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI), 
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, or hypopituitarism, in addition 
to those with relatively more common perinatal stress hyperinsu­
linism: birth asphyxia, intrauterine growth restriction, or toxemia 
or infants receiving total parenteral nutrition (Box 39.8).
The PES suggests a plasma glucose concentration of 50 mg/
dL (2.8 mmol/L) or lower as an appropriate threshold to trigger 
further diagnostic testing in a child less than 48 hours old and 60 
mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L) or lower after 48 hours of age.315 Neverthe­
less, many will criticize that it is a relatively conservative threshold 
and others that it may lead to overtreatment of many neonates, 
but in the neonatal period, the threshold is intended to avoid dis­
charging newborns who may be at risk for recurrent and severe 
hypoglycemia.315,317
The diagnostic evaluation for neonatal hypoglycemia should 
contain a critical sample that includes plasma confirmation of a 
low blood glucose value and simultaneous measure of HCO3 to 
determine if there is an associated acidosis, an insulin level and 
ketone bodies to determine if there is evidence of hyperinsulin­
ism and measure of the counterregulatory hormones (cortisol 
for cortisol deficiency and growth hormone for growth hormone 
deficiency), as well as FFAs to see if there is a defect on fatty acid 
oxidation, and lactate and ammonia levels. If outside of the new­
born period, a C-peptide level should also be measured. A gluca­
gon stimulation test at the time of hypoglycemia after the critical 
sample is obtained, can provide very useful diagnostic information 
about glycogen stores and possible hyperinsulinism. In such a test, 
0.03 mg/kg of glucagon is given intravenously or by IM injection 
when the child is hypoglycemic. Plasma glucose levels are mea­
sured before the injection and 10, 20, and 30 minutes after. A rise 
in plasma or blood glucose of more than 30 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L) 
within 30 minutes after glucagon administration suggests the 
child has hyperinsulinism, because during hyperinsulinemia 
there is inappropriate buildup of hepatic glycogen stores that are 
released in response to glucagon administration. In the case of 
a child with hypoglycemia of unknown cause, measurement of 
acylcarnitine profile, urine organic acids, and serum amino acids 
should be considered. In addition, always ensure that acylcarni­
tine level is normal before performing a diagnostic fast because 
coma can occur during fasting in children with inborn errors of 
metabolism including defects in fatty acid oxidation. Duration of 
the fast will vary according to patients age (12-hour fast for a term 
neonate >3 days of life, 18 hours for children 1–12 months old, 
and 24 hours for children >1 year old).
It is essential to treat patients with persistent low plasma glu­
cose to prevent adverse outcomes. If the patient is conscious and 
able to drink and swallow safely, they can be treated with adminis­
tration of 10 to 20 g of rapidly absorbed carbohydrates by mouth 
or by a gastric tube if available. This process may be repeated after 
15 minutes if hypoglycemia persists. However, if the hypoglyce­
mia does not improve within 30 minutes, parenteral glucose is 
recommended. In infants and children with altered consciousness, 
IV dextrose should be given. A slow bolus of 2 mL/kg of 10% 
dextrose solution can be given followed by a continuous infusion 
of dextrose at 6 to 9 mg/kg per minute. If IV access is not readily 
available and the patient has documented hyperinsulinism, then 
IM glucagon (0.03 mg/kg up to a maximum of 1 mg) should be 
given.
Close monitoring for further evaluation and treatment is 
needed in children found to have low plasma glucose concen­
trations. In neonates, monitoring should continue until plasma 
glucose concentrations can be maintained with regular feedings 
above 50 mg/dL (2.8 mmol/L) in newborns less than 48 hours 
old, and above 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L) in newborns more than 
48 hours old. However, the mean plasma glucose concentration in 
the postabsorptive state of children and neonates after 48 hours of 
age does not differ from that in adults (70–100 mg/dL [3.9–5.5 
mmol/L]). Thus, in children with the diagnosis of a disorder caus­
ing persistent hypoglycemia or a known risk of a persistent hypo­
glycemic disorder, the goal of treatment is to maintain a plasma 
glucose concentration above 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). Therefore, 
a safety fast (6–8 hours for a term neonate >3 days of life, 12 hours 
for children 1–12 months old, and 18 hours for children >1 year
