cess cannot occur unless perilipin 1, a protein that coats small 
lipid droplets, is phosphorylated by protein kinase A. Defects in 
PLIN1, the gene encoding perilipin 1, are associated with a form 
of familial partial lipodystrophy.13,14 Adipose tissue lipolysis is 
depicted schematically in Fig. 41.4. Human mutations in either 
ATGL or CGI58 are responsible for two variants of neutral lipid 
storage disease that are characterized by hepatic steatosis; lipid 
accumulation in skeletal muscle; cardiomyopathy; neurologic 
problems; and, in one variant, skin defects. 
Lipoprotein Lipase
Most lipids are delivered to peripheral tissues, such as muscle and 
fat, through the activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL). LPL has a 
pivotal role and is a rate-limiting step in the clearance of plasma 
TGs carried in TG-rich lipoproteins (TRLs)—very low-density 
lipoproteins (VLDLs) generated in the liver and chylomicrons 
generated in intestinal cells. LPL hydrolyzes the fatty acids in 
TGs from the glycerol backbone (and to a lesser extent, fatty acids 
in phospholipids) present in circulating TG-rich lipoproteins to 
allow peripheral sites access to preformed fatty acids.
The regulation of LPL mass and activity is determined in an 
extremely complex manner by both genetics and metabolism. 
Optimal LPL activity is needed to effectively and efficiently 
distribute fatty acids for both metabolic needs and appropriate 
storage, and its activity is thus regulated by multiple inputs. LPL 
is synthesized in adipose tissue, muscle, and the heart and to a 
minor, but potentially important extent, in macrophages. Much 
of this lipid flux is controlled by insulin, which increases LPL in fat 
and decreases LPL in muscle. Exercise tends to have the opposite 
effect,15 ensuring appropriate energy supplies to meet metabolic 
demands. LPL activity is also regulated by a number of apolipo­
proteins, which both enhance and inhibit activity. Apolipoprotein 
C2 (APOC2), encoded by APOC2, is an obligate activator of LPL. 
Glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored high-density lipoprotein 
binding protein (GPIHBP1) is a key protein that transports LPL 
from its site of synthesis in smooth muscle cells and adipocytes 
across the endothelium and anchors it on the endothelial luminal 
surface, where it can interact with TG-rich lipoproteins. On the 
other hand, apolipoprotein C3 (APOC3) has been shown to be a 
key inhibitor of LPL activation. In addition, recent studies have 
increasingly provided evidence of a family of angiopoietin-like 
proteins—namely, ANGPTL3, ANGPTL4, and ANGPTL8—
that are important and complex regulators of TG metabolism 
by virtue of inhibiting LPL activity and partitioning the distri­
bution of FFAs to adipocytes, muscle, and liver.16,17 Apolipo­
protein A5 (APOA5), encoded by APOA5, is another important 
activator of LPL. APOA5 also lowers TG levels via suppression 
of ANGPTL3/8-mediated LPL inhibition.18 FFAs released from 
lipoproteins by the action of LPL at the luminal surface of capil­
lary endothelial cells must then cross the endothelial cell barrier to 
be captured by resident cells via conversion to acyl-CoA species. 
Tissue uptake of fatty acids at low concentrations appears medi­
ated by cell surface transporters such as cluster of differentiation 
36 (CD36), also known as scavenger receptor B2 (SR-B2), whereas 
at high concentrations, fatty acids may enter and transit the mem­
brane in a nonregulated, nonsaturable process, sometimes referred 
to as flip-flop.19 Fatty acyl-CoAs are then either stored as TGs or 
subjected to fatty acid oxidation. The role of LPL in disorders 
of the TG-rich lipoproteins is discussed later in this chapter (see 
“Severe Hypertriglyceridemia” section). 
Cholesterol Metabolism
Most diets include animal products, the source of dietary cho­
lesterol. However, in humans, dietary cholesterol is not required 
because most tissues are capable of sufficient cholesterol synthe­
sis to meet their structural and/or metabolic needs. The liver and 
intestine are quantitatively the most important sites for cholesterol 
metabolism in humans, although a very small amount of choles­
terol is also lost through the normal turnover of skin.
Cholesterol Absorption, Synthesis, and Excretion
Cholesterol is absorbed through a process that requires formation 
of bile salt micelles. The efficiency of absorption varies widely in 
humans. There is a gradient of absorption through the intestine that 
is greatest in the proximal small intestine and least in the ileum. 
This gradient parallels the expression of the protein Niemann-Pick 
C1–like 1 (NPC1L1), a transmembrane protein with a sterol-sens­
ing domain that is involved in cholesterol absorption.20 NPC1L1 is 
the target of ezetimibe, a drug that lowers cholesterol and has been 
shown to decrease CVD. NPC1L1 also absorbs phytosterols such 
as sitosterol. The function of NPC1L1 in cholesterol absorption 
requires an interaction with the LIM domain, an acronym of the 
three genes (LIN-11, Isl-1, and MEC-3) in which it was first identi­
fied, and the LIM domain and actin binding 1 (LIMA1), which, 
when mutated in humans, are associated with low LDL-C.21
Plants do not have cholesterol, but their membranes con­
tain phytosterols, which are structurally similar to cholesterol. 
Although sterols, including phytosterols, are absorbed by humans, 
they are pumped out of the enterocyte and back into the intestinal 
lumen by two ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters: ABCG5 
and ABCG8. Human mutations in these transporters cause the 
rare disorder sitosterolemia,22 which is characterized by increased 
absorption and circulating levels of sitosterol (and other plant 
sterols) and cholesterol and can cause xanthomas and CVD (see 
“Rare Lipoprotein Disorders” section).

Fig. 41.5A illustrates cholesterol synthesis. Acetate is converted 
to HMG-CoA, which is a substrate for HMG-CoA reductase, 
the enzyme that is rate limiting for cholesterol biosynthesis and 
is inhibited by statin drugs. Cells exquisitely regulate their inter­
nal cholesterol levels by regulating its synthesis and acquisition.23 
When levels are low in the endoplasmic reticulum, the transcrip­
tion factor sterol response element–binding protein (SREBP) 
translocates from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi, where 
it cleaved by proteases, allowing it to then translocate to the 
nucleus to activate genes that both increase cholesterol biosyn­
thesis and import cholesterol from the extracellular environment. 
Statins, which are the major LDL-lowering agents, work by inhib­
iting cholesterol biosynthesis in the hepatocyte, thereby lower­
ing intracellular cholesterol levels, which results in an increase 
in LDL receptor expression and transport to the hepatocyte cell 
surface, where they bind and internalize plasma LDL, thereby 
enhancing LDL removal and both maintaining cell cholesterol 
and lowering plasma LDL (see “Drugs to Treat High LDL-C” 
section). Free cholesterol in cells is esterified to form cholesteryl 
esters for storage. This esterification reaction is carried out by 
acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferases (ACATs). These endoplas­
mic reticulum enzymes exist in two forms: ACAT1 is present in 
macrophages and implicated in atherosclerosis; ACAT2 is present 
in the liver and intestine. ACAT2 in the intestine is implicated in 
cholesterol absorption. Nonspecific ACAT inhibition in humans 
does not affect serum lipids and does not have beneficial effects on 
atherosclerosis.24
Cholesterol, which is nonnutritive and cannot be catabolized 
to carbon dioxide and water within cells, is either secreted into 
the bile as free cholesterol (about half of which is reabsorbed) or 
converted to bile acids for secretion into bile. Most bile acids are 
reabsorbed in the terminal ileum. This enterohepatic circulation 
of cholesterol and bile acids is shown in Fig. 41.5B. The rate-lim­
iting enzyme for bile acid synthesis is cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase, 
which is under feedback regulation by bile acids. Interruption 
of the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids through the use of 
bile acid–binding resins reduces the farnesoid X receptor (FXR)-
mediated inhibition of 7α-hydroxylase, resulting in a subsequent 
induction of bile acid synthesis. There is also an associated increase 
in cholesterol biosynthetic rate, perhaps to compensate for the 
cholesterol diversion to bile acids, and a concomitant increase 
in LDL receptor synthesis, which then mediates enhanced LDL 
removal from plasma. Bile acid sequestrants were the first effective 
LDL-C–lowering agents that reduced CVD events in a random­
ized placebo-controlled trial.25 In many patients, the use of bile 
acid sequestrants is associated with a mild and often transitory 
increase in TG synthesis, explaining TG elevations seen with this 
group of drugs. At least in mice, evidence suggests that plasma 
cholesterol can be transferred from the basal surface of enterocytes 
directly to the apical surface for excretion from the body in feces. 
This has been shown to be independent of the biliary system, 
working through an active metabolic process called trans-intestinal 
cholesterol excretion.26 
Plasma Lipoproteins, Apolipoproteins, 
Receptors, and Other Proteins Involved in 
Lipoprotein Metabolism
Lipoproteins, which are spherical particles that circulate in the 
blood, transport vital non–water-soluble nutrients, such as lip­
ids, as well as vitamins, structural components, and proteins with 
specialized functions from the liver and gut through the plasma 
compartment to remote tissues. Appropriate concentrations of 
lipoproteins are essential for health, but increased circulating con­
centrations of certain lipoproteins are associated with increased 
risk for CVD. Absent or low levels of some lipoproteins may lead 
to vitamin deficiency syndromes. The roles of the various lipopro­
teins are discussed in detail in the following sections.
Major Lipoproteins
A prototypical lipoprotein is shown in Fig. 41.6. The funda­
mental structure of a lipoprotein exploits biochemical character­
istics of its components. The surface consists of a monolayer of 
charged molecules that interact with the aqueous environment, 
such as phospholipids, as well as free cholesterol buried in the 
lipophilic membrane. Amphipathic proteins (with both hydro­
philic and hydrophobic domains), called apolipoproteins (or sim­
ply apoproteins, often abbreviated as APOs), are also present on 
the surface, with hydrophilic domains oriented toward the plasma 
and hydrophobic domains toward the core of the particle. Apo­
lipoproteins regulate the lipoprotein interaction with metabolic 
enzymes and cellular receptors. The lipoprotein core consists of 
neutral (uncharged) hydrophobic lipids, such as TGs and choles­
teryl esters.
Humans spend most of their lives in the postprandial state. Eat­
ing is associated with generation of lipoproteins and the induction 
of enzymes that metabolize those lipoproteins. Within the circula­
tion, lipolysis of TGs within TG-rich lipoproteins, VLDL from 
the liver and chylomicrons from the gut, leads to rapid reduction 
in the size of the TG-rich lipoproteins. Along with loss of core 
TG, excess surface components of the TG-rich lipoproteins are 
shed and transferred to other lipoproteins, and both nonesterified 
fatty acids, released by action of LPL, and fat-soluble vitamins are 
delivered to tissues.

CHAPTER 41  Disorders of Lipoprotein Metabolism
The major classes of lipoproteins are listed in Table 41.2. They 
were initially identified based on flotation in an ultracentrifuge, 
and thus their names were defined based on density, for example, 
low-density lipoproteins (LDLs). An alternative original classifica­
tion scheme, which is no longer used, involved electrophoretic 
mobility in agarose gels or paper. Chylomicrons, chylomicron 
remnants, and VLDLs are rich in TGs. Intermediate-density 
lipoproteins (IDLs), LDLs, and lipoprotein(a) (Lp[a]) are rich in 
cholesterol. HDLs are enriched in phospholipids. TG-rich lipo­
proteins such as chylomicrons are large and refract light when 
plasma is viewed in a test tube, which accounts for the cloudy 
appearance of plasma when TG levels are above ∼400 mg/dL 
(4.5 mmol/L), as can occur in plasma of nonfasting subjects or 
in fasting plasma of subjects with elevated levels due to impaired 
clearance of VLDL and chylomicrons. Table 41.2 provides general 
ranges for particle size, which differ substantially among lipopro­
teins and within each class. The relative amount of protein versus 
less dense lipids correlates with the size and also the buoyancy of 
the lipoproteins. For example, large VLDLs contain much more 
lipid than the smaller HDLs. The subspecies of these particles sim­
ilarly differ in size and protein/lipid content. Although all forms 
of LDL are atherogenic, one LDL subtype, small dense LDL, is 
associated with insulin resistance and hypertriglyceridemia and 
may be particularly atherogenic.27 
Chylomicrons
Chylomicrons originate in the gut. They are lighter than water 
and float to the top of a plasma sample without the need to do 
centrifugation. The TGs in chylomicrons are normally cleared 
rapidly (within minutes) after a meal, whereas the whole parti­
cle takes a few hours for removal by the liver. Normally, there 
should be almost no chylomicrons present after an overnight fast. 
Their distinguishing apolipoprotein is APOB48, which is the only 
form of apolipoprotein B produced by intestinal cells in humans. 
APOB48 is so named because, as a splice variant, it is 48% of the 
size of the entire APOB100 protein found in VLDL and LDL. 
Chylomicrons acquire APOCs and APOE by transfer from HDL 
particles, a process that promotes chylomicron metabolism and 
conversion to chylomicron remnants. Chylomicron remnants, 
also characterized by the presence of APOB48, are cleared over 
several hours after they have lost most of their TG. Remnant par­
ticles, as well as LDL, can promote atherosclerotic CVD. 
Very Low-Density Lipoproteins
VLDL particles are of hepatic origin. Smaller than chylomicrons, 
their distinguishing apolipoprotein is full-length APOB100, the 
form of APOB produced by the liver. VLDLs are also enriched in 
APOC molecules that play an important role in the conversion of 
VLDLs to IDLs, which are enriched with VLDL remnants and 
are also atherogenic. IDL particles contain APOB100 and APOE, 
and they are either taken up by the liver or converted at the liver 
surface to LDL.

SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Low-Density Lipoproteins
LDL particles are characterized by essentially having APOB100 as 
their only apolipoprotein and are the major carriers of cholesterol 
in most humans. Measurement of the cholesterol content of LDL, 
termed LDL-C, forms the basis for coronary heart disease risk 
stratification and treatment goals. For most clinical laboratories, 
LDL-C measurements include cholesterol in both IDL and LDL 
particles, as well as the cholesterol content of Lp(a)—an LDL-
like particle to which a large protein termed APO(a) is attached. 
Lp(a) is described in greater detail later in the chapter (see 
“Lipoprotein(a) as a Major Cardiovascular Risk Factor” section). 
High-Density Lipoproteins
HDL particles have a complex biology. They can be generated 
by the liver and intestine or assembled in the plasma as a conse­
quence of surface lipids being released during the catabolism of 
the TG-rich lipoproteins. They are divided by density into HDL2 
(less dense, at 1.06–1.123 g/mL), which typically contains both 
APOA1 and APOCs, and HDL3 (more dense, at 1.12–1.21 g/
mL), which typically contains APOA1, APO2, and APOCs. 
There also is a minor subclass known as HDL1 that carries a large 
percentage of plasma APOE. Higher HDL levels are associated 
with lower CVD risk in population studies, but it is unclear if 
HDL plays a direct role in atherosclerosis. HDL can be assessed 
by its cholesterol content; by measurements of its major apolipo­
protein, APOA1; or more recently by functional assays, such as 
its ability to protect LDL from oxidation or its ability to promote 
cholesterol efflux from cells in an in vitro assay. This latter activ­
ity, reflecting the movement of labeled cholesterol from a cultured 
macrophage cell line to APOB-depleted plasma, which still has its 
content of HDL, may be inversely associated with CVD events 
(see “Abnormalities of HDL Metabolism” section).28 It has been 
suggested that the disparity between HDL-C concentration and 
function might in part explain why genetic markers associated 
with HDL levels do not associate with CVD risk.29 
Lipoprotein(a)
Lp(a), which was discovered as an immunologic variant of LDL 
in 1963, is an evolutionarily recent lipoprotein only found in old-
world monkeys and humans. It was termed Lp(a) because it was 
found that it was an LDL-like particle attached to a novel anti­
gen termed “a,” and hence it was called Lp(a) to distinguish it 
from the usual LDL. The function of Lp(a) and the reason for its 
evolutionary selection are unknown. Lp(a) is APO(a) covalently 
bound to APOBI00 by a disulfide bridge, and generated in the 
liver to form the Lp(a) lipoprotein, as shown in Fig. 41.7. APO(a) 
should be distinguished from APOA1, the major apolipoprotein 
of HDL.
APO(a) has a high degree of homology to the coagulation pro­
tein plasminogen and contains various repeating structures com­
mon in coagulation proteins termed kringles (K) because their 
structure is similar to the Danish pastry of this name. APO(a) 
is highly polymorphic; one particular kringle-encoding sequence, 
KIV2, is repeated as few as 4 times in a given allele or as many as 
over 40 times in another allele, creating many different isoforms. 
More than 80% of individuals express two different APO(a) iso­
forms, each inherited from one parent.
APO(a) has a complex structure, with 10 similar components 
named KIV1 through KIV10 and two additional components, KV 
and a protease domain. Additionally, the KIV2 domain can be 
present in 4 to 40 duplications called repeats, as noted previously. 
APO(a) isoforms with fewer repeats, such as the KIV2 with four 
or eight repeats shown in Fig. 41.7, are synthesized and assembled 
with APOB100 more efficiently than larger APO(a) isoforms 
with, for example, 24 or 40 repeats. Thus, smaller APO(a) iso­
forms generate higher Lp(a) plasma levels, and conversely, larger 
APO(a) isoforms generate lower Lp(a) plasma levels.
The metabolism of these lipoprotein classes is described in the 
“Lipoprotein Metabolism” section. 
Major Apolipoproteins
The chromosomal location, size, sites of synthesis, and major func­
tions of important apolipoproteins are summarized in Table 41.3.
Apolipoproteins A1, A2, A4, and A5
APOA1 is the most abundant apolipoprotein in HDL. It is syn­
thesized by the liver and intestine, and aside from its structural 
properties, it activates the enzyme lecithin:cholesterol acyltrans­
ferase (LCAT), which transfers a fatty acid from lecithin (also 
called phosphatidyl choline) to the free hydroxyl group on choles­
terol to generate cholesteryl esters. HDL particles mature when 
discs containing phospholipid and APOA1 acquire free choles­
terol. Cholesterol in the surface of the nascent HDL is converted 
through the activity of LCAT to cholesteryl ester, which moves to 
the hydrophobic core of the nascent HDL, leading to expansion 
of the discs into spheres. APOA1 mediates efflux of cholesterol 
from peripheral tissues, an important step in the process of reverse 
cholesterol transport.30 Human genetic mutations in APOA1 
cause low levels of HDL and corneal opacities (see “Causes of Low 
HDL-C” section). Although APOA1 is considered an antiathero­
genic protein, genetic defects leading to low levels of APOA1 are 
not consistently associated with coronary artery disease (CAD).
APOA2 is present with APOA1 in some HDL particles. Syn­
thesized mostly in the liver, it has been implicated in the activation 
of hepatic lipase (HL), an enzyme involved in HDL metabolism, 
and in the inhibition of LCAT activity. APOA2 disrupts the ability 
of HDL to promote reverse cholesterol transport, but the genetic 
absence of this protein in humans does not seem to be associated 
with a phenotype.31
APOA4 originates in the gut, and its secretion is induced by 
consumption of a high-fat meal. It has been implicated in many 
physiologic functions, including a role in chylomicron assembly 
and lipid metabolism, as a mediator of reverse cholesterol trans­
port, as an acute satiety factor, and as a modulator of blood glu­
cose homeostasis. Much remains to be learned about APOA4 in 
humans.32
APOA5 is encoded by a locus near the APOA4 gene in the 
ApoA-I/C-III/A-IV/A-V gene cluster on chromosome 11. It is pro­
duced by the liver and circulates at low concentrations in asso­
ciation with VLDL particles in humans. APOA5 is an important 
activator of LPL, which promotes hydrolysis of TGs in TG-rich 
lipoproteins. Its expression is inversely related to plasma TG levels, 
and it promotes lipoprotein clearance by hepatic proteoglycans.33 
In humans, homozygous mutations in APOA5 result in reduced 
LPL activity and increased risk for hyperchylomicronemia and 
pancreatitis.34

There are two forms of this apolipoprotein, APOB100 and 
APOB48, which are encoded by a single gene. A unique mech­
anism that involves RNA editing allows translation into these 
two forms of APOB Fig. 41.8. In both liver and intestinal cells, 
the same messenger RNA is transcribed, but an editing protein

In humans, APOB100 is synthesized in the liver, where it is co-
translationally associated with lipids to coordinate the formation 
of VLDL particles. VLDL assembly and export, which affect the 
levels of circulating atherogenic lipoproteins, are determined not 
by transcriptional control of the APOB gene but by a mechanism 
involving stabilization of the APOB protein by lipid. VLDL pro­
duction is shown in Fig. 41.9. Assembly is thought to involve two 
distinct processes. First, as the APOB message is translated on the 
rough endoplasmic reticulum, it binds to lipids that are provided 
by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP). MTP is essen­
tial for effective VLDL production, and rare deleterious muta­
tions in MTP result in abetalipoproteinemia, a condition in which 
APOB is synthesized but, because it is not lipidated, is completely 
degraded intracellularly in hepatocytes (or intestinal cells), result­
ing in absent secretion of VLDL from the liver or chylomicrons 
from the gut (see “Rare Lipoprotein Disorders” section).
Lipidated APOB is then acted upon by protein disulfide isom­
erase (a homodimer with MTP in the endoplasmic reticulum), 
which remodels the APOB protein by rearranging the positions of 
disulfide bonds in the molecule to accommodate incoming lipid. 
Much of this lipid originates in adipose tissue, where TG lipoly­
sis releases FFAs that are transported to the liver. Phospholipids 
and cholesterol also associate with APOB at this step. If sufficient 
lipids are not available in the liver, APOB (which is constitutively 
produced) is ubiquitinated and degraded in the proteasome. Sec­

the Golgi; this process is not completely defined. Transport of 
this large lipoprotein (25–70 nm in diameter) from the endoplas­
mic reticulum to the Golgi body occurs in specialized, large coat 
protein complex II (COPII) vesicles. The complex intracellular 
itinerary of VLDL requires quality control at several points and 
the involvement of numerous proteins, including MTP and trans­
membrane 6 superfamily member 2 (TM6SF2), which appear 
crucial for proper lipidation of nascent VLDL, and several pro­
teins involved in transport from the endoplasmic reticulum to the 
Golgi apparatus. Abnormalities in any of these steps can lead to 
the targeting of VLDL for degradation. The TG-rich particles are 
then secreted into the space of Disse. Throughout this process, 
VLDL may be degraded by autophagic or other poorly character­
ized pathways. However, fully lipidated VLDL particles ultimately 
gain access to the circulation, where the transfer of apolipopro­
teins, such as APOCs and APOE, from other lipoproteins modi­
fies VLDL structure to promote metabolism in the periphery.
Increased VLDL production, fueled by the increased avail­
ability of lipid, is predominantly responsible for the dyslipidemia 
seen with obesity and diabetes. There is one copy of APOB100 
on each VLDL particle, and this relationship is retained as these 
lipoproteins are metabolized to IDL and then to LDL. Therefore, 
measurements of APOB100 in plasma reflect the particle number 
of potentially atherogenic lipoproteins, and higher levels of APOB 
are associated with CVD.36 
Apolipoproteins C1, C2, and C3
The small apolipoproteins C1, C2, and C3 are encoded by loci 
residing at two different locations in the genome. APOC1 and 
APOC2 are transcribed from a site on chromosome 19 near the 
APOE gene. The APOC3 gene is a component of the apoAI/C-
III/A-IV/A-V gene cluster on chromosome 11. APOCs, which can 
be exchanged freely among lipoprotein particles, are important 
for regulating lipoprotein metabolism in many different spheres. 
APOC1 is the only known endogenous inhibitor of cholesterol 
ester transport protein (CETP) activity.37 APOC2 plays a vital 
role in mediating TG clearance from plasma because it is an obli­
gate activator of the enzyme LPL. Humans with biallelic loss-
of-function mutations of APOC2, which is extremely rare, have 
severe hypertriglyceridemia, mimicking LPL deficiency. Heterozy­
gous mutations in APOC2 cause variable TG levels ranging from 
normal to high 186.
On the other hand, levels of APOC3 are important modulators 
of plasma TG levels. APO3 is a major inhibitor of LPL activity 
and, in addition, inhibits hepatic uptake of TG-rich lipoproteins 
by a mechanism independent of LPL activity. Thus, APOC3 raises 
plasma TG by both LPL-dependent and LPL-independent mech­
anisms. This explains why levels are increased in the setting of 
many dyslipidemias and, in turn, why many TG-lowering medi­
cations lower APOC3 levels. Extensive epidemiologic and genetic 
data demonstrate that lower plasma APOC3 levels are associated 
with both decreased plasma TGs and decreased CVD events,38 
suggesting therapies targeting APOC3 might provide clinical 
benefit. Indeed, in patients with extremely high TGs, resulting 
from either familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS) or mul­
tiple genetic and environmental causes (also called multifactorial 
hypertriglyceridemia), inhibiting hepatic APOC3 synthesis by use 
of antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) targeting APOC3 mRNA 
results in substantial TG lowering39 (see “Severe Hypertriglyceri­
demia” section). 
Apolipoprotein E
APOE biology is also complex. APOE expression is highest in the 
liver, followed by the brain. In the brain, astrocytes and microglial 
cells synthesize APOE, which can also be produced by injured 
neurons. Many other cell types synthesize the protein, includ­
ing macrophages.40 APOE circulates in plasma on all lipopro­
teins, with the probable exception of LDL. Its principal function 
involves interactions with the two major receptors mediating the 
clearance of plasma lipoproteins: the LDL receptor and LRP1. 
Therefore, APOE is primarily responsible for clearance of intesti­
nal-derived lipoproteins after a meal and for clearance of VLDL 
and IDL particles before they are converted to LDL.
There are three major APOE isoforms: E2, E3, and E4. They 
are encoded, respectively, by alleles referred to as ε2, ε3, and 
ε4, with charge differences caused by variations in amino acids 
at residues 112 and 158 in the protein. APOE3 is the predom­
inant isoform; it has a cysteine at residue 112 and an arginine 
at 158. APOE2 has cysteines at both 112 and 158, and APOE4 
has an arginine at both 112 and 158. These variations have struc­
tural and functional consequences (Fig. 41.10). The protein has 
two domains: an amino (NH2)-terminus that interacts with

presence of the ε4 allele slightly increases risk. These observations 
are interesting for two reasons. First, ε2/ε2 individuals, although 
they are protected from CAD on a population basis, are at risk for 
dysbetalipoproteinemia, with greatly elevated TG and cholesterol, 
which occurs in about 5% of ε2/ε2 individuals and is associated 
with aggressive vascular disease (see “Combined Hyperlipopro­
teinemias” section). Second, the E2 protein binds less well to the 
LDL receptor than APOE3 and E4. This suggests that LDL-C in 
patients with the E2 protein should be higher (because it is less 
likely to be cleared by this receptor), yet the opposite is observed. 
These data suggest that APOE2 may be involved in the remodel­
ing and conversion of IDL to LDL and/or that other receptor-
mediated processes, such as those mediated by heparan sulfate 
proteoglycans (HSPGs), may be critical for clearance of APOE-
containing lipoproteins.42

Major Receptors Involved in Lipid Metabolism
LDL Receptor Gene Family
Because of its central role in biology, few molecules have elicited 
more study, or more Nobel prizes, than that of cholesterol. Among 
these many advances, the elucidation of the cellular LDL recep­
tor pathway to control cholesterol metabolism was a watershed to 
our understanding of and ability to control plasma LDL-C levels. 
Much of this fundamental knowledge was pioneered and devel­
oped by Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein, who were awarded 
the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1985 for their dis­
coveries. This knowledge has led to a revolution in our ability to 
lower plasma LDL-C and thereby treat and even prevent com­
plications of atherosclerotic diseases, including myocardial infarc­
tion, stroke, and peripheral artery disease. Here, we will outline 
the roles of the LDL receptor and related proteins.
Although the LDL receptor was the first member of this fam­
ily discovered, we now know that there are at least 10 members 
of the LDL receptor family; the LDL receptor and LRP1 are the 
two most important ones for systemic lipid metabolism. The LDL 
receptor recognizes APOB100 and APOE, whereas LRP1 recog­
nizes only APOE. Other core family members (those that share 
considerable structural homology) include the VLDL receptor, the 
apolipoprotein E receptor 2 (APOER2 or LRP8), LRP4, LRP1B, 
and megalin (LRP2; also known as gp330 and as the major Hey­
mann nephritis antigen).
Three family members lack some of the structural features of 
the others. They are sortilin-related receptor L1 (LR11/SORL1), 
LRP5, and LRP6. Along with the LDL receptor and LRP1, sor­
tilin receptors participate in brain development, synaptic func­
tion, and neuroprotection, making them relevant to Alzheimer 
disease.44 LRP5 and LRP6 are both co-receptors for a family of 
G protein–coupled receptors known as frizzled receptors. Frizzled 
receptors bind the Wnt molecule to induce an important signaling 
cascade upstream of the transcription factor β-catenin. Genetic 
variants in LRP5 are associated with obesity,45 and a human 
mutation in LRP6 results in metabolic syndrome and CAD.46 
Loss-of-function mutations in LRP5 or LRP6 cause osteoporosis 
in humans, whereas gain of function in LRP5 causes osteopetro­
sis. These observations suggest that insulin resistance, CAD, and 
osteoporosis, which are common comorbid conditions in patients, 
may be related to abnormal Wnt signaling. 
LDL Receptor
The LDL receptor is a large (160-kDa) glycoprotein expressed on 
the surface of most cells. Because it recognizes APOB100 as well 
as APOE, it is involved in the uptake of LDL, chylomicron rem­
nants, VLDL, and IDL. The observations in the 1970s by Brown 
and Goldstein that fibroblasts from patients with FH, who have 
the highest plasma LDL-C, could not bind and internalize LDL 
and thereby decrease endogenous cholesterol synthesis, whereas 
normal fibroblasts could, were the key findings that led to the 
discovery of the LDL receptor on the surface of cells.47 The elu­
cidation of the LDL receptor pathway defined receptor-mediated 
endocytosis as a novel paradigm for providing cells with critical 
components from the external environment and was a fundamen­
tal discovery in the history of cell biology.
The LDL receptor shares functional domains with other 
members of this receptor family, including the ligand-binding 
domain, the epidermal growth factor (EGF) precursor domain, 
the O-linked sugar domain at the cell surface, the membrane-
spanning domain, and the cytoplasmic domain at the COOH-
terminus (Fig. 41.11). The ligand-binding domain includes seven 
repeats of approximately 40 amino acids, each containing six cys­
teines that form three disulfide bonds within the repeat to stabilize 
the structure. The repeat also includes negatively charged amino 
acids that interact with positively charged residues on the ligands 
APOB and APOE and with calcium ions. The EGF precursor 
domain consists of three EGF-like repeats (see Fig. 41.11) with 
a structure known as a β-propeller located between repeats B and 
C. The O-linked sugar domain is the site at which carbohydrate 
moieties attach to the molecule, and this is followed by a short 
membrane sequence. The cytoplasmic domain consists of 50 resi­
dues that include an NPXY (asparagine, proline, any amino acid, 
tyrosine) targeting sequence where adapter proteins dock, which 
leads to receptor clustering in coated pits.
Coated pits are specialized plasma membrane regions in the 
cell surface characterized by the presence of the protein complex 
clathrin. When LDL receptors bind lipoproteins, they migrate 
to coated pits, and clathrin directs the complex to a cell mem­
brane region that folds inward, creating an intracellular vesicle or

Lipoproteins are degraded in lysosomes. Cholesterol is trans­

lipoprotein hydrolysis in the lysosome and moves this sterol to 
the membrane-associated NPC1 for subsequent release to the cell, 
where it serves structural and regulatory functions.
Sterol response element–binding proteins (SREBPs) are a fam­

protein (SCAP), which is a sterol-binding protein and binds to 
SREBPs in the endoplasmic reticulum. SREBP2 is most impor­
tant for LDL receptor transcription; its NH2-terminus contains 
a leucine zipper–type transcription factor structure that binds to 
a sterol regulatory element (SRE) in the promoter of the LDL 
receptor gene. When cells are sterol depleted (Fig. 41.14, left side), 
SCAP migrates from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi 
apparatus, where sugar moieties attached to the protein are modi­
fied. This allows SCAP to transport SREBPs to the site-1 protease 
(S1P) compartment. There, two proteases, S1P and site-2 protease 
(S2P), sequentially act on SREBPs to release their NH2-terminus, 
which migrates to the nucleus and binds to the SRE in the pro­
moter region of lipid genes, such as the LDL receptor and HMG-
CoA reductase, increasing transcription and subsequent levels of 
functional proteins. Thus, when cell cholesterol is low, the synthe­
sis of both cholesterol and LDL receptors is increased, leading to 
an increase in cell cholesterol. In the presence of cholesterol (see 
Fig. 41.14, right side), SCAP does not cycle to the Golgi structure, 
it cannot move SREBPs to the S1P compartment, and SREBPs 
are not cleaved to allow their transcription factor to migrate to the 
nucleus. This disruption of SREBP activation in the presence of 
cholesterol decreases both cholesterol and LDL receptor synthesis 
and thus protects cells from excessive accumulation of cholesterol. 
Not shown in Fig. 41.14 are other crucial endoplasmic reticu­
lum proteins, insulin-induced genes (INSIG1 and 2), which are 
oxysterol-binding proteins that sense endoplasmic reticulum ste­
rol levels and promote endoplasmic reticulum retention of SCAP, 
thus preventing its migration to the Golgi. In addition, INSIGs 
promote ubiquitin-mediated degradation of HMG-CoA reduc­
tase, thus inhibiting cholesterol synthesis. These complex mecha­
nisms maintain cellular cholesterol homeostasis by exquisitely fine 
regulation of cellular membrane sterol content.50 
Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin Type 9
Another milestone in efforts to develop effective therapies to lower 
LDL-C grew out of basic research that uncovered the role of the 
protease PCSK9 in regulating the level of LDL receptors expressed 
on the hepatocyte cell surface. Genetic studies seeking to identify 
the gene locus of patients with a phenotype of heterozygous famil­
ial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) but with normal LDLR geno­
types and population studies seeking to identify the gene locus 
of individuals with low plasma LDL-C both identified the same 
PCSK9 locus. Subsequent studies identified gain-of-function 
mutations in PCSK9 that were associated with increased athero­
sclerosis, whereas loss-of-function mutations in PCSK9 were asso­
ciated with dramatic decreases in CVD.51,52 These observations 
propelled a dramatic investment in basic and therapeutic research 
that rapidly led to the development and approval of novel thera­
peutics targeting PCSK9 (see “PCSK9 Inhibitors” section) that 
have been incorporated into clinical practice to optimally lower 
LDL-C.
PCSK9 is a member of the proprotein convertase family of 
proteins that activate other proteins. Although it is secreted by a 
number of tissues, it is the hepatic secretion that is of relevance 
to regulation of plasma LDL concentrations. PCSK9 is inactive 
when first synthesized but then undergoes autocleavage to activate 
it before hepatic secretion. At the surface of hepatocytes, it binds 
to the LDL receptor, which affects the subsequent intracellular 
fate of the LDL receptor, targeting it for lysosomal degradation. 
This binding does not require catalytic activity. As shown in Fig. 
41.13, when plasma LDL binds to the hepatic LDL receptor, it 
induces internalization of the LDL-LDL receptor complex within 
an endosome. The acidity of the endosomal environment induces 
the LDL receptor to adopt a conformational change, which causes 
the LDL to be released and directed to the lysosome for degrada­
tion. The LDL receptor, free of its LDL ligand, is then recycled 
back to the hepatocyte surface for a new round of binding to LDL. 
However, in the normal situation, when the secreted PCSK9 is 
present at the hepatic cell surface, it binds to the LDL receptor 
and prevents the conformational change of the receptor-ligand 
complex within the endosome. This inhibition redirects the LDL 
receptor to the lysosome instead of recycling back to the cell sur­
face, thus effectively reducing the number of LDL receptors on 
the hepatocyte surface. Thus, at steady state, the LDL receptor 
concentration at the cell surface is a function of LDL receptor 
synthesis and degradation, which is regulated by the concentra­
tion of free PCSK9. Importantly, the presence of typical plasma 
levels of PCSK9 in the general population results in about a 50% 
reduction in LDL receptors available to bind LDL.53
Thus, when the free PCSK9 concentration in plasma is 
decreased, either by the presence of therapeutic monoclonal 
antibodies binding to PCSK9 or by either antisense- or siRNA-
mediated inhibition of hepatic PCSK9 synthesis, more of the 
internalized LDL receptor can then be recycled back to the

LDL Receptor–Related Protein 1
LRP1 is also known as the APOE receptor or the chylomicron 
remnant receptor. LRP1 is large, containing components of four 
LDL receptors with a multiplicity of ligand-binding domains. 
The major cell types expressing LRP1 include hepatocytes, neu­
rons, and placental syncytiotrophoblasts. Multiple ligands bind to 
LRP1 and participate in both nutrient flow and signaling. These 
ligands include amyloid precursor protein (processed to form the 
amyloid-β of plaques in Alzheimer disease), bacterial by-products, 
tissue plasminogen activator (which interacts with LRP1 to pro­
mote inflammation in the setting of brain ischemia), plasminogen 
activator inhibitors, and α2-macroglobulin (which contributes to 
inflammation, in part by inactivating matrix metalloproteinases). 
LRP1 is associated with receptor-associated protein, a small pro­
tein that binds to several regions of LRP1 to chaperone this large 
protein during intracellular processing.
LRP1 binds APOE but not APOB100. Therefore, it medi­
ates the metabolism of the major APOE-containing lipoproteins, 
including chylomicron remnants and IDL (VLDL remnants), 
but is not involved in LDL metabolism. The interaction between 
LRP1 and lipoproteins is more complex than that between LDL 
and the LDL receptor. Multiple copies of APOE on a lipopro­
tein are required for LRP1 binding, and this interaction requires 
an initial binding of the lipoprotein to proteoglycans on the cell 
surface. 
Other Enzymes and Transfer Proteins Mediating 
Lipid Metabolism
Hepatic Lipase
HL is primarily a phospholipase with some TG lipase activity. It 
is synthesized in hepatocytes but found mostly attached to endo­
thelial cells in the liver and on heparan sulfate proteoglycan in 
the space of Disse. It is also found in steroidogenic tissues but is 
not synthesized at those sites. Unlike LPL, which is mostly pres­
ent in tissues remote from the liver, thereby ensuring the periph­
eral delivery of lipids and vitamins, HL coordinates lipoprotein 
metabolism centrally. Functions include conversion of IDL to 
LDL, conversion of HDL2 to HDL3, and probably the final 
metabolism of chylomicron remnants to facilitate their uptake by 
LDL receptors and LRP1, at least in mice. Also unlike LPL, HL 
does not require a cofactor such as APOC2, but both enzymes are 
displaced from their endothelial sites of activity by injection of 
heparin (post-heparin lipase activity). High levels of HL decrease 
HDL concentrations, whereas high levels of LPL increase HDL. 
Endothelial Lipase
Evolutionarily related to HL and LPL, endothelial lipase (EL) is a 
phospholipase with almost no TG hydrolase activity. It is expressed 
at high levels in embryonic endothelial cells, with expression 
declining during maturation. In adults, expression is highest in 
endothelial cells, thyroid, lung, liver, placenta, and gonads. In 
mice, overexpression decreases and inactivation increases HDL-C. 
EL is expressed in the aorta, where it may increase with athero­
sclerosis. Human loss-of-function mutations are associated with 
increased HDL,54 and EL elevation in humans has been observed 
in multiple pathophysiologic conditions, including metabolic syn­
drome, obesity, and CAD.55–57 Recent studies have demonstrated 
that ANGPTL3 inhibits EL and that decreasing plasma ANG­
PTL3, either genetically or by therapeutic targeting, in turn low­
ers plasma HDL. In addition, these studies uncovered a novel role 
of EL in processing of VLDL, which, in the presence of the LDL 
receptor, is apparently not of importance. However, in LDL recep­
tor–negative mice and humans, inhibiting ANGPTL3 uncovers 
an important EL-mediated processing of VLDL that promotes 
LDL receptor–independent particle clearance.58 This leads to sub­
stantial lowering of LDL-C in patients with homozygous familial 
hypercholesterolemia (HoFH), and targeting ANGPTL3 with a 
monoclonal antibody is now an approved adjunctive therapy in 
such patients (see “Drugs to Treat High LDL-C” section). 
Lipoprotein-Associated Phospholipase A2
Phospholipases hydrolyze the ester bond at the sn-2 position of 
phospholipids, usually resulting in the release of a fatty acid and 
generation of lysophosphatidylcholine, which can induce inflam­
mation. Phospholipases were originally identified as a component 
of snake venom, and many distinct classes have since been charac­
terized. Membrane phospholipids are the substrate for most phos­
pholipases. Lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A2 (Lp-PLA2) is 
an exception because it can hydrolyze substrate in the aqueous 
phase. Lp-PLA2 binds to both LDL and HDL and is a biomarker 
for CAD.59 In humans, inhibition of this enzyme decreases the 
expansion of the lipid core of atherosclerotic plaques60 but does 
not decrease CVD endpoints.61 
Cholesteryl Ester Transfer Protein
CETP promotes the exchange between lipoproteins of two classes 
of neutral lipids: cholesteryl esters and TGs. HDL-cholesteryl 
esters are transferred to VLDL, IDL, and chylomicron remnants; 
in return, TGs from VLDL, IDL, and remnants are transferred to 
HDL. TGs from VLDL can also exchange with cholesteryl esters 
from LDL, leading to cholesteryl ester–enrichment of VLDL and 
their remnants and TG-enriched LDL. Humans and other pri­
mates have CETP activity; the transfer of cholesteryl esters from 
HDL to APOB-containing lipoproteins ultimately leads to most 
of their cholesterol burden being carried by LDL, and this has 
been postulated to result in atherosclerosis. Rodents and dogs 
do not have CETP. Most of their cholesterol is carried in HDL; 
LDL-C is low, and these animals are resistant to atherosclerosis 
in the absence of extreme measures to raise LDL levels. Humans 
with nonfunctioning mutations in CETP have high HDL-C. 
These and other theoretical observations led to the development of 
therapeutic agents inhibiting CETP activity as a treatment to raise 
HDL-C and decrease atherosclerosis in humans. However, results 
with these agents have been disappointing to date (see “Approach 
to the Patient With Low HDL-C” section). 
Lecithin:Cholesterol Acyltransferase
Lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) is an enzyme syn­
thesized primarily in the liver; it circulates in plasma associated 
with HDL and, to a lesser extent, with LDL. LCAT is activated 
by APOA1 and serves the important role of generating most of 
the cholesteryl esters present in lipoproteins. LCAT uses a fatty 
acid derived from lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) to esterify free 
cholesterol to cholesteryl esters, with lysophosphatidylcholine as a 
by-product. Rare human mutations in LCAT result in low HDL 
levels. The role of LCAT in atherosclerosis is uncertain, and some 
1643
CHAPTER 41  Disorders of Lipoprotein Metabolism
reports suggest humans with loss-of-function LCAT mutations 
do not appear to have an increased risk for atherosclerosis,62 per­
haps because their residual HDL is functional in assays of reverse 
cholesterol transport. (See “LCAT Deficiency in Abnormalities of 
High-Density Lipoprotein Metabolism” section.) 
Lipoprotein Metabolism
Lipoproteins regulate a dynamic flux of multiple lipid species 
from the external environment, for example, from the intestine 
to the liver, from the liver to peripheral tissues, from peripheral 
tissues back to the liver, and eventually back to the external envi­
ronment through the excretion of bile acids and biliary cholesterol 
via the intestine. Integrated views of the major pathways involved 
are shown in Figs. 41.15 and 41.16.
Chylomicrons carry dietary-derived (exogenous) lipids to the 
liver, whereas endogenous lipids produced in the liver are exported 
to peripheral tissues as VLDL. Chylomicrons, with their signa­
ture protein APOB48, are assembled within and secreted from the 
small intestine, first into the lymphatic system and then via the 
thoracic duct into the circulation. They transport vital non–water-
soluble nutrients, vitamins, structural components, and proteins 
with specialized functions from the gut to remote tissues. Their 
major lipid cargo is TG that has been reassembled from fatty acids 
generated by hydrolysis of dietary TG in the lumen of the small 
intestine. Chylomicrons deliver TG to adipose tissue, skeletal and 
cardiac muscle, and the liver. Hepatic-derived VLDLs, with their 
signature protein, APOB100, transport endogenous lipids from 
the liver to peripheral sites, particularly adipose tissue and both 
skeletal and cardiac muscle. Their major component is TG, which 
is derived from the esterification of plasma fatty acids but also 
from the internalization by the liver of chylomicrons and VLDL 
remnants and from the synthesis of fatty acids by DNL. A major 
difference between the metabolism of chylomicrons and VLDLs

is that essentially all chylomicrons are internalized by the liver 
after delivery of the bulk of their TG to peripheral tissues, whereas 
VLDLs, after delivery of much of their TG to the peripheral sites, 
have two possible fates; on average about 50% are internalized by 
the liver, and the other 50% will undergo further loss of TG in 
the peri-hepatic circulation and become IDLs and LDLs. In turn, 
LDLs carry most of the plasma cholesterol in a typical individual.
HDLs are composed of particles with a wide range of size, den­
sity, and composition; they regulate the flux of lipids, particularly 
free and cholesteryl esters, from peripheral tissue to the liver. HDL 
is the most complex lipoprotein class for several reasons. First, 
HDLs do not enter the circulation as mature lipoproteins; their 
signature protein, APOA1, is secreted from the liver and small 
intestine, either as a free protein or complexed with the phos­
pholipid phosphatidyl choline (PC) as a disc. In the circulation, 
nascent HDLs go through an iterative series of steps until they 
become mature HDLs, acquiring cholesterol and phospholipids 
from cellular sources. In turn, the free cholesterol is esterified by 
the enzyme LCAT to generate cholesteryl esters, which form the 
core of the HDL particles. Although the intestine and the liver 
secrete chylomicrons and VLDLs in a range of sizes and densities, 
mature HDLs exist in several discrete size and density classes that 
differ not only in the content of cholesteryl ester, their major lipid 
cargo, but also in both the number of APOAI molecules present, 
as well as specific combinations of several other apoproteins on 
the surface of the particles, such as APOA2, APOCs, and so forth.
Appropriate concentrations of plasma lipoproteins are essen­
tial for health, but elevated levels of circulating APOB-containing 
lipoproteins and decreased levels of APOA1-containing lipopro­
teins are associated with increased risk for CVD. Absent or low 
levels of lipoproteins may lead to vitamin deficiency syndromes.
Exogenous Lipid Transport by Chylomicrons
Dietary fatty acids and free cholesterol are absorbed into the duode­
num and proximal jejunum after hydrolysis of TG and cholesteryl 
esters by lipases in the lumen of the intestine (see Fig 41.15, top left). 
The fatty acids and monoglycerides generated in the intestinal lumen 
are reassembled within enterocytes into TG, and the cholesterol is 
reesterified. These neutral lipids, together with APOB48 and phos­
pholipids, make up the chylomicrons that are secreted at the lateral 
borders of enterocytes and enter mesenteric lymphatics. They access 
the plasma via the thoracic duct and are rapidly metabolized by LPL 
in the capillary beds of adipose tissue and muscle to produce chylomi­
cron remnants. These remnant particles contain 10% to 30% of their 
original TG. In contrast, the cholesteryl ester content of the chylomi­
cron actually increases, both relatively and absolutely, because of the 
transfer of HDL-cholesteryl ester to the remnants via the action of 
CETP. The chylomicron remnants are taken up by the liver by several 
pathways, including LDL receptors, LRP1, and heparan sulfate pro­
teoglycans, including syndecan-1. Fatty acids liberated by the action of 
LPL on chylomicron-TG are available for storage in adipose tissue and 
for uptake into skeletal and cardiac muscle for use as energy substrates. 
Chylomicrons also can be taken up by arterial endothelial cells in a 
scavenger receptor B1 (SR-B1)-dependent manner, after which they 
undergo lysosomal degradation. The resulting lipids can then be stored 
in endothelial cells or released to adjacent cells such as macrophages.63 
Endogenous Lipid Transport by VLDLs
Fatty acids released from lipolysis of TG stored in adipose tissue, 
fatty acids derived from the uptake of remnants, with their small 
TG cargo, and fatty acids from DNL are reassembled in the liver, 
with phospholipids and APOB100 (see Fig. 41.15, bottom left), to 
generate VLDL particles, which are secreted into the circulation. 
Fatty acids from adipose tissue dominate as the source of fatty 
acid incorporated into TG for both VLDL assembly and hepatic 
lipid droplets. Fatty acids from the internalization of chylomicron 
and VLDL remnants play a very small role, but this source of 
fatty acids can be increased when peripheral lipolysis by LPL is 
diminished. DNL provides about 5% to 10% of VLDL-TG in 
normal, healthy individuals but can be the source of as much as 
30% to 40% of VLDL-TG in individuals who are obese and have 
insulin resistance or diabetes. Elevated levels of circulating TG in 
insulin-resistant people are mediated in large part by overproduc­
tion of VLDL, an event that results from both increased hepatic 
TG synthesis and disruption of normal signaling downstream 
of the insulin receptor and the insulin receptor substrate (IRS) 
adapter proteins.
VLDL particles are metabolized in capillary beds of adipose 
tissue and muscle by LPL to produce VLDL remnants, most of 
which are present as IDL. A portion of these VLDL remnants is 
further metabolized by LPL and HL to yield LDL particles. Thus, 
LDL is derived from VLDL, which helps explain why treatments 
that increase LPL activity to lower TGs (carried by VLDLs) are 
frequently associated with transient or even sustained increases 
in LDL. IDL can be taken up by the liver through an APOE-
dependent process, and LDL is taken up by the liver through the 
binding of APOB100 to LDL receptors. Small VLDL particles, 
IDL particles, and LDL particles may be taken up by peripheral 
tissues to deliver nutrients, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins. 
When present in excess, each of these APOB-containing lipopro­
teins may be atherogenic. 
Reverse Cholesterol Transport
Whereas chylomicrons and VLDLs transport TG, a major energy 
substrate, HDLs’ cargo is cholesterol, an entirely different entity, 
which is involved in maintaining the structural and functional 
integrity of cell membranes and the synthesis of hormones and vita­
min D. Importantly, cholesterol cannot be degraded by peripheral 
tissues, or even hepatocytes, and must be returned to the liver for 
excretion as biliary cholesterol, either directly or after conversion 
to bile acids. The process of moving cholesterol from peripheral 
tissues and arteries to the liver is called reverse cholesterol transport 
and is dependent on HDL and its precursors (see Fig. 41.16). 
Excess unesterified free cholesterol (FC) in tissues can be effluxed 
to lipid-poor APOA1, mediated by the protein transporter ATP-
binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), to generate nascent 
HDL particles. This process can be repeated in the presence of the 
enzyme LCAT, which esterifies the FC, allowing it to move into 
the core of the HDL and thereby creating space for more unesteri­
fied FC to efflux to the particle surface. After the nascent HDL 
matures into a spherical particle, additional FC efflux from tissues 
can be mediated by ATP-binding cassette transport G1 (ABCG1) 
or SR-B1 (the gene product of SCARB1). Efflux, when measured 
from cultured cells to human plasma as a biomarker of CVD risk, 
is thought to mostly reflect the activity of ABCA1. There is also 
evidence that cholesterol can be acquired by HDL without the 
assistance of transporters by following a concentration gradient at 
the cell surface. At this point, HDL particles have three pathways 
for transporting sterols to the liver. First, they can directly bind 
to SR-BI at the surface of hepatocytes, which induces cholesteryl 
ester delivery through a mechanism involving selective lateral 
1645
CHAPTER 41  Disorders of Lipoprotein Metabolism
lipid transfer and not receptor internalization. Second, cholesteryl 
esters be transferred to APOB-containing lipoproteins by CETP, 
and these particles can deliver cholesterol to the liver through the 
LDL receptor. Third, based on ex vivo data, a small portion of 
HDL can acquire APOE, particularly when CETP is deficient, 
and bind to the liver LDL receptor.64 Once in the liver, where the 
HDL-cholesteryl ester is hydrolyzed to FC, it can be added to bile 
directly or converted to bile acids for excretion.
Cholesterol is the principal lipid component of atherosclerotic 
plaque, and thus atherosclerosis might be treated by promoting 
the efflux of cholesterol from lesions. HDL participates in this 
process, but static levels of HDL are poor predictors of reverse 
cholesterol transport. Dysfunctional HDL particles incapable of 
mediating cholesterol efflux could explain why some HDL-elevat­
ing interventions have not been associated with decreased CVD. 
Measurements of the rate of flux of cholesterol from the periphery 
to the liver, which may be possible in humans, would represent a 
better predictor of beneficial therapies. Experimental studies have 
suggested that in vitro cholesterol efflux capacity might be useful 
for assessing risk28,65 but does not appear to be inversely associated 
with disease in all instances nor to predict therapies that success­
fully reduce CVD.66,67
In addition to participating in reverse cholesterol transport, 
HDL has other properties that could be impaired by a variety of 
processes leading to a dysfunctional particle (see “Abnormalities 
of High-Density Lipoprotein Metabolism” section). They include 
the induction of endothelial nitric oxide synthase, the ability to 
inhibit oxidation of LDL thought to be involved in atherogenesis, 
the transport of proteins involved in the acute phase response and 
inflammation, and the suppression of thrombosis through induc­
tion of prostacyclin (which decreases thrombin production via the 
protein C pathway and decreases platelet activation). 
Clinical Approach to the Diagnosis and 
Treatment of Dyslipidemias
Laboratory Analysis of Lipids and Lipoproteins
The term dyslipidemia is used to refer to abnormal distributions 
of lipids and lipoproteins in plasma. The initial step in diagno­
sis relies on the measurement of plasma lipids and lipoproteins, 
which is necessary for CVD risk evaluation and for assessing 
the response to treatment. Most CVD guidelines are based on 
the measurement of a standard lipid and lipoprotein panel, which 
consists of measurement in the fasted state of plasma total cho­
lesterol and TG levels, and LDL-C and HDL-C levels. In most 
assays, the LDL-C is determined indirectly after measurement 
of total and HDL-C and then calculating LDL-C using the 
Friedewald equation that takes into account the cholesterol in 
VLDL.68 There are also assays in which LDL-C can be measured 
directly.
LDL-C measured by the Friedewald equation can be inac­
curate in the presence of hypertriglyceridemia, and the standard 
lipid panel is not recommended for use with TGs over 400 mg/dL 
(4.5 mmol/L), although inaccuracies are present even at lower TG 
levels.69 The Sampson-NIH equation overcomes many of these 
difficulties, at least until TG levels are 800 mg/dL (9.0 mmol/L) 
or greater.70 Assays for LDL-C also include Lp(a), a lipoprotein 
that is genetically determined and increases CVD risk. High levels 
of Lp(a) can lead to the overestimation of LDL-C values when 
measured as part of the standard lipid panel.
Nonfasting plasma lipids are sometimes used for initial screen­
ing because nonfasting TGs have been shown to be of value in 
predicting CVD risk.71 However, TG levels can vary widely 
depending on the baseline fasting level, the amount and type of fat 
in the meal, and the time since consumption of the fat-containing 
meal. Therefore, individuals with elevated nonfasting TG levels 
should ideally be retested in the fasted state.
Non–HDL-C, which represents the cholesterol content of all 
APOB-containing lipoproteins, can also be calculated from the 
standard lipoprotein panel. When plasma TGs are low (e.g., low 
VLDL and remnants), the non–HDL-C primarily represents 
LDL-C, but as fasting TGs rise, or when chylomicrons are pres­
ent, as in the nonfasted state, the non-HDL is increasingly discor­
dant from LDL-C. Under such circumstances, non–HDL-C has 
been shown to be an excellent predictor of CVD.72 Discordance 
between LDL-C and non–HDL-C also can result in misclassifica­
tion of patients in risk categories, which by and large have been 
based on LDL-C calculated by the Friedewald formula.
Because each atherogenic lipoprotein particle (VLDL, rem­
nant, Lp[a], and LDL) contains one molecule of APOB, measure­
ment of plasma APOB is a useful measure of CVD risk. Both 
non–HDL-C and APOB have been shown to be better risk pre­
dictors than LDL-C in some studies.73–75 Measurement of non–
HDL-C provides a useful index of APOB levels for individuals 
with low to moderate TG levels.
The reference method for measuring LDL-C relies on its isola­
tion by density gradient ultracentrifugation, so-called β quantifi­
cation. This is still an important method for accurately measuring 
LDL-C in patients with TGs above 400 mg/dL (4.5 mmol/L) 
and is widely used in clinical trials to test TG-lowering agents in 
hypertriglyceridemic patients. However, it has little current use in 
standard clinical practice other than for the diagnosis of remnant 
removal disease, also known as dysbetalipoproteinemia, or type III 
hyperlipoproteinemia in the Fredrickson classification system.
Several companies offer advanced lipid testing, which includes 
the determination of LDL particle number, LDL particle size, and 
lipoprotein distribution (including HDL subfractions), by nuclear 
magnetic resonance (NMR) or ion mobility, in an attempt to bet­
ter stratify patients’ level of risk. Although these can be of use 
in research studies, there are few data to recommend that they 
are useful for risk prediction in clinical practice. Therefore, they 
are not recommended for routine diagnostic testing at the present 
time.
Measurement of specific apolipoproteins can be of use in rare 
genetic disorders and is discussed in the sections devoted to those 
disorders.
Detailed reviews of current and future laboratory tests are given 
by Feingold and Grunfeld76 and Lucero et al.69 
Pure Hypercholesterolemia 
(Hypercholesterolemia Without 
Hypertriglyceridemia)
This section will commence with a brief overview of the athero­
sclerotic process and its relationship to hypercholesterolemia. It 
will then proceed to deal with primary causes of hypercholester­
olemia due to increased levels of LDL-C. A discussion of Lp(a) 
will follow, and the roles of the TG-rich lipoproteins and HDL in 
atherogenesis are described later in the chapter.

SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Hypercholesterolemia and Atherosclerosis
CVD is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in the West­
ern world. Although it is an exceedingly complex and multifacto­
rial disease, there can be no doubt that elevated plasma cholesterol 
levels play the dominant role in promoting atherosclerosis and 
its manifestations, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and 
peripheral artery disease. It is beyond the scope of this chapter to 
discuss the extensive experimental and clinical literature describ­
ing the literally thousands of papers investigating the etiology of 
atherosclerosis. However, in the midst of all this work, one fun­
damental fact remains: although investigators have now identified 
many hundreds of genes and metabolic and environmental effects 
that both accelerate and inhibit atherogenesis in animal models, a 
basic observation that underlies all of these studies is that it is impos­
sible to generate atherosclerotic lesions in any animal model with­
out dramatically raising plasma cholesterol levels. It is only in the 
background of marked hypercholesterolemia that the influence of 
genetic and other factors has been shown to modulate atherogen­
esis in animal models.
Similarly, there is now overwhelming epidemiologic, experi­
mental, and therapeutic data that plasma cholesterol, and spe­
cifically LDL-C, is the major causal factor responsible for the 
complications of atherosclerosis that are the leading causes of 
death and morbidity in the Western world. Because total choles­
terol levels correlate with the risk for coronary heart disease over 
a broad range (Fig. 41.17), normal levels are preferably defined as 
those associated with minimal CVD risk rather than population 
averages, suggesting that most people in the developed world have 
cholesterol levels that put them at risk for atherosclerotic CVD. 
Epidemiologic studies indicate that total cholesterol below 150 
mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) is associated with low risk of CVD. Decades 
of randomized trials conclusively show that lowering LDL-C 
in both primary and secondary prevention trials reduces CVD. 
Indeed, recent intervention studies producing dramatic reduc­
tions of LDL-C to values well below 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) even 
cause regression of established disease.77,78 Thus, the adage that 
“the lower the LDL, the better” is now the guideline for treatment 
goals in high-risk patients.
The dramatic success of LDL-C–lowering therapy suggests that 
this should be sufficient to cause regression of established disease 
and/or halt its progression in populations as well. Conceivably this 
might be true if plasma cholesterol levels had always been low 
from a young age or were chronically reduced to very low levels, 
for example, LDL-C levels well below 70 to 100 mg/dL (1.8–2.6 
mmol/L). Nevertheless, there is great variability in the expression 
of clinical disease in individuals with values above this, which 
includes the vast population of the Western world. Although it 
is clear that elevated LDL-C is a major risk factor for CVD, as 
in studies with animal models described earlier, there are likely 
hundreds of genetic and other influences that affect the clinical 
expression of atherosclerosis, even among individuals with similar 
cholesterol levels. Although this seems rather intuitive for those 
with only mildly elevated LDL-C values, it is even true for those 
with very high LDL-C as well. This is dramatically exemplified 
by two HoFH subjects with the same founder-gene defects and 
plasma cholesterol levels of over 1000 mg/dL (25.9 mmol/L), who 
developed CAD and died at vastly different ages. One, a male, 
died of a myocardial infarction at age 3 years, whereas his sister, 
despite developing symptoms of CAD, died of unrelated cause at 
age 33.79 Thus, clearly, although elevated LDL may be the pre­
requisite for development of CVD, there are many other factors 
influencing the development and progression of atherogenesis.
More than 100 years ago, investigators first showed that feed­
ing cholesterol to animals caused atherosclerosis. Since that time, 
there have been two main themes that have emerged as to the 
etiology of lesion formation. The oldest is the so-called lipid infil­
tration theory, and the second that has garnered increasing sup­
port is that atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease.80 As 
now agreed by most investigators, these two themes in fact go 
hand in hand. It is the hypercholesterolemia that is a prerequisite 
and driver of atherosclerosis because hypercholesterolemia itself 
promotes inflammation, but at differing absolute cholesterol lev­
els, the degree of inflammation and the responses to this differ in 
different individuals. Thus together, hypercholesterolemia and the 
inflammatory response to it establish atherosclerosis as a chronic 
inflammatory disease.81,82 In broad outline, atherosclerosis can 
be considered a form of chronic inflammation resulting from a 
complex interplay between elevated circulating LDL that becomes 
modified after entering the artery wall, and nearly all of the clas­
sical elements of both adaptive and innate immunity, including 
monocytes and macrophages, T-cells and antibodies derived from 
both adaptive B-2 and innate B-1 cells, as well as other circulating 
cellular and blood elements, and cells of the artery wall. It is now 
apparent that each of these may play key roles in a given setting 
and can modulate the extent of inflammation within the artery 
wall, providing responses that not only promote atherogenesis but 
are protective as well. The pathologic mechanisms involved are 
exceedingly complex.
Lipoproteins, chiefly LDLs, continuously flux into and out of 
the arterial intima. As hypercholesterolemia progresses, there is 
continued accumulation of LDLs within the intima, where LDLs 
are bound by collagen and proteoglycans, becoming trapped, 
prolonging their residence times, thus providing an enhanced 
opportunity for the LDLs to become modified.83 The genera­
tion of oxidized LDLs (OxLDLs) in the artery wall is one of the 
best-documented modifications in animal models and humans, 
and it occurs via cell-mediated, enzymatic, and other as yet unde­
fined mechanisms. The formation of OxLDL confers numerous 
atherogenic properties to LDLs.84–87 Native LDL uptake into 
macrophages is usually very limited because arterial macrophages

express low levels of LDL receptors, and excess cellular choles­
terol downregulates LDL receptors. However, OxLDLs bear novel 
oxidation-specific epitopes that serve as ligands recognized by 
scavenger receptors on macrophages,88 such as CD36 and scav­
enger receptor A (SR-A), mediating enhanced and unregulated 
uptake by macrophages, leading to cholesterol loading and foam 
cell formation (Fig. 41.18). In addition, the oxidized lipids of 
OxLDL, including oxidized phospholipids and oxidized choles­
terol, are both toxic to cells, promoting macrophage apoptosis and 
death. They also mediate extensive inflammatory gene expression 
in neighboring macrophages and endothelial cells,89,90 which, 
among other properties, promotes further recruitment of yet more 
monocytes into the intima. OxLDLs in turn promote differentia­
tion of the monocytes to macrophages and possibly conversion of 
smooth muscle cells into macrophage-like foamy cells as well. In 
addition, OxLDL and its products may inhibit normal mecha­
nisms that should promote cholesterol efflux from macrophages 
that otherwise would reduce cholesterol burden. An alternative or 
additional mechanism creating foam cells is the aggregation of the 
proteoglycan-bound LDL, which is mediated by both enzymatic 
mechanisms and by oxidation. In turn, the aggregated LDL is 
taken up at greatly accelerated rates by macrophages via a combi­
nation of receptor and nonreceptor mechanisms, further promot­
ing cholesterol accumulation.91,92
In the presence of hypercholesterolemia, enhanced LDL trans­
fer into the intima progresses, and LDL becomes associated with 
both collagen and proteoglycans, along with arterial cells. In time, 
acellular lipid-rich areas develop, as a result of both lipoprotein 
accumulation and death of lipid-laden macrophages. There are 
phenotypic changes in smooth muscle cells, which synthesize 
variable amounts of overlying collagen-rich connective tissue, 
forming a cap over the lesion. Although the arterial lumen can be 
progressively narrowed by the accumulation of macrophages, the 
proliferation of smooth muscle cells, and the deposition of choles­
terol, the truly dangerous lesion (the culprit lesion) may not cause 
marked luminal narrowing.93,94 As atherosclerosis progresses, 
there is a compensatory expansion of the lumen that maintains 
an almost constant lumen size. As the lesion develops within the 
intima, the complication of rupture of the overlying intima or 
endothelial erosion leads to exposure of the lesional contents to 
platelets, initiating thrombosis. It is the acute thrombosis that is 
responsible for infarctions in most patients. Rupture or erosion 
occurs where the fibrous cap covering the underlying thrombo­
genic lipid is thin.
The surfaces of complicated lesions can become thrombo­
genic as endothelial cells are lost or the fibrous cap ruptures and 
the subendothelial space is exposed. Platelets can adhere to this 
exposed surface, promoting thrombus formation. In these unsta­
ble plaques, blood actually dissects into the artery wall, leading to 
the formation of a large thrombus. Calcification is also a feature of 
late lesions. Advanced lesions can weaken the elasticity and integ­
rity of the artery wall, potentially creating an aneurysm of the ves­
sel. Removal or reduction of the atherogenic stimulus can result 
in plaque regression and stabilization, leaving a residual lesion 
depleted of lipid that is capped by collagen and less likely to serve 
as a nidus for thrombus formation.78
