SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
Lowering LDL-C is the cornerstone of both primary and 
secondary prevention and is of proven value. Nevertheless, it is 
apparent that lowering cholesterol, especially when started later 
in life, is not as effective as a lifetime of low cholesterol levels, 
and in almost all clinical trials, there remains a major “residual 
risk” among even the treated subjects. This has led to the search 
for additional therapies to add to the cholesterol lowering, as well 
as to starting LDL lowering sooner in individuals with genetic 
disorders, in whom exposure to elevated LDL levels occurs early 
in life. A major focus has been to develop effective therapies to tar­
get the inflammation that accompanies the hypercholesterolemia. 
A recent clinical trial studied the use of canakinumab, a human 
monoclonal antibody targeting interleukin 1β in patients with a 
previous myocardial infarction and an elevated high-sensitivity 
C-reactive protein level. Canakinumab, given every 3 months for 
a median of 3.7 years, significantly lowered the rate of recurrent 
CVD events versus placebo, independent of lipid-level lower­
ing. Unfortunately, canakinumab therapy was associated with a 
higher incidence of fatal infection than was placebo.95 This trial 
was important because it demonstrated, in principle, that target­
ing inflammation can provide additional CVD benefit above and 
beyond lowering LDL. Further support that targeting inflam­
mation is of benefit comes from a recent meta-analysis of ran­
domized trials using low-dose colchicine in secondary prevention 
trials. The addition of low-dose colchicine to standard medical 
therapy reduced the incidence of major CVD events, although 
not cardiovascular mortality, when compared with standard 
medical therapy alone.96 However, in another study, the antiin­
flammatory agent methotrexate failed to reduce CVD events,97 
suggesting that specific antiinflammatory approaches are needed. 
These early attempts to treat inflammation as one of the targets 
to reduce residual risk will no doubt expand. Targeting oxidation 
is another obvious strategy but is difficult to achieve because we 
currently lack effective antioxidants targeting the specific mecha­
nisms involved in atherogenesis. Analyses of earlier studies using 
vitamin E purposed for other noncardiovascular endpoints did 
not find evidence of benefit. Newer approaches targeting oxidative 
processes of relevance to atherogenesis may need to be tried. Neu­
tralizing oxidized phospholipids, which in murine studies reduced 
macrophage uptake of OxLDL, decreased arterial and systemic 
inflammation, and reduced lesion formation and necrotic cores,90 
might be an example of a potential future target. 
Etiology of Hypercholesterolemia
Hypercholesterolemia usually is discovered during routine blood 
testing or during analyses performed following the onset of clini­
cal CVD. Exceptionally, patients with genetic forms of hypercho­
lesterolemia, or occasionally patients with obstructive liver disease, 
will present with distinctive xanthomas. Elevation of LDL-C may 
be broadly categorized as due to distinct genetic disorders, such as 
FH, to so-called polygenic hypercholesterolemia, to as yet poorly 
defined metabolic, dietary, and environmental effects, and to con­
tributions from each of these general categories.
Hepatic LDL receptors are the primary determinate of plasma 
LDL levels. In most cases, increased LDL levels are the result of 
defective LDL clearance due to decreased hepatic LDL receptor 
number or activity. Rarely, gain-of-function mutations in PCSK9 
that lead to enhanced degradation of LDL receptors, or muta­
tions in APOB that affect the LDL receptor–binding site, pre­
venting LDL from binding to normal hepatic LDL receptor, can 
lead to elevated LDL levels. Increased LDL-C also can result from 
increased VLDL secretion leading to increased LDL production, 
as occurs in familial combined hyperlipidemia (see “Combined 
Hyperlipoproteinemia” section), which can sometimes manifest 
as primary elevations of LDL-C. Greater LDL production due 
to greater absorption of dietary cholesterol, abnormalities in the 
regulation of lipid-regulated nuclear transcription factors, or gain-
of-function abnormalities in cholesterol and APOB lipoprotein 
assembly pathways are all possible contributors but remain poorly 
defined. 
Polygenic Hypercholesterolemia
Although patients with FH have the highest LDL-C levels (typi­
cally over 190 mg/dL [4.92 mmol/L]), the vast majority of hyper­
cholesterolemic patients do not have monogenic FH due to 
mutations in one or more of the LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9 genes. 
In fact, in most patients, the etiology of the hypercholesterolemia 
is likely to be a complex combination of environmental, meta­
bolic, and genetic etiologies. In population-based samples with 
severe hypercholesterolemia, only 1% to 5% of patients have a 
pathogenic FH-causing mutation in the LDLR, APOB, or PCSK9 
genes.98 Among the 95% to 99% of patients with hypercholester­
olemia who lack major gene defects, less than 50% have elevated 
polygenic risk scores.98 Polygenic risk scores are tallies of com­
mon small-effect single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) alleles in 
a person’s genome. These alleles each act to slightly raise the level 
of LDL-C, and the effect of a given SNP on LDL-C in a given 
individual is minimal. Thus, for the majority of patients with 
elevated LDL, we do not fully understand the genetic, metabolic, 
and environmental factors, such as diet and lifestyle, that influ­
ence their elevated LDL-C levels. Nonetheless, irrespective of the 
mechanisms responsible for the elevation of LDL, the increased 
LDL-C is associated with a higher risk of CVD; the higher the 
level, the greater the risk. 
Monogenic Familial Hypercholesterolemia
Patients with FH have up to a 10-fold increased prevalence of 
CAD if untreated. They have the most elevated levels of LDL-C 
among all hypercholesterolemic patients, with LDL-C values usu­
ally well above 160 mg/dL (4.14 mmol/L), often above 500 mg/dL 
(12.9 mmol/L), and even exceeding 1000 mg/dL (25.9 mmol/L) 
in those with HoFH. Among patients with FH, 80% to 85% of 
cases are caused by loss-of-function mutations in the LDLR gene, 
and another 5% to 10% are caused by missense mutations in the 
LDL receptor–binding domain of APOB-100 that reduce the 
ability of LDL to bind to hepatic LDL receptors (familial defec­
tive APOB [FDB]). Rarely, gain-of-function mutations in PCSK9 
are a cause of autosomal co-dominant FH and biallelic loss-of-
function mutations in low-density lipoprotein receptor adaptor 
protein 1 (LDLRAP1) also can generate an FH phenotype.99
Heterozygous FH (HeFH) is the most common monogenic 
cause of high plasma LDL-C levels. Although the prevalence of 
HeFH was previously thought to be about 1:500, more recent 
population data suggest a prevalence of about 1:250.100 In con­
trast, biallelic LDLR mutations causing HoFH are rare, with 
an estimated prevalence of 1:250,000 to 1:360,000.101 Biallelic 
mutations may be either two identical copies of the same allele 
(true homozygote, very rare) or two nonidentical mutant alleles 
(compound heterozygote). FH has a co-dominant mode of inheri­
tance with a gene-dosage effect. There are more than 1200 differ­
ent LDLR mutations identified to date, each of which potentially 
leads to different levels of LDL receptor function, varying from 
null alleles resulting in no receptor activity to mutations reduc­
ing residual activity from 10% to 80% of normal function. This 
1649
CHAPTER 41  Disorders of Lipoprotein Metabolism
leads to a wide variation in plasma LDL-C levels depending on 
the degree of impairment of LDL receptor activity. Heterozygotes 
have one normal LDLR allele, in addition to the mutant LDLR. 
Therefore, they generally respond well to therapies such as statins, 
which effectively increase hepatic LDL receptor activity. In con­
trast, patients with HoFH, who have two mutant alleles, respond 
poorly, depending on how much residual LDL receptor activity 
their mutant alleles retain. Individuals with two null alleles do not 
respond at all to standard therapies that alter LDL receptor activity. 
However, the finding that treatment with an ANGPTL3 mono­
clonal antibody, evinacumab, had significant efficacy in hypercho­
lesterolemic individuals led to studies that included patients with 
HoFH. Importantly, the monoclonal antibody reduced LDL-C 
by about 50% in such patients, including those who had two null 
mutations, which is important because such patients are usually 
resistant to all LDL-C–lowering treatments other than plasma­
pheresis.102 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and 
the European Medicines Agency (EMA) both approved this agent 
for the treatment of HoFH in 2021.
Patients with HeFH may have LDL-C levels that vary from 
160 mg/dL (4.1 mmol/L) to levels that exceed 300 to 400 mg/
dL (7.5–10.3 mmol/L). Most patients with HeFH do not have 
clinical or physical findings of hypercholesterolemia, particularly 
when young. However, those with higher LDL-C levels and with 
advancing age and those who are not on effective LDL-C–lower­
ing therapy can develop tendon xanthomas (Fig. 41.19). They 
most commonly occur on the Achilles tendons and appear as a 
convex thickening of the tendon or can be detected as a bump 
or generalized thickening of the tendon by palpation (see Fig. 
41.19, left). Tendon xanthomas can cause recurrent episodes of 
Achilles tendinitis. Xanthomas also can occur on extensor ten­
dons of the hands and are best appreciated on the knuckles after 
flexing and extending the fingers (see Fig. 41.19, right). The tib­
ial tuberosity is another site where xanthomas can occur. Patients 
with FH also can have xanthelasmas (Fig. 41.20, left) and pre­
mature corneal arcus (i.e., in persons younger than 40 years) (see 
Fig. 41.20, right), but these latter findings are not specific for 
FH. Before the development of effective therapy to lower LDL-
C, premature CAD was common but variable. Some patients 
with HeFH develop CAD in the third or fourth decade of life, 
especially if they have other CVD risk factors, such as cigarette 
smoking or elevated Lp(a) levels. Even before the introduction 
of statin therapy, some patients with HeFH (especially women) 
only developed CVD later in life or not at all. Incomplete pene­
trance, protective genetic factors, or other lifestyle modifications 
may have been contributing factors.
In one health care system in the United States, the HeFH 
form was detected with a prevalence of 1 in 256 in unselected 
participants and 1 in 118 in cardiac catheterization laboratory 
patients.2 HeFH is a major cause of early-onset CAD in those 
who are not treated. In addition, HoFH and some other severe 
forms of LDL receptor deficiency are associated with aortic valve 
calcification and stenosis. It is important to emphasize that early 
detection of elevated LDL-C levels in children and younger adults 
with FH and establishment of effective therapeutic programs to 
lower LDL-C are very effective in negating the adverse effects of 
the hypercholesterolemia.103,104 These data advocate for early cas­
cade screening of all family members in FH families and early

Homozygosity for FH is not common but is likely to occur more 
frequently than previously appreciated.105 These patients come to 
clinical attention early in life because of the appearance of tendon 
and planar xanthomas, as well as tuberous xanthomas (Fig. 41.21), 
marked hypercholesterolemia apparent at birth, very premature 
CAD, and/or aortic valve disease. Plasma LDL-C concentrations 
range from 500 to 950 mg/dL (13.0–24.6 mmol/L). Symptomatic 
CAD can occur as early as 3 years old and often before age 10 years. 
If not treated, these homozygous patients usually die from myo­
cardial infarction by age 20 years. Aortic valve disease in homo­
zygotes can be valvular or supravalvular. The diagnosis of HoFH 
should be suspected in any child with extremely high plasma cho­
lesterol (typically above 500 mg/dL [13.0 mmol/L]) or those who 
have the xanthomas characteristic of HoFH. Both parents are obli­
gate heterozygotes and should manifest the phenotype of HeFH. 
What distinguishes treatment of HoFH is the need to start therapy 
as soon as the diagnosis is made, in very early childhood when 
possible.101 In general, patients with HoFH respond less well to 
LDL-C–lowering therapy, and in the past, repetitive LDL apheresis 
was the only effective therapy. However, depending on the extent of 
residual LDL receptor activity expressed from their mutant alleles, 
they may respond to statins, PCSK9 inhibitors, ezetimibe, and 
bile sequestrants, as well as varying combinations of these agents. 
Lomitapide, an MTP inhibitor, also has been used to treat patients 
with HoFH.106 Recently, inhibiting plasma ANGPTL3 with a 
monoclonal antibody, evinacumab, was found to lower LDL-C 
rather dramatically in many patients with HoFH.107,108 Addition of 
evinacumab to two adolescents with HoFH, on background treat­
ment of statin, ezetimibe, and weekly apheresis, resulted in substan­
tial LDL lowering and marked regression of total plaque volume 
measured by coronary computed tomography angiography after 6 
months.109 As a result of these therapeutic modalities, used in com­
binations, the use of repetitive LDL apheresis is declining. In rare 
patients, liver transplantation has been used.110 
Rare Mutations Associated With Elevated LDL 
Levels
Familial Defective Apolipoprotein B-100
Familial defective apolipoprotein B-100 (FDB) is an autosomal-
dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in the LDL 
receptor–binding site on APOB100 that reduces the bind­
ing affinity of APOB100 for the LDL receptor, thus inhibiting 
LDL clearance by the liver. The R3500Q variant in APOB100 is 
most commonly associated with familial defective apolipoprotein 
B-100 and occurs in approximately 0.1% of Northern Europeans 
and U.S. Caucasians; it is thought to make a significant contribu­
tion to FH phenotype. The clinical phenotype is frequently milder 
than that of HeFH due to mutations in the LDLR gene, possibly 
the result of a partial defect in receptor binding attributed to the 
mutation or the continued ability of APOE to mediate lipoprotein 
uptake. Familial defective apolipoprotein B-100 is subsequently 
underdiagnosed according to standard FH diagnostic criteria.111 
Autosomal-Recessive Hypercholesterolemia
Autosomal-recessive hypercholesterolemia (ARH) is a very rare 
cause of elevated LDL-C caused by mutations in LDLRAP1, the 
gene encoding an adaptor protein required for internalization of 
LDL bound by the LDL receptor on the surface of hepatocytes. 
The mutation in this protein was discovered in studies investigat­
ing children with the clinical features of HoFH who were born 
from normocholesterolemic parents, strongly suggesting a reces­
sive transmission of FH. In these patients, the involvement of 
LDLR and APOB genes was excluded. Several patients identified 
in Sardinia led to the elucidation of the genetic defect, which has 
subsequently been identified in other patients around the world. 
These patients present as typical patients HoFH (although LDL-C 
levels can be less elevated than typical HoFH), but whose parents 
both have normal LDL-C values.112 
Gain-of-Function Mutations in PCSK9
As described earlier in the section on the LDL receptor, mutations 
of PCSK9 lead to alterations in LDL receptor expression because 
this secreted protein binds to the hepatic LDL receptor and medi­
ates its enhanced degradation when the receptor is internalized, 
preventing it from recycling to the hepatocyte surface.113 Gain-of-
function mutations increase the ability of the secreted PCSK9 to 
mediate enhanced degradation of hepatic LDL receptors, reduc­
ing LDL receptor number, which leads to reduced plasma LDL 
clearance by the liver and a clinical picture of FH. These rare 
mutations probably account for about 1% of FH phenotypes.114 
PCSK9 inhibitors, either monoclonal antibodies or siRNA oligo­
nucleotides that reduce PCSK9 synthesis, should be particularly 
effective therapy for this genetic form of hypercholesterolemia.115 
As noted earlier, loss-of-function mutations in PSCK9 are associ­
ated with low total cholesterol and LDL-C and decreased risk of 
CAD.52,116 
Approach to the Patient With High LDL-C Levels
Clinical trials clearly demonstrate benefits of LDL reduction in 
both primary and secondary settings.117,118 The initial evalua­
tion for all patients consists of a history and physical examina­
tion, including assessment of diet, exercise, and traditional CVD 
risk factors (Box 41.1) and measurement of plasma lipoprotein 
levels. Exclusion of secondary causes of hypercholesterolemia (see 
“Secondary Forms of Hyper- and Dyslipoproteinemia” section) 
is important. Obesity is an independent risk factor for CVD, 
particularly central obesity, as reflected in the waist circumfer­
ence measurement used to define metabolic syndrome (Table 
41.4). Obesity aggravates dyslipidemia, hypertension, and insulin 
resistance and is a target of therapy regardless of the severity of 
traditional CVD risk factors. However, although obesity may be

A crucial part of the initial exam should be to obtain a detailed 
history of CVD and history of elevated cholesterol or TGs, not 
only of the patient but of all first-degree relatives. A family history 
of CVD is a major factor enhancing CVD risk, aside from the 
degree of hypercholesterolemia. In primary care, a child–parent 
screening strategy is effective in identifying FH with high CVD 
risk.119 The examination should emphasize the cardiovascular 
system, with careful examination for tendon xanthomas, xanthe­
lasma, and corneal arcus and for features of disorders causing sec­
ondary lipid abnormalities.
Patient Selection and Treatment Goals
It is widely accepted that LDL-C reduction prevents CVD 
and reduces clinically important CVD events in patients with 
established disease or at increased risk. Guidelines on who to treat 
and to what lipid targets have evolved as more effective therapeu­
tic options have been developed and clinical trial data have been 
expanded. The National Cholesterol Education Program, first 
established by the National Institutes of Health in the late 1980s, 
created a standard for cholesterol levels and pioneered a practical 
approach to treatment by dividing the population according to 
cardiac risk based on lipid and other cardiac risk factors. More 
recent clinical trials have shown greater reductions of plaque, and 
even plaque regression, with aggressive and safe LDL reduction. 
In the setting of mounting evidence that lowering LDL-C by any 
of multiple approaches leads to further reductions in CVD events, 
future guidance will likely lead to recommended therapeutic goals 
that are ever more aggressive to achieve the adage that “the lower 
the LDL, the better.”
Almost all guidelines now agree that the LDL-C goal for sec­
ondary prevention in patients with existing CAD should be less 
than 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L). Some guidelines recommend even 
lower targets (below 55 mg/dL [1.4 mmol/L]) in the setting of 
documented atherosclerosis, very high risk (recurrent events and/or 
multiple other CVD risk factors), or evidence of continued disease 
progression despite LDL of less than 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L).78,120 
Cardiovascular outcome trials using aggressive approaches to LDL 
lowering, including combination therapies and PCSK9 antibodies 
or siRNA, which can reduce LDL-C to very low levels, support 
the recommendation that in those with existing CAD, lowering 
LDL-C to below 50 mg/dL (1.3 mmol/L) may not only stabilize 
existing disease but can even cause plaque regression.81
Guidelines for treatment of patients with type 2 diabetes mel­
litus consider their increased risk of CVD events. Patients with 
established CVD and diabetes mellitus are considered to be at 
very high risk.121,122 CVD disease accounts for a high percentage 
of deaths in the geriatric population, and there are clear survival 
benefits for the treatment of elderly patients, even if frail.123,124 
Moreover, the relative clinical benefit of lowering LDL-C for pri­
mary prevention of major vascular events is similar in individuals 
≥70 years as in those aged <70 years.124a
Previously, some guidelines focused on the use of high- versus 
low-dose statin therapies, as well as the percentage of LDL reduction 
achieved, rather than on LDL goals. Guidelines from the American 
Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) 
and other societies125 and the European Atherosclerosis Society 
(EAS)120 at the time of writing focus more on achieving absolute 
LDL-C goals, although they differ in that the lower target in the 
U.S. guidelines was 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) versus 55 mg/dL (1.4 
mmol/L) in the European guidelines. Various potent therapeutic 
options to lower LDL-C are now available, including statins, ezeti­
mibe, a variety of PCSK9 inhibitors, bile sequestrants, a mono­
clonal antibody to ANGPTL3, bempedoic acid, and even LDL 
apheresis. Therefore, effective therapies to optimally lower LDL-C 
are available for nearly all hypercholesterolemic patients, including 
patients with HeFH and even many patients with HoFH.
Most guidelines recommend drug treatment for any patient 
with LDL-C greater than 190 mg/dL (4.9 mmol/L), irrespective 
of risk score.
In general, desirable levels of LDL for primary prevention of dis­
ease should be less than 100 mg/dL (2.59 mmol/L) for most people 
and even lower for those with multiple risk factors. When lipid-low­
ering therapy for primary prevention should be initiated is unclear.
The 2018 AHA/ACC guidelines provide a categorization of risk 
and need to initiate therapy based on a variety of factors enhancing 
the risk for CVD.125 Risk calculators based on current AHA/ACC

Specific Therapies for High LDL-C
Specific therapies include lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, and 
weight management) and drug therapy. 
Lifestyle Treatment, Including Diet
Lifestyle changes, including dietary intervention, moderate exer­
cise, and weight loss, are first-line therapies for hyperlipidemia 
(Table 41.5) and may be sufficient for mild dyslipidemias in low-
risk patients. All other treatments should build on therapeutic life­
style changes.125 The role of exercise is discussed in more detail in 
the “Management of the Patient with Mild to Moderately Severe 
Hypertriglyceridemia” section.
Most experts recommend restriction of saturated fatty acids 
to below 7% to 10% of calories because their intake is associ­
ated with increased plasma cholesterol levels and increased CVD 
risk. The optimal dietary recommendations are continually being 
“fine-tuned” in various guideline recommendations but in gen­
eral emphasize restriction of dietary saturated fat and cholesterol, 
utilization of liquid vegetable oils (but not tropical oils such as 
coconut and palm oil) and nuts, and consumption of at least two 
servings of fish a week. Almost all guidelines recommend restric­
tion of cholesterol intake to below 300 mg/day. The most recent 
AHA guidelines at the time of writing are the 2018 guidelines.125
Fatty acids and TGs that circulate in the blood in lipoproteins 
primarily reflect the fatty acid composition of adipose tissue TGs, 
and both sources reflect dietary fatty acid composition. Dietary 
saturated fats are found in animal-based foods, such as beef, pork, 
poultry, and full-fat dairy products, which are all greatly enriched 
in cholesterol as well. Importantly, tropical oils like coconut and 
palm, frequently used as substitutes, are in fact highly saturated, 
and they raise plasma cholesterol by decreasing plasma clearance 
of LDL. If the dietary recommendations for reduction in satu­
rated fats are followed, this will result in reduced dietary choles­
terol intake because cholesterol is often present in foods rich in 
saturated fats. In place, it is recommended to eat foods made with 
liquid vegetable oils but not tropical oils, which are highly satu­
rated.128 In contrast, olive oil, found in Mediterranean diets and 
associated with reduced CVD, is composed of 60% to 70% ole­
ate. In addition, olive oil also has on average 10% linoleic acid 
(C18:2), an omega-6 fatty acid, and below 1% linolenic acid 
(C18:3), an omega-3 fatty acid. Olive oil therefore is rich in essen­
tial fatty acids.
Trans-fatty acids are unsaturated fatty acids with at least one 
or more double bonds saturated artificially by the addition of 
hydrogens attached in trans configuration across the double bond. 
This configuration causes the molecules to act more like fully satu­
rated fatty acids. They are produced when liquid vegetable oils are 
hydrogenated to produce semisolid fats used in some margarines 
and shortenings. Such trans-fatty acids raise LDL-C, lower HDL-
C, and have been associated with increased CVD.128 Their use in 
the diet has been dramatically reduced in the past 2 decades. Very 
low intake of trans-fatty acids is recommended for the prevention 
of CVD.
AHA guidelines and other guidelines recommend eating 
at least two servings/week of fatty fish to achieve sufficient 
omega-3 fatty acid intake associated with both decreased all-
cause mortality and CVD risk. The role of omega-3 fatty acid 
supplements for the prevention of CVD is discussed in the 
“Treatment of Mild to Moderately Severe Hypertriglyceride­
mia” section.
Other dietary components also influence plasma lipids and 
lipoproteins. For example, soluble fibers such as psyllium or oat 
bran, which can bind bile acids in the gut and promote net cho­
lesterol excretion, decrease LDL modestly, by about 5% to 10%. 
Margarines made with sitostanol or sitosterol, which are plant ste­
rols that inhibit cholesterol absorption, reduce serum cholesterol 
by up to 10%.
Together, a rigorous diet that restricts cholesterol and satu­
rated and trans-fatty acid intake and utilizes plant sterols and 
soluble fiber can reduce LDL-C levels by up to 30% in dedicated 
patients.129 However, more easily achieved changes in dietary 
composition reduce LDL-C levels by about 10% to 15%, depend­
ing on the content of cholesterol and saturated fats in an indi­
vidual’s baseline diet.

HMG-CoA Reductase Inhibitors (Statins)
Statins inhibit cholesterol biosynthesis, upregulate hepatic LDL 
receptors, enhance LDL clearance, and reduce lipoprotein secre­
tion from the liver, thereby decreasing LDL production. Statins may 
decrease TGs by reducing VLDL secretion and enhancing VLDL 
clearance from the circulation, which also decreases LDL production.
Statins are the cornerstone of therapy to lower LDL-C and 
have been in use since 1984. They are useful in all types of hyper­
lipoproteinemias in which LDL-C is elevated. They have an exten­
sive safety record and have been shown to reduce the risk of CVD 
and all-cause mortality. A statin is almost always the primary drug 
to be used in any patient with elevated LDL-C, and statins are 
the drugs of choice for lowering LDL as primary or secondary 
prevention. They remain effective in patients with HeFH and are 
even effective to a variable degree in many patients with HoFH, 
depending on the level of residual LDL receptor activity on their 
two alleles. Many of the statins are approved for use in children 
with FH as young as 8 years of age and may be considered in 
young people with high LDL-C without an FH history but with a 
significant family history of premature CAD.
Table 41.7 provides the relative potency of various statins when 
used at different dosages, and Table 41.8 lists expected effects of 
various statins on LDL-C. They reduce LDL-C by 20% to 60%, 
increase HDL-C by 2% to 16%, and reduce triglycerides by 7% 
to 37%. Statins can also raise Lp(a) levels on average by approxi­
mately 10%.130,131 The LDL-lowering effects vary by drug, dos­
age, and in the case of TG, baseline values. Effects also vary among 
patients, with greater or lesser degrees of LDL-C reduction even 
at the same dose. For each statin, doubling of the dose typically 
produces an additional 6% reduction in LDL-C.132 LDL lowering 
is seen within 1 to 2 weeks after the start of therapy and is stable 
in about 4 to 6 weeks. Pitavastatin, atorvastatin, and rosuvastatin 
have long half-lives, about 12 hours, 14 hours, and 21 hours, 
respectively. The other statins have half-lives of about 2 to 3 hours. 
First-generation statins with short half-lives should be taken in the 
evening. Atorvastatin and fluvastatin have minimal renal clearance 
and may be more suitable for patients with renal insufficiency. All 
the statin drugs are now available as generic drugs in the United 
States. Table 41.9 shows specific features of available statins.
The statins are among the most widely prescribed medica­
tions worldwide and are usually very well tolerated, with minimal 
side effects. The most common substantive complaint relates to 
muscle symptoms, and although up to 5% to 20% of patients 
complain of muscle side effects, randomized placebo-based trials 
have suggested that many, if not most, of these issues are due to 
a nocebo effect, which is the anticipation of a side effect lead­
ing to altered perception.133,134 The adverse effects associated with 
statin use correlate with drug dose,135 but many large random­
ized, placebo-controlled clinical trials have not shown differences 
in rates of myalgias and creatine kinase elevations between statin-
treated and placebo groups. Regardless, muscle complaints are a 
common reason for statin discontinuation by patients, perhaps 
related to misinformation about the risks of statin therapy pro­
mulgated through the internet.136 Many people take statins for 
years without complaints but then develop muscular complaints 
and stop the statin. A careful history may reveal an alternative 
explanation for the symptoms or, occasionally, the introduction of 
another medication that impairs the metabolism of the statin or 
the presence of renal disease. In many, if not most, patients, the 
statin can be successfully restarted over time in stages. An alternate 
approach is to use a low dose of rosuvastatin on alternate days or 
even as infrequently as once or twice weekly. This can achieve a

15% to 25% reduction in LDL-C, which can be increased by the 
addition of a non-statin such as ezetimibe.137
In patients with muscle complaints after statin administration, 
creatinine kinase levels will be within normal limits in over 99% 
of cases. Disorders that might influence skeletal muscle or present 
with muscle symptoms must be excluded, such as hypothyroid­
ism, vitamin D deficiency, rheumatologic conditions, and per­
haps depression. Inhibition of statin catabolism is associated with 
increased myopathy risk. Drugs metabolized through the cyto­
chrome P450 (CYP) system, such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, 
clarithromycin, and erythromycin, increase statin plasma levels, 
particularly of older statins that are more extensively metabolized 
by the liver. Other drugs that increase the risk of statin myopathy 
include gemfibrozil, cyclosporine, digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem, 
amiodarone, colchicine, and protease inhibitors. Also, a sudden 
dramatic increase in exercise can cause symptoms, with associated 
high creatinine kinase levels.
The most serious potential side effect of statins is rhabdomy­
olysis leading to myoglobinuria and renal failure. Rhabdomyol­
ysis is rare and more likely in patients with renal insufficiency, 
advanced age, other comorbid conditions, or polypharmacy, as 
well as during perioperative periods.137 It is also occasionally seen 
after endurance exercise, such as marathon running. Routine sur­
veillance of creatine kinase is not useful in most patients.
Management of dyslipidemia in patients with muscle-related 
complaints is challenging and may include using a different statin, 
decreasing the dose, giving the medication less frequently, or con­
sidering other LDL-lowering drugs. Asians appear to be sensitive 
to rosuvastatin, and lower doses should be used initially. Higher 
doses of simvastatin should be avoided. The FDA recommends 
that simvastatin 80 mg not be used, and simvastatin should be 
limited to 10 mg in patients taking amiodarone, verapamil, and 
diltiazem and limited to 20 mg in those taking amlodipine and 
ranolazine.
Liver toxicity is uncommon with statin use. Hepatic amino­
transferase elevation is usually mild and does not require discon­
tinuation of the statin. It may be dose dependent, as demonstrated 
in clinical trials that showed rates of persistent elevations of liver 
aminotransferase greater than three times the upper limit of nor­
mal occurring in 0.1% to 1.9% of patients, depending on the 
statin and the dose. Routine monitoring of hepatic transaminases 
is not required and should only be obtained at baseline if there 
is a clinical indication for their measurement. Only about 1% of 
statin-using patients have aminotransferase increases to greater 
than three times the upper limit of normal, and the elevation often 
decreases even if patients continue on the statin.138,139 Statins 
can be used cautiously in the presence of liver disease that is not 
decompensated, and nonalcoholic hepatic steatosis is not a contra­
indication.140 If aminotransferases remain greater than three times 
the upper limit of normal, consider lowering the dose or changing 
to a different statin, and identify other contributing conditions or 
drugs. Irreversible liver damage resulting from statins is extremely 
rare, with a liver failure rate of 1 case per 1 million person-years 
of use.140
Statin therapy is associated with a small increased incidence 
of type 2 diabetes mellitus in patients,141 especially in those with 
a predisposition to developing this disorder, such as individuals 
with metabolic syndrome.142 This association was most evident 
with the use of the highest doses of atorvastatin (80 mg) and rosu­
vastatin (40 mg).139,143,144 Genetic studies indicate that variants 
in the LDL receptor, PCSK9, and HMG-CoA reductase (the tar­
get of statins) that lower LDL-C levels are associated with type 2 
diabetes mellitus risk,145,146 suggesting that promoting uptake of 
LDL might affect diabetes pathogenesis. Nonetheless, the large 
reduction in major CVD events with statin therapy markedly out­
weigh the risks of small increases in glucose in all but those at low­
est atherosclerotic risk.147 Attention to diet, exercise, and weight 
can mitigate the diabetes risk, and glycemic-lowering therapies 
can be initiated.
There is a large litany of alleged side effects promoted on the 
internet, and patients often have complaints that may or may 
not be due to statins. Complaints about confusion, memory loss, 
or peripheral neuropathy should be appropriately evaluated for 
causes of these symptoms. There is no evidence that statins cause 
direct adverse effects on renal function beyond those due to rhab­
domyolysis. Statins are contraindicated during pregnancy and 
nursing and in patients with significant hepatic dysfunction. 
PCSK9 Inhibitors
There are two approaches to targeting PCSK9. The first includes 
fully humanized monoclonal antibodies to PCSK9 that lower 
LDL-C levels by preventing lysosomal degradation of the LDL 
receptor, increasing recirculation of the receptor to the surface 
of hepatocytes and consequent lowering of circulating LDL (see 
Fig. 41.13). Alone or in conjunction with statins, they increase 
removal of LDL from the circulation, leading to a nearly 60% fur­
ther reduction in circulating LDL beyond that achieved by statins 
alone, a reduction in CVD events, and as noted earlier, atheroma 
regression in patients with known atherosclerosis.
Clinical trials with both monoclonal antibody PCSK9 inhibi­
tors (alirocumab and evolocumab) marketed in the United States 
demonstrate reductions in atherosclerotic CVD events, particu­
larly in patients with recent acute coronary syndrome, multivessel 
CAD, or peripheral arterial disease.148,149 Reductions in LDL-C 
to levels less than 25 mg/dL (0.65 mmol/L), which occurred 
in more than a quarter of the patients in the clinical trials, are 
associated with even lower CVD event rates,150,151 thereby estab­
lishing no lower limit for LDL when using PCSK9 alone or in 
combination with a statin. No adverse effects of lowering LDL to 
these low levels have been observed. PCSK9 inhibitors are recom­
mended for high-risk patients with LDL levels of 70 mg/dL (1.8 
mmol/L) or higher on maximally tolerated oral therapies, includ­
ing statins and/or ezetimibe. They are invaluable for patients with 
high LDL-C who are intolerant to statins. PCSK9 inhibitors are 
especially useful in HeFH, where carriers have a high prevalence of 
premature death and can otherwise be challenging to treat. They 
are effective to varying degrees in most FH homozygotes, except 
the estimated 10% who have biallelic null alleles. Evolocumab is 
approved for use in HoFH in the United States. Unlike statins, 
PCSK9 inhibitors decrease Lp(a), although modestly, in the range 
of 15% to 30%.152 These drugs are injected every 2 to 4 weeks. As 
with many new biologics, insurance restrictions and expense pro­
vide barriers to use, but because of their proven ability to reduce 
CVD risk, their availability and use are increasing. Aside from 
injection site reactions, side effects of this therapy thus far appear 
minimal.
Recently, a small interfering RNA (siRNA), inclisiran, has 
been developed to inhibit hepatic synthesis of PCSK9. Inclisiran 
effectively reduces plasma PCSK9 levels.153 The siRNA is targeted 
to the liver by an attached triantennary N-acetylgalactosamine 
(GalNAc) complex, which binds to the asialoglycoprotein recep­
tor present on the hepatocyte surface. The internalized siRNA has 
an extended biological half-life, and injections of inclisiran are 
given at baseline, 3 months, and then only at 6-month intervals. 
1657
CHAPTER 41  Disorders of Lipoprotein Metabolism
A meta-analysis of data from three randomized clinical trials dem­
onstrated that inclisiran decreases LDL-C levels by 51% and is 
associated with a 24% lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular 
events.118 Inclisiran is well tolerated, with no significant adverse 
events other than mild injection site reactions. A major CVD 
reduction trial is now underway. It has recently been approved by 
the FDA to lower LDL-C and adds another important agent to 
the growing list of drugs that inhibit PCSK9’s detrimental effect 
on LDL receptors. 
Ezetimibe
Ezetimibe inhibits cholesterol absorption by binding to NPCL1, 
the intestinal cholesterol absorption transporter. Ezetimibe lowers 
LDL by 14% to 25% when used alone or in combination with 
statins. It is a very useful drug to add to baseline statin therapy for 
optimal LDL lowering. For example, in one study of combina­
tion therapy, LDL was reduced from nearly 70 to 54 mg/dL (1.8 
to 1.4 mmol/L)154 and further reduced CVD events beyond that 
achieved by the statin therapy. Ezetimibe can be particularly use­
ful in patients who are intolerant of statins. Ezetimibe undergoes 
glucuronidation, leading to extensive enterohepatic circulation. 
Absorption is not affected by food.
Side effects are relatively uncommon but may include diarrhea 
and abnormal liver function. Myopathy is rare and, like myalgias, 
is not clearly related to the medication.155 Ezetimibe can increase 
cyclosporine levels. Fibrates can increase ezetimibe levels, a find­
ing with unknown clinical significance.156 Ezetimibe is contrain­
dicated in pregnancy and in severe liver dysfunction. 
Bile Acid Sequestrants
Bile acid sequestrants were the first LDL-C–lowering drug class 
shown to reduce CVD in a randomized clinical trial, which sup­
ported the cholesterol hypothesis of atherosclerosis and provided a 
crucial early rationale for the development of LDL-lowering ther­
apies.157,158 The bile acid sequestrants have been used since the 
1970s but now are primarily reserved for patients unable to take 
statins and for those who require additional cholesterol reduction.
They work by binding negatively charged bile acids and bile salts 
in the small intestine to interrupt the enterohepatic circulation of 
bile acids, which leads to increased hepatic synthesis of cholesterol 
and conversion into bile acids. Despite the increase in cholesterol 
synthesis, there is decreased hepatocyte cholesterol content, which 
results in increased LDL receptors, leading to reduced circulat­
ing LDL levels. VLDL-TG synthesis also increases,159 which is 
temporary in many patients. Enhanced VLDL clearance returns 
VLDL to baseline, although in selected patients, the increased 
TGs may persist.160 For this reason, these drugs should be used 
with caution in patients with baseline hypertriglyceridemia.
As monotherapy, sequestrants lower LDL by 5% to 30% in 
a dose-dependent manner. Cholestyramine, colestipol, and cole­
sevelam are available in the United States. Colesevelam has greater 
bile acid–binding capacity and affinity than cholestyramine or 
colestipol and is used at lower doses. LDL reduction is typically 
15% at 3.8 g/day (six 625-mg tablets) and 18% at 4.3 g/day (seven 
625-mg tablets).161,162 Bile acid sequestrants also lower fasting 
blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c levels in patients with diabetes 
mellitus.163 The mechanism underlying this effect is unclear but 
might relate to activation of a bile sensitivity receptor (TGR5) in 
the colon.
Gastrointestinal disturbances are common and include consti­
pation, nausea, bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, and aggrava­
tion of hemorrhoids. Initiation with low doses, patient education, 
and use of stool softeners or psyllium can increase compliance. 
Gastrointestinal symptoms occur less with colesevelam. These 
drugs are not absorbed, so they can be used in pregnancy. Bile 
acid sequestrants affect absorption of a wide variety of drugs; other 
medications should be taken either 1 to 2 hours before or 4 to 6 
hours after the sequestrant.
Bempedoic Acid. Bempedoic acid, a small molecule that acts as a 
selective antagonist of ATP-citrate lyase, catalyzes the ATP-depen­
dent conversion of citrate and coenzyme A (CoA) to oxaloacetate 
and acetyl-CoA, which is a crucial precursor for the biosynthesis 
of cholesterol. Thus, bempedoic acid inhibits cholesterol synthesis, 
which in turn leads to an increase in hepatic LDL receptor synthe­
sis and reduced plasma LDL-C.164 In various patient populations, 
it reduces LDL-C by 18% to 30%, either alone or in combina­
tion with other LDL-lowering agents. It may be especially use­
ful in statin-intolerant patients.165 Bempedoic acid may lead to a 
decrease in hemoglobin; increases in blood urea nitrogen, creati­
nine, and uric acid; and an increase in gout. A phase 3 cardiovas­
cular outcome trial in patients with statin intolerance is underway. 
ANGPTL3 Inhibitors. Recent studies reveal that targeting ANG­
PTL3 is very effective in lowering LDL-C in patients with HoFH 
and does so by promoting LDL clearance by the liver in a nonca­
nonical manner independent of the LDL receptor. This offers an 
important and novel addition to our armamentarium to effectively 
lower LDL-C in HoFH. Evinacumab is a monoclonal antibody 
against ANGPTL3166 and produces up to a 50% reduction in 
LDL-C in patients with HoFH, with good safety and tolerability 
and infrequent, mild, and transient adverse events. Its high cost and 
requirement for intravenous administration may limit use.108,166 It 
is only approved by the FDA for use in patients with HoFH at pres­
ent. Gene-silencing strategies directed against ANGPTL3 are also 
being developed, including both antisense and siRNA oligonucle­
otide approaches, that may offer alternative ways to target ANG­
PTL3 in the future, with possible application to other patients. 
LDL Apheresis. In the past, in the absence of effective pharma­
cologic ways to lower LDL-C, LDL apheresis had been the cor­
nerstone of therapy in HoFH for over 40 years. LDL apheresis 
produces an acute decrease in LDL-C by 50% to 60%, but because 
the LDL levels are rapidly repleted after the procedure, this leads 
to a mean decrease of 20% to 33% averaged over 2 weeks, the 
usual interval over which apheresis is performed. In some coun­
tries, apheresis is done at weekly intervals, resulting in a better 
integrated LDL lowering over time. Resolution of xanthomas was 
seen in 83% of cases in one review of 76 studies.167 Although ran­
domized studies have not been done, retrospective studies suggest 
a reduced CVD event rate.168 An advantage of LDL apheresis is 
that it also lowers Lp(a), which is often elevated in patients with 
FH. However, although it will likely continue to play an impor­
tant role in some patients with HoFH, particularly in those with 
null alleles, with the advent of new and more effective therapies 
and combinations, the role of LDL apheresis as the mainstay of 
FH therapy is changing, and its use is being reappraised.169 
Combination Therapies for High LDL-C
Combination therapy (see Box 41.2) is indicated for patients with 
severe lipid elevations and those who have an insufficient response 
to monotherapy. Patients with FH, baseline LDL-C over 190 mg/
dL (4.92 mmol/L), or familial combined hyperlipidemia (see “Com­
bined Hyperlipoproteinemias” section) are at particularly increased 
risk of CVD and may require LDL-C reductions that cannot be 
achieved with a statin alone. LDL levels lower than 70 mg/dL (1.8 
mmol/L) or 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L), as per the European guidelines, 
can be difficult to achieve with a single drug. Higher statin doses may 
be associated with increased side effects. If the highest tolerated statin 
1658
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
dose does not produce adequate LDL reduction, adding an agent 
from a different class may produce the desired result. Statins, ezeti­
mibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, and sequestrants work through different 
mechanisms and can be more effective in combination than when 
used alone. Because very high-risk patients often require a reduction 
of LDL-C by more than 50% to reach their LDL-C goals when start­
ing therapy, the concept of upfront combination therapy is gaining 
traction.169a,169b Therapy with ezetimibe plus a moderate dose of 
statin produced greater reductions in LDL-C, total-cholesterol, non-
HDL-C, APOB, TGs, and greater achievement of LDL-C levels <70 
mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) than high dose statin alone.169c,169d 
Lipoprotein(a) as a Major Cardiovascular Risk 
Factor
The enhanced risk of Lp(a) for CVD is thought to be related to 
its LDL-like and APO(a) moieties, which independently and 
together promote atherogenesis; to its enhanced content of oxi­
dized phospholipids, which promotes both inflammation and aor­
tic valve stenosis; and possibly to its APO(a) moiety independent 
of LDL, which, because of its homology to plasminogen, might 
theoretically interfere with thrombolysis.
As described earlier (see “Laboratory Analysis of Lipids and 
Lipoproteins” section), the current clinical measurement of 
LDL-C in fact measures not only classical LDL particles but also 
Lp(a) particles. Thus, the measurement of LDL-C includes the 
levels of both LDL and Lp(a), and only in the past few decades 
have we learned that each lipoprotein independently confers risk 
for CVD. In fact, Lp(a) is probably the most prevalent lipoprotein 
risk factor worldwide for CVD for which no specific therapy is 
currently available. Furthermore, the fact that statins lower con­
ventional LDL but may raise Lp(a) by 10% to 15%170 illustrates 
the importance of thoroughly understanding what Lp(a) is, how it 
is measured and distinguished from LDL, and how one evaluates 
its importance as a risk factor in the context of other CVD risk 
factors. Importantly, there are current therapeutic approaches that 
alter Lp(a) levels and novel molecules in clinical development that 
specifically and effectively lower even greatly elevated Lp(a) levels.
Lp(a) Epidemiology
As opposed to the distribution of LDL, which is Gaussian, the dis­
tribution of LDL is highly skewed (Fig. 41.22),171 with the major­
ity of individuals having low values and about 20% having values 
above 50 mg/dL (107 nmol/L). Until recently, few clinicians even 
measured Lp(a) values, both because its importance as a risk factor 
was not widely known and because no specific therapy was available 
to lower elevated values. However, in the past few decades, extensive 
epidemiologic and meta-analyses, as well as Mendelian randomiza­
tion and genome-wide association studies, have established that 
Lp(a) is an independent, causal, and genetic risk factor for CVD in 
both primary and secondary settings. Some experts interpret existing 
data to suggest there are Lp(a) thresholds above which risk is greatly 
accelerated, which in general correspond to the top 20th percentile 
of distribution, as shown in Fig. 41.22. However, other recent analy­
ses suggest a continuous independent association between Lp(a) and 
CVD outcomes (Fig. 41.23).172 These data have important clinical 
implications. If risk for CVD increases with increasing Lp(a) inde­
pendent of LDL-C levels, then high Lp(a) is a risk factor even at low 
LDL-C levels and should be considered in all CVD risk assessments. 
Second, aside from LDL-C levels, patients with Lp(a) values above 
the 20th percentile (50 mg/dL, 125 nmol/L) have the highest abso­
lute increased risk for CVD, and for pragmatic reasons, these are the

hypothesis that lowering Lp(a) will prevent major CVD events.
The increased risk of Lp(a) applies widely to all manifesta­
tions of CVD, including myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, 
peripheral artery disease, and even heart failure.173 There is also an 
unusual association of very high Lp(a) in some children with isch­
emic stroke. In addition, high Lp(a) is associated with an increased 
risk for calcific aortic valve stenosis and, with faster progression 
of this disease, with an increased risk for aortic valve replacement 
therapy. Although APO(a) has been linked to potential increased 
risk for arterial thrombosis because of its high homology to plas­
minogen, evidence that this occurs in vivo is lacking. Similarly, 
most studies have not found an association with venous thrombo­
sis,174 although some emerging evidence supports promotion of 
venous thromboembolism.175,176 
Regulation of Lp(a) Levels
Lp(a) levels vary widely between below 0.1 mg/dL and over 
300 mg/dL (0.25 and 750 nmol/L, respectively), and levels are 
approximately 90% determined by genetic variation at the LPA 
locus. The LPA locus codes for a wide variety of different APO(a) 
isoforms, from very short to very large APO(a) proteins. This 
results in a range of molecular masses of APO(a) from about 200 
to 800 kD. In the hepatocyte, it takes longer to synthesize and 
release larger APO(a) isoforms, resulting in lower plasma Lp(a) 
levels, whereas shorter isoforms are synthesized and released 
more quickly, leading to higher plasma Lp(a) levels. Most people 
express two isoforms, and although synthetic rates between given 
isoforms vary widely, in general, genetically determined synthetic 
rates of APO(a) in large part determine plasma Lp(a) levels. The 
mechanisms by which Lp(a) lipoproteins are cleared from the 
plasma are not well understood but appear to be mediated by 
a combination of mechanisms, including in part by plasmino­
gen receptors and possibly LDL and LRP1 receptors. Adult levels 
of Lp(a) are usually fully attained by 5 years of age, although 
occasionally they may continue to increase into adulthood. Levels 
are strongly influenced by ethnicity. In the UK Biobank, median 
Lp(a) increased sequentially in Chinese, White, South Asian, 
and Black populations (6.4, 7.6, 12.4, 30 mg/dL [16, 19, 31, 
75 nmol/L], respectively). These differences are believed to be 
due to Lp(a) isoform size and genetic variation at the LPA locus. 
Although these observations reflect differing prevalence of high 
Lp(a) levels by ethnicity, all data to date suggest that despite the 
racial differences in absolute medians, it is the absolute plasma 
Lp(a) level that determines individual CVD risk attributable to 
Lp(a), irrespective of ethnicity.
In adulthood, Lp(a) levels remain relatively constant in men 
and women, although levels may increase in women during meno­
pause and decrease with postmenopausal estrogen replacement. In 
general, nongenetic influences on Lp(a) levels are minimal/mild, 
although pregnancy and growth hormone therapy can double lev­
els, as can nephrotic syndrome or peritoneal dialysis.
One unexpected and still unexplained observation that has 
emerged from extensive epidemiologic and genetic studies is 
that very low Lp(a) levels, below approximately 5 mg/dL (12.5 
nmol/L), are associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabe­
tes mellitus. Potential mechanisms for this association are not 
explained by known risk factors or genetic variants. Of impor­
tance, this association is only observed in patients with very low 
Lp(a), and because therapies to lower Lp(a) will initially only 
target individuals with Lp(a) above approximately 70 mg/dL 
(175 nmol/L), it is not likely that even the most potent therapies 
will lower Lp(a) to target values below 5 mg/dL (12.5 nmol/L). 
Nevertheless, whether potent Lp(a)-lowering therapy might 
uncover an exaggerated diabetes risk will have to be evaluated. 
Testing for Lp(a)
Thinking has evolved dramatically over the past decade in the 
approach to Lp(a). Currently, few clinicians, even cardiologists and 
endocrinologists, measure Lp(a), even in individuals at high risk for 
CVD. However, as now recommended by all recent guidelines or 
position statements (European, Canadian, National Lipid Associa­
tion [NLA]), Lp(a) should be measured at least once in all adults, 
preferably at the time of the initial lipoprotein profiling aimed at 
identifying individuals at high CVD risk. Because it is a genetic risk 
factor, in the absence of changing metabolic conditions, repeated 
measurements are not required for those with low Lp(a) values. In 
young people, measurement of Lp(a) is recommended in the unusual 
setting of a history of ischemic stroke and when there is a history of 
a parent with a history of CVD, either premature or at an older age.
All subjects with genetic hyperlipoproteinemias, particularly 
those with FH, who frequently have increased levels of Lp(a), 
should also be profiled.177 Cascade testing for Lp(a) should be 
considered when very high Lp(a) values are found, in the setting 
of strong family history of high Lp(a) and/or CVD, and in all FH 
subjects with high Lp(a). 
Management of the Patient With High Lp(a)
At present, there are no approved therapies to specifically lower 
elevated Lp(a) levels, and therefore the approach advocated here 
is to consider the elevated Lp(a) as an independent risk factor 
that amplifies other existing risk factors, with the understanding 
that the higher the Lp(a), the greater the conferred incremental 
risk. For example, an Lp(a) level of 100 mg/dL (250 nmol/L) 
approximately doubles the risk for CVD, irrespective of the abso­
lute baseline risk. For individuals with higher baseline risk, the 
magnitude of absolute increase in CVD risk is greater (20–40%) 
than for those with lower baseline risk (5%–10%). Thus, all CVD 
risk factors should be optimally addressed according to the various 
guideline recommendations. Because of Lp(a)’s importance as a 
risk-enhancing factor, strategies to maximally lower LDL-C levels, 
as described earlier, should be employed.
A number of therapeutic approaches have been advocated to 
lower Lp(a) levels. Statins do not lower Lp(a) and, in fact, can 
raise Lp(a) by approximately 10%, but this increase can be up to 
20%.131 However, statins form the cornerstone of LDL-C–lower­
ing therapy and are well documented to reduce CVD morbidity 
and both CVD and all-cause mortality and therefore remain the 
foundation of CVD prevention and treatment. They should not be 
stopped in order to negate the mild Lp(a)-raising potential. Thera­
pies targeting PCSK9 lower Lp(a) by about 20% to 30% and pro­
duce absolute CVD risk reduction that is greater in individuals 
with higher baseline Lp(a) levels. Niacin lowers Lp(a) by 20% to 
40% and has long been used by experienced endocrinologists and 
lipidologists in selected patients with very high Lp(a) and existing 
CVD. However, niacin is associated with marked side effects and 
morbidity and was not associated with a reduction in CVD in ran­
domized trials, although these studies were not designed to specifi­
cally test the hypothesis that Lp(a) lowering was cardioprotective. 
Finally, as noted earlier, lipoprotein apheresis, which binds APOB-
containing lipoproteins, can effectively lower Lp(a) as well. It is 
approved in Europe and in the United States in specialized centers 
for use in select patients with very high Lp(a) levels and progressive 
CVD despite the use of optimal therapies for other risk factors. 
Uncontrolled studies indicate benefit in very high-risk patients.178

Emerging Therapies
As noted earlier, hepatic synthesis of APO(a) determines plasma 
Lp(a) levels, and therapies inhibiting hepatocyte APO(a) pro­
duction effectively lower plasma Lp(a) levels. Pelecarsen is an 
antisense oligonucleotide conjugated to a triantennary N-acetyl­
galactosamine (GalNAc3) moiety, which is a high-affinity ligand 
for the asialoglycoprotein receptor on the surface of hepatocytes. 
This effectively targets pelacarsen to the hepatocyte and reduces 
systemic dosage and side effects. In a clinical trial in patients with 
existing CVD and high Lp(a) values (median Lp[a] of 82–99 mg/
dL [204.6–246.6 nnmol/L]), at a dose equal to 80 mg/month, 
pelacarsen generated a mean 80% decrease in Lp(a), and at 
this dose, 98% of patients attained a level below 50 mg/dL (20 
nmol/L).179 The FDA requires demonstration that lowering Lp(a) 
reduces CVD morbidity for approval. At the time this chapter 
was written, pelacarsen is being studied in an international car­
diovascular outcome trial—Lp(a) Horizon—to determine if it can 
reduce CVD morbidity in patients with CVD and very high Lp(a) 
levels. Other GalNac-conjugated siRNAs also are under active 
development. Olpasiran dramatically reduced Lp(a) levels in a 
dose-dependent manner in patients with established CVD and 
Lp(a) above 60 mg/dL (150 nmol/L),180 and another siRNA tar­
geting Lp(a) is also under active development.181 Because nearly 
1.2 billion people worldwide have Lp(a) values above a threshold 
of 50 mg/dL (125 nmol/L), if Lp(a) lowering reduces CVD risk, 
there would be important individual health benefits, and there 
will be a great demand for therapeutic agents to lower Lp(a).

with TG levels of 50 to 150 mg/dL (0.6–1.7 mmol/L), the patient
