greater than 750 mg/dL (8.5 mmol/L), pathogenic mutations of 
one or more genes directly involved in TG metabolism may exist, 
but environmental modulators will continue to be very critical 
(see Fig. 41.24A). Finally, as TG levels increase further to 1000 
mg/dL (11.3 mmol/L) and above, very few individuals will be 
homozygous or compound heterozygous for mutations in genes 
that alter LPL activity (see Fig. 41.24B). Although these individu­
als may not be obese, be insulin resistant, or have diabetes mel­
litus, and their diets may be very healthy, their genetic defects will 
result in the extreme phenotype. The key to optimal identification 
and treatment of moderate to severe hypertriglyceridemia, includ­
ing the importance of targeting therapy to prevent CVD versus 
preventing pancreatitis, is to understand the changing pathophysi­
ology across the spectrum of mild to moderate to severe hyper­
triglyceridemia. The discussion that follows attempts to offer a 
roadmap to address the complexity of the regulation of plasma 
TG and the causes of hypertriglyceridemia.
Moderate to Severe Endogenous Hypertriglyceridemia
Epidemiology of Moderate to Severe Hypertriglyceridemia. 
TG levels of 150 to 500 mg/dL (1.7–5.6 mmol/L) have gener­
ally been considered to be abnormal, but the actual cutpoints that 
appear in various official guidelines seem to have resulted from 
“expert opinion” rather than having a strong scientific basis. This 
range was provided in the National Cholesterol Treatment Pro­
gram’s Adult Treatment Panel (ATP III) report in 2001,182 with 
very high TG defined as levels of ≥500 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L). 
However, previous guidelines from the AHA/ACC and from the 
European Society of Cardiology and European Atherosclerosis 
Society (ESC/EAS) and Canada have varied slightly in their defi­
nitions of moderate to severe hypertriglyceridemia. To put this in 
perspective, studies in the United States and Europe indicate that 
65% to 70% of adults have TG levels of less than 150 mg/dL (1.7 
mmol/L), approximately 25% to 30% have TG levels between 
150 and 500 mg/dL (1.7 and 5.6 mmol/L), and under 2% have 
levels above 500 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L). 
Pathophysiology
The earlier “Endogenous Lipid Transport by VLDL” section pro­
vided a brief overview of the secretion and plasma catabolism of 
VLDL. If optimal steady-state levels of TG are below 100 mg/dL 
(1.1 mmol/L), why do approximately 40% of adults have levels 
between 150 and 500 mg/dL (1.7 and 5.6 mmo/L)? What are 
the driving forces for increased secretion and/or decreased catabo­
lism of TG-rich lipoproteins that result in elevated plasma levels 
of TG? What are the relative impacts of genetics and the environ­
ment that lead to moderate and severe hypertriglyceridemia?
The rate of VLDL secretion is a key determinant of plasma 
TG levels, particularly at levels up to 300 mg/dL (3.4 mmol/L), 
which account for about 90% of the population (see Fig. 41.24A). 
VLDL secretion is the culmination of several steps, including 
co-translational and posttranslational addition of core lipids to 
nascent APOB100, described earlier in the “Apolipoprotein B” 
section. The increased secretion of APOB100 and TG that initi­
ates dyslipidemia, however, is secondary to the effects of insulin 
resistance and environmental factors listed previously. Insulin 
resistance, which is typically a polygenic disorder, is a main driver 
of hepatic steatosis, which is highly correlated with VLDL-TG 
and APOB100 secretion.183,184
Although increased VLDL secretion is a critical factor in the 
genesis of dyslipidemia, the range of APOB secretion is about 
threefold, and that of TG secretion is about sixfold. Why, then, do 
plasma TG levels span a range from 50 to 2000 mg/dL (0.6–22.6 
mmol/L) or greater across the general population and reach as high 
as 10,000 mg/dL (113 mmol/L) or greater in a few individuals? 
The simple answer is that the plasma concentration of any mole­
cule derives from its rate of entry into plasma and the efficiency of 
its removal (fractional clearance rate [FCR]). The FCR of VLDL 
is determined by lipolysis of TGs in VLDL, as well as removal of 
VLDL particles from the circulation. Thus, whereas VLDL secre­
tion is the major cause of the fivefold to eightfold elevations of 
TG present in moderate hypertriglyceridemia, even greater-fold 
increases of plasma TG, particularly those leading to TG levels 
in the range of 500 to 10,000 mg/dL (5.6–113 mmol/L), are 
inversely related to rates of lipolysis and remnant removal, in part 
due to saturation of TG-removal systems (see Fig. 41.24A).185
VLDL and chylomicron catabolism involve the actions of 
several lipases, including LPL, HL, and EL. These enzymes dif­
fer in their optimal lipoprotein substrates, with LPL being most 
active in larger TG-rich lipoproteins, whereas HL and EL prefer 
the smaller VLDLs, IDLs, and HDLs. LPL is required for the 
initial conversion of chylomicron TGs into fatty acids. Normally, 
lipolysis of nascent chylomicrons in nonhepatic tissues removes 
approximately 70% of the core TG and converts chylomicrons 
into smaller remnant particles that are then cleared by the liver. 
VLDL lipolysis generates smaller particles that are often referred 
to as VLDL remnants, present mainly in IDL. Partly through the 
actions of HL, these particles can be converted to LDL.
Effects of Hypertriglyceridemia on LDL and HDL Levels and 
Metabolism. Hypertriglyceridemia also modulates the circulat­
ing levels and the composition of LDL and HDL. In humans, 
LPL activity is clearly required for both efficient conversion of 
TG-rich lipoproteins to LDL and the generation of surface lipids 
and proteins that are acquired by HDL.186 CETP-mediated trans­
fer of TG from TG-rich lipoproteins to LDLs and HDLs, with 
cholesteryl esters from LDLs and HDLs moving in the opposite 
direction, is driven by the quantity of TG in TG-rich lipopro­
teins (VLDLs and chylomicrons). When LPL-mediated lipolysis 
is inefficient, CETP-mediated exchange of TG and cholesteryl 
esters between TG-rich lipoproteins and LDLs and HDLs results 
in reduced LDL-C and HDL-C but also increased TG content, 
providing substrate for HL- and EL-mediated lipolysis. This gen­
erates the smaller, denser subpopulations of LDLs and HDLs that 
are characteristic of the dyslipidemia present in individuals with 
high plasma TG levels. 
Genetics of Moderate to Severe Hypertriglyceridemia. Stud­
ies conducted over the past 60 years have clearly demonstrated 
the interplay between genetic and environmental factors, mainly 
related to nutrient intake and energy balance, in the regulation of 
both the secretion and the catabolism of TGs in TG-rich lipopro­
teins. However, most genetic forms of mild to moderate elevations 
1662
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
of plasma TG levels are due to the presence of multiple common 
gene variants, each with small phenotypic effects.187 These gene 
variants can interact with lifestyle measures, such as diet and phys­
ical activity, and with secondary forms of hypertriglyceridemia 
(see “Secondary Forms of Hyper- and Dyslipoproteinemia” sec­
tion). Although these minor gene variants can be quantified using 
a polygenic score,188,189 such gene scores are not yet in widespread 
clinical use. However, they may be useful in the future as a means 
of identifying individuals with modest elevations of plasma TG 
who are at risk for rapidly developing severe hypertriglyceridemia 
and pancreatitis. 
Approach to Management of the Patient With 
Moderate to Severe Hypertriglyceridemia
The initial approach is to confirm the presence of hypertriglyc­
eridemia and rule out secondary conditions and drugs that can 
elevate TG levels (see “Secondary Dyslipidemia” section). A care­
ful family history can be of value in determining whether the 
condition has a genetic basis. Physical examination should be per­
formed to evaluate the presence of abdominal obesity, after which 
other features of metabolic syndrome should be sought. The pres­
ence of eruptive xanthomas, especially on the buttocks, can sig­
nify the presence of severe hypertriglyceridemia. The presence of a 
distinct buttock shelf above which fat is present and below which 
it is absent, together with an absence of adipose tissue on the arms 
or legs, can help with the diagnosis of the Köbberling variety of 
familial partial lipodystrophy (FPLD).
Diet and Lifestyle Measures
Moderate to severe hypertriglyceridemia derives from the com­
bination of increased secretion of VLDL APOB and TG and 
reduced efficiency of TG clearance by lipolysis and particle uptake 
by the liver. Both of these pathways, particularly the secretory 
pathway, are significantly affected by energy balance and insulin 
sensitivity. It is logical, therefore, that lifestyle changes, including 
dietary intervention, moderate exercise, and weight loss, should 
be first-line therapies for moderate to severe hypertriglyceridemia 
(see Table 41.6). Indeed, improvements in diet, exercise, and body 
weight may be sufficient therapy for patients at low risk for CVD 
with moderate hypertriglyceridemia. All other treatments should 
build on therapeutic lifestyle changes.190
Hypertriglyceridemia will almost always respond to a decreased 
intake of saturated fats, simple sugars, alcohol, and calories. In 
patients with established CVD, lifestyle changes should also tar­
get LDL-C, with drug therapy to lower LDL-C commonly insti­
tuted along with diet therapy. Response to lipid-lowering drugs, 
whether those drugs target LDL-C or TG, may be disappointing 
in patients who do not follow dietary and other lifestyle recom­
mendations. However, the initiation of drug therapy to reduce 
levels of plasma TG per se with the goal of reducing CVD risk is 
an area where uncertainty and even controversy exist.
As noted earlier, no controversy exists regarding reduced 
caloric intake and increased caloric utilization as foundational 
lifestyle approaches to reducing plasma TG levels because energy 
imbalance—specifically, energy overload—is a major contribu­
tor to plasma TG levels.191 The question of what nutrient classes 
should be reduced is where differences of opinion have existed 
for decades, particularly regarding whether low-carbohydrate or 
low-fat diets are more effective in reducing plasma TG levels, body 
weight, and CVD risk. It is generally agreed that saturated fats, as 
well as trans-fatty acids, raise LDL-C levels, but there is a large 
body of evidence that saturated fats also increase plasma TG lev­
els. Saturated fats should be limited to less than 10% of calories 
in most people, with reductions to less than 7% recommended 
for people with established CVD. The question of what nutrient 
should replace saturated fat is a second area of controversy. Dur­
ing active weight loss, reducing saturated fats without replacing 
them with another nutrient source might be the simple answer 
to this question. However, there are strong data demonstrating 
that diets high in carbohydrates, particularly simple sugars high 
in fructose or sucrose, are especially potent in raising plasma TG 
levels because of an unregulated effect of fructose on hepatic DNL 
(i.e., conversion of glucose to fatty acids). These data support low 
dietary carbohydrates regardless of the caloric content. Although 
there are extreme views and extreme diets that have been champi­
oned, such as very high-fat keto diets or very high-carbohydrate 
diets rich in fiber, a reasonable compromise would be a diet with 
moderate reductions in simple, refined carbohydrates that also has 
reductions in saturated fats balanced by increases in mono- and 
polyunsaturated fats. Overall, current recommendations are to 
restrict saturated fats and trans fats and substitute with complex 
carbohydrates, polyunsaturated fats, and monounsaturated fats.128 
The Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) and Med­
iterranean diets are appropriate examples. The response to very 
low-fat diets may be disappointing in patients with impaired glu­
cose tolerance, unless the diet is hypocaloric.
Fish oils are rich in eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) or docosa­
hexaenoic acid (DHA) (see Table 41.1). Daily doses of 4 g of EPA 
plus DHA lower VLDL levels and can be effective in the treatment 
of moderate to severe hypertriglyceridemia other than in patients 
with proven FCS. Observational data support the use of diets high 
in fish to reduce CVD risk in those with and without known CVD. 
Many experts recommend eating two or more servings of oily fish 
each week. The issue of fish oil supplementation to prevent or treat 
CVD is less clear and is discussed in the “Drug Treatment for Mild 
to Moderately Severe Hypertriglyceridemia” section.
Daily moderate exercise, such as walking, may help reduce 
TG levels. Exercise may be particularly useful in obese, insulin-
resistant patients with high TG, low HDL-C, and moderately 
elevated LDL-C. An exercise program combined with a moder­
ately hypocaloric diet leading to modest weight loss may improve 
dyslipidemia, as well as glucose tolerance and blood pressure, 
especially in patients with metabolic syndrome. Team manage­
ment that includes nutritionists and dietitians is likely to enhance 
dietary therapies. 
Drug Treatment for Mild to Moderately Severe 
Hypertriglyceridemia
Statins. Statins are at the top of the therapeutic list for lowering 
LDL-C and reducing risk for CVD. Therefore, it is an appropri­
ate and guideline-based approach to start treatment of moderate 
or moderately severe hypertriglyceridemia with a statin when a 
patient has a significant risk for CVD or has had a CVD event. 
After initiation of statin treatment, if the TG is greater than 200 
mg/dL (2.3 mmol/L), the physician and patient should discuss 
the need and the rationale for adding a more specific TG-lowering 
drug to the statin. The data supporting this approach follow. How­
ever, it is important to remember that statins can also lower TG 
levels by 10% to 25%, depending on the baseline level of TG. In 
general, TG levels of 150 to 200 mg/dL (1.1–2.3 mmol/L) will be 
reduced by about 20% in parallel with a reduction in LDL-C, and 
this degree of TG lowering may, along with lifestyle approaches, 
be adequate. 
1663
CHAPTER 41  Disorders of Lipoprotein Metabolism
Fibrates. Fibrates are ligands for the PPARα, which, in combi­
nation with the retinoid X receptor (RXR), activates or suppresses 
the transcription of many genes. Binding of fibrates to this recep­
tor increases fatty acid oxidation in rodents and increases LPL 
activity and the expression of the genes for APOA1 and APOA2 
while decreasing APOC3, an inhibitor of LPL in humans. Impor­
tantly, fibrates lower TGs by 25% to 50% and raise HDL-C by 
5% to 20%, depending on the baseline levels of TGs. Fibrates may 
sometimes lower LDL-C modestly in patients with significantly 
elevated levels, but more commonly, when fibrates are adminis­
tered to individuals with moderate to moderately severe hypertri­
glyceridemia, LDL-C levels increase modestly, more so with severe 
hypertriglyceridemia.
Fibrates are well-known TG-lowering drugs; the class includes 
fenofibrate, bezafibrate, gemfibrozil, and pemafibrate, which has 
been used only in Japan. Several prior randomized controlled tri­
als produced inconsistent results regarding CVD risk reduction, 
particularly among patients on statins. However, a meta-analysis 
demonstrated that fibrates may reduce CVD risk by about 10% in 
the subgroup of patients with high baseline plasma TG levels.192
In the Helsinki Heart Study (primary prevention) and the Vet­
erans Affairs–High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol Intervention 
Trial (secondary prevention), the use of gemfibrozil without back­
ground statin treatment significantly reduced fatal and nonfatal 
cardiovascular events and did not increase mortality from noncar­
diac causes.193,194 In the Fenofibrate Intervention and Event Low­
ering in Diabetes (FIELD) study, although fenofibrate did not 
reduce the composite cardiovascular outcome of cardiovascular 
death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and stroke in patients with 
type 2 diabetes mellitus, fewer nonfatal events were observed.195 
However, a post hoc analysis suggested that fenofibrate provided 
benefit to patients with diabetes with TGs over 200 mg/dL (2.3 
mmo/L) and HDL less than 40 mg/dL (1.0 mmol/L).196 In the 
Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes (ACCORD) 
trial, fenofibrate plus simvastatin did not reduce the primary 
outcome of fatal and non-fat myocardial infarction and stroke 
compared with simvastatin plus placebo. However, a prespeci­
fied analysis of approximately 17% of study patients in both the 
upper tertile of TG (over 204 mg/dL [2.3 mmo/L]) and the lower 
tertile of HDL-C (below 34 mg/dL (0.9 mmol/L]) had a 28% 
reduction in the primary outcome.197 Both studies indicated that 
fenofibrate slowed the progression of retinopathy in patients with 
diabetes.198,199 The underlying mechanism for the beneficial effect 
on retinopathy is unknown and does not appear to be related to 
effects on circulating lipids.
Fenofibrate may be taken once daily. Gemfibrozil is given 
twice a day with meals but is used less often due to a less favor­
able drug-interaction profile. The combination of gemfibrozil 
and most statins is associated with an increased risk of myopa­
thy due to increased statin blood levels, whereas fenofibrate 
does not interfere with statin metabolism and is preferred in 
fibrate/statin combination regimens.137 Fibrates are contra­
indicated in patients with liver or gallbladder disease because 
they increase the lithogenic profile of bile, and thus the risk of 
gallstones may be increased. Liver transaminases may increase, 
particularly with fenofibrate, but significant hepatotoxicity is 
very rare.197 Fenofibrate increases creatinine by about 15% on 
average, but this was completely reversible even after several 
years of treatment in both FIELD and ACCORD, and pro­
teinuria was reduced. Because of the effects on protein binding, 
warfarin doses may need to be adjusted when fibrate therapy 
is started. Gemfibrozil may be used beginning in the second 
trimester in pregnant women with severely elevated TGs who 
are at risk for pancreatitis.200
Pemafibrate is a selective PPARα modulator; its PPARα acti­
vation is more than 2500 times stronger compared with fenofi­
brate.201 Pemafibrate reduced plasma TG levels in the range of 
40% in several Japanese trials, and similar results were seen in 
a European cohort with plasma TG levels between 175 (2.0 
mmol/L) and 500 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L); the highest dose of 
pemafibrate tested, 0.2 mg BID, reduced plasma TG levels by over 
50% from the baseline.202 However, a phase 3 cardiovascular out­
come trial involving more than 10,000 statin-treated patients with 
type 2 diabetes and plasma TG levels between 200 mg/dL (2.3 
mmol/L) and 500 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) and HDL-C less than 
40 mg/dL (1.0 mmol/L) was stopped early in 2022 for reasons of 
futility. Despite the fact that pemafibrate treatment was associated 
with a placebo-corrected 26% reduction in both plasma TG and 
remnant cholesterol levels, the hazard ratio for the primary major 
adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) endpoint of nonfatal myo­
cardial infarction, ischemic stroke, coronary revascularization, or 
CVD death after a median follow-up of 3.4 years was 1.03 (not 
significant).203 The lack of efficacy of pemafibrate for MACE was 
possibly due to a 12% increase in LDL-C and a 4.8% increase in 
plasma APOB. The lipid changes were, overall, similar to those 
seen in the ACCORD subgroup with high TG and low HDL at 
baseline, and therefore it is unclear why the CVD outcomes were 
so different in the two trials. This negative trial raises questions 
about the value of fibrates in patients on statins for the prevention 
of CVD in patients with hypertriglyceridemia. 
Omega-3 Fatty Acids. Omega-3 fatty acids decrease TG secre­
tion from the liver through unclear mechanisms and are indicated 
for TGs higher than 500 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L). Four-gram com­
binations of EPA and DHA lower triglycerides by 20% to 50% 
depending on the baseline levels. There is minimal effect on HDL-
C. LDL-C may increase as VLDL is converted to LDL.
Over-the-counter preparations have variable quantities of 
EPA and DHA. Prescription formulations usually contain twice 
the content of omega-3 fatty acids than nonprescription prepara­
tions. Preparations contain EPA and DHA, unesterified EPA and 
DHA, or only EPA. Unlike fibrates, EPA and DHA do not affect 
statin metabolism and do not increase the risk of myopathy. Side 
effects with omega-3 fatty acids include eructation, diarrhea, and 
abdominal discomfort. There is potential for increased bleeding, 
but this has not been seen in clinical trials. Importantly, omega-3 
fatty acids have been linked to a modest but significant increase in 
the risk for atrial fibrillation.204,205
Although fish-derived omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) 
reduce circulating TGs, their effects on CVD events are less clear. 
Some very large meta-analyses suggest that fish oil supplements 
may result in a reduction in CVD events of about 10%,206 whereas 
others find benefit only in studies using higher doses for long peri­
ods of time.207 Two studies of EPA alone have raised the question 
of whether this omega-3 fatty acid is specific for CVD benefit. 
The Japan EPA Lipid Intervention Study (JELIS) showed that 
combined treatment with a statin plus EPA (1.8 g/day) reduced 
major coronary events by 19% compared with a statin alone in 
patients with CAD.208 Other earlier clinical outcome studies 
with fish oils, however, did not show mortality or cardiovascular 
health benefits.209–211 However, a more recent study, Reduction 
of Cardiovascular Events With Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial 
(REDUCE-IT), using 4 g of icosapent ethyl, a synthetic EPA, 
in mildly to moderately hypertriglyceridemic participants with 
known atherosclerosis or high risk (e.g., diabetes), dramatically 
1664
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
reduced coronary events.212 Importantly, a study using a similar 
design but with an agent that contained both EPA and DHA was 
stopped early for futility.213 At face value, these studies indicate 
major differences between the two types of omega-3 fatty acids, 
but there is controversy regarding the use of mineral oil as the 
placebo in the icosapent ethyl trial, where levels of inflamma­
tory biomarkers and LDL-C increased in the placebo group.214 
Nonetheless, icosapent ethyl has been approved to reduce CVD 
in people with TG levels greater than 135 mg/dL (1.5 mmol/L), 
although it was not related to a decrease in plasma TG levels. 
Niacin. Nicotinic acid, or niacin, is a B-complex vitamin that 
was found to lower plasma cholesterol in humans in 1955. The 
mechanism underlying the effects of niacin is not understood 
beyond the physiologic observation of decreased VLDL secre­
tion. Niacin lowers TGs by 10% to 30% and increases HDL-C 
by 10% to 40%. Niacin also lowers Lp(a) by up to 25%. In the 
pre-statin era, the niacin arm of the Coronary Drug Project showed 
a decrease in nonfatal myocardial infarctions in men with CAD 
during the 6-year trial and a decrease in total mortality rate in the 
9 years after the study had ended.215 However, more recent trials 
of slow-release niacin in subjects whose LDL was already markedly 
reduced by statins failed to show additional clinical benefit with 
niacin,216,217 despite improvements in HDL-C and TGs, including 
the Atherothrombosis Intervention in Metabolic Syndrome With 
Low HDL/High Triglycerides: Impact on Global Health Outcomes 
(AIM-HIGH) and Heart Protection Study 2–Treatment of HDL 
to Reduce the Incidence of Vascular Events (HPS2-THRIVE) 
studies. This lack of proven efficacy and the introduction of new 
agents to lower TG levels (fibrates, omega-3 fatty acids) or LDL-C 
(statins, ezetimibe, and PCSK9 inhibitors) have reduced niacin use 
except in refractory hypertriglyceridemia and hypercholesterol­
emia or for patients with extreme elevations of Lp(a).
Cutaneous flushing, most notable with the first doses, is the 
most common side effect. Flushing generally occurs 15 to 60 min­
utes after ingestion, lasts 15 to 30 minutes, and may be related 
to release of dermal prostaglandin D2. Ingestion of niacin with 
food, and taking aspirin (preferably 325 mg) 30 to 60 minutes in 
advance of niacin, minimizes flushing,218 whereas alcoholic bever­
ages and hot and spicy foods potentiate it. Prescription extended-
release niacin (Niaspan) may be better tolerated than short-acting 
crystalline niacin. Tolerance can occur with gradual increases and 
consistent dosing, so starting low and gradually increasing the 
dose improves tolerability.
Niacin has additional adverse effects. Hepatotoxicity is the most 
serious, and although not common, it is seen more with crystalline 
niacin compared with prescription slow-release forms. Worsening 
of glucose tolerance and hyperuricemia also may occur. Niacin 
is contraindicated in active peptic ulcer disease. Rare side effects 
include blurred vision and a reversible condition known as cystoid 
macular edema. Myopathy is rare with niacin alone or in combi­
nation with statins. Niacin is contraindicated during pregnancy. 
Drugs Targeting APOC3 and ANGPTL3. Extensive epidemio­
logic and genetic data demonstrate that lower plasma APOC3 
and ANGPTL3 levels are associated with both decreased plasma 
TGs and decreased CVD events,219,220 suggesting therapies tar­
geting APOC3 or ANGPTL3 might provide clinical benefit in 
patients with moderate to moderately severe hypertriglyceridemia. 
An antisense oligonucleotide to APOC3, volanesorsen, showed 
significant efficacy in patients with moderately severe hypertri­
glyceridemia. However, trials focused on patients with FCS and 
multifactorial chylomicronemia syndrome (MFCS), are discussed 
in the “Drug Treatment for Severe Hypertriglyceridemia” section. 
At about the same time, a monoclonal antibody to target ANG­
PTL3, evinacumab, was also developed. Clinical trials of this drug 
also focused on severe hypertriglyceridemia, although because 
LDL-C lowering was observed, a parallel series of studies was con­
ducted showing efficacy in patients with moderate hypertriglyc­
eridemia and moderate to severe hypercholesterolemia. In initial 
studies, TG levels were reduced significantly, along with moderate 
reductions in LDL-C and HDL-C. Further evaluation of these 
approaches is required before marketed use. 
Severe Hypertriglyceridemia
Causes and Pathogenesis. Three major groups of conditions 
can lead to severe hypertriglyceridemia, often defined as TG levels 
above 1000 mg/dL (11.3 mmol/L): FCS, previously called type 
1 hyperlipoproteinemia; multifactorial chylomicronemia syndrome 
(MFCS); and familial partial lipodystrophy (FPLD).221
In FCS, the absence of LPL activity leads to severe fasting 
hyperchylomicronemia due to the inability to hydrolyze TGs in 
both chylomicrons and VLDLs. MFCS is nearly always the result 
of exacerbation of genetic forms of mild to moderate hypertri­
glyceridemia by disorders or drugs that can adversely affect TG 
levels (see “Secondary Forms of Hyper- and Dyslipoproteinemia” 
section), leading to saturation of TG-removal systems and hence 
accumulation of additional TG-rich lipoproteins that enter the 
plasma pool.185,221 Much less is known about the pathogenesis 
of the hypertriglyceridemia seen in FPLD, which often is severe. 
Genetics of Severe Hypertriglyceridemia. The role of genetic 
factors is of great importance in individuals with TG levels above 
1000 mg/dL (11.3 mmol/L), the top 1% of the population. In 
MFCS, also called type V hyperlipoproteinemia or polygenic late-
onset chylomicronemia, heterozygosity for pathogenic loss of 
function of the major genes in the LPL pathway (LPL, APOC2, 
APOA5, GPIHBP1, LMF1) may be present along with a profile of 
high polygenic risk, but this is often not the case. This combina­
tion of major and minor loss-of-function variants or simply an 
extreme preponderance of minor variants that raise TG may make 
responsiveness to environmental therapeutic approaches or even 
existing medications less effective. However, there are no clinical 
trial data indicating that genetic testing would inform therapeutic 
approaches. At present, genetic testing might be informative for 
the diagnosis of FCS in a patient with TG levels in the several 
1000s (mg/dL) but who does not have the classical history of diag­
nosis in childhood or recurrent pancreatitis at an early age, which 
is characteristic of FCS (see “Section Familial Chylomicronemia 
Syndrome” section).
FCS, also known as type I hyperlipoproteinemia or LPL defi­
ciency, is an extremely rare autosomal-recessive genetic disorder 
characterized by absent plasma activity of LPL, which results in 
marked degrees of hypertriglyceridemia. TG levels typically exceed 
1000 mg/dL (11.3 mmol/L) and often are in the range of 5000 to 
10,000 mg/dL (56.4–113 mmol/L). FCS is associated with acute 
pancreatitis and other complications of chylomicronemia. Patho­
genic biallelic mutations in the LPL gene that result in deficiency 
or loss of catalytic activity of LPL account for more than 80% 
of reported FCS cases, with over 180 mutations identified. The 
incidence of homozygous loss of function of LPL is thought to be 
about one per million people. In addition to the amount of active 
LPL protein, other proteins modulate TG-rich lipoprotein lipoly­
sis and LPL activity, including APOC2, APOA5, APOC3, ANG­
PTL3, ANGPTL4, GPIHBP1, and LMF1. Their role in lipolysis 
is discussed in more detail earlier in the “Lipoprotein Lipase” sec­
tion. Genetic variants that cause complete loss of mass or activity 
1665
CHAPTER 41  Disorders of Lipoprotein Metabolism
of APOC2, APOA5, GPIHBP1, or LMF1 significantly reduce 
or abolish LPL-mediated lipolysis of chylomicrons and VLDLs, 
mimicking complete loss of LPL function. However, homozygos­
ity for loss of function of these genes or compound heterozygosity 
is even less common than that for LPL.222,223 Increasingly, autoan­
tibodies to GPIHBP1 are recognized as a cause of FCS.224
Diagnosis of FCS is based on presentation with features of 
chylomicronemia syndrome, the onset of which usually but not 
always occurs early in life. Diagnosis is confirmed by the absence 
of LPL activity in plasma after the injection of heparin but ide­
ally requires genotyping for mutations in any of these genes, 
which is now readily available. Other findings include low levels 
of APOB.
The third cause of severe hypertriglyceridemia is FPLD, sev­
eral forms of which can lead to severe hypertriglyceridemia and 
marked insulin resistance. FPLD is a relatively uncommon cause 
of severe hypertriglyceridemia; the exact incidence is not clear. The 
two most common forms are the Dunnigan (type 2) and Köbber­
ling (type 1) varieties. The diagnosis is based on the clinical phe­
notype. However, the diagnosis is often missed, so it may be more 
common than is appreciated. The Dunnigan variety of FPLD is 
due to mutations in the LMNA gene, encoding for Lamin A/C or 
PPARA, so genetic testing can be useful. Generalized lipodystro­
phy, which is very rare, also can be associated with severe hypertri­
glyceridemia,225 although its incidence is unknown. 
Chylomicronemia Syndrome. TG levels above 1000 mg/dL 
(11.3 mmol/L) can be associated with features of chylomicrone­
mia syndrome, which is a constellation of features that can occur 
when TG levels are severely elevated (reviewed by Chait and 
Eckel221). It is characterized by such clinical features as abdominal 
pain, acute pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas (Fig. 41.25, left), and 
lipemia retinalis (see Fig. 41.25, right).226 Eruptive xanthomas are 
yellow papules that characteristically appear on the buttocks and 
extensor surfaces of the upper limbs and can be itchy. Because 
they can be localized to the buttocks, failure to examine the but­
tocks, as often occurs during an outpatient visit, can lead to them 
being missed. Eruptive xanthomas are loaded with lipid derived 
from chylomicrons63,227 and signify the presence of long-standing 
chylomicronemia. Lipemia retinalis is a whitish appearance of the 
optic fundus and retinal vessels that is sometimes observed in the 
presence of severe hypertriglyceridemia (see Fig. 41.25, right). It 
is of no pathologic significance and seldom is detected without 
knowledge of the existence of severe hypertriglyceridemia. Other 
less well-described but frequent features of chylomicronemia syn­
drome include mental fogginess, memory loss, peripheral neurop­
athy, and arthralgic symptoms.226,228
However, by far the most serious consequence of severe hyper­
triglyceridemia is acute pancreatitis, which can be recurrent if TG 
levels are not adequately managed. In the general population, 
there is a stepwise increase in the cumulative incidence of pan­
creatitis as TG levels rise from 1000 to 1999 mg/dL (11.3–22.6 
mmol/L), through 2000 to 2999 mg/dL (22.6–33.9 mmol/L), 
to greater than 3000 mg/dL (33.9 mmol/L).229 However, many 
patients with even higher levels often do not get pancreatitis. In 
patients who present with pancreatitis at TG levels below 1500 to 
2000 mg/dL (17.0–22.6 mmol/L), a careful history often indi­
cates the onset of pain several days before presentation, followed 
by reduced or absent food intake, which would lower TG levels.
Acute pancreatitis has a mortality rate of about 2% to 5%,230 
with TG-induced pancreatitis having an approximate doubling 
of renal and respiratory failure, a nearly fourfold increase in 
shock, and a near doubling of mortality.231 Thus, outcomes for 
pancreatitis due to severe hypertriglyceridemia are far worse than 
for other causes of pancreatitis. The mechanism by which hyper­
triglyceridemia causes pancreatitis is speculative. However, based 
on experiments in animal models, it is proposed that pancreatic 
lipases hydrolyze lecithin and TG to yield lysolecithin and FFAs, 
respectively, in pancreatic capillaries. Lysolecithin and fatty acids 
could lead to a form of chemical pancreatitis,232,233 which would 
liberate more pancreatic lipase, thereby establishing a vicious 
cycle.
CVD risk can be increased in chylomicronemia syndrome, 
depending on the cause. Most patients with FCS do not have a 
greatly increased risk of CVD in the absence of other risk fac­
tors, such as cigarette smoking and diabetes,234,235 because chy­
lomicrons have been considered too large to cross the endothelial 
barrier. However, recent studies have demonstrated an SR-B1-
dependent, LPL-independent uptake of chylomicrons by endo­
thelial cells resulting in lipid accumulation in those cells, provid­
ing a potential mechanism for atherogenesis and the formation of 
eruptive xanthomas in this disorder.63 In contrast, patients with 
MFCS and FPLD have an increased risk of CVD, in part due to 
their ability to form remnants of the TG-rich lipoproteins by the 
action of LPL (reviewed by Chait and Eckel221). More moderately

Approach to Management of the Patient With 
Severe Hypertriglyceridemia—Diet and Lifestyle 
Measures
Chylomicrons, which are assembled in the intestinal entero­
cytes, transport dietary-derived fat through plasma. Therefore, it 
seems intuitive to limit the intake of dietary fat in patients with 
severe hypertriglyceridemia and chylomicronemia syndrome. This 
clearly is the preferred treatment in FCS, in which there is an 
absence of functional LPL to hydrolyze dietary TGs. Indeed, in 
FCS, total dietary fat (all types, including saturated and unsatu­
rated) intake should be limited to less than 5 to 10 g/day, which 
is difficult to maintain on an ongoing basis and is a major burden 
to patients.237 Moreover, this often fails to keep TGs below 500 
mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L), a level below which the risk of TG-induced 
pancreatitis is very low. Therefore, breakthrough pancreatitis can 
occur even at this very low level of fat consumption when TG 
reductions are inadequate. Because of their shorter chain lengths, 
medium-chain TGs (MCTs) do not require chylomicron forma­
tion for their absorption and transport and travel directly to the 
liver via the portal circulation. Therefore, they can be used in FCS 
to improve the palatability of the diet and, in patients who are not 
in need of weight reduction, maintain caloric intake.
In MFCS, total fat intake should initially be restricted to 5 
to 10 g/day, together with management of aggravating factors, 
until fasting TG levels fall to below 750 mg/dL (8.5 mmol/L), at 
which time attempts to somewhat liberalize the fat intake can be 
tried. Simple sugars and large amounts of carbohydrates should 
be avoided because they can further increase TG levels. Alcohol 
should be strictly avoided. In contrast to FCS in which LPL activ­
ity is absent, there is residual LPL activity in MFCS. Therefore, 
although diet therapy remains important in MFCS, drug treat­
ment with fibrates, omega-3 fatty acids, or other TG-lowering 
drugs can be effective in maintaining TG levels below 500 mg/
dL (5.6 mmol/L).
Much less is known about dietary therapy for severely elevated 
TG levels in FPLD, the mainstay of which is therapy with TG-
lowering drugs. However, because insulin resistance is typically an 
important component of this disorder, the use of the PPARγ ago­
nist pioglitazone can be efficacious in lowering TG levels. Because 
CVD risk is increased in both MFCS and FPLD, strategies for 
the prevention of CVD events should include a diet that is low 
in saturated fat and cholesterol, as well as drug treatment, as dis­
cussed in the following sections.
Drug Treatment for Severe Hypertriglyceridemia. The initial 
goal of drug treatment for the patient with severe hypertriglyceri­
demia is to prevent the development of TG-induced pancreatitis, 
the onset of which will not occur at levels below 500 to 750 mg/
dL (5.6–8.5 mmol/L).238,239 Saturation of TG clearance at lev­
els above 500 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) can lead to rapid increases 
to much higher levels associated with pancreatitis. Therefore, in 
order to prevent pancreatitis, the goal is to get below this level, 
when possible. The approach in the individual patient depends to 
a large extent on whether FCS, MFCS, or FPLD is the reason for 
the severe hypertriglyceridemia.221 Therefore, a critical first step is 
to diagnose the cause of the severe hypertriglyceridemia because 
the specific treatment will differ depending on the cause. 
Familial Chylomicronemia Syndrome. As discussed earlier, 
the mainstay of therapy for FCS is severe restriction of all dietary 
fat, including saturated, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated 
fats, which includes fish oils that can lower TGs in other condi­
tions. Fibrates, which effectively lower TGs in most situations, are 
largely ineffective in lowering TGs in FCS. Gene therapy using 
alipogene tiparvovec, an adeno-associated virus encoding a variant 
of the human LPL gene, led to some improvement in postprandial 
TGs in a few patients with FCS.240 However, fasting TG levels 
only fell by about 40% and subsequently returned toward base­
line,241 leading to discontinuation of its development in 2017. 
ANGPTL3 inhibition is effective in MFCS but does not work in 
FCS because these patients lack LPL, which ANGPTL3 inhibits, 
and there is no known effect of ANGPTL3 on hepatic uptake of 
TG-rich lipoproteins.102
However, promising results have been obtained with weekly 
subcutaneous injections of volanesorsen, an antisense oligonu­
cleotide against APOC3, a known inhibitor of LPL, in patients 
with severely elevated TGs due to either FCS or MFCS.39 
Because APOC3 had also been shown to inhibit TG-rich lipo­
protein uptake by the liver in murine models, the efficacy of 
volanesorsen in three patients with FCS with well-characterized 
LPL deficiency242 suggested the drug could remove the block 
on hepatic uptake of TG-rich lipoprotein mediated by APOC3 
(discussed in the “Exogenous and Endogenous Pathways of Triglyc­
eride Metabolism” section). In a subsequent study of 66 patients 
with FCS, volanesorsen lowered TG levels to less than 750 mg/dL 
(8.5 mmol/L) in over 75% of patients.39 The small size of that trial 
did not permit firm conclusions about the effect of volanesorsen 
on pancreatitis, although the magnitude of the TG reduction sug­
gests pancreatitis rates would be decreased.39 However, because of a 
significant incidence of low platelet concentrations during volane­
sorsen treatment, the FDA did not approve it for treatment of FCS, 
although the EMA did approve the drug for the treatment of FCS in 
2014. Ionis Pharmaceuticals, the company that developed volane­
sorsen, modified it with a triantennary GalNac moiety that targets 
the antisense oligonucleotide specifically to hepatocyte asialoglyco­
protein (ASPG) receptors, allowing administration of much smaller 
doses with similar efficacy and essentially no uptake by other organs, 
which seems to have significantly diminished the low-platelet issue, 
and this drug olezarsen is in phase 3 trials in patients with FCS and 
MFCS. Future approaches may include the use of a newly devel­
oped dual APOC3 inhibitor and APOC2 mimetic.243 
Multifactorial Chylomicronemia Syndrome. The initial step 
in the management of the severe hypertriglyceridemia seen in 
MFCS is to identify and treat any modifiable secondary cause(s) 
that may be contributing to the hypertriglyceridemia. This 
includes treatment with estrogen or estrogen-like compounds, 
consumption of alcohol, treatment of disorders such as diabetes 
or hypothyroidism, and substitution of β-adrenergic agents and 
diuretics with alternate agents for the treatment of hypertension, 
where possible. Because MFCS almost always results from exac­
erbation of a genetic form of hypertriglyceridemia by secondary 
causes, TGs seldom fall to normal levels without management 
of underlying conditions. The most effective way to reduce the 
residual hypertriglyceridemia is with fibrates, which usually lowers 
TGs sufficiently to eliminate the risk of pancreatitis,244 although 
other TG-lowering agents such as omega-3 fatty acids and niacin 
also can be effective. Treatment with volanesorsen, an APOC3 
antisense oligonucleotide, also led to substantial TG reduction 
in non-FCS hypertriglyceridemic patients245 and also led to a 
significant reduction in TGs in patients with MFCS, including 
those on fibrates.246 Volanesorsen is not yet FDA approved for this 
indication. Treatment with evinacumab, a monoclonal antibody 
1667
CHAPTER 41  Disorders of Lipoprotein Metabolism
targeting ANGPTL3 (an inhibitor of LPL), was also effective in 
patients with MFCS.102 However, at this time, it is only approved 
by the FDA for the treatment of HoFH. 
Familial Partial Lipodystrophy. The hypertriglyceridemia 
seen in this group of disorders can be severe and very resistant to 
lipid-lowering treatment. These patients also often have insulin 
resistance, which can be severe. Aggressive measures to treat the 
diabetes should be undertaken, and fibrates should be added to 
lower TG levels. Omega-3 fatty acids can be used in addition. 
Although niacin can reduce TG levels, it worsens insulin resis­
tance247 and therefore is not recommended. In our experience, 
the addition of thiazolidinediones and glucagon-like peptide-1–
receptor analogues sometimes helps lower TG levels. There is 
little rationale for the use of leptin in the Köbberling form of 
FPLD, in which leptin levels are normal or high,248 although TG 
levels may fall with leptin therapy in generalized lipodystrophy 
and in some patients with partial lipodystrophy who are leptin 
deficient.249
Although CVD risk is not usually increased in FCS, patients 
with both MFCS and FPLD are at increased risk of CVD in 
addition to pancreatitis.221 After TG levels have been lowered 
sufficiently to reduce the immediate risk of pancreatitis, the 
residual elevated remnants and VLDL may still be atherogenic. 
In addition, the dramatic decreases in TG often are associated 
with elevations of the initially low LDL levels. Therefore, strate­
gies to prevent CVD should be employed, including addition 
of a statin to the fibrate244 that the patient is on for pancreatitis 
prevention. Although there is a theoretical interaction of statins 
and fibrates to cause myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, this seldom 
is observed in practice,250 especially with the use of fenofibrate, 
which is the preferred fibrate for treatment of hypertriglyceri­
demia in patients who are on a statin.125 Many patients with 
both MFCS and FPLD also have other CVD risk factors, such 
as diabetes and hypertension, which should also be aggressively 
treated.
An algorithm for the management of the patient with severe 
hypertriglyceridemia is shown in Fig. 41.26. 
Combined Hyperlipoproteinemias
Combined hyperlipoproteinemia usually refers to the simultaneous 
elevation of LDL and VLDL levels. LDL-C and TG usually are 
above the 90th percentile for age and sex, with elevated APOB 
levels.251 On rare occasions, combined elevations of cholesterol 
and TGs also can be caused by the presence of increased levels of 
remnant lipoproteins and HL deficiency.
Combined elevations of LDL and VLDL occur commonly and 
often are associated with increased susceptibility to CAD. It can 
be the result of underlying disorders, such as hypothyroidism and 
nephrotic syndrome, or some of the drugs described in the “Sec­
ondary Forms of Hyper- and Dyslipoproteinemia” section, partic­
ularly immunosuppressive agents. When it occurs within families, 
this phenotypic pattern has historically been termed familial com­
bined hyperlipidemia (FCHL). These individuals characteristically 
come from families with various hyperlipidemias that include 
increased isolated TG or increased isolated LDL-C. Moreover, 
the abnormal lipoprotein pattern (increased TGs, cholesterol, or 
both) can vary over time in an individual. Metabolic syndrome 
and type 2 diabetes mellitus are commonly found in association 
with combined hyperlipidemias.
Although FCHL was originally believed to be a monogenic 
disorder based on family studies, this is no longer believed to 
be so. Early genetic studies revealed several loci linked to sus­
ceptibility genes in FCHL, the major one being a locus on 
1q21-q23, with the upstream transcription factor 1 (USF1) 
being the major gene underlying this linkage.252 Modifying 
genes, especially those influencing TG levels, include APOC3 
and APOA5, the latter being a downstream target of USF1 
(reviewed by Naukkarinen et al251). More recent studies using 
next-generation genetic analytic methods indicate a polygenic 
basis for combined hyperlipidemia, with a clear large contri­
bution from the accumulation of small-to-moderate-effect 
common SNPs throughout the genome that is associated with 
raising TGs and probably also LDL-C levels (reviewed by Gill 
and Hegele253). Although genotyping does not currently have 
a role to play in its diagnosis, there is some utility in making 
a clinical diagnosis of FCHL in appropriate families because it 
can identify individuals and families at markedly increased risk 
for developing premature CVD who likely would benefit from 
lipid-lowering therapy.254
In the absence of secondary causes, kinetic analysis has 
demonstrated that this lipoprotein pattern is primarily due 
to overproduction of APOB-containing lipoproteins rather 
than defective clearance.255 Regulation of APOB produc­
tion involves several steps (see the “Apolipoprotein B” sec­
tion), including increased fatty acid return to the liver and 
reduced degradation of newly synthesized APOB as a result

Familial Dysbetalipoproteinemia (Remnant Removal 
Disease, Type III Hyperlipoproteinemia)
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia is an uncommon disorder of lipo­
protein metabolism that is characterized by plasma TG and cho­
lesterol levels typically in the range of 300 to 400 mg/dL (3.4–4.5 
mmol/L), due to the accumulation in plasma of cholesterol-rich 
remnant particles. It is rarely detected in persons younger than 
20 years, and the disorder is more common in men than in pre­
menopausal women because estrogens appear to facilitate remnant 
removal in this disorder via unknown mechanisms.256 Palmar 
xanthomas (Fig. 41.27), which are present in more than half of 
affected subjects, are pathognomonic for this disorder. Tuberous 
or tuboeruptive xanthomas (see Fig. 41.21) also can occur but are 
less specific for this disorder. Unlike FH, in which peripheral vas­
cular disease is uncommon, premature peripheral vascular disease 
occurs in addition to premature CAD in patients with familial 
dysbetalipoproteinemia.
This condition usually requires homozygosity for the APOE2 
allele. However, because the phenotypic expression of the disorder 
is limited to approximately 5% of patients with the ε2/ε2 geno­
type (see “Apolipoprotein E” section), expression of the pheno­
type of remnant accumulation requires the concurrent presence of 
other genetic or environmental factors that lead to overproduction 
of APOB-containing lipoproteins or prevent their clearance, such 
as genetic forms of hypertriglyceridemia, diabetes, excess alcohol 
consumption, or hypothyroidism.187 The hyperlipidemia is caused 
by a defect in clearance of remnant lipoproteins,257 whose liver 
uptake requires APOE interaction with the LDL receptor, LRP1, 
and heparan sulfate proteoglycans (see the “Apolipoproteins and 
Major Receptors Involved in Lipid Metabolism” sections). The 
remnants that accumulate have lost much of their TG through 
LPL-mediated TG hydrolysis and therefore are relatively choles­
terol enriched. A clue to the accumulation of these remnant par­
ticles is that cholesterol and TGs are elevated to roughly the same 
extent. The predominant remnant particles, previously termed 
β-VLDLs, can be identified by abnormal migration on gel elec­
trophoresis or by other specialized tests, including identification 
of an APOE2/APOE2 phenotype on isoelectric focusing or an 
ε2/ε2 genotype, the presence of a VLDL cholesterol/plasma TG 
ratio over 0.30, or an APOB/plasma cholesterol ratio below 0.33. 
Because these tests are seldom routinely performed in patients 
with combined elevations of cholesterol and TG, it is likely that 
the diagnosis of remnant removal disease is often missed.
In addition to homozygosity for the APOE2 allele, some rare 
mutations in the APOE gene can lead to the dysbetalipoprotein­
emia phenotype in an autosomal-dominant fashion.258,259 In such 
cases, the phenotype manifests at an early age without exacerbat­
ing factors. 
Hepatic Lipase Deficiency
HL deficiency is a rare disorder associated with a lack of hep­
arin-releasable HL activity in the plasma.259a Because this 
enzyme mediates the final step of conversion of IDL to LDL 
and is involved in chylomicron remnant clearance, its deficiency 
causes elevated plasma cholesterol (250–1500 mg/dL [6.5–38.8 
mmol/L]) and TGs (395–8200 mg/dL (4.4–92.6 mmol/L), a 
phenotype that sometimes resembles dysbetalipoproteinemia. 
Patients also can have palmar and tuboeruptive xanthomas, cor­
neal arcus, and premature CAD (see Figs. 41.20, 41.25, 41.27). 
Because HL also affects HDL metabolism, HDL-C levels can be 
increased. The demonstration of HL deficiency requires in vitro 
assays of enzyme activity in post-heparin plasma or DNA analy­
sis to identify mutations. A clue to its presence is the absence of 
the ε2/ε2 genotype in a patient with a clinical picture of familial 
dysbetalipoproteinemia. 
Approach to the Patient With Combined Hyperlipidemia
As with other forms of hyperlipoproteinemia, it is important to 
rule out potential secondary causes (see tables in the “Secondary 
Forms of Hyper- and Dyslipoproteinemia” section later in this 
chapter), treatment of which can lead to normalization of the 
dyslipidemia.
A careful and detailed personal and family history should be 
obtained to look for evidence of premature CVD, which often 
is present in individuals with combined hyperlipidemia. Obtain­
ing or measuring lipid levels in relatives can help with the diag­
nosis. An elevated APOB level usually is present in individuals 
with combined hyperlipidemia who are prone to develop prema­
ture atherosclerotic disease. The presence of palmar xanthomas or 
tuberous or tuberoeruptive xanthomas (see Figs. 41.21, 41.25, 
41.27) should raise the suspicion for dysbetalipoproteinemia due 
to the accumulation of remnants of the TG-rich lipoproteins. In 
such cases, APOE phenotyping or genotyping should be obtained, 
and the other test noted earlier should be performed. If the patient 
has features of dyslipidemia but does not have the APOE2/2 iso­
form, a dominant form of dyslipoproteinemia or HL deficiency 
should be considered.
Because the patient with combined hyperlipidemia due to 
increased VLDL and LDL is at increased risk of atherosclerosis, 
treatment consists of the lifestyle measures discussed earlier for 
the prevention of CVD plus the use of statins, which have been 
shown to be effective in reducing CVD endpoints, regardless of 
the cause of the increased risk. Statins usually reduce LDL-C lev­
els by 20% to 50%, depending on the baseline level and strength 
and dose of the statin used. The decision of whether or not to add 
an additional medication for any residual hypertriglyceridemia 
is controversial. Although TG values will fall with both fibrates 
and omega-3 fatty acids, current recommendations are to add 
icosapent ethyl to a statin in very high-risk patients, despite some 
concerns about this approach (see “Drug Treatment for Mild to 
Moderately Severe Hypertriglyceridemia” section).

Fewer data are available about the best approach to treat­
ment of dysbetalipoproteinemia. Although fibrates are effective 
in reducing the abnormal lipid values, combination therapy of 
fibrates and statin appears to be more effective260,261 and is cur­
rently recommended. Because this condition often requires the 
presence of additional factors over and above the APOE2/APOE2 
genotype, it is important to treat conditions such as diabetes and 
obesity with appropriate lifestyle measures and drugs to attempt 
to correct the lipoprotein abnormalities and reduce CVD risk, 
although randomized controlled clinical outcome trials as to the 
effectiveness of these approaches are lacking.
There is no known treatment for HL deficiency. 
Abnormalities of High-Density Lipoprotein 
Metabolism
Epidemiology
HDL consists of a heterogeneous group of particles of varying 
size, density, and composition. The standard metric for HDL is 
measurement of HDL-C, which has been shown to be inversely 
associated with CVD risk in multiple studies over several decades. 
HDL-C was firmly established as a negative and independent 
CVD risk factor in the Emerging Risk Factor Collaborative 
Study.262 When corrected for either TGs or LDL particle number, 
the relationship between HDL-C and CVD persists, although it is 
diminished.263,264 Although isolated low HDL-C levels are seen, 
low HDL-C is more often part of an atherogenic lipid profile that 
also includes hypertriglyceridemia and increased levels of APOB 
due to the presence of excessive numbers of VLDL remnants and 
small LDL particles.265
For every 1-mg/dL (0.03-mmol/L) decrease in HDL-C below 
the mean, CVD risk appears to increase by 2% in men and 3% 
in women,266 and low levels are common in both males and 
females with premature CVD.267–269 However, some observa­
tional studies show that very high levels of HDL-C are actually 
also associated with an increased risk of CVD and an increased 
mortality rate. In the Cardiovascular Health in Ambulatory Care 
Research Team (CANHEART) study, overall mortality increased 
at HDL-C levels of over 90 mg/dL (2.3 mmol/L),270 and in the 
Copenhagen Heart Study, women with HDL-C levels of over 
135 mg/dL (3.5 mmol/L) and men with levels of over 97 mg/
dL (2.5 mmol/L) demonstrated an increase in overall and CVD 
mortality.271 Thus, a U-shaped relationship between HDL-C lev­
els and CVD risk appears to exist.272 The relationship between 
HDL-C and CVD risk persists after the development of CVD 
over a wide range of LDL-C levels in some studies,273–275 but 
HDL-C loses its predictive effect in established patients with 
CVD on intensive statin therapy.276 However, some Mendelian 
randomization data suggest that HDL-C may not play a causal 
role in CVD. For example, variations in ABCA1277 and LCAT 278 
that are associated with reduced HDL-C levels are not associated 
with a corresponding increase in CVD risk, and genetic varia­
tions in HL that are associated with increased HDL-C levels do 
not show a corresponding decrease in CVD risk.279 Furthermore, 
individuals with the APOA1milano variant, who have low levels of 
HDL-C, are not at increased risk of CVD.280 In addition, rare 
variants in the SCARB1 gene that codes for SR-B1 increase both 
HDL-C and CVD risk.281 Taken together with the observation 
that clinical trials that increase HDL-C levels generally do not 
improve CVD outcomes, the findings suggest that the relation­
ship between HDL-C and CVD is not necessarily causative and 
is more complex than originally believed. How to manage the 
patient with low HDL-C levels is discussed in more detail in the 
“Approach to the Patient With Low HDL-C” section. 
Functions of HDL That Might Protect Against 
Atherosclerosis
For many years it was widely believed that the inverse relation­
ship between HDL-C and CVD could be explained by the role 
of HDL in reverse cholesterol transport. In the process of reverse 
cholesterol transport, free or lipid-poor APOA1 comes in con­
tact with ABCA1, which facilitates the uptake of excess FC from 
cells of the artery wall, after which LCAT mediates its conver­
sion to cholesteryl esters and the conversion of discoidal HDL to 
spherical HDL particles. Cholesteryl esters in HDL can either be 
delivered to the liver via SR-B1 or be transferred to lower-density 
lipoproteins by CETP and delivered to the liver via LDL receptors 
for excretion in bile.
HDL has other potentially cardioprotective effects, including 
antiinflammatory, antioxidant, antithrombotic effects and protec­
tion against endothelial function (reviewed in References 266 and 
282). Most of these properties of HDL, including reverse choles­
terol transport, have been studied using in vitro systems or animal 
models and have not been studied to a major extent in humans.
In vitro studies show that HDL and APOA1 inhibit inflam­
mation in endothelial cells,283 macrophages,284 and adipocytes.285 
These antiinflammatory properties could potentially play a role in 
protection against atherogenesis, in which inflammation plays a 
prominent role.80–82 However, several antiinflammatory proper­
ties of HDL are impaired in individuals with established CAD, 
including marked changes in the HDL proteome.286 One pro­
tein that markedly reduces HDL’s antiinflammatory properties is 
serum amyloid A (SAA).285 Thus, the concept has been proposed 
that because HDL might be dysfunctional in inflammatory condi­
tions, it might be contributing to atherosclerosis rather than hav­
ing an atheroprotective effect. Data from the Copenhagen Heart 
Study show that low HDL-C levels are associated with an increased 
risk of autoimmune diseases,271 suggesting that HDL might be 
playing an antiinflammatory role in diseases other than CVD. 
HDL-C levels also fall in acute and chronic inflammatory states, 
in which HDL also loses its antiinflammatory properties.287,288
HDL also has antioxidant properties. HDL inhibits LDL 
oxidation in  vitro,289,290 in part related to the HDL-associated 
enzymes paraoxonase and glutathione selenoperoxidase.291,292 
This function of HDL may play a role in protection against ath­
erosclerosis, in light of the role of the presence of oxidized LDL in 
the artery wall and its role in atherogenesis.
Several other functions of HDL may play a potential role in 
limiting atherogenesis. These include beneficial effects on vaso­
relaxation, cell survival, cell adhesiveness, angiogenesis, and syn­
thesis of antiatherogenic and antithrombotic molecules such as 
nitric oxide and prostacyclin.282,293 Many of these effects can be 
attributed to sphingosine-1-phosphate, a bioactive lipid that accu­
mulates in HDL.293 
Causes of Low HDL-C
The mean HDL-C value for men is 45 mg/dL (1.2 mmol/L), and 
for women, it is 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L). Levels are equivalent, 
at about 55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L), in prepubescent children but 
fall by about 10 mg/dL (0.3 mmol/L) after puberty in males. Low 
HDL-C, often defined as below 40 mg/dL (1.0 mmol/L) in men 
and below 50 mg/dL (1.3 mmol/L) in women, can either be due 
1670
SECTION VIII    Disorders of Carbohydrate and Fat Metabolism
to lifestyle issues or be genetically determined as a result of small-
effect, common variants. Large-effect genetic variants, which often 
are monogenic, are more common with HDL-C levels below 15 
to 30 mg/dL (0.4–0.8 mmol/L) in men and in the low 30s (∼0.8 
mmol/L) in women.
Factors often associated with reduced HDL-C levels include 
obesity, weight gain, cigarette smoking, high-carbohydrate diets, 
metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes and other insulin-resistant 
states, acute infections, chronic inflammatory states, systemic 
lupus erythematosus, multiple myeloma, monoclonal gam­
mopathies, and hypertriglyceridemic states. Several drugs, such 
as β-adrenergic blocking agents and anabolic steroids, can also 
reduce HDL-C levels, the latter to a profound degree.294,295
Isolated Extremely Low HDL-C
HDL-C levels are usually considered extreme when below 10 
mg/dL (0.3 mmol/L). This can be due to several genetic con­
ditions and secondary causes (Table 41.10), including familial 
hypoalphalipoproteinemia due to mutations in APOA1, LCAT 
deficiency, and fish-eye disease due to complete or partial non­
functioning mutations in the LCAT gene, respectively, and Tang­
ier disease, due to absence of ABCA1. Secondary causes include 
multiple myeloma; monoclonal gammopathies, including 
monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS); 
the presence of monoclonal antibodies to APOA1, a protein 
essential for HDL integrity and normal HDL metabolism; and a 
rare paradoxical response to fibrates, especially fenofibrate, used 
in combination therapy.296,297 A recent decrease in HDL-C lev­
els is suggestive of a secondary cause. Because APOA1 activates 
LCAT, the activity of this enzyme is reduced in some mutations 
in the APOA1 gene.298,299 
LCAT Deficiency and Lipoprotein X
Rare mutations in the LCAT gene can lead to either complete or 
partial LCAT deficiency (fish-eye disease). Because of its role in 
the esterification of cholesterol in HDL, patients with these dis­
orders have very low but variable levels of HDL-C. In complete 
LCAT deficiency, there is an inability to esterify cholesterol in all 
lipoproteins, whereas in fish-eye disease, cholesterol in the APOB-
containing lipoproteins becomes esterified.300 Thus, LDL-C levels 
can be normal in fish-eye disease. In both conditions the ratio 
of free to esterified cholesterol is increased, although to a greater 
extent in complete LCAT deficiency. Measurement of LCAT 
activity or the finding of a known mutation in the LCAT gene is 
required for confirmation of the diagnosis.
The clinical manifestations are heterogeneous, but affected 
individuals can present with corneal opacification (Fig. 41.28), 
proteinuria, renal disease, and hemolytic anemia, with variable 
LDL-C and TG levels.301 The role of the very low HDL-C lev­
els in LCAT deficiency remains unclear.301 However, the higher 
amount of cholesteryl esters in LDL in fish-eye disease may pre­
dispose individuals with this disorder to CVD more than those 
with complete LCAT deficiency.
In complete LCAT deficiency, the excess FC can lead to the 
formation of an LDL-sized lipoprotein, LpX, that is rich in phos­
pholipids and unesterified cholesterol. It has albumin in its core 
and APOCs on the surface of the particle, but it is devoid of 
APOB. The renal manifestations of LCAT deficiency, which can 
include end-stage renal disease requiring transplantation, may be 
related to the presence of LpX.
LpX also is seen in cholestatic liver disease, where its concen­
tration is related to the degree of cholestasis and liver function.302 
In this instance, formation of LpX may be related to the reflux of 
bile into the plasma compartment. It can also be found in plasma 
following the infusion of lipid emulsions.303 LpX has an unusual 
cathode mobility on agar gel electrophoresis,304 which can be use­
ful to diagnose its presence. 
Familial APOA1 Deficiency
Total deficiency of APOA1 is a rare condition that results from 
homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the APOA1 
gene, leading to undetectable plasma levels of APOA1, a marked 
decrease in HDL-C, and an increased risk of premature CVD.305 
Some heterozygous mutations in the APOA1 gene are associated 
with an increased CVD risk, whereas others are not. 
Tangier Disease
Tangier disease results from biallelic homozygous loss-of-func­
tion or compound heterozygous mutations in the ABCA1 gene. 
Although affected individuals have a near absence of HDL-C due 
to the inability to transport cellular FC to APOA1, they do not 
appear to have a major increased risk of CVD, possibly related 
to the very low levels of LDL-C that also are present in these 
patients.306 Patients with Tangier disease have enlarged yellow- 
or orange-colored tonsils and enlarged livers, spleens, and lymph 
nodes, presumably due to inability to export cholesterol from tissue 
macrophages. With heterozygous mutations in ABCA1, HDL-C

Other Genetic Causes of Low HDL-C
Very low HDL-C levels can also occur in the presence of severe 
hypertriglyceridemia, such as is seen in FCS due to mutations 
in the LPL gene and associated proteins that result in absent 
or very impaired LPL function (see Table 41.4). In such cases, 
cholesteryl esters in HDL are replaced with TG exchanged from 
the TG-rich lipoproteins, mediated by CETP. Less severe reduc­
tions of HDL-C are present in heterozygous mutations in the 
LPL gene.308 Very low HDL-C levels can also be seen in familial 
combined hypolipidemia due to biallelic mutations in the ANG­
PTL3 gene, in which LDL-C and TG levels also are reduced. 
Individuals with elevated CETP activity due to a polymorphism 
in the CETP gene, as well as increased HL activity, in which TGs 
and phospholipids in HDL are hydrolyzed by HL, also have low 
levels of HDL-C. 
Causes of Elevated HDL-C
Occasionally, patients who present with hypercholesterolemia 
primarily have elevations of HDL-C with normal LDL-C levels. 
Usually, individuals with this pattern have little CVD in their 
families. Several conditions can be associated with high levels 
of HDL-C, not all of which are associated with protection from 
CVD (Table 41.11).
Nongenetic Causes of High HDL-C
HDL levels can increase as a result of physical activity; alcohol 
consumption; weight loss; smoking cessation; use of oral estro­
gens, phenytoin, or phenobarbital; insulin therapy in some 
patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus; and treatment of some of 
the disorders or discontinuation of the medications (discussed 
later in the “Secondary Forms of Hyper- and Dyslipoproteinemia” 
section) that suppress HDL-C levels. Interestingly, consumption 
of diets rich in saturated fat also can increase HDL-C levels while 
also raising LDL-C levels.309 
Genetic Causes of High HDL-C
Genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified com­
mon variants in several genes at numerous loci associated with 
variations in HDL-C levels.310 These account for some of the 
variation in HDL-C levels in the population. In addition, rare 
variants in several genes can also be associated with high levels of 
HDL-C.
CETP Deficiency. Homozygous mutations in the CETP gene 
that result in complete loss of enzyme activity lead to increased 
HDL-C and reduced LDL-C levels because of impaired transfer 
of cholesteryl esters from HDLs to lower-density lipoproteins. 
This would be expected to result in a reduced CVD risk. Although 
it generally appears that genotypes associated with high HDL-C 
levels are more likely to be associated with a lower CVD risk,311 
and several loss-of-function SNPs in the CETP gene that are asso­
ciated with increased HDL-C and concomitant decreases in TGs 
and LDL-C, are associated with corresponding risk reductions in 
CAD events,310 the findings of other studies have not been con­
clusive (reviewed by Shaw311). Moreover, several clinical trials 
with CETP inhibitors have shown limited clinical benefit, in part 
due to potential off-target effects. In addition, as noted earlier, 
the CANHEART study showed that very high levels of HDL-C 
can be associated with an increased risk of CVD and an increased 
mortality rate.270 
SR-B1 Deficiency. As described earlier in this chapter, SR-B1 
mediates the selective uptake of HDL-cholesteryl esters into the 
liver and also provides a substrate for steroidogenesis in the gonads 
and adrenal glands. Deficiency of SR-B1 leads to elevated HDL-C 
levels as a result of loss of function of one limb of the reverse 
cholesterol pathway. This is a likely explanation for increased 
atherosclerosis despite increased HDL-C levels in SR-B1 knock­
out mice.312,313 Rare variants in the SCARB1 gene that codes for 
SR-B1 increase both HDL-C and CVD risk.281 
Hepatic Lipase and Endothelial Lipase Deficiency. Complete 
loss of function in the LIPC gene that encodes for HL leads to 
an increase in HDL-C, accompanied by elevations in the APOB-
containing lipoproteins and accumulation of remnant-like par­
ticles.279 Premature atherosclerosis has been documented in some 
families with this disorder,279,314 likely due to the increase in lipo­
proteins other than HDL. Human loss-of-function mutations are 
associated with increased HDL-C, and the experimental use of 
an EL inhibitor was found to increase HDL-C and HDL par­
ticle number, size, and functionality.315 However, a Mendelian 
randomization study failed to show an association with reduced 
risk of myocardial infarction,316 although carriers of mutations 
in LIPG, which codes for EL, exhibited trends toward reduced 
CAD.317
Other than for patients who come from families with high 
HDL-C levels and little history of CVD, there is no good evi­
dence that these rare mutations that lead to high HDL-C lev­
els confer protection against CVD, and in some instances, they 
appear to increase the risk. 
Approach to the Patient With Low HDL-C
An initial approach is to consider other conditions that can be 
associated with low HDL-C, such as metabolic syndrome, dia­
betes, hypertriglyceridemia, obesity, weight gain, cigarette smok­
ing, high-carbohydrate diets, acute infections, and systemic lupus
