Endocrinology of HIV/AIDS
TAKARA STANLEY AND TODD T. BROWN
H
uman immunodeficiency virus (HIV) disease affects up 
to 38.4 million patients worldwide and over 1.2 million 
in the United States. In many parts of the world, for 
example, in eastern and southern Africa, HIV remains epidemic, 
with an estimated 20.6 million people infected. In addition, the 
number of people with HIV (PWH) is growing rapidly in Asia 
and other parts of the world. Endocrine dysfunction is common 
among PWH. Adrenal, gonadal, thyroid, bone, and metabolic 
abnormalities have all been reported. HIV itself, related infectious 
organisms, immune activation, cytokines, and antiretroviral medi­
cations may all affect endocrine function. Endocrine disorders in 
HIV disease, for example, hypogonadism, adrenal insufficiency, 
diabetes, and bone loss, may cause significant morbidity and are 
thus important to diagnose. Interactions between antiretroviral 
therapy (ART) and specific medications may also contribute to 
endocrine disturbances. Endocrine strategies may improve quality 
of life and long-term survival through effects on critical metabolic 
and body composition parameters, including loss of muscle mass 
(sarcopenia) in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) 
wasting, fat redistribution with loss of peripheral and abdominal 
subcutaneous fat, and relative or absolute gains in central (vis­
ceral) adiposity among some patients. However, diagnosis and 
treatment may be difficult because of varying nutritional condi­
tions and effects of the varied medications used to treat HIV dis­
ease. As PWH live longer as a result of the success of antiretroviral 
medications, adverse effects resulting from these very medications 
and HIV-related immune dysfunction have resulted in increased 
cardiovascular risk and metabolic changes that may require 
1767
CHAPTER 46  Endocrinology of HIV/AIDS
intervention and long-term management by the endocrine spe­
cialist. This chapter will review the prevalence, mechanisms, and 
optimal treatment strategies for endocrine abnormalities in PWH.
Adrenal Function
Adrenal dysfunction has been described in individuals with 
advanced HIV and/or AIDS, but it does not appear common in 
those with treated HIV and virologic control. Although clinical 
adrenal dysfunction is relatively rare even among patients with 
AIDS, subtle impairments in adrenal reserve may be seen in this 
population. Adrenal dysfunction most often is caused by destruc­
tion of adrenal tissue by cytomegalovirus (CMV) in patients with 
advanced HIV disease but may also be caused by medications, 
hypothalamic/pituitary disease from opportunistic infection, idio­
pathic inflammation or tissue destruction, or in rare cases, by cor­
tisol resistance. In addition, some features of Cushing syndrome 
may be seen among PWH with fat redistribution, but true Cush­
ing disease is rare.
Adrenal Insufficiency
Adrenal insufficiency occurring in the context of advanced HIV 
disease is most often caused by tissue destruction of the adrenal 
glands from opportunistic infections. CMV adrenalitis is the most 
common cause, seen in approximately 40% to 90% of patients 
with CMV infection at autopsy. However, adrenocortical destruc­
tion caused by CMV is usually less than 50% and therefore 
unlikely to cause adrenal insufficiency,1 and CMV disease is rare 
with well-preserved immune function in patients on ART. Other 
organisms and processes that have been associated with adrenal 
destruction in advanced HIV disease include Mycobacterium tuber­
culosis, Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (MAI), Cryptococcus, 
and hemorrhage. Additionally, pituitary/hypothalamic destruc­
tion resulting in secondary adrenal insufficiency may be caused 
in rare instances by opportunistic infection (e.g., toxoplasmosis, 
Cryptococcus, and CMV). Idiopathic adenohypophyseal necro­
sis was observed in a minority of patients (approximately 10% 
at autopsy) who had untreated HIV early in the epidemic and 
could be related to a direct effect of HIV.2 In the current era, data 
on adrenal function in individuals with virologically controlled 
HIV are sparse, and there is insufficient evidence to support an 
increased prevalence of clinically relevant adrenal insufficiency in 
this population.3,4 
Glucocorticoid Excess: Adrenal Shunting and 
Cortisol Resistance
Like adrenal insufficiency, glucocorticoid excess was described in 
association with HIV in the pre-ART era, but there is no evidence 
to suggest an association in those with virologically controlled 
HIV. In untreated or advanced HIV, increased cortisol levels may 
be seen, most commonly as a stress response, in association with 
low weight or increasing degree of illness.5 Cytokine modulation 
of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis may also con­
tribute to increased cortisol levels.6 Glucocorticoid resistance has 
also been shown in rare patients with advanced HIV disease, who 
demonstrate addisonian symptoms, including hyperpigmenta­
tion, in the setting of hypercortisolism and increased adrenocorti­
cotropic hormone (ACTH). Of note, individuals living with HIV 
may experience socioeconomic and health stressors such as stigma, 
substance use, metabolic diseases, and immune dysregulation that 
could lead to chronic activation of the HPA axis, but this currently 
is not well understood.3 
Medication Effects
Medications may contribute to adrenal insufficiency in HIV 
patients (Table 46.1). The most common adverse event associated 
with the combination of antiretrovirals and other medications 
is iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency caused by the combination of 
boosted antiretrovirals and inhaled corticosteroids.7 The resulting 
reduction in metabolism of the inhaled corticosteroid, via inhibi­
tion of CYP3A4 by ritonavir or cobicistat, can result in glucocorti­
coid excess, adrenal suppression, symptoms of Cushing syndrome, 
and potentially severe adrenal insufficiency with discontinuation 
of the inhaled corticosteroid. Similar effects have been reported 
with combinations of ritonavir or cobicistat and intraarticu­
lar steroid injections.8,9 Ketoconazole, an antifungal agent, may 
also cause adrenal insufficiency by inhibiting side-chain cleavage 
enzyme and 11β-hydroxylase.10 Phenytoin, opiates, and rifampin, 
among other drugs, affect cortisol metabolism. For example, adre­
nal insufficiency may be precipitated by the use of rifampin for 
treatment of tuberculosis in patients with reduced adrenal reserve. 
Megestrol acetate, a potent synthetic progestational derivative 
used as an appetite stimulant, has glucocorticoid properties and 
decreases ACTH. Abrupt withdrawal of megestrol acetate may 
precipitate adrenal insufficiency, and such patients should be 
tested for adrenal insufficiency and receive physiologic glucocorti­
coid administration as needed after megestrol withdrawal.11 
Clinical Assessment
Patients with HIV with symptoms of adrenal insufficiency and 
particularly those with hyponatremia and risk factors for adre­
nal insufficiency (e.g., known disseminated CMV or recent use 
of megestrol acetate) should be evaluated. Cosyntropin testing is 
usually an adequate first step, except in those patients in whom 
hypothalamic or pituitary insufficiency of recent onset is sus­
pected. In such patients, use of morning cortisol levels, metyra­
pone, or insulin tolerance testing may be necessary, if there are no 
contraindications. If adrenal insufficiency is documented, ACTH 
testing and appropriate imaging are used to localize the defect. 
In patients with clinical symptoms of adrenal insufficiency and 
elevated cortisol levels, cortisol resistance may be present and the 
diagnosis may be made by glucocorticoid receptor studies in blood 
monocytes. Conversely, in patients with symptoms of adrenal 
excess and low cortisol and ACTH levels, exogenous steroid use or 
interactions with ART should be suspected. 
Gonadal Function
Male Gonadal Dysfunction
Gonadal dysfunction is common among men with HIV with 
weight loss and advanced illness. Initial studies indicated bio­
chemical hypogonadism in approximately 50% of men with 
AIDS, in association with increased disease severity. Among men 
with HIV and low weight, hypogonadism was seen in 20%.12 
Studies in the modern ART era suggest a lower prevalence of 
hypogonadism.13–17 The mechanisms of hypogonadism in men 
with HIV may relate to severe illness or effects of undernutrition 
on gonadotropin secretion, medication effects, or more rarely, 
tissue destruction from opportunistic infections. Most often,

hypogonadism is secondary in nature, with low or inappropri­
ately normal gonadotropin levels, as seen in 91% of patients with 
reduced free testosterone levels during initiation of ART in the 
Swiss HIV cohort.18 Primary hypogonadism is seen less often and 
may be caused by cytokine effects on the testes, including effects 
of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) to inhibit steroidogenesis via 
effects on the side-chain cleavage enzyme and of interleukin (IL) 1 
to inhibit Leydig cell steroidogenesis and luteinizing hormone 
binding to the Leydig cell. Indeed, among young men, median 
age 45 years, using an early morning total testosterone as a test to 
define hypogonadism in a large Italian cohort, Rochira and asso­
ciates demonstrated that gonadotropins were elevated in 16% of 
patients studied14 (Fig. 46.1).
Increased prolactin levels and gynecomastia have been dem­
onstrated among men with HIV. In a case-control study, gyneco­
mastia was seen in 1.8% of 2275 consecutively screened men with 
HIV and was associated with hypogonadism, hepatitis C (HVC), 
and degree of lipoatrophy (subcutaneous fat loss associated with 
ART).19 Of ART medications, efavirenz (EFV) is most closely 
associated with gynecomastia,20 which is due to direct activation 
of the estrogen receptor.21 Hyperprolactinemia has been reported 
in 21% of men with stable HIV disease and was significantly asso­
ciated with opioid use and increased CD4 count but not with 
changes in body composition or gynecomastia.22,23
Sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG) levels are increased in 
30% to 55% of patients with HIV. Therefore, use of bioavail­
able or free testosterone is recommended to diagnose hypogonad­
ism, because use of total testosterone assays may underestimate 
the prevalence of true hypogonadism in this population. As a 
caveat, analogue assays of free testosterone may not be indepen­
dent of SHBG and should not be used. In contrast, determination 
of free testosterone by equilibrium dialysis or calculation by an 
accepted equation are more useful strategies to detect hypogonad­
ism among those with HIV. For example, Monroe and colleagues 
conducted a large study in the Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study 
(MACS), comparing normal-weight men with and without HIV 
in the current era of ART. In this study, total testosterone lev­
els were similarly HIV serostatus, but free testosterone calculated 
using the Vermeulen equation was significantly lower in the men 
with HIV. Reliance on total testosterone alone would have missed 
33% of patients with hypogonadism.13 Use of total testosterone or 
free testosterone analogue radioimmunoassay to diagnose hypogo­
nadism among men with HIV is associated with poor sensitivities 
of 25% and 33%, respectively.15
In patients in whom acute and chronic illness may contrib­
ute to hypogonadism, retesting of gonadal function by measur­
ing an early morning free testosterone level is recommended upon 
resolution of the illness, as endogenous function may return with 
improved health. In patients who remain hypogonadal, adminis­
tration of physiologic testosterone replacement after appropriate 
diagnostic workup for the cause of hypogonadism is appropriate. 
Female Gonadal Dysfunction
Gonadal dysfunction is common among women with HIV. In a 
study from early in the HIV epidemic, amenorrhea was described 
in approximately 25% of women with advanced HIV, whereas 
anovulation may be seen in up to 50% of women with HIV in 
association with reduced CD4 counts.24 Among anovulatory 
women with HIV, changes in menstrual function are three times 
as likely compared to normally ovulating patients. In a more recent 
meta-analysis, amenorrhea was seen in 2% to 7% of premeno­
pausal women with HIV, and the odds of amenorrhea were 62% 
higher in women with HIV compared to those without.25 Early 
menopause has been reported in up to 15% to 26% of women 
with HIV, and most studies show an earlier age of menopause 
in women with HIV, but many studies did not use biochemical 
confirmation of menopausal status.24,26

Androgen levels are often reduced in women with HIV. In one 
study, androgen levels, assessed with the use of a free testosterone 
assay, were reduced below the level seen in age-matched healthy 
women in over 50% of women with HIV with significant weight 
loss and in over one-third of women with HIV without weight 
loss.27 The mechanisms of androgen deficiency in HIV disease 
may be caused in part by intraadrenal shunting toward cortisol 
production and away from androgen production, particularly in 
women with significant weight loss.28 
Thyroid Function
Individuals with untreated or advanced HIV commonly have 
altered thyroid function tests (TFTs).29 Abnormal TFT results 
in advanced HIV are most commonly caused by the stress of ill­
ness in patients with advanced HIV or concomitant disorders, as 
found in other patients with nonthyroidal illness (“euthyroid sick 
syndrome”). However, among adults, some studies have shown 
that reverse triiodothyronine (rT3) levels do not rise in associa­
tion with decreasing T3 levels, as one would expect in nonthy­
roidal illness.30 Additionally, thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) 
levels are increased in individuals with HIV in association with 
reductions in CD4+ counts.29,31,32 Patients with progressive HIV 
disease therefore exhibit decreased T3 levels, increased TBG, and 
decreased rT3 levels with increasing illness.
Thyroid dysfunction may also occur in individuals with HIV 
as a result of immune reconstitution syndrome following ART. 
This most commonly manifests as Graves disease, estimated to 
occur in 3% of women and 0.2% of men following treatment 
with ART, or less commonly results in autoimmune hypothyroid­
ism.32 Graves disease may develop several years after initiation of 
ART, with a median time between ART initiation and Graves of 
29.5 months in one cohort33 and 63 months in another.34 Graves 
disease has also been described after IL2 therapy in patients with 
HIV.35 Patients with HIV and Graves disease due to immune 
reconstitution have been successfully treated with radioactive 
iodine.33,34 Recent guidelines on thyroid dysfunction following 
immune reconstitution do not recommend routine surveillance of 
thyroid studies in those initiating ART; rather, clinical suspicion 
should guide screening decisions.31
Opportunistic infections may also cause thyroid disease. 
Pneumocystis thyroiditis has been reported to cause a painful 
thyroiditis-like picture, with hyperthyroidism followed by hypo­
thyroidism, decreased uptake on scanning, and a firm but tender 
gland. Pneumocystis thyroiditis may result from the use of inhaled 
pentamidine, which is associated with extrapulmonary Pneumo­
cystis infections. CMV, MAI, Cryptococcus, and Kaposi sarcoma 
(KS) have been demonstrated in the thyroid on autopsy but have 
not been related to clinical thyroid disease. Clinically apparent 
thyroidal abscesses from Aspergillus and Rhodococcus equi have 
been reported. Hypothalamic/pituitary replacement from oppor­
tunistic infections, such as toxoplasmosis and CMV, has also been 
reported to cause secondary hypothyroidism. Medications may 
affect thyroid function. Rifampin influences hepatic clearance of 
thyroxine (T4), and interferon is associated with an increased inci­
dence of autoimmune hypothyroidism.
In ART-treated individuals with virologic control, studies do 
not support an increased prevalence of overt thyroid disease com­
pared with the general population.36–38 Although some studies 
have suggested an increased incidence of subclinical hypothyroid­
ism in people living with HIV,39,40 others demonstrate no asso­
ciation between HIV-status and thyroid-stimulating hormone 
(TSH).36,38 At present, evidence does not report routine screening 
of thyroid studies in adults living with HIV.31,38,41 Children living 
with HIV may also demonstrate thyroid dysfunction. Increased 
TSH has been demonstrated in young children with average 
age 1.5 years and failure to thrive. T4 levels were normal, but 
­thyrotropin-releasing hormone testing showed exaggerated TSH 
responses, and growth rates increased in response to thyroid hor­
mone.42 Fundaro and associates demonstrated increased antithy­
roglobulin antibodies in 34% of symptomatic children with HIV, 
along with elevated TSH levels in 28%, particularly those with 
severe immunosuppression.43 A more recent cohort has also dem­
onstrated increased rates of subclinical hypothyroidism and non­
thyroidal illness in children with HIV compared to controls.44 A 
large study in perinatally infected children demonstrated reduced 
total T3, total T4, and free T4 and increased rT3, TBG, and TSH, 
with negative autoantibodies, suggesting a euthyroid sick pattern, 
particularly in those with severe immunosuppression.45 Children 
with HIV with failure to thrive should be screened for true hypo­
thyroidism, but more often the TFTs will reflect nonthyroidal ill­
ness and the severity of immune compromise.45 
Fluid Balance and Electrolytes
Disorders of fluid balance and electrolytes are common among 
patients with AIDS. Hyponatremia may be seen in upward of 
50% of patients and is most often related to the syndrome of inap­
propriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). Hyperkale­
mia is also frequently reported and may be seen in association with 
various drugs, such as trimethoprim. More rarely, hyperkalemia 
may be associated with adrenal insufficiency.
Sodium
Hyponatremia (sodium <130 mmol/L) is seen in 40% to 60% of 
hospitalized patients with AIDS and 20% of outpatients. SIADH 
(volume-replete patients with low levels of serum sodium, and 
inappropriately elevated levels of urine osmolarity) is seen in 23% 
to 47% of hyponatremic patients. SIADH may be caused by vari­
ous infections and tumors and is treated with fluid restriction and 
hypertonic saline if severe. The vasopressin receptor 2, tolvaptan, 
has also been used in the treatment of hyponatremia in a patient 
with advanced HIV disease.46
Adrenal insufficiency is documented in 30% of volume-
depleted, hyponatremic patients with HIV.47 Volume depletion 
(diarrhea, vomiting) with excessive free water and impaired water 
clearance (HIV nephropathy) may cause hyponatremia among ill 
patients with HIV, especially those in the hospital. Volume reple­
tion is the treatment. Hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism,48 more 
typically associated with hyperkalemia, may be another cause of 
hyponatremia and is treated with mineralocorticoids. 
Potassium
Hyperkalemia occurs in 20% to 53% of AIDS patients on tri­
methoprim because of structural similarities to amiloride and 
inhibition of tubular potassium excretion.49 Other potential 
causes include pentamidine-associated tubular nephropathy, 
HIV-nephropathy (glomerular sclerosis), primary adrenal insuffi­
ciency, and rarely, hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism. Physiologic 
studies investigating potassium balance in patients with HIV also 
suggest an inadequate aldosterone response to hyperkalemias. A 
drug interaction between ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (PI) 
1771
CHAPTER 46  Endocrinology of HIV/AIDS
and eplerenone has also been associated with hyperkalemia.50 A 
Fanconi-like syndrome with tubular dysfunction, phosphate wast­
ing, and hypokalemia has been described with the use of tenofovir 
disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and more rarely with adefovir, cidofo­
vir, and didanosine.51 
Calcium Homeostasis and Bone Changes
Calcium Homeostasis
Hypocalcemia is common in with advanced HIV disease. Hypo­
calcemia, based on albumin-adjusted total calcium levels, was 
demonstrated in 6.5% of a large cohort of individuals with AIDS. 
Calcium levels decreased progressively with stage of disease. Among 
patients with hypocalcemia, 48% were vitamin D deficient, and 
the expected increase in parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels was 
lacking in the majority.52 Jaeger and colleagues also demonstrated 
decreased PTH secretion in severely immunocompromised 
patients with AIDS, but the mechanism is unknown.53 In addi­
tion, decreased PTH levels may occur in the setting of hypomagne­
semia during severe illness or in association with renal magnesium 
wasting. Vitamin D deficiency may be caused by malabsorption 
from AIDS enteropathy or by specific effects of antiretroviral 
drugs (e.g., inhibition of 1α-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvita­
min D by PIs or increased conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 
24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 by efavirenz).54–56
Severe vitamin D deficiency of nutritional origin has also 
been described in individuals with HIV. Osteomalacia has been 
associated with use of rifabutin for MAI in a patient with HIV. 
Rifabutin induces cytochrome P450, which may affect vitamin D 
metabolism. Other drugs that induce P450 could have a similar 
effect, including the nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibi­
tor (NNRTI), efavirenz, which has been associated with lower 
25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations.57 A number of drugs may 
affect calcium homeostasis (see Table 46.1). Foscarnet complexes 
with calcium to decrease ionized calcium levels and may also 
induce severe hypomagnesemia. Pentamidine therapy has been 
associated with renal magnesium wasting and severe hypomagne­
semia, which may, in turn, cause hypocalcemia, through decreased 
PTH release and resistance to circulating PTH. Ketoconazole 
inhibits 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D synthesis.
Among patients with HIV disease, hypercalcemia can be 
caused by excessive 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production in the 
setting of granulomatous disease (tuberculosis) or lymphoma; by 
local osteoclastic bone resorption from disseminated CMV; or by 
human T-cell lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1)-related activation 
of PTH-related protein (PTHrP). Immune reconstitution–asso­
ciated hypercalcemia has been described in the setting of ART 
initiation among patients with known tuberculosis, in whom 
immune reconstitution results in increased granulomatous activ­
ity and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production.58 
Bone Loss: Prevalence, Etiologic Factors, and 
Treatment Strategies
Studies performed in the current era of ART give an estimate of 
the prevalence and risk factors for progression of bone loss among 
PWH. Bonjoch and associates investigated 671 PWH and dem­
onstrated osteopenia in 47.5% and osteoporosis in 23%.59 Pro­
gression rates to osteopenia and osteoporosis were 12.5% and 
15.6% over 2.5 years of follow-up and 18% and 29% over 5 years 
of follow-up. In this large cohort, factors associated with pro­
gression of bone loss were age, male sex, lower body mass index 
(BMI), PI use, and TDF use.59 Significant bone loss has also been 
shown among postmenopausal women with HIV, with time since 
menopause and traditional risk factors most significantly associ­
ated with bone loss. In a longitudinal analysis of postmenopausal 
women with HIV, Yin and coworkers demonstrated increased 
markers of bone resorption and annualized bone loss in women 
with HIV versus those without HIV (Fig. 46.2).60

Specific antiretroviral strategies may affect bone in populations 
with HIV. Studies demonstrate that switching to a TDF-based 
regimen is associated with bone loss and increased bone turn­
over61 (Fig. 46.3). Strong evidence for an effect of TDF is shown 
in studies in which patients at risk for HIV are given TDF and 
emtricitabine (FTC) for preexposure prophylaxis. In these indi­
viduals, bone loss averaged approximately 1% compared to con­
trol subjects over 2 years of follow-up. Larger effects might be seen 
in less healthy PWH with other comorbid contributors.62
Current recommendations suggest that TDF should be 
avoided for the initial or continued treatment of PWH at risk for 
fracture.63 ART switching from TDF to abacavir, raltegravir, or 
the tenofovir prodrug tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) are associated 
with improvements in bone mineral density (BMD) in PWH on 
effective ART.64–66 In addition, because of their negative effects on 
BMD, PIs should be avoided in PWH at risk for fracture.67
Immunologic factors including T-cell activation,68 low CD4 
cell count,69 and coinfection with hepatitis B (HBV) and HCV 
are strongly related to reduced bone density, particularly among 
women.70 These data suggest the need to assess and follow bone 
density in patients with HIV with specific risk factors, for exam­
ple, older age, long-term ART use, low BMI, hypogonadism, 
hepatitis, low CD4 count, and TDF use.

in patients with HIV, including hypogonadism, relative growth 
hormone (GH) deficiency, and vitamin D deficiency. GH pulse 
area determined from overnight frequent sampling was reduced in

trial. PLoS One. 2012;7:e32445, Fig. 2.)

CHAPTER 46  Endocrinology of HIV/AIDS
with vertebral bone density.71 This relationship may explain in part 
the inverse association between increased visceral adipose tissue 
(VAT) and reduced bone density in PWH.72 Vitamin D deficiency 
is common among patients with HIV. In a study of ambulatory 
clinic patients in London, the prevalence of 25-hydroxyvitamin 
D deficiency (<20 ng/mL) and severe 25-hydroxyvitamin D defi­
ciency (<10 ng/mL) was 58.5% and 12.6%, respectively.73 In a 
large cohort of 2044 consecutively followed patients with HIV 
in Brussels, the prevalence of severe vitamin D deficiency using 
the 10-ng/mL cutoff was 32.4%.74 Among PWH in the study, 
advanced disease (CD4 < 200 cells/mm3) and current use of EFV 
were significantly associated with severe vitamin D deficiency.74,75 
TDF may increase PTH and bone turnover, potentially related 
to effects on proximal tubule phosphate reabsorption or other 
effects. PIs may also inhibit 1α-hydroxylase and result in vitamin 
D deficiency.54
Studies in PWH receiving highly active ART (HAART) have 
investigated markers of bone resorption and formation and found 
evidence of increased bone turnover.76 Tebas and colleagues eval­
uated serum and urine bone markers in 73 PWH receiving PI 
therapy.77 Increased serum bone alkaline phosphatase and urine 
N-telopeptide were found to be inversely correlated with BMD 
T- and Z-scores measured by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry 
(DXA), suggesting an increased rate of bone turnover among 
PWH receiving PI therapy.77 Dysregulation of the production of 
nuclear factor κB ligand (RANKL) and osteoprotegerin by B cells 
is associated with lower BMD in PWH, validating a preclinical 
model of HIV-related bone loss.78,79
Increased risk of fracture has been observed in PWH compared 
to those without HIV. In a U.S.-based data registry study, the 
overall fracture prevalence was 2.87 versus 1.77 per 100 persons 
for persons with and without.80 In a large cohort study performed 
in Europe, significantly increased adjusted hazard ratios for hip 
and major fracture were 4.7 and 1.8, with an increased relative 
risk (RR) of fracture among older PWH in the study81 (Fig. 46.4). 
In a Veterans Administration (VA) cohort of men, Womack and 
coworkers demonstrated that increased fragility fractures were 
strongly associated with higher frailty score, low BMI, alcohol-
related diagnoses, White race, proton pump inhibitor use, and 
PI use.82 In a study limited to women, lifetime fragility fractures 
were significantly more common in women with HIV compared 
to those with HIV (odds ratio [OR] 1.7, 95% confidence interval 
[CI] 1.1–2.6)83 and among older men in the MACS, age-related 
increases in the risk of fragility fracture occur about 10 years ear­
lier in men with HIV compared to those without HIV.84
Use of the FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool) score to 
predict fragility fracture has shown relatively poor sensitivity 
but good specificity among PWH. Among PWH, the estimated 
10-year risk of fracture using FRAX tends to underestimate actual 
fracture risk.85 When using FRAX without a BMD measure­
ment, accuracy can be improved by including HIV as a second­
ary cause of osteoporosis.86 These results suggest that other factors 
unassessed by FRAX may be contributing to fracture risk among 
PWH, which may include immune dysfunction, ART exposure, 
and concomitant infection such as HCV.
Limited data are available on treatment strategies to reduce 
fracture risk in PWH. In short-term studies, alendronate and zole­
dronic acid have both been shown to improve BMD in PWH with 
good safety and tolerability.87–89 In one study of zoledronic acid, 
significant improvements in BMD and suppression of bone turn­
over persisted 5 years after initial dosing, suggesting that dosing 
intervals greater than 1 year may be effective in this population, 
but the efficacy for fracture reduction has not been clearly demon­
strated.90 To date, there have been no studies examining the effect 
of teriparatide, abaloparatide, or denosumab in populations with 
HIV. Among men with AIDS wasting, testosterone at high doses 
(200 mg/week) has been shown to increase bone density.5
The first 2 years after the initiation of ART is associated with a 
2% to 6% decrease in BMD with the larger decreases in this range 
observed in those receiving TDF or PIs.67,91–93 Advanced HIV 
disease at the time of ART initiation has also been associated with 
greater loss on BMD in this period.94 In addition to avoiding TDF 
and PIs, as well as starting ART at a higher CD4 cell count, sev­
eral strategies have been tested to mitigate bone loss during ART 
initiation. In a randomized controlled trial, high-dose vitamin D3 
(4000 IU/d) and calcium (1000 mg/d) at the time of ART initia­
tion with TDF/FTC/EFV was shown to attenuate ART-initiation 
associated bone loss by 50%.95 In another randomized trial, a sin­
gle dose of zoledronic acid (5 mg) before ART initiation prevented 
bone loss over 96 weeks;96 this may be an important strategy to 
maintain bone health in those patients with HIV initiating ART 
who are at risk for fracture because of older age, lower BMD, or 
the presence of other fracture risk factors (Fig. 46.5). 
Bone Metabolism in Children With HIV
Reduced bone density has also been reported in children with 
HIV compared to those without HIV with reported prevalence 
of “low bone density,” defined as a Z-score <−2 for bone mineral 
content (BMC), areal BMD (aBMD), or BMD, ranging from 
4.1% to 15%.97–100 Although growth delay may partially account 
for lower BMD seen on DXA scan in children with HIV, reduc­
tions in BMD compared to controls persist following adjustment 
for body size, suggesting altered bone physiology independent of 
differences in growth.99,101 Children with HIV also demonstrate 
impairments in bone microarchitecture and bone strength assessed 
by peripheral quantitative computed tomography (pQCT) and 
high-resolution pQCT (HR-pQCT).100,102 Jacobson and col­
leagues also recently demonstrated increased fracture risk among 
children with perinatally acquired HIV younger than 6 years, 
with adjusted incidence rate ratio compared with an HIV-exposed

The etiology of reduced bone density in children with HIV 
is multifactorial. During childhood, bone formation should out­
weigh bone resorption. Immune activation and subclinical inflam­
mation can alter this balance, however, and children with HIV 
demonstrate reduced markers of bone formation, with markers 
of bone resorption variably reported as increased or reduced com­
pared to controls.104,105 Factors associated with lower bone density 
among children with HIV include lower nadir CD4+ count, lower 
CD4/CD8 ratio, delayed initiation of ART, and orphanhood.97,98 
As in adults, exposure to TDF is associated with low bone density 
in children. Rukuni and colleagues demonstrate that detrimental 
effects of TDF on bone are dose and duration dependent: children 
exposed to TDF for 4 or more years demonstrated a deficit of 0.52 
standard deviations in total-body-less-head bone mineral content, 
a magnitude that would confer a 50% increase of fracture risk in 
childhood.99 Also similar to data in adults, bone density is related 
to insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) in children with HIV, sug­
gesting a potential effect of low GH on bone.106 Importantly, 
deficits in bone density in children with HIV likely translate into 
reductions in peak bone mass, which confers a lifelong increase in 
fracture risk. Among young adults with HIV age 20 to 25 years, 
Tanner stage 5, infected either perinatally or during adolescence, 
volumetric bone density and cortical and trabecular thickness on 
HR-pQCT was reduced, suggesting lower peak bone mass among 
patients with HIV.100 Vitamin D supplementation has been tested 
as a strategy to improve BMD in children and adolescents with 
HIV, with modest effect to improve bone density in one study107 
and no effect in other studies.108,109 A systematic review of 20 
studies addressing vitamin D supplementation in individuals aged 
0 to 25 years with HIV concluded that vitamin D supplementa­
tion does not appear to improve bone outcomes, although larger 
studies, potentially with longer follow-up, are needed.110 One 
randomized, placebo-controlled study administering alendro­
nate to 52 children with HIV ages 11 to 24 years with lumbar 
spine BMD Z-score <−1.5 demonstrated that increases in lumbar 
spine BMD were greater over 48 weeks with alendronate (20% 
[14%–25%]) than placebo (7% [5%–9%]).111 No safety concerns 
appeared over 48 or 96 weeks of treatment with alendronate, and 
the gains over 48 weeks of alendronate were largely maintained 
after treatment. These data suggest that bisphosphonates could 
be considered in a pediatric patient with HIV and osteoporosis 
(using the pediatric definition of BMC or aBMD Z-score <−2 
plus a clinically significant fracture history),112 but larger studies 
would be required to establish whether bisphosphonates should be 
used in children with HIV and low bone density who do not meet 
the pediatric definition of osteoporosis. 
Avascular Necrosis of Bone
Miller and coworkers demonstrated a 4.4% prevalence of avas­
cular necrosis (AVN) among 339 asymptomatic individuals with 
HIV.113 A significant relationship was reported between AVN 
and prior use of systemic corticosteroids. Other potential factors 
significantly associated with an increased risk of AVN included 
the presence of anticardiolipin antibodies, as well as routine body­
building and its associated mechanical stress. Alcohol use may also 
be a factor associated with AVN among patients with HIV.114 In 
an analysis among patients with HIV, osteonecrosis of the bone 
was associated with exposure to one or more ART drugs and high 
triglyceride and cholesterol levels, as well as high serum immuno­
globulin (Ig) E.115 A role for altered coagulation and inflamma­
tion was also suggested by the observation of increased d-dimer 
among patients with osteonecrosis,116 and that past history of 
immunosuppression was a major risk factor for AVN incidence.117 
The Growth Hormone/Insulin-Like Growth 
Factor 1 Axis
Significant abnormalities in the GH/IGF1 axis occur in patients 
with HIV. Among patients with AIDS wasting and significant 
weight loss, GH levels are increased in association with reduced 
IGF1 levels, a pattern typical of GH resistance seen with malnu­
trition. In contrast, patients with VAT accumulation and/or obe­
sity in the context of HIV demonstrate relative GH deficiency, 
with reduced mean overnight GH and GH pulse amplitude com­
pared to controls.118 Relative GH deficiency is strongly predicted 
by increased VAT, with a multifactorial etiology likely including 
GH suppression from increased free fatty acids (FFAs) due to 
increased lipolytic rate, increased somatostatin tone, and reduced 
ghrelin.119,120
Growth and Puberty in Children With HIV
Children living with HIV, the majority of whom reside in resource-
limited settings, often exhibit short stature and/or stunting, as well 
as delayed puberty. Stunting is defined as length-for-age Z-score 
< −2 according to World Health Organization (WHO) growth

is found in up to half of ART-naive children and adolescents with 
HIV in resource-limited settings.121–123 Among ART-treated chil­
dren with HIV, estimates of stunting range from 6% in higher 
resource settings to 39% in lower resource settings.124
Compared to children born to mothers without HIV infec­
tion, children who acquire HIV from their mothers have lower 
length-for-age and weight-for-length at birth, as do children 
who were exposed to HIV in utero but uninfected (HEU).125 
Low birth weight (LBW) prevalence is also increased in infants 
with HIV.125,126 During the first 2 years of life, linear growth 
and weight gain are lower in those with HIV infection and, to a 
lesser degree, in HEU compared with controls.125,127 Infants and 
young children with HIV also have decreased head circumference 
compared to uninfected controls.128 Deficits in height are seen 
throughout childhood and adolescence in those with HIV and 
persist at least through age 5 years in HEU cohorts.129 Initiation 
of ART results in “catch-up” growth and improved height-for-age 
Z-scores.130 Large pediatric cohorts demonstrate that, even in chil­
dren who started ART relatively early, catch-up growth may not 
completely reverse early statural deficits.124,131,132 In one cohort of 
children starting ART by age 11 years, only those children with a 
height-for-age Z-score of −1 or above at ART initiation were able 
to achieve heights similar to WHO reference ranges.131 Younger 
age of ART initiation, higher CD4+ count, lower HIV viral load, 
female (vs. male) sex, and nutritional supplementation are associ­
ated with better linear growth over time.122,124,130,133,134
Children with HIV may also demonstrate pubertal delay com­
pared with controls, often in close correlation with their growth 
delay.135 Compared with HEU children, girls with HIV enter 
puberty 6 to 8 months later and boys 10 to 11 months later with 
regard to both gonadarche and adrenarche.136 Completion of 
puberty also occurs about 6 months later in children with HIV 
compared to HEU children.135 Lower CD4+ count and higher 
viral load predict later pubertal timing,136 and older age at ART 
initiation is associated with delay later peak height velocity,122 
also suggesting an association between ART timing and pubertal 
timing.
Many factors contribute to the perturbations in growth and 
pubertal timing in children, the largest of which appear to be poor 
nutrition, HIV disease activity and severity before ART, and other 
infectious burden including opportunistic infections. Literature 
does not support an increased prevalence of GH deficiency in 
children with HIV, although children with undernutrition and 
wasting may have GH resistance and lower circulating and/or 
bioavailable IGF1. Evans and colleagues describe lower IGF1 in 
HEU infants, in association with increased C-reactive protein 
(CRP) and CMV viral load, suggesting that, independent of HIV 
itself, inflammation and immune activation may disrupt the GH 
axis.137 Continued research in the HEU population, which repre­
sents a significant and growing percentage of children worldwide, 
is necessary to elucidate alterations in growth and puberty in this 
group. 
Glucose Homeostasis and Pancreatic 
Function
Disorders of glucose homeostasis were relatively infrequent before 
the institution of potent ART but may result from use of specific 
antiretroviral agents and are commonly seen in association with 
dyslipidemia and fat redistribution in the current era of ART (see 
discussion under “Body Composition Changes in People With 
HIV”). The pancreas is a frequent target of opportunistic infec­
tions and malignancies in patients with advanced HIV disease. 
However, clinical endocrine dysfunction rarely results, except in 
cases of massive pancreatic replacement from lymphoma or KS. 
For example, opportunistic infections of the pancreas are seen on 
postmortem examination but are rarely clinically relevant. More 
commonly, pancreatitis and hypoglycemia follow use of certain 
drugs, such as pentamidine, didanosine, or zalcitabine. Hypogly­
cemia can result from pentamidine administration secondary to 
islet cell inflammation and insulin release, especially in the context 
of high-dose therapy and azotemia. Subsequently, chronic hyper­
glycemia from pancreatic β-cell destruction may follow pentami­
dine use. Megestrol acetate use has been associated with new-onset 
diabetes mellitus (DM) because of its potent glucocorticoid 
action. Pancreatitis is common among patients with advanced 
HIV and most often related to a drug effect (i.e., pentamidine, 
trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, didanosine, and zalcitabine). In 
a large study of almost 6000 patients followed for 23,460 person-
years at the Johns Hopkins HIV Clinic, the incidence of acute 
pancreatitis was 5.1/1000 person-years between 2001 and 2006. 
Low CD4 count, aerosolized pentamidine, and female gender 
were associated with pancreatitis. In contrast, specific antiretro­
viral medications were not.138 In the EuroSIDA study, a lower 
incidence of pancreatitis was seen since 2001, 1.27/1000 person-
years, and again low CD4 count was predictive. Similar to the data 
from the Hopkins cohort, no association was seen between cumu­
lative exposure to ART and exposure to didanosine and stavudine, 
nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) that have been 
associated with pancreatitis.139 Amylase levels may also be elevated 
in PWH secondary to macroamylasemia and salivary amylase.
Epidemiology of Diabetes Mellitus and Insulin 
Resistance
Insulin resistance and DM are common among PWH. In an early 
longitudinal study, DM was 3.1 times more likely to develop in 
PWH receiving combination ART than in control subjects.140 
Later studies confirmed increased risk of DM before 2000 but 
found equivalent rates among persons with and without HIV in 
the era of modern ART with agents less likely to contribute to 
glucose abnormalities.141 These estimates suggest a peak incidence 
of 23.2/1000 patient-years immediately before 2000 that has 
decreased to less than 10/1000 patient-years, with no difference 
between subjects naive to and those using ART (Fig. 46.6).142 
However, an analysis comparing a large nationally representative 
population of PWH had an adjusted DM prevalence of 11.8%, 
which was significantly higher than 8.0% DM prevalence in the 
NHANES.143 BMI, lipodystrophy, low CD4 counts, and expo­
sure to specific, older ART medications including stavudine and 
indinavir are predictive of DM in the HIV population.141 PWH 
with impaired glucose tolerance demonstrate hyperinsulinemia, 
suggesting that insulin resistance contributes to the development 
of impaired glucose homeostasis in this population, and PWH 
with prediabetes are more likely to progress to DM than those 
with HIV.144
Hemoglobin A1c (A1c) has been shown to underestimate lev­
els of blood glucose in patients with HIV, particularly those with 
increased mean corpuscular volume resulting from specific ART 
agents.145,146 In one study, use of an A1c cutoff of 5.8% optimized 
the area under the curve for the diagnosis of DM and increased 
sensitivity from 40.9% to 88.8%, while simultaneously decreasing 
1776
SECTION IX    Polyendocrine and Neoplastic Disorders
specificity from 97.5% to 77.5% compared to use of a cutoff of 
6.5%.147 As a result, A1c should be used with caution as the sole 
method of diagnosis in those with HIV.
Insulin resistance among PWH may be caused by the abnor­
mal fat distribution itself (e.g., increased central adiposity, loss of 
peripheral subcutaneous fat, and associated molecular changes). 
These changes include altered cytokines (e.g., low adiponectin, 
increased resistin, or elevated TNF) or changes in other processes 
such as mitochondrial dysfunction, increased lipolysis, increased 
proteolysis, increased expression of suppressor of cytokine signal­
ing 1 (SOCS1),148 and increased accumulation of fat in the muscle 
and liver. Increased inflammation after initiation of ART is associ­
ated with development of DM among PWH,149 and metabolic 
changes may result from persistent microbial translocation across 
the gastrointestinal barrier resulting in increased levels of lipopoly­
saccharide (LPS) in the blood, despite viral suppression.150 Meta­
bolic abnormalities in HIV have been shown to be associated with 
increased levels of retinol-binding protein 4 (RB4), which may 
further contribute to insulin resistance.151 Rarely, insulin receptor 
autoantibodies may develop among patients with HIV experienc­
ing an immune reconstitution syndrome during ART initiation.152 
In addition, significant evidence suggests direct effects of specific 
antiretrovirals to reduce insulin sensitivity. PIs have been shown 
to decrease glucose uptake by inhibiting the transport function 
of GLUT4 (glucose transporter type 4) in vitro153 and have been 
shown to reduce insulin sensitivity in vivo.154 Effects to decrease 
β-cell apoptosis and compromise insulin secretion have also been 
postulated.155 Earlier NRTIs are associated with insulin resistance, 
which may be a direct effect, potentially related to mitochondrial 
toxicity156 or through effects on subcutaneous fat,157 and these 
effects may persist after discontinuation.158 Most recently, inte­
grase strand transfer inhibitors (InSTIs), which are used widely, 
have been associated with diabetes risk.159,160 Further studies are 
needed to understand the underlying mechanisms. As discussed 
later, InSTIs are also associated with weight gain. It is unclear 
whether this is the key underlying factor associated with DM risk. 
For more details of the metabolic effects of specific ART agents, 
see Table 46.1. The specific manifestations and course of DM 
in HIV patients have not been well studied, but initial studies 
suggest an increased risk of albuminuria in patients with HIV, 
particularly those with increased viral load, independent of blood 
pressure.161 In general, the treatment of PWH with DM should 
be similar as the general population, although newer agents with 
potent end-organ benefits, such as GLP1 receptor agonists and 
SGLT2 inhibitors, have not been extensively evaluated in this 
population to date. 
Body Composition Changes in People With 
HIV
Patients with HIV may demonstrate a number of changes in body 
composition. These changes are present to varying degrees among 
patients with HIV and are multifactorial in nature related in part 
to the HIV virus itself, inflammation, specific antiretroviral drugs, 
and the interplay of these factors.162,163 Of importance, some of 
these changes may contribute to increased cardiovascular disease 
(CVD) and respond to variably to changes in ART or lifestyle 
modification (LSM).
The AIDS Wasting Syndrome and Loss of Lean 
Body Mass
Wasting was initially a common feature of advanced HIV disease, 
which was known originally as “slim disease.” The AIDS wasting 
syndrome is defined by weight less than 90% ideal body weight or 
weight loss greater than 10% over 3 months. It is characterized by 
a disproportionate loss of lean body mass, with a relative sparing 
of body fat, particularly in men. In women, fat mass may be lost 
disproportionately with disease progression. The loss of lean body

weakness, and increased resting energy expenditure of 8% to 9% 
are also features of this disease. Cytokines associated with severe 
illness may increase energy expenditure and decrease appetite. In 
addition, chronic weight loss may be associated with gastrointes­
tinal disease, including malabsorption. Weight loss is a significant 
predictor of mortality rate in HIV infection, with BMI less than 
18.4 kg/m2 associated with a 2.2-fold increase in mortality rate 
and BMI less than 16.0 kg/m2 associated with a 4.4-fold increase 
in mortality rate.164 Hypogonadism is observed in 30% to 50% of 
men with AIDS wasting and may contribute to loss of lean body 
mass27 (see discussion under “Gonadal Function”).
Treatment of AIDS Wasting and Loss of Lean Body Mass
Testosterone has been used successfully to increase lean body mass 
in men with AIDS wasting. Randomized studies of intramuscular 
testosterone for hypogonadal men with AIDS wasting suggest a 
beneficial effect of testosterone administration on lean body mass 
(2.0 kg over 6 months) and improved quality of life.165 Short-
term use of anabolic steroids may also be considered in eugonadal 
patients with severe wasting but may be associated with adverse 
effects and should generally be avoided.
A number of studies have investigated androgen administra­
tion to women with HIV and low weight. These studies have 
investigated testosterone using a transdermal patch designed to 
deliver low physiologic doses of 150 to 300 μg/day. Among stud­
ies using the 150-μg/day dose, functional capacity and strength 
significantly improved with a trend toward increased lean body 
mass over 6 months. Hirsutism was not seen, and virilization did 
not occur. An 18-month randomized, placebo-controlled study 
conducted among relatively androgen-deficient women with HIV 
demonstrated that 300 μg/day increased lean body mass and bone 
density at the hip and improved depression indices without aggra­
vation of lipid or glucose parameters.166
Megestrol acetate is a synthetic progestational agent with 
glucocorticoid-like properties. Randomized studies in the litera­
ture show that megestrol acetate increases weight 3 to 4 kg over 
12 weeks with an increase in caloric intake.11,167 However, the 
change in weight is almost entirely fat mass without an increase 
in lean body mass. In addition, megestrol acetate, because of its 
glucocorticoid-like properties, is associated with a number of side 
effects, including hypogonadism and hyperglycemia, and abrupt 
withdrawal can precipitate adrenal crisis. In children, megestrol 
acetate promotes weight gain without improving linear growth.168
In addition, patients with AIDS wasting may demonstrate 
a typical pattern of nutrition-related GH resistance (see discus­
sion under “The Growth Hormone/Insulin-Like Growth Factor 
1 Axis”). These patients exhibit elevated GH levels but decreased 
IGF1, the primary hormone mediating the action of GH on mus­
cle, suggesting GH resistance.169,170 GH has been used in patients 
with HIV to increase lean body mass in sarcopenic patients with 
AIDS wasting. Among patients with AIDS wasting, high-dose, 
supraphysiologic GH (0.1 mg/kg/day) has been investigated. Rel­
atively small but significant effects on weight (1.6 kg) were seen 
over 3 months in a placebo-controlled study.171 GH administra­
tion at 0.1 mg/kg has also been shown to increase work output 
during treadmill exercise171 and quality of life, as well as periph­
eral muscle oxygen extraction and utilization in patients with 
AIDS wasting.172 These studies suggest that large doses of GH 
may be necessary to significantly increase lean mass in patients 
with AIDS wasting and nutritionally mediated resistance to GH. 
However, high-dose GH is associated with side effects including 
hyperglycemia and fluid retention173 and is not well tolerated in 
the long term. For these reasons, caution should be used with 
respect to long-term high doses of GH for treatment of AIDS 
wasting, because this treatment may cause acute and chronic side 
effects of GH excess.
A multidisciplinary approach to the AIDS wasting syndrome 
is most useful. Optimization of ART is paramount in conjunction 
with provision of adequate nutrition and protein intake. However, 
even in this context, weight and muscle loss may occur, because of 
the highly catabolic nature of the disease. In such cases, endocrine 
evaluation should include assessment of gonadal function, which 
will often be reduced. GH levels are increased in AIDS wasting, 
but supraphysiologic administration, as approved by the U.S. 
Food and Drug Administration (FDA), can further increase lean 
body mass. This strategy is best reserved for severe wasting refrac­
tory to other treatments. Other therapeutic strategies that increase 
weight by stimulating appetite, including megestrol acetate, are 
not associated with gain in lean body mass and may be associated 
with side effects. 
Changes in Fat Mass and Distribution
Early in the ART era, loss of abdominal and peripheral subcu­
taneous fat, including loss of subcutaneous fat in the face, was 
very common.174 Other changes have also been seen including 
relative preservation of central fat, with relative and absolute 
accumulation of excess VAT and excess upper trunk fat.174,175 
In addition, ectopic fat collections can be seen, including in 
the dorsocervical area. Increased fat deposition in the liver and 
muscle is also seen and is associated with insulin resistance. In 
prospective studies of ART-naive patients beginning treatment 
in the early 2000s, including an NRTI and PI, initial gains in 
both peripheral subcutaneous and central fat depots are seen 
with reversal of the catabolic wasting state in association with 
control of viral infection. These changes are followed by subse­
quent decreases in peripheral fat and relative preservation and 
even absolute gains in central fat,176 which generally improve, 
but not completely, after switching to ART with fewer metabolic 
side effects.177 More recent data of ART-naive persons initiating 
treatment with more modern regimens suggest increase in both 
subcutaneous and VAT over 96 weeks.178 Data from the Study 
of Fat Redistribution and Metabolic Change in HIV Infection 
(FRAM study) demonstrate that increases in VAT and reduc­
tions in limb fat are independently associated with increased 
mortality rate in PWH (Fig. 46.7).179
The cause of relative central fat accumulation remains unknown. 
For example, it remains unknown whether this is a direct effect of 
specific antiretroviral drugs and whether abnormal nutrient parti­
tioning to relatively preserved central adipose stores, less affected 
by NRTI administration and mitochondrial toxicity, may contrib­
ute. In contrast, a number of mechanisms have been shown to 
contribute to the fat loss seen peripherally. NRTIs variably inhibit 
mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma and contribute to mito­
chondrial dysfunction. Use of specific NRTIs, including older 
NRTIs such as stavudine, has been associated with apoptosis of fat 
and reduced mitochondrial DNA in vitro and in vivo, as well as 
reduced expression of lipid metabolism genes, and clinically with 
reduced subcutaneous fat and lipoatrophy.157,180 PIs may have 
direct effects on adipogenesis (via inhibition of nuclear localiza­
tion of sterol regulatory element–binding protein 1 [SREBP1] 
and reduction in peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor-γ 
[PPARγ] expression).181 NRTIs and PIs have been associated with 
1778
SECTION IX    Polyendocrine and Neoplastic Disorders
increased lipolysis in vivo and in vitro, although new agents in 
these drug classes are less likely to lead to these problems.
Genetic polymorphisms may predispose to changes in body 
composition and metabolic alterations in PWH receiving ART. 
Such findings could indicate a gene-environment interaction con­
tributing to such changes. For example, single nucleotide polymor­
phisms in the resistin gene were seen to predict the development 
of dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and limb fat loss in response 
to a specific antiretroviral regimen.182 In the same study, poly­
morphisms in the hemochromatosis gene and specific mitochon­
drial gene haplotypes were also associated with increased limb fat 
loss.183 Specific haplotypes of the Fas gene (APOC3), PPAR gene, 
and adrenergic receptor have also been associated with the devel­
opment of lipoatrophy.184
Other studies suggest early molecular changes in the fat of 
patients with subsequent peripheral adipose tissue loss. Kratz and 
colleagues showed that reduced expression of messenger RNA 
(mRNA) encoding lipoprotein lipase and the transcription fac­
tors SREBP1, PPARγ, and CCAAT/enhancer binding protein C/
EBPα in thigh subcutaneous fat were associated with the loss of 
fat, before it became evident clinically, whereas increased levels 
of mRNA encoding hydroxysteroid 11β-dehydrogenase 1 and 
the transcription factor C/EBPβ were found in adipose tissue 
from patients with preservation of subcutaneous fat mass.185 The 
expression of the endoribonuclease Dicer, which modulates brown 
and white adipocyte differentiation, was found to be reduced in 
subcutaneous fat of PWH with lipodystrophy, providing a novel 
mechanism for adipose dysfunction in HIV.186 In addition, stud­
ies suggest increased activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldoste­
rone system associated with visceral adipose accumulation in HIV. 
Further evidence of the potential role of the renin-angiotensin-
aldosterone system is provided by evidence that administration 
of the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist eplerenone reduces 
immune activation and improves select metabolic indices in 
PWH.187
Changes in fat distribution have been most widely recognized 
since the introduction of potent ART, but abnormal fat distri­
bution can be seen in ART-naive patients, suggesting that viral 
factors also may contribute. In this regard, adipose tissue dysfunc­
tion may be related to a viral accessory protein, Vpr, which may 
simultaneously coactivate the glucocorticoid receptor and repress 
PPARγ.188
The changes in fat distribution seen among patients with HIV 
bear some similarities to those in Cushing syndrome, with dorso­
cervical fat accumulation and centripetal fat distribution. How­
ever, more specific stigmata of true Cushing syndrome, including 
proximal muscle weakness, facial plethora, thin skin, bruising, 
and violaceous striae, have not been seen, and thus these changes 
constitute a pseudo-Cushing syndrome.189 Miller and cowork­
ers observed normal cortisol levels and adequate suppression in 
response to dexamethasone among PWH with cushingoid fea­
tures.190 Yanovski and associates compared individuals with HIV

with PI-associated lipodystrophic changes in fat to PWH without 
fat changes and those with true Cushing syndrome.191 In contrast 
to patients with true Cushing syndrome, PWH with PI-associated 
lipodystrophy demonstrated normal diurnal variation in cortisol 
levels. Twenty-four-hour urine free cortisol levels were reduced 
and 17-hydroxysteroid levels were increased compared to levels 
in control individuals. Among PWH with changes in fat distri­
bution, increased 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase expression 
in subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) has been demonstrated in 
association with an increased ratio of urinary cortisol to cortisone 
metabolites and may also contribute to increased cortisol produc­
tion.192 In addition, as noted earlier, viral proteins may activate 
the glucocorticoid receptor in specific fat depots.188
Other abnormalities of steroid metabolism have been noted 
in association with changes in fat distribution. In a longitudi­
nal evaluation, the development of lipodystrophy was associated 
with reduced dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), increased cor­
tisol/DHEA ratio, and increased interferon-alpha (IFN-α).193 
Increased cortisol regeneration from affected fat depots may con­
tribute to insulin resistance and further fat redistribution.
Treatments for Visceral Fat Accumulation
LSMs, including exercise, may improve lipid levels and visceral 
adiposity among PWH.194 Progressive resistance training (PRT) 
may also significantly improve glucose homeostasis in PWH 
through a reduction in muscle adiposity.195 Studies of LSMs in 
PWH modeled after the Diabetes Prevention Program demon­
strated improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness and levels of 
high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) and CRP196 but 
did not show significant effects on body composition.
GH has also been used to reduce VAT in PWH with central fat 
accumulation. Lo and coworkers investigated low-dose, long-term 
GH over 18 months in PWH with central fat accumulation and defi­
cient responses to growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH)-
arginine testing. Low-dose GH was shown to reduce VAT by 9% over 
18 months, simultaneously lowering blood pressure and triglyceride 
levels. Even with low-dose GH, however, 2-hour glucose increased, 
demonstrating that GH is potentially useful in decreasing central fat 
accumulation but is hard to titrate in a population with significant 
insulin resistance.197 Largely because of its ability to aggravate glu­
cose, GH was not approved by the FDA for HIV lipodystrophy.
In contrast, GH secretagogues have been used successfully to 
increase lean body mass and reduce visceral and truncal fat, with­
out significant effects on glucose. In the combined analysis of two 
large, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of over 800 
patients, GHRH(1–44) (tesamorelin) reduced VAT by 15.4% rel­
ative to placebo in PWH with central fat accumulation. Improve­
ments were noted in triglyceride levels, equal to 43 mg/dL, total 
cholesterol (TC), and cholesterol-to-HDL ratio. Further improve­
ments in body composition were seen over 12 months (Fig. 
46.8).198 Interestingly, no clinically significant effect to reduce 
SAT was seen, and thus GHRH(1–44) was selective for VAT. 
Use of GHRH(1–44) was associated with physiologic increases in 
IGF1 levels and was not associated with increased glucose or insu­
lin levels, in contrast to low-dose GH. Larger reductions in VAT 
were associated with improvements in lipid and glucose levels, 
as well as adiponectin, suggesting metabolic improvements with 
VAT reduction.199 GHRH(1–44) has also been shown to improve 
liver fat in association with VAT, suggesting beneficial effects on 
other ectopic fat depots.200 Discontinuation of both GH and 
GHRH result in reaccumulation of VAT back to baseline levels, 
demonstrating that the effects of these agents do not outlast the 
treatment period.201,202 GHRH(1–44) was approved by the FDA 
for the treatment of central fat accumulation in PWH in 2010.

SECTION IX    Polyendocrine and Neoplastic Disorders
Treatment of Lipoatrophy
There are no established treatments for lipoatrophy except for 
switching off contributing ART, such as stavudine. However, these 
fat changes are often not completely reversible. Thiazolidinedione 
medications have been associated with increases in subcutaneous 
fat in clinical trials, but generally the magnitude of these changes is 
not clinically relevant.203 Leptin levels are low in association with 
fat loss and lipoatrophy in PWH. Initial small studies of leptin 
administration to PWH with lipoatrophy and reduced leptin 
levels demonstrated significant improvements in insulin sensitiv­
ity, HDL, and triglycerides and reduced truncal and VAT.204,205 
Among patients with mixed lipoatrophy and lipohypertrophy, but 
low leptin levels, leptin administration improved TC and non-
HDL cholesterol, as well as glucose parameters, but not HDL or 
triglyceride or lipid kinetics.206 Because leptin reduces appetite, 
administration may be associated with weight loss. Metreleptin is 
FDA approved for treatment of complications related to congeni­
tal and acquired lipodystrophy, not related to HIV infection or its 
treatment. Further studies are needed to understand the clinical 
potential of leptin to improve metabolic parameters and fat redis­
tribution among PWH. 
Weight Gain in the Modern ART Era: Potential Effects of 
Tenofovir Alafenamide and Integrase Strand Transfer 
Inhibitors
Compared to medications used in the early ART period, such 
as first-generation PIs and thymidine analogues, like stavudine, 
modern ART medications have relatively fewer metabolic com­
plications. However, recent data suggest that some of these widely 
used medications may be associated with weight gain.
The medication class of ART that is most implicated in weight 
gain in PWH is InSTIs. In randomized controlled trials of PWH 
initiating ART, InSTIs, most notably dolutegravir (DTG) and 
bictegravir, have been associated with more weight gain than other 
regimens.207 In the ADVANCE study, for example, ART-naive 
individuals with HIV in South Africa were randomized to one 
of three arms: DTG with TDF/FTC, DTG with TAF/FTC, or 
EFV plus TDF/FTC. Over 96 weeks, those persons randomized 
to DTG gained more weight (mean 7.1 kg with a TAF-containing 
regimen and 4.3 kg with a TDF-containing regimen) compared 
to those randomized to EFV (mean 2.3 kg).208 Obesity incidence 
was also higher in the DTG arms (28% and 18%) versus EFV 
arms (12%) among women, with similar trends in men. Simi­
lar results have been observed in switch studies in which persons 
with controlled HIV on ART are switched from one medica­
tion to another. In an observational study of people switching 
from one ART medication to another, those who switched to 
an InSTI-containing regimen gained an average of 2.9 kg at 18 
months compared with 0.9 kg for those who continued taking 
EFV.209 Preclinical evidence also suggests a direct effect of InSTIs 
on adipose tissue. In a study of InSTI-exposed macaques with­
out HIV infection, DTG exposure was associated with increases 
in adipose tissue fibrosis, adipocyte size, and increase adipogenic 
marker expression, which may be related to inhibition of adipose 
beiging.210,211
Most of the clinical data implicating InSTIs in weight gain 
have compared against EFV. There is some evidence, however, 
that EFV may have specific weight suppressive effects, so when 
compared to InSTIs in ART initiation or switch studies, InSTIs 
show greater weight gain. In a substudy of ADVANCE (described 
above), the investigators examined EFV concentrations in study 
participants to determine whether those with the highest drug 
concentrations would have the least weight gain when initiat­
ing ART; EFV concentrations were inversely related to weight 
gain with ART initiation with an EFV-based regimen.212 Varia­
tions in EFV concentrations in PWH on treatment are related 
to polymorphisms in P450 CYP2B6. In an additional study of 
the ADVANCE population, individuals with CYP2B6 variants 
leading to slower metabolism of EFV (and therefore higher drug 
concentrations) showed the least weight gain.213 Taken together, 
these results suggest that some of the apparent effect of InSTIs 
on weight may be due to weight-suppressive effects of the com­
parator drug, EFV. Ongoing studies that examine whether weight 
decreases after switching off of InSTIs will be essential in evalu­
ating the causal role in InSTIs and provide an evidence base for 
antiretroviral management for weight gain in PWH.
Among drug in the NRTI class, the tenofovir prodrug TAF had 
also been implicated in weight gain in PWH.207,208,214 In the Swiss 
HIV Cohort Study, for example, weight trajectories for those who 
switched to TAF were compared to weight trajectories of people 
who continued on TDF. After 18 months, switching to TAF was 
associated with a greater weight increase compared to continued 
use of TDF. The between-group weight gain difference was 1.1 
kg.215 Although these studies suggest that TAF is associated with 
weight gain, additional evidence from HIV prevention studies in 
which TAF or TDF is given to people without HIV suggests that 
TDF may have mild weight suppressive actions.216,217 Similar to 
switch studies off of InSTIs, studies that examine switches off of 
TAF on weight will be instructive to understand any potential 
direct effects. 
Lipids and Cardiovascular Disease in People 
With HIV
PWH face roughly twofold risk of CVD compared to the general 
population.218 Research over the last two decades has identified 
increased rates of myocardial infarction (MI), cerebrovascular 
events, heart failure (HF), and sudden death among PWH com­
pared to controls.219 Although traditional cardiovascular (CV) 
risk factors like dyslipidemia and cigarette smoking account for 
some of the increased risk, other mechanisms including chronic 
inflammation and immune activation also appear central to CVD 
in PWH. This section briefly describes lipids and CVD risk in 
PWH, with an overview of emerging strategies for management.
Lipid Abnormalities
Lipid abnormalities are highly prevalent among PWH, attrib­
utable both to effects of HIV infection itself and effects of vari­
ous antiretrovirals. Those with HIV not receiving ART generally 
demonstrate reductions in TC, HDL-C, and low-density lipo­
protein cholesterol (LDL-C).220 Hypertriglyceridemia is also 
reported, particularly in those with advanced HIV disease, in 
part to increased hepatic de novo lipogenesis and decreased clear­
ance.221,222 The causes of lipid alteration are not fully elucidated 
but may relate to the effects of viral infection itself and resultant 
inflammation.219,220,223–225 Individuals with HIV receiving ART 
experience increases in TC, LDL-C, and HDL-C compared to 
pre-ART.220 Whereas this may be a “return to health” phenom­
enon in part, antiretrovirals themselves also affect circulating lipid 
levels, with effects varying by ART class and specific antiretrovi­
ral agent. First generation PIs significantly increased LDL-C and 
triglyceride,226 whereas newer PIs atazanavir and darunavir have 
1781
CHAPTER 46  Endocrinology of HIV/AIDS
less adverse effect on circulating lipids.227,228 With regard to the 
most commonly used NRTIs, TAF increases LDL-C, HDL-C, 
and triglyceride compared to TDF, without changes in the ratio 
of TC to HDL-C.229 Compared with TDF, TAF does not increase 
the rate of cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events, such that the 
clinical significance of lipid changes is unclear.230 Some NNRTIs, 
such as efavirenz, may raise TC and LDL-C but also raise HDL 
cholesterol.231 Newer NNRTIs, such as rilpivirine, and etravirine 
have less pronounced effects on the lipid profile compared to efa­
virenz.232–235 Integrase strand transfer inhibitors, such as raltegra­
vir, DTG, elvitegravir, and bictegravir, have a more favorable lipid 
profile compared to PIs.236–239
Current recommendations suggest obtaining lipid levels before 
initiating ART, within 1 to 3 months after starting ART, then up 
to every 6 to 12 months if lipids are abnormal and/or cardiovascu­
lar risk factors are present.240 Management of frank dyslipidemia 
can follow general population guidelines. Of note, however, exist­
ing risk calculators that direct lipid management underestimate 
the risk of CVD in PWH.219 
Atherosclerosis, Myocardial Infarction, and 
Stroke
PWH exhibit increased rates of atherosclerosis compared with 
matched controls, with a relatively higher proportion of plaque 
that is noncalcified and has features causing vulnerability to rup­
ture.241,242 Additionally, individuals with HIV have increased 
arterial inflammation compared to matched controls, in associa­
tion with markers of increased immune activation (Fig. 46.9).243 
Increased vulnerable plaque and inflammation translate into 
increased risk of acute myocardial infarction (AMI), with roughly 
twofold risk of AMI among PWH compared to controls.218,244,245 
Increased risk of AMI in PWH is described in men and women 
across the age spectrum and among individuals with undetectable 
viral load. Further, even “elite controllers” who achieve virologic 
suppression without ART demonstrate increased atherosclerosis 
and immune activation compared to controls.246 Individuals with 
HIV often have multiple traditional risk factors for CVD, includ­
ing cigarette smoking, insulin resistance or DM, atherogenic

dyslipidemia, truncal adiposity and/or obesity, and hypertension 
(HTN).
Traditional risk factors do not fully account for the increased 
risk of AMI in PWH, however. In a large study of patients in a 
major U.S. health care center, Triant and colleagues demonstrated 
an RR of 1.75 (95% CI, 1.51–2.02; p <0.0001) for increased 
MI in individuals with and without HIV in a model accounting 
for age, gender, and race245 (Fig. 46.10). Increased rates of tradi­
tional risk factors, including DM (11.5 vs. 6.6%, HIV-infected 
vs. non–HIV-infected), HTN (21.2 vs. 15.9%), and dyslipidemia 
(23.3 vs. 17.6%), were seen, and each contributed to the increase 
in MI rates (RRs of 1.62, 1.98, and 3.03, respectively, for each 
risk factor). However, regression modeling, accounting for HTN, 
DM, and dyslipidemia, demonstrated that these three risk factors 
contributed to only 25% of the excess risk related to HIV serosta­
tus, suggesting that other factors might contribute. Freiberg and 
associates demonstrated an increased hazard ratio of 1.48 for MI 
among a large cohort of men with HIV in the VA system, control­
ling for Framingham Risk Factors.244
Inflammation and immune activation play an important role 
in increased CVD risk among patients with HIV. Increased CRP 
levels are observed among PWH and predict increased MI rates,247 
and elevated circulating inflammatory cytokines are associated 
with atherosclerosis in PWH.248,249 The SMART (Strategies for 
Management of Antiretroviral Therapy) Study Group demon­
strated an increased rate of cardiovascular events among patients 
randomized to interrupted therapy with less strict goals for con­
trol of immune function.250 Indeed, a 2014 study suggests that 
low CD4 and nadir CD4 are important contributing factors to 
CVD among patients with HIV, suggesting an important role for 
immune dysfunction.251 Markers of monocyte activation, includ­
ing soluble CD163 and CD14, and bacterial translocation have 
been associated with atherosclerotic indices, including carotid 
intima-media thickness and noncalcified coronary plaque among 
PWH.252,253 As in the general population, diabetes is strongly 
associated with CVD risk in PWH, and greater visceral adiposity 
also predicts measures of atherosclerosis in PWH.254,255
PWH also face increased risk of stroke compared with the gen­
eral population, with adjusted hazard ratios ranging from 1.2 in a 
large cohort of men with HIV256 to 1.9 in a large cohort of women 
with HIV.257 Whereas these data are from cohorts primarily com­
prising individuals with treated HIV, data from Malawi demon­
strates increased stroke risk in untreated HIV, as well as in the 6 
months after starting ART, suggesting that immune reconstitu­
tion syndrome could play a role in pathogenesis of stroke immedi­
ately following ART initiation.258 Low CD4+ count substantially 
increases the risk for stroke among PWH, whereas higher CD4+ 
and adequate viral suppression are protective.259,260 
Heart Failure and Sudden Death
Men and women with HIV also have increased risk of HF com­
pared to the general population—both HF with preserved ejec­
tion fraction (HFpEF) and HF with reduced ejection fraction 
(HFrEF).261,262 A recent meta-analysis demonstrated an RR of 
1.8 (95% CI, 1.51–2.15) for HF in PWH compared to con­
trols, with higher RR among younger adults, women, and those 
with low CD4+ count.263 In another recent report, Go et al264 
report an increased risk of incident HF of similar magnitude, also 
reporting higher RR among women and those ≤40 years. Of note, 
increased risk of AMI among PWH explains some but not all of 
the increased risk of HF.262,264
PWH also have increased risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD) 
compared to controls without HIV.265–268 In one large cohort 
study, increased SCD risk was limited to those with CD4+ counts 
<200 cells/mm3 and/or HIV viral load >500 copies/mL, whereas 
others with HIV had a risk similar to the general population.265 
In another recent study, Sardana and colleagues demonstrated 
that HIV confers a 2.5-fold increased risk of out-of-hospital car­
diac arrest (OHCA), after adjustment for risk factors and existing 
comorbidities, including existing CVD. In this cohort, women 
with HIV, younger individuals with HIV, and those with concom­
itant HTN, HF, or chronic kidney disease experienced even higher 
RR of OHCA compared to controls.268 The etiology of SCD in 
PWH is multifactorial and may include existing HF, arrythmias, 
subclinical structural or electrical abnormalities, or substance use. 
Treatment of Hyperlipidemia Among PWH
Treatment for hyperlipidemia among PWH is indicated to 
reduce cardiovascular risk and should proceed according to cur­
rent guidelines. CVD risk prediction equations established in the 
general population, such as Framingham CHD or the American 
College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA 
ASCVD) perform poorly in PWH and tend to underestimate 
true risk269 (Fig. 46.11). An HIV-specific risk prediction equa­
tion established in the Data collection on Adverse Effects of Anti-
HIV Drugs (DAD) Study, which includes HIV-specific variables 
may improve risk prediction compared to the Framingham CHD 
score,270 although this has not been seen in all populations.271 As 
in all patients, healthy nutrition, smoking cessation, regular physi­
cal activity, and limiting alcohol consumption should form the 
foundation of both primary and secondary prevention of CVD.
As in the general population, statins (3-hydroxy-3-methylgl­
utaryl coenzyme A [HMG-CoA] reductase inhibitors) are first-
line for LDL-C reduction and reducing CVD risk among PWH. 
Potential interactions between statins and ART are important in 
selecting therapy. Some antiretrovirals, including ritonavir and 
cobicistat, inhibit cytochrome P450 (CYP450) and can raise 
the concentration of certain statins by severalfold. Simvastatin 
and lovastatin are highly metabolized by CYP450 and should 
generally be avoided in PWH.219 Pravastatin has minimal ART

current antiretrovirals. The high-intensity options of atorvastatin 
and rosuvastatin both have modestly increased serum concentra­
