cautiously in PWH, starting at lower doses.219,240
Although an early report suggested that statins may have 
slightly less efficacy in terms of LDL-C lowering in PWH,272 mul­
tiple studies have since demonstrated beneficial effects of statins to 
improve measures of atherosclerosis and reduce markers of inflam­
mation and immune activation. In the INTREPID trial, men and 
women with HIV were randomized to receive pitavastatin 4 mg 
versus pravastatin 40 mg orally for 52 weeks. Pitavastatin showed 
superior lipid lowering, with a 31% reduction in LDL-C over 12 
weeks and a 30% reduction over 52 weeks, compared to reduc­
tions of 21% and 20.5%, respectively, for pravastatin.273 Both 
pravastatin and pitavastatin reduced oxidized LDL and decreased 
lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A2 (Lp-PLA2) over 52 
weeks, with greater reductions in the pitavastatin group, and 
pitavastatin also decreased soluble CD14.274 Neither pitavastatin 
nor pravastatin significantly affected glucose metabolism.273 The 
SATURN-HIV trial investigated the effects of rosuvastatin 10 mg 
daily vs. placebo on markers of CVD risk and immune activa­
tion in PWH receiving ART. Compared with placebo, 48 weeks 
of rosuvastatin decreased Lp-PLA2 along with the proportion of 
activated monocytes and T cells.275 Rosuvastatin use in PWH is 
associated with increases in fasting insulin and HOMA-IR, but 
it is unclear if this translates to an increased risk of diabetes.276 
A randomized trial of atorvastatin treatment for 1 year in PWH 
demonstrated that, compared to placebo, atorvastatin reduced 
noncalcified plaque volume and high-risk plaque features.277
Effects of statins on clinical events have not yet been reported 
in large randomized controlled trials. A large, placebo-controlled 
randomized trial examining the effect of pitavastatin on clinical 
events, called REPRIEVE, is underway in PWH who do not have 
an indication for statin therapy.278 Inhibition of proprotein con­
vertase subtilisin kexin-9 (PCSK-9) offers an additional treatment 
strategy for PWH at high CVD risk.279 PCSK-9 levels were found 
to be higher in PWH compared to matched HIV-uninfected 
controls and were related to markers of monocyte activation.280 
Further, PCSK-9 levels decrease with initiation of ART.281 In a 
randomized, placebo-controlled trial of the PCSK-9 inhibitor 
evolocumab in PWH, Boccara and colleagues reported that evo­
locumab reduced LDL-C by 57%, achieving LDL-C <70 mg/dL 
in 73% of patients, with good tolerance and similar adverse events 
between placebo and evolocumab.282
Severe hypertriglyceridemia should be treated to reduce the risk 
of pancreatitis. An initial option in patients with severe elevations 
in triglyceride levels is to switch to an ART regimen less likely to 
cause dyslipidemia. Triglyceride levels are reduced approximately 
20% by diet283 and 30% by exercise284 in those with HIV. Neither 
diet nor exercise is likely to normalize triglyceride levels in those 
with severe dyslipidemia, however. Fenofibrate resulted in a 40% 
reduction in triglyceride levels and a 14% reduction in TC levels 
over 3 months in patients with HIV and hypertriglyceridemia.285 
Lesser but nonetheless beneficial effects may be seen with gemfi­
brozil or other fibrate derivatives. Niacin also significantly reduces 
triglyceride level but may worsen glucose tolerance in PWH, 
although such changes in glucose may only be transient.286,287 
Studies also suggest the efficacy of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty 
acids, which were shown to reduce triglyceride levels by 25.5% and 
be well tolerated in a randomized, placebo-controlled study.288 In 
a study investigating combined therapy, triglyceride levels were 
reduced by 65.5% among hypertriglyceridemic patients with HIV 
receiving simultaneous fenofibrate and fish oil.289 Comparing fish 
oil to gemfibrozil, fibrates, and atorvastatin in hypertriglyceride­
mic patients with HIV, fish oil was shown to decrease triglyceride 
by 45 mg/dL, whereas fibrates (−66 mg/dL), but not atorvastatin 
(−39 mg/dL), were more effective in this regard.290 
Antiinflammatory Strategies for Cardiovascular 
Disease in HIV
Given the important role of inflammation and immune activa­
tion in CVD pathogenesis among PWH, investigators have more 
recently pursued antiinflammatory strategies to improve endothe­
lial function and reduce arterial inflammation. Aspirin therapy 
over 12 weeks at doses of 100 mg or 300 mg did not affect circu­
lating markers of immune activation or inflammation;291 to our 
knowledge, no primary or secondary prevention trials of aspirin’s 
effect on CVD events exist specifically in PWH. A randomized 
trial of the dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor sitagliptin in 
PWH also showed no effect on soluble CD14 or markers of lym­
phocyte or monocyte activation, although sitagliptin decreased 
the inflammatory chemokine CXCL10.292 Ruxolitinib, which 
inhibits Jak 1/2, decreased markers of immune activation and was 
well tolerated, although larger studies are needed to fully elucidate 
clinical effects.293 Cenicriviroc, a dual CCR2 and CCR5 antago­
nist, improved circulating markers of fibrosis in individuals with 
HIV and currently is being tested in a larger study to assess effects 
on inflammation and immune activation.294 Other possible strat­
egies include use of pentoxifylline, canakinumab, and methotrex­
ate, but safety and efficacy of these agents in the HIV population 
remain unclear. Use of statins may also be beneficial as an antiin­
flammatory strategy, as they may lower CRP and have pleiotropic 
effects on monocyte activation.

KEY POINTS
 • 
SARS-CoV-2 can target all endocrine tissues either directly or 
indirectly.
 • 
Obesity and diabetes mellitus are major risk factors for disease 
severity.
 • 
Thyroid and pituitary damage is underrecognized after SARS-CoV-2 
infection/vaccination.
 • 
Islet cells may also be targeted by viral infection and this may 
cause de novo occurrence of diabetes mellitus.
 • 
Low vitamin D levels have been associated with acute COVID-19 
outcomes, long COVID occurrence, and decreased persistence 
of immune response to COVID-19 vaccination.

Acute and Chronic COVID-19 and the 
Endocrine System
ANDREA GIUSTINA AND CLIFFORD J. ROSEN
Introduction and Overview of COVID-19 and 
Endocrine Disorders
Since January 2020 nearly 1 billion people have been infected 
worldwide with the SARS-CoV-2 virus, the vast majority of 
whom have developed COVID-19, the disease.1 COVID-19 has 
also resulted in nearly 7 million deaths, primarily as a result of 
pulmonary injury and its subsequent cardiovascular comorbidi­
ties. Despite the availability of several vaccines and boosters, the 
pandemic continues, and the cost to society mounts.2 Recent viral 
subvariants of omicron have rapidly spread across most countries, 
with significant morbidity and mortality. These subvariants (e.g., 
BA.4 and BA.5) resemble BA.2 but have greater infectivity than 
the original omicron, albeit potentially less lethal. The clinical 
characteristics of the acute syndrome of SARS-CoV-2 infection 
can be variable, but predominantly begin with upper respiratory 
symptoms that are associated with gastrointestinal complaints, 
fatigue, loss of taste and smell, malaise, and fever.2 Multisystem 
involvement can follow the acute onset, particularly pulmonary, 
cardiovascular, and hematologic, and tissue damage is further 
complicated by release of potent immune-mediated cytokines.3 
The endocrine system is not immune to the acute inflammatory 
response to the virus, especially metabolic aspects. Treatments for 
acute COVID-19 can worsen the metabolic response, but it is clear 
that the pituitary, thyroid, and pancreas can be targeted directly by 
the virus, as well as being involved the immune response.4 More 
longer term respiratory disease further stresses these responses and 
is often manifested by glucose intolerance or frank type 2 diabetes 
mellitus (T2DM).5
Although the majority of individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 
recover, there is a significant subpopulation of patients with per­
sistent symptoms 4 weeks and beyond after infection, even among 
those who suffered from mild to moderate COVID-19. Symptoms 
include brain fog, exertional fatigue, dyspnea, chest tightness, 
gastrointestinal disturbances, and vertigo.2,3,6 Those symptoms 
and their resultant clinical signs (e.g., glucose intolerance, sleep 
disorders, postural hypotension, cardiac arrythmias, neuropathy) 
may also represent prodromes to future health threats such as the 
development of autoimmune diseases. In addition, gender, age, 
and social determinants of health are certain to be determinants of 
longer term symptomatology.6 The term post-acute sequelae of CoV-
2 (PASC) is a label for those who suffer from symptoms after acute 
COVID-19, although the lay terminology “long COVID” is often 
used interchangeably. However, because the clinical spectrum of 
COVID-19 continues to evolve due to differences in substrains, 
vaccines, and susceptibility by ethnicity and race, post–COVID-
19 syndromes also have changed.7 Since October 2021 there has 
been an ICD-10 code UO9.9 for PASC, which can be applied 
1785
CHAPTER 47  Acute and Chronic COVID-19 and the Endocrine System
from common diagnostics, treatment-oriented procedures, symp­
toms, and medications associated with these patients. The N3C 
consortium has algorithmically clustered three major categories of 
PASC using machine learning and the U09.9: cardiopulmonary, 
neurologic, and metabolic.8 Nevertheless, the overall syndrome 
complex remains to be fully defined. Moreover, because of the 
variable presentation, symptom complex, and duration of PASC, 
it has been a challenge to develop therapeutic approaches beyond 
conventional support. There is, however, emerging evidence that 
glucose intolerance and/or T2DM is more likely during the first 
year after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Other endocrine manifestations 
are just emerging, beyond the metabolic syndrome and T2DM, 
including autoimmune thyroid disease, adrenal insufficiency, and 
pituitary disease.9
In this chapter we characterize how the pathophysiology of 
acute COVID-19 and how it relates to endocrine complications, 
as well as the bi-directional nature of the interaction between 
viral infection and host metabolic state. We critically examine 
whether the vitamin D pathway is involved in the acute and 
chronic syndrome and whether therapeutic vitamin D has an 
impact on the clinical course of COVID-19 and PASC. 
COVID-19 and Diabetes Mellitus
Prevalence of Diabetes Mellitus in COVID-19
Diabetes mellitus may predispose to infections, the risk of which 
can be reduced by appropriate glycemic control. In fact, all patients 
with diabetes (over 2 years old) should undergo influenza vaccina­
tion.10 Diabetes mellitus is one of the most frequent comorbidities 
in hospitalized COVID-19 patients ranging from 7.3% in China 
to 18% in South Korea and 43.3% in U.S. veterans.11,12 In fact, 
the most frequent phenotype of a COVID-19 patient requiring 
hospitalization is an aged male with metabolic comorbidities, 
including diabetes mellitus and obesity, as well as hypertension, 
coronary heart disease, and cerebrovascular disease.13 There is no 
evidence, however, that diabetic patients are at greater risk of con­
tracting SARS-CoV-2. Rather, the clinical course is worse (see fol­
lowing discussion).14 It may be different for obesity, where at least 
one study suggests a greater risk of infection.15 
Increased Risk of Morbidity and Mortality in 
Patients With Diabetes and COVID-19
Experimental data suggest that diabetes causes several structural 
changes, such as increased vascular permeability and collapsed 
alveolar epithelium in the lung.16 Hyperglycemia may also induce 
respiratory dysfunction that is worsened in patients with diabetes 
affected by COVID-19, who may show deteriorated pulmonary 
radiologic scores.17,18 Moreover, renin-angiotensin system dys­
regulation, excessive protein glycation affecting immunoglobu­
lins, the degree of expression of angiotensin-converting enzyme 
2 (ACE2), procoagulative state, bacterial superinfection, and 
low vitamin D levels may also contribute to worse outcomes in 
patients with diabetes and COVID-19.19,20 Recent evidence sug­
gests that endotrophin, a peptide fragment of Col6A3, is associ­
ated with T2DM and chronic inflammation of adipocytes with 
fibrosis,21 although evidence that endotrophin is a marker of acute 
or long COVID-19 is lacking. Pulmonary fibrosis during SARS-
CoV-2 infection includes extracellular matrix remodeling with the 
deposition of collagen fragments that induce scarring and may be 
exaggerated in patients with diabetes.22 In a cohort of deceased 
hospitalized COVID-19 patients from the UK, 32% had T2DM 
and 1.5% had type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) with male sex, 
older age, renal impairment, non-White ethnicity, socioeconomic 
deprivation, previous stroke, and heart failure being risk factors 
for increased COVID-19–related mortality.23 Diabetes was also 
associated in a U.S. cohort with longer hospital stay and the need 
for assisted ventilation and intensive care unit (ICU) admission.24
Higher mortality rates in either T1DM or T2DM with SARS-
CoV-2 can be traced to coexisting comorbidities, but may also be 
associated with deranged glycometabolic control.25,26 Indeed, the 
most recent HbA1c before COVID-19 occurrence was shown to 
have a linear relationship with outcomes and in particular with 
mortality when HbA1c was greater than 10% in either T2DM or 
T1DM. Conversely, low HbA1c was significantly associated with 
an increased mortality risk in T2DM.23 The impact of obesity 
on the background of diabetes was reported to worsen mortality 
and other relevant clinical outcomes.23 Current glycometabolic 
control and fluctuations of blood glucose during the first days of 
hospitalization were reported to be determinants of length of stay, 
ICU requirement, and mortality, particularly in patients treated 
with high-dose glucocorticoids and consequent need of concomi­
tant intensive insulin treatment.27
Interestingly, preexisting microvascular diabetic damage 
including severe retinopathy, which has also been associated with 
low vitamin D,28 may predict adverse outcomes in COVID-
19 patients.29 In fact, in hospitalized COVID-19 patients with 
poorly controlled diabetes, retinopathy was independently associ­
ated with a higher risk of intubation. Therefore, it may be hypoth­
esized that diabetic microangiopathy could be a surrogate marker 
of endothelial dysfunction/damage, which may in turn predispose 
to severe tissue damage seen in COVID-19.30 However, it is also 
possible that the damaged retina in diabetes predisposes to viral 
persistence in the eye, as has been noted for other viruses such as 
HIV.
In people with diabetes, SARS-CoV-2 infection may induce a 
worsening of glycometabolic control as can occur with virtually 
every infectious disease, but may be exaggerated with COVID-
19.31 Therefore, close monitoring of blood glucose and urinary 
ketones measurement is recommended in T1DM patients with 
fever and hyperglycemia who should also proactively adapt insulin 
(basal and/or bolus) dose to maintain euglycemia.4 Insulin is the 
most effective antihyperglycemic agent in hospitalized seriously ill 
patients such as those with COVID-19, particularly when under 
high-dose dexamethasone treatment, although recently potential 
negative effects of its use on disease progression in patients with 
T2DM have been hypothesized.14,32,33
Use of metformin and statins was reported to be associated 
with decreased disease severity and mortality, suggesting the 
opportunity to continue these treatments during hospitalization 
for COVID-19, if there are no specific contraindications.34,35 
Controversial data were reported on the use of GLP1 analogues 
and DPP4i on outcomes of hospitalized COVID-19 patients with 
diabetes.36–38 In fact, some studies showed protective effects on 
severe disease,36,37 and others an associated higher risk of poor 
prognosis with DPP4i but not GLP1 analogues.38 Treatment of 
patients with diabetes with antihypertensive drugs, including 
ACE inhibitors, was not associated with increased mortality.39 
COVID-19 and New-Onset Diabetes
A possible bidirectional relationship between diabetes and 
COVID-19 has consistently been reported.40–42 SARS-CoV-2 can 
1786
SECTION IX    Polyendocrine and Neoplastic Disorders
directly damage pancreatic β-cells, which abundantly express the 
ACE2 receptor and/or increase insulin resistance.43 Therefore, this 
may be an additional cause of worsening hyperglycemia observed 
in patients with known diabetes affected by COVID-19. Such 
deterioration can lead to other clinical consequences such as keto­
acidosis with greater insulin requirements.44 New-onset diabetes 
in COVID-19 patients who were previously nondiabetic has been 
widely reported, leading to the hypothesis of a potential diabeto­
genic action of SARS-CoV-2.45–47
Recent research has highlighted several potential mechanisms 
related to hyperglycemia during acute COVID-19. Overwhelm­
ing cytokine release can lead to glucose intolerance, as well as glu­
cocorticoids that are used to treat moderate to severe infections.48 
Transient β-cell dysfunction, particularly in individuals who are 
obese, may also contribute to hyperglycemia.49 Much work has 
focused on adipose tissue alterations that can drive insulin resis­
tance. Obesity and the metabolic syndrome are associated with 
a proinflammatory state, and as lipid storage increases in adipo­
cytes, macrophage recruitment occurs. These can induce adipo­
kine and cytokine release, and further hyperglycemia with insulin 
resistance.50 The transient or persistent nature of this new-onset 
hyperglycemia in COVID-19 as well as its true incidence and 
metabolic characterizations are still not entirely known, and inter­
national registry efforts are ongoing in order to collect and analyze 
cases of COVID-19–related diabetes worldwide.40 Importantly, 
persistent hyperglycemia and insulin resistance may predispose to 
postacute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection.51 
Obesity and COVID-19
Impact of Obesity on Susceptibility to SARS-
CoV-2 and on Clinical Outcome of Patients With 
Acute COVID-19
It is well known that obesity, particularly when severe, is com­
monly associated with altered pulmonary function, pneumonia, 
and respiratory failure.52 Furthermore, T2DM, hypertension, 
cardiovascular disease, hypovitaminosis D, and kidney disease are 
common comorbidities in obesity and could negatively affect out­
comes in respiratory infections and COVID-19.20,53 Additionally, 
elevated expression of ACE2 in adipose tissue may lead to pro­
longed exposure to SARS-CoV-2 making obese patients more sus­
ceptible and vulnerable to the infection.54 Obesity is also known 
to be a state of low-grade chronic inflammation, cytokine activa­
tion, with altered adiponectin versus leptin ratio, innate and adap­
tive immunity dysfunction, and hypercoagulability with increased 
risk of thrombosis, may all be relevant contributing factors to poor 
prognosis in obese COVID-19 patients.55–57
Limited evidence has been published on susceptibility to SARS-
CoV-2 infection in patients with obesity, whereas there are several 
reports showing the negative impact of obesity on the clinical his­
tory of COVID-19. A study of a large Spanish cohort of persons 
diagnosed in an outpatient setting with COVID-19 reported an 
obesity-associated increased risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection (haz­
ard ratio 1.23 [1.21–1.25]).12 In a recent meta-analysis of 19 stud­
ies 32% prevalence of obesity in hospitalized COVID-19 patients 
increasing to 41% and 43% when COVID-19 patients admit­
ted to intensive care or needing invasive mechanical ventilation 
were considered, respectively. Finally, a 33% prevalence in those 
patients who died was reported.58 A comparative assessment of 
over 900,000 U.S. COVID-19 hospitalized patients reported that 
in 63.5% cardiometabolic conditions were present as risk factors, 
with obesity accounting for 30.2% of the cases independently of 
age for body mass index (BMI) up to 40 kg/m2.59 On the other 
hand, severe obesity represented a stronger risk factor for hospi­
talization in the youngest women.59 Furthermore, several meta-
analyses pointed to obese people as being at increased risk of poor 
outcomes, including hospitalization, admission in ICU, and need 
for mechanical ventilation (odds ratio 1.39–2.4).58,60,61
However, data on impact of obesity on COVID-19 mortality 
are not conclusive. The American Heart Association’s COVID-19 
Cardiovascular Disease Registry collected 7606 patients’ data with 
a 17% mortality rate and reported that severe obesity may be asso­
ciated with increased risk of in-hospital death (hazard ratio, 1.26 
[95% CI, 1.00–1.58]), particularly in relatively younger patients 
(age less than 50 years).62 This currently prevalent view is confirmed 
by the UK Biobank study on more than 500,000 persons (hazard 
ratios for obesity and COVID-19 mortality 2.21 [1.69; 2.88] for 
females and 1.78 [1.44; 2.21] for males),63 although other studies 
were not able to find a significant impact of obesity on mortality 
in COVID-19 patients.64,65 These discrepancies in mortality data 
were also reflected by different meta-analyses60,61 reporting either 
significantly increased relative risk (1.09) in COVID-19–related 
mortality in obese people60 or only a trend toward this associa­
tion that did not reach statistical significance.61 This is likely due 
to differences in included study populations with variable degree 
of obesity and of disease severity. Finally, the potential protective 
effect of mild obesity on COVID-19 mortality (obesity survival 
paradox) has been suggested but not yet clearly demonstrated.66-68
Based on these caveats, it has been suggested that anthropo­
metric parameters should be assessed in patients with a positive 
SARS-CoV-2 test as a part of routine risk profile evaluation since 
obese patients with COVID-19 should be considered as a high-
risk population who may undergo specific prevention, detection, 
and follow-up/treatment measures in order to avoid unfavorable 
outcomes.4 Importance of weight control, as well as of blood pres­
sure or glucose control, was further emphasized in the context 
of the COVID-19 pandemic.69 Management of COVID-19–
hospitalized patients with obesity, particularly in the ICU, was 
complicated by difficult venous access, weight limits of imaging 
machines, and small number of bariatric beds.14 Finally, lockdowns 
and mobility restrictions, together with preventive social isolation 
measures (with their behavioral and emotional implications), 
resulted in lifestyle changes that aggravated weight problems in 
obese people and increased the chances for weight gain in previ­
ously normal-weight subjects, particularly if inadequate dietary, 
physical activity, and sleep regimens were followed.70 Sarcopenic 
obesity has been recognized as a state of frailty,71 and although its 
definition is still not precisely defined, sarcopenia is reported in 
systematic reviews and meta-analyses to be highly prevalent and to 
have negative prognostic significance in COVID-19.72–74 
Bone and Mineral Metabolism in COVID-19
Hypocalcemia, hypovitaminosis D, and vertebral fractures 
were the three components of the osteometabolic phenotype of 
COVID-19 that were recently described.75,76
Hypocalcemia
Hypocalcemia is a major biochemical finding in COVID-
19.77,78 It was first reported in an Italian patient hospitalized with 
COVID-19 showing very low calcium levels in whom subclinical 
1787
CHAPTER 47  Acute and Chronic COVID-19 and the Endocrine System
hypoparathyroidism also was suspected due to previous total thy­
roidectomy.79 Thereafter, in the first study conducted on a series of 
more than 500 COVID-19 patients, hypocalcemia was found to 
be highly prevalent80 and associated with inflammatory markers. 
Hypocalcemia was also found to be an independent predictor of 
hospitalization.80 These data were confirmed by many other subse­
quent studies showing low calcium levels in SARS-CoV-2–infected 
subjects with independent association with poor prognosis in terms 
of ICU admission and mortality.76 Importantly, this predictive role 
was observed also for ionized calcium,80 because low albumin due 
to severe illness could complicate interpretation of total calcium 
levels.81 Finally, it was suggested that hypocalcemia may represent 
a peculiar feature of COVID-19 being more frequent than in non–
COVID-19–hospitalized patients.82 Mechanistically, widespread 
vitamin D deficiency associated with an impaired PTH compensa­
tory response may predispose to the occurrence of hypocalcemia,83 
which in turn may be triggered by intracellular and extracellular dis­
turbance in calcium handling due either to calcium-dependent viral 
mechanism of action or to tissue changes such as calcium deposits 
and precipitation in muscle, altered coagulative (prothrombotic) 
status, acute malnutrition from critical illness, or elevated levels of 
unbound and unsaturated fatty acids due to systemic inflamma­
tion.84–88 COVID-19 hypocalcemia, although infrequently severe, 
may have a potential impact on COVID-19 patients with cardiac 
and neurologic disorders.75,89 Therefore, people with postsurgical 
hypoparathyroidism, also if mild and untreated, and particularly 
if obese/overweight,90 who are infected with SARS-CoV-2 should 
undergo strict calcium monitoring on hospital admission and dur­
ing hospitalization.75 Acute COVID-19 could represent an event 
in which treatment of the underlying disease may be even more 
important in order to prevent acute hypocalcemia, and calcium 
should not be discontinued or downtitrated (e.g., for tolerability 
or compliance issues).90,91 
Vitamin D and COVID-19
Vitamin D deficiency is widespread in Mediterranean countries 
in which food is not fortified with vitamin D as in the North of 
Europe where vitamin D levels in the blood are higher (the so-
called Scandinavian paradox).92 COVID-19 was reported to be 
more prevalent and severe according to latitude and sun irradia­
tion.93 Moreover, the pandemic forcing many elderly subjects to 
home confinement may have further contributed to the deterio­
ration of their vitamin D status, and hypovitaminosis D was in 
turn suggested to have negative clinical effects in ICU patients 
in whom supplementing vitamin D could improve their out­
comes.94,95 Because vitamin D plays a relevant role in regulating 
innate and adaptive immune response, its deficiency may predis­
pose to systemic infections such as COVID-19 with a possible 
protective role of vitamin D supplementation in acute respiratory 
infections.96,97 Moreover, vitamin D may also play a further spe­
cific role in COVID-19 downregulating ACE2 and modulating 
proinflammatory cytokines, which may result in counteracting 
the cytokine storm.98
Several studies from different geographic areas reported from the 
beginning of the pandemic showed that low vitamin D levels were 
present in hospitalized patients even after adjustment for confound­
ing factors compared with the general population.20,99 Low vitamin 
D status was consistently reported to predict severity of COVID-19 
in terms of clinical outcomes and lung involvement (as defined by 
chest computed tomography stages)100–103 and even mortality. It 
was also associated with endocrine comorbidities such as diabetes 
and obesity that impair prognosis of COVID-19.104 Whether low 
vitamin D is a consequence and a marker of acute illness or may 
have a causal role in this clinical context remains to be established. 
In fact, impaired vitamin D status predicts poor outcomes in 
patients hospitalized with mild acute COVID-19.104a However, in 
individuals at high concomitant risk of COVID-19 and hypovita­
minosis D (elderly with diabetes and obesity), particularly if living 
in areas characterized by widespread vitamin D deficiency, reinstat­
ing through supplementation adequate vitamin D status may have 
a preventive role in the context of COVID-19,105 much like other 
acute respiratory tract infections.106 Interestingly, recent meta-anal­
yses of interventional studies in the context of acute illness (i.e., 
in hospitalized COVID-19 patients) consistently report a positive 
effect of vitamin D supplementation on clinical outcomes,107,108 
although specific trials have led to conflicting results. In some 
clinical trials, vitamin D administration significantly improved 
clinical outcomes in COVID-19–hospitalized patients with pneu­
monia109,110; however, in other studies, no significant effects on 
some endpoints were reported.111 Differences in baseline vitamin 
D status and other confounding factors such as differences in doses 
(high vs. standard, single bolus vs. daily) or types of vitamin D used 
as well as in disease severity may at least in part explain these con­
flicting results. 
Vertebral Fractures
Vertebral fractures detected opportunistically on cross-sectional 
chest x-rays performed at admission and submitted to mor­
phometric analysis were reported to be highly prevalent (36%) 
in a single-center cohort of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 
suggesting that such fractures were among the most common 
comorbidities in this population.112 Moreover, COVID-19 
patients with vertebral fractures, particularly if severe, at hospi­
tal referral showed a higher mortality risk compared with sub­
jects without vertebral fractures. Finally, fractured subjects were 
older and with more compromised clinical pictures including an 
increased need of mechanical ventilation.112
Vertebral fractures may predispose COVID-19 patients to 
develop more severe impairment of respiratory function, also 
increasing the pneumonia risk. Vertebral fractures may also repre­
sent a marker of frailty, thus predicting poor outcome.112 There­
fore, it was recommended not to stop antiosteoporotic therapy 
during the pandemic, including the monoclonal antibody deno­
sumab. In regard to this drug there is no evidence that osteopo­
rosis treatments predispose to severe COVID-19.113 Finally, since 
vertebral fractures are often asymptomatic and largely frequent in 
the general, and male, population, it may be worth proactively 
searching for vertebral fractures on chest radiograms in order to 
better predict the risk of severe disease.112 
The Pituitary and COVID-19
Recent autopsy studies detected SARS-CoV-2 antigens and 
its genome in two-thirds of pituitary glands from patients who 
died from COVID-19, but not in controls,114 whereas pituitary 
hormone mRNA and their regulatory genes were found to be 
suppressed in all COVID-19 cases independently from virus posi­
tivity.114 This direct involvement of the gland in COVID-19 is 
likely due to the expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 receptors in 
pituitary tissue.115 The result of this targeting includes the clinical 
syndromes of pituitary apoplexy, hyponatremia, and hypophysitis, 
which in turn may cause hypopituitarism.116 Moreover, pituitary 
1788
SECTION IX    Polyendocrine and Neoplastic Disorders
diseases including acromegaly, Cushing disease, and hypopitu­
itarism may indirectly expose affected patients to higher risk to 
develop COVID-19 due to comorbidities such as diabetes mel­
litus, obesity, and vertebral fractures, which may per se predispose 
to severe disease.116
Recently, several series of cases of pituitary apoplexy in asso­
ciation with COVID-19 were reported in the context of the neu­
rovascular manifestations of COVID-19, either in the presence 
of or without a preexisting pituitary adenoma.117,118 Endothelial 
cells of the cerebrovascular system may be damaged by SARS-
CoV-2. The virus can also enter the brain via the olfactory nerve 
or through the median eminence.119 In addition, SARS-CoV-2 
infection is able to trigger pituitary autoimmunity and was 
associated with immune-mediated hypophysitis.120,121 Moder­
ate to mild hyponatremia (serum Na range 130–135 mmol/L) 
was observed in up to 50% of COVID-19–hospitalized patients 
causing presenting signs in some cases, and predicting severity 
of the disease.122,123 Hyponatremia was related to syndrome of 
inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) possibly mediated 
by increased interleukin-6 (IL6) and consequent nonosmotic 
secretion of vasopressin.124 Therefore, in all patients admitted 
to the hospital with COVID-19, monitoring and, in case of 
clinically relevant hyponatremia, adequate sodium correction 
are recommended.125
According to an international survey,126 COVID-19 negative 
effects on acromegaly care included delayed neurosurgical cure 
similar to all pituitary tumors. In fact, SARS-CoV-2 infection 
dramatically impaired the operations of neurosurgical depart­
ments, which were functioning only for urgent surgical proce­
dures with consequent long delays of interventions for benign 
tumors, such as pituitary adenomas. However, this could be dan­
gerous particularly for patients with aggressive tumors, although 
neurosurgery may be burdened by the risk intrinsic to endonasal 
surgery due to intraoperative SARS-CoV-2 aerosolization.127,128 
These risks can be minimized if adequate preventive measures are 
implemented.129
Patients with Cushing disease were reported to be at higher 
risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 due to the excess 
glucocorticoid-mediated immunosuppressive effect.130 Moreover, 
as in acromegaly Cushing comorbidities such as hypertension, 
obesity, and diabetes, which are all known to be negative prog­
nostic factors for COVID-19, could contribute to this increased 
risk.131,132 In fact, severe disease was reported particularly in active 
Cushing patients.133
The existence of a bidirectional relationship between hypo­
pituitarism and COVID-19 has been hypothesized because, in 
addition to direct or indirect SARS-CoV-2–mediated pituitary 
damage, it is characterized by the aforementioned metabolic 
comorbidities, which also affect conditions of hyperpituita­
rism.116 Among the single hormonal components of hypo­
pituitarism, adrenal insufficiency was thought to be a risk for 
COVID-19, as for other infections, due to impaired immune 
activity.134 However, an Italian survey on more than 200 patients 
showed that, in either primary or secondary hypoadrenalism, 
there were similar clinical manifestations linked to SARS-CoV-2 
infection as well as COVID-19 outcomes versus controls.135 
These data, which were obtained in patients submitted to strict 
follow-up, monitoring, and adequate training for infection 
prevention, suggested that optimal hormonal management of 
this condition, including correct and early application of sick-
day rules, can be crucial in prevention of COVID-19 in these 
patients.14 
Thyroid and COVID-19
Thyroid abnormalities that may occur in COVID-19 patients 
include either direct damage due to SARS-CoV-2 or indirect 
through immunologic mechanisms and in some instances also 
sick euthyroid syndrome.136 Subacute thyroiditis reported in sev­
eral patients with COVID-19 was defined as atypical because it 
is painless and may be characterized by thyrotoxicosis followed 
in some instances by hypothyroidism without elevated thyroid 
autoantibodies.137,138 Nevertheless, SARS-CoV-2 cytokine storm 
may be associated also with thyroid autoimmunity that may be 
complicated by thyrotoxicosis, Graves ophthalmopathy, and pri­
mary hypothyroidism.139 Euthyroid sick syndrome was frequently 
observed in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, particularly when 
admitted in ICUs, who show low to normal thyroid function and 
thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) without clinical manifesta­
tions of hypothyroidism.140
Symptoms of agranulocytosis (a rare side effect of antithyroid 
drugs used in the treatment of Graves disease) may overlap with 
those of COVID-19, and therefore close monitoring is suggested 
in hyperthyroid patients starting medical treatment during the 
COVID-19 pandemic.141 Long-term outcomes of COVID-19–
related delays in diagnostic procedures of thyroid nodules as well 
as thyroid surgery, particularly for differentiated thyroid tumors, 
remains to be assessed prospectively.142 
Sex Hormones and COVID-19
Epidemiologic data suggest that women and men are similarly sus­
ceptible to SARS-CoV-2 infection.2,143 However, there is evidence 
that men are at higher risk of COVID-19 morbidity and mortal­
ity, with an odds ratio of 2.8 to 3 and 1.4 to 1.7 for ICU admis­
sion and death in males versus females.144 Behavioral aspects such 
as smoking might contribute to these differences in COVID-19 
outcomes, as well as higher prevalence of comorbidities and lower 
frequency of treatment with vitamin D in males versus females.143
Sexual dimorphic COVID-19 outcome may be based on the viral 
entry into the body as well as on immune system differences.2 SARS-
CoV-2 enters the cells through ACE2 and TMPRSS2, the transcrip­
tion of which is influenced by androgens in epithelial cells of the 
lung.145 On the other hand, different responses to infection in males 
versus females were previously reported.146 Women with COVID-
19 appeared to have more effective T-cell response than men.147 
COVID-19 Vaccination and Endocrine 
Diseases
COVID-19 vaccination represented a population worldwide effort 
and its risk/benefit profile in clinical trials was excellent.148,149 
However, possible endocrine side effects of thyroid, pituitary, and 
glucose metabolism have emerged during its widespread use. In 
particular, in the former, several sporadic cases of subacute thyroid­
itis and of Graves disease occurring after COVID-19 vaccination 
were recently reported, likely linked to ASIA, that is, the autoim­
mune syndrome induced by adjuvants.150,151 Interestingly, in a 
recent relatively large monocentric series there emerged distinc­
tive clinical features of patients in whom Graves disease occurred 
within 4 weeks after COVID-19 vaccination.152 These included 
greater age at onset, male sex, and rapid hormonal and immune 
response to methimazole. Moreover, for the pituitary several cases 
of hypophysitis and pituitary apoplexy in temporal relationship 
1789
CHAPTER 47  Acute and Chronic COVID-19 and the Endocrine System
with COVID-19 vaccination were also published.153,154 In the 
first instance, an autoimmune mechanism was suspected; in the 
latter case, a vascular origin of the disease was hypothesized.153–155
Concerning glucose metabolism, several reports of new-onset 
T1DM possibly complicated by ketoacidosis were reported 
shortly after receiving the COVID-19 vaccination in the Japanese 
and U.S. populations.156–159 Loss of endogenous insulin secre­
tion, positivity for autoantibodies, and specific at-risk haplotypes 
were reported in those cases.156–159 Since both severe hyperglyce­
mia and Graves disease may possibly be triggered by COVID-19 
vaccination, screening of subjects at risk and early detection of 
related symptoms after COVID-19 vaccination may be recom­
mended.152,160 Finally, it was recently reported that patients with 
hypovitaminosis D may have reduced persistency of immune 
response to COVID-19 vaccination.160a 
Post–Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2
Definition and Prevalence
There is no one definition for the symptoms related to a previ­
ous SARS-CoV-2 infection. Generally, symptoms that persist 
beyond 4 weeks in a mild or moderately SARS-CoV-2–infected 
individual could be considered as part of the post–acute sequelae 
of CoV-2 (PASC) syndrome.7 However, there are a number of 
variables that make establishment of that time point difficult to 
accept. For example, moderate to severe patients who are hospital­
ized will often take weeks for resolution of their original acute ill­
ness. Their residual symptoms and signs, such as dyspnea or heart 
failure, which may be considerable, could be construed as part 
of the PASC syndrome, as much as mild fatigue or brain fog 6 
weeks after a mild upper respiratory infection would also be clas­
sified as PASC.161 For the better part of the first 18 months of the 
pandemic, it was a challenge for clinicians to label the symptom 
complex that in lay terms was often called “long COVID.” Origi­
nally issued early in 2021 by the World Health Organization, the 
ICD code U09.9 was officially recognized on October 1, 2021, as 
the “Post COVID-19 condition, unspecified.” It is an attempt to 
enable providers to establish a coding link between the coronavi­
rus and lingering symptoms after the virus is no longer active.162 
For coding purposes, U09.9 also includes common diagnostics, 
treatment-oriented procedures, and medications along with symp­
toms. As such, PASC or long COVID is now defined by ongoing, 
relapsing, or new symptoms or other health effects occurring after 
the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection (i.e., present 4 or more 
weeks after the acute infection). Heterogeneous symptoms may 
include, but are not limited to, fatigue, difficulty breathing, brain 
fog, insomnia, joint pain, and cardiac issues.
The prevalence of PASC is unknown. Several cross-sectional 
and longitudinal studies have estimated that 10% to 30% of 
patients with acute SARS-CoV-2 will develop symptoms that 
could be considered as PASC.163 However, much like the defini­
tion of this syndrome, the true prevalence is unknown and awaits 
longitudinal studies. Several variables make this effort difficult. 
First, there are now at least five distinct viral strains (alpha, beta, 
gamma, delta, and omicron), as well as several substrains of omi­
cron. Little is known about the differences in postviral symptoms 
across the SARS-CoV-2 variants or whether coexistent influenza 
or other cold-related viral infections might produce similar symp­
toms or signs. Also, repeated SARS-CoV-2 exposures are not 
uncommon, so symptom complexes may occur with one or more 
infections and one or more variants, or be present only as a sum 
of multiple infections. Second, PASC can occur with minimal or 
no symptoms, making the tracing of symptoms to initial onset 
difficult if not impossible. Conventionally, symptoms persisting 
4 weeks after infection positivity (PCR-positive) are considered 
within the realm of PASC. Yet this too is an arbitrary definition 
that must await longitudinal studies Third, with the advent of 
widespread vaccination efforts, symptoms related to the vaccine 
versus symptoms related to the virus (as noted with subacute thy­
roiditis or Graves disease) complicate classification. Furthermore, 
vaccination can ameliorate, lessen, or worsen PASC symptoms. 
Thus, attempts to fully define prevalence or incidence of PASC 
await an accepted definition of this complex and the overall time 
course. Nevertheless, there are endocrine manifestations of PASC 
that complicate complete recovery from SARS-CoV-2 infections. 
Pathophysiology
The etiologies of PASC are not known. Current theories revolve 
around several key tenets: chronic inflammation from viral per­
sistence; autoantibody production; reactivation of previous latent 
virus; T-cell dysfunction, coupled to viral persistence; endothe­
lial inflammation; dysbiosis from an altered gut microbiome; or 
hypercytokinemia. More studies are necessary to better under­
stand the pathobiology of long COVID. 
Symptomatology
The three main symptoms that characterize PASC are brain fog, 
fatigue, and dyspnea. But others are also part of this yet to be 
named syndrome. These include postural orthostatic tachycardia 
syndrome (POTS), cough, chest pain, confusion, neuropsychiat­
ric components (see later discussion), weakness, anosmia, dysgeu­
sia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and pain.164 Relatively new data 
suggest that neuropsychiatric components are the most frequent 
and are often unresolved months to years after acute SARS-CoV-2 
infections.165 These are important to delineate even in an endo­
crine practice as many are included in the differential diagnosis 
of endocrine disorders. The largest and most powerful data come 
from electronic health records. In an analysis of 2-year retrospec­
tive cohort studies, Taquet et al165 extracted data from the Tri­
NetX electronic health records network, an international network 
of deidentified data from health care records of approximately 89 
million patients collected from hospital, primary care, and spe­
cialist providers (mostly from the United States, but also from 
Australia, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, India, Malaysia, and Tai­
wan). A cohort of patients of any age with COVID-19 diagnosed 
between January 20, 2020, and April 13, 2022, was identified and 
propensity-score matched (1:1) to a contemporaneous cohort of 
patients with any other respiratory infection. Matching was done 
on the basis of demographic factors, risk factors for COVID-19 
and severe COVID-19 illness, and vaccination status. The study 
found that the increased incidence of mood and anxiety disorders 
was transient, with no overall excess of those diagnoses compared 
with other respiratory infections. In contrast, the increased risk of 
psychotic disorder, cognitive deficit, dementia, and epilepsy or sei­
zures persisted throughout. The differing trajectories suggested a 
different pathogenesis for post–SARS-CoV-2 disease versus other 
postviral infections. Similarly, others have noted that patients 
with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/
CFS), which is of unknown etiology, in many ways resemble long 
COVID patients, particularly in respect to fatigue, muscle weak­
ness, and brain fog165–167 (Fig. 47.1). Studies are under way to 
1790
SECTION IX    Polyendocrine and Neoplastic Disorders
assess those similarities, particularly in hopes of identifying the 
pathogenesis of both chronic disorders. 
Endocrine Determinants of PASC
Numerous risk factor predictors have been enumerated to help 
clinicians in the acute management of COVID-19. Particularly 
noteworthy are obesity, older age, hypertension, a compromised 
immune system, hypovitaminosis D, and diabetes mellitus. 
Although these are not associated with a greater risk of contracting 
SARS-CoV-2 infection, each predicted potential risk for severity 
of disease. As noted earlier in this chapter, the relationship between 
the body’s endocrine systems and the virus is bidirectional, such 
that coexisting morbidity enhances further the likelihood of acute 
infection severity and may predispose to long COVID.14 Particu­
larly for obese and T2DM patients, the preexistence of a chronic 
inflammatory state, with high cytokine and adipokine levels, cou­
pled to viral persistence and hyperglycemia, almost certainly con­
tributes to the greater morbidity and mortality from COVID-19. 
Less clear is the relationship of endocrine dysfunction to duration 
and severity of PASC, although based on numerous small studies, 
metabolic dysfunction could play an important role. 
Thyroid Dysfunction
Graves Disease
Several case reports noted that within 4 weeks of SARS-CoV-2 
vaccination, there was evidence of Graves disease. Although the 
classic definition of long COVID is onset 4 weeks or more after 
infection, the Graves disease reports were notable. Speculation 
centered on the relatively acute timing of disease onset, its rela­
tively mild clinical course, and the type of patient that suffered 
from hyperthyroidism. Although there are no direct longitudinal 
studies, a large series from Milan for the 2021 time period revealed 
a high frequency of Graves disease after vaccination, subsequently 
termed postvaccine early-onset Graves disease (PoVEO GD).152 
Sixty-four first diagnoses of Graves disease were made in a large 
endocrine referral center in Milan in 2021; 20 patients (31.2%) 
with Graves disease had onset within 4 weeks following vaccina­
tion administration. Median age of this subpopulation of PoVEO 
GD was 51 years; compared with the other 40 patients, these 
patients were older and more frequently male (40%). Whereas 
baseline biochemical and immunologic profiles were similar in the 
two groups at diagnosis, 3 months after the start of methimazole, 
the PoVEO GD group showed a lower percentage of patients with 
persistent TSH less than 1 and none of this group had a sustained 
fT3 elevation.152 Moreover, PoVEO GD patients showed a signif­
icantly lower TRAb titer and were taking lower doses of methima­
zole. It is likely that these cases were an autoimmune syndrome 
induced by adjuvants (ASIA). More studies are needed to confirm 
PoVEO GD as a relevant syndrome. 
Subacute Thyroiditis
Postviral thyroid dysfunction is a well-known clinical syndrome 
that has been known for nearly half a century. Generally, the 
patients present with neck or jaw pain, thyrotoxicosis, and an 
elevated sedimentation rate. A history of a previous viral infec­
tion is often reported. This type of thyrotoxicosis, in contrast to 
GD, is associated with very low or absent radioiodine uptake 
and a more transient, benign course. Often hypothyroidism fol­
lows before resolution. Glucocorticoids reduce the magnitude 
of symptoms and may shorten the course of the disease. Recent 
case reports suggest that subacute thyroiditis can also present 
after SARS-CoV-2 infection, although no large series have been 
published.138,168 Notwithstanding, autoimmunity seems almost 
certainly the underlying pathophysiology of subacute thyroiditis, 
whether post–SARS-CoV-2 or other viral infections. 
Metabolic Dysfunction
Patients with obesity or T2DM are more prone to have severe 
acute SARS-CoV-2 infections. This almost certainly is a function 
of altered immune function. Both conditions are associated with 
adipose tissue inflammation and a more chronic immune reac­
tivity.169 Whether viral persistence plays a role in the sustained 
response to infection is still unclear. In respect to PASC, there is 
evidence from retrospective cohort studies that there is a higher 
frequency of glucose intolerance. Xie and Al-Aly170 demonstrated 
an increased burden of disease related to glucose intolerance and 
antihyperglycemic medications from electronic health records 
at the Veterans Administration Hospital. Finally, people with

CHAPTER 47  Acute and Chronic COVID-19 and the Endocrine System

Pathophysiology of Metabolic Dysfunction in PASC
Exactly how obesity or glucose intolerance drives PASC is still 
very uncertain. Two targets that might be susceptible to postviral 
disease are the fat cell and the pancreas.5,9,18 It is likely that expan­
sion of adipocytes drives an inflammatory response, as evident by 
the presence of macrophages near or adjacent to adipocytes. And 
at least one paper reports SARS-CoV-2 viral presence in macro­
phages close to fat cells. Viral persistence may be present in adipo­
cytes as well. Some work has shown that viral RNA can be detected 
in adipocytes taken from individuals during bariatric surgery who 
previously had acute SARS-CoV-2.171 There is evidence, at least 
in immune-compromised individuals, that SARS-CoV-2 viremia 
is present out to at least 6 weeks, suggesting an impairment in viral 
clearance, and there are circulating viral proteins.172,173 Inflamed 
adipocytes release adipokines that might promote chronic inflam­
mation or cytokines that exacerbate a chronic inflammatory state. 
Several studies have suggested that the ratio of adiponectin to 
leptin is reduced in patients with PASC.174,175 Other work points 
to endotheliitis as a mechanism of impaired fat cell function and 
altered adipokine release.176 It is also possible that fibrosis of adi­
pose tissue is a major driver of both insulin resistance and PASC. 
Small studies have shown hyperinsulinemia in PASC patients, 
even in the absence of chronic hyperglycemia.8,177 Long-standing 
inflammation can cause fibrotic changes in adipocytes and pre­
fibroblasts. Importantly, many PASC patients with pulmonary 
manifestations and respirator support develop a fibrotic lung con­
dition due to myofibroblast conversion to lipofibroblasts.178 These 
can be a source of insulin resistance. Antifibrotic agents that are 
experimentally being used to treat the pulmonary fibrosis could 
enhance glucose tolerance. Recombinant adiponectin is also being 
considered as a therapeutic modality to improve insulin resistance 
in peripheral adipose depots.
In regard to the pancreas, it is notable that there is an increased 
incidence of T1DM after SARS-CoV-2 infections in children.179 
This may not be totally surprising because viral and postviral 
responses are often considered as etiologic agents in islet cell 
destruction. There is currently no evidence that SARS-CoV-2 
directly targets the islet cells or persists from autopsy series, 
although the number of subjects is very small. More studies are 
needed to understand whether T1DM is a bystander effect of 
SARS-CoV-2 infection or a direct result of injury. Notwithstand­
ing, the circulation of the pancreas can be involved due to endo­
thelium involvement, and this could in turn impair first or second 
phase insulin release. Whether this contributes to a higher preva­
lence of T2DM is still unclear. At the present time, regardless of 
the etiology, treatment of T1DM and T2DM should remain the 
same. Recently, it was reported that prevalent vertebral fractures at 
hospital admission for COVID-19 were not only able to predict 
acute negative outcomes but also to negatively affect spirometric 
performance of survivors of COVID-19 at 6 months after hospital 
discharge, further supporting the importance of vertebral fracture 
assessment on thoracic x-rays in COVID-19 patients.112 
Summary
The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic led to significant morbidity and 
mortality over a 36-month period.2 The virus did not spare endo­
crine tissues, and it affected all secretory glands from the islets, 
to the thyroid, to the pituitary. The manifestations of endocrine 
dysfunction during and after this virus infection range from 
severe to protean, but all can lead to significant illnesses. There 
might also be endocrine dysfunction after vaccination, particu­
larly Graves disease.167 Obesity complicates the clinical course of 
acute COVID-19 and likely contributes to postacute sequelae of 
SARS-CoV-2. Diabetes mellitus is more prevalent after the acute 
infection, although its true prevalence and relationship to SARS-
CoV-2 are not known. More research is needed to understand 
the pathophysiology of long COVID and how endocrinopathies 
may complicate the clinical picture. The National Institutes of 
Health and other funding institutions are now driving efforts to 
understand the pathobiology of PASC and to develop therapeutic 
options. For clinicians, a clearer understanding of the clinical signs 
and symptoms of COVID-19, acute and chronic, will help in 
guiding treatments for patients with secondary endocrinopathies.

Introduction
As a consequence of severe medical illness, major surgery, or 
trauma, critically ill patients need vital organ monitoring or sup­
port to prevent or treat life-threatening insults, in order to main­
tain or restore homeostasis. As part of the stress response, profound 
endocrine alterations occur, including neuroendocrine changes, 
insulin resistance and stress hyperglycemia, and alterations in vita­
min D, which have been assumed to be adaptive. However, in 
patients who remain dependent on intensive care for a prolonged 
period of time, a different endocrine phenotype develops, which 
may be maladaptive. The illness-induced endocrine alterations 
often complicate the diagnosis of preexisting endocrine disease 
and may have important therapeutic implications. This chapter 
provides a review of the most prominent endocrine changes dur­
ing acute and prolonged critical illness, as well as the diagnostic 
and potential clinical implications. 
Alterations in the Somatotropic Axis
In the acute phase of critical illness, growth hormone (GH) secre­
tion increases, with increased pulse frequency and amplitude and 
elevated trough concentrations.1,2 Similarly, peripheral growth 
hormone resistance occurs, with lowered expression of hepatic 
GH receptors, leading to low concentrations of insulin-like 
growth factor 1 (IGF1), IGF-binding protein 3 (IGFBP3), and 
acid-labile subunit (ALS) (Fig. 48.1).1,2 Low levels of binding pro­
teins also lead to increased elimination of IGF1, enhancing low 
IGF1 bioavailability.1 High GH concentrations directly induce 
lipolysis and gluconeogenesis, hence increasing substrate to vital 
tissues for survival, while indirect and energy-consuming anabolic 
effects of GH—mediated by IGF1—are postponed.2 Systemic 
inflammation is likely a main driver of these changes, although 
the concomitant fasting response may also play a role.2
In patients developing prolonged critical illness, IGF1 con­
centrations remain low, predominantly explained by a lack of 
hypothalamic stimulation, since GH pulse amplitude and trough 
concentrations decline while peripheral GH responsiveness at 
least partially recovers.1,2 Administration of the ghrelin-like GH-
releasing peptide 2 (GHRP2), and even more the combination of 
GHRP2 and GH-releasing hormone (GHRH), restore the pul­
satility of GH secretion with a proportional increase in IGF1, its 
binding proteins IGFBP3, and ALS.3 When coadministered with 
thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), GHRP2 infusion also 
decreases markers of catabolism in prolonged critically ill patients, 
suggesting that central hyposomatotropism and hypothyroidism

KEY POINTS
 • 
In critical illness, characteristic endocrine alterations develop; 
these alterations differ in the acute versus prolonged phase of 
illness and complicate the diagnosis of preexisting endocrine 
disease.
 • 
Acute critical illness is characterized by low levels of thyroid 
hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1, and high levels of 
cortisol, which is presumably adaptive and mainly brought 
about by peripheral alterations in hormone metabolism.
 • 
In patients with prolonged critical illness, a central suppression 
of the somatotropic, thyrotropic, and adrenocorticotropic 
axes progressively develops, which may impair rehabilitation, 
although treatment indications and regimens remain to be 
studied in adequately powered trials.
 • 
Safe blood glucose control in critically ill patients requires a 
validated protocol, with accurate and frequent blood glucose 
measurements and avoidance of insulin boluses.
 • 
The ideal blood glucose target in critically ill patients not 
receiving early parenteral nutrition remains unclear.
 • 
Critically ill patients have low vitamin D concentrations, which is 
probably adaptive in the acute phase of illness.

may contribute to the wasting phenotype of such patients.4 How­
ever, whether this translates into clinical benefit requires confir­
mation in larger studies that are powered for clinical endpoints. 
Theoretically, administration of hypothalamic secretagogues may 
be safer than administration of GH, by allowing downstream 
adaptations to overdosing. In this context, two randomized con­
trolled trials (RCTs) revealed that high-dose GH treatment, initi­
ated after 5 to 7 days in expected long-stay critically ill patients, 
significantly increased mortality, which may be explained by GH 
overdosing in a state of recovered GH responsiveness.5
In the intensive care unit (ICU), therapeutic interventions also 
may affect the somatotropic axis. The administration of dopamine 
treatment, commonly used as vasoactive strategy in the past, cen­
trally suppresses the somatotropic axis.6,7 Tight glucose control 
by intensive insulin therapy in a fed state further increases GH 
resistance in both critically ill children and adults, with suppres­
sion of IGF1 and the ternary complex proteins IGFBP3 and ALS, 
and results in a concomitant increase in GH.8,9 Yet, in a context 
of early full nutrition, tight glucose control with insulin therapy 
improves outcomes.10–12 It remains unclear whether the con­
comitant effects on the GH axis reduce the outcome benefit of 
the intervention or not. Withholding parenteral nutrition until 
1 week after ICU admission further suppresses the GH axis by 
decreasing the nonpulsatile GH secretion and attenuating a rise in 
IGF1.13 The suppression of the GH axis statistically attenuates the 
outcome benefits of the intervention.13
After recovery from critical illness, the somatotropic axis 
largely normalizes. In a 5-year follow-up study, survivors had com­
parable levels of GH and IGF1 as age-matched controls, although 
IGFBP3 levels were slightly but significantly higher in former ICU 
patients.14 Higher IGFBP3 concentrations were independently 
associated with improved handgrip strength.14 Hence, although 
speculative, increased IGFBP3 levels after recovery from critical 
illness could be a compensatory protective response. 
Alterations in the Thyroid Axis
In acute critical illness, levels of the active form of thyroid hor­
mone, triiodothyronine (T3), rapidly decline, explained by altered 
peripheral metabolism (Fig. 48.2).15 Mechanistically, the activity 
of type 1 deiodinase is attenuated while type 3 deiodinase activ­
ity increases, leading to increased peripheral conversion of thyrox­
ine (T4) secreted by the thyroid gland to the biologically inactive 
reverse T3 (rT3). Simultaneously, degradation of T3 is increased, 
altogether leading to low T3 levels and a decreased T3:rT3 ratio.15 
Concomitantly, concentrations of the pituitary hormone thyrotro­
pin (thyroid-stimulating hormone [TSH]) and of T4 briefly rise, 
followed by rapid normalization of TSH and T4.16 These altera­
tions have been designated as euthyroid sick syndrome, nonthyroidal 
illness, or acute low T3 syndrome. Triggers of this biochemical con­
stellation are systemic inflammation and fasting accompanying

severe illness.2,15 Of note, fasting evokes similar alterations in thy­
roid hormone metabolism and is thought to reflect an adaptive 
response preventing hypercatabolism.17,18
In prolonged critical illness, alterations in peripheral metabo­
lism often persist: T3 concentrations further decline due to the vir­
tually absent pulsatile TSH secretion, and this results in low TSH 
and T4 concentrations.15 The low pituitary hormone secretion 
is explained by hyposecretion of thyrotropin-releasing hormone 
(TRH). An autopsy study revealed low TRH gene expression 
in patients dying after prolonged critical illness compared with 
sudden death.19 Moreover, TRH administration can augment 
nonpulsatile TSH release in prolonged critically ill patients, and 
TRH coadministered with GHRP2 also reactivates pulsatile TSH 
secretion.3,4 The drivers of central suppression of the thyroid axis 
in prolonged critical illness remain unclear. Endogenous dopa­
mine and hypercortisolemia may play a role.6,20,21 In addition, an 
altered setpoint for feedback inhibition may be present through 
increased local type 2 deiodinase activity.22,23 Apart from the 
critical illness–induced alterations, TSH secretion and/or thyroid 
hormone production may be suppressed by iatrogenic factors, 
including iodine-containing wound dressings and contrast agents, 
and drugs such as glucocorticoids, somatostatin, dopamine, and 
amiodarone.24
The common alterations in thyroid hormone metabolism in 
critical illness have important diagnostic implications because the 
diagnosis of true thyroid dysfunction and preexisting thyroid dis­
orders can be extremely difficult.25 In critically ill patients who 
do have overt primary hypothyroidism, the TSH concentrations 
may be lower than expected. Hence, a low or normal TSH does 
not exclude primary hypothyroidism.25 To facilitate diagnosis, 
history, physical examination, and the presence of autoantibod­
ies may provide diagnostic clues. However, repeat thyroid tests 
after recovery from critical illness are usually necessary to confirm 
the diagnosis.25 Conversely, elevated T3 concentrations are highly 
unusual in critical illness and should always lead to suspicion of 
hyperthyroidism or even thyroid storm.25
From a clinical point of view, the question is whether altera­
tions in thyroid hormone secretion and metabolism should be 
treated or not. In the acute phase of critical illness, these altera­
tions are assumed to be adaptive.2 Interventional studies supple­
menting thyroid hormone in the acute phase of critical illness have 
not shown benefit on outcomes.26–30 Moreover, several metabolic 
interventions that improve the outcomes of critically ill patients—
tight glucose control, as well as withholding early parenteral nutri­
tion supplementing insufficient enteral nutrition—further lower 
T3 and the T3:rT3 ratio, which seems to be a beneficial adaptation, 
whereas a lowering of T4 appears to be deleterious.31–33
In contrast to the adaptive response in critical illness of short 
duration, several observations suggest that prolonged low T3 
levels and low hypothalamic TRH secretion in prolonged criti­
cal illness may be harmful.4,34–36 Observational studies revealed 
potential signs of adaptation to prolonged low T3 in some tissues, 
including increased expression of thyroid hormone transporters,34 
a relatively increased expression of the active thyroid hormone 
receptor TRa1 over the ligand-insensitive isoform TRa2,36 and 
altered local deiodinase activity resulting in increased local thyroid 
hormone availability.35 Moreover, pilot studies found suppressed 
markers of catabolism by administration of TRH in combination 
with GHRP2 to prolonged critically ill patients.4 However, RCTs 
that are powered for clinical endpoints are lacking.
There is currently no solid evidence on how to adapt endo­
crine treatment for patients with preexisting thyroid disorders 
who are admitted to the ICU. Hence, practical guidance is 
based on expert opinion.25 In patients with preexisting hypo­
thyroidism, chronic hormone substitution is usually contin­
ued at the same dose, whereby T3 concentrations expectedly 
decline, as is the case in critically ill patients without hypothy­
roidism.25 The substitution dose is usually not adapted unless 
clinical signs attributable to hypothyroidism would develop. 
When the patient is in need of intravenous substitution, the 
substitution dose is usually reduced by approximately 25%, 
to account for an oral bioavailability of roughly 75%.37 For 
patients with hyperthyroidism, thyroid hormone concentra­
tions need to be closely monitored. There may be a need for 
dose reduction of antithyroid drugs because critical illness by 
itself lowers T3.25
In patients recovering from critical illness, a rise in TSH pre­
cedes normalization of T3.38 Five years after critical illness, survi­
vors have normalized circulating TSH, T4, and T3 concentrations 
as compared to age-matched controls, whereas rT3 is still elevated, 
leading to a significantly lower T3:rT3 ratio.14 Moreover, the lower 
T3:rT3 ratio was independently associated with lower handgrip 
strength and shorter 6-minute walking distance.14 Hence, insuffi­
cient recovery of the thyroid axis after critical illness may be a risk 
factor for long-term impairment. Whether hormonal treatment 
may prevent or alleviate such long-term alterations remains to be 
studied. 
Alterations in the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-
Adrenal Axis
Critically ill patients undergo profound changes in the hypotha­
lamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Following acute stress, adre­
nocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) briefly rises, accompanied by 
elevated cortisol concentrations (Fig. 48.3).39 Thereafter, ACTH 
concentrations rapidly decline to low levels, while cortisol concen­
trations remain persistently elevated.40 The persistent hypercor­
tisolemia in the presence of suppressed ACTH (ACTH-cortisol 
dissociation) after the hyperacute phase is explained by suppressed 
breakdown of cortisol. Moreover, less cortisol binding to the bind­
ing proteins cortisol-binding globulin (CBG) and albumin due to 
lower levels and CBG binding affinity will increase the active free 
cortisol fraction.40–42 High cortisol availability during acute stress 
is adaptive, as illustrated by the development of adrenal crisis in 
patients with no or insufficient adrenal reserve to mount a cortisol 
increment to stress.43 As part of the vital “fight or flight” response, 
hypercortisolemia promotes hemodynamic stability by provok­
ing fluid retention and by sensitizing the response to catechol­
amines, and it aids in shifting the body from energy-consuming 
anabolism to a catabolic state with liberation of energy substrate 
to vital tissues.44 Recent evidence indicates that the rapid sup­
pression of ACTH following acute stress is explained by negative 
feedback inhibition through stress-induced hypercortisolemia on 
the pituitary gland, while ongoing stress-induced hypothalamic 
stimulation through corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and 
arginine-vasopressin (AVP) leads to ongoing expression of the 
ACTH precursor pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), which is no 
longer processed into ACTH.45 Unprocessed POMC leaks into 
the circulation, leading to elevated circulating POMC concentra­
tions.45 The potential role of elevated POMC in critical illness 
remains largely unknown. POMC may stimulate adrenal cortisol 
production and secretion to some extent,46 although in vivo evi­
dence in critically ill models is currently lacking.
1795
CHAPTER 48  Endocrine Disorders of Critical Illness
In prolonged critically ill patients, central suppression of the 
HPA axis develops while cortisol breakdown remains reduced.41 
The central suppression of the HPA axis is illustrated by the pro­
gressive decline of total and free cortisol concentrations to even 
normal concentrations after 4 weeks in the ICU in the absence 
of elevated ACTH, despite persisting illness.41 Moreover, 
the ACTH response to a CRH stimulation test significantly 
decreases beyond the first week in the ICU,47 whereas POMC 
remains elevated.45 Adrenal glands from patients dying after pro­
longed critical illness are characterized by a reduced expression 
of ACTH-regulated genes and a severely disturbed adrenocorti­
cal structure, potentially explained by the reduced trophic effect 
by low ACTH.48 One week after ICU discharge of long-stay 
ICU patients, both ACTH and cortisol concentrations rise to 
supranormal concentrations, which corroborates a central and 
reversible suppression of the HPA axis by a yet unknown fac­
tor.41 Five years after critical illness, alterations in the HPA axis 
normalize in survivors.14
Apart from alterations in cortisol production and degradation 
in acute and prolonged critical illness, recent evidence also reveals 
tissue-specific alterations in cortisol effects through altered local 
cortisol production by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 
1 (11β-HSD1) and through altered expression of the glucocor­
ticoid receptor and its co-chaperone FK506 binding protein 51 
(FKBP51).49 A study in samples from critically ill patients docu­
mented reduced glucocorticoid action in human neutrophils based 
on the reduced expression of glucocorticoid-induced leucine zip­
per (GILZ).49 Such reduced glucocorticoid action in neutrophils 
is accompanied by reduced gene expression of the glucocorticoid 
receptor α (GRα), which mediates most glucocorticoid effects, 
and by increased expression of the GRα-sensitivity–regulating 
co-chaperone FKBP51, which negatively regulates GRα action.49 
Moreover, very high glucocorticoid availability, as defined by 
receiving high-dose synthetic steroids (≥30 mg methylpred­
nisolone over 48 hours) or free cortisol concentrations ≥3.096 
μg/dL (the 75th percentile of untreated patients), is not associated 
with increased glucocorticoid activity in human neutrophils.49 
In contrast, in monocytes, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue 
obtained from critically ill patients, and in vital tissues of septic 
mice, glucocorticoid action was mostly increased, with a tissue-
specific regulation of local glucocorticoid availability through 
altered expression of 11β-HSD1, GRα, and its negative regula­
tor FKBP51.49 Interestingly, very high glucocorticoid availability 
in patients (see prior definition), and hydrocortisone treatment 
in mice is only associated with increased glucocorticoid action in 
human and murine adipose tissue, as well as in murine lung and 
diaphragm, but not in human and murine skeletal muscle, and 
neither in murine heart, kidney, or liver.49 These tissue-specific 
alterations in expression of 11β-HSD1, GRα and FKBP51, and 
glucocorticoid action, as deducted from expression of GILZ, 
occurred in the acute phase of critical illness and largely persisted 
in the prolonged phase of critical illness.49
