SECTION IX    Polyendocrine and Neoplastic Disorders
These novel findings have important diagnostic implications. 
First, the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency in critical illness is very 
difficult, because high cortisol concentrations are largely mediated 
by peripheral adaptations and not by increased cortisol produc­
tion.40,41 Hence, random cortisol measurements can be difficult to 
interpret because elevated cortisol concentrations do not exclude 
adrenal insufficiency. In addition, the ACTH stimulation test, 
assessing the increment in cortisol to a supraphysiologic dose of 
the ACTH-analogue tetracosactide (cosyntropin), is not useful 
in critically ill states because the lower concentrations and bind­
ing affinity of cortisol-binding proteins increase the distribution 
volume of cortisol, as well as the active free cortisol fraction and 
its associated glucocorticoid availability.40,41 Hence, although the 
total incremental cortisol response to ACTH is usually lower in 
critically ill patients than in healthy subjects, the increment in free 
cortisol was found to be similar.41 Free cortisol is, however, not 
measured by routine laboratory assays. The cosyntropin stimula­
tion test does not identify patients who would benefit from treat­
ment with glucocorticoids. Although an observational study in 
patients with septic shock associated a lower incremental corti­
sol response to cosyntropin with increased mortality risk,50 large 
RCTs did not show significant impact on mortality in patients 
with low incremental cortisol response.51,52 This suggests that the 
association of a low cortisol response to cosyntropin with adverse 
outcomes is likely explained by more severe illness, which is asso­
ciated with lower cortisol-binding proteins and a higher cortisol 
distribution volume, and it does not support the concept of adre­
nal failure in septic shock.
Recent evidence also questions the presumed general glucocor­
ticoid resistance that has been assumed to occur in septic shock, 
based on reduced GRα expression in blood cells.53 Observations 
documenting tissue-specific alterations in local glucocorticoid 
availability and action, as well as differential responses associated 
with increased glucocorticoid availability in human critically ill 
patients and in a septic mouse model, argue against generalized 
glucocorticoid resistance in sepsis.49 Moreover, RCTs in patients 
receiving hydrocortisone in septic shock have not shown consis­
tent benefit on hard clinical endpoints.51,52,54,55 Although most 
RCTs demonstrated faster weaning of vasopressor support, which 
could be expected based on the well-known blood pressure–aug­
menting effects of steroids, only one RCT found significant mor­
tality benefit.52
These findings may have therapeutic implications. Indeed, 
stress doses of hydrocortisone to prevent adrenal crisis and as 
adjunctive treatment of septic shock far exceed the cortisol pro­
duction rate in hyperinflammatory patients without adrenal insuf­
ficiency, which has been estimated to be approximately 60 mg 
per day.40,43,56 One could speculate that lower doses may suffice, 
potentially with fewer side effects, a hypothesis that needs to be 
investigated.44
Altogether, recent evidence questions the traditional concept of 
critical illness–related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI), which 
has been assumed to be present in septic shock, and has been 
related to a decreased incremental cortisol response to ACTH, as 
well as to generalized glucocorticoid resistance.50,53 On the other 
hand, the central suppression of the HPA axis observed in long-
stay ICU patients, and the rise of ACTH and cortisol 1 week after 
ICU discharge, suggest that central adrenal insufficiency may exist 
in a subset of long-stay ICU patients, which could clinically mani­
fest as a persistent need for vasopressors, impaired consciousness, 
and electrolyte abnormalities.44 Future research should investigate 
the potential drivers of the central suppression of the HPA axis in 
prolonged critical illness, and how to diagnose and optimally treat 
potential CIRCI in long-stay ICU patients. Although speculative, 
central suppression of the HPA axis in the prolonged phase of 
critical illness could be mediated by an endogenous factor or exog­
enous factor, which needs further investigation. 
Insulin Resistance and Stress Hyperglycemia
In response to severe inflammation and elevations in counter­
regulatory hormones, critically ill patients usually develop hyper­
glycemia, which has been associated with poor outcomes.57,58 
However, the ideal glucose target remains unclear, because RCTs 
have yielded at first sight nonconcordant results.10–12,59 Whereas 
three single-center RCTs performed in Leuven, Belgium, have 
shown benefit from lowering blood glucose to the healthy, age-
adjusted fasting range (50–80 mg/dL for infants, 70–100 mg/
dL for children older than 1 year, and 80–110 mg/dL for adults) 
compared with tolerating hyperglycemia up to the renal thresh­
old (215 mg/dL),10–12 the NICE-SUGAR RCT subsequently 
showed harm by tight glucose control compared with maintain­
ing blood glucose below 180 mg/dL.59 The outcome differences 
between these landmark RCTs have been attributed to differences 
in glucose targets in the control group, differences in accuracy of 
the glucose monitoring and the insulin protocol, and differences 
in feeding strategies (Table 48.1).60 In this context, a benefit of 
tight glucose control was only demonstrated in a context of early 
parenteral nutrition supplementing insufficient enteral nutri­
tion,10–12,61 which has been abandoned after RCTs showed harm 
by this feeding strategy, even when feeding-induced hyperglyce­
mia is treated.62,63 Hence, it currently remains unclear whether 
tight glucose control is beneficial in the absence of early parenteral 
nutrition, when provided with a validated protocol that minimizes 
the risk of hypoglycemia and of large glucose fluctuations.60 This 
is currently being studied in the TGC-fast multicenter RCT (clin­
icaltrials.gov, NCT03665207).
Some evidence suggests that the glucose target may need to be 
individualized according to the chronic level of blood glucose con­
trol. Of note, observational studies have shown that the association 
of blood glucose with outcomes is affected by diabetic status and 
the pre-ICU level of glucose control, as derived from hemoglobin 
A1c concentrations (HbA1c).64–66 Patients with poorly controlled 
diabetes may be more vulnerable to severe and relative hypogly­
cemia,67,68 and observational studies have shown that the lowest 
mortality risk in these patients associates with blood glucose con­
centrations that are closer to their preadmission glucose levels.64,66 
However, solid evidence supporting individualized glucose con­
trol is hitherto lacking. Whereas a before-after implementation 
study suggested benefit by implementing looser glucose control 
in diabetic patients,69 a large RCT did not demonstrate benefit 
of individualized, HbA1c-guided glucose control as compared to 
conventional control with a glucose target of less than 180 mg/
dL.70 However, in this RCT, there was a large overlap in blood 
glucose between groups, in part because of delayed randomiza­
tion, and the study is likely underpowered to detect or exclude a 
benefit of individualized blood glucose control.71
Although the optimal blood glucose target for critically ill 
patients remains unclear, recent evidence illustrates that safe and 
effective glucose control requires frequent and accurate glucose 
monitoring and a validated insulin protocol. Arterial blood glu­
cose measurements are preferred, because venous measurements 
can be falsely elevated in cases of concurrent intravenous glucose 
infusion, and capillary measurements are potentially unreliable in 
1797
CHAPTER 48  Endocrine Disorders of Critical Illness
patients with poor capillary perfusion.60 Evidently, the measure­
ment device needs to be accurate, with measurement errors within 
recommended standards.72 Insulin is preferably administered 
through continuous intravenous insulin infusion while avoiding 
boluses, to slowly progress toward blood glucose target and to avoid 
hypoglycemia and large glucose fluctuations, because both have 
been associated with poor outcomes.73–75 The quality of glucose 
control can be improved with use of (nearly) continuous glucose 
monitoring and computerized decision-support algorithms.76,77 
However, the additional cost of (nearly) continuous glucose moni­
toring and the discussion about the ideal glucose target, as well as 
potential concerns regarding point accuracy of subcutaneous sen­
sors due to inherent lag time compared with intravascular sensors, 
preclude widespread adoption of this technology.60,77–79
The universal presence of stress hyperglycemia impedes the 
diagnosis of preexisting diabetes based on glucose determinations 
alone. Moreover, recent studies have shown that a considerable 
amount of critically ill patients may have previously unknown 
antecedent diabetes mellitus, as derived from elevated HbA1c 
levels on ICU admission.70,80 Therefore, routine HbA1c measure­
ments may aid in discriminating pure stress hyperglycemia versus 
stress hyperglycemia superimposed on diabetes mellitus, which 
could be important for post-ICU follow-up. Traditionally, insu­
lin resistance induced by stress has been considered to be fully 
reversible.81 However, recent studies suggest that the development 
of stress hyperglycemia may be a risk factor for developing sub­
sequent diabetes mellitus.82,83 However, HbA1c was not system­
atically measured in these studies, which could be a confounding 
factor. Moreover, the definitions of hyperglycemia varied, and 
studies insufficiently corrected for known risk factors of diabetes, 
so it is not clear whether and to what extent stress diabetes inde­
pendently associates with long-term diabetes.82,83 Future research 
should investigate this in greater detail and needs to elucidate 
which patients may need specialized endocrine follow-up. 
Alterations in Vitamin D
Critically ill patients develop low vitamin D levels, an alteration 
that has been associated with adverse outcomes.84 Moreover, part 
of the clinical phenotype of prolonged critical illness could be 
mediated by vitamin D deficiency. Prolonged critically ill patients 
have signs of increased bone resorption and increased fracture 
risk.85–87 Moreover, vitamin D plays a role in innate immunity 
through regulation of inflammatory mediators, whereby altered 
vitamin D levels could play a role in immune dysfunction in 
prolonged critical illness.88,89 Recently, interest in vitamin D 
has increased, because patients with severe COVID-19 also have 
low vitamin D levels, as do non-COVID critically ill patients.84 
However, RCTs have shown that substitution of vitamin D3 and 
25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD) in critically ill patients is unable 
to normalize concentrations of the active hormone 1,25-dihy­
droxyvitamin D (1,25[OH]2D),87,89 whereas intravenous admin­
istration of 25OHD did increase concentrations of the inactive 
metabolite 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.89
Administration of much higher doses of vitamin D3 in large 
RCTs powered for clinical endpoints did significantly increase 
25OHD or 1,25(OH)2D in critically ill patients with baseline 
vitamin D deficiency, although there was no benefit on clinical 
endpoints.90,91 Moreover, despite high supplementation doses, a 
considerable number of patients still had very low concentrations 
of 25OHD and 1,25(OH)2D after supplementation.90,91 With 
regard to COVID-19, there is no solid RCT evidence to support 
vitamin D supplementation.92 Altogether, current evidence sug­
gests that low vitamin D concentrations are adaptive during acute 
critical illness and do not require pharmacologic correction on top 
of a normal maintenance dose. Importantly, until now, clinical 
studies have focused on vitamin D supplementation initiated in 
the acute phase of illness. Whether persistently low vitamin D 
concentrations are maladaptive and require treatment in long-stay 
ICU patients remains to be investigated. 
Conclusion
Critical illness is accompanied by neuroendocrine abnormalities, 
insulin resistance and stress hyperglycemia, and low vitamin D 
concentrations. These illness-induced changes are proportional to 
the severity of illness and are largely adaptive during acute severe 
illness, although the optimal blood glucose target remains to be

defined. In patients who do not recover swiftly and remain depen­
dent on intensive care for a prolonged period of time, a different 
endocrine profile develops, which may be maladaptive by contrib­
uting to the hypercatabolic phenotype and immune suppression 
associated with this condition. Nevertheless, RCTs powered for 
clinical endpoints that specifically interfere with the endocrine 
phenotype in prolonged critically ill patients are lacking. The 
illness-induced alterations often impede the diagnosis of preexist­
ing endocrine disease. In patients surviving critical illness, selected 
endocrine abnormalities may persist for years after randomization. 
However, currently it remains difficult to determine at the time of 
discharge from the ICU which patients need specialized endocrine 
follow-up and treatment.
